review: Another great RE game
Fabulastic <3

Games are the only art form that lets you rehearse the grotesque comedy of fatherhood, survival, and how quickly civilized pretense collapses when something tall, elegant, and very hungry decides you look like a good vintage. Resident Evil Village leans all the way into that madness and somehow emerges as one of the most confident, deranged love letters the series has ever produced.

You return as poor, long-suffering Ethan Winters—still somehow functional despite the amount of bodily trauma he’s endured—and get dropped into a snow-dusted Eastern European nightmare where fairy-tale horror meets grotesque family drama. The village itself is the sermon: a living, breathing hub of dread that shifts from eerie rural quiet to all-out siege as the Lords of the region come calling. Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters turn the castle into a gothic cathedral of camp terror and predatory elegance. Heisenberg brings chaotic, magnetic swagger that somehow makes fascist-adjacent robot murder feel like the most entertaining family reunion you’ve never wanted to attend. And then there’s House Beneviento… that section doesn’t just break the tension—it reaches into your chest, squeezes, and laughs while it does it.

The gameplay is a glorious, irreverent remix. Tight, weighty gunplay that rewards careful resource management without ever feeling punishing for its own sake. Exploration that actually feels rewarding—backtracking through the village as seasons and story shift the landscape, uncovering secrets while the Duke peddles his suspiciously well-stocked wares like the ultimate horror merchant. Boss encounters range from towering, unforgettable spectacles to intimate psychological gut-punches that leave you questioning your own sanity. One moment you’re feeling like a capable survivor carving through lycans; the next you’re running from something that makes you feel very, very small.

The dark philosophy sneaks up between shotgun blasts and desperate inventory scrambles. What does it mean to protect what you love when the world itself has been rewritten by something ancient and cruel? How much of our humanity survives when we’re forced to become monsters just to keep going? The game never preaches. It just keeps throwing increasingly unhinged set pieces at you while the story twists like a broken spine, culminating in a finale that somehow manages to be both ridiculous and strangely moving.

Resident Evil Village isn’t flawless. It occasionally loses its nerve in the back half, swinging wildly between tones like a drunk at last call. But that wildness is part of its charm. In a medium full of safe, predictable design, this one dares to be messy, horny for tall vampire ladies, terrified of dolls, and weirdly heartfelt about a man who just wants to get his daughter back while everything tries to eat him.

It’s interactive art that understands the best horror isn’t always quiet dread—it’s sometimes a nine-foot-tall dominatrix in a fancy hat chasing you through her wine cellar while you cackle and scream in equal measure.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
✅ Strongly Recommended
I finished Resident Evil Village on Steam, including the story DLC Shadows of Rose. This was my first time ever playing the game and my first full playthrough. It took me 14.5 hours to finish everything, and I enjoyed it more than immensely.

I’m a big fan of the Resident Evil series. Recently I finished Resident Evil Requiem, and compared to Village, Requiem worked much better for me in both gameplay and story. But even with that comparison, Village still holds up very well. I’m glad I finally experienced the closure of Ethan Winters’ story.

[h2]My history with the game[/h2]
[list]
[*] Finished Resident Evil Village on Steam
[*] Finished the Shadows of Rose story DLC
[*] First playthrough ever
[*] Total playtime: 14.5 hours
[*] Big Resident Evil fan
[*] Enjoyed it a lot, even though Requiem clicked with me more
[/list]

[h2]Quick signals[/h2]
💸 Value: ✅ Great package with base game and story DLC
🖥️ Requirements: ✅ Medium
🎨 Graphics: ✅ TOP visual presentation
📖 Story: ✅ Strong ending for Ethan Winters’ arc
🎮 Difficulty: ✅ Balanced modern Resident Evil experience
🎧 Audio: ✅ Music and voice acting are TOP
🐛 Bugs: ✅ No issues worth mentioning
⏱️ Length: ✅ 14.5 hours for my full run with DLC

[h2]What I liked[/h2]
[list]
[*] I really enjoyed the whole experience from start to finish
[*] The Romanian setting gives the game a strong identity
[*] The medieval horror vibe fits Resident Evil Village beautifully
[*] I’m glad Ethan Winters’ story got proper closure
[*] Music, voice acting, and visuals are all TOP
[*] The Shadows of Rose DLC was worth playing as part of the full experience
[*] The mannequin sequence in the DLC, where they move behind your back, was a really cool mechanic
[/list]

[h2]What didn’t work for me[/h2]
[list]
[*] After playing Resident Evil Requiem, Village felt weaker to me in both gameplay and story
[*] I only wish Big Momma Dimitrescu had more screen time, because her part deserved more space
[/list]

[h2]Is it an endless game? How long to beat?[/h2]
Not endless — it is a story-driven Resident Evil game with a clear ending, plus the Shadows of Rose story DLC. Although you can play mercenaries mode and there you can spend you free time.

My full playthrough, including the DLC, took 14.5 hours. For me, that felt like a solid length: not too short, not too stretched, and with enough variety to stay enjoyable.

[h2]Who will love it[/h2]
[list]
[*] Resident Evil fans who want to continue Ethan Winters’ story
[*] Players who like modern first-person Resident Evil gameplay
[*] People who enjoy horror mixed with action and strong atmosphere

[*] For me personally: definitely worth experiencing, even if Requiem became the stronger game for me overall
[/list]

The atmosphere is excellent, and a few sections show real craft. But then you hit areas that are just downright asinine from a gameplay perspective, breaking the flow and killing the tension.

I think that the biggest problem with this game is the shift away from RE Biohazard’s focused horror toward something closer to a first‑person shooter. It doesn’t suit the game, and it makes Village feel unsure of what it wants to be. It's not terrible, but just inconsistent and quite dull at times. It's worth playing if you enjoy Resident Evil as a franchise, but only if you catch it on a good sale.

The RE4 Connection
If you grew up playing the original Resident Evil 4 on the PlayStation 2 (like I did!), this game give me massive nostalgia. hahaha. The nostalgia hits hard because RE8 brings back that classic sense of exploration and puzzle-solving. Oh and the vibes and locations are very similar. It has that classic village atmosphere, the castle, the swamps, and even industrial factory buildings.

One of the highlights is the hidden bosses and secret areas. In RE4, some secrets were locked behind difficulty settings, but in RE8, they are integrated into the world, rewarding players who take the time to explore.

The Story & Lore
The plot of this game is actually quite solid, though if we’re being honest, most of the problems could have been solved if the characters just talked to each other! It’s a classic case of "lack of communication," which is honestly a bit funny.

However, for the lore hunters out there: this is a must-play. RE8 connects a lot of dots and makes the overarching storyline of the series much clearer. If you care about the history of the RE universe, you cannot skip this one.

Ethan Winters: RE7 vs. RE8

I bounced off this pretty hard a few years ago but after giving it another go I'm really enjoying it - at least for the first half of the game.

It's a bit of a departure from regular RE (although Redfield pops up in the beginning and resurfaces throughout) and it's weird-ass as hell, and all the better for it. The puzzles aren't exactly taxing and as usual it's a case of exploring the environment and taking note of some very basic clues to get through it. Lady Dimitrescu - a fantastic character, feels criminally underused (maybe a case of less is better?). 'The Duke' pops up as a merchant to sell you more stuff, offer (mostly) useless advice and generally acts a sage and an irritant - sadly you can't put a bullet in him.

The atmosphere - as expected is top notch with plenty of audio of things-that-aren't-crows, mist and wind to immerse you in the environment. The problem is, where am I in the game now, the village itself outside of the early story beats becomes a place to farm stuff for crafting and collect random things hidden in drawers, outhouses and scattered around the environment. Characters you meet early on aren't encountered again leaving the whole place feeling a bit empty - and slightly wasted. The sections where you explore to 'collect' the essentials for the game (I'll leave you to discover what those actually are) are nicely done. Atmospheric, but not particularly challenging. 

The game suffers from a bit of tonal shift just after the midpoint in the game. The more mechanical opponents don't sit well with the what felt more supernatural at the beginning. There's a section where you control a motorised turret - which frankly is just awful. And getting to play as another character seems a bit of a misstep. Towards the last act the narrative jumps off a cliff, things become incredibly surreal and depending on your point of view - either wraps the whole thing up in an epic conclusion.... or completely jumps the shark. Personally I think there's elements the story could have done without and it would have been better for it. 

Despite all that its decent survival horror (less survival, more shooty on the easier difficulties) and  an entertaining enough story for the price. Worth a punt.

Resident Evil Village is an interesting package. Story wise, it's an absolute mess. The entire story is pushed through bad decisions by Chris and Miranda, but the structure of it is good enough for Ethan to follow through an interesting set of locations and enemies. 

I thought Lady D was going to be a bigger antagonist in the story, but Heisenberg ended up being my favorite. He even gets more screen time than Miranda, the main enemy of the story. There's a little bit of miss potential with the story here. And they, as in Requiem, tried to add more into the Resident Evil lore with diminishing returns.

But that's the story. The gameplay is pretty good. In only a few exceptions I felt the annoyance of having such a small FOV. Ethan moves a little faster than Resident Evil 7, which helps a lot in this game. He was a push mechanic, besides his blocking. There's also a crafting system and a merchant. Those two help to create a more interesting gameplay loop than Resident Evil 7 and Requiem (the most recent RE I've played). Gunplay feels tight and responsive, although the lack of proper ironsights is strange in a game like this one.

The overall presentation has some ups and downs. I get why the colors are muted, compared to other Resident Evil games, but it makes the game look a little bland in a lot of the main areas. That being said, the factory looks absolutely amazing. Same with characters models: Capcom has created very detailed characters. Also, facial animations are absolutely fantastic. They've been doing some insane stuff since Resident Evil 5 in this regard.

Overall, the game is better than I expected. While the story and characters are lacking, the gameplay is pretty good. You do have to suffer through the worst opening section of any Resident Evil. While the game is very fast paced after the initial hours, your first playthrough is going to drag due to the amount of cutscenes or forced gameplay sections in the beginning.

I recommend it for sure. While the highs and lows are not as extreme as other Resident Evil games, the game steadily gets better, and better after the castle. I do feel you need to play Resident Evil 7 before this one to get the most out of Ethan.

I've been playing through all the Resident Evil games since RE9 came out. I played. RE9 as my first RE game, as I always viewed it from the outside as just a "hell yeah" game series which isn't really my thing. After playing RE9, the world was so much deeper than I could have imagined from the outside, so I was compelled to play all the other mainline games. At the time of this review, I've played all the mainline RE games except for RE0, 1, and 6.

Oh RE8, shares many of the shortcomings of RE7, but still remaining to be a solid game. RE8's flaw is that its trying to be everything, making it feel diluted in ways. RE8 opts for first-person as the intended way to play the game wanting to be a tense survival horror experience, but simultaneously wants to be action horror like RE4. The result is watered down puzzles and level structure, less tension, and minimal enemy variety. The minimal enemy variety also extends to very sparse enemy encounters for the half-action oriented experience they were aiming for. Most of the time in the castle I felt like I was playing RE7. The boss fights and action sequences felt like they wanted to make a third-person action game, but didn't want to pivot from what they set up for Ethan and his gameplay in RE7. I can hear comments saying "well play in third-person if you hated first person so much," but I clicked what the dev's vision was for the game, not the accessibility option. What realllllly made me upset on the level design front is when the game opens up, and you have to tackle the different members of the family. They present 3 icon on the map, and I was like "oh wait, are they going metroidvania on this and letting my choose my own paths to take out the family where I get knew tools to explore side areas?" No. You need keys in a sequential order and are forced to take out specific bosses at specific times with no player agency. That was the real "awe man, that could have been way cooler." 

With the things I disliked about it out of the way, the game still isn't bad. I quite enjoyed my time still, but it just left me underwhelmed in so many ways like RE7. Great foundations, a good story, expands the world of RE in meaningful ways, but ah. I just wish Capcom wasn't so torn on the direction for the gameplay on this one. If they weren't so focused on splitting this game between action horror and survival horror, maybe my vision of the metroidvania style village would have come to fruition. The DLC... was probably my least favorite DLC I've played for an RE game, but I really did like the story. The story was good and gave a meaningful/fulfilling end for Ethan, and I did like the mold powers as a gameplay mechanic, but for the love of god why did Rose have to move so slowwww. I got confused because I missed one thing, and spent like 15-20 minutes hobbling around the castle to find out I just missed one spore thing. Though, I felt like Rose did not feel very convincing for the situation she is in, comparing to someone like Grace at least. She's a kid thrown into a mold hell, but seems a lot more collected and better with weapons than Grace. I honestly felt more scared in this DLC than all of the base game at times though, props to that.

I would probably put it below RE7 on my list at my 5th favorite mainline RE game. There were far more moments in this game where I was like "ah, that coulda been so much better" than in RE7. I still enjoyed my time with this one though. I'd give it a strong 7, maybe a light 8.

[h1]While I recommend the game, it's under certain circumstances.[/h1]


This game left me the most confused about how I felt in the entire franchise, not because it was divisive or some sort of controversial experience, but it's been a game I wasn't sure if I liked or disliked at the simplest.

Story is about the best part of this game, and it's a very simple but very wholesome (in principle) message about a father doing whatever it takes to save her daughter. It's not a deep story, there's some twists and gotcha moments that are entertaining on the first pass but they don't add anything aside keeping you engaged in the first playthrough - and while that is great that the first time is honestly rather exciting, the replay value hurts dramatically the more it leans on these twists.

Gameplay in my opinion is a sidegrade to RE7 at best for a couple of reasons; most of the guns don't feel all that great to fire/accurate to where you want them to fire but the ones that do feel fun to use feel [i]fantastic[/i], the enemies themselves are a mixed bag of either fun or frustrating where the Lycans are all shooting up whatever the most twitchy substances they can get their hands on to make themselves harder to hit, the bog standard zombies are anemic in nearly every sense and are target practice - however by the start of the last third of the game there's some genuinely fun and interesting enemies in both design and gameplay that start to crop up. 

Trading/upgrading in this game feels worse than RE4 in only because the guns clearly weren't balanced around this system, in RE4 where nearly every gun is in some way usable/comparable to the weapons you find towards the end, Village instead takes a weird left turn where every new gun you get is a direct upgrade to your latest version no matter what parts you got for it or how many upgrades you purchased, to me it feels like now with that hindsight if I play the story again there's no reason for me to invest deeply into upgrades until the very end of the game aside [spoiler]The Sniper Rifle and the Wolfsbane[/spoiler] since I'll be pushed to treadmill my older weapons anyways.

OST and soundscape is pretty OK, it wasn't exactly anything to write home about as it felt a little more generic horror sting/suspense music whenever combat music wasn't actively blaring, the safe room music isn't bad but it doesn't stand by the bigger more enjoyable saferoom jingles in the series.



All in all, despite some of the griping I do still enjoy this game, and I'd recommend it on a sale to anybody who wants the part 2 to the winters saga, however I don't think this game has earned full price purchase in my book.

It's a good game, but an average Resident Evil. 

The best parts of it are the graphics, the atmosphere, and how detailed the levels are. However, this game doesn't hit the same notes as other RE games. It lacks the exploration and the inricate level design of games like RE2, while falling short on the combat mechanics when compared to RE4. 

I can't say I'm a fan of the Winterses' plot, either. Ethan is a character whose writing feels confused. On one hand, the game refuses to show his face, suggesting that he is an avatar for the player. But on the other hand, he is a character of his own, with his own arch, personality and development. It seems like Capcom wanted to have their cake and eat it too, and the result feels weird and incoherent, especially in a series that is so well-known for its charismatic characters. 

The replayability of this game is also not very good. While you can play RE2 and RE4 ten times and never get tired of them, this game feels like a chore to replay. Capcom tried to create a successor of sorts to RE4 with Village, but instead of going for its gameplay focus, they focused much more on atmosphere and on the cinematic aspect. The result is an experience with lots of moments where there is little to no gameplay involved, many unskippable cinematic moments, and other sections with no particular replayability value. The Mercenaries mode is there, but personally, I find that mode breaks too much with the atmosphere, and it can get rather silly. 

It's a game worth playing through once, but overall I didn't find it particularly memorable.

Resident Evil Village is a game steeped in an exceptionally dark and immersive atmosphere. 
The village in which the story unfolds is crafted with remarkable attention to detail, showcasing a masterful gothic horror style that both enhances the narrative and draws the player in. It creates a unique emotional tension, making you feel both unsettled and captivated by your surroundings at the same time. 
The map design stands out as one of the game’s strongest elements, alongside its consistently gripping atmosphere.
The story is engaging and manages to hold your attention all the way through. However, as it progresses, it becomes clear that it leans toward a more over the top, action driven “Rambo-style” narrative. 
This may appeal to some players, after all, it is a Resident Evil title but for someone like me, playing their first Resident Evil game on PC, the story can feel somewhat exaggerated.
The enemies you encounter are excellently designed, with the werewolves being a particular highlight. 
The variety of weapons and useful items is impressive as well, although unlocking everything in the game requires a fair amount of effort and dedication.
For completionists like myself, earning the platinum trophy is exceptionally challenging. Some of the achievements feel somewhat unforgiving, requiring at least three full playthroughs to unlock everything.
It’s important to familiarize yourself with the map and optimal routes during your first two runs, as this will make it much easier to achieve the under-three-hour completion challenge later on.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to fans of horror and dark, atmospheric storytelling.

It takes the best parts of Resident Evil 4 and 7 and adds some new flavor and makes what might be my favorite game in the series. Outside of a story that at times is a little bit silly (nothing new for the series) and one section towards the end that dragged just a hair, I really don't have any problems with this game at all. The story is amazing, the world is mesmerizing, the characters are some of the most memorable in the whole series, and the game features not only some of the scariest moments in the whole series, but some of the best action sequences as well in my opinion. If you're a fan of Resident Evil this is an absolute must play. 

[h2] Presentation [/h2]

Not only does the game look incredible graphically, the world design is top notch. The village where you spend a lot of your time is full of destroyed homes, full of remnants of a more peaceful time. You can easily get lost just looking at these empty homes and piece together what life was like for the villagers before it all went wrong. Then once the first enemy appears, you get to see what's responsible and they're truly terrifying. More than the normal zombies, the enemies in Village look and feel like truly life threatening threats. You can hear them crawling around you, jumping on roofs, or surrounding you as you try and find an exit. This exceptional world and enemy design doesn't let up as the game goes on. Every area feels unique and true to the monsters who call it home. The big threats are brilliantly designed and you know so much about who they are just be looking at them for the first time. The game also has great sound design, with the game going silent at times, adding to the tension when you can hear the distant footsteps of your stalker a couple rooms away from you.

[h2] Story [/h2]

Talking about this game's story without spoilers is difficult so I'll just share my thoughts about it without spoiling anything. The game is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, and I'd say you should 100% play that before this if you haven't. More so than any other games in this series, 7 and 8 are connected to each other. Very early on the game isn't afraid to take risks and while I can see why some people don't love aspects of the story, I actually found it to be gripping, and really well done. It does get a little silly and dumb but for the most part, it actually tells a pretty serious story with some really powerful and shocking moments, I didn't see coming. 

[h2] Gameplay [/h2]

Village's gameplay is outstanding. It takes the action heavy parts of 4 and mixes in the horror focused first person gameplay of 7 really really well. The fights are tense, with you having to keep track of multiple enemies, and always stay moving to stay in good positions, but the game isn't afraid to slow things down at times. One of my favorite sections in the game actually takes all your weapons away and plays out like an escape room with some of the best atmosphere and horror in the whole series. I think it does a great job of balancing the two sides of the series, and has enough to leave the horror fans and the action fans happy. There are some solid puzzles too, and lots of exploration. The environments are full of little secrets and I always felt rewarded for taking the time to dig a little deeper.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]

Overall I absolutely loved this game, and I think it's one of the best in the whole series. I know many others aren't quite as fond of it as I am maybe, but this is an incredibly well done game that doesn't waste your time and had me on the edge of my seat from start to finish. I never wanted to put it down and I think it's well worth your time and money, especially with how cheap it is on sale. I beat Resident Evil Village on Village of Shadows difficulty and all I got was this lousy inventory full of trauma.

So you’ve finished Resident Evil Village on Hardcore. You’re feeling pretty good about yourself. You’ve memorized every Lycan ambush, you’ve crafted a surgical attachment to your sniper rifle, and you know exactly how many shots it takes to make Lady Dimitrescu’s daughter say that satisfying “crunch” sound. You look at the main menu and see it: Village of Shadows difficulty. You think, “I’ve played a lot of Resident Evil. I have infinite ammo for the Dragoon. How bad could it be?”

Famous last words, spoken approximately four seconds before a Lycan rips your face off and wears it as a little wolf hat.

Village of Shadows does not just raise the difficulty; it looks at the concept of “fairness,” lets out a wet, guttural laugh, and buries it in the snowy Romanian soil next to the remains of your self-esteem. Playing VOS is like being in a horror movie where the director actively hates you and keeps rewriting the script so you die more creatively. Remember that very first Lycan ambush at the beginning of the game? On normal difficulty, it’s a tense scramble for survival. On VOS, it’s a prologue to your own obituary. There are more of them, they have more health, and they all apparently graduated summa ♥♥♥ laude from the School of Eating Ethan’s Hands While Three Other Wolves Also Eat His Hands.

The opening siege in the village became a 20-minute exercise in cowardice. The strategy isn’t “fight.” The strategy is to run laps around that one house with the ladder, shrieking like a malfunctioning teakettle, occasionally firing a single pistol round behind you to remind the wolves that you are, technically, armed. I looped that house so many times that by the time Urias showed up, I didn’t even see a giant hammer-wielding monster; I just saw a gentle, hairy usher finally putting me out of my misery. I cheered when he killed me because it meant I could stop running.

And then there’s Lady Dimitrescu’s castle. Oh, the castle. The daughters, who on Hardcore are a manageable “pop the window, shoot the sparkly lady” routine, become full-blown Dark Souls invaders with a vendetta. They take so many bullets that you start to wonder if you’re supposed to be performing an exorcism instead. I dumped entire magazines into Cassandra’s smug, swarmy face while backpedaling through pools of blood, only to realize my Dragoon with infinite ammo was doing the damage equivalent of aggressively flicking a chickpea at her. The only reliable way to kill them is sheer attrition and praying to whatever dark god keeps bringing Ethan’s hands back. By the time I reached Lady Dimitrescu’s boss fight, I wasn’t scared of her. I was just tired. She’s also a massive damage sponge, and the fight devolves into circling a crumbling tower shouting “EXPLODE, YOU TALL NIGHTMARE” while she shrieks about how insolent I am. Lady, I’ve been here for 45 minutes. I’m not insolent, I’m unionized.

Let’s talk about the Beneviento house. Normally, this section is a masterpiece of psychological horror. On VOS, it’s a war crime. That fetus baby thing—the one that swallows you with a sound that makes you want to unplug your console and become Amish—now moves at a speed that defies biology. It isn’t crawling; it’s commuting. I hid under that bed for so long I started drafting a will. “To my loving wife Mia: please don’t shoot me in the beginning of RE9. To Chris: please learn to communicate like an adult.” The elevator at the end wasn’t a set piece; it was an emotional rescue vehicle. I have never loved a slow-moving wooden box more in my life.

The Moreau section, surprisingly, is almost a break, but only because VOS conditions you to accept misery as a default state. You’re just navigating a rainy obstacle course while a giant sad fish-vomits acid at you. Standard Tuesday. But then you reach the stronghold. The stronghold on VOS isn’t a combat encounter; it’s an academic dissertation on the limits of human patience. The armored Lycans—those massive, hammer-swinging, plate-wearing nightmares—redefine what it means to be a “bullet sponge.” I put so much lead into one that I’m pretty sure I violated several international environmental treaties. Eventually, you just learn to run past them while yelling “NOT TODAY, SATAN!” and lobbing pipe bombs behind you like a demented wedding guest throwing rice.

And now, the Heisenberg fight. We need to have a serious conversation about Karl Heisenberg on Village of Shadows. This fight on easier difficulties is a power fantasy: you’re in a homemade tank, blasting a magnetic Magneto-dad with a cannon, feeling like a hero. On VOS, it’s a Sisyphean punishment designed by someone who thinks “fun” is a four-letter word. Heisenberg moves like he has a personal grudge against your entire bloodline. His weak points are the size of postage stamps and your cannon takes approximately eight business days to fire. He does a charge attack that covers the entire arena in two frames. I couldn’t even get truly angry, just philosophically broken. I imagined Heisenberg monologuing, “I will use you to destroy Miranda!” while I sobbed, “I’m not even going to survive your cutscene, buddy.” When I finally beat him, I didn’t feel triumph. I just stared at the screen, a hollow shell, listening to the sound of my own breathing and the faint, distant cackle of someone at Capcom who definitely lost a bet.

Even Chris Redfield’s section, where you are presumably playing as a bio-weapon-punching god, is a kick in the teeth. The final gauntlet before the Miranda fight pits you against seemingly infinite waves of bulletproof Lycans while you have the audacity to exist. I used Chris’s targeting drone so frantically that I’m pretty sure the in-game military fired me for waste of resources. The final Miranda battle itself is an endurance test: you dodge her spider-ball-scream attacks while trying to remember what hope felt like, all while praying your block button holds up long enough for Ethan’s arms to not simply detach from existence. Spoiler: they almost do, and so do you.

So why five stars? Because Village of Shadows is, against all logic and self-preservation, an incredible experience. It forces you to learn the game inside out, to treat every bullet, every herb, every kitchen knife of a block animation as a precious resource. It makes a game you’ve already beaten feel brand new, in the same way that a new allergy makes a meal you’ve eaten a hundred times suddenly thrillingly dangerous. It’s a masterpiece of masochism, a love letter to anyone who has ever thought, “I wish survival horror made me survive less and horror more.” You’ll finish it with shaking hands, a depleted inventory, and a profound respect for anyone who has ever done this without bonus weapons. Those people are not gamers. They are cryptids.

Would I play it again? Absolutely not. Let me boot up a fresh New Game+ right now. Ethan, grab your hands. We’ve got a village to burn. Slowly. After dying seven times to the same wolf.

This game is great, in terms of Resident Evil games I think this may be my favorite. It has the correct blend of horror and suspenseful moments mixed with the action we all love in Resident Evil games. I will be splitting my review up because I got a lot to say about every section. 

Main Game: I think that this game has my personal favorite main story, just based on locations, puzzles, and weapons. The locations are designed wonderfully to fit the lord they house.

Castle Dimitrescu is a great beginning segment to get you settled into the vibe of the game, the puzzles are fun and the layout of the castle is just big enough to make it feel fun and engaging to explore, not too big to make it feel like a chore but still big enough to feel rewarding. 
House Beneviento does a complete 180 from the action packed, bright, and "pursuer" filled castle and throws you into a dark, defenseless horror segment. I think this section personally is my least favorite section of the game but that's not me saying it's bad, it's a very good segment and does a great job at making you feel anxious. But the "threat" in this segment is a very easily avoidable enemy and one that is literally scripted to disappear after certain segments. If this segment just had one threat that was ever-present it would be WAY better, the puzzles are fun and after returning to the main floor the hide and seek segments starts which is pretty boring, literally 4 locations for Angie to be and it's easy to find her.

Salvatore Moreau's segment might be my favorite segment of the entire game, the anxiety of this huge mutated fish creature jumping out of the water and hearing him splash right behind you or seeing him breach is such a cool way to do an environmental threat. It's a simple segment but it's not boring, this segment is incredibly short but the short moments that you're jumping on and off of floating boards dodging this huge creature's attacks is enough to make this entire segment both more action packed than House Dimitrescu and more scary then House Beneviento. The boss fight is a simple but fun fight, shoot the fish, dodge his attacks, and grab an umbrella, after this we have to deal with Temu Magneto.

Bryan Cransto- I mean Karl Heisenberg, honestly this segment doesn't really deserve anything super special. You run through this giant factory going between floors grabbing molds to forge your key items. The Propeller Head enemy shows up and chases ya a little bit but you always lose him...until you don't and you have to fight him not a super special fight also not a very hard section just tedious. The mech fight you have with Heisenberg is pretty cool. I love a good ol' Tank vs Mech fight. 
The final segment of this game has you play as Christ Redfield taking a final stroll through the village you once knew in ruins, fighting through some enemies, blowing ♥♥♥♥ up, then handing the Torch back off to Ethan to fight his final battle against Mother Miranda. 
Just for the main game I would recommend buying this game 10/10 will play again.

Shadows of Rose: The "Shadows of Rose" DLC is a fairly short story following the events of the main game you play as Rose who is all moldy and powerful, you go through familiar segments you played as Ethan but everything is taken over by this red and black mold that you have to destroy the "Cores" of. I really like how it feels more like RE2 or RE3 with the 3rd person POV. Unfortunately they also took a page out of RE2 and 3's book and made the arsenal super lack luster, which I understand with it being a DLC but Rose deserved so much more love (I want to see her use the Lightning Hawk or some cool ass magnum like that). Not too many puzzles outside of the Dollhouse segment which was very cool to see how they redid House Beneviento, turning my least favorite segment into my favorite segment. Using the powers to interact with the environment to open up pathways and knock down objects was really fun to experience. I would recommend playing this for anyone trying to get the full RE Village experience.

The Mercenaries: The Mercenaries has always been my favorite part of the series, playing as different characters, using the different weapons, and playing the different stages trying to get a high score has always been such an addicting gameplay loop. This game's Mercenaries has the smallest roster of characters compared to the other games but they made up for it in the perks you get for each character. Playing as any of the characters is super fun and each of their kits are entertaining to use. The LZ answerer is a super fun weapon to use and carries anyone going for the "Knives Out!" Achievement.

Overall: If you own the game play it, if you don't buy it. If you're a die hard fan of the series (I would say I'm a part of this group) I would recommend 100%ing this game, each playthrough is fun and engaging and as you play more the armory expands. 10/10 will be putting many more hours into this game and I'll hopefully start speedrunning this game. Have Fun y'all, enjoy your time.

Analyzing the gameplay of the new-generation Resident Evil games is quite an interesting process, because it’s clear that Capcom takes elements from older games that don’t work very well, or that were never implemented very well, and tries to improve them. Here, it takes elements from the original Resident Evil 4, combines them with what was reinvented in Resident Evil 7, and even includes some features that were eventually improved upon during the remakes. On a larger scale, Village takes elements from 7 and expands upon them; one of the best things they’ve likely done here is the free exploration of the Romanian village itself, where every detail and location is clearly very well polished, and the immersion of the village works quite well. Village also returns to embracing the franchise’s more campy elements, in terms of dialogue and narrative, though it’s perhaps one of the most cynical entries in the series, starting with the opening cutscene itself, creating shock value for shock’s sake without much substance to back it up. I could also point out that there’s something here, which has been present since the 7th game, where at certain moments the game wants to be an action game when it switches to Chris’s perspective, and it’s perhaps in those moments that I dislike it the most, because if you have the skills to make a horror game, the concept of action will never, ever be suitable enough for that. Anyway, Village is necessarily more appealing than the previous entry, although the second half of the game leaves something to be desired. Looking forward to play Requiem soon.

[h1] This game confused me [/h1]

Capcom decided to go for a sequel of Ethan Winters story, it was an odd decision for them, since replicating the charm of Resident Evil 7 survival horror was almost impossible to do, Re7 was basically lightining in a bottle and considering ethan was not nearly as popular as the other big names in the Resident evil universe.
With that being said, Capcom nailed it, the sequel felt less like a continuation of Re7 and more of its own thing, i can understand why some people didnt like it, they expected another Re7 style game and they didnt get what they wanted, i think its pretty stupid to expect the same classic survival horror format of resident evil for every new game, that incentivizes the devs to not expiriment and not try new things that might be a game changer, for example the first person mode on Re7 felt weird since we are used to a third person prospective, but that first person managed to captivate me and make the experience more horrific.
This game should be judged as its own thing, and as i said, not specifically as a sequel of Re7, because even tho its a continuation, in my opinion feels and plays way different.
The story talks about Ethan Winters, a man willing to go thru hell and back for the sake of loved ones, in Re7 it was for mia, an here its for the daughter, and that is it, i wont say more to avoid spoilers, but as usual for Resident Evil games the story is simple and compelling, so i will leave it at that.
Ethan's character somehow managed to be intresting, its not that intricated of a personality, but the fact that the devs avoided to show his face and the first person prospective made me feel like i was the one going thru all that, and that made me connect with the character way more than i expected, a man with clear ideals, loving father and loving husband.
The visuals are absolutly stunning, the scenery is goergous and the world building is very well done.
Frome the gothic architecture of the Dimitrescu castle to the gritty and dark factory of Heisenbergh, it takes space in 4 different sections of the map, each one different from the over, each one has personality, beautiful enviromental story-telling, The eery music, the background noises make you feel like you are always being watched, the atmosphere made me stressed and always on edge, this game is just artistically stunning, nothing less than that.
The combat is in my opinion, a massive step up from the previous game, you can tell Ethan went thru military training by how much the pace is faster and just from the reload animations of the guns, its just feels better, the game doesnt shy away from giving you ammo and different weapons, you might notice during your gameplay that there is no storage options, it bothered me at first, but you get so much space and i think the devs wanted to make the game more fast paced and less "tactical".
I still enjoyed the puzzles and the exploration, they added a very nice verticality to the game, and the map design are nicely done, even tho i wished we spent more time im the Dimitrescu castle, dont get me wrong i liked it but i definetly wanted more of it, especially if you consider how goergous and big the castle is.
I like the basic enemies on the central area, the village, they didnt go with the usual zombies but with Lycans, a mix between wolf and human, and honestly it felt refreshing, they look scarier and you can feel the bloodlust coming from them, its a nice change,  each section has its own enemy type, and its lovely, a critique of mine in the previous game was the enemy diversity, do its a bigt plus in Re8 for me.
The boss fights are absolutly AMAZING, the are cinematic, goergous and ingaging, the boss designs are insanely well done, the only thing i didnt like is that they were a bit too easy.
With all that being said, the game confused be, in the best way possible, somehow the devs managed to stray away from the formula of Re7, but not so much so that it woudlve been way to different, they managed to mix action and horror factors masterfully, each section feels different, one gives you survival horror, one gives you tense horror, one pure action and another one with a mix of both, its just amazing how Capcom balanced all of these factors, and in my opinion this game feels better than re7, i enjoyed it much more, one thing that i didnt like is that one part near the end felt a bit too much like a call of duty mission, but in th great picture it made total sense.
So if you are wondering if you should buy this game, its totally worth your money and its a good Resident evil game overall, i loved it.

With werewolves, charismatic vampires ladies, and evil dolls, it’s a much more fantastical setting than the usual zombie epidemic. The only time I was actually creeped out was in a blood cave with hooded enemies; otherwise, it’s far too over-the-top to be scary.

That said, I actually enjoyed this more than Resident Evil 7. The gameplay loop is improved, and I liked the merchant system. The graphics are stunning, and I was impressed by how well-optimized the PC version is! Playing as Ethan again, you really see him take a beating, in a crazy way. Village takes the RE4 formula that already works brilliantly and blends it with the horror DNA of Biohazard. 
RE4 was tense but never truly scary. Biohazard was terrifying but a different kind of game. 
Village strikes an almost perfect balance between the two.

The pacing across its 10 hours is tight. 
Every area has its own identity and threat level, but Heisenberg's factory stands out.
Tight corridors, relentless enemies, and constant tension. 
Even the backtracking feels rewarding thanks to well-placed treasures and challenges that make exploration worth your time rather than a chore.

The villains are genuinely memorable. 
Lady Dimitrescu is the clear standout, part Mr. X, part theatrical horror icon. 
Her chase sequences ratchet up the fear and anxiety, and the voice and mocap performance behind her is excellent. 
The boss fights across the board are fun and exciting, though I would've liked hers to be a little more challenging.

Where Village isn't a jump scare game, it builds dread through atmosphere, unsettling environments, eerie sound design, and deeply unnerving character designs. 
That's the harder, better way to do horror, and Village does it well.
Ethan Winters went from a character I didn't care much about to sitting at the top of my list by the time the credits rolled. 

The payoff at the end of this game is satisfying to earn.

My one gripe: the weapon tier system. 
Higher-tier guns are just plain better every time, which removes any reason to stick with earlier weapons. 
RE4 handled this better, every weapon felt viable through endgame. 
Here, upgrades feel like a straight replacement rather than a meaningful choice.

You can go into this blind, but it hits harder if you've played Biohazard first. 

Already planning my next run on a harder difficulty, and I haven't even touched the DLC yet.

After securing a 100% completion rate, it is safe to say Resident Evil 8 isn't just a phenomenal game—it takes the survival horror formula and injects it with a massive dose of heart, creating an experience that lingers long after the credits roll.

A Father's Relentless Journey
The absolute core of this game, and its greatest triumph, is Ethan Winters. Watching a man endure unimaginable, gruesome horrors—pushing past every physical and mental breaking point simply to save his little girl—elevates the narrative far beyond standard survival horror tropes. Having a daughter makes this hit entirely differently; the primal, unconditional instinct to protect your child at all costs resonates on a profoundly personal level. Ethan isn't an elite mercenary or a superhero; he is just a desperate father refusing to let go.

Mechanics
The gameplay loop in Village is incredibly satisfying, striking a balance between resource management and exploration.

The Inventory System: The return of the grid-based "Attache Case" (expertly managed by The Duke) adds a layer of "inventory Tetris" that makes every find feel impactful. Deciding whether to carry more ammo or save space for high-value treasures keeps the tension high without being cumbersome.

Environmental Puzzles: While the puzzles are more streamlined than some of the older titles, they serve the pacing perfectly. They offer a necessary breather from the intense combat, requiring just enough environmental awareness to feel rewarding without grinding the momentum to a halt.

The Savior of the Franchise
Ethan’s overarching arc is nothing short of brilliant. He didn't just breathe new life into the Resident Evil franchise; he completely revitalized a personal passion for the series. Moving from a relatively faceless protagonist to an absolute legend is a masterclass in character development. Village was so good that it forced my return to Resident Evil 7, turning what was just a YouTube watch-through into a full 100% completion run as well. While I had 100% completed the RE2 and RE3 remakes and played through the action-heavy RE5, none of them ignited my passion for the franchise quite like Village. It strikes a perfect balance, bridging the gap between classic atmospheric dread and fluid, modern mechanics.

The Late-Game Action Shift
Even a masterpiece has its rough edges. If there is one notable flaw, it is the third-act shift from survival horror to pure action. As the game pushes into Heisenberg's Factory, the gothic dread is replaced by prolonged, industrial shootouts with cyborg-zombies. This culminates in the Chris Redfield section; while undeniably cathartic, suddenly handing the player an assault rifle and tactical air support momentarily strips away the chilling vulnerability of survival horror, briefly turning it into a Call of Duty campaign.

The Perfect Capstone: Shadows of Rose
A phenomenal base game deserves an equally stellar expansion, and the Shadows of Rose DLC delivers completely. It offers a beautiful, melancholic, and deeply satisfying closure to the Winters family saga. Stepping into Rosemary's shoes perfectly wraps up the emotional themes established from the very first moments of the main campaign.

The Verdict
Achieving 100% in a game is the ultimate stress test of its quality, and Resident Evil Village remains gripping from the first lycan encounter to the final boss. Despite momentarily losing its horror roots near the end, it is an unforgettable blend of terrifying atmosphere, satisfying progression, and an unexpectedly beautiful story of fatherly devotion.

The impact of this game is so profound that it’s turned me into a completionist for the entire series. Between my plans to 100% RE4, diving into the roots with RE0, RE1, and Revelations, to revisiting RE5 and RE6 before finally getting to RE9.

Resident Evil Village continues the “rebooted” format of the series, while also paying homage to the previous entries in the series. It feels like a blend of Resident Evil 4 and 7, in the best ways possible. The weapons are all classic, but feel fun to use. The environments are great throughout, with enough diversity in both feel and gameplay. The bosses are introduced at the beginning of the game, and you get a glimpse of what you’re up against. A shout out to the shop keeper in this game, who is also an awesome character. 
	The star of this game has to be the story. The initial mystery at the beginning of the game, to the village location you end up in. It’s a joy to piece together what is going on, along with the sub stories of each adversary throughout the game. The twists and turns throughout are enough to keep you engaged, and want to continue on. 
	The main issue with this game that keeps it from being perfect is the pacing. This is a major issue in what would have otherwise been near perfection. The first half of the game is FAR more interesting than the second half. The enemies and the locations just feel much more thought out. The last couple of locations feel annoying at times, and do not give off the same magic the first couple did. It’s also worth noting that the best location and characters are introduced at the beginning of the game. While this is disappointing, there is no doubt this is one of the best Resident Evil games released. It blends both the newer horror focused direction, with some action and exploration features from the earlier games. This is a game that can be appreciated by both fans of the original games, and the new ones alike.

[b][u]INTRODUCTION[/u][/b]
I first played Resident Evil 4 as a kid around the time it came out, all the way back in 2005. Despite really enjoying it, I never dove deeper into the rest of the franchise until just a few short years ago.

With 4 being a favorite game of all time, my experience with the rest of them is that they are pretty great but nothing groundbreaking. If you asked what I believe are the ingredients that make Resident Evil, Resident Evil, I’d say it's a very recognizably unique horror tonality, best-in-class survival horror gameplay loops, lovable protagonists, an acceptable but usually forgettable story, and a few snippets of lore about the greater RE universe that always get you hooked waiting for more.

Interestingly, I believe this new duology of 7 and Village really reshapes and ultimately makes me rethink a lot of that for the better.

[b][u]THE REVIEW[/u][/b]
Resident Evil Village was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. While I knew the game was connected to 7, I never expected just how much of a direct sequel this would be—I loved every second of it. This really comes full circle in blending my favorite elements of Resident Evil 4 with its Eastern European vibes, ridiculous action, and over-the-top characters/creatures with the innovations of 7, making for such a wildly entertaining experience.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
This really is just if Resident Evil 7 and 4 had a baby. I don't have much to add, but I loved every moment of it.

[b]Difficulty[/b]
This was the first Resident Evil game that playing on the standard difficulty meant that I had essentially no trouble whatsoever throughout the entire game. Maybe I’m just getting better at games (copium), but this really felt inappropriate for the series. I think I only died two or three times in the entire playthrough? While I’m not super bothered by this, as I felt combat was difficult enough most of the time for my taste and I had loads of fun, I just never felt that survival horror trap really close in on me at any point. I always had the resources to kill every enemy I came across, I almost always had the money to buy the things I wanted, and ultimately I just kind of breezed through every encounter I came across with the exception of a few boss fights.

[b]Characters[/b]
All of the new and returning characters besides our protagonist are amazing. All of the antagonists you come across in the story have such a massive range of personalities with interesting backstories, are full of life with their own unique charms, and are backed by phenomenal performances. I really can't believe how all-out and eccentric they went with the ensemble cast of this game.

However, one major criticism I had with 7 that still holds true here is Ethan Winters. I can’t for the life of me understand why they had to make the protagonist such a lifeless blank slate. In a series dominated by protagonists with main character syndrome, I’m just stunned by this decision. My only assumption is that with the games being first person, perhaps they felt it would allow the player to embody Ethan and relate to him more?

[b]Story and Lore[/b]
Just like with 7, perhaps the thing that stands out the most in reshaping what I expect from a Resident Evil game is the incredible human writing in the stories supporting the game's plot. A continuation of what 7 built in the best way possible, adding up to the series' best story yet.

As the story goes, we get more and more interesting tidbits of lore until one final big drop at the end that is really quite earth-shattering for the RE universe. I really hope to see more.

[b]World-Building and Visuals[/b]
The art direction backing this mysterious snowy Eastern European mountain village was stunning. Lady D's Castle, the dilapidated villager homes and windmills, the modernization happening with Heisenberg's factory, and the hidden medieval tunnels branching underneath it all. It all tells such an interesting historical story and kept me wanting to explore every corner of it. Also, coming from 7, just shows the extreme diversity Capcom has been able to capture with the series while maintaining its iconic tone.

[b][u]CONCLUSION[/u][/b]
Resident Evil Village is a phenomenal continuation of 7—the first game in the series to break the boundaries of being more than just a cliche horror story to support the necessary plot. The series' freshest and most human story, all while combining recent innovations and the vibes/over-the-topness of classics to create another phenomenal and unique Resident Evil experience. Excited to continue with the DLC and then onto Requiem!

… why does Ethan have four arms? Once I saw it, I couldn’t unsee it for the life of me, and it bugged me like crazy the whole time. It bugged me so much that I did a second playthrough in third-person mode, and my guy Ethan doesn’t behave like a human being in that either. It took about five different mods to make it not look amateurishly broken. Official Capcom DLC, by the way.

With that pedantic tangent out of the way - how was the game?

Well, it flows smoothly the first time around. It’s very pretty, and something entertainingly mad is happening all the time; nothing is in the game enough to become stale. Ethan’s one-liners are so horrendously lame that they’ve gone full circle and become adorable, plus Lady D and all that. It’s like a fun roller-coaster.

But, dear God, this roller-coaster becomes such a drag in repeat playthroughs. It’s genuinely brainless; the whole thing is on complete autopilot. There is no real exploration, no decision-making, and no resource management. The game leads you by the hand on a rigid, preplanned route while throwing very modest handfuls of enemies at you every once in a while. It’s a middle point between classic REs and RE4 -without nearly anything that made both playstyles fun in the first place. I somewhat woke up from the autopilot coma in the final third, when the game started to demand paying attention somewhat, but it was too little, too late.

And it’s not that I can fall back on the story, because the story is about Ethan’s plight, and he is not written like a human being either, I’m sorry.

Let me start by saying this is not really a survival horror game. Don't get me wrong there are some moments where it almost feels like it is one but then they quickly go away and it feels like an action-shooter again. This is a bit disappointing to me since resident evil 7 did such a good job with the survival horror aspects and I was hoping to get more of that. That said, I still had a great time because this is a very fun action-shooter. Just make sure you go into this not expecting a scary survival horror game. 

The Good:
- The areas are really well crafted. 
- The enemies have a fair amount of variety. 
- The visuals are absolutely stunning. 
- The game is very well optimized. 
- The game is fairly immersive. 
- The overall feeling and gameplay remind me of resident evil 4 remake but in first person. 

The Bad:
- The story is pretty good, but has some really needless/bad plot devices that are just there to either keep the player in the dark or add a dramatic effect. I wont go into details because it would be spoilers. 
- There was some pretty bad/annoying voice acting. I liked it better when Ethan was mostly silent in resident evil 7.
- I HATE HATE HATE the yellow paint/tape on all the interactable objects in the game. It's like capcom thinks its players are incapable of figuring things out themselves, so they feel like they need to put this yellow garbage everywhere to show you where to go or what objects are lootable and thereby not even give you a chance to put your brain to work. It really hurts the immersion and the joy of figuring things out yourself.

Overall: I really had a great time with most of the game but it was slightly bogged down by bad plot devices. I'd give it a 7/10

TLDR - game is great overall, story is decent and so is gameplay, DLC is OK, pacing of main game could be better at points but that's personal preference. Overall rating: 8.5/10 or 9/10, depending on the area of the game.

As the second Resident Evil game I have managed to 100%, I think that RE Village is overall quite a good game. The story, while in my opinion not as interesting as RE7 or RE9, is still quite an enjoyable plot with the context of RE7 behind it. The gameplay is fun and the semi open world with the Village and the other major areas is rewarding to explore for all treasures and collectibles etc. Boss fights are good in my opinion, Lady D's bossfight was probably the best with Urias Strajer's fight against Chris coming in at second, the rest aren't really special but they aren't half bad either.

Shadows of Rose is a nice epilogue to the Winter's storyline but if I wasn't going for 100% achievements I definitely would not have replayed it. It's not a bad DLC but I just found it quite boring to play for a second time, since it is a very very linear experience.

I think the pacing of RE8 is a bit weak at times especially towards the end. The Castle is great and definitely the best area in the entire game. House Beneviento is a good interlude first time around but on subsequent playthroughs it becomes more irritating as all of the encounters within it are scripted and there's not much you can do to skip sections. Reservoir is similar but its not a Puzzle A, Puzzle B simulator so it's still a decent area. After there I think the game loses its footing a bit however. Stronghold is a kind of pointless section to me because it's so short and easier than I think it should be to get through. In my opinion, Factory is a slog to get through and my least favourite part of the game. Maybe it's just me but I thought that the whole running back and forth for molds just felt really unintuitive despite the area being actually quite complex compared to the other sections of the game. I found it to be the most boring area but I think it comes down to primarily a matter of personal opinion.

I don't write many reviews because I largely just don't care enough, but when I saw that this game has overwhelmingly positive reviews, I had to do my part to lower that score in what little way I can. Bit of a rant for a 4 year old game incoming...

I hated this game - I think it's very easily among the worst in the franchise.

I dislike almost everything about it - The lycans are frustrating as hell to fight (that dodge drives me NUTS), the village is awful to navigate, nearly half of the game is moving around a location just avoiding a big thing that's following you, the animal hunting is the worst kind of busywork, the amount of backtracking for treasure is too damn high, the story is a complete mess, the vampires and werewolves don't belong in RE, and entire sections of the game are just plain boring to replay because significant chunks have no enemies and are analogous to scripted sequences like a walking simulator.

I just want to give a special dubious honour to Ethan Winters. A character so devoid of personality, with so little to say about anything that he may as well be a cardboard cut out painted beige. Everything he says throughout the game had me muttering "Ergh you're so f'ing lame." I can't recall the last time I hated a protagonist as much as him. His responses to antagonists amounts to "NO U." . [spoiler] I'm glad he died at the end, and I truly truly hope Capcom leave him to rot [/spoiler]. If he appears in a future instalment, I will boycott on basic principle. He is worse than a blank slate. He is a void that sucks the atmosphere from the world around him. ♥♥♥♥ that guy. His existence in this franchise is a stain. I can't put my disdain into sufficient words.

Combat is retrograde too. RE7 had very disappointing Mould enemies that barely reacted to most damage (the rest of the game made up for it), and here that returns except now they also come equipped with a light speed dodge that would make Wesker proud, and they can do it as often as they like with no telegraph. They are profoundly aggravating to fight, and unsatisfying to kill. Capcom nigh perfected this with RE4 nearly 2 decades prior. How did they arrive at THIS?!

Another special mention goes to the map design of the village itself: It's utterly loathsome. I'm sure they thought that returning to this area over and over again was a clever bit of design. To an extent it is. It's cool re-exploring an area under new context, but at certain points its an insufferable maze. Blocked paths that arbitrarily force you through long (and uneventful) detours through multiple buildings, in the front, out the back, through windows, up a ladder, down through a hole in the roof. None of this is visible on the map., and its all because a new wall appeared. When you finally fumble your way through you're rewarded with a MacGuffin and sent back the way you came. The pacing of this game is a complete mess anyway, and this Great Value Silent Hill map design serves only to compound the issue further.

Exploration overall is such a drag I actively avoided it where I could. Those treasure chests on the map? No thanks, I'd rather just get the game over with.

Unfortunately this stuff comes together to create a game that actively makes me angry to play.

There are some good things to note, which I'll do quickly: The game looks truly terrific, has lots of post game content and unlocks for those that bought this game by mistake instead of RE4, and that opening cutscene with the story book is a delight. The four lords are great character designs (sadly wasted here), with the Beneviento horror house section being a particular standout (the first time), 

There's the core of a great game here, but it constantly trips over itself in every aspect.

Lady Dimitrescu herself is the perfect mix of elegance and terror, stalking you through her castle like a relentless, towering nightmare that you almost do not want to escape from.

House Beneviento is a completely different flavor of horror, and I absolutely love it for that. The weapons stripped away, the suffocating silence, the twisted doll imagery and that one unforgettable sequence in the dark… it all turns into pure psychological horror that sticks in your head long after you are done. It is one of those sections where I slow down on purpose, just to soak up more of the atmosphere and notice all the little environmental details hidden in the gloom.

Across the whole game, the level of detail is incredible. From the snow-covered village streets to the interiors of each lord’s domain, every area feels distinct, hand-crafted, and full of things to discover if you take your time exploring. I am still working on achievements, and that just gives me the perfect excuse to go back in, try different routes, poke into every corner, and appreciate how much care went into the visuals, sound design, and world-building.

The Shadows of Rose DLC definitely tested my patience, especially on Hardcore, but in a way that fits the series’ brutal charm. There were moments that genuinely pissed me off with how punishing they felt, but once I pushed through and watched everything come together at the end, I ended up really enjoying the experience as a whole. In the end, Resident Evil Village is one of those games I am happy to keep replaying for years, whether it is to chase more achievements, get scared all over again in House Beneviento, or simply walk the halls of Castle Dimitrescu one more time.

It is never too late to drop a review for a game this good. Even as a longterm Resident Evil fan who actually finished RE9 before circling back to finish 8, and even knowing exactly how Ethan’s story ends, this game still moved me to tears. There is something so deeply affecting about watching a father put his life in total danger just to piece his daughter back together; it holds a very special place in my heart.
The structure of the five villains is a brilliant hook, though I definitely had some critiques on how their arcs wrapped up. Lady Dimitrescu is easily the most iconic Capcom even brought her voice actor back for lines in RE9 because of it, and her castle is a series highlight. However, I found her ending a bit underwhelming. For a character that strong, having her turn into a flying creature felt like a cheap way to go out. From there, you hit the dollhouse, and while I appreciated the psychological horror of losing my weapons, it didn't scare me as much as I thought it would. I honestly wish we had fought  Donna Beneviento directly rather than just the doll; I think it would have been a much scarier and more personal experience.
The sea monster, Moreau, actually broke my heart. Hearing him cry about Mother Miranda hating him and the others laughing at him made him feel so pathetic and sad, which is a testament to the writing. Then you have Heisenberg, who felt like he got the "special treatment" compared to Dimitrescu. His section was so much more extensive and long; while the constant monsters were pissing me off every two seconds, I loved the design and the sheer scale of the factory.
The gameplay balance is nearly perfect, the puzzles weren't overdone, and the action stayed right in that sweet spot where it never felt like too much. My only major gripe is how they handled Chris Redfield. His character felt off; he could have saved Ethan so much pain if he had just explained himself. Even his own soldiers repeat three times that he should have told Ethan what was happening, so you know, even the writers knew it didn't make much sense. I really wish Chris had a bigger, more complex role that got his hands a bit dirtier.
Overall, this is a 10/10 experience for me. The emotional weight of the Winters family saga is incredible, and despite my small critiques, I enjoyed every second of it.

Resident Evil village is pretty good. Uneven, but pretty good. Resident Evil 7 is among my favorite Resident Evil games and after beating it I more or less jumped right into this one. 

Like RE7, RE8 starts with a heavily scripted intro, and it's almost as long-winded as the RE7 opening act. I do however, believe that RE8 is better about getting you into the action sooner than RE7 is. The walking segment is much shorter, you get a big moment right at the start of the game where Chris comes in and seemingly kills off Mia, takes Rose away, and leaves Ethan alone in the dark on what just happened. Afterwards you get to explore the village weaponless for a bit, and then to end the opening segment off, you get into a hold out against the new enemies of this game, reminiscent of the opening from RE4.

Bringing up RE4, RE8 is heavily reminiscent of it in a lot of ways. Primarily in
1. Enemies in RE8 drop items upon killing them, so the game is subtly encouraging you to engage in its combat mechanics.
2. RE8 has a merchant "The Duke" who sells you supplies, upgrades your weapons, and lets you sell him treasure. Like RE4, you can combine certain treasures for even more Lei
3. Like RE4, RE8 has a centralized area "The Village" and the levels branch off from the main area, acting self contained, but at within the game's world. This isn't like RE7 where it's all the Baker Estate. RE4 has that main town area at the beginning of the game, and you loop back around to it sometimes to progress, that's the set-up with RE8 here.

To a degree I can see how this game tries to have its cake and eat it to. On one hand, RE8 attempts to continue the survival horror gameplay from RE7, but since I can't stop comparing this game to RE4, it also has RE4's action. This doesn't really bother me though because RE8 is just so fun, and tbh it doesn't even really clash tonally a lot of the time. I think from a gameplay and story perspective, RE8 knows what it wants to be and it balances the action and the horror decently well.

The story of RE8 is a mixed bag, mainly because Chris Redfield is DUMB in this game. First of all, him not wanting to get Ethan involved in this mess is all well and good, but he (seemingly) kills off Mia, abducts Ethan's daughter, doesn't tell him anything about what's going on, and just expects Ethan not to go after Rose. 2ndly, when you meet Chris again later in the game, he acts incredibly antagonistic towards Ethan and berates him for making it as far as he did up until that point. This would be a good time for Chris to explain ♥♥♥♥ since Ethan has already taken out 2 of mother Miranda's lords up to this point, but alas. It isn't until the 3rd time they meet that Chris explains to Ethan what's happening. I just think the writing on Chris here is baffling, especially because the rest of the story surrounding it is largely decent, but not as tight as RE7s. Lady D in general is the highlight, but she's barely in this game. Heisenberg honestly is a cool villain, I think his warehouse is a great level, and his desire to rebel against Miranda is honestly a standout thing about his character. Ethan Winters though, RE8 did such a good job at improving him. I thought Ethan was a boring protagonist in RE7, he just barely reacted to most of what was going on around him. RE8 is a much better representation of that, because after Big Boss battles Ethan will always have something to say, he's not afraid to talk back & raise his voice against the 4 lords, & he will do anything to save Rose no matter how dangerous or life threatening it is.

I haven't really spoken on the gameplay much, and that's because it's good. The guns are all satisfying to use, the exploration from 7 is still there, combat encounters are exciting because the guns feel good. The enemy variety is improved 10-fold from RE7, & RE8 just really comes together neatly as a package. It continues with the First Person POV from RE7. I don't think the FP POV is as essential to what makes me like this game as it is to RE7, because RE8 isn't as much of a straight up horror game as RE7 is, but I like the FP POV and the game is clearly designed around it, so that's all good. The boss fights are all a highlight, they're pretty good about staying in the action and not having long stretches where you just can't do anything. They're all huge story moments, the monster designs for these bosses are actually insane in how good they are, RE8 just has some really good bosses.

I recommend RE8. I had a lot of fun playing this game and I look forward to coming back to it in the future

The yellow paint on important stuff isn't a huge deal and admittedly helped me out a lot in some head-scratcher situations. The guns feel nice and I appreciate having a strange salesman around again to sell me more. The story is actually decent and there's a few cool twists along the way if you don't think too hard about them.

The werewolf zombies piss me off, but are better once you realize how to play around them effectively. A lot of the bestiary is pretty typical RE stuff, though the bosses are pretty awesome design-wise. But gameplay-wise, they sadly suffer there. 

The bosses (most of them) boil down to being a giant monster with a pretty damn obvious weakpoint sticking out and telegraphed attacks. None of them really gave me a hard time besides the Final Boss, but mostly because I wasn't armed to the teeth in power weapon ammo. She's pretty frustrating to fight against and some attacks did feel like me getting blindsided. I'm sure it's a skill issue, but all it did was compound my eternal hatred of FPS bosses.

The visuals are beautiful and it played like a dream on my 3440x1440 ultrawide, with no aspect ratio shenanigans to speak of. I didn't really notice the ray tracing enough to care to keep it on, but your mileage may vary on higher settings. The wintery environments were calming at times, despite the world that they subside in being horrifying.

TL;DR If you really like your action horror FPS games, go for it. If you're expecting RE7 but better, look elsewhere. Bosses suck, but everything else is good when ignoring any premonitions I may personally have.
