Resident Evil: Village is a horror-filled and action-packed shooter game, marking itself as one of a kind among a plethora of already respected games.

Ethan stands alone as the best Resident Evil protagonist, because of his backstory and funny one-liners. Village feels amazing to play for the first time, and brings a modern reinterpretation of elements from classic RE titles. Ethan has to defeat four lords while trying to save his beloved daughter Rose. Our main character is greeted with bio-weapons both him and his ally Chris Redfield, have never seen before. Determined to look for his daughter, Ethan embarks on his adventure in the village where he was brought to search for Rose. Ethan experiences supernatural events that no ordinary being should survive, but he stands strong throughout the whole story, in spite of getting his hands gets cut off clean or where his heart is literally ripped out. 

The first part of the game in Castle Dimitrescu feels like Resident Evil 2, 3 and 7; with the Dimitrescu family stalking you inside the castle. The puzzles in this area are some of the best ones in the whole franchise; filled with confusion and suspense, the one where you have to find and shoot 5 bells within a time limit comes to mind. When Ethan stabs Lady Dimitrescu she mutates into a massive, unrecognizable dragon. You fight her on the castle's balcony, where she charges at you and spits flies directed towards you: that fight ranks among the top ten in the whole franchise, for me at least.

We transition over to House Beneviento, which in my opinion has to be the scariest area in Resident Evil history; it might not be the longest area in the game (or in general), but what it lacks in size it makes up for in rich and worthwhile content. You solve puzzles in a basement trying to escape, while a disgusting large baby chases you in cramped hallways. The fight with Donna the Doll is just an easy version of hide and seek, depending on the difficulty you are playing on. 

Then we get to Moreau, who is one of the most disturbing characters overall. His character design is unsettling and his dialogue is filled with desperate pleas of approval to Miranda while hunting down Ethan. Moreau turns into a massive fish and tries to eat you, while attempting to drain the dam. The boss fight itself is kind of underwhelming, there isn't much action nor is it particularly difficult to kill him. 

The next lord, Heisenberg, talks to Ethan through a TV and tries to persuade him into becoming an alliance. Ethan says "nah im good", and gets launched into the depths of Heisenbergs factory. This location marks another gold standard in Resident Evil games, in terms of diffulcuty. You have to climb the factory while Heisenbergs' machinery come grabbing at you with razor sharp metal. I must confess; when I got to this part while playing on Village of Shadow, it would've been impossible for me to complete without unlocking infinite ammo. The robots take around three magnum bullets to fend off, and the machines get tougher the higher you climb up. The fight with Hesingberg is mid because of the tank that is given to you by Chris, you basically have unlimited ammunition making it super easy to defeat the boss. 

After the fight, Ethan dies (for the 2nd time) yet somehow enters a dream-state where he meets Eveline from RE:7. She shares a secret that is beyond comprehension, Ethan Winters actually died back in the previous game to Jack Baker, it was the mold that brought his body back to life. With the help of Chris, he is able to restore Ethan's consciousness, setting up the final segment of the game. Back at the Ceremony site, Mother Miranda tries to resurrect her dead daughter using Rose's flasks, before being put to a halt and initiating the final battle. This was absolute cinema, not only is Miranda in my top five for hardest bosses in the series (it took me dozens of attempts on my first playthrough to defeat her), her attacks are spontaneous and hard to counter. She has multiple forms, including her normal one, spider, bird, and dark mode form. Mother Miranda is a challenging one, and is one of the best foes the series has to offer.

Village is my 2nd favorite game in the whole franchise, and truly does feel like a proper Resident Evil experience. I rate Resident Evil: Village a 9/10.

BONUS: If you interact with the Duke, he says "What are you buying mate?" this is a callback to the merchant in RE:4. I also love how the menu progressively changes as the game goes along, more games should totally keep doing that.

Resident Evil Village Review

Resident Evil Village is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, but it feels completely different.

The game moves away from pure horror in favor of action and variety.
There are several different zones, and each feels like a separate story.
Dimitrescu Castle is a classic survival horror.
Beneviento House is almost a psychological horror.
The rest is closer to action.

The plot has become more expansive and unfolds properly by the end.
Ethan finally stops being an empty character and gets proper development.
The ending is strong and memorable.

Gameplay-wise, it's a mix of shooting, exploration, and a bit of survival.
Resources aren't as stifling as before.
More dynamic, less tension.

Bosses vary in style, but not all are difficult.
The game focuses more on atmosphere and staging than hardcore.

In the end, it's not as scary as before.
But it's more varied and spectacular.

Suitable for those who want more than just horror but also action

I really tried to like Resident Evil Village, but it just didn’t feel right at all.

Coming from Resident Evil 2, 3, 4, 7, and even 9, this game feels like a downgrade in core gameplay.

-Movement feels floaty and lacks weight. Ethan doesn’t feel grounded at all.
-Gunplay has almost no impact. Shooting enemies doesn’t feel satisfying and reactions are weak.
-Enemy behavior feels off. Lycans dodging and moving like that makes the combat feel unnatural.
-Loot visibility is poor. Items are hard to see and I constantly had to rely on the map turning blue. Even when I knew something was missing, I had to run around multiple times to find it.
-Pickup range is inconsistent—you can grab items from far away, which breaks immersion.
-Not controller-friendly. Movement feels off, aiming is inconsistent, aim assist doesn’t function properly, and only properly supporting Xbox controllers is disappointing for a modern release.

Overall interaction with the world feels clunky and inconsistent.

What confuses me the most is that the game is more action-heavy, but the mechanics don’t support that shift.

Resident Evil 7 worked because everything was slow, tight, and cohesive. Here, they increased the pace and enemy behavior but didn’t improve the movement, shooting, or feedback to match it.

The visuals are great, no doubt. But gameplay-wise, it feels like style over substance.

Resident Evil Village or Resident Evil 8 is a sequel to the Resident Evil 7 and continues Ethan's journey. This time set 3 to 4 years after RE7's story.
In RE8 Ethan have to yet again pick up weapons, craft potions and fight with monsters, undead and very strange hybrids. But just like in RE7, Ethan has a lot to lose if he fails. Even more than in his debut game...

== Pros ==
1. Gameplay - Vastly superior than RE7. Ethan handles weapons better, especially knives and is able to actually push away enemies from him after guarding. 
2. More weapons - Unlike RE7, Ethan's arsenal is way bigger and he has more means to fight and defeat his enemies. From handguns, shotguns and rifles to assault rifles, pipe bombs and even mines!
3. Vendor - Just like in RE4, and later RE4R, Ethan can buy and sell from a Vendor, but he can also upgrade his weapons to enhance them and make their upgraded selves superior. Besides that, this clearly was a test for how shopping would be like in RE4R, though there are no missions given by a Vendor, but at least we can bring him ingredients to cook stat boosting meals!
4. Boss fights - Fun and every single one have a different theme, making them feel fresh and not annoying, boring or copy pasted.
5. Exploration - similar to RE4, in Village Ethan can explore levels to find valuable items he can (combine and) sell, or he can look for ammunition, herbs, chem fluids, etc. There are also hidden jewels stuck on walls or ceilings a'la RE4.
6. Great rewards bought using CP - You can buy unlimited ammunition for your guns (have to upgrade them first), new weapons you can use in main campaign, new knife. It is pretty neat!
7. NG+ - Yes, you can replay main campaign as buffed Ethan with everything you had previously and with everything you unlocked in a CP Shop. Makes replaying this game easier but also more fun. It allows you to prepare yourself for VoS (hardest difficulty) as well.
8. Mercenaries mode - great mode, very fun. You get couple characters to choose like Ethan or Chris, have couple maps to clear and on every single map you can destroy blue orbs which will upgrade your character; you can choose which upgrade you want. 

== Neutral ==
1. Boss's presence throughout the game - Although you're meeting your antagonists, talk to them and sometimes have to run away from them, baddies of the story aren't really visible all that much and when nemeses perish (not a spoiler, you know you have to kill them) their locations are becoming even more quiet.
2. Lady Dimitrescu - She was used to create hype for RE8 using fanbase's horniness to generate clicks and views. But she's not really somebody important and [spoiler] you kill her and her daughters first [/spoiler]. 
3. Dimitrescu Daughters - dissapointing, really. Not bad, so I won't put them in a "Con" section but I expected more from them than what we got. 
4. Your hub - It is cool we get an area where we can rest a little bit and gather our thoughts, but after clearing it from enemies and valuables + items, this location becomes barren and you will have to travel through it a lot. It is not annoying, or even badly designed but it might get a little boring.
5. Story - Ethan has a lot to lose like I said, but this is still a Resident Evil story so don't think you're getting SSS writing and depth. It is nice, but not very deep. 

== Cons == 
(oh boy, I might piss some people off)
1. Stalker enemy (Castle) - So, in Castle you got Lady D in a role of a stalker enemy. At least I think because on a Standard difficulty she was absolutely not an issue. Basically I barely even saw her, and when I did all I had to do was run to the safe zone, or just dodge her (which was really easy). She's better than RE3R Nemesis, but worse than RE2R's Mr.X. 
2. Enemies are bullet sponges - You shouldn't have issues with ammo on Standard difficulty, but it is quite annoying how tanky some enemies are, especially lykans. I was using a mod giving me 1.5x more headshot damage and still had to unload half a pistol mag at them. 
3. Mini bosses - AKA bullet sponge enemy part 2. I don't know what Capcom thought but for some reason I had more problems dealing with a "mini" boss than with main bosses. They take so much damage that at one point in a game I almost was out of bullets; it was that bad!
4. House Beneviento - From a horror perspective great, interesting and ambiance was very nice. But, this is RE8's Boat section = it is linear as fck, and not even scary (at least to me) but annoying. Can't really tell you much without spoiling so I will say this: you will either like it or dislike it. Moreover, its linearity kills replay value of RE8 because you can't skip anything and have to follow its scripted path.
5. Mia - again. Seriously, I don't know why but Capcom refuses to make her a better character. She looks way, way better than in 7, but she is still a dumb b1sh who basically kickstarted all of this. And she did something so stupid I couldn't believe... Spoiler - [spoiler] So, she never told Ethan or Chris that Ethan is molded. Like ever. She only revealed that to Chris at the end of the game when it really didn't matter to Ethan anymore... [/spoiler]. And of course nothing happened to her after what she has done in RE7 (and prior to it)...
6. Ending - Technically speaking ending was great. I just didn't liked what happened to one guy... Poor dude, homie did not deserve it...
7. DLC, Shadows of Rose - Hot garbage, sadly. Basically we're playing as Rose, Ethan's and Mia's daughter, who [spoiler] has molded powers [/spoiler] but wants to get rid of them. Gameplay is way different than in RE7 or RE8; it is more of a survival horror than action horror. You get less ammo, less weapons, no shop and have to craft ammo using ingredients to do so. It is a very short DLC, about 3 hours or less but I had to stop because yet again House Beneviento had to ruin everything it. Now, just like in the main game, HB's horror atmosphere is great but because it is a linear section in a linear DLC, it makes go through it even more tedious. But that's not the worst thing - we get stalker enemies, mannequins. They're cool and move weird and creepy like. Later dolls join, and that's where sh1t hits the fan because we're in a stealth section where you don't have any healing items and have to perfectly go from point A to point B without being seen. You have basically one hit, because the second hit is death so you have to do it flawlessly. This section broke me, it was boring, annoying, and not fun. Besides that, Rose is a weaker Ethan - she can't guard or even heal during gameplay, is slow (speed, I mean) and her [spoiler] powers [/spoiler] are fcking ridicoulus even for RE standards...

It was a fun game. I recommend it but not for a full price. Buy it with expansion to get better Mercenaries.

Overall, I had a good time, and think it is worth the price especially considering how often it goes on sale. Recommended!

[h1] Resident Evil Village [/h1]

As someone who's played the majority of titles in the Resident Evil series, I thoroughly enjoyed Village. It's not without its flaws, but I'd be lying if I said I didn't have a lot of fun playing it -- because I certainly did. Most of what fans love about the series is here. But, depending on what you want and expect from a Resident Evil game, your love for Village may vary. I want to begin by talking about all of the things that this game undoubtedly gets right:

[h2] The Positives ▼ [/h2]

[b] 1. The Graphics [/b]
Like every other Resident Evil and Capcom game that uses the RE Engine, Village looks incredible and runs great. Character models are highly detailed, and even on the lowest settings, this game still looks phenomenal. 'Nuff said. 

[b] 2. The Gameplay [/b]
What has brought me back time and time again with each title has always been the gameplay, and with Village, it's no different. The loop of exploration, discovery, fighting monsters, solving puzzles and obstacles, and uncovering lore is all here. If you love previous Resident Evil games, there's a good chance you're going to enjoy Village. 

[b] 3. The Environmental Design [/b]
Village has to have some of the most beautiful locations and environmental designs I have ever seen in a Resident Evil game. From the hub village to Castle Dimitriscu, House Beneviento, Moreau Reservoir, and Heisenberg's Factory, each area is stunning, boasting its own distinct atmosphere and identity. I can't say enough good things about it. 

[b] 4. Weapon & Enemy Variety [/b]
Compared to its predecessor, RE7, Village boasts a much healthier and more interesting group of enemies to fight. Lycans of various forms, zombies, monsters created by fusing man and machine, and other mini-bosses; it's a great mix of enemies and a meaningful step up from the last game. And the weapons you'll be using to fight them are equally fun to use as well, with each having attachments and various categories to upgrade. I always looked forward to each combat encounter, and these are the reasons why. 

[h2] The Negatives ▼ [/h2]

[b] 1. Bad Writing Trope [/b]
Village suffers from a writing problem where no one tells anyone anything to drive up artificial tension and to give the plot a reason to exist, and it's annoying. It doesn't get used once, but multiple times throughout the story and DLC. Capcom could've achieved and gotten similar narrative and emotional results without having to rely on this old and tiring trope. I'm disappointed they didn't put more care into the story and its execution. 

[b] 2. Lack of Puzzles [/b]
Solving puzzles has always been one of my favorite things to do in a Resident Evil game, so I was pretty surprised to learn that they don't really exist outside of a handful. And what can be considered as puzzles are simply too easy. Considering how varied and beautiful each location is, I really wish Capcom could've spent more time designing more interesting and creative puzzles to suit the theme of each area.

[b] 3. Lack of Music [/b]
Unlike other Resident Evil games, Village opted for a more ambient-focused soundtrack for the sake of immersion. Truthfully, I don't like this creative change. Music has always played an important role in building a thick and memorable atmosphere in each game. And while I do see the benefit in some cases, I simply don't think the tradeoff is worth it for this series. 

[b] 4. Disappointing DLC [/b]
For anyone who bought the gold edition and got the Shadow of Rose DLC, you're going to be let down by its quality. Most, if not all, of the locations are reused, including a boss fight, with later parts literally boiling down to a series of trial and error chase sequences. Fun thing about one of those chases: if your frame rate is set higher than 60 FPS, it is literally impossible to beat. It's a well known and documented bug, and I can't believe Capcom hasn't fixed it yet. Not to mention the whole DLC is incredibly linear to the point of feeling like an on-rail shooter. It certainly does have its redeeming qualities, but overall, it's going to be hard to consider it as anything more than a disappointment. 

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3]

Despite its flaws, I really enjoyed my time with Resident Evil Village. It's a solid entry that delivers most of what players have come to expect and want from the series. And while it might not satisfy all fans, it certainly will with most. I am one of them, and I strongly recommend buying it on sale. It is certainly worth your time and money.

RE8 is an overall recommend from me, but a lot of weird choices were made about the game. It's a really strange Resident Evil, even by Resident Evil standards. Thankfully the good outweighs the bad, so let's start there.

Village looks astounding. I especially loved the village and castle maps, with Ethan arriving at the village in the dead of night being a stand-out for me. The game also runs really well, so the experience of moving through the environment feels smooth. Gunplay feels great, and the simple act of shooting enemies is a lot of fun. RE8 is much more action-oriented than RE7 and remains first person, which I enjoyed. Hunting for secrets and cash while I filled out the map felt rewarding and satisfying.

I'd go as far as to say that all of the core gameplay systems here are excellent. Village runs like a dream and plays clean.

Yet there's so much odd in RE8 that I just don't understand.

The story is a total mess. I couldn't empathize with any of the characters because their conflict always seemed to stem from complete absurdity. Nobody develops as a person, nobody grows in character, instead it's one deus ex machina after another until the required heroic sacrifice at the end.

These plot problems compound with the game being intensely linear, with an unreasonable amount of cutscenes that act as unexpected points-of-no-return. Bosses are generally uninteresting and act only as bullet-sponge gatekeepers to the next zone. I had high hopes for the villains in this game, but Lady Dimitrescu is gone in a flash, Heisenberg reminds me of the kind of person who would argue on internet forums, and I barely remember the rest.

Ethan is no better as our protagonist with the personality of a piece of cardboard. He's constantly making the most inane comments about the environment or, more likely, screaming as his body is brutalized in yet another cutscene. And somehow Chris is still the worst-written character of them all. It's like he speaks a different language than everyone else; he blatantly ignores or talks past others in a way that I think was supposed to read as "cool and aloof" but instead comes across as if he's got some kind of disorder.

It's expected for Resident Evil games to get funky, but RE8 doesn't handle its progression well. It moves on from the well-grounded village too quickly and into too much absurdity. As a result, RE8 isn't a game that feels like you're doing stuff, rather it's a game where stuff is constantly happening to you. The story and characters are so absurd that it's better to turn off that part of your brain and instead treat it as a gorgeous shooting gallery. If that sounds fine to you, then I would recommend Village to you on sale, but never full price.

I absolutely loved [i]Resident Evil Village[/i]. It's quite whimsical and unabashedly follows classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] and video game formulas. The opening of the game is one of the absolute best parts, and scratches that more classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] formula in the village and castle where there are rooms to clear out, search for treasures, you'll have to find all your favorite returning characters like Crank, Jack, Wheel, Key, Fuse, and probably a few others I'm forgetting. Of course, this section has a few stalker enemies in the form of Lady D and her daughters. The game is actually quite linear, and after this section they essentially tell you "that was 1 out of 4 bosses, you're gonna get the other 3 in this order now". So you move into a more classic horror experience, which is quite terrifying, but memorable, before going into more action heavy sequences that feel a little more [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. In general, from the opening village section to the last area, RE4 is a huge inspiration here. 

It's quite refreshing that [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] feels a bit less connected to the overarching RE plot, similar to [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] and Ethan gets a bit of a redemption arch as a character here as he is undoubtedly a little more interesting and charismatic than he was in his debut. Honestly, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] might be my favorite game in the series, it's a short experience, but with so much variety, and many reasons to replay with the challenge runs. If you're an RE fan it's a necessary play, but even for new players if you jump in here you'll have an awesome experience and get to see more of the full spectrum of gameplay experiences the series has to offer. 

[b]Highly Recommended[/b]

This has been the most intense feeling Resident Evil game so far. It blends the action and adventure of Resident Evil 4 with the pure horror and tension of Resident Evil 7, and with its variety of settings (village, castle, factory...) and creature designs, it truly feels like a massive game. Weapon upgrades, inventory management, and even cooking dishes with fish, pork, and beef through our dear Duke’s “let him cook” recipes that boost health and stamina make this horror focused experience surprisingly fun as well :D

Before starting the game, I only knew about Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, but it turns out they only occupy a small portion of the story. The game actually dives into the origins of the Resident Evil universe, touching on how all these mold, virus, and mutation events began. That’s why it’s worth reading the notes you find.

Mother Miranda’s Cadou experiments, aimed at reviving her daughter Eva through parasites, resulted in both failed creatures and the so called “Lords,” who were successful but still not suitable hosts. Dimitrescu is just one of them. Each Lord has their own motivation and incredibly well crafted environment. If you really want to feel fear, wait for the “House Beneviento” section. Lord Heisenberg feels like a Magneto type character. And then there’s the grotesque Moreau... those parts can be quite disturbing.

They also finally explain something about Ethan Winters that caught my attention throughout both games. His limbs keep getting severed, he gets seriously injured, yet he continues like nothing happened. It turns out that when Jack Baker “killed” him at the beginning of Resident Evil 7, he actually died, and the mold altered his body. However, his mind, memories, and identity remained intact. That’s when everything clicked for me.

After Ethan’s first encounters with Mother Miranda, the operation led by Chris and his Wolf Squad to destroy the Megamycete, despite BSAA’s involvement, gave me strong “Bravo Six, going dark” vibes from Call of Duty :D The game shifts so aggressively from horror and boss fights into full on action that it sometimes leaves you wondering what just happened.

In short, it’s a great game that ties many things together and significantly expands the universe. Definitely play the Shadows of Rose DLC. It’s important for Requiem and for Rose’s character development.

Resident Evil Village is very confusing but very good. It felt a lot like they were experimenting for a lot of their future games, making this title very interesting with the hindsight we have now that RE4 Remake and Requiem have both released. The game takes a lot of inspiration from the OG RE4 with its more combat heavy gameplay, and similar merchant system. You run through Romanian mountains committing massacres against the entire local village population for the sake of saving your daughter Rose. You collect lots of fun weapons that are pretty standard for your typical Resident Evil romp, and you upgrade them or trade them in for new ones throughout the campaign. In this game you also hunt animals and collect ingredients for your merchant to cook with, and they provide you with permanent effects like stat increases. The gameplay blending both puzzles and gunplay was fairly consistent throughout the game, with a few notable moments near the end where it kinda dragged in the factory section, but otherwise I had a lot of fun playing this game. The story like the entirety of this game is kinda mixed. I found some parts of it very interesting and fun, and I found other parts of it to be kind of annoying and sometimes straight up dookie. There were a lot of plot choices that really confused me, and not in a profound or interesting way, but in a dumb and thoughtless sort of way. Ethan Winters returns from RE Biohazard and his main plotline I found to be very simple but very effective, while everyone else is just there along for the ride. [h1]Resident Evil Village Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Resident Evil Village is a really cool sequel to Resident Evil 7. It absolutely hits in a lot of places, even if it misses in a few others. I definitely recommend this game, no question there.

That said, I also think Village could have done some things better. It follows up on Resident Evil 7 in a very interesting way, but it also shifts the series even more toward action, and that is either going to work for you or make you miss the pure horror of the previous game.

For me, it was a mixed bag in the best possible way. Very fun, very memorable, sometimes ridiculous, sometimes genuinely creepy, and occasionally it feels like the game looked at Resident Evil 4 and said, "Yeah, I want some of that too."

[hr]
[h1]What It Is[/h1]
Resident Evil Village once again follows Ethan Winters after the events of Resident Evil 7. This time, he is searching for his kidnapped daughter, Rose, after a brutal opening that throws him into a remote village full of monsters, cult-like figures, and some extremely questionable local hospitality.

As Ethan explores the village, he is forced to deal with four powerful lords, each ruling over a different area. This takes you through several distinct locations, including Castle Dimitrescu, House Beneviento, the reservoir, and Heisenberg's factory. The result is a game that feels like one long haunted tour through chaos, and honestly, it works more often than it doesn't.

[hr]
[h1]World and Exploration[/h1]
The world of Village is one of its biggest strengths.

The village itself is a great hub area, and the game does a really good job making each major section feel distinct. One minute you're exploring a gothic castle, the next you're in one of the creepiest houses in the series, and later you're dealing with much more industrial and action-heavy areas. It is a very different ride compared to Resident Evil 7, but I personally liked that variety.

Exploration is also very rewarding. There are treasures, optional items, puzzles, keys, upgrades, and hidden routes to look for. Resident Evil in general tends to do exploration well, and Village keeps that going. Even on repeat playthroughs, going back through the map and collecting things still feels fun.

[hr]
[h1]Combat and Gameplay[/h1]
Village leans much harder into action than Resident Evil 7.

The gunplay is solid, you get a much bigger arsenal this time, and the game gives you more tools to handle enemies. Ethan feels more capable here, and the overall flow is much more combat-driven. You still have inventory management and survival elements, but this is clearly a more action-focused game.

The addition of the Duke also helps a lot. He acts as the game's merchant, letting you buy weapons, upgrade gear, sell treasure, and stock up on supplies. It is not exactly the same system as Resident Evil 4, but the influence is very obvious, and honestly, I liked it a lot. If a large mysterious merchant is offering me more firepower in the middle of absolute nightmare fuel, I am not asking questions.

Enemy variety is decent overall, but some of the lycan enemies early on can feel a bit too spongy, especially when your weapons are still weak. A few boss fights also lean more into shooting until the health bar finally gives up, rather than doing anything especially deep mechanically.

[hr]
[h1]Atmosphere and Horror[/h1]
This is where Village gets a bit tricky.

There is horror here, absolutely. The atmosphere is strong, the locations are memorable, and some sections are genuinely tense. House Beneviento in particular is easily one of the scariest parts of the game and probably the closest Village gets to the full horror style of Resident Evil 7. That section is fantastic and horrifying in exactly the right way.

But outside of moments like that, Village is much more action-heavy than scary. It has creepy imagery and strong presentation, but it does not keep you on edge the same way Resident Evil 7 does. If you are hoping for pure horror all the way through, Village is probably not going to give you that.

[hr]
[h1]Characters and Story[/h1]
The characters are one of the reasons Village stays memorable.

Lady Dimitrescu became the face of the game for a reason. She has a strong presence, the castle section is great, and the way she stalks you around parts of the area definitely gives off Mr. X energy in a very good way. The other lords also help give the game its unique identity, even if some are more memorable than others.

As for Ethan, I still feel mixed about him. I do not dislike him at all, and I can appreciate what he represents. He is basically just a normal guy going through absolute hell to save his family, again, which is respectable, but also maybe somebody should stop letting this man go on family trips.

Story-wise, Village is enjoyable, but it can feel a bit over the top and a little inconsistent. It also follows a structure that feels similar to Resident Evil 7 in some ways, with Ethan moving through a series of major threats tied to his family situation. It works, but it does feel familiar.

[hr]
[h1]Pacing and Replayability[/h1]
I actually liked the pacing quite a bit overall.

Each major area has its own tone and style, which helps keep the game moving. Even when one section is not as strong as another, the game usually changes things up before it gets stale. Some parts are definitely more replayable than others, though. A few later sections can feel weaker on repeat runs once the surprise factor is gone.

Still, Village remains very fun to replay thanks to the exploration, upgrades, weapon variety, and the general flow of the campaign.

[hr]
[h1]DLC and Extra Content[/h1]
The post-launch content is worth mentioning too.

The main expansion is Winters' Expansion, which adds Third Person Mode for the main story, The Mercenaries Additional Orders, and Shadows of Rose. Shadows of Rose is a story expansion focused on an older Rose Winters and takes place years after the main game. It is a cool addition and gives the game a bit more story weight, especially if you were invested in Ethan and Rose.

Third Person Mode is also a nice feature if you wanted Village to feel a bit closer to some of the older Resident Evil games, even though the game was clearly designed around first person first.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]Great exploration with rewarding secrets, puzzles, and treasures
[*]Excellent variety between the major areas
[*]Strong atmosphere and memorable set pieces
[*]House Beneviento is terrifying in the best way
[*]The Duke upgrade system adds a lot to progression
[*]Very fun combat with a much bigger arsenal than Resident Evil 7
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]Leans too much into action compared to Resident Evil 7
[*]Not consistently scary outside a few standout sections
[*]Some enemies and bosses feel too spongey
[*]Story can feel over the top and a bit inconsistent
[*]Certain later sections are less replayable than the early game
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Resident Evil Village is a very fun and highly memorable sequel. It is not as consistently scary as Resident Evil 7, and I do think it leans too hard into action at times, but the exploration, atmosphere, level variety, and overall pacing make it absolutely worth playing.

It is a mixed bag, but a very entertaining one. If Resident Evil 7 was pure nightmare fuel, Village is more like a haunted roller coaster with a shotgun and a very large woman chasing you through a castle.

And honestly, that still sounds like a good time.

Bella - Hardest Boss - The first boss and you fight her with minimum weapon upgrades inside a tiny room
Daniela & Cassandra - Hard but manageable Bosses - They have viscious attack speed

Overall Resident Evil Village is a wonderful continuation of the franchise with great emotional story, good action and a fantastic setting. The introduction to the game is immediately engaging. You begin in a new village after leaving the area featured in *Resident Evil 7*. Ethan now has a child, and things quickly spiral when his wife is shot in front of him and his baby is taken, all by the very person who had promised to protect them.

From there, the story revolves around your attempt to get your daughter back. As you progress, you face four major bosses before reaching the final confrontation with the fifth.

The ending is decent, although the final cutscene does a much better job of setting up the direction for any future *Resident Evil* story connected to this one.

Overall, the story is strong enough to keep your attention throughout. The main frustration comes from the fact that reaching 100% completion requires roughly three to six playthroughs, and some of those runs can feel very repetitive and tedious.

Visually, the game looks excellent, especially in 4K. However, while the graphics are impressive, some of the gun audio sounds surprisingly poor and lacks impact.

The harrowing saga of the great and heroic Ethan Winters continues in RE Village, a tale of monsters and madness in the snowy mountains of Europe. Lycans have overtaken the village, and high up in Castle Dimitrescu terrors await around every corner. A direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, Ethan Winters must once again set out into the heart of danger, not for money or because it's his job like that loser Leon Kennedy, but for love and honor. Will Ethan survive the battle scarred village and overcome the Lycan empire? Will he escape the castle and the allure of the sexy vampire babes therein? Will he find his daughter Rose and defeat the giant baby, fish man and other weirdos? Well... you can't spell Winters without W..I..N.

While the previous title was a pure horror masterpiece, this entry leans closer to being an action game while continuing the compelling story of Ethan Winters. Many elements of the game are clearly inspired by Resident Evil 4, and the village-centered level design is well-crafted. Its iconic characters are something I will never forget.

Gameplay : Standard Resident Evil gameplay but it can't make up its mind whether or not its an action game or a survial horror game, you pretty much get access to every gun you'll need before you even finish the first main Boss

Antagonists : Goth Mommie and Hillbilly Magnito and Crazy Angel lady are the only standouts, the rest could have been cut and you could have extended those 3's areas and storylines.

The main HUB village you spend a good portion of time in, could have had more going on in it, you clear it out one time and then you have free reign of the place outside of one or two unique encounters.

# 7/10

SPOILER FREE:

There are two games in RE8-- action, and horror. IMHO the action parts just don't work and everything boils down to bullet sponging enemies. With that being said, the horror parts carry the rest of the game

If this is your first RE game then I would by far recommend the RE2 remake as opposed to this since its story is much more coherent and actually well written, and the horror parts linger until the endgame

My main gripes are with the narrative as a whole, and the way the characters get written. The protagonist is quite literally a 0 dimensional character.
Some actual quotes from the protagonist:
"It's dark"
"What the hell?"
"What the hell is wrong with this place?"
"What the hell?" (again)
"What the hell?"
"What the hell do--" (again)
"Man, screw this castle"
"What the hell...?"
etc etc, more "what the hell" moments and that's all he says.

He gets irrationally angry every chance he gets and even gives up his advantages because of it. He cannot even be a self insert character because the choices he makes don't reflect my own

With that being said, the story is best when Ethan (protagonist) is not speaking. Unfortunately, this only happens for the first half of the game. However, the reason for the 7/10 is because the early to mid game is fantastic. The vibe is just on point for everything up until the first of five big boss battles. I think some of the content just got half baked along the way in the later areas. 

I can only recommend the first half of the game :(



## SPOILERS AHEAD

Overall, the early - mid game is fantastic. The length is short but it didn't feel that way. The reason I give it a bad review is because the story is just so bad that it took me out of the game far too many times to count and I ended up rolling my eyes multiple times throughout the game. Individual sections are fine on their own but the four bosses and one main boss concept just doesn't work at all. It feels like Nuka World DLC for Fallout 4. Each section is underbaked (with the exception of the Castle) and each "vibe shift" which is what I believe they were going for could've been a part of the same section. ie: if you want to shift from Lady Dimi's atmosphere into House Beneviento, just make an expanded part of the Lady Dimi lore instead of making a whole new character and boss fight. That would safely remove 1-2 bosses since they tend to get very repetitive and make a mockery of the narrative as a whole.

I hate all of the characters involved in this story except Heisenburg (who was a rational guy and Ethan didn't listen to), and Dimi. Ethan, bro, you're not Leon, just give up ATP

This one is painful for me; I am a huge Resident Evil fan, especially since did a semi-reboot and starting remaking the series. Except for Resi3R, they have all been straight A's. Another exception comes with Resi8. 

I know I'm in the minority here, but I hate this game. Capcom have reinvented Resident Evil several times now, and this one just feels like they jumped the shark and just added whatever the hell they felt like into. I think I would look at it far more favourably if this wasn't part of the RE series. 

Story first: It's an absolute mess. The whole plot stinks of several rewrites. Nothing in the game makes sense. Resident Evil has so far managed to contain itself in it's own internal logic; but this just doesn't seem like it gives a ♥♥♥♥. Werewolves, vampires... because mold? What? My suspension of disbelief just can't accomodate that much ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 
Or maybe it could have if the game didn't follow Ethan - arguably the worst RE protagonist of all time. Ethan worked for RE7. A random dude, dragged thoroughly out of his depth into a nightmare rendition of Texas chainsaw massacre. I get it, it works. 

This one, he's just painfully boring. He just wanders from one set-piece to another, constantly tricked into bad situations, and has zero likability. Even Punished-Chris over here, acting like a Metal Gear Solid villain, is more charismatic here. And he gets done dirty here as well, for absolutely no reason other than the plot demands that Ethan have no idea what he's doing until 15 minutes before the game ends. It's truly painful. If Ethan were written out entirely, and this was just Chris' rendition of Resident Evil 4, I would have enjoyed it more. 

- Stuck in some Eastern European hell-hole, trapped with virus monsters driven by nutty cult. winner. Boulder punch your way to victory. That's an easy dub. But we didn't get that. 

Gameplay wise, it's fine. Fist person mode does NOT suit this game in the slightest. This is definately not a horror game. Ethan can now tank literal deathblows and shrug them off. Enemies are everywhere, ammo is plentiful (despite mobs being absolute bullet sponges). The classic explorative section that every RE game is easily the best section of the game (Castle Dimitrescu), but remains painfully short. Then a quick almost on-rails horror section. And after that it's just a straight enemy/boss rush until the final section of the game. 

DLC wise: This is where it gets tricky. The actual 'new content' is dogwater. The expansion focused on Ethan's daughter is just a bizzare additon, made almost entirely out of cobbled together RE8 assets, and has no impact on the anything going forward. You do however get third-person mode for both Ethan and Rose's campaigns. It's a nice addition; but it doesn't feel as fluid as RE2/3/4R. The game's movement just wasn't designed for it. 

Overall, If you're just here to shoot things - this game will probably give you what you're looking for. I knew going into this I wasn't going to be happy with where they took the franchise here, and I wasn't proven wrong. With that said, the game is absolutely gorgeous and the actual moment to moment gameplay is very good. Take this review for what it is: one mans opinion.

Got it with RE7 during a Capcom sale some time back, so I played both this week back to back.

It was interesting to see how much grander and more ambitious this RE game was following the events of RE7. You can clearly feel the bigger budget in this one: gorgeous art direction, creepy when it needs to be, top-notch voice acting from most of the main cast of villains, and a much bigger map to explore with level design that made sense and didn’t make me feel lost.

Gameplay-wise, it’s a much smoother and cleaner experience following RE7, with more enemy variety, which was my main criticism of the previous game, the addition of the merchant "The Duke" was cool and certainly better than tossing some coin inside a cage in RE7 to buy stuff. The boss fights are much more engaging this time around and much larger in scope. I'm a sucker for gothic horror aesthetics, so this game easily jumps into my top five favorite RE games.

I can’t think of anything that negatively impacted my experience while playing, but I do have to point out that the game starts a bit slow in your first two hours or so. However, it really gets better and better as you play and progress. My favorite section, and arguably the scariest, is within a certain house full of "dolls"—no spoilers.

Overall, a very enjoyable RE game that features both creepy survival horror and big action spectacle. Oh, and Chris is there.

This game is a combination of Resident Evil 4 and its other predecessors, including Resident Evil 7. More of the game is RE4 than any other Resident Evil game -- you have to manage a tile-based inventory system throughout the game in order to hold multiple weapons, ammunition for those weapons, and other items; you fight horror creatures a lot more than you experience horror; your player character engages a lot in corny, campy dialogue more than being scared or serious; there is an eccentric, zany merchant; etc. The story directly follow Resident Evil 7 where the protagonist, Ethan Winters, has moved away from the events from what happened in the last game, where he has become a dad in addition to being a husband, but the effects of the last game drag him back into being a force of nature with an arsenal of guns.

I would have to say that the first half of the game is a lot stronger than the second half of the game. One setting is an interwoven, nonlinear castle where you can progress a couple of different ways or explore to find additional treasures -- all while being chased by a giant woman; another setting is an escape room as you deal with horrific imagery and enemies. Afterwards, the other settings are more centered around using your expanded arsenal in how you choose to best pick apart the various enemies in your path.

Overall, I can recommend this game if you enjoy RE4 with little bits of something actually horrifying mixed into the action or if you are a fan of Resident Evil in general. I can also recommend it if you are interested in the main characters of Resident Evil 7 and want a continuation of their story.

Resident Evil Village is a solid addition to the franchise and the second main entry to feature Ethan Winters as the protagonist.

Like Resident Evil 7, the game sticks with a first-person perspective, which changes the overall feel compared to the more traditional third-person titles. The restricted field of view makes enemy ambushes harder to spot and generally increases the tension. Enemies also feel more threatening up close, as the first-person perspective allows you to see far more detail during encounters and cutscenes. This results in a thrilling horror experience, especially on higher difficulty settings.

However, the game is structured into several different sections, each with its own scenery and design. While this variety keeps things fresh and interesting to explore, it also has a downside. Because there are so many distinct areas, some of them end up feeling shorter than they should. Even though they are polished and well designed, the pace can make certain sections feel rushed.

The weapon progression also feels overly linear. Each new weapon you obtain within the same category tends to be a direct upgrade in nearly every aspect compared to the previous one. Because of that, fully upgrading earlier weapons often feels pointless, since the game soon offers a stronger replacement—sometimes even for less money than some of the upgrades for the previous weapon would cost.

There are also a few moments that break immersion. One example is a scene where Ethan reattaches his hand, and somehow his jacket is magically restored along with it. Small details like that don’t ruin the game, but they can make you stop and question what just happened.

That said, the game does offer replay value. Even if you already know where the scares are, a second playthrough reveals small pieces of foreshadowing and story clues that are easy to miss the first time. Seeing those details in hindsight adds a new perspective to the narrative.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a strong entry that combines tense first-person horror with varied environments and a story that rewards paying attention.

I just finished Resident Evil Village (RE8). Its a beautiful and mysterious game that blends action, horror, and suspense perfectly. The story is rich and full of secrets that keep you thinking until the end.

The Story and Atmosphere

The story is emotional and very well written. You travel through a strange village that looks enigmatic and beautiful. Capcom is excellent at creating atmosphere. Sometimes the game feels like a psychological thriller, and it is very successful at making you feel scared.

Gameplay: Variety and Action

The best thing about RE8 is that the game is always changing.
Constant Variety: You visit many different levels, and you fight different types of enemies and bosses. The gameplay never feels boring because something new is always happening.
The Merchant and Weapons: Just like in other games, there are many weapons available. You can buy, sell, and trade with the merchant (The Duke). This makes the progression feel very satisfying.
Story Length: The campaign is about 20 hrs long, which is a perfect length for this kind of adventure.

Visuals and Performance

The graphics are 10/10. The environment design is a visual masterpiece. You can see that the developers paid meticulous attention to every small detail in every room and forest.

Performance: The game is extremely stable and runs perfectly. I did not face any bugs or performance issues. The frame rate is smooth even in heavy areas, and the optimization is flawless.

Value for Money

With a 20 hrs story and amazing visuals, the game is definitely worth it. Its a high quality experience from start to finish.

Pros (The Good Stuff)

* Perfect emotional story with a lot of mystery.
* Beautiful graphics and masterpiece environment design.
* Constant variety in levels, enemies, and bosses.
* Great weapon system with the Duke.
* Flawless performance and perfect optimization.

Cons (The Not-So-Good Stuff)

*The game is too linear, you are often forced to follow one single path.
*Puzzles are way too easy and do not challenge your brain.

Note:
Imo, you must play the previous part RE7 to understand the story, its directly connected to this part.

Final Rating: 9/10

They say it takes a village. To do what? I'm not sure. I have ADHD and this means I sometimes miss things that people are saying to me - an unfortunate side effect. 

It was a cool summer afternoon. I took a walk to my local cafe. It was nestled between a laundromat and convenience store, both of which were highly overpriced. The cafe was no exception, however it was one of the few that was still open. Cafes that continued to serve past noon should be celebrated for the rarities that they are, particularly those that knew how to make a consistent brew. I made idle conversation with the joint barista and owner. We soon found we had nothing to discuss, however. I ordered my usual and sat down outside. Double espresso with a dash of hot water. Many cafes will pull the shots so that they pour onto the side of the mug. The resulting crema that forms would therefore be consistent and smooth across the top of the brew as it settled, like a field of cream. Maybe it was inexperience, or laziness, but this cafe neglected to do so. Instead the double espresso would be served with two evenly spread abcesses from where the coffee and poured. These disruptions to the crema formed two ‘snake bites’, which tended to disipate as I poured in the dash of hot water myself. It’s the little imperfections that you can count on which build connection, familiarity, and appreciation. 

The neighbourhood was empty, as usual. These visits to the cafe often left me feeling depressed. It wasn’t the coffee, it was the loneliness that crept into me. Looking at the scene, you wouldn’t have thought there existed another soul in the universe than my own, and the barista. The amber light of the sun filled my field of view. The many homes in the area were clearly those of wealth. Where was everyone? This seemed to be a common experience for me, or, at least something I found entered my mind. It just didn’t fit. Like having a restaurant which faced a brick wall. To sit and enjoy a moment such as this required people. It required passing connection with those sharing the spaces you inhabit. It’s the same feeling you get when you see an old man on his own. Even though you know nothing of his circumstances, you feel sorry for him. It feels wrong to see someone, who should be surrounded by others, solitary. You wish not to be like him in the future, dreading the passage of time. Yet you fail to consider that he might just be waiting for a niece, son, or partner. 

There’s something to be said for experiences in life which just don’t add up. Moments of unease where you can’t quite place what is wrong, yet you know deep down that something simply is not right. I am glad, nay, exuberant to say that Resident Evil Village is not one of these experiences, not at all! In fact, it is a game that oozes the feeling of rightedness. The gears of this game are well-oiled, moving in harmony without a hint of rust nor the whine of inefficient metal-on-metal. Sure, it has its moments, but all-together it’s a fine experience and a wonderful addition to the resident evil lineup. Overall, Resident Evil Village is a fantastic entry in the series. It balances horror, action, exploration, and story really well. If you enjoy survival horror or liked Resident Evil 7, this is absolutely worth playing.

I didn't get to play through Resident Evil 7 when it first came out and to this day I've not been able to play it. There's only been a handful of games to ever give me motion sickness and unfortunately RE7 and 8 were both on that list. (Wolfenstein 2014 is another game that initially gave me issues if you are curious.) With no FOV sliders, no alternate camera options, the best I could do is turn off as many of the simulated camera movements as I could but in the end it was still giving me a migraine after an hour of play. 

So I chose to ignore both games and assumed I'd never get to play them...

Until the Shadows of Rose DLC dropped and brought with it an entirely new third person mode for RE8. Now granted I am still missing out on RE7, but I'm not about to look a gift horse in the mouth. I've been wanting to play this game for years and I frankly didn't know that this DLC included a third person camera for the entire base game. With RE9 around the corner (at the time of my starting the game) I saw a perfect opportunity to jump in. 

So, does RE8 hold up? Does RE8 work as a third person game? Should you play RE8 if you've never played RE7? 

The answer to all these questions is... well its complicated. 

I'll address the last question first: should you even play this game if you haven't played RE7. These two games are pretty directly linked and honestly kind of exist off on their own. Some classic Resident Evil characters that you will recognize show up and are mentioned but for the most part 7 and 8 are pretty stand alone from every other game in the series. RE8 does a good job of recapping the events of RE7 and you should at the very least know what happened in that game before you start this one or you may be a little lost. (Especially with regards to the end of RE8...)

I watched a friend play through a good amount of 7 and watched the recap that RE8 provides and I feel that was more than enough get me through the games biggest story beats. 

That brings us to: Does it hold up?

Absolutely. This game feels as fresh today as I imagine it felt back in 2021. While I don't think this game ever really reaches the scary levels that RE2 Remake reaches I do think this game has its own unique feeling of dread that just never goes away. Everything feels super claustrophobic (even in third person) and you are constantly left feeling like you're being watched at all times. It leaves you with this uneasy feeling that really never goes away throughout the entire playthrough. There are definitely moments where they load you up with ammo and resources to give you a power trip, but its nothing on the level of what RE4 Remake does. 

The individual levels that you go through are all incredibly well designed and if you'll permit me to be a bit hyperbolic for a moment: I honestly feel this game has some of the best puzzles in the entire series. With one entire section more or less dedicated to it with nearly zero combat. The only thing that I didn't love and kind of struggled with was the main hub area. I think a good amount of that could be attributed to the visual clutter that this game embraces. It looks wonderful in the individual areas with tables covered in items, floors littered with little objects and debris, beautiful particle effects, some of the best water and blood I've ever seen in a game, and (at least until RE9) best in class lighting and shadows all bringing everything together. But that main hub area was really tough for me to navigate with many of the paths looking a little too samey. A small mark on an otherwise stellar presentation. 

Lastly: Does RE8 work as a third person game?

I'd say so yeah, but not without caveats. Look I'm not gonna blow smoke up your butt here, this game was never meant to be seen or played this way. They will tout that this mode was built from the ground up for the game and that might be true but this game was not built from the ground up for third person. This game was certainly not rebuilt in any significant way to accommodate third person either. Big things like transitional animations between crouching, side strafing, mantling, all look and feel very awkward with extremely harsh camera movements. Cutscenes are all still in first person which can very often taken away from the impact of what's happening in game. Moments that might be scary are somewhat ruined when the camera punches into first person because you KNOW that something is going to happen giving you plenty of time to brace. 

But despite all that if you are like me and cannot experience this game any other way: this is truly the best way to do it and in the end its better than nothing. Don't continue to miss out on one of the best games in the entire series. 

4/5

I have mixed feelings about this game, even though I haven't played a lot of the RE series, but amongst them, I would rate this being one of the weakest.

The most glaring flaw would be the pacing of the game. Some areas can be completed in an hour or less, whereas some are significantly larger. Even though the story is set within a day or 2, it doesn't make sense to just 'simplify' certain areas. Furthermore, there are many points of no return but thankfully the game accounted for the player skipping exploration. It is totally possible to finish the game by just rushing without exploring. However, it annoyed the hell out of me as I was saving some spots to explore later only to get locked out.

The encounters don't really get more interesting and by the end of the game they just end up being irritating. Even in the beginning, the enemies felt unnaturally tough, not sure if that is the intention. I would appreciate it more if the game difficulty didn't come from enemies taking more bullets to take down, but rather having less resources to work with? The first-person perspective felt very janky, with awkward movement. That's why the horror elements felt 'forced' to me.

The game introduced a mechanic to increase survivability, but with how tanky the enemies are, each encounter ended up unnecessarily prolonged, with me living longer and the enemy just eating my shots, usually with them in my face, blocking the camera. The enemies will sometimes dodge when you are aiming but it felt like they were input-reading at times, making it more frustrating.

All in all, the game just felt average I guess? Not exactly a good shooter experience, the horror is standard jump scares or being stalked while disarmed, and lastly the story is just weird. I would still recommend to buy it on a discount, especially if you are a fan, but otherwise, I think you are not missing out on a lot.

Resident Evil Village is the direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, but it feels more like the spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4, which makes it both weird and awesome at the same time. It also reached a wider audience thanks to the addition of Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, so I have to give credit to the developers for their creativity.

Even though the game leans heavily toward action-oriented combat, it still tries to satisfy fans of both styles with sections meant to make the player feel vulnerable, such as the introduction before entering the village and the House Beneviento segment. However, the direction of the game is clear: Capcom wanted to recapture the lightning in a bottle that made Resident Evil 4 so popular. You have a village where you must survive an ambush while being severely underprepared, four enemies you must hunt down before reaching the endgame and facing the true villain, a relentless stalker inside a huge explorable castle, open areas with different enemy types, optional encounters that are worth checking out, and a mysterious merchant who sells weapons, upgrades and resources. Combined with the variety of powerful weapons available, the game clearly borrows the right ideas to create a memorable experience.

RE8 is enjoyable, but it’s far from perfect. The story sometimes feels forced and doesn’t always make sense, some elements don't connect with each other and it feels all over the place. Ethan Winters is also not a particularly well-written character. He’s just a regular guy who often has no idea what’s going on, and he feels like a bland protagonist compared to Leon S. Kennedy. This might just be my perspective, but as a Romanian, I don’t feel like the village is as well-defined as the one in Spain from Resident Evil 4. It resembles villages from Transylvania, which makes sense given the theme (vampires and lycans), but there could have been more details and localized elements to make it feel authentic. There are only a few written Romanian words in the game, and the locals don’t speak the language or even have an accent. Another downgrade is that weapons are mostly direct upgrades rather than meaningful alternatives while also having no infinite storage. This hurts replayability because you’ll almost always choose the best weapon available.

In the end, Resident Evil Village is still a solid game like the other modern entries in the series. It’s definitely worth playing at least once for the main story and multiple times for players who enjoy challenge runs.

[h3]TL;DR[/h3]
[h2]Resident Evil Village is an incredibly fun horror-action game with fantastic art direction, memorable environments, and strong replay value—but the story and dialogue are shockingly weak and often undermine the experience.[/h2]

I've played Village about six times on PS5, and returning to it on PC with mouse and keyboard (plus mods) was really fun. The art direction is outstanding, the graphics still look fantastic, and a couple sections of the game are especially memorable—Castle Dimitrescu and House Beneviento specifically.

This said, the game's weaknesses are significant enough that it's worth setting expectations going in.

The biggest problem is the story. The narrative setup relies on a character refusing to explain what's happening during a traumatizing situation for no good reason. It's a frustrating and lazy storytelling device that feels especially strange because it's completely out of character for this classic Resident Evil Protagonist. The mystery never becomes compelling because the foundation for it is so weak.

Now there's Ethan.

Ethan Winters was a serviceable protagonist in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard because his simple motivations and minimal dialogue helped immerse the player in the setting. In Village, however, his bland personality and awkward dialogue become genuinely irritating. He throws out one-liners throughout the game that aren't clever, aren't funny, and land with a painfully flat delivery.

One of the strengths of Resident Evil has always been its charismatic protagonists, so Ethan's execution here feels especially jarring.

The core structure of the game also creates narrative problems.

The premise is simple: you collect four items from the four lords of the village in order to confront the main villain. The issue here is that these lords—aside from Heisenberg—have no narrative weight beyond their immediate function. The director has said in interviews that Village was designed to feel like a "horror theme park," and I think the team absolutely succeeded. Each lord's domain feels distinct and creatively designed but absent of stakes with shallow connections to the main plot.

Fortunately, the ending lands with some emotional weight and ties up a few threads that set up future developments for the series. That said, I would strongly recommend playing Resident Evil 7: Biohazard first—not only because it's a stronger game overall, but because Village spoils several major story elements from it.

Ultimately, I still had a lot of fun with Resident Evil Village. It has great atmosphere, secrets to uncover, and a New Game Plus system that makes it highly replayable. As long as you go in expecting a stylish horror blockbuster without a tight story, there's a lot to enjoy here.

Cheers.

[h3]A fantastic ride full of folk-horror spooks.[/h3]

RE Village is the direct continuation of 7 and it’s the conclusion of one of the most compelling RE protagonists yet, Ethan Winters. This game has a fantastic storyline with great pacing, perhaps it moves a bit too fast to let you bask in the glorious folk-gothic atmosphere this game offers.

From a gameplay perspective, it’s a weird hybrid of old and new, almost plays like RE4 in first person and the amount of enemies you encounter are WAY more numerous compared to 7, which the game more than compensates with the arsenal you’re given.

This game is structured in a way that you need to deal with 4 Lords with the village itself serving as the main hub area, each lord has their own thematic structure, like a castle, a house, a lake and a factory, each with their own set of challenges and puzzles to overcome.

One of the more common criticisms is the early encounter with Lady Dimitrescu, with many people arguing it should've happened much later, which I can understand to a degree, but her fight needed to be at the beginning if they were sticking to the formula of “the day passes throughout the story” and I get the feeling she needed to be a daylight fight. 

Other than that, I wish there were more areas like the castle Dimitrescu and Hisenberg’s factory due to how fun and challenging they were to explore and delve into.

Great performance with equally great graphics, you can run from one side of the village to the other without seeing a single stutter. Perhaps the only areas where I saw a few framedrops were near the end where things get pretty crazy and hectic.

Tons of unlockables and incentives with great replay value once the main game is done and over.

Overall, a fantastic entry in this great franchise, I can't really think of many negatives to say about it, I greatly enjoyed this game from start to finish.

I played through Resident Evil Village after finishing RE7, and it felt like a natural follow-up but with a bit more action mixed in.

The game keeps the first-person perspective from RE7, but the overall scale feels bigger. Instead of being mostly stuck inside one house, you’re exploring the village and several different locations around it. Each area has its own style and atmosphere, which keeps things from feeling repetitive.

The characters are definitely a big part of what makes the game memorable. Lady Dimitrescu and her castle were probably the most talked-about part before release, and honestly that section is really good. The castle has that classic Resident Evil exploration feeling with locked doors, puzzles, and slowly unlocking new paths. But the other areas stand out too. The Beneviento house in particular was one of the creepiest sections in the game and felt very different from the rest.

Combat feels a bit more action-focused compared to RE7. There are more enemies and more situations where you’re expected to fight your way through. The weapon upgrade system through the Duke was a nice addition since it gives you a reason to keep improving your loadout as the game goes on. It feels good slowly turning Ethan into a much stronger character as you progress.

The story continues directly from RE7 and expands a lot more on the overall lore. You start learning more about the bigger picture behind the events, and by the end it ties into the series in some interesting ways. Some parts of the story get a little wild compared to the more grounded feeling of RE7, but it still kept me interested.

Enemy variety is definitely better here than in RE7. You fight several different types of enemies depending on the area you’re in, which helps keep combat fresh throughout the game. The boss fights are also pretty memorable and feel bigger in scale.

If I had to point out a couple downsides, some sections feel a bit shorter than I expected, especially the castle. Also, because the game jumps between different styles of gameplay depending on the area, the pacing can feel a little uneven at times.

Overall though, I really enjoyed Resident Evil Village. It keeps the horror elements from RE7 but mixes in more action and variety. The different locations, memorable bosses, and expanded story make it a really fun entry in the series. It might lean a bit more toward action than pure horror, but it still manages to keep that Resident Evil tension throughout most of the game

This is not a review of the gameplay this is a review of the story.

As stated in my review of RE7, I did not pay for this game nor did I play this game. I refuse to support Capcom for these entries because they are not Resident Evil, they are a new IP that amounts to generic action horror with no unique identity of its own. I do not recommend this for anyone wanting to experience Resident Evil.

*Spoilers*

Negatives:

1. Annoying modern trends: 

- The player character speaking of their own accord outside of cutscenes, especially in horror. As the player, I should be the one reacting, the player character should not be telling me what I should be feeling or how I should be reacting. Many people argue that the play character speaking is realistic but in reality what is is doing in a horror game is breaking the tension, reducing the fear, and removing the isolation for the player by taking them out of the moment and allowing them to react to the character rather than the atmosphere. Stop neutering horror experiences.

- Hand holding and sign posting with interaction icons and with yellow/white paint/fabric, and spelling everything out for people who are unable to think for themselves. I don't like being told where to go or what I can and can't pick up or interact with. The idea that these are included in most games now and people still claim to be "exploring" is ridiculous on the face of it. Following icons and paint to your next destination is not exploring. Not knowing where you are going and getting lost is intergral to exploration and in a horror game heightens tension and fear. Stop neutering horror experiences.

- Over explaining the backstories of the antogonist and other bad characters to make the player sympathize with them. The reason a person does a bad thing does not excuse the bad thing, they do not deserve sympathy. Stop confusing understanding with rationization, the only reason to understand why people do bad things is to try to prevent it in the future. Many serial killers had a terrible childhood, not all but many, but they don't deserve sympathy. Nothing can rationalize or excuse their actions. Even more people also experience a terrible childhood and don't take it out on other people. In horror especially, understanding the why reduces the horror. Fear of the unknown is universal and the greatest fear because in not knowing the viewer/player gets to imagine their own personal worst fears. Unfortunately, too many people have no imagination and need to be spoon fed everything. 

- Turning all long running franchises into "Dad" games. Stop turning fun and interesting protagonists into sad, depressed, burned out, tired, and boring old men. Stop turning fun and interesting everyman characters into super soldiers.

2. Worst protagonist in the entire franchise: Ethan is still a faceless, milk-toast, nothing-burger of a character and we are given no reason to care about him or his family. He stayed with Mia even though she was a bio-researcher working for an illegal arms and biological weapon dealing organization and is directly responsible for the events of the previous game. Ethan therefore deserves no sympathy or empathy in this game when Mia is again responsible for his predicament. And the cherry on top Mia, the guilty bio-terrorist, survived both the previous game and this game and Ethan apparently didn't even survive the opening of the previous game.

3. Plot Hole: It makes no sense that Chris and his organization didn't know that Ethan is made entirely of mold. They checked both him and Mia and, according to the documents in the game, were analyzing Rose for traces of mold. If they were that inaffective at identifying it then how do they know that the only remaining mold on earth exists under the village? Isn't that why they blow up the village and everything in the vicinity at the end, because its the last of the mold? How can they know that when they didn't even know Ethan was entirely mold? Terrible writing.

4. Tonal Whiplash: The game cannot decide what genre it wants to be. Gothic Horror, Cultist Horror, Biological Horror, or Action. It has just as much action as RE5 which is great for an action game but terrible for a Resident Evil game. 

5. Enemy design: The enemy variety is better than the mold but when the bar is on the floor, crawling over it is really isn't an accomplishment. The mold and evrything related to the mold is lame compared to the viruses. Its not even as interesting as the Plagas parasite which I also don't like but prefer infinitely to the mold. The mold now has supernatural powers not just biological mutation. One of the reasons they canceled the haunted castle version of RE4 is because Resident Evil isn't supernatural, its science fiction, viruses, mutations.

6. More Character Assassination: RE8 brings the the real Chris Redfield back after RE7 used a weird imposter that surely was designed by AI. The return of Chris should be a positive but instead Chris is turned into an idiot as a contrivence to justify the events of RE8 even happening. Chris creates more problems simply by not telling Ethan the truth in the beginning. There was no reason for Chris to not to tell Ethan everyhing at the beginning except that the game needed to happen and the writers couldn't figure out a way to make that happen without Chris being stupid. I don't have a favorite character in this franchise, and I am not a Chris superfan but this is a character assassination of Chris who with decades of experience would have known better.

7. Lazy and contrived writing: Overexplaining and adding to the origins of Umbrella is at best getting old and at worst lazy writing to force a connection between RE7/8 and pre-RE7 games. RE5 did this to connect itself to RE4 and both RE4/5 to the previous games and it felt contrived there too. If the story they are telling cannot naturally connect to the previous mainline games then they should just accept that it is a different IP or side story and not give it a mainline number. They messed up the numbering way back with RE3 and CV.

- RE3 is basically an RE2 side story or DLC taking place at the same time as RE2. It should have just had a subtitle "Nemesis" or "Last Escape" as it was originally intended, its fine that it has a number but CV really deserved a number more.

- RECV should be RE3 or RE4, maintaining the subtitle is fine but unnecessary.

- RE4 should not be numbered it should be called RE: Las Plagas or RE: Los Illuminodos, its a side story at best, but its really a different IP.

- RE5 should not be numbered  it should be called RE: Uroboros, its a side story at best, but its really a different IP.

- RE6 could be called RE4 as it follows the Progenitor family of viruses again or RE: Chrysalid (C-Virus) if seen as a side story. But really it should just be ignored because it is bad. The game moved so far from the franchise in both gameplay, atmosphere, and story, that Capcom overcorrected when making RE7. 

- RE7 is a side story at best but really Capcom back peddled so hard after RE6, they actually created a new IP, but got scared it couldn't stand in its own so they threw in discount Chris Redfield and stapled it to Resident Evil again.

- RE8 should just be called Village, its a side story at best but its really a different IP and shouldn't be title Resident Evil at all.

- The mainline numbering should only be at 4, possibly 5 but mainline numbers should focus on the Progenitor viruses.

Positives:
