Resident Evil Village is a story about a man who has some really awful luck. Continuing the story of Ethan Winters from the last Resident Evil. I had come up with some kind of silly name for this somewhere in the 11-ish hours it took me to finish it. Something about locked doors. That's where the story ought to be. Ethan has a solid skill in finding doors that must be opened.
Anyway... The game starts off pretty intense, sending you on your journey to save your daughter Rose. Simple enough purpose, but the execution was not really all that engaging. As a father, there's nothing I wouldn't do to save my daughters. So I thought this would be a story that'd really resonate with me. But, nope. It just kind of falls flat due to the extreme lack of urgency and an odd decision to use the story as a dangling carrot that you never quite catch.
I think, perhaps, the biggest failure is that the absolute best characters in the game are not featured for nearly as much time as they deserved. Ah well. In any case the story plays out in general RE fashion. Notes, some cutscenes, dialogue, and progression through some weird and spooky places.
In the end I don't think the story was very good. Characters felt like they existed only to be thrown away, forgotten about rather quickly. There's never a real explanation as to why Ethan and his family ended up in Europe, and the ending was fairly disappointing. Mostly felt like a setup for the DLC which you may or may not play. I guess after playing 7 I really expected more with 8.

This is probably one of the least spooky Resident Evil games. A few jump scare moments, but nothing that actually gave me a shiver. It follows in 7's footsteps with the FPS perspective, unless you choose a third person view. Your call. Walk round, run, shoot things, solve puzzles, open doors, navigate fairly large areas, and of course shoot more things. Also boss fights. It works.
And, I don't really dislike the presentation. The game's environments are pretty well designed, so they were mostly a pleasure to explore. Sometimes I had some trouble finding my way around, but that's probably due to my lack of map reading and navigation skills.
I think the gameplay suffers from presenting so many situations that don't feel like they matter. We're introduced to characters that have the impact of a wet fart. There's this idea of characters having some deep layers, followed very quickly by a "lol, just kidding."
Combat is not difficult. Several different weapons to use, plenty of ammo, with mostly incompetent enemies. Aside from the boss fights and a few enemies there weren't many challenges. Fairly entertaining to fight the enemies though. I guess the short version is just to say it's fun-ish.

There are some really beautiful areas in the game, and great character models. I'm playing this almsot 5 years later, and I think it looks fantastic for 90% of the game. There are some character models that look a little off, and some animations that look silly from afar. But overall? Great locations, cool enemy designs, and very pleasing to the eyes.

Something about the voice acting here just didn't mesh with me. Some characters are great. Some, eh... not so much. I think it's just the emotional aspects falling a bit flat at times. Good music. Subdued sound effects for guns, which was disappointing.

It won't be my favorite Resident Evil for sure. It's not a satisfying conclusion of this part of Resident Evil's story, and also falls in that "barely Resident Evil," category.

A fantastical departure from what you normally see in Resident Evil, becoming a delightful Theme Park of Horror. In the end, it still manages to completely feel like a Resident Evil game, both in tone, themes, and tying in to the greater story and world. 

+ The Village location is the most delightfully varied in any Resident Evil game. The 4 lords each have their own completely unique, absolutely gorgeous lairs.
+ A sort of soul successor of RE4, with similar item shop and gun upgrading gameplay to add a bit of fun and levity. As well as a similarly interconnected world. 
+ Higher budget from the success of 7 means plenty of enemy variety this time around. 
+ Overall atmosphere is amazing. It never feels like it's gone full fantasy horror. Everything is still rooted in Resident Evil lore and science fiction. The twists that bring it all back around are a treat.
+ The 4 Lords are a delightful creature feature. It creates a larger variety of aesthetics, scares, and locales then we've ever seen, or probably ever will see, in a Resident Evil game. 

- This game is not very scary, outside of a few segments (one standout). While still certainly iconic and suspenseful, Lady D just doesn't instill the terror that the Bakers of 7 or Tyrant of 2 remake did as the "unkillable stalker". Most of the zones are too well lit and the gun upgrade focused system makes things more in line with RE4's "tensity" than actually scary or uncomfortable.
- There's a segment similar to the "Boat" of 7 that similarly just isn't that fun. 
- Ethan worked as a mostly silent player-surrogate in 7, but now that he's more of an MC, he's definitely bottom tier for RE. Still, he works plenty well as the player surrogate role.

  Overall I am VERY happy with this departure for the normal zombie-infested, completely rundown settings of Resident Evil past. Especially now with the knowledge that RE9 is more in line with RE of old, it really makes this a standout, unique entry. It is an absolutely delightful carnival ride from start to finish, and is one of the most re-playable Resident Evils. (Spoilers) I hope to return to the mold, and Rose, someday, but even if not, this was a very worthy departure to help fully revive Resident Evil.

Amazing Resident Evil Experience: Lady D Stole the Show

I had an incredible time playing Resident Evil Village. From start to finish the game kept me hooked with its atmosphere, action, and story. It honestly gave me a lot of strong Resident Evil 4 vibes, which I absolutely loved because that game is legendary. The mix of horror, exploration, and intense combat felt very similar in the best possible way.

One of the biggest highlights of the entire game for me was Lady Dimitrescu. She was amazing and easily one of the most memorable characters in the whole experience. Her presence, design, personality, and the castle section of the game were honestly some of the best parts. The atmosphere inside the castle felt classic Resident Evil and it was such a fun and tense area to explore.

To be completely honest, I was actually a little sad that her part of the game was relatively short. She was such a strong and interesting character that they almost could have made a huge portion of the game focused entirely around her and the other castle monsters. That section had so much personality and uniqueness that it left me wanting even more.

That being said, the rest of the game is still fantastic. The different areas, enemies, and bosses all bring something unique to the table. The pacing keeps things fresh, and the story has enough mystery to keep you curious about what’s going on next. It constantly felt like the game was throwing new surprises at me.

The gameplay itself feels great too. Combat is satisfying, exploring the village and different locations is really fun, and the overall horror atmosphere is done extremely well. Sometimes it’s creepy, sometimes it’s intense, and sometimes it’s just straight up wild.

Overall this was an amazing entry in the Resident Evil series. The game managed to feel modern while still capturing the classic spirit of the franchise. And again, Lady D was absolutely incredible and unforgettable.

If you’re a fan of Resident Evil or loved the style of Resident Evil 4, this game is absolutely worth playing.

Resident Evil: VILLAGE, also known as Resident Evil 8: Village, is a 2021 horror first person shooter that isn’t in the right place in my steam library and it’s actually making me mad.

Ethan Winters is back! And this time more dead wife than ever. After Chris and pals shoot up his house and steal his baby (also his wife got shot, this is important, remember this.), Ethan is abducted by Hound Wolf Squad and soon finds himself waking up in a secluded Eastern European village. Soon, Ethan finds out that its NO GOOD and he must fight for his life in order to save his baby Rose from weird Resident Evil shenanigans.

Village was kind of refreshing after playing RE7 right before. A continuation of the “First person resident evil” only this time there was a lot more effort put into the combat and exploration/puzzle solving. You can play the game in Third Person as well, but it feels weird to me compared to other Resident Evil games so I just stuck with First Person.

We’re also very far removed from the “Oh no scary monster time to run!” craze, the games still get made but not as much as they were back in RE7 came out. This time the run and hide aspect of the games was toned down to one level and maybe one other encounter much later in the game.
The first major area in the game is Castle Dimetrescu, which has the big lady that everyone likes in it. You spend a good chunk of the level running away from her and her daughters, or running into them if you’re into that.

Your female wiles won’t work on me, big lady, you remind me of spoiled bacon.

For the most part, its a pretty straight forward Resident Evil affair, you need to find solutions to a bigger problem (Your daughter has been kidnapped) and you solve those problems with various solutions (You have a handgun).

The enemies in Village are a pretty big improvement compared to RE7, moving away from the dumb mold monsters and instead making Resident Evil versions of ye olde horror movie/ fairy tale monsters. Lycans replace the main mold monster now, werewolf men who fight in packs and move quickly and aggressively to keep you on your toes.
They also hang corpses from posts and burn people at the stake, so I kind of have beef with their animosity.

The game basically justifies werewolves, zombies, and ghouls (yes, they’re different) being monsters you have to deal with with RE logic. My main problem is that they still have the mold monster problem of not being all that fun to fight. But keep in mind I’m coming from the Resident Evil 4 Remake and things like that where shooting someone in the face and then drop kicking them was a viable option.

Ethan being very much a scooty and shooty man with enemies that have a few canned animations when they take damage feels like a severe downgrade from even the meaty and crunchy shooting from Resident evil 2R, a game that was 2 years old at the time when RE8 first came out.

On normal mode, this game should take you around 8 or so hours, like the last game. I did die less in RE8 compared to 7 and when I did I got caught in an instant kill or two. Its a funner, goofier story than the Baker house and I would say, outside of ONE specific area, its probably not going to scare you as a horror game. But as an action game with spooky elements and fun exploration and puzzles? You’ll probably have a good time.

There isn’t much else I can say that I didn’t say already when I reviewed RE7, its a good time. I like Ethan, he’s a dumb idiot but he’s MY idiot. The big twist near the end of the game was really funny because a buddy of mine called it when I was playing RE7.

Do I like the Ethanuology? Yeah, I like them, would I play them over the classic or other Resident Evil games released recently? Probably not.
Would I play a Resident Evil Outbreak 3 with 7/8’s gameplay? Absolutely. Also, this game makes me want more games with military guys with cool military gear shoot monsters. 

Also, a merchant is back in Village. I don’t know how exactly they modeled a 1:1 recreation of me but I expect royalties any day now, Capcom.

Resident Evil Village isn’t just another survival horror game. It’s Ethan Winters’ story, and honestly, he carries the entire franchise on his back.

Ethan goes through absolute hell in this game, like the last game. The amount of physical and emotional punishment he endures is insane, yet he never stops. No dramatic speeches, no superhero attitude but just pure determination. He feels more human than most protagonists, and that’s exactly why his journey hits so hard. By the end of the game, it’s impossible not to respect him.

Now let’s talk about Chris Redfield… I get that he’s supposed to be the “legend”, but here? His actions are questionable at best. Instead of communicating properly, he keeps everything vague, makes reckless decisions, and ends up creating more problems than he solves. A lot of the chaos Ethan has to deal with could’ve been avoided if Chris had just been honest from the start. It honestly feels like Ethan is cleaning up after him most of the time.

What really elevates this game, though, is its theme. Resident Evil Village isn’t just about surviving monsters. It’s about family, loss, and sacrifice. Every major antagonist represents a twisted version of family. Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, Donna Beneviento’s isolated grief, Heisenberg’s rebellion against control, and Mother Miranda’s obsession with bringing back her child. It all connects back to one central idea: how far someone will go for family, and what happens when that love becomes corrupted.

Ethan stands in complete contrast to all of them. While the villains are broken by their past and consumed by their desires, Ethan keeps moving forward for one simple reason: his family. That contrast gives the story real emotional weight, especially towards the ending, which hits way harder than you’d expect from a Resident Evil game.

Gameplay-wise, the balance between horror and action is nearly perfect. The castle section builds tension beautifully, House Beneviento is pure psychological horror, and later areas shift more into action without completely losing the atmosphere. It constantly changes pace, so it never feels boring or repetitive.

Visually, the game is more than I expected. The environments are detailed and full of personality, and the sound design does an incredible job of pulling you into the world. Every creak, every distant noise adds to the tension.

In the end, Resident Evil Village is more than just a horror game. It’s a surprisingly emotional story about a man who refuses to give up.

Ethan deserved better. And honestly? He’s one of the most underrated protagonists in gaming.

Another great entry into the Resident Evil franchise. I only have two complaints with this one. First, you cannot load saved data without going back to the main menu; however, there are mods available to remedy this. Second, I wasn't as big of a fan of the Lycan-Vampire theme over the traditional T-Virus, G-Virus, and Nemesis stuff Resident Evil is known for. Regardless of those issues, Resident Evil Village offers one of the best replay values out of all the titles in my opinion. The way the gameplay loop is designed, the amount of content, and the many unlockables to chase makes the world more enjoyable to keep going back to. It has a great open world-sandbox to explore (like Resident Evil 4), which I also enjoy, as I am a fan of scavenging the areas and spending time enthralled in the environments instead of just speed running through them. Nevertheless, it does offer an arcade mode to get that speed run fun in with its own unique unlocks! This title also allows the player to play as Chris, if only for a moment. It would be amazing If all the Resident Evil titles had this much content to chase, game modes, and replayability factors. Just don't be restrictive with the save loads, or the stash boxes Capcom. RE8 is in a weird position. Clearly it's trying to emulate the design of RE4 with the perspective of RE7. And honestly, I don't think its good at either of those lol. Overall it's a fine and enjoyable game but in the deapartment that matters most, i.e the gamepalay itself- it's much weaker than the previous ones. There are also so many missed oppurtunities with this game, it makes me really sad.
Since this is not a cheap game, I will elaborate a bit for anyone interested in trying out RE8.

1. Graphics- I think RE8 is significantly better looking than previous entries. This is a truly beautiful game with very minute details. I highly recommend playing this in first person mode. The first person perspective is so immersive and all the props and interiors are so deatiled it'd honestly be a disservice to not play it from that perspective. Not to mention the 3rd person animations imo are not good at all, atleast compared to other games. 

2. Story and characters- I don't think most people play RE games for the story, but as this is a direct sequel to RE7 which had a pretty good story and characters, I feel some might have some expectations regarding this aspect. Well, it's the complete opposite of RE7- I mean- In RE7 Ethan was like an unseasoned boiled vegetable, he had no character, and most of the story was focused on the Baker family. In RE8, Ethan is significantly more likeable with actual personality. I was very much rooting for the guy. However, all other characters are massively under utilised....I cannot believe how much marketing went behind some of these characters but they had like 5 min of proper screentime (that's with me being generous). Not to mention, they could've easily solved this shortcoming by making some short DLCs around these characters like they did in RE7 but they didn't- instead we got this half-assed and mediocore, nay, worse than mediocore Mercenaries mode and a single DLC about a chaacter that has like 2 min of screentime at the very end of the main game. While the existing lore behinf the characters was good, but it was seriosuly such a shame that Capcom didn't even bother to give some decent post-launch support.
About the story itself- without spoiling anything, the premise and setup was more or less stupid imo but they clearly made an effort to make the ending good. I liked the ending a lot- I think this one of the better endings in the franchise. I think most people will also like the ending.

3. Gameplay- Imma be honest, the gameplay here is not very good. There are many guns, but they dont feel good to use. Most of the enemeies except the bosses up until the very last section of the game, are just not fun to fight. The gunplay feels much worse than any mainline RE game, maybe even RE6.
There is a central hub and 4 major boss areas- the design of the hub is pretty good but most of the boss areas are not that good. Lady D's castle for example- while graphically looks beautiful, has no sense of identity and uniqueness, there is no mysetry and all of the rooms are identical. Lady D herself as a stalker type enemy is also laughably easy. Overall its just a pale imitation of what came before, but never reaching remotely anywhere their quality or design. Rest of areas all try to do different things- some are better than others. There's an attempt at a horror sequnece, where I felt the buildup was really good but the actual climax was not so good. Other than that you have yoour RE4 style merchant-weapon upgrade system, valuable/loot system, and a new barebones hunting system that has the similar functions as that of the yellow herbs. Overall, RE8 is best when it's not trying to imitate the previous games and just trying to do it's own thing. 

4. Extra content- Not much extra conent- as mentioned earlier, a massive shame there wasn't good post-launch support like RE7 had. There's a pretty poor Mercenaries mode (the gunplay sucks) and a DLC set 16 yrs after the main game where you retread old grounds and acts like an epilogue. The expansion pass/gold edition overall is not worth it imo, the base game is fine enough and the base ending is perfectly fine. (What's funny is that with this bare amout of content this is still significantly more than what RE3R offers)

TLDR, RE8 is an enjoyable game, with exceptional graphics, good lore and ending, and an interesting but massively underutilised cast of characters. It has good exploration alebit with not so interesting level design, and unfortunately, a quite poor or atbest servicable combat system(gunplay).  If you go in simply to enjoy the adventure without the expectations of classic RE level design, or combat from RE4, I think you'll have a good time with RE8. I'd still recommned getting this on a sale only, or the bundle that includes other RE games.

After years of watching playthroughs and speedruns, I finally sat down and properly played Resident Evil Village from start to finish, and nine hours later I was staring at the credits wondering how the hell that flew by so fast. It genuinely felt closer to five hours. That alone tells you how tight this game is. 

The biggest thing that hooked me was the atmosphere. Village commits fully to its gothic horror vibe and never lets up. The setting is cohesive, the pacing is sharp, and characters like Lady Dimitrescu and Karl Heisenberg are not just visually memorable, they actively keep the momentum going because each lord section feels distinct. 

What surprised me most is how small the game actually is, but in a good way. It is dense rather than bloated. Every area has purpose, every encounter feels placed with intent, and the game almost never wastes your time. You sit down, you make progress, and it keeps paying you back for your attention. I still enjoy massive games and have sunk serious hours into titles like Horizon Zero Dawn and Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, but the reality now is those games demand a lot more mental bandwidth. Village does not. It delivers a complete, polished experience in under ten hours, and right now that kind of tight design hits way harder. 

This is one of the few games in years where I sat down intending to play a bit and ended up losing an entire day without noticing. Tight, polished, and genuinely hard to put down.

Released in May of 2021,  "Resident Evil Village" is the official follow-up to 2017's "Resident Evil 7".  It serves as a conclusion to Ethan Winter's story arc, the protagonist of Resident Evil 7.  

In just 8-10 hours, Resident Evil Village manages to meet and even sometimes surpass the bar set by its predecessor.  Almost everything that made RE7 work can be found here, with more enemy variety, more weapons, more bosses to take down, and a much bigger area to explore. 

The game's premise is very simple.  Mia is presumably shot dead, and Ethan and his daughter Rose were taken by Chris Redfield's team for unknown reasons.  Shortly after,  Ethan wakes up after an accident that separated him from his daughter, and now Ethan has to explore the village to get her back. 

What made this game work in particular, and what I believe to be this game's high point, are the bosses.  During the course of the game, you will encounter 5 different bosses that you will have to defeat to get to Rose: Lady Dimitrescu, Donna Beneviento, Salvatore Moreau, Heisenberg, and finally Mother Miranda.

You can not fight these bosses in any order other than the one listed, but each of them will take you to a different area in the village, usually with new enemies and mini bosses to encounter.  This may sound similar to the structure of RE7, where you had to deal with the different members of the Baker family, but Village takes it even further by having each area be its own gameplay style.

[spoiler] Lady Dimitrescu will chase you around her manor along with her three "daughters"  (similar to the encounters with Jack Baker in RE7), and her boss battle will have you battling her in her monster form at the top of a tower. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Beneviento will take your weapons away and drug you with a hallucinogen, where you'll have to solve puzzles and hide from a giant fetus monster to escape. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Moreau will transform into a fish monster, where you'll have to lower the water level to escape his area, and Heisenberg will throw various mini-boss level monsters at you in his factory, which ends in you controlling a tank to kill him in his final battle. [/spoiler]

I found myself enjoying each boss sequence, even the ones that are seemingly less popular with other players. 

Now with all of that in mind, this game should be an easy 10/10, right? 
 
In my opinion, it is very, very close.   Unfortunately, I think it falls just a bit short due to one major thing:  the writing.  

Resident Evil 7 (and the series in general, I'm sure)  has its own moments of corniness, but I think because we hear characters speak more often in this game, it ends up feeling much more present.  The voice direction also just sounds off to me.  Characters in this game don't really speak like human beings—this is especially noticeable whenever Ethan is talking.  There were multiple times where I was being rage-baited by Ethan and Chris's dumb decisions throughout the story as well. 

So, as far as gameplay is concerned, this game is peak, and I absolutely recommend anyone interested in survival horror to play it before they die.  But due to the problem mentioned, I think it's just shy of my personal GOAT list.

Survival in a Gothic Nightmare – A Review of Resident Evil Village

Overall Rating: 9.25/10

Resident Evil Village builds directly upon the foundation of its predecessor while expanding its scope, scale, and spectacle. Where Resident Evil 7 thrived on intimate isolation, Village embraces gothic grandeur without abandoning survival tension. Set in a remote European settlement plagued by mythic horror, the game blends classic monster iconography with the franchise’s bio-organic roots. The result is an experience that feels both nostalgic and modern—an ambitious fusion of action and atmosphere.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 10/10

Village is visually striking from start to finish. Snow-covered paths, crumbling stone architecture, and looming castles establish a tone steeped in gothic horror. Each of the Four Lords governs a distinct region, creating varied environments that prevent repetition and maintain momentum. Castle Dimitrescu exudes aristocratic decay, while other areas lean into psychological horror, industrial dread, and open combat spaces. Lighting and environmental detail elevate immersion, and the art direction confidently blends folklore aesthetics with the franchise’s science-driven mythology.

Story and Narrative: 9/10

Continuing Ethan Winters’ story, Village shifts from desperate survival to a more mythic, almost fairy-tale structure. The narrative is divided into chapters centered on each Lord, creating a clear progression that mirrors classic Resident Evil design. Themes of parenthood, sacrifice, and manipulation run throughout the story. While some late-game revelations stretch believability, they remain consistent with the series’ evolving lore. The pacing is strong, balancing character moments with escalating horror.

Gameplay and Combat: 9/10

Village leans further into action than Resident Evil 7 but retains survival fundamentals. Resource management remains important, though ammunition and crafting materials are more generous. Combat feels weightier and more responsive, particularly during large-scale encounters with Lycans. The addition of the Duke merchant system adds strategic flexibility, allowing players to upgrade weapons and tailor their approach. Exploration is encouraged through optional treasures and hidden upgrades, rewarding careful observation. Notably, the game’s pacing shifts dynamically. One section strips combat almost entirely in favor of pure psychological horror, demonstrating the developers’ confidence in varying tension rather than relying solely on gunplay.

Sound Design and Music: 9/10

Audio design enhances both atmosphere and combat. The distant howls of Lycans, the echoing halls of the castle, and sudden environmental shifts sustain tension. Music swells during confrontations but remains restrained during exploration, allowing silence to build unease. Voice performances are strong across the board, lending credibility to both grounded and exaggerated characters.

Replayability and Extra Content: 9/10

Multiple difficulty modes, unlockable weapons, and post-game content extend longevity. Mercenaries mode offers an arcade-style challenge that contrasts with the campaign’s tone, providing additional replay value for combat-focused players. New Game Plus options encourage experimentation with upgraded arsenals, making subsequent playthroughs more dynamic.

Conclusion: 9.25/10

Resident Evil Village successfully balances horror tradition with modern spectacle. It honors the franchise’s survival roots while confidently expanding into gothic action-horror territory. Though less restrained than its predecessor, it compensates with variety, visual ambition, and mechanical depth.

Final Verdict:

Resident Evil Village is a bold continuation that blends folklore, bio-horror, and action into a cohesive experience. It may not be as intimate as Resident Evil 7, but its ambition, atmosphere, and memorable set pieces secure its place among the franchise’s strongest modern entries.

Light discussion of bosses and locations, but no story spoilers.

---------------------------------
Verdict
---------------------------------

One of the most ambitious and memorable Resident Evil games so far.

---------------------------------
Opening and First Impressions
---------------------------------

This is my favourite Resident Evil game so far alongside Requiem.

From the beginning I felt engaged. The opening Lycan assault is intense — being relentlessly chased before the sequence ends with Urias sets the tone perfectly. On a first playthrough it’s chaotic, overwhelming and full of tension.

---------------------------------
Castle Dimitrescu
---------------------------------

The Castle Dimitrescu section is easily my favourite part of the game.

Lady Dimitrescu is an excellent antagonist and has a strong presence throughout the castle. 

My only criticism is that she was used too early as a boss. Given how heavily Capcom marketed her, I expected a larger overarching role. Defeating her as the first major lord felt too soon.

---------------------------------
House Beneviento
---------------------------------

Donna Beneviento’s section was another standout. Her arc feels tragic and different from traditional Resident Evil villains.

The House Beneviento sequence — especially the Giant Fetus monster — is one of the scariest moments in the entire franchise. The realism of the baby crying combined with the grotesque design works incredibly well and genuine panic.

---------------------------------
Moreau and the Swamp
---------------------------------

Salvatore Moreau (the swamp lord) was less compelling as a character for me. I enjoyed the boss fight itself — one of the stronger arena encounters — but the water section leading up to it wasn’t as enjoyable.

That said, his mutated form during the battle was visually interesting.

---------------------------------
Heisenberg and the Factory
---------------------------------

My least favourite lord was Heisenberg. His magnetic powers felt slightly out of place — more X-Men than Resident Evil.

However, the factory still delivers tension. The Soldat Jet enemies, especially in tight spaces while they charge and breathe fire, create stressful combat moments.

The factory overall was probably my least favourite area. By that point the game felt like it was stretching slightly too long, although the section is actually shorter than it initially feels.

---------------------------------
Village Hub and World Design
---------------------------------

One thing I really liked was how the bosses were tied into an open-zone village hub rather than a completely linear structure.

The story progression remains linear — which works for Resident Evil — but being able to revisit areas adds a semi-open feel that improves immersion.

---------------------------------
Mother Miranda
---------------------------------

Mother Miranda was fine as a final boss, but she felt more forgettable compared to Lady Dimitrescu. Given how much Dimitrescu featured in marketing, expectations were naturally high.

---------------------------------
The Duke and DLC
---------------------------------

I also liked The Duke. He’s a unique and entertaining take on the Resident Evil merchant.

I do wish the main story explored him more, although the Shadows of Rose DLC expands his character slightly.

Speaking of the DLC — I enjoyed it. Not as much as the main game, but it was a solid addition. Seeing Rose grown up and revisiting locations Ethan once fought through was nostalgic. I’d be interested to see her return in a future Resident Evil title.

---------------------------------
Mercenaries Mode
---------------------------------

The Mercenaries mode was enjoyable but not as strong as the version in Resident Evil 4 in my opinion. It felt slower — intentionally so — but I preferred the faster pace of RE4’s Mercenaries.

---------------------------------
Final Thoughts
---------------------------------

Overall, Village is one of the strongest Resident Evil games for me. The variety of enemies, the tonal shifts between the lords, and the blend of horror and action kept the experience consistently engaging.

For me, this is Resident Evil at its most ambitious — and one of the most memorable entries in the series.

I will give this game a very tentative "yes." I have played all of the mainline RE games and REmakes, and I'd say this game is about a B- to B tier comparably. In my opinion, RE Village contains both the worst and best aspects of the series.

The BEST:

- Intricate level design with clever shortcuts and backtracking that feels rewarding ([spoiler]Castle Dimitrescu and the Factory)[/spoiler]
- The 1st person POV is more immersive and was a great decision back in RE7 to bring the series back to its horror roots after whatever the f*** RE6 was
-Lady Dimitrescu
- The inventory and crafting system is engaging as always, and resources feel scarce
- Lady Dimitrescu
- They continue to bring back legacy characters without them feeling shoehorned in or like the devs are just saying "MeMbEr ThIs??"
- Optional side content that is both challenging and rewarding
- Lady Dimitrescu

The WORST:
- The hide and seek gameplay of the dollhouse is horrid. After finishing Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Outlast over a decade ago, I was already sick of that peekaboo bulls**t
- One of the best areas of this game fumbles hard in the final fight. A brilliant survival horror level is finished with vehicle-based, "just hold shoot until they die" slop, almost exactly the same as the ending of The Evil Within
- The opening ambush sequence is a chore, especially on returning playthroughs. It is so much worse than the village ambush in RE4. I keep save files on each difficulty right after the ambush just so I don't have to play it again when I revisit RE Village

Overall, I had a lot of fun with RE Village and will probably continue returning to it. If certain design choices were different, it could have had the potential to be the best game in the series so far. As a strapping young lad from rural Europe, I have to say that Resident Evil Village presents the closest representation of my daily walk to the nearest grocery store to pick up some bread and vodka. I'm not sure where the developers got the idea that my gamer body is being stalked by 4 charming young ladies who can't seem to get enough of me, but I'll let that slide just this once, merely because everything else is depicted with such pinpoint accuracy.

While I'm not impressed with the technical side of this game, as it drops frames way too often for my liking. The "animal hunting" minigame. How long certain characters wait to tell certain other characters the "real plot". Ethan's insistence on commenting on every obvious thing in front of him. Nor how little time the game spends characterising its memorable boss encounters, with most of their backstory being lazily dumped into your lap via notes a couple of minutes before the game ends. And a few other bits and pieces here and there. RE:8 still does enough things right for me to overall enjoy the experience. It somehow manages to have some of the scariest and most tension-filled moments of the franchise, all the while a good chunk of the game succeeds in bringing a bit of levity to the mix, being a really great spin on the horror-fantasy genre. Vampires, robots, werewolves, giants, dolls, and more are all intermixed with a surprising degree of nuance and logic that makes about as much sense as a setting with all of these types of enemies can potentially make sense. Not only do all of these make sure that there is more than sufficient enemy variety for the entire game's runtime, but each one of these enemies also poses as their own unique and formidable threat towards Ethan's life, with you having to learn their individual strengths and weaknesses in order to survive.

This game is like a consistently fun roller coaster that never really dips into tedium nor strives for excellence in my eyes. The initial section that serves as the usual Resident Evil chase from an unkillable antagonist is done about as well as in RE2 or RE7, yet it is not nearly as scary as those. The psychological horror parts of this game are top-notch, yet, unfortunately, also heavily telegraphed, with lockers for Ethan to hide in being placed in those parts alone, taking away from the sting of that section. The more action-packed parts where you just mow down enemies (which bothered me in RE7) are now even more action-packed, but I don't think the guns pack enough of a punch for those to be any more than good. And the entire experience can just be summed up by saying that I felt it was consistently engaging, with a few bright spots here and there shining above the rest. Nothing more, nothing less.

After the success of [b] Resident Evil 7: BIOHAZARD [/b], the public would be right to assume that Capcom would keep this train going and that the next game in the series would be just as fun and even scarier than the last. However, the public would only partially agree with that assumption. 

[h1] Story [/h1]
Ethan Winters returns as the main protagonist of this new entry. After the events of the Baker House Incident in Louisiana, Ethan and his wife Mia are placed under witness protection and moved to an undisclosed location in Europe. It isn’t just Ethan and Mia now too; the two of them welcomed their new bundle of joy into the world, Rosemary Winters.  

The game opens on a normal day in the Winters’ household. Mia is cooking dinner, and Ethan goes to put Rosemary to bed for the night. Breaking glass is then heard, and a bullet strikes Mia in the shoulder. Mia is then fired upon by more weapons while Ethan ducks and takes cover, wondering what the hell is happening. Chris Redfield then enters the house, knocking Ethan out and taking both him and Rosemary with Chris and his team. 

Ethan then wakes up after the truck transporting him and Rosemary crashes. With no sign of Rose anywhere nearby, Ethan treks off further into the snow. Ethan eventually stumbles upon the titular Village and is left to explore it whilst hearing the howling of wolves nearby. With no other options, Ethan is left to explore this Village and find Rosemary, no matter what it takes.  

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Like [b] Resident Evil 7 [/b], this game is entirely in the first-person, something not entirely normal for the series. Despite this, the game still feels like a [b] Resident Evil [/b] game. All the ingredients are here: herbs, combining different items to make ammo or healing items, and a few puzzles here and there. But while [b] Resident Evil 7 [/b] channeled the energy of the first three games, [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b] channeled [b] Resident Evil 4 [/b] in its gameplay style. You’re encouraged to make good use of your ammo, but the addition of The Duke as the merchant means that you buy more ammo should you ever run out. While you can’t roundhouse kick enemies like Leon did; after a successful guard, Ethan can shove enemies away, allowing the player to put some space between them and their attacker.  

Replacing the Molded from the previous entry are the Lycans. Now you may hear that and think of werewolves, but you couldn’t be more wrong. The lycans are strong, mutated humans that have been experimented on and kept out of the village. Compared to the zombies from previous Resident Evil entries, the lycans are a bit more unique in the fact that they’re able to move a lot faster than the zombies do. In addition to this, the lycans will be using weapons like machetes and bows and arrows against Ethan.  

I have no huge qualms about the gameplay of [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b]. I thought that it succeeded in what it was trying to achieve. Most of my issues from [b] RE7 [/b] were resolved, Ethan can finally move faster than a snail, and all the weapons have some use. There is one gripe I do have about this game, though: all the enemies are complete sponges. Almost every enemy you come across will take at least half a clip of your pistol to kill, and that’s assuming you’re getting all headshots. Some enemies move slowly enough to get consistent headshots, but the lycans are always jumping back ‘n forth, sidestepping from left to right, it's incredibly difficult to get consistent headshots on them. Ammo is less of a concern in this installment, yes, but you still need to be conscious about it. I can’t be using all my shotgun ammo to take down common enemies when I could use it for the boss of the area.  

[h1] Gamefeel [/h1]
Continuing the trend from [b] Resident Evil 7 [/b], the design of [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b] is incredible. All the character models look fantastic, just looking at some of them can instantly put you at unease from how disgusting or creepy they look. The juxtaposition of the cozy village being filled with the countless horrors you face works incredibly well for this game. You are constantly on the edge of your seat while navigating the village, because you can’t be certain if you’ll be ambushed by another enemy or if you’ll be able to peacefully explore the area. The sound design is great too; the ambience of certain areas works well to put the player at unease. Being in the cellar of Castle Dimitrescu and hearing far away hissing along with the clattering of chains made me hesitant to keep moving forward. 

Similar to what I said for [b] Resident Evil 7 [/b], I’m not the biggest fan of the first-person perspective in this game. It succeeds in what the game is aiming to achieve. I’ll always prefer third person with fixed camera angles, though. 

Ethan gets a little better as a protagonist in this game. He does a better job at reacting to his situation like a normal person would, but he still acts over the top in some scenarios. However, for a Japanese game, over-the-top is normal for them, so I can’t complain too much about that. I still don’t understand Capcom’s obsession with not showing his face. They want the player to be able to identify with Ethan, but they also give him his own identity and motives? It’s incredibly confusing and does nothing but hurt his character. In the end, though, I felt I was able to like Ethan enough to care about his plight and want to see him succeed. 

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
I greatly enjoyed playing through [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b]. While it was a step back from returning to a more horror-centric experience, it was a more consistently enjoyable experience from start to finish in comparison to [b] RE7 [/b]. [b] Resident Evil [/b] games aren’t the longest games out there, and they encourage the player to replay them and get faster times with bonus items that you can unlock. [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b] was more of a time sink, though. The game felt so huge that trying to replay and rush through it feels like it would be a major disservice to the overall experience. Despite this, I do see myself going back to [b] Resident Evil: Village [/b] in the future, just for a nice gaming experience, much more often than I would go back to [b] RE7 [/b].

First of all, the visuals and overall atmosphere are genuinely impressive. The environments are detailed, the lighting is fantastic, and the creepy tone is maintained well throughout large parts of the game. It definitely looks like a high-quality horror experience.

However, what really held the game back for me was the lack of proper hints for certain puzzles that are required to progress the main story. Some of them felt unnecessarily obscure, to the point where I had to look up walkthrough videos just to move forward. For a horror game, this completely ruins the immersion. Having to pause and check YouTube destroys the tension and the scary atmosphere the game tries so hard to build.

The most outrageous example was how some key items initially appear completely unusable. To make them work, you have to open the inventory, manually rotate the object, and trigger an “examine” prompt before the item suddenly becomes usable as a key. There’s no tutorial, no clear hint, and no indication that the key you’re trying to use needs to be altered or interacted with in a specific way beforehand. Instead of feeling like clever puzzle design, it comes across as poorly communicated and unnecessarily frustrating.

On top of that, I was frequently lost due to poor navigation and unclear direction on how to progress the main mission. Instead of feeling suspenseful, it often felt frustrating.

One of the most irritating design choices was the difficulty system. After dying twice in a challenging section, the game prompted me to lower the difficulty — which I did. The problem is that once I passed that part, the game no longer felt challenging at all. When I tried to increase the difficulty again, I realized you can’t raise it back mid-playthrough. That restriction makes absolutely no sense. I wasn’t even playing on the highest difficulty (which only unlocks after completing the game), so I don’t understand why the game locks you into an easier setting with no option to return. It completely ruined the balance of the experience for the rest of my playthrough.

By the end, I found myself completely uninterested in the story progression and even the twists. Instead of feeling invested, I just wanted it to be over. A big reason for that was how both Ethan and Chris kept making avoidable mistakes and questionable decisions that felt increasingly careless and illogical as the game went on.

Overall, while Resident Evil Village looks great and has a strong atmosphere, frustrating puzzle design, unclear progression, and a poorly handled difficulty system made it a disappointing experience for me. I wouldn’t recommend it.

As much as I love the franchise, out of the newer games this one sits at a weird spot for me. I truly love the first person from RE7 and from Village as it makes it feel more in your face. Yet something about Village feels.... well "off".

WHAT I DO LIKE:
--------------------------
- I love the lords of the village as well as Mother Miranda, especially her different forms. The design of each character is so well made, especially with how they represent classic horror movies. Dracula/Vampires, Creature of the Black Lagoon/ The Deep, Frankenstein, as well as psychological horror. I love these tropes and I think it's a bit different from the classis zombie formula which I like. 
- I really liked the DLC with Rose. 3rd person is a little weird as you go through area's you played through as Ethan in first person. And the end cutscene playing again carries new meaning with what you see after the base story vs after playing as Rose. 
- Heisenburg. I love how he is written, and voiced. His side of things are so different from the other lords and I like the conflict within them. His charismatic and chaotic take on things feels like a showman preparing a huge performance, even if its just for his entertainment. And I'm really glad he was the last lord you deal with, adds to his grand plan. 

WHAT I DON'T LIKE:
--------------------------
There isn't much surprisingly. However that feeling of the game being "off" is definitely something I want to talk about. In RE7, everything felt so set in place and it never felt like something was there just to be there. It all felt natural, from the house setting feeling as it was a family home for years, the swamp being active with bugs and ambiance. However in Village....I just don't feel the same after the castle. 
-The flooded area with the light platforming felt rushed and wonky, the factory felt kinda out of place with the old village aesthetic. 
- I kinda wish we got an option to choose whether we helped Heisenburg with Mother Miranda. I felt like there were multiple times a choice could of been made to change the story a little, especially with Moreau. He was so out-casted from the other lords and he just wanted the attention of Mother Miranda. Ethan just taking the flask seemed kinda, well wrong. He wasn't much of a threat and he wasn't hostile until Ethan ♥♥♥♥ talked him. 
- Another small thing I wish we got more of is The Duke. He's such a unique character who knows so much and has a business connection with Lady D with her wine, yet doesn't reveal anything else. He knows about just about everything Ethan needs to get Rose back yet seems not involved with the lords. He makes a comment when Ethan askes him, "Who-what are you?" and he gives such an ambiguous response of "Even I can't quite answer that!" I wish we got small tid-bits as the story went on as to who he really was like when finding a letter regarding him and his business with Lady D located in the castle. His DLC appearance feels kinda odd to be there yet I understand why he is there. 

TLDR:
--------------------------
I really like the game and the new characters, loved the DLC because it adds to the finale of the game with new weight. dislike some decisions made regarding Heiseinburgs interactions with Ethan especially at the Factory. Want to know more about The Duke and his place within the village.

I think RE8 basically ranks in the center of every RE games released to date. It's nowhere near as bad as RE6 or RE3R, but it's also nowhere near as good as RE4(or Remake), RE2R. Is it worth playing? Yeah, sure, at a decent discount (20-40 USD?), and the DLC is pretty nice too.

It kind of tries to be RE4 in the RE7 gameplay style. You have a lot of enemies and generally barely enough ammo/resources to make it through for nearly 2/3rd of the game. One section of the game is scary, but mostly because it strips you of everything first, and the fact that this section MUST be replayed on every playthrough is really annoying.

A lot of survival horror games tend to be pretty short, but have high replay value. It's kind of inherent to the genre that there's only so much time you can keep the player's tension and attention before they get familiar with the horror and it's less effective. RE8 is really short, but it kind of ends up not being great for replays either. There's upgrades and "cheats" that make every playthrough better, but that segment of the game that strips you of everything makes every re-run annoying because it's the one part you can't use all of your resources to breeze through.

Another annoying issue is that guns that are sold/given at the later part of the game are much better than the starting ones, meaning that spending a LOT of money to upgrade the early weapons is wasted, and that's disappointing.

Either way, the game has good highs and the first playthrough is pretty exciting and fun. The story is campy as all hell ( Resident Evil Cheese), fights are tough, and the environment designs and atmosphere is great. Just be aware that it is no where near my favorite Resident Evil game to re-run and thus getting your money's worth will depend heavily on how much you want to get time out of the game.

Ethan's Bizarre Adventure.

That is the one sentence that perfectly sums up the whole experience of this game. They were not joking when they said that RE4 was the main inspiration here. Compared to 7, this entry leans much more into action, throwing you into bigger encounters and more intense set pieces, though it still manages to deliver a few surprising and tense moments waiting for you to experience. As with most RE games, there are puzzles, and I really enjoyed what the game offers. They are not overly complex, but they break the pacing nicely and give you a breather between combat sections, making the overall journey feel more varied and engaging. One thing I  really disliked in this game is our MC himself, Ethan Winters. His character and personality felt incomplete at times, as you can see emotions coming from him, and then there are moments where he seems very clueless. This builds up to something that I’m going to talk about later for the DLC. Overall, it’s a wild ride from start to finish, balancing action, horror, and absurdity in a way that makes Ethan’s journey feel memorable and uniquely entertaining.

Now for the DLCs:

The Mercenaries

It’s a classic RE Mercenaries experience, you kill enemies within a time limit while managing your kill streak and aiming for high scores. It’s a fun mode, though I didn’t play it that much. Still, it’s an enjoyable mode overall.

Shadow of Rose

Shadow of Rose offers a unique take with a story I genuinely liked. Coming back later after finishing the main story felt refreshing, especially revisiting some areas. Still, it feels like a missed opportunity — more focus on Rose’s early life and a more expressive Ethan could have made the narrative hit much harder. It’s a good experience overall, but it definitely could have been longer and more developed. It basically concludes the whole 7/8 story.

By and large, an improvement upon the foundation and groundwork laid by Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, the sequel Resident Evil Village is almost the perfect Resident Evil game by my account. While I still prefer the theme and setting of 7, Village takes what made its predecessor great and builds upon it in almost every aspect. The combat feels much better this time around, and the improved inventory system (inspired by the classic Resident Evil 4) makes the survival element far more engaging for the player.

The Lycans make for more interesting—and simply better—enemies than the predecessor’s Molded, and each of the unique villains helps keep the player engaged in the story. In particular, the combat that takes place within the village setting is where this title really shines. The complex layout of the village, combined with its tight corners and overall cramped atmosphere, makes fights feel more intense and uncomfortable (in a good way).

The story of Village is usually where the game receives most of its criticism, but I found it to be just as fun as Resident Evil 7: Biohazard’s story and more than serviceable as a follow-up. It serves as a conclusion to Ethan’s story, and while I won’t get into details, his goal of finding Rose is relatable to most players, and I found the ending to be quite fulfilling. The only element I didn’t enjoy was Ethan’s questionable actions at the beginning of the game, which aren’t explained until the tail end of the narrative but could have—and should have—been clarified much earlier.

Overall, this has quickly become one of my favorite releases in the Resident Evil franchise, and I foresee myself returning for multiple replays. Despite its somewhat flawed narrative, I felt Village improved upon its predecessor in every way that matters, and I hope to see this style of survival horror return in future entries.

Resident Evil, as a series, tends to go in cycles or seasons. The first 3 resident evil games were all fixed camera horror games, 4,5 and 6 were all over the shoulder action horror titles (as were the revelation titles but lets not worry about those right now) and 7 marked the start of a new cycle with the shift to first person horror. Resident Evil 8 is the second game in this cycle. We return to the shoes of Ethan Winters to once again save your family from a conspiracy that is way above his pay-grade.

Like 7, Resident Evil 8 is an homage to a specific genera of horror movies although unlike 7 which was clearly based on the slasher movies of the 80s it is referencing the classic Universal Monster pictures. This has a noticeable effect on the gameplay as unlike 7 which had one very cohesive, dense but generally smaller map. 8 returns to the large varied environments of games like Resident Evil 4, taking place in the remote mountain settlement of Suckstobehereville, Eastern Europe. Also unlike 7 enemy variety is quite high and combat is more a focus. No pushing past nonthreatening slow-walking mold piles, you're going to be killing a lot of irate farmers. Each of the sections of the village centers on a different theme and so repetition is low, and the respective antagonists of these sections are unique and make for good translations of the creature feature creatures into the videogame space. 

While I think near the end it falls into the Resident Evil trap of getting too convoluted for its own good, I think it's a strong game. Less focused than 7, sure, but more loose and indulgent. Given it appears to be the final game in this particular cycle of Resident Evil games, and we're returning back to the tried and tested waters of Resident Evil 4, I think it's a suitable send-off for this specific era.

I can finally breath a sight of relief, no longer fearing anything spoilery in discussions of the franchise at last, after finally having completed the last chronological entry in the series and what a ride it’s been. While I’m certain is no news that the RE Engine is an amazing engine for visual fidelity, give or take a few hiccups with HDR on PC, the way it’s used to facilitate the most gorgeous art direction I’ve seen in the franchise thus far is something to behold. I, like most gamers am kind of tired of most developers and publishers sometimes pushing graphics over gameplay, and while I’m glad to report that is most certainly not the case here, I feel like that I should get out of the way now that this game warrants a playthrough for its level design and art direction alone, easily one of the most beautiful games I’ve played, especially on the castle section.

The horror while still present, heightened even in a few key areas, does take a back seat once again in favor of action in a similar vein with 4 and the original trilogy. I think for the most part it was the right call, as while the tight corridors of the Baker Estate and the claustrophobic atmosphere they provide are great, they wouldn’t be the right fight for the quasi-open world approach this game took to its setting.

While I’m overjoyed to see some features from RE4 return like a merchant character and the attache case, I do think that you can exploit them very easily up until the very late game and that made their inclusions a bit less impactful. 

In classic RE4 the storage upgrades were spaced out enough that you had to make constant judgments calls with regards to what you picked up and had to make a point to keep it orderly in order to maximize space. I’ve never once had a full inventory here and while I did keep my inventory mostly tidy, there’s hardly a need for it as there’s always enough space for anything you might want to pick up, I feel like if crafting components took inventory space, you would have to actually engage with both mechanics far more as choosing what and when to craft would introduce a whole new dynamic to both mechanics but it is what it is. On a lesser note, it just doesn’t hit the same to have the greyed-out representation of the items visible as opposed to the 3d models themselves.

While character wise I like the way the Duke is far more involved in the story than the merchant ever was, like wise I feel it’s way too easy to max out everything, with how generous this game is with giving you Lei, you will quite often be running around with everything that he has to offer cleaned out as opposed to be forced to make judgment calls about what to upgrade and when which removes a lot of the friction that made the feature great in RE4, and when the time comes that you can’t just buy anything and will probably need a couple of playthroughs worth of currency to upgrade anything you are sufficiently equipped and deck out to deal with the remainder of the game easily. I can see how more casual players might enjoy the way both the mechanics I talk about were streamlined but I can’t help to feel like something special was lost by taking away the challenges they offered.

In the notes on the concept art, the art director made a point that the objective with this game was to move away from the more realistic horror of 7 into a more fantastical approach to keep things fresh and while admittedly I don’t think the narrative hits as hard, it’s a good change of pace and I dug the fairy tale approach they went with here, especially with how closely the final boss fight felt like a continuation of the opening recounting of the story book. 

This game also felt like a great addition to Ethan Chopped-Limbs Winters, in 7 I just didn’t get enough from his performance to actually care and the supporting cast did a whole lot of the heavy lifting to make the story impactful, here however they flipped the switch and I really bought his father on warpath deal here far more than his “concerned” husband character of the previous game. And I quite liked how they concluded his story here in a way that not only was great in its own right, but also elevated the tragedy of the events that took place in the previous game.

I do feel like the story did a disservice to Chris, from the concept art I feel like at one point in development he and his team where way more involved in the story, specially with him apparently no longer having any ties to the BSAA, but in the final cut he just comes across like a really out of character ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ up until he does a complete 180 close to the final act of the game. Hell, in his segment of the game, which is admittedly pretty fun, even his team and himself admitted they should have acted differently. Anyway, I always felt like being a bit dumb was an important character trait of his since RE1 so I’ll just chuck his behavior here to a continuation of that and be glad his character model actually feels like and evolution of RE5 and 6 instead of whatever they were thinking with 7.

Overall while I don’t quite think this entry is a once in a generation hit that 7 was, it still is an incredibly fun, creative and beautiful game, that’s certainly worthy of you time if you liked the previous game or action horror in general.

I really liked Resident Evil 7 when I played it years ago, and Village is a worthy successor, that rare beast, a sequel that not only matches but in some ways exceeds the original. Village is more action oriented than 7, and right from the start it brought up a lot of good memories of traditional RE games from many years ago. Desperately trying to craft a few more shotgun shells, trying to stuff just a few more items in your inventory, running around in a blind panic, barricading doors, it's all here.

The game is visually striking, with every environment minutely detailed and carefully lit. Gameplqay is a satisfying combination of combat, exploration and loot gathering, and in addition to the main story levels there are side areas you can explore with a few extra miniboss fights and some good rewards. But the overall emphasis is on combat, with some truly epic battles and boss fights that make this game the leader in survival horror.

The only thing missing here are the traditional main characters like Chris and Jill. While Chris makes a few appearances he's not really part of the main story. I think that Ethan is a limited protagonist, but a few weaknesses in story and character are more than made up for by all the other game elements, which combine beautifully to create an entertaining, immersive, and exciting game, and I strongly recommend it for all fans of survival horror.

How do you follow-up the 'soft reboot' of REVII? A game that received universal praise and resuscitated the franchise from the criticisms of RE6? By making a direct sequel with the same cast.

	8 (I refuse to call it 'VIIIAGE') gives us a brief epilogue to 7. I don't consider anything that happens within the first 15 minutes spoilers so here goes: Ethan and his wife have been moved by the BSAA to Europe. They have a daughter. The events of 7 still hang over the young couples' heads, with neither able to move on from such a horrific event. Chris and his BSAA troops break into Ethan's home, kill his wife, and abduct his child. En route to who knows where the vehicle crashes and Ethan is the only one left alive. His daughter is missing.

	You're in some remote European village, and its clear the game is trying to somewhat relive RE4's village scenario. There's a church, a cult (of sorts), villagers that seem to have gone crazy and 'transformed'. It's familiar territory. It's surface level similarity, but it seems to have affected the maps.

	RE1-3, 7, and CV had maps that were built on backtracking; you acquired key items in areas by solving puzzles, which had you running back and forth using whatever new item you unlocked somewhere else. 4-6 were built on mostly proceeding down a linear path, with combat being the center piece. 5 and 6 were co-op XBOX shooters.

	Back in my RE7 review I praised the game, but found the beginning and ending too linear to be truly perfect. RE8 attempts to amp up the combat, but it also amps up the parts of 7 that I least liked. And maybe this would be excusable if the game had interesting enemies. But they mostly aren't. 

	It takes around a fifth of the game until you feel you are 'off-rails' and actually exploring an area (Dimitrescu Mansion). And even then, it's pretty linear with no complex navigation required.

	The next two levels drop the pretext of exploration and are extremely linear. There's the house by a cliff, with no enemies and one puzzle (a mannequin). The third level is a slightly more chaotic affair, but just as linear with a very simple puzzle. Once done, you get giant arrows telling you precisely where to go. Literally planted on the stage itself, directing you to the final boss (not really). Because the game thinks if it doesn't have you on-rails at all times you might get lost.

	It's not that RE8 doesn't have its moments, it's that the meat of the experience is basically one long corridor. Castle Dimitrescu has some opportunity to get lost, but it's a really small level. Dimitrescu follows you (like Nemesis), so that's interesting. Not amazing, but interesting. The second level attempts to spook you with a short linear experience, and the payoff is a very unique....well, I'd rather not spoil. But none of this supersede's the criticism. Which is that empty corridors are boring.

	The game isn't a total waste. I've already praised the house by the cliff, but I think the factory level is also praise-worthy. It's as linear as anything else, but it's beautifully eerie. And the Soldat enemy type is like the Regenerators of RE4: a threat that requires precise shots. Most enemies in the game are basically zombies, so the Soldat's are the first real threat. And that's all you need to frighten the player: threaten them with a powerful foe around the corner.

	The Rose DLC, while being interesting from a story perspective, is just Dimitrescu castle with walls that have to be taken down in a specific order. There's more puzzles, but it's still fairly linear. The only reason the DLC takes 2 to 3 hours to pass is because Rose's run speed is Ethan's walk speed cut in half. She's practically crawling with how slowly she moves. 

	The mercenaries game mode is funny, because the developers refuse to give the player any sort of agency. You run from A to B to finish the level. There's a timer, but there's never any threat of it running out. And you don't have to kill all enemies to finish the map (just half). You should kill ALL for the points, but it's more a mode about seeing how quickly you can get to the end of the map. 

	I would stop short of calling this game bad. I think it's average. The production values are there, and it's a solid linear experience. But this is RE. I expect a little more than a 'solid' experience. This would be a decent game if it was some no-name indie company. It's a disappointing game given that it's the RE franchise. After RE7 it feels like a step back. Here's hoping that if they go down this linear route, they at least make the enemies interesting. Add more variety. Because they're trying to have slow pacing whilst also being an action game, and it just didn't click this time.

The game successfully explores a new subgenre of horror, that has not been a major part of Resident Evil so far, though the game cant find a good balance between the series' typical mix of horror and action and falls behind most other modern Resident Evil entries. It is worth a play for sure though.

Story:
As always, story and plot are not Capcom's primary concern. They are all over the place - slow paced horror, hide and seek, hectic chase sequences and a one man army. At one point you are the villains' punching bag far out of his depth, at the next you are Batman working himself through his rogue gallery. It is not a big deal and actually advantageous, given the variety of locations made for the different characters and scenarios, but the majority of objectives being fetch quests makes it clear, that the plot was developed around independent ideas and set pieces rather than the other way around. The only noticeable effect on gameplay is the ridiculous amount of points of no return. You definitely need to be thorough with exploration on a first visit to new locations, because the central area aside, you cant trust in backtracking opportunities (dont use the lift below a certain windmill immediately after beating a nearby boss!).

Gameplay:
The general game mechanics all fit the environment and enemy design well. The mentioned blend of diverse setpieces create great variety. A more unified experience would not have been a bad direction though, because the mechanics never feel perfectly sufficient to fit and deal with every scenario, which is made most apparent by the option to switch between first and third person perspective. The atmospheric horror is a lot weaker than in RE7, while you feel to slow in comparison to your enemies to properly deal with the action encounters. Together with appropriate weaponry and supplies, the game still manages to achieve a balanced difficulty, but the stark contrasts in tone make it impossible for RE8 to peak at either one - it neither comes close to RE7 in horror, nor RE4R in action. The forced 3rd person perspective of the DLC improves the more unified focus on horror noticeably. Removing the ridiculous bloom would have been a great additional improvement for the combat.
Where the game shines is its weapon variety. There are many different weapons, each feeling unique, you can upgrade over the course of multiple subsequent playthroughs and use to work on the challenges. They certainly increase the game's replayability by a lot despite its general linearity.
What dampens the experience a little - again - is the inclusion of bonus weapons. Again, it only takes a normal playthrough with a few finished challenges to earn enough points for some overpowered weapon with unlimited ammo. Unfortunately, the highest difficulty and plenty of the challenges are designed around using those, trivializing a lot of the combat encounters and making achievements more of a grind than... well, an achievement. I would prefer the RE2R approach, where bonus weapons locked you out of the highest rating, which made it necessary to actually improve at the game - combat, movement, puzzles, navigation.

Graphics & Optimization:
The graphics look as good as in any other modern Resident Evil and the performance is consistently good. UI, HUD, settings and controls all fulfill their purpose, the inventory management and map are significantly weaker than in other entries though. The game does not even have an auto-sort option. The standard keybinds for menuing are pretty unintuitive. It is great, that we can skip cutscenes again after having to sit through them in RE7 on every playthrough, though it takes away a lot of the tension on a first playthrough, when the game is constantly showing you, when a cutscene is playing and stuff is out of your control anyway. Unless you are interested in a far fetched story, you are no longer glued to the screen in case you have to do something and just wait for the skip-prompt to disappear.

Resident Evil Village is a solid experience, especially if you have the hardware to really push it. I played this a while ago and it still stands out as one of the best looking games I have run.
Visuals and Performance
 * I was playing at 4k with every setting maxed out and the detail is incredible. The ray tracing is really where the game shines. Seeing the way the light hits the floors in the castle or how reflections work in the darker areas makes the atmosphere feel way more immersive.
 * Even with everything pushed to the absolute limit and ray tracing on, I was easily getting 100 plus frames on a 5070 and a 9700x. The game is incredibly well optimized for the level of graphics you are getting.
Gameplay and Story
 * The gameplay is fun and feels like a more modern take on the Resident Evil 4 style. It moves from tense survival horror to more action-heavy sections pretty smoothly.
 * That said, the story definitely has some "Resident Evil logic" going on. There are some plot points that feel a bit forced just to keep the mystery going, and some of the character decisions, most notably from Chris, can be pretty baffling if you actually stop to think about them.
 * The pacing is mostly good, though it does feel a bit disjointed at times. You move from one "horror trope" area to the next, like going from a Gothic castle to a weird doll house. It is all fun, but it feels more like a collection of different horror themes rather than one cohesive journey.
 * Some of the late-game sections lean a bit too hard into being a straight-up action shooter, which might not be what everyone is looking for in a Resident Evil game, but the combat is solid enough that it still works.

If you want a game that looks beautiful and runs great on high-end hardware, this is a must-play. The ray tracing alone makes it worth the experience. It has its goofy story moments and some weird writing, but the fun gameplay and the visuals definitely make it worth your time.

For first-time players, expect around 9–12 hours for the first playthrough,
and 4–6 hours when replaying.

[h3] On the Good: [/h3]

I loved Village. RE:VII was and still is my favorite RE game, and I was very happy that Ethan got a continuation of his storyline in a more action-packed style that still kept to the horror appropriately, keeping both your attention and dread constantly. The ambient was a masterpiece of art design, from the run down Eastern European brick and thatch buildings of the Village, to the Gothic Horror of Castle Dimitrescu, then to the House of Dolls in Beneviento, the flooded plains of Moreau's Marshes and finally to Heisenberg's Factory of Lucas-lite madness. Everything felt interesting, unique, with individualistic identities instead of the Baker's never-ending Hallways of Jack and the occasional Molded freaks. Nowhere felt 100% safe. Even with Duke, I was always anxious that something would try to break down the doors of safety while I was trading for Lei. This, I would say, is the best and strongest part of RE:VIII. If you liked RE:VII, but wanted more shooting instead of running endlessly from Jack and Black Molded freaks, then I am certain Village will be a great time for you.

[h3] On the Bad: (spoilers) [/h3] 
Dimetrescu and her daughters exist for one hour, and then it's over. Honestly, I would unironically say that even just her and her daughters should have been one seperate game. The Castle is beautiful, and it's a damn shame that in the end it was nothing more than the standard RE formula of doing puzzles, running from the thing, getting the shotgun, and then doing the same gimmick 3 times with the daughters, find where the cold air is coming from, bring it inside, and then just shoot them to freeze and then kill them. Very big shame. It's pretty obvious that Capcom just was way too ambitious probably in the board room by adding four Lords, giving two of them an actual personality, and then being unable to really develop them properly from there. It goes without saying that the 9'6" Vampire woman was the face of the game for a lot of people (me included) and it just felt really dirty that she was criminally underused, beyond her boss fight. Frankly, she probably should have been the last, with you doing Heisenberg's Factory first (after all, he's the one to find you first), then Moreau's Swamp, then Beneviento, and then as Climatic Peak, the 3 daughters, Dimitrescu, and then Miranda. As for the "Village" part of Village, you quickly realize that beyond the intro and the very early game, it also suffered the same fate as the Dimitrescu's. The fear is quickly gone when you realize that it serves as nothing more than quasi-walkways into the Lord's Arenas, with some gear to find and some infected freaks to kill. Lastly, the story was horrifically butchered to add drama and tension when all it would take is for Chris to be honest with Ethan, even at the start. He legit could have just said [spoiler] "Don't worry Ethan, I didn't actually kill your wife in front of you, it's actually Miranda and she took her form as Molded"[/spoiler] at any point (though, there's no game if he does that, now is there?), but I digress. Speaking of Ethan, sadly, his character is still really just a brick wall. Despite seeing his wife gunned down, his infant stolen, his hand, three fingers, many other parts of his body mutilated, he really doesn't care. [spoiler] And no, I'm not excusing this as him being Molded, seeing that if he was dead from RE:VII, conceived a child with his wife, and then lived in some bliss, that Mould would have a personality).[/spoiler] He's still steadfast, not a care in the world, no reaction to horrific events that constantly occur to him, and no real "fury" of being stuck again in hell on earth from Umbrella shenanigans.

[h3] On the Ugly: [/h3]
It's a pain to run the game. I have an I9, a 4080 Super, 64GB of DDR5, and still, I suffered some lag spikes here and there, and some horrific frame drops when entering in and out of Lord Arenas. Beyond that, however, there's not much to whine about, however. Just don't try to run the game with HDR or else all your in game screenshots get washed out later.

[h3] In conclusion: [/h3]
-Yes, it's good.
-Wait for a sale to buy, as with everything.
-Expect mediocre-ish performance.
-Probably has the best twist in RE history. (which I don't even want to write about, just play it yourself and find out.)
