I really expected to hate this. It seemed like RE8 was taking a bypass of the superb and intimate horror of its predecessor in favour of just copying RE4 (like every other game since) and that seemed a damn shame. RE7 was at its best when it was quiet and atmospheric, it was grungy and disgustingly realised, and it shined despite its ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a protagonist. 

Make no mistake, this game really, REALLY does take notes from RE4. You have the rural village in ‘Europe,’ you have the big castle with an oddly proportioned ruler, you have the bit in the boat with a big fish, you have the strange, eccentric shopkeeper (although the duke is not even comparable to my beloved merchant.) So much of this game is strikingly familiar, so why would I like it when it just steals from RE4, has a terrible protagonist, and has middling combat?

Well, it just isn’t that simple. I feel as though I have become the RE4 guy because I have to compare everything to it, and although it is more warranted here than ever, Resident Evil Village won me over with its scale, its setting, and its operatic characters. I cannot believe I am saying this, but this game made me (almost) like Ethan Winters as a protagonist. Yeah, he still says stupid ♥♥♥♥, and the writing in general is still absolute piss, but the grand scale and exaggerated caricature of its characters fits him well.

Writing in Resident Evil games is pretty bad across the board, but it works when it is on the far end of a very long scale. It works when it is simple, reduced, intimate, and it works when it is grand, over the top, almost comical. This here is the latter. RE8 has a rogues gallery of misfits, from the dominating, sensual violence of Lady Dimitrescu, to the pitiable waste of Salvatore Moreau. Each of these lords hold their corners in this isolated snowy town, and they are the beating heart of this game.

Lady D in her grand gothic castle. Seeing it immediately outlined against the fog on the horizon as you enter the Village is one of the best moments in Resident Evil history. Its grand main hall and open grounds a welcoming counterpart to the blood-flooded basements, filled with the roaming remains of a once noble house. 
Donna Beneviento in her hidden manor, nestled by a waterfall in a path through a misted grove. Its quiet melancholy turning into a nightmare as you creep around surreal rooms, tormented by some monstrosity. 
Water wastelands and industrial hellscapes follow, each area having a strong visual identity, and all of them reflecting their respective rulers.

You become intimately familiar with the setting and these locations over the course of its 8-12 hour runtime, visiting the central Village often, opening locked rooms and finding secrets as you move between these disparate lords. That is something I really want to hammer home. The combat is not great, enemies just do one of two things, and they don’t really react when you shoot them. It has the intentional clunkyness of RE7, but without the horror and anxiety to back it up. The game actually gave me motion sickness due to its low FOV, and the excuse “oh, its for the horror and atmosphere” simply does not hold up when the previous game had an FOV slider, and had horror and atmosphere in droves. Some parts of this game are far too long, while others are far too short. Ladies D and Beneviento had by far the most interesting story and locations, and they are both far too short. Moreau I actually quite liked, and I think it was a perfect length, while Heisenberg’s factory felt too long. 

As I said before, you can hammer on its criticisms, but when a major one is ‘i wish I had more’ then you know you must be doing something right. This is one of the best games I have ever played in terms of setting and environment. It is so unbelievably stunning, all of the way through, and any complaint is nullified by simply looking around. That is why you should play this game.

The Resident Evil franchised really picked it up with its last two releases. Both Biohazard and Village tell their respective story from the first person, placing the setting front and center. Paired with some truly messed up circumstances and events, the last two iterations bring a level of twisted horror that did not exist  in the series prior. Before you would watch truly horrific things happen to a character. Now those things are happening to you. I actually had one moment where a jump scare got me pretty damn good and I cannot tell how many moments had my skin crawling as I processed what was happening or just happened to me. Although I feel the horror aspects are peak Resident Evil, the series is, and always has been, a resource management game at its core. 

The survival/resource management side of the game felt easier than past RE games. I could not tell if it was because they softened it up or this being my 4th RE game I have experienced. I usually hit a  point in RE games where I feel like I am soft locked, but in this one I found myself with an abundance of resources throughout my entire playthrough. [spoiler] When the credits rolled I still had so many valuable resources in my inventory I felt I  could have done a whole additional chapter without picking a single thing up. [/spoiler] Maybe I have learned my lesson and managed my resources effectively, but my gut says it was easier.

Progression felt good overall. I liked how the systems worked and I felt I scaled properly with my enemies throughout the story. [spoiler] The only problem I had was how many upgrades were left on the table in the end. I like to max out my character and it was just impossible in the end. [/spoiler] 

The story was pretty good, but not without its flaws. It had me interested. I did not skip any cutscenes. I found a lot of them progressed the story and kept you engaged in its setting.  [spoiler] The ending was fine. It had this weird way of making me tired towards the end, but also leaving me wanting for more as if it ended too soon. I found myself begging for the end and also mad that it ended that quickly. A little unbelievable as well, I did not like how they explained Ethan's ability to take so much pain. It felt like a copout dressed up as a sincere Eureka moment. [/spoiler] 

Graphics wise this game was beautiful. I found myself walking through it for most of the game. There are very few times when I play a video game will I walk.  I am a sprinter through and through, but this game had me pacing my steps, even stopping at points to admire my surroundings. The mountains, the village, the underground, etc. were all gorgeous to look at. Not to mention the use of light and how it brings it all together to be one of the best uses of modern graphics to date. 

Overall, I enjoyed this game a ton and would recommend it to anyone who is interested in the series. You could start with this one first, but I would suggested Biohazard. If you do start with this one it brings you up to speed pretty quickly and the story feels connected even with limited context.

Honestly, just another great Resident Evil game. It successfully mixes the campy quirkiness of Resident Evil 4 with the perspective and horror of Resident Evil 7.

That said, I still prefer the RE7 aesthetic. It felt more realized and focused. After leaving the Castle in this game, no other area feels quite as detailed, with the possible exception of parts of the Factory. It feels very front-loaded. House Dimitrescu and the vampire family were extremely interesting, but everything that follows feels progressively more watered down.

House Beneviento was said to be the scariest part of the game, and while it was definitely creepy, it goes by way too quickly. I enjoyed the return of the upgrade system and the ability to customize a loadout similar to RE4, but it doesn't feel quite as essential or impactful as it did in that game. Ultimately, it feels like they tried to force the RE4 mold onto the RE7 engine; some parts fit perfectly, while others feel slightly out of place.

As for the story, it’s honestly pretty ridiculous. I preferred the grounded mystery of 7. They clearly wanted to connect Ethan’s journey to the rest of the series lore, which isn't bad per se, but the execution is bizarre. Ethan’s arc feels a bit aimless here, and the twists regarding Mia and Mother Miranda were so over-the-top that I actually laughed. Chris Redfield feels like he was included mostly because of his cameo in the previous game; his presence leads to some weirdly hilarious moments, like when he suddenly blows up the entire village with BSAA high-tech military force lmao.

This game needed a little more time in the oven to feel fully realized. It’s definitely not a bad game, but it left me feeling slightly underwhelmed by the end.

A note on the Shadows of Rose DLC: It’s largely a reskinned tour of main-game areas. The voice acting is hilariously campy, and while there are some cool moments, it doesn't compare to the massive amount of creative DLC RE7 received. Still, I hope Capcom continues this trend. This era has honestly revitalized the Resident Evil franchise as a whole.

The graphics are absolutely stunning, the game ran really smoothly for the vast majority of the time, and the story was really intriguing and well paced!

The story did remind me a lot of Silent Hill, honestly, since it involves a dad trying to find his daughter who is being used for a ritual to be reborn. It has a bit of a twist to it but it still is pretty reminiscent of Silent Hill at that core story element. All the different characters popping up was pretty cool though, I enjoyed how they all had their own "dungeon" to go through and different abilities that those areas reflected well. I can tell a lot of thought went into all of it. I really liked how much of the story tied back to not just RE7 but other RE games as well. It's not as simple as a random Chris cameo, rest assured. There was one part in particular that I was kind of fanboying over, not gonna' lie.

The gameplay was decent enough, but there were some annoyances here and there. There were a lot of areas that had infinitely respawning enemies where you had to just through them and it was never clear that was what you were supposed to do exactly. It seems like a weird hold over from a bygone era of gaming and there is a reason why games don't tend to do that anymore. A lot of the enemies just seemed to take way more hits than they should as well, even on the regular difficulty. I only died a few times, but if I had to play the game again for the first time I would pick the easy difficulty just to make combat go a little bit faster. It isn't deep enough to warrant how drawn out the encounters can feel, even in the boss battles. Enemies just feel really bullet sponge-y. I shouldn't have to dump 5 or 6 shotgun rounds into a basic zombie lol.

Oddly enough, I think I may have actually preferred to play the game in 3rd person. People said to not do that for a first playthrough because it does obviously change the vibe of the game and it makes it a lot easier, but gameplay-wise I think third person would fit WAY more for what they were going for. Compare that to RE7 which was designed very intrinsically for first person since it was a VR game (and one of the best, mind you). The combat here felt more like a traditional RE game that they just decided to make first person, so I think 3rd would have been better in that regard. However, you'd kind of lose the immersion and some of the cool cutscenes that result from playing in first person, so it would be a bit of a trade off for sure. Maybe one day I'll do a NG+ run in third person and see how it compares.

Anyway, overall, really good game that I had a good time with. About 18 hours (12 IGT) for my completion. Give it a try if you haven't already and are a fan of the other RE games, especially 7!

Capcom managed to capitalize on the series' revival with Biohazard, and made it bigger, better and creepier.
Welcome to the Village, which is this time around set somewhere in Romania, my homeland, and to be fair, it was represented incredibly! The village is re-created to the detail: the houses, the pots, the carpets, every single aspect of the homesteads of remote villages. It also gets recipe representation through Duke's shop, recipes that give you pretty important benefits throughout the story.
The village is the center of the map, from which you can visit a castle, fishing huts and a really big underground factory.
The story takes the Winters family through another struggle, because of the events in Louisiana. They tried hiding out in Romania, but because of Mother Miranda, a scientist set around the area, that wants to resurrect her long-dead daughter, tries to steal the Winters daughter, and Ethan has none of it. The virus that Miranda brought upon the village is of a local origin, not being related to the one found in the US.
The gameplay and exploration is what you'd expect from a Resident Evil game: treasures, looting every house, completing puzzles, destroy hidden items, and having the merchant(this time, someone called "The Duke"), as one of the few friendly faces you meet throughout the story. 
Of the villains, of course the ones who stand out the most are Lady Dimitrescu and Heisenberg: Lady Dimitrescu is a tall vampire lady, with her three vampire daughters, residing in the castle with the same name, in my opinion the best location of the game. And Heisenberg is the one that created the underground undead soldier factory, with an army that could have taken over if it wasn't for Chris and Ethan. The two villains being voiced by two future award-winning voice actors.
Village, alongside RE4 are in my opinion the two most memorable entries in the Resident Evil franchise. Because both take their predecessors and make everything 10 times better!

It's quite easy to see that Capcom poured a lot of love and work into making RE Village a bigger and better experience than RE7. The game has more exploration, more flushed out story moments, more combat, more puzzles and more side content, and yes it's also good if not better.

Truth be told, I was not at all into the game until I finished the castle segment and the game opened up. The start of the game can be quite slow and boring, but if you stick with it you will see why people love this game so much. The second half of the game delivers incredible plot twists, combat, horror and exploration in spades.

Personally I still rank RE7 higher than this game because I simply like the vibes better. I felt that the baker family was a far more memorable cast of characters and the overall game worked more coherently as a vehicle for immersion to sell the baker house as some kind of surreal place that might actually exist somewhere, rather than this totally made up village with a host of not so likeable characters other than Dimitrescu and Heisenberg. Either way I recommend playing both games because they are excellent video games.

EDIT: Extra points for eye popping HDR implementation. If you have a proper OLED TV/monitor with HDR, this game delivers incredible contrast, visuals and highlights and is a shining example of great HDR

My favorite RE games are 1, 2, and 4 plus all 3 of their remakes. I liked 7 but I never replayed it beyond the initial playthrough (while I've played 1, 2, 4 countless times, specially 4). 

So if you're a fan of those games, you'll love Village. I really didn't follow much of the release press for this game when it was coming out (just had too many other things to play at the time, I knew I would have to revisit it later). So I went into 8 almost blind (of course I knew it was another Ethan Winters game and I knew Lady D was gonna be in it from all the coverage she got). 

It was a blast, this game is exactly like a marriage of 4 and 7, but 4 wears the pants in the relationship. Unlike the more traditional RE games, you most likely will be killing everything you see rather than preserving ammo. Enemies almost always drop materials you need to craft more ammo. The horror and puzzle is light - there's a part in there that's very much like the Amnesia games where you have to hide from something big and subjectively scary and can't fight back. But that part lasts about maybe 10 minutes or less. Rest of the game is definitely ACTION horror and I had a great time. I really enjoyed the setting, the cast of characters, and the story is super entertaining. I wanted to know what was gonna happen with Ethan, I wanted to know what Chris's deal was, where and what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on with Rose. Who the hell are these villagers and what do the lords want. The game is just vary varied and doesn't get stale. The way the game has you go hunt down the different lords and come back to more explorable parts of the central "Village" is great, I loved that aspect a lot. Some of the "segments" are weaker than others sure but none of them are bad imo. Sure some could be more fleshed out but I think as a whole they deliver great pacing. I especially loved the ending. You go through one of the more "grueling" areas of the game and you get rewarded with a GREAT setpiece starring an RE favorite. 

My only complaints about the game has to do with the gameplay itself. It's fun and all but its SO damn similar to RE4 that it HURTS the game, coming from a massive fan of RE4. Ethan will get guns and upgrade them like Leon but he can't roundhouse kick and he can't suplex. It just makes me wanna play RE4. There's other stuff that I could nitpick but it's honestly fine. My only other complaint was the Shadow of Rose DLC. It's pretty much an asset flip which I think is pretty lame. Same exact areas from the game with slightly different mechanics. The story is a little touching but predictable and meh from a villain pov. At least its short and it gives you some closure between the dad and daughter. 

Anyway, I'm hyped for Re9uiem. Ethan can't do a roundhouse kick but muh Leon can.

Also it ran great on the Deck with some tweaking. Played the entire game on it.

It seems like Capcom can't resist making everything action packed because yet again the dread, urgency, and powerlessness from their most recent game's predecessor is almost entirely gone, almost. The best moments are those where Ethan feels way too underequipped for the situations he's in, which really only happens with a few of the bosses and certain segments (if you've played the game you know that one boss that does this perfectly). Don't get me wrong though, the action itself is still pretty fun. The gameplay and level design, especially the level design, are great, but I'm not sure if it really works great coming off the heels of the most "horror" Resident Evil game. The puzzles are also basically non-existent, as they are easy enough for a toddler to solve.

Other than that, the only other problems are pretty normal for Resident Evil: the writing and voice acting. The whole thing with framing Chris as a "bad guy" is just dumb and if you're surprised to find out that he's still a "good guy" then you might just be dumb too. I honestly have no idea who thought that it would be interesting to try and frame one of the most altruistic characters in the franchise as an antagonist. No, just no. Every major plot point that involves Chris is just dumb, and could've totally been avoided with Chris telling Ethan like three things. Also, I don't know what happened, but Ethan's voice actor just doesn't seem to be putting in the work here, but it could just be because the writing is bad too. Also maybe it's because he has way more lines in this game but the whole time, very few actually sound good. I really loved Biohazard's self contained plot with the Baker family, and having the "bigger scale" stuff only come out at the end.

It's got a pretty great ending, and for the first time in the franchise I actually felt a little emotional. Resident Evil 8: Village is a good game overall, but not one that fully clicked with me. The atmosphere, visuals, and sound design are excellent, and some locations are genuinely memorable. Exploration is enjoyable, and the mix of combat and puzzles mostly works. However, the game often leans more into action than horror, which made parts of it feel less tense and more straightforward than I expected. Still, the main campaign is solid and generally fun, even if it’s not my favorite entry in the series.

The DLC (Shadows of Rose / Winters’ Expansion), on the other hand, was a big letdown for me. Instead of expanding on what worked in the base game, it feels slow, repetitive, and surprisingly boring. A lot of the gameplay relies on limited abilities and reused environments, which quickly gets old. The pacing drags, and encounters feel more tedious than engaging. Rather than feeling challenged in a good way, I often felt restricted and uninterested.

Story-wise, the DLC tries to add emotional weight and close the Winters storyline, but it didn’t really land for me. The narrative moments are there, but they’re stretched across gameplay that doesn’t feel strong enough to support them. By the end, it felt more like something to get through than something to enjoy.

Final thoughts:
The main game is decent, visually impressive, and worth playing. The DLC, however, feels underdeveloped and dull, offering little in terms of fun or replay value.

I got the game super cheap on a pricing error a few years back. I'm a broke, but I think at $10-15, I still would think it's a decent price. I definitely think playing through it was worth my time. 

Game is split up into multiple sections, so it feels a bit disjointed looking back. I think the classic Resident Evil style sections were stronger, but the action parts were fun too. 

I played on Hardcore difficulty, and I felt like it was an enjoyable level of challenge for me. The only real standout part is the very beginning of the game, which is significantly harder and more frustrating than anything else the game has to offer. Once you get past that, remember it tells you your objective is to survive, I felt like Hardcore was a good balance for me. 
I don't play very many Survival Horror games, I'm not a terrible shot but I'm definitely missing heads here and there. I felt resource pressure at some points, but not overwhelmingly so. I'm not sure how much harder Village of Shadows is, but Hardcore might not be as satisfying if you're a veteran Resident Evil / Survival Horror player. 

I don't think very hard about the story in this type of game, just kind of took it at face value, so I found it fun and engaging enough. If you're looking for like deep lore or a good/consistent addition to the Resident Evil universe, you might be disappointed on that front.  

The game does have some technical issues I encountered, primarily in the DLC. Enemies are harder to squeeze around at higher framerates, and the DLC has some areas that were seemingly impossible on Hardcore until I capped my FPS at 60. Like literally the monster chasing you runs too much faster/sooner above 60 FPS that you can't escape it. 

The DLC was more story based, again taking things at face value, and I enjoyed it. The gameplay is a bit more limited, and honestly probably more frustrating overall. Enemies don't seem to stagger or have the chance of critical hit 1-shots, at least on Hardcore. Definitely takes some getting used to, especially when you have the full arsenal at the end of the main story.  


tl;dr
Somewhere in the range of 15-18 hours of gameplay to beat the main game + DLC for me (I suck at puzzles tbh). Definitely enjoyed my time  with it. Not a perfect game by any means, but no point which I'd personally say was a major negative. A bit disjointed/unfocused style, has classic Resi style and more modern action parts. 
Start on at least Hardcore difficulty if you're looking for some challenge, but wait until after (and/or struggle through) the initial "survive" section to actually judge the difficulty.

Resident Evil Village (RE8) — это тот случай, когда Capcom взяли всё лучшее из классического хоррора, приправили экшеном и подали в очень красивой обёртке.

Идея с мрачной деревней и «семейкой» антагонистов работает отлично: каждая локация ощущается по-своему, атмосфера держит напряжение, а история затягивает так, что хочется идти дальше, даже когда уже поздно и «ещё один сейв — и спать».

Графика — просто 🔥. На HDR игра выглядит шикарно: свет, тени, туман, интерьеры замка — всё выглядит дорого и кинематографично. Иногда ловишь себя на мысли, что просто стоишь и рассматриваешь окружение… пока тебя не сожрут.

Геймплей бодрый, баланс между страхом и стрельбой удачный, враги разнообразные, а бои не скатываются в тупой тир. Это не чистый хоррор, но именно в этом и кайф.

DLC — ну… скажем честно, без восторгов. Не плохое, но довольно скучное и явно не обязательное. Если брать — то строго по скидке, иначе ощущение, что можно было спокойно пропустить.

Итог:
Отличная основная игра с сильной атмосферой и впечатляющей картинкой. Один из тех RE, которые реально хочется пройти до конца. DLC — опционально.

The sequel to Ethan's story, which saved the franchise, so to speak. The one that everyone waited for so badly. The one where the antagonist became a legend before the game was actually released. Well, I can say a lot, and I don't know where to start. I liked my overall experience, but I am not floored by it. It was a decent Resident Evil experience, sometimes surprised me in a good way, but at the end of the day, I feel that something was missing to be amazed by it.

The story continues and closes Ethan's adventures, and answers interesting questions; it would be very spoilerish to talk about it. Let's say there are many twists and turns, and even if some of them are not too hard to figure out, still adds to the adventure. The game binds certain previous happenings together and explains a few main events as well. It was a bit longer than RE7, but definitely shorter than RE4 remake, which left me a bit disappointed. Another aspect I didn't like was the pacing of the story. It started well, the middle section slowed down, while the ending was interesting again.

I really cannot complain about the atmosphere and the visuals. This wasn't clearly mentioned anywhere, but it is crystal clear that the main inspiration for the setting was based on Romania and its myths. For example, Lady Dimitrescu's castle was based on Castle Peles in Romania. We saw braided garlic in games before, but a lot of pickles in jars, so the authenticity is top notch. Walking on the streets and in the houses of the village, where the poverty and the war-torn history are still palpable, really adds a nice extra. Even when it feels still, you can't be sure when you be attacked by something or someone. The soundtrack is also nice, my personal favourite was the final boss's music, which literally gave a good Dark Souls vibe with its gravely tones, combining with that defining moment by multiple reasons.

The gameplay, as always, brings the well-known classic Resident Evil motives; there's no need to talk about it. It was enjoyable (exploring every nook and cranny is always fun for me), but comparing to, for example, RE4 Remake, the gunplay was way too underwhelming, the shots had no real impact on the enemies. On the other hand, the main boss fights were creative (even if they're not too challenging), just as their territories were. And in my opinion, here comes the big pro and con. The main horror experience comes from different classical fear elements which the "Four Lords", aka the main bosses of the village, represent, such as vampires/beasts, dolls, monsters, and mechanical/body adjustments, so a wide range of the audience can find their likings or not so much their likings. Village puts these elements together, and while it feels like one big comprehensive solution, it has no real unique identity, which I think is a missed opportunity.

Coming from RE7, my experience with RE Village was drastically more engaging. Where RE7 felt thematically disconnected from the franchise I’ve followed for years, Village brought me back into the world I love. I was genuinely invested in the story this time, the pacing, the environments, and the narrative twists all pushed me forward with excitement rather than exhaustion. Seeing Chris Redfield again, and seeing him remain consistent with his origins, was incredibly satisfying. Alongside Leon and Jill, Chris continues to represent the true core of the Resident Evil legacy. His presence grounded the story and reinforced that Village belongs within the larger series in a meaningful way. Ethan also received a bold and emotional conclusion. Whether players personally love him or not, it’s undeniable that Capcom took a courageous step in how they ended his arc. It gave weight to the events of both RE7 and Village, ensuring that Ethan’s journey would not be forgotten or overshadowed. For me, RE Village now stands alongside RE1–4 as one of my absolute favorite entries ever. It respects the roots of the franchise while confidently pushing forward, something RE7 tried but didn’t quite achieve.

Resident Evil Village is more action-oriented, but honestly not much more than RE4 when you think about it. What really made it work for me is its structure: the game feels like four distinct acts, each with its own identity, tone, and villain.

I loved that approach. The gothic horror of Lady Dimitrescu’s castle is pure, classic excess — dramatic, stylish, almost operatic. The haunted-house section with the dolls is genuinely unsettling and psychological, easily one of the strongest horror moments in the series. Then comes the bayou-like section with the creature, and that one really stayed with me. It made me uncomfortable in a different way — not through fear, but through empathy. I honestly felt a bit like a bully there, even a bit ashamed, in the same way you might feel facing the Frankenstein creature: monstrous, but tragic and deeply human underneath.

Finally, you get the industrial horror with Heisenberg — full-on Magneto energy — leaning into spectacle and action without completely losing its edge. Even with the increased action, RE8 balances its tones incredibly well and experiments with horror in varied, memorable ways. For comparison RE2 Remake had my heart racing often but in this one I was fairly calm most of the time. 

Some of the things I didn't like:

- I'm not happy about this not having an FOV slider. Had to install a mod to get rid of motion sickness it caused me. Why is it so hard to implement such a simple accessibility setting? 

- Factory level ruined the pacing for me. They couldn't have made a more disorienting and confusing level if they tried. I was constantly getting lost and found myself running in circles trying to get to where I needed to be. Looking at the map didn't help much. You'd think that after so many games in the series there would be some innovation in map design but no, it's the same old design making you scratch your head trying to figure out what stairs lead where. For example, Borderlands series do this well with their 3D map.

Overall well worth your money.

Anyway, it's 4 Years after I bought this game, and my gosh does it still hold up. I come back every couple of months wanting to do a speed run or a Village of Shadows playthrough. Or even just for a slow walkthrough to take in the incredible scenery of a rural, haunted Romania. 

The atmosphere is magnificent. Castle Dimitrescu is one of the most beautiful places in any of the Resident Evil games. So much so that I find myself standing still in the main hallway, hearing the chandelier above creak as it gently swings from side to side, a masterpiece of small, intricate details that add up to an outstanding game. Though the castle segment feels a bit short, maybe it's because I enjoy that part the most, and time flies when you're having fun. Either way is still excellent. The game is still filled with puzzles: going to get a key that unlocks a cabinet that has another key in it. You know, the classic Resident Evil gameplay. While RE8 leans more into action than RE7 at times, the horror never entirely disappears. You will know what I mean when you walk through those castle doors for the first time.

The boss fights also feel innovative and are a significant improvement from the past titles. I'll try my best to prevent spoilers, but the boss fights are an equal mix of disgusting (such as Moreau's fight in the reservoir) and cool and different (Heisenberg, in the factory). It's easy to get the hang of the weak spots in the fights, and it gives a satisfying and climactic resolve once you finally defeat them. Between the boss fights, the game doesn't let you have too much rest time, unexpected enemies behind doors or hiding in the shallow water below you are sure to keep you on your toes and your ammo... dwindling.

The game also offers a variety of difficulties, so casual players can roam and have a good time. In contrast, hardcore players can really get along with the more complex difficulties.

I recommend this game to everyone, but it should go without saying that you play RE7 before this one. You certainly won't be disappointed in that game either. 

Overall a very firm 9/10 from me :)

Resident Evil Village is a masterclass in modern horror gaming, seamlessly blending spine-chilling atmosphere, gripping narrative, and exhilarating gameplay. From the very first moment, you’re drawn into the eerie and haunting world of the village, where every shadow, creaking floorboard, and distant howl reminds you that danger lurks around every corner. The attention to detail is simply astonishing — from the weathered textures of the villagers’ homes to the opulent yet sinister design of Castle Dimitrescu, every location is meticulously crafted and brimming with personality.

The gameplay strikes an incredible balance between survival horror and action. Resource management, tense exploration, and heart-pounding combat keep you constantly engaged. Each encounter feels meaningful, whether you’re sneaking past enemies, planning your attacks, or facing off against massive, unforgettable bosses. The combat mechanics are fluid and satisfying, offering a depth that rewards careful strategy while still delivering adrenaline-pumping action.

One of the standout aspects is the variety in environments and challenges. From the snow-covered village to the eerie catacombs, and the towering Castle Dimitrescu, each area feels unique and fully realized. The pacing is excellent, with moments of intense fear interspersed with quieter, tension-building exploration. This ebb and flow makes every step of the journey feel significant.

The narrative is another highlight. The story is engaging and layered, with compelling characters who leave a lasting impression. The twists and revelations keep you on the edge of your seat, and the emotional stakes make the horror elements even more impactful. Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, among other iconic characters, are not only terrifying but fascinating, blending horror with unforgettable personality.

Visually, the game is breathtaking. The lighting, textures, and cinematic presentation elevate the experience to almost film-like quality. Combined with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack and ambient sound design, the game fully immerses you in its world. Every creak, scream, and whisper contributes to an atmosphere of tension and dread that is rare to find in games today.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a triumph. It honors the legacy of the franchise while pushing boundaries in storytelling, design, and gameplay. Whether you’re a longtime fan or new to the series, this game delivers a horror experience that is both terrifying and unforgettable. From its epic locations and thrilling combat to its rich story and unforgettable characters, it’s an absolute must-play for anyone who loves high-quality horror.

A complicated hybrid. So I played this game back when it came out on the PS4, but after recently replaying 7 and completing its madhouse difficulty, it made me want to go back and revisit this game. I loved the game back when I first played it, as it gave my long awaited sequel to 7 and it brought back many of 4’s gameplay elements, which is my favorite entry in the series. But sadly, it all just didn’t hit as hard for me as 7 did, which even now many years later, it felt just like the first time I played that game. So let’s talk about it.

Visually, the game still looks good and continues to showcase the REEngine at its best. I loved the design of the levels with each biome having its own distinct feel and vibe. Lady D’s castle and the village itself were my personal favorites.

One thing I did really love too was the game's semi-open world structure. I like that the game gives you the time to explore the environment, hunt animals and treasures and just take in the sights, but not feel too bloated like many big open worlds do. And it’s rewarding when after you finish a major story section and boss fight, you can come back to the village and see what new areas or open locked chests you couldn’t before and see what new bosses have spawned in older areas for you to take on.

Combat I’m a little mixed on though. It still feels like a decent first person shooter, but it’s a lot more action oriented to fit 4’s gameplay framework, with you being able to upgrade guns and eventually replace them with more powerful versions. The issue is, the enemies in this game are just bad, especially the Lycans, who on paper are cool as it’s the series take on Werewolves, but they are so annoying to fight. They're too fast when moving towards you, making landing headshots on them very tricky, and they also just take way too many bullets to go down. Like one lycan can just take a direct blast from the shotgun like it was nothing and they get back up on their feet in like a second. It was just so infuriating, especially the fight in the stronghold or when you play as a Chris, and you have to call down like 5 Call of Duty air strikes on a target while being swarmed by dozens of lycans. Ya, no thanks.

And ya the survival horror gameplay is there but it’s used very sparingly and not to the effect that 7 did. But there are some great moments like Lady D’s castle which feels like classic Resident Evil and then the Donna basement section. If you know, you know.

(SPOILERS AHEAD FOR THE STORY)

Then it’s onto the story, which I just didn’t enjoy that much this time around. Like I said, the Lady D castle section is the best and she is a standout villain, but they don’t do all that much with her and she’s dead before you’ve even gotten to know her that much. I liked how you fought Jack multiple times in 7 and still had to deal with him towards the end of the game. It would have been nice if they did something similar with Lady D.The rest of the villains you fight are okay but none hold up to Lady D really. Heisenburg a little bit but just because his voice sounds like Nicolas Cage which always made me grin, and some of his one liner’s like in reference to Chris, "I'm going to murder that boulder-punching a*hole, but you're first.". That line had me laughing lol

I liked how Ethan just had a ‘I’m done with this bull***’ attitude in the cutscenes and in some of the boss fights, but it kind of mimicked me just being like I’m done with this game. And then there's also the twist with Ethan being a Molded. Honestly, it’s just dumb and the game does nothing with it. Like they explain that Jack killed Ethan in the guest house in the last game, but I’m like okay but then how did he come back as a Molded? Did Eveline bring him back to be her “daddy” with her whole family plotline? Who knows because they don’t bother explaining any further.

But ya, overall I wouldn’t say this is a bad game by any means, but it’s definitely been knocked down quite a lot for me.

The short and dirty for this game is that it's really well made, and really boring. Resident evil as a franchise is torn between the classic puzzle solving, exploration, and inventory management survival horror of the ps1 era games and the action horror of post resident evil 4 until RE 7 went back to survival horror. This game tries to pay homage to both eras with middling success. 

On the classic survival horror side: Village has maps that slowly open up and loop back to earlier sections as you obtain more puzzle items and keys. The problem is, with the exception of the main hub area, that the maps are too short and basic due to this game being split up into different sections that all have different vibes that they're going for. You don't have much time to really familiarize yourself with the layout of the level before being pushed into the next gameplay chapter. The puzzles are also very basic.

On the action horror side: Village pays a lot of homage to RE 4. You have upgradable weapons, an eccentric merchant, and a moment early in the game that is very reminiscent of the opening segment of RE 4. The problem is the combat isn't very good. Guns have minimal impact and village doesn't have the arcade-y movement and melee options from RE 4. You just shoot enemies until they're dead.

The game does have good parts, the hub area you revisit between main segments is the highlight of the game as it slowly opens up each time you revisit it. I also won't go into spoilers, but there is a segment in this game that probably the scariest the franchise has ever been. unfortunately, this part is a slog on replays.

Buy on a deep sale, or better yet replay RE 4 or its remake.

After completing the main RE series 100% (except RE5 Multiplayer / RE6 because it sucks) I have to say, and I know it might be a hot take: RE 8 Village is my favourite one in the series.
Why?
Because it picks up on almost everything previous titles do and expands on it. Examples?
The horror of RE7
The puzzles from RE1
The crafting system of previous titles
The mercenaries mode of previous titles
The hordes of enemies that pursue you from RE4
The treasure system from RE4 (but simplified)
Iconic antagonists close to the ones like Nemesis and Mr X in RE 2 and RE3
No annoying superslow segments that hurt replayability (AshleyRE4/SherryRE2)

This game does so much right: the atmosphere is captivating, the variety of bosses is refreshing (in contrast to RE2 and RE3), the interactivity of the overworld is great by giving you the ability to hunt certain animals or look for treasure etc.

Even though people either hate this entry due to it experimenting with different enemies other than zombies and some people glazing it for Lady Dimitrescu (who only takes up like 20% of the game) it should be judged by more than just these two criteria.

And although I really love this title, I have to admit that it is not perfect. Examples for this:

The knives (except the LZ answerer to some extent) are almost completely useless. While you were able to parry or defend yourself with knives in previous title, 7 and 8 somehow managed to make them feel exceptionally useless by dealing no damage, not staggering enemies and making you more vulnerable to grab-attacks when using them.

Furthermore, the guns (unlike RE4 for example) are not treated as alternatives from one another but rather straight up upgrades. So instead of having one deal more damage and be inaccurate or one firing fast and dealing less damage, most of the time as soon as you unlock or find the next pistol/shotgun etc. you are better of just selling your current one and upgrading the new one because it will always be objectively better in every regard.

Also, there is no item box, so you are forced to carry all of your items (even ressources like meats) in your inventory which take up unneccessary space until you either deliver them to the trader or purchase an inventory expansion. [Thankfully crafting materials don't take up inventory space]

In addition to that Mia is unbearable as a character, making you feel like you were playing gaslighting simulator whenever she is on screen. (But I also hated her in RE7 already so that is a bias)

In conclusion, this title does A LOT right and is REFRESHING for the series. Even if you hate this title you can't argue against it having plenty of different enemy types and bosses and unlike previous titles A LOT of interesting personalities within one game. If you haven't played this title yet I strongly advise you to try it out and if you have been hating on it maybe give it a second chance.

Impeccable atmosphere. The snowy village, the opulent castle, the feeling of a place stuck in time where something isn't quite right. There's an unsettling stillness to everything that lingers even when you get attacked by the monsters, a constant feeling of being watched by whatever might be lurking in the shadows. 

It can be peaceful at times, but the tension is always there. You know it's not safe, but you can't help but be mesmerized by the overwhelming beauty of the landscape. 

Inside the village itself, you might feel somewhat too big, out of place, but as soon as you look around and truly take in the size of the mountains and everything surrounding you on a larger scale, an inescapable feeling of loneliness and hopelessness takes over. And yet, Ethan keeps pushing on. His resilience is so raw, so human. So powerful.

Would have loved an option to team up with Heisenberg. His defiant demeanor is extremely appealing, and I feel that with enough tactfulness involved, he could have been convinced to elaborate a new plan to take down Miranda together with Ethan, without weaponizing Rose. Despite his roughness, his anger and resentment towards Miranda, he's incredibly smart and shows a level consideration towards others and life itself that you don't see in the other lords, especially regarding his own experiments. His focus on using Rose's powers in order to defeat Miranda seems to come from a place of self-doubt and insecurity. Despite being the most powerful of the four Lords, he still doesn't believe he's strong enough to take Miranda down for good, even with Ethan's help. His diary entries are particularly heartbreaking; Heisenberg just wants to be free, to be in charge of himself, and after decades of being mistreated, abused and experimented on, he knows he will only be able to rest if he takes down the person who inflicted all that pain on him with his own hands.

I truly hope someday we get a DLC/spin-off focused on the four Lords. There are endless possibilities for such interesting characters, especially in the Resident Evil world, and it would be a shame to see all that potential wasted.

The creation process of this game seems less like a carefully executed plan and more like the result of chaotic creative debates within the studio. In the early stages of development, no one on the team had a finalized story, a defined tone, or a clear gameplay formula. Because of this, every time they held a meeting, people started suggesting ideas inspired by their favorite horror games, and without even realizing it, the project gradually turned into a blend of three different horror traditions. One developer talked about the pacing of Resident Evil 4, another was influenced by the enclosed and claustrophobic atmosphere of Resident Evil 7, and someone else argued that adding disturbing psychological elements from P.T. would benefit the game. Since the creative director didn’t reject any of these suggestions, the project evolved into a hybrid experience combining multiple horror styles. 
This lack of direction caused a long-running debate within the studio. One group pushed for “more action,” while the other insisted on “pure horror.” This conflict lasted for months, leading management to partially include both ideas in the final product. This decision gave the game variety, but also turned it into an unusual structure that never fully settled into a single identity. The studio’s budget allocation strategy added another layer to the confusion. The lead producer believed that “even if players don’t fully understand the story, they will love the game if the atmosphere is strong enough.” Because of this mindset, most of the budget went into graphical quality, environmental design, and creature modeling. The narrative team was downsized, while the environment, lighting, and animation teams were expanded. As a result, the game’s environments are incredibly detailed, the lighting is almost cinematic, and the creature models are absurdly polished. However, because the same level of care wasn’t applied to the story, the narrative naturally ended up thinner and more shallow.The creature design process is especially noteworthy. The team working on this section approached it with almost academic precision. They reportedly stayed late at the studio drawing in dim rooms, referencing real autopsy footage, and directly copying and distorting real biological anatomies. That’s why the creature resembling the fetus baby from P.T. appears almost identical. Early feedback warned that it looked too similar and needed to be changed, but the team only made minor adjustments because they “didn’t want to break the spirit” of the concept. This resulted in monsters that feel both familiar and deeply unsettling in their own way. On the gameplay side, the most interesting detail is how the ammo balance was designed. The testing team collected hundreds of hours of gameplay data to analyze how much ammo players typically used, at what points they struggled, and when they experienced fear of running out. Using this data, they created an adaptive ammo distribution algorithm. Factors like the damage you took in the last section, how many enemies you killed, and how many healing items you had determined how much ammo the game would give you next. Because of this system, the player is never completely helpless, but never fully comfortable either. This artificial equilibrium acts like a constant electric tension running through the entire game. The reason boss fights ended up weak has everything to do with production pressures. In early development, boss battles were shorter, more intense, and more cinematic. But because the investors wanted to artificially extend the total playtime, the bosses were stretched out. Their health values were increased, their attack cycles were lengthened and made more repetitive, and transitions between phases were slowed down. That’s why the final boss battle feels extremely long not challenging but exhaustingdirectly due to this commercial intervention. The fact that the TPS camera wasn’t included in the main game and was sold later as DLC wasn’t actually a design choice but a technical issue turned into a business opportunity. The camera system was developed by two different teams, and while the FPS camera was completed, the TPS camera wasn’t technically ready. Instead of delaying the game to fix this, management decided to finish it later and sell it as paid content. Naturally, this caused backlash among players, since TPS feels like a core gameplay option rather than optional DLC. From a horror design standpoint, the game is highly professional. It doesn’t rely solely on jump scares; it uses low-frequency background sounds, subtle noises behind the player, barely noticeable motion effects, and subconscious lighting techniques. So the fact that the game made you unable to play alone is not surprising at all. At some point, people genuinely feel the need for someone else in the room. The fact that you had to invite friends over and only three out of six could even watch the screen shows how strong the atmosphere truly is. In the end, the final product is not perfect but an impressive mixture. Visually and atmospherically, it’s strong; in creature design and horror presentation, it’s highly successful. The gameplay balance is carefully crafted, though the boss fights and certain business decisions slightly limit the game’s potential. Despite the lightweight story, the intensity of the overall experience, its ability to keep players constantly on edge, and the way it blends its inspirations into its own identity make it a striking game. Even though you’re not a big Resident Evil fan, you were able to clearly recognize the technical achievement and fear crafting ability behind this project. And despite saying you can’t handle horror games, the reason it kept you playing is because its atmosphere and mechanics are constructed so skillfully. In that sense, the game leaves a strong impact despite its shortcomings.

This is a careful recommendation, and the main reason is... I can't choose what sort of person to recommend this to. There's such a variety of you, I can't quite pick one.

As an RE game, it has some of the mechanical hallmarks that you're likely familiar with. Smart ammo preservation, finding key items to progress, combining treasures. It's all there, but the campiness... I can't tell whether it's campy in a new but similar flavor, or not at all.

Ethan's such a weird protagonist, being the wimpiest or at least physically weakest protagonist the series has seen, while overcoming some of the worst odds any RE protag has been in. I'd almost call him John McCoolGuyAmerican as a joke, but I have a hard time being really reductive about him. The most precise thing I can say though, is that Ethan's never having a good time, not even when he's just at home being a Daddy. Dude's gonna join Guts in the Can't-Catch-A-♥♥♥♥♥♥'-Break club.

As an FPS, I feel like I am fighting the controls most of the time. I wouldn't say that's a failing on the design, as it seems intentional, meant to ramp up the tension. Ethan's just a civilian using guns well past his competency (even though he's had military training between 7 and 8? or did I just imagine that?), so he's got that awkward ol' weapon sway and imprecision past the first shot. It's annoying, it throws me off and I don't like it, but having tight shooting controls would undermine the atmosphere the game's working so hard to set up. I'm not conflicted on the matter, it should be this way, even if I don't like it.

It was rather recent (let's say Months) since I finished RE7. As a new experience, I respect its chops but felt some fun was lacking. Turning RE into a straight-played horror was an interesting choice, just too bad I don't care at all for swamp environments in videogames. Personal aesthetic preference notwithstanding, RE8 across the board felt like an improvement on it. RE feels at its best when it throws the surreal at your normal mug, and forces you to deal with it spectacularly. Or as the old adage says: "When in doubt, C4". RE8 feels like it's all about that. It's not your 'human gumption' that overcomes these supernatural threats, it's that your contemporary means (ramped up to 11) were enough to deal with the situation. Except for that poison dagger, that just felt a little too convenient if you ask me.

So I guess I need to review this based on the conclusion of its merit as an RE game, and as a horror fps shooter.

As a horror shooter, it doesn't keep as organically tense as 7, I feel. Duke's Emporium game-ifies your resource management enough that any time I felt worried was back at the start, when I had little to trade, and the second major section where it was all scares and no combat. After that, tougher enemies are less frightening as more annoying, or a 'problem' for you to either navigate around or deal with directly. They become combat challenges instead, which makes Ethan's poor gun handling stand out more as a sore point then.

As an RE game? Yeah, RE7 didn't feel like much of an RE game mechanically, and RE8 completely addressed that through all of its improvements. Upgrading guns, unlocking unlimited ammo, simple crafting. Really, it felt as though RE4 had been given the horror treatment and toned down the campiness. Is it bad? Better? It's different, that's what it is.

Is this a good game you should play? That's going to depend what you want out of it, and hopefully the above review helps a little with that.

[i]What do you expect from a survival-horror shooter game? [/i] Village manages to do everything in a certain style and quality. Great thrilling moments, lots of action with a wide variety of monsters and many different locations to explore in just 7-8 hours of playtime. But most importantly, this game connects the dots of the series' story and makes a fine conclusion to Biohazard.

[h3] Best One in the Franchise [/h3] 
Village may not be the one with strongest atmosphere, but it certainly has the best action mechanics and the scariest, PT style horror section. While Biohazard achieves the right dose of thriller, can't maintain it for the rest of the game. But pacing is never the problem with Village. It makes you feel like prey, then hunter, then prey, then hunter... Until a certain point in game where the story began to reveal and it's all you care.

[h3] Apart from RE, what makes RE: Village one of the best in Survival-horror genre?[/h3] 
This game never bore me, and I think it's very hard for someone who's into this genre to get bored. Simply because, Village never lets you stay too long in the same place, you'll constantly experience new places, enemies, bosses and plots for the story. There are [spoiler]4 lords[/spoiler] before the main enemy in this game, which you see very early, and they have totally different and appropriate places for their personalities. Basically, you'll meet someone new, begin to understand your enemy and its territory while investigating the main plot, along with nicely designed action sequences. And when you finish that part, totally different experience awaits. Sometimes it will be scary, sometimes disgusting, sometimes thrilling, sometimes fun and intriguing, but it will never be the same.

[h3] What About Cons? [/h3] 
This game doesn't have any major flaws as I see it. It doesn't have constant horror scenes and you probably won't run out of ammo in standard difficulty, but these are personal preferences. I agree that this game could be longer, at least 10-12 hours would really be great. But Village already does a great job and offers variety in weapons, places, bosses, enemies and concludes story in a nice way. There are no meaningless time-spending sections nor rushed plots, so the length is just how it should be.

A first person survival horror game that puts you in Ethan Winters' shoes once again, now more battle hardened than before and better equipped to take down all the evil residents. This time around you have a more open map (or maybe just larger than usual) set in a rural European village with much to admire in terms of scenery, and as these things go you get to explore an absolutely gorgeous gothic castle as well. The design of it all is just superb and the level of graphical fidelity also plays a big part in bringing it out and the atmosphere is often excellent as well.

In terms of gameplay, you have exploration, inventory puzzles and combat. The puzzles are as you would expect and engaging if that is your sort of thing. The combat is a usually tense affair that will need you to both act quickly and aim carefully to take down enemies without letting your limited resources run dry. The sound design and the way enemies react to being shot in different body parts does a lot to make the gunplay feel satisfying. You also have an upgrade system for weapons based on getting money from enemies or optional puzzles, sort of like Resident Evil 4. This game's flavour of zombies make for intimidating adversaries, and when it comes to some of the major antagonists they are stylish, terrifying and highly entertaining villians. As far as the story goes it is pretty standard for the series but still engaging and a good reason to partake in all the sci-fi survival horror shenanigans the series is known for.

Overall I can strongly recommend it to fans of first person shooters and survival horror games.

[h1]Village Is A Masterpiece of Survival Horror[/h1]

[i]Experience survival horror like never before in the 8th major installment in the Resident Evil franchise - Resident Evil Village. With detailed graphics, intense first-person action and masterful storytelling, the terror has never felt more realistic.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Taking place a few years after Resident Evil 7, Ethan and Mia Winters try to live a quiet life with their infant daughter, Rose, under the protection of Chris Redfield. One night, Chris unexpectedly storms their home, kills Mia, and takes Ethan and Rose into custody. Their transport is attacked, and Ethan wakes up in the woods near a mysterious, decaying European village overrun by werewolf-like Lycans. He then starts his search for Rose and the truth.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil Village is a first-person survival horror game. Later, a third-person perspective was added, giving you a choice which perspective you prefer.

The inventory system works much like Resident Evil 4’s briefcase layout, letting you move, rotate, and arrange items to maximize space. There’s no item box, so smart organization is key. However, key items, crafting materials and collected treasures have their own inventory.

Resident Evil Village offers a wide range of weapons to suit different playstyles. Handguns handle general combat, shotguns deliver powerful close-range blasts, sniper rifles provide long-range precision, and magnums deal massive damage to tougher foes. You also get pipe bombs, mines, and a grenade launcher for groups or large threats.

Weapons can be upgraded and fitted with attachments to improve power, accuracy, and other stats, giving you a steady sense of progression as you take on the village’s many dangers.

You can buy weapons, upgrades, supplies, and crafting materials from The Duke, a mysterious merchant who appears throughout the world. He also cooks meals using animals you hunt, granting permanent stat boosts like reduced damage or faster movement.

Exploration is heavily rewarded with treasures and collectibles scattered across the village. These valuables can be sold to the Duke for Lei, creating a satisfying loop of exploring, looting, and upgrading your gear.

[b][u]Mercenaries[/u][/b]
The classic arcade-style Mercenaries Mode returns in Village, offering fast-paced, timed stages where you chain kills to build combos and earn high scores. Between rounds, you can visit The Duke’s Emporium to buy weapons, upgrades, and supplies, creating a fun loop of optimization and intense combat.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The game’s main enemies, the werewolf-like Lycans, are fast, smart, and often attack in packs. They can wield weapons and overwhelm you quickly, forcing careful decisions about when to shoot, fight up close, or simply run. Enemies can drop crafting materials, treasures or Lei when killed, and bosses drop very valuable treasures that can be sold.

The village is ruled by four mutant lords, each controlling their own territory. Lady Dimitrescu, a towering vampire aristocrat, lives in Castle Dimitrescu with her three daughters. Donna Beneviento commands House Beneviento through her eerie puppet Angie, using hallucinations to torment intruders. Salvatore Moreau, a grotesque “merman,” lurks near the reservoir. Karl Heisenberg manipulates electromagnetic fields and leads an army of mechanical Soldat soldiers from his factory.

All four answer to Mother Miranda—the village’s witch-like ruler and the supreme figure the villagers worship. These five serve as the main bosses, though mini-bosses appear throughout the game as well.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The game world might seem straightforward at first, but it’s cleverly built so that different areas connect back to each other in surprising ways. This looping design keeps exploration interesting and makes the world feel more real. The village consists of a majestic castle, Lycan strongholds, a factory, and more.

Exploring the environment is made easier by an excellent map system. Rooms that still have items to find show up in red, and once you’ve collected everything, they turn blue to show they’re cleared. If your inventory is full, any items you couldn’t pick up are automatically marked on the map so you can come back later. Doors are clearly labeled too—red for locked, blue for unlocked, and special key symbols show what key you’ll need. It’s an incredibly smart system that helps you keep track of what’s left to do and where to go next. Simply put, the map is one of the game’s best features.

House Beneviento is for sure the game’s most scary and intense section. The atmosphere and the paranormal encounters inside that place is a masterclass in horror and tension. It starts slow, with flickering lights and a creepy radio, before it escalates and the whole house goes dark. It holds both jump scares and running and hiding mechanics from a giant baby creature that really freaked me out, while trying to solve the puzzles to escape.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
One of the standouts from this game is House Beneviento. It’s full of creepy dolls, an eerie voice talking through a radio, a basement including a dark well, and a giant baby creature that is one of the most disturbing enemies I’ve ever seen in a horror game. The slightly distorted screaming baby sounds it makes really made my skin crawl. Imagine a severely deformed, fleshy, bloody, drooling baby, which is at least twice the size of two grown people with an enormous head, crawling and chasing you through the hallways of the house, leaving behind a giant trail of blood. Truly terrifying and unforgettable.

The Lycans are designed to look both wild and unsettlingly human. They mix classic werewolf features with hints of the villagers they used to be. Their matted hair, long jaws, sharp teeth, and clawed hands make them look brutal and animal-like, but details such as torn clothes, human-shaped bodies, and expressive eyes remind you they were once ordinary people. Their rough appearance—muddy skin, blood-stained mouths, and patchy fur—fits perfectly with the game’s harsh rural setting. Lycans communicate with a mix of snarls, growls, and howls, mixed with faint, twisted hints of human voices.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
Nothing worth mentioning.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil Village delivers an outstanding mix of atmosphere, horror, and action, making it one of the most memorable games in the series. Its environments are detailed, varied, and incredibly immersive, featuring some of the best horror moments the franchise has ever pulled off. The visuals and sound design work together beautifully, building tension, fear, and awe throughout the entire experience.

The story and characters are some of the strongest in modern Resident Evil, with each major location offering its own style, personality, and surprising twists. Combat feels powerful and satisfying, backed by a wide range of enemies and well-crafted boss fights that keep the game exciting from beginning to end.

[h2]Rating: 10/10[/h2]

In the case of the Resident Evil series, they tend to have a great story timeline with plenty of combat stirred in. With RE Village, the story is a tad lackluster but the combat and other game play aspects make up for the story deficiencies. There are multiple bosses and multiple "mini bosses" throughout the game. Overall, this game feels like any other Resident Evil game and I would definately recommend this game to others.           8/10

Van Helsing meets Resident Evil.

This is the story of, inarguably, the best father in gaming.

Ethan Winters is back with a bang, his character freshly adorned with an actual personality this time, in quest of his daughter’s much needed rescue. He’s no longer the blank canvas he used to be back in Louisiana- our papa has grown to show his resilience and fiery tendencies with confidence alongside the painful one-liners. 

I’ve come to love the moldy man’s grit.

 I couldn’t have possibly thought of a better ending for him. Imperishable as we’ve known him, we all knew this moment was coming. Touching, poignant and sure to make you drop a tear.

I love Mia and always have since my first time playing RE7 in 2020, witnessing her tough and pragmatic side in the tapes.
I've legitimately seen people defend Wesker's actions more than Mia's, which is a comedic  indicator that some people cannot fathom the idea of a female character being morally grey. 

In any case, Mia pulling through to see the day her family is safe once again is something I can admire and especially so from an individual who's made considerable mistakes. Who are we to blame her for trying to fix her mistakes and to seek normality?

Gameplay wise, re-incorporating aspects of the revolutionary and beloved survival horror game Resident Evil 4 (2005), Village is a bejewelled (wink) love letter to the iconic entry. It offers us similar mechanics and references I naturally appreciate as a die-hard fan. I mean, a teleporting merchant? Del Lago rip-off? Attaché case? Treasures? The list goes on.

Chris Redfield, having suffered a regrettably botched plastic surgery in RE7, has returned looking more like himself this time. Character wise, I inquire the direction they went in with him, or rather what he now stands for. Redfield has always been as caring and protective as a man can get ; unstoppable in his tracks if it means saving lives. The twist that makes him such a tragic character? He's an angel, one of prowess and safeguard, certainly ; but nonetheless, one that is the catalyst for a plethora of death. 
It seems that the events of RE6 have been our hero's turning point and final straw, forcing him to set aside the one beautiful thing that has led to the perishing of many that mattered to him- his heart. Chris is attempting to shield Ethan the best way he can, and that is by taking a step back and operating in the shadows. A cruel decision, but a necessary evil in his eyes.

In a much less sophisticated tongue, Chris is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hot in this entry.

Being plunged into this snow-ridden Romanian village has been nothing short of terrifying, but a delight nonetheless ; the imagery is splendid. From the vampiric Dimitrescu castle to Heisenberg’s oppressive factory, the design team have given it their all to amaze us.
Speaking of design, as an artist, I’m feeding off of the character designs. Lady D, Miranda, the lycans...list goes on. My favorite was Heisenberg’s, as Van Helsing is a guilty-pleasure kind of movie for me and I’m ready to go as far as saying that Karl has one of the coolest antagonist designs in RE. As someone who loves virtual photography, I’m so going to have a field day with this gem. I love exploring every nook and cranny of this gorgeous universe. 

My favorite part about any video game has always been the soundtrack. Resident Evil, since 1996, is known for the haunting yet calming effect its soundtracks have always possessed. Village’s, well, was rather unmemorable to me. I love ambient music, but this one leans on the “too imperceptible” and generic side in my humble opinion.


The beauty of the Resident Evil franchise is the absolute diversity of every single entry. Capcom always tries new things, and I respect that. 

Village combines action and minimal horror to create what seems to be a combination of the fourth and seventh entry. I've seen people complain, seen people praise it. What do I think?

It's a solid game. It has artistic merit. It tried something new.

...It has Chris Redfield.

There’s lots of goods in this game idk from where to begin, the pacing and gameplay are also beautiful. I love the lvl design and how well installed it to the theme this game is taking compared to 7 especially in the first 2 areas. Castle Demitrescu is such a classic with its re vibe area that reminds me alot of the training facility, but ALOT better. House benviento is also incredible and shows how unhinged village could’ve been if capcom wanted to make this game scary.  

The First and Second acts shows how capcom can perfectly pace horror and action in one game, the first one being horror and the 2nd being horror and their both nearly as good as one another, I would say Moreau section is just a lil off vibe for me but it’s still decent, the Lycans hideout Carrie’s the 2nd act for me and it’s such an awesome action section. 

Not to mention The 3rd act, Heisenbergs factory feels like we went back to the classic RE style with the fun of backtracking and puzzle searching, same with Castle Demi but in a very different vibe, and despite what everyone says I think this is one of the best locations in the series, the enemy variety is great and the puzzles are good, the backtracking is fun and the lvl design is very complex and unique, the bosses takes it down a notch tho because the spinning fan dude is hitting and Heisenberg was a massive disappointment, idk why such a great section had very mediocre bosses, not to say they were bad but they were not as good as they should’ve especially for the 3rd act.

the reason why I think the game doesn’t fall off because of Chris is simple, the showdown against Miranda will forever stay as the best finale in any re game for me, it gave me sigrun vibes and in a good way.
