Resident Evil Village is the 8th entry in the survival-horror series Resident Evil. After the 6th game, which received backlash for not following the series’ survival-horror roots, Capcom decided to make a game with a smaller scope, and one that was more horror focused. That game was Resident Evil 7. It was widely praised, and Capcom had the unenviable task of following it up. Resident Evil Village was their followup.
I 100% recommend playing Resident Evil 7 before Village. While there is a recap of the story of 7 in Village, you should play it yourself to know the story. It is an incredible game. But this review is about Village, not 7. Is it as good as 7? Is it better perhaps? I guess you’ll have to read this long ass essay.
Now, if you don’t like reading (like 80% of everyone I’ve met), you can skip to the last paragraph. If you do like reading, here’s my review.

Story
Village takes place a couple of years after 7. You still play as Ethan Winters. Mia, Ethan’s wife, is reading a book to Rose, their newborn daughter. It is a local book, as they’ve moved somewhere in Europe. It creeps Ethan out, but evidently not Rose, as she is put to sleep. Just after Ethan puts Rose to sleep, Mia is shot and killed by… Chris Redfield? Without explaining, they capture Rose and a bewildered Ethan. 
Ethan wakes up outside a crashed Umbrella van, in a snowy forest in the middle of nowhere. He ventures to a village where all of the residents are evil. There are some who are not, but they’re extremely paranoid. He soon finds out that an epidemic has come over this village, where the people turn into beasts called Lycans. They worship a being known as Mother Miranda as some sort of way to keep them sane. Ultimately, everything goes to ♥♥♥♥ and Ethan is captured once more, this time by the Lycans. He is then brought in front of Mother Miranda, where four of, seemingly, her children argue on how to kill him. Ethan is chased by Lycans throughout a dungeon after this argument, and he ends up in one of the children’s (Lady Dimitrescu, who you’ve probably already heard of before) castle. Your goal (for now) is to escape Castle Dimitrescu and find Rose.
This story has a lot more moving parts than the last story. It’s much more complicated. It also has way more cutscenes than the last game did. It also characterizes Ethan more, where in the last game, he was pretty much just a silent protagonist who would echo your thoughts occasionally, in this game, a crazy development occurred and he actually has a personality. 

Gameplay
Resident Evil has always been a survival-horror series. Village is no different. You explore the areas, sliming opps, solving puzzles, and being scared, now in the 1st person, just like the last game. Village leans a tad more into the action side of the series than 7 did; it’s not full-blown RE4 levels, but it’s more than 7. The general pace of the game is faster, and I think this is actually worse for the horror experience. You can get away quicker, and the gunplay feels less good as a result. Also, the physics are dumbed down. You can’t shoot off individual body parts like you could in 7. There are also no storage boxes, which I find odd. My last complaint is that cutscenes are often intrusive, like some of them take forever. I get it’s a horror game and it’s about atmosphere, but sometimes I just want to play the game, you know?
That seemed negative, but Village gets a lot of things right. For starters, there is a shop system. In 7, there were some cages you could open. Here, a fat man named the Duke sells you things, such as resources, upgrades, and foods, and he can buy various treasures you can collect from enemies. I know this system existed in prior games, but this is my first experience with it, and it’s a welcome addition. Also, the greater focus on action leads to some pretty sick setpieces, one of which you’ll see at the very start of the game. Probably the game’s biggest strength is its exploration. In 7, it would gate certain areas off from you. In Village, while it occasionally does that, you will always be able to return to the areas later. There are a lot more secrets and hidden areas in this one, which is just flat-out cool. They also reworked the inventory system slightly so that key items don’t take up space in your normal inventory. You also have to slide resources around in order to make space. Some people don’t like this, but I think it’s pretty alright.

I’m not sure if I could call either game’s general gameplay loop better than the other. They are separate experiences meant to cater to different parts of their audiences. What I will say, at the very least, is that the gameplay loops are similar enough so that if you liked 7’s, you will like Village’s.

Presentation
Village is set in a rural, mountainous area somewhere in Europe, speculated to be Romania, but there’s no way of knowing. Village is beautiful. This is what they’re talking about when they say a “9th-gen game”. All around it’s very pretty. It’s also good at establishing an atmosphere, a lot like its predecessor. It’s odd, because the settings are polar opposites, but its atmosphere feels similar. I hear that Village tries to be 4, which takes place in a similar setting and has a similar atmosphere, so good on you, Capcom.
I wanted to mention this somewhere, but I didn’t know where, so here it is. In the last game, they never actually showed Ethan’s face, which sort of became a joke in the community, and in this game, they double down on it. There are a handful of renders of him, but his face is always covered or shadowed. I thought that was really funny. This series certainly is good at inside jokes.
The sound effects are good, but not as good as the previous game. In 7 they just seemed to stand out more. Here, they’re very solid though, and add to the ambience. There’s very little music, and when there is music, it fits. As for the voice acting, besides for one character, I would say it’s very, VERY good. 
There’s even a photo mode so you can take cool screenshots of this game and make them like your wallpaper or something.

Content
According to Howlongtobeat.com, RE Village is roughly 10 hours long, which is a good length. There is much more to explore in this one than in 7 though. The new focus on exploration leads to it being much easier and much more fun to dig through and 100%. There are a lot more optional treasures and secrets in the village. It actually does a really good job at keeping those hours distinct, too. Another thing this game (and this series) does well is the pacing. In a 10 hour game, it isn’t too hard to have good pacing, but this one keeps you hooked throughout the whole thing. I was always curious to see what would come next.
In the way of story DLC, there’s only 1, being the Winters’ expansion. It’s about 3 hours long. I have not played it, and chances are I won’t, because it costs too much to justify its runtime for me. I hear it reuses lots of areas as well, and the only big difference is it being in a 3rd person camera angle.
There are also some side modes, the most well known being Mercenaries. Village’s version of Mercenaries is less replayable than previous iterations of it, but it essentially tasks you with defeating all of the enemies in an area as efficiently as possible. You can play as either Ethan or Chris in the base game, and get more characters with DLC.
There are a handful of other DLCs, but I frankly don’t care about them enough to cover them. They aren’t story expansions, so I don’t care. 
This game has a lot of DLC. But it has a lot of base-game content, as well.

Positives:
-Incredible atmosphere and setting
-Fun exploration
-Intriguing story that characterizes Ethan well

Negatives:
-Faster gameplay and worse gunplay
-Long and sometimes obtrusive cutscenes

What a game! This is the perfect title to get your blood rushing, and it also has an engaging story that, no matter how scared you are, will make you come back to it.

This Resident Evil game is a direct sequel to RE7, so even though you get a little refresher at the beginning, it’s best to have played the previous game for a more immersive experience.

Ethan, Mia, and their newborn baby are now living in Romania, and as a Romanian, I loved the little nods to our culture scattered throughout the game; from the design of the houses and the names of foods to the famous Castle Dimitrescu, which seems like a mix of several iconic Romanian castles.

The action kicks off when Mia is shot, and Chris Redfield and his team show up to take Rose and Ethan away. On the way, the vehicle transporting them crashes, killing everyone except Ethan. Now it’s his duty to find Rose, save her, and get the hell out.

The game is filled with mystical creatures, from lycans to vampires, ghouls, and all kinds of horrifying mutations. The roster of villains is amazing. Lady Dimitrescu will send shivers down your spine, and after you manage to deal with her, the rest of the family feels like a breeze. It might be because you spend so much time in her castle, and the developers likely shortened the others’ stories in her favour, which I honestly don’t mind. The second scariest villain, after her, is the puppet. Puppets are already creepy, but that chapter of the game will give you nightmares.

The art is stunning, from the intricate details in the houses to the fluid character animations and breathtaking landscapes, it all feels like a true labour of love. The soundtrack and voice acting are equally spectacular.

If I compare my experience with RE7, I enjoyed Village more. It felt more forgiving than the previous game, and as someone more invested in story than survival horror mechanics, it was satisfying knowing I had a higher chance of making it through.

Is Resident Evil Village a perfect game? I don’t know. But it’s definitely up there among the best I’ve ever played. Give it a go, it’s an awesome experience.

This is RE 4 played from the perspective of Survivor/Dead Aim, with a tone that settles closer to C:V. Goofy but takes itself serious. So generally not scary in tone like 7 could be at times. 8 is more focused on putting you into a state of excitement or panic if anything. That said, 8 does do a decent job of pacing, giving some downtime to build tension at parts before dropping the hammer.

Main downside is that the game is half the length of RE4 and has little of the charm that RE4 had. Though I will give it credit for being one of the least verbose RE titles in memory, over half of the script is probably some variant of "Where is Rose?".

The weapon system doesn't become as interesting as RE4, partially since the enemy combat design doesn't go anywhere too interesting from a NG story perspective. You'll go from bullet sponge to bullet sponge with some armor on it all with a weakness to being shot in the face repeatedly. RE4 OG had enemies carrying shields. One section required a thermal scope to shoot "tumors" hidden in the enemies. Ganados also had their heads pop when it was dark, making head shots become a downside in a NG without a flash grenade available.

The most interesting thing, for me, is that the game actually ended up feeling like I was playing a FPS version of SH1 visually when I was fighting the final boss. There's actually a decent amount of parallels between the story of SH1 and RE8. Which is neat?

Also the RE4 village attack intro this is not. It is the most scuffed part about the entire playthrough, at least on a NG hardcore blind play, probably the hardest part of the run. In RE4 the timer would decrease by killing Ganados or running out of time. RE4 also gave you more room to run about, covering 6 or so buildings. RE8's village attack has you run, shooting enemies does not reduce the timer, between two buildings and a river until you randomly appease the game in order to progress the game. Don't try to trick the game either because the timer also stops when doing things like sitting on the ladder, however there's speedrun gimmick strats apparently. All of it combined makes for a pretty deflating opener by the time you complete it, teaching you how to fight an enemy type that will immediately disappear for the next 3-4 hours. Also don't worry, you'll be armed to the teeth by the time they come back as well, so it didn't matter if you learned anything at all!

That said when on sale, you could do way worse than this, especially as a fan of the series. Better than 5, but not as good as 7 personally. But one could say 7 is to 1 as 8 is to 4.

There's so many features I like in Resident Evil Village, particularly its setting, combat, and visuals, but my enjoyment of it is crippled by its flaws.

The story and dialog are astoundingly bad and make no sense.  It wouldn't be such a problem if the story was in the background such as with RE 1, but Village keeps putting weight on its narrative foot.  And the writing is not laughably bad, it's just an annoying bad.

I haven't played the previous few RE games so I don't know if this is already a trend, but I am disengaged by the way Village relies on extreme fake stakes and fake harm.

Cut scenes will have monsters do shockingly brutal things to the player, then the player walks away with "merely a flesh wound".  After the third or forth fatal injury the shock has been lost.

And if being effectively immortal isn't enough, so many times the protagonist should have failed his mission but is spared because the villains have contrived idiocy.

Ethan has enough plot armor to swallow a nuke.

Having auto-regeneration in a Survival Horror game takes both the survival and the horror out of the gameplay.  There's no better way to remove tension then by allowing players to tank damage with no repercussions.

While RE games tend to be fairly linear, the ones I've played did a good job of hiding it and making the player feel in control.  Village feels like a bait-and-switch, where its layout appears non-linear but is gated to be linear.  Part of the problem is with Village's "theme-park" layout with separate lands, it's like a Mega Man game without being able to choose which level to play next.

I'm not a big fan of boss battles so I am biased, but for me Village's boss battles are an annoying tangent.

It goes without saying that Resident Evil Village is a damned behemoth in the genre. It is a direct continuation of the story that Resident Evil 7 established. Whereas Resident Evil 7 went for a slaughterhouse horror vibe (think The Hills Have Eyes and Texas Chainsaw Massacre), Resident Evil Village goes for a "classic Hollywood horror" kind of atmosphere. Vampires, Frankenstein, Werewolves.

On top of that, it blends the gameplay styles of RE7 and RE4. Incredibly intense, claustrophobic first person scarefest crossed with campy and fun action horror. Then add just a touch of Silent Hill 2. Freaking brilliant combo. This was a very bold new direction for the series at the time, and is legitimately the coolest set up for Resident Evil game since RE1 nearly 30 years ago.

The idea behind the game is brilliant, but what of the execution? Well, where to start? 

Well, what about the graphics. The art direction. The environments have always been such a major highlight in REV for me. Mild spoilers here, but you have snowbound destitute Romanian villages that are acutely splattered in blood, slime covered fishing docks that exist to disgust you with every step, underground facilities that house untold mechanical nightmares that were hidden away from the light of the world, and then you have an gigantic gothic castle sitting at the apex of this twisted world. Amidst the mountains. Observing the horrors underneath. The environments of REV are very good. They are inspired and varied, rendered to perfection. They all have this extremely distant, unbearably cold, terrifyingly chilling and slightly supernatural feeling that I've come to really appreciate as the years go by. I can physically feel my body grow a little colder as I walk around the village. A nightmare covered in a murderous winter's snow. What should be a healthy relationship between father, mother and daughter turned into a frozen hellscape that only exists to torment and hinder every effort to make things right. I haven't really seen anything else in gaming like it. Not to this extent at least. This game looks incredible, it is impossible to not take it all in and immerse yourself in the terrors that await you. Ethan Winter's hands have never looked better, especially when they aren't constantly being mutilated and severed, of course.

Speaking of Ethan, the story here is actually good. It is extremely campy and fun, which is all a story for a Resident Evil game needs to be. The characters are great. You'll feel empathetic towards Ethan and his struggle to get his daughter back. Heisenberg is a mysterious and highly charismatic hobo magneto with some crazy voice acting to boot. Moreau is disgusting. Chris is a boulder punching badass. The Duke is a seriously lovable fat guy. Lady Dimitrescu grabs your attention in literally every single scene she's in, and yes, this is partially (mostly) because she's a really iconic hot 10 foot tall vampire wearing a low cut dress that takes pleasure in violently dommy mommying the ♥♥♥♥ out of Ethan via slamming him relentlessly into the ground, slicing his 4k rendered hands apart with wolverine style nails, and rizzing him up with gratuitious cleavage shots while threatening to feed his filthy man-thing hands to her vampire daughters. I guarantee you that Lady D's bust canonically weighs more than Ethan himself. She is HUGE. Seriously, the dev team clearly loves Lady D. You can see it in every camera angle. You can see it how Lady D is still SOMEHOW in Resident Evil's marketing even 4 years after Village's launch. And guess what is one of the preorder bonuses for RE Requem? Of course. Lady D costume for the new lead protagonist Grace Ashcroft. Thank you, Capcom. I'm sure Maggie Robertson is absolutely loving the attention now. (Justifiably so, Lady D's voice acting is incredible.) Ok, I've gotten off topic. Enough about Lady DD. Music.

The music is actually really good. Feels cold. Distant. Occasionally really blood pumping. It really gives you a yearning for dark shadows. (GET IT? BECAUSE ONE OF THE SONGS IS CALLED YEARNING FOR DARK SHADOWS HAHA-)

The fact of the matter is that the game looks, sounds and feels good in the moment. You won't have a bad time with the game from start to finish. In the moment. But then you will eventually have the moment you look back on the wild rollercoaster ride, and then you realize that there's a few screws loose on the ride upon closer inspection. And then you don't really look at that same rollercoaster ride you loved the same way again. There are definitely flaws.

As good as the gameplay blend of RE4 and RE7 may sound, it's not as good as it sounds. RE7's gameplay was strong because it's incredibly scary and claustrophobic despite how basic it is. RE4's gameplay was strong because it was mechanically really fun and goofy and gave you many "non-linear" ways to fight enemies in your own unique way. So these 2 approaches are at odds with each other. Village's gameplay is simultaneously not scary enough and not mechanically in depth enough, so it kind of comes off as way too easy and basic. Mechanically, it's the exact same as RE7 but without the scare factor that made RE7 great. (that isn't to say that REV isn't totally bloodcurdling at times, it very much can be) REV also has RE4's weapon upgrade system without understanding why RE4's upgrade system worked so well. How? Well, every weapon in RE4 was viable throughout the whole game while the weapons in REV are more of a direct upgrade to your previous weapon. In REV, whenever you find a new weapon, you are pretty much expected to ditch your old weapon because it will never be as powerful as the new weapon even when fully upgraded. So you don't get that sense of "personal playstyle" in Village in comparison to RE4, which damages replayability.

Another way replayability is heavily damaged is how the areas in Village are set up. They are mostly linear. It's kind of like an amusement park. The only area that is (kinda) nonlinear is the village but that is mostly used as a hub area for you to traverse in order to get to the next very linear area. Go through linear area, wander around village, go through next linear area, wander around village some more, go through next linear area. Playthroughs will always remain the same. And there are more than a few areas in the game that feel EXCELLENT during the first playthrough but feel like a slog in the next. You try going through House Beneviento on the 2nd playthrough. Gets tedious very quickly.

Also, Village's mercenaries mode is lame as hell. Ethan handles way too clunky for an agility based gamemode like this and it feels like major trial and error spawn enemy spawn memorization ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when you are attempting to S rank levels. This is the worst mercenaries mode in the series.

.....And that's the gist of what RE Village gets right and wrong. There's a lot more flaws to talk about (like just how many plotholes there are but I'll let you see that for yourself) but then again I've rambled for long enough. Hopefully all of that gives you an idea of what to expect. The game is very much worth playing. Feels great, sounds great, looks great. In the moment at least.

Resident Evil Village is a first-person survival horror game that continues the story of Ethan Winters. The plot centers on the search for his kidnapped daughter in a remote European village. The narrative mixes gothic themes with modern bioweapon lore, creating a structured progression through distinct regions.

Exploration balances linear paths with optional rooms. Players collect keys, solve simple puzzles, and unlock shortcuts. Resource scarcity shapes decision-making. Ammunition and healing items are limited, pushing cautious aim and route planning.

Combat emphasizes weapon upgrades and enemy crowd control. Ethan can block attacks to reduce damage. Enemy types vary in speed and pressure. Boss encounters are scripted set pieces with clear weak points. Progression through the merchant system improves firepower and inventory.

Atmosphere relies on lighting, sound design, and environmental detail. The village hub changes over time as threats increase. Audio cues warn of danger. Level themes range from classic horror to action-focused segments, maintaining pacing variety.

Character upgrades use currency gained from exploration and combat. Inventory management returns as grid-based organization. Crafting supplements supplies but cannot replace poor aim. Weapon attachments alter recoil, reload, and spread.

Story delivery uses cutscenes and collectible files. Dialogue remains concise. Familiar franchise characters appear briefly. Plot twists escalate toward a high-intensity finale. Emotional tone is present, but delivery remains functional for pacing.

Resident Evil Village targets players who want hybrid horror and action. It may feel less tense than earlier entries but offers strong atmosphere and progression. Replay value comes from higher difficulties, new game+ upgrades, and extra challenges.

RE8 is the last stop in the chronological story in Resident Evil saga so far and caps off my month of re-playing the modern RE games.  This was my second playthrough and I found this to be an incredibly strong RE game but a weak sequel to RE7 that actually, in my opinion, undermines a lot of the gut punch in the Louisiana narrative.  RE8 has a stellar stage set in yet another undisclosed village in Europe.  The comparisons to RE4 are inevitable and RE8 is overall a fantastic package that addresses almost every complaint I have with RE7.

(+)  RE8 is arguably the best designed game in the series.  I found the entire game lovingly constructed with some areas being the most well-realised and executed you can find in the horror genre.  The castle of Lady Dimitrescu with its rotten dungeons and the waterfall Beneviento manor with it's accompanying graveyard are the stand-outs for me.  I was swallowed in the exploration side of RE8 and engrossed in the gameplay as it only gently guides you through giving you the agency of being stuck with Ethan and having to map out your plan and adapt when it all inevitably goes wrong.  The fidelity of display is a real punch up from RE7 and the character design is stunning, Mia has thankfully lost her spaghetti hair!  The creatures that overwhelmed the village and that spill out of the dungeons are incredible and the variety of enemy design has seen the most love and care.  The gameplay is a lot more responsive and even though we've tipped into action there's still a lot of surprises, twists and turns waiting for you.  Creatures can literally rise from their graves, fall out of trees and smash through walls and it always kept my eyes on the spectacular world design which was a nice way of keeping you in Ethan's shoes.  There's a lot lifted from RE4 but I personally think this is what RE should be shooting for when going for an action game so I loved how exploration led to upgrading weapons, how killing enemies fuelled the gameplay loop and how you've always got control in the action, you're rarely in cutscenes for anything other than story.  The gameplay is a lot more energetic and I was never sure headshots were the way to go, the Lycan's literally gyrate like they're in the Thriller music video and they pushed pressure onto me which always kept me on the backfoot.  The sound design has also seen some bulking and it's some of the best in the series.  Wind can whip around buildings and through the castle, snow is constantly crunching underfoot and footsteps echo off stone floors.

(-)  I don't have much to gripe about other than the game pulling the emotional rug out from under RE7 and, at least in my opinion, completely muddying the fresh take on RE by sloppily tipping the old lore into the story and undoing a lot of the delicate emotional crafting done in RE7.  The twist with Ethan left me salty when I first played the game four years ago and I haven't replayed RE8 until now.  I still hate the twist and think it really takes away from the Winter's story as well as partially ruining my favourite moment in the entire series with Ethan emotionally connecting with Jack in RE7.  I've mellowed out on it now but I really think they should have hesitated in tying this to the old games, especially as RE7 was the breath of fresh air that saved the series.  The game also cheekily locks areas off behind you and is obviously baiting a new game plus playthrough which was infuriating to my beaver-ish OCD as I like to collect everything in each area before moving on and I didn't finish upgrading anything despite ticking all but a few areas off being fully searched.

Overall, I was with the game through giant Vampires, through werewolves, through giant fish and through talking dolls but it lost me right at the narrative's crescendo.  The gameplay is engaging and the atmosphere is electrifying so I would absolutely recommend this game.  I was finished in 11 hours but that was me completing the game as thoroughly as I could with a lot of backtracking.  I had zero technical problems with it and is yet another example of the fantastic RE Engine.  It worked perfectly with my X1X controller I would recommend this game to all horror fans.

Resident Evil Village is the second title in the Ethan Winters Resident Evil saga. Ethan, his wife, and his kid are trying to recover from the incident in Louisiana back in RE7 by living out in the European countryside,  when their quiet life is loudly disrupted. His wife shot, his kid taken, Ethan must find a way to reunite his family and finally put the past fully behind him.

Resident Evil Village was a very fun continuation of Resident Evil 7's story. Almost all the characters in this story felt very lively and captivated my attention whenever they were on screen. The story sees you traverse primarily through a village, where there are some evil residents lurking about. Outside of the village though, you'll be taken through a gothic manor, a house filled with dolls, a rusting broken-down factory, and more. The settings felt great to walk through, from a visual standpoint there was enough standing out between each that I was consistently treated with something new, but they were never so distinct that I felt like the atmosphere was disjointed. The gameplay is a tad more action-oriented compared to RE7, with a bit higher ammo availability and less horror-focused boss fights compared to the first game, which isn't inherently bad it's just different.  The inventory system is also more in line with Resident Evil 4's, where Ethan carries around a large briefcase to manage all his items. I very rarely had too much issue with managing the space in the inventory, if you're consistent about buying the increased space you'll usually have enough for everything. The puzzles in this game are pretty good, though arguably a tad easy, as normally I have to look up one or two guides during Resident Evil playthroughs for the harder puzzles but this one I don't think I did that once.

I liked Village overall, but there's two things that I wasn't the biggest fan of. For one, I didn't feel like Ethan had any major character development over the course of the game. He starts the game thinking "I will kill anybody who hurts my family" and ends the game thinking "I will kill anybody who hurts my family". Over the course of the game, he of course kills people that threaten his family. There's this big climactic moment towards the end where he screams out about how he's going to protect his daughter no matter what, and it just didn't feel very impactful to me because as the player that seemed like a given. It wasn't any change from where I thought his motives lied at the beginning of the story. This negative isn't helped by the fact that Ethan's VA's line delivery tends to use the same tone for almost every line. My second negative is that the Rose Winters expansion is just kinda okay. It was an interesting premise, but it was a bit too fantastical and magical to feel distinctly "Resident Evil" to me.

Despite those two negatives, I think Resident Evil Village is an incredibly solid Resident Evil game, definitely in my top 5 of the entire mainline series. I feel like Village hits a really solid middle ground by taking a few elements from every type of Resident Evil game in the past and mixing them into one cohesive experience. Definitely recommend for any long-time Resident Evil fans and new enjoyers of the series.

[h1]TL;DR NO SPOILERS[/h1]

RE8 is a good game, but unfortunately bloated. If there's ever any point where you feel like the game is dragging, it'll get better in a while
Graphics are amazing, the story is bad (though you can skip the cutscenes), but the good portions are real good, which softens the blow of the bad parts

[h1]SPOILERS AHEAD[/h1]

I legitimately think this game would've been better with just 3 Lords, maybe even 2. The Castle is great, the Factory is great, coming back to the Village every time is great, I think the Doll House is very meh and one-note (the kind of thing that once you know what the deal is it just feels like a waste of time) but understand its appeal. I don't think the Sluice/Fish part has any merits whatsoever. It's very linear, very stupid, and not fun, in all the ways RE8 gets to be not fun when it wants to
I've mentioned the story being bad before, and I really mean it. Not just Chris refusing to engage and explain from the start, leading to needless confusion. Not just the camp (that part's actually kinda fine here and there), but Ethan's interjections being always the equivalent of "neener neener" or "what the hell is going on!?" is painfully annoying, and somehow Eveline shows up to be even worse. The structure is very obvious - so much so it's called out in-universe - but since it leads to plenty of good scenarios, I don't mind it too much. Whenever it's actually trying to not be a game is where the problem lies
Gameplay-wise this is a bit of a rollercoaster. The early parts are extremely linear, cutscene heavy, and middling. The Castle is great, though I think the 'roaming big villain' thing is just a waste of time that wants to force you to go around them but really just makes you wait in the safe room until they go away, or literally run past them because they're so slow. Coming back to the village and slowly fully exploring it is always good (though I think the map could use some work), the Doll House is fine for what it is but you can be done with it extremely fast if it's not scary for you, the Sluice part is just linear instant kill avoidance until an unexciting fight, and then the Factory is back to being as good as the Castle. Maybe it's better, even
The reason the Factory can be even better than the Castle is the combat. Being a first person horror means RE can't get too creative with its combat - RE7 is often somewhat lambasted for this, with people mentioning the lack of enemy variety making the combat boring. RE8 comes to prove that that wasn't the only issue - lycans, ghouls, flying ghouls, big lycans with hammers, a big fish, a big wolf, they're all boring to do combat with. It's somewhat on purpose - being a horror game, it's supposed to be a real choice whether you engage with an enemy or just run away. But if you do choose the combat, it's easy to cheese and just not very engaging. Until the factory, which gives you armored enemies and enemies with specific weak spots, and arenas with explosives. It takes that little to make it more interesting!
For a completionist there's a LOT in this game. I thought I was being thorough but clearly missed a lot, and I took my sweet time checking most things. That's good! It does lead to a surplus of resources but that's par for the course for this kind of gameplay, and means you can take it easier on that front and still do well
Overall I had a positive experience but still did have some 2 to 3 spots where I really had to think "the game can't be this bad the whole way forward, right?" and I'm glad the bad parts eventually go away, even if they could've just not been there to begin with

Resident Evil 9 was around the corner, and, feeling nostalgic while also wanting to keep up with the vast and somewhat understandable plot of the recent Resident Evil storyline, I decided to get the "latest" game in the installment, Resident Evil Village, or 8. I'm not a die hard Resident Evil fan, despite Resident Evil 4 REmake being one of my favorite action orientated games of all time. And I'm not a horror fan, although I enjoy games series such as Alan Wake and it's sequel, and some of the Resident Evil games. The point I'm making is, take this review with a grain of salt.

The story of the game isn't confusing, and, considering the fact that I did skip most of the previous Resident Evil games (5, 7... etc.), it was pretty ok to keep up with the events and story of the game. Really though, if you really want to know what's going on for immersion, playing 7 would probably be better before Village, and you just gotta know Chris Redfield, and what he's done before the past years of the game. The characters can feel quite... weird, sometimes? Sometimes, the dialogue is really good, and then sometimes, the dialogue some characters make is just... eh, for me. But for the most part, I really like all the characters. I like the antagonists, I like the main character, and the side characters. Chris was also pretty cool, and I can see why a lot of people like him, although, I'm more a Leon fan.

The gameplay is as expected, as per a Resident Evil game, ala a bit more... action orientated. It's not like the older new games with 2 and 3 Remake where every ammo preservation needs to be carefully taught out to see if it's worth wasting, although, of course, it's still a survival horror where ammo isn't an infinite resource. It's just, ya know, you can go a bit more ham on the occasion. A gripe I had with the game (which does get fixed with newer game in the line) is the inventory scroll wheel. You can have 4 equipments tied to your mousewheel to use. The problem is, there's more than 4 equipment. Let alone, if you're using guns, you have a pistol, a shotgun, a rifle, a grenade launcher. But you'd be conserving ammo for those higher powered weapons, and furthermore have other considerations to shortcut such as your knife, your pipe bombs, or your mines. And scrolling through your case just to take back the item kind of kills the flow between the game and you.

The horror level for this game fluctuates for me. I feel different levels of horror for the game, but it's rather mild for me. It's not bad to start, for horror, but if you're looking for a scarier game, then I wouldn't recommend Resident Evil 8, and would point you more down the line of Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Overall, the game is a great Resident Evil entry, and I still await with bated breath for the next entry. Hopefully it'll be as good, if not better.

A direct follow-up to RE7, is it better than its predecessor?
Well, it depends in your own taste.
If you liked the horror presented in RE7, then you're gonna think it's a worse game.
But, if you prefer the action-oriented titles, especially those RE4 die-hard fans, you might like this better than RE7. 
Speaking of action-oriented, they definitely upped the aspect of it with this entry, not excessively -- to their credit. The body horror that's a signature of this franchise is definitely here, I love how we're left with 8 fingers most of the game, a clever nod to the eighth title. There are also some parts where they really emphasised the horror, but obviously it's going to backfire, though not thoroughly. 

The gunplay is definitely better than RE8! I love how balanced they are, you can pretty much use the trusty LEMI up until the end as your handgun. 
Given that you know how to manage your resources and enemies, of course. 
That's the beauty of survival horror, resource management.

I will explain further down this review.

Obviously with the game titled "Village", you cannot look past the fact it is indeed a nod to RE4.
They are not even ashamed of it and I'm glad they weren't! Because it was done right.
The opening sequence with the Lycans displayed how powerless we are and not just simply outnumbered by a large margin. In contrast of RE4, even getting outnumbered simply doesn't take away the fact we could just roundhouse kick the ♥♥♥♥ out of everyone in our sight.

Next is definitely my favourite part of the game: Castle Dimitrescu.
Everything about it is beautiful, the interior exuded such beauty, the exterior towered the village -- showing the clear objective after the sequence at Luiza's house. Well to be fair, the castle was locked in our sight ever since when we first arrived there.
I loved the sequences introduced here, the amputation of our hands, the remolding of our own limbs, the structure of this level. For a bit there, we got to experience the signature Resident Evil game progression. Even though it really is not that non-linear, at least there is an aspect of backtracking in there, you will be rewarded with the azure gem for backtracking to the basement.
Arguably the best part of the game too, not just my favourite. 
It sucks that Lady D was our first Lord out of the four to be defeated, you cannot even go back there after you're done with the castle.

The second Lord is at the Beneviento House.
Simply put, this was indeed a horrifying experience, it is very well-crafted.
There is unfortunately a glaring problem: it is a hide-and-seek simulator.
When you're past your second playthrough, this part is a total slog and would be a boring 20-minute segment, especially given that it is the followup of the Dimitrescu Castle.

My least favourite part is definitely Moreau's.
Another slog after the second playthrough with the scripted walking simulator at the windmill segment and it ends almost immediately after that.
The only good thing that comes out from this segment is literally the magnum.

The stronghold part is fine.
I liked it, it felt right at that point for the game to throw every Lycan in our faces.

Last but not least, Heisenberg's -- I'd argue that this is on par with the Castle.
New enemies are introduced, you're really, really incentivised once again to aim for the weak points, with some enemies having it in the worst places possible. I love how the game throws a little curveball at you, especially with you already becoming a one-man army at that point.
It's just not my favourite because it was quite disorienting for me to get through during my first playthrough, just my personal gripe.

Miranda is an okay boss fight. 
Just incredibly bullet spongey.

Regarding the difficulty, it definitely did not hold the candle when compared to RE7's Madhouse.
Hardcore's actually easy, while Village of Shadows is clearly designed for New Game+ with infinite ammo weapons. I mean, you have the liberty to do it with your regular weapons with finite ammo, but it is unfairly difficult. It's a flaw in design. But I guess they want you to replay this game a lot, which I guess they succeeded. They did add some enemies in different places in VoS compared to the lower difficulties, but I think it really is not enough. Simply just inflating the HP of every enemies while making almost all of them able to one-hit KO you is pretty infuriating at least.

I don't know how, but they really managed to hit the strides with Madhouse, man. 

The extra content is actually a lot of fun, Shadows of Rose was surprisingly easy but can also be a slog in the second half. I'd give a pass for the asset recycle since they had a good in-game explanation for it. But man, it's glaring.

The Mercenaries are a lot of fun... I am glad that this is my first taste of this franchise's Mercenaries.
I believe that there are better ones in other entries, but giving us the opportunity to hack-and-slash with Lady D is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ peak. She made every levels, including the hard levels a joke. SSS'd all of them first-try.

100%-ing this entry was definitely easier when compared to RE7.
Though replaying the main story can be a slog at times, it's still replayable.

It is a good game, though not an essential entry of the franchise -- it remains as one that is course-correct.
Though I would still recommend playing RE7 first or at least acknowledge the events prior to this. Otherwise, the reveal at the end wouldn't be that impactful.

Resident Evil 8 is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, where we once again play as Ethan Winters on a mission to save our daughter, Rosemary Winters, who was kidnapped by the bioweapon Miranda.

The gameplay is more or less similar to its predecessor, using a first-person shooter format but with a greater focus on action and less on horror. Ethan is more tactical, having been trained by Chris, and is more emotional and responsive than before. The weapon variety is expanded, featuring multiple pistols, various shotguns, a sniper rifle, and new explosive throwables to combat enemies.

The game world is stunning and grand, set in a village with a medieval vibe mixed with an 80s aesthetic and extreme weather conditions. It feels reminiscent of Resident Evil 4, where we explore the village, fight enemies, search for easter eggs, and meet The Duke to buy and upgrade weapons.

As for the enemies, Miranda is the main villain who kidnaps our daughter, and she has four subordinates we must face one by one. 

First is Lady Dimitrescu, a tall monster with claws. Fighting her is the most fun, in my opinion, with a mix of puzzles, hide-and-seek, and the grand, luxurious design of Castle Dimitrescu. Facing her three daughters is also exciting and relatively easy, culminating in the final boss fight against Dimitrescu, who transforms into a dragon-like creature.

Second is Donna Beneviento, a doll manipulator. This section is pure horror, where we have no weapons and rely entirely on hide-and-seek. The dark atmosphere and a giant baby monster make this level genuinely terrifying. However, the Beneviento section feels very short. 

Third is Salvatore Moreau, an insecure fish-like monster, reminiscent of the fish villain from Resident Evil 4. This part feels brief and less seriously developed compared to the previous two villains.

Lastly, there’s Karl Heisenberg, who wields magnetic metal powers. This section is entirely action-oriented with no horror elements. Fighting his forces and Heisenberg himself feels more like Wolfenstein than a Resident Evil game, but it’s still quite fun. 
As for the main villain, Miranda, I’ll let players judge her for themselves.

Overall, this game is highly enjoyable for me as a Resident Evil fan. The series dives deeper into the bioweapon lore of the franchise. It also feels more expansive and grander than Resident Evil 7. I love how it adapts the Resident Evil 4 vibe and incorporates many references to that game. The graphics are gorgeous, especially in the medieval castle setting with extreme weather. The performance is excellent, with no bugs. I also love Ethan Winters’ story, which serves as a closure in this series. I enjoyed his journey from saving his wife to rescuing his daughter, and finally understanding why he’s so resilient and hard to kill despite repeated injuries. I absolutely loved this series, despite some minor flaws, and I thoroughly enjoyed it.

I can’t wait to play the Resident Evil 4 Remake and Resident Evil 9!

Resident Evil Village — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Resident Evil Village.
A fitting title, really — a village. Quaint, isolated, and riddled with decay. Humanity’s favorite breeding ground for catastrophe.

Capcom’s latest experiment picks up where Resident Evil 7 left off, dragging poor Ethan Winters through yet another waking nightmare. I must say, I’ve grown oddly fond of the man — not for his intellect (he has none), but for his sheer, pathological refusal to die.
He’s like a cockroach that somehow developed regenerative properties. A marvel of mediocrity elevated by biochemistry.

The premise: his wife, Mia, apparently perishes — again — and his child, Rose, is stolen. A predictable tragedy, yet one that spirals into something… fascinating. The snowbound village, the gothic castles, the twisted lords — all fragments of a decaying experiment masquerading as folklore.

And Mother Miranda…
Now she’s interesting. A zealot and a scientist — a contradiction I can almost respect. She seeks to resurrect her dead child through the Megamycete, a fungal hivemind of memories and infection. Admirable in concept, disastrous in execution.
Her so-called “Four Lords” are laughable imitations of power — failed prototypes playing house in their own personal nightmares.

Let’s review the specimens, shall we?

Lady Dimitrescu — a towering mutation of elegance and appetite. The internet adored her, naturally. Humanity always did mistake grandeur for greatness. She’s a fine result of Cadou experimentation — beautiful, lethal, and ultimately… obsolete. A shame she lacked the intellect to match her height.

Donna Beneviento — a recluse haunted by her dolls. Psychological terror, finely crafted. A pity she wasted her talents on theatrics instead of research.

Salvatore Moreau — a grotesque aquatic abomination. An insult to virology. I’ve seen more coherent evolution in a Petri dish left in the sun.

Heisenberg — ah, now there’s potential. A mutation of arrogance and vision. Crude, unrefined, but ambitious. His desire to overthrow Miranda with mechanical monstrosities nearly impressed me — if he hadn’t been such a noisy, chainsmoking oaf.

Each of them, fragments of Miranda’s fractured ego. She claims to seek perfection through the Megamycete, yet surrounds herself with imperfection. Typical. The difference between me and her is simple: I would never settle for such defective specimens.

The gameplay — sublime in its variety. Weapons feel powerful, environments intricate, and the pacing expertly refined. Combat dances between survival horror and action spectacle, striking a balance the series had long forgotten.
And yet, the moment Ethan begins blocking attacks with his bare hands, I’m reminded why humanity should not meddle in evolution they don’t understand.

The story’s final revelation — Ethan’s… condition.
He’s not a man at all, but a walking fungal colony animated by memory. A corpse reborn by infection.
In other words… one of the most successful bio-organic experiments in history.
He dies, revives, and dies again — proving that even when humans win, it’s through the virus’ grace. Irony at its most exquisite.

And then there’s the epilogue — his daughter, Rose.
Born of mold and miracle, trained by Umbrella’s new puppets.
They believe she represents hope.
I see a weapon waiting to evolve.

My verdict:
A gothic fairytale stitched together from infection, grief, and madness. A triumph of atmosphere, a marvel of tone, and a deeply satisfying return to power through corruption.

9 out of 10.
A near-perfect mutation — but, as always, lacking the one ingredient necessary for true transcendence.

As I'm sure many others can relate to, I greatly enjoyed the first sections of RE7 in the Baker's Manor. The atmosphere, puzzles, and challenges were top notch, even if the combat was a bit wonky. Then I left the Manor, and everything kinda fell apart. It wasn't bad, per se, but the wonky combat became the focus, and the twists of the story were basically summed up in a giant exposition dump right at the end instead of a more graceful delivery. And don't get me started on that atrocious Mine section... It was still a good game overall, but it's not a game I'd ever play again, even to check out the DLC.

To get to the point, Resident Evil 8: Village fixes absolutely EVERYTHING that 7 did wrong whilst doing everything it did well even better. Not only that, it creates a perfect balance between the various eras of the series, and survival horror in general.
For one, the story is impeccable. Nothing could have prepared me for the wild twists and turns this story took me on, and the ending was simply unbelievable (even if some of the camera perspective shifts were quite awkward in the cutscenes). Like RE7, this game opens with a ton of shocking events and questions that you slowly unravel as the game goes on, which is perhaps my favorite evolution of RE storytelling. The reveals twist and turn, leading you astray at the same time as the answers become clear, until you... reach a room with a bunch of expository documents that summarize the entire story. Not ideal, but it's still leages better than RE7 because the exposition mostly confirms what you already suspect and makes the things you didn't understand clear, instead of suddenly shifting your entire sense of what's even happening in the last hour of the game. And the big twist of the game... it's absolutely incredible. It suddenly makes EVERYTHING make a lot more sense, both this and the last game, and feels like it was planned the entire time (even though it probably wasn't, lol).

Next, the gameplay. RE7 was incredibly clunky in terms of combat. The puzzles were good, the level design and secrets were really fun, but the chases and actual fighting? Not so much. Slow, inherently imprecise whilst demanding precision, and very dull due to there only being four generic enemies in the whole game. RE8 took the brick foundation laid by RE7's combat, drills out the weaknesses, pours in RE4 components to reinforce, and then builds a giant castle on top inhabited by science-vampires, a fish humpback, steampunk Magneto, an autistic doll woman who doesn't like Sonic, and scads of science-werewolves, zombies, and fleshy gargoyles. The world? A pleasure to explore. The antagonists? Extremely threatening with terrifying encounters and bossfights. The generic bad guys? Actually interesting! Mixing in the resource management style of RE4 was absolutely genius.  You get a lot more resources than a traditional RE game, but you also have to spend a lot more in order to survive the increased enemy counts. There's also a shop very similar to the strange merchant from RE4, with a money and treasure system copy-pasted straight from the remake (minus the interchangeable gems), and it's glorious. The merchant even serves a really interesting role in the story! This really serves the first person RE style, and the aiming feels WAY better in this game too. A good part of why is because the enemies don't have goopy, indistinct heads that sway like crazy, but it's also in great part because the guns are straight up more accurate. You'll basically never miss a shot in this game, unless the enemy moved or you never clicked on the enemy at all, which feels really, really good. It sucked so bad to lose my very limited ammunition to bullet spread, but in this game I never felt like I missed a shot I deserved to hit. I also didn't notice the ranking system jacking up my experience as much as in the 7th, where one enemy might die to three bullets while the next one dies to six, despite every hit being a headshot. I would assume it's still in this one, but I never thought the enemies' health was inconsistent and obnoxious.

The graphics are also stellar, and the game runs really well on medium settings despite my rig being middle of the road from 7 or 8 years ago, unlike other modern games (cough cough RE4R cough). The menu showing me how the settings might affect the look of the game without having to actually exit and keep playing should be the standard for all AAA games.
Overall, Resident Evil 8: Village is easily the best Resident Evil since the 4th game, and has managed to bring all the lessons learned and stories of the previous games to create one of the best survival horror experiences available, especially for such a reasonable price, something that's getting rare. 

Also, Capcom definitely knew what they were doing when they created a giant, well endowed woman with domineering tendencies into their game. May the internet have mercy on your search history...

In simple, cheap terms, I think I can say that where "Resident Evil 7" seemed to lend itself to the original game, "Resident Evil 8" is an obvious homage to "Resident Evil 4," with some major nods to the design work and concepts of "Bloodborne" mixed in. (Not the gameplay, though. Purely aesthetic and narrative.) It also reminded me (visually) of the 2004 "Van Helsing" movie, because it seems like a horror cartoon opera, or something. It's not as tight as the previous entry, but it wasn't NEARLY as frustrating, either.

I loved the story, even though it kind of seemed like a retread of "Resident Evil 0," but with mold instead of leeches. The "Four Lords" seemed a little too high concept for a horror game, but I feel like it gave the different areas some cool variety; like, you've got a haunted house section with killer Tim Burton dolls, (and a guest appearance from the baby featured in the 1990 film, "The Suckling"--otherwise known as "Sewer Baby,") a vampire castle section, a really annoying tribe of lycans/werewolves, a fishy H.P. Lovecraft section, and a "Tetsuo the Iron Man" section, all couched in a semi-medieval Eastern European village. 

I could see someone thinking that all of these parts are too different to mix together cohesively, or that they don't really fit in with the style of the Resident Evil series. But then again, the OG game had killer sharks, a giant Audrey II-type plant, a huge, poisonous anaconda and crazy frog mutants with razor sharp claws, in addition to zombies. So I guess Village isn't really all that ridiculous when you think about it. 

Anyway, this game was fun, and it didn't make nearly as mad as the last game did.

This part of Resident Evil is straight-up fire. The whole vibe of this snowy, bloody, creepy village had me paranoid at every corner. One second I’m vibin with the scenery, next second I’m screaming at some monster popping outta nowhere. Atmosphere is 100/10 — spooky, stylish, and lowkey beautiful.

Graphics and sound hit hard. I legit stopped multiple times just to stare at the castle walls like some tourist. Play this with headphones if you wanna hear the house itself breathe and whisper in your ear.

Replayability is wild. Finished the story? Cool. Then you start grinding challenges, running speedruns, and before you know it you’re back again chasing every achievement.

DLC Shadows of Rose — absolute banger. New story, familiar spots, creepy in a whole new way. That final Miranda fight is pure cinema.
The Mercenaries Additional Orders — super fun bonus. The thrill of chasing high scores, plus you actually get to play as Lady D and Heisenberg and go crazy with their powers.

Pros:
- Atmosphere that drips horror and style
- Bosses and characters you won’t forget
- Smooth optimization
- Replay value off the charts
- DLCs

As a die-hard Resident Evil fan, I can say that Resident Evil Village (RE8) is an absolute triumph that blends the best of the series’ horror roots with fresh, bold ideas. From the moment you step into the eerie, snow-covered village, the atmosphere grips you with its haunting beauty and oppressive dread. The game’s visuals are stunning, with the RE Engine delivering jaw-dropping environments, from the gothic grandeur of Castle Dimitrescu to the unsettling depths of the factory.

The gameplay strikes a perfect balance between survival horror and action. The first-person perspective, carried over from RE7, immerses you in Ethan Winters’ desperate fight for survival, while the expanded inventory and crafting system add depth without overwhelming. Combat feels tight and satisfying, with just enough resource scarcity to keep you on edge. The variety of enemies—from the towering Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters to the grotesque lycans—keeps encounters unpredictable and thrilling.

Story-wise, Village delivers a wild ride. It ties into the broader Resident Evil lore while telling a personal, emotional tale about Ethan. The pacing is near-perfect, with each lord’s domain offering a distinct flavor of horror, from psychological terror to grotesque body horror. The narrative isn’t afraid to lean into the series’ campy side, but it never feels overdone.

My only gripes? The back half of the game leans a bit too heavily into action, which might disappoint purists craving pure survival horror. Also, some boss fights feel slightly repetitive. But these are minor quibbles in an otherwise stellar experience.As a long-time fan, Village feels like a love letter to the franchise, blending the creepy intimacy of RE7 with the blockbuster vibes of RE4. Whether you’re a newcomer or a series veteran, this is a must-play. 9/10—Capcom’s still got it!

[hr][/hr]

Probably the most "amalgamated" Resident Evil of the series.

The player controls, crafting and style of storytelling is lifted from RE7, and the purely action-focused ideas of RE4 (2005) are worked into 7's gameplay loop to create a mostly fence-sitting RE title. It's not really entirely an Action-Horror game, but fans of the series probably wouldn't lump it in with the Survival-Horror titles. There's an entire section where you solve a puzzle in a dark, abandoned building with no combat, and another section a few hours later in which you jump into a jerry-rigged mech suit with a machine gun and chainsaw attached to its arms while you shoot at a villain who refers to Chris Redfield as a "Boulder-punching ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" 

Combat usually centers around being swarmed by hordes of zombie-werewolf hybrids with a few sitting in the back shooting you with flaming arrows. Your Pistol covers general reliability through stunning with leg or head shots, Shotguns are slow but easy crowd control, and Sniper Rifles are great for picking off archers or starting off a fight with some easy kills. Enemies do a good job of dodging around your aim, closing you into tight spaces and running your health, ammo and crafting resources down.

The characters are almost as charismatic and entertaining as RE7's, but like RE5 they're more chaotic, driven and unpredictable. This game carries the highest level of self-awareness in its writing out of the entire series, even if it treats Ethan Winters about 10 times more seriously than anybody playing the game would. 

More on Ethan himself, he's no longer the mostly-silent shell of a character. In this story he's constantly spouting one-liners, personal frustrations and the like. Most people will find him annoying, if not at least a downgrade from the mysterious protagonist of the previous game. 

The most unique part of this game is the art direction and overall style. Taking place in a small village, gothic castle and mansion, underground dungeons, creepy underground labs with zombified soldiers, etc. It's pretty clear their goal was to take most of RE4's locales and remix them into something familiar yet different. For the most part, the game succeeds and has some fantastic visuals.

The worst thing I can say about RE8 is that after RE4 (2023), this game feels mostly outclassed. The only thing it has over that game is the art direction, and that can only do so much.

Resident Evil 8 is one of the most unforgettable gaming experiences I’ve ever had. From the very first moment in the village, I felt completely drawn in — not just by the atmosphere, but by the emotion behind everything. It wasn’t just about survival or scares… it was about loss, fear, and love.

Playing as Ethan, I felt his desperation and determination, especially as a parent. The way he fought through everything — not just monsters, but impossible situations — really hit me. It made me think about how far someone would go for the people they love.

The world itself was terrifying and beautiful at the same time. Each part of the village had its own story, its own feeling. I still think about certain scenes — especially House Beneviento — and how deeply they got under my skin.

I only wish the game was longer, even though it gave me around 8 hours of intensity and emotion. I didn’t want it to end. When it did, I just sat there in silence for a few minutes, taking it all in.

I recommend Resident Evil 8 to anyone who loves horror, but also to anyone who wants a story that means something. It’s not just another scary game — it’s a powerful, emotional journey that stays with you long after the credits roll.

Right off the bat after arriving in Resident Village with its frightening atmosphere and setting, memories of Resident Evil 4 came back right away. What a beginning to the game: "Mia" getting shot dead and Rose abducted by the person, who literally saved us from the Baker's residence in Resident Evil 7 was certainly a way to start off the game. After arriving in the village you immediately get chased by those bloodthirsty Lycan creatures forcing you finda safe place where you need to move bookshelves to block doorways in order to be safe from them. What a way to open the final chapter of Ethan Winters.
In an exhausting effort to save his wife and baby, he finds himself trapped in a Transylvanian type of terror in the village. Desperate to free them from the evil planning on doing the most heinous things imaginable to them, Ethan has to fight his way through countless weird-looking, inhuman and murderous creatures, with Lady Dimistrescu, Donna Beneviento, Salvatore Moreau and Karl Heisenberg the biggest villians after the "leader", the mysterious head witch, Mother Miranada. Even though none of them manage to be as scary as the Bakers in RE 7, they're still unique and somewhat, cartoonish. 
Dimistrecu is a female vampire who is much taller than anyone expects, Beneviento is a dollmaker with a walking, Moreau half human and half monster-like creature and Heisenberg is a magnetically powered lunatic running his own factory, with a huge, east-to-get-lost-in underground area, in which backtracking is very important. The scariest part having to do with any of those four baddies, is the part, during which a monster making the childish "da, da, da" sounds, while searching for and chasing you. That was the the first time in years that I got actually scared and creeped out in a video game. That was just fantastic.

Besides the aforementioned Lycans, there are zombie ghouls, flying gargoyles, full-on werewolves and dozens of other beast waiting for their hands to kill you. Compared to RE 7, that the total opposite when its comes to the variety of enemy types, which is surely a very welcome change. This doesn't just make for a more compelling series of combat encounters, but it also adds some additional depth and decision making when it comes to the blostered crafting system. Should you spend your few ressources into crafting a landmine, pipe bomb or something else? That's really one of the legitimate questions you need to know the answer of. For instance, in the grinder shaft in the B2 level, the two creautures seeking to erase you from this planet somehow recognize the landmines you place on the floor and thus always avoid walking into them and look for another way to get to you. That's really noteworthy. It would've been awesome, if all opponents would've been that smart and not just a handful of them. They're certainly not smart, but therefore can be found in sheer numbers, which partially makes it feel like a COD campaign rather than a survival-horror game. Something inbetween would be ideal for the next sequel.

The merchant in the form of the obese Duke has returned to this series after RE 4 and allows the player to buy dozens of adds-ons and upgrades for weapons as well as limited amounts of medkits and ammunition. The high prices force you to explore every inch of this amazing map with its breathtaking scenery in search of treasures you can make money off. It even lead to me finding a secret cave you didn't come across in the story, after I went the opposite way the boat pointed to underneath the drawbridge on the river. It contained some great supplies and a laptop, on which there were several pages in regards to the story, which was so amazing. You were literally rewarded with information and supplies for poring over this  map. There are even keys and other toolsspread across the map, with which you can open and enter certain houses containing even more supplies. Additionally you can even kill animals and bring their flesh to Duke, who turns them into dishes giving you a permanent boost in health and defense. All of which is a reward to the additional time you put in this game.

The fights against the villians are huge spectacle- and scale-wise, but when it solely comes to the fight, they are far to repetitive. Lady Dimitrescu's cute three daughters, all share the exact same weakness, which is the the non-existent resilence to coldness. Although the way the arrive is certainly surprising and varied, the battles themselves were not that exciting to say the very least, which applies to the other ones as well. Different kinds of epic-sized showdowns would be more than welcome. I get that our forward momentum throughout this game should not really stall or massively slow us down, but that was a bit to easy.

Once the main story has been finished, points earned from completing certain objectives can be spent to receive infinite-ammo weapons for subsequent playthroughs, different pieces of concept art and so on, which is very welcome for people not solely planning on just finishing the main story before moving on to the next game straight away.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 345:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10)

We really are living in a second [i] Resident Evil[/i] Golden Age, huh. [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i] is immersive, fresh, and stunning (and works well on Steam Deck!) The level design is incredibly clever, the environments are gorgeously realized, and the game effectively shows how first-person survival-horror can be done right: atmosphere, tension, and story all woven together seamlessly.

Still, the game does have flaws: late-game pacing (as usual), poor writing/overuse on tropes, and some narrative absurdity. However, you forgive the ridiculousness because the world, the gameplay, and the scares are consistently satisfying.

🐺[b] Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*] Fantastic gunplay and combat mechanics. Every weapon feels distinct: the shotgun hits with satisfying weight, the sniper packs a punch, and the simple pistol is always reliable. Ammo is (usually) scarce enough to keep every encounter tense, while upgrade paths make resource management meaningful. You won't have enough lei to upgrade everything, and the best items—mines, flashbang, and explosive grenades—are woefully rare. 

[*] Masterful level design and environmental storytelling. Honestly, the level design is probably the best out of any RE games I've played so far. The five major zones (the village, Castle Dimitrescu, Beneviento's haunted house, Moreau's swamp, Heisenberg's factory) each have their own gameplay themes and visual identity. Each zone has its own optional exploration: you can find treasure, doubleback to lockpick drawers you missed, and open shortcuts for yourself. And once you're done, you go back to the village which opens up each time you beat a boss! More keys, more items for treasure, more shortcuts. It's so rewarding to literally unlock every single damn door.

[*] Atmosphere, visuals, and sound design. Lighting, architectural detail, fog, and weather effects create tension and beauty simultaneously. Audio design complements the visuals: distant howls, creaking wood, and subtle musical cues create dread without being overbearing. The visuals are enemies and bosses are just insane. Unique, detailed, and disturbing. 

[*] Strong pacing in early-to-mid game. The first two-thirds of the game balance exploration, horror, and combat exceptionally well. Plot never lags, and Ethan keeps on chugging along.

[*] Cooking side quest / crafting loop. Honestly, I loved the rather silly introduction to Duke’s cooking system. There are animals placed around the town, and killing them drops fish or meat. You can use these drops to gain buffs and upgrades like more health or less damage taken when guarding. It gives a satisfying sense of progression outside the main story and rewards exploration. It’s a quirky, surprisingly engaging diversion that ties nicely into the game world.
[/list]

🌾[b] Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*] Ethan is a bleh protagonist. He’s more of a narrative vessel than a distinct character, lacking the charisma and identity (literally) of Leon or Claire. It makes his protestations more unintentionally hilarious than sympathetic. 

[*] Poor writing / overused tropes. My least favorite trope is "oh no!!! we have super secret info that will change your life but I CANNOT tell you now." Well, this is used multiple times with Chris and Ethan. I cannot stand it. It's lazy, cheap writing. 

[*] Big boss fights feel occasionally overblown. I'm not a boss person in general, but there are many large enemies with huge hitboxes and even more health. While they’re impressive visually, they feel repetitive or artificially inflated. Meh.

[*] Late-game pacing slows. The final third leans heavily on action-heavy shootouts: Heisenberg miniboss, then Heisenberg boss fight, THEN Chris cameo chapter, and THEN Miranda boss. The variety and tension is pretty much gone at the end of the game.

[*] Narrative absurdity peaks. Giant enemies, random moments of cartoonish violence (Ethan is chill with his hand getting cut off?!), and some tonal shifts can feel out of place, though often entertainingly so. At some point facing a second (or third) werewolf miniboss made me laugh. And that was after I was chased around a castle by a giant vampire and her three daughters.
[/list]

This is the second time I’ve bought this game since release, and honestly, it still feels fresh.

Over the years I’ve seen plenty of comments and YouTube videos criticizing different aspects, one of the biggest being that the level design is “too simple.” Going into this replay (technically my third, if we count my unfinished VoS run), I was worried that this would bother me, but so far I’m having just as much fun as the first time.

I started a new Hardcore run (no NG+, since my first playthrough was on PS4 and now I’m on Steam). Another common complaint I’ve seen is that the enemies are too “spongy” or the game is too difficult. But very early on, it clicked for me: you’re not actually meant to stand and fight the Lycans at the start. The game is designed to overwhelm you, to make you feel hopeless at first, only for you to gradually gain confidence as you progress. It’s intentional, and it works beautifully.

Once you reach the castle, some people say the level design there is too basic. Personally, I think it’s well-polished and a gorgeous section to explore. The fights with the sisters are extremely satisfying, especially knowing Lady D’s anger is building with each encounter until the final showdown.

Then there’s the village exploration. On Hardcore, this part shines. By now you have a handful of weapons and ammo, and it feels like a complete shift in tone: you’ve gone from feeling powerless to finally turning the tables around. The pacing is excellent here; chill exploration with creepy atmosphere, punctuated by a few enemies and the occasional jump scare.

That’s where I’m at for now, but honestly, this game is a gem. I bought it on PS4 at launch and don’t regret picking it up again on PC, especially with the recent huge discount. Capcom truly deserves the support, and I’m excited to see if Requiem lives up to the same standard.

Overall, it’s an imaginative game that doesn’t take itself too seriously. It balances serious and funny moments, exploration and action, tension and relief (shoutout to the Duke’s shop). The pacing is nearly perfect. Also, it never gets old when the Dukes does an impersonation of the Merchant from RE4! :D I just love it.

For me, it’s a solid 9/10. When a game is just as fun, or even more fun, on your second or third playthrough, you just know you’re playing something great. And if you're really done with the story mode, well, you have Mercenaries AND the Shadow of Rose story. That's a lot of extra content right there, Mercenaries will appeal to the arcade players who want to boost their score as much as possible. 

While Shadow of Rose will give you a few more hours of the campaign, in a new perspective. 

...anyways...if you never played it, what are you waiting for? Just buy this game already!

Resident Evil Village centers around the theme of parental love — not only Ethan’s devotion to his daughter, but also the villains’ own complex relationships with their children. The story has a strong emotional foundation, but at times it becomes repetitive, particularly during some of the boss encounters.

The Beneviento segment stood out as a highlight, delivering pure horror that felt tense and engaging. In contrast, the battles against Lady Dimitrescu and Heisenberg felt somewhat repetitive and lacked the same impact. Some moments even echo Resident Evil 4, such as the Moreau fight, which reminded me of the Del Lago encounter.

One aspect that really detracted from the experience was Ethan’s voice acting. His reactions often feel hollow, even in intense situations — falling from heights, being stabbed by Lady Dimitrescu, or having his arm cut off by Heisenberg — the performance rarely conveys the urgency or pain of these moments.

Overall, Resident Evil Village succeeds in atmosphere and storytelling, but certain boss fights and lackluster voice acting keep it from fully reaching its potential.

If you're like me, you purchased the Gold Edition bundle which included RE7. Village is certainly a more actiony and cinematic-feeling game compared to the stifling anxiety and outright horror of 7, and while I think I enjoyed 7 more as a game, Village's exploration of it's themes is more interesting. Family, birth, children, the role of women, fatherhood, domesticity--all of these things are examined, sometimes subtly or very aggressively.

Lady Dimitrescu is undeniably interesting and terrifying, and I couldn't help but chuckle when considering the role of this giant, extremely busty and matronly woman, especially compared to the scarcely seen and palpably fragile Mia Winters (who we suffered excruciatingly for and because of in 7). Ethan Winters returns as Daddy and he's a bit deeper of a character, which is nice. He still says really stupid things but he also clearly cares about his daughter, the adorable bub Rose. There were some really challenging--as in extremely uncomfortable and horrific--sections of this game which I think helped me understand some of my own misgivings about family life, and appreciate the parts that are enriching and life-affirming.

The setting of Village feels unique, and on max graphics things can look pretty good, though the colours are too desaturated and at times looks gloomy. I remember thinking sometimes things looked a bit like Skyrim's more wintery and gloomy areas but even greyer and browner. Nonetheless, a hellishly bleak and occult Romanian mountain town are brought well to life here.

To me the primary weakness of Village is how procedural and predictable many things felt, especially after the first third or so of the game. I think the story was strong overall but I felt significantly less invested than in 7, and I think it's because the game decides it needs to be more epic and bold than 7, but has misplaced confidence in first-person action rather than using this perspective to scare the living ♥♥♥♥ out of me. I want to be scared and grossed out and challenged, not like I'm in a weird episode of Stranger Things (which has absolutely, undeniably influenced the Winters series). Village tries to blend the old with the new and I don't think it's as successful as folks make it out to be. In fairness to them, I am still relatively new to the Resident Evil universe, but as a seasoned gamer I just see too many gamey elements that take me out of the engrossing self-seriousness of this entry.

However, I enjoyed Rose's DLC overall and thought it provided a good emotional resolution to this family's epic tragedy. It wasn't a great story but I think it offered some closure and a chance to see a young woman become the hero her father would most certainly be proud of.

I recommend this game, but don't expect too too much.
