The horror element is almost non existent which doesn't give you the feel of playing an RE game. The monsters dropping sellable loot which you can trade for upgrades in the shop made me feel like I was playing an RPG title rather than an RE game yet again. The shooting is one of the best in the series if not the best. I loved shooting the shotgun which was OP as hell. The unlocking of guns made this even feel more like an RPG. Sure, the previous games had a simular concept, however this one due to the marking on the map made it feel like an RPG yet again. The story was pretty generic and blant. I really like Ethan Winters as a protagonist, so the decision to kill him off should have been a big deal in the game which the story actaully makes you feel like the game is coming to an end...and he rises from the dead. This was really, really stupid. After his "death" we had what felt like a COD story mission where you play as Chris and kill everything that has two legs with basically no effort at all. The plot twists in the storyline felt really forced. "Oh, Chris wasn't the bad guy. Ethan was just living with a psycho witch this entire time" does that mean that Rose (The baby about which this whole mess is about) was Ethan's and Miranda's kid? The way the characters talk about Rose would contradict that, however logically speaking, if Miranda pretended to be Mia this entire time whilst holding the real Mia in a basement, then who did Ethan have a kid with? Well, that never seems to be explained. The doll boss fight had to be one of the goofiest "boss fights" I have seen in a horror game yet. This was so stupid. I would say that most of the boss fights were terrible. The Heisenberg fight was...made me feel like I was playing an FPS shooter rather than a horror game. This game litearlly gives the player a tank to defeat him. The sacrifice that Ethan made at the end was very heroic and make it feel like it was an ending that he deserved. He saved his family and ended the upcoming chaos. The credit scene in which you see a grown up Rose who gives tribute and respect to her father for his birthday was beautiful and the end credit which stated "A father's journey ends here" made for a great ending to the story. Overall, I really enjoyed it not for it's horror aspects (which the game should have had) rather for the great gameplay that it had to offer.

9 hours of some of the best level design I've ever seen in a game. Great game play, fun elements of classic puzzle solving and pretty well done enemies too.

There are moments where the game slows down to a halt almost, I guess to allow you to explore and find treasure (Treasure Hunting is fun too btw). I missed a couple of them, only did Moreau and Heisenbergs Labyrinth puzzles, couldn't find the other 2 spheres anywhere, I didn't want to use a guide for my first play through either. The reward is only money however, so it's not bad.

Was positive i'd found all the gun upgrades for the LEMI pistol but as it turns out, I guess I was 1 shy? couldn't tell you where. Also, the game does have 1/2 moments where you cannot access an area you have already cleared, so if you see treasure, assume you can grab it now (in 9/10 cases, you can) and if you're really bothered, bring up a guide, the game does sometimes have moments of nonsensical difficulty when it comes to enemies and finding stuff to sell (Gemstones are diabolical).

My MAJOR issue with the game is, The pacing is garbage. Utter garbage. It shifts tone so suddenly, you meet all these characters at once and it's like "HEY HERE WE ARE, YOU KNOW US NOW, BYE" and then you're off to kill them. The Dollhouse boss is... pathetic. that entire section exists just for the giant baby reveal (which is awesome and made me genuinely run away in horror) and you can 100% beat the entire segment in a half hour or less if you know what to do. Moreau's area too, which comes hot off the heels of the Dollhouse...

We're never given time to meet these villains properly (bar Dimitrescu). Mother Miranda's story gets explained in the last hour, Heisenberg is interesting but JARRINGLY contrast to the rest of the game.

It's still a solid 8.5/10 I'd say, Better than RE7 (which is good... just lacking).

Things the game also has I didn't mention that I enjoyed:

>Weapon Upgrades
>Head Popping Action
>Collectables
>Post-Game Challenges
>very nice enemy design
>Hunting Animals for Health Upgrades

THE SHORT REVIEW:
What does it matter what I say? You're probably going to buy it regardless, because it's AAA "horror" and there's naff-all else in the genre at this level of production. Or because it has pretty graphics and you like gore, and you think the story isn't dog-sh*t but is actually "cool"

Gosh! Maybe you even find it scary...who knows! 

THE LONGER REVIEW: 

A-ha-ha-ha-ha....ha-ha-ha-ha!

Oh, that's funny reading the description of this on Steam. "Experience survival horror like never before" and "masterful story-telling".....the former is debatable unless you were literally born about five minutes before playing the game, and the latter is just a plainly ludicrous claim.

Resident Evil has never had "masterful story-telling" and after about a trillion games tripping over themselves trying to tie the "plot" *coughs* together they never will. By now it's an abysmal bunch of things just shoved into one utterly stupid and unwieldy approximation of a narrative that keeps the series rolling on to what is about the twentieth game by now (if not more) 

Attempts to link to this the other games are awful and cringe-inducing, and appear incredibly desperate as they try to explain how a series that started off as being about biological mutations now has vampires that can turn into a swarm of flies and werewolves thrown into the mix. With the likes of zombies, lickers, the nemesis and whatever else seemingly being derived from the parasitic insects that created the Ganados in Resi 4, that are also somehow linked to the mould that explains the monsters in Resi 7 and 8.

Ultimately by the time it gets to Resident Evil 50 it will no doubt be Mitochondria that are to blame, and they will either be a good thing that create the Jedi and the Force, or be responsible for turning humanity into horrible mutants that are un-killable unless you shoot them in the vast number of terrifyingly unnecessary eyeballs they have sprouted.

So, no, it isn't "masterful story-telling" It isn't even vaguely good story-telling, but who in their right mind plays a Resi game for the story? It was awful for the first game (I should know, I was there playing it as a young'un) and it has never got any better since. Maybe in terms of slightly better dialogue, but plotting that isn't nonsensical guff? fugged'about'it!! 

Anyway - that's quite enough about a plot that wasn't ever worth more than the amount of critique you could fit on a postage stamp. What about this claim of the game-play being "survival horror like never before"...well....that's a strange claim to make, since (a) it isn't scary beyond about the first ten minutes (which are genuinely effective at a jump-scare or two) and (b) this is just the combat of Resi 4 in first-person but minus a whole lot of what made that game so good almost twenty years ago.....

Sure, the enemies duck and weave just like they did in Resi 4, but what else? Uh...well...that would be nothing. You shoot werewolves and they die. You shoot some zombie-esque humans and they die. Whatever it is you shoot...it just dies. There's none of the crimson heads (?) from Resi remake of about twenty years ago, where they come back as super-vicious creatures if you don't burn the bodies. 

They don't sprout monstrous barbed tentacles like they did after shooting their heads off in 4, or mutate like the Necromorphs in DeadSpace. They just drop dead and that's it. Can you shoot weapons out of their hands before they throw them, or blow up sticks of dynamite that they're holding? Nope. If you took out the crazy QTE's of 4 + 5, along with any nuance to the combat, along with iconic things like the chainsaw wielding bag-man, and then replaced all of that with....nothing, then that is apparently "survival horror like never before"

You would literally either have to be a baby or utterly adverse to horror games to have never before experienced 100% of what is in this game. Other than it being in first-person this is a weaker version of 4 and 5 when it comes to the action, and it has traded off most of the tension and relatively restrained narrative from 7 (which wasn't all that in the first place)

Most of the enemies are nothing special to look at or frightening to encounter, and the boss-battles are about as bog-standard as you can get. Personally I don't find this at all surprising, since any game series with this many incarnations was always likely to run out of ideas and originality, and make no mistake - just because this is numbered 8 it is actually way, way, waaaay more than that and just as tired as you'd expect.

Is it fun? Sure, who doesn't like decapitating monsters with a shotgun. Is it worthy of any hype, or a score of more than, say, 7 out of 10? Nope. I would say I don't know long Capcom can go beating this dead horse, but the fact Resi 9 is on the way suggests people still lap it up. But as an older gamer seeing this do set-pieces and AI that aren't even a step above the 1998 release of Resi 2 (Lady Dimitrescu is basically Mr X with the exact same dumb and slow behaviour) is disappointing.

I decided to challenge myself by finishing the game with nothing but the knife. No pistols, no shotguns, no grenade launchers—just a hunk of sharpened metal and a lot of stubbornness.

What surprised me most is how well the game lets you do this. Every encounter becomes a tense dance: learning enemy patterns, baiting lunges, and striking at just the right moment. Lycans go from terrifying to sparring partners, and even bosses—yes, all of them—are beatable with enough patience and footwork.

Highlights:

Blocking actually matters when you’re not spraying bullets. You feel every claw and wing swipe.

Boss fights become endurance tests where victory feels earned, not just bought with ammo.

The knife upgrade path gives just enough edge to make it viable without breaking the challenge.

I'll try to keep this review short since it is a CAPCOM game after all and has received THOUSANDS of positive reviews since it's release in 2021, I'm just a bit late to the party. However I did want to say that among ALL of the Resident Evil games I have played Village (a.k.a. 8) was EASILY the BEST! For context my friends got me into this franchise of games two months ago and I played all of them excluding 5 & 6 for obvious reasons (bad) as they watched. It was a really great time and we all had a blast. In my time playing each game I realized that Resident Evil excels in a few categories per game. You have some that are superb in puzzles like Resident Evil 2 Remake, Some that are horrifying like Resident Evil 7 and its family of nightmares and some that excel in its gameplay/combat like Resident Evil 4 Remake. Each game has something unique about it that differentiates itself from the rest of the franchise somehow. So playing each game was always a delight and I was in for a surprise each time. Village is different in this aspect however, not only is it the top of each of those categories for me (YES! I think this game is better than 4!) the game also excels in its characters, art direction and story far more than any other game I played. Each area of the game is mesmerizing and every character drew me into their own unique story and motivations. The plot is amazing and a major upgrade to what I found to be the lackluster one in 7 (although I think playing 7 is necessary to love this game properly). The combat is smooth and not irritating in any manner unlike 7 or 3R where things can stun lock you or there is invisible walls where there simply shouldn't be. I even think the combat in this game outranks RE4R in that department, which is a hard thing to do as it's the titan of this series. It shares the same level of fun in puzzles with RE2R and I think the game is just as scary as RE7 at times. It's everything I could've ever wanted in a Resident Evil game without having a contrived story or annoying features. Even the extra gamemode "Mercenaries" which is akin to the side stories in RE2R is much better than any other one I played as it is genuinely fun and not draining or grating to try and achievement hunt. The game is fun to speedrun, fun to achievement hunt in and the characters are lovable and memorable. I can't describe how much joy being in Dimitrescu's castle each run brings me. Or how about talking to Heisenburg, or being scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of Beneviento? Feeling bad for Moreau? The characters bring such a quality of life to this game it's not even funny. They're much better than just insert funny joke here from normal guy #4 (Looking at you Chris/Leon/Carlos/Whatever) It's the perfect Resident Evil game and I don't know how they're going to top this in 9. I've seen a lot of people say this game is budget/diet Resident Evil 4 and I MAJORLY disagree. Yes, the setting may be similar (man in crazy village find & save girl) but the characters are not nearly as enjoyable in 4 and frankly Leon has no real ties to Ashley. Ethan being Rosemary's father makes him deeply entrenched in the issues of the game. Where as you have to just kind of wonder why the hell is Leon risking his life for Ashley in 4? Why does he even care? Money? Okay, I guess? I enjoyed 4, but it's not comparable to the perfection 8 is. Also, Resident Evil games all take from each other. Almost all of the games have a lab or water section for reference. I don't see how 8 and 4 are more comparable than 2 and 3, or even 1 and 7? I genuinely have no complaints, no comments... This game is perfect. It was a pleasure to play and 100% in achievements. Never felt frustrated, didn't think it was too easy either. This game is more than I could ever describe, and this is what I would consider the SHORT of my opinions about the game. In 2025 the game is $10 on sale. It'll give you your money's worth, I can't recommend it enough. It's the best of Resident Evil.

Resident Evil 8 is a good game. It feels like capcom for this Resident Evil combined Resident Evil 4 og & Resident Evil 7 Biohazard together. Personally I love Re4 & re7 so I was a big fan of this design decision. Resident Evil Village is probably the most atmospheric Resident Evil yet, it feels as if you could easily get lost in the scenery and environment if you let yourself. Resident Evil Village captures the fun combat, weapon tune up, and treasure system from Resident evil 4; at the same time it captures some of the true horror of Resident Evil 7. Overall a good game!

This game is basically a prototype for Resident Evil 4 remake, which is a bit of a bummer but it stands on its own pretty well. The story is good, the graphics are great, runs really well and has more enemy variety than RE7. Now, compared to RE7, this game is less scary overall (although it has a section that is way more scary than anything seen in RE7) and becomes more action oriented, with a structure very similar to RE4 which rewards exploration, it even has a merchant that sells you stuff, but sadly no item box. The game can be played in both first person and third person perspective which is a plus.

The game starts slow and serves as a direct sequel to the story of RE7, once you get to the Village and you get a gun the game kicks in with a survival segment. Some time after that you must go into Castle Dimitrescu which is where the game shines, because it's gameplay segment is very similar to the police station in RE2 Remake: a mysterious place with danger every corner and you have to solve puzzles while being stalked by both zombies and a tall and posh vampire lady (evoking Mr. X). After this, you can explore the village itself a bit more before going to your next objective: House Beneviento. This segment is not for the faint of heart and is very spooky, because the game forces you out of your weapons while you have to solve puzzles through dark corridors and a creepy ambience. In my opinion this part was way scarier than the entirety of RE7, but after this, the game starts to drag a bit, forcing you into long battles against vampires and zombies in almost linear sections until you get to the end, which I found very fitting to end the story of the Winters family.

Overall, the game is very good and very replayable due to its New Game+ feature that preserves your inventory after every playthrough, but it gets a bit tedious after a while due to its linearity. If you liked RE7, you will like this, but if your favorite is RE4 or it's remake, you might feel a bit disappointed because it feels like a watered down version. I give it a 8.5/10.

The game's format sends you to the village, to another place, then back to the village, repeat. Any time you head back to the village, whatever place you left is locked out for the rest of the game, making any leftover loot unavailable.
The game follows the RE4 tradition of having treasures that can be combined to make far more valuable ones. You can tell if this is true by the item description, if they are named as "combinable". Some of the second halves of those items are spaced far apart, so don't sell off the pieces unless you are truly desperate.
The map will have each room go from red to blue when all items are taken from it. Said items can be anywhere. Under chairs, inside drawers, even glinting gems in the ceiling. If you want to clean the place out make sure you look up.
Some horror games demand you stop and fight enemies. This is not one of them. If you can just book it right past enemies then do so. Yes you can get items and cash from their bodies, but a bullet you don't have to spend is often better than one you have to buy.
Some weapons have upgrade parts that increase capacity. These also fully refill your weapon, so holding off on equipping them will let you use them as an instant reload in a fight.

* If possible, play on **PS5, Xbox Series X**, or a good PC for the best visuals and performance.

Resident Evil Village is an atmospheric triumph—equal parts terrifying, gorgeous, and unforgettable. Capcom has truly outdone themselves with this Gothic horror symphony. The Lords and Mother Miranda deserve standing ovations for their unforgettable performances.

👑 Lady Dimitrescu – Towering elegance meets razor-sharp menace. Every hallway in her castle drips with tension and decadence. Her presence alone is worth the price of admission.

🔩 Karl Heisenberg – A mad inventor with Magneto-tier flair. His factory is a brutal industrial nightmare and his character arc is unexpectedly compelling. He’s chaotic, brilliant, and totally badass.

🪞 Donna Beneviento – Her section is straight-up psychological horror genius. The Beneviento house is the scariest, most mind-bending part of the game. Angie's twisted puppet show lives rent-free in my nightmares.

💀 Salvatore Moreau – The tragic monster. Equal parts grotesque and sympathetic, his section feels like classic RE with a beautifully sorrowful undertone. Don’t underestimate the King of the Reservoir.

🌸 Mother Miranda – The puppet master herself. Mysterious, powerful, and divine. Her influence seeps through every shadow in the village, and her final confrontation is a glorious crescendo. Hail Miranda!

Beyond the Lords, the game nails pacing, visuals, and gameplay. It’s a love letter to horror fans with just the right mix of action, puzzles, and lore. If you're a fan of the RE series—or horror in general—this is unmissable.

So I came to this charming Eastern European village looking for my kidnapped baby, like any responsible dad. First red flag? The welcoming committee was a pack of werewolves. Second red flag? Everyone in town dresses like they’re in a Tim Burton fever dream.

A creepy doll that runs an Airbnb full of hallucinations.

A fish man with self-esteem issues and too many teeth.

Heisenberg, who looks like Magneto’s cousin with a vape pen.

And of course, Mother Miranda—because what’s a village without an evil god-tier bird lady?

I solved puzzles, got attacked by furniture, crafted ammo from literal trash, and somehow my fingers were constantly getting chopped off. Ethan Winters has the healing ability of a Marvel character and the emotional range of a potato. Iconic.

In conclusion: I came for survival horror, stayed for the wine cellar aesthetic, and left deeply concerned for my fingers. 10/10, would yell “WHY IS THIS HAPPENING?!” in a snowstorm again.

I've played almost all Resident Evil games, and I generally enjoy them, because I can play them through over a weekend. I usually also feel pretty entertained by them, although the story is also usually bizarre.
'Resident Evil Village' is one of the weaker parts of the series though in my opinion.

On a positive note, the graphics are very nice, you can play in 1st or 3rd person perspective ( - I prefer the classic 3rd person view), and, as always, there are many extras and addons offered for those players who already completed the main storyline.

This being said though, I feel that the series starts moving away from its roots. It is not a horror game anymore, but more a shooter. Especially one of the later chapters in the (Heisenberg) factory was rather annoying  to me. The possible assumption of the developers that it would be fun running through a confusing maze of assembly lines I personally can't fully understand. I didn't like those parts at all.

The final chapters and end bosses were good again though, and as always, Resident Evil finishes with a bang. No comments regarding the story: It is somehow always the same, but getting weirder and weirder. 

I started and finished the game over the weekend. I don't have any regrets playing it, I overall felt good. However, for players who don't know the series well, I would recommend playing the remakes of parts 1-3 first as well as Resident Evil 7 - these parts are much better in my opinion.

In sum, I would choose a 'thumb-in-the-middle' icon if there was one. 

My final rating: 7/10

Resident Evil Village is one of those experiences that you remember forever no matter how much time passes since you first played it.

I’m not particularly good with survival horror games but Village’s storytelling and characters were something that kept me going even during the scariest sections of the game. With the progression to each new area, you get more and more attached to the main character. Ethan is an incredibly-written protagonist who easily convinces you on why his journey is so important. His character is the reason that initially made me stick around and play this game from beginning to the end in a week.

The themes that the game explores were also very close to some of my personal experiences which made its story impact me in a special way. I imagine a lot of other players will have the same experience.

As a Resident Evil game, Village is extremely different. You get all of the familiar Resident Evil mechanics and gameplay but the context they’re put in is so different that at times you wonder if the game you’re playing is really Resident Evil. The gothic horror snowy environments give this game its individuality not seen beforehand in the previous instalments of the series.

Universe wise, the game is of same importance as 7. While drastically different, this is pretty much the most important RE game you can play lore-wise. The game also provides a lot of context via in-game resources about the events of 7, so while I recommend playing it before, technically you can easily catch up on the story by just playing Village.

I thought that 100% the game would be tedious but the achievements that require replaying the game change your playstyle so drastically that the experience feels fresh.

My least favorite part was the bonus mode “Mercenaries” in its entirety as well as one of the achievements to 100% the game being tied to it. It was extremely hard to get and I didn’t feel like I had fun or was even playing Resident Evil due to how drastically different the gameplay is. I really hope this won’t be the case in Requiem.

I recommend you to play Resident Evil Village and experience the story of the Winters Family. It is my currently my favorite single-player game I’ve played this year.

[h1]Rituals of the Living Dead[/h1]

¿Am I dead? Or am I a dead man — one who refuses to die?

After Miranda tore the heart from my breast — whilst I witnessed her transformations through the ages — this pain, so piercing and vertiginous, seemed to be my end. I had failed to rescue my daughter, Rose. And yet, without mercy for my suffering, I faded as I watched her use my heart to slake her thirst. She proclaimed herself a mother: mingling my daughter with her own long-dead child.

Though she tore the heart from me, the organ is not the seat of love — only its symbol. Nor could bathing in it — that vampiric act I perceived before my swoon — ever achieve motherhood. I saw everything burn. I saw the earth split asunder so that the tentacles of the Megamycete might emerge, in this night of wolves and madness.

I closed my eyes.
I died.

And yet — I awoke.

I had my questions. I am alive — so I see. So I believe. I move. I crawl. It is not a matter of what happened — I know they extirpated my heart. Something that cannot be repaired upon a physical level. What is it that they have not taken from me? That is my question. Or rather: what has befallen me?

I am in the snow, walking once more, and I realise that I have my hand and my fingers. Upon arriving at this place — the beautiful and lugubrious winter that seeps into my mouth, freezing my lips and nose as I exhale warm vapour — I know it is Romania. I travelled here by car, thinking of my daughter; and the legends take on strength, flesh, and blood. A werewolf tore away my fingers. All this time I had been lacerated, these wounds burning upon my skin — yet they never turned me from my purpose: to find Rose.

‘What am I?’

Eveline answers — though I am more concerned for my body. Her laughter already tells me: a body that refuses to die. But what truly died? I saw with my own eyes that Miranda extirpated my heart. No one lives without that organ.

Eveline insists, with a mocking yet sincere tone, that I was already dead. In the Bakers’ house — there I died. Once more I ask: what am I?

Mould, she says. Only that. Nothing more.

I am reduced to mould, and yet I maintain the form of who I am: Ethan Winters. But how is it possible that this mould clings to its purpose? Eveline does not yet understand — though she is no longer vengeful, no longer seeking her family, nor wishing for them, nor imposing them, nor playing house and tea with her dolls, believing them to be her family: cadaverous puppets. She forgets something.

It is not what I am, but who I am.

Before I go for my daughter — before I look Miranda in the face — I need to recover, to regain my strength. What died? The body, only that; and the mould restores it. But why am I not merely fungal matter, without voluntary movement and without desire for an end? How do I know who I am? Why am I not like those who were once villagers, until they became mould and werewolves?

The Duke rescued me. He carried me within his merchant’s caravan. We arrived — and before facing, confronting, revealing myself — I asked him to prepare me a meal.

This action tells me what I am; yet it returns the question and the answer through the intimate experience of warmth. It does not merely heal me. I appreciate its flavour, texture, aroma. I possess the ingredients: pork, poultry, fish. The Duke has the seasonings and vegetables.

The firm, almost liturgical blows of the knife upon the board — that steady rhythm as the ingredients are sliced — restore to me a fragment of who I am.

If the lycanthropes merely bite to devour their prey, I live the rite: the preparation, the purification, the cooking, the serving, the eating — with calm and measured rhythm. If Dimitrescu and her daughters could not sate their hunger and required yet more blood, I, by contrast, recognise the taste. I recognise who I am when I eat — whether I am sensible and moderate, or whether I am not. The food is metabolised to sustain my being. I tell myself I am satisfied. I desire no more.

Unlike Dimitrescu, who wants more — slaking her thirst in a bottomless pit whilst dressed in dandy elegance. Unlike Heisenberg, who no longer eats at all.

The Duke says, “To eat is to live.”

It is the most marvellous thing I have ever heard. It leaves me thinking, feeling, creating. Only those who eat, live. Or rather: food is movement perceived as action, and life brims with movement.

A dish preserves that movement — life. The warmth, the unfolding aroma, the bubbling heat. And I — my heart beating, within my mouth like the frothy wave of a wind-driven sea.

The Duke slices. He does not speak. He allows the silence to be shaped by the ingredients, to reveal their essence as they become a dish. The meal is art with its own purpose: to metabolise my being. Yet it also expresses our personhood.

It is not merely a matter of biting into meat or vegetable. It is ritual.

The being of the dish exists thanks to the living potency within the ingredients. I hear the hiss of the oil — that soft tsss resonating even within me. I hear the water come to the boil, splashing as the vegetables fall.

“Here you are: Ciorbă de porc.”

What a delight.

If one merely wishes to swallow food, it is soup. But not for me — it is Ciorbă de porc. It bears a touch of acidity from yoghurt and lemon. The meat is tender. The heat stings my tongue slightly; the softened vegetables grant it that added flavour — the sweetness of carrot, its colour — like contemplating a mobile work of art. The flavour lingers.

I am satisfied.

Then he prepares — I can already scent the seasoned, marinated meats — mititei. He serves them, inviting me to enjoy. I accompany them with bread and plum juice.

Whilst I ate — the Duke scarcely daring to interrupt — I felt the weight of my thoughts.

Food reminds me of my origins. It evokes the feelings of who I am. Mia, my wife, was happy with our daughter — though I did not truly know what had befallen her. Miranda was cooking in her stead. She still desired to be a mother. But when one loses a child — it is the most thorned tragedy that can pierce the soul and leave an incurable wound.

That wound is what cannot die.

I feel pain in my body even as I hold warmth in my mouth — the warmth of homely, ritual food. This pain resides not in the body, but within. Thus I know there are experiences that grieve me, and others that please me — and they are not of the flesh.

I might have eaten without asking the Duke to cook — merely to fill my stomach, thirsty, lost like a beast in unconscious hunger. But I did not.

Therefore I know what I feel. I know what my will desires. And though this body be dead, there remains something within me that cannot die.

Who am I?

That is my question.

I have not sunk into the misery of hunger, nor into the absence of appetite. If these simple things persist, then there are other movements — other actions — that tell me I have a purpose. Better still: I know what I desire because I do not lose myself.

I remain whole. I maintain my being — my personhood living in my daughter, as she lives in me.

It is sorrowful to hear how the villagers prayed to their Holy Mother, when it was she who brought horror upon the hamlet. Miranda is the beast who, wishing to be a mother, knows not how to feed nor nourish. She casts them into misery — into the extremes between craving and apathy — instead of helping to refine that within us which cannot die.

It is not merely love for my daughter. It is the knowledge of how to nourish that appetite — the seed that germinates the ultimate will with purpose: love. Love for my daughter. My desperate steps that seek her, that want her back.

Without an appetite formed, educated, metabolised through effort, I would be no different from the beasts of this village.

Before I go for my daughter, I remember who I am: one who acts, one who persists.

The form of my appetite is love.

Love for my daughter.

Although I have been a long time Resident Evil fan ever since the very first game on PlayStation 1, I stopped gaming in general for over a decade sometime after the Resident Evil 3. I never went into PlayStation 2 and beyond and I did not play Resident Evil 4, 5, 6 or 7 nor the other titles in the series. For me Resident Evil is always the classic survival horror with Jill, Chris, Leon and Claire and Raccoon City, Umbrella, the zombies and other monsters. 

When I came back to gaming few years ago then I looked into what the series had become and at first the Spanish village and African village action horror style of Resident Evil 4 and 5 (or 6) did not appeal so much to me because as I said for me the series meant classical survival horror as was portrayed in the first 3 games. I just looked some game play videos of these new titles and that was it. I did not intend to play them. When Resident Evil 7 came out then that sparked my interest in the sense that this game went back to a more survival horror setting and the first person view approach seemed a good way to go in my opinion. But there were no classical zombies and Ethan had to constantly run away from most of the enemies. While good horror style in itself it again did not appeal to me so much as the first 3 games. I liked as in the original games that I could shoot all the enemies dead if needed. So I skipped Resident Evil 7 as well.  

Well there was the remake of Resident Evil 1 as well but since I did not own a console to play it (at the time of it's release) then I skipped that also. Then came the remakes of Resident Evil 2 and 3 and I was able to run them on my laptop computer quite nicely and there I was back in Raccoon City with my favorite Jill, Leon and Claire. It was a great experience to go through those classical story lines in a new graphical and engine setting. Yes, Mr. X was chasing the characters around but it was properly integrated into the game play with plenty of shoot to kill moments with zombies and other monsters. 

Then I heard about the new Resident Evil Village and I saw some videos of it in the internet. It looked great and interesting but it seemed to me that all it mainly has is poor Ethan constantly running away from the big vampire lady D and her daughters. Again I can not obliterate the enemies if needed. But years later, now in 2025, I decided to give it a go and I was very pleasantly surprised by the actual good contents of Resident Evil Village. Yes, there was some running away from big enemies but it was not a constant thing and it was actually done very well. Plus there was plenty of action and shooting to be had in addition to the well designed chase parts. The whole atmosphere, characters, game play of the Village and it's story, beautiful and mysterious locations are very interesting and well arranged. Enough for me to be playing another play through on the hardest difficulty later on and the Mercenaries mini game is a really cool addition. So for survival, action horror fans out there I highly recommend this game. It is very good and it is worth it.

Resident Evil Village is the 8th mainline Resident Evil game, where it continues the story of 7's protagonist Ethan Winters. This time, he has to rescue his daughter from the rulers of a snowy, mysterious European village infested with monsters. But unlike 7, this game is more like RE4 if 7 was 2. Other than the change to European village from an American setting, it's more action-packed and has less inventory management. Key items are stored separately, and there is a shop system in which you can get money from fallen enemies. And no item boxes, so prepare to sell outdated weapons.

What I find interesting about this game is the variation of levels. Each of the rules have a different style, so their levels reflect that. Like you get to explore a huge castle, but later also a metal factory. The boss fights are pretty great, and you don't really have to worry about ammo since you can craft, buy, or just find a lot of them. However, the game still manages to be scary, with the multiple types of deformed enemies and overall creepy and dark atmosphere. It won't be as action-y as RE5 for example.

After you finish the game once, you'll get an extra game mode, The Mercenaries. It's similar to modes of the same name from the previous games, but also has elements of Raid Mode like in Revelations 2 where they have visible health bars and the area is not as circular. You can use money to upgrade your weapons, but sadly unless you have the DLC, you can only play as Ethan. Though it's more reason to buy it, as it has an extra story mode.

If you enjoyed 7 or other RE games, Resident Evil Village is definitely a title you should play. The change of pace is actually kind of a nice touch if you want a more combative RE game, but still maintains the scariness. It also manages to be emotional at several parts, mainly the ending. A great game all around, though I wish there were item boxes since I love hoarding and changing weapons.

I really enjoyed the horror aspect. Personally, I'm not a fan of jumpscares, but the creepy atmosphere and ominous enemies and monsters really get me. The overall design of the map and the whole world was magnificent, and the attention to detail was insane. Even some spots that many players could have missed (unlike me, obviously) were so nicely and realistically designed. Dimitrescu’s castle was insanely luxurious, and the graphics were actually some of the best I’ve seen. Like, there was no need for all those little details in every room you only had to enter once, but they did it anyway.

The Village itself was very disturbing and mentally challenging. Having to backtrack through the same spots over and over just to unlock certain things was exhausting, but so rewarding once you actually got to them. It really resembled the village from Resident Evil 4, just like the castle did. But for the castle, I have zero complaints since I really enjoyed that part of RE4. The map was so confusing at first, I had to pull it up every two seconds just to figure out where I was, but it was smartly and realistically designed. I didn’t like how some entrances were blocked but didn’t show up as blocked on the map, like it does for a locked door, for example.

Just from what I’d seen and heard online, I thought Lady Dimitrescu was the main boss and got all the attention, but that wasn’t the case at all. I really liked how the game had multiple big bosses, each with their own unique way of being defeated. Some required strategy, like Beneviento. You had to solve a pretty complicated puzzle, and that part really reminded me of the ‘Happy Birthday’ video puzzle in RE7, which I also very much enjoyed, so no complaints there either.

Moreau was quite different too. He needed a bit of both worlds: puzzle-solving with the bridges on the water and combat. I actually felt bad for how pathetic he was, trying so hard to prove himself to his mama. The ‘mother’ tattoo was a nice touch, he definitely would’ve gotten that.

Moving on to Heisenberg, that was actually the best part of the game, and I’m surprised how little people talk about it online. One minute you’re at the top of the map entering his lair, exploring this huge underground factory filled with modified humanoid VR-wearing zombies through endless mazes and corridors, and the next, you look at the map and realize you’ve crossed the entire thing. He was super cocky and it really suited him. His power was so interesting and cool. His character design really stuck with me, especially that old Soviet hand-scale hanging around his neck. And the fact that he was AGAINST Miranda the whole time? That was nice. If I were in Ethan’s place, I would not be going against him, I’d team up with him and then backstab him before he sacrificed my baby.

I loved how sometimes you just knew you were in some deep sh*t. You’re looking at this creepy monster with a chainsaw for a hand, plugged into a computer, just sleeping there, and you know he’s gonna wake up and fight you. So you’ve got, like, ten seconds to prepare mentally.

I hated how you could miss treasures after passing a certain point. I’m a bit of a perfectionist about that, and when I couldn’t go back for Beneviento’s treasure, I started tweaking, same thing when I missed some fish and couldn’t get all the upgrades.

Speaking of upgrades and cooking, DUKE. He is a marvelous creature. I’ve always been a huge fan of the merchant from RE4 and got disappointed when I realized he wouldn’t be here, but when I saw DUKE, my heart stopped for a second. He was everything. His disgusting design, mischievous attitude, and cocky manners really grew on me. His huge little toes, his sausages, his stacked shop, his heavily deformed BELLYBUTTON, and his ‘I don’t give a sh*t’ attitude were all so fun to experience. You’re fighting for your life and he’s just smoking a cigar, reading a book, admiring his ginormous rings on his fat fingers, and waiting for you to show up and make him richer. Yeah, he’s the best. I also really liked how small crystals were hidden throughout the map. It was challenging at first, but when you spotted that little sucker you’d be like, ‘Yeahhhh, more money for me and more goodies from Duke.’

Moving on to a pleasant surprise, Mr. Chris Redfield. I’m gonna be honest, I haven’t played the RE games that had Chris in them, but even for me, he was a symbol of hope, glory, and muscles. I can only imagine how his fanboys felt when he started smoking that cigarette like the edgelord he is.

Lastly, Miranda. First of all, she was beautiful. I don’t get how Lady Dimitrescu and her goth daughters got all the hype. The word I’d use for Miranda would be divine. I really liked her phases as a bird and as a spider, hella cool.

Overall, I’d give the game an 8.5 out of 10. The horror, combat, concept design, creepiness, art, and details were all top-notch, definitely way better than RE7. Also, low-key glad Ethan finally got to rest in peace, he had some tragic stories to tell. Would’ve been cool if Rose was the main character of Requiem. Maybe she is, and just changed her name?! lol. Because of the different concepts, bosses, and maps, it felt like a collage of many games in the best way possible.

Resident Evil Village is one of the best modern entries in the series. It strikes a great balance between the intense, claustrophobic horror of Resident Evil 7 and the more action-heavy style of Resident Evil 4. The result is a game that keeps you on edge but rarely feels overwhelming.

The environments are a standout, each major area has its own distinct style, tone, and type of threat. From the gothic castle to the unsettling dollhouse, the game constantly shifts in ways that keep things interesting. It’s clear Capcom put a lot of care into world-building and pacing.

Combat feels tight and satisfying and while some of the later segments lean more into action, they still maintain tension. The puzzles are a bit light compared to classic RE, but they’re a welcome break from the shooting.

Narratively, it’s more out there than previous games, but it still manages to tie things together in a surprisingly emotional way. Long-time fans will appreciate how it connects with the larger RE universe.

Overall, Village is a polished, well-paced survival horror experience that doesn’t overstay its welcome. Whether you're new to the series or a long-time fan, it’s absolutely worth playing.

[b]Resident Evil Village[/b], o oitavo título principal da franquia [b]Resident Evil[/b], chega como uma experiência que mistura horror, ação e uma narrativa cheia de reviravoltas. Lançado em 2021 pela Capcom, o jogo continua a história de Ethan Winters, protagonista de [b]Resident Evil 7[/b], mergulhando-o em uma vila assombrada por criaturas sobrenaturais e segredos macabros. Com uma atmosfera densa, vilões memoráveis e uma gameplay que equilibra tensão e ação, [b]Village[/b] se consolida como um dos melhores títulos da série.

[h3]História e Narrativa[/h3]
A trama começa com Ethan e sua família vivendo uma vida tranquila, até que um evento trágico os leva a uma vila isolada na Europa Oriental, dominada por seres grotescos e governada por figuras enigmáticas, como a icônica Lady Dimitrescu e seu coven de "filhas". A busca de Ethan para resgatar sua filha, Rosemary, é o motor da narrativa, que mistura elementos de horror gótico, folclore europeu e ficção científica.  

A história é envolvente, com cutscenes cinematográficas e documentos espalhados que aprofundam o lore. Embora alguns fãs critiquem o tom mais "fantástico" em comparação aos jogos anteriores, a narrativa mantém a essência [b]Resident Evil[/b], com conspirações bioterroristas e reviravoltas surpreendentes.

[h3]Gameplay e Mecânicas[/h3]
[b]Village[/b] mescla elementos de survival horror e ação, sem abandonar totalmente o terror psicológico. O combate é mais dinâmico que em [b]RE7[/b], com um arsenal variado (pistolas, espingardas, rifles) e a possibilidade de melhorar armas no Mercador (um retorno bem-vindo de [b]RE4[/b]). A exploração é recompensadora, com quebra-cabeças inteligentes e segredos escondidos.  

Os inimigos variam de lobisomens frenéticos a criaturas biomecânicas, garantindo diversidade nos confrontos. Os chefes são pontos altos, cada um com mecânicas únicas – a perseguição de Lady Dimitrescu e a sequência de [b]House Beneviento[/b] (um capítulo assustador e quase sem combate) são memoráveis.  

[h3]Gráficos e Atmosfera[/h3]
Visualmente, o jogo é deslumbrante. A vila e seus castelos são ricamente detalhados, com iluminação e efeitos sonoros que ampliam a imersão. A direção de arte oscila entre o gótico opressor e o industrial perturbador, criando um mundo coerente e assustador. A dublagem em inglês é competente, mas a versão em português poderia ter sido mais completa.  

[h3]Pontos Negativos[/h3]
Alguns fãs podem estranhar o tom mais "action" em certos momentos, especialmente na reta final, que lembra [b]Resident Evil 6[/b] em seu excesso de explosões. Além disso, o modo [b]Mercenaries[/b], apesar de divertido, não é tão robusto quanto em jogos passados.  

[h3]Veredito Final[/h3]  
[b]Resident Evil Village[/b] é uma experiência eletrizante, que honra o legado da série enquanto inova. Ele pode não assustar tanto quanto [b]RE7[/b], mas compensa com personagens carismáticos, level design criativo e uma campanha cativante. Se você gosta de horror com pitadas de ação e uma narrativa envolvente, esse jogo é imperdível.  

[h2]Nota Final: 9/10[/h2]
[b]Destaques[/b]: Vilões marcantes, atmosfera imersiva, gameplay variada.  
[b]Pontos fracos[/b]: Reta final muito "action", modo Mercenaries limitado.

[h1]Stranger in a Strange Land[/h1]
Evil returns once more in the eighth mainline entry of the franchise. Following a well-received return to form with [b]Resident Evil VII[/b], [b]VIIIage[/b] had the heavy task of proving that the series was truly back on track after years of both narrative and quality missteps... Mission accomplished?

A direct continuation of the seventh game, it once again features Ethan Winters, who thought he could finally enjoy some peace in his new European home with his (rather ungrateful) wife and their newborn daughter, the latest addition to the Winters family. Alas, poor Ethan doesn’t seem to be a lucky man: neck-deep in trouble once again, things go from bad to worse when, one night, a squad forcibly kidnaps his daughter and guns down his wife in the chaos.

Dragged away by the mercenaries to an unknown destination, Ethan wakes up in the middle of a snow-covered forest after the van transporting him crashes, with only one goal in mind: to save his daughter...

[h3]The eyes of horror[/h3]
Once again, the game opts for a first-person perspective, just as effective and well-executed as before, with a generous number of cinematic sequences that fully capitalize on the immersive viewpoint. The immersion is total, and the adventure gripping. That said, a DLC offers the option to play in third-person mode, à la [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] or [b]Resident Evil 4[/b], for those who prefer it. A nice bonus, though it would’ve been even better if it had been free. But hey, Capcom's gotta be Capcom.

[b]VIIIage[/b] builds on the solid foundation laid by the seventh entry but avoids falling into copy-paste territory. Gone are the Louisiana swamps - this time, the action moves to Poland, and the result is visually stunning. If [b]Resident Evil VII[/b] sometimes felt like a clumsy love letter to [b]The Texas Chainsaw Massacre[/b], its sequel takes its cues from classic gothic horror, with [b]Nosferatu[/b] being the most obvious influence. The series thus returns to something closer to its roots, with settings ranging from sprawling manors to opulent castles, and a few new environments that are as intriguing as they are debatable when it comes to coherence.

Not that I’m complaining: in fact, quite the opposite, but one major segment of the game is clearly inspired by [b]Tetsuo: The Iron Man[/b], a sharp tonal shift from the rest of the adventure, both in atmosphere and gameplay. Super cool! But it does come at the cost of immersion.

[h3]"What!... What is this?"[/h3]
This is once again where [b]VIIIage[/b] stumbles: I’ve never expected [b]Resident Evil[/b] to deliver a deep, moving storyline, but the series at least used to offer a lovable cast and a well-maintained, consistent lore, up until the narrative U-turn that was [b]Resident Evil 4[/b]... The plot disasters of the fifth game forced Capcom to revise a lot to keep things going, and it’s clear they’re still struggling to make everything fit, often veering into absurdity while trying. [b]Resident Evil VII[/b] and [b]VIIIage[/b] form a parallel storyline that’s passable at best, but ultimately add little to the greater saga, and what little they do attempt, they don’t do very well.

That said, once the damage is done and can’t really be undone, you might as well go wild and make the ride thrilling.

Compared to the seventh installment, this sequel leans more heavily into action. On higher difficulties than normal, you'll still need to manage your resources carefully during the game's first half, which is no walk in the park. Things get much more explosive after the midway point, opening up the gameplay and giving players more freedom, all while maintaining a solid challenge.

[h3]Gone Shooting[/h3]
[b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a major influence on [b]VIIIage[/b], and its spirit is felt throughout. The first big action sequence is a shameless callback, as intense as it is entertaining. Gameplay-wise, the game borrows heavily from the cult classic: enemies drop ammo, healing items, and money upon defeat, and a traveling merchant offers his services throughout the game, selling gear and upgrading your arsenal.

It’s a bold choice that pays off. While not perfect, the game is undeniably fun, striking a palatable balance between pure Survival Horror and full-blown First-Person Shooter.

A few words about the side modes: The Mercenaries makes its return in a functional, if slightly lazy, version. You’re given a variety of levels where your goal is to go from point A to point B while dispatching enemies along the way, ideally chaining combos to boost your score. The action is intense, and a bit of strategy is needed to optimize your final result. Ethan Winters is the only playable character in the base game, but the DLC adds three distinct characters with unique playstyles: Chris Redfield, Karl Heisenberg, and Lady Dimitrescu, the game’s charismatic antagonists. Each character is fun to play and clearly designed with care, but the mode struggles with balancing issues. Since the levels remain identical regardless of who you play, earning top scores with Ethan is noticeably more challenging than with Lady Dimitrescu. Depending on your patience, going for perfect scores with every character might quickly feel repetitive, but that’s just the nature of score-based modes.

Finally, the story DLC “Shadows of Rose” gives you 4 to 6 hours of gameplay with Ethan’s daughter, sixteen years after the events of the main game... I’ll be honest: it doesn’t add anything meaningful to the main story, and while not bad, it’s rather average. Played in third person, Rose revisits some familiar locations and explores new ones. She has supernatural powers that come in handy on her journey, which is far less intense than her father’s. The story veers into full-blown B-movie territory, flirting with the absurd and supernatural, further weakening ties to the franchise’s origins, but at this point, who’s counting?

One highlight worth mentioning: the DLC includes what is arguably the scariest moment in the entire game: a short but excellently crafted sequence where Rose is stalked and watched by deeply unsettling entities in the Beneviento mansion... Absolutely brilliant!

[h3]Mission accomplished[/h3]
Visually stunning, undeniably fun and intense, [b]Resident Evil VIIIage[/b] is a generous, well-crafted game that’s easy to recommend. Don’t expect much from the story, and be ready to accept some of the usual modern gaming annoyances (yes, we’re talking about the infamous yellow paint), but all in all, there’s little to complain about in this eighth entry. It wraps up the Winters arc in style: perhaps not perfectly, but with confidence, and cements the franchise’s comeback.

Today is a good day: a good day to die.

He’s not the hero we expected. He’s the duct-taped, emotionally exhausted icon we got.

Resident Evil Village taught me two things: trust no one, and first aid juice fixes everything.

Imagine binge-playing every Resident Evil game from 2 through 7, getting hyped by the momentum and then... running headfirst into this. It’s like the series took a long, suspenseful inhale with RE7, then coughed up a confusing mess of tone shifts, awkward writing, and zombies who walk faster than the plot.

The pacing is so slow, I was pressing my analog stick through the controller hoping the character might break into a jog. The tension that once defined the series, causing you to take your sweet time peering around every corner and opening every door, now replaced by open areas and plenty of daylight... yet still thought it was a good idea to keep your movement speed the same as the other games, giving you nothing but time as you nature walk between objectives to critique every detail of every bit of the story... so that's exactly what I did.

Without spoiling anything—let’s just say it feels like it was written by someone who read a one-paragraph summary of RE7, ignored the entire series lore, and then shouted vague emotional keywords at an AI until a script fell out.

There are moments where the game almost shines… and then it trips over its own mold-covered boots. If you love Resident Evil, you’ll either be heartbroken, confused, or too numb to care by the time the credits roll.

Capcom, I love you… but this one deserved a rewrite, a retcon, and a reality check. EMPHASIS ON THE RETCON!!!

So why do I recommend the game after that trashing? Because the game is gorgeous and fun and the map design is really well done. The rant above is for the story fans. If Capcom keeps going down this path, they'll end up like Disney—irrelevant, alienating their core audience, and wondering why no one shows up to watch their next Snow White reboot. Don’t piss off the fanbase, folks.

Also there was too much focus on looking for objects... felt like an Easter egg hunt for plastic eggs filled with vegetables placed in the most diabolical locations... like the fiberglass sheets in the attic. I just don't wanna.

[b]Overall: [/b] 6/10

RE8 is a significant improvement; however, it is a poor man’s RE4 copy. If you want to finish Ethan’s story, be my guest; however, afterwards, play R2R and R4R and see the vast difference in storytelling, gameplay, and character growth.

[b]Music: [/b] 6/10

Voice acting is, for the most part, a significant improvement. More so for Ethan who actually has some lines now and at least feels more like a human being. The music is different. NPC’s have distinct voices too, and weapons are satisfying to listen.

[b]Visuals: [/b] 7/10

It looks good overall. Each zone is diverse on it’s own way, character design is great, weapons look unique, and their upgrades too. However, considering everything Ethan goes through, he could have had at least some visual changes through the story (besides the first one). This is more prominent in 3rd person where he gets (by story cutscenes) cut, stabbed, impaled, and more, yet his clothes only have one minor change.

[b]Gameplay: [/b] 5/10

I feel like this is barely passable. Gunplay is good, movement and interactions can be a bit clunky in 3rd person. Maps that tell you that you are missing stuff or what is locked is always a plus. However, my biggest complaint is the lack of diversity with the enemies, more so considering that it is basically the same formula as 4.

Here is a list of all the enemies, bar bosses, you face. Melee werewolf, ranged werewolf (so rare you forget they exist), werewolf with a helmet, big wolf (mini boss), giant werewolf (miniboss), vampire ghoul, vampire ghoul with helmet, flying bat, tin soldier. And with the exception of the flying bat, all enemies are bullet sponges that can take 3 - 4 headshots.

On contrast, let’s see at just the simple villagers in RE4. Melee villagers (both female and male versions), crossbow villagers, dynamite villagers, bullhead (mini boss), chainsaw man (mini boss), chainsaw sisters (mini boss), villagers parasite phase 1, villagers parasite phase 2, wolves. I have just as many enemies within the 1st third of the game in RE4, than RE8 has throughout the whole experience. Plus they have more diverse designs.


[b]Story: [/b] 5/10

The story relies on character assassination to succeed in a way so stupid that if you have known Chris from previous games (let’s not count 7) you really need to power through it. Outside of that, let’s see the positives. It’s a more personal story, it has some great interactions with the villagers (short as they are), some NPC’s are really great and fun, the 1st and 4th lord are interesting, they practically dropped and ignored the mold (which was a dumb idea to have it in RE7, so that is a big plus).
Now, on to the negatives. If you have played 7, then boy, the two plot twists won’t surprise you at all. They were so blatant that you can’t help by laugh at them repeating a plot point from the previous game. Absolutely abysmal world lore. Again, using RE4 as an example, even though the villagers have been under the thrall for a significantly shorter time than in RE8, you have a lot of info about them, the impact it had in their lives, the way the parasites work, how everything happened. Here, they up the ante with 4 lords a village that has been under their joke for at least 80 years, and somehow, have even less information. You basically learn nothing about the lords, the villagers might as well be indoctrinated for how so little they add to the story.
What’s the next thing, BOW’s so to say, previous games, anyone, had “science” behind them, and the BOW’s made sense. Here, it makes zero sense and might as well just say it is supernatural or witchcraft. You have werewolves expy’s, ladies that turn into bugs and have to drink blood,  a woman that possesses dolls, a metalbender, an abomination and it is basically glossed over. There is absolutely no reason for that to happen as per the lore, and are basically asspulls.

My other objection is that the Resident Evil games always have been about being desperately low on ammo and health, but there are far too many moments in this game where you spend 75% of your resources only to realize that you are in a situation with infinitely respawning foes and you have to follow the scripted path exactly to progress, or an enemy that is invulnerable and again you have to follow a scripted path or it's insta-death.

I am giving this game a negative review not because it is a bad game (it isn't), but because this game does not deserve its "overwhelmingly positive" Steam rating. Halo 2 deserves its overwhelmingly positive reception. Expedition 33 deserves its overwhelmingly positive reviews. Factorio deserves its overwhelmingly positive reviews. But this 7/10 game? No way.

CAUTION SPOILERS AHEAD

First, to give the game credit where it is due. The atmosphere of the game, particularly in the first half, was quite good. I experienced a few good scares exploring Dimitrescu's castle and Beneviento's house, and the general tension being built up (through setting, sound effects, lighting, etc.) was great. Additionally, exploring the village for the first time was creepy and intriguing. Heisenberg's factory (4th area) was not particularly scary for me, but it was still cool visually -- the "cyber-zombie" aesthetic from Warhammer 40K was present and well done here. I also enjoyed the puzzles and backtracking/exploration, which RE has always done well. Lastly, I think the bosses were better than RE7 overall -- though that isn't saying very much. Two bosses that stuck out to me positively were Sturm and Miranda.

Now, to talk negatives. Firstly, the characters in this game are just not good. The voice acting is bad and the dialogue is stupid -- a particularly offensive example that comes to mind is Ethan telling Dimitrescu "No you're the one who's cursed" while they are in a fight to the death. Chris' character is also pretty bad; he feels like a tryhard sigma in the same way as the main character of Atomic Heart. The lore snippets/journal entries are also written in an unrealistic and stilted way, feeling more like something you would find on a fan wiki page than in a triple-A game. The actual narrative is decent -- I liked Miranda's story and the way in which they tied the mold back to the original Umbrella story -- but it is presented in a stilted and uncompelling way. The dialogue, storytelling, and voice acting feel like something you would hear at a local D&D table. Immersion and atmosphere wise, the game fell off a cliff for me starting in the third region (Moreau's swamp).

As I mentioned above, parts of the gameplay loop are fun. Shooting enemies is mostly fun, and buying upgrades from the Duke is rewarding. However, the game still has a certain jankiness that is unacceptable coming from a studio as large as Capcom. The gunplay and gun sound effects feel like something pulled from 2010 Xbox or from present-day COD Mobile. No weight to the weapons, stiff animations, tinny sound effects. The sniper rifle literally feels and sounds like the Intervention from Black Ops 2, a game from fifteen years ago. The interactivity with the environment is similarly stiff and lacking. The knife doesn't leave marks in the wall, plant vases can't be broken by a gun, patrolling boss enemies don't react to the player shooting the environment and making tons of noise. It feels like you are walking around inside of a diorama rather than an active world.

In conclusion, I would buy this game on sale, or if you are looking for something to kill the time in the disappointing modern gaming landscape. The first half of the game is quite good, and I feel like I got my $10 worth from it. However, this game is absolutely [i]NOT[/i] any kind of masterpiece that deserves an overwhelmingly positive score.

I really enjoyed Resident Evil Village. It’s undeniably entertaining, full of creepy moments, awesome boss fights, and a ton of atmosphere. The visuals are stunning, the environments are varied, and there’s always something new around the corner to keep you on edge.

The bosses are a major highlight : Lady Dimitrescu is iconic, and Donna Beneviento absolutely steals the show. Her section is hands-down one of the scariest in the game, and the DLC takes that horror to a whole new level with those horrifying Mia Winters mannequins. Seriously, I wasn’t expecting that level of psychological terror in an RE game.

Ethan is still a likeable protagonist, even if he's kind of bland. He’s a solid everyman, easy to root for, but not particularly exciting. Rose, in the DLC, falls into that classic “troubled teen with a dark past” trope. Her story wraps up nicely, but she felt more like a plot device than a fully developed character.

One thing that really disappointed me was the castle section. It had so much potential, it could’ve easily been the climax of the game, but instead it’s over way too soon. Meanwhile, we spend forever in Heisenberg’s factory, which just felt tedious and overstayed its welcome. Also, the Chris section was cool, but painfully short, felt like a missed opportunity to add some weight to the story.

Now, here’s my biggest gripe: as fun as the game is, it doesn’t really feel like Resident Evil anymore. Lycans, vampires, ghost stuff, weird fungus powers, it all feels like we stepped into another franchise entirely. Besides Chris, some Umbrella references, and Miranda’s backstory linking to previous games, this could’ve been its own IP. It’s horror, sure. It’s action, definitely. But is it RE? I’m not so sure.

Still, Village is a very solid game. The scares are real, the combat is satisfying, and the world is super immersive. Just don’t expect the same Resident Evil flavor we’re used to, this is more like RE gone full gothic fantasy.

Resident Evil 8: Village is a standout entry in the long-running Resident Evil franchise, successfully balancing the slasher horror of Resident Evil 7 with the more action-oriented gameplay of Resident Evil 4. A continuation of Ethan Winters’ story from visceral slasher story from Resident Evil 7 Biohazard with a spiritual follow up to the magic that Resident Evil 4 brought. Capcom has managed to create an experience that feels both familiar and fresh, delivering a game that is a thrill full of campy horror along with genuine unsettling terrifying story beats. The RE engine continues to absolutely blow me away and is so underutilized when it comes to the first person perspective. The FPS perspective in Resident Evil is controversial but this game is the best argument for it because the RE engine feels effortless here. Not only is the game incredibly optimized but it looks and feels like god. This is truly a simulator where the controls are just that effortless. From the moment you step into the eerie, snow-covered village, the atmosphere grips you and it pretty much turned into a ‘Try Not To Screenshot Challenge’ for me. The game’s visuals are stunning, with beautifully crafted gothic architecture, creepy dollhouses, humble yet eerie village homes, grotesque underground factories and most of all character and monster models. Something that I don’t think gets enough talk or praise for this game is how detailed and beautifully horrifying the lycan enemies are. There is so much love and care that is put into this game but something that really has always shined were the lycans. They might be my favorite in the series for how intelligently they move and avoid the players gunfire. I actually love how visceral and “in your face” some of these enemies get. If you allow a lycan to get close enough to take a chomp out of Ethan it’s terrifying and completely detailed. Lycans also might be my favorite in the game for how satisfying it is to land a fatal shotgun blast to the head to these guys. Might be just as good as landing a headshot with the sniper in RE4 on a villager. The sound design earns praise as every creak, growl, and whisper throws players deeper into the experience. One of the game’s greatest strengths is its distinct sections of the village. The story brings Ethan to face 4 lords of Village and each of them provides different genres of ‘Resident Evil horror’, alternating between classic Resident Evil exploration puzzle-solving, and high-intensity combat. In my experience some of the pacing of these sections could be jarring as some get too overindulgent. Prime example being late in the game when playing as Chris Redfeild the game straight up turns into Call of Duty and the dollhouse very briefly does a serviceable at best imitation of Silent Hills P.T. On one hand this keeps the experience engaging and rarely allows for a dull moment but at times it will pull you out of the experience. The cast of villains are great especially Lady Dimitrescu as her screen presence demanded attention. Lady Dimitrescu in particular, became an instant icon not just for her towering presence, but for the charisma and terror she brought to the experience. I also enjoyed her section the best by far as it was most in line with classic survival horror. There aren’t really stand outs in the overall cast of characters. This is definitely the case for Ethan, the protagonist. My first experience with this game back upon its release I hated Ethan in this game as he came off like a clueless idiot; the stereotypical naive horror story character. Upon this repeat experience I’ve grown to appreciate Ethan as he does add to the campiness and the sense of the game not taking itself too terribly serious but he definitely is just another bland young ‘dude’ in a game. His willingness to continue on fighting these horrors for the sake of his daughter carries the narrative and upon the completion of his arc the emotional payoff is one of my favorite moments in any Resident Evil game. Combat in Village is fluid, satisfying and incredibly underrated. Weapons feel powerful, and managing resources like ammo and healing items adds a strategic layer that makes every encounter meaningful just like RE4 felt all those years back. You begin the game with little to no supplies to your inventory and finding materials in the village, upgrading guns, upgrading Ethan was an extremely satisfying gameplay loop. It’s a shame The Duke has to always be compared to the merchant in RE4 because I think The Duke is super interesting and stands as a great addition to the wacky cast of this game. The biggest flaw with this game is how the story completely incinerates if you think about it for more than a second. Why doesn’t Chris just tell Ethan the situation from the beginning? I understand the reason is because Chris killing Ethan’s ‘wife’ and taking his daughter Rose is all to drive the narrative and Ethan forward but the only reason Chris can give later in the story is the whole “I couldn’t get you involved bro.. you’d get yourself hurt. Ok bro?” cliche. Really? Resident Evil was never about the story and actually is more well known for having “it’s so bad it’s funny” kind of charm to their narratives but this is just incredibly cheesy. Overall very dumb and just the easiest way to plot twist “Chris Redfeild wasn’t all of a sudden the villain of a Resident Evil story.” No one believed for a second that Chris was a bad guy especially those that are long standing fans from the first game. For what this game is, it’s a great experience. A wacky, campy, take on vampires, werewolves, monsters and spooky environments. Resident Evil 8 is a thrill ride and is an entry that frustrated me at first with its direction, but I now appreciate what it is and that’s plain ol’ good video game fun.

I really enjoyed RE7 for the big changes it made to the RE formula. That game was much more focused on pure horror, trying constantly to unsettle the player and be as utterly terrifying as possible. I was, however, not a fan at all of the combat, which I felt was very one-note with a severe lacking in enemy variety. Granted, there were not a ton of enemies in general, but there were multiple times where I would skip entire combat encounters by running past them. Most importantly regarding RE7, I was really invested in the Winters family, and that was what excited me about RE8, among other things that have been meme-ified on the internet (looking at you, Lady Dimitrescu).

RE8 reminded me a ton of RE4, which was clearly the main inspiration. There's a much larger emphasis on combat, with a lot more weapons and enemy variety. It also brings werewolves and mechanized zombies into the fold as enemies, and I love it. The lycans in particular look awesome and scary. Similar to RE7, there's quite a bit of exploration and puzzling solving, but none of it is particularly challenging or intricate. RE8 also has a ton of really detailed and atmospheric locations, and it's clear the love and attention that was poured into all these places. 

Lastly, I really enjoyed the story in this game. Ethan makes for a great protagonist, and this game does what few other RE games have done in establishing a colorful and interesting cadre of villains. There are still some weak points to be sure, such as Mia being completely underwritten across these two games, but I overall loved it. This is probably the most fun I've had playing an RE game since RE4, and that says quite a lot.

First playthrough review time.

Resident Evil Village is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, continuing the story with a first-person perspective and improving on many aspects of the previous game. Later, they have also added a third-person perspective, giving players a new way to experience the game. The environments are detailed and well-crafted, ranging from large castles to dense forests, with a main area that connects different locations. While some areas are more impressive than others, the overall design creates a strong and immersive atmosphere.

The horror elements are less intense compared to Resident Evil 7, which I found to be the scariest due to its intense atmosphere and jump scares. However, the action and level design build on the previous game, adding more depth and variety. The story unfolds steadily, with new details becoming clearer as the game progresses. The game also includes two DLCs. One is The Shadows of Rose, a new story campaign DLC, and the other is The Mercenaries: Additional Orders, a survival mode where players must defeat waves of enemies within a time limit.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is an engaging survival horror game with impressive visuals and a compelling narrative. 

Note: The game does not explain how to counter-push enemies or how to swap grenade launcher ammo. I play most games using keyboard and mouse, and after checking the entire menu without finding this information, I found it in a guide. To counter-push an enemy, you need to hold Space to block as the enemy is about to attack. Immediately press Space again to push the enemy back if the block is timed correctly. To swap grenade launcher ammo, aim the launcher with the Right Mouse Click and press F, which is the interaction key, to switch the ammo type.

[h1]A Balance Hard to Get Right[/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a phenomenal game through and through, featuring magnificent level, environment, and enemy design, thrilling action, and a strong art style. However, while the first half offers a great survival horror experience, the second half leans too heavily into action for my taste. Resident Evil 4 has stood for 20 years as the pinnacle of action-focused survival horror, and that formula sadly hasn't been fully replicated since. That said, Resident Evil Village comes very close, close enough that it stands out as one of the best attempts yet. That alone makes RE8 a great game in its own right.

As mentioned, the game has two very distinct halves. Castle Dimitrescu has become one of my favorite hub areas in any survival horror game. Given that the castle section in RE4 is my favorite location in the genre, I might be a bit biased toward that kind of setting, but still, Dimitrescu castle is simply marvelous in its design. While the rest of the game doesn't quite reach the same heights, it's still impressive. I especially enjoyed the non-combat segment in House Beneviento, though the Factory section felt significantly weaker by comparison.

Overall, RE8 is a very solid survival horror experience, even if it occasionally struggles with balancing its action elements. Still, I have to say that the combat is easily the second best in the series, right after RE4, and that's no small feat.

After finally playing Resident Evil Village (RE8), I can confidently say it’s an amazing experience and definitely lives up to RE7. While it’s generally less scary than RE7, it still delivers a fantastic balance of horror and action—never leaning too heavily into either. One major exception is House Beneviento, which was pure psychological horror and puzzles—easily my favorite part of the game.

On the downside, I found some of the bosses on Standard difficulty a bit too easy. I managed to first-try every boss except the final one, which made combat feel a little less tense at times. That said, it didn’t take away from how much I enjoyed the game overall.

RE8 is now one of my favorite entries in the franchise. Highly recommend giving it a shot!
