Resident Evil Village: A Triumph of Gothic Dread and Modern Design

Resident Evil Village stands tall as a masterful blend of survival horror and modern action, pushing the boundaries of the franchise while respecting its roots. The game transports you to a world steeped in atmospheric dread, where every shadow and echo tells a story of dark secrets and relentless terror.

Atmosphere and Visuals
From the first glimpse of the mist-shrouded village to the imposing silhouette of its mysterious castle, the visuals in Resident Evil Village are nothing short of breathtaking. Capcom’s attention to detail shines in every environment—from the quaint, eerie hamlets to the grotesque, labyrinthine interiors of ancient fortresses. The superb lighting and texture work not only anchor you in a world of gothic horror but also play a pivotal role in building suspense, where every crevice and candlelit corridor promises both beauty and danger.

Gameplay and Mechanics
The gameplay in Resident Evil Village strikes a perfect balance between visceral action and strategic survival. The refined controls and intuitive over-the-shoulder perspective deliver intense, heart-pounding combat encounters while maintaining the delicate resource management the series is known for. Each enemy, whether humanoid monstrosities or supernatural abominations, forces you to adapt and plan, keeping the adrenaline high. The game’s mix of exploration, puzzle-solving, and open combat sequences ensures that no two moments feel the same—continuously evolving the experience in ways that reward both cautious planning and daring risk-taking.

Narrative and Immersion
At its core, the narrative of Resident Evil Village is an engrossing tapestry woven with threads of folklore, tragedy, and mystery. You assume the role of a determined protagonist on a quest that blurs the lines between human malice and supernatural horror. The story layers the personal stakes against a backdrop of ancient curses and eerie legends, creating an emotional journey that is as compelling as the adrenaline-fueled encounters. The richly detailed character interactions and subtle narrative nods to earlier titles further enrich the lore and deepen the immersion.

Audio and Sound Design
Sound design in Resident Evil Village is masterfully crafted to evoke a constant sense of unease. From the creaking of old wood in abandoned structures to the distant, haunting laughter echoing in dark corners, every sonic detail is a deliberate choice to enhance the terror. The dynamic soundtrack shifts between haunting melodies and pulse-pounding rhythms, perfectly syncing with the game’s shifting moods. These auditory cues are not just background ambiance—they are integral to the storytelling, heightening anticipation and rounding out the immersive experience.

Conclusion
Resident Evil Village is a shimmering beacon in the world of survival horror—a game that dares to innovate while holding firm to the elements that made its predecessors legendary. Its impeccable marriage of stunning visuals, immersive sound design, and multifaceted gameplay creates a thrilling, unforgettable experience that both honors tradition and redefines the genre. For those eager to lose themselves in a meticulously crafted world where every decision could mean the difference between salvation and doom, this entry stands as a must-play masterpiece of gothic terror and modern design.

In exploring the evolution of horror gaming, consider how modern mechanics can coexist with the chilling aesthetics of classic tales. What personal moments of dread or triumph have defined your journey through horror, and which elements of narrative intrigue keep you coming back for more?

The story begins in a truly unexpected and shocking way, which immediately hooks the player. Then there's the village—of course. The scenery is stunning, and I loved the mysterious Slavic aesthetic. I took my time exploring and capturing screenshots throughout.

However, I encountered my first problems during the initial battle. It was confusing and frustrating to fight the Lycans with practically no proper weapons. I had to search online just to figure out that the goal was to survive the seemingly impossible attack by running from one house to another until a cutscene triggered.

Then came Dimitrescu Castle. Once again, the aesthetics and interior design were amazing. But I ran into more issues, this time with the Daughters. It was confusing and frustrating because the game provides no information or hints on how to deal with specific enemies, you have to figure it out yourself somehow (I played on standard difficulty). I wasted almost all my ammo on Cassandra before turning to YouTube and learning that you’re NOT supposed to fight her at that point, but rather run or avoid her.

Several side quests were equally infuriating—like the one with the hanging lamps you’re supposed to light up somehow. The effort rarely felt worth the reward too. That’s one of the core issues with this game: you’re constantly running around collecting items, unsure of when or where to use them, and exploring areas without knowing if you’re even meant to yet. The game allows it, which adds to the confusion and often makes you feel lost. There were times when I thought there was still more to do in a specific location—I had unused items—but the game gave the impression that the story in that area was wrapping up. A major reason for this confusion, I think, was the way optional treasures (like crystals or cabinets you needed lockpick for) were marked on the map the same way as key story items and puzzle elements.

After finishing the Castle mission, I began to understand the game’s mechanics and how it expects players to navigate, which made it more enjoyable. Still, the design is not very intuitive.

As a PC player, I also experienced technical issues with fullscreen mode—it was best not to touch anything during gameplay, or the game would lag or even crash. The achievements are also horrendously bugged. I followed YouTube tutorials step-by-step to shatter all the windows in Dimitrescu Castle for the "Hooligan" achievement and destroy all the goats for the "Heretic" one, but neither unlocked.

In summary, the story is genuinely captivating, and the in-game world is beautiful and atmospheric. But the mission design and certain side quests can be poorly executed and unintuitive, sometimes to the point of making me want to quit entirely. I do recommend the game overall, but you might need some help from other players or YouTube content creators. :)

RE8 is fittingly RE4(2005) 2.0, an on-rails action experience that takes you from one set-piece to the next; except that Ethan Winter is comparatively bland compared to Leon S. Kennedy.

Writing is pretty bad, and the game mentioning the plot contrivances doesn't really fix it. The boulder punching a-hole should have told Ethan what was going on, but doesn't for the sake of an early-game mystery. The antagonists' plans are about as absurd and nonsensical as RE4, and felt the need to give Ethan a Jar-collect-athon instead of utilizing what was already in their possession; and then Ethan conveniently gives the Jars back under the mere suggestion of some guy who wasn't playing a part in the main antagonist's plans. Shadows of Rose continues on the bad writing through miserable attempts to pull at the audience's heartstrings, failing to actually add to the main game's ending, and the increasingly absurd decision to not give Ethan a face.

Gameplay-wise it's one of the more action-oriented RE, with faster-moving werewolves this time instead of shambling zombies (though it does have those too, moroaica). The castle is reminiscent of RE2r(2019), with you exploring and puzzling through a large building from attic to basement, whilst an unkillable entity occasionally chases you about. Beneviento house strips you of weapons and transitions  into a more traditional & atmospheric horror. The reservoir is a water level with platforming puzzles that ends with you fighting a big fish, reminiscent of the lake in RE4, though you do get to shoot more than harpoons this time. The last set-piece shifts to industrial setting, which I guess complete's RE4's set-piece list (village, lake, castle, military camp).

Difficulty option is rather poorly balanced for first playthrough, trying to play on hardcore or VoS on the first playthrough is inadvisable due to everything being ridiculously bullet-spongy with un-upgraded weapons from NG+, coupled with less ammo; if you're avoiding fights (e.g. optional bosses) to conserve ammo, you are missing out on content. On the other hand you can breeze through VoS on NG+ with the easiest-to-unlock infinite ammo weapon. I think the difficulty options could use better descriptors (e.g. include health increase percentages) or be more customizable.

I like inventory tetris and all, but making crafting ingredients stack outside of inventory takes away from it a bit. Part of RE4 was crafting herbs together to save space in the inventory, in RE8 Ethan can store large quantities of metal scraps, herbs, gunpowder, and chemical fluid in his pocket dimension, which conveniently only takes up space if he crafts them into something.

If you're going to design for replayability, please let players skip the long-@$$ opening on subsequent playthroughs.

After the terrifying experience I had with Biohazard, I gotta say that Resident Evil Village has to be the most fun I had in this franchise. It's not as scary as 7 but I still had a blast playing it. It’s creepy, chaotic, and kind of insane in the best possible way. It doesn’t always hit perfectly, but when it works, it really works.

First off, I really liked the pacing, it's definitely one of the game’s biggest strengths. It constantly throws new environments, enemies, and gameplay styles at you, and somehow it all blends together without feeling disjointed. The village setting is incredibly atmospheric, and I loved how it acted as a central hub that slowly opened up as you progressed. Each area tied to the Four Lords felt distinct, from the gothic horror of Castle Dimitrescu to the psychological nightmare that was House Beneviento. It keeps things fresh without dragging any section out too long.

The combat is satisfying, especially once you start upgrading your weapons and crafting more efficiently. It’s not as slow and claustrophobic as Resident Evil 7, but it still has that survival horror edge. I also liked how much more confident Ethan feels this time around. He’s still not a super soldier, but he can hold his own.

That being said tho, I feel like the story is completely off the rails this time around, and while that’s not necessarily a bad thing, some moments definitely feel like they stretch the suspension of disbelief a bit too far, even for Resident Evil standards. The tone shifts can be jarring. One second you're in a full-blown horror sequence, and the next you're in a shootout that feels pulled from an action movie. It doesn’t ruin the experience, but it does make the story feel a bit uneven. Also, a few of the boss fights, especially later on, feel more style than substance.

Overall, I had a great time with Resident Evil Village. It’s fast-paced, entertaining, and packed with variety. It might not be as grounded or scary as RE7, but it makes up for it with style, creativity, and straight-up fun. If you’re into survival horror with a bit of madness thrown in, this one’s worth playing.

Resident Evil Village veers a little off course from the return to horror that RE7 provided, but its prioritization of fun gives it the edge over its predecessor. Past its story and first person perspective, Village seems to take more inspiration from RE4 than RE7.

Village could be disappointing to a fan of the claustrophobic and dark corridors of RE7. It's more action focused, with a surplus of ammo and enemies to use it on, and only a few (but great) horror segments. Ethan is no longer an everyman, losing his most immersive trait, and he lacks the charisma found in other RE protagonists. A more immersive horror experience could have been expected after RE7, but it does not detract from how good of a game Village is.

Importantly, Village is crazy fun. Enemies and encounters are varied, and the gunplay itself is akin to a first-person RE4. The story is standard Resident Evil; melodramatic and paced kind of strangely, but entertaining. The Four Lords of the Village have well-written dialogue and lore, making them great antagonists to the slightly stiff personality of Ethan. Their respective locations are diversely designed and allow for their unique characterization through the setting. Horror may take a backseat, but the segments where it shines through are strong.

Resident Evil Village's jack of all trades approach makes it one of the most accessible and yet strongest entries in the series. It's pure, well-designed entertainment that is fun and hard to put down.

VIIlage is a strange entry in the RE franchise. It's a hybrid of RE7's movement and combat mechanics (although sped up) and RE4's exploration, progression and encounter design. In theory, this should be an instant win, an absolute classic, but RE8 feels like it's not sure how to properly combine those design ideologies.

[h3]Combat[/h3]
The most grating component of this game, specifically, enemy design. Your main foe, the lycans, are hyper agile, tanky, deal a crapload of damage and seem to have this nasty habit of reading your inputs whenever you take aim at them, so EVERY single one of them requires aim correction. They also suffer from a severe lack of appropriate feedback upon receiving damage, with this issue being even worse in terms of thralls (zombies) and mini-bosses.

[h3]Bosses[/h3]
Speaking of bosses, while they are a visual spectacle each, they are not very exciting in terms of mechanics or personality. Lady D does most of the heavy lifting both in marketing materials and the first act of the game, and when you're done with her there's a void left in her place until you get to Heisenberg, who I personally like a whole lot for his banter and taunting.

[h3]Environments[/h3]
Environments seem to be heavily "inspired" by RE4, with a village, castle, lake and factory/military base; however they are fairly constricted in terms of exploration and scale. The vilage is also more of a hub area, as after first clearing it, very little interesting encounters happen there and most of your time there is spent alone, just rummaging through the abandoned houses.

Boy, for how much negative stuff I have to say about this game, it must not be worth it, yeah? Well, if you're looking for an action survival horror fix it's hard to beat an entry in the Resident Evil franchise. The first playthrough of VIIlage is really magical, it checks all the boxes and it's a good conclusion to the story of Ethan. Don't try it of Village of Shadows difficulty though, you're gonna hate yourself.

Resident Evil Village is a wild, ambitious ride through a nightmare landscape of gothic horror, fairy tale grotesquery, and relentless action. As the direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, it retains the first-person perspective and intimate terror but broadens its scope considerably—both in narrative scale and gameplay variety.

You once again step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, now a man worn thin by trauma and tragedy. After his peaceful life is shattered (again), Ethan finds himself in a remote European village teetering between reality and dark folklore. What unfolds is part Bram Stoker, part Grimm Brothers, and part Resident Evil 4 on steroids—and somehow, it works.

Visually, the game is stunning. The RE Engine continues to impress, rendering icy mountains, decaying mansions, and fog-choked forests with terrifying beauty. The village itself is a character, evolving and unraveling as you explore its corners, meet its twisted inhabitants, and uncover its secrets.

And then there’s her—Lady Dimitrescu. Towering, charismatic, and instantly iconic, she’s just one of four lords ruling over the village. Each lord’s domain is distinct: Castle Dimitrescu oozes classic vampire dread, House Beneviento delivers psychological horror at its peak, Moreau’s reservoir is tragic and disgusting, and Heisenberg’s factory leans into mechanical madness. It’s this variety that keeps the game fresh throughout its runtime.

Gameplay-wise, Village strikes a deft balance between survival horror and action. Ammo is scarce but not cruelly so, enemies are dangerous but manageable, and the combat feels more refined than its predecessor. Inventory management, weapon upgrades, and crafting return with satisfying depth, bolstered by the Merchant-like Duke—a welcome homage to RE4.

Where Village stumbles slightly is in tone. The jump between grounded horror and near-fantastical action might feel jarring for some. The story, too, leans into the absurd more than ever, especially in its final act. But in the context of Resident Evil’s long, campy history, it’s all part of the charm.

Resident Evil Village is a confident, stylish sequel that successfully blends atmospheric horror with pulse-pounding action. It may not always play it safe, but its boldness pays off. A gothic horror thrill ride that both honors and reinvents the franchise’s legacy.

It's named "Village" because the most beloved area of Resident Evil 4 is the village. It has the same merchant, who even calls back to one of the RE4 merchant's lines and says he's an old friend of his. The same inventory, shooting crows, shooting treasures that are hanging from places, combining treasures to sell them for more, upgrading weapons, even the same opening sequence where you're against overwhelming odds and are literally saved by the bell.

   So, make no mistake. This game is trying to replicate what made RE4 so successful. That'd be fine. I love RE4. But it fails by a wide margin. You don't use the merchant to upgrade your favourite weapon. You use the merchant to upgrade the latest weapon, which is so significantly more powerful than the previous one, that sticking with what you had because you think it's cooler is a big handicap. Also, the guns feel like they have no impact. The shotgun sounds like you popped some confetti, and taking an enemy's head off with it feels like you just punctured a bag of urine. Lastly, the combat situations aren't interesting enough like in RE4, where you have multitudes of different area layouts that have a unique feel to them, and different strategies that you can try. 

   But that's not all. The game doesn't just try to replicate RE4's success. It also tries to be a survival horror game. And it fails even harder at that. It's just so linear and scripted. The pieces of the puzzles are just given to you when you need them. The chase sequences just require you to go around your pursuer, which takes no effort. There are no decisions to be made, just walk along the only available path. No decisions, no chance of failure, no tension. The spooky environmental sound effects have no actual meaning. It's not like, for example, hearing the zombies moaning in the next room and being afraid to open the door. In this game, if you hear a piece of glass breaking behind you, there's no one actually there. It's just a sound effect. The writer's pen is too visible, and the illusion falls apart too easily.

   Then there are the characters and the story. I don't expect much in this department in these games, so this is my least important gripe. But it's all bad. Ethan's remarks are just plain stupid most of the time. The villains aren't bad in concept, but they are amateurishly written and acted. The plot doesn't make sense and yes, even a zombie game has to make at least some sense. Characters withholding information from other characters, for no good reason other than to keep the player guessing, is just bad writing.

   So yeah, I'm dumbfounded by how bad this game is. It gets nothing right. I don't like writing too much on Steam reviews, but sometimes I feel like I have to prove I'm not just being a contrarian. Prove it to whom? To you, kind stranger, who might receive this message in a bottle on your quest for your next game to play. Skip this one. It's a waste of time.

This is a good game. A good game that I can't personally recommend because of how much it disappointed me, especially in comparison to resident evil 7.

By far my biggest issue with this game is how it completely ditches the kind of self-serious, true horror tone that its predecessor revolutionized and perfected. RE7 wasn't just serious scary horror, it was grotesque and personal. Like your wife chopping off your hand. Like being fed maggot soup until you die. The framing of it, the intimacy of it, the skin-crawling creepiness of it. It was just so much darker, so much more calculated in constructing a horrifically phenomenal experience that no other game had ever come close to accomplishing. So to see this sequel completely ditch and abandon all that brilliance for the sake of standardized and toned-down experience felt very very disappointing. It felt like I was playing a discounted version of RE7 that just happened to have a much higher budget. 

To be clear, if this is your first resident evil game or you're someone that isn't that invested in the franchise, you will most likely love this game. Most people will probably love this game. It's got good puzzles, good graphics, great set pieces filled with memorable cut scenes, excellent character designs, fun shooting and a very by-the-books story that the average person will enjoy. This game is essentially a theme park style ghost train of horror that will cart you from exhibition to exhibition, giving you that same short-lived adrenaline rush you’d get from a roller coaster. And yet it never achieves the sort of tonal or thematic congruence that RE7 had. and thus just ends up feeling like a downgrade compared to it.

For every feat this game achieves, it fails on two others.  This game has a very weak and forgettable cast of characters, laughably embarrassing plot lines and very disappointing boss encounters that took me out of the experience and robbing me of the X-factor that Resident Evil games live and die by. This one certainly dies by it for me.

It's difficult to start a review of these modern Resident Evil games without taking a moment to mention the impact that Resident Evil 7: Biohazard had on not just the franchise, but the genre as a whole. While survival horror had never truly gone away, it was essentially dead in the AAA space, and RE7 had proven an excellent example of what a high-budget, modern survival horror experience could be. While not all of these newer RE games have entirely hit the mark, the series is certainly back in full force. For around four years, Capcom largely focused on remaking older titles rather than pushing the franchise forward, so Resident Evil Village finally continues the story of Ethan Winters while bringing back the first-person perspective that made RE7 unique for the franchise.

This, to an extent, is why Village feels so strange as a sequel to RE7. RE7 and Resident Evil 2's remake had pushed for classic survival horror game design in a modern context, something that Resident Evil 3's remake would push against yet largely fall in line with. Village opts to eschew this entirely in favor of action-horror gameplay drenched in survival horror window dressing. I've never strictly had a preference between these two gameplay styles (although I generally find the survival titles far better), but considering the historical context behind the game Village is following up on, this move is an odd one. Despite that, I would say Village's game design is largely well executed. Copy-pasting RE7's gameplay into much larger levels would lead to disaster, which is why Capcom has rather tastefully upgraded the combat system to favor more intensive situations with more enemies at once. Your weapons, even the more powerful ones, all feel appropriately rinky-dink and you never entirely feel safe behind the trigger. Even so, shooting feels just good enough to make the moment-to-moment gameplay still rather fun even if it's not exactly silky smooth by design. The enemies in this game, particularly the Lycans, are demanding and require the player to learn and adapt quickly, leading to some surprising early game difficulty. I played on hardcore, and not only are Lycans tanky, but they bob and weave throughout the environment actively dodging your crosshair and this makes fighting them both tricky and tense. Mastery of timing, blocking, and pushing away at the right time is essential to success here and this difficulty is very welcome after RE3make's hardcore mode was a breeze. The game follows a semi-open-world structure where the player can return to the titular village after completing each major area, and while I do find this aspect somewhat underbaked, it is nice to be able to come back and explore newer areas after acquiring new items. This open-ended structure means that exploring your environment is just as crucial as ever, as you'll need to find treasure, lei, and even hunt for food to purchase supplies, weapon attachments, and stat upgrades. Despite the genre change, Village is still chock full of classic-style puzzles and they're generally fine. Some are fairly clever, such as the statue puzzle in Castle Dimitrescu, whereas many are a little too simple. I wasn't particularly stumped by any of these, but some of them did stick out to me as being more interesting than others. RE puzzles are not exactly known for being Silent Hill mind-benders, but I would like a few more "a-ha!" moments than I got here especially compared to RE7's generally more interesting puzzles.

It seems, then, that Village's main flaw is its lack of consistency. Developed partly during the COVID-19 pandemic, I get the sense (but don't have much proof) that the game was kneecapped by this. The game is split primarily into four different areas led by different members of the cult of Mother Miranda - Lady Dimitrescu, Salvatore Moreau, Donna Beneviento, and Karl Heisenberg. Capcom tries a lot of different things in these levels, but unfortunately, they are far from equal. Castle Dimitrescu is by far the best part - the gothic horror setting and deeply cold winter vibes help it stand out while also providing an experience that feels like classic Resident Evil. The exploration, puzzle solving, and backtracking deeply echo the survival horror roots of the franchise, and despite the action-oriented gameplay stands out to me as perhaps one of the highlights of the entire franchise. Unfortunately, this is also the peak of Village, and from there, it's downhill to varying degrees. Moreau's area is ultimately fine for what it is, but far too on-rails with very little in the way of interesting gimmicks outside of a pretty interesting puzzle involving levers and platforms that only shows up once. It's criminally short and never truly gets to experiment with the promise of a water-based setting, though thankfully he has the best boss fight in the game - a stressful hide-and-seek around a small arena that ends up tense and exciting. House Beneviento was my least favorite part of the game, a severe drop in quality that I found to be boring and cheap. While I understand to some extent why people have found it so memorable - the house itself is rendered beautifully and the infamous baby has a terrifying design - it's largely a non-threatening level with very little in the way of any real tension or stakes. Heisenberg's Factory is when the game picks up for me again, providing tense combat scenarios against formidable enemies and an oil-crusted, steamy atmosphere. The game certainly has excellent peaks, and at its worst, it dips its toes into mediocrity, but it's never downright bad. It's a game that tries to do many things but due to possible development troubles, doesn't manage to entirely hit the mark in terms of consistency. For what it's worth, the variety the game tries to pull off is certainly admirable.

Resident Evil Village, for better or for worse, is one of the most unique Resident Evil games by far. Completely unlike anything else in the franchise, what it brings to the table is fresh, new, and generally interesting. The excellent atmosphere, great action horror gameplay, stellar graphics and art direction, memorable characters, and solid scoring ultimately make for a good, if flawed Resident Evil experiment. Unfortunately, lazy and sloppy scriptwriting, inconsistent level design and overly basic puzzles are noticeable and difficult to ignore. Still, it's a game that tries a lot of things, and while it doesn't always succeed, I'm glad to see Capcom further experiment with the series. Obviously highly recommended to RE fans, but generally recommended to fans of action horror games as well.

The game is a perfect mix between horror and action game, but unlike RE7, it's leading onto the latter rather than a horror game. The characters and plot is solid, silly but solid. You can like one less than another but everyone had their charm. The gameplay is sincerely fun and even the standard difficulty can pose a threat if you find yourself cornered, but the challenge is not that high. I really enjoy how the game gives you sufficient ammo to feel like you constantly need to watch out but also kinda relaxed.
My only complaint but also a good point for the game is the Village of Shadows difficulty. If you really want to play a horror game, play that. Bullets do not suffice, the simplest enemies require *three* grenade launcher shots to die, and they are agressive and fast. It makes the game feel absolutely different and I will recommend playing it 100%. It's not impossible, but I'd recommend some Infinite ammo weapon before doing that. It can be really frustrating at some points without it, but don't exploit it, I tried doing saves to compare the gameplay with one and another and some become a joke. Resident Evil Village: Magnificent Gothic Horror, Action, and a Little Bit of Madness (Steam Review)

Resident Evil Village is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, and it once again offers players the chance to step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, who is dragged into a new nightmare. This time, instead of a creepy mansion in Louisiana, we're treated to a mysterious European village full of gothic castles, terrifying creatures, and charismatic villains. Village is a bold mix of horror, action, and even light humor, offering an unforgettable adventure.

What I Liked:

•  Captivating Atmosphere: The village and its surroundings are crafted to the smallest detail and are imbued with the atmosphere of gothic horror. Each location is unique and presents its own threat.
•  Charismatic Villains: Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters became true stars even before the game's release, and they fully live up to expectations. The other members of the "Four Lords" are also very memorable and colorful.
•  Varied Gameplay: Village skillfully combines elements of survival horror (limited resources, puzzles) with action scenes. There are moments when you need to hide and save ammo, and there are moments when you need to shoot your way through hordes of enemies.
•  Engaging Story: The story of Ethan and his family is full of secrets and unexpected twists. The ending of the game leaves a strong impression.
•  Mercenaries Mode: This arcade mode offers dynamic gameplay, weapon upgrades, and numerous challenges.

What You Might Not Like:

•  Story: Although the story is generally engaging, it has some illogical moments and plot holes.
•  Lack of VR Support: Unlike Resident Evil 7, Village does not support VR, which is a bit disappointing.
•  Linearity: After completing some locations, it's impossible to go back, which limits the freedom of exploration.

Conclusion:

Resident Evil Village is a magnificent game that successfully continues the traditions of RE7 and offers an unforgettable survival horror experience. The game combines a chilling atmosphere, charismatic villains, varied gameplay, and an engaging story. If you are a fan of the Resident Evil series or just love horror games, then Village is a must-buy.

Should you buy it? Absolutely YES!

Continues the story of Ethan from Resident Evil 7. It does some things better and some worse but ends up being a solid entry that mostly improves from its predecessor. 

The game and locations look amazing. The pacing was well done and I never got bored all the way till the end. There is more action and less scares than 7, but gameplay wise its very similar with solid sound design and animations. I do wish they would make puzzles more interesting (they are mostly just fetch quests). 

They wanted to hit a specific theme of gothic horror and sort of sacrificed the story and characters to do it. It’s cheesy but also tries to take itself too seriously which ends up not working, especially when it comes to the dialog.

There’s a vendor this time around with a currency system to upgrade and buy weapons and ammo. I was so rich early on that it basically eliminated the balance of resources that I usually enjoy from these games. 

Inventory management returned to Tetris style, and keys and crafting items don’t take up space, which I prefer.

AI of some enemies are easily abusable. A stalker boss will just ignore you if you walk into safe rooms, and the basic enemies won’t attack you if you sit on the top of ladders. 

Small changes like gathering ingredients to increase your health or having a prompt to break boxes without having to swap to your knife were great.

[i][b][h1] Resident Evil Village [/h1][/b]

[b][h3] Direção de Arte e Ambientação - Jogo Base [/h3][/b]
A direção de arte e ambientação de RE Village são muito bons. O clima nevado combinado a estética visual do jogo encaixam perfeitamente.

[b][h3] Level Design - Jogo Base [/h3][/b]
O level design e todos os elementos que o compõem me agradaram muito. A conectividade entre os ambientes, casas, quartos e cômodos foi muito bem feita, nada é desperdiçado, e a resolução de puzzles também foi bem trabalhada.  

[b][h3] Trilha Sonora e OST - Jogo Base [/h3][/b]
Trilha sonora muito boa, mas nada que ganhe um destaque.

[b][h3] História [/h3][/b]
4 (quatro) anos se passaram desde os acontecimentos de RE 7: Biohazard, Mia e Ethan foram transferidos para a Europa e estavam sob a proteção da BSAA. Durante esse período, Mia engravidou e deu à luz a Rosemary Winters. Em uma noite que até então parecia ser normal, Chris e seu esquadrão "Hound Wolf" (uma força-tarefa de elite da BSAA) invadem a residência dos Winters, executam a Mia e levam Ethan e Rose. Durante o percurso, a van que transportava Ethan e Rose é interceptada por uma figura misteriosa, Ethan acorda em meio a neve, com seu comboio tombado, com os guardas mortos e Rose em lugar nenhum. Seguindo uma trilha composta por neve, sangue e carcaças, Ethan se depara com uma grande vila deserta, esse é o lugar mais provável em que aquela figura pode ter levado a Rose, mas só existe um jeito de descobrir.

[b][h3] Bosses - Jogo Base [/h3][/b]
[b]Principais/Obrigatórios:[/b] Quase todos os bosses principais/obrigatórios são únicos e muito bem trabalhados em mecânicas e design, o único que me desapontou foi o Karl Heisenberg, esse era um personagem que desde o início do meu primeiro playground eu estava absurdamente hypado pro desenrolar dele, mas pessoalmente não gostei do design da forma mutante dele e nem da boss fight em si, eu inclusive preferia ter enfrentado a sua forma humana.

[b]Secundários/Opcionais:[/b] Os bosses secundários/opcionais são bem legais no geral, mas nada de mais, infelizmente o moveset deles é uma cópia de outros bosses ou inimigos.

[b][h3] Gameplay [/h3][/b]
A gameplay de RE Village segue todos os padrões semelhantes a RE 7 e FPS, você deve economizar o máximo de munição possível e evitar confrontos diretos, você não deve gastar munição ou recursos com qualquer inimigo que estiver no seu caminho, tente baitar ou apenas correr dele. Você poder defender ataques pra tankar mais dano e você deve coletar itens espalhados pelo mapa, e ao combiná-los você consegue munições, primeiros socorros e entre outros recursos. Com o único diferencial sendo uma DLC que te permite jogar o jogo base em terceira pessoa, por mais que o jogo fosse feito e pensado pra se jogar em primeira pessoa, eu acho muito mais confortável jogar em terceira pessoa.

[b][h3] Conteúdo Secundário - Jogo Base [/h3][/b]
O conteúdo secundário de RE Village é preenchido por tesouros e cristais de crânio espalhados pelo mapa, protegidos por puzzles ou bosses, eu achei muito legal e recompensador coletá-los.

[b][h3] Shadows Of Rose - DLC [/h3][/b]
Direção de arte e ambientação bons, level design agradável. Aqui, acompanhamos parte da história de Rosemary Winters, 16 (dezesseis) anos após os acontecimentos de RE Village Base. Seguindo o conselho de Charlie "K", Rose é levada a um laboratório do governo que está manipulando um pedaço sobrevivente de Fungal Root recuperado da Europa. Seguindo as instruções de "K", ela deve tentar se conectar mentalmente com o Fungal Root e encontrar um Cristal Purificador que pode remover seus poderes completamente. Essa é uma sinopse não muito interessante mas promissora, que infelizmente foi totalmente prejudicada pela falta de criatividade e um roteiro mal feito. Muitas coisas do jogo base foram reutilizadas aqui, o que é totalmente condizente com o fato de que o Fungal Root tem o poder de armazenar memórias, mas nem tudo é bem trabalhado ou elaborado, o final boss também é reutilizado do jogo base, com o mesmo design e alguns movesets novos, o plot twist final é decepcionante e deixa bem escancarado que os roteiristas não queriam se esforçar muito nessa DLC. 
Mesmo com muitos pontos negativos, Shadows Of Rose tem muitos positivos também, eu gostei da forma como as inseguranças e traumas de Rose foram representadas em formas de puzzles na casa da Donna Beneviento. O design dos inimigos me agradou, e por mais fácil que tenha sido eu gostei muito da boss fight contra o Amalgam. E outro ponto positivo aqui é a gameplay, diferente do jogo base você não consegue defender ataques físicos diretamente, e durante a campanha você vai poder contar com a ajuda da pistola "LEMI", a espingarda "M1897" e bombas de tubo, armamentos já conhecidos do jogo base. Você pode usar os poderes de Rose pra paralizar inimigos, uma mecânica bem simples mas agradável, durante a boss fight final os poderes de Rose já estão mais fortes e você ganha algumas habilidades novas, o que consequentemente melhora a boss fight.

[b][h3] The Mercenaries - DLC [/h3][/b]
[b]Normal Stages:[/b] Seu objetivo aqui é aprimorar seu armamento e enfrentar grandes hordas de inimigos e inclusive alguns bosses dentro de um tempo limite, que pode ser aumentado eliminando inimigos, ganhando assim um pequeno tempo bônus. Cada fase vai te colocar em um lugar diferente, com inimigos diferentes um objetivo de abate diferente. Você pode jogar como Ethan ou Chris, cada personagem possui seu proprio armamento e estilo de gameplay. É muito fácil, mas mesmo assim me agradou muito.

[b]Hard Stages:[/b] Além de deixar as coisas um pouco mais desafiadoras, toda diversão aqui é triplicada, você desbloqueia novos personagens que inclusive podem ser usados na dificuldade normal.

[b][h3] Conclusão [/h3][/b]

[h1] [b] I don't follow all of the Resident Evil saga, RE8 is probably one of the RE game I've played since a long time. Here's my thoughts about it [/b] [/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a thrilling mix of action and horror that continues Ethan Winters' story after Resident Evil 7. If you don't follow the story from the previous title, they give a short movie about the story recap. The game shines with its stunning visuals, atmospheric environments, and memorable villains, including the iconic Lady Dimitrescu. The gameplay is a solid blend of action and survival horror, with refined combat and a satisfying progression system. Here's my pros and cons about this game:

Pros:
- [b] Atmosphere & Visuals: [/b] The haunting village and detailed environments create an immersive experience.

- [b] Story & Characters: [/b] Engaging plot with interesting villains and connections to the Resident Evil lore. Also, character design seems solid AF, like the Wolf Hound squad and the bosses.

- [b] Gameplay: [/b] Fluid combat, crafting, and intense boss fights. My most favourite part is the Chris's mission. It resemble CoD mission or any other tactical game but they execute it pretty well and it trully give depth to Chris character on how he handle the situation.

- [b] Pacing & Replayability: [/b] Well-balanced between action and exploration, with lots of unlockables and difficulty options.  The extra content IMO is very rewarding and worth it.

Cons:
- [b] Reduced Horror: [/b] The action-focused gameplay reduces the tense, survival horror experience.

- [b] AI Issues: [/b] Enemy AI can be predictable, making some encounters feel repetitive.

- [b] Dialogue & Storytelling: [/b] Some cheesy dialogue and lackluster character reactions detract from the immersion. Heisenberg is the solid example, and Chris's mission dialogue feels like they're a bunch of LARPer, too many unnecessary dialogue and given the context that they're some Tier 1 Operator who handle zombies, they don't feel like it.

- [b] Difficulty Spikes: [/b] Some sections feel overly punishing, with inconsistent difficulty. Especially the "Village of Shadows" difficulty.

[b] Conclusion [/b]
Resident Evil Village is a fantastic game for fans of the series, offering an exciting, visually impressive experience, but it lacks some of the pure horror that made previous titles iconic. I've never played any Resident Evil games so am not familiar with the lore. I purchased Resident Evil Village on a sale due to a recommendation from my brother. I can't say I have completed the game fully as I am currently stuck at the end level boss (no spoilers here). But I have seen the ending (again no spoilers here) and it seems to be satisfactory.

I don't usually like the horror genre but apart from one single jump scare that caught me off guard I did not find the game very scary, just a bit tense. The gore is also way over-the-top and a bit comedic so unless you faint at the sight of blood and things that go splat I wouldn't worry about being grossed out. The only real critique I have is the convenience of items that allow you to level up and the fact that you will need to revisit the game through New Game Plus in order to go back and find all the secrets if you missed them on the first play through.  For instance there were a couple of puzzles I was unable to solve because I was missing a certain item that I never managed to find playing through the main story (also make sure you examine every item you collect because they hold secrets to solving the puzzles). 

I am unsure on the replay-ability of this game once you get to the end. It really depends on if you wish to go back and complete every aspect of the game and gain every trophy.
The other aspect of the game is that you cannot change the difficulty once you start the game. It does ask you if you wish to change the difficulty level to an easier mode if you die a couple of times though but once you say no it may not ask again depending on what boss fight you are in.
The graphics are good, audio is serviceable and the acting a little hokey but suits the mood of the game. The game-play can be a little clunky at times and the lack of the ability to jump or dodge and roll etc makes boss fights very linear. The difficulty on normal is not very hard and when you die it is usually because of the ability to escape an enemy due to being locked into a confined space. You can also run away from enemies and they don't re-spawn after you move on to the next section of the game. At least in some sections.

One thing I would advise for anyone new to the game is to save at every save checkpoint that you can as you will not find it fun being thrown back to the last auto-save checkpoint which can sometimes be substantial. Also concentrate on building your armoury. It's quite easy to end up running out of ammo leaving you lacking in firepower for the big boss fights. Use ammo sparingly. There is no shame in running away here if it saves you from using up all of your resources.

All in all an enjoyable game that does not take itself too seriously. It's 'light' horror in the vein of a B movie. If you are looking for something more souls like and challenging look elsewhere. But if you just want a bit of a fun thriller type romp with horror elements this is an entertaining distraction.

I dove straight into Resident Evil Village: from the very first seconds you’re thrown into a cold, unfamiliar village with no explanations, and you have to figure everything out on the fly. I was immediately hooked by the question, “Who is this Duke and why does he have all these strange treasures?”—it drove me to explore every corner.

The locations stood out: the frozen village, Lady Dimitrescu’s gloomy castle, and the eerie Beneviento estate. Two bugs haunted me in Beneviento all the way to the end. First, one of the plaques refused to activate—I couldn’t trigger it, so I missed out on some treasures and bizarre creatures. Second, the animal area was blocked by thick roots that I couldn’t clear—access stayed locked until the finale. These issues ruined the experience a bit, since I knew there were secrets I couldn’t uncover.

Another weird moment was enemies hitting through walls: you take cover, and suddenly you get struck without ever seeing the attacker. It felt like the textures were letting attacks pass through, breaking the immersion.

The final battle with the mega-mycetium roots also had its glitch: the roots themselves “lagged”—their animations jumped and stuttered even though my FPS stayed solid, creating a distracting effect during the fight.

The progression imbalance also stood out: you spend the whole game gathering resources and leveling Ethan to take down enemies with well-placed shots, and then Chris shows up in the end and kills them in one or two bullets—making all your previous efforts feel pointless.

Despite these technical flaws, Resident Evil Village is pure gothic horror. The creaking floorboards, shifting shadows, icy corridors, and echoing footsteps build unbelievable tension. It’s an atmosphere every horror fan should experience, even if you have to tolerate a few bugs.

The best Resident Evil game.... for people who doesn't like Resident Evil games. They even dowgraded "Resident Evil" to a subtitle. This doesn't look, feels or plays like a RE game, and also lack the polish we always saw in the recent RE games, which bland characters, confusing story, and supernatural elements that would be better used in a spin-off.

The zombies and mutants were replaced by werewolfs, ghosts and vampires and I honestly expected to see jack'o lanterns and black cats too as I played this game. The mix of horror and action is not homogeneous, with sections of pure survival horror alternating sections of FPS. The lycan cannot hold a candle for the ganados of RE4: they are way more annoying than scary, constantly dropping the player on the ground and with an attack animation that takes forever.

The story is interesting, but told in a weird way. You spend most of the time without any idea about what is happening (besides the "rescuing Eva" part) but then after 2/3 of the game a bunch of information about the monsters and characters began to be throw at you. I am not kidding, I think half of the lore of this game is told in a single room before the final boss as scattered documents. Usually in RE games this kind of lore is more dispersed across the areas, slowly feeding the player with information about the world and its characters. Without giving spoilers, they also tried to make the main villain some key characters to the entire franchise, but based only in a few documents inside said room.

Speaking of characters, they all suck hard. Most of Ethan's dialogs are just him asking things, like "who are you?, what is happening?, why is this happening?". He has no personality and sounds like a annoying dude trying to say something smart but can't. Or better saying, whowever wrote his dialogs could not think about something badass, smart or funny for Ethan to say. Some people argue that the idea was to make him sound like a average dude forced to be a hero...but that his second game, just give me the hero. Besides, who the hell wants to play an action/horror game as some boring dude? Even Chris looks and sounds boring AF.
The villans are a joke, they talk WAY too much during the boss fights and is the dumbest cliche dialogs ever. Of all japanese things they decided to keep during this "westernization" of the franchise, why pick the "anime villain monolog"?

The maps are almost metroidvania like, with a HUB area and four "dungeons" that you need to explore, with a boss fight at the end. Not necessarily a bad thing, but increases my feeling of "this is not RE". They still  add collectibles around the maps, something I personally found distracting and immersion breaking, but I can understand why people may like those.

Combat is mostly fine, but the weapons aren't well balanced. What I mean by that is that the next handgun you find is always better than the one you already have. In R4 some guns have higher firepower, others bigger magazines, they could shot 3 rounds at time or pierce enemies..here is just direct upgrades which gives me this feeling of wasting money when upgrading a weapon. Ethan also moves like a snail, which definitely doesn't help when fighting enemies that looks that they were ripped from a FromSoftware game.

They also added cooking to the game....for some reason. They also removed the herbs, with only one healing item available (with HP increase done by cooking now).

Review of Resident Evil 8: Village (NO SPOILERS)

Introduction
Resident Evil 8: Village is the next installment in the cult series, which has been balancing survival horror with more dynamic action. This time Capcom takes us to a dark, mysterious village somewhere in Eastern Europe, continuing the story of Ethan Winters from “seven.”

Plot and narrative
The story is neatly constructed, full of secrets that we discover as we explore. The twists and turns manage to surprise you and keep you curious, and the whole thing has an engaging, cinematic twist. The lords - the adversaries who rule the village - are colorful, though at times they lapse into the grotesque. The characters are expressive and each brings something unique to the plot. Still, their characters rarely go beyond well-known archetypes, leaving them lacking in depth or surprise. Resident Evil 8: Village takes a stronger turn toward the fantastic - supernatural elements dominate, which for some may undermine the story's credibility, especially when compared to the more down-to-earth tone of earlier installments. Village opts for a grim adventure with action elements, rather than building a dense atmosphere of horror. For action fans, it's still a treat, but those hoping for thrills of unease may feel disappointed.

Gameplay mechanics
Mechanically, Village stands at a very high level, as befits the Resident Evil series, although it introduces some simplifications. The inventory is much more capacious than in previous parts, making it easier to manage items. Finding the things you need also no longer requires as much effort as it used to - the game almost leads us by the hand, often marking key items with yellow paint - a mechanic already familiar from “Seven,” but in Village it is even more visible and conspicuous. This makes the gameplay clearer, but sometimes all too much so - one gets the impression that the developers are treating the player as someone who needs obvious hints. Combat is fluid and satisfying, though simpler than in its predecessors. Bosses, of which there are more than in “Seven,” differ in style and behavior, but are easier to defeat - I think I died only twice in the game, including once in a clash with a boss. Maybe this is a result of my experience with the series, or maybe the game was actually designed with a wider audience in mind. The economy, on the other hand, is brilliantly balanced - we never have an excess of money for ammunition or upgrades, which forces us to manage our resources wisely. The mini-games and puzzles have also been simplified and are not as rewarding as they once were.

Game world
The Village world seems larger and more diverse than in previous parts. The village, Dimitrescu castle, Heisenberg factory - each location has its own unique atmosphere and style. However, instead of being unsettling, it is often more stunning in its details and architecture. The interior of the castle, for example, impresses with its majesty - the rich decorations and spacious halls are impressive, but they don't inspire the horror one might expect. The exception is the plot of Donna Beneviento - this passage, brilliantly builds a feeling of unease and is undoubtedly the best moment of the game, but it does not last long. The rest of the locations, while interesting, allow us to go through them like a tank, without much sense of danger or relief once the threat is gone.

Audiovisual setting and technical aspects
The soundtrack in Resident Evil 8 sounds good - It fits the reality and atmosphere of each location. The graphics are beautiful and extremely detailed. Character models, textures and lighting are very impressive. Unfortunately, towards the end of the game, it happened that the more distant animations moved noticeably less smoothly, as if they had a much lower frame rate - this effect disappeared only after zooming in. Nevertheless, the visuals still remain one of the game's strongest assets. Technically, the game performs superbly. I did not encounter a single bug or underdevelopment, which testifies to the refinement of the production.

Summary and subjective assessment
Resident Evil 8: Village is a great, polished game with beautiful graphics, high-level sound design and solid mechanics. However, its simplifications - larger inventory, easier bosses, clearer gameplay - make it less satisfying than its predecessors. The plot is intriguing, but the twist towards paranormal phenomena takes it away from realism. The biggest downside is the lack of tension and horror that defined earlier installments - aside from Donna Beneviento's storyline, the game doesn't hold in the anxiety and feels more like an action shooter in a bleak world than a full-fledged horror game. It's still a good game, but as a horror game it falls short of the previous installments. For fans of action and beautiful sights - a revelation. For fans of survival horror - a slight disappointment.

His connection with Ethan is tense and mysterious at first, but it grows into something much deeper.The relationship between the two becomes an important part of the overall narrative.

In short, Resident Evil Village is a masterful blend of old and new. Terrifying, emotional, and endlessly engaging— and a beautiful nightmare worth experiencing.

The story, the gameplay, the level design, the secrets, the bosses. It's all just magnificently crafted together.

While not a requirement, it's best played right after Resident Evil 7. The stories are very connected, and there will be some lore stuff you will only understand if you played Resident Evil 7 before. I Highly suggest getting the RE7 and RE Village Gold Edition bundle, and if you can get it at a discount, even better. Village borrows heavily from Resident Evil 4. From the very style of the game being heavily action focused from start to finish, to the enemy heavily reminiscent of El Gigante and there's even a fight with a fish like creature right after you drive somewhere with a boat. Definitely RE4 inspired, which, dare I say it that this game is better? I know, I know. Huge claim, but give it a try and you will see for yourself.

The Shadow Of Rose DLC has a nice story and it all ties in nicely with the ending of the game. The final boss fight is interesting, but the levels are mostly reused and the gameplay doesn't really feel as good as the base game to me. I also don't like that this DLC forces you to play in 3rd person. Should have been a toggle for people that want that but not mandatory.

The game is also highly replayable as is RE tradition. There's a mercenaries mode, but I will let other reviews speak on that as that was never really my cup of tea.

But yeah, all in all a very nice package. A great addition to the series and my favorite game in it so far.

Atmosphere and Environment
One of the game’s absolute strengths is its atmosphere. Resident Evil Village is set in a mysterious village in Eastern Europe, and the environments are so detailed that they almost feel alive. Dark forests, dilapidated castles, and narrow caves create a constant sense of unease. The sound effects and music enhance this further—a sudden noise in the silence can easily make your heart skip a beat. It’s a perfectly crafted horror atmosphere that keeps you on edge throughout the entire adventure.

Characters That Linger
The characters are another highlight. The protagonist, Ethan Winters, is a sympathetic figure whose fight to save his family gives the story a strong emotional core. On the other side, we have the antagonists, with Lady Dimitrescu standing out for her imposing and terrifying presence. She is undoubtedly one of the most memorable villains in the series, and her role makes the game even more captivating.

Gameplay That Balances Horror and Action
The gameplay is a successful mix of horror, action, and puzzles. The combat is intense, requiring both strategy and quick reflexes, while the puzzles are clever without being frustrating. There are also plenty of weapons and upgrades to collect, which gives a sense of progression as you explore the village. The balance between these elements makes the game feel fresh and engaging from start to finish.

A Story for Everyone
Despite having no prior experience with the Resident Evil series, I had no trouble following the story. The game introduces new players to the world smoothly while offering enough depth and references for fans. The narrative is filled with unexpected twists that keep you hooked right until the credits roll.

Visually Impressive
The graphics are also worth highlighting. The character models are realistic, the environments are rich in detail, and the lighting effects are masterful. It’s clear that a lot of love went into creating a world that is both beautiful and terrifying.

Conclusion
In summary, Resident Evil Village is a fantastic game that combines horror, action, and adventure in a way that’s hard to resist. Even as my first Resident Evil game, I felt welcomed and completely immersed in the experience. It’s truly worth buying, whether you’re new to the series or a longtime fan. Now, I’m eager to dive into the earlier games—that’s how good it is!

I've played every main Resident Evil title and a few of the spin-offs. I have pages of complaints about this game but nobody would read them, so I'll just say this has dethroned RE6 as the worst. Here's a summary:

-The story is awful. The dialogue is awful. Every potentially interesting character gets killed off before they can get fleshed out at all. Everyone is an idiot. The ending is bad. 
-The immersion and interaction with your environment sucks. Everything is aggressively linear by even RE standards. Other than two parts, the game is not good horror, while also not being a good action game. 
-The combat is the worst to date. Everything is a bullet sponge. The boss fights are boring. 

As hollow as they were, I actually had more fun with RE6 or RE3R. On Village, I had to bump the difficulty down to casual just so I could quickly beat it and I still hated it. Under The Mayo on Youtube does a decent job of breaking it down.

How on God's green earth this has overwhelmingly positive reviews, I have no clue.

Resident Evil Village attempts to please every kind of Resident Evil fan at once, by including elements from past Resident Evil games, like puzzles and survival horror elements from Resident Evil 1, 2, 3, and 7, as well more action heavy gameplay, like Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6. But since it tries so many different things at once, it fails to find a proper focus, and the whole experience feels incredibly shallow as a result.

There's a lot of combat in this game, especially during the last third, however, none of it feels particularly good. The weapons feel weightless and weak, just like they did in Resident Evil 7. However, RE7 had far less combat encounters, and was a more puzzle focused game overall, so it isn't that much of a glaring issue in RE7, as it is in RE8. The minibosses are especially bad, since they do not react to your shots at all. It doesn't even seem like your dealing any damage, until they suddenly drop dead. 

Combat encounters in general feel very dull and empty. You usually have a relatively open area, where you have to fight a couple of copy pasted enemies at once, and sometimes there is a singular enemy that is armored or has a unique weapon. Yet every encounter feels the same, because they don't give you unique ways to deal with them. Every time you simply take shots at the enemies, then you block, then you take a few steps back, rinse and repeat. Every. Single. Time. 

You can also upgrade your weapons at the merchant, a mechanic taken from Resident Evil 4, and yet this game offers you no unique upgrades, unlike RE4. No 1,5 damage increase, no 100 slot magazine, no triple shot, nothing. Just regular stat increases that are sometimes just straight up useless. There's one upgrade for the magnum revolver that decreases the reload time by a tenth of a second. Why? You are barely going to use this weapon, and when you do, that tenth of a second is not going to make any difference. I'd much rather have something that actually shakes up the gameplay a bit. The merchant's a fun character though, i like him.

The titular village acts as the games hub world of sorts. You get to explore the village before every major area, and every revisit offers some slight changes, and new items to find. It's nothing special, but it does its job decent enough, even if there are no truly interesting things to find in it. It is pretty basic overall.

The castle tries to be a classic puzzle box dungeon, just like the mansion from RE1, the police station from RE2, the city streets from RE3, and the Baker house from RE7, but it fails to understand what made these dungeons special. They didn't hold your hand, guide you along a path, or give you any major hints. They let you explore and get lost in their halls at your own pace. The castle doesn't do that. It just gives you the illusion the illusion of choice. You may think that you can explore the castle as you please, but the game constantly keeps you on a scripted, linear path. In every playthrough, your journey through the castle will be the exact same. When you found an item in older RE games that was needed for a puzzle, then you usually had to look through the dungeon to find out where you can use it. Sometimes you had to store it away and keep it in your mind, until you find out where you have to use it. Sometimes you find an item in one corner of the map that you then have to in the opposite corner. The castle doesn't do that. If you find an item, the game usually proceeds to guide you straight to the puzzle that requires it. No critical thinking or problem solving needed. Just let the game take your hand and tell you what to do. The castle also has the worst stalker enemy in the franchise, Lady Dimitrescu. She is slow, doesn't have any unique tricks, and you only encounter her for like 5 minutes, in a dungeon that lasts about 2 hours.

The boss fight against Lady D at the end is also pretty mediocre. You mostly just run around in a big circle, while you have to take shots at her weakspot. Sometimes you gotta snipe her from afar, but that hardly makes the fight more exciting.

House Beneviento is the worst area in the entire game, especially on repeat playthroughs. There is no combat, and the whole thing is an escape room like puzzle, followed by a stealth section. The puzzles itself aren't bad, and the stealth section can be pretty scary...on your first playthrough. On repeat playthroughs, the Beneviento house quickly turns into a chore that takes about 20 - 30 minutes to complete every time. And since it's only puzzles and one very simple stealth section, it feels the exact same every time you go through it. No, it doesn't feel the exact same. It IS the exact same, which sucks, because RE games are meant to be replayed multiple times. 

Donna Beneviento also has the worst boss fight in the game. You just have to look for her doll, while you're under a time limit. The whole thing can be done in a minute or two.

Moreau's Reservoir is...weird. Again, there are hardly any combat encounters, but this time there's also a glaring lack of puzzles. So what do you do instead? Well, you go through a "parkour" section with an instakill monster. I don't even know what to say about this area. I don't hate it, but i don't like it either. It's just kinda there. 

The boss fight against Moreau is alright. Again, it mostly has you run around in circles, but there's more dangers this time, compared to Dimitrescu's boss fight. 

The fortress sucks. It is one big combat encounter, where you'll have to fight against hordes of enemies, followed by a boring mini boss. Nothing else to say, other than that i do not like it in the slightest.

Heisenberg's factory is the last major area in the game, and a lot of people dislike it...and i don't know why. Sure, the visuals get boring pretty quickly, but the factory comes much closer to the classic puzzle box dungeons than the castle ever could. Sure, it is still pretty linear, especially when you compare it to the classic dungeons, but it doesn't take your hand as much, and while the puzzles still aren't difficult in the slightest, they are at least a bit more interesting than the ones in the castle. The factory also has the best and most unique combat encounters in the game, since every type of enemy has different weak spots and attack patterns. There are enemies with protective gear around their head, enemies that can dash, enemies wearing heavy armor, and they all offer a unique combat experience, when compared to the dull encounters you had to go through thus far.

Heisenberg's boss fight, while simple and super easy, is also pretty fun. Something about destroying his weak spots with a tank just tickles my brain the right way. Probably my favourite boss fight in the entire game.

The final boss sucks though. As a character, that is. The fight itself is alright. Not the worst final boss we've had in the RE franchise. 

The story is a hot mess, and the entire game could have been avoided, if they didn't turn Chris into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ idiot. Ethan is also super annoying with his constant quips and his attitude. I prefer the mostly quiet Ethan from RE7.

Resident Evil Village is a near-perfect blend of action, horror, and storytelling that takes everything great about Resident Evil 7: Biohazard and builds upon it, creating one of the most unforgettable experiences in the entire franchise. For me, it’s a worthy successor and an incredible follow-up that balances the survival horror roots of the series with more thrilling action-packed moments, while still delivering that same atmospheric tension and suspense.

The story picks up with Ethan Winters as the protagonist once again. taking him to a remote, eerie village filled with terrifying creatures and bizarre characters. The setting an isolated Eastern European village shrouded in mystery. The environments are wonderfully designed, from the dilapidated village streets to the intimidating castles and snow-covered mountains. The world feels alive. 

What truly sets Village apart, though, is how it blends the best elements of survival horror with intense action. The game doesn’t shy away from heart-pounding combat and intense shootouts, but it still maintains a careful balance with the resource management, puzzle-solving, and exploration that made the series famous.

The game’s pacing is another highlight. Village expertly moves between horror, mystery, and action sequences, keeping the game-play fresh and engaging throughout. The first half of the game is dripping with atmospheric tension as you uncover the secrets of the village, while the second half leans more into action and exploration, offering a variety of different game-play styles and environments.

The gameplay itself feels fluid and responsive, building on the solid mechanics of Resident Evil 7. The first-person perspective works beautifully here, keeping the player immersed in the action while maintaining that sense of vulnerability when facing the unknown. While the combat does get more action-heavy than its predecessors, the horror is still ever-present, and the game doesn’t let you forget that you’re constantly fighting for your life.

Another notable improvement is the game’s inventory and crafting systems. They’ve been refined to provide more freedom in how you approach combat and resource management, adding a layer of strategy to how you use ammunition, healing items, and upgrades.

If you loved Resident Evil 7, Village feels like a natural evolution. It expands on the formula and offers more of what made its predecessor great while introducing new elements that keep the gameplay exciting. The game delivers a fantastic mix of horror, action, and adventure, all wrapped up in a beautifully designed world that’s as terrifying as it is stunning.

Resident Evil Village (or RE8 as I interchangeably call it from time to time) is a worthy successor to its' predecessor Resident Evil 7 that outshines it in almost every way you can think of. The gameplay is vastly improved, it looks great as every game in the RE engine does, the atmosphere, while not as overtly 'scary' as 7 (with one exception) still manages to do a lot over its' varied locations that gives the game an experimental feel that not many others in the series have.

I really adore this game because they took almost everything that was good about RE7 and some prior games and expanded upon it, starting from the story, down to the gameplay loop. Its all really well done.

We got hands down the best Resident Evil characters in a long time. Everyone felt real, mysterious, and interesting. Not a single character felt fake, everyone was really competently written. The only minor complaint about the characters I have, is I wish we got to learn more about them. I especially appreciate the enthesis on the side characters, [spoiler]Lady Dimitrescu, her daughters, the Duke, and Heisenberg [/spoiler] in particular were stand outs for me because of their incredible aura and design. 

[b]The environments[/b] are extremely detailed and consist throughout the whole game this time around, something which I couldn't say about Resident Evil 7 where the quality fell off after we left the houses. The village was really fun to explore and loot around, but the Castle in particular was simply god tier to me. I hardly remember the last time i enjoyed exploring a location in a game so much as castle Dimitrecu. Its beautiful, intricate, and detailed no matter where i looked. It was so immersive to be there that I was sad when I had to leave. I really wish it was expanded upon further, the castle is gigantic, we got to explore maybe less than half it. This is a common complaint i have with a lot of games. There were so many windows, rooms, towers, and interesting looking places that it saddened me that i couldn't explore more. I really wish Capcom leaned further into the Metroid Vania genre in regards to exploration and maybe even gameplay. We already have a great inventory system. It would've been really fun to find other items that would allow us to open secret rooms or paths and experience more of what this games' various areas have to offer. 

[b]The gameplay[/b] was fun and it times even tense on the medium difficulty, however it becomes easier the more you invest into your gear, which was something i enjoyed. The enemy variety is actually amazing this time around, I liked basically every single enemy type with maybe the exception of the [spoiler]flying gargoyles[/spoiler]. Enemies move around, encircle you, try to anticipate your attacks, and are overall fun to fight. There is a bit of rudimentary stealth system which i thought could've been expanded upon with silenced weapon attachments (no takedowns please). It irks me that we couldn't destroy ANY of the light sources to improve our chances of stealthing through some areas. Such a missed opportunity to add further depth to the otherwise amazing package. I really wish the environments were more interactive and complimentary to the gameplay loop outside of a few braindead explosive red barrels placed around. 

[b]The weapons[/b] were simply great, amazing even! One of my biggest gripes with RE7 was how there was basically no weapon variety and no way to meaningfully upgrade your weapons either. This game on the other hand nailed it for me. I was also delighted to learn that the merchant system from RE4 has made a come back with improvements. [spoiler]Not only is the Duke an incredible character design, he's also really interesting and charming. I love him.[/spoiler] The addition of rudimentary hunting and cooking was also a welcome surprise. [spoiler]I think the Duke was a stroke of former genius, I enjoyed everything the Duke had to offer. Also the fact that he canonically is friends with the Merchant from RE4 was great too~[/spoiler]

[b]The story was great[/b], well written and interesting throughout. I loved every second of every character I saw on screen, everyone looked so charming and interesting. Rose, I really did not expect Rose to get kidnapped a chopped up into pieces,[/spoiler] as if we're making a stew. So about RE8, as we all know by now there's two styles of RE, RE0-CV the survival puzzle horrors, and RE4-6 the survival action horrors. RE8 falls in with the latter group of RE4-6 survival action horror. Similar to RE4R it's correcting the things it got wrong the first go around, except in this case with 8 making sure they don't happen. 

There's 3 fanbases for RE. The OG RE fans 0-CV, the action only RE fans 4-6 and than there's the RE fans who love both styles. I would argue the last one are the true fans, while the first ones are the purists and the middle ones the mainstreamers. Anyways pointing this out because it's important to note RE4 fractured the fanbase and its why we have 3 groups now. Ever since than sales had been weird for RE. RE4 lost alot of the survival horror only enthusiasts and initially sales for the game were lackluster, while it gained a bunch of the new fans it lost plenty, so instead of outdoing the previous REs it just sold around the same. But thanks to the critical acclaim and the ports letting a whole new economy learn about RE4, things changed it sold well and RE5 was born. Still the horror portion of the fanbase never came back and when the action focus started getting tiresome Capcom sought to get the horror fans back with RE7. Ever since than Capcom has avoided past mistakes(for the most part) RE8 while playing like the action style of later REs, out of RE4, 5, 6 and 4remake this one meets a middle ground of the original style of RE0-CV and RE4-6 the most. It legitimately plays like a perfect blend of both while also expanding the formula by making the game more open world like. The game plays like RE4 but brings back the puzzles and riddles of RE0-CV that RE4 abandoned, it also brings back gameplay in tight corridors and smallers more slower paced enemy encounters, most importantly tho it retains the horror factor and scares. The game is scary and oozes with atmosphere. The game only has one con, they reintroduced puzzles to the action formula but my god are the puzzles in this game the weakest in the franchise, some are alot of fun but god this was missed potential. A mixed feeling is the difficulty, Capcom programmed the difficulty weird in this game. Usually you get Normal, Hard, Very Hard/Hardcore and Professional. This time however Normal is Easy, Hardcore is normal and Hard is Very Hard. So I suggest doing your first playthrough on Hardcore. The game has alot of replayability, not as much as RE4-6 but it's definitely up there with them just slightly behind. I like that when you beat the game you can't unlock everything and has to be unlocked with an additional playthrough, and everything carries over to new game plus, so when I went from Hardcore to Professional, I still had stuff left to do in the game. Than there's the 3rd person mode. This game easily gives you 3 almost equally fun playthroughs and a decent mercenaries distraction. 9.75/10
