RE8 is a fantastic game. The biggest compliment I can give it is there's not a section of the game I thought was bad. There's sections I prefer, but I think the whole game is good.

I find it strangely hard to compare the game to other RE games because of how... "fresh" a take some aspects of the game are. It does lack some tonal consistency & trades this off with variety & excellent pacing. The "Village" of the game works as connective tissue to help bring it together though, I don't know if the game would've been as good if you, for example, went linear straight from area to area. The hub Village works to help transition you from the different tones of each area, I actually think without the Village the game would've been a lot worse. It's made me think a lot about game design, since in earnest the developers words of, "Theme Park of Horror" describes RE8 near perfectly.

I do notice each part of the game taps into aaspect of Resident Evil.

The opening prologue hour taps into the sorta "cinematic opening" chapters RE has been doing recently, between RE7, RE:2, RE:3.

Dimitrescu's Castle is an expansion on the "Classic RE Unlocking Survival-Horror" area, like Baker's House in RE7, or RPD Police Station in RE:2, giving a stalker enemy with rooms to solve, puzzles, shambling enemies.



And finally, the final boss & sequence just felt like they wanted to make a good final boss fight, & a better than usual RE ending.

I can actually see pretty clearly that RE8 was them further developing a lot of individual elements the series has toyed around with in the last decade, & the biggest compliment I can give RE8 is I feel it's a successful one. I think each area pretty successfully manages to be an improvement of what came before.

And I think the Village helps round it out. I've concluded I really like horror games with "small hub areas", I personally loved it in Silent Hill Downpour, Evil Within 2, & now Resident Evil Village, where there's side areas to do, mysteries to solve, hidden events off the main path to just explore. The Village in RE8 isn't big, but it's very dense, and as I said, I actually think it was the perfect solution to help connect the tonal contrast and help the game feel thematically consistant and connected, as otherwise the huge tonal whiplash between the various areas could've been done a lot more poorly.

I do think the boss fights also end up being stronger than usual for the series, it does feel there's a bit room for improvement, but the series has a rocky, uneven history with boss fights, & I can say Village has more consistently good boss fights than other entries, helped they're all pretty varied to each other.

I really like Ethan's story, 



RE8's story is kinda' out of focus until the last hour or so, but I think it's held up by an interesting cast of villains. I'm actually sad the RE8 villain cast only get so much screentime, each one of them felt like they had potential to do more, but that's a huge step up from boring villains the series had going for it compared to some of the recent past entries.

I know I loved RE8, but I need a bit more time to digest where I'd place it on my series chart. Most RE games have a consistent tone that kinda degrades in the last third. RE8 doesn't suffer this problem, but in exchange it switches multiple tones during its course. The Village does help connect them, but they're still quite different to each other. Village is held by its core themes, Village setting, & characters, but the actual gameplay experience goes a bit all over the place.

Compared to, say, RE7, which nailed its hillbilly found footage horror aesthetic & focus on the Baker Family, RE8 is a bit more all over the place. This leads to greater variety, & I think RE8 nails what it's going for, but it's very different, & actually makes them hard to compare for me. I think RE8 virtually solves all of RE7's problems, IE it has a good final boss fight, Chris is really interesting in RE8, new much more interesting enemies, with new enemy types introduced through the whole game, with a better back-half, but it's such a different game than RE7 in so many ways I still find it hard to compare the two.

Which I guess is also interesting, since RE8's foundation is so clearly RE7, that the fact it feels so different speaks to them doing a lot with that foundation to make it something entirely new that doesn't feel like a retread at all.

I'm very curious what fans & Capcom ultimately pull from RE8, but my immediate impressions are glowing. I think it makes the series future exciting. I think it's a very good game, a weirdly experimental RE, but a successful one.

PSA: The achievement "Frugal Father" is either incorrectly worded or incorrectly coded. According to Steam and the in-game achievements menu, to earn it you must "Finish the story without spending more than 10,000 Lei." In pseudocode, this would look like if (leiSpent <= 10000) { earn achievement; }. 

HOWEVER, if you spend precisely 10,000 Lei, which is not more than 10,000 Lei and happens to be the exact price of the first inventory size expansion, the only really essential purchase of the game, you will not get the achievement. The achievement should say "Finish the story without spending 10,000 or more Lei", as the actual check being made is if (leiSpent < 10000) { earn achievement; }.

In other words, don't bother trying to get that achievement on your first run. Save it for some cheesed out utterly broken new game plus speedrun, and temper your expectations accordingly.

While this game is a great experience to play through, I do have some gripes about some of its defining characteristics(SPOILERS INVOLVED IN SOME SECTIONS):

1. The story feels really drawn out and seems to never end, especially towards the end of the game when certain events take place. You understand that [spoiler] killing Miranda [/spoiler] will most likely end the game. It's just a matter of when that is actually going to happen.

2. Some of the story beats don't really line up. At the end of the game, Chris's team asks Chris why he didn't just tell Ethan about their plans. Chris told Ethan he, "didn't want to get civilians involved" knowing damn well that Ethan was the one who killed the entire Baker family in the first place, proving he is more than capable at handling himself. Then there's the conflict with Heisenberg. [spoiler] If they wanted to work together to kill Miranda, why didn't they? [/spoiler] Ethan just acts like a prick the whole time even though they essentially have the same goal.

3. Maybe it was just the brightness level I set before entering the game but the visuals felt a little blurry. Everything seemed to blend together and the colors didn't pop as well as I would have liked. Each location felt too similar because they didn't have a distinct pallet that set them apart from the rest. To give an example of good design, in the RE4 Remake, the village section had a brownish hue to the surroundings with a grey sky hovering over the map. During the castle section, the lit torches and royal colors made you feel as if you were in an old, renaissance-style castle. The island section had more of a greenish blue hue to it, with glowing red dots signifying the high tech equipment scattered throughout the map. RE8 doesn't have a strong enough color pallet to distingush locations. It also doesn't help that the entire game is covered in a layer of snow.

4. Speaking of RE4, this game draws almost too many similarities. The map is sectioned off to essentially the same style as RE4, just in a different order. Each game starts in a village, involves a giant castle, takes you through a mini village on the water inhabited by a giant aquatic monster, visits a manor far removed from the village, and ends by traversing through a more technologically advanced area. When I played this game, it kept reminding me of how much better RE4 felt to traverse and explore.

Overall, this game is an amazing game to experience. Just note that if you're looking for the signature Resident Evil experience the first 4 games(and sometimes the 5th) brought, you might have a harder time enjoying this game.

So I've been streaming this recently on YouTube and been having a real good time. At the time of my writing this review, I'm still replaying it AND I'm streaming the DLC of "Shadows of Rose" and might even try out Mercenaries to give people a look at what the game has to offer. For now, my streams are here: https://youtube.com/live/kuhr2xXlE3s

So in this game we come back to Ethan who is enjoying family life with his child, Rose and the true villain from RE7, Mia. I honestly hated this because of how, considering the events of that game (all of which were her fault) and how I didn't feel much of a connection to this character that if I was Ethan, I would've dumped her and instead gone after Zoe!

Chris Redfield comes in and saves the day, however, being Chris "Boulder-punching" Redfield, he decides not to explain anything and kidnaps you all, but your transport gets attacked and you end up in a creepy village that is swarming with werewolf-like creatures known as Lycans.

Without getting into spoilers, you will be looking for Rose, leading you to battle the very tasty Lady Dimitrescu of the many curves and the other three lords who work under Mother Miranda such as a Creepy Puppet, a fish-like monstrosity and someone who looks like a low-budget magneto with his powers of magnetism.  Mother Miranda herself is a creepy figure, equipped with six black wings and was once seen as the pillar of the community until these creatures attacked.

The game feels closer to RE4 than how the previous game was closer to the earlier RE games as you have no shared storage box, there's more enemies and they even drop items that can benefit you for crafting materials (similar to the previous games) or treasures to be sold to the merchant. A VERY big man named "The Duke" who operates like the Merchant from RE4, even making a reference by saying "What're buyin'? Heh, just a joke a old friend of mine used to say." but he also will buy ammo, weapons and will upgrade your weapons too. Later you unlock a kitchen where hunting animals and collected meat can be used in recipes that give your character a passive boost either to HP, block or even movement speed.

Another function that's from RE4 is the ability to look at your treasures and other items closely, taking parts of them apart or adding parts to them to make certain treasures even more valuable and even uncovering keys to some secrets of hidden treasures. It pays to look at most things to do this as I know there were many things I completely missed in my first playthrough and even missed again in my second playthrough.

After finishing the game many of your in-game actions will have unlocked challenge points (CP) which are used to buy special things for the game, such as infinite ammo for a weapon you have fully upgraded (purchasing all the damage, ammo, reload and fire-rate enhancements) which can certainly help on subsequent playthroughs since you'll probably be selling ammo for weapons that don't need it and there is only one sniper in the video game, but there is also a insane hand-cannon you can get that uses rifle ammo and does more damage too!

There are a lot of really fun weapons to unlock, especially if you try to go for the higher difficulties like Village of Shadows where the enemies are even tougher, which is what I'm grinding for currently. Your inventory system, again, harkening back to RE4, is a large suitcase that can be upgraded so you need all the space you can ask for, however, there's always the chance you might most stuff around. Either because of limited space or you have Autism+ADHD like I do!

Another really good thing I quite liked was, unlike RE7, whenever I alt-tab out of things (which as a streamer, I might be prone to do) it doesn't change the screen resolution from Fullscreen to windowed, which was a pain in the ass. That said, doing a New Game+ isn't as simple as you'd think because, unlike other games where there's a New Game+ option on the main menu, you have to go into the load options where you would've made that "Complete" data save after the end of the game and load from there, choosing the difficulty and you start the game with all the weapons you had at the end, fighting the final boss so I hope you didn't completely empty all of your ammo or you might be a little stuck...

The challenges are pretty easy to sus out before you finish the game as many of the achievements are tied to it, so it won't take you too much to look up. Not to mention, I really helpful thing is that you can look up the challenges whilst in game so you are covered in case you forget or want to double check that it's ticking down for certain actions.

Mercenary's mode makes a return as I referenced above and I have not yet touched this, but it gives you access to getting more CP and also even unlocking special upgrades that make your weapons even more powerful (if you can believe that) resulting in some weapons becoming absolute beasts, even in the highest difficulty setting, however, this is totally up to you as you can toggle infinite ammo and these upgrades on or off individually.  I love that this is a option because you can have a whole-lot of fun!

Resident Evil Village is a thrilling, action-packed entry in the Resident Evil series that successfully blends horror and action while staying true to the franchise's roots. 
While it leans more heavily into action than survival horror, it delivers a visually stunning, emotionally engaging, and often terrifying experience that will keep players on the edge of their seat!
The game picks up with Ethan Winters, the protagonist from Resident Evil 7, as he embarks on a journey to rescue his kidnapped daughter, Rose. 
The plot may seem simple on the surface, but the twisted, gothic setting of the village and its bizarre, nightmarish inhabitants help elevate the narrative into something more compelling. 
The game does a great job of balancing the tension and emotional weight of Ethan’s journey with an eerie atmosphere and haunting setpieces.
Visually, Resident Evil Village is a standout. 
The village itself is beautifully designed, with detailed environments that feel alive, from the snow-covered mountains to the eerie, claustrophobic interiors. 
The lighting and shadows contribute to the foreboding mood, enhancing the horror elements. 
The game’s enemies, especially the towering Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, have become iconic, and their designs reflect the gothic horror influences that permeate the game.
Gameplay-wise, Village strikes a fine balance between action and survival horror. 
Ethan has a wider arsenal of weapons than before, and combat is more dynamic, especially in terms of movement and aiming. 
The game brings back some of the classic Resident Evil elements, like exploration and puzzle-solving, but also introduces intense shootouts and boss battles that will appeal to fans of more action-oriented gameplay. 
The pacing can be a bit erratic at times, with some sections being more action-heavy than others, but the tension rarely lets up.
The game’s tone is an interesting mix of horror, folklore, and action movie spectacle. 
While some areas, particularly the village and castle, are deeply unsettling, other segments, especially the latter half, lean more into action and even supernatural thrills. 
The shift in focus can feel jarring for some fans who enjoyed the claustrophobic tension of Resident Evil 7, but there’s no denying that Village brings a fresh perspective to the series.
On the downside, Resident Evil Village can sometimes feel like it’s trying to do too much. 
While the variety of environments, from the vampire-infested castle to the werewolf-filled forests, is impressive, it occasionally detracts from the sense of dread that the earlier parts of the game establish. 
Some of the side characters are underdeveloped, and the story, while entertaining, can feel a bit predictable and clichéd at times.
However, Resident Evil Village still delivers a captivating experience, bolstered by a solid performance from the voice actors, a well-paced narrative, and moments that will genuinely scare players! 
The game’s technical polish is apparent, with smooth controls and immersive sound design that heighten the tension.
In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is a worthy continuation of Ethan Winters’ story and a compelling entry in the series. 
While it may lean a little more into action than its predecessors, it balances those moments with excellent horror sequences, memorable characters, and stunning visuals. 
It may not be as terrifying as Resident Evil 7, but it’s a thrilling ride that’s hard to put down once you’ve started.

Resident Evil Village, the eighth main installment in Capcom's legendary survival horror series, is a thrilling blend of action, horror, and atmosphere. Building upon the first-person perspective introduced in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, it expands the scope while retaining the series’ signature tension and terror.

Set in a mysterious, isolated village in Eastern Europe, the game follows Ethan Winters as he searches for his kidnapped daughter, Rose. The narrative weaves together personal stakes with the overarching lore of the Resident Evil universe, offering both newcomers and longtime fans plenty to savor. The village itself is the star of the show, an intricately designed hub that connects a series of unique and haunting locations, each ruled by one of the game’s four lords.

The game’s pacing is one of its greatest strengths, seamlessly blending moments of nail-biting tension, exploration, and adrenaline-pumping action. From the gothic opulence of Castle Dimitrescu to the psychological horror of House Beneviento and the industrial nightmare of Heisenberg’s factory, each area offers distinct gameplay styles and a fresh sense of dread.

Combat feels refined and responsive, with a robust arsenal of weapons and a crafting system that encourages resource management. The enemies are varied and horrifying, ranging from werewolf-like Lycans to grotesque abominations. Boss battles are memorable and cinematic, pushing players to adapt their strategies while delivering some of the game’s most intense moments.

Visually, Resident Evil Village is breathtaking. The RE Engine brings the village and its surroundings to life with stunning detail, from the eerie flicker of candlelight in the castle to the oppressive fog of the forests. The sound design is equally masterful, with every creak, growl, and whisper heightening the sense of unease.

The game does lean more toward action than pure horror, echoing the style of Resident Evil 4. While this may not sit well with fans seeking a more traditional survival horror experience, the balance of scares and spectacle ensures the game remains gripping from start to finish.

One of the game’s standout features is its cast of characters, particularly the enigmatic Lady Dimitrescu and her vampiric daughters. While her screen time is relatively short, she leaves a lasting impression, and the other lords are equally compelling in their grotesque and tragic ways.

If there’s a drawback, it’s that the story occasionally leans into melodrama, and Ethan’s character remains somewhat bland compared to the vibrant personalities around him. However, these are minor blemishes on an otherwise outstanding experience.

Resident Evil Village is a triumph of design, atmosphere, and gameplay. It respects the series’ roots while forging its own path, offering a thrilling and varied adventure that will keep players hooked until the very end. Whether you’re a die-hard fan or new to the franchise, this is a journey into darkness that’s not to be missed.

A very solid single player game through and through. This is my fourth RE game in the series so far and I gotta thank the remakes for getting me into this franchise. Like all the prev revival games, this one follows a similar pattern so existing fans can easily warm up to it. I gotta say though, the beginning of the game is NOT friendly to new players. The first portion had me fighting against an army of respawning werewolves all by myself for a few minutes but since the mission objective isn't exactly clear, I initially and painfully, had to go through this segment lost and frightened. 

It's crazy to say this though but the game actually gets easier after that. I admit I had to use a walkthrough for the most part but it's not really a hard game but more action-oriented compared to RE7. The story is a great run as you once again take control of Ethan (who's still masked) and now have to locate your daughter taken from you. I'd call the story a bit generic and over-used though for a horror setting (the typical find your loved one plot line... I mean who else would dare venture into this nightmare right?). 

There's only one pain point I have with this game and it's the most major change in the core RE mechanic: the new merchant system. This time round, you don't have an infinite loot box you store your stuff in. Your inventory is limited to only what you can carry. Anything else must be sold off or discarded. It works well in some cases but not always. For example, since the merchant's inventory is also limited, it may be wiser to save up ammo than prioritize on money. One other thing I disliked is how the merchant introduced waaay better guns only very late into the game and without the player knowing about it. This meant most players would've used their cash to instead upgrade their existing guns and be unable to buy the new guns at all (or get worse versions of them). If Capcom was trying to encourage replayability with this cheap tactic, I guess it works but for those who wanna be opportunistic, it's a loss. 


Overall I could just summarize that this game is basically the RE4 to RE2 remake. It's heavier on the action yet features some scary segments that are really well done. The campaign length is more than decently long enough and the crazy boss encounters are just great. I also loved how this game ventured into the most diverse set of themes and enemies you'd never expect from the RE franchise. From werewolves to vampires, to creepy dolls to steampunk horror... it's all there. But ok, there's no zombies. RE8 takes everything right from RE7 and the past two remakes and makes things even better by amping everything up on a greater scale.

Não é um jogo ruim, mas é uma grande decepção dada a qualidade CAPCOM, a própria existência desse jogo é algo duvidoso.
Resident Evil 7 foi um banho de água fresca na franquia, com uma temática mais de terror, visão em primeira pessoa, perseguições e como o jogo, num primeiro momento, não tem muita relação com a conturbada história dos jogos anteriores. Eles tinham tudo para dar certo nessa continuação, mas jogaram tudo por água abaixo.
Começando pelo enredo de Village, é a coisa mais desnecessária possível. Pois simplesmente joga fora tudo o que aconteceu no RE7, criando uma nova fonte para o fungo. Isso poderia ser bom, mas logo somos levado a um enredo cliché estilo filme de Liam Neeson, uma odisseia para salvar sua filha. Tudo é muito bizarro e sem lógica, com organizações secretas, assembleia dos malucos e uma temática meio medieval que foi uma cópia super mal feita de RE4. É como uma cópia mal feita de RE7 e RE4. Lady Dimitrescu tinha potencial como vilão mas nunca é aproveitada, sendo, novamente, potencial descartado e todos os outros vilões vão ficando cada vez pior.
O gameplay: é péssimo, convenhamos que o gameplay em RE7 já é ruim, mas agora em Village é foco em combate é bem maior e os problemas do gameplay são imediatamente aparente. Seus tiros não possuem impacto algum, tudo é muito duro e lento, sua movimentação é extremamente lerda, os bosses são todos batalhas genéricas sem graça, é um combate pior que King's Field. Depois de ter jogado o remake de RE2 e RE4 voltar pra jogar Village foi doloroso.
Algum ponto positivo ao final de todo o jogo: não, nenhum. O enredo fica cada vez pior e eu pensava que DLC pudesse dar algo decente ao jogo, mas não, piora ainda mais. O modo Mercenaries desse jogo é o pior que já teve, com mapas labirínticos demais (os mapas desse jogo não funcionam para esse modo, deveriam ter criado mapas novos e não apenas reaproveitar) e a história extra é a coisa mais inútil já feita. Você simplesmente joga umas 4 - 6 horas de mesmas partes do jogo para voltar a estaca zero da história pré DLC, mas para isso passa por mais combate ruim e a pior sessão de stealth que já vi num jogo.

[h1]Resident Evil Village is a mediocre game [ENG and Pt-Br review] [/h1]
It's not a bad game, but it's a huge disappointment given the quality of CAPCOM. The very existence of this game is somewhat questionable.
Resident Evil 7 was a breath of fresh air for the franchise, with a more horror-themed approach, first-person perspective, chases and, for the most part, doesn't have much to do with the troubled story of the previous games. They had everything they needed to succeed in this sequel, but they threw it all away.
Starting with the plot of Village, it's the most unnecessary thing possible. It simply throws away everything that happened in RE7, creating a new source for the fungus. This could be good, but we're soon led to a cliché plot in the style of a Liam Neeson movie, an odyssey to save his daughter. Everything is very bizarre and illogical, with secret organizations, an assembly of freaks, and a medieval theme that was a very poorly made copy of RE4. It's like a poorly made copy of RE7 + RE4. Lady Dimitrescu had potential as a villain but she was never used, once again her potential was discarded and all the other villains got worse and worse.
The gameplay: it's terrible, let's face it, the gameplay in RE7 was already bad, but now in Village the focus on combat is much greater and the gameplay problems are immediately apparent. Your shots have no impact whatsoever, everything is very stiff and slow, your movement is extremely slow, the bosses are all boring battles, the combat is worse than King's Field. After having played the remake of RE2 and RE4, going back to play Village was painful.
Any positive points at the end of the game: no, none. The plot gets worse and worse and I thought the DLC could give the game something decent, but no, it gets even worse. The Mercenaries mode in this game is the worst it's ever had, with maps that are all literal mazes (the maps in this game don't work for this mode, they should have created new maps and not just reused them) and the extra story is the most useless thing ever made. You simply play about 4-6 hours of the same parts game to get back to square one of the pre-DLC story, but to do so you go through more bad combat and the worst stealth session I've ever seen in a game.
[b][u]I don't recommend this game, just read half a paragraph about the plot on Wikipedia and you'll know everything interesting about the game and save your time and money.[/u][/b]

Have no idea why this game is so well reviewed. Absolutely none.

The good:
It looks very nice, runs well and the atmosphere is generally very good.

The bad (spoilers from here):
The sound design is anemic. Every weapon sounds and feels like a toy. While in RE 2 or 4 for example a a shotgun shot would take a zombie in half, here it knocks them down. Nearly everything is a bullet sponge even on the Standard difficulty. Boss fights are horrendously boring. Shoot, move a little, put up your kevlar arms and block everything.
There is no tacticality to anything. While in RE 2, 4 or even 7 you had to ration your ammunition, use your weapons wisely, here nothing matters. Shoot them in the leg/head/torso all the same. You never gonna run out of bullets, because you get plenty outright and then you can always craft if you need more. You never gonna run out of storage space either. Didn't even buy the biggest storage upgrade as it was completely unnecessary. You have no melee moves at all, weapon switching is slow, sometimes inputs are dropped especially when you want to throw a pipe bomb quickly. In short the combat is bad.
Okay, so maybe puzzles, exploration or the story is good? Bah.
First of all, there are no puzzles here. Every item you need is put right in front of you, on the only path you can take. Literally some of them, you can't miss even if you wanted to, because you can only progress if you have picked them up. While you may be able to go back to certain areas later on, there is really no purpose to this. Apart from collecting some dodads and gigas to sell for some lei, that you absolutely don't need.
Uhh, don't even get me started about the story. The RE series was never really strong in this department, but this one? Dear lord a ten year old could write a better one. Ethan's wife gets mowed down by Chris? Sure, don't take the 10 seconds to say that that wasn't Mia but a shape-shifter. Why bother right?
What your baby was divided into 4 pieces and distributed among the bosses. Why exactly? Why not do the big ritual from the start. Because then the "story" can't happen!
Ethan is an immortal beast, that can apparently live without a heart, reattach his cut off hand, but loose two fingers, that can't be fixed.
The end? Ethan as the big macho he is, takes the REMOTE detonator from Chris so he can blow up the monster point blank range? Excellent choice. Much sacrifice, true glory.
By the by why can Ethan only say "What the hell/heck?" all the time? You saw like the 100th supernatural creepy thing that day, after you magically reattached your hand. Surely you can't be that surprised.

Bah, this isn't a Resident Evil game. Only in the title and the general story. It is not survival horror, not a shooter, not a story rich game. Have no idea what it is. Avoid it, unless you can get it at a steep discount. Turn off brain, maybe get drunk and have at it. If you are looking for anything more, just avoid this one.

RE7 & RE8 really solidified my love for resident evil as a whole. I definitely consider RE8 to be the best of the series as the Ethan saga hits all of my [u][b]favorite points:[/b][/u]
[list]
[*]A grotesque world with truly horrific creatures and implications.
[*]Constantly struggling to survive leaving you scrounging for ammo and consumables.
[*]A goofy main character that is tough as nails while also somehow dumb as rocks.
[*]This game has some truly terrifying moments and encounters that tap into primal fears, but didn't feel as scare heavy as RE7. (Most likely bias)
[/list]
While I love this game to its core it still has some [u][b]problems and shortcomings:[/b][/u]
[list]
[*]Ethan is [b][i]SLOW[/i][/b]. It becomes much more apparent the longer you play and is also present in RE7.
[*]Many of the games areas are amazing at setting up a horror atmosphere but some struggle to keep that same appeal in consecutive playthroughs due to gimmicks and cutscene heavy encounters. [spoiler]House Beneviento really became a chore for me after my first few playthroughs due to the amount of running around with no true combat.[/spoiler]
[*][b]3rd person POV shouldn't be paywalled behind a DLC![/b] (Even though I never used it)
[*]The Shadow of Rose DLC doesn't really fit the same vibe as the game. It has less focus on gunplay and more focus on [spoiler]the abilities that Rose has[/spoiler]. On top of this the plot is very strong in some areas and weak in others; losing that same kick-ass horror feeling as the base game. (More info in my DLC review)
[/list]

Overall its terrifying, enjoyable and did a really good job [spoiler]wrapping up the Ethan saga[/spoiler]. I thoroughly recommend you try it if you're a fan of first person survival horror, and check out Resident Evil 7 if you want more of Ethan's story. 9.5/10

[code]While not as tight of an experience as its predecessor, Resident Evil Village provides a great mix of horror, exploration and action elements in an unique setting that constantly comes up with new surprises to keep things fresh, with only a few minor missteps along the way[/code]

Originally released in 2021, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] marks the return of Ethan Winters, his second appearance as a protagonist in the long-running franchise since 2017’s [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i]. While [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] can be considered somewhat of a “soft reboot” in the sense that it was a return to survival-horror roots of the franchise, which had long moved it’s focus to action beforehand, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is more about expanding upon it’s well-received predecessor – quite literally, as the well-designed but small house of the Baker family is traded in for a much larger snowy European village with vastly different locations to explore.

However, a word of warning first: Even if [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] provides a recap of the events from [i]Resident Evil V7: Biohazard[/i] at the beginning, I heavily recommend playing the game beforehand – not only because it’s an excellent [i]Resident Evil[/i] title but also due to it laying the groundwork for many plot points that are followed up on during the sequel. On that note, keep in mind that both games include paid DLC that offer new canon story content, if you want the full narrative experience. Additionally, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is only playable in a third-person perspective if you bought the Gold edition/”Winter’s expansion” of the game – although I’d personally suggest using the first-person perspective for your first playthrough anyway, since that’s what the game was initially designed for (also, cutscenes stay in first-person during both perspectives).

Moving on to the game itself, set three years after the incident at the Baker’s house, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] once again brings back the iconic mix of survival horror, rewarding exploration and tense action the franchise is known for - even if the individual combination varies per game. In this case, starting out at the titled village, protagonist Ethan Winters is naturally low on resources, which makes enemy encounters much more intense as you only got one pistol with little ammunition to defend yourself. But even as your resources grow little by little through careful exploring, the game uses boss fights to make you spend them just as you think you’re going to be fine for a while – or includes locations that strip all your weapons away, forcing you to rely on puzzle-solving and hiding from enemies instead.

Without going into spoilers here, it’s refreshing how the game shifts the gameplay experience slightly with every new location, as it keeps things from becoming stale. You also acquire new weapons at a decent pace, not too long for you to get bored, but also not too short for you to refrain from upgrading them. A dubious duke, serving as the merchant in this game, also allows for weapon upgrades through coin or stat upgrades through food exchange, making exploration much more interesting than just finding ammunition. Additionally, a crafting system allows you to create new helpful items on the fly, such as ammunition or first aid potions, if you found the required resources. As the traditional grid-based inventory system from the franchise makes a return, you also have to think about what you’re actually able to carry, although I personally never ran into any actual limitations here.

In terms of combat, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] offers a nice variety of guns that also play very well, although the enemy variety is a little on the low side. Regardless, due to a constant lack of ammunition, you want to make each shot count and thus switch weapons according to the situation – it never feels like you get to rely on one gun alone. This makes exploration more rewarding as well, with the game offering a handy map that shows you which rooms you fully explored and where you might want to take a second look. Compared to some of the previous games in the franchise however, it’s quite easy to figure out where you need to head next, which might come as a disappointment to some. Similarly, puzzles in this game are also not only few in numbers but also way too easy, usually of “use visibly marked key at the door obviously marked with the same symbol” difficulty. It’s nice that they’re included to shake up the pace, even making up the majority of gameplay in one location, though having a little more faith in the abilities of the players wouldn’t have hurt.

In terms of horror, I personally never really thought of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise as scary games, although this [url=https://youtu.be/Fvx2RPdYajk?si=kP-JwYjGFwi0D8fI]just a subjective view of course[/url]. This is mainly thanks to the ability to defend yourself, as long as you’re careful with ammunition management - although I do want to note how much I appreciate the tense atmosphere some of these games manage to build up, like [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] or the remakes of [i]Resident Evil 1 & 2[/i]. The reason why I mention all this is because [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] does feature a sequence that I did find unexpectedly scary, which was a positive highlight for me.

While I really enjoyed the mix of exploration, combat and survival horror in [i]Resident Evil Village[/i], there are two things I do want to talk about that unfortunately diminished my overall experience with the game: The boss fights as well as the pacing.

In terms of boss fights, the problem mainly boils down to movement and perspective of the player. While normal enemies are usually quite slow and give you enough time to aim for their weak spots, the boss fights mostly feature huge enemies that also move around a lot. While I wouldn’t call them too difficult, they usually make me feel like I must fight against the slow movement and limited (first-person) view of the protagonist as well to properly hit my shots. On that note, if you’re playing on a controller like I am, I recommend changing the default settings to making looking around more responsive.

The issue with pacing correlates with [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] offering much bigger and more varied locations compared to its predecessor, despite both being mostly linear: While each location also features a unique big bad with their own story, they vary in size and things to do. As a result, the storytelling suffers, with some villains receiving a lot more attention than others. Subsequently, some locations feel rushed while other too drawn out. In addition, the main plot slows down significantly in the middle of the game, only picking up pace again towards the end. And as the story of [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] culminates, the game also switches gears to an action-heavy approach entirely during the final hour, which just feels too abrupt and forced even if it’s unfortunately a common occurrence in the franchise.

Despite these missteps however, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is a very enjoyable and fully recommendable entry in the franchise, although it should not be treated as a starting point – pick [i]Resident Evil 7: Biohazard[/i] instead. [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] plays well, it runs great and although the boss fight and overall pacing could be improved, it’s a great showcase of why the entire franchise remains beloved by many.

Resident Evil Village is more than just a horror game — it is an emotional odyssey that pulls you through an intensely chaotic and deeply personal journey. It’s the culmination of the modern Resident Evil saga, blending supernatural terror with a visceral, survival-focused narrative. As the eighth main installment in the series, it stands as a brutal testament to both the evolution of the franchise and the emotions at its heart: the cost of survival, the depths of parental love, and the complex nature of grief. From the moment you step foot into the eerie and oppressive world of Village, you are confronted with more than just terrifying monsters and grotesque environments; you are confronted with yourself — with the relentless fight to protect your family, to cling to what little humanity remains in a world consumed by darkness.

The story begins with Ethan Winters, the protagonist from Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, finding himself thrust into yet another nightmare after a peaceful moment with his wife, Mia, and their infant daughter, Rose. The tranquility is shattered when a mysterious force attacks their home, stealing his daughter away and leaving devastation in its wake. The quest to save Rose and uncover the truth behind the horrors of the village becomes not just a fight for survival, but a journey of grief, loss, and redemption. Ethan, a seemingly ordinary man, is drawn into a world where grotesque beings, ancient forces, and sinister motives challenge everything he thought he knew about the world, about humanity, and even about himself.

What stands out most about Resident Evil Village is how it manages to deliver its horror in emotionally charged bursts. From the very beginning, you feel the emotional weight on Ethan’s shoulders. As a father, the driving force behind his actions is his unyielding love for Rose, his daughter. But beyond the blood-soaked battles with werewolves, vampires, and other grotesque creatures, Village delves into the emotional cost of survival. Ethan’s journey is one of personal sacrifice, the kind where every step forward feels like another piece of him is being lost to the horrors surrounding him. It’s about the price of love, of a father’s willingness to go through hell and back to save his child, even if it means confronting the deepest, darkest parts of himself. The visceral, personal stakes of the narrative make every monster, every horror, hit far harder than any of the series' previous antagonists. This isn’t just about surviving; this is about a man who will do anything to protect what’s left of his humanity.

The setting of Resident Evil Village — the isolated and gothic village nestled deep in the snow-covered mountains — is a character in itself. The atmosphere of desolation and helplessness permeates every moment. The village feels like a forgotten place, steeped in ancient curses, lost lives, and secrets that the people within are too afraid to confront. But this isn't just a haunted town or a mansion full of zombies — it’s a place that feels alive with malevolence, where everything from the weather to the very architecture seems designed to oppress and terrify. The snow that coats the ground and the towering castles on the horizon offer a chilling contrast: beauty intertwined with dread. The game gives you brief moments of tranquility, but they never last. The oppressive sense of isolation hits you hard. You’re alone in a world that’s been abandoned by hope, and it’s just you against an insurmountable force.

And then there are the villains — powerful, terrifying figures who each represent something deeper than mere monsters. Lady Dimitrescu, the towering vampire matriarch, with her seductive but deadly presence, is a symbol of the corrupting nature of power. Beneath her imposing beauty lies a creature who has long since abandoned any notion of mercy. The grotesque, nearly motherly figure of Mother Miranda, the shadowy figure behind the chaos, represents a godlike desire for control and rejection of human fragility. And the werewolves, the lichens, add another layer — they are relentless in their pursuit, wild in their unpredictability. The monsters in Village are not simply creatures to shoot; they are embodiments of emotional and psychological terror. They represent the twisting of the human form, a perverse reflection of how far people are willing to go for power, immortality, and control.

However, what makes Resident Evil Village stand out even more is how it doesn’t just scare you — it makes you care. Ethan Winters is an ordinary man thrust into an extraordinary situation, and you feel every moment of his exhaustion, his fear, and his loss. As the story unfolds, you begin to realize just how deeply the events of Resident Evil 7 have affected him. His journey in Village is a continuation of grief, of coming to terms with his own identity and the trauma of losing loved ones. The narrative isn’t just about stopping the antagonist; it’s about Ethan reconciling with his own humanity, his very essence as a father and husband.

The emotional grief Ethan carries is reflected in the game’s tense, horrifying gameplay mechanics. The combat is still as intense and frantic as ever, but it’s the moments of quiet despair that really hit hard. When you step into the cold, abandoned halls of Castle Dimitrescu, or the eerie, cavernous spaces of the Beneviento house, the atmosphere isn't just tense — it's suffocating. The sound design enhances this, with every creak of the floorboards, the howl of the wind, the distant growl of a monster, and the occasional whispers that make you feel like you’re not alone. The lack of a traditional safe zone, the constant danger of the hunt, makes each encounter feel more personal — it’s not just about surviving the monster; it’s about surviving the emotional trauma of the nightmare.

As Ethan ventures deeper into the village, the dread continues to mount, not just in the form of grotesque creatures but in the unraveling of Ethan’s own identity. He is confronted with the reality of what he’s become — what he’s had to do to survive. The game cleverly weaves in the emotional toll of constant loss, confronting Ethan (and the player) with the fact that survival often demands terrible sacrifices. There are moments where you’re forced to question your morality, where the stakes aren’t just about life and death but about the essence of who you are.

The final act of Resident Evil Village is both a triumph and a tragedy. Ethan’s journey is not just one of physical survival but of emotional transformation. In the end, you realize that his journey has been about redemption and the human ability to love in the face of overwhelming darkness. The game’s shocking and emotional conclusion leaves you breathless, and it doesn’t offer easy answers. The sense of loss is profound — you’re left with the feeling that no matter how much you fight, no matter how many monsters you kill, the scars of the journey will remain forever. Resident Evil Village isn’t just a horror game. It’s a story of love, sacrifice, and the unyielding will to protect those you care about, even when the world has gone to hell.

Resident Evil Village is a breathtaking, emotional experience that showcases the power of storytelling in the survival horror genre. It’s not just a game about defeating monsters; it’s about the cost of survival, the weight of responsibility, and the journey of healing. It’s a beautiful, terrifying, and heartbreaking exploration of humanity in a world gone mad. Every step forward in the village is a step deeper into the emotional depths of a father’s love and a fight to preserve what little humanity remains in a world of endless nightmares.

Resident Evil:Village, is mid tier at best.

What starts as a strong premise for a spooky time, soon becomes dull, bland, and formulaic in the execution of story.

Starting out in the village, there's a true sense of being isolated, outnumbered, and in danger. There were times I found myself making choices to fight enemies, or try sneak past them to conserve ammo. This very much reminded me of RE:4 (A game I hold in very high regard). This changed pretty quickly as the game progressed however, as ammo is littered everywhere, so I felt no inclination to not blast everything in sight like I was Judge Dredd.

Moving on to the castle, this whole act was confusing, very long winded and ultimately a little pointless. Being as this section was what the entire marketing campaign focused on, it felt quite weak.

What followed was a series of different boss fights, which to their credit, were all varied and felt unique.

After defeating 3/4 of the lords of the village however, just when you the think the story will ramp up to some epic Resident-Evilness, what actually follows is a very quickfire series of encounters to speed through plot holes, interjected by a Call of Duty section where you play as Chris, and then wham bam into the finale boss fight (Which was lacklustre and I just pressed left click a lot).

In Conclusion, a lot of the survival aspects of RE's roots have been lost in my opinion, there's very little variation in the weapons (which mostly feel slow, under powered, and Ethan's aim is about as good as Stevie Wonders'), and the story is full of ultimately forgettable characters who you meet once, kill. and then move on with your life.

The small homages to RE:4 and other parts of the franchise are nice, but ultimately I felt RE:Village relied too heavily on aspects of these games to keep it interesting.

Worth picking up in a sale, but definitely over hyped by the community.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil Village strikes a near-perfect balance between survival horror and action. The resource management mechanics of the series return, requiring careful planning when dealing with enemies or navigating environments. However, the game also leans more heavily into action than its predecessor, with a more extensive arsenal of weapons and a greater variety of enemies to combat.

The pacing is excellent. Intense, action-heavy sequences are balanced by slower, exploration-focused sections. One standout area, House Beneviento, shifts the focus entirely to psychological horror, delivering one of the most memorable and spine-chilling moments in the series.

[h2]Graphics and Performance[/h2]
The RE Engine shines again, delivering photorealistic visuals and smooth performance across platforms. Character models, particularly Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, are stunningly detailed. Lighting plays a significant role in creating a foreboding atmosphere, while subtle environmental details draw you into the world.

[h2]Replay Value[/h2]
Village offers plenty of reasons to return after the credits roll. Additional difficulty modes, the fan-favorite Mercenaries mode, and a host of collectibles provide hours of extra gameplay. The game also features excellent voice acting and a compelling story that rewards multiple playthroughs to fully appreciate its nuances.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Resident Evil Village is a worthy successor to the franchise, blending its roots in survival horror with modern action elements. Its rich environments, diverse gameplay, and memorable characters make it one of the best entries in the series to date. While some might prefer the pure horror of Resident Evil 7, Village’s approach offers a broader appeal without sacrificing the tension fans expect.

Score: 9/10

I love the first person survival horror genre and RE 7 and village are at the top in my opinion. 

In terms of story, I waited 3 years and avoided all spoilers to be fully immersed in the story, and even though a random review accidentally gave away a part of the ending, I was still pleasantly surprised by the outcome.

It's not required, but it is an experience that will set you up for the ride of your life. Village is another strong entry in the Resident Evil series that almost feels like RE Greatest Hits: it takes inspiration from the various, most notable and acclaimed characteristics, mechanics and environments from the earlier games, nicely combines them and wraps them up in an intriguing setting with a few unique segments and a newer protagonist that provides a different perspective.
Comparisons with RE4 are hard to avoid, as that is what it seems to borrow from the most, both mechanically and aesthetically, however as the game progresses, it does enough to set it self apart. Similarly, it has a fair balance between action and (survival) horror, but is a bit more grounded and simpler when it comes to combat and instead of having consistent proportion, what takes the front spot is more based per section.
The setting here is my favourite in the series - it is intriguing, charming, unnerving, with exceptionally good looking environments, solid level design, creative enemy design and character aesthetic and an adequate amount of scary. The village serving as a central, returning point that slowly opens up and connects all the other domains works very well. There is plenty of engaging exploration, both mandatory and optional, in the village itself as well the castle and factory. It alternates between providing exploration on your own terms and while being pressured or hunted by enemies, which works well for relieving and building up tension. Puzzles are on the simpler side, but they're still plentiful and generally serviceable for what Village was going for. Gunplay is as solid as ever and although the weapons are mainly clear upgrades in each category, there's still a respectable amount of options for player to choose from, especially with bonus content unlocks. The enemy design, variety, placement and distribution is quite good, managing to keep a consistent theme and slowly ramp the difficulty up in an interesting, but suitable way as you progress. It has some of the most impressive set pieces in the series and I personally enjoyed the boss fights, as they had a good mix of gimmicky and classic approach with cool arenas.
The Beneviento Mansion is one section that deserves a separate mention, as it's the most unique area in the game and it might just be peak Resident Evil survival horror with the atmosphere, backstory and gameplay there.
Story in Village is among the best in series in my opinion - both when it comes to discovering more about the setting and its characters and Ethan's personal arc. It grabs your attention right from the start drawing you to find answers and learn more about what's going on, as well as push through with Ethan's personal quest. The strong setup with recurring characters is then built upon by introducing new intriguing places and figures, whose designs and backstories I found some of the most interesting Capcom has done so far. The payoffs and conclusion are actually pretty decent too, even though it doesn't stray far from the usual theme.
Voice acting and cutscenes are quality work as per usual and the UI, controls and performance are decent.
Shadows of Rose DLC is also pretty great and very much in line with what I've said so far, although it leans more into survival horror. The infected and changed parts of previously visited zones are even creepier and the Beneviento section was once again executed super well with its extremely eerie ambience. Fights with Rose's newly acquired powers now at player's disposal were decent, especially the final one - a shame you get to play with them so little. I enjoyed the insight it provided into Rose's mind and her relationship with Ethan, as well as the aftermath of the base game. I appreciate the addition of 3rd person mode with this, as that's how I prefer playing Resident Evil. Obviously, it shows the game was really meant for 1st person in some places, but it's serviceable and I liked being able to actually see Rose's face during cutscenes and gameplay, unlike Ethan's.
While Village doesn't necessarily do anything the best in its entirety, it offers everything the Resident Evil series has to display on a more than competent level and has several stand-out sections. I consider it to be the most beautiful RE game, both visually and narratively and even though it might not be the best starting point, if you enjoyed any of the older or similar games - this should be a pretty safe bet.

This is a mixed review from me.
Game is well optimized and has great graphics, but the downsides and nitpicks made it a slug for me.

I can start with the story, which feels underwhelming, especially Mirandas motive. It was such a cliché.. some parts feel like the devs were just rushing to get the game over with [spoiler] Mia is still alive, despite being a prime candidate for Miranda's tests, even if just to create another strong bioweapon [/spoiler]
Heisenberg and the factory do not feel like they belong to this RE world either. It gets even more out of place when you consider how he got his powers...
Donna's playhouse was by far the most creepy and interesting place to visit, but I can see why they picked Dimitrescu to be the face of the advertisement and trailers this game had. The first impact of Ethan going through a crumbling village in contrast to a huge, pristine castle is incredibly well made and the peak of this game. Unfortunately, castle Dimitrescu is the first zone, so the game never lived up to that area again and honestly, it was a huge snoozefest near the end.

Weapon progression caught me by surprise and I did not like it, I was expecting a similar game to RE7, upgraded the LEMI and suddenly I am met with a better pistol, leaving my upgraded one, as a sidegrade. It should be fine, but the game also scales enemies to make sure you either use the newer weapons, or you have to spend more ammo. I ended up being more cautious about upgrading whatever I had and that hindered my playthrough.

Also, fire rate is just code, there is no mechanical part of any weapon, even the rifle, that justifies why you have to wait X seconds to fire again.. they could have added a proper weapon system, cocking the next bullet in the chamber for the rifle for example. They were lousy and it made the guns feel super awkward.

Lastly, the game wants you to be mobile/agile at times, but the engine does not behave how the devs wanted, and it feels really awkward at times (trying to create space for example).

I haven't played the DLC yet, but I am honestly not all that excited for it.

A Thrilling Masterpiece – Resident Evil Village is a Triumph for Horror Fans

Resident Evil Village is a stunning achievement in survival horror, offering a perfect blend of chilling atmosphere, intense action, and captivating storytelling. Building on the success of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, this latest installment in the iconic franchise elevates the series to new heights, delivering a terrifying yet thrilling experience that both longtime fans and newcomers will adore. Here’s why Resident Evil Village is a must-play for any gamer:

Engaging Story and Immersive World:
One of the standout features of Resident Evil Village is its captivating story. Following Ethan Winters' journey after the traumatic events of Resident Evil 7, players are thrust into a new nightmare as Ethan searches for his kidnapped daughter, Rose, in a mysterious village. The narrative is rich with twists and turns, building on the series' lore while introducing new, intriguing characters. From the towering, menacing Lady Dimitrescu to the eerie folklore of the village, the game keeps players hooked with every chapter, creating a gripping and emotional journey that adds depth to the horror experience.

Chilling Atmosphere and Stunning Visuals:
The atmosphere in Resident Evil Village is nothing short of terrifying. The game’s visuals are breathtaking, with each environment meticulously crafted to heighten the sense of dread and unease. Whether you’re exploring the fog-covered village, navigating the claustrophobic halls of Castle Dimitrescu, or venturing through dark, snow-covered forests, the attention to detail is exceptional. The lighting, sound design, and environmental storytelling combine to create a world that feels alive with danger, where every creak of the floorboards and distant howl in the night sends shivers down your spine.

Varied Gameplay and Dynamic Combat:
Resident Evil Village excels at blending classic survival horror elements with modern action gameplay. The game strikes a perfect balance between exploration, puzzle-solving, and intense combat. Players will encounter a wide range of enemies, from grotesque creatures to terrifying bosses, each requiring different strategies to defeat. The combat feels fluid and satisfying, with a wide variety of weapons to choose from, including shotguns, pistols, and even explosives. The addition of crafting and resource management adds depth, making each decision feel consequential as you balance limited ammo and health.

Terrifying Yet Memorable Enemies:
The enemy design in Resident Evil Village is one of its greatest strengths. From the terrifying Lady Dimitrescu and her vampiric daughters to the grotesque Lycans that roam the village, the game offers a variety of disturbing foes that keep players on edge. The variety in enemy design and behavior ensures that combat always feels fresh and unpredictable. Each encounter is different, requiring players to think on their feet and adapt to the threats around them. The boss battles are particularly noteworthy, with each one delivering epic, memorable moments that challenge both your combat skills and your nerves.

Action and Horror in Perfect Harmony:
Unlike some previous entries in the series, Resident Evil Village is a seamless blend of action and horror. While the game features plenty of heart-pounding moments and jump scares, it also introduces exhilarating combat sequences that make you feel powerful as you face off against terrifying monsters. The transition between slow, methodical exploration and intense action sequences is handled perfectly, ensuring that you never feel overwhelmed by either the fear or the combat. It’s a delicate balance that makes Resident Evil Village both exciting and terrifying in equal measure.

Excellent Level Design and Exploration:
Resident Evil Village continues the series’ tradition of excellent level design, with multiple interconnected areas that reward players for thorough exploration. Whether it’s finding hidden items, solving environmental puzzles, or uncovering secrets that expand the story, the game encourages you to explore every nook and cranny of its world. The environments are not only beautiful but functional, offering a variety of settings, from gothic castles to underground laboratories, each offering new challenges and experiences.

Incredible Replay Value:
Resident Evil Village offers a high level of replayability, especially for players who enjoy completing challenges and uncovering all the hidden content. After completing the game once, players can unlock new modes, weapons, and difficulties, which make replaying the game both rewarding and enjoyable. The inclusion of Mercenaries mode adds a fun, action-packed side activity, while the extensive item and weapon upgrades provide an extra layer of depth for those looking to master the game.

Exceptional Sound Design:
The sound design in Resident Evil Village is truly top-notch, playing a critical role in building tension and atmosphere. From the unsettling creaks of the floorboards to the chilling growls of approaching enemies, the audio keeps you on edge throughout the game. The haunting soundtrack perfectly complements the action, amplifying moments of horror and excitement. The careful attention to sound helps immerse you in the world, ensuring every footstep and whisper feels loaded with meaning.

Conclusion:
Resident Evil Village is a triumph for the franchise, blending the best aspects of survival horror and action gameplay into an unforgettable experience. With its captivating story, terrifying enemies, beautiful world design, and thrilling combat, it’s a game that will keep you hooked from start to finish. Whether you’re a longtime fan of the series or new to the Resident Evil world, Village delivers everything you could want in a modern survival horror game. It’s a perfect balance of fear, action, and storytelling, and it firmly establishes itself as one of the best games in the Resident Evil series. If you’re looking for a heart-pounding, immersive adventure, Resident Evil Village is an absolute must-play.

Resident Evil: Village is an interesting case. I would certainly recommend this game to people, however I would put a heavy asterisk next to that for die-hard Resident Evil fans. It's undoubtedly a "good game." All the elements are there. The combat is nice, the setting is interesting and visually appealing, the characters and monsters are fun! There are tons of unlockables and replayability packed into this game. That said, if RE7 was a step in the right direction for the series, RE8 was just a little bit too far of a step. The inspiration taken from classic monster novels and films are just a bit too on the nose. Gothic castles, vampires, werewolves, etc, are all cool, but they're definitely a strange fit in the fairly well-established world of Resident Evil. We have to reach a point where viruses and mold can't be an excuse to do whatever the hell you want to do. Still, I like the game a lot! I can just understand if fans of the series are just a bit put off by some of what's presented here.

I understand why. *
+ Pacing is great, you never get stuck for too long at one place
+ The riddles are simplified, which is great as I personally don't want to spend a lot time to figure out how to solve xyz
+ The controls are "simple" as in PC players will get immediately familiarized 
+ A horror survival "1st person shooter" kind of feeling. It is very different and interesting
+ Not everything evolves around THE village. The castle concept is very well made, as well as Heisenberg's factory
+ Capcom's graphics engine is superb with plenty of options and configurations to meet your needs and your PC specs
+ There are some jump scares and certainly "oh shxt moments" what we know from Resident Evil games
+ I really do appreciate THE DUKE and his shop
+ Interesting encounter with "armored zombies"

Resident Evil Village: Ethan Winters Deserves a Vacation

Welcome to Resident Evil Village, where Ethan Winters proves he’s either the unluckiest dad alive or secretly made of indestructible duct tape. His baby’s been kidnapped, his hand gets chopped off (again), and his European Airbnb is crawling with werewolves, creepy dolls, and a fish that looks like it swam straight out of someone’s nightmares.

And let’s talk about Lady Dimitrescu, the internet’s favorite nine-foot vampire mommy. She’s elegant, terrifying, and probably the only villain who could murder you while you’re busy saying, “Wow, she’s so tall.” Until she starts chasing you—and suddenly, you’re screaming, “I TAKE IT BACK!”

The gameplay is wild. One minute you’re solving puzzles like a genius, the next you’re unloading shotgun shells into Lycans while screaming, “WHY IS THIS HAPPENING?!” Meanwhile, The Duke, your jolly traveling merchant, rolls in like Santa with grenades and cooking tips.

The plot? Pure nonsense. [spoiler]Babies in jars, robot zombies,[/spoiler] and Ethan just casually reattaching body parts like it’s no big deal. But who cares? It’s a chaotic, hilarious thrill ride, and you’ll love every insane second of it. 10/10 would lose a hand to [spoiler] Lady D [/spoiler] again.

A masterpiece through and through.

After almost thirty years, it still feels and plays like a pure Resident Evil game: the gunplay still has this arcady feel to it, and the progression still spirals around some sort of hub that expands with those good ol' Capcom puzzles. The truly amazing graphics are just the cherry on the top.

I love how each segment tries to introduce new gameplay elements but I have to congratulate the Devs for the whole Donna Beneviento segment. This right here is a gold nugget of true survival horror and environmental storytelling and will stay with me for years to come.

Finally, the game (and the REngine more generally) runs flawlessly, even on a 2019 PC. 

tl/dr: I highly recommend it !

Resident Evil Village : By Triple F

"Resident Evil Village," the eighth main installment in Capcom’s iconic survival horror series, pushes the boundaries of the franchise with a blend of atmospheric horror, intricate storytelling, and action-oriented gameplay. Released in 2021, the game directly follows the events of "Resident Evil 7: Biohazard" and continues the story of protagonist Ethan Winters, who, after barely escaping the horrors of the Baker family estate, finds himself searching for his kidnapped daughter in a mysterious Eastern European village. While "Village" incorporates elements from "Resident Evil 4" in its structure and pacing, it builds on the first-person horror foundation established in "Resident Evil 7," bringing players closer than ever to the action and atmosphere that define its new horror direction.

The setting of "Resident Evil Village" is among its most compelling features, drawing players into a richly detailed, Gothic-inspired village that feels both expansive and claustrophobic. The village acts as a central hub, surrounded by foreboding environments that each host distinct, horrific threats, such as the lavish Castle Dimitrescu, the eerie Beneviento House, and the mechanical horrors of Heisenberg’s factory. These diverse locations allow Capcom to showcase different styles of horror, from psychological tension and body horror to grotesque monstrosities and combat-driven encounters. The attention to detail in each area is meticulous, with atmospheric lighting, haunting sound design, and environmental storytelling that make each corner of the village feel alive and dangerously unpredictable.

Gameplay in "Resident Evil Village" strikes a balance between survival horror and action, echoing the structure of "Resident Evil 4" while retaining the first-person perspective from "Resident Evil 7." Combat is more refined and flexible, giving players access to an array of weapons, from pistols and shotguns to sniper rifles, that encourage different approaches to encounters. Ammunition and resources are scarce enough to keep players on edge, but more readily available than in "Resident Evil 7," allowing for a greater focus on action without entirely losing the series’ survival elements. This shift brings a layer of empowerment to Ethan while still demanding resourcefulness and tactical awareness, particularly during encounters with the game’s more powerful enemies and boss fights, which require careful use of space and ammunition.

The enemies in "Resident Evil Village" are a highlight, showcasing some of the series’ most varied and inventive designs to date. Each major area of the game is controlled by a unique “Lord,” with distinct enemy types associated with each one, from the vampiric daughters of Lady Dimitrescu to the grotesque, mind-altering creations in House Beneviento. These enemies force players to adapt their strategies, whether it's conserving resources against the relentless Lycans that roam the village or solving intricate puzzles in Beneviento’s disturbing, psychological horror-themed section. The Lords themselves serve as unforgettable boss fights, each with unique combat mechanics and backstories that enhance the narrative. The variety in enemy design and behavior helps to keep the game’s pace dynamic, ensuring that no two sections feel the same.

The narrative of "Resident Evil Village" is a compelling blend of mystery and horror, expanding Ethan’s story while weaving connections to broader franchise lore. Ethan’s journey to rescue his daughter unfolds like a dark fairy tale, gradually revealing the village’s twisted history and the purpose of the four Lords under the control of Mother Miranda, a powerful figure with her own haunting motivations. As Ethan uncovers more about the village’s origin and his connection to it, the game reveals ties to "Resident Evil" mythology that will resonate deeply with longtime fans. The storytelling is elevated by strong voice acting and cinematic moments that make the stakes feel personal, grounding the horror in a tale of love, loss, and survival.

One of the most effective and unnerving parts of "Village" is House Beneviento, a chapter that dials back combat in favor of pure psychological horror. Here, Ethan is stripped of his weapons and forced to navigate a series of surreal, chilling puzzles that evoke classic survival horror elements, such as limited resources, oppressive atmosphere, and a sense of helplessness. The experience of House Beneviento is unique within the game, relying on subtle, slow-building tension and disturbing imagery rather than direct confrontation. It’s a standout sequence that proves "Village" can deliver both heart-pounding action and deeply unsettling horror, showcasing the range of scares Capcom is able to achieve in a single game.

"Resident Evil Village" also brings back the merchant system with the character of the Duke, a mysterious vendor who assists Ethan by selling weapons, upgrades, and supplies. The Duke adds an intriguing layer to the gameplay loop, giving players an opportunity to spend the currency gained from looting treasures and defeating enemies on valuable upgrades that enhance survival. He also provides cooking services that grant permanent health and stamina boosts, making exploration and resource management feel rewarding. The Duke is a welcome homage to the merchant from "Resident Evil 4," and his cryptic hints and connections to the story add another layer of mystery to the game.

Ultimately, "Resident Evil Village" is a masterclass in balancing horror and action, merging the best elements of the franchise’s past with modern gameplay mechanics and an engaging story. Its meticulously crafted world, varied gameplay, and unforgettable characters create an immersive experience that appeals to both horror purists and fans of action-oriented gameplay. While some sections lean more heavily into action than horror, the game maintains a suspenseful atmosphere throughout, ensuring a thrill from beginning to end. With "Village," Capcom has proven that "Resident Evil" can continue to evolve, offering players an ambitious, polished, and multifaceted horror experience that both honors its roots and pushes boldly into new territory.

[h1]My Review of Resident Evil Village[/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a memorable entry in the series, blending horror with a gothic aesthetic that stands out. This review covers five parts: the first half and second half of the game, the Village itself, the story, and the overall presentation.

[h2]The First Half[/h2]
The first half of the game is fantastic—exactly what I want from Resident Evil. It’s creepy, with eerie spaces to explore, undead enemies, and a survival-horror style inspired by RE1, 2, and 7, even taking some cues from Silent Hills PT. In one particularly creepy section, the game hits a series high for atmosphere, almost surpassing RE7 in sheer tension. However, resource management could have been better balanced. In classic Resident Evil, every bullet and herb felt crucial, but here, resources are so plentiful that I rarely felt pressured or concerned about running low, which took away some of that classic Resident Evil survival tension.

[h2]The Second Half[/h2]
The second half is where the game lost its grip on me. While it maintains a horror theme, it shifts away from the tense survival elements of the first half and moves into more of an action-adventure with horror elements. This change dialed back the tension, and I found myself no longer on edge or reluctant to peek around the next corner. The scares became less impactful, and the shift in tone felt like a departure from the survival horror experience I expected.

[h2]The Village[/h2]
The Village acts as a central hub that opens up with new areas and secrets over time. This progression is rewarding, though basic, and would have provided a great reprieve if the horror-survival style had continued throughout. However, as the game shifted in tone, the Village felt more like a place to check off items than a necessary retreat.

[h2]Presentation[/h2]
The presentation shines—Resident Evil Village excels both visually and audibly. The clean audio and stunning visuals add a lot to the game’s atmosphere, and performance has been excellent, especially after recent optimizations.

[h2]Story[/h2]
The story missed the mark for me. While there are some twists that could have had a bigger impact, they fall flat without strong character connections. Ethan remains a faceless character, and his lack of development made it hard to invest in his journey or the supporting cast. The main story features interesting lore callbacks to RE1-3, though these are relegated to optional background rather than integral to the central plot.

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
For me, the first half of Resident Evil Village is peak Resident Evil, delivering creepy, well-paced horror with a balanced use of the Village as a break from the tension. I could even overlook the story flaws because the horror worked so well, making it a 10/10 up to this point. However, when the game shifts to a horror-themed action-adventure, it loses its identity, and the flaws become harder to overlook. By this point, the second half feels like a 6/10.
I somewhat believe the developers see it similar as the entire advertisement focuses almost exclusivly on the first half of the game so you'll be a little suprised how fast you'll leave the trailer stuff behind you. 

Overall, I’d rate Resident Evil Village an 8 out of 10.

[h3] Final Thoughts[/h3]
I hope Resident Evil 9 brings back the tension and survival elements from Village’s first half, keeping the action sequences to a minimum until the end. I’d also love to see Resident Evil 1, Code Veronica, and Zero remade, which seems possible given the series’ current direction.

This game was mostly designed to feel like "Resident Evil 4: Ethan Winters Edition" and I dig that A LOT.  While not being able to roundhouse kick enemies (nor sneak up on them like in RE4:R), combat feels varied and snappy, and serve as good preparation for RE4:R. The Beneviento and Heisenberg sections are my favorite, the former is a nice switch-up from all the game's action-heavy gameplay whilst the latter I simply find to be sick; that ♥♥♥♥ played out like an IMAX film and I don't care if others find it to be out-of-character, it's not RE6's level of "big thing go boom and also we're piloting a damn plane".

Main game's story is great. I really like Ethan Winters as he slowly became more witty and determined as the game progresses; not in the same way as Leon, but close enough. Chris's actions were a bit odd, but I didn't mind that a whole bunch.

As for nitpicks, collecting items can be disorienting because they can be acquired over a longer distance than expected, so in the heat of battle that threw me off a lot. Audio proximity is also not the most distinct in terms of enemy encounters, but not a big deal. Lastly, mini bosses don't chase you around if you're far enough away from a designated area, so while it's easy to cheese them it can also come off as a hassle if unprepared.

The DLC campaign is...eh. Certainly feels less like an RE game as it feels more fantastical and dream-like. Gameplay is more akin to a traditional survival horror as ammo and resources are more limited, which is nice. And the Beneviento section this time around was amplified by 10 in terms of how frightening the enemy encounters were. The story I could care less about, wasn't very moving and the whole "Michael" thing was kinda off too even by the end of the campaign.

And Capcom, please don't lock 3rd Person mode behind a paywall. How else am I supposed to get a good look at Ethan's face when being chased down by a tall woman???
