Despite not being a huge fan of zombie games or anything zombie in general, modern Resident Evil games have a formula that simply hits just right for me. The horror atmosphere and the action/adventure parts are well-balanced, the game rarely feels cheap. The story can reach absurdities, but it never really bothered me and everything overall just sort of clicked in the end. 

This eighth instalment in the series has a very interesting setup, the environments are greatly varied and there is a lot of interesting characters. The voice acting was again amazing. Where I found a lot of improvement is how diverse the enemy encounters were and how well the graphics (vastly improved) were used to emphasize the atmosphere of many places. I had no issue with lighting this time around – the artistic direction is great. What was also made better was exploration and backtracking – I was complaining about boring and empty parts last time – this time I never really felt safe during backtracking as the game made sure to keep the danger imminent at all (…well, most of the…) times.

This is the 8th mainline Resident Evil game, but it really feels like the second game to a completely new IP that pays homage to Resident Evil.

RE8 is bit of a mixed bag. One the one hand, it has a lot of improvements over RE7. I has more interesting and varied locations, it has more involved bosses (and an actual final boss fight), it has more enemy types, it has marginally better puzzles, and it has more content to engage with. But, there's another, mangled, less functional hand to consider. The FOV is shockingly low. The intro sequence is painfully slow. One fairly big section of the game is a non-combat interactive puzzle, where you interact with a boss to win. The penultimate section of the game is awful, which such slow movement speed I thought the game bugged. Also, there's the story.

The game opens with a moment that will confuse both Ethan and the player. However, it could be cleared up in one sentence. The problem is that in universe, they would have just cleared up the misconception right there. But because "Ethan" and "the audience" are the same person, the information is kept from Ethan for the audience's benefit. It just doesn't work. The story is both about rescuing your baby, and why the baby even needed to be rescued. And I found pretty much everything in that department to be hugely unsatisfying and boring. All that really matters is Ethan is stuck in a weird European village, but it would have been nice if the surrounding story was a bit more intriguing.

But, I think the scales tip to the game's favor. Lady D is just such an awesome character, and she steals the show. Her castle is amazing, so vividly detailed, and so coherently organized. It was disappointing that she represents 25% of the game, is the best part, and is also first. It's hard to top her character and location, but everything else is pretty good.

I'd recommend the game, but I'd also recommend an FOV mod.

Resident Evil Village takes players on a thrilling and atmospheric journey that blends horror, action, and an engaging storyline. Set in a desolate Eastern European village, the game masterfully builds on the lore established in Resident Evil 7 while introducing new elements that breathe fresh life into the franchise.

The graphics are stunning, showcasing intricate details in both character models and the haunting environments. The village itself is beautifully crafted, with an eerie ambiance that keeps you on edge. The sound design enhances this experience, with ambient noises and chilling music that perfectly complement the game’s tension.

Gameplay strikes a balance between exploration and combat. Players will find themselves solving puzzles, scavenging for resources, and engaging in intense battles with a variety of grotesque enemies. The combat mechanics are satisfying, offering a range of weapons and upgrades that allow for different play styles. Boss encounters, particularly with the iconic Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, are both challenging and memorable, each requiring unique strategies.

One of the standout features is the game’s ability to shift tones and gameplay styles. From survival horror to action-packed sequences, Resident Evil Village keeps you guessing and invested throughout your journey.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a triumphant addition to the series that successfully merges classic horror with modern gameplay mechanics. It’s a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike, offering a hauntingly beautiful world filled with suspense, mystery, and excitement. Whether you’re in it for the scares or the story, this installment delivers on all fronts.

Resident Evil Village or RE 8 as it it’s known, is a direct continuation of the story of the Winters that began in Resident Evil 7. You reprise the role of Ethan Winters as you explore a monster infested village in search of his daughter, Rosemary Winters and ultimately discover the origins of the Mold (with some help from RE Vet Chris Redfield).

Gameplay is similar to RE7 with puzzle solving and exploration in horror themed environments but a bit more action focused this time around. In fact this game pulls a lot from RE4 and if you enjoyed RE4, chances are you’ll enjoy this one too.

Pros:

+++ The Visuals. My god the graphics and visual direction in the game are top notch. Capcom really knows how to make the most out of their RE Engine. The world is incredibly detailed, dirty, bloodied, and a gorgeous macabre sight to behold in just about all areas. Lighting is done well too as no place feels too dark to be a bother or lighted unnaturally.

+ Performance even with those impressive visuals is optimized quite well. You’ll still need a decent rig to get the most out of it and make use of RTX features, but even at lower settings the game still looks and runs great. (The interlace option is a great way to boost your FPS with little loss of visual fidelity). You also get previews of the graphic options too which should become a standard. 

++ Sound design is excellent is for a game of this type as it should be. The guns sound good, flesh and bone getting chewed on sounds meaty and visceral and the directional audio works well enough to let you know where threats are.

++ Voice acting is also done quite well throughout with just enough camp to not be too cheesy or dull to hear on repeat playthroughs. 

++ Level design is also on point with main paths often looping you back around to starting areas naturally with a few side paths here and there for extra goodies. The Village itself acts a bit of a hub to the other regions that serve as “stages” for that Lord’s area. Each area also feels distinct from the others.

+ Decent accessibility options

+ Puzzle design is decently done. There’s nothing too complex here, it fact some might the puzzles a bit too easy but I found them adequate and not frustrating or too obtuse. The base game’s puzzles really shouldn’t stump most players familiar with the series.

+ The shopkeeper, the Duke is a well set shop and upgrade system. New weapons can be bought, upgraded and even food crafted for stat boosts. While the amount of money that can be gained in a session is limited, I never felt like was strapped for cash in the game and could upgrade at a steady rate.

+ The boss fights overall are done quite well and nicely varied with maybe a couple exceptions

+ The Story overall is done well IMO. It does a decent enough job of expanding the lore of the Mold from RE7 with a small nod to the OG villains of the franchise. 

++ The antagonists for the most part I found to be interesting and varied. While Moreau is probably the least interesting, the rest all provide some story interest. While Dimitrescu certainly dominates the media for this game, I found Heisenburg a far more compelling and complex antagonist for Ethan with his own subplot running in the background.  

++ Extras. There’s a good amount of extra content here, especially if you got the Gold edition. There’s additional weapons to unlock, infinite ammo unlocks, galleries with game still and artwork with dev notes and a model viewer. Mecenaries mode also exists for more gameplay. It’s very similar to the Mercenaries mode from previous games. 

++ The Shadows of Rose DLC provides a nice post-game expansion to the events of the main game and in IMO provides a better final confrontation with the game’s main baddie. 

+ Third person option exists if you prefer. I find it a bit weird to use but some may prefer it.

+ Difficulty options are decent. You have your basic push over mode, “Normal”, and Hardcore which is more like the classic RE games. Village of Shadows, the hardest difficulty option does change up a few things beside the basics so it can feel like a fresh experience to the other options. 

Cons:

-- Typical Capcom UI jank plagues this game. Fake scroll bars, slow mouse scrolling, no confirmation for resolution changes in graphics settings, right click to go back instead of ESC, DEL key to quit the game and mouse focus lock is lost anytime you enter a menu or look at the inventory. Capcom, please hire someone who knows this stuff as it’s apparent the person you have right now doesn’t.

- No FOV adjustments for a first person game is sacrilege 

- As usual in most RE games, the knife is nearly useless. Short range, minimal damage,  and it doesn’t stun enemies so you’ll almost always get grabbed if you try to use it. (Yes, I know Chris’s knife is way better but you don’t get that on the first playthrough)

- The story with Chris Redfield in this game is… not great. While the whole intro sequence is certainly intriguing it makes Chris come off as a huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for most of the game. In fact the game even pokes at this towards the end that Chris should had just come clean with Ethan and maybe could had avoided half of this mess. It just comes off that this particular side of the plot wasn’t thought out very well.  

- The plot twists… I don’t want to spoil in my review, but to be honest, I don’t think they’re that great. One has continuity issues and the other felt so obvious to me that I didn’t even think it was a twist.

- The mid section of the game definitely drags a bit, especially on repeat playthoughs.

- While most boss fights are enjoyable, there’s a couple that are a real nuisance to deal with and it mostly comes down the area you’re forced to fight in. 

- The Shadows of Rose DLC is a lot more puzzle focused than the main game and some of them are a bit too obtuse and filled with too many instant kill moments. 

Overall, I very much enjoyed my time with RE Village and had more fun with than I expected. I think I may prefer this over RE7, which was also surprisingly good. I don’t think this quite tops RE4, but it’s still a very good RE game and highly recommended.

RE8 not only is a great action horror game with good feeling combat, interesting exploration, and a decent story; but it also leans into the campy nature of the franchise. Ethan's stubborn "I'm over this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" attitude and cheesy one liners fit right in with some of the most beloved moments of the series. Different parts of the game lean on different strengths, mixing things up a bit throughout keeping things from getting too stale or repetitive. One moment you have the classic "move around this area while avoiding a large invincible adversary" the next you get your tense escape room-esque puzzles with no way to fight back against the horror looking for you and then you get your wild over the top action shootouts and giant bosses, which all feel unique and distinct, sprinkled in. A great memorable experience that shouldn't be missed.

No but really, Ethan is the best part of the game for me. I haven't touched RE7 yet because I know that it's the scariest RE game out there and I'm actually the biggest chicken to exist, so I went in not really knowing Ethan's character, but this game made me fall in love so quickly because you just feel for him. Poor guy just wants to have a normal life with his sus wife and his daughter, and then Chris comes in and doesn't explain a thing for the longest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ time. Of course Ethan is gonna be cranky and confused, fights his way through the whole village to get his daughter back. The emotional impact of the father-daughter bond really got to me, and Ethan's trashtalk is so dumb and I love it so so much. His character just resonated so well with me. Got done with a boss fight, what does he say? "Eat ♥♥♥♥." Hell yeah. 

Anyway, there weren't a lot of parts that had me scared, the most obvious part being the dollmaker house with the baby monster. But not being afraid doesn't mean it wasn't good or fun. I enjoyed the heck out of this whole game, it's just fun to shoot enemies in the face with a good shotgun, and the mercenaries mode lets you play as Dimitrescu??? Hello??? That's so awesome. 

All that aside, I am going to compare it to RE4 Remake, because they are similar in a lot of ways. First off, village setting, plus castle. Second, religious cult. Third, more action than horror but still fun. Fourth, merchant character, and with that comes the currency and treasure hunt. I feel like they were really counting on people who loved the original RE4 to love this one too because there are so many similarities, or maybe they were testing some stuff out to see how it would be received, since about 2 years later, the RE4 remake would be released. 
My personal pet-peeve is that finding items is such a pain. In the other games I've played, if you walk past items, they get marked on the map. However, in this one, I don't think it does? Maybe I'm just dumb, but I've walked past items so many times because they're just harder to spot than in any other RE game for some reason, and I had to go back and search areas so many times because I was still missing something and couldn't find it. 
Also I think some of the achievements are bugged, like shooting all destructible windows in the castle. 

Anyway; the OST is great, the graphics are great, the gameplay is fun, wasn't afraid but had a really good time, I love Ethan and he deserves so much better, and Chris is a big doofus. 10/10.

My review does contain partial spoilers. Please beware.

As far as the game goes, it's fun. Enjoyable story and characters, boss fights are fun, and the story is interesting. It still holds a lot of Resident Evil qualities, such as the limited ammo/crafting system, while borrowing the "Merchant" idea from the original Resident Evil 4 (even nodding to him via a voice line!). 

The story is heart warming and the game is fun, but it honestly does not feel as if it can fit in the typical Resident Evil franchise. They attempt to make a strong argument as to why certain characters have supernatural-like qualities, despite just being bioweapons, but it honestly feels hard to believe (as far as the universe that has been created). 

The first half of the game was phenomenal, and really set the stage, but the second half was subpar, with the final boss fight being outright boring. The ending was touching, and almost redeemed the game for me; however I cannot overlook such an underwhelming boss fight.

I've played this game multiple times and will always return to it as a Resident Evil fan, but as a successor to Re7 (an AMAZING addition to the franchise with the introduction of Ethan Winters), this game was a 4/10 at best.

Obviously, you're welcome to your own opinion, and I think the game is still enjoyable, but in comparison to former Resident Evil games, it just didn't meet my personal expectations.

[h3] Overview [/h3] 
Resident Evil Village is the 8th mainline game in RE franchise, and is a direct sequel of RE7. The game has you continuing the story of Ethan Winters, the protagonist from RE7, after the events of the last game. I would recommend playing 7 first before Village, but the game does play a recap video of 7's plot in order to catch the player up to speed - so it is possible to play Village without having played 7 first. If you enjoyed RE7, there is a good chance you will also enjoy Village; however, I personally prefer the Southern Gothic horror theming of 7 over Village.

[h3] What to Expect [/h3] 
Like 7, Village maintains the first-person perspective. While it is still a survival horror game, it feels more action-focused than the previous title. Where as RE7 felt like it was RE1 but an FPS, Village feels like RE4 but an FPS. In RE7, you spent a lot of time exploring, solving puzzles, fearful of single enemies due to limited resources, and utilized an item box system to manage your limited inventory.

Village, like RE4, eschews the item box in favor of grid-based inventory system that you can expand and organize in a Tetris-like manner. I was always able to afford the next inventory upgrade whenever it became available, so I never once found myself not able to put something in my inventory.

Like RE 4, there is a merchant NPC that you can buy new guns from, upgrade your guns, buy gun mods, and sell treasures you find hidden in the world for additional currency. Like RE4, defeated enemies will drop crafting materials, money, or treasures.

Also like RE4, Village takes place in a non-specific country in Europe. The main map of the game uses the titular village as a hub that you can gain access to more of as you progress through the other 4 main "dungeons" of the game that each end in a boss fight. Each of these major areas has a different theme of horror: werewolf infested village, Gothic vampire castle, creepy possessed dolls, aquatic monster horror, and industrial body horror. The different areas vary up the gameplay slightly, with one area having you avoid a Nemesis-like pursuer, another being purely puzzle-focused with no combat, and another that is heavily combat focused.

[h3] Criticisms [/h3] 
The KB&M controls are really unintuitive, predominately with a lot of the UI. I don't remember RE7's controls being this bad. I powered through the game with them, but I never really felt I got used to them. For example, to open the map you hit "V," and to move on the map screen you need to hold down the middle mouse button to drag the map... instead of the left click. Also, to exit this screen you lick the right mouse button instead of the "V" key again. There were many times I'd open up the map screen, try to drag/move the map with left click, realize it was not moving, then try to drag with the right click - only to then be exited out of the map menu entirely. 

*While Village definitely feels like a mash-up of RE7 and RE4 to be more combat-focused, it was rather odd that they did not add any more melee/unarmed combat options that were present in RE4. 
*The puzzles and exploration in Village feel a lot weaker compared to RE7.
*Because the game is split into smaller, distinct sections, they tend to feel a littler more linear and railroady than in some of the more survival horror focused RE games.
*The factory level's industrial design left many of the halls, corridors, and mezzanine levels looking the same, making it a little difficult to navigate even with the map.

[h3] Other Features [/h3] 
*At some point the game added a 3rd-person mode, so now it can be played just like the RE2 through RE4 remakes (I personally played it in 1st-person mode as that is what it was intended for).
*The Shadows of Rose DLC serves as an epilogue to the main story where you play as a different character with unique powers in the 3rd person. This campaign took me about 2.5 hours to complete. Much of it has you exploring zones from the base game, but has some unique enemies and gameplay elements.
*There is a mercenaries mode with 4 playable characters (Ethan Winters, Chris Redfield, and 2 unlockable characters that are bosses from the base game). Each character plays differently and has its own unique set of weapons, attacks, and abilities. I got a few hours of fun out of it. I beat all the normal mode areas with Ethan and tried the other characters at least once.

[h3] Final Thoughts [/h3] 
 I got the the Gold Edition with the DLC on a steep discount and felt I got my money's worth. I beat the main game on the standard difficulty with Steam saying it was under 15 hours played (though the in-game completion time was around 10 hours). I've a veteran of the RE games and it felt pretty easy for me at this difficulty. There were a few tense moments, but I feel I probably should have played it on the next difficulty up. Overall, I enjoyed my time with the game.

As someone who has been playing the Resident Evil starting with the first game on the PS1 back in 1996:  Resident Evil Village hits the same way that your favorite band's Greatest Hits release does.  You realize how long this has been around, how much the culture around music/gaming has changed [in addition to how much really hasn't changed], and how this is only another step because there's definitely more to come.

NGL, I'm really impressed with the quality of Capcom's RE Engine games.  The fact that the last FIVE Resident Evil games have all been bangers seems unreal to me because at some point, we'll hit that point of [strike]global[/strike]over-saturation just like we did before RE4 released.  Yeah, Code Veronica was technically impressive, but tank controls on the Dreamcast in full 3D?  C'mon now...  

Either way, I have nothing but praises to sing for Village.  Ethan and Mia's story is brought back and is concluded in an especially satisfying manner.  The gameplay beats and progress remind me of other 3D Metroidvania's, most notably: Batman - Arkham Asylum.  The audio is on another level.  The way the wind echoes through The Village causing tree branches to snap, windows and doors to jitter and rattle.  It just completes the atmosphere.  

I fully hope that Capcom embraces more Metroidvania concepts for RE9.  Also, I'm hoping they will give Code Veronica the RE Engine treatment because the game certainly deserves some love.

Ethan returns to a sh!tshow yet again, as the man with the worst luck in Resident Evil history. 

If you haven't played RE7, then I believe you should wait on playing this until after that game. Although it's not 100% necessary, it certainly adds to the experience and gives you a better idea of what's new and what's different. I'm gonna compare it to 7 a lot because it's structured very similarly. 

HORROR: 7 takes this one easily. 8 has many unsettling areas, especially [i]one[/i] in particular; but for the most part it's quite a bit more action and light tension focused. Not a bad thing, just different.

ACTION: Obviously, this goes to 8. Many times I had my jaw near the floor like WTF IS HAPPENING

STORY: Neck and neck with 7. After all, it's a sequel, and equally builds upon and creates new mysteries and intrigue within the new European village. 

SHOOTING / PUZZLES: Yet again, pretty even and consistent with 7. I think some puzzles in 7 were more difficult to figure out, but 8 makes it very accessible. Boss fights are a separate discussion. I feel like for players who like to do everything and find as much stuff as they can, the game will become much easier as it rewards you more than it punishes you. 

BOSS FIGHTS: Very much improved. Without spoiling, I'll say that the major ones feel very tested and satisfying to play. Not a single one was a pain or frustrating. I give the point to 8. 

With that, RE8 is ahead for me personally in a couple categories. However, those categories are highly up to your own interpretation, and I think that both RE7 and RE8 have their own respective strengths that make sense both thematically and technically. Very impressed; can't wait to see more in the future.

Resident Evil Village delivers an exhilarating blend of survival horror, action, and exploration that both honors the franchise’s roots and pushes it forward. Here’s my breakdown:

Pros:

	1.	Atmosphere & Visuals: The gothic, European village setting is stunning, from the eerie castle to the creepy woods. The attention to detail and atmosphere is top-tier, amplified by excellent lighting and environment design.
	2.	Varied Gameplay: From tense horror sections to action-packed firefights, the pacing keeps you on edge. Each section has its own distinct vibe, giving you different flavors of horror throughout the game.
	3.	Memorable Villains: Lady Dimitrescu and the other Lords are standout antagonists, each with their own unique personalities and settings, adding a lot of character to the game.
	4.	Inventory & Crafting System: The return of the attache case is a welcome nostalgia hit, and managing your inventory feels satisfying without being tedious.
	5.	Performance: Even with its jaw-dropping visuals, the game runs smoothly on a wide range of hardware, thanks to great optimization.

Cons:

	1.	Lack of True Survival Horror: While there are horror elements, some sections lean more towards action than fear, which may not sit well with fans craving pure survival horror.
	2.	Short Playtime: The main story can feel a bit short, especially if you’re used to taking your time. However, replay value with New Game+ and Mercenaries mode helps balance this out.
	3.	Ethan’s Character: While Ethan Winters gets more development, he still feels a bit flat compared to the series’ iconic protagonists.

Verdict:
Resident Evil Village is a must-play for both long-time fans and newcomers. It’s a thrilling, visually stunning experience with enough twists and turns to keep you hooked. While it skews more towards action at times, the game’s incredible atmosphere and engaging story make it one of the best entries in the series.

The overall progress in the game is pretty linear, where you go from area to area, and while you have some freedom to go down branching paths in general you need to go a certain way to progress. You spend most of the game fighting cannon fodder enemies that still pose a challenge because of how limited your ammo is and a lot of the game is spent exploring for more resources. That is the main part. The other chunk of the game is what I would call "set pieces" where the normal flow of the game is suspended as you puzzle out something while panic running from a monster. There are some truly memorable moments (house beneviento for example) within that formula. I waffle back and forth whether the health sponge enemies are good or bad horror, because on one hand they are annoying and frustrating but on the other hand I did feel tense about the amount of resources I was wasting on them, and having me run from enemies because I just don't think i have the resources to deal with them is actually pretty effective. My only complaint is that the "ending" is like a two hour sequence where a lot of this gets kind of boring because the gameplay elements get removed. 

Storywise the game is pretty good, though it is very "out there". There are vampire and werewolf like creatures, but also bioweapon experiments and super powered humans with magneto powers. Its not exactly cohesive or grounded, but it is all part of the story. The horror does not have one foot in reality, it has both feet in space, and while that is not my favorite type of horror, it is well done here.

This game does work as a standalone game without needing to play previous titles, but you probably benefit from playing RE7. [h3] Base Game [/h3]

The game's atmosphere is absolutely chilling, with every location with tension and dread. The combination of stunning visuals, haunting sound design, and a truly terrifying story makes for an unforgettable experience.

The gameplay is a perfect blend of survival horror and action, offering a satisfying balance of exploration, puzzle-solving, and intense combat. The enemies are both terrifying and sometimes challenging, forcing you to use your reflexes to survive.

The story is well-paced and filled with twists and turns that keep you on the edge of your seat. The characters are memorable and well-developed, and the game's lore is rich and intriguing.

[h3] The Mercenaries [/h3]

For those seeking a more action-packed experience, the Mercenaries Mode is a classic return. Players can choose from four legendary characters: Ethan Winters, Chris Redfield, Lady Dimitrescu, and Karl Heisenberg. Each character has their own unique abilities and playstyle, making for a diverse and exciting experience.

This is a good entry in the franchise.

Combat starts out some what frustrating, but gets better when the weapons become more powerful. Aiming and head-shots are important, as well as player position in relation to enemies.

Crafting items and upgrading weapons is a major component, which helps to serve as reason to fully explore the game world. Resource management is implemented well, wasting ammo is not a good idea. Every purchase from the merchant should be weighed carefully.

Exploration is great, with large sections of the valley partitioned out. The paths can seem a bit restricted and linear, but not enough to mind considering the franchise has always been that way. Maps are big squares as apposed to say early Call of Duty with skinny paths.

Cut-scenes no longer appear in modern Resident Evil, replaced by in-engine scripted events. This is better because it is far less jarring than to be taken out of the first person perspective. However, the scripted events are quite frequent, especially early on. Would prefer to have less of them and more free movement like in Half-Life.

Story is entertaining, but is going far beyond the original idea of a city over-run with zombies. Would like a less fantasy premise that is difficult to believe. Just stick with a virus infecting people and turning them into zombies.

Enjoyable overall.

Resident Evil Village successfully revitalizes the series by blending its classic survival horror roots with innovative gameplay and an engaging narrative. For those who found Resident Evil 7 intriguing but felt it fell short in certain areas, Village delivers a more refined and exhilarating experience.
One of the standout features of Resident Evil Village is its gameplay. The game builds upon the solid foundation laid by Biohazard, offering an expanded and more dynamic experience. The diverse range of enemies keeps players on their toes, making each encounter unique and challenging. The variety not only enriches the combat but also enhances the overall sense of dread and unpredictability.
While the gameplay is impressive, it’s the story that truly sets Resident Evil Village apart. The game excels in crafting a compelling narrative that is both gripping and emotionally satisfying. Ethan Winters’ journey comes to a meaningful conclusion, providing a fitting end to his arc. The storytelling is deeply immersive, with a rich lore that adds depth to the world and its characters. This strong narrative focus distinguishes Village from its predecessor, making it a more memorable and impactful experience.
Final Thoughts
Overall, Resident Evil Village stands out as a superior entry in the series, surpassing Biohazard in gameplay and in story. The combination of varied enemies, a captivating plot, and a satisfying conclusion for Ethan’s character makes this installment a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike. If you’re looking for a modern survival horror game that balances tension with innovation, Resident Evil Village is an exemplary choice.

Resident Evil Village is a great, but incredibly uneven game with some significant flaw. Some story related and some mechanics related. A lot of the flaws are more obvious on replay.

The gothic castle theme, despite being heavily used in the game promo and in the teaser, only accounts for the first 20-25% of the game. It’s enjoyable and has classic RE elements but it feels over very fast compared to how much is left when you’re done. The villain of the castle is gone from the game far too soon, and it’s tremendously to the game’s detriment.

The Doll-maker House is enjoyable the first time but on replay it loses ALL its good notes. There’re no enemies to fight and you just run from one piece of the puzzle to the next to get it over as fast as possible so you can get your equipment back and actually play the game. It’s also an extremely short part of the game and almost feels like a separate game entirely stitched into RE Village, but it doesn’t quite fit. The boss fight is also disappointing and gimmicky.

The fish man is fun but also short, like the Doll-maker House. Much of the area is spent just trying not to fall in the water. The side areas you can do after the fish area are more fun than the actual fish area.

The factory (as with the Doll-Maker House) seems like an entirely different game when compared to the actual Village and the gothic castle. It has good RE themes and level designed but the mini boss is also very gimmicky. The final boss of the factory falls apart hugely on replay. You spend time (often multiple full runs worth) getting powerful weapons but you cannot use them at all in this section. You are stuck in a mech-tank and it has the same power as always. It feels like a downgrade after building up so much power. 

Speaking of downgrades, in the section right after the factory, on your first play through you feel super powered, but on replay it’s the opposite. The weapons that once felt OP feel weak in comparison and when you get to higher difficulties, you’re at a huge disadvantage. It was a significant lapse to not let you keep your own equipment on NG+ when you get to this section. For me it’s the single biggest flaw in the game that makes the end of any replay a chore to get through. 

The final boss is also disappointing. They do some nice tie-ins lore-wise but she just doesn’t feel like a final boss should. Also the lore is left for you to read on notes as a “lore dump” close to the end of the game.

On top of that not only did they cut down the horror they also completely removed the sense of inventory management by removing chests and moving crafting materials to another tab, which honestly sucks because its such a huge part of the resident evil spirit. I have only been encumbered once which I could easily solve by moving items around. However it is very actiony, if RE7 was RE2 RE8 would be RE4 though the combat is nowhere detailed like RE4’s but still a major upgrade from RE7. One of the things I disliked the most about RE7 was that there were very few enemy types. That got fixed thankfully and its still not as varied like RE4 but at least you don’t only fight enemies with the same texture like in RE7. All of the boss fights were fun and different from each other even the minor boss fights were varied. Exploring the whole village was so fun and rewarding I also love that instead of finding coins for upgrades like in RE7 you hunt animal meats and bring them to duke for him to cook with and you get upgrades from the meals he cooks, that was interesting. Another thing I disliked about RE7 was its pacing and I think RE8 pacing is absolutely amazing like its too good, probably my favorite part. Insane prologue that will make you say wtf, amazing introduction to the village and the chaos state that its in, crazzyy introduction to the antagonists, chateau dimitrescu (the first big level), open world and exploration section with beneviento and moreau levels (beneviento and Moreau levels are smaller than those of lady dimitrescu and Heisenberg but as a whole with the open world its the second big level), the factory (3rd big level), Chris section and final boss are the end game. Its the most story heavy resident evil game and they made a great job with the pacing if it wasn’t this long I probably could finish it one sitting. Shadows of rose dlc was really fun, emotional and lowkey the most scary RE has ever been featuring a great final boss fight and it makes a great job wrapping up Rose’s story and preparing it for future installments. To fully grasp this review, here is what "non-resident evil fans" need to know...

[b]RE1, RE2, and RE3[/b] were the "original" survival horror games in this series, where you had to CAREFULLY manage inventory, and avoid enemies if possible.
[b]RE4[/b] went a bit more "action oriented" with its design, and made you into a killing machine, that killed enemies left and right, which felt refreshing at the time.
[b]RE5 and RE6[/b], went 100% over the top with an action focus, and had "horror" being more of a minor theme, and fans HATED it...

Resident Evil is at its best, when it commits to survival horror. In RE7 we finally went back to survival horror, after the atrocity of RE6, where CAPCOM went fully into a more action oriented playstyle... And fans were happy!

RE:Village is hard to review, on the basis that it still IS survival horror... But at the same time also starts diving back into a much more action oriented playstyle again, similar to RE4 and RE5... :/

While RE:Village tries to keep things scary... It doesn't feel like RE7s incredible survival horror focus... And I was REEEALLY hoping CAPCOM would stick to that direction. ':D

On top of that, the gunplay feels VERY flat in RE:Village... :/ When you shoot enemies, it doesn't feel satisfying... Kind of as if it was developed by people, who were still "figuring things out" when it comes to action combat.

So is RE:Village good? 

Short answer is yes. But don't expect the same level of survival horror, as RE7. RE:Village is a horror based action shooter.

Oh boy where do i start with this one. the pacing, the way the game is VERY linear, the heavy scripted sequences. Let's start with the positives shall we.

Graphics: The graphics looks so nice crisp and clean, especially when you enable the RTX in the game. It's just beautiful to look at with these small details to the world, the game looks beautiful in both first and third person views. Just Really a gorgeous looking game in general with high level of details.

Gameplay: The gameplay is way faster than the original, and way better and much smoother. And the exploration of the village is so cool, it makes you feel that your playing a metrovania game mixed with The Evil Within 2 where the game feels like a mini open world, with a lot of hidden areas and optional bosses and areas as well making it the biggest RE game to date. Man at this point Capcom really need to explore an open world re game, it would be a nice idea and i can see it happens after Village semi open world design.

I'd say the biggest plus in this game is the exploration of the village and the side content hidden in the village, every time something new happens making the experience fresh and unique. With many nice surprises that can and will happen with you in the village.

Combat: Combat has been improved, like heavily improved. Movement, shooting, the guns now feel very impactful and satisfying to shoot. Same goes for the movement Ethan is way faster than 7 and very agile, given this time the game takes place in a big village, unlike 7 where it took place in a massive house complex. Same goes with the reloading animation just high quality stuff.

Sound: Sound design is fantastic, the atmosphere of the village, the windmills, the monsters sound is well designed as well and creepy. The guns sound is beautiful from the Grenade launcher to the heavy shotgun to the magnum all sexy sound you just wish to hear man. 

Enemies: The enemy variety is better this time, unlike Re7 from enemies design to bosses, there is a good variety here, its still smaller than the previous RE games but still there is a good amount of variety.

Additional Content: Man the achievement system is well designed, and the mercenaries mode is so cool and fun to play, reminds me a lot of RE5 merc mode and Shadows Of Rose is a good lengthy dlc, which is really cool. so yeah that's it for the good.

The bad.
Structure: The game sits between a rock and a hard place, where it cant decide if want to play out like RE4 or RE7, it has a merchant, currency system just like RE4/5 and ALOT of weapons, but the game throws these bullet sponges enemies, where they just waste your resources, because of how bullet sponges they feel. Which is a shame because RE4 ( the original) did a great job of being a survival horror game and an action horror game. But the one who made that game is none other than ma boy Shinji Mikami. And that guy is a living legend. 

It's shame though how poorly this is balanced, because the guns in this game feels really really good, sometimes it feels like your playing a shooter game because of how smooth they feel.

Level design: Man this one hurts. Where the village was really cool idea and concept, unfortunately the same can't be said to The Castle, The Reservoir or The house. i'll stick to the castle to avoid spoilers. It sadly gives you the illusion that you are exploring this massive castle and that you are backtracking and your looking for the items. Instead it does not it gives you the illusion not MAKES you, it's HEAVILY scripted section that you move from A to B where the game HANDS/GIVE you the key items you need in order to progress the castle, which is a shame that they went with this design choice it makes no sense why would they do this in RE game, its like the game is just holding your hands throughout these sections.

Puzzles: puzzles are very few and very easy to solve, you give it to a toddler and he will solve it in mere minutes, especially the dam "puzzle". Jesus don't get me started on this one.

Story: I dunno where to start with this one. it's just bad, like really bad man. If capcom is headed for this direction where RE games want to be VERY serious in tone and no longer becomes a B movie cringe like it used to be. Then they need to hire better writers to write the story for these games. Because the writing in the this game is really really bad and stale. It takes it self too seriously and this doesn't work in RE game, and Ethan is really boring protag, i wasn't invested in his quest to save his family at all, because he is bland very bland. 

If this game had 3rd person cutscenes ( there is only 3 in the final hour of the game btw, in case someone wants to argue) than maybe we would have cared for Ethan as a player.

Here's my spoiler-free review of Resident Evil Village. I've completed the game five times, finished all available challenges, played through all difficulties, and explored everything the game has to offer. I've enjoyed the overall package, so I'll focus mostly on its faults.

Duration: Depending on your chosen difficulty and play style approach, the game could take anywhere from 10 to 20 hours to complete. For my first playthrough, I picked Hardcore, did extensive exploration, and finished with 15 in-game hours and even more on Steam playtime due to restarts and deaths. The segments always felt top-notch, with no rushed moments.

Enemy Variety: Unlike RE7, which had a limited variety of monsters, Village offers a decent roster. The designs and attack patterns of some enemies can be annoying, especially during the first playthrough, but overall, the variety is good.

Exploration: The Village looks gorgeous, and the exploration is entertaining. Similar to Souls games, you can see the areas you'll visit in the distance. The pacing is excellent, balancing action, exploration, and horror.

Gunplay: The gunplay is okay, but there are issues. There's stuttering (see P.C. Specifics), and enemies on higher difficulties become too spongy. However, the arsenal has been expanded, and weapons are upgradable, making the progression satisfying.

Difficulty Levels: Standard difficulty provides plenty of ammo, while Hardcore requires better resource balancing but can be frustrating for new players due to an unfair difficulty spike at the beginning. Village of Shadows difficulty is challenging and geared towards returning players with completion unlocks.

Soundtrack: The soundtrack felt generic, lacking distinct themes that complement a survival horror title.

Predictability: Some scenes felt cliché and predictable, occurring a bit too often and even in cutscenes. This may be due to intentional toning down of the game's scariness.

P.C. Specifics: The game runs mostly at a locked 60 FPS and scales well with older hardware, providing a good level of performance and a vast options menu for tweaking settings.

RE8: Village is the last chronological entry in the franchise thus far. It takes the gameplay sensibilities of RE7 and combines them with some aspects from the much beloved RE4 (2005). It is much more action-oriented than some games prior, and it shows.

The story takes place in 2021, in a remote Romanian village overseen by a lavish castle. Its citizens live in constant fear of the local lords, who demand frequent offerings. Ethan Winters, having survived the events of RE7 and made it out of Louisiana alive with his wife, settles down in the village outskirts hoping to raise their daughter in peace. Unfortunately for Ethan, he's forced to watch his wife get shot in front of him and his infant taken away and is sent on a long and painful journey trying to rescue her. 

The game shares most of its gameplay elements with RE7: Biohazard, though with the addition of many fan-favorite features from RE4, such as an attache case-style inventory, where you can sort your items manually in a grid of slots, a mysterious but affable merchant who offers you new items and weapon enhancements, and collectable treasures to sell for more money. There isn't a whole lot I can really say about it besides what I already have, but there is also a cooking system, where you can bring the Duke (this game's merchant) ingredients such as fish to fix you up some meals, that give you permanent stat increases, much like the stabilizers from 7. There are many hidden and powerful weapons and valuable treasures scattered around the many maps, as well as dropped by enemies, giving you more elaborate trinkets depending on the threat level of the beasties you fell. The enemy variety is decent, the most common being the werewolf-like bioweapons created in the village, but also the more frankenstein-esque mechanized horrors from Heisenberg's factory. Puzzles are much more simplified this time around, with there being a larger focus on exploration and collecting resources. When it comes to side content, you have a DLC expansion, not unlike the past couple of RE games since RE5, having you play as Ethan's daughter Rose, an added third-person perspective you can toggle that comes bundled with the Winters' Expansion/Season Pass, as well as the glorious return of the Mercenaries mode for the first time in nearly a decade, if you don't count the Raid modes from the Revelations games. 

The story is where the game sadly fumbles. The premise isn't the problem, it's just not paced all too well and can be inconsistent, with some laughably cheesy dialogue- but not the good kind of cheese. Characters make questionable decisions, the writing comes off as fanfiction in some parts and it overall knocks the experience down a peg. This doesn't ruin the game, but it does take away what could've been a lot more cohesive. You play as Ethan Winters once again, trying to live his life in peace at the outskirts of a supposedly Romanian remote village with his infant daughter Rose and wife Mia, but is ambushed by Chris' platoon for unknown reasons and has Mia gunned down, and is loaded onto a transportation convoy. The vehicle is suddenly destroyed, no signs of Chris and his squad, and most importantly Rose is nowhere to be found, and so Ethan must venture into the village to find answers on where his child is. He learns that the ringleader of the local nobility, Mother Miranda, wants his daughter for some scheme, and he must go through her four lieutenants- the nobles of the village, house Heisenberg, House Moreau, House Dimitrescu and House Beneviento, to find the information he's looking for.

It's a fairly good game, definitely a fun play the first few times, but also has a fair few flaws. I recommend it despite my minor gripes. You can buy it for full price, but as usual you'd be better off waiting for the common Capcom publisher sales.

Resident Evil 8 makes no attempt to hide the fact that it’s a video game. It’s kind of refreshing. The game is littered with nonsensical game mechanics that feel completely disconnected from the plot, or logic. Such as not being able to crawl through a hole because thin strips of bandages block your path, which require scissors to cut - naturally. 

If you’re interested in an experiencing an immersive story, look away. If you’re searching for a solid first-person survival horror game that doesn’t take itself too seriously, and you’re willing to deal with some sillier and rather contrived game mechanics, this is well worth a playthrough. 

While I don’t really want to spoil anything, there’s one thing that happens in the game that I must mention, to make my point clear. 

At one point in the story, Ethan (the protagonist) gets his hand cut off. Shortly after, he puts the hand right back on and pours a health potion on it. This doesn’t just heal his hand, but also mends his jacket right where the cut was. This is the kind of blatant disregard for physics the game contains, and I thought it had some charm to it in that campy and absurd kind of way. 

One of my favorite features of the game was how they handled the map. Rooms will be marked in red on your map until you’ve found all the items in that area, which then turns the room blue. It’s super useful when exploring and ensures that you always have resources at your disposal. It’s both fantastic and terrible for completionists, as it can be hard to leave an area without finding everything. Unfortunately, there is some wonkiness to the system, and it isn’t always perfect – some areas are split in awkward ways, and clearing the map only becomes possible when clearing another connected area. It’s been a while since I played Resident Evil 7, so I don’t remember if this feature was in 7 as well.

If you like poking around every corner of the map and taking notes while you play, this is a great game for that. How much sense solutions make will vary, and the game won’t really tell you where to go or what to do. So, you need to figure out a lot of things on your own or refer to a guide. 

The average playthrough should take about 10 hours, which you can easily cut down to 3 hours using the knowledge and power you gain from the first playthrough. 

Throughout my playthroughs I encountered zero technical issues, bugs, or crashes. In fact, I was pleasantly surprised by how well optimized the game was even with raytracing turned on. 

The game is very cinematic in its presentation, and does take control away from the player frequently, which can feel a bit annoying at times. 

There are also some, albeit very short and few, sequences with what feels like infinitely respawning enemies which I really dislike.

In terms of story, Resident Evil 8 continues where Resident Evil 7 left off, and while it’s probably fine to play this without having played 7, I personally wouldn’t recommend that. Being familiar with the story and characters will make the story more enjoyable and rewarding. 

At the very least, I recommend playing both, even if you start with this one. They’re both great games, and blasphemously perhaps, the two are my favorites in the franchise after the original Resident Evil 4.

I was very careful not to be spoiled, I did not know absolutely anything about it, how it was going to be or the characters, except ethan was going to be the protagonist. When I started playing, I though it was going to be similar to RE7, which switched to a more classical survival horror adventure. RE8 kind of started like that and the style was the same. However, short after the start you realize that it is much more prone to action than RE7. Also, there are SO MANY similarities with RE4, some of them overly blatant [spoiler] (duke in RE8 =  Merchant in RE4, Village intro scene with infinite hordes of enemies, even being saved by the bell..., a castle, a lake with a huge monster, a factory with a terrifying new enemy, the treasuring and combining, the suitcase space management, etc... [/spoiler]. Even though at first I was a bit disappointed, after a while I found out it was a very fun game to play, similar to RE4, but with the graphics from RE7 and some similarities with the RE2 engine. It even has some sections with a more classical survival horror tone [spoiler] I absolutely loved house Beneviento [/spoiler]. The story is a bit meh, most characters are forgettable and not engaging at all, and it has many instances where you are thinking wtf were they smoking? However, again, it is a very fun game to play, and very replayble. The DLC is also very good and adds into the story. Mercenaries is fun but a bit repetitive and not rewarding. 

Overall, if you liked RE7 because of its survival horror environment you will be disappointed (still you will enjoy many parts of it), but if you loved RE4 this is basically the spiritual RE4 sucessor and you will absolutely love it.

Review:

Resident Evil Village is a top-tier action-horror shooter, delivering an extremely high level of quality in every conceivable aspect.

Story:

Resident Evil Village is the direct sequel to Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, heavily building on the events of the previous game. However, it can also be enjoyed without prior knowledge, as the game frequently includes flashbacks to the predecessor, and any missing context only occasionally affects the understanding of certain connections.

The story is thrilling, action-packed, and dark, yet also partly emotional, allowing players to experience a wide range of emotions in a cinematic manner.

The characters are all uniquely interesting and fit seamlessly into the story. This often leads to genuine interest in learning more about their backgrounds and roles within the narrative.

Gameplay:

The gameplay is as varied and engaging as in the recent Resident Evil titles, characterized by constantly evolving opportunities. There are well-designed shooter segments with a variety of enemies and several boss fights. As you progress through the game, you can find loot, such as new weapons and treasures, scattered across the map. Occasionally, you’ll encounter small puzzles to solve. Everything runs smoothly, providing an excellent gaming experience.

Graphics:

Resident Evil Village stands among the most visually impressive games I've ever played, alongside titles like Witcher 3 and Batman: Arkham Knight. The breathtaking landscapes of the village, both day and night, the interior design of buildings—especially Lady Dimitrescu's castle—and the detailed character models are all visually stunning.

Conclusion:

In summary, Resident Evil Village is a worthy successor to Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, matching its quality in many aspects and even surpassing it in some. I appreciate that Resident Evil Village has managed to establish its unique atmosphere, giving both games their own distinct right to exist.

Personally, I was thoroughly captivated and entertained while playing Resident Evil Village and can wholeheartedly recommend it to everyone.

That’s it for this review. Until next time.

The variety of enemies keeps encounters fresh and thrilling, while the strategic crafting system adds depth to the experience. I found myself constantly weighing my options—should I use my limited resources to heal or to craft ammo? This adds an extra layer of tension that every horror fan will appreciate.

Ethan Winters as a protagonist continues to impress. His journey through the village is both harrowing and compelling, filled with twists that kept me guessing. The supporting characters, including the various Lords of the village, are uniquely crafted and memorable, each bringing their own flavor of horror.

Moreover, the game balances its horror elements with moments of dark humor and action, preventing it from becoming too grim while still delivering genuine scares. The pacing is excellent, with plenty of moments that leave you breathless and others that allow you to catch your breath—before plunging you back into the chaos.

In summary, Resident Evil Village is a breathtaking and immersive journey that every fan of the genre should experience. It pays homage to the beloved franchise while forging its own path, delivering both nostalgia and innovation. Whether you’re a long-time fan or new to the series, this game is an absolute must-play!

For everyone that have the d3d crashes.

Since i tried everything and nothing worked i spend hours/days and i found a solution at least on my end.

I had to lower my core clock slightly in order to play the game with MAX settings. Playing on a laptop with 1660 ti.

I was monitoring the game with MSI afterburner and realise that the core clock was getting around 2100. Apparently that causes the crash on my end.No other games were providing any issues with my core clock being around 2100 so this was the first time i came up to an issue like this. I lower it to 2075 and game is stable.
Before that i would be around 3.6gb vram usage and still crash.

Optimisation Guide :

Optimise your settings(Plenty videos in Youtube etc.),lock your fps around 30 and use looseness scaling.
Texture Vram based on the internet should be 1GB or 2Gb based on graphics Card. 
This Recommendation is for mid to low Laptops/Pcs.

Game now plays super smooth and no crashes at least for me.

So check your core clocks if your Vram ain't even exceeding half of it.

There are so many references in Village that can be tied to RE4; like the Duke (the Merchant), the Village,  the Castle, Lady Dimitrescu ( Big Chief), the giant fish (Del Lago), and finally Mother Miranda ( Osmund Saddler). Even gameplay wise, its similar to RE4. So I guess what I'm trying to say is, as a fan of RE4, I loved this.

But whats even better is the story. I love how to clearly ties to RE7, and answers so many questions. Ethan had a major character development, from a civilian in the previous game, to a badass who would do anything to protect his daughter. Mother Miranda is one of the best written RE villains I've seen in a long time, and I love how she is the polar opposite of Ethan in so many ways.

The larger theme of this game revolves around "Family", and I honestly love that. The Ethan Winters saga is one of the best things the RE team has done in a long time. 

The DLC however felt short, but it was extremely terrifying. Wish they had the option to switch to first person. There were some annoying moments too. I would recommend getting the DLC, or the entire Gold edition on sale.

[h1] Positives [/h1]
[list]
    [*]Incredible world & enemy design
    [*]Brisk narrative pace
    [*]Good amount of post-story content
    [*]Fantastic voice performances
    [*]Expansion on the universe's lore
    [*]Worthwhile sequel
    [*]Great technical performance
[/list]

[h1] Negatives [/h1]
[list]
    [*]Paper-thin characters (especially Ethan Winters)
    [*]Some sections feel less-favoured than others
    [*]Weak villain
    [*]DLC expansion feels out of place with the franchise
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion [/h1]
[i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is another meaningful entry in the titular series, instead taking a step towards action in an incredibly well-executed Gothic setting. Like with most of the well-received games in the franchise, [i]Village[/i] maintains an engaging pace to convey its story and introduce new weapons, enemies, and world changes in a manner that feels smooth, naturally progressive, and accessible. With the RE Engine once again bringing wonderful technical achievements to near-perfect visual storytelling, [i]Village[/i]'s narrative does well to conclude the story begun in [i]Resident Evil 7[/i], and move the series' overall plot in a meaningful manner, with a bang.

However, [i]Village[/i] suffers from having nearly no interesting characters, and those that do draw your eyes are left with the most basic treatment. Ethan Winters especially grows from an audience surrogate into a full-fledged character on his own right here, but the stark contrast brought forth by how the narrative switches away from first-person makes the decision to keep Ethan paper-thin even more confusing. He, along with the game's main villain (whose appeal pales when compared to the other antagonists), don't truly grab your attention. This treatment extends to the DLC expansion [i]Shadows of Rose[/i], where players will also have to grapple with the straight-up reuse of levels from the main game in a story that evokes the franchise's more infamous wacky qualities.

All in all, fans of first-person (or third-person) survival-horror-actions are in for a great time with [i]Village[/i]. Despite its flaws, which are very in line with common criticisms of other games in the series, [i]Village[/i] has a lot of good to offer for fans, or would-be fans, of [i]Resident Evil[/i] and the action-horror genre.

In general, I absolutely love horror games so I couldn't wait to start Resident Evil Village. The game continuously brings up the events from the previous game's entry, Biohazard, which if you haven't played yet, should definitely check it out if you want far greater context to the ongoing story.

The story is very captivating and I always feel so anxious walking around the map, waiting for something to pop out and startle me. Performance wise, the game runs great, just like previous entries of RE, optimization is very good and I've ran into zero issues with bugs or crashes. The gunplay is fun and you really need to depend on hitting your shots at a pretty high percentage as ammo can be quite limited upon the starting couple hours.

Puzzles are quite simple but don't overstay their welcome, and there is enough curveballs thrown around to keep you curious about what/where to head off next. Bosses are presented in high quality and the soundtrack keeps you on your toes as you find ways to use your guns are environment to take these creatures down.

For fans of the Horror genre, I would highly recommend you check this title out, as it's often on sale you can get a great deal.

If you remove the two instances of finding the umbrealla corp logo in the game world, as well as removing Chirs Redfield as a ingame character, then you wouldn't know it was a resident evil game. Could as well be the next Alone in the Dark of Silent Hill game or any generic survial horror shooter. 

To be clear i did not finish the game. After 3 hours of running around in the factory level i was just burnt out with the game. That section just dragged on and on. The scrapfield mecha monster battle broke me. Like wtf does this have to do with Resident Evil? I quit the game after you were given control of Christ Redfield and im probably not goign to finish it. The POV is way too narrow.

The game pads the playtime alot with making you backtarack from a place to another. This makes Ethans running speed very annoying. Yet you need to do alot of backtracking and exploration to get it.

The Boss fights are the low point of this game. Bland, boring, unimaginative, tedious. 
 
TLDR: The game is barely enjoyable enough to keep playing. Graphics are excellent. Story not good. If you like survival horror youll like this game, as long as you forget its supposed to be a Resident Evil game. If you can get it below 30 euros give it a try.

Resident Evil Village: A Stunning Evolution of Horror

As a longtime fan of the Resident Evil series, experiencing Resident Evil Village was nothing short of exhilarating. This latest installment not only lives up to its predecessors but surpasses them in many aspects, making it arguably the best Resident Evil game to date.

One of the most striking improvements is the shift to a first-person perspective, which adds a heightened sense of immersion and tension. This FPS aspect completely transforms the gameplay dynamics, placing you directly in the heart of the horror. Every encounter feels intensely personal, whether you're navigating dark corridors or facing off against grotesque creatures. The decision to embrace this perspective pays off tremendously, making each moment pulse-pounding and unforgettable.

Visually, Resident Evil Village is a masterpiece. The graphics are breathtaking, with intricately detailed environments that evoke a hauntingly beautiful atmosphere. From the eerie village streets to the dilapidated castles and mist-covered forests, every location is meticulously crafted to immerse you in its sinister world. The character designs are equally impressive, especially the formidable and nightmarish enemies you encounter, each more terrifying than the last.

The sound design and music further elevate the experience, enhancing the game's chilling atmosphere. The subtle creaks of ancient wood, the distant howls of unseen creatures, and the ominous score all contribute to a pervasive sense of dread. This attention to audio detail is crucial in building tension and keeping you on edge throughout your journey.

Gameplay-wise, Resident Evil Village strikes a perfect balance between survival horror and action. The exploration is rewarding, encouraging you to scour every corner for resources and secrets. Combat is intense and satisfying, requiring strategic use of limited ammunition and resources against formidable adversaries. The variety of weapons and upgrades add depth to the gameplay, allowing for different approaches to each encounter.

Moreover, the narrative is gripping, weaving a tale of mystery and intrigue that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The protagonist, Ethan Winters, is a compelling character whose journey is fraught with peril and revelations. The story seamlessly connects to previous Resident Evil titles while introducing new and unexpected twists that will leave fans eager for more.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is not just a game; it's a masterclass in horror gaming that sets a new standard for the genre. With its groundbreaking FPS perspective, stunning graphics, immersive sound design, and engaging game play, it surpasses all expectations. Whether you're a longtime fan of the series or a newcomer, Resident Evil Village is an absolute must-play and undoubtedly the pinnacle of the Resident Evil franchise.

RE Village is basically a mix of Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7, its not a complete walking simulator and has gameplay. There are some attempts at depth too (weapon upgrades, stat upgrades) but to me the whole thing just felt...not great. Why?

TL:DR Version - 
Average gameplay
much walking sim
Interesting bosses (lore, design) and good graphics
Cant be played without FOV fix/RE Framework
Nonsense boss fights/plot
Little enemy variety

- To make this even PLAYABLE you need RE Framework because by default your FOV is at like 80 or less and if you zoom it goes even further (like 65) so enjoy playing through binoculars because THE GAME HAS NO FOV SLIDER! Yes, seeing LESS is scary! Oh and guess what? in this limited FOV there is also a forced vignette effect and much like film grain, it adds absolutely nothing except for making you see EVEN LESS! Who needs a FOV slider if you can just SEE LESS OF THE GAME :) this is tech from 2008 or so missing.

- Alot of the plot and the bosses make no sense at all and will ruin your immersion. Gameplay mechanics are unique in that they dont make any sense at all and you just have to accept it since the explanation for that comes after beating the game. Great. What I mean by that is that in cutscenes bosses literally can easily deal with you but once its your turn they are all weak or why cant the boss just stomp me for example? No it goes all around me lol (I know this sounds weird but I dont wanna spoil bosses)

You have to run around or block with your hands, your hands are magically so powerful they reduce the damage taken by like 80% or so and can withstand drills, claws or anything the game can think of. Very unintuitive and even with normal FOV its hard to "dodge" enemies. On hardcore they are also bullet spongey and there is not much reaction to them getting hit alot of times.

- Gameplay feels like the worst thing out of all Resident Evils, it doesn't know what it wants to be so it took the worst out of both worlds. Some bosses and parts are pure walking simulator, you can finish the one "boss" without firing a bullet and others with barely firing any bullet. Wow.

- You fight the same enemies the entire game. Over and over and over will you fight the basic enemies in like 2 variations with sometimes a special enemy appearing but only sometimes.

- The last normal boss location was the most enjoyable part to me since its much more gameplay heavy but even then or afterwards fighting bosses and so on its just not all that fun because the gameplay doesn't feel that great, shooting and such is not as enjoyable. Enemies lack reaction to what you do as well.

- EASY to cheese game, a bunch of enemies can literally not go beyond a door or invisible border so you can just let them turn around and shoot them again and repeat the process. There were enemies that could not walk around a fence so I could knife them through it lol. This happened overall like 5 times?

Now, those all were negative points but there were some positives too:

- The graphics are very good
- The characters are very interesting and their design is cool
- Good voice acting and towards the end the story picks up which is nice
- Combat is acceptable but can be annoying

But as you see, not a whole lot. So what is my final verdict? If you wanna play a game, this wont be all that much fun for you but there is still something to  be found. If you enjoy walking sim and the "cinematic" experience this game will blow you away. For me personally I got it on a cheap sale and would rate it a 6/10 and im happy I wont have to play it again. 

Whats most memorable to me are the bosses and their lore/design as well as some characters like Chris.

Disclaimers. I'm writing this review while playing through a hardcore campaign. I am a HUGE resident evil slut. I consumed nearly all the material the universe has to offer and enjoyed every bit. Until Village that is.

Now there are 2 types of resident evil games. There is the horror / inventory management with sprinkle of action (RE2, RE4, RE7 etc.) and there is the other way around. Infinite resouces, massive amounts of enemies and going haywire with them (RE5, RE6 etc.). Now I love all of them. But something these games have is that they dont try to be the other games themselves. You never find 150 pistol ammo on an area in RE4, or you dont see backflipping handsome dudes on RE7. Village is trying to be both these resident evil types and failing miserably.

Lets get the good out of the way. RE7 was amazing and it still is. First person camera with the horror setting RE puts you in is an amazing sight to see for any horror enjoyer. REVillage is no different. The background noises, atmosphere, its all there. And the Doll chapter actually got me goosebumped all the way from the start to the end bec of how absolutely dreadingly creepy it was. Reminded me of Silent Hills PT.

Now the bad and OH the bad. Gunplay. This game feels like Capcom made a first person horror game that had no combat in it whatsoever, saw RE2 and was like 'Hey, people really like combat so lets just add it to our game!!!!' and micropatched it last second. Guns feel terrible, enemies sometimes show some reaction but most of the time its just shooting at moving walls. Each enemy dies to MINIMUM 7 8 headshots which makes encounters feel horrible. Now RE2 had the same 'problem' too, but that game forced you to decide if you were gonna clear out an area or not. You could just run past your enemies bec zombies were slow as hell. But that meant that the area would be infested and when X was chasing you, you could get grabbed. It was a choice. Lycans run faster than you, they dash around and they have a long reach. And most encounters are forced on you too so there is no 'Hey ima just skiddadle out of here'. And unlike RE4 where killing zombies -sometimes- rewards you with either herb's or ammunition, Village ONLY rewards with money. Which is worth absolute ♥♥♥♥. Gun upgrades dont change the impact of the weapons, most worthwhile upgrades themselves are found as treasures on the world. So combat overall is just there as a nuisance. The absolute worst part of the game. Dude. Shotguns dont one shot useless zombies. In a resident evil game. It should be a sin. 

Inventory. Why is it even there? Cleared 3 chapters and on the last chapter atm but I have NEVER felt the importance of my inventory space at all. There is no stash so you can't really store your weapons too. The game forces you to carry all your weapons on you and gives you a massive inventory space to go with it. So what is the purpose? Why is it even in the game? Where is the stash? It is just dumb to be able to carry literally everything on the map all on you for any scenario. (Which again all weapons feel ♥♥♥♥ either way so it doesn't change much but still)

The story. Personal opinions from here weewoooweewooo. I liked the way RE7 was. It was a fresh spinoff that was away from the chaotic rock punching, zombie kicking, asian dressed agent filled universe of RE. We def did NOT need this game to be connected to the original RE universe at all. Then we saw the Redfield at the end of RE7 and I said oh no. It wasn't CHRIS Redfield however. Then the DLC dropped and the game was bound to be connected. And now the village. The core of the problem is Ethan. Ethan was not supposed to be a main character. He was just a nobody that you were supposed to take control of on the lonely and horrifying place that was Bakers' mansion. You were a nobody who tried to be somebody. Now when you make this character a very important MC, it feels...rushed? Ethan got military training in the prologue so he can now use any weapon he can find!! or Ethan was very special from the beginning!! I dunno. I don't like Ethan as a main character. He feels dull, uninterested and boring to listen to.

Overall, as a resident evil slut who saw that the game was in a discount, I was extremely dissapointed to play through a worse RE7. It's definitely not the WORST game I played, absolutely not. But compared to any other RE (and I am including RE6 bec f you all haters) this was BY FAR the worst one yet.

[u]Fair warning[/u]: The first act is clunky, confusing, and unfun. As a newcomer to Resident Evil games, I almost put Village down at the start from frustation and not really vibing with the gameplay. (Spoilers act 1: [spoiler]walking in 90% darkness on a straight line, opening empty drawers in a cabin, going in circles in a village fighting lycans with no objective was a chore[/spoiler]). But I'm very glad I gave it a second chance.

After the unfun opening act, things get much, much better! Soon the objective becomes clearer and less murky, which helps immensely. I had to restart on casual difficulty because I was so unfamiliar with the RE combat mechanics. But then I quickly realized casual was too easy, so I did a 3rd start back on normal. That felt perfect for a first playthrough. After 2 hours and 3 starts, things were finally rolling.

This game is a gem in my eyes, but not so much for the gameplay. The actual gameplay of Village - the combat, survival mechanics, puzzles, crafting, etc -  although very good, don't particularly outshine the gameplay of other all-time great games.

Rather, what makes Village really special and worth the time is the game design. Starting from the top, the atmosphere and environment is exquisite and a genuine rush to explore. I haven't had so much fun in a spooky Slavic hamlet since the Trastamara Estate Ruins in the Witcher 3: Blood and Wine. That's very high praise for any game to be held in the same category as the Witcher 3.

Village's world is haunting, foreboding, creepy, and makes your skin crawl with dread. Every setting feels so very thoughtful and artfully crafted. That's important because although the combat may not be the greatest ever, the environment truly amps up every encounter. Small noises and rustles, bells, doors creaking will startle you, placing you on the edge of your seat and making it an enthralling experience.

Aside from the phenomenal atmosphere, Village also has a great attention to detail and good quality of life features that earn my praise. Every area has been dotted with a number of resources and secrets, which feel carefully and lovingly placed. It's like finding stars in Mario 64, except in a horror game for adults. (The loading screen with a model typewriter is another small but delightful touch). As for QoL, the map shows individual rooms with a red color indicating more items/secrets, and a blue color indicating it's cleared. That's a really nice QoL feature that I appreciate because it cuts so much of the guesswork and tedium out of it.

All in all I feel like this game deserves to get a 9/10 from me. Yes, I know that's high and some diehard RE fans may differ, but when I take the experience as a whole, appreciating all the morsels and flavor this game offers, I feel it's well-earned in my book. So if you're looking for a fresh experience of Resident Evil, and not coming in with expecations from other RE games, I highly recommend Village. Just watch out for that first act, and make sure to choose your difficulty properly!

Welcome to Resident Evil Village, where the only thing scarier than the monsters is your lack of ammo. Our protagonist, Ethan Winters, continues his unlucky streak, stumbling into a creepy European village where everyone either wants to kill him or suck his blood. Spoiler: it’s usually both.

This game serves you a cocktail of nightmares: towering vampire ladies, werewolf hordes, and dollhouse horrors, shaken not stirred. Lady Dimitrescu, the 9'6" tall vampire queen, is the star of the show—she’s got legs for days and enough charm to make you forget she’s trying to slice you into Ethan-tartar.

Combat is intense, but the real challenge is managing your inventory. Just when you think you’ve mastered the art of Tetris with bullets, herbs, and fish (don’t ask), you’re back to square one. Pro tip: always keep a shotgun shell for those “Oh no” moments, which happen approximately every five minutes.

The plot is a rollercoaster of twists, turns, and "WTF" moments. One minute you're solving puzzles in a castle, the next you're fighting a giant fish in a flooded village. And just when you think you’ve seen it all, the game throws in mechanical monsters because why not?

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is like a haunted amusement park: terrifying, thrilling, and occasionally ridiculous. It’s a screamfest that’ll keep you on the edge of your seat, mostly because you’re about to fall off in terror or laughter. Highly recommended if you enjoy heart palpitations and the sweet sound of Ethan Winters screaming "WHY?!?" every few minutes.
