Resident Evil: Village is messy in a way the main Resident Evil series very rarely ever is, however, the things that make it messy are also the reasons why I found myself loving it more than any other game in the series. While it is not as scary as Resident Evil: Biohazard and not as well-paced as Resident Evil 4, the series' twin masterpieces, its commitment to Eastern European horror and attempts at balancing out everything the series has become lead it to having some of the series' highest highs and lowest lows.

Gameplay-wise, the game is as good as first-person Resident Evil can get. The blending between action and horror is done in the best way I think the series ever has outside of Resident Evil Four. The horror serves the action sequences and vice versa in the best way possible, leading to boss encounters and gameplay areas that are equal parts stress-inducing as they are genuinely fun to play. However, the game's structure plays with the idea of allowing you to go about clearing each biome in any which way you like but still simply snaps back to a level of linearity that kind of harms the overall flow of this more combat-focused entry. 

The game's visual identity, world, and characters are more interesting than the core 'Resident Evil' story nestled underneath all the village's mystery. More so than any other Resident Evil game, exploring the world of Village had its moments of duress as well as moments of pure atmospheric bliss. You can genuinely see the personal impact the Mold has had not just on Mother Miranda and her underlings, but on the people of the village themselves as you pick through the ruins of a town lost within its own remoteness. This is something they did as well with the Baker family in Biohazard, but there is a different sensation when you see how Umbrella's dark experiment can affect the entirety of society in a way that's much more personal than any other game in the series has let on. 

Not only did I love that, but the lore surrounding Mother Miranda and the Four Lords was enchanting. Exploring every room, admiring the visual storytelling on display whilst the game's enchanting soundtrack played was incredibly mystifying. I would 100% just come back to this game to simply exist in the world, the snowy setting and gothic inspirations setting itself apart from most other survival-horror games on the market.

However, the actual story is held together by glue, duct tape, and a hope that you'll pass off its failings as just more Resident Evil goofiness. Village tries to focus the story more on Ethan Winters and front him as less of a vehicle for the player to impress themselves upon and more of a character of their own, but they don't fully commit. We don't get enough time with Rose to care about her, we don't get enough time with Mia to understand why Ethan and her are lovers, and we don't have enough time with Ethan to really understand why he'd go to these lengths to save his daughter yet the main plot is written in a way that expects you to have these connections to the Winters family. Where Biohazard was the story of the Bakers perceived through the eyes of Ethan, Village is Ethan's story yet he doesn't feel present within it. What I found myself caring about was not what the story spent enough time focused on. The most engaging aspects of the story emotionally were when Chris was involved, and that didn't occur really until the game's last third.

Overall, what I love about the game is the direct cause of what holds the game back from being as good as the series heights, but keeps it from being in a race for the bottom with Resident Evil 6. resident evil village might be capcom’s greatest feat yet for the franchise. 

resident evil 7 took players by surprise, steering the series in a markedly different direction. up until seven, the resident evil games were primarily action-oriented survival horror experiences. this approach wasn't inherently flawed, as it aligned with capcom's vision for the franchise. however, when seven was released, it astonished players by deeply embracing horror elements, setting a high bar for it’s sequel.

this is where it gets tricky. while seven was largely successful, some fans found it “too scary” or considered it a deviation from the franchise’s roots. village had to balance appeasing fans of seven and long-time enthusiasts who preferred the classic survival horror with an action-centric style.

so, what became of village? it largely adhered to the classic style. the house beneviento section, where the game truly leaned into horror, was particularly notable. stripped of all tools, players found themselves helpless in a dark, eerie setting, a homage to seven that resulted in a gripping experience. besides this, moments of genuine fear occurred when facing lycans, thanks to their element of surprise. the village environment allowed lycans to camouflage perfectly, often necessitating a second look to spot them. the game skillfully used music to build tension and surprise especially during the blood-soaked basement section. while the game leaned more towards action than pure horror, this wasn’t necessarily a drawback. in the end, resident evil village turned out to be phenomenal.

even though this game was released for last-generation consoles, it stands as one of the best-looking games capcom has ever produced. from the intricately crafted romanian architecture of castle dimitrescu to the old-school layout of house beneviento, every environment is meticulously crafted, offering a visual feast. heisenberg’s factory, with its modern look, still manages to awe with its detailed design.

as for gameplay, ethan moves particularly the same as before, but there's a wider array of firearms available this time. this includes classic handguns, rocket launchers, a laser sword, and more, marking a step up from seven. ammo scarcity remains a concern, maintaining the survival aspect. the firearms complement this game well, much like the firearms of seven did to themselves. the lycan are particularly unique and agile, providing a fresh challenge compared to the zombies of previous games.

the game also rewards players for exploration. village is filled with open areas that are fairly linear yet interconnected. hidden treasures and a optional boss fight await those who venture off the beaten path. revisiting areas with new keys and items often reveals previously inaccessible treasures and weapons, enhancing the sense of discovery.

let’s talk about karl heisenberg as a character. everything about him was phenomenal, the character design complimented with neil newbon’s voice acting. his motivations throughout the game and his factory, everything about him was just memorable.

additionally , there’s a mercenaries mode. all resident evil games could benefit from this mode, which offers an arcade-like experience centered around fun. players can control characters like alcina, heisenberg, chris, and ethan, each offering unique abilities. I wasn’t particularly impressed with chris redfield and the BSAA’s involvement throughout the game. they accompanied ethan but mostly stayed idle, only contributing at the last minute. their aid in the fight against heisenberg was noteworthy, but chris’s sporadic appearances felt underwhelming. surprising, yes but underwhelming.

capcom concludes the ethan winters saga with a splendid narrative. ethan’s character  and the overall storytelling are exceptional, despite some corny dialogue. most resident evil games pit protagonists with supernatural foes against seemingly ordinary humans. whilst offering fun gameplay, these characters seem flawed in design; chris is the boulder-punching a-hole, leon was practically superhuman in four, and ethan has insane regenerative abilities. however, village explains ethan’s abilities as the game nears its end. additionally, providing a satisfying conclusion to his story.

village has borrowed elements from its predecessor, such as the duke’s emporium, among other things. however, I feel these are basic components of a well-established franchise that more games could benefit from. just as resident evil 7 served as a sketch for resident evil 2 to some extent, resident evil village does the same for resident evil 4. nevertheless, both games have managed to stand out uniquely on their own.

thank you, ethan winters.

Ultimately, I chose not to recommend this game because it simply doesn't deserve its 'Overwhelmingly Positive' rating on Steam. In fact, of the ~250 titles in my Steam library, this is the first I've reviewed negatively. [u]Unless you want AAA devs to continue to release such underwhelming games that insult the intelligence of the player, I suggest you do the same.[/u]

RE VIII starts off incredibly strong with Castle Dimitrescu... and falls off equally sharply after that. (To be fair, I did enjoy the doll workshop for its originality and spookiness, though it doesn't hold up to the castle's gorgeous aesthetic and atmosphere.) 

[b][u]But the main problem with this game is that it treats the player like an imbecile, hand feeding him/her all along the way.[/u][/b] Allow me to elaborate.

- Every environmental object with which you can interact (breakable crates, climbable ladders, etc.) is wrapped in bright yellow tape. 'Hidden' areas are likewise draped with bright yellow cables. Beyond that, every lootable item is illuminated with an arrow icon once in proximity, and fully looted rooms/buildings transition from red to blue on the map. While I understand the game makes regular use of dark milieus, the design choices here remove any challenge/thrill from scavenging supplies or identifying traversable routes.

- The puzzles are embarrassingly simple, with solutions always placed directly adjacent. Take, for instance, the [spoiler]birthday[/spoiler] puzzle. Not only is the solution in the next room, a clue is scribbled on an unrealistic note [i]directly in front of the container[/i].

- Completed areas become closed off for no apparent reason. I first noticed this with the castle and had to load an old save to complete the missed rooms. Some of these events involve frustratingly narrow windows of opportunity, such as that related to the Beneviento treasure.

- The boss battles are disappointingly easy (played on Standard difficulty). I realise this isn't Dark Souls, but, c'mon! When you don't die a single time during boss encounters, it says something about the game’s design. Isn’t RE supposed to be a challenging franchise?

- The game's GPS-style map is totally unnecessary and, again, insulting to the ability of the player. [i]Why does every modern AAA game need to incorporate this feature?![/i]

- Redfield's sequence is much closer to Call of Duty than RE. In this section, the gameplay and even the dialogue feels forced.

+ The castle and doll workshop sections truly did well in preserving the survival horror character of the RE franchise. They were also beautifully designed. Alas, they represent less than half the game, with the latter part really becoming a chore to finish.
 
[b]My verdict:[/b] if you must play this game, wait for a good sale (at least 50% discounted), and expect to be treated like a child.

This is where I draw my connection. Could RE8's setting recreate this uncanny feeling that RE7 evoked? Unfortunately, no. Not for me. But RE4 could. Playing RE7 constantly reminded me of the first village-section of this gem of a game. It was also an atmospheric work of art. RE4's transition of the campaign leading to the Salazar Castle was fluent, I really enjoyed it and this kind of change also worked well for RE7 and RE8. 

The events of Ethan's nightmare in the U.S. were connected alright-ish to the current snowy european location in what seems to be Romania. To me, it felt weird at the start but it did not take long for me to get hooked by the medieval village-and-castle-theme resembling the Romanian wallachia and Dracula's castle, which definitely is the game's highlight when it comes to level-design. Titlu: O Continuare Înfricoșătoare și Captivantă a Seriei - "Resident Evil Village"

★★★★☆ Recomand

"Resident Evil Village" este o călătorie înspăimântătoare și captivantă în lumea sinistră a seriei "Resident Evil", oferind o experiență de joc echilibrată între horror și acțiune.

Un aspect notabil al jocului este atmosfera sa înfricoșătoare și misterioasă. Jucătorii preiau controlul asupra lui Ethan Winters într-o căutare disperată pentru a-și salva fiica într-un sat izolat din Europa de Est. Povestea plină de întorsături și surprize menține suspansul pe tot parcursul aventurii.

Gameplay-ul este o combinație reușită de elemente de supraviețuire și acțiune. De la explorarea încăperilor întunecate și rezolvarea puzzle-urilor până la confruntările intense cu inamicii, fiecare moment oferă o tensiune constantă și o satisfacție înfricoșătoare.

Grafica jocului este impresionantă, cu peisaje înfricoșătoare și modele detaliate de personaje și monștri. Satul european de est este redat într-un mod autentic și înspăimântător, contribuind la atmosfera sumbră a jocului.

Atmosfera jocului este amplificată de sunetele înfricoșătoare și de coloana sonoră tensionată, care îți mențin inima în alertă în timp ce te afunzi în întuneric.

Un avantaj semnificativ este varietatea de inamici și boss-uri, care adaugă diversitate și imprevizibilitate experienței de joc. De la zombie și licării până la creaturi mitice și monștri gigantici, fiecare confruntare este un test al abilităților și al curajului jucătorului.

Un dezavantaj potențial poate fi durata relativ scurtă a campaniei principale, care ar putea să nu satisfacă complet fanii seriei în căutarea unei experiențe de joc mai lungi.

În concluzie, "Resident Evil Village" este o continuare reușită și înfricoșătoare a seriei, oferind o combinație perfectă de horror și acțiune într-un cadru înspăimântător. Indiferent dacă ești un veteran al seriei sau un nou venit în lumea "Resident Evil", acest joc te va captiva și te va menține lipit de ecran până la sfârșitul aventurii.

Resident Evil 7 was the game, that prompted me to give a chance to other games in the franchise. Resident Evil 8 was the game, that prompted me to solidify my belief, that it was a mistake, and that I should not do that again. The only thing I really liked in this game was the night-vision filter.

It's not like I was expecting much of the story. I've been shown time and time (and time) again, that it's not the strong suit of the franchise. But where other games had atmosphere or at least somewhat interesting experiences, this one was... Generic? It felt like a b-movie of b-movies, completely and utterly silly. I hoped, that it being much shorter than RE4 will be a saving grace, but no, it was not. Especially considering the utter dump of the ending that this game got. So many stupid things, so many poor dialogues...

And the gameplay felt completely unoriginal, too. It was not necessarily bad, but it was even more tedious, than in RE4, and that's considering that RE4 was tedious simply because it was padded out. But, at least, in RE4 you always felt like you are going forward thanks to its level design. Here, though, you are forced to backtrack by that same design. Don't get me wrong, level design in general is still quite strong here, there is a definitive attention to details, and areas mesh together quite nicely, but the fact that you kind of have a "base of operations" in a survival horror (as the ads claim) just does not work in my head.

Of course, this could be a complaint with RE7, too. But what got me with that game was this thick sticky atmosphere, especially in the very beginning and, to an extent, during the ship episode. They also used first person perspective quite nicely there, it really felt immersive. But in RE8 all of that was lost. It's now some kind of a stupid fairy tail with werewolves and vampires, that do not even fit anything that was previously in the franchise.

There were only 2 moments in the game, that felt like they were trying to be atmospheric. One with Angie, where you are in kind of escape room scenario, but it was ruined by for me by introducing this ugly baby-thing, that you need to escape at certain points. What was bad about it was that... There was no real challenge with that thing, you just needed to run in a specific pattern, and that's it. The other one was with Moreau, which was bringing a sense of danger, but it was highly scripted and timed. It's probably not noticeable for most people "in the moment", but I noticed it right away.

To be honest, I think this game just got overhyped by teens salivating on Dimitrescu and her daughters. Granted, they could have been an interesting quartet, but in the end they were completely flat as characters and utterly forgettable. And somewhat annoying, since they were similar to lots of other "unkillable" enemies, that the franchise has used so far. It all would have been much better, if they created a game that would be a pure-blood shooter as what we had during Chris's section. Then I might have recommended it. If it was not desyncing during cutscenes if your FPS is low.

[h1]Esse jogo perdeu a essência de Resident Evil[/h1]

Eis um jogo que saiu COMPLETAMENTE do tipo que Resident Evil passou ANOS construindo. Na trilogia Raccoon City, e ainda no 0, o principal aspecto dos jogos era o terror e apesar do RE4 dividir essa faceta com a ação, ainda havia o terror como um aspecto principal. Ignorando o quinto e o sexto, RE7 voltou com um foco quase q completo ao terror, mas agora Resident Evil 8, um jogo que eu esperava que seguisse a mesma dinâmica do jogo anterior, não encontra um equilíbrio entre o terror e a ação e, na minha percepção, se torna algo semelhante ao RE4, o que me faz ter medo do próximo jogo.

[h2]O Jogo em si[/h2]

No começo é fácil de ver o terror pq ele ainda existe. Até chegar ao castelo fiquei um pouco apreensivo com as minhas decisões e o que poderia vir a acontecer. No castelo em si esperava mais da perseguição da Dimitrescu e das filhas dela, mas não foi bem assim. Existem MUITAS salas em q elas sequer entram e mesmo q entrem é fácil de contornar ambas, oq tira a tensão dos momentos que viriam posteriormente e mais ou menos desde o começo o castelo eu não tinha mais medo e mt menos apreensão caso eu morresse, não entenda errado, o jogo é bom e ainda é divertido, mas eu não consegui ver isso como um Resident Evil. Ele mantem a história das armas biológicas e todo aquele bla bla bla sobre mutações, traz um passado ainda mais interessante para a Umbrella, mas q é facilmente esquecível já que é um detalhe idiota e que não afeta em NADA em NENHUM dos jogos, ou seja, fica mais como uma curiosidade.

[h3]Bosses[/h3]

Os bosses são, em sua maioria, esquecíveis. Eu acabei de terminar o jogo, derrotei a Dimitrescu ontem, a donna, o peixe e o Heinsenberg hj e sendo sincero eu mal me lembro dessa batalhas, já que a exploração do mapa, os inimigos e os puzzles são mt mais entretivos e divertidos. Esse jogo falha em fazer bosses dignos de Resident Evil, mas ainda assim cria bosses que são divertidos.
Apesar de saber q algumas pessoas não curtem pelo fato de que parece q existem lobisomens e poderes, de alguma forma, exceto pelo heisenberg e parte do q é a Miranda, são todos plausíveis e não tem nada de fadas, magos e essa encheção de saco de quem gosta de reclamar de tudo. Os bosses não estão tão distantes do que RE costuma trazer, eles só não são tão marcantes como o Mister X, G (do RE2), Nemesis, Salazar, Wesker, Jack, mas são excelentes inimigos. Inclusive, parece que eles seguiram uma dinâmica semelhante ao RE7: O Jack e a Dimitrescu são semelhantes, apesar de o Jack ser mais persistente. A MArgareth tem uma dinâmica bem diferente do Peixe, mas eles tem um padrão que deve ser seguido que é justamente uma espécie de perseguição cronometrada, já q existem momentos em q se deve ficar escondido e momentos em que se deve agir. E o que foi mais semelhante q é o Heinsenberg e o filho dos Baker fazendo todo um joguinho e colocando inimigos q foram experimentos do próprio personagem. Enfim, não é uma crítica, é mais como um padrão q eu percebi (Provavelmente eu viajei forte, mas ta aí kkkkkk)

[h3]Mapas[/h3]

Os mapas são MARAVILHOSOS! Eu adorei vagar pelos mapas, buscando os mistérios e itens q eu poderia ter deixado pra trás. Enfim, desse aspecto não tenho mt do que comentar já que mapas de RE nunca são uma decepção e a exploração é recompensadora o suficiente.

[h2]Conclusão[/h2]

Resident Evil Village é um jogo excelente e que vale mt a pena, mas na minha opinião ele falha em ser um bom Resident Evil e se torna um jogo mais similar à um jogo de ação com certos inimigos irritantes q são uma marca registrada de RE. Vale a pena jogar, mas não vale esperar um jogo de terror ou algo como o RE7 já que como terror esse jogo falha. O tempo de jogo tambem é mei curto já que eu zerei em menos de 10 horas, mas é bem divertido. Vale mt a pena. O quarto melhor RE q já joguei.

In my mind, after enjoying RE7 so much that it turned me into a Resident Evil fan, there was no chance in hell that Village wouldn't be a home run. Unfortunately, this is the only Resident Evil game I've played so far I can't even say I like.

The setting is cool and I can appreciate the pseudo-fantasy elements as someone who couldn't care less about the series' overarching plot, but other than that, there's so little about this game I can appreciate. Even its intro leaves bad first impressions, being much too long and on rails and then culminating in a surprisingly difficult semi-wave defense section that is way harder than the pretty easy regular gameplay to follow. I'm not particularly good at Resident Evil games, but even I found this game to be pitifully easy on Normal after the intro and went to restart in the hopes that a bit of challenge would make me actually enjoy the game. Nope.

RE8's combat is pretty dull. Kills don't feel particularly satisfying and it feels stiff and clunky in a way that doesn't gel well with the first-person point of view. It's not awful, but it's not good either. What is awful are the boss fights I've encountered so far. They're easy and the characters themselves don't stick around long enough to begin to feel like any kind of threatening presence before you off them in truly miniature arenas. Lastly, it's a very linear game and it loves to hold your hand. There's no sense of self-discovery or ingenuity as it explains even the simplest of tasks as if you're 5... which considering the modern gaming audience struggles to think for themselves for even a second, is an understandable approach for Capcom.

Graphically, the game can look good, but it's nothing to write home about. The more recent RE4R blows it out of the water. My biggest problem with the visuals is how static the world is. It feels astonishingly plastic as very few items have physics properties and it's rare that anything will result in a unique animation or effect when shot at or otherwise interacted with. It's as if everything's made out of indestructible metal. This may sound like an odd complaint and even I'm surprised it bothered me, but it really does make the game's world feel hollow and superficial. By 2021 standards - let alone the standards of a triple A developer - this is weak.

What's also inexcusable by 2021 standards is a field of view so pathetically puny. Even previous Resident Evil games at this point had had a field of view slider. Why on earth would you make it so tiny and then not give us the option to change it? This isn't 2007 anymore. 70 degree lens' don't cut it on PC in the modern age. It's disorienting and very uncomfortable and actively detracts from the experience in every moment. Thank God for mods. I'd also like it if this modern practise of darkening the surrounding inches of the screen (vignette?) would die in a fiery ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pit. How am I supposed to see what I'm ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ looking at when half of the screen is obscured by a shroud of blackness?

I regret the money and time I spent on this game. It's not quite the disaster I'm making it out to be and there is fun to be had, but it's a pretty hefty disappointment in an era of endless disappointments.

Another thing that might just be me but why on earth is the game titled "Resident Evil Village" instead of "Resident Evil 8" I personally hate this as all the other main stream entries are numbered titles (Unless you consider "Code Veronica" a main stream entry to the franchise, which I personally do). I just think calling it "Village" instead of just "8" was a mislead decision.

Overall I'd give this game a solid 6.5/10 as it is a significant downgrade (in my opinion) to the horror that was present in "Resident Evil 7" that I and many others loved. And while still being an enjoyable game it is extremely linear, with only the illusion of non-linear progression, and although this has worked in other Resident Evil games such as "Resident Evil 4" and its recent remake it just doesn't really work with Village. I also think the story isn't the most thought out. I love what it brings to the table for future games in the franchise though, especially the ending with Chris on the plane-copter-thing, (And even though I saw the Ethan-mould twist from a mile away i still adored it).
I personally don't think this is a "good" Resident Evil game, but overall it is still a very enjoyable experience.
I also strongly suggest using a mod that mutes Ethan so you don't have to ever listen to that cocky bastard.

TLDR: Mediocre Resident Evil game. Alright game overall, eh story, mute Ethan.

This is in stark contrast to RE2 Remake, RE7 and R3make (although that game had different issues)

[h2]Scariness[/h2]
Unlike the first half of RE7 or almost all of RE2, this game just isn't really scary at all. All the villains are more likely to make you laugh with their dialogue and voices etc, they're just a bunch of whiny babies... ironically a literal whiny baby was about the only scary sequence in the game, but I won't spoil that for you. Anyway, it's just odd for a horror game to not be very scary at all, especially a AAA series like Resident Evil.

[h2]Variety[/h2]
In theory this game actually does a lot right. You get different times of day, different locations/settings throughout the game, different enemies, a section or two where you do puzzles, a section or two where you gotta run/hide from monster (though not as adrenaline filled as the first third of RE7, or avoiding Tyrant in RE2), boss fights, but mainly a lot of action in this game; a little too much action-focused is the issue for me. Also I swear this game has way more in-game cutscenes than the previous entries.

It also has a mini game-mode you unlock after finishing the game called The Mercenaries, but it doesn't seem like it'll take up much of your time unless you're obsessive about getting the absolute best score

[h2]Length[/h2]
Thankfully this game didn't commit the sin of R3make by being too short. Hard to judge the length because it was about 17 hours for me (Hard to tell because I had to leave the game on pause and go do stuff various points. The typewriter says my final save was 12 hours but that doesn't seem right) and for many games 17 hours would be short, but because I wasn't overly enjoying this one... if anything it felt too long. So I'm gonna say length isn't an issue.

[h2]Story[/h2]
I don't really play these games for the story, and it was indeed a mid story; but it's cohesive enough and it brings together previous entries in the franchise by the end which I'm sure long time fans will get a little kick out of.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
By now you should be used to the formula, nothing is really different in this one apart from having a store to buy and sell stuff from which seemed weird to me at first (because it is... a ridiculously obese giant man follows you everywhere even into dark dungeons, just to sell only you things... not a great business model) but it was nice to have item and weapon and upgrade choice after several games of not.

The combat was what you'd expect, though man it's annoying how many bullets to the head even a lowly enemy can take; I think the earlier games were better with the zombies being not powerful, but always in giant swarms. These ones are powerful and really bloody good at jumping around right as you're aiming at them, but they're never in a horde.

I was relieved when at the end of the game it didn't keep track of how many times you used the typewriter; hated being penalized for being a habitual saver in RE2make.

[h2]Replayability[/h2]
There are no story choices to make in this game unlike the one main one in RE7, there is no different version of the main story like in RE2, there is no particularly interesting New Game+ mode... you can just complete 'challenges' which unlock cheats for you to use in story mode like unlimited ammo or give you different weapons to buy.

Like I said I already was forcing myself to get through it the first time round, so I'm definitely not gonna replay it.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
I did have good expectations for this game based on reviews etc, and it's not a bad game or poorly made by any means. However it just wasn't what I was hoping for in a Resident Evil... it neither scared or puzzled me, nor impressed as a shooter. And so that is why ultimately I can't bring myself to give it a recommend. I might be being a little harsh but I'm going to give it a [b]6/10[/b] as a Resident Evil game

REVIEW FOR RESIDENT EVIL 8:VILLAGE
-------------------------------------------
WARNING WILL CONTAIN SPOILERS: As an unprofessional reviewer i like to say that i feel that it is essential to finish a game to the very end before feeling justified in "trying" getting certain things off my chest. I will say that i'm still not over with the ending of this game, not to say that the ending disappointing because i don't think it was even a little bit, but it makes me feel this tingly feeling like i'm standing in boots that don't quite fit or that i have bottled tears or concerns that i toss around within my head.
As a non-Resident Evil-fan (which i apologize for) i will say this is my favourite Resident Evil game so far, and i will do my best to explain why i think that. Remember well that this is all in my opinion and i'm not the kind that comes saying that any opinions are sh!te. First of all the only Resident Evil games i have played are RE0, RE7:Biohazard, both the original and remade RE4, then finally RE5 with a friend. 
So for those that disagrees with me, that is probably why. (i'm not sorry)

STORY:
Following the events from Resident Evil 7:Biohazard, Resident Evil:Village takes place 3 years later in Europe after Ethan and Mia Winter's involvance with the Bakers. They now live in Europe because of a relocation provided by Chris Redfield (that showed up in the ending of RE7:Biohazard) together the Winters have an infant daughter together named Rosemary Winters. One night Mia reads a storybook for Rose before bedtime, after Ethan carries Rose to her crib he gets into an argument with Mia having to do with the memories of the Bakers incident, then suddenly Chris and his men opens fire at the Winters household. Mia is seen being shot to death by Chris in front of Ethan, then the baby, plus the father in the household are escorted out of there. Later Ethan wakes up in a car wreck and sets off to find both Chris and his daughter Rosemary. He then finds an abandoned-looking village (hence, the name of the game) full of Lycans: infected humans with werewolf-behaviour but still intelligent enough to use firearms, melee weapons and other kinds of items. Ethan soon discovers that there are 4 lords and a leader within the ghost town that has kidnapped Rose with unknown intentions towards her, it's up to Ethan to defeat all 5 of them and save his daughter.

GAMEPLAY:
Resident Evil:Village has similar functions and layout like Resident Evil 4 with Ethan Winters improved skills in weapons and climbing-abilities due to military training also provided by Chris Redfield. Certain buildings and obstacles can be climbed, squeezed through and crawled under. The whole slum can be explored for crates and barrels destoyable with a knife to gain supplies and many treasures found elsewhere for selling to the Duke, an overweight mysterious man that shows interests in buying and trading for money, ammo, supplies such as healing salves and resources to build ammunition, bombs also improved endurance abilities through meals made of meat from pigs, chickens and fish that Ethan can harvest plus weapon upgrades (The Duke does not offer any side missions like the trader in RE4 to gain money though) 
Furniture can be pushed to block entrances and explosive barrels are widespread all over the whole place, unlike RE4, Ethan Winters can and will block certain attacks without the knife to tank the damage down to a decreased percentage, not all attacks can be blocked some will actually need to be avoided to take damage from by taking cover. The boss battles are epic, i love how different they all are from each other, however i thought 2 of them were a little too simple to be boss fights (Lady Alcina Dimitrescu & Donna Beneviento with Angie) The first one that i found to be hard was against Salvatore Moreau. The most fun ones were Karl Heisenberg and Mother Miranda.


NEGATIVES
I like to give this game the benefit of the doubt in having flaws, but all games have flaws and i think the strongest flaws in Resident Evil:Village are predictable plot-twists and certain holes in the DLCs that hadn't fully reached an conclusion to end at (not all explanations or plot-spoilers will be given) One other thing that i like to point out is that to change rounds in the flashbang-launcher rifle you need to aim the rifle in order to change the rounds with the player's preferred key-button, which i think is dumb because it took me until the end of the game to know that. And also one that i already pointed out where it felt like the boss-fight with Donna Beneviento and Angie was the point where Capcom gave up, because it was only to find Angie thrice in a game of Hide-and-Seek. I found it a little disappointing that if Ethan sneaks up on a lycan or enemy you don't get the option to stealth kill (like in the remake of RE4)
POSITIVES
And now onto the positive things about this game, firstly of all i feel like in RE7:Biohazard Ethan's lack of character was one of the weak points because i barely got to know anything about and feel a connection to him. And that is where i think RE:Village stepped up the game and actually made him one of my most likeable characters in the series with both Todd Soley's amazing voice acting, lines and background with one certain unpredictable plot-twist in the end.
With cheap jumpscares aside, the Donna Beneviento and Angie-house did have a stong point with being actually scary TWICE. The giant jaw-hinged multiple limbs-Feutus actually made me terrified for a long time and the Mia-Mannequins in the DLC made me scream loudly. The last one i found to be scary too was The Varcolacs, the first one jumps out at you when you don't expect it and tries to tear you to pieces.
The Cutscenes in this game builds great tension and IMO alot of emotional moments also, which makes it feel like a film that you take an important part in (if that makes any sense) the cutscenes feels like a reward for the effort you put into getting from A to B.

I think Resident Evil:Village is a fantastic survival-horror game that feels way more like a full place to explore and actually works well as a continuation for Ethan Winters. It throws many unexpected surprises for you along the journey with scary monsters that aren't just the Lycans... I think it does it right to make you feel threatened and not always inclined to take risks.
9.6 OUT OF 10

When someone mentions Romania, most things that come to people’s minds are varying stereotypes: vampires, immigration, and the other ones who switched sides during WW2.

However, Resident Evil Village goes beyond that. It takes some of those very know stereotypes, such as vampires (god bless Lady DUMITRESCU since Dimitrescu is not a proper Romanian name), small villages, rich culture, and orthodox religious affliction and builds a world upon it that is scary, complex, and... rich. Rich in story, rich in detail, rich in culture.

As a fellow Romanian, I was very eager to play this. Not only for the fact that it was clearly situated in Romania but since it also represents a castle I visited often as a kid, Peles Castle. The small village felt real, just like it did when I grew up. The fireplace/stoves looked just like they did when my grandma used to heat the house, all the pots and earthenware looked exactly like they when my grandma used to cook for me and most importantly... the eerie atmosphere reminded me of the cold late autumn nights.

For good or worse, Resident Evil is far from what it tries to depict. You can tell that the developers did not visit Romania, that they did not spend time with the locals (ignoring the fact that most have Romanian names but speak perfect English) and the design team could not get a proper grasp of how things look. The wooden orthodox churches depict a very muddy, kitsch-styled art, the household appliances are a mix between other Balkan countries, and even the gates in front of each house are sometimes far from what you can find in various corners of Romania.

However, it shouldn’t take away from what Resident Evil is. An insanely well-crafted game, with simple yet functional game mechanics, very well-detailed characters, and an atmosphere like no other. I’m not a fan of survival horror games but I deeply enjoyed exploring, analyzing, and interacting with the world: it felt alive.

The story, while intricate, is one of the very few that tackles the fact that sometimes, in life, no matter how hard you try, there are no happy endings. I would like to talk about it more, since it is one of the greatest points of the game, but that would spoil the beauty of it.

Besides some small caveats, like the shooting system being absolute garbage at times, and the linearity of the game preventing you from fully immersing yourself in the game, I truly believe RE8 is a must-play for anyone.

And yes, Alcina Dimitrescu (ALINA DUMITRESCU FOR CHRIST’S SAKE) is very well modeled.

Resident Evil Village is an electrifying rollercoaster ride through horror and action that will leave you on the edge of your seat from start to finish.  I can confidently say this game delivers an experience like no other.

The attention to detail is incredible, making every environment feel alive and hauntingly beautiful.

But it's not just about the looks - the gameplay is where Resident Evil Village truly shines. The controls are smooth and responsive, allowing you to navigate the treacherous landscape with ease. Whether you're solving puzzles, scavenging for resources, or taking on hordes of terrifying enemies, every moment feels intense and exhilarating.

And let's not forget about the story. Resident Evil Village continues the saga of Ethan Winters in a gripping tale of survival and mystery. From the moment you step foot in the village, you'll be drawn into a narrative full of twists and turns that will keep you guessing until the very end. And with memorable characters like Lady Dimitrescu and the enigmatic Chris Redfield, you'll find yourself invested in their fates every step of the way.

Of course, it wouldn't be Resident Evil without its signature brand of horror, and Village delivers in spades. From jump scares to tense encounters with grotesque monsters, this game will have you jumping out of your seat one moment and nervously peeking around corners the next. It's the kind of adrenaline-pumping thrill that horror fans crave.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a must-play for any horror enthusiast, you're in for one heck of a ride. With its stunning visuals, gripping gameplay, and spine-tingling scares, it's an experience you won't soon forget. So grab your controller, brace yourself for the horrors that await, and prepare for a gaming experience like no other.

Rating: ★★★★★

If you're looking for a game that will give you the heebie-jeebies while simultaneously making you question the laws of physics (specifically, boob physics), then look no further than Resident Evil 8! This game is a rollercoaster ride through a nightmare-inducing village filled with monsters, mysteries, and, of course, some seriously impressive assets.

Let's start with the graphics – wowza! Resident Evil 8 boasts some of the most stunning visuals in gaming history. From the eerie mist that hangs over the village to the grotesque details of the monsters, every pixel is a masterpiece. But let's be real here, the real MVP of the graphics department is undoubtedly the, ahem, "character models." Let's just say that if you're into... um, ample assets, you won't be disappointed. Those polygons have never looked so... perky.

But it's not all about the eye candy (though it certainly helps distract you from the terror). The story is a blast to play through, filled with twists, turns, and enough scares to make you jump out of your seat – and possibly knock over your snacks in the process. From uncovering the secrets of the mysterious village to facing off against some truly terrifying bosses, every moment is a thrill ride.

Of course, we can't talk about Resident Evil 8 without addressing the elephant in the room (or should I say, the elephants). Yes, the character designs in this game are, shall we say, generously proportioned. It's like the developers took one look at the script and said, "You know what this game needs? More... assets." And hey, who are we to argue? It's not every day you see a survival horror game where the biggest threat isn't the monsters, but the risk of getting smothered by some seriously big... distractions.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 8 is a must-play for any fan of the series – or anyone looking for a good scare and a few laughs along the way. With stunning graphics, a gripping story, and some seriously impressive... character development, it's an experience you won't soon forget. Just be sure to keep your eyes on the screen – and try not to get too distracted by the, uh, scenery.

[h1] Review[/h1] 
After the success of the 7th instalment in the main franchise it was a no brainer that for one there will be a sequel and two it will continue the same gameplay mechanic. I always liked every mainline resident evil game, even most of the weird spin offs. Be it the traditional ones, the action oriented or the new generation.  

[u]Gameplay[/u]
The gameplay feels like a culmination of some of the aspects of 4 and 7. Which means you not only have weapons to find, smaller areas to explore but also some interconnectivity between the levels to a certain degree. While the main playthrough is very linear there are a lot of side objectives to do or find hidden objects. From hunting animals to finding treasures to killing additional bosses.

The main combat did not change at all. Including the great idea of the blocking feature makes the combat simple yet really fun. Although the healing mechanic got dumbed down and there is an abundance of crafting resources. This does not mean that you can’t run out of ammo, but there is a lot to pickup.

On your way you fight a few different bosses with their own quirks including a chainsaw battle while driving a makeshift tank. I always respected resident evil for making the very over the top encounters and cutscenes absolutely a blast to play through even though they might break with the horror atmosphere. 

This might also be the only real flaw of the game for me. While I like the enemy design way much more than the previous game, generally its not such a scary game. At least for me. I think its hard to recreate the dread of the mansion in the first game without trying to do the same thing again. The baker mansion felt a bit like repeating the same setup and I’m glad they opted for exploring a very rural and foreign village as its core design although that one sets up to be a metroidvania esque game but actually plays mostly linear and never does anything with it despite setting it first up for the player.

Your goal later on is to defeat 4 bosses who each have their distinct setting and mechanics around them adding a huge amount of variety. Although you cannot choose who to beat first whatsoever.

Also the points shop from re 3 remake is back again. In the same manner. With its nice ideas and cons. Unlocking infinite ammo is done after the first playthrough, making the highest difficulty just way too easy. There is also not that much fun stuff to unlock aside a few weapons. Most of it is just models and concept art, not even cosmetics.

[u]Story[/u]
Its quite a mess. I found the loosely umbrella connected story in 7 very decent and fun to experience. Although that one went partially a bit into the esoteric it still was focused on horror caused by scientific experiments. Village adds some of the occult but the whole story feels more magical. There is barely any satisfactory information why the enemies look like werewolves or involve vampires. The antagonists story seems interesting at first but the end result is just a story that does not really engage me that much. There are interesting points in there, especially the setting and some of the characters. But instead the story just initially appears to make a great mystery but its one of those games where you have to save your child and even worse toddler whom you don’t have any connection towards and it culminates into one of the most unsatisfactory endings and general story in the franchise. Not to mention how they wrote both Ethan and Chris into slightly annoying characters.

[u]Sound[/u]
Unlike the older resident evil games, the new ones tend to be way much more environmental. There are barely any action tracks and few trying to setup horror. Instead, its mostly focusing on sound effects. 

[u]Graphics[/u]
Absolutely gorgeous and well optimized game. It runs absolutely flawless for me and looks at times photo realistic, especially scenes featuring mountains and the general surroundings of the 

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
Village is for me a game that exceeds in some parts the previous game but having also equally more bad parts. The rather unsatisfactory story which in turn is implemented into a game with probably the best horror combat in the franchise with a very fun gameplay loop that entertained me from start to finish. Some more horror sequences wouldn’t have been too bad but overall I think its a highly entertaining videogame

Village is a fine game. Not great, not awful. However, it is by far the worst Resident Evil game.
Not in terms of gameplay but in terms of lore and the rules of the universe it takes place in. Which is weird to say about a series that features a naked ant-lady that shoots flaming blood at you, a giant mutant T-Rex man that is down REAL bad for his assistant, and underground facilities so massive that their construction surely awoke a Balrog.
Given that, I feel like the more you know about Resident Evil and the more invested you are in the series the less you will like this game, but you probably won't hate it. Conversely, if you don't know jack about RE and could care less about anything other than some nice presentation, shooting werewolves, and getting chased by big lady you'll really enjoy this game.
On that note, the presentation is the real selling point of Village. The atmosphere and setting are fantastic. There is some spookiness to it, but Resident Evil hasn't been the place to find scares in a LONG time.
The gameplay on the other hand is just okay. It's not a great survival horror game and it's even less so a great action game. Puzzles are... well let's just say this game is journo-proof.

Mercenaries is pretty good if that's your cup of tea.
Shadow of Rose is just okay. Not really important story/lore wise.
Replayability of the story isn't as appealing as other entries but you do get some new toys to play with. 

This next bit is just some examples and nitpicks about what bothers me with this game. Probably some spoilers ahead.
-The bastardization of Chris. He is written as an idiot and an ass just for some contrived shock and drama.
-Literal Magneto character. No need for further bioweapons, guys, we've peaked. Why would anyone be interested in second-rate weapons like T-Abyss when they could have Magneto?
-Magneto has a one-man Horzine operation in his massive underground facility. See this sort of thing works for Umbrella or Tri-Cell because they're multi-billion dollar international corporations with thousands of employees, Heisenberg is one guy. Maybe he had all the scrakes and fleshpounds help him build it.
-Magneto calls Chris a, "boulder punching ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥." How did he know Chris was there? How did he know it was Chris who blew up the factory? How did he know Chris punched a boulder? How does he even know who Chris is? [i]I get it, it's funny.[/i] But there are better ways to make call-backs and references, like Claire causing Moira to cringe with a Jill Sandwich joke.
-Literal Magneto is apparently not strong enough to defeat Miranda, so he wants Ethan's help. Ethan ends up just killing Miranda by simply unloading a shotgun in her face. Remember in the last game when you had to inject Evaline with a serum to weaken her to even stand a chance?
-Some terrible and hamfisted revelations about O. Spencer and the origins of Umbrella that revolve around Miranda.
-Miranda, a terribly generic and underdeveloped villain that is essentially only in the game for about 20 minutes with 10 of those minutes being you feeding her buckshot.

If there is one thing I will remember about this game years from now it will be Heisenberg saying, "That ♥♥♥♥♥, Miranda!"

Resident Evil Village stands out as one of the best entries in the series in recent years. Continuing the story started in Resident Evil 7, we once again step into the shoes of Ethan in this thrilling first-person adventure. The game's campaign is excellent, offering an immersive and satisfying gameplay experience with a decent length. While completion times can vary depending on the player, it typically lasts around 16 hours. Personally, it took me about 20 hours to complete, as I thoroughly explored each area to find all the items and upgrades. While the beginning can be a bit confusing, the plot unfolds into a compelling and satisfying narrative.

One of the most interesting additions is The Duke, a character reminiscent of the merchant from Resident Evil 4, providing commercial services such as weapon upgrades and selling essential supplies.

In summary, Resident Evil Village offers an exceptional experience that captures the essence of the series without feeling repetitive. With a complete story, stunning visuals, and excellent gameplay, it's a compelling option for fans of the franchise. For those looking to delve into the world of Resident Evil, this installment is a great choice, as it provides a recap of the events of Resident Evil 7.

As for the rating, I would give it a solid 8/10. The graphics are up to modern standards, the story is engaging, the game offers a substantial length, a wide variety of enemies and challenging puzzles, and the gameplay is fantastic.

Personal Notes:

I would say my favourite title in the resident evil franchise until 4 was released, village is a fantastic edition to the series. I loved the map with it being what could be described as a marketplace with the central village being the epicentre and the story leading you to each corner with you circling back to move to the next. I loved the design of the village and just how good it looked with it being well laid out to support the aforementioned story design with it being designated as a "hub". By far however my most loved area was the castle, I loved the design of it and its layout as well as its general feel and sound. Capcom built it very well with its gold accents and elegant furniture. It is a shame they did not further develop this area with new DLC. The other areas are also good with there being a horror type house on a cliff involving dolls which is well structured and by far the most disgusting aspect of a game I have seen. A large lake and more water focused area with caves and windmills followed by a factory built into the ground with a more mechanical feeling, I did like how each area had its own feeling and design not copying the others.

I would without a doubt recommend this title, it is less linear and more open world than resident evil 3 but more linear and less open world than resident evil 4. But none the less a fantastic game in the series with its unique game play, graphics and sound as well as a brilliant take on an older game play design with a more medieval feel, it is again just a shame they did not pursue the castle more. The only downside I did find was I did not at all enjoy the DLC story for Rose and found it quite boring, only completing it for the achievements which is a massive shame. Bar that I can recommend the game to any resident evil fan.

The only thing I didn't like is the difference in areas:
 - First area becomes the hub area, the same Village the game is named after. Great place.
 - Second area - The castle the game is known for. Again, an amazing area.
 - Third area - the forced horror sequence, and just doing small puzzles while avoiding enemies. Too short and too simple. 
- Forth area - few puzzles in the start, and a very prolonged boss battle. A lot more world building could have been made here, and just battling one enemy (the boss) here feels just bad. The area itself is large and could have been a really cool place to explore, but oh well, ended way too soon. 
 - Fifth area - combines a very long combat arena and probably the 2nd best designed area in the game after the castle. Really amazing place, on par with the second area. 

But except these small nitpicks of how the game could be even better, I really don't have anything else to add. Great experience through and through.

Out with the bad first because it's a short section before going with what I loved about the game. There were minor bugs relating to lycan weapons clipping into the models of the enemies sometimes. Anyway, those problems affected maybe 1-3% of my playtime, the other 97-99% of the time I had an absolute blast. The visuals are absolutely amazing, same with the animation. The story, the level design, soundtrack and characters are extremely captivating. Resident Evil Village is much like Resident Evil 4 in that it plays much more like an action-adventure game than a survival horror game. I did my first play-through on hardcore and ammo and healing wasn't particularly scarce at any point. Granted there are times when you find yourself short handed but they are few and far between. There is much more emphasis on shooting your way out of situations than avoiding enemies by sneaking by.  Actually I cant think of a single point where you were able to outright avoid a fight. Resources are also abundant, with almost every enemy dropping loot, which further incentives killing them instead of avoiding them. 

I'm not bringing this up to disparage the game, but its important to understand that this is not a traditional Resident Evil game. If your expecting a survival-horror experience like that in say, Resident Evil 2, you will be disappointed. If you are a fan of more action oriented games than Village will almost certainly be an enjoyable experience. It still features mechanics like crafting and inventory management from previous Resident Evil games, however it is more simplified than in previous entries. Your inventory, for example, is much less constricted.  

The graphics are very good and, more importantly, the game ran well on my decent but not top of the line PC with everything maxed out. This cannot be said for many older AAA titles. The game is, however, missing an FOV slider which is unacceptable. Granted I didn't find the default FOV to be horrible, but being locked in without the use of mods is frustrating. Most of the voice acting is pretty good (some small exceptions) and the motion capture is excellent. Definitely don't skip the cut-scenes.  

Gameplay is very fun and with a good variety of weapons and enemies. The several boss fights were also quite good and didn't feel too formulaic. The puzzles are abundant and fun as always. Another standout feature is collecting loot to sell to the merchant. There is a lot of it and it can be quite satisfying to see just how much money you can make which can then be used to upgrade weapons and purchase items. The only thing I didn't really like was the Call Of Duty campaign-like segment around the end. It isn't too long but it felt very out of place and kinda lazy. 

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is a fantastic game that I highly recommend to anyone who enjoys more action-oriented experiences.  There are still plenty of scary moments if that's more your thing, but again, this is not a true survival horror game if that's what your after.

A sequel to RE7 that gives continuity to the Winters’ spooky adventures and explains the origins of the fungus that made Mia go cuckoo. RE Village goes so wacko mode that it makes RE7 seem restrained by comparison. Whether that’s good or bad is up to the player.

[h3]General notes:[/h3]
[list]
[*] It’s considerably more action-oriented than its predecessor. Killing enemies is encouraged by the guarantee of one drop per kill (either money/treasures or crafting materials), and ample availability of ammo and resources. Do mind that I say this having played it on Hardcore difficulty
[*] That being said, the game doesn’t give up its survival horror elements - there’s still puzzles that make no sense, lots of backtracking to open weird gates with weird items, and plenty of going around the map to unlock doors that were previously [i]locked from the other side[/i]
[/list]

[h3]What’s good:[/h3]
[list]
[*] The inventory and the crafting system. Crafting materials no longer take up inventory space - they have their own little neat section in which you can see all the materials and [i]recipes[/i] you have, allowing you to strategize accordingly. It’s a well designed and intuitive UI
[*] Despite what I said about resource availability, it was frequently necessary to ponder [i]which kind[/i] of ammunition/item I needed to craft based on the available materials, the type of enemies inhabiting my current location and how those enemies behave (for example, I would favor explosives if they constantly attack in groups). This is the game’s greatest and most enjoyable puzzle
[*] Enemy variety. All my homies hate the same 4 molded variations RE7 had throughout the whole game
[*] The bonus content. There’s the Mercenaries game mode, 3D figures, concept art (with commentary, which is pretty sick and should be the norm), and unlockable weapons
[*] Replayability. I don’t often enjoy replaying games, but the challenges, extra content/guns and the bonus difficulty were enough to make me play RE Village again
[*] Tall, big tiddy mommy
[*] Her daughters
[/list]

[h3]What could be better:[/h3]
[list]
[*] A lot of the dialogue, especially Ethan’s one-liners, is wack. The start of the game made me think it would take itself seriously (Ethan asking himself [i]“Why does everyone keep dying on me?”[/i] got me in the feels, highkey), but the dialogue and interactions get progressively cornier
[*] Puzzles in general. I’d never expect RE puzzles to make sense, but it would be nice if they posed a challenge
[*] At a certain point (after exiting the first/best zone), the game gives you a checklist of the evil [strike]exes[/strike] bosses you must defeat to get your lil Rose back. Since you have no choice of which one you’re going to face first, there is 0 need for this kind of exposition. It feels tacky, and I don’t want to know exactly how much game is left
[*] Some of the bosses’ designs could be improved to better match the game’s mechanics. Uriaș Strӑjer and Miranda come to mind. They reminded me a lot of Dark Souls’ boss fights because learning attack patterns and dodging is essential to survive/perform well in their battles. However, this is a first-person game in which you can only run in a forward direction, thus requiring you to look away from them while they are executing their string attacks. It just feels weird, like they belong in another type of game
[*] Heisenberg is so cool, and then they turned his boss fight into [spoiler]a giant robot battle[/spoiler]. Shame.
[/list]

As always, the Resident Evil game franchise continues to deliver in spades with their survival-horror genre, and this release takes the baton from their previous titles flawlessly.  

Gameplay: Greatly increasing Ethan Winters' abilities, a much larger variety of weapons and strategies are now at your disposal. Continuing the 1st person view from previous works, up to 4 weapons may be quick-equipped, allowing you to select the most optimal equipment to deal with certain foes while preventing damage by dodging, hiding, or blocking. 

Combat: In typical horror fashion, failing to adequately defend yourself often leads to severe punishment or outright death, courtesy of the games' custom execution animations. This becomes most evident on the highest difficulty, where increased enemy health and damage are now accompanied by additional enemy spawns, earlier scripted battle scenes, upgraded enemies, and increased enemy combat intelligence (such as staggering towards the player when shot), mitigating extra content cheats such as infinite ammo. The mid-bosses are slightly repetitive but occur at far enough intervals where they don't become too much of an annoyance. The boss fights, however, are the main focus; a wide variety of specialized attacks serves to uniquely personify their character along with other background information you may discover throughout the map, especially regarding a certain 8 foot tall vampiress.  

Exploration: While not required, adequately exploring the map and pursuing side-missions is heavily recommended, and serves to greatly reward the attentive player, yielding riches of money, supplies, critical enemy information, or specialized tools. Puzzles, treasure maps, and optional combat scenarios await your inquisitive nature should you so choose...

Immersion: The vastly larger and isolated mountainous exterior serves as a stark contrast to the dark and oppressive interior, a classic feature of Resident Evil. Player movement is surprisingly human, displaying small pauses for vaults, movement reversals, or opening doors in addition to other actions. Disgustingly detailed enemy models are accompanied by hyper-realistic combat animations, ranging from attacks to movements to deaths. The nearly overwhelming number of detailed and distinct sound effects serves to root your attention to your screen at all times as you listen to Ethan's nervous breathing or the breaking of sticks in the woods.

Non-gameplay: The game is graphically gorgeous, with falling snow, player/enemy characters, tools, and more. As mentioned before, the sound quality and content is insanely immersive. Quality of life aspects are quite user friendly, with save and loading screens conducted nearly immediately other than the initial load in from the main menu. Finishing the game rewards the player by unlocking additional challenge perks that will serve to greatly alter traditional gameplay, including unlocking a mini-mercenary game or the aforementioned infinite ammo. A DLC with additional story and gameplay content is also available for download (Winters' Expansion - Shadows of Rose).
The trade-off is the high temperatures this game will generate; it is highly recommended to throttle your CPU or graphics cards (reducing electric consumption = less heat), and even then my own computer was hovering in the mid-50 degrees Celsius. You will most likely hear your computer fan running at full blast to cope with this large game, so make sure to have some temperature monitoring software running. 
This website serves as a great guide to bring down your computer temperature: https://www.ultrabookreview.com/31385-the-throttlestop-guide/
  
All in all, a fantastic continuation of the Resident Evil series, and it is clear that a staggering amount of effort was put into the makings of this game. As a RE fan, you will enjoy the continued and surprising changes to the plot and characters in the RE universe, and if you're new to this franchise, this game is user friendly enough where it does not require you to play previous titles to enjoy its content. 

10/10 would highly recommend playing this masterpiece.

If you are a producer or contributor to the makings of this game, know that you deserve a pat on the back and more for your efforts, and I hope you keep up the good work. I look forward to supporting your future products when they are unveiled. 
As a long time fan, thank you for your efforts and service. Please go eat some ice cream or something similar.

A game that tries a little too hard to be Resident Evil 4, but I'd hardly call that a flaw, because that is by far the best mainline RE title in the series.

People always complained about RE5 and RE6 being too action-y and it's like they have a gap in their memory that makes them forget that RE4 started that trend. Leon literally does backflips in that game, he's like an Olympic gymnast with firearms training.

This game is a little more grounded, oddly enough. Ethan certainly isn't a master of quips like Leon, either, but I find his basic irritation with the crazy cultist weirdos around him to be oddly endearing in a way. Whereas Leon would mock his opponents, Ethan prefers to tell them to go ♥♥♥♥ themselves and it's that sort of energy I can get behind in a protagonist. Other people find him to be bland, but especially considering he's a first-person (technically faceless) protagonist that's easier to implant your own personality onto at times, it's less of a problem than people make it out to be. He talks a lot, has a lot of dialogue like any FPS protagonist from the 2000s era, but is otherwise quite moldable (heh) to your own tastes. But I guess that's subjective and I can see the problems with it, but even where his personality overtakes that, I find his motivations to be fairly relatable or at least easy to empathize/sympathize with. His entire goal throughout RE8 is to find and rescue his daughter, so it's not hard for me to like him. I wouldn't say the writing is award-worthy, but it's satisfying enough that I've played through the game three times now (including two PS4 playthroughs where I replayed immediately after beating it the very first time).

The game itself is pretty fun. It doesn't do everything as well as RE4 did, that's just the honest truth. Even presentation of, say, the inventory management, is quite bland visually by comparison. All that being said, I would rather replay RE8 than the RE3 remake. It feels like a complete game. On a quick casual run for my first time replaying in a while it only took 10 hours for me to beat the game completely while grabbing most of the extra goodies I could find along the way (semi-thorough; I did miss some parts for my magnum somewhere, I'll have to grab that in another run). Considering the Extra Shop you unlock for beating the game allows you to buy more weapons, infinite ammo for the weapons you do have, and some basic extra content like viewable figures and concept art, you'll have some good motivation to come back and replay the game in the future, if not immediately afterwards.

I never felt frustrated with the combat, it always felt reasonable and fair. Enemies make sense being a bit bullet-sponge-y unlike the zombies in the RE2 remake who just... didn't make much sense for how durable their faces were to bullets. Fighting enemies always feels responsive, too. A shotgun blast knocks enemies back and it looks decent, too. Stop, aim for the head and let the reticule narrow and you can cause a lycan's head to turn to mist. Plenty satisfying.

So, yeah, haven't really sold the game as much as I probably should, but this isn't a hard game to figure out if it's for you. Don't let it being somewhat of an RE4 clone turn you off. If anything, it's a nice homage to one of the best RE games we've ever had and a solid one of its own. Also, don't forget that mods are very much an option, as this is an RE game. Plenty to choose from to enhance your experience. Just don't be surprised at the perverseness of the mod selection. RE fans are a desperately thirsty bunch. I really don't get it, but I try (key word TRY) not to judge.

Decided to change the review since I had a chance to finish the game and, while the combat is still frustrating, the quality of the rest of the game is more than good enough to warrant a recommendation. Original complaints below.

----
Game doesn't support refresh rate above 120hz but that's not the reason behind my overall negative experience. Much greater concern is combat, which is the second worst in the whole RE series. This is mostly due to enemies being generally unresponsive to your attacks while also spazzing out with comically over-the-top swaying animations designed to make you miss your shots just after you've finished lining it up. Letting them get too close means getting hit by grab attacks that grant them invincibility frames... all of this makes for very tedious and unrewarding combat sequences: what worked for the slower paced and more puzzle oriented RE7 definitely doesn't here (the people comparing this to RE4 - original or remake - are out of their minds). Also the third major boss in the game will often use attacks that always hit through geometry - you may have an entire wall between you and him and you'll still take lots of damage (please note that I am not talking about his acid rain attack, that one is clearly telegraphed and the hiding spots work as intended).

That said, the straw that broke the camel's back was the "logic" behind House Beneviento treasure being only obtainable if you purposely screw yourself over (revisit an already explored and out of the way area of the map, which leads to new enemies spawning out of the ground, one of which will eventually open a gate containing a key item). That in itself wouldn't be too bad if it wasn't for the fact the event is one-time only: if you didn't revisit said area during a specific time, it's lost forever in that playthrough. 

It's clear the designers intended for the player to return there by giving the player a clue to a rare hunting bird's location (it's perched high up among the branches); having noticed and killed said bird on my first visit there, I had no reason to backtrack and unknowingly missed the window of opportunity (and thus the associated treasure/mini boss fight) for a completely unrelated treasure/event. There's absolutely no logic behind punishing the player in such a way and I assume it's a developing oversight, given the many options available to prevent a lock-up: for example, enemies could've been made to spawn during any of the player's revisits and not during a specific point of the game. Or the gate could've been opened automatically if done at a late enough point during the campaign. Whatever: as it is, being keen-eyed and straying off the intended path punishes you.

At the time of writing this review I have played all 8 mainline Resident Evil games and some of the spin-offs. I love this franchise so much, however as much as I enjoyed this game I can safely say that if this is the end of the Winters' story I will be happy. I don't believe I am the only person that thinks Ethan isn't as strong of a protagonist as the other series veterans, and find him to be a bit lame. In a franchise full of so many cool action hero-esque characters it feels strange playing as an everyday Joe.

I personally find it odd the amount Chris is used in the marketing, for crying out loud hes on the box art. I personally love the section where you play as Chris and his new Hound Wolf Squad, I just wish it was the whole game and or lasted longer than it does. Besides my personal disliking of Ethan, this game is great all the way through, I have never felt more fear playing a game when I was doing the doll house section. This whole game is full of RE 4 inspirations, whether its the isolated European village full of locals turned monsters, or the four bosses you must beat before you reach the "mastermind" of the story's operation. It can't be a coincidence that the RE 4 remake came out after this game.

The first person camera also isn't my jam, while it sucks you into the game and immerses you I still like being able to see the designs of the characters as well as more of the world around me, I just associate Resident Evil with third person cameras personally. So if this is the sendoff to the Winters' family and story in the Resident Evil universe, I'd say it is a good sendoff to the story that started all the way back in 2017 in Louisiana.

I'd call this one "Resident Evil's Greatest Hits", because in many ways it feels like an amalgamation of all the best bits of the entire series in one game. 

In some ways it's great seeing all those good bits work together. In others it feels like retreading old ground. Yes there's a Resident Evil 4 village. Yes there's another Resident Evil mansion. Yes there's an unstoppable behemoth stalking the map. Yes there are somewhat ludicrous puzzles and gates that open when you jam things-that-don't-look-like-keys-but-are into them. And yes there's some other bio-engineered bug turning people into monsters - because of course. Right? It's a Resident Evil game!

As a game it still holds together extremely well and Capcom have finely tuned what makes a great Resident Evil experience down to a fine art now. My only real complaint is that the tone of the game goes from dark and grisly, to somewhat cringe as Capcom strays into self-parody with some of the character designs and dialogue. I wish they could settle on a serious tone and not let it get too ridiculous. It's jarring especially when you see the great build up, tension, and horror that they've put into this game - only for them to wreck it with something completely nonsensical.

Resident Evil Village was a very notable game with very few flaws. Below is a list of pros and cons that I noticed. This is not meant to be controversial, but is my opinion of the game. (Based on the 3rd person play through)
Pros:
-Gameplay mechanics are fluent enough
-Story was riveting (Based off playing RE7)
-Numerous different enemies throughout game
-Huge map
-Every different area is original
-Still has the enclosed scary feeling from other RE games
-The four lords all have their own quirk (making the different bosses new and always a different fight)
-Always on the edge of my seat
Cons:
-Boss battles are a little lack luster and provide little for tactics (all seem to be closely related other than the boss)
-Sprinting while going from W to WD or WA has an awkward movement (still very playable)
-Playable characters don't sprint as if it is life or death (I prefer player models to run like hell)
-Some moments I find myself wondering WTH do I do? (this is not the worst but can also be a pro)
-The game goes by a little quick in terms of what is truly happening in the story.
-Not as scary as some of the older games
-No storage box (Forced to sell items)
-Final boss is not the most enjoyable fight (me personally)

It may seem like there is a lot of cons, but these are not game ruining nor are they that bad. Most of the pros make the game awesome.

The graphics aren't mind-blowing but still visually appealing; the RE Engine never disappoints! The story is also surprisingly heartfelt, much better than the dud 7's story left with me. I enjoyed every minute of the story, even if the middle part of Village could be more precise. Horror-wise, Village has some of the tamest set pieces in the series while also having the scariest horror moment of the last few years; you KNOW what I'm talking about if you played. 

One of my favorite parts of the RE series is how it's not afraid to get campy & ridiculous & Village doesn't hold back in that department; it was very clearly inspired by RE4 & in a few ways, also set the table for the remake we just got. Aside from the flimsy middle portion of this game slowing things down after the AMAZING castle level, I can't think of too many negatives for the base game. Also, playing as Lady D in Mercenaries is AMAZING, **** that the DLC doesn't advertise itself as having to grind to unlock her instead of at purchase. -_-As for the Shadows of Rose DLC, it's much more horror-focused than Village's action-packed moments, and it was enjoyable, just not all that fun to play. I get Rose is a young girl just trying to help herself & she won't control as smoothly as an adult like Ethan, but things felt significantly clunkier, jumping right into the DLC after finishing the base game. I appreciate the horror focus & there are some genuine moments of terror in the DLC (THOSE FORSAKEN MANNEQUINS)... But other than that, you only get to fully experience Rose's powers at the literal end of the story. It feels great, but I wish we could skip to RE9 to play as a powered-up Rose trying to save the world or whatever they introduce in that sure-to-be jam-packed game. 

Overall, the DLC was an excellent addition but not necessary ****. Village is the most fun I've had with a Resident Evil game.
