I'm glad I did it.

I finished my first playthrough of the game in 12 hours, which doesn't seem all that long considering the price I paid. Other AAA games double or triple this with ease. But where others (like AC Valhalla) bored me to death with their empty, interchangeable characters and story, Resident Evil 8 shines as a quality experience. Especially this grotesque cabinet of well-written and acted characters, the villains could be taken straight out of a Tim Burton film. Not to mention the pacing and plot twists I didn't expect to be so compelling. All in all, definitely an unforgettable adventure.



Graphics, oh my god, graphics. I've rarely found myself so surprised by a game. For me, Resi 8 ranks with Horizon Zero Dawn, Control, Cyberpunk 2077, Tomb Raider and AC Odyssey/Valhalla. (I know there are others, but these were the most amazing looking ones I've played). It's not just that the textures, lightning, reflections, and all the technical shenanigans are great, but it's the balance of light, shadow, color, reflections, etc. that makes this game truly shine. Capcom managed to find the sweet spot to set the perfect tone for Ethan's second journey through Marcabra.

The sound design is always special for me. From the roar of animals or the sound of guns to small rustles, clicks, creaks and cracks. All these little details that were added, Capcom absolutely added them. I found myself cowering in my seat, holding my breath in tense situations too often, thanks in large part to the excellent sound design and musical composition.

Last but not least is the gameplay. For the most part, Resi 8 follows the same steps. Get to a new area, kill the boss, explore for more loot, upgrade things, repeat. Sounds simple... and, well, it is. But you don't really need much innovation when the structure you've built is filled with quality content, like balancing loot and currency/treasure to upgrade. I never felt like there was too much of either, but I also never felt like there was too much of a lack as long as I played smart (on standard difficulty). This is kind of symbolic for the entire gameplay. I should also mention that I've probably killed a thousand bosses in my gaming career, but after some of the Resi 8 bosses I was just smiling, thinking, "Damn, that was amazing..." Capcom must have done something right by achieving this. I think it's a mixture of all the things I mentioned above.

Bottom line, Resident Evil 8 follows a simple recipe, but a simple recipe done right... completely. Sound, graphics, story, map, puzzles, gunplay, etc... it's all great. And unfortunately, currently you have to claim that (at least in my example) they did it without errors.

A lot to love, and a lot to be annoyed by. The game world is exceptionally designed, full of atmosphere, mystery, and style. The combat is solid, and RE8 features all the features you'd want in a lite survival/crafting action game - inventory organization, limited supplies, crafting decisions, and lots of upgrades to move from a vulnerable twig into beast mode. The early sense in the game that there are lots of treasures to come back and find later on was very satisfying. It's fun unspooling the map and revealing all its secrets.

Acting is good, cinematic sequences are engaging, and the overall pacing felt about right. Although RE8 features much bigger maps than RE7, the playtime is about the same, and I'm not sure the game world really IS bigger ... they mostly just added lots of tunnels to walkthrough between the larger rooms and objectives. Still, it's really beautiful to look at and explore.

But damn does this game have some annoying design decisions. My least favorite was the pointless killing domesticated animals for upgrades system. It's not even hunting; you just walk up to some poor beast and blow its brains out. Felt needlessly sadistic and is unsatisfying as a mechanic.

After you explore a major area off of the hub map, you get locked out of that area -- even if you left essential treasures and obtainable meats ungathered, which can really hamstring you from accessing upgrades later in the game. Yes, I know this was the case in RE7 as well, but it felt less punitive in that game. Here, a lot of the cool things can get permanently missed until the next playthrough.

A real loss from RE7 is the survival horror elements. Gone are any real sneak mechanics. There's very little suspense or surprise in this game; it's mostly just full-on vampire hunter and such. It's still fun to play, but I really think the survival horror in the first three sections of RE7 were glorious, and I wish they had retained some of that. Instead, in this game we get far more wave shooter moments and overall run 'n gun sequences. Most are enjoyable, but I didn't care for the moments when a mini-boss battle took place in a cramped arena. Those were unnecessarily tedious.

Finally, the story is a disappointing morass of retconned elements. It's hard to make sense of anything in this game if you haven't played RE7, but the story basically undercuts that whole game. I won't give it away, but suffice to say that RE8 sacrifices a lot of the significance of the actions in the previous game to come up with some cheap plot twists. While I *love* the Village of Shadows story-within-the-story, the rest of the plotline felt like lazy writing to me.

Still had a blast running through it, but it is definitely not as good as RE7, especially if you're looking more for survival horror than action.

[i] Village [/i] is definitely a good way to return to the old RE roots of exploration and survival. You can see this title takes a lot of inspiration from [i] Resident Evil 4 [/i] and if anything the Remake of that solidifies it in how to approach this title. 

As its namesake, the main HUB of this game is a Romanian Village. You return playing as Ethan Winters, the new RE protagonist who was introduced in RE7. You can see he had ended up with Mia Winters regardless of the baggage she had brought from the 7th Installment (if anyone was Team Zoey, I am sorry, I was conflicted about that choice as well). This game made me realise, in my least bias, that Ethan is one of the only people who can love and accept Mia. She was a jerk in RE7 and caused Ethan and so many people a lot of problems.

However, Ethan is more interested in building a life with her and even trusts she is private or closed off on certain things despite their history. Mia and Ethan now have a baby, Rosemary Winters. They kind of consider her a miracle and I think it is because of all Mia and Ethan went through in RE7 and I think it is simplified they were worried if The Mold made them infertile or caused mutations that would consider basic reproduction a risk. 

 However, all the events in 2017 Dulvey, Louisiana, has shaken Ethan to the core. He is not the same naive, optimistic person. Rather, he even says "It is not paranoia if they are really out to get you." He is scared for himself and his family and this creates some frictions with him and Mia who, despite being a key proponent to Dulvey, is somewhat over it.If you played RE4 Original and RE4 Remake you can see how Leon had changed significantly after the events of Raccoon City in RE2. A similar shift has happened to Ethan, he is no longer inexperienced and not the shy and passive systems engineer from 2017. Things go South, when Chris Redfield, someone Ethan trusts without a doubt, comes into his home and kills Mia Winters and kidnaps Rosemary, his daughter. These are not spoilers, this is the setting of the game as showcased by Capcom. 

Ethan is SHOCKED at Chris's betrayal and wants to find his daughter again who is further kidnapped by a group of mutants in an isolated Romanian village run by this weird Prophetess/Saint of a Black God named Mother Miranda. Hence, [i] Village [/i] is you, playing as Ethan Winters, uncovering the treacherous secrets of this remote Draculinian place in out of nowhere. I would say the atmosphere, ambiance and setting is quite GOOD for this kind of game. Unlike the heated and fetid swamp backwaters of Louisiana, Ethan now is in the arctic cold of Romanian Winters (his namesake) and must adapt to the weather and dangers that have come into this place. 

[b] GAMEPLAY: [/b] The game is designed around Stoker like symbolism, Romanian myths and iconography. It is Gothic in nature and blood and viscera play a deep role in creating the environments but also enhancing levels of fear, immersion and play. Unlike the visceral entanglements of the virus you have seen as large massive sacs of putrid flesh in RE2 Remake, [i] Village [/i] takes its influences from the medieval and European imagery of dungeons, torture devices and torment. It also has amazing artwork and paintings to heighten that kind of atmosphere and give it an architectural narrative. 

Speaking of architecture, this game is a visual feast. From Castle Dimitrescu and House Beneviento, you can see the creators have shaped it as a tour de force and to show the graphical excellence of the RE Engine. Even though this game was released in 2021, you can see that it has a lot of craft and care that still stands up today. The ambiance and cold of the Village, of castle walls and the houses, all beautifully detailed, are also somewhat hauntingly beautiful. You feel Ethan's sadness and isolation and as you play him in a village surrounded by werewolves and mutants, you feel his pain and dread. 

Gameplay enhances this with Ethan having thrust in cruel and unforgiving situations. His reactions to them are not like Leon, Jill and Chris. They seem to a mix between Claire and a younger Leon, in that he shows shock more often and despair, reminding you, underneath it all, Ethan is still a software guy who is way over his head. It actually makes him more relatable and enjoyable to play at times given that he is not trained exclusively by BSAA and also FBI or is not a cop in any shape or form. The enemies are well detailed and you can see that the first person view is meant to show you their nasty physiques and blood drenched mouths. As European lore is more into this game, the 'zombies' are more Lycans (werewolves), Vampires (mutants) and bizarre beings who fly and swim. They are a far cry to the non-intelligent zombies of RE2 and an upgrade to the Ganados of RE4, having more concentrated behaviour and abilities. New Game + allows you to explore the village more and get tons of goodies as weapons and such!

[b] CHARACTERS: [/b] I am not going to lie. I was never really a fan of Ethan Winters. I found him lacking in certain ways that Chris, Leon, Jill, Ada and Claire were not. Hell, revamped Carlos and Luis is WAY interesting to me. I noticed it also did not help that first person hides a lot of nonverbal stuff about Ethan. So, the new third person addition is awesome. It allowed me to like Ethan more and the secrets surrounding him are also quite appreciated. I loved that Capcom added that twist and I was waiting for something like that in the RE franchise. 

Though, I would not input so much into other characters aside Chris, Mia and The Duke.  Mother Miranda is very one dimensional. Even though she has a rich history apparently in this new RE mythos, she is annoying and kind of makes less sense than Wesker, Birkins and Spencer.  This is a trend in Capcom villains I noticed in their animated movies recently as well.  Miranda has the same sort of appeal as the main baddie from [i] Infinite Darkness [/i] Netflix show. Just there to be culled by you the gamer. Too much powers and less 'meat' to her motivations. 

The Lords, her 'children', are also quite forgetful in a way. You wish to learn more about them and their motivations but you can forget them. They function as obstacles to get to Rose rather than characters in their own right. Disappointingly, Lady Alcina Dimitrescu, who was the game's promotional villain, seems more like that, an ad hoc poster than a character.

Now, in [i] Shadows of Rose [/i] I have to say, older Rosemary Winters, leaves an impression on you. She is very complex and actually has complicated feelings and emotions. You can see her childhood was hard and she pines a lot for acceptance but is not really valued by ordinary people. I get the sense she is a kind of character who we will see more in the RE universe and I am grateful for it. Maybe, I am being a bit too hopeful, but I would want some of the complex philosophical questions RE putting out there to be fleshed out than just binary black and white. 

[b]  LORE: [/b] Lore needs work I think RE has a lot of ideas but does not wanna give them ALL at once. This a problem in modern gaming in general. Before, Games were not made by AAA studios and taking a franchise approach kind of ruins the storytelling process so I hope Capcom works on this. 

Overall, I will give [i] Resident Evil: Village [/i] an 8/10. I think it does show Ethan's (later on Rose's) journey from being unsure about themselves and the world, to being more formulated. It also shows a great way of understanding Chris aside than classic hero figure and we see him mature as well. Learning to trust and move forward in a world where bioweapons and eccentric beings live side by side an uninfected humanity or rather humans waiting to evolve and mutate as well.

It's definitely up there with the RE4 remake when it comes to my favorites in the franchise. I've loved everything about RE7, but this brings out so many great sequences and I'd be lying if I said I didn't have more fun with this game. It's a great showcase of what a big budget production Resident Evil looks like. Not a big production game that follows trends, like RE6, but that is everything Resident Evil is supposed to be. Terrifying, spine-chilling atmosphere, immersive level designs with gruesome, realistic graphics and details, a great story with characters that each develop and have an interesting plot for themselves.

I was fully drawn into the gameplay. Such a smooth and beautiful experience. Usually, for me, every Resident Evil game had at least one section for which I would say it drags on too long or is just uninteresting - here, I absolutely loved every part of it. What I loved the most is that you're finally free to explore and backtrack as much as you really want. Almost nothing is just plain linear and focused. From the village, to the amazing and very memorable sequence at Dimitrescu castle, to the crazy, mental experience at house Beneviento, to a seriously unsettling experience at Heisenberg's factory, and everything in-between - I honestly loved every segment of this game. It's not just because of how well designed everything is. There have already been other games in the RE franchise that are both this lengthy and introduce such a big number of new characters, but I don't think there is one that checks all the marks on my must-have list. Most of them usually had one or two great sequences and then the quality would drastically fall off, it would go off too far from the survival horror genre into the action horror genre, sometimes even straight up being just an action game. This one might be the one that checks it all. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3135608034

Sure, the story could be a bit better, and Chris, once again, turns out to be the big douchebag, but it doesn't really bother me that much. What mattered to me is how detailed all of these sequences were and that it's what I love the most about the way RE does survival horror. Exploring and puzzle solving all through the game, with some of the nuttiest and most rememberable characters in the series, with intense and diverse combat including a ton of new enemy types in each sequence, unforgiving boss fights, with a lot of inventory and resource management, an amazing trading system with a new merchant and new treasures to find. The sound design is outstanding and way too damn immersive, you will hear and feel every single creak, whisper, growl, even a drop of water.

What I must mention completely separately is the baby stage at the house Beneviento. I have played and will continue to play some really crazy ass horror titles, but that part has to be up there with some of the most nerve-wracking and unsettling parts I've ever experienced. Period. I was very glad it did not last any longer than it did. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3135189676

While I'm mentioning boss fights - here, they might be some of the best boss fights too. All of them are challenging and unforgiving, but at the same time, spectacular and magnificent.

[h1]The Gameplay: [/h1]
Basically take RE7 and just add in more engaging combat because Lycans do not play with you. You now have a push mechanic when enemies grab you, as well as having some Quality of Life upgrades such as being able to break boxes without having your knife out. This is coupled with an inventory system similar to RE4 where somehow you don't feel like your choking for space. Overall it's a big improvement from 7's controls and gameplay loop.

[h1]The Story:[/h1]
Bringing back Ethan Winters was an interesting choice, but it allowed us to play someone who wasn't built like a brick ♥♥♥♥ house and does this every day. It builds up a good mystery and even has a good piece of bait to keep the story going. The big bad also had a nice twist as to the implications of who she is, however, she fell a little short to her underlings. It sort of had a Farcry 3 effect where once Vaas was gone, the big bad didn't matter as much.

[h1]The Visuals:[/h1]
Gorgeous, with their scenery and enemy models. The Lycans were indeed top tier and some of the enemies looked like they came out of Bloodbourne which was a welcome change of pace. This is probably the strongest aspect of this game, and somehow outdoes it's other RE Engine predecessors, which is quite the feat since they are all using the same engine.

[h1]The Sound:[/h1]
The voice actors did an excellent job of making the experience feel magical. They really sucked me in and kept me locked in immersion so hard I forgot this was just a game and not a real exchange at times. The sound effects are truly satisfying and terrifying all at the same time. The music was that and I could not remember it, but it did it's work well.


[h1]The Experience:[/h1]
This game was both not what I expected but also exactly how I imagined it would be. This is gives me hope for the future of Resident Evil in terms of an ongoing story that doesn't rely soley on it's remakes. I am glad they are making those remakes, but I am also glad they are looking to make solid titles for the future. This new vision for Resident Evil is one I am glad has matured to this almost fine wine of a game series. This is an obvious recommend for the game.

The level design was incredible in this game. One thing that I think makes a Resident Evil game amazing is the level design and utilizing the different areas to their fullest extent, which is something I think the OG Resident Evil games mastered and Capcom seemed to forget for over a decade after RE4. Capcom redeemed themselves with recent titles, specifically RE2 Remake and RE7. RE2 remake specifically with the RPD section did so well with this and forcing the player to back track constantly to find clues, solve puzzles or complete objectives while combining this with horror elements. Village does an amazing job providing incentives to go back and search areas you were at before to find things you may have missed and implementing things like secret boss fights and new loot. 

Some of the puzzles in this game were trickier than we've seen in recent RE games and I appreciate the effort they put into this with village. OG RE games had some of the most difficult puzzles and it felt refreshing to feel lost again in an RE game.

1. This doesn't strike me as a Resident Evil zombie game. It seems more like a Lovecraftian story. I'm not complaining (much), just commenting on it. The bad guys seemed more like fairy tale horrors than zombified. (In fact, there aren't any zombies in this game at all.) There are werewolves, witches, fish men, cyborgs, giants, etc. etc. .... it's just a different genre.

2. Ammo and supplies could be more plentiful, but the shop feature seems to fill in the gap for the most part. 

3. Some of the puzzles and obstacles need improvement. The most glaring example of this is where you have to change the order of six cylinders in a music box so you can gain access to a door key in it. All of the parts look the same, so it's hard to figure out which order to use. Another example would be in Moreau's Reservoir. Here, you have to throw some switches in order for pieces of a bridge to rise up out of the water so you can reach a little island in the middle. The issue is that the bridge pieces will drop back in the water after a few seconds and there's just not enough time to throw the switches and make it to the other side. A few extra seconds would have spared me countless nights of swearing to the Heavens because I couldn't finish this part.

4. The story was excessive, to say the least. The cutscenes go on for WAY too long and reference things from previous titles that just don't make any sense if you haven't played them. The whole story seems to almost have a strange "lost in translation" feel to it, like when you watch a subtitled foreign film and it's just too difficult to interpret. Fortunately, you can skip cutscenes.

It's not as good as RE7, but taken as a whole, the Ethan Winters duology is a strong two-punch return to form from Capcom. The lore and series continuity is as convoluted and as contrived as ever, and I can't help but wonder if 7 could've been their chance to do a complete reboot -- it tried the soft reboot thing with a new first person perspective, a new protagonist in Winters, and taking cues from the likes of Kojima's P.T. and more recent flavours of horror (instead of originally ripping off Romero's zombie canon) but the Umbrella connection is still shoehorned in, Chris still shows up, and it still follows the Mikami formula of tension and dread in an enclosed space >> which opens up to a larger space as more puzzles and combat is laid on >> finally a climatic shoot-out in a high tech lab or some such, etc. Not that any of this matters with how loosey goosey RE can be in its own storytelling logic (and who plays RE for the story amirite).

Ethan Winters is a bit more compelling as a protagonist this time around and the Shadows of Rose DLC is a nice coda to it, to say nothing of its smart reuse of 8's assets, as I felt even Capcom knew they underutilized the fantastic Castle & Beneviento maps, the latter of which gets a chance to truly shine in its redux.

The Steam/PC version is a mixed bag. If you install RE Framework or similar mods to say, unlock the FoV, you may run into system instability like I did (perhaps caused by Denuvo rearing its ugly head if you have the DLC installed?). And really that console level FoV of like, 10, is inexcusable for a PC port in 2023. Playing on KB+M always feels off, while the controls on gamepad aren't great either (something to do with mouse acceleration or some such, IDK). Enabling RT will cut your framerate down by a lot, and offers subtle but barely noticeable differences to my untrained eye, so I'd say leave it off. Lack of Nvidia DLSS support, or an updated version of AMD FSR (stuck on 1.0), or hell, Intel XeSS is also unfortunate. Capcom will go through the effort of having sliders that show the performance impact of each setting on your system components -- great! -- but then bizarrely make you click RMB to back out of its options menu instead of using Esc, or bind Ctrl by default as a Use key instead of crouch -- wth??

Can't say I'm optimistic for RE9, knowing Capcom's history with this series, but 8 isn't any worse than previous games and is a strong, if uneven entry.

After Act One, I stopped being horny and was just straight up scared. I beat Alien Isolation on max difficulty and assumed this would be a cakewalk in comparison. I was partially right, I wasn't TERRIFIED but I cowered in hidy-holes and procrastinated walking down a hallway for an hour because I no longer had my emotional support shotgun. RE7 WAS terrifying, this was a step down in that regard. 

The atmosphere and visual storytelling is top tier. This is one of the two W's eight takes over 7. I felt like a lone rat scurrying form place to place, always at risk of getting pinned by one of the cat's many claws. The world is beautiful and unsettling. I prefer it over the bayou.

Combat, what this game lacks in fear, it more than make up in panic. Overwhelming forces constantly kept me on edge. I never knew where an enemy was going to pop up and on higher difficulties a single hit will put you on the brink of death. The bonus content, additional orders, is nonstop action combat, and unlocking the special knife is a challenging but worthwhile quest. Additional orders alone is worth getting the gold edition for. The Rose DLC isn't bad either, not great but not bad.

Overall, get this game on sale so the gold edition is worth it. Otherwise, just replay RE7 and RE4. It's not the best game in the series but it's far from the worst.

Okay so... I avoided this game for about 2 years because quite frankly outside of a few aesthetic choices, the game looked pretty boring. Having played through the whole thing now, I can say it's not as boring as I expected. As games in general go, it's a bit flawed but pretty good, but as RE games go it's just kinda mid. Honestly I'm 90% sure people just meat ride Village because it's the slightest tinge scarier than RE 5 and 6.

So in regards to story and themes, this game's all over the place. It tries to recreate the vibes RE4 had by redoing a lot of scenes from that game while also trying to expand the enemy variety beyond just zombies, giants, and bugs by taking inspiration from Werewolves, vampires, bog monsters... I think you get the idea. As far as "Civilians who find themselves suddenly in the thick of it" protagonists go, Ethan's reactions and confusion are at least plausible and potentially realistic if nothing else. Frankly only a small handful of moments in the game are actually properly scary (that baby can ♥♥♥♥ right off), and I think this is mostly because it lacks the nuance that games like RE4 had. RE4 wasn't scary just because you were fighting freaky monsters in a forested village and ancient castle, it was also scary because of little things like the creepy synth music sounding haunting and unnatural, because of things like the bug monsters and regenerators looking inhuman and making you question if you could even win in the first place, because you yourself were infected as well and were essentially a ticking time bomb even if it didn't reflect in gameplay. In Village, you have what? Lady D? Who looks pretty much like a normal human albeit pale and abnormally tall? The majority of people just fap to her rather than fear her. Most of the time the game just relies on gore to try to scare you, and frankly that isn't scary, it's just gross...

Gameplay-wise there's very few actual flaws at all. Most of the flaws that are present are from the puzzles themselves. They're all pretty easy to be completely honest. The few major enemies that deviate from that that aren't bosses are the gargoyles, some cellar zombies, and some mechs. Really good installment in the franchise. This game takes a step towards being a military shooter again rather than survival horror, something which RE7 was trying to prevent being a sorta hard reset in the series as that game was purely a survival horror experience, however, I thought this game did a good job at blending the genres together, making the game feel like a survival horror when it wants the player to be scared, while in other sequences your character will be blasting magnito in a mechanized tank. 

Game play (8/10) -
If I had to compare the game to other installments in the series, I would say that it plays like RE4, taking a lot of the game play mechanics like the merchant and the crafting system, but toned it down as you are not a MMA special forces agent. The combat system is not my favorite, but at the same time making Ethan into a one man army that can right hook enemies across the room would've drastically impacted the tone Capcom was going for in this game

Story (10/10) - 
This game probably has the best story in the franchise, there are constant twists and turns that will keep the player on their feet while not feeling too cheep or contrived. Ethan is a very sympathetic character that you really do root for while you are playing through, and the villains and monsters feel like they have a lot of development. I don't want to get too deep into the story as there would be a lot of spoilers, all I can say is to play the game and experience it first hand.

Overall (9/10)
I really enjoyed this game, and like the direction the franchise is headed in, my only worry is that Capcom may go back into making full military shooter games again like the notorious RE6, but as long as they balance their game play as well as they did in this game, it will be yet another great installment in my favorite game series.

Resident Evil 8 tries to emulate a lot of things, but in my opinion doesn't succeed at most of them. Don't get me wrong, it's still a good game and I wish Steam gave me a "mixed" option, but for me this game is just kinda disappointing. The initial village section and the "4 lords" being the initial motivation for Ethan, try to make you think that you'll be able to explore around and choose where to go, but you will quickly realize that this game is just a one, very long corridor with maybe 2 or 3 side rooms. 

The Village of Shadows difficulty is more of a chore than a challenge, especially once you get to the factory section of the game, as enemies and especially bosses are just bullet sponges. 

The inventory management tries to emulate RE4, but I don't remember ever needing to actually manage it, and I picked up pretty much every weapon I found, only selling the old ones, because for some reason RE8 also decided to make new weapons in the same type (as in for example a 2nd pistol you find) just straight up better than their predecessor, so there's no real reason to keep them anyway. 

Lady Dimitrescu tries to emulate Mr X/Nemesis in her section of the game but she's rarely an obstacle and I swear she has to be blind because more than once, I would stand more or less directly in front of her, like in the door frame with the doors open, and she would fail to notice me. Then you have to add the silly cutscenes where (SPOILER) Ethan stands pretty much next to her, on the other side of the window, in a position where she should easily notice him in her mirror, and she's just completely oblivious to his presence. At least it made me laugh, I guess.

The House Beneviento is scary at first, but once you realize that the enemy chasing you just disappears after a while it turns into a loop of getting to a point where it spawns, hiding for a while and then continuing your journey because it despawned. The final encounter with it does force you to "survive" for some time, but once again it's not really hard to move around the furniture in the mandatory chase section. The boss of this section is also kinda bad, but the whole section feels like some weird Silent Hill/PT adaptation and trying new horror related things is always good to see, even if they don't end up great.

I'll admit tho, I still had a lot of fun, especially since the design of those locations was really cool and thematic, but after that part the game just kinda falls over and peaks at the CoD section where you play as Chris and slaughter everything in your way. Apart from those things, the combat never really became that enjoyable, the 1st person perspective of shooting stuff just feels stiff. The puzzles in this game are just mind-numbingly simple. Overall, I feel like my problems with this game are not fully with what it is, but with what it could be and what it tries to make you think it will be in the beginning section of the game. A very big part of the "horror" (and there's honestly not a lot of horror in this game anyway) also seems to just be around Ethan's limbs getting damaged because we established that he can heal it so why not make him lose his leg/hand/fingers for some additional tension.

I'd still probably recommend it to most people but only on a good sale, but I hope RE9 (because we all know it will come out eventually) is a step up when it comes to the series and survival horror in general.

Also don't mind my play time/achievements, I played it previously from a legal source of course.

It’s a game not like any other, if you haven’t experienced other RE games that is. I can imagine playing this for the first time without having any knowledge or experience in the RE games and what an unique experience this must be. RE7 walked so Village could run. I experienced the same sense of twisted wonder as I had in Dark souls (3). 
The areas are extremely detailed, super immersive and varied. It feels like playing through a mix of an Evil dead type action and horror movie. There’s an element that is unique to the series that I feel can't be tied to an existing piece of media. You'll be exploring insanely tense close quarter horror to spectacular gothic setpieces, fighting off enemies that vary in behavior and size. This is what creativity and passion in the AAA space can do and I'm extremely here for it. If you're still indecisive, give it a chance. It really is an impressive true-to-gaming experience.

As for difficulty, if you aren’t as familiar with the tense and sometimes frustrating RE gameplay loop where you manage your resources and often barely survive encounters, where you just want to experience what the game has to offer without significant hicc-ups: go with standard. I often like to play games on their harder difficulties but if I’d started out with hardcore I would’ve probably dropped the game and missed out on this unique experience. I now feel more inclined to replay the game in hardcore as I’ve already experienced the game and its story.

If you are looking for the classic RE gameplay with all its (extremely) tense moments and you like bumping your head at certain sections because of it do go with hardcore.

[h1]8/10[/h1] RE 7 is the pinnacle of atmosphere and unsettling locations in Resident Evil but RE 8 takes its gameplay formula and creates an awesome action adventure.

The puzzles and exploration are really well done, they reward you for visiting old areas by sprinkling new enemies and resources around. Even the main objective isn't super spelled out for you. A lot of stuff you have to figure out yourself. The snowy Romanian village with werewolf monsters is such a unique setting and the environments are gorgeous. There's 4 areas in the game + the main village area. Each location has its own unique personality, its own enemies and bosses. There's 4 bosses in the game (+ some mini-bosses), including the final boss. Each one has its own set pieces and abilities. One of the areas of the game is a puzzle + horror segment and it's easily scarier than most moments in RE 7.

I hated the inventory system and inventory UI. Give me item boxes. Having useless key items and having to scroll through to find the one you're actually looking for is annoying.

Enemies drop treasure that can be sold to the merchant from whom you can buy ammo, meds and upgrade your weapons and character. This incentivises you to kill enemies, instead of trying to conserve ammo and avoid them like other RE games. This works really well considering the more action heavy focus. It feels more consistently fun throughout, instead of being like RE 7 where the second half of the game is painful to get through.

TLDR: First person action/horror. While similar in many points to its predecessor, manages to tweak the gameplay so it feels different. If you played the 7th title but would have liked more action at the expense of some of the scare factor, you might favor this one over the 7th.

Story: Direct continuation of RE 7, so I suggest playing it beforehand. 
At first, and I do mean the first few minutes, you feel like it's going to really be a continuation... You see Mia, realise which ending was cannon, become pretty happy for Ethan with his lil' baby... Then, it all gets thrown out the window and you feel forced into events that are completely unrelated to the previous entry. But eventually... It manages to reel you back in with just enough clever pulls at your heart strings and interesting character developments to make it interesting and coherent (enough). After all, it is Resident Evil, so story was never their forte, but after Resident Evil 7 and 2's remake, I expected amazing quality. So much so that I was probably being unfair.

Gameplay: The combat is VERY similar to RE 7, like, ridiculously so. The only changes are in the weapons selection and their upgrades and customisation (similar to RE 4 & 5), collectable treasures that are sometimes combinable for much more resale value (again, like RE 4), a sales person and an inventory system that is like RE 4. No need to find backpacks to increase inventory size like in RE 2 (the remake) and 7, simply purchase the bigger cases available in the in game store. There is also food/ingredients you can collect from animals which you can craft recipes from to obtain permanent buffs; health, speed, block dmg, etc. I wish the game told me earlier because I'd been selling it since it had no use. The food is finite btw so don't sell it like I did.
The game feels balanced on normal. Though I was never out of bullets, I felt the squeeze when I would miss too many shots. The areas you visit are varied, not so much in locations but more as in you'll have tight quarters one minute and have room to fight the next. A couple of enemies here, and a crowd there. An easy fight here, and an optional big boss there. It keeps things much fresher than in RE 7 where all you had was moldy fellas.

Graphics: Looks good! It's no master piece but it looks really good. Some textures looked a bit off but 99% looks like what you'd expect from any game with RE engine. It's also noteworthy that the game isn't always having you creep around at night. Lots of the game takes place during the day and outside. 

Audio: A lot of the guns sounded a bit wimpy, but then again... maybe it's just that I haven't unlocked some more powerful guns. It might also not help that I've never fired the magnum. I was saving the bullets for later... But then the game was over :( I'm one of those people that save up 99x potions and end up never using them.
The voice actors are ok, and the ambience is as good as RE 7. 

What I initially was let down by was simply that the game did not  INITIALLY feel like a horror game. It threw a few curve balls at me and whenever they were happening I couldn't see myself growing to like them. But when you take a step back and just appreciate it at its face value, the game is actually great. I think this game is very similar to RE7, but it's like the difference of opinion between COD and Battlefield... Same thing, but oh so different.

[h1] Technical performance [/h1]
This game runs really well. It can push the hardware to the limits. I suggest using FSR with adequate resolution and limited filtering options. Otherwise - like all RE games, Village looks satisfying and runs well with support of many modern technologies.

The game runs perfectly well on Linux, with absolutely 0 issues on GE-Proton8-16 (but probably any version really). The FPS is stable, textures are detailed. I had lots of fun.

[h1] Technology [/h1]
FSR and RTX, the game allows a broad selection of settings. I think everybody can find something adequate.
Graphically it's not the Crysis of 2000s, but it was never the major point in this game I suppose. The game does look pretty and I imagine with all "HQ" options enabled it would present itself as one of the best looking games in 2022-2024. Great job for a RE game. Capcom has bought a Customer by delivering high quality games with great controls, animations and polished experience.

On the note of AI - it is not the brightest at the times, but absolutely sufficient. I wish Dimitrescu was a bit smarter in her castle, but otherwise everything's OK.

[h1] Gameplay/bugs [/h1]
Absolutely no issues in terms of controls or gameplay, at least if using the keyboard. Controller is also just fine (technically), but aiming is difficult. Being a mostly FPS type of game, Village just doesn't feel good without mouse/keyboard. It's the reverse Elden Ring situation...

I noticed just one bug on Linux. The mouse would sometimes go a bit crazy in the menu. Everything works fine in the game, but I would experience a jumping cursor in the shop or game's menus. Could be Proton acting up a bit or some kind of incompatibility in between the window compositor and Wayland.

[h1] Genre [/h1]
I never played RE games and started with Village. I bought a couple of different RE titles during the sales. 0 regrets. Absolutely one of the best purchases ever. The lore is great, the enemy design is interesting. Every boss is unique, has a specific style and comes in a different environment. Some of the areas remind me of different games. Having played RE 0 (Resident Evil Zero) I would say that Village is MUCH better and yet still resembles the original games from early 2000s.

[h1] Value [/h1]
100% great value. If bought on a discount then it's even better. It's one of few games that actually delivers what it promised. If you're disappointed with the "AAA" (more like AAA jokes) titles in 2023 then I suggest trying out RE. Additionally there is no mandatory online play, no encrypted textures or anti-cheat ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and the game does not require 10 different accounts. It reminded me of playing games in my childhood.

A small drawback - the game is not very lengthy, although it can be played multiple times with different difficulty settings, some DLCs etc. I would say playing it twice is the recommended scenario.

PS: Perhaps the biggest question 'not answered' directly in the game's lore is...
[spoiler] Whose child is Rose after all? It's a moldy subject, for how long did Miranda pretend to be... her mother? [/spoiler]

Capcom's Resident Evil Village, released in 2021, takes players on a nightmarish journey through a gothic and hauntingly beautiful village. Building on the success of its predecessors, Village not only continues the gripping narrative of Ethan Winters but also introduces new elements that elevate the Resident Evil franchise to new heights of horror and grandeur.

Visually, Resident Evil Village is a stunning triumph. The RE Engine showcases its prowess with atmospheric lighting, detailed character models, and intricately designed environments that seamlessly blend the eerie beauty of the village with the grotesque horrors that lie within. The diverse settings, from the dilapidated village to the opulent castle and beyond, create a visual spectacle that is as unsettling as it is captivating.

The narrative weaves a tale of desperation, loss, and survival as Ethan Winters embarks on a quest to rescue his kidnapped daughter. Village introduces a compelling cast of characters, each with their own dark secrets, and the unpredictable twists keep players on the edge of their seats. The enigmatic Lady Dimitrescu and her vampiric daughters, among other horrifying creatures, contribute to the game's atmosphere of constant dread.

Gameplay mechanics in Village strike a balance between survival horror and action, offering a diverse range of challenges. The first-person perspective enhances the immersion, with responsive controls and intense combat encounters. The game introduces a merchant called the Duke, adding an intriguing economic element that allows players to purchase and upgrade weapons, further enhancing the strategic aspect of gameplay.

Village excels in level design, offering a mix of tight corridors, open landscapes, and intricate puzzles that keep the player engaged. The interconnectedness of the various areas encourages exploration, uncovering hidden secrets, and solving environmental puzzles that reward the curious and thorough player.

The sound design in Resident Evil Village deserves special mention. From the unsettling ambient noises to the bone-chilling roars of monstrous adversaries, the audio elements contribute significantly to the game's immersive horror experience. The voice acting is superb, adding depth to the characters and amplifying the emotional impact of the narrative.

While some purists may find the game's departure from traditional survival horror mechanics and its increased focus on action to be a deviation from the series' roots, the balance struck by Village allows it to appeal to a broader audience. The varied pacing, unexpected scares, and the constant feeling of vulnerability contribute to a horror experience that is both thrilling and emotionally resonant.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village stands as a pinnacle in the Resident Evil franchise. Its breathtaking visuals, captivating narrative, and refined gameplay mechanics come together to create a horror masterpiece that pays homage to the series' legacy while boldly venturing into new and terrifying territory. Village is not only a must-play for fans of the genre but also a testament to Capcom's ability to evolve and redefine survival horror in the gaming landscape.

[h1] Wasted Potential. [/h1]

[b] Warning, yapping ahead. I could've said MUCH more though. TLDR: The game is overrated. [/b] 

First two hours of the game are needless cutscene spam. RE7 already started off slow but this one is on another level. They introduce characters that don't matter within the story, so why waste so much time with them?

[b] Combat is underwhelming. [/b]
One of the big issues with RE7 was it's lack of enemy variety. Village does it better, barely. While yes, there are more enemies in this game, most of them are reskins of already existing enemies or they have basically the same counter play as all of the others. Moroaicǎ are your basic ass resident evil zombies, and Samcă are basically the exact same thing but they're in the air (and are super tame lol). Lycans also just feel like regular zombies, but with a bit more movement. Such wasted potential. I mean, you have Werwolf and Vampire inspired enemies and the devs don't do anything interesting with them? Archers apply almost no pressure on the battlefield.

Large Lycans and maybe the standard Soldiers are more interesting, but do little to really spice the gameplay up. The Soldiers enrage mechanic is underutilized as a point black headshot to their core is enough to instakill them, with those guys it's just a waiting game that plays out the exact same each time.

The rest of the common soldier enemies are more interesting, but they only appear in one section of the game. [spoiler] Jets are really cool enemies that are only used in ONE room in the ENTIRE CAMPAIGN and then never again. They don't even have their special ability in the mercinaries. [/spoiler]

[b] Bosses suck. [/b]
Bela is extremely underhwelming and the fight and has barely any build-up. 
[spoiler] Seen many people just go ''oh wow she's dead already...''. You just brawl with her in a really short room and block on occasion, such a lame fight. [/spoiler] Her sisters don't hold up much better. Cassandra is the best of the bunch but it's not a very memorable encounter, at least you have an actual arena to fight her in, but they did nothing to really spice it up. Daniella can be cheesed by just keeping the window open, she is harmless LOL.

Dimitrescu is boring. Moreau is alright but he's too tanky and his acid rain attack has uninteristing counterplay. Miranda is a better fight but her constant talking will make your ears want to jump off a cliff. Urias is a decent encounter, but I don't understand why they had to copy paste him two more times as mini bosses but okay. Varcolac is an enemy who's counter play literally consists of camping in a house that he can't get you in, same applies to the boss variant too. Sturm is cool but the fight drags on for a bit, Heisenberg is mid.

[b] The writing is of very poor quality. [/b]
[spoiler] Miranda is one of the most forgettable villains that I have ever seen. Her character is barely explored. The later issue also applies to the other villains. They're all fancy and quirky, but none of them go beyond the surface level. The more you pay attention the less sense the story makes. I still don't get Chris' reasoning behind never telling Ethan anything until the last 45 minutes of the game. Of course he's gonna get in your way if he sees you killing his (presumed) wife right in front of him with now explanation, you dumbass! Heisenberg can move metal, yet he never uses it to kill Ethan, who is carrying a large arsenal of guns in his pockets at all times, [b] which are made out of metal [/b]. The antagonists had sooo many chances to kill Ethan and they never take it, with barely any good reasons as to why. The entire plot of this game falls apart so quickly once you think about what is actually happening, it's comical. I could probably write a novel about the amount of issues. [/spoiler] Ethan also needs to shut up. I don't mind them fleshing him out as a character, but damn can his voice lines be corny. This is some of the laziest writing I've seen yet.

[b] Puzzles, exploration, inventory, survival, horror. [/b]
The Resident Evil franchise was known for all of these things, RE8 excells in none of it. Most puzzles are basically designed for toddlers to a comical extend. The game has some exploration but feels extremely linear. Most of the treasures you can find are just for selling, so you can spend a ♥♥♥♥ ton of lei on a 5% damage upgrade... amazing really.

Inventory management is pretty bare bones. Crafting, healing, treasures and key items don't take up any inventory space. Chests are gone too. It's very rare that you will actually have to make choices on what you want to bring along your journey, which defeats the whole point of that system.

The horror aspect is only well done in ONE area which lasts maybe half and hour. In general the Estate and the Reservoir are way too short.

[b] Extra content [/b]

Mercinaries can feel very underhwelming unfortunately. Not enough weapon variety, only a handful of repetitive stages. I personally find it fun but I have to admit that mercinaries is mid, sorry. You need to buy an overpriced DLC to get new characters and like two or so new stages. Wow Capcom, how generous!

Shadows of Rose wasn't very memorable but there are some things I liked about it. It had better puzzles from what I remember.

In RE7 you got lots more extra game modes and bonus campaigns for that same price, wheras RE8 makes you pay 20 or so bucks for a 3rd person mode, character selection that should've been in the base game and a mediocre side campaign.

In the words of Karl Heisenberg: Truly, truly dissapointing.

Yet another great horror title from Capcom.

I liked the game even though it had its issues like hard-locked 81 degrees FoV. It caused me to have motion sickness in the very beginning of the game to the point where I couldn't carry on playing anymore.

I had to download 'Lazy FoV' from NexusMods.com in order to fix the hard-locked FoV because Capcom didn't include a slider option for FoV in the vanilla game.

After fixing the FoV back to 90 degrees (acceptable value for first person view games), I have eliminated motion sickness. However, you shouldn't set the FoV greater than 90 degrees, because then it causes visual glitches like your view being obstructed by Ethan's character model or having a fisheye-like screen/the edges of your screen gets visually distorted as you increase the FoV. Next up, you'll want to enable manual flashlight on/off prompt which can be enabled through RE Framework tool which you can also download from NexusMods.com and after this, lastly, you'll want to remove the Vignette effect whenever you crouch, because both sides of your screen gets darker and it becomes difficult to see around. For that, what you'll need is 'Vignette Fix' from NexusMods.com

After these adjustments, you're good to go. The gameplay and story telling is just as much as you'd expect from any other Resident Evil title.

Upon completing the main story, I've played Shadows of Rose DLC, which unfolds the events after Ethan Winters' story ending. You play as Rose Winters, Ethan's daughter. But this time you are playing from a 3rd person perspective, so you get to see Rose and the vanilla game doesn't cause motion sickness. It offers about 3 hours of content on top of the main storyline which was roughly about 9 hours. (not rushed) The Shadows of Rose DLC also doesn't have the issues I've mentioned above, which the vanilla RE Village main game does.

I hope Capcom will perfect their next Resident Evil game in the series, like including an FoV slider, giving player the basic ability of manually turning on/off flashlight and removing the Vignette effect.

Overall, I'd give Resident Evil Village & Shadows of Rose both a solid 8 out of 10.

This is a good game but with two major critical points: screenplay and combat system (with some kind of enemies).

Don't get me wrong, I was liking RE8 up until the first half. I really thought that the beginning was perfectly made and the first encounter too. But, for me, everything else has been so lazily written that it eventually got to me. 

I'll say this, though: the Dimitrescu castle and the Beneviento mansion were really well made and I have liked their structure and feel. Each room felt neatly structured, and not simply a random arrangement of objects.  Especially in the castle, I've felt that the actual storyline was being constructed accordingly. 

After that, apart from the aforementioned mansion, everything has gone downhill. Massively. To the point that it began feeling less of an horror story, but rather an average anime saga. Really. 

Dialogues got more and more cartoony, and I can't understand why. I was only laughing whenever people spoke in the second half of the game, as it felt like none of the characters were taking anything seriously. This culminated in the final battle which, even without considering the cringy part with Redfield, was definitely a chore. 

This is the worst part of RE8, for me. And, for a game that wants to be narrative, it makes me really not want to recommend it at all.

The other thing I haven't liked at all was the combat system. I mean, not that RE7 had the best gameplay ever, but here the arsenal was just too vast and pompous for a "normal" guy like Ethan. I wouldn't have minded it, if most of the weapons were completely useless against bigger enemies. I can't stress how many bullet sponges I have encountered. I have played in hardcore difficulty, yes, but I expected something different. Some enemies will literally make you waste mines, pipe bombs, explosive ammos, bullets... everything. A waste of time.
Not only that, but the overall worldbuilding was definitely more spot on in RE7 than here. The story is very predictable.

Excluding the bullet sponges, though, normal enemies were okay. You could kill all of them only with a pistol, if you had enough bullets. And new enemies were always presented in an interesting way, at least for me.

A worthy mention could be made for the DLCs. RE7's ones were kinda genious, here... not so much. It almost feels like a Thirteen Reasons Why + Life is Strange screenwriting, at best.

I'm upset not because the game is bad, but because I was getting invested in it and it changed structure so much that it didn't feel serious at all, at one point. If I had to make a review half into the game, it would have been almost certainly positive.

Not that RE7 is perfect. I still remember how goofy the final battle was. I can't understand why Capcom can't seem to mantain seriousness more than a couple of hours. Well, I hope that the next iteration will be more narration-focused with less flashy weapons and quirky characters. I think that, today, it doesn't work anymore as it used to in past titles.

Hot take: Resident Evil Village is one of the best entries in the series, and it’s in my top 10 favorite games of all time. I originally played it on Series S back when it came out, but recently took advantage of the Halloween sale and picked it back up again on PC. This is one of the best horror games I’ve played and I’ll explain why (spoiler free.) 

Story: The story is top notch. Ethan Winters is probably my favorite Resident Evil protagonist. He’s just a normal guy. Not a John Wick esque, roundhouse kick giving, boulder punching BA. Just a normal dude trying to save his wife and daughter and doing whatever he can. I love it. 

The story takes many twists and turns, including a ton of jaw dropping moments and action set pieces. Without spoiling anything, the game is split up into different “zones” that encapsulate different horror themes and gameplay styles. There’s survival horror, psychological horror without the ability to fight, straight up epic action sequences, and much more. In my opinion, the game stayed fresh throughout and the story kept me engaged the entire time. 

The bosses are excellent. Voice acting is superb. Set piece design is A+. The roster of characters in the game is fantastic, most of them are very well written and memorable. 

The game is a mix of action and horror. The game is overall not the scariest game I’ve ever played, but it has one section… oh God… one section that is THE scariest thing I’ve ever played. I speedrun this game and EVERY time I get to this certain section I dread it. 

The finale left tears in my eyes and really resonated with me emotionally, especially as a new father myself. I was a huge fan of RE7 and RE8 and I loved the Ethan Winters storyline. He truly is the greatest dad ever. 

Gameplay: The combat is top notch. I will say, it is much easier on PC than console because of mouse and keyboard. Part of what made it scary on console is how difficult the aiming was on the game pad. If you have decent aim, the combat is much easier on PC. 

The game is loaded with puzzles and treasures that reward exploration and sharp wit. If you take your time and search every inch of the game, you won’t be lacking in money, supplies, and really cool weapons. 

The game is difficult, but exponentially more so if you just try to barrel your way through the game as fast as possible. 

Presentation/Graphics: I personally think this game is one of the most visually appealing games I’ve ever seen. Whether it’s a dank, dimly lit basement illuminated solely by flickering candles, a gorgeous castle hall, snowy forest, or a factory corridor lit by flashing red lights, the game is gorgeous and makes fantastic use of light. 

Textures are gorgeous. If you run the game on max settings with ray tracing, you’d be hard pressed to find a horror game with better looking textures and light effects thanks to the tremendous RE engine. 

Enemy designs are amazing. Every enemy looks unique and terrifying. Not only do they look terrifying, but their movement is very lifelike and immersive. Enemies don’t just sit still and wait for you to kill them. They sway  from side to side, attempting to dodge your bullets. The blood and gore effects are top notch. Exploding a werewolf’s head with a shotgun always feels nice. 

This game is really fun to speedrun. The whole Resident Evil franchise is consistently a good choice for speed runners because it rewards skillful play and you can really breeze through it if you commit the puzzles and fights to memory. 

Things you might not like: The game is very good, with the exception of a few stale segments that don’t hold up as well as the rest. (Fishing Village, I’m looking at you.) 

Some people might not like the B movie cheese, but those people have clearly never played a Resident Evil game before. 

As mentioned earlier, the game is meant to be played slowly. If you just want to barrel through a story, the game is probably not for you. 

Conclusion: Give this game a chance! It’s a wonderful addition to the series, and in my opinion it’s up there with RE4 in terms of quality. Hope you enjoy as much as I did!

"Resident Evil Village" is a standout title in the storied Resident Evil series, and there are numerous reasons why it should be at the top of a gamer's must-play list.

Firstly, the game expertly blends classic survival horror elements with modern gameplay mechanics, creating an experience that is both nostalgic and innovatively fresh. The game's setting, a desolate village overshadowed by a looming castle, is not only rich in atmosphere but also in mystery, compelling players to explore every dark corner and unravel the secrets within.

The narrative is another strong point, continuing the story of Ethan Winters from "Resident Evil 7" and expanding the lore of the series in surprising ways. The storytelling is personal and gripping, with twists that keep players engaged until the very end.

Visually, "Resident Evil Village" is a marvel, showcasing breathtaking graphics that bring its gothic horror setting to life. The attention to detail in the environment is impeccable, from the decrepit state of the village houses to the opulent decay of the castle, every location is a feast for the eyes and sets the perfect stage for horror.

Gameplay-wise, the game introduces new enemies and creatures that are both terrifying and intriguing, each with their own unique challenges and weaknesses to discover. The game also sees the return of the franchise's beloved inventory management, encouraging players to think critically about what resources they carry.

Moreover, the game innovates by incorporating a hunting and crafting system, allowing players to hunt animals in the village to create dishes that provide permanent upgrades to the character. This adds an additional layer of strategy to the game, rewarding exploration and resourcefulness.

The character of Lady Dimitrescu, in particular, has become an iconic figure in the gaming community, and her presence in the game adds a charismatic yet fearsome antagonist that players will love to encounter.

Finally, "Resident Evil Village" offers a high replay value with its additional content, including the return of the Mercenaries mode, which challenges players to achieve high scores in combat-heavy runs through various levels.

In conclusion, "Resident Evil Village" is a masterful blend of horror, action, and storytelling that is both respectful of its roots and ambitious in its new directions. It provides an immersive gaming experience that is sure to satisfy long-time fans of the series and newcomers alike with its atmospheric world, challenging gameplay, and compelling story.

[...] Nous incarnons donc Ethan Winters qui mène une vie isolée avec sa compagne, Mia (dans cette histoire, vous l’avez forcément sauvée alors dans le 7), et sa fille Rose. Isolée parce qu’ils ont été mis en sécurité par Chris Redfield, arrivé à la rescousse à la fin du 7. En sécurité de quoi ?  On ne sait pas trop, mais bon de toutes manières, Chris va débarquer au cours d’une soirée d’hiver et abattre froidement Mia d’environ trente balles dans la poitrine et faire kidnapper Rose et Ethan. Ce dernier se réveille suite à un accident de voiture à proximité du fameux « Village » (qui n’a pas de nom, nous voyons juste que la monnaie utilisée est le « Lei », wikipedia me dit Moldavie ou Roumanie) où il va rapidement se faire attaquer par des lycans (loups-zombis-garous) et par Hagrid (ou le père Noël à vous de voir), dans une scène d’introduction qui ressemble ENORMEMENT à celle de RE4. Il rencontre les derniers villageois en vie qui finissent massacrés et Ethan, est lui-même capturé par les 4 seigneurs du coin : Lady Dimitrescu, Donna Beneviento, Salvatore Moreau et Karl Heisenberg. Ces quatre seigneurs sont aux ordres de Mother Miranda qui, il se trouve, comme par hasard, ça alors, a récupéré Rose et laissé Ethan pour mort car c’est elle qui a fait attaquer apparemment le convoi (on notera au passage que le plan de Chris est de mettre à l’abri Ethan, Mia et Rose à côté du domaine de Miranda… Génie).[...]  
Ceci dit, ce qui vient gâcher un peu tout ça, c’est l’écriture de certains personnages… enfin, non, pas certains… Juste celui d’Ethan ! S’il n’a pas de visage, il est assez loquace, mais raconte rarement des choses intéressantes et se retrouve plus à réagir comme un spectateur Twitch plus que comme héros de l’aventure. [...] 
Concernant le système de jeu, on se retrouve devant celui du 7 avec quelques ajustements pour le rapprocher du 4 et du remake du 2 [...] Pour avoir fait le jeu en difficulté « hardcore », j’ai appliqué ma méthode habituelle des RE canoniques : je regarde ma vie, mes balles et j’utilise ce que j’ai de disponible en plus grande quantité pour passer, en esquivant les combats inutiles. Alors ça a fonctionné mais avec le très bon équilibrage du jeu, je me suis retrouvé dans une assez bonne attrition durant les premiers 80 % du jeu, mais c’est exactement ce que j’étais venu chercher ! [...] 
	De temps en temps, mais c’est assez inhérent à la série des RE, il y a des séquences où le système de jeu empiète les intérêts de la cohérence, ainsi les ennemis traînent toujours avec eux dans leurs poches des objets utiles (même s’il y a plus de corbeaux avec des grenades par exemple…), il n’est pas possible de fermer des portes, il n’y a pas de dégâts de chute, la viande n’est pas empoisonnée, un ruisseau n’est pas traversable à pied, il arrive aussi de se retrouver coincé devant un tas de petites babioles, ou une énigme (notamment les labyrinthes à bille) qui techniquement pourraient se résoudre juste en tendant le bras, sans compter les grillages qui nous empêchent de passer et résistent à tous les explosifs sur Terre, ou encore, des lustres à incendier en les poussant péniblement sur des flambeaux alors qu’il y a trente bougies dans la pièce etc. Le jeu est parfois engoncé dans son moteur et son gameplay, et il devrait y avoir un peu plus de développement devant certaines situations, pour les présenter de manière moins frustrantes. 
	Les énigmes sont à mi-chemin de tout cela, il n’y en a absolument aucune qui ne soit vraiment difficile, et il semble toujours bizarre d’avoir un environnement qui fonctionne avec des clefs improbables que l’on obtient de manières incongrues, mais ces énigmes ont le méritent d’exister et sont relativement réalistes et crédibles à dire vrai, dans la localisation des objets, la nature de ces objets et la manière dont ils sont utilisés, même s’il y a ce problème de la grosse pince coupante qui disparaît de l’inventaire au début du jeu et dont on aurait eu l’utilité une dizaine de fois sans doute, ou encore cette scène incroyablement stupide avec la voiture... Ceci-dit, cela reste regrettable que la série des RE semble avoir renoncé à laisser vraiment le temps de se creuser la tête, surtout que le rythme du jeu n’est pas tonitruant, mais il est calibré pour que quelqu’un qui y jouerait une heure par si par là y trouve son compte. Je reste étonné à chaque RE que la solution à la Silent Hill, celle de calibrer le niveau de difficulté des énigmes en début de partie, n’ait jamais été tentée pour les RE. Le symptôme de ce refus de laisser réfléchir les joueurs se retrouve dans les myriades de marques jaunes et d’items scintillants qui indiquent les directions à suivre ou quelques objets à récupérer. [...] 

	Concernant le moteur graphique, le RE Engine, RE8 est sorti au démarrage de la diffusion du Ray Tracing, mais à la fin de l’aire PS4/XOne, et au démarrage de la génération suivante. Le jeu a désormais trois ans et avec les graphismes poussés à bloc, il reste vraiment impressionnant [...] À ce très bon moteur graphique s’ajoute un excellent travail sur les sons [...] Dans les maisons abandonnées, le vent qui siffle, le plancher et le toit qui grincent etc. viennent ponctuer la partition des bruits de pas, des borborygmes et cris des monstres qui sont affreux, hurlants et stressants. Les musiques sont globalement discrètes mais pesantes et tournent vraiment sur un rythme angoissant, elles sont capables de précipiter nos actions assez aisément, même s’il n’y a pas de thème principal qui s’en dégage. 

	Les ambiances sont posées efficacement et sans aller jusque dans le registre de la peur, il y a une angoisse régulière qui vient empêcher d’être serein au moment de la découverte d’un nouvel environnement. Sombre, sale, très emprunt de l’imagerie de la fin du XIXème siècle – les petits villages paysans des tableaux polonais, les palais des anciens seigneurs qui perdent leurs privilèges peu à peu, les constructions en briques, les sidérurgies massives chaudes et étouffantes, un peu de steampunk par là, le loup-garou et l’ambiance gothique générale, des monstres types abomination du Dr Frankenstein – RE8 brille clairement car il est à la fois bourré de références à des opus précédents de la série, mais parce que son ambiance est unique aussi. [...] Dans la zone du Village notamment, il n’est pas inconcevable que des gens vivaient ici : la nourriture est stockée, il y a un lit, un poêle de chauffage en fonte sur lequel faire à manger, des décorations uniques à chaque bâtisse, faite parfois en brique, parfois dans des matériaux traditionnels, les toilettes sont dehors et les gens vivaient avec les deux-trois animaux qu’ils élevaient pour le lait ou les œufs. 
	Ce RE offre une belle transposition de la même critique de la modernité que l’on a dans les anciens épisodes (après-tout, le premier RE paraît au moment où les études sur les gènes, les virus et les scandales alimentaires -vache folle- se font parfois échos dans les débats publics). Le fait d’y ajouter un filtre de lecture spirituel continue de filer la longue métaphore dans laquelle s’est lancée la saga, et ce, de manière intéressante puisque n’appelant pas de réponses franches aux questions que se posent les joueuses et joueurs, RE8 laisse une part d’interprétation et donc, de doutes, et par conséquent, d’angoisse puisque les limites de l’envisageable s’élargissent. Par ailleurs, le fait de se situer dans un environnement archaïque mais assez générique pour être familier des occidentaux implique tout de même efficacement, autant qu’il va sans doute intriguer celles et ceux complètement étrangers à ce type d’endroit et qui seront sensibles à l’imaginaire que peuvent invoquer un village ancien à côté d’un château en ruine, ou d’un vieux moulin qui tourne à présent à vide. [...]

As an ardent fan of Resident Evil, I was eager to step into the terrifying world of Village, and I can confidently say that this game is a masterclass in horror and storytelling.

Gameplay in Resident Evil Village is a perfect blend of classic survival horror and modern action elements. The combat is both satisfying and challenging, with an array of weapons at your disposal, but scarce resources that keep you on edge. The story itself is engaging and takes some surprising twists and turns, blending elements of folklore and the supernatural seamlessly with the traditional Resident Evil universe. The game's pacing is excellent, offering moments of tense exploration, terrifying encounters, and poignant storytelling, all in perfect balance.

The audio design in the game is exceptional, from the unsettling sounds of creaking doors to the haunting melodies accompanying the action. The voice acting is top-notch, adding depth to the characters, making them more relatable and convincing. Resident Evil Village's use of RE Engine, Capcom's proprietary technology, allows for smooth character animations, realistic physics, and stunning particle effects. The game also features remarkably detailed textures and environmental effects that contribute to the overall sense of immersion. Whether you're exploring the dimly lit interiors of a foreboding castle or navigating the foggy marshes, the graphics consistently impress.

In my humble opinion, Resident Evil Village is the apex of the franchise. It successfully blends the series' signature elements with fresh innovations, providing a terrifying and immersive journey that keeps players on the edge of their seats. Whether you're a long-time fan or a newcomer, Resident Evil Village stands as the finest Resident Evil title, offering a captivating and unforgettable gaming experience.

[h1]Not as spooky as RE7, nor as action heavy as RE4, but a good middle ground between the two and a delightful time for the most part.[/h1]

RE8 ditches the low stakes setting of a single household, in favour of a more fairy tale-esque setting set in a village.
The village itself feels very similar to RE4, albeit less malicious and more tragic, with everyone looking towards a godly figure known as Mother Miranda [spoiler],basically just this games equivalent of Saddler,[/spoiler] for help.
And looming over this village however are a variety of main locations, such as a flooded watermill, the imposing Castle Dimitrescu, a messed up doll house, and a bit more beyond that.

You've got werewolves, vampires, standards zombies and more, and these are by far some of the most aggressive [spoiler]and tankiest[/spoiler] enemies in the franchise.
You've also got the return of the merchant system from RE4, meaning currency makes a return, along with weapon upgrades and the ability to sell excess supplies and valuables.
Despite the different coat of paint, it's definitely closer in tone to RE4, but where it differs is in the action.
While RE4 throws a lot of enemies at you, RE8 handles its survival aspects better in my opinion by throwing harder enemies at you. These guys are aggressive, they're faster than most RE enemies and they can take quite the beating on average.
Until you get comfortable towards the later half of the game, you may find yourself a bit low on ammo unless you're willing to part with a bit of coin. I genuinely liked this as it made running from battles feel more viable, or if I'm going to fight, I need to make every bullet count.

[h1]Continuing with the positivity, the level design is quite strong, some of my favourite in the series[/h1]

While the game could be divided into chapters, the game keeps funnelling you from major locations back towards the village, with more locations being unlocked each time you come back.
The rest of the game also has this winding level design mentality, what with having plot progression tie into backtracking, but the Village is in the title for this game, and I feel its thematics and level design are enough to justify that. 

[h1]Sadly while I quite like the setting itself, the actual plot/hook is nowhere near as strong as the games I'm comparing it to[/h1]

The games main way of hooking you from the start is shock value, I won't go into massive spoilers here but I will say that the game plays its hand way too early, for the vast majority of the game it feels like what I'm going up against is easier than the last thing when it comes to scale and sheer threat.

Comparing it to the Baker residence from RE7, the persistent threats are nowhere near as menacing, nor do they have any surprises to catch you off guard.
Lastly, the boss fights against the bigger bads here are often pretty annoying, they're usually quite tanky, their mechanics are lame and I felt only one of these had appropriate mechanics to match its absurdity and scale.

I just feel it's a step down considering how well built up the Bakers in RE7 were compared to these guys, a little bit sad but not a deal breaker.

[h1]There's one last thing to mention, and that would be the DLC[/h1]

Aside from the expansion, this DLC also brings in the option of a 3rd person camera, something that I feel should've been included for free, but regardless, is a fair selling point for enough for some people to warrant a mention.

Next is the expansion, the epilogue for the game.
Because of it's place in the plot, I can't go into detail about the plot, but I will say that I found it highly unnecessary, [spoiler]even if it did have some sweet moments,[/spoiler] and concerning for the plot moving forward since in theory, we'll know about the timeline of some characters for a long time to come.
But in gameplay, it's a lot of weak weaponry, reused assets, forced walking and bland hallways.
None of what makes the main game shine is present here, and it makes it feel pretty boring, even if the experience is only 2 - 4 hours long.

[h1]Despite some issues, I still feel this is one of the better games in the series[/h1]
I have no idea what will come after this game, as it feels like RE as a series typically tries to reinvent itself every 2 - 3 games, but these latest entries in the franchise have felt like some of the best they've had to offer, very high quality.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

• [u]Resident Evil 4 Influence[/u]: Resident Evil Village seamlessly incorporates the best action elements of Resident Evil 4 into its modern, first-person perspective, offering an intense and combat-heavy experience reminiscent of Shinji Mikami’s magnum opus.

• [u]Visually Distinctive Villains[/u]: Each of the main villains, from the towering Lady Dimitrescu to the grotesque Salvatore Moreau, presides over visually distinctive domains, providing a variety of settings that demand different approaches, contributing to an engrossing and mysterious story.

• [u]Expanded Enemy Variety[/u]: Village addresses the lack of enemy variety in Resident Evil 7, introducing a diverse range of foes, including Lycans, werewolves, zombies, and more, resulting in evolving and interesting combat encounters.



[hr][/hr]

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

• [u]Predictable Puzzles[/u]: The puzzles in Village are either straightforward or entirely spoiled by instructional notes, lacking the complexity or challenge that could enhance the overall experience.

• [u]Ease of Standard Difficulty[/u]: On the standard difficulty setting, Village feels less challenging compared to Resident Evil 7, with fewer deaths and a sense of reduced overall difficulty, potentially impacting the satisfaction for veteran players.

• [u]Limited Lady Dimitrescu Presence[/u]: Despite Lady Dimitrescu's popularity, her appearance is short-lived and not as impactful as expected, with her three daughters sharing similar weaknesses and encounters.
