Resident Evil Village: The Rollercoaster of Horror and Hilarity

Resident Evil Village is like that one bizarre party where you end up laughing hysterically and crying in a closet at the same time. It's a rollercoaster of horror and hilarity, with a dash of existential crisis thrown in for good measure.

First, let's talk about the hero of the game: Ethan Winters. This guy is the master of deadpan humor, facing the creepiest horrors with the enthusiasm of a Monday morning meeting. He's less "Action Hero Extraordinaire" and more "Why did I even come to this village?" But, oh, the absurdity! From stapling his hands back on to nonchalantly carrying liters of health-restoring soup, Ethan's sheer ridiculousness makes you snicker even in the face of grotesque monstrosities.

Now, the village itself. It's like someone thought, "Let's put vampires, werewolves, and a giant metal chicken lady in the same place!" It's as if they spun a wheel of mythical creatures and just threw it all in. You'll find yourself questioning the game's sanity as you dodge Lady Dimitrescu's attempts at a close embrace and fend off her freakishly tall daughters.

And don't get me started on the Duke, the jolly traveling merchant who somehow manages to be a comic relief buffet in this carnival of horrors. He's got the magical ability to turn everything you find into cash, like a hoarder's dream come true. He's the friendly neighborhood capitalist, reminding you that even during a zombie apocalypse, someone's gotta make a profit.

But for all the hilarity, there's an underlying sense of dread. As you uncover the mysteries of the village, you'll realize that beneath the absurdity lies a tale of despair and loss. It's like trying to laugh through a terrifying therapy session that's slowly unearthing your deepest fears.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is a game that's so funny, it's depressing. It's a wild, sometimes absurd, often terrifying ride through a village that redefines the meaning of "wacky horror." So, grab your stapler, load up on soup, and get ready to laugh and cringe your way through this horror-comedy extravaganza. Just be prepared for a few nightmares along the way, both in-game and in your sleep.

[h1] Resident Evil Village: A Chaotic Blend of Horror and CInema [/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a mixed bag of horror elements that caters to a wide range of tastes, but this concoction, while intriguing initially, becomes overwhelming and unbalanced as you delve deeper. Just like sipping a complex smoothie, the first few sips are delightful, dark, and brooding, but as you continue, it turns fiery and wild, leaving you with a confusing aftertaste.

In this game, you once again step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, the same resilient yet bewildered protagonist from Resident Evil 7. This time, he's found himself in a chilling, snow-covered village teeming with lycanthropes instead of kids playing. The game manages to blend action and fear effectively during its first half. It starts with a hair-raising introduction that leads you through a village that's as monstrous as its furry inhabitants. Silence dominates the atmosphere, and every creak or snap of a twig sends shivers down your spine. Resources are scarce, firepower is limited, and fights are genuinely perilous. It's an unsettling crime scene that defies understanding, but you know you'll return to uncover the truth. Resident Evil Village shines when it embraces this patient, eerie atmosphere.

One of the early locations you explore is Dimitrescu's Castle, a grand fortress inhabited by a formidable lady, her diabolical daughters, and classic Resident Evil puzzles. More importantly, the castle preserves the village's eerie ambiance. The pacing is superb as you navigate its enigmatic puzzles and hidden passages, all while trying to ignore the suffocating silence.

But not everything in this game is flawless. Some moments prioritize action over fear, with boss fights feeling choreographed rather than genuine tests of survival. This pattern continues through most of the game, where significant encounters feel more like rehearsals with strict cues to follow. However, one location stands out as an exception.

As you progress, Resident Evil Village takes a turn. The village transforms into a hub world with four different zones, each home to one of the game's villains. The area you visit right after escaping the castle is especially exceptional, but I can't reveal any details about it without spoilers. Suffice it to say, it's a nightmarish and inventive experience that will keep you on your toes. It's a moment of vulnerability in the game, and it's masterful in how it plays with your fears.

Each return to the hub world keeps things fresh. The village subtly evolves to reflect your absence, with weather changes and subtle alterations that make revisiting areas feel rewarding. You may find new tools, like keys, during your adventures, making it satisfying to unlock previously inaccessible spots. These moments of discovery, such as finding new weapons or mysterious treasures, add depth to the gameplay.

Resident Evil Village is visually stunning, with detailed environments and intricate objects that bring its world to life. While the game ran smoothly on my RTX 2070-equipped system, I experienced one crash during a cutscene. This occurred during an early review build, so it may not reflect the final product.

The change in tone during the latter half of the game is kind of jarring. Action increasingly supersedes the horror aspect, and the abundance of weapons feels out of place. The introduction of the Duke, a shopkeeper who offers supplies and gun upgrades, makes resource scarcity less meaningful. By the end, the game prioritizes shooting over suspense and unpredictability.

As Resident Evil Village nears its conclusion, it spirals into chaos, with sequences that feel more suited to Call of Duty than a survival horror game. The transition from a chilling, unknown world to action-packed shootouts is unsettling, and the fear of running out of ammo replaces the fear of the unknown. The game sacrifices its unpredictable, chilling atmosphere for more straightforward gunfights.

Despite this shift, the game's story remains engaging. Ethan Winters' predicament hooks you from the beginning, and the conclusion, while messy, ties up loose ends and leaves room for more questions, a challenging feat for a long-running series.

In the end, Resident Evil Village tries to cater to a broad audience, but this ambition comes at the cost of balance. The early horror-focused sections are exceptional, but the game loses its way as it approaches the end, favoring action over fear. Despite this, it remains compelling.

Overall it's a wonderful game and it's a nice change of pace. The serialization and cinimatic focus of recent Resident Evil titles is something I'm enjoying and I'm hoping to see where Ethan's daughter plays in the next game.

Resident Evil Village is an electrifying addition to the iconic Resident Evil series that promises to take you on a heart-pounding journey. While it might not deliver the same bone-chilling scares as its predecessor, Resident Evil 7, it compensates with a more action-packed experience that masterfully maintains the series' signature atmosphere.

As a long-time fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I stepped into Village with high expectations, and I wasn't disappointed. Right from the start, the game immerses you in a beautifully realized, eerie village and its surrounding environments. The attention to detail in the graphics, sound design, and environmental storytelling is impeccable. Every creaking floorboard and distant whisper adds to the pervasive sense of dread.

What sets Resident Evil Village apart from its predecessors is its shift towards a more action-oriented gameplay style. While it may not be as terrifying as Resident Evil 7, it delivers in terms of heart-pounding action sequences, intense boss battles, and an arsenal of weapons that makes you feel like a one-person army against the horrors that await. This evolution in gameplay adds an exciting twist to the series while retaining its core essence.

The storyline is engaging, filled with intriguing mysteries, and memorable characters. Ethan Winters, our protagonist from Resident Evil 7, returns to face a new nightmare as he searches for his kidnapped daughter. The introduction of new characters like Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters adds depth to the narrative, making you question the motives of every character you encounter.

The game's pacing is impeccable, offering moments of respite amid the chaos to explore and solve puzzles. The merchant, Duke, provides a welcome dose of humor and acts as your one-stop shop for weapons and upgrades. Managing your resources and making strategic decisions about which weapons to buy and upgrade adds a layer of depth to the gameplay.

While Resident Evil Village may not reach the same levels of horror as its predecessor, it excels in creating a tense and eerie atmosphere that keeps you on edge throughout. It's a roller coaster ride of adrenaline-pumping action, unexpected twists, and unforgettable moments that will keep fans of the horror genre and the Resident Evil series thoroughly entertained.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village may take a different route in terms of horror, but it doesn't sacrifice the franchise's identity. It's a thrilling, action-packed adventure that continues to build upon the rich lore of the series. If you're a fan of Resident Evil or enjoy a mix of horror and action, don't miss out on this unforgettable journey through the village of nightmares. Grab your weapons, brace yourself, and dive into this captivating and atmospheric experience.

I'd say more survival action. Capcom finally nailed it with RE7, they brought back all the horror and anxiety from real RE classics, while adavncing and innovating the survival horror genre. It was a miracle but they already decided to squander it all to appeal the masses. So forget all about the tension, claustrophoby and helplessness that made RE7 great. In RE Village, they wanted to strike a balance between horror and action, and they obviously failed although not entirely. Capcom thought RE7 was good (in terms of sales) but they wanted the next RE to sell even more, so they tried the obvious: they imitated their most (wrongly) acclaimed title in the series, RE4. RE4 was an ok game, but it was also where the series started to rush into the abyss of forgettable crap.

Anyway, given the premises, they did an amazing job. Young and old fans will probably enjoy this RE, even if it is far from the genius of the 7. Enjoyable is a fit adjective for this game, entertaining is too. It isn't survival horror though. In a real survivor horror you need to explore cautiously and make hard strategic decisions and keep your cool else you ♥♥♥♥ up. Here you are just required to have fast reflexes and act fast. Assuming you play on hardcore, else it's no challenge at all. "Survival action fps with a bad aiming mechanic" is more adequate for RE8. Yeah you cannot aim down sight like in RE7 Not a Hero for some reason, you always fire from the hip and the aiming just restricts the aiming reticle. There are a few very nice puzzles, but never too hard and most puzzles are absolute no brainers. Difficulty is toned down to meet the needs of the casual gamer, so I suggest hardcore diificulty for veterans of the series, which equals normal difficulty in RE1, RE2, RE3, RE7. Even the most basic enemies are bullet sponges, but you'll be given a replenished arsenal so you won't worry too much about that after a while. The hardest section of the game is at the very beginning, so after that you're golden till the end.
The RE engine is amazing as ever, with a 1080ti I had almost everything maxed out and still a stable 140fps. Visuals are great and for the most part even improved, except a few things like the explosive red barrels which look cartoonish (RE4 style).

To conclude: great game, but very mid when compared to the previous entry RE7.

What we actually got was incredibly linear in it's approach and it pains me every time I replay this game. 

With that said this is still a modern Resident evil game so we have fantastic atmosphere (albeit it a much less scary game which was intentional.), fun gun play and cool locations and bosses. I do really like the enemy variety this time round as RE7 did lack in that department and the amount of fun unlockables is great. 

This is also the end of the winters story and the dlc leaves the game in an interesting place, will we see RE9 pick up from the dlc and will we see really old versions of the characters we love? Who knows. 

But what I can say this that this is a disjointed, tonally inconsistent mess with loads of wasted potential that is still really fun to play, even a bad resi game is a fun time, unless it involves anything multiplayer.

Resident Evil, being one of my favourite gaming franchises, it was only normal I went with high expectations for this title, after all, I enjoyed myself quite a bit of RE7 years ago.

Pros:
+ Fantastic graphics and optimization, the game runs with pretty much everything set to ultra with no dips or stuttering, hats off!
+ Ethan is now a fully fleshed character.
+ Voice acting (at least in English) is REALLY good, but I do wished there was British accents thrown in since the game is, in y'know, Romania.
+ They learned from RE7 and now we have decent enemy variety, nothing to write home about but they heard.
+ Awesome level design and atmosphere.
+ The Merchant returns! (well, it's not HIM, but hey!).

Cons:
- Combat is clunky as all hell, I think is even clunkier than in RE7!
- Weapons don't feel good and lack the proper accuracy to make them feel like you're shooting something.
- The whole vampire dommy mommy was a fiasco, she showed up for like 2-3 hours and that's it. Which brings me to...
- Boss fights in RE7 were lackluster (except for Jack's) but here... man, what happened? They're lame af. Villains in this game had plenty of potential to become one of, if not, the best cast in the series, but we ended up with lame and short fights.
- Puzzles are WAAY too easy.
- The whole House Beneviento DOESN'T BELONG to the game, or any RE for that matter. If I wanted to play smth like that I'd play SH/PT. 
- Ending was meh (still better than RE7's).

Overall, I feel like they tried so SO hard to emulate RE4 perfectly-balanced formula they ended up with a game that is, in the end, dissapointing, as it doesn't know what it wants to REALLY be. Sometimes, it wants to be SH, sometimes RE4, and then, sometimes, its own thing. Game lacks the direction needed in order to be a good RE in my eyes.
Even if I love RE4 and I consider it one of the best games ever, its formula shouldn't be replicated, but rather, inspiring.

Final score: 5.5/10, first time since RE6 I didn't enjoy a RE title.

A Masterpiece of Horror

Resident Evil Village isn't just a game; it's a spine-tingling journey through the darkest depths of survival horror. This title stands as the pinnacle of the genre, delivering a thrilling experience that leaves players both awestruck and utterly terrified. Capcom has truly outdone themselves with this masterpiece, and it's the perfect ending to the winter's chilling story.

From the very moment you step into the shoes of Ethan Winters, you're thrown headfirst into a nightmare that is both hauntingly beautiful and profoundly disturbing. The village itself is a character, a living, breathing entity filled with secrets and horrors that will keep you on edge throughout your entire journey. The attention to detail is nothing short of remarkable, with every cobblestone, flickering torch, and eerily decaying building contributing to the game's overall atmosphere.

The storyline, which continues the gripping narrative from Resident Evil 7, is a rollercoaster of emotions. As Ethan Winters, you're driven by a relentless determination to rescue your daughter, Rose, from the clutches of an unforgettable cast of villains, each more twisted and nightmarish than the last. Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters, Karl Heisenberg, and the puppet-master himself, Mother Miranda, are characters that will haunt your dreams long after you've put down the controller.

What truly sets Resident Evil Village apart, though, is its masterful blending of horror elements. From the tense and claustrophobic encounters with hordes of lycans to the heart-pounding chase sequences with Lady Dimitrescu, this game keeps your adrenaline pumping. Yet, it also manages to weave in moments of profound unease and psychological horror, making you question what's real and what's a product of your fear-fueled imagination.

The gameplay is a perfect balance between the old and the new, incorporating the best elements from previous Resident Evil titles while introducing fresh mechanics that keep the experience exciting. The inventory management, resource scarcity, and puzzle-solving are back, but they're complemented by an improved combat system and stunningly realistic graphics. The RE Engine deserves special mention for bringing the game's environments, characters, and gore to life in a way that's genuinely breathtaking.

Resident Evil Village doesn't just excel in its individual components; it excels in making them all work harmoniously to create a symphony of fear and tension. The sound design is impeccable, with every creaking floorboard, distant scream, and unnerving silence contributing to the feeling that something sinister lurks just out of sight.

As for the culmination of Ethan Winters' story, it's a gut-wrenching and emotionally charged climax that wraps up the narrative in a way that will leave you contemplating it long after the credits roll. Without giving away spoilers, I can say that Resident Evil Village delivers a conclusion that's both satisfying and bittersweet, providing closure while leaving the door open for the series to explore new horizons.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is not only the pinnacle of horror games but also a stunningly beautiful and hauntingly captivating experience. It's a fitting end to Ethan Winters' winter nightmare and a testament to Capcom's commitment to delivering top-tier survival horror. If you're a fan of the series or simply a lover of horror games, this title is an absolute must-play. Just be prepared to face your fears like never before.

THE MOMMY MILKERS STRIKE BACK

The Resident Evil franchise has experimented with many aesthetics and styles of horror, all being based in the realm of cinematic presentation. RE 7 really tried something new with a focus on visceral horror akin to Tobe Hooper’s Texas Chain Saw Massacre. So, it was fitting for the franchise to return to more gothic, fantastical horror, but keeping in the established canon of the Ethan Winters storyline. However, does it improve upon its predecessor?.. 

Ehhhhhhhhh not really.

Resident Evil: Village is an incredible game  with great aesthetic and familiar gameplay. Adopting a more gothic design akin to Stoker’s Dracula meets Dario Argento, the updated location of a castle and village grounds is expansive and expertly designed. It is gorgeous to look at too! The only problem I have with it is that the map feels too big for the atmosphere to be effectively scary. The brilliance of Biohazard’s map(s) was that the farm and ship felt uncomfortably intimate. The scares were more invasive instead of grandiose, but that’s probably due to the different styles of horror. However, there are moments in Hammer’s Dracula or other cult horrors like Suspiria that are far scarier than the jumpscare-y blandness of Village. Also, the horror is lessened by the reduced difficulty of standard, which felt more like easy than anything else. Despite it taking me longer to complete this one than 7, everything felt rushed and quick. 

The design is brilliant though. The creatively found in the characters is truly inspired with extreme levels of detail and nuanced voice performances. Even the mommy milker vampire lady  is a fully-realized minor antagonist with depth. The rest of the intrigue is kind of a let-down, but it’s a decent bookend to the the plot established in Biohazard, making a good two-parter for the franchise.

I will say just like the first game, use the knife to save ammo as I found saving ammo this time around was harder than the first because UNLIKE RE7 this game has a shop but NO CHEST to store items. It is trying to replicate RE4 and it works but I think the chest being missing sucks.

This game kind of encourages you to go on the offensive more and given enemies now drop money or other treasures it is encouraged to clear enemies. There is no consequence other than ammo for killing enemies. 
The game has a good story but it has some issues. Chris kills Mia in front of Ethan without giving him any time to know why Chris did such a traumatic thing leaving Ethan in the dark and then getting mad Ethan gets involved to save his daughter. A Umbrella agent even calls Chris out on this decision. Some people think this is bad writing. Some say this action by Chris is built into his personality as a flaw. I lean to the former as he should be more professional at this point in is career given the situation and how he knew Ethan would respond. I mean he even takes Rose from Ethan and talks to Ethan like a dog.  
Also Lady D is the first boss and she isn't in the game very long which can be a disappointment to some given she was a big sell for the game and the main face that people simped over. But she has a presence and a lot of personality.
Also the Lords are broken up into their own different territories and once you leave the castle you can't go back to it. But the village is a hub for the other Lords' territories. 
The DLC mostly sucks. You have to pay for a Third person view, gun charms that don't matter, and an Albert pistol you can't get in the main game that gets easily outclassed damage wise by the starting pistol. Some aspects of the DLC are neat like unlocking things you would have to unlock through challenges for free in the main game with no dlc attached.
The Shadows of Rose dlc expands upon the ending and lore. As well as Rose herself. As well as her relationship with Ethan. Its a good dlc for that but the gameplay is too linear and gimmicky to keep you busy.  
Its a solid game but some weird game design choices stop it from being really great but definitely worth a shot.

Edit: I wanted to add this game is less like the Resident Evil games of old and understandably fans, including myself don't like this direction. The devs even admitted to pulling back the horror elements from RE7 that scared little babies. The game is not very scary. It does have some survival horror elements but it is too action packed to be tense. Even RE4 outshines this game in some ways. 
This game is too generous with inventory space. You can have three guns in your inventory, one being a sniper rifle before you need to add more space. 
The castle of Lady D is lost potential as it seems bigger on the outside. You don't explore all of it. The Castle should have come last in the game or Lady D should have had more of a presence as you kill her daughters maybe her patrols around the castle become more aggressive and she isn't too hard to run around. 
You even are tricked into a more linear game where you walk into big rooms with many doors but there is usually only one way to go. Puzzles are braindead easy and the game gives you the answers to them. The game directly hands you a ring with an eye on it solve a simple door puzzle as you are progressing through the basement. Puzzle items and crafting materials don't even take up inventory space. There is even a section where you play as Chris and you just storm the front and gun down enemies without a care for supplies. The game lies to you about how big it is and the directions you take. Oddly enough the factory section is more well designed with more places to go and secret rooms to find resources. 
Crafting has become so simple as not only does it take up no inventory space unlike older titles or even RE7 but now the chem fluid mainly is used to make healing items and certain ammunition. Scrap metal plus gunpowder is used to make ammo now making crafting less of a decision making process on how you use your limited resources.

I love Resident Evil 8. It's a fantastic game: The graphics are amazing, the Gameplay is solid and fun, and the Story is a great sequel to RE7. Boy, where do i start? The Characters you meet along the way, such as the Duke, Lady Dimitrescu, Heisenberg or the old hag, they all have their own taste, especially the bosses. Never have i ♥♥♥♥ myself this much, with things where you expect it to happen. I've played alot of Horror games, and you expect alot of things - jumpscare wise, and yet, the game managed to make me almost ♥♥♥♥ myself from fear, in a certain part of the game. 

Though, with every great game, come flaws:

I hate the Lychans. Literally, they're the most annoying and ♥♥♥♥ enemies, just like the Molded were in RE7. I love that there's more than just one type of enemy, but the Lychans are some of the most disgusting, annoying and boring enemies to fight. I just hate how they work, and every time you have to fight them, after the first playthrough, they're just a tideous roadblock in your way through the game. 

Then, there's the difficulties. In all honesty, i've played every gamemode, except for casual - because i didnt see a reason for it yet. Normal is a very well made gamemode, in terms of difficulty - it doesn't feel unfair. Hardcore, as it's said, is harder. Still, fair. But, Village of Shadows is a jump in difficulty which makes me question: "Who the hell came up with this? A 10 year old?". Im aware, hardest difficulty, hardest enemies etc. but, if you start a NEW game, without your "completed" savestate, where you have the items of the last playthrough, it's basically impossible, unless you're a god at the game. I couldnt beat the game on Village of Shadows without the savestate, because the LEMI and the Shotgun from the beginning arer just way too weak. And even after getting past the beginning, every enemy is just a pain in the ass to fight, because it feels like you waste your bullets repedeately spamming your pistol and or shotgun at the specific enemy, just to not die with one hit - like always. This is also a reason i just hate the Lychans, because in the beginning of the game, you just always get one-hit by them. It's so annoying, it made me quit the game for a few days, just to not get upset and uninstall it.

Oh, and i'd like to mention that the S.T.A.K.E. is way too OP, when fully upgraded. You can speedrun Village of Shadows with only the S.T.A.K.E. if you have infinite ammo, without issues. It turns the game into a joke, because you can basically one- or two shot most enemies.

What i also have to mention is the blocking mechanic. Lychans (at least for me) seem to ignore my block in 25% of the cases, just getting a hit on me, despite me facing, and blocking their attacks. If it's just me, or the game, is not up to me to say, but it defenetely is a thing that breaks the immersion in the game.

For an Achievement hunter like myself, the fact Some achievements are locked behind a hefty paywall is devastating aswell. I won't pay like 60€ for a game i already paid 40€ for. And, reading the reviews to the DLC's, i'm pretty sure it's not worth the time to even buy and play them. CAPCOM, why make way-too-expensive DLC's for an already very expensive game, that then is effectively ruined if you can't play all that there is. In RE7, the DLC's were alot more fleshed out, and funnier. (THOUGH, aswell as RE8, RE7 had paywall-locked achievements aswell). The only good Minigame in RE8 defenetely is Mercenaries, as it just makes you play: "Resident Evil: DOOM edition."

All in all, i still love this game, even with the flaws and things i just tend to hate.

Resident Evil Village encapsulates you in its gameplay loop, making this one of the most games to replay I've ever played. While this game does have a lot of issues with its story, characters and horror elements, they are not mind-numbingly stupid to the point where this game is bad.

First, the how the game plays. The combat is fun and pretty rewarding. You shoot enemies; they drop loot. More difficult enemies will drop better loop that has more selling value. Some drops will be ingredients that you can use to craft ammo, healing or explosives. Surprisingly, enemies never drop ammo. There is still a problem with ammo over-abundance, however, even if you don't factor in the Duke's ammo supply. [spoiler]The game does a good job of making you face the medium difficulty enemies first, to give you a glimpse into how hard these mid-range enemies are at your current level. After defeating two of these enemies in separate one-on-one battles, you are faced with a swarm of them. The problem with the Haulers, Moroaice and Lycans is that their grab attack animations are too fast that you don't get enough of a reaction window to block them. Their regular weapon attacks are just fine, but if you anticipate a grab attack and instead they perform a weapon attack, you're forced to keep blocking for an uncomfortably long time. Most of the boss fights are pretty good, but it feels like some of the villains should have gotten more boss fights, such as Lady Dimitrescu9 in her human-escu form.[/spoiler]
Exploration is really good in this game that I even enjoy it on multiple playthroughs of the game. It's just fun to run back through parts of the map you've already been to, so that you can get treasure that becomes available. Sometimes there are even new enemies or animals available at said parts. Upgrading all the weapons is fun because of this, although I wish there was an item box to store weapons, because if you sell them, you have to buy them back at full price, complete with all attachments and upgrades (provided you have fully upgraded the weapon).
This leads me to a major gripe I have with the game, the storage space. You simply have way too much storage. I never found myself discarding items or picking what to take with me because:
a) Key items don't take up space nor do crafting items
b) Storage space is huge
c) You get storage upgrades before you need them
One fix around they tried in RE7 with the generous storage space was limiting the stack amount for ammo as well as giving you a lot of item variety to work with.
Another problem with this game is that income is scaled. You get more money on harder difficulties for some reason. This doesn't really matter, as no achievements require you to play on New Game except for your first playthrough. Still kind of stupid for players who want a challenge. If they wanted to make Village of Shadows easier for people playing New Game, they could just make the weapons start with extra upgrades or give you more weapons and items at the start of the game like in RE3R.
The story is just not that great. It's not bad, but it leaves something to be desired. [spoiler]The factory feels out of place and it could have been cut down to allow more time for Moreau or Lady Dimitrescu, who I thought were more interesting characters. The theming just didn’t work for the medieval atmosphere the game was going for. The factory is industrial but it could have gone for the Frankenstein Castle look, which also could have cut out the Lycan fortress and given more time to the aforementioned villains. Village’s story also has a problem with not explaining crucial information to the protagonist. This segways into being a problem for the characters.
Ethan has no idea what is going on the whole game, so he’s constantly asking the same thing, “What the heck is going on?” It just gets really annoying after the 29th time. Mia is also barely in the game, so you still don’t really care for her by the end of this game. Chris is just completely stupid. He doesn’t tell Ethan what is going on when he has two chances that would benefit both of them if he just spoke. The villains are interesting but they don’t have enough screen time except for Heisenberg. Heisenberg has this plan to use Rose and team up with Ethan, but he never fully explains his plan, nor does Ethan try to hear him out.[/spoiler]
Horror is hardly present in this game. Some parts are pretty scary, [spoiler]like the Vârcolac fights, the dungeon and house Beneviento (before you encounter the baby).[/spoiler] But for the most part, this game just doesn’t really try to be scary, especially with the game taking place almost entirely during the day. This was probably because too many people stopped playing Resident Evil 7, due to being too scary.

Overall, this game is worth it and I do enjoy the story even if it is lacking. The progression is what really drives this game for me.

[h1]Resident Evil: Village[/h1]
[i]Village People - this time it's not just disco[/i]

[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b], the latest instalment in the iconic survival horror franchise from Capcom, continues to push the boundaries of the genre with its innovative first person camera view. Set in a chilling, Gothic European village, the game takes players on a roller-coaster ride of thrills, intrigue, and heart-pounding action while also delivering the franchise one of its most iconic, if not iconic villains, Countess Alcina Dimitrescu. From the moment she appeared in an early trailer for [b]Resident Evil: Village[/b], Lady Dimitrescu captured the attention of the internet: her towering, sultry frame; her sickly-sweet smile; her massive hat; her proper yet authoritative tone. 

Viewers were instantly obsessed, labelling her "tall vampire lady" and demanding to know everything about her, which prompted Capcom to reveal her exact height — 9'6" including her hat and heels — months before [b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] launched in May of 2021. Lady Dimitrescu, and her murderous three daughters preside over Castle Dimitrescu which towers over the village protagonist Ethan Winters (the lead from [b]Resident Evil 7[/b]) finds himself in at the start of the game. Countess Alcina Dimitrescu is not the only villain Ethan Winters will need to outsmart in this sequel, but she definitely is the most memorable. From the get go [b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] manages to deliver an intense and memorable experience that should keep fans of the series on the edge of their seats.

[u][b]Graphics and Atmosphere[/b][/u]:
One of the standout features of [b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] is its stunning visual presentation. The RE Engine once again proves its prowess, delivering detailed character models, breathtaking environments, and impressive lighting effects. The titular village itself is a masterclass in environmental design, seamlessly blending decrepit architecture with eerie ambience. The transition from the village to more fantastical locales is seamless and adds to the game's sense of mystery and foreboding.

[u][b]Gameplay and Mechanics[/b][/u]:
[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] continues the franchise's shift towards a more action-oriented approach, akin to [b]Resident Evil 4[/b]. The gameplay strikes a balance between tense survival horror and intense combat sequences. Ethan Winters, the protagonist, is more agile this time around, allowing for smoother movement and dynamic evasive actions. The inventory management system returns, adding an extra layer of challenge as players must strategise on the fly.

The weapon variety is satisfying, with each firearm feeling impactful and unique. However, the game occasionally suffers from pacing issues, with certain segments feeling too action-heavy, diminishing the sense of vulnerability that defines the series. The addition of crafting and merchant mechanics adds depth, but the inclusion of some survival elements may alienate purist fans of the franchise.

[u][b]Story and Narrative[/b][/u]:
[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] boasts an intriguing narrative that combines supernatural horror with [b]Resident Evil[/b]'s signature bio-terrorism plotlines. The enigmatic Lady Dimitrescu and her vampiric daughters steal the show with their eerie charm, but some secondary characters lack development. The overarching story sometimes struggles to maintain a cohesive tone, veering between chilling horror and campy action. While the central mystery is compelling, some plot twists may leave players scratching their heads.

[u][b]Horror and Atmosphere[/b][/u]:
[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] excels at creating an unsettling atmosphere, with its haunting sound design, meticulously crafted environments, and relentless tension. The first-person perspective heightens immersion, making encounters with grotesque enemies genuinely terrifying. The game's psychological horror elements, especially in the dollhouse segment, are spine-chilling and showcase the developers' mastery at crafting scares. However, some areas lose their fright factor due to predictable jump scares and reliance on shock value.

[u][b]Technical Performance[/b][/u]:
[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] runs smoothly on current-gen hardware, maintaining a consistent frame rate even during intense action sequences. However, I did experience severe frame drops when fighting one of Lady Dimitrescu daughters who deploys swarms of insects during the fight with her. This swarm lowered my framerate in to single digits which was jarring.  Load times, for the most part, are minimal, and the game's visuals remain impressive throughout. Some players may also experience minor glitches or texture pop-in (as I did), though these issues are infrequent and don't significantly impact the overall experience.

[u][b]Conclusion[/b][/u]:
[b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] is a worthy addition to the franchise, offering a visually stunning and atmospheric journey through horror. While the game occasionally strays from its survival horror roots and stumbles in its narrative execution, it still manages to deliver an intense and memorable experience that will leave players eagerly anticipating the next chapter in the [b]Resident Evil[/b] saga. With its exceptional graphics, spine-tingling moments, and a gripping sense of dread, [b]Resident Evil: Village[/b] solidifies itself as a must-play title for both series veterans and newcomers alike.

Feels like Capcom attempted to mix the terror and horror of Resident Evil 7 with the fast-paced action of Resident Evil 4 and ended up with this mediocre convoluted mess.

Combat is an unsatisfying, clunky mess; even with mid/late game upgrades, Ethan is marginally faster than he was in RE7 yet the enemies he fights (primarily lycans) can close the distance by weaving through your shots, tanking them, and eventually surrounding you in groups of ~3, which in itself wouldn't be a problem if the lycans didn't just awkwardly stand around staring at you and wait until one of them individually takes a swing at you. These lycans are meant to act like pack animals yet they feel more brainless than the molded from RE7 which completely breaks any potential intensity or immersion. The lack of a FOV slider doesn't help either since the FOV is so low and therefore the screen is zoomed in way too much, which many online claim was omitted in order to maintain and enhance the horror atmosphere by limiting what you're able to see on screen at any one time. However, RE7 was also first person and features a FOV slider despite being more horror-focused than RE:Village and much more claustrophobic, taking place in the tight hallways and basement of the Baker residence, a rusty tanker ship, and a mine rather than RE:Village's relatively open areas such as the central village or Moreau's Reservoir. There's simply no excuse why Capcom chose not to include a FOV slider in RE:Village even with the DLC since the default FOV is so low and its gameplay is more action oriented than horror oriented.

Another major issue I have with RE:Village is the over saturation of monster archetypes. Over the course of this game, you fight werewolves (lycans), vampires, a ventriloquist and the hallucinations of her doll, a grotesque fish-man, an electromagnetic steampunk man, cyborgs, and a shape-shifting witch, most of whom are ridiculously explained as results of human experimentation with mold-altered parasites. This mishmash of vastly different monster archetypes into one game makes this game feel like a cheap haunted house or theme park ride rather than a relatively consistent and coherent horror experience. In comparison, in earlier RE games most enemies were zombies/undead or bioweapons like Mr. X, in RE4 all enemies were humans infected with a mind-altering hive mind parasite or the parasite itself, and in RE7 the Bakers were infected with and mutated by the mold and other enemies consisted of humanoid masses of sentient mold. All RE scenarios feature some level of ridiculousness which require you to suspend your disbelief to a certain degree, but such suspension is impossible when one moment you're fighting a vampire (who later also turns into a dragon no less), then a deformed fish-man, and then a steampunk electromagnetic man; it is simply too much for one game to be even slightly immersive or believable and by extent scary.

Other major issues with RE:Village are the underdeveloped areas of the map and its linearity. Apart from the central village, Castle Dimitrescu, and Heisenberg's Factory, all other areas of the game feel incomplete or rushed, like all resources were poured into the development of the three aforementioned areas while House Beneviento, Moreau's Reservoir, and the lycan Stronghold received the short end of the stick. House Beneviento is stunning visually but it loses all value after one playthrough since it just serves as one big glorified puzzle, the fetus that chases you is entirely scripted and thus poses no real threat or induce fear after the first playthrough, and the pathetic Donna "boss fight" is just hide and seek on a timer. Moreau's Reservoir boils down to a boring linear run to retrieve a few machine parts to drain the water from the reservoir and immediately fight Moreau; you don't get to explore the flooded village even for some loot. At the very least, Moreau is a better boss fight than Donna. The lycan Stronghold feels like completely pointless padding which fails as an intense action segment due ti generally clunky combat and the aforementioned brainless AI of the lycans who surround you and take turns attacking individually rather than as a pack. Though Castle Dimitrescu is great and is one of the few highlights of this game since it's beautiful visually, features a few puzzles, and lady Dimitrescu actually pursues you through her castle, it is the first area you're forced to visit since this game is completely linear and thus is way too short and over way too soon, leaving only Heisenberg's Factory as the only area other than the central village to look forward to because of its great atmosphere, cyborg enemies which are more interesting in comparison to the lycans, and some decent enough exploration and backtracking compared to the rest of the game.

Apart from those three major issues, here are some other issues worth mentioning with RE:Village:

- Ethan's dialogue is dull, cringeworthy, and somehow worse than RE7,
- Guns sound weak and are poorly animated,
- The scope of the sniper rifle is a complete joke as it barely zooms in,
- Horror elements have been toned down considerably from RE7,
- Movement feels twitchy and unrefined compared to RE7,
- Third person point-of-view included in the DLC is very amateurish and looks like a fan-made mod completely unlike the fantastic third person perspective of RE2/RE3/RE4 remake,
- Enemies in the Mercenaries game mode all spawn on set points unlike RE4's Mercenaries, thus every Mercenaries attempt feels the same,
- Chris' action shoot-em-up section at the end of the game tries too hard to be cool and ends up feeling corny.

The only things I can praise about this game are the jaw-dropping, near-photorealistic graphics, its great art direction, and the Duke who's a great mysterious character. Other than that, RE:Village feels like a poor, overambitious mishmash of RE4 and RE7 that fails to live up to either the intensity of RE4's combat and its charm or RE7's terror and horror. 

Overall, I would only recommend buying RE:Village at a hefty discount for one playthrough and instead would recommend saving your money for RE4 (original or remake) if you're looking for a phenomenal action-horror third person shooter or RE7 if you're looking for a terrifying outstanding first person horror experience.

The game follows Ethan Winters, the protagonist of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, as he travels to a mysterious village in Europe to rescue his kidnapped daughter. Along the way, he encounters a variety of enemies and bosses, such as werewolves, vampires, dolls and mutants. The game play is smooth and responsive, with a first-person perspective that enhances the sense of immersion and tension. The game also offers a variety of weapons, puzzles and secrets to discover, as well as different endings depending on your choices. The game also connects to the previous Resident Evil games in clever ways, while introducing new characters and lore. The only downside of the game is the story, which is too much of a fairy tale horror for me. The game deviates too much from the realistic and grounded horror of Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, and instead opts for a more fantastical and over-the-top approach that feels out of place in the series. However, this is just my personal preference, and some people may enjoy this style of horror more. Resident Evil Village is a great game for fans of the series and horror games in general. It is a game that will keep you entertained and amazed.

Definitely one of the weaker Resident Evil games especially if you take replayability - something that Resident Evil as a franchise has always been known for - into account but that’s not to say this is a bad game because there are no bad Resident Evil games. 

Right off the bat you can tell this is aiming for a completely different feel than its predecessor by taking the player away from the damp, claustrophobic Louisiana swamp house and dropping them under broad daylight in the titular Village, where the game opens up almost immediately and you’re (mostly) free to explore whichever direction that your heart’s desire. Which imo is both a good and a bad thing. 

The good being I’ve always liked the idea of having a central hub area where you can come back to for a sense of safety and brief respite from whatever crazy ♥♥♥♥ that’s going down on the outside world since my early days of playing Demons Souls, and despite being a fairly rudimentary implementation of that idea the "village" still serves that function. It’s weirdly comfy just strolling through this snowy, dilapidated village tucked away in some far away mountain ranges in Romania that probably hadn’t seen any outsider set foot in until a random team of video game developers from Japan pulled up and started taking pictures. What’s more the open nature of the map really allows them to play around with optional encounters. There’s now quite a few completely optional and fittingly challenging mini bosses that just roam around freely in some far away corner of the map that you’d have to go out of your way to find like in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Souls game. That sense of player discovery is unique to Village and I appreciate it. 

The bad being, well almost everything else, really. It hasn’t been that long since my most recent playthrough of RE7 and it really solidified what a masterclass particularly in level design that it was. There’s a lot of intricacies within the Baker House that make it feel like it was designed by a group of veteran architects whose main concern was not to build a house that could realistically exist, but one that’s fun to get around in; intricacies that are sadly lost within the wide, open field geography of the village. Open area with a lot of freedom to move around in is just infinitely less interesting to me and probably requires considerably less effort to design, too, than a confined space where you have to constantly rely on your map to navigate, like in RE7. There are some resemblance of that here in the factory section which is a step in the right direction, but it’s a step too small, and too late because within two hours of you getting there the game is over. 

But I’m getting way ahead of myself. This is where I need to start talking, or complaining, rather, again, about the four different sections that this game is split into. I wanna preface by saying all four of these sections are good, just not in ways that make a RE game good. 

First off we have the castle, which for all intents and purposes is your "traditional" RE experience. Or so I’ve heard, until I played it for myself. Because aside from the gothic visuals this entire section is a pretty far cry from your classic RE formula. The layout is too linear and there’s no routing involved whatsoever. All that branching paths is merely an illusion, a ruse to trick your brain into thinking the map is more open ended than it actually is. When in reality it’s pretty much on rails with the occasional, very scripted appearances of a pursuer type enemy to funnel you down a single corridor. It’s a thrilling haunted house ride but none of it feels very organic like in RE7 or the RE2 Remake. Speaking of enemy unless my eyes are deceiving me I’m pretty sure the hooded blind dead (yes that is a Tombs of the Blind Dead reference) share the same animation skeleton with the possessed medieval armor in the RE4 Remake. I would know because as soon as I saw that sword swing animation my muscle memory kicked in and I almost went in for a parry, until I realized I was playing as Virgin "where is my wife and daughter" Ethan, not Chad "Kill zombies. Behead zombies. Roundhouse kick a zombie into the concrete. Blow zombie heads with magnums. Suplex zombies. Feed zombies to lickers. Throw zombies into lava. Blow zombies up with rocket launchers" Leon. Shame. Another nitpick I have to get out of my system is that the castle doesn’t feel very… castly. It may resemble a castle on the outside but as soon as you step through that castle gate it’s like you’re transported to an entirely different structure where the interior could best be described as Spencer Mansion meets Goldener Saal. Now I don’t mean to endlessly heap praise on the RE4 Remake but this is where I have to once again for it really nailing the look and feel of being inside of a medieval castle. 

On to the next section House Beneviento which I think is masterful. Not in terms of gameplay because there barely is any since it’s just a walking simulator with some light puzzle elements thrown in but the buildup of tension is masterfully done. It’s almost 90% buildup with a very gradual escalation and a simmering score in the background but without that buildup the remaining 10% payoff wouldn’t be as worth it. It’s so good in fact that they remade this entire segment pretty much beat for beat in the Shadow of Rose DLC, and it’s just as terrifying if not more so the second time I tell ya. 

Then there's the reservoir which is a platforming section that plays like a 2D Mario game with the most jank boat control you’ll ever experience in a video game. There’s nothing more to say about it really because it’s a nothing burger of a segment that exists only to pad out the length. At least it’s mercifully short. 

Finally we arrive at the factory which I think is the best section for reasons I’ve mentioned earlier. It’s the only section that resembles a classic RE game with its own unique twist on the key hunting and a non linear progression. The rusty, industrial aesthetic, the killer ambiance, and the literal Frankenstein's Army that are the enemies you face off against also do a lot of heavy lifting in making this entire area my absolute favorite. 

At this point you might begin to notice the biggest issue I had with this game overall and that’s a complete lack of tonal consistency and consistency within the locations. Aside from the fact that geographically they all link back to the same village there really isn’t any cohesion between these locations. They feel and play so different from one another it’s hard not to pit them against each other and choose a favorite, like I just did. Hell even RE Revelations, the LITERAL episodic RE game, feels less disjointed than this one. Now I don’t like being overly analytical or worse yet overly critical on things that I’ve enjoyed since I did very much enjoy this game, but it’s hard not to given it bears the RE name, and directly following up RE7 no less - a game that not only revitalized an almost 30-year-old franchise, but one that lots would consider the single greatest survival horror game ever made.

After the absolutely terrifying tour-de-force of classic survival horror that was Resident Evil 7, I was really excited for what was next in this re-invigorated franchise. RE is one of my all-time favorite series, but one I felt began to lose sight of its trajectory around RE4.

I have to admit, seeing the trailers was highly discouraging. Werewolves, vampires, evil dolls -- it was all a step in the wrong direction. Playing the game I realized just how much of a spiritual remake of Resident Evil 4 it was, in all the right and wrong ways. Similarly to RE4, the action-oriented gameplay is a blast and a nice change-of-pace from claustrophobic survival horror. But the more grounded story trajectory they were building toward in RE7 has been thrown out the window and immediately returned to the over-the-top ridiculousness of middle series.

The game is gorgeous and at times, truly scary, though not nearly often enough. Given that they knew they were going to remake RE4 and that it would of course be a smash hit, I just wish they would have stuck to the rootsy terror of RE7, which itself harkened back to the original and timeless classic entries in the series. While Village is a great game, I'm trepidatious about what's in store for the future of the series.

- Really interesting characters and story. They all feel alive and unique, and all the cutscenes and the story are interesting.
- Very pretty. There are some quite imperfect areas, such as clearly 2D grass and other things the game does not manage to hide very well and slightly break immersion, but, at least, the performance is very acceptable even with ray tracing on, so it's still pretty fair.  The game really misses DLSS though, being the main graphical downside of this game.
- Very cool and/or badass cutscenes, and very cool extra Village of Shadows story. One significant issue is that you can't re-watch the dubbed version of it on the Extras menu, as it is hardcoded to english on the main menu version, so that's a significant and annoying oversight.
- Gameplay is usually around a 7/10. Some parts of the game are too easy to get lost in, or you have to walk all the way back, and that could be better, The default difficulty is a bit too easy and most bosses died on the first or second try, yet I'd be scared of the hardest difficulty so I couldn't go for it.
- Some of the "water boss" section is very annoying. The water platforms that fall and instakill you are unfair, tend to oneshot you and just aren't fun, alongside with some similar mechanics on that area. That boss fight itself was pretty meh too so it felt like that entire section was not worth it and not as good as the rest of the game
- Good atmosphere and gameplay balance overall. Fun progression.
- Several bits of good AI, enemies that already attack you as they're coming out of the ground unlike other games or being dragged out of your safe spot by an enemy that knows he can't reach you there just makes the game so much more scary as the enemies are not robotic and those interactions really caught my attention by how much they improved my experience. On the other hand, there are a few bits of bad AI, like Dimitrescu being extra dumb when chasing you, or that clunky fight in a small space against the giant near the end of the game - though if those bits were improved AI-wise, the section would become too hard or too annoying on the current design, and the game ended up going with the dumb route - though thankfully that is only in a few minor parts of the game.

⚫Soundtrack is AMAZING. Especially the ending song for Resident Evil Village is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. I just cannot get enough.
⚫They also added back in the popular mercenaries mode which adds TONNES of replayability.
⚫You can grab yourself even more content as there is a decent DLC for Village - Winters Expansion.

This is an alright third person shooter with a horror setting but a pretty terrible Resident Evil/Biohazard game. Spoilers:
[spoiler]
This game has literally no purpose in the RE universe other than "Oh wow, werewolves and vampires are canon now."  RE isn't a series I hold to a strong story with consistent narrative and plot; but this one doesn't make even a single ounce of effort.  Oh, Miss D. and her 3 daughters are weak to cold?  Good thing they live in the mountains where it's perma-winter.  Oh, and Miss Ds bugs are weak to cold except in the last fight against her where you have to hide inside, away from the cold, to disperse her bugs because the devs have no consistency ever in this game.  

Oh, and Miss D's weakness?  A knife with a bunch of poisons on it that she keeps in her house and never cleaned the poisons off of for...reasons...and then she waits to attack you until you open a coffin and grab the knife in the slowest animation ever.  Because the devs couldn't bother making her first phase weakening her enough that the knife isn't guarded anymore.  They also couldn't make the mansion a mission of getting the poison so you can stab her...instead you get masks to get the knife that has the convenient poisons.  Like...ANY EFFORT...ANY EFFORT AT ALL...and the game could make sense but the writers are not good at their jobs.

Oh, and Miss D that got Twitter all horny, the only reason this game is well reviewed and liked is because twitter got horny for Miss D btw, is only in the game for about 30 minutes.  She's the first boss.  She's not important to the plot at all other than she was there.  

This RE entry also features more walking simulator segments than anything I've ever seen in RE before.  If you really like walking around doing nothing but listening to dialogue and avoiding a giant insta-kill fish...this game has you covered.

There was exactly one (1) fun segment in this whole game: Heisenberg.  The voice actor for H had so much fun with his role and you could really feel it.  The combat in that section was genuinely engaging, the progression felt like old RE progression, and the final fight for that segment felt so epic that they should have just ended on it tbh.  It was perfect.  That section should have been the whole game really.  Just expand it. 

The actual final fight was extremely mid however.  Run in a circle, shoot, run in a circle, shoot, shoot 3 orbs, run in a circle, shoot, repeat.  RE final fights tend to be a let down, so I wasn't surprised, but I wanted a bit more after how epic the preceding fight had been.

Lastly, the DLC.  The DLC was complete garbage.  50% walking sim, 40% Dragon's Lair love letter (QTE sim), 10% actual gameplay.  The final boss was the same final boss from the base game too; which didn't help.  The game tried to make Miranda returning a plot twist; but it was incredibly obvious that Rose was being manipulated by her from the start.

I’m really conflicted about this game. There is so much to like, the setting the characters, the callback to RE4 are all very well done. The return of the “Merchant” titled “The Duke.” The music and sound effects are well done and most of the battles are entertaining. I think my issues with the game it that it tries to be Resident Evil 4 without trying to be its own thing and unfortunely relies of the nostalgia factor. To me RE7 is flat out the better game because of how fresh it was and while the feeling of helplessness was tough at first it eventually became understandable on how to play the game.

RE8 meanwhile just feels off in how they want you to play the game. At first you are completely helpless just like in the last game but over time it becomes much more of a run and gun time game. With that said however the aiming is not great and the general idea of just running in circles to avoid an enemy gets very repetitive especially with most of the boss battles at the end.

I also don’t understand why Chris Redfield’s character becomes so absolutely useless to our main character and the lack of information characters share with each other becomes quite a nuisance. With that said the game certainly is not bad but I would argue unfulfilling. While the characters are interesting we barely get much time with each of Miranda’s “children.” It’s also a big point that there is just a lot of empty parts going on in the game and it feels less like an exploration and more of a to do list. Having so many things revealed early on doesn’t help things either.

Spoilers: I’m not sure how I feel about Ethan, Mia or Rose. I guess Ethan’s story makes sense and it certainly explains a lot of things but Mia still being alive and the mystery of Rose that is just never explained becomes frustrating. Miranda in general is really boring because we flat out do not interact with her at all until the very end. Heisenberg and really all the other children were far more interesting and much more interaction with our main character.

All in all the game does a lot of things right but I think in an effort to recapture the RE4 magic it lost what had made RE7 so refreshing and we are left with a game that doesn’t know what it wants to be.

I enjoyed this a lot after having played the RE4 remake. RE Village is more of the same style of gameplay, though with significantly worse writing (though that mostly adds to the entertainment). This game is lots of fun, and has a couple of truly memorable scary moments.
OUTSTANDING GAME

Good, but disappointing.
The entire game is a mashup of different concepts from several other Resident Evil games:[list]
[*]Storywise is reminiscent of Barry's European excursion from Revelations 2: extremely similar main plot, setting, AND themes. Though the Eastern European setting is more original in Rev2, since it isn't just RE4's village+castle combo, it's a post-Soviet era town with surroundings.
[*]Speaking of RE4: the setting, the desperate defense from a horde of enemies in the beginning, a merchant, upgrading weapons and inventory capacity, no item box, finding treasures, a fish boss. Even the head explosions are similar. There's also a doll based "boss", which seems to be a concept from one of the early versions of RE4.
[*]Mercenaries mode is Revelations 2 Raid Mode with 2% of the content. At best.
[*]RE7's first person camera and a few characters like Ethan.[/list]

There are many problems with simple mechanics:[list]
[*]Enemies are fairly damage spongy even on Standard difficulty.
[*]Hitboxes on enemies and their attacks are inconsistent, e.g. sometimes they attack you through walls (Moreau’s spit), their attack which is supposed to be blocked by terrain, isn’t (Urias), they can damage you in cutscenes (going inside the safe room for the first time in the castle while being chased by Lady D), enemies with thrusting drill attacks (Soldats) have hitboxes so large you’d swear they were swipes.
[*]Some of the boss arenas are poorly designed. What are these areas with the Urias fights supposed to be? Small, cramped spaces against a giant wielding a huge double handed hammer who can spin to win? 2 of the 3 fights against Dimitrescu’s daughters are also 2x2 meter rooms or corridors so narrow you have absolutely no room to maneuver.
[*]There are locations where the enemies just stop pursuing you and walk away after you cross an invisible line. They do not regenerate their health, so it’s easily exploitable.[/list]

My other issues:[list]
[*]No FoV option, even though it was present in RE7. 
[*]To quit the game you have to press Delete; you cannot use the mouse.
[*]Inventory management is pointless. If you buy the larger attache cases, you will only run into inventory issues on your NG+ runs. On your fresh save you don’t have to do anything.
[*]Takes a while to get to the game proper. A ton of cutscenes and scripted sequences at the beginning make repeated playthroughs a chore.
[*]Enemies spam grab moves which have animations so long you'd think they're death animations. Some of them are nearly 10 seconds long. On Village of Shadows difficulty it's even worse.
[*]Puzzles are lackluster. There's one statue puzzle in the castle that has a description more confusing than the actual puzzle.
[*]Ethan behaves either like a badass or a total wimp. It's really jarring and inconsistent. He's also constantly commenting on everything, in contrast to RE7 where he barely reacted to anything: I preferred him mostly silent.[/list]

Biggest positives:[list]
[*]Looks absolutely gorgeous.
[*]I like the Metroidvania gameplay of the village itself.
[*]The combat is satisfying.[/list]

They tried to appeal to both horror and action fans, and while RE6 failed spectacularly in this endeavour, Village appears to have succeeded when looking at the general reception. For me, however, while it's a significantly better game than RE6, it's still unfocused. Each section is distinctly different from the other. It’s theme park horror by design. RE7 was laser focused: it knew what it was and what it wanted to be from start to finish. RE7 was a labor of love. Village seems a corporate creation.

It's still a good game. I finished it several times in a row. But it's a disappointment and I don't think I'll ever touch it again after unlocking all achievements.


Shadows of Rose[list]
[*]The mannequin bit was outstanding. Too bad it lasted only a few minutes and was followed by an awful stealth section that was way too long.
[*]Great scares ruined by a protagonist who doesn't shut up.
[*]Constant re-use of locations.
[*]Unfulfilled potential with the Mutamycete storing memories: they could’ve shown more Lord backstories, or even the Bakers again.
[*][spoiler]Capcom went to comedic lengths to hide Ethan’s face.[/spoiler][/list]

I've heard others describe this game as a "horror theme park" and I think that's an apt analogy. Each section sees you going against a different villain in a different theme, from vampires in a Gothic castle to a factory producing mechanical abominations. It's fun to see the RE/Biohazard take on classic horror monsters, like werewolves and fishmen, while not going too overboard. 

In terms of horror the game gets nowhere near the 7th game (other than one section that is scary the first time but not on repeats), but the pacing is mostly excellent and the action combat feels great. There are a bunch of unlockables that provide a great incentive to play multiple times, and your weapons and tools can carryover into new runs to make even the highest difficulty manageable.

I don't think I will be coming back to this game as much because of the release of the Resident Evil 4 remake, but that's fine. I think this game stands on its own and is worth a couple playthroughs.

It's always challenging to follow up on greatness, which [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was for the survival horror genre. Sadly, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] failed. And I know, I know, [i]"Weird slav man, who haveth a glorious moustache and a smile that brightens up even the blackest abyss, this review of yours has a blue thumbs up, yet it failed? Que?"[/i] Well, thank you. But yes, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] did fail... in being a good survival horror game — [b]still a damn good action game tho.[/b]

So, let's talk about it.

[h3][b]Remember, no horny[/b][/h3]
Village picks up shortly after the last game. Ethan's chilling in his new funky house with Mia, his lovely wife, and Rose, his baby girl, all the way in Europe. Life is good for our boy, as he's far away from all that mold shenanigans. Anyway, [i]pew-pew-pew, punch, baby grab, car crash,[/i] and [b]bam![/b] Ethan's now staring at a giant medieval castle which looms over a small village and has but one thought on his mind, [i]"Where the heck am I?"[/i]

Oh yeah, and he also needs to find his daughter, Rose.

This is a return of the cheese, and lots of it, with outlandishly ridiculous backdrops and villains. And I didn't really care for the main baddies and their silly monologues, except for Lady Dimitrescu. There was just something different about her. Something [i]big[/i], voluptuous, and arresting of my gaze, but I couldn't quite grasp them.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2996106328
And after two games of seeing him flung around like a prop, Ethan grew on me like mold on a stale loaf of bread. Once again, without hesitation, he runs head-first, bare, into a burning building as the fires are being extinguished with gasoline, risking life and limb for those he loves, laughing in the face of death. And that ending... just [b]perfect[/b], that's all I'm gonna say.

Presentation-wise, [i]Village[/i] is a sensory blessing. I don't even need to worry about RE Engine delivering the goods — [b]it's a done deal.[/b] The design of the characters, enemies, the sheer amount of gore and other nasty effects are just incredible. I feel blessed to have my sight, so I can enjoy the brilliance of the RE Engine.

[i]Capcom's[/i] audio game is also on point, with every voice actor doing a great job, especially the villains. They really doubled down on the cheesy delivery and corniness. I liked it. As for the sound effects, look, my ears busted a nut every time I pulled off a headshot on one of the enemies in the game. Do with that graphic imagery what you will.

Now, onto the gameplay.

[h3][b]Spreading American culture in Europe[/b][/h3]
With a more significant focus on action, the freedom arsenal had to expand. And it did. With many guns at his disposal, Ethan effortlessly spreads the gospel of the freedom church, whether these residents like it or not. [b]Shooting still feels meaty[/b], with heads exploding like pinatas, showering me with all their juicy, gooey brain pulp if I'm standing in the splash zone, and I always am!

The pew-pew did stay the same, with only the [i]"parry"[/i] mechanic being new. You can now push enemies away by quickly pressing the block button after an enemy attack lands. So, not really a parry, but also kinda is... Anyway, other areas of the gameplay were slightly tweaked to complement this shift in focus from survival horror to action.

For one, [b]you can now upgrade every gun's stats[/b] (damage, reload speed, etc.) and even outfit them with [b]special attachments[/b], improving their quality. But guns aren't the only thing you can enhance. A delicious meal will not only quench Ethan's appetite for some good ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ food but improve his health, stamina, and so on. And all you need to do is find some wild game and bring its meat back to the Duke — [b]he'll cook you up a fancy meal in a jiffy.[/b]

[b]Resource management[/b] is no longer necessary, with the game showering you with items. And the famous inventory management mini-game returns, with Ethan carrying one spacious man purse. It can hold many items, big and small, and I got to play tons of Tetris, rotating and shifting my things around, all in the name of having everything compact and my inventory looking clean. Pure pleasure!

[h3][b]We're going to Villageland![/b][/h3]
[b]The game resembles a theme park[/b], with Ethan, the (un)lucky kid, getting to enjoy all the fancy rides. So, each level will have its own tale to tell, and will do so on its own terms. [b]The game doesn't have a single concept for every level.[/b] It loves tinkering; each level will deliver a different experience than the one you just beat. One may be super scary, while the next will douse you in water, probably also guts. One may even require you to look inward and start asking yourself the big questions, [b]"Do I have a giantess dominatrix fetish?"[/b] [i]—Yes...[/i]

But, to not spoil what awaits you, I'll briefly summarise the first level, excluding the village (hub area), to tease you a bit.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2993033059
[b]The castle section blends spooky and action[/b], not committing to full-on horror, like one later level, only flirting with it occasionally. And a [i]Resident Evil[/i] map not interconnected as heck is like going to a slava in Serbia and not drinking rakija until you see your ancestors. You just don't do that. So, it's good to see the castle section deliver in this area.

But this is also home to a few horrors and Lady D, who stalks the halls. She was hunting me as I leisurely roamed her residence, breaking stuff (some on accident, I swear) and looking for that next key story item.

And I'mma be honest, while she thicc, [b]her AI also thicc[/b], if you catch my drift. It's super easy to avoid her (not that I wanted to). She doesn't even have an [i]Ethandar[/i]... it's like a gaydar but used for instantly finding Ethan instead of hunky men. So, without one of those, unless I made eye contact with her big... eyes, yes, those, she wouldn't know I was sniffing the air behind her. And with the castle having plenty of rooms, some of which she can't even enter, despite it being [b]her[/b] castle, avoiding her was easy.

So, while Lady D's presence made [i]something[/i] rise, it wasn't the tension.

Thankfully, my biggest issue with [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was addressed as [b]Village boasts excellent enemy variety.[/b] Fighting the same three moldy boys just didn't please me, but [i]Village[/i] pleased me — [b]I'm pleased.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2993516311
And [b]most levels introduce a new enemy[/b], giving combat a new spin. I now had to learn how to deal with this new, different foe from the ones I faced previously. [b]There are even hecking mini-bosses!?[/b] And boy, do they like eating bullets, love 'em, in fact. But feed them enough lead, and they'll eventually end up dead.

But what about them big tidd- I mean, big bosses... Yeah, they're pretty big. Definitely above 5'11''. And while still relying on the lazy [i]pump-and-dump-my-load-into-the-boss'-weak-spot[/i] strategy, each had a cool little gimmick for me to do, which made these fights fun. There's even a fricking mech fight! It was just a blast to blast these big baddies.

So, to end this high-quality review, a conclusive answer to the question, [i]"Is Resident Evil Village good?"[/i] must be given.

I dunno... [b]it's fun tho.[/b] And you know what rhymes with fun — [b]gun...[/b] And you use a gun here. So, make of that what you will.

I was one of the many RE fans that didn't really like how the series went with the success of 4. I liked 4, found 5 to be meh and I didn't play 6 because I heard from reviews that it was basically a pure action game and the survival horror bits from old were pretty much all thrown out, and those were my favorite parts from the RE series. The claustrophobic feeling, finding keys and solving puzzles, all the while killing monsters and worriedly watching your precious ammo dropping, wondering when you'll find more. Those were my favorite parts of the RE games. And they were slowing moving away from that, and with 4, started in a new direction. So I figured 6 killed the franchise since I'd heard it didn't do well and so wrote RE off. But like the zombies of old, they rose again with RE 7. At first I was excited, they were coming back to their survival horror roots, yay! They were bringing back the keys, puzzles and central locations, yay! And it was FPS... crap!
The thought of an FPS Resident Evil filled me with dread and confusion. I thought they were just jumping on the bandwagon of those survival horror games like Alien Isolation, the Amnesia series, Slenderman and all those other FPS games that pitted you against some horrible monster that you couldn't kill, or didn't even have weapons like with some games of the genre. So I wrote off 7 and 8 and just hoped for something better. Then the remakes came along and I was revitalized. With the 40th anniversary of Capcom putting all the RE games on sale, I decided to bite the bullet and fill out the rest of my collection and snap up 5, 6, 7, and 8 for the PC. 7 and 8 are very damn good. I was, quite frankly, shocked and amazed at how good they are. They are pure Resident Evil, all the keys and puzzle solving, limited ammo but enough to kill everything you run into if you aim right and make the right crafting choices. I also was ashamed of myself for not giving 7 or 8 a chance and ignoring them all these years. I might be late to the party, but I finally got here and I am completely enjoying myself.
Bottom line, if you are a fan of the game style of the older games, the puzzle solving, the keys and the claustrophobic feeling of the environment, then 7 and 8 will be welcome editions to your Resident Evil collection!
