Resident Evil Village is the sequel of the outstanding Resident Evil 7, a game that brought me back to enjoying and loving the franchise as I once did some years ago. Raising the bar of its predecessor would be challenging, but certainly not impossible considering Capcom has some of the best talent today among the gaming studios.

Village's story continues where 7 left off and although I'm a pretty strong proponent that story is the franchise's weakest point, I'll always enjoy it for what it is, either serious or in some cases dumb fun. The charm hasn't come off yet and even though the developers are rehashing ideas and swapping them around, I can still go into a new title interested to see new characters and enjoy the story as they present it. This hasn't changed, yet and Village is another game that can boast about characters that one day will be defined as classic.

Gameplay has always been the strongest positive the series had on its belt, which is simple action with an emphasis on shooting, rather than running away. The game can provide a challenge, but unless you're pushing for the hardest difficulty, at a point in the game, you'll be having a blast, blasting enemies, with no sweat present. Everything is quite well streamlined and makes sense, with enough weapons to give satisfaction to those like me who want variety, whether it is because you want to approach an enemy in a particular way or simply because you want to change it up a bit. Speaking of changing, upgrades are available, giving you an advantage over your enemies and making it easier to annihilate them. If upgrades are not enough, do not fret, the shop has returned and there you can buy the necessary tools that will no doubt help you - bullets, for one thing is certain, and that is that if bullets are not enough - buy as much as it will finish the job. Bullets are never enough.

The sound department is exemplary, with voice acting and effects being always a highlight in these series, the soundtrack is very well-suited. There are some great tracks, but here, I have to admit am not a fan of every single one, which will not stop me from saying that is quite a rare occurrence and isn't a big negative in my book.

Overall, Village was a great ride that passed quickly without realisation, and recommend it strongly to those who are looking for more Resident Evil or are wondering if they should commit after finishing 7, but if you haven't played the predecessor, I suggest coming back after, although not required, you'll enjoy it far more. The game is often on sale and the price it goes down to is more than adequate for the quality you're receiving and if you're someone who enjoys replaying games, the game has plenty of content to keep you busy for a while.

Resident Evil 7 was clearly a reimagining of the first Resident Evil, with the mansion, the relatively few monsters and the overall scariness. This one is Ethan Winters' very own Resident Evil 4. You get the intro with a village filled with monsters, the castle tour, the giant aquatic monster, the hordes of monsters, the merchant of dubious origins seemingly everywhere, the weapon upgrades... I like both formulas so I'm fine with it, but it's interesting to see how different those two games are.

I very much liked this opus. It might be because I don't play that many AAA games, but I'm quite impressed by the level of graphical quality. I think it's a very beautiful game. I feel it's important to note that the game handles brightness much better than Resident Evil 7 did. You can actually see what's happening, and you don't have to wait every few seconds for the silly simulated eye adaptation to stop fiddling with the luminosity. The gameplay is standard action Resident Evil fare, except for the lack of melee hits. The progression is a tad weird because the game plays the four heavenly kings one emperor card straight but only two of those five enemies really feel fleshed out. The other three mostly look like quickly thrown-together arcs made just to keep to the original five arcs plan.

The game is of standard Resident Evil length: 2-3 hours if you rush, 8-16 during your first run. After your first run you unlock a new game mode, a new difficulty and a bunch of cheats that become available by getting the game's achievements like in the Resident Evil 2 remake. The additional game mode isn't that good in my opinion, and is mostly about speedrunning through the story levels with different enemy placement and weapons to earn a high score.

The main complaint that I have after putting down the game is about something relatively small, but it really sours my entire impression of it: you're forced to watch a bunch of stuff countless times over. I find it particularly irritating that despite the fact that the developers put in a way to skip cutscenes, they made a conscious effort to make it crappy. They introduced a system that makes it so that for most cutscenes, there will be a pretty long delay between the start of the cutscene and the moment when you can actually skip it. The way they do this is by disabling the game's menu for a time. They also use the same system quite often when you're grabbed by an enemy, making it impossible to go to the menu and choose restart for a few seconds. It is a problem common to lots of games and it is always very irritating, but for this one I'd even call it puzzling, because it's clearly not a mistake or an oversight, but truly intentional, and I just can't begin to comprehend what could go through a guy's head that'd make him waste time to implement something actively bad like that. There's also the issue of some cutscenes not being identified as such and thus being unskippable by default.

In short, it's pretty good but who's the idiot that thought forcing players to sit through cutscenes and grabbing animations was a good idea? Especially in a game series that has always strived for replayability. Please fire that guy. Really.

Resident Evil Village is probably best described as a blend of the first-person perspective and control scheme of 7 with the set pieces, action, and general tone of 4. As a way to conclude the story of protagonist Ethan Winters, it doesn't get too wrapped up in the potential novelty of its villains, providing Ethan room to grow and develop through the story, resulting in a satisfying end to his tenure as the protagonist of the franchise. Taken as a complete package with its DLC, Village feels like a send-off for this era of the franchise, clearing the board for another reinvention whenever 9 comes around.

The gameplay is a clear evolution of 7, taking numerous cues from 4 - upgradeable weapons, a massive inventory thanks to an attaché case, a shop maintained by a mysterious observer to the events of the story, and a much, much faster pace in terms of both combat and story. This is far more of an action game than a horror game - the primary grunts all take what feels like a million bullets to put down, and the lycans in particular move extremely fast and very erratically, creating tension rather than fear. There are elements of the game that evoke horror, particularly the second mansion, but on the whole, horror certainly takes a backseat again here in favor of more intense gunplay. It felt right to me - Ethan certainly isn't a supersoldier or government agent, but he's done this before, and it makes sense that he would be better equipped to fight the horrors head-on, compared to the raw fear and claustrophobia of 7.

Story-wise, it's Resident Evil - fun and campy, but with strong attempts at having heart and genuine emotion at its core. Village is the story of a father trying to save his daughter, and the thread of parenthood follows throughout, reflected in the game's villains as a sort of dark mirror to Ethan's journey, manifesting in different ways for each of the four Lords of the village. There's some nonsense, of course, and the way the game seems to speed up exponentially after the second mansion speaks to some sense of wanting to just get on with it after putting a great deal of work into the first few major set pieces of the game, but despite this, I felt like the game remained well-paced. I do wish we had a bit more time with each of the Lords, though - even Dimitrescu felt like she could have had more screentime. 

There are frustrations, certainly - the lycans got tiresome very quickly, especially in the early game where you are simply not equipped to efficiently deal with them, and parts of Dimitrescu's castle and ESPECIALLY Heisenberg's factory in the late game felt like absolute labyrinths - the factory is probably the worst-designed part of the game, being hard to navigate with a lot of stupidly-strong enemies following behind you and forcing you to blindly run ahead into bad situations lest you get slashed across the back by their stupid drills. I've seen this section be described as "classic Resident Evil" and if that's the case, sheesh. Don't want to go back to that. The central village also felt hard to navigate at times - new sections were un-gated with every Lord taken down, but the game didn't feel like it made it clear how to get to those new areas or where to go in general a lot of the time.

Overall, though, Village is another great game in the modern iteration of this franchise, continuing Capcom's streak of quality releases over the past several years. Memorable villains, a story that kept me engaged enough to give a ♥♥♥♥ where it was going, very satisfying late-game gunplay, and a conclusion to the story of Ethan Winters that left me glad he was given two games to develop. And the DLC is fine, too, which admittedly is all I really have to say about it.

Resident Evil Village, the latest installment in the long-running Resident Evil franchise, takes players on a chilling and intense journey through a world consumed by horror. Packed with a captivating narrative, stunning visuals, and heart-pounding gameplay, this game manages to strike a delicate balance between the familiar and the innovative, resulting in a truly immersive and unforgettable experience.

One of the most impressive aspects of Resident Evil Village is its visual presentation. From the hauntingly beautiful environments to the meticulously crafted character models, the game is a visual feast that pulls you deeper into its nightmarish world. The attention to detail is remarkable, with each location oozing with atmospheric tension and providing a constant sense of dread.

The storyline in Resident Evil Village is both engaging and intriguing. Building upon the events of its predecessor, the game introduces new characters and further explores the lore of the series. The narrative is filled with unexpected twists and turns, ensuring that players are constantly on the edge of their seats. The addition of iconic characters from the franchise's past adds a nostalgic touch that fans will appreciate, while still allowing the game to stand on its own.

Gameplay is where Resident Evil Village truly shines. The combination of intense combat, resource management, and puzzle-solving keeps players engaged throughout their playthrough. The game strikes a fine balance between action and survival horror, providing moments of adrenaline-fueled battles against grotesque creatures as well as more tense, suspenseful sequences. The introduction of the merchant character, Duke, adds a new dynamic to the game, offering upgrades and supplies that enhance the gameplay experience.

The enemy design in Resident Evil Village is truly remarkable. Each encounter with the game's various monstrosities is a harrowing experience that tests your nerves and reflexes. From the relentless Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters to the hulking lycans and other creatures lurking in the shadows, the game's enemies are a constant threat that keeps you constantly on the run.

However, the game's pacing can feel uneven at times. While the initial sections are filled with tension and horror, there are moments in the middle where the pace slows down, and the game loses some of its momentum. Nonetheless, the breathtaking finale more than makes up for any minor lulls, delivering an explosive and satisfying conclusion to the story.

In terms of replayability, Resident Evil Village offers multiple difficulty settings and unlockable bonuses that encourage players to revisit the game. The inclusion of the addictive Mercenaries mode adds an extra layer of longevity, providing a fast-paced and action-packed arcade experience.

In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is a must-play for fans of the survival horror genre and the Resident Evil series. With its captivating narrative, stunning visuals, and exhilarating gameplay, it successfully manages to both honor its roots and carve a path of its own. Despite a few pacing issues, the game delivers a terrifying and unforgettable experience that will leave players eagerly awaiting the next installment in the franchise.

This comparative review will explore these parallels and their implications for the overall gaming experience.

Firstly, the visual design of Resident Evil 8 is reminiscent of BioShock Infinite's distinctive aesthetic. The game's setting, a mysterious European village, is imbued with a sense of eerie beauty that mirrors the floating city of Columbia in BioShock Infinite. The architectural design, color palette, and atmospheric lighting in Resident Evil 8 all echo the art direction of BioShock Infinite, creating a similarly immersive and visually stunning environment.

The gameplay mechanics of Resident Evil 8 also bear a striking resemblance to those of BioShock Infinite. Both games blend elements of exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat in a seamless manner. The player is encouraged to explore their surroundings thoroughly, uncovering secrets and resources that aid in their survival. The combat in both games is intense and strategic, requiring the player to make effective use of their limited resources against formidable enemies. The presence of powerful, unique adversaries in both games—akin to BioShock Infinite's Handyman or Resident Evil 8's Lycans—adds an additional layer of challenge and unpredictability to the combat scenarios.

Also, the narrative structure of Resident Evil 8, while retaining the franchise's signature horror elements, incorporates themes of existential dread and moral ambiguity that were central to BioShock Infinite's storyline. The player is confronted with complex characters and moral dilemmas that blur the line between good and evil, echoing the narrative depth and complexity of BioShock Infinite.

However, it is important to note that these similarities do not detract from Resident Evil 8's unique identity. The game retains the franchise's core survival horror elements, such as the tension-filled exploration of hostile environments and the constant threat of gruesome enemies. Furthermore, the game introduces new mechanics, such as the ability to block and counter enemy attacks, which add a fresh dimension to the gameplay.

Lastly, Resident Evil 8's aesthetic and gameplay similarities to BioShock Infinite contribute to a rich and immersive gaming experience. These parallels, combined with the game's unique elements, result in a compelling blend of familiarity and innovation. It's a game that doesn't really know what it is, but the end result is a good game if a bit unfocused and uneven in quality. It's strong atmosphere and good horror (at times) make it well worth playing, but it falls short of the top tier of RE games.

The highest highs and the lowest lows of the whole experience are showcased in the first few hours of gameplay. Castle Dimitrescu is a masterpiece of unique and engaging level design, while the re4 inspired Village fight is one of the most frustrating experiences I've had in an RE game (at least on hard dificulty).

The reason one area works and one doesn't, is that the movement and combat mechanics are similar to Re7, designed for slow paced oppressive horror. However the game has multiple zones taking design inspiration from re4, which is to say, they're designed like combat arenas. But Ethan isn't an action character. In these areas which feel like a crossover of 4 and 7, the character mechanics and level design simply don't mesh like they should, resulting in the gameplay feeling less tight and satisfying than other areas, and often quite frustrating. Village is at its best when it's being more like 7 than 4. 

In the marketing leading up to release, Capcom made it quite clear RE4 was a big inspiration for Village, but if this was really their intention, they didn't go far enough in turning Village into an action game. Capcom actually intended for Village to be both like 4 and 7. This is shown in their 'themepark of horror' design philosphy. Basically, 'do everything', 'be everything residen evil has ever been'.

This 'themepark of horror' philosophy the game is built on is actually the whole reason the game feels so uneven. Beyond mechanics, its effect on world design means Village tries to divide the game into 4 different themed zones, but it clearly puts varying amounts of effort into each area, resulting in an uneven level of quality throughout, as well as a general feeling of disjointedness that the extremely tightly put together RE7 never had.

At it's strong points, Village is an immensely atmospheric game, with a unique identity, and there are far more high points than low points. For that reason it is well worth playing, among RE games its definitely on the higher end. However when compared to 7 before and 4 remake afterwards, it feels like its in a strange midpoint where it's trying to do what both do while not quite as good as either. I would consider it a 'second rung down' re game.

Rating: 9.6/10 (It's scary good, but not without a few creaky doors)
Resident Evil Village takes the beloved survival horror series to new heights, delivering a spine-tingling adventure that will have you clutching your controller for dear life... and occasionally snorting with laughter. With its mix of creepy ambiance, pulse-pounding action, and a story that's a little more out there than usual, this game is a wild ride that deserves its almost-perfect score of 9.6 out of 10.
Prepare to be immersed in a world of gothic horror and supernatural weirdness. From the moment you step into the village, you'll be greeted by towering castles, mist-filled forests, and a bunch of weirdly friendly locals. The stunning graphics bring every grotesque creature and hauntingly beautiful environment to life in vivid detail. It's like a haunted house comes to life with slightly better Wi-Fi.
The storyline of Resident Evil Village is a deliciously campy mix of Gothic literature, folklore, and B-movie horror. You'll encounter mysterious witches, hulking werewolves, and a certain tall lady who's captured the internet's attention for reasons we won't discuss here. It's a narrative that balances between genuinely creepy and downright hilarious, keeping you engaged while occasionally making you question the sanity of the developers.
The gameplay in Resident Evil Village is a heart-pounding rollercoaster of fear and action. The gunplay feels satisfyingly punchy, and the enemies are delightfully grotesque. Whether you're running for your life from a pack of werewolves or engaging in a tense boss battle, the adrenaline rush is real. And let's not forget inventory management, where organizing your herbs and shotgun shells becomes a strategic puzzle worthy of a Ph.D. in Tetris.
Speaking of puzzles, Resident Evil Village offers a mix of brain-teasing challenges that range from clever to "seriously, who designed this?" Some puzzles are brilliantly designed, requiring you to think outside the box and uncover hidden secrets. Others might leave you scratching your head, desperately trying to find the one obscure item you missed while accidentally throwing explosive barrels at yourself. But hey, it's all part of the fun!
Now, let's talk about the real star of the show: the larger-than-life characters. From the gruff but lovable protagonist Ethan Winters to the delightfully eccentric Duke, the cast of Resident Evil Village oozes personality. And, of course, we can't forget Lady Dimitrescu, the towering vampire queen who has become an internet sensation. She's tall, she's elegant, and she's the reason everyone's upgrading their monitors. Kudos to the developers for creating a character that has taken the world by storm.
While Resident Evil Village is a masterclass in horror and hilarity, it's not without its quirks. Some of the voice actings can be a little... let's just say "charmingly wooden." And there are a few moments where the game takes itself a bit too seriously, causing unintentional bursts of laughter. But hey, it's all part of the charm and adds to the game's unique flavor.
In summary, Resident Evil Village is a spooky, silly, and thoroughly entertaining experience that deserves high praise. It's a game that will make you jump, laugh, and possibly question your sanity. With its hauntingly beautiful visuals, engaging gameplay, and memorable characters, it's a must-play for horror aficionados and fans of the series. Just be prepared to embrace the scares and enjoy the hilariously eerie ride. With a rating of 9.6

Among re7, re2r and 3r, 8 is imo best of them all.

7 felt too short, locations felt really small and, compared to 8, it felt very much like an interactive movie - which isn't bad in itself if the game has some crazy story or spectacle going on that will make use of linearity of the game but alas that didn't really happen in 7. It was just aight.

8 improves on basically everything except the fact that horror elements are rather more sparse (which is not bad in itself too, just different). Big improvement in this game compared to 7 IMO is player agency - weapon progression/upgrade system is MUCH more robust than one in 7 and u will make more of your own choices on what u will want to get first, which items to craft etc. Enemies drop currency which makes killing feel rewarding. There is also a sizable amount of hidden currency items to find in the environment - that too fuels the progression system considerably. You have lots of options to deal with encounters and to power yourself up. Combat feels way better all around, there is much more weapons too.

Difficulty, for a horror game scaredy-cat like me, was really great on Standard mode, I was trying my best and felt rewarded for it without the game feeling like a cakewalk. 

Story is similar in quality to 7 but imo a bit more intriguing. It has some very wacky stuff in it that made me go like "why would you do that" (same in 7) and i did not like such moments but overall it is cool. Characters (mostly antagonists) are neat and some plot reveals were great even though i was confused for the big part of few last hours and had trouble telling who is who lol. What. A. Masterpiece. 

This game is best described with the word: evolution. My first impressions were somewhat mixed - why is this a Resident Evil game? It went kinda-sorta fantasy, there are some character elements that are outright magical, the creatures are all over the place because the devs thought it would be fun to have X or Y type of monster too and didn't bother to keep to a coherent world and lore direction that fits into the world of Resident Evil. Then, you start to see the signs, which I will not spoil here to preserve the experience of exploration for you. Then the signs become hard facts, and you are allowed to peak behind the curtain from time to time, and as you piece together the "meta puzzle" about how this game connects to the rest of the franchise, it starts to transform into an integral part of the overarching story, which is best enjoyed if you played Resident Evil 7 - this is a direct continuation of that, in more ways than just the protagonists (Ethan and his family).

This evolution as your perception of the game changes over time does not stop at lore and presentation. It also applies to gameplay - what starts out as a linear cinematic experience will evolve across multiple stages of semi open world, full open world, and more linear sections that change in perfect rythm and harmony. What I could've lived without was the RPG elements (collecting money to upgrade weapons) but it's really not too bad, frankly, you can ignore it entirely if you want to - your pistol doing 150 damage to 190 fully upgraded means what, 2-3 bullets difference? The game also explores horror in a way that most other horror games do not: for each of it's major parts (I'm avoiding words that would identify what parts I mean), there is a different type of horror. One is psychological, another is mechanical bodyhorror, yet another has an invulnerable pursuer in a labirinth (a la RE2), and even some lovecraftian elements in another, but the thing is, naturally exploring the game, you won't get a sign that "here starts this part". It's seamlessly melting into each other of course, nobody warns you that here starts this or that kind of experience, and that's a huge part of what keeps tension up, hand in hand with trying to wrap your head around a hundred "but how?" questions as you try to make sense of how these seemingly fantastical elements fit into the "realistic" world of Resident Evil. Lots of time we - me and my fiancé - said, yeah that's just lazy writing, and turns out it was done that way on purpose because of a twist later on.

Then you finish the game, and it's wonderful ending ties it all up. And if you are like me, you stop here. But VILLAGE keeps throwing things at you to fill that, RE3 style: you get a shop with points you get from achievements, where you can buy new weapons and upgrades, buy 3D models and concept arts (which come with tons of developer notes explaining the design choices, it's not just art), how it's made videos for cutscenes, things you usually find in collector's edition boxes on a separate disc but it's part of the core game here and I very much appriciate it. In fact, I'll replay it in the future on higher difficulty because of these. There is also a weird survival arena game mode called Mercenaries which is unlocked after the story, if that's your thing. 

One little negative is that enemies cristalize and turn to dust upon death - unlike in RE2, RE3, RE7 - and when they don't, they can still drop items like ammo. This took away a large part of the tension, because you just *know* they died, while in previous games you could not know if they'll wake up again, and again, and maybe bite your leg when you walk by. The game is generous with ammo aswell so aside from the start and maybe later in a certain location, you won't feel like "oh god I don't know what's ahead of me and I have 2 shotgun shells", you'll have hundreds of ammo and that kind of made the game more Rambo style after the early village areas / first major location after the village. 

So to summarize:
+ RE Engine: graphics and optimization is god-tier.
+ Highly varied style / approach to horror as a genre
+ Amazing story which is the most surprising part of the positives, easily the best across the franchise
+ /- Best enjoyed if you played and finished Resident Evil 7
- Enemies disappear / drop loot upon death, decreasing tension, because you know they won't wake up
- Generous with ammo: decreasing tension as you progress and become a walking one man army.

Resident Evil Village is a strong follow-up to Resident Evil 7, delivering an engrossing horror-action experience with some of the series’ most memorable locations. The standout feature here is the variety and creativity of the environments — from the gothic grandeur of Castle Dimitrescu to the unsettling psychological horror of House Beneviento, each boss location feels distinct and engaging. The exploration in these areas is atmospheric and fun, pulling you in with strong pacing and environmental storytelling.

However, while the settings are fantastic, the actual boss fights tend to fall short. Most of the major encounters devolve into fighting large, grotesque blobs with glowing weak spots — a formula that becomes repetitive, especially considering how unique the build-up to each boss often is. There’s a clear contrast between the creativity of the journey and the simplicity of the final fights.

Performance-wise, the game mostly runs well, but there are noticeable FPS drops in certain areas — particularly on the upper floors of Castle Dimitrescu. This is disappointing since the castle is not only the first major area but arguably the best in the game. On a high-end GPU like the 3080 Ti, this kind of stuttering feels out of place.

Despite these issues, Resident Evil Village still excels in immersion, atmosphere, and pacing. It’s a polished horror-action hybrid that pays homage to past entries while pushing the series in an exciting direction. A must-play for fans of the franchise.

In the hallowed annals of the gaming pantheon, there emerges a beguiling opus known as Resident Evil Village, an ambitious endeavor that, alas, stands as a valiant attempt to recapture the transcendence that was Resident Evil 4. Verily, it must be said that this endeavor hath not achieved the zenith of its predecessor's brilliance. However, in the realm of relative comparisons, it doth soar above the lamentable shortcomings of Resident Evil 7, thereby illuminating a glimmer of promise within its sprawling tapestry.

Within the vast expanse of this intricate creation, one finds oneself inexorably drawn into its dark embrace, ensnared by the intermingling threads of nostalgia and novelty. Its visual opulence, meticulously crafted and rendered with an attention to detail that borders on the ethereal, stands as a testament to the wondrous potential of contemporary graphical prowess. From the foreboding shadows that dance upon ancient corridors to the sinewy textures that breathe life into the uncanny inhabitants of this macabre realm, every pixel reverberates with a sense of foreboding and visual splendor.

Yet, it is not merely in its visual majesty that Village finds its potency, for the audial symphony that accompanies this harrowing journey is an orchestral marvel in its own right. The soundscape, a delicate fusion of haunting melodies, spine-chilling ambience, and bone-chilling sound effects, ensnares the senses in a vice-like grip, heightening the atmosphere of dread and trepidation. It is in this synergy of sight and sound that the true horror of this realm manifests, leaving an indelible imprint upon the very fabric of one's psyche.

Among the rogues and miscreants that populate this twisted landscape, a particular figure emerges with an air of resplendent magnetism. Heisenberg, a villain of enigmatic allure, exudes an aura of cool detachment that captivates the discerning eye. Clad in a sartorial elegance that befits his status, he commands attention and leaves an indelible impression upon the annals of gaming antagonists. His enigmatic presence, coupled with his formidable abilities, stands as a testament to the imaginative prowess of the game's designers.

As one delves deeper into the intricate web of Resident Evil Village, it becomes evident that the echoes of Resident Evil 4 reverberate throughout its corridors, seeking to rekindle the fire of adulation that once burned so brightly. Alas, despite its earnest endeavors, it falls short of replicating the transcendence of its forebear. The magic that made Resident Evil 4 a timeless masterpiece remains elusive, casting a shadow upon this valiant attempt to capture lightning in a bottle once more.

Nevertheless, it would be remiss to dismiss Resident Evil Village entirely, for within its flawed tapestry lie moments of undeniable enjoyment. The ebb and flow of gameplay, the heart-pounding encounters with grotesque abominations, and the spine-tingling exploration of its treacherous environs coalesce to form a compelling experience. It is in these fleeting instances of triumph and discovery that the game shines, pulling the player deeper into its haunting embrace.

In conclusion, while Resident Evil Village may fall short of the lofty standards set by its illustrious predecessor, it does possess a measure of merit that outshines the lamentable missteps of its immediate predecessor. As one traverses its winding corridors and grapples with its harrowing challenges, the visual splendor, haunting audial tapestry, and the charismatic allure of certain individuals within its nightmarish domain create a captivating experience that deserves recognition. Embrace its flaws with tempered expectations, and thou shalt find a journey worth undertaking within the tenebrous heart of RE: Village.

The pace continues the theme since RE4, where you begin in a seemingly unwinnable situation but then a cut-scene takes over and the game truly starts. Great story line, won't make you pull your hair out in frustration and comes packed with great characters. Script could be a bit cringey at times but did not detract from the fun.

[b]Cost, AUD:[/b] N/A, gifted.

[b]Time to finish:[/b] Finished the story in just over 10 hours.

[b]Difficulty setting:[/b] Normal.

[b][u]PC specs[/u][/b]

Motherboard: ASUS ROG STRIX Z490-E
CPU: Intel i7 10700K @ 3.8GHz
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 3080 10GB
RAM: 32GB DDR4 1600MHz
Drive: Silicone Power 500GB M.2 PCIe SSD
OS: Windows 11

[b]Performance:[/b] Surprisingly smooth. I played with everything on Ultra, and even had raytracing enabled and I still got 100-120 FPS. The devs did a great job of optimising this game's performance. The one small thing I noticed was near the end of the game where you see [spoiler]the megamycete flailing around in the background, it looked like it was playing at considerably less than 30 FPS.[/spoiler] 

[b]Graphics:[/b] I don't much care for snowy landscapes and environments in games, so I won't do the designers a disservice by commenting on that, however, the other environments were done very well. In particular, [spoiler]Castle Dimitrescu[/spoiler] had so much attention to detail, and [spoiler]Heisenberg's Factory[/spoiler] had so much character to it. Although there were many different designs, each of them felt very Resident Evil. 

And of course, the enemies. Wow, these were really something to look at. I liked how each area had their different enemy type that fit in with it. The bosses, especially were so incredible. To see them [spoiler] transform into their mutations[/spoiler] was both disturbing and awe inspiring. 

[b]Story:[/b] I enjoyed the story in this game. While the general story line itself ([spoiler]save daughter, kill the bad guys[/spoiler]) wasn't anything revolutionary, it was the characters themselves, the world that they built and the way that it was all put together that made it fit right in to the Resident Evil world. I enjoyed it every step of the way.

[b]Gameplay:[/b] This game is Resident Evil through and through. From the inventory management (you DID keep your inventories sorted nicely, didn't you?) to the gun upgrades, the light crafting, the item combining, the weird (but admittedly quite nice) merchant, the puzzles, the bosses...it was all so....Resident Evil. I know, I've said that 3 times in this review, but dammit it's applicable. My ONLY gripe with the entire experience was that some areas are (seemingly) arbitrarily closed off once you leave the area, which sometimes isn't exactly all that obvious, until you realise you forgot to go check out that one thing in the castle, so you try and go back but....nope, door's locked. What about through the front? Nope! Mildly frustrating.

[b]Bugs:[/b] None.

[b]Final thoughts:[/b] Resident Evil Village is a great addition to the franchise and I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. It doesn't revolutionise anything, but it does what it does well. It's just a great Resident Evil game, plain and simple.

[b]Do I recommend this game?[/b] Since I didn't purchase this game myself, I can only infer its value, but looking at the current price of the game on sale websites, (approx. $20 AUD) I can wholeheartedly recommend this game. It's short, but it's very well done!

Ah Resident Evil, licence culte du genre  Survival Horror. 
Me concernant, j'ai commencé la licence au 5  J'avais adoré Resident Evil 5 à l'époque sur Xbox 360, même si le Gameplay était particulier, et même ici l'ayant refais sur PC avec les DLC's, je continue à adorer ce jeu, et je vais le dire, c'est celui que je préfère de la Licence. 

Avant de vous parlez de ce Resident Evil Village, je me dois de vous donnez mon ressenti sur les différents Resident Evil auxquels j'ai pu jouer:

J'ai découvert Resident Evil 4 il y a quelques mois seulement sur PC, et personnellement, je ne comprends absolument pas son succès et pourquoi tout le monde considère que c'est UN des meilleurs de la Licence, les gens ont critiqué violemment RE5 car trop d'action et le côté Survival Horror a été délaissé, alors qu'entre nous, RE4 c'est la même chose mais à mon sens en pire. J'ai passé un mauvais moment sur le 4 car principalement je trouve les environnements franchement pas dingue (notamment la dernière partie sur l'Île qui est infâme), les Boss sont pas dingues non plus (excepté U-3 et le Verdugo que j'ai beaucoup aimé), les musiques sont pas marquantes quand tu les compares au 5... Bref, je n'aime pas le 4 et c'est UN des pires auquel j'ai pu jouer.

J'ai pu me faire récemment Resident Evil 6, et on ne va pas se mentir, c'est pas un Resident Evil, c'est un jeu d'action TPS, y a réellement la Campagne de Léon qui représente Resident Evil avec une ambiance angoissante et horreur, la Campagne de Chris est catastrophique (c'est Call of Duty), la Campagne de Sherry j'ai personnellement bien aimé (sauf le passage dans la Neige qu'est pas ouf) et la Campagne d'Ada je l'ai trouvé très moyenne. Bref, c'est un très mauvais RE mais un jeu d'action sympathique.

Concernant Resident Evil 2 Remake (je n'ai pas fais l'original), j'ai énormément apprécié le jeu, le seul défaut qui m'a franchement dérangé, c'est le backtracking (notamment t'as plus de place dans ton inventaire, donc il faut que tu retournes dans la pièce de Sauvegarde pour déposer ton stuff dans le Coffre), pour ma part, c'est un très bon Resident Evil. 

Pour Resident Evil 3 Remake, j'ai personnellement apprécié la partie de Jill mais j'ai détesté jouer en tant que Carlos (car une fois de plus, c'est du Call of Duty), et le Nemesis et ses 3 ou 4 affrontements sont bidons (sauf le 1er que j'ai plutôt apprécié), en conclusion, je n'ai pas aimé RE3 Remake (même si ce n'est pas une merde, mais c'est très très moyen).

Voilà, nous allons pouvoir passer à Resident Evil Village, je n'ai personnellement pas joué au 7.

Je vais commencé par les Qualités du jeu puis j'enchaînerai sur les Défauts du jeu:

Qualités:

Le Lore, c'est personnellement UNE des choses que j'ai le plus aimé dans le jeu , l'Univers à la Castlevania, le bestiaire (Lycans, "Vampires", Gargouilles... y compris la majorité des Boss à l'exception de Moreau), les Environnements proposés (le Village, le Château Dimitrescu, Maison Beneviento...)

- Son Ambiance, c'est lié aussi au Lore mais j'ai trouvé l'ambiance franchement génial, mention spéciale au Meilleur moment que j'ai pu vivre dans un Resident Evil tous jeux confondus de la Licence (passage Beneviento), ce passage est exceptionnel, ça respire du Resident Evil à l'état pur.

- L'Histoire, j'ai trouvé le Scénario plutôt intéressant, alors certes c'est tarabiscoté par moment (notamment sur la fin), mais je l'ai trouvé intéressant et plaisant à suivre.

- Les Graphismes + La Direction Artistique, le moteur RE Engine est magnifique (mais c'est pas étonnant, on a déjà pu voir ce moteur sur le 7 ou sur RE2 et RE3 Remake), les Textures sont très jolies et mention spéciale aux effets.

- L'Optimisation, elle est bonne, j'ai quelques chutes d'FPS de quelques millisecondes à certains moments bien précis mais c'est pas dérangeant, en revanche, le jeu consomme beaucoup de VRAM (j'en ai 12 et j'ai pas pu mettre au Max les Textures, le reste des Options Graphiques aucun souci).

- "L'Exploration", j'ai adoré me perdre dans ce Village ou dans les autres environnements afin de récupérer tous les Trésors ou à affronter les Boss Optionnels.

- La Bande Son, elle fait le taf, les doublages sont bons (notamment la VO mais la VF est bonne), les Musiques sont sympas mais beaucoup d'armes manque d'impact, c'est le petit reproche de cette bande son selon moi.

- La Durée de Vie + La Rejouabilité, j'ai terminé le jeu une première fois en 10 heures environ (en Hardcore et ce qui est bien), trop ça aurait été chiant (j'y reviendrai dans les Défauts), concernant la Rejouabilité, cela va dépendre de vous, vous débloquerez le Mode Mercenaire et puis vous débloquez la Boutique Spéciale ainsi que les Défis (qui vous donnent des Points pour acheter des Figurines, des Arts Works mais surtout acheter la possibilité d'avoir munition infinie sur l'arme que vous voulez, cependant vous devrez améliorer au maximum l'arme que vous voulez ce qui est très chère). J'ai refais le jeu 4 fois au dernier niveau de difficulté soit Village of Shadows puis j'ai joué au Mode Mercenaire un peu, j'ai donc terminé mon "Aventure" en 37 Heures environ.


Je vais désormais passer aux Défauts:

- Le Gameplay, il n'est pas mauvais, il est plaisant mais j'entends par là que dans les phases ou ça dégueule d'action, le gameplay n'est pas adapté car tu te fais défoncer et c'est bordélique.
- L'Effet Sacs à PV, c'est ce qui m'a le plus gonflé dans le jeu, tous les ennemis sont beaucoup trop résistants (en Hardcore, comptez 8-10 balles en Headshot sur un simple Lycan (même lorsque votre Pistolet est amélioré, en Village of Shadows j'en parle pas, c'est terrible), c'est la même chose pour les Boss (qui ont tendance à traîner en longueur à l'exception de Beneviento et Heisenberg).

- Le Game Design (notamment le Passage de l'Usine d'Heisenberg, je trouve cet environnement mal pensé, je m'y suis perdu plusieurs fois tellement c'est mal fait).

- La Progression du Jeu, j'entends par là que le jeu m'a fait rager à plusieurs moments et ça chauffe le chaud et le froid: 
 le début est catastrophique (où vous devez survivre à l'assaut des Lycans), c'est catastrophique car ici c'est Call of Duty mais t'as pas de balle donc tu peux rien faire. Ensuite, le passage au Château Dimitrescu est relativement bien (l'exploration), mais les Combats contre les Filles Dimitrescu et Dimitrescu elle même sont pas fou).
Le passage avec Beneviento est exceptionnel, je n'ai rien à redire.
Le passage avec Moreau est pas dingue du tout, l'environnement est très dégueulasse et n'est pas intéressant, et le combat contre Moreau est beaucoup trop long et n'est pas très palpitant.
Le passage de la Forteresse est d'une nullité affligeante, là sans rire, vous affrontez une soixantaines d'ennemis, c'est très mauvais car le Gameplay n'est pas du tout adapté à de l'Action pure contre des dizaines d'ennemis).
Idem pour l'Usine d'Heisenberg, environnement pas intéressant et bordélique avec beaucoup trop d'action, l'exploration reste cool et le combat contre Sturm et Heisenberg je les ai bien aimé).
Le passage avec vous savez qui je l'ai bien aimé mais c'est également du Call of Duty avec du Gears of War, ça dégueule d'action.
Et la dernière partie où l'on affronte le Boss Final est sympathique.


Pour conclure, j'ai passé un bon moment sur le jeu, j'ai quand même presque 40 heures mais honnêtement, il n'y aurait pas eu les Défis et le Mode Mercenaire, j'accorderai au jeu un 13-14/20, ici grâce à la rejouabilité et j'ai pu plus apprécié le jeu, je lui accorde un 15/20. C'est un Resident Evil que je trouve sympathique mais loin d'être incroyable, si vous aimez la Licence, je vous le conseil mais en promo, pas au prix fort.

Resident Evil Village is a good game from start to finish with nice combat mechanics that felt really good and satisfying. While the horror elements could have been more consistently terrifying throughout the game, the unforgettable House Beneviento chapter sent chills down my spine. Though on the shorter side, the inclusion of New Game+ and its replayability factor made every moment worth it.

Unlike RE 7, the game does draw you to play a second time and it's not boring at all.

About the combat system, I loved it, it felt the best combat system so far in a resident evil game, guns are all interesting and feel good shooting them, there was plenty of strategic resource management, 
and some intensive enemy encounters, making those encounters a white-knuckle experience.

I feel like I have to talk about the horror aspect, and my feeling there are mixed.

1. The castle level does not feel as scary as let's say the Baker's house of re 7, even though Dimitrescu is tall and scary, they way she 
walks in the house feels like she doesn't actively chase you as with Mr. X or Jack Baker. It's ok but could've been better.
2. House Beneviento level saves the situation since it was an actually scary level, immersing me in an atmosphere of dread and psychological horror.

The game could have benefited from a longer overall playtime. While not as short as its predecessor, it felt like it ended too quickly even with me looting everything out of existence...

From a technical perspective the game for me didn't have any problems and there weren't any bugs as far as I can tell.

Conclusion:

Resident Evil Village provides an enthralling experience with its captivating combat, satisfying replayability, and unforgettable moments of terror.
The House Beneviento chapter stands as a masterclass in horror, leaving a lasting impression on everyone about to play the game.
While the game could have been longer and scarier throughout (which is my main complaint), the inclusion of New Game+ make it a title worth revisiting.

Game is an easy 8/10 for me and worth getting it.

Note: I haven't played the DLC with Rose but I doubt that would change anything on the above review.

1. Defrost your steak (in less than an hour)

I’m not a great planner, so there are plenty of nights I’m in the mood for steak but the only steaks in the house are in the freezer. Not a problem. I fill a bowl of water (not warm) and place it on the counter and put the frozen steak (in its package) in the water for an hour. Sometimes I’ll change the water halfway through - and 60 minutes later my steak (or ground beef, or chicken breast) is thawed. Tip: There can be small holes in the cryovac plastic wrap so inspect your meat package before placing it in the bowl of water. 

Never defrost your steak in the microwave or on the kitchen counter - for food safety reasons.

2. Don’t cook a cold steak
To ensure the steaks cook evenly, it’s important to let your steak come to room temperature before cooking it (if you have time). You don’t need to wait until the meat is exactly 72 degrees. And you certainly don’t need to take its internal temperature with a meat thermometer. I usually try to leave my steaks out for an hour or so before cooking.

3. Pat your steaks dry before cooking
Before placing your meat on the grill or in a pan, pat them dry using paper towels. This is particularly important if the meat is seeping a bit of blood. One method I use is to place a stack of paper towels under the steak and another stack on top. Press down gently and pat down the sides of the meat. 

Drying the meat with a paper towel just before cooking will ensure good contact between the steak and the pan. If it’s not dry it won’t get crispy on the outside.

4. Don’t over-season your steak
I’ll admit it right off - the only seasoning I use on my steaks is salt. Salting is a crucial part of the seasoning process. Salt releases moisture in the muscle of the meat and releases the natural flavors of steak. I season my steaks with kosher salt just as I put them in the pan - but some chefs suggest adding the salt right after you take the meat out of the refrigerator. I don’t think that matters a whole lot - but whatever you do, don’t wait to season until you’re serving.

Even top steakhouse chefs limit their seasoning to salt, black pepper and, perhaps, garlic. You want to let the wonderful flavor of the steak be the star.

5. Use the right cooking oil
I was doing this one wrong until very recently! I was using olive oil but it was always smoking. I discovered that’s because it has a low smoke point (300 degrees). The best oils for cooking steak are avocado oil, soybean oil, and canola oil - all of them have a high smoke point between 400 and 520 degrees. Another alternative is clarified butter - with a smoke point of 450 degrees. 

6. Use the right pan and make sure it is very hot
These days, many steakhouse chains  use infrared broilers with their steaks to ensure extremely high temperatures and even heat distribution. Unfortunately, most of us don't have the luxury of such kitchen gear at home. I recommend using cast iron skillets  because they hold heat, which ensures the right sear and caramelization. Since cast iron is a dense metal, it also ensures even heat distribution. This, in turn, translates to evenly cooked and browned steak. No matter what, insure your skillet is very hot, but not smoking.

7. Don’t worry about how often you flip your steak
You’ve probably heard that you shouldn’t flip your steak too often. I’ve read up on this and it seems top chefs say not to worry about it - and, in fact, flipping it often might improve the final result (because it will cook more evenly through the center).

8. Don’t overcook your steak
My daughter recently told me she was nervous about cooking some Ribeyes and I reassured her there was only one really bad thing she could do - she could overcook it.

It can be tricky - This is because how fast your steak cooks depends on the thickness of the cut and the temperature of the grill or skillet. Sure, you can cut into the steak to check whether it's ready but I don’t recommend doing that since it lets out the juices.

I use a meat thermometer - always. Available in either digital or analog versions, meat thermometers are inserted into the center of the meat to gauge its internal temperature. In the case of a medium-rare steak, this should be around 125-130 degrees Fahrenheit. However, because the steak will continue to cook on the plate, it should be removed from the source of heat when it's 5 degrees Fahrenheit lower than the desired temperature.

9. Let the steak rest before serving
When you prepare a steak on a scorching hot skillet or grill, you're forming a crust that locks in moisture. If you cut into your steak right after it's removed from heat, you risk losing all these wonderful juices. Thin steaks should rest between five and seven minutes, while thicker cuts of meat should sit out on the plate for at least 10 minutes. You can even use a meat thermometer to check if your steak is sufficiently rested. No matter how thin or thick the steak, ideally you want its center to cool down to 120 degrees Fahrenheit.

10. Cut against the grain and serve on a warm plate
How you present a steak can have a huge impact not just on its visual appeal but also on its flavor and texture. If you want to cut the meat prior to serving, always cut against the grain or perpendicular to the direction of the muscle fibers. Since muscle fibers can be on the tough side, slicing through them will make the beef more tender. Slicing along the muscle fibers, on the other hand, will have the opposite effect, making the steak chewier.

Another trick to elevating your home dining experience is by warming the plate prior to serving. This is because a warm plate helps to maintain an even temperature of the food while a cold one absorbs its heat, which could translate to a lukewarm steak. One of the best ways to warm your plates is by stacking them in the oven set at a low temperature or by placing them on the stovetop burner.

In summary, Resident Evil Village is a fantastic addition to the long-running series that both honors its roots and pushes the franchise forward. The game's exceptional graphics, immersive music, and superb voice acting create a captivating world that's difficult to leave. Although the story can be a bit convoluted, it doesn't take away from the overall enjoyment of the game, especially for those familiar with the series. Resident Evil Village is the 8th installment in the franchise. The series has had dynamic shifts since its original releases, from camera angle to genre shifts. While Resident Evil 7 was an entirely new package with lots to explore and get scared for, its promising first act leaves the finale less than desirable. With this newest installment, I was excited as to how the game would play out. At first glance, there was immediately an emphasis on more open world and a particularly dashing vampire mother. The trailers built up major hype, and I was more than ready for the release. After playing, I'm sad to say a lot of the hyped aspects of the games such as the castle and horror fall flat. Almost pathetic puzzles ruin any sort of brain usage, and the ammo and health crafting is completely foreign in comparison to its horror SURVIVAL label as a game. That being said, it's hard to fault the story, considering this is Resident Evil, but my main complaint I still hold is how Chris was butchered. The writers forced things that left me confused and angry. In terms of strength, this game still has many. MOST of the bosses are cool and their fights enjoyable. A large weapon variety builds on that Resident Evil 4 feeling of being an action hero in a desolate battlefield. Enemies are engaging and mostly well designed. The horror aspect is there, especially in the factory. I genuinely felt fear for the first time in a long time from a game. Exploration, while limited, is rewarding and fun. The game runs vert smoothly with beautiful graphics. Witty banter is exchanged between the Duke and Ethan, which lightens rather dark moments. But that brings me to Ethan. As much as I ignored his dry attitude in the last game, I simply can't help being pulled out of the thrill by his empty remarks. He simply cannot shut his mouth during awesome parts of this game, immediately ending any immersion. Overall, I'd say new players will enjoy quite a bit, while returning players may feel it to be repetitive and nuanced. 8.5/10.

The RE franchise tries to do more horror in their games, and this is one of the entries that tries and almost fails that attempt. While doing so, almost ruins the gameplay loop to boredom and repetition but only almost.

This game is more horror and intense, but also not. My advice would be : ignore certain story points. The story is weakness and strength. On one hand it has intense moments that let you feel the horror and on the other you think the protagonist has severe brain damage and needs a doctor or a severe blow to the head. Another thing is certain NPC and the PC are "over acted" in their voice, and it feels cheap and/or annoying but other times and sounds amazing, and you can hear the emotions clearly.

Gameplay wise there are some good points: the look and the atmosphere, but sadly the shooting feels not good. The problem goes for the whole fighting system. As if the game was designed at the base without fighting and the fighting added later. It is clunky, slow, unresponsive. BUT at some points the fighting feels right (certain bosses). As if the game knew "Oh Lord, he/she will ALT+F4 any moment I need something to keep him/her on the game" and throws a good moment or boss at you. 

As you can see there is a pattern of "boring and/or annoying" and "cool, give me more" that repeats until the end of the game. For me it was enough to carry on.

TLDR or short verdict:
The Story is badly written, with sometimes good dialog and ideas surrounded by boring clutter. The optic and atmosphere is most of the time great. The performance is okay, but sometimes there are some FPS drops, but only for a moment (at least for me). 

So all in all a solid experience 6.5 out of 10.
(For reference, a good game begins at 8 and a bad is below 4, ergo everything between "above 4" and "below 8" is a solid experience with some drawback)

The level design of this game is immaculate. You always know where to go next, while you are also encouraged to explore and find secrets. You never have to backtrack, unless there is something waiting for you along the way, and you revisit a lot of places for a sense of nostalgia throughout the game. There is a kind of hub area as well, that you come back to fairly frequently, and throughout the game you unlock new paths around the village so that exploring becomes easier. I'm a sucker for good level design and this game just does it perfectly.

Combat is really fun as well, especially because you can explode the heads of certain enemies, which is really satisfying. Enemies also react to where you shoot them, so you can develop your own strategies against different enemies, depending on how you want to play or if maybe, you're short on ammo.

The pacing of the game is great as well. Areas usually start off a bit slow and ramp up until a climax where you can have some peace of mind, before either continuing that sense of serenity to give you an opportunity to enjoy the environment or give you a hint that the worst is yet to come. Some areas show this type of curve through combat, where you kill a few smaller enemies, then some larger ones or greater numbers, leading into a bigger fight later. Other areas contain no combat, but play more into fear and panic to give the same sort of tension.

In terms of gameplay elements, there are only a few (seeing as it is an first person horror game, that shouldn't come as a surprise). You shoot enemies with your weapons, explore to find resources and valuables, which you can use to upgrade your weapons. For me, this type of gameplay loop is a big hit. It's simple and to the point, but every element of it has been mastered. Exploring is really fun, killing enemies is really fun, and getting upgrades makes you feel powerful, which, you guessed it, is really fun.

The story is a give or take. The very short version of the story is that your daughter is kidnapped and you have to go through five lords in order to get her back. Of course, there is much more to it, most of which you have to read in files that you find throughout the game. Either you like it or you don't, I won't say much more about it.

I can't exactly explain why, but the game has incredible replayability value. I've replayed the story around 15 times and I still think I'll play it again. Worth every last penny.

My favorite Resident Evil so far.

I probably haven't got much to say that hasn't been said already, but the game is fantastic.

Graphics are amazing indoors but outdoors it suffers a little, making terrain and nature look very weird and unrealistic sometimes. Sound design is very well done. Gameplay and controls? As you would expect of the RE franchise. Nothing new really, but it's very well done.

Level and game design are also great, innovating on each area whilst unlocking treasures in old ones. Progression and objectives are clear, there are no tedious sections or puzzles and I really value that. The game is way more action-based than RE7 losing a bit of the puzzle aspect of the previous one; whether that's good or bad is up to you. There's one area in particular in which the game turns into a survival, but other than that, you'll probably have a good stock of ammunition throughout your playthrough.

I loved the story. In fact, RE8 is one of those games in which I even read all the documents I found scattered throughout the game. It's well integrated and brings new perspective to the old games as well.

Content-wise, again, it's as expected of a RE game. You have your relatively "short" campaign that you can replay with many unlockables after you beat it the first time. It took me eight and a half hours according to the game's stats. There's some DLC which I won't get but I'll definitely watch the Rose one on YouTube.

And finally, of course, I had a lot of fun playing this. To put it into perspective, in 2021 I gave RE7 an 8.2/10, in 2022 I gave RE2 an 8.9/10 and RE3 an 8.6/10 and now, in 2023 I give RE8 a 9/10.

The game has no real tutorial, you're travelling from cinematic to cinematic for the first hour instead, the story make absolutly no sense, and do not tie together in any way shape or form. You're then forced to flee enemies for over 5 minutes without the game giving you any hint that is what they intend you to do, so prepare yourself to die over and over and over until you ran away a certain amount of time and find the exact right spot for the next cinematic to occur as there are infinite enemies (they go Dark Soul on your ass). You're then spared for the stupidest reason (actually an easter egg referencing RE4, the bell rang you see?). Then, you encounter NPCs with absolutly no sanity, the story make even less sense, only to make less and less sense as you progress.

This game is closer to a fantastic-horror fairytell than a Resident Evil, from which it only borrow the name, and that twice by taking over Chris Redfield and the protagonist of RE7 and doing an intro "linking it together", when in actuality it doesn't matter at all, doesn't relate to it, and would make MORE SENSE if they didn't tried to. It is sad nowadays companies fear that their game will not be "as popular" if they do not borrow names from established franchise, because it would be a good game on it's own storywise, but as a Resident Evil, it is a senseless shame that doesn't build into the world nor lore of RE. The only way it would make any sense lore-wise, is if the protagonist wake up and it was all just a dream, and THAT tells it all. It totally feel like somebody had a great idea for a game, and the company told him to use the RE name on it, and forced him to do something to make it seem it was supposed to be related while it definitely was not.

To summarize : The game style and lore can't integrate into the RE series. Some features that try to make this "RE" relate to others are just half-assed gimmicks. The story make no sense. The controls are terrible. The graphics are terrific at the expense of player accessibility. There is way too much cinematics and character interaction animations for no real good reason other than to amaze people, and that ultimately end-up making you feel the loss of character control as well as a loss of imertion (sit back and watch the movie rather than actually play a game). Level design is not good at directing you nor building up intrigue, only tension. The game doesn't introduce you properly to any of its mechanics. It takes way too much time before you can ACTUALLY start to really play the game and not run from cinematic to cinematic, but that will still happen ALOT throughout the whole game.

My advice? Remove the entirety of introduction, stop pretending it is Resident Evil, make your own characters with more defined personnality traits other than being the "victims of RE7", properly map the controls, rework the tutorial, and BOOM, it become a 9/10 with the only flaw being WAY too much cinematics and not enough gameplay. As a Resident Evil though... I'd give it 6/10, and story-wise, a 3/10, best way to enjoy it is to turn your brain off and forget the name along with any expectation coming from it.

"Resident Evil: Village" has very high highs, and very low lows. It takes a while before it gets going, but then it throws you into a middle of an awesome castle level. Soon enough it transitions into a non-combat horror section that will scare the pants off of most players, just to then transition into a weird, setpiece-driven water level. By this point you start to realize that you haven't really had many opportunities to shoot monsters because the games sprinkles the encounters very conservatively. "Village" seems to take note, because it then throws you into a long combat-heavy section, and does not let up the pace until the end. What I'm saying is that it's a rollercoaster, and that's good. Some sections are boring and overdone though, especially late in the game, which is not great, but only really becomes grating during subsequent playthroughs. Still, "Village" kind of lost me in the third act, not because it cranked up the absurdity, but because it felt more dumb than fun. The plot is the weakest link of this game, and that's including Ethan Winters, the unfortunately-not-silent protagonist. It's clear that Capcom was going for "Resident Evil 4"-type vibe, but the combat feel is too close to the slow survival horror entries and does not allow for enough creativity. I'm mixed on "Village", but I still find it worthy of recommendation.

Better than its dumpster fire predecessor in almost every single facet.
Pros: I'm running this on two 3080 RTX's with 15 gigs of ram on a 10 year old motherboard and was able to play in ray tracing mode with no loss in frame rate or loss in performance. 
The first play-through was in Hardcore Mode and felt well balanced, forcing you to be conservative with ammo and strategically combining items according to whatever dilemma you're in. Like a true survival horror, you always had barely enough to push forward even after missing a few shots. 
This game has near photo-realistic graphics. The level and sound design are absolutely terrifying and kept me on edge even after enemies have been cleared out - especially Heisenberg's factory and the cellars/dungeons throughout the game.  
Loot, treasures, and puzzles are actually worth trekking back for - often with a few surprises along the way so you never let your guard down. Also, that lock pick you've been anticipating for a few hours might actually open something worthwhile and not like 3 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hand gun bullets as in RE 7. 
Also, unlike its predecessor, this game actually has enemy variety.
Cons:
The latency after hitting space bar to block feels unresponsive and can be extremely frustrating when anticipating an attack you see coming. Even more frustrating is when swarmed on all sides and Ethan is moving like a sloth with a load in his pants, getting stuck on boxes, railings, and what not.  On that same note, the game sometimes confuses the player with obnoxious camera rattling, noise, and other vision obscuring screen overlays - this is often in combination with cut scenes where you're not sure if you're actually playing or not. In short, it feels like they're breaking the "fourth wall" to effectively cheat the player in the name of immersion. 
Also, historically RE games would give you some kind of warning before perma-leaving an area - like RE 2 before departing on the train - but this was left out  in this installment, so even if you're persistent in finding everything you may have to reload previous saves (something to keep in mind in Luiza's house before the chaotic cut scene or opening the sarcophagus after finding all the masks in Castle Dimitrescu).
Overall, I would recommend. This game is well-polished and an absolute trip.

Bought RE 7 and 8(village) together in a bundle while it was on sale. I initially wanted to finish RE7 first to play them through in proper order but I was extremely disappointed in RE7 for various gameplay related seasons that I abandoned that game after about 2 1/2 hours. RE7 disappointed me so much that I was even hesitant to try RE8. I'm glad that I decided to give the game a chance though as I actually had a pretty good time with the game.

In many aspects it feels very similar to what RE4 did years ago. You have a somewhat similar inventory. Enemies drop loot that you can use to buy and upgrade stuff and even the whole atmosphere of the village is very similar to what RE4 did from what I remember. The movement and overall combat of RE8 is faster than in RE7. It actually looks and feels like you're running. The game also switches the focus from time to time. Some sections are more action oriented while others are designed to be creepy horror. The game sometimes uses jump scares but it's rare. My favorite section is a part where there isn't even any combat. It's just pure constant tension buildup where things get crazier and crazier while it then ends with a pretty satisfying finale and gives you some room to breath afterwards.

The overall story is coherant and servicable but unfortunately also has some problems. I can't really get into it without spoiling to much. I'm just gonna say that I would've handled some sections and character interactions differently as at least one character is a bit wasted within the story even though there's a cool boss fight. RE8 also has quite a few puzzles, most of which are easy or at least reasonable in terms of difficulty. There were one or two puzzles that left me scratching my head looking for a guide though. In addition there are quite a few hidding items. There have been a few rooms in my playthrough that still indicated something was there but I couldn't find it.

There are some parts I don't like in RE Village. The heavy use of video sequences in some parts of the game can be pretty annoying as it constantly takes away control from me as a player and there is no indication that you might run into a extensive video sequence. You open a door and *bam* you're watching a movie for the next few minutes...

Also there heavily scripted events as well. In one situation Ethan ends up in a cave with a deathly trap while being shackled. After dying the first time because I had no idea what to do I though about using the trap to unshackle myself. So I went closer to the trap and then ended up dying again because this was not the right solution. What the game expected me to do was crawl into a specifically prepared corner of the room that left a bit of space so I wouldn't be killed by the trap and then the game did for me what I wanted to do before with the shackles. I feel cheated in these kind of situations as I would like to figure something like this out on my own and actually do it myself instead of just watching a movie sequence doing it.

Also with boss fights it often comes down to "cause enough damage to the enemy to trigger the kill movie" because basically all bosses are the same in this regard where you shoot them for a while (maybe hit a specific spot) and then at some point the finisher sequence will start and you can watch a movie of the boss dying with Ethan doing something outside of your control.

And while I can criticize the game I had a good time with it and played it through in 2-3 days (about 15hours) and I added another 2 1/2 hours with the DLC right afterwards. So I would easily recommend RE Village if you can get it while it is on sale.

Wow! I usually wait until I've played through the game 2 or 3 times with a resident evil title before I give my full thoughts. But I've just finished my first playthrough and wanted to give them now. This is spoiler free. 

Resident Evil 8 feels like Capcom sat down and said "Okay, we feel like our best games in the series were 2,4, and 7. So let's take the best parts of all those games and mash them all together." And they absolutely hit it out of the park on delivering that!

it has a merchant (called the duke) with buying, selling, upgrading, and finding treasure like resident evil 4 with some sections in the game where you are shooting multiple enemies with plenty of ammo again like 4. 

It has sections with really interesting puzzles and backtracking with barely any shooting while being stalked by a mr x type stalker enemy (lady D) which reminded me of Resident Evil 2. 

And it also had a big section where they took inspiration from Resident Evil 7 which had quite intense horror and puzzle rooms (think the birthday puzzle room in Resi 7). While yes on the whole this game is less scary than the previous entry. This section in particular made me feel more scared and uncomfortable than even Resi 7 (people who have played probably know the section I'm talking about)

The story was fantastic and is of course a sequel to 7. While they do a brief rundown from the events of 7 I still recommend playing 7 first to understand every reference and story callback to that game (also it's just an amazing game you should play). Though it isn't necessary if you watch the 7 recap at the start (or a youtube video to explain 7 if you really don't want to play it for some reason)

The only thing I noticed was usually in past entries the standard difficulty mode was REALLY well balanced for a first playthrough before ramping it up on a second or third playthrough. I noticed here the standard felt a slight bit too easy, especially on boss battles. So word to anyone buying who likes a fair challenge, I would recommend going on the difficulty above standard. Not really a complaint just something I noticed. 

Overall this is a great Resident Evil game. and just a good game in general. As with all these games, new difficulties, cosmetics, weapons, and beating your time, all await you after the credits roll and I look forward to further playthroughs.
