Before I finish off Shadows of Rose, I thought I might as well update my review after spending 30 painstaking hours of doing achievements for this stupid game.


[b]First off: Denuvo.[/b]
It's gone, No more need to ♥♥♥♥♥ about it anymore.
But I don't understand why they'd wait 2 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ years just to remove the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ DRM.
A DRM, mind you, that is capable of being easily cracked in just measly hours or so.

[b]Second on the list, The length.[/b]
6 hours may be an average length for a first time playthrough, but once you compared this to other Resident Evil games, That length is SHORT in comparison.

Compare this to my times with games such as RE4R (8-10 hours max), RE7 (7-8 hours max), or RE5 (10-12 hours max), It's abysmally short, and this really doesn't paint a good picture for a game that costs around $50+ AUD or even at launch when it came out with a ridiculous $90 AUD price tag.

[b]Third, The content.[/b]
Main campaign and Mercenaries. That's it.
The post-game content for this game is minimal and pales in comparison to RE7's content, even without DLC.

The Extra Content shop doesn't even have anything good either, and at worst: The guns you can buy from the Duke can EASILY OUTPERFORM any gun the Extra Content shop offers you.

Case in point, The Handcannon PZ. One of Village's ONLY returning guns after being missing from Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil 6. Maxed out, it can deal around 3200 damage to enemies and even have one of the best reload speeds in the entire game...

...That is, until you buy and fully upgrade the S.T.A.K.E Magnum.

All of a sudden, the Handcannon easily became redundant as the S.T.A.K.E has 4500 damage, almost nearly close to the Handcannon's damage in Resident Evil 5 (that being 5000 when maxed out) and on top of that, also bearing a MUCH higher ammo capacity, fire rate, and even reload speed. (28 rounds compared to Handcannon's 5 rounds.)

Somehow, they nerfed one of Resident Evil's best post-game unlockables for a weapon you can just buy from the shop without even finishing the game. Why.

[b]Fourth, the story.[/b] (Spoilers here)
Out of the many times I went and ran through the game's story to speedrun, I swear even skipping the cutscenes alone accounts for the fact how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ long Lady D's portion is, only *a cut* above Heisenberg's section. And yet the "Big Bad" [spoiler] Miranda [/spoiler] doesn't even show up until you finish off Chris's assault on the village, and that's the last 5% portion of the game.

Besides that, The story isn't even remotely good. 

You play as Ethan (who is now a dad), and you have to save your infant daughter against a group of cult maniacs in a enclosed European town.

(I wonder where they got this from... [spoiler] RE4 and Silent Hill 1 [/spoiler])

Once you enter said town, You find a group of survivors and spoiler alert: [spoiler] They die, big whoop. But one of those survivors, Elena, could EASILY become an important character if Capcom tried. But they didn't. She died and Ethan didn't do ♥♥♥♥ to save her. [/spoiler]

After that, You meet up with Dimitrescu, [spoiler] kill her three daughters, then she turns into a furious dragon. Fast forward, You find a jar with your infant daughter's limbs, and then you go on a wild goose chase to find them all. [/spoiler]

Beneviento was probably the most interesting section of the game, But it wears out quickly on your second run through of the game. [spoiler] One scary baby section of the game, and she's dead. Great. [/spoiler]

Moreau is boring, plain and simple.
Somehow even taking away a boat still can't make the fish fight any less boring than it needed to be.

Heisenberg is the first and only good character you'd meet in the story.
His dungeon is long, and for a good reason.

But I swear, they did him dirty for not giving him an alternate scenario which I'll drop now.

[spoiler] So when you meet Heisenberg again in the dungeon, You (supposedly) have a choice to join him and kill Miranda. which Ethan automatically declines. [/spoiler]
It's a stupid thing that I am disappointed for. If you could choose Mia and [spoiler] Zoe [/spoiler] in RE7, Then surely they could've done it again for Village. But since this is Capcom, who is notorious for reusing assets in games. Why am I even surprised.

Anyway, [spoiler] you kill Heisenberg, and THEN, Miranda shows up again. Only to kill Ethan in 3 minutes. What a record. [/spoiler]

It was then revealed that [spoiler] Ethan had died since RE7 and has mold regeneration inside of him. [/spoiler] And I'll give the game credit, they did a good job explaining how Ethan can even reattach his limbs. Good job.

[spoiler] You kill Miranda, save Rose, and then end the game with a sacrifice of Ethan Winters. [/spoiler]
(This choice alone will be a mistake for what comes next.)
 
So they made an story that's actually average, That's my one of only good points I'll give to this game. Moving on...

[b]Fifth, DLC Content.[/b]
1 campaign and a third person mode that is literally a mod you can download off from Nexus Mods, and extra Mercenaries characters.

I'm not going into detail about the campaign or the third person, because I am saving that for the DLC review when I get to that. What I will go into detail, however, is comparing the DLC to what RE7's DLC offers.

Resident Evil 7 Gold Edition offers:

-Resident Evil 7: Base Game
-Resident Evil 7: Season Pass (which itself offers:)
   -Not A Hero (Campaign)
   -End of Zoe (Campaign)
   -Nightmare (Minigame)
   -Bedroom (Minigame)
   -21 (Minigame)
   -Daughters (Minigame)

All for the low, low price of $56.89 AUD. The same price you can get if you were to buy Village.
All I'm saying now, is that if you can buy Village, you can buy RE7: Gold Editon, which has FAR more content than what Village can offer for the same price.

[b]Sixth, and finally, the Achievements.[/b] (and my problem with Mapmatician)
Effortless, That's what I'm going to say.

You got your usual Frugalist and Speedrun for X hours achievement, even bringing back an achievement where you knock an arrow with your knife from RE5.

But even on the Hardest difficulty: Village of Shadows. It's either a mix of the most effortless and easy parts, to the most ridiculous and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ parts in the entire game, and the reward you get for it is what should've been a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ confetti gun.

The Rocket Pistol is absolutely worthless, can't even kill on the easiest difficulty with it's low damage (500) and low fire rate. It's almost like a sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke.

In the meanwhile, the Mapmatician achievement can go ♥♥♥♥ ITSELF.
What should've been an easy achievement, became 3 hours of pure agony trying to find any missing items in a room, only to softlock myself and end up restarting an hour's worth of progress due to my own paranoia. 

Noticed how I said "should've"? Because the MAP ITSELF, is HINDERING YOU.

That's right, The map got ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gutted right after how useful it was for Resident Evil 2 and Resident Evil 3's remakes. It used to show you where you missed ammo and even key items you missed. Only for it to never do that in Village for no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ reason.

I can understand this for RE7 because that came out before the REmakes.
That, is not an excuse for Village. 

The only reason it's even possible to get the achievement was to repeatedly check the Challenges menu and see how much progress you have gained for said achievement.
But it should've been an easy QoL change to add it on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ map itself.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]
I can easily say this is literally the third worst Resident Evil game I've ever played, behind Resident Evil 0 and Resident Evil 6. My disappointment with this game is unfathomable.

If you really want to buy this game. Please, please get this on a discount. It is not worth the full price by a long shot.

[h1] Introduction [/h1]

First my knowledge with Resident Evil started from 7-th part, and I really enjoyed this game. I have played Resident Evil Village twice: first time I passed this game when it was released on Mac and second time - now in Steam.

[h1] Main Plot [/h1]

The story of Village is a direct sequel of part 7. From the very beginning I had many questions to what is happening. The game very beautifully sets the tone and the formed questions after the introduction make you run forward for answers.

We don’t have straight answers until the very end, and only before the last fight game gives us all answers and admirably connect this part with the whole RE saga.

RE Village doesn’t give all answers in cutscenes, in turn, more answers are given in notes. This is done in the spirit of the old parts, where there were no beautiful cutscenes, and all the answers had to be given in the form of notes scattered throughout the game.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

When I was playing the first time - I really was scared almost all the game. This game doesn’t have many screamers, in turn it casts a mood of constant anxiety. During the passage, my mood changed very quickly from panic and apathy to peace and tranquility in the save rooms. So all gaming experience may be explained as emotional rollercoaster.

The game is based on Village [spoiler] and 4 extra locations with 4 boss fights + the final boss. In the house of Beneviento game takes all our weapon and we need to pass it only by solving puzzles. [/spoiler] And it was the most scary part of the game.

The last location is [spoiler] Heisenbergs factory [/spoiler] and it is the only location during which I was tired from the game. This location is very big and long. And due to this location I felt boring. When I played this game second time, only [spoiler] Heisenbergs factory [/spoiler] was stopping me from playing.

[h1] DLC and third person view [/h1]

DLC Shadow of Rose is made perfectly in all canons of DLSs. Where taken already Ken locations, has been changed to fit the new story and was realized as a new small game. And it was done perfectly. The second location which is [spoiler] Beneviento’s house [/spoiler] I was really scared and got all emotions which I wanted to have.

I haven’t played the RE village with a third person view, but have seen few play throughs, and what I have understood is - all screamers and cutscenes are done for a first person view. So those who really want to try it as s new old experience may lose a big part of emotions. As well need to notice that in all cutscenes camera moves to a first person view, even if you play with third person view. According to this I believe that this is a detriment to the player immersion.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I have really enjoyed Resident Evil Village, that’s one of those games which I enjoyed to play second time. DLC Shadow of Rose is not bad, it had many good moments, but I haven’t seen in it any of revealing hidden storylines. For all my gaming experience I haven’t seen any of gaming bugs or optimization problems. So from technical side game looks really perfect.
I may easily recommend this game if you enjoy some horror.

Resident Evil Village, despite its high expectations as a follow-up to the acclaimed Resident Evil 7, disappoints with its lackluster execution and missed opportunities, resulting in a game that fails to fully capitalize on its potential.

One of the most significant issues with Resident Evil Village is its uneven pacing. While the game starts off strong with a captivating introduction, it quickly devolves into a disjointed and repetitive experience. Players are forced to backtrack through the same environments multiple times, leading to moments of tedium and frustration. This lack of variety in gameplay mechanics makes the overall experience feel stale and uninspired.

Additionally, the game's narrative fails to fully engage players. While the premise of a rural village overrun by werewolves and other supernatural creatures is intriguing, the story fails to deliver any meaningful payoff. Characters lack depth and development, and key plot points feel rushed or underdeveloped. This lack of investment in the narrative makes it difficult for players to care about the outcome, diminishing the overall impact of the game.

Furthermore, Resident Evil Village suffers from a lack of innovation. While it introduces some new gameplay mechanics, such as a merchant system and a larger focus on action, these additions feel tacked on and shallow. The game fails to push the boundaries of the survival horror genre, instead opting for safe and predictable gameplay mechanics that do little to differentiate it from its predecessors.

Visually, Resident Evil Village is a mixed bag. While the game boasts stunning environments and impressive character models, it also suffers from technical issues such as texture pop-in and frame rate drops. These visual inconsistencies detract from the overall immersion and can pull players out of the experience at crucial moments.

In conclusion, while Resident Evil Village may have its moments of excitement and intrigue, it ultimately falls short of delivering a truly memorable gaming experience. With uneven pacing, a lackluster narrative, a dearth of innovation, and technical issues, it's hard to recommend this title to anyone other than the most dedicated fans of the series.

The rewarding exploration and problem solving of the previous games is largely absent, replaced with monotonous trudging around a linear path of houses and sheds or stone hallways. The village is not fun to explore; you don't get to just walk around it because that would too convenient, instead half the areas are blocked off by a tree or something meaning you have to go through a house and into the backyard where there is a shed that has a small hole on one side that you have to go through (although its easy to miss because there are a ton of sheds and outhouses that don't have anything in them). Resident Evil Village is the latest addition to the iconic Resident Evil franchise developed by Capcom. This survival horror game takes place a few years after the events of Resident Evil 7 and puts players in the shoes of protagonist Ethan Winters, as he tries to rescue his daughter from a village plagued by supernatural beings.

The first thing that stands out about Resident Evil Village is its stunning graphics. The game features incredibly detailed environments, character models, and visual effects that create a hauntingly beautiful atmosphere. The game's sound design is equally impressive, with an eerie soundtrack and terrifying sound effects that help build tension and create a sense of dread.

One of the most impressive aspects of Resident Evil Village is its level design. The game is split into different areas, each with its own distinct look and feel. From the spooky village to the creepy castle and the disturbing dollhouse, each area is expertly crafted and offers a unique gameplay experience. The game's puzzles are also well-designed, providing a good challenge without being frustrating.

In terms of gameplay, Resident Evil Village delivers a solid experience. The game combines elements of survival horror and action, with players having to scavenge for resources while also fighting off hordes of enemies. The combat is visceral and satisfying, with a variety of weapons and upgrades available to customize your playstyle. The game's bosses are particularly memorable, with each one offering a unique challenge that requires players to think strategically and use their resources wisely.

The game's story is engaging and well-written, with plenty of twists and turns to keep players on the edge of their seats. The game's narrative is also tied into the wider Resident Evil universe, with nods to previous games and characters making appearances throughout. Without giving away too much, the game's ending sets up some interesting possibilities for future installments in the series.

One potential downside to Resident Evil Village is its length. The game can be completed in around 8-10 hours, which may disappoint some players who were expecting a longer experience. However, the game's high replayability factor makes up for this, with players able to unlock new game modes and items by completing the game multiple times.

Another potential issue with Resident Evil Village is its difficulty. While the game can be played on a variety of difficulty levels, even the normal difficulty can be quite challenging at times. Some players may find themselves getting frustrated at the game's more difficult sections, which require precise timing and quick reflexes. However, for those who enjoy a good challenge, the game's difficulty is a plus.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is an excellent addition to the Resident Evil franchise. With its stunning graphics, well-crafted level design, engaging story, and solid gameplay, the game is sure to please both long-time fans and newcomers alike. While its length and difficulty may be an issue for some players, these minor flaws are more than outweighed by the game's strengths. If you're a fan of survival horror games, Resident Evil Village is definitely worth checking out.

After having played and beaten RE7, I was finding myself disappointed in how that game failed to capture the horror and feeling of hopelessness I found in previous RE titles. Gun play felt forced, and scares were placed everywhere so obviously that nothing really gave me a feeling of terror I had come to know and enjoy, even in more action heavy titles like RE4 and RE6. So after that experience I was left with fear that RE8 would be more of the same, since it built off what RE7 had "done so well." And after having played through RE8, I find that my fears had come true, and in not the horrifying way that they were going for.

Starting with the character himself, Ethan Winters: In RE7 I found him to be an insufferable "self-insert" of a character that it brought me out of every single moment I had even begun to feel accomplished in, and that character trait stays true and is amplified in the sequel. Giving him such amazing one liners as "In death as he was in life. Disgusting." that completely makes you forget that you had just cleared a boss, and instead remind you that you're playing through what can only be described as a poorly written middle school performance. These lines are a far cry from anything RE4 brought in its amazingly campy humor. And this game violently reminds you of that every time Ethan begins to speak.

And while Ethan is poorly written, It does not help that his character is placed in the most cardboard flat world written, With characters quickly introduced with seemingly only one trait, and then they completely dismissed within the hour. The advertising leads you to believe that you have to deal with Lady Dimitrescu for the game and much of it shows her as the main antagonist. And that is true, for about an hour and a half before she is completely forgotten about and maybe offhandedly mentioned once more for the rest of the story. The pacing of the story is not exempt from being poorly done too, as it makes you bounce around 4 different areas for about an hour or two before returning to the hub area like you’re playing Super Mario 64.

All of this could just possibly be excused if the gameplay itself is good, RE4 arguably didn't have that much of an amazing story if we took away the great character writing from it right? Well unfortunately, I think that’s where RE8’s biggest sin is shown, as the gameplay is filled with terrible choices and problems that haven’t been issues in gaming since the early 2010s.

Starting with one of the biggest offenders that no doubt everyone has heard about, The lack of an FOV slider. Sure with 3rd person games, the need for an FOV slider could be an afterthought, as you typically don't think about needing that if the camera is far enough away from your character. But with a 1st person game, it is almost a necessity, as some people need a different FOV if they experience motion sickness if the FOV is too low. As you may have guessed, RE8 shipped with a locked 80 FOV that, as far as I know, still cannot be changed in the settings, causing motion sickness in some players, and generally looks bad. Most esports games are played at around 110, and a typical first person FOV is 90-100.

This isn't the only thing stopping me from enjoying playing the game, a personal grievance is that I play with a particularly low DPI on my mouse, 700 to be exact, that means I need to move my mouse farther physically to move my camera. Nearly every game I have played, including RE2R, I had no issue with my low DPI and the camera controls. But with RE8, the default settings had my mouse almost geriatric, leaving me to swipe my mouse across my desk several times to even turn my camera 180 degrees. That has me diving into the settings to change my mouse sensitivity, in which there are 3 different options, one of which is on a scale from 0-9 and the other two on a scale from 1-50. Completely unintuitive at minimum, and downright annoying to fiddle with at worst. I found myself pausing over and over again for 20 minutes trying to dial my mouse settings in a way that I found comfortable.

With my settings successfully set, I was finally free to experience the gunplay.

I cannot fathom how they possibly did this, but they made the weapons quite possibly the worst weapons I have used. No weapon felt satisfying to use, except for maybe the revolver as it had the stopping power of an entire 18 wheeler. With every weapon, it felt as if I was kicking myself in the crotch in an enemy’s direction and they were feeling sympathy pains. The default shotgun was the biggest offender, as even if the reload animation finishes, Ethan takes an extra second before firing the weapon, almost as if he’s contemplating if he left the stove on before his daughter got kidnapped. The sniper rifle has about maybe the same amount of recoil as a base pistol, it makes you feel as if you’re shooting a glorified nerf rifle at a boss until he falls over like a father playing dead when his kid doesn't stop shooting him with his McDonald’s happy meal toy gun.

None of the failures in the gun play, however, detract from how piss easy the game is on the base difficulty. As I found myself having an abundance of healing items and ammo for my weapons. This was without even crafting any of the health or defense upgrades, as I did not know that system existed until I randomly killed a chicken, harvested it, and unlocked a menu in the shop. The only times I actually struggled was with mechanics that felt were unpolished or sluggish to the point that I felt as if the game didn't want me to play it.

With all of these problems stacking, what does the game leave me with after everything is said and done?

Well to its credit, the RE engine that capcom has developed makes for some outstanding visuals and RE8 does still manage to look pretty good in sections that have a lot of details placed in them, I found myself in the village looking around legitimately enjoying the scenery, until eventually I had to fire another couple of foam darts at yet another group of enemies, and hearing another Ethan Winters’ classic one liners for me to groan too. The performance is also great, As I have everything maxed out at 1440p with a rock solid framerate. Granted this is with a RTX 3080, but I still find myself impressed that the game rarely stutters, even with Denuvo.

That leaves us with my last thoughts about RE8

The game fails to provide anything of note that I would expect from a survival horror game, especially one from the RE franchise. With gunplay and writing leaving more than enough to be desired, I simply think many would be fine to simply not play this entry into the series. I believe there are simply better games within its own series that provide a better experience. RE4 has simply just a better combat system and story that really give more to the action to the RE franchise than any game has. The RE2 remake takes the action down a notch, but makes up for it in simple atmosphere and enemy designs alone that set it apart from the other games in its genre. And if neither of those, RE1 simply is a must play for anyone that wants into the franchise or is looking for a survival horror game that really defined its place in the genre. RE8 provides almost nothing of value to any of the aspects of survival horror or to the RE franchise to warrant playing it through.

Boy does this game live up to its literal title:

Your home life is interrupted by some evil residents,
You make your way through the titular village, inhabited by many evil residents,
You find yourself in a spooky castle whose residents are (promiscuously) evil,
You get the picture, many residents of evil.

Stupid eye catching intro aside, Resident Evil Village is a great addition to the series we all know and love, and a fantastic sequel to its predecessor released back in 2017. This is another one of a game where I felt compelled to write a long review no one will read because I had such a fantastic experience with it, but more so because I was on the fence about even getting it up until 4 weeks ago when it was on major sale.

To put it bluntly, I thought a lot of the hype around this game was purely because of the "big mommy vampire meme hehe," wave that EXPLODED and was inescapable when the trailer dropped. That compiled with this horror setting from the 1930s (feudal village and spooky castle) paired with classic movie monsters (vampires, werewolves, swamp creatures), had me confused about what this game was going for and how it fit into the series. I wasn't particularly interested and it took a super sale, coupled with my longing for the RE:4 Remake and needing something to tide me over before its release for me to pull the trigger. Simply put, I've got no regrets: I beat the game multiple times, completed every challenge minus DLC, and frankly should have jumped on the Dimitrescu bandwagon earlier. 

Going back to my previous point: how does this game fit into the series? While it contains everyone's favourite boulder punching a-hole, I view RE:7 and 8 as separate from the main series. They're their own unique games and it's not just because of the shift to first person. I think what sets these games apart is that Capcom really struck a perfect balance of ridiculous, over the top, WTF plots, with fantastic characters, amazingly portrayed and brought to life, set in truly unique environments, which can be considered characters themselves. Take RE:7, the focal point of that game was the Baker family and their disgustingly beautiful Louisiana plantation manor. The three antagonists in that game were incredibly iconic, making for scenes ranging from unsettling, to hilarious, to terrifying. It also helped the player build up these twisted relationship with each of them, ultimately culminating in memorable showdowns.  

That formula is repeated here, but built out further with Mother Miranda and her "family." This is where RE:8 truly shines: here's a cast of truly memorable misfits, each one more unique than the last, but most importantly, all fantastically voiced and acted. I know everyone loves to talk about Lady D (for obvious reasons, memes or not), and yes she is an amazing character (Maggie Robertson killed), but honestly all the children do such a fantastic job. I'd argue Neil Newbon as Heisenberg is equally fantastic and makes for such a fun villain. How he enunciates "Mother Miranda, that b**ch," will forever by stuck in my head and his showdown was quite the- experience to say the least. My point is that these wild and wacky characters, brought to life by passionate VA's make this game such a fun time. On my first playthrough, I couldn't wait until my next encounter, but there were moments in subsequent playthroughs where I'd happily watch cutscenes in their full length.

The other thing to point out is that this game never takes itself too seriously, and that's why it truly shines compared to other RE games. They really nailed the precedence RE:4 set back in 2005, but the series seemed to lose shortly thereafter *cough* RE:6 *cough*. There's actually a lot of parallels to RE:4 and this game and probably the reason why I had such a great time with it. But in terms of plot, this game takes place in a spooky village straight outta Transylvania a la 1800s with werewolves and vampires, there's no way to play that seriously and thank god they don't. You can tell the devs had a lot of fun coming up with the story, characters and setting, and honestly if it weren't for the title and one character, this could just as easily not be an RE game. Aside from that, this plot has more twists and turns that a daytime soap opera. There's drama, romance, highs/lows, aforementioned memorable characters, plot twists, ect- my god it's got it all and never seems to hold back. In fact as the game progresses, it gets even more ridiculous, but again it embraces it and is even able to poke fun at itself at times. I think a fair comparison could actually be how Metal Gear treats its stories: serious plot/setting, sprinkled with moments that come out left field. 

In terms of gameplay, just like the characters and plot, it's a wild ride. This game has something for everyone. One minute it's survival horror, then it takes a complete 180 and suddenly you're playing something akin COD, mercilessly blasting everything in sight. It can be a walking sim, then a looter shooter, hoarding every penny for an insane weapon upgrade. It has horror moments hiding in lockers straight from Amnesia and then classic RE puzzle moments solving nonsensical/overly complicated door locks with statue pieces. Then you're fighting a boss that violently transforms into some eldritch abomination- it's all here and you better be ready. Caught up in this whole mess is our protagonist turned super dad Ethan Winters (also fantastically voiced), and if you loved how much of a literal punching bag he was in RE:7, this game is your wet dream. It's an absolute roller coaster of emotions seeing how much abuse poor Ethan takes in this game, yet inspiring how he perseveres through it all. I don't want to spoil the fun, but they really up the punishment compared to what he endured in RE:7 and don't hold back at all.

Now I mentioned RE:4 and yes, this game screams of RE:4 and I'm all for it. I'll admit it's a bias on my part- RE:4 was my official introduction to the series on GameCube back in 05 and it left quite the impression on me. That game introduced a lot of elements to the series that are now quintessentially "Resident Evil," and it was such a welcome surprise to see them back in this game. There's the setting of course (castle, village, swamps), but also treasure hunting/combining is back, along with a currency to spend at a merchant for buying/upgrading weapons. Special shout out to The Duke- he is an absolute pleasure to deal with and sucg a fun side character encountered throughout the game. Also, love it or hate it, the RE:4 attache case and inventory management is here too, which is a fun minigame on its own. It's interesting because the RE:4 remake was clearly in development while this game was, and while there are a lot of parallels between the two (btw: the Remake is phenomenal and I'll be reviewing it as well), RE:8 offers its own unique flavour to the mix.

My only critiques with this game are first; the movement speed. My god is Ethan slow, its RE:7 all over, and even with a supposed "speed increase perk" you move at a snails pace, which can be especially frustrating during enemy heavy encounters (the ending for example- yikes). Second, sound design for weapons is hit or miss. A lot of the guns sound like peashooters, even after maxing them out, and it just seems off. Thirdly, while the game looks fantastic and runs superbly on damn near max settings (even on my older 2070), how certain things are rendered in the RE engine can be weird. You'll go from beautiful, hyper detailed interiors, to smoke/clouds that look like literal pixels, or animations being jerky/stop motion like when viewed at a distance. I'm sure it's to help performance, but it kills immersion at times.

Anyway this is long and I'm rambling. TL;DR, come for the vampire mommy, stay for the wild ride of a story and engaging gameplay it has to offer

1) Gorgeous areas. The first and second areas that the game will take you to (After the side-boss characters are revealed) are truly something else. This is not to say that the others are bad, but those are spectacular.

Cons:

1) While the graphics in general are really good, some random textures can look especially rough, almost like they belong to a game from 2008. These are random textures on environmental objects though so its not the worst thing.

3) There is a certain area when you go to a 'stronghold' region in the main story. For that small section, the game becomes far too action-oriented in my opinion. It is jarring compared to the rest of the game. Regardless, once you get past that, it goes back to being solid.

Resident Evil: Village. I still remember when I thought to myself once the game was revealed, that this entry in the franchise looked just like a copy/paste of the forth chapter, only with a different protagonist and better graphics and controls. I spent 4 years simply reading reviews --both from specialised critics and players--stating that this was an amazing game without letting that hype persuade me to spend a single dollar on it.Last year, however, I decided to give this title a try after buying a Steam Deck. Before my handheld console arrived, I only had 15 or 20 games on my account (I'm primarily a PS user), so when I finally got the chance to hold it in my hands, I knew I needed more, and because the Resident Evil games were on sale, I bought the only one i had never played, which was about to receive an amazing DLC that not only expands the Mercenary mode with new characters or give us an epilogue starring the Winters' daughter, Rose; but also includes a third person view of which I'm in love with in regards of this saga.For 35$, I bought the bundle (base game + DLC). As soon as I started playing choosing the Hardcore difficulty, I realised I was wrong about something, this game doesn't feel like Resident Evil 4 at all. I'm not going to dive into the plot because I think it's better to play RE8 knowing nothing about it, just the basics from the trailers, but one thing I want to say is that Ethan Winters isn't Leon S. Kennedy, so the way he interacts with what's happening around him, from the perspective of a man caught in a situation that slips out of his hands, sounds so natural that the player ends up sympathising with him, and I'm very glad they went this way since RE7. Shout-out to all the actors and actresses who voiced these characters though, because they nailed the level of threat, friendship and mystery necessary to immerse yourself in the story.Secondly, the gameplay mechanics are truly marvellous, as it is along all of the games in this franchise. Starting with the use of guns, I must say that I was shocked at how smooth the combat can get when you adapt yourself to the different scenarios and come up with the right strategy depending on the kind of enemy you're dealing with. From handguns and shotguns to rifles and even grenade launchers, all these tools provide you the fire power you need to enhance the feeling of "badassery" that keeps you going forward. It's amazing the pace at which you find new weapons because as soon as you get used to one, another shows up which improves in every aspect that which you're holding.But not everything relies around the combat. Yes, you can buy upgrades for your guns, become a man of action similar to what our beloved Leon was at the end of Resident Evil 2, but some hours into the game also unlocks a new ability which is related to the Duke, the merchant of this eight entry, and the animals you see across the Village and its surroundings. Anytime you decide to "hunt" one of these, you receive a piece of meat, chicken or fish, which then you can trade for a dish that improves Ethan in a certain way: more health, better defense... It gives you a reason to explore the scenario a bit more in search of this wild life apart from the treasures hidden in the map (or those obtained by defeating the final bosses and mini bosses, which there are.)Lastly, I just wanna give you a brief summary about how it feels like when playing Resident Evil: Village on the Steam Deck. With a little bit of tinkering, I was able to achieve a stable and smooth 40FPS experience from beginning to end, inside and outside, with many or none enemies on screen. The RE Engine is probably the most optimised graphics engine out there when it comes to the Steam Deck. RE2, RE3 and RE7 also play as if you were holding a PS4 in your hands. The lighting, shadows and textures all benefit from the small screen and its 800p resolution, so with a Medium-High mix of settings, you're gonna be left jaw-dropped. Trust on this one.All in all, I must say that this game is truly an amazing choice if you're thinking of buying an action/adventure --with a few drops of RPG-- game set in the Resident Evil universe, and an even better choice if you want it for your Steam Deck. I guarantee you're gonna enjoy a very nice time unfolding its secrets and helping poor Ethan Winters in his journey to fight the evil which lies in this Village.GAME SCORE: 8.5 / 10STEAM DECK SCORE: 9 / 10

I started Resident Evil 8: Village on it's release date in 2021. I finished it the nearly 2 years later. Just one day before the RE4 Remake comes out. It took me 2 years and multiple restarts with giant gaps between play sessions. It probably doesn't seem like I love Resident Evil 8...but I do love Resident Evil 8.I can't entirely explain how i got so distracted so many times but every time I sat down to play this game i had an absolute blast and yet I didn't come back for some time. Resident Evil 8 is not particularly scary...at all really. I mean there's that one level that everyone talks about. It's spooky once. I certainly jumped a few times but none of this game really scared me. RE8 is very campy horror. It's fun horror but maybe that's why it's so fun. I love the aesthetic of horror even when it doesn't scare me.Resident Evil 8 is also not particularly challenging. This is one of the easiest RE games i've ever played. Resource management isn't really a thing. Maybe on the higher difficulties and maybe i'll try those some day but i barely died in this game. Barely ever ran out of ammo. Not that you can't instantly craft more with your bottomless crafting inventory. It's not ideal but it's in no way a deal breaker for me. The shooting is fun and the enemies are fun to shoot. I'm not complaining. So what worked for me if the game wasn't scary and the gameplay didn't challenge me? Just being in this world. It's just fun. The 4 antagonists are a lot of fun with huge personalities and their own personal domains. Each sporting a different campy horror theme. 2 of them clearly have more love given than the others. So basically you have 2 well crafted villain domains and the other 2 are shorter set piece driven sections. That's where the Village itself comes in. It's ever expanding as a sort of central hub that you keep returning to. Sporting more treasure and threats every time you return to it. So besides the charm of the setting, themes and villains the other part that really worked for me was the story and Ethan Winter's himself. As a Father the story of village really effected me way more than it would have a few years ago. I know it's become a meme to make fun of Ethan but he's easily my favorite RE protagonist. Sure he's goofy and arguably kind of stupid sometimes but he's an every man. A dad who will do anything to save his daughter. I unironically love his cheesy trash talk that he spits out every time he takes out a big enemy. "Hell yeah brother! Tell em!" His insults are hilariously tone deaf and sometimes unnecessarily nasty and they never ceased to make me laugh or sometimes they just buffed my ego. Give me Ethan Winters over Chris Redfield any day. Village currently still has Overwhelmingly Positive reviews on steam and I remember people being super positive on it when it came out but recently the discourse seems to have soured on it significantly. Not so for me. It certainly doesn't fit with old school RE games in terms of tone or themes but when you reach the 8th mainline game in a series (more if you include all the remakes and spinoffs) you have to reinvent yourself. Without this new direction and the remakes I doubt the series would still be going this strong. I love the og RE titles and we can have both but for my money I'd prefer Resident Evil to keep being this Horror Bio Weapon Anthology series over the endless "evil corporation with zombies vs 80's action movie characters" thing. Keep being weird and keep being fun and that's all i can really ask for.

Let's just summarize this in a TLDR

If you want Resident Evil 4R then go play that. If you've already played that then go back and replay that. Because this is a shallow imitation of what made Resident Evil 4 good back in the day.

Onto the lengthy breakdown, still let's try to be brief:

The plot doesn't make any sense. Too much information is withheld from you and from a narrative structure I was confused as to why I should care about anything that happens. 

And there are plenty of moments in the game where they just wanted to have something cool happen and did not care one iota for how logical or sensible it'd be. And for me the game very early on broke that immersion completely to the point that I could not take its setting seriously at all. It's just a string of "wouldn't it be cool if?" and "and then this happened and then this happened!"

The game exposes its "villains" very early on and basically kills any idea of surprise by doing it. One of those villains is a doll. You know, an inanimate object? But now 'I know' that the doll is alive... So... The whole point of an inanimate object being alive isn't scary anymore, because you've exposed it too early.

Another villain is literally just dommy mommy. A pale(lol) imitation of Mr X from REvil 2R. Oh and she has 3 daughters that are basically just MGS villains. (she does have a lot of amazing R34 however and that's nice)

The third is a bumbling idiot, very scary.

The fourth is a Metal Gear Solid boss. I dunno why he's here but voice acting is atrocious. I guess he needed to get hired somewhere after Konami stopped making MGS games.

The game is not a survival horror game but rather an action game in a horror setting. The problem with that is that its action? Well, it's not good. The shooting in the game feels wonky, enemies are too spongy and unresponsive and the weapons feel anemic as a result. There are plenty of enemies that have bullet sponge health but no indicator as to how much progress you're making or whether what you are attacking with is even effective in the first place. Meaning that a lot of your weaponry feel meek. The worst part is probably bosses that go on forever and ever and you wonder if you're just wasting your ammo away.

And in regards to the action in the game it is the kind of action game that takes control away from the player far too often to razzle and dazzle you with its shiny first person cinematics that create narrative dissonance from how Ethan acts in the gameplay.

The most common enemy that you will fight will be the standard "werewolf", and you know the type of game where there is an enemy that is just plain damn annoying to fight? Maybe it is the attack pattern it has, maybe the animations, maybe the hitboxes, maybe the status effect or how persistent its AI is, regardless of what it is you know what I'm talking about... THAT enemy, the bane of the game. Well in this game that is the standard enemy.

They are ridiculously aggro. There is no indication as to how much damage you've done to them. They don't get weaker as you damage them in different parts. They got grab attacks that lock you into an attack scene where control is taken away from you. They are fast when they want to but but slow otherwise which means there is a lack of consistency as to how much time you're allowed to line up shots. They move in weird patterns which can make aiming at them a chore. And they are so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ many. Like when the game throws them at you there are so ungodly many of them.

I found them to be extremely annoying to deal with. They're not scary. They're not satisfying to fight. They are just plain damn annoying and just a waste of ammo.

Why do you want to play this game? Because you played REvil 2R, 4R, 7 and want more? Well, Village isn't more. Village is the equivalent to back in the day when they made a really great film in the 80's and when it popped off massively they created a cheap sequel to cash in on its success. That's 8. It is not a good action game. It is not a good horror game. It does not have a good story or worldbuilding. 

As I'm re-writing my review (as I reviewed it once before) I am about 80% through the game and I'm just bored and annoyed by the stupid enemies. I don't want to play this game anymore but will for completionist sake since it's so close to being finished. But do I advice anyone to play this even if it were to be free? No. Not even if this game was free would I suggest you play it. Because you're paying for it with your time. And it's not worth it. [h1]Resident Evil [i]Village[/i][/h1]
Is the newest chapter in Capcom's popular survival horror franchise. The game follows on from RE 7: Biohazard, (2017), and is full of blood, fright and a lot of action.

[h1]Complex plot...[/h1]
In this new Resident Evil game, once again the player lives a story starring Ethan, the main character of RE 7 After the torturous events of the 2017 game, the character tries to return to normality alongside his wife Mia and daughter Rosemary . However, right at the beginning of Village, he is surprised by the already known Chris Redfield, who murders Mia and kidnaps Rose.

Knocked out in a fight with Chris, Ethan wakes up in a village completely in ruins, which seems to have a special fondness for a quasi-religious figure named Mother Miranda. There, he starts his journey in search of Rosemary, facing several enemies and unraveling countless secrets.

[b]Although it looks simple at first glance, the plot is actually quite complex. Under the premise of a father's search for his daughter, several mysteries are kept that involve even the history of the formation of the main company of Resident Evil, the Umbrella Corporation. The entire unfolding of the narrative deepens as we advance in the game, and the icing on the cake is its completely surprising outcome.[/b]

Despite its complex story, the game is relatively short and can be beaten in about ten hours. As usual in Resident Evil, however, Village keeps some treasures and small parallel missions, which make the user want to play it more than once. In addition, there is also the return of the Mercenaries mode to challenge the player even more.

It's worth saying that even those who don't know Resident Evil 7 can play Village without major problems. This is because the game presents a retrospective of previous history right at the beginning, situating those who did not live through the horrors of Biohazard. However, for better understanding and even affinity with this new storyline, it might be a good idea to play the 2017 game.

[h1]Powerful and well-varied enemies[/h1]
In the demo released, Capcom knew how to hide the depth of the story of Resident Evil Village very well. If we started the gameplay with the certainty that our biggest enemy would be the already known Lady Dimitrescu, we were soon surprised: there are at least three other villains that we must defeat.

They are Donna Beneviento, Salvatore Moreau and Karl Heisenberg. They are Mother Miranda's followers, and each poses different difficulties to the player. It is worth mentioning that, for TechTudo, the most terrifying moments were due to Beneviento, while the greatest battle difficulties were found with Heisenberg.

Furthermore, Resident Evil Village is also interesting for the variety of types of enemies. In this game, there are vampires, witches, killer dolls, creatures that resemble werewolves and even robotic villains, in a striking cyberpunk aesthetic. The tip here is that the headshot is not always the main way out - however, it's always a good idea to keep your aim properly calibrated.

[h1]Guaranteed horror with terrifying soundtrack[/h1]
This new Resident Evil game is definitely one of the scariest in the franchise. To keep a comparison in mind, the last time I felt so terrified of a game in the series was with Resident Evil 2, released for PSOne in 1998.

In addition to having several jump scares to scare players, Village also has a haunting soundtrack that keeps players in a constant state of tension. It is even possible that this is the scariest track of all the games in the series, delivering a magnificent job of setting in survival horror.

[h1]Excellent graphics in realistic scenarios[/h1]
As expected, the RE Engine did an excellent job on Resident Evil Village, which features exquisite lighting and realistic environments. The video game engine was launched in 2017, for Biohazard, and now comes with a game that runs well even on more limited hardware consoles - as is the case with the PS4.

Although the very characterization of the characters, such as Lady Dimitrescu and Salvatore Moreau, for example, is interesting in itself, what most called attention during the tests was the beauty and realism of the scenarios. From the tense scenes in the Dimitrescu castle to the unpleasant moments in the Heisenberg factory, the game maintains neat environments full of details at practically all times.

In Resident Evil Village, even the ugly is beautiful. The only exception to this logic is perhaps a moment present in the second boss of the game, Donna Beneviento. However, although it involves a frightening situation, the setting of the scene is still impressive, making its horror justified.

[h1]Traditional and expected franchise mechanics[/h1]
Like any other game in the franchise, Resident Evil Village demands a lot of curiosity and exploration from the player. It is always necessary to look closely at each object collected, as some must be assembled and/or disassembled to actually be used.

It is interesting to note, however, that in this new chapter of the Capcom series some items have extended lifespans. In addition, there are regions that, although they appear at the beginning of the game, must be explored later.

To facilitate the trajectory, the map of Resident Evil Village is quite intuitive. It shows in a simplified way if there is still something to be explored in each of the available areas, but its simplicity can be a real headache for players who like to collect any and all items.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Resident Evil Village is an excellent new chapter in Capcom's traditional franchise. With mechanics already known and loved, the game made a beautiful debut in the new generation.

Although it has a slightly long ending, all the hours invested are justified by the complexity of the story. With beautiful graphics and well-developed villains, Resident Evil Village ends Ethan Winters' journey with a flourish, pleasing a lot with its surprising and terrifying gameplay.

Resident Evil Village is an excellent, well - paced, and tense continuation of Ethan Winter's endeavors to yet again rescue another member of his immediate family. Having played Village immediately after completing Resident Evil 7, The Ethan Winters Saga came to a meaningful and satisfying close (albeit with enough unanswered questions to allow the series to continue). 

      From the onslaught, Village's excellent presentation in terms of visuals and audio design is impeccable. Story moments are immersive due to the superb animation, made possible by motion capture technology. Furthermore, Each member apart of the wide cast of characters was performed exceptionally by their respective actors, especially by that of the four lords. Enemy encounters and atmosphere are made far more tense due to the great audio design, allowing for needed tension and horror to build when needed. The variety of environments in which this game takes place in also add to the experience, in areas such as Victorian Castle Dimitrescu, the dilapidated Village, and Heisenberg's underground factory. The level of detail and polish that went into each of the environments by the team at Capcom is phenomenal, made possible by the latest version of the RE engine. 

      Combat this time around, when compared to Resident Evil 7, is the forefront of the experience. The gunplay is satisfying and fairly balanced overall, although continue to expect enemies to act as "bullet sponges", a staple of the resident evil franchise. Ammunition and weapon variety is increased considerably over Resident Evil 7, allowing for a more action - oriented experience. As a direct result of this, enemy encounters are less scary this time around, mostly due to the fact that they can be easily disposed of due to the emphasis on combat. Moreover, the jarring nature of many of the enemies found throughout the game also become less tense as the experience progresses, as you will see many of the same enemies due to the lack of variety. This was an issue with Resident Evil 7 as well, although this is a minor gripe. Furthermore, boss encounters are a delight and a considerable leap forward from Resident Evil 7, having mitigated the use of weak points which I find quite basic. Each combat encounter is still fairly streamlined and simple however, allowing for the game to progress at a fairly quick rate. The difficulty can be increased, to the extent of the inclusion of "Village of Shadows" which in itself is a much more challenging means to play the game. 

      Post launch content has been a treat as well, due to the likes of "Shadows of Rose" DLC, the expansion of the mercenaries mode, VR support, third person perspective, and more. This further adds to the replay value of Village, although this has always been a given for most Resident Evil titles. 

      Overall, I have had an incredible experience with Resident Evil Village and look foward to see what the team at Capcom will continue to with the Resident Evil Franchise! I thoroughly recommend!

I can not believe what I am seeing. It feels like my eyes are playing tricks on me but no, it's legit. I had my FPS counter up the entire time to confirm I wasn't crazy.

In short, this game runs like f*cking butter. Holy sh*t it is so, so smooth. Rock solid 144 FPS in my 3 hours of playing (at the time of this review) and it never dipped once. Not even from gameplay to cutscene transitions (which is typically when FPS dips occur), or even when moving from one area of a map to the next (another common offender of FPS stutters). 

I am nowhere even close to finishing the game but the performance alone gets a thumbs up from me. It's extremely rare I say that in this day and age with all the god awful PC ports constantly being released. I do recall hearing back when this game originally launched that there were performance issues regarding how Denuvo was implemented or something along those lines. So, I came into this game wary and with expectations tempered. Either it was fixed or those FPS drops only affected a small selection of people. Regardless, as it stands this game is unbelievably well optimized. 

I got this game for sale along with RE7 for roughly 60 bucks and that includes the gold edition of both of them. If you were like me and got any of those 2 games on sale, they are an absolutely steal. Yes I recommend Resident Evil: Village, it is fantastic. May or may not come back to update this review when I finish the game but like I mentioned before, the performance is so good it gets a thumbs up from me regardless.

Alright 10 hours later I have finished the main game and everything I wrote before still applies. There were a couple instances where the FPS would dip for a second but those instances were so rare it doesn't matter. It's not like I expect games to run flawlessly 100% of the time without any single hiccups. This game still runs like a dream and is an absolute blast to play. 

In comparison to RE: Biohazard, this game is a little less scary in favour of more action. Not necessarily a bad thing depending on how you view it, but something to think about. I personally didn't mind and found the wide arsenal of guns and the implementation of a shop system quite a fun departure from what was done in 7. 

I really liked how each antagonist had their own area and theme surrounding said area. The game has a village in the middle and surrounding it are 4 areas that each of the lords occupy. Beneviento's was my personal favourite, though it was shorter than I expected. For a roughly 10 hour game there is a surprising amount to do and see. It certainly felt much longer than 10 hours and it's one of those games where it's so good you wish there was more. However, it's easy to miss collectibles and with the game's challenges system, it incentivizes repeat playthroughs.  

On the topic of playthroughs, I finished my first game on standard difficulty. Definitely consider ramping up the difficulty if you're considering doing more playthroughs because at that point you are familiar with the game's systems and layout. I think I can count on one hand how many times I died in this game on my first playthrough. That is certainly a byproduct of the game giving you lots of resources during combat, but it's also a testament to how well the game gives instructions. There's plenty of chase sequences and puzzles to solve where it's not like my ammo or guns would even matter in those scenarios. But the game does an excellent job of nudging you on the right path to take when you're being pursued, or dropping subtle hints when trying to piece together clues to solve a puzzle. 

So I had a very smooth and pleasant experience with this game. Certainly part of it was the abundance of resources, but also the game itself just does a really good job of guiding the player without frustrating them. I could have all the ammo and healing in the world but if I kept dying to some chase sequence or stuck in a room for an hour it would be a very different discussion. None of this is to imply that the game is boringly easy or anything like that, it's just a solid experience all around and it strikes that perfect middle ground of challenging but fair.

In short, Resident Evil: Village is fantastic and I recommend it to anyone who isn't afraid to try some survival horror.

The story once again follows Ethan Winters, who grows from being a blank slate for players to immerse themselves into a really likeable fellow, once again having to deal with horrific sights and non-sensical stuff that's more than he signed up for (and still coming out on top). The new enemy design and variety is a much welcome step up from the regular three type molded from 7. The main baddies also have a lot of personality sewn into them, the highlights being the nine feet tall vampire lady, Alcina Dimitrescu and the nihilistic Karl Heisenberg, as well as the cold and manipulative Mother Miranda who is the baddest of baddies. Just as with it was in 7, Village also brings the family theme once again, having all of these characters have some kind of bond to one another even if they don't particularly are fond of each other that also relates to Ethan and his family. During his time at Capcom, Shinji Mikami created two great things - survival horror with the classic RE, and its reimagining with RE4. It's been almost 20 years now Capcom is exploiting these concepts, again and again. To the point that if you played RE4, you played Village as well:

Dirty village? Check
Majestic castle? Check
Modern factory? Check
Boat and giant fish boss? Check
Weapon upgrades? Check
Finding and combining treasures? Check
Shooting chicken for stuff? Check
and the list goes on

All that, to an extent, would not be a problem if Village was a good RE4. It isn't.

1) Setting. It's no secret that RE came to be heavily associated with Raccoon City, Umbrella, and zombies - to the point of everything that came later seen as heresy. That said, RE4's Ganados were pretty much "zombies with weapons" so it worked well. However, Village throws in too many stuff that feels like it belongs in a different game - including vampires, werewolves and scary dolls.

2) Combat. There is not much difference to where you shoot anymore, you won't be crippling or disarming your enemies, they merely get staggered every 3rd shot so the combat feels much less nuanced and a step back on the whole. The weapons likewise lack nuance and each new one is simply a straight upgrade over the previous one, even with all the improvements - making the system superficial. 

3) Identity crisis. There are generally two kinds of horror games - in first, you are a weak schoolgirl with no or barely any weapons and the fear factor comes from the fact any engagement might prove fatal; in second, you're a spec ops with a machine gun and you're only ever scared of one thing - running out of ammo. Village tries to be both at the same time, and it doesn't work. The segment where your weapons are taken away and you spend about an hour solving puzzles and hiding in closets from a giant monster feels super disconnected from the rest of the game - the existince of this segment alone is enough to discourage replayability.

4) Pacing. Which is all over the place. It starts slowly, with village itself serving as a prologue/tutorial. The Castle, first actual area, is everything you'd expect from a RE game - action packed, fun puzzles, memorable characters, decent lengh. In contrast, House Beneviento and Reservoir are fairly short and straight to the point. And when you're already tired and are ready to watch the credits, the game throws a lengthy tedious labyrinth called the Factory at you. Imagine if Resident Evi 1/2l's laboratories were longer than the mansion and the police station respectively, and you'll see what I'm getting at. 

5) First person. I only got Village after discovering they added a third person view, but to be honest - it's not good, definitely not what the game was designed for. The Mercenaries mode is still first person only, giving me heavy PS1-era Biohazard Gun Survivor vibes, and that's not a compliment.

TL;DR Village tries to copy RE4's successful formula, but feels underwhelming in the most core aspects and as just a clone in the others.

[h1]Resident Evil Village[/h1]

With the success of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, a upcoming sequel was practically guaranteed. Resident Evil Village continues the survival horror line of recent Resident Evil games by combining the survival horror properties of RE7 with fast paced aspects taken from RE4 to make this a critically successful title in the franchise.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]The story of Resident Evil Village takes place a little over three years after the events of RE7 and is set in Romania. Ethan and his family were relocated under Chris' orders to protect their existence from the public (and unsavory organizations) after the events of RE7, but when Mia is killed by Chris and Rosemary, Ethan's infant daughter, is kidnapped, his chase leads to a nearby deserted village where Ethan's search begins.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]I found much of the story's structure well-constructed and interesting thanks to Ethan's individuality as a more fleshed out character instead of the self-insert image he held in RE7 and the neopagan cult that was prominent within the village. Ethan is a much more relatable and compelling character in which he is basically the best father ever and is also more composed for someone who has faced BOWs already. The village in relation to the cult is an idea that goes as far back as RE4 and it does okay here, although not much is done with it outside of some files and one cutscene with the last remaining human villagers.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]For other characters, they're all great but I think they could have been given more screentime. For example, the Four Lords: Lady D, Donna, Moreau, and Heisenberg. Outside of one scene, they never make contact with each other ever again and are exclusively tied to their respective set pieces. I was expecting Lady D to be more of an overall threat through the game due to how much trailer time she got, but she's done and over with after the Castle section. It's the same case for the other lords (Donna and Moreau especially). Miranda is the most obvious one with this issue; outside the one scene you see her along with the Four Lords, Ethan and Miranda never have encounters with each other until near the end of the game - hell, Ethan barely acknowledges her existence until she actually appears before him as Mia after killing Heisenberg. As for Chris, I was already not buying the possible heel turn from the most iconic RE character into a villain when the trailers came out and of course, the subversion was there. I'm all up for seeing Chris, but there were times where I felt like there was no reason for him [b]not[/b] to explain everything to Ethan early on or to act hostile towards him so it just feels contrived.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

The gameplay is similar to RE7 except it's now built for much faster pacing. There are more enemies thrown at you, albeit with more ammo drops, you're given a lot more leeway to your movement, and you can now push back enemies after you successfully block their attacks. There are set pieces here like the first village fight which reference parts of RE4 that are still fun and challenging to play through. Monsters range from Lycans to the Cadou-powered Soldats in the Factory, but it's too bad some of the enemies are derived from the common enemy type in terms of design. Despite its similarity to RE7, it's still a very solid and enjoyable gameplay system.

The map is a wide arrangement of different settings that never feel too similar from each other. There's the widely explorable Village, the Gothic-styled Castle, the Beneviento Manor, and more varieties of places to progress towards. The levels are designed different aesthetically and mechanically so you'll have different tastes to the gameplay as you continue forward. It does, however, stagnate near the end when you enter the Factory. And yes, horror is still present in this game despite the added action aspects: [spoiler]The gameplay segment with "Baby" kept me in an anxious state for a few days...[/spoiler]

Weapons are a lot more varied now with different handguns, shotguns, magnums, proximity mines, and more. The inventory system is similar to RE4's too: an attache case system where items are organized by tiles. Ammo is common, but still should be managed due to the increased enemy count. There's a treasure system where you can collect treasures (and sometimes combine them) to sell them to Duke, the Merchant character of this game. You can buy a variety of items from ammo to modifications for your guns from Duke and even give him ingredients for food recipes which can give benefits like increase your maximum health or make you run faster.

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

Resident Evil games in the RE engine still look as great as ever. In fact, I'd say it's getting better as time goes on. Many of the background graphics in lightly lit places like the Castle or the Manor are exquisite. Flashlights shining dimly in dark areas are always a tense moment and really bring out the refined lighting and shadow effects in this game.

The sounds are quite crisp and clean. Each enemy has their own sound cues to assist you in detecting them and the soundtrack for Resident Evil Village overall adds a lot to the tone of Gothic and eldritch horror already shown through the atmosphere the game gives off.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Aside from a few issues I have with the flow of the story, I found myself satisfied with the time I spent playing Resident Evil Village. Even with the minor negative points I've noted, this game is still a solid addition to the series. The combined gameplay mechanics from RE7 and RE4, the extended exploration, and the added Winters' Expansion DLC makes this game an enjoyable experience with high replayability. 

Recommended for all players who enjoy survival horror with some action sprinkled in.

Resident Evil, Metal Gear Solid, and Mass Effect are my 3 favorite video games series of all time. I've played all there games many times. Easily thousands of hours invested, so I'm going to be a very harsh critic when it comes to games I care about.  Resident Evil Village is going to receive that same treatment. I've read the reviews both good and bad and finished the game. I'm now ready to jump into my pros and cons list. 

Pros:
 * Game looks gorgeous, environments are exciting. You visit lots of locations, you aren't stuck in a village like the title implies. 
* RE8 is a mix of RE7 and RE4, both solid games in the franchise. There's no item box, you buy and sell items to a vendor. You have plenty of item space on your person and it's up-gradable. (Also a con) 
* Lots of different weapons to find, to buy or unlock with many different upgrades for each weapon
* You can craft things: health, ammo and other goodies 
* Ethan is back from RE7 and he's a very likable character, he makes a great protagonist because he behaves like a normal human being would given the situations he's put in over and over again
* The main story is more lengthy then I was expecting, I think it's a couple hours longer than RE7, but that's because there is a lot more to find in RE8 (the length is also going to show up in the cons too)
* Treasures are back, just like 4 and 5, I can't remember if RE6 had treasures (who cares that was garbage game anyway) remember some treasures can be combined and they sell for significantly more, always check each item before selling
* A wide variety of enemies and there is also a minor animal hunting aspect to the game (you'll collect meat from them)

Cons:
* Honestly, not a fan of the story. I see how they tied it in to the rest of the RE Universe but pretty uninspiring I thought 
* As far the story goes, who on Earth can keep track of what villains or evil corporations are doing what, and how they relate to the rest of the universe. We started with the T-Virus and Umbrella (game release chronologically) and now we have black mold and good corporations turning bad and bad ones turning good. Children are infected, children are important, children are evil. I don't know, we just keep getting the same damn rehashed stories! 
* I did mention length as pro, but it's also a con. I think the game went on for about 2 hours too long. The first several hours of the game was a ton of fun but then near the half way point I was ready for it to be over and the last couple of hours I hated. It brought me back to the nightmares of playing RE6. WAY WAY WAAAAY to action oriented. [spoiler] Seriously, just F*** the whole factory part, I hate the cyborg BS or whatever you want to call those enemies. [/spoiler] 
* As I just mentioned the first few hours of RE8 is great, but this game completely lost touch with what made RE so awesome. It was scary, there was tension being built through excellent story telling and the use of unique cinematography. Simply put, RE8 runs out of gas and does the old let's just throw all this stupid ♥♥♥♥ at the player and see what sticks. It lost it's survival horror feel quickly.  
* I remember when RE had only zombies, or zombified creatures. Now we have [spoiler] werewolves, vampires and paranormal ♥♥♥♥ [/spoiler] It doesn't really feel like RE anymore. 
* They did Ethan dirty SPOILER INCOMING [spoiler] he was basically made of mold, because he was killed at the beginning of RE7 so he went for several years and never knew that? Even had a child?! WHAT?! That's the big deal of RE8?! That's ♥♥♥♥ story telling! [/spoiler]
* There is zero point to inventory management, you can craft things whenever and the crafting materials don't take up inventory slots. It's easy to save on space so I ask you why bother removing the item box when you never run out of room in the first place? They took that idea from RE4 for zero reason, because it truly has no effect on how you play. 
* Interacting with enemies other than shooting them is pretty dull. There are very few times where you can shoot environmental items so they effect enemies. Even shooting different body parts doesn't hinder or play any effect on them. A lot of the enemy interactions are seriously subpar compared to other RE titles. 

I could list a few more things on the cons list, but I think everyone is getting the gist of my review. It's not good, it's not the worst RE game but it's not in the top 3 like many people are saying it is. FYI, so you understand my standards, I'd say the pinnacle of the RE Universe is RE2 Remake (as of the time of this review). It got so many things right and arguably did it better than the original. With that being said, I can't give RE8 a free pass because it did several things right. I have to look at both sides of the coin. Was this game a step forward or a step backward? Unfortunately, I think it was not as good as RE7. SO, I'd buy this game on sale and that's about the only way I'd recommend this game. Otherwise, it gets a thumbs down from me.

Resident Evil: Village is the definition of disappointing.

On a mechanical level, the game is competent and fun. Gunplay is smooth and polished (if lacking some punch), just like the other RE titles built on the RE Engine. Enemy encounters are functional and, in isolation, often enjoyable. Village clearly positions itself as a spiritual successor to [i]Resident Evil 4[/i], leaning harder into action over survival horror, and at times this approach works well enough.

However, its weapon system is a clear downgrade from what RE4 achieved nearly two decades earlier. Instead of offering sideways progression where different guns serve different purposes, Village opts for a linear upgrade path. What that means is that each new weapon is simply a direct, objective upgrade of the previous one, rendering older weapons obsolete. There is little incentive to experiment, and upgrading early weapons becomes pointless when they are guaranteed to be outclassed in every single way by whatever's coming next. RE4’s arsenal encouraged diverse playstyles and situational choices; Village’s arsenal encourages saving your money for the last weapon of each category and never using anything else.

Where the game truly falters is in its pacing. Structurally, Village feels disjointed and poorly thought out. Major sections—with the most notable one being Castle Dimitrescu—are shockingly short for how much narrative and marketing weight they carry. The game constantly lurches between tones and gameplay styles without allowing any of them to fully develop. After a slow opening desperately copying RE4's opening hour, the game finally begins to gain momentum in the castle, only to slam the brakes entirely with the House Beneviento segment, which brings progression to a near standstill and makes repeated playthroughs a chore.

The story itself is also awful, with delivery so clumsy that it borders on unintentional comedy in the [i]bad[/i] way. Dialogue is awkward and unnatural, as if written by a 14 years old imitating dramatic storytelling without understanding how people actually speak. Characters interact in ways that feel emotionally hollow and strangely artificial, even for this franchise's standards. Mystery is achieved not through intrigue, but through excessive vagueness, withholding basic information for no reason other than to manufacture surprise (I'm looking at you, Chris). The late-game "twist" only carries weight for players who either skipped RE7 or played it while drooling all over the floor from zoning out. For anyone who paid the bare minimum attention, however, it lands with a dull thud.

The soundtrack is similarly underwhelming. Most tracks are forgettable and fail to do anything for the game and its atmosphere. The standout has to be the soundtrack for The Mercenaries mode, which is genuinely energetic and memorable, but unfortunately still an exception in an otherwise bland score.

And speaking of The Mercenaries mode, it represents one of the few genuinely successful parts of Village and, in my opinion, the most underrated and overlooked aspect of the game. Capcom attempts to blend classic (as in [i]Resident Evil 3: Nemesis[/i]) Mercenaries with the Raid mode from Revelations, and the result is surprisingly enjoyable. Its structure encourages constant engagement with the game’s strongest element (its combat) while the RNG-based builds promote adaptation and variety. It is easily the most replayable and consistently fun portion of the package, even if it lacks the depth it could've had. Also, for as bad as the Winters' Expansion DLC is as a whole, it does improve Mercenaries by introducing new playable characters with genuinely distinct playstyles and mechanical gimmicks. It injects the mode with personality and even more replay value, turning it into the DLC’s only success.

Yes, [i]only[/i] success. The official third-person mode added by the DLC feels unpolished and awkward, with stiff animations and camera behavior that is somehow worse than the fan-made third-person mod that existed long before Capcom's version. Movement lacks fluidity, combat feels less precise since the aiming is off, and the perspective often clashes with level design that was clearly never meant to be viewed this way. Rather than a new way to experience the game, it comes across as a rushed novelty feature added for marketing value since they had nothing else to justify the pricing.

Worse still is the [i]Shadows of Rose[/i] expansion, which is genuinely terrible in every respect. Its gameplay is shallow and repetitive, its stealth-heavy design strips away what little mechanical strength Village had, and its narrative is even more incoherent and melodramatic than the base game’s. It feels like self-indulgent fanfiction, relying on recycled assets, contrived emotional beats and underdeveloped mechanics to justify its existence.

In the end, Resident Evil: Village is a game that plays well but thinks poorly. Its mechanical foundation is solid, but it is dragged down considerably by weak narrative design, erratic pacing, and an oversimplified progression system. It feels less like a confident sequel and more like a collection of ideas stitched together without a clear vision other than appealing to Resident Evil 4 nostalgia.

Village may still provide some short-term entertainment if you enjoy the RE Engine games, but I wouldn't recommend getting it without a decent discount attached to it. But for players seeking a cohesive, well-rounded Resident Evil experience, Village is one of the last games in the entire franchise I'd ever recommend. It is serviceable at best, fun for short-lived moments, and often frustrating. An entry that settles for spectacle and mimicry instead of depth and consistency.
