Resident Evil Village, or as I like to call it, 'Resident Evil: The Hills Have Eyes Edition', is a game that'll have you questioning whether you're playing a survival horror game or a fever dream. From the opening moments where you're chased by a giant werewolf with a thirst for blood, to the final boss battle against an eight-foot-tall vampire lady, this game is full of moments that'll make you say, 'What the hell is going on?'

But don't worry, you won't be alone in your confusion. You'll have Ethan Winters, the game's protagonist, to guide you through this nightmare. And by 'guide you through', I mean stumble around blindly while muttering to himself and getting his hands chopped off for the fifth time. Seriously, if Ethan Winters is the only hope for humanity, we're all screwed.

The real stars of the show, though, are the game's villains. You've got Lady Dimitrescu, the aforementioned eight-foot-tall vampire lady who could crush you like a grape but instead wants to seduce you (hey, whatever floats your boat, Lady D). Then there's Heisenberg, a guy who's basically Walter White if Walter White was a mad scientist with a metal arm. And let's not forget the dollhouse, which is... well, let's just say it's a whole thing.

As for the gameplay, it's your standard Resident Evil fare - lots of exploring creepy environments, solving puzzles, and fighting off hordes of monsters with limited resources. But Village amps up the tension by constantly putting you in tight spaces with enemies that can jump out at you from any angle. And if that's not scary enough for you, there's a mode where you can play the entire game in VR. Because who needs sleep anyway?

All in all, Resident Evil Village is a wild ride that's sure to leave you with more questions than answers. But hey, at least you'll have Lady Dimitrescu to keep you company in your nightmares. Just don't expect her to cuddle with you. Unless you're into that kind of thing.

I had an enjoyable time with Resident Evil 8. I feel as though the jump from RE8 to RE7 was how RE4 jumped from RE 1-3 was; a more action horror focus rather than survival horror, but in the good way like RE4 did. Good action sequences while not completely diminishing the horror aspect of the series. 

You can tell RE8 is very much inspired from RE4 when you contrast the similarities in locale (European Rural setting), Set Pieces (Castles, Village, Fortified Strongholds), collecting coins and treasure from the environment to sell to a mysterious merchant to upgrade gear etc. There were some aspects I liked with this such as the added cooking mechanic to upgrade Ethan's stats like Health or Blocking by encouraging you to explore the locations a little more.

My only noticeable criticism with the game was the extremely strong game start, with a meh midway, and then an adequate finale. It's obvious they used the start of the game for the marketing since it's the most interesting aspect of it (IMO), it has a very strong hook to lure you into the rest. But I enjoyed the game enough to not be completely dis-satisfied either. The game does eventually tie in the lore between RE7-RE8 and even into the greater Resident Evil universe. 

It's definitely worth playing for any fan of Resident Evil.

You can argue a lot of these are growing pains as the series evolves and finds it's comfortable medium, or say that I am nitpicking, but hey, YMMV.

[b]However[/b], despite all this, the game absolutely shines. The story is compelling, the environment rich and bone-chilling no matter where you go, the incredibly crisp and smooth graphics that are highly-optimized and the animations and transitions are smooth as butter. Everything you would expect from a AAA game and more. Have I mentioned the combat? What is a Resident Evil game without satisfying zombie (or in this case, lycan) destruction, as well as challenging & creative boss fights? There is no shortage of either action or horror in this entry and I couldn't be happier with how it plays out. I could go on, but I don't think it's necessary. Final verdict is this:

If you're on the fence, wait for a sale. I mean, you've waited this long, right?

Resident Evil Village is a game that certainly has its ups and downs, and as someone who enjoys the game, you are aware of both its strengths and weaknesses. The graphics and lighting in the game are indeed impressive and contribute to the overall atmosphere of the game. The game's replayability through its new game+ feature is also a definite plus, allowing players to continue to enjoy the game after completing it once.

However, it's impossible to overlook the fact that the game's launch was marred by significant performance issues caused by Denuvo DRM, which went unacknowledged by Capcom for an extended period of time. It's frustrating when a game's performance is negatively impacted by an intrusive DRM solution, especially when it takes so long for the developers to address the issue.

Finally, it's disappointing to hear that the VR version of the game will be exclusive to the PS5 and PSVR2, which limits the accessibility of the game's full potential to a specific group of players. Nevertheless, despite these drawbacks, the game's interesting story and impressive graphics make it a game that is still worth playing.

Recommend dialing down most shadow options, moving to medium-high for mesh/model and lighting options and turning off Ray tracing and vertical sync to start. If you're not familiar with the impact the settings each will have just go one by one until you have the best settings for your rig and try to get all of those settings settled on before continuing any further past that first typewriter checkpoint. Howdy, y'all! Gather round the campfire, 'cause I got a story to tell about a new game that's got the Wild West buzzin': Resident Evil Village.

All in all, Resident Evil Village is a game that'll make you jump out of your skin one minute and cheer with excitement the next. It's a wild ride that's perfect for anyone who loves horror, action, or just a good old-fashioned western shoot-em-up. I really enjoyed this game. I don't know if it has enough content in it to justify the price, this game was EXTREMELY short. Rose's DLC adds a lot to it and I absolutely loved it but that's an extra charge for more gameplay. The environment in this game is downright beautiful, there's still some scares (although I don't think we'll ever get as scary as RE7 was), and a really neat storyline if that sort of unconditional familial love is something that tugs at your heartstrings. I was very compelled by Ethan's love for his daughter and I don't know if a father daughter relationship will ever rock me as hard as theirs did.

Resident Evil VILLAGE follows Ethan Winter's story as he searches for his missing daughter. Having just left the events of Louisiana behind, his past comes back to haunt him once again. Once again, we experience the events unfold through The World's Best Father's eyes. if Resident Evil's 7 inspiration was the Original Resident Evil with its looping level design and focus on gore and horror then Resident Evil VILLAGE's inspiration was RE4. Throughout my playthrough I felt a sense of familiarity from its level design and gameplay, which was very welcome. It combines some of the best aspects of past games to create an overall great package: Persuers from past RE games, gameplay and level design from RE4 and a really nice story. If you've played RE7 (which I recommend you do if you haven't) you know what to expect. Memorable characters will haunt, torture and mock you as you traverse each of their twisted dungeons. I recommend turning aiming reticles off for a much more immersive experience. Family plays a very important role in the story and seeing Ethan overcome daunting obstacles in the name of love really moved me. I'm still in awe at how much I cared about Ethan, Rose and Mia.  Speaking of Rose, she gets her own DLC story which further strengthens the family bond. At first, she comes off as a bratty teenager going through an emo phase but by the end of it, I came to really like her and felt nothing but compassion towards her. Resident Evil Villllllllllillllilllllllage is what happens when a committee meets and decides to make a sequel by trying to smash together the best bits of two of the best entries in a series and hope it makes an even better game. I can't help but feel that this was originally going to be a whole different game (i.e. Not Resident Evil) then Capcom got hold of it, chucked Ethan Winters into it, and made it a sequel that never needed to happen.

RE7, and before it RE4, were great because they changed up a tired and increasingly cliched format. RE4 knew not to take itself too seriously and was fun, scary and challenging. RE7 got (slightly) more serious, at least until the end, and was a pretty horrifying experience. You know whats not scary? Being able to craft your own ammunition from scrap metal and chemical fluid. Or having various parts of your body impaled, removed or mutilated and having it not impact your ability to perform tasks in the slightest. Again; this worked in RE7, but it just feels silly now.

Remember zombies? Zombies were pretty important in RE games. Now we have werewolves and vampires and....zombie vampires or something. Again, this would be fine if it actually made any sense in the context of the world, but it doesn't. The designers obviously realised this and just gave up making any attempt to explain it beyond "umm umm mould or something". And don't get me started on Chris F-ing Redfield.

In summary: too short, too mad and not very challenging or scary. But hey, go play it. Its Resident Evil! Apparently.

[b]"Resident Evil Village" is a technically and artistically flawless blockbuster cinematic game. Visuals are breathtaking. Its world is amazing with a lot of unique locations and strong, surreal atmosphere. Sound design is a masterpiece. Gameplay is fluid with addictive battles. It's a game incredibly fun and that partially its problem. In order to become more popular it lost many of the series' characteristics. Plenty of supplies and a huge inventory make the experience less survival. Also, It's too linear, with limited freedom and easy puzzles. The series has evolved into a run and gun action that is less frightening and needs no thinking at all. That's not necessary bad, but it's certainly different.


Manometer: 8/10[/b]


The good
- Breathtaking visuals. Amazing detailed models and textures, awesome lighting. It's a piece of art.
- Fantastic world with weird, haunted atmosphere. From the creepy, abandoned in a hurry, village to the imposing castle above it and so many other unique locations, everything will make you feel stranded and alone.
- Fluid, fun gameplay with responsive controls. Each level has different approach which makes it interesting enough. Some locations prioritize action and others puzzles. The overall pace is great and never lets you get bored. Shooting is addictive and kills are rewarding.
- One of the best sound designs ever in a video game. Amazing job with the environmental sounds. Every bush's rustling, every door's crackling will make you sweat. It never feels excessive. Everything is super realistic with attention to detail. Battles' sounds, shooting, enemies' roars are great. Ethan's sounds, heavy breathes, struggling makes it even more suspenseful. 
- A stunning cinematic experience with great flow and high quality cut scenes. Fantastic direction and photography.
- Great characters design. Although mobs are a little bit boring, the bosses are pretty unique visually. The main five enemies have a weird, grotesque style that helps on creating an eerie, almost surreal atmosphere. They're all absolutely unforgettable. The Duke is such a cool guy.
-  Very good job on motion capturing. Great animations. Very good facial expressions. Everything feels super smooth and realistic.
- Nice, convincing voice acting performances.
- The main story isn't anything special but the lore surrounding this small village is pretty rich. A combination of traditional legends, medieval vibes, modern gear and sci-fi elements make the game's atmosphere even more unique.
- The "Village of Shadows", that small animation video at the beginning is pure art and could easily be a stand alone short movie.
- A menu full of extras gets unlocked the first time you finish the game. It includes challenges, concept art, 3d models, videos and more.

The bad
- It isn't survival horror. Unlike older games of the series that you have to survive with whatever you find, here there is a shop, you can loot enemies' bodies and sell trophies in exchange for bullets and gear. The supplies are plentiful and the inventory is huge. You don't need to count your bullets anymore. The game has evolved into a run and gun action shooter which is entertaining but not exactly what you expect from a "Resident Evil". Especially the last part with all those stuns, blockbuster battles, bombarding and tank driving threw me completely off.
- This cinematic approach is great for selling to bigger audiences, but it doesn't have that raw horror feeling of its predecessors. It feels too restricted, too guided. There are many scripted sequences with predetermined path of movement and others that look like QTEs. It just keeps reminding you that it's a movie and not an actual experience that you have to find your own way to escape.
- Puzzles are easy with completely linear and uninspiring structure. Usually you don't need to think or even open the map cause the game automatically guides you to the next object that you have to find. A little bit more freedom is offered at some locations but it never really "opens up".
- A lot of things that Ethan does make absolutely no sense if you think about them. It's like he doesn't have a certain plan and tries random things. Furthermore a lot of things seem to happen completely by accident. Luckily all the monsters throw him at the right place.

A wonderful mix of Resident Evil 2 Remake, Resident Evil 4, and 7.
From start to finish I had a very enjoyable time, it's cheesy and knows it, but it can be creepy at times, not exactly a survival horror game but still has the gameplay elements of them with excellently juicy combat mechanics, fluid movement, and just great overall environmental design on top of it all that I often just stopped to admire while exploring.

My favourite aspects were exploring/scavenging/unlocking areas like the central Village that reminds me of the police station in RE2R, the Castle, and the Factory, those felt like the core gameplay loop, hunting for key items and resources while navigating a complex area with plenty to discover while dodging and engaging enemies.
My least favourites were the gimmick sections, mainly Beneviento's doll house escape room while unarmed being chased by an instakill monster, and Moreau's "floor is lava" swamp section, though that one did have a tiny bit more exploration with regular combat and a more standard boss fight. But those sections didn't take advantage of the core systems that are the strongest areas of the game.
Luckily those sections were relatively short and more in the middle of the game (first a bit in Village, then Castle, Village, Doll house, Village, Moreau, Village one last time to unlock the last areas, then Factory, and finale) which meant overall none of it left a bad taste in my mouth, and I can see the rationale for trying to put some variety in the middle to make sure nothing gets too stale.

Your movement feels so satisfying, even though you aren't sprinting like the Doom Marine, the speed and detail in all the animations from weapon sway to subtle camera sways and your quick turn and such made it feel smooth and great to sprint around, you don't really get stuck in geometry.
How guns feel to use, their animations, the flash of a muzzleflash and seeing a flash on bullet impact, and blood spurts coming out of enemies that visibly twitch and fly backwards and get knocked back, all the stuff is just a testament to the fact that you can have good combat even in a game that is living in the borderworld space of survival horror/action horror games, you don't have to have bad combat if you're making a survival horror game, please, I beg you devs.

It's a bit sad that REVillage doesn't take more inspiration from RE4, mainly in weapon variety/progression. 
In RE8 all weapons you find are in a linear manner improvements to your previous ones, simply better stats overall even without upgrades. When RE4 tried to differentiate them, make it so that you would maybe even want to stick with an earlier one and keep upgrading that one, because it had the best crit chance, or could penetrate enemies, or was the most well rounded, or did the most damage but took up the most space and had a slower firerate. RE8 also is maybe a tiny bit too generous with its inventory space, could have used a smaller inventory perhaps, and more thought put behind the size/shapes of different items to make players think about their inventory management more.

I hope Capcom makes more in this vein, RE2R vein, full complete games with no hacked off endings in DLCs or entire gamemodes people have been used to getting with the standard edition, just a solid fully fleshed out complete singleplayer package, they've been kind of nailing it with these and it makes me excited for RE4R.

But, compared to RE2R, RE3R, RE7, Village is a bit more technically unstable, I don't know if it's Denuvo DRM, or something else, but previously I tried playing it and it just was constantly crashing randomly-- Had 60fps almost locked, could even play with settings at relatively high (MAX object detail, med shadows & volumetric effects, med0.25GB textures, contact shadows and cache on, CACAO on, rest off, vsync on, 1366x768res) but before it just crashed no matter the setting, low or high, despite running super smoothly. 
I upgraded my RAM, from 8 to 16GB, and well, crashing seems to have stopped? 
Laptop, Win11, i5-11400H 3050RTX 4GBVRAM otherwise.
Could also be just some magical driver update, or Windows update difference, or REFramework version I used (seems mandatory, also you need it to turn off Vignette and edit FOV, highly recommended), but I suspect 8GB RAM is just too little for this game, that, or Denuvo, which hopefully gets patched out later this year just like Capcom has patched Denuvo out from RE7-2-3R before.
Hopefully Capcom also work on their settings menu UI a bit for future titles. Though all the options available are very much appreciated, it's clunky to navigate them and change your settings (e.g. changing resolution isn't a drop down menu but you clicking arrows cycling through resolutions which actually change immediately and ask if you want to keep it, meaning you are forced to do that constantly for each resolution until finding the one you want)-- RE2&3R had this issue as well, but it stood out less there because I set it and forgot it because those games ran so hassle-free, whereas I kept tweaking RE8 out of paranoia with all my crashing history (wanted to put graphics higher, but scared to go over memory limits in case that caused the crashes, but I had 60fps with my tests with even higher settings).
Oh, also game doesn't close properly, it just stays open when you exit (delete key...) and you are forced to shut it down via your task manager, so again, not all is completely right and stable with RE8

But, game's gorgeous with great art, environments, animations, gameplay feels so good with fun varied enemies and good weapons, runs super smooth on my laptop, apart from one final crash at the very end (didn't crash otherwise after the RAM upgrade).
Recommended if you like the modern RERemakes & RE4.
Oh, and the demo seems representative of the current build, it crashed a ton before my RAM upgrade, and stopped after, so give that a shot.

The game's levels are expertly designed to create a sense of unease and tension, and the game's creatures are truly terrifying. The game also features a strong narrative with complex characters and a well-written story.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a horror game that will not disappoint fans of the franchise. I just went back and rated RE3 Remake again and I feel so invigorated that I'm gonna write a full review for this one too. It's been a minute since I played it so this won't be a great review (but who's gonna see it anyway?) I'm no OG player but as someone who's completed about 4.2833333 RE games, (33.333% of RE4 remake, 95% of Biohazard and all of 2 Remake, 3 Remake and Village) I think I'm qualified enough to say this game is pretty subversive as far as the series goes. This is the most recent entry in the main series and the most recent chronologically as well. It is the second and final game involving Ethan Winters, a boring but sweet protagonist who will forever live in Leon's shadow. This game is very good. I like how much it goes against things it already establishes during the game, from lord to lord in new and wacky scenarios. I love the ending, the lore, and the possibility of seeing Rose in future installments. I actually have less to say about this game than I thought so I feel stupid right now. What's new? Anyway, I liked my first experience with having a dedicated shop where you could collect treasures to sell for money. I love games with collectibles, especially when they appear on the map. I forget if they appear on the map here or not but uh. Cooking was an interesting mechanic which I enjoyed. Every area felt unique. The voice acting for everyone except Ethan and a couple of other characters was kind of mediocre. Interestingly enough, this game introduces the megamycete as the source of all of the chaos seen in the franchise thus far but actually does a lot less explaining or rationalizing the effects it has on the enemies and characters seen in this game compared to the previous ones. My fingers are freezing because of the vent underneath my desk so I'm gonna end this review by saying that this game is, for a Resident Evil game, a breath of fresh air and a good ending to the new experimental first-person horror style, even if this one was kind of a departure from horror and more into action territory.

Resident Evil 8 continues the Winters family storyline that was first presented on Resident Evil 7. This time, the title is more ambitious than its predecessor, but, is it able to improve the results of the previous entry of the series? Well, so so…

RE8 has the same outstanding points of RE7, but does not deliver a title that is able to cope with the less brilliant aspects that RE7 had problems with too. Again, we have a game with a brilliant start, but then it seems that the developers could not bring to the rest of the experience the same quality. The atmosphere and the story of the game is pretty good, as it is the general gameplay, but it is sad that again we have a kind of a rollercoaster experience, with the highest point in the first hours of the game and then we slowly go down. I think that this may be more of a franchise problem other than just a few titles with this problem, because something similar happened with RE2 Remake.

Anyway, the title is still pretty solid and very good (one of the best games of the last years, probably). It is just a bit sad that we are talking about a very good game and not an instant classic, because it really had the material to become something like that.

The game has decent story, gameplay, and replay value similar to the previous two entries that came out recently. Unfortunately, the game suffers from the same downside than its predecessors, the game is just way too short and linear. The game can be beaten easily in 2 hours without exploring, If you explore the game completely it will take you somewhere between 4 to 5 hours depending on your speed.

Gameplay wise, if you played previous entries, you know what you are getting into, since it has not change much since RE7. The only new thing add it is the upgrading system similar to RE4. You can upgrade weapons to do some serious DMG. The only thing I dislike about it, is that where RE4 weapons were almost all useful once upgraded, because once you finish upgrading they had special perks. In this game there is no perks once you finish upgrading the weapons, so the best weapons are the ones you receive last and that is it.

The mercenary mode is intriguing but the HARD scenarios are just way too hard and annoying. I got SSS rank on the 4 basic scenarios in hard mode, but honestly I would rather not play that again. The game goes out of its way to make it hard by just allowing you to use the first handgun you receive in the game, and the rogue lite elements are almost pointless since you will be choosing the same abilities  every time anyway.

The DLC is interesting and makes the game feel more like real survival game than the main entry. Bullets are hard to come by and you actually need to make a choice between running or shooting and sometimes making the wrong decision will kill you. Also, sports some new elements to it in its second part but I won't spoil anything. The DLC has two bosses and both are hard to fight, specially in Hardcore difficulty.

Overall, I would give the game a neutral rating or a 7 out of 10.

Easily the laziest game I've ever played. Need to cross a gap? Push a cart into it. Still can't cross because the gap is too wide? No problem, just run around in a circle until that exact same cart respawns with no explanation. Now you can cross with both carts in the gap. That was a lazy puzzle.

At one point you are in a werewolf den completely surrounded. No worries though, as there are exploding barrels all over the place. Want to shoot them? You can't! The gun just locks onto the nearest enemy and not where you are trying to point. Why? Auto aim is turned on by default, even if you don't have any controllers installed. I'd say that there's a mix of RE4, Dead Space and the Evil Within sprinkled throughout the game. Overall RE8 feels very polished, the puzzles are intuitive and not annoying, there's a great factor of exploration and getting valuables, which is very rewarding when you manage to find that hidden treasure. 

You'll still be fleeing from some enemies, especially in some regions and on higher difficulty. You still have the options to hide and avoid conflict but if you're prepared, having guns and actually fighting your way through scary environments while trying to survive can't help but remind me that that's what horror games are all about. That's what makes them enjoyable and RE8 encapsulates that perfectly.

Capcom and the RE Team took a huge risk when they caveated from the traditional 3rd person formula they had going on for years and made RE7 not only in the 1st person, but created an original character and set it all in a different environment with a different story as well. It worked, and a few years later we get greeted with Resident Evil Village. 

Much like other RE games, this one (story wise) is insane and over the top, as most of them have been since RE4. The characters are crazy, the setting is creepy and beautiful and the game play is a lot of fun. It still has the same campy/cheesy dialogue you'd come to expect by now from an RE game, but whether or not you're someone who scares easily or you just enjoy the franchise, I think they did a very good job with this game. 

With sudo open world exploration, the ability to buy and upgrade weapons as well as prepare meals to boost your stats, treasure hunting, puzzle solving, larger-than-life enemies, it's all here. 

My complaints would be that a lot of the boss fights are kind of one-dimensional and the story is sort of all over the place in terms of consistency. But, it's not enough to hold me back from recommending this game to anyone who, a year or so after it's release would still be on the fence about buying this game.

Resident Evil 8 is a decent enough action romp which kept me hooked until the later stages of the game, where it became a bit of a trudge and I was hoping it would end. I waited until now to play it as I hate RE being a FPS, so the third person was welcome and I enjoyed that side of it.

However, as others have said, this is NOT Resident Evil anymore. Maybe they could continue this as some kind of spin off series, but then go back to roots making a true successor to the original survival horror genre that Resident Evil founded. Come on Capcom, show us some innovation, shake up the original style somehow to make it relevant today, give us something fresh while still keeping that creepy, isolated feeling of days gone by. There were no chills to be found in RE8, which is really unfortunate.

As an action adventure game I give this 7/10, due to there being very little chance I'll play it again, though it was highly polished and overall an enjoyable affair.
As a survival horror game I can't give it a rating as it really isn't one.

Unexpectedly slightly disappointing. The game takes from RE4 and RE7, but it's not scary like 7, and the combat and game mechanics are nowhere near as fun, tense and satisfying as 4. 

I think that village concentrated on visual presentation over gameplay in terms of level design. While visually interesting it's very cluttered resulting in combat being much less tactical and less fun.
 Combat feedback and reaction of enemies to where you shoot them is years behind RE4, a game that came out 17 years ago. I do feel that village was also trying to go for this style of combat.

The castle is great but comes to an end too soon. Lady Dimitrescu is a really cool cutscene character, but gameplay wise she's a lame duck. Unfortunately she has a single slash attack that she takes about a minute to wind up to. She only ever walks at you and once you realize you can gently trot away she ceases to be scary or interesting. 

Then she turns into a very boring and uninspired monster, making for a boring boss fight and is gone early. It could have been amazing if she'd kept her same form for the fight and you battled her in some very tense scenario similar to the right hand in RE4. This would have been a great payoff for all of the buildup of her character that was wasted. 

Some quite uninspired level design - Moreau's level in particular. None of the main bosses are satisfying or tense/well designed fights. While the rest of the level is decent and creepy, the doll boss is crap; run around the house for a couple of minutes to find her a few times. Moreau - boring. Lady and Heizenberg - waste their characters and turn into generic monster/machine bosses that are not fun to fight. Miranda - visually very cool but not fun/interesting to fight, and some dodgy sound mixing.

There are some decently designed enemies: soldat with heart you have to hit are better than any of the main bosses in terms of combat design, but in general I don't find the combat mechanics to have a good feel to them. I think that the combat they went for would work better in a third person view, but it would have to be designed from the ground up with this view in mind.

There is a really great game map with color-coded completion status. All games that have a map should learn from this! Enjoyable poking around the map to find everything, and how new things appear back in the village.

Great graphics, generally good sound design although sometimes I think mixing levels between different effects/music are a bit off.

It was an ok game but I think that the visuals should have been built around gameplay, not the other way around.

The story of this one was great, as well as the sound design, characters, visuals, and voice acting! Gameplay-wise, it is basically just like the previous game. I love how this one brings back Chris and mentions a few other characters from the older Resident Evil games (you'll see which ones if you read the documents). I also love how Duke says "What are you buying? Just something an old friend used to say", in reference to the iconic merchant from Resident Evil 4, that used to say "What are you buying?".

When it comes to the characters, each one of them is unique in their own way, we have Lady Dimistrecu and her three daughters (the Internet went crazy about these), the charismatic Heisenberg, Mother Miranda with her tricks, Duke and his deals and items that can save your life, Chris Redfield making a comeback, Ethan - who was the playable character from Resident Evil 7, the horrible Moreau with loser complexes, and Beneviento with her creepy dolls.

Although the game doesn't have as much horror as the classic games, it was still scary, especially with the chasing phases with Dimitrescu and that weird big baby in Beneviento's house.

Overall, it was a fun game to play, and very engaging, yet still with some of the essential Resident Evil elements in it to remind us that yes, it is still a Resident Evil game.

I wish I had read more of the negative reviews before buying this game, but I was bewitched by the amazing screenshots and the "Overwhelmingly Positive" rating. Only after playing the game did I come back here and read the critical reviews and realize they were so right.

This game is deeply flawed in two main areas.

The first is technical. It was clearly designed for consoles and controllers and does not work well on PC with mouse/keyboard. They didn't seem to spend any time at all adapting it to a PC environment, so adjusting things like screen size, brightness, volume, even mouse sensitivity are difficult or even impossible. I've never seen a modern game with such a minimal, useless settings area.

The second major problem is the game itself. If this was billed as an "interactive movie" I would have gone in with different expectations and I might have found it better. But it's basically a walking simulator with in-game cutscenes every few seconds. You walk from place to place, then the camera is taken over and you watch an NPC say or do something, then you are given permission to walk to the next place. The graphics, the art, environments, all of the visuals are BEAUTIFUL!! but... they are just nice drapings on what can hardly be called a game.

There are moments of action, of course. But rather than challenges which you can pass or fail, they are also essentially cut scenes. The first big one you get to throws a horde of baddies at you that is so big you wonder what is going on, until you realize, "Ah yes, this is the plot piece I am being railroaded into." Then, instead of trying, you sit back and let the cutscene take place so you can be taken into the next scene. It feels terribly staged and not like a game at all.

In fact, the game doesn't seem to make any effort to hide the fact that it is a game. Level design is painfully linear, so you have pretty much one way to go the whole time. There isn't much effort to hide "game elements" or integrate them into the story or world in order to preserve immersion. There is a weird shopkeeper who lives in the castle whose sole purpose is to sell you healing potions and gun upgrades... Which works for a game of course, but is comically absurd if we're trying to suspend our disbelief for the story.

It really is a beautiful game, and that makes me regret giving it a thumbs down. But the game itself is not good, and it is not formatted well for the PC either. You could probably enjoy this better by watching someone play it on Twitch or YouTube and treating it as a movie.

[i][b]I just wanted to share that even if you’re not familiar with Resident Evil 7, you can absolutely enjoy Village without feeling lost. The game is so thoughtful and kind in offering a little recap of the previous story right at the beginning, so anyone new to the series can easily get up to speed. However, if you’re looking for a deeper emotional connection and a richer understanding of the storyline, playing Biohazard from 2017 might make the experience even more special.[/b]

At first, the plot might seem straightforward, but it’s so much more than it appears. At its heart, it’s a touching tale of a father on a desperate journey to find his daughter, full of twists and mysteries that uncover the roots of the dreaded Umbrella Corporation. As the story unfolds, it becomes even more captivating, with an ending that will leave you absolutely stunned. Although the game isn’t overly long—about ten hours—you’ll find yourself wanting to return to uncover hidden treasures and side missions that add a little more magic to the experience. And with the return of the Mercenaries mode, there's always something fun to challenge you.

As for the characters, there’s something so intriguing about figures like Lady Dimitrescu and Salvatore Moreau. But what really seemed to take the breath away of those who tested the game were the breathtaking, realistic environments. From the chilling atmosphere in Dimitrescu Castle to the unsettling beauty of Heisenberg’s factory, every corner of the game is filled with so much detail and care. Even the eerie moments are crafted so beautifully—it's as if the game finds a way to make the scary feel strangely beautiful. One exception might be the encounter with the second boss, Donna Beneviento, but even in these dark moments, the setting’s richness really stands out.

As with every game in this series, Resident Evil Village gently encourages you to be curious and explore every nook and cranny. You’ll need to pay close attention to the items you find, as some of them require a little assembly or disassembly to be truly useful. One lovely thing about this chapter is that many of the items you find have longer-lasting uses, which makes everything feel so meaningful. Plus, there are areas that you’ll want to revisit later, which adds to the charm, almost like building with Lego blocks.

The map in Resident Evil Village is incredibly intuitive, making it easier to navigate and discover areas you’ve yet to explore. But I have to admit, for those who love collecting everything, it can be a little tricky to stay on top of all the hidden treasures.

Even though the ending might feel a bit drawn out, every minute of time spent is so worth it. The story is rich, emotional, and complex, with stunning visuals and villains who are beautifully developed. Resident Evil Village brings Ethan Winters' journey to a close in a way that’s truly satisfying, with gameplay that’s both terrifying and exhilarating. Above all, it’s a powerful story about family, hope, love, and the strength to never give up.[/i]

Joke aside, the two games do share a lot of similarities in terms of overall design, gameplay mechanics, even some story elements. Even though I no longer associate any Resident Evil titles with the word "horror" anymore, Resident Evil Village is still a great first-person survival shooter. The visuals are stunning. Two of the major levels are really detailed and full of personality. The characters, albeit too pompous, are quite charming. And of course, the tall vampire mommy. It is, however, not short of flaws regarding level designs and the overall story. 

[h1]Things I Like About Resident Evil Village:[/h1]

[b]1. The Tankiness Of Mobs[/b]
Disclaimer: I complete the game on Hardcore difficulty.
It is a rather rare occasion in which I would go and praise the sponginess of normal enemies in a video game without much criticism, but I genuinely like how tanky the lycans are. In the past titles, the regular enemies, zombies, are just fodders for players enjoyment of popping heads. Only hunters and lickers can give players some inconvenience. Now imagine all the regular enemies are replaced with hunters, and you can get a head start of Village's difficulty spike. Forcing players to go for weak spots as well as being aware of the surroundings where you can safely loop around really tickles my likeness. I am aware not everyone like this kind of difficulty, but I really think this design brings out the "survival horror" for Resident Evil.

[b]2. Rewarding Backtracking[/b]
Ever since 7 and 2 remake, I am quite looking forward to see how will this franchise handle and evolve the backtracking. Looking at Village I would say the dev does a good job at it. After the major levels, players can go back and unlock supplies, treasures for sales, and weapon parts using the key items found in those levels. Finding these items can drastically reduce the difficulty the lycans apply, and in general, players will feel rewarding when they explore the small semi open-world. I wish the game can drop the balls and don't auto-mark the point of interest on map when players get close to it.

[b]3. Other Compliments[/b]
→Again, the visuals are really good.
→That one scary part in Donna's house.
→Suitcase management and expansion are back.
→A merchant equivalent of Resident Evil 4, also the reference.
→Lady D, of course ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°).

[h1]Things I Dislike About Resident Evil Village:[/h1]

[b]1. Disproportionate Level Design [/b]
I'll describe how I feel about the length of each main levels with capital.
[b]DIMITRESCU→beneviento→moreau→HEISEnberg.[/b]
Maybe it's because Castle Dimitrescu is so flamboyant and memorable, maybe the other major levels focus on other stuff, the overall level design in each area feels disproportionate to me. I can vividly remember exploring room through room in the castle. I can only remember one part of House Beneviento. I only remember the boss fight in House Moearu. And I remember first half of Heisenberg's factory simply because of his performance. In terms of level complexity, I don't know why Lady Beneviento and Lord Moreau and their respective levels receive less attention than the other two.

[b]2. That Cliffhanger, Man... [/b]
A cliffhanger would be fine, if it gets addressed properly. Resident Evil Village starts off with Chris shoot Mia to death, knock Ethan unconscious, and take him and Rose away. This could've been a great yet brutal opening, if only it wasn't resolved in such generic way. I really wish the story after the event could have more twists, especially Chris' part. Something like he was forced to act, or simply calls Ethan in secrecy. I just don't think an apology and a really short explanation are enough.

[h1] The BEST modern Resident Evil. [/h1]
Resident Evil 8 blew me out of the way with everything it did. This is one of the few games I've completed this year, and I loved it. Everything it does is great. Let's break it down though.

[h1] Presentation/Graphics [/h1]
The game looks gorgeous, from castles to factories to the woods to the swamps, it always is brilliant with the art. I wish I could own this art book and just gawk at all the pieces of art. The characters look great, and I could say "Haha big boob woman!" but no. That would be ignoring the way better Heisenberg who is handsome as hell. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Village follows the same gameplay as Biohazard, but it is way more improved. The combat is fluid and the movement is great as well. The controls are responsive and the guns are amazing. I could end the review here and say get it for these two, but there's more.

[h1] The Village [/h1]
The Village is the only area that you constantly go back to, and it's not that good. It flip flops between being great and bad, but it's overall alright. Not the worst one, but what can you do when it's the only area you constantly go back to? It changes every time you kill a boss, but it's bland. I can't say anything negative in the end however, since it's not supposed to be grand. 

[h1] Castle Dimitrescu [/h1]
Starting the game at the part everyone talks about is the greatest decision in this game, and even greater how this is the longest section of the game. Exploring the castle is spooky and fun as well, this is the best area in the game, and even one of the best areas in Resident Evil entirely!

[h1] The Doll House [/h1]
This area is not good, hence why I didn't even bother to remember the name to it. The puzzles are annoying, and the boss fight is awful. [b] BUT OH MY GOD. [/b] this was the scariest area, and the shortest too! The area never overstays its welcome, not to mention the...the baby. It's great, and I'm glad it's 1 hour< 

[h1] The Reservoir [/h1]
Arguably my least favorite area, it's quite gross as well. I feel as if the puzzles aren't that good and the boss fight is dreadful. This is also the only part of the game where my game constantly crashed, but the villian here makes up for it entirely. Moreau is my favorite villain in the game, he's the funniest lil guy. But he definitely gets worse at the end. The worst area, but that doesn't make it bad. 

[h1] Heisenberg's Factory [/h1]
An AMAZING final area, with the best character in the game. Forget what I said about Moreau, [b] HEISENBERG [/b] is the best character. His voice actor fits his personality great and his design is amazing too. The whole area is perfect, completely matching the industrial feel of a factory. The end boss is perfectly well done too, and it looks amazing. The game ends on the highest note possible

[h1] The End (SPOILERS) [/h1]
From this point, the game made me lose my mind. [spoiler] once Ethan dies, Chris makes the game way more intense. [/spoiler] The endless horde of enemies made me scared, simply because I wasn't ready for it. Storywise, finding out what happened to Ethan in Biohazard made it a great twist. [spoiler] The ending, where everything ended for the Winters, was beautifully done. Ethan dies, and Rose becomes a government tool. [/spoiler]
Ethan Winters is a perfect character, and he is perfect in this game.

[h1] Finale [/h1]
Resident Evil 8 is a great game, and one of my top 3 Resident Evil's of all time. (4, 2, 8, 0, 7, 1, 5, 6, 3) It's a perfect game for people looking to get into the series, but it should be played AFTER Biohazard. There's a recap in Village, but Biohazard is an opener to this gameplay.

I will admit that this one surprised me, I rather enjoyed. The setting and mood was amazing (although, I enjoyed the more focused and singular locale of Resident Evil 7). I was surprised that the game took place in more than just the castle and it's titular Village prelude, but rather the village as a whole (the castles surrounding houses, a "factory," a home on the outskirts of town, etc)

As a side note, I was expecting Lady Dimitrescu to be the main villain of the game, considering all the hype she had gotten as well as the focus on her daughters, and virtually no mention of the games REAL villain despite their appearance pretty early on in the game. I was pretty surprised that Lady Dimistrescu was simply just a side character.

The gameplay of RE7 was carried over to this one, so if you played that one you know what you're getting into here. It's still Resident Evil, but in the first person. There's plenty of slow paced exploration, inventory management, moody & creepy atmospheres, and a few action sequences. I'll admit that I enjoyed the creepiness of RE7 a little more, but I loved many of the set pieces of this game (the castle is definitely the highlight of the game).

The story is definitely the weakest part of this game, and I feel that it comes to the questionable actions and occurrences of the main character, Ethan Winters. To give an early game example, Ethan gets his right hand cut off, and a little while later he simply just "sticks it back on" and keeps on fighting. I know that there's an explanation for it, but it ends up feeling thin and insinuated (and that same argument can be applied to RE7 as well, as the same thing happens to Ethans left hand. Honestly, I think Ethan is the only character I have ever played as who got both his hands cut off and was still able to fire a gun with a fully functional hand).

The replay value of this game is very good because it has A LOT of stuff apart from the main story mode. After beating it once you unlock Mercenaries mode, which is quite good, but also very different from other RE games's mercenaries, making it a pretty original one!
You have a lot of stuff to watch from the menu; unlockables, characters's models, extras, etc etc

Probably most casual players will play it and beat it only once, while most RE players will beat it many times, the other modes too, and try to unlock as many stuff as possible. But of course to each their own experience!

Another great entry for the RE Series!
The story follows Ethan Winters and his journey to save his daughter from the twisted inhabitants of an old village. The characters can very from one another. I found that the protagonists such as Ethan and Chris Redfield turned out to be either bland or pretty boring compared the colourful antagonists such as Heisenburg or Lady D with their over the top (and really enjoyable) performances. The story itself is pretty great at the start with it being very mysterious and intriguing, however i do think that it looses its steam around the ending as it just results into a generic mission. 
The setting of the village is very reminiscent of RE 4, but does enough to stand out on its own. Each part of the map that is owned by one of the antagonists in the game are uniquely designed and keeps things from getting repetitive. I think that the best part of the map was the castle as it can be seen from the design choices made that there was a lot of work put into this section alone. I'm not saying that the other parts of the map aren't that great, but i do think that the Castle is a fantastic standout. 
Visually, the game is gorgeous in the RE engine. Performance wise, the game ran really smoothly and i never ran into any bugs or glitches that would have taken me out of the experience. The art directing was also really well handled in making a believable European village and making such memorable villains such as the previously mentioned Lady D and Heisenburg. 
Sound and Audio aren't really a stand out, but suited the game really well. The soundtrack managed to deliver the right tone throughout the runtime and the audio for things such as guns and enemies also felt very fitting. 
In terms of gameplay, its pretty fun. Now if you didn't like the combat in RE 7 there's a good chance that your not going to enjoy this either, however i do think that they have somewhat improved upon it and have added more options for the player to mess around with. Guns feel great to use and the upgrade that can be bought do feel that they aid in combat. The inventory system is your classic affair which is great as it is Resident Evil's strongest gameplay mechanics. I also like how resources are scarce which offering a crafting system for the player to be able to make things on their own accord (depending if they have enough resources). At the start, the enemies in this game are pretty well varied and are fun to engage with, however the further you progress there really isn't much more variety than there was at the start. The Duke is a brilliant addition with there being options to buy, sell, upgrade guns and even upgrade things such as health and blocking. This definitely encourages more exploration in order to be the best of the best in order to fight against enemies. Finally, the boss fights are pretty great. The only one i wasn't a huge fan on was Donnas', but apart from that, the rest of them were a fun challenge. 
Overall, while i doesn't do anything to revolutionise the series that its apart of, Resident Evil Village is a nice addition with its core gameplay and atmosphere being as solid as some of the greatest in the RE lineup.

All style, no substance.
As for a game advertising itself on being the best of RE4 and RE7, it underdelivers on both action and survival.
But, lets get to the beginning.
It begins with quite long walking-simulator section, which interesting on the first playthrough, kills any subsequent rounds just on how dragged and linear it is. There's literally no items to find and as for file hunting, yeah, AAA entertainment right there. After a ton of jumpscares over-relying on  1st person perspective, we're straight up thrown into the action, and all the worst flaws of the game are immediately made known. Fist - pacing. We fight 1 enemy, next door over 4 of them, next a whole horde, then - nothing, some 3 enemies right after, and a TON of walking with no combat for about an hour or two. The game doesn't know what it wants to be - a bunch of encounters thrown together and then LOOONG section with nothing happening at all. Pacing sucks horribly. And when it comes to the fight there's so much BS... 2 types of grunt enemies - 1 fast and 1 slow, that have little to no variety amongst each other, which is as well, since you can't do anything to them besides trying to shoot in the head. Nothing besides blocking and pushing away, which doesn't even stun them! Now I get why people complained about RE2R combat. You can't even knife them when they're down! They're back up in 2 seconds! You still need need to politely wait for them to get up so you'll have a first row to the peak RE8 experience of busting a whole clip to their head and hope for a headshot, since aiming anywhere else is a waste of ammo thanks to horrible hitboxes. What were they thinking?! They're all left to chance (?). Body shots can be shrugged off or make enemies swirl arund like ballerinas. Such tactics, so satifaction. It's a pleasant surprise if you score a headshot or a down, because mostly they tank pistol to the face like nobody's business. 
And you just stand there reminiscing better times.
Times, when there was such a thing as level design, where encounters would be immediately distinguishable and memorable.
There's no level design here 80% of the time. The first horde and last and that's all, and that's stretching. Mostly it's just a plain, flat field, or a tunnel for a change. One instance of grass obscuring your view. You CAN barricade doors, but it neither a common occasion or particularly sound from a tactical standpoint. One differerence is with flying enemies, appearing 3 times, where overhead cover matters, and piss poor AI emerges in its full - awfull glory. No door breaking, window barging, ladder climbing, it only has the enemies simply walk (even run on harder difficulties) in the straight line at you. If their 2 braincells meet they manage to strife. They have two attacks if they're armed, otherwise they just bite. And for a mini boss there's a version that has helmet on that you have to blow up and grill with your guns a little longer. No worries though, usually you can just fall back behind a certain line and they obediently go back to their spawn spot. YEP. Even on the Village of Shadows you can reliably crouch and shank the slow zombies' ankles away. Truly, a worthy succesor of RE4! 
Granted, at the last section of the game a new type of enemies are introduced, which is a breath of fresh air. The trick with them is to bait an attack so they expose their weak spot, which is both a reliable and exciting tactics, but noting can save the overall picture by then.  
Bosses telegraph poorly if you're doing anything to them, so you question if their poorly telegraphed weak spots are weak spots at all. Only final boss is geuinely ingenious encounter.
There're optional bosses, but don't worry, they go back to their spawn if you run away, such obedient little pups they are! You can juke them like that, they don't regenerate health or anything!
Exploration is ok, I guess, a little bit of hoarding for bosses, which rewards smart conservation of resources, extremely nice, no way you're going to have to choose what to keep and what to get rid of since you're virtually never going to run out of inventory space because raw materials are unlimited and separate from your normal inventory bag. Crafting's ok, I guess.
There's one "stealth" section mixed with old school find and use item section. On first time it's intriguing, but once you realize how linear it is it becomes a chore and all pretense of horror are replaced by boredom.
And it's a shame, because the scenery they chose is quite unique. The snow fallen Eastern European village leading to a homey castle, a riverbank and industrial factory. You rarely ever see socrealism represented as an aesthetic in a video game, and contrasted with gothic castle, yum! It's AAA perfect setting for a horror story (trust me)! Attention to detail is great. However, RE3R curse rears its ugly head yet again, there's a plenty of beautiful barren locations! The drawn-out begining and unreasonably glorified "horror" sections are the best examples, the whole point is to input a few on-rails clicks, you're stripped of all your agency (you're literally mysteriously stipped of all your weapons because the game says so), and unable to engage in any optional interaction. The "scary stalker" appears in scripted moments and follows scripted paths. You drain the water from a lake and reveal a village underneath, you know what happens? Boss battle and adieu! You can't even enter the area you traversed on the rooftops before. It's insulting. 
Story is contrived, with a transparent red herring. "I didn't tell you the truth to protect you. I knew you'd seek vengence"- when the protagonist has almost single-handedly destroyed the main antagonist's lair. This is literally Wesker's reveal in OG RE1. You know it would be bad, but you fool yourself into hoping for any improvement. No, scratch that. This is big budget, big news AAA game, they dropped the ball, indesputably. 
Such a shame.
The enviroment design and graphical fidelity is obviously the main, and with time it becomes clear - the only selling point. It's a tripple A a hounted house ride mixed with indie gameplay.
Such a shame because it doesn't bode well for RE4R - Capcom don't do gameplay anymore, they do graphics and marketing campaign. And RE4 was... A brilliant gameplay based on genius level design, reliable gunplay and overall well though out pacing. Everything sung together and it took people out of left field.
RER4 doesn't advertise any of those things.
Overall, if you're not into shooting zombies and love escape rooms instead - give it a try. For anyone who craves an engaging gameplay, avoid.

Resident Evil Village is an incredibly fun game, with somewhat of a retarded story, most noticeably in the second half. The villains are quite fun, even when ignoring all the memes although I have to admit that Lady Dimitrescu has awakened things inside me I really don't want to talk about, and the environments can really look quite gorgeous, and the signature Resident Evil gameplay is here, with lots of items and secrets and puzzles strewn around the well-built levels and environment. That is all awesome. But for someone whose favourite Resident Evil game is unequivocally Resident Evil 7, Village is a step backwards in many aspects. Ethan was in 7 too, but he wasn't too bad as a protagonist, and even though he isn't as bad as some would make him out to be, he can still be unbelievably obnoxious at times, especially after everything he's already been through at this point. The story is nowhere near as tight and compelling either, and especially in the second half, all the cracks really start to show, quickly descending into the almost nonsensical. Another thing that was sadly sacrificed for a more expansive setting is the atmosphere, which was masterfully textured and layered in 7, every nook and cranny of the bayou oppressive and foreboding, fear lurking around every corner, which sadly resulted, at least for me, in Village feeling and playing like more of an action game rather than the unbelievably tense survival-horror experience that made Resident Evil 7 so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible. Where 7 was about tension, and fear and atmosphere, Village opts for spectacle and throwing enemies at you. Mostly. The doll house chapter was superb, horrifying and tense and hitting all the right spots of paranoia, by far the best chapter in the game for me personally, and it just kinda soured the rest of the experience a bit, realising how different the whole experience could have looked. Now this sounds like I'm just crapping all over the game, but the truth is I actually had a lotta fun playing it, and I realise most people really loved it, and everything it sets out to accomplish it does accomplish more or less, this is more about personal taste rather than actual faults. I recommend Resident Evil Village, even if I vastly prefer 7, and I really hope Capcom goes back to the survival-horror experience I loved so much, in the next game.

RE8 Village is a good game, but it's a really weird Resident Evil game. It picks up awhile after RE7 and the gameplay is mostly the same mechanically. However, it is heavily inspired by RE4 stylistically. It starts with suspenseful horror and carries that until about the halfway point, where it largely curbs into action. The awkwardness is mostly centered around a much more supernatural/fantastical approach to the characters and story rather than the established Resident Evil sci-fi. Village tries to fit into greater plot of the series in a very loose way and it creates some weird implications going forward. Depending how invested you are in the story, you may or may not care about this.

RE7 seemed like a return to old RE form. This is like a RE4 take on RE7 and it works really well. Would heartily recommend.

RE:BIOHAZARD tried (with some mixed results, IMO) to recapture some of the claustrophobia and helplessness of RE1. It was a step in the right direction, even if nobody was going to put it in their "top 3 RE" games list. RE:VILLAGE is channeling prior success, but this time the other side of the franchise coin: RE:4 and its 'action shooter' vibes. There are easter eggs, references and homage to everything from Ganados to "Whaddayabuyin" Merchant... multiple modes, winding village maps with timed survival horde attacks. In this case, I have to say, I think Cap was more successful than 7. This is adrenaline pumping, non-stop, pull-you-forward story mode, with enough mystery thats not mired in dumb, nonsensical monologues of RE4. 

I'm not gonna risk getting my lips slapped off for saying its "better" than RE4... I mean, Ethan has about as much personality as a brick, but the QOL is certainly better, and the formula still works. The backtracking is satisfying, the sequences are varied, and the basic game loop is just as good as it was in Spain... with 100% fewer controller smashing Quick Time Events. While I'm slightly bothered that everyone in this 'mysterious' 'European' 'village' all speak unnaccented American English, and we're not in any identifiable country/location... c'mon, we know what series this is...RE-diculous. Honestly we'd expect nothing less. Plus there's a castle with oh-so-thicc Dommy Mommy, who I'll take over Salazaar any day! Double thumbs up...

RE7 was a huge change for the series, confining itself to smaller scale encounters, toned back enemies, and relying more on atmosphere for its horror elements. Village on the other hand is almost like jumping from RE1 to RE4 in terms of tone and pacing (albeit with minimal cheesiness). While it's definitely a great game, there's some game design choices that really held it back compared to 7. It's better than I expected, but I still prefer 7 for its slower pace and better storytelling. 

While 7 mostly followed Ethan's motivations, in Village he's more railroaded by outside forces using and abusing him. They give you hints at self-determination at the beginning, showing you how you have to defeat the four lords to save your daughter, when in reality it's actually very linear. They not only force you to fight them in a certain order, but you're locked out of their "lairs" once you finish the boss of the zone. This was probably the most disappointing part of the game for me because you can clearly see rooms with untouched loot on your map... Unfortunately, once you trigger that lair boss fight they might as well disappear. 

FOMO wasn't a huge deal though because playing on Standard difficulty gives you plenty of ammo to deal with everything the game throws at you, including the optional mini-bosses that you can instead sneak around. Despite the narrowness of the world and level design, there's always options for dealing with situations, including old-fashioned dashing to the save room. You might want to save your supplies for the mandatory boss fights anyway because there's a lot of big, bombastic fights here. 

The internet was salivating over Lady D before release but funnily enough she's the first boss in the game, with things only getting more ridiculous as the game continues. Getting chased by Big Vampire Mommy and her three daughters is actually light-hearted compared to some of the later encounters... Most of the game manages a consistent tone and pacing outside of the ridiculous boss fights. However, the last boss jumped the shark completely into JRPG territory (but at this point in the series that's to be expected).

Village was surprisingly very good apart from the lack of player agency. RE7 & 8 have been an excellent new direction for the series and I hope 9 doesn't return to "co-op zombies with a Resident Evil skin" like some of the previous entries. As long as you can handle the excessive jump scares (including some literal monster closets), there's enough action here to satisfy the average gamer when compared to 7's slower paced approach. While I preferred 7 more, both games get a big thumbs up from me.

I personally don't like RE8, but I recommend it. Honestly, it made me sort of dislike RE7, even though I love that game. 

Personally, I think Capcom just used RE as a franchise to sell their previous 2 installations, because from a narrative standpoint, they have nothing to do with RE. Simply changing the title, and some names (like Chris Redfield), one wouldn't guess it had anything to do with RE. The connection is very, very shoe-horned. Some spoilers ahead: 

The main antagonist of RE8 is Mother Miranda. She was born in the agrarian mountains of Transylvania, Romania, during the 19th century, and she lost her daughter during the Spanish flu in 1919. As she went to end her life in some arbitrary cave, she stumbled upon some giant fungal-colony, what she refers to as the "Black God." It's a fungus that goes by many names, such as "the mold" in RE7, or more appropriately, the Megamycete. Apparently, it's conscious, and it collectively holds the consciousness of its victims, even the dead buried nearby in a local cemetery, like her daughter. She recognizes her daughter's consciousness as being a part of this thing, so she makes it her life mission to resurrect her. In order to do that, she needs a vessel of some sort, and spends much of the 20th century conducting experiments on villagers and curing them of their ailments. Eventually, she is viewed as some sort of messiah. They abandon their Christianity in favor of "Mother" Miranda. In truth, she was infecting them, and many of the villagers turned into Lycans. Some feudal lords of the lands became her most successful experiments, and they make up many of the bosses in this game. An example is House Beneviento (the doll house).

At the turn of the 21st century, Miranda was approached by the crime syndicate, The Connections, who had been made aware of her research and wished to collaborate with her. Miranda provided DNA samples of her daughter, and some of the mold, and in return, they made Eveline.. you know her from RE7. As it so happens, Mia (Ethan's wife) was Eveline's caretaker, and she met Mother Miranda during all of this, well before she reunited with Ethan. Big spoilers: Apparently, Ethan died during RE7, right after his fight with Mia during the opening hour. This entire time, he's been infected with the mold, and Mia seemed pretty aware of this, as she was also infected.. not to anyone's surprise. So, when they conceived a child, Rose, Mother Miranda wanted her as a vessel for her daughter. Rose was essentially Evenline 2.0.

Now, opinion part, this is where the story really bothers me. None of this is related to RE, and merely changing a few references, like Chris' name, and the title, it would have been a great franchise on its own, completely independent of RE. When I played just RE7, much of it was a mystery, so the story didn't bother me. I figured Evenline was the product of Umbrella Pharmaceuticals or something, but it didn't pan out that way. So, how does the game make a connection to the rest of RE? Well, toward the end of RE8 village, when you're playing as Chris, you find Miranda's little underground dungeon, where she looks like she's been doing experiments for the past century. In there, you find Mia, and rescue her... but if you really look around the room and read notes like a good ole' completionist, there's a letter (must be DECADES old at this point) in plain sight for you to see. Right there, opened for anyone to read. It's from an admirer of Mother Miranda's. In fact, it's from a former protege of hers. It was a British medical student, who was lost during a hiking exercise, and Miranda just happened to find him. Did she infect him? No, quite the opposite. He was now her assistance, and he knew about her nigh-immortality and the megamycete. What's the significance of this? Nothing. He left and parted ways, because she just wanted to resurrect her daughter, but he wanted to further human evolution and change the world, and apparently, the mold wasn't good enough for him. In his letter he informs her that he is starting a pharmaceutical company, Umbrella. SIgned, Ozwell Spencer. I mean, really? Mother Miranda knows Spencer because he got lost hiking in some agrarian, Transylvanian village during the 50s? He doesn't even really collaborate, leaves, and then goes out to form Umbrella and discover the progenitor virus, and nearly ended the world. All of what he did is completely irrelevant to their meeting. Capcom just wanted to say, "tehe, Miranda knew RE's former big-time villain." The mold and t-virus are unrelated and originate from different places in the world. What are the odds this immortal, fungal witch knows Ozwell Spencer? I guess, pretty likely. 

Despite all of this, what really bothers me, is that Mia met Mother Miranda during her time in Romania, prior to the events of RE7. On top of this, Chris Redfield knew about mother Miranda. He and the BSAA were investigating her. So, why the ♥♥♥♥ would Chris move Mia and Ethan right next door to her in Translyvania, on the other side of the world from Louisiana, where RE7 took place? That's an artificial plot-point that is just forcing the story along. The excuse is that BSAA HQ just happens to be in the area.. I guess they wanted the same Translyvanian-esque experience Leon had in Spain. It still makes no strategic sense, whatsoever. Surely you have other places where you have setup shop, in the US, and can leave Ethan and Mia there.. rather than moving them next door to Miranda. Which, by the way, kidnapped Mia prior to the game's opening, so when the game starts and Mia is reading Rose a story, that's Miranda.. disguised as Mia. That's all possible because Chris moved them next door to each other. This witch spent 150 years in Romania, so why the hell would make Ethan her neighbor? 

RE8 isn't nearly as nasty and horror-driven as RE7, self-admitted by Capcom. They received complaints that RE7 was "too scary," and they wanted, "everyone to feel comfortable playing their game." That's not really something you want to hear as an RE/horror fan. Again, the game would be great as part of its own franchise, but it really feels like they're just taking advantage of RE. It's taking the same turn as the second trilogy, and most of RE8 is a giant fap fest dedicated to RE4. Even the Merchant makes a return as "the duke," but in same game files in the menu, he's still referred to as the merchant. lol. 

Castles, bizarres monsters like Lycans, Banshess, and Vampires.. plenty of ammo and guns for upgrade at the merchant.. it's an FPS version of RE4. If that's for you, BUY this game. For many similar reasons, I don't like RE8 and RE4. My favorite is REmake, and I doubt that will change. To reiterate, the game is good, and the story would be phenomenal with a few changes and removal of RE references (like Chris existing and also being a dumbass). Honestly, I just pretended like I wasn't in the RE universe and it worked wonders. I don't like it, but I recommend it.

Resident Evil Village is an awesome game in many places.Lets start with its pros.
-Graphics
RE Engine is one of the best engines in the gaming world it is both beautiful and runs very well.Detail on textures and animations are great.
-Sound And Music
Sound is a must have for horror games.Because most of the time sounds are the the one who sets up both tension and horror.From craking of winds and doors to growl on enemies.Sounds will put you in the edge of your couch.As far as for music not really that anytihng stands out.Dont get me wrong they are not bad but they are not highlights of the game either.
-Combat
This topic in my opinion is the bread and butter of this game.RE series has a very distinct gamestyle persists since 2000's and multiple games.Even with the new style of RE7 and this game it very much works.From its inventory management to sounds and impacts of the guns.For a firstcomer to the series it may be slow process to like it.But if you are veteran of the series you are gonna love it.
-Performance
I didnt really encounter performance issues but i will advise yo to go look for your own computer since i played this game on a powerful pc(3070,I9-10850K)
-Enviroments
Village done an amazing job for its enviroments.From an abondont village filled with monsters to very well lit castles from eastern european architectures to creepy houses.I can assure you you are going to spend several minutes to watch the beauty of the game when enviroments goes thourgh your eyes.
Cons
While i love RE Village i have some few criticism about the game
-Atmosphere
I love RE series and one the prominent features of the series that its atmosphere.While i do love Village(this is an opinion everyone can have their one)i dont think its atmosphere is scary enough especially compared to 7.Love it or hate the louisiana swamps you cant dent that RE7 has a very scary and tensefull atmosphere.While Village is succesfull for what its is showing to you in my personal opinion atmosphere is a bit of setback from its previous installment.
-Story
Story of Winters family is easily one of my favourite ones in RE series.Ethan is such a good,lovable and relatable chracter.While i do love Ethan itself very good i do no share the same feelings for the villians of this game.Dont get me wrong their Voice Acting is superb but as far as the story goes they are pretty weak forgettable villians.
-Mercenary Mode(This is also a very personal opinion)
I feel like this mode itself heavly relies on the combat itself.I do think that combat of the game is pretty good for the first playthourgh its not really offer any replayability.While i do get for some people is coming from this is a great way to increase game time without adding already existing content i feel like %90 of the player base would play this mode more than an hour.So i ask myself wouldnt be better to put developers time to better places such as improvements and upgrades to combat or even to dlc
-DLC Shadows Of Rose
[spoiler]While the games ending sets up Rose really well i dont really think this dlc done a great way to show it.First of all dlc is super short around 2-3 hours max.Second when they announced this that we will play as Rose i was super exited.Since Rose is a superhuman being i assumed we would have cool superhuman abilities boy i was wrong it was just more RE gameplay while its good for what it is i feel like devs could go more crazy with the gameplay since we were playing as Rose.[/spoiler]
So overall my score for this game is 8/10

Village is a superb game, in terms of graphical & production quality, storytelling, and gameplay. But, I don't think that makes it strictly a great *Resident Evil* game. I feel you could slap any other survival horror game title on this and it'd still work. Maybe I'm just high on nostalgia from the original series, but that's just me.

Back to the game, the production quality is great, and the game is very refined, clean, and has no issues on the face of glitches or bugs, and it runs smoothly. My only gripe is the graphical issue with the antialiasing, where with certain settings, it makes the game look like it's being seem through a moist camera lens. But that's a solveable, issue that I can't say I care about it too much.

The range of weaponry the game offers is great as well, and the customization is good, but nothing noteworthy. I'd like to have had an option to ADS regularly, rather than just zooming in, but that's just me being overly attached to FPS games.

The game's length felt a little bit too long for me as well, and I was almost happy when the game ended (not to say I hated it or disliked it, I simply felt it started to drag).

On the front of the environment, I'm not sure how to feel. I think it was very well made, and fit its role, but I, personally, didn't quite care for the entire secluded village and ancient castle & remnants setting. Again, well made, but just not my thing.

The story was well done too, and it left an opening for a RE9, whether that be it follows Chris or Rose, and I'm intrigued to see where it leads. And although the Ethan storyline was short lived, only going 2 games, it still felt like more than enough for his character, and he went off like I felt he should've; tragic and sacrificially. 

I do feel there were some plot elements that were iffy at best, namely how Chris just tells Ethan to ♥♥♥♥ off after he murders his thought-to-be-wife in front of him, and gives genuinely no explanation whatsoever, until Ethan has run through Hell and back to find out what's occurring. Also how Chris doesn't bother to help Ethan at all, even when they meet later in the game, he just gets on his case and and gets mad at him for trying to survive, which completely goes against the whole witness protection thing they had going, and ultimately makes no sense for his character.

The cast of characters is super fun as well, and I thoroughly enjoyed versing all the bosses, and could even sympathize with Heisenberg to a degree, what with wanting to escape his slavery to Miranda. I also enjoyed the Duke, as mysterious as he is, and he was a good reprieve from the chaotic and frigid world.

All-in-all, RE:V is a great game, and even better survival horror, although I felt it was a loose fit for the Resident Evil franchise. Definitely worth the play on all accounts.
