The thing with Resident Evil 4 is that it was something new and different for a series which, as the received wisdom goes, had run out of ideas.

Out with the fixed camera angles, the limited ammunition, the creeping horror; in with Spanish villagers, cultists, chaingunners, 'your right hand comes off?', chicago typewriter-fuelled camp nonsense. An entry in the series so fresh, so new, so [i]fun[/i] that they did it again, bigger and even more off-the-wall mental in RE5, where Chris Redfield repeatedly punches a boulder in a volcano (after the laser pyramid and the aeroplane fight) in order to avoid COMPLETE. GLOBAL. SATURATION. Then - so it goes - RE6 came along and was a bit too much (read: aggressively jumped the shark), shrugging survival horror off entirely where it had desperately clung on before, and signalled the creative death of the series for many - until, of course, RE7 completely refreshed everything. All of this long-winded intro is to say: I Reckon That RE8 Village is the RE5 of the newest iteration of the series.

Unhelpful? The ramblings of a madman? Yeah, okay, maybe - let me be more specific.

Resident Evil 7 recognised the reaction - in some cases, the [i]anger[/i] - that a lot of fans had to its predecessor, and gave them something back. No more obnoxious secondary character, no more infinite launcher: just you, Some Guy, looking for his wife in a swamp somewhere in the southern US; the body count (and number of extremely over-the-top daft moments) was drastically reduced and the suspense ratcheted up, with elements like 'persistent enemies who follow you around' becoming a new staple and fan favourite. Survival horror was back, babey (awooo).

RE: VIllage, the direct sequel, is still in that lineage - but it's very clear (to me, at least) that whereas RE7 was looking to the future and represented a clean break with the past, the developers of RE8 looked directly at older entries in the series to innovate, with particular attention to that venerated classic RE4. Sure, there are some tropes which make a reappearance which are in virtually every game - lockpicks, for example, or herbs, or unrealistically large buildings with far too many rooms, or 'that puzzle where you have to replace a key item with a broken/similar item in order to keep the door open' - but there were parts of RE8 which made me think 'I've been here before'. Parts like entering a village and waiting out a swarm of enemies until an arbitrary time limit; parts like rearranging your attache case to fit more junk; parts like going into a castle, then an abandoned mine, then a human experimentation lab; parts like dealing with a merchant who, despite not really having any good reason to be there, can sell or tune up your weapon and seems to always have an absolute maximum of 2 first aid kits on hand. 

This isn't limited to similar gameplay, but also to tone and plot: it's been a while since i played it, but I don't think RE7 Ethan would have idly shrugged off [spoiler]having his hand removed, then vaguely stuck back on with first aid liquid, with absolutely no ill effects[/spoiler], nor do I remember him making quite so many unintentionally dumb - or intentionally camp - quips. Near the end, the game fully does away with everything that's been happening for the past 8-ish hours, and - after a really protracted period of exposition cutscenes - [spoiler]hands you a rifle and tells you to go have some stupid fun[/spoiler]. 

None of this is to say that RE8 is bad, it's not; in fact, it's a fantastic way to spend a bit under 10 hours (especially as someone who sank a considerable amount of time 100%ing RE4 across multiple platforms), at least until you hit the factory level and it all starts going a bit downhill. But we are once again seeing the slow stray from survival horror - where it had been reclaimed in RE7 - back into action horror, as Ethan guns down hordes of whatever flavour of not-technically-zombies we have this week, quipping and being generally daft along the way - and if you're into that (like me), that's great, you're going to have a blast. But I can't shake the feeling that the series might be about to jump the shark again, as it did before - nor the question of whether we'll be able to cope with the return of the incredibly tedious 'but is it really survival horror?' arguments again.

RE8 follows the same game-play as RE7 with a few adjustments to how the difficulty effects your play-through, RE7 would change up where loot was located and how much was available where as from my understanding RE8 increases strength and health of the creatures you face while leaving the available loot in the same areas.

Graphically the game is stunning the atmosphere of the varying levels/zones is great but can be tough to spot some things in the dinginess in the darker areas right away.

The map does give you a reasonable amount of area to explore within each level/zone but you do get locked out of some areas if you progress to far so its worth exploring everything in its entirety to make sure you arent missing simple loot like ammo you may need going forward. 
The game did a reasonable job of keeping you at a decent level of ammo as long as you dont miss a bunch of shots on stuff you'd be fine even if you only have a couple rounds left at the end of larger fights. Tip: explosives are very helpful if saved

Gameplay length wasnt the longest I beat the base game in just under 10 hours and I wasnt trying to speed through anything I did a fair amount of searching around to find loot wherever possible.
The Winter DLC was about 2.5 hours of playtime and unlike the base game the DLC is more of a linear story not so much exploring as the base game provided.

I dont mind replaying story games so I could easily replay this multiple times and enjoy it each time but for those that don't like replaying stories there are some extra bonus options once you finish the base game (some stuff provided by the DLCs)
There is a mercenaries mode you can unlock which is wave based, you can unlock different characters to play as from the story like chris or lady dimitrescu. you also can unlock different guns and mods like infinite ammo of course.

If you enjoy'd RE7 this is worth picking up and giving a chance, I'd recommend picking up the gold addition just because you can get the dlc for a discount as well

INTRO - 11-24-2022, Morning:
So, I've been playing Resident Evil: Village (PC/Steam), taking my time & soaking in this game in. I'm some 18.5 hours in so far, on the 8th main entry here in this RE series (Resident Evil). Got some thoughts on it, of course...so, let's get this show on the road.

WINTERS...WINTERS IS COMING.
In this game, you play as Ethan Winters, the protagonist from the awesome RE7. So, yes - you should play RE7 first if you haven't, as that game's awesome & since this is a direct sequel to that. Without giving a ton away here, this is after those events from RE7 and he has now found his way to a Village, to go find his daughter & hopefully save her. In doing so, he's going this village that has a ton of things going on, without going too far into this & into Spoiler Turf.

GAMEPLAY, COMBAT, ENEMIES & MORE.
This feels basically like RE7, combat-wise & gameplay-wise. In the OG version of RE: Village here, you're in first-person perspective here, seeing through Ethan's eyes. Like RE7, the combat's awesome in 1st person and flat-out just feels great; it's extremely satisfying. A lot of times here, you'll be exploring areas, defeating enemies, solving puzzles, combing items to make another item, and other things of the typical survival-horror sort - and it's awesome. So far, this game is nothing short of that.

Enemies here are not always the typical RE enemies here either, which is great...and they are often not of the zombies sort here. You don't always deal w/ zombies & those type of RE enemies, since...this Village has a lot more on-going than that. Just know, since the game is split up, more or less, into 4 major different areas in this Village, each area often has its own enemy types - such as Vampires, Lycans/Werewolves, Cyborg type of Frankenstein-like creations for monsters, and more. Simply put: I love what this game is doing w/ the enemy type variety here.

There's even a section that feels mostly like a small puzzle section almost entirely, as if it was right out of an adventure game like Myst - but oh, is it so a lot more creepy and indeed does have a bit of combat here & there, too.

Also, you'll be running into a Merchant named The Duke a lot, from whom you can buy, sell, and upgrade your assortment of items (guns, equipment, etc.) - in which this mechanic of running into him so reminds of the merchant from my favorite RE game (Resident Evil 4). 

PERFORMANCE.
My PC's have no problem w/ this one pretty much. On my desktop loaded with i7 10700KF, 16 GB RAM, 8gb RTX 3070, 1 TB SSD - yeah, easy 1080p60fps here & eating around 7-8 GB VRAM on the regular, with Ray-Tracing On paired with either DLSS or FSR - I'd have to check again but I normally use DLSS, if both options are there. My Gigabyte gaming laptop loaded with R5 5600H, 16 GB RAM, 6gb RTX 3060 (laptop-GPU), 1 TB SSD & W11 runs this no problem at Medium settings w/ RT and either DLSS or FSR On. Flat-out, this game both looks & runs great. Can't say anything bad here about any of that stuff, as the game runs & looks great here.

OUTRO...FOR NOW.
And, that should conclude what I've got to say for now, on RE: Village. So far, it's been great and has been awesome. This is so far a fantastic sequel to the awesome RE7 - and all of this RE: Village talk & partial-reviewing makes me want to go finish the game up, since I'm probably getting there & I am probably close to the end anyways. More to come, when I finish this - but so far, it's awesome & looks like a certain "Must Play" and a very easy recommendation, provided that sticks the landing & ending.

ADDENDUM - 11-24-2022, 4:55pm EST:
After 21 hours, I have completed RE: Village. And in the grand scheme of things, it was awesome overall & is definitely "Must Play" and an easy recommendation here. While the main story does wrap up here & the conclusion to this game's story is satisfying, there's obviously going to be more to come b/c there's always something going on w/ the Resident Evil/Biohazard Bio-Weapons. Certainly, I do look forward to at some point buying the Winters Expansion & to the inevitable Resident Evil 9, whenever that's going to be coming.

Another great modern RE game that blends action with puzzles and complex nonlinear levels. If you liked RE 7, 2 Remake, or 3 Remake, you will like this. In particular, I love how replayable this game is and how the ingame challenges give you a reason to play it over and over again in different ways. The castle is one of the greatest levels in Resident Evil history and the village and factory are good as well. House Beneviento and the Reservoir are alright, but feel a little unfinished and not as fleshed out as the other levels. 

My biggest complaint about this game is the huge number of missable treasures and upgrades, and the game's inconsistency regarding backtracking. With a linear game, it's obvious that you need to find everything on your first go through the level, and in a fully open game, you can backtrack at any time. But in RE Village, it's an awkward hybrid. In some areas, you can't get everything in your first run and are required to leave then come back later to get the rest. In other areas, however, you are punished for doing this as leaving the area will lock you out of ever returning to get what you missed. And you can't tell which is which ahead of time. This issue is the only major blemish on an otherwise excellent game. My advice to anyone playing would be to just play without walkthroughs the first time and accept you're going to miss a bunch of stuff and get locked out of unfinished areas, then replay with walkthroughs to find all the secrets you missed the first time. 

Ultimately though, despite this issue, it's still absolutely worth playing for anyone who likes Resident Evil or survival horror games.

I waited until the DLC to come out for this before I made my review, but in my humble opinion, (and I fully expect to get ratio'd,) but I thought Village was better than RE4. ONLY because it took the best parts of 4 and expanded on them, while creating genuinely terrifying moments (Beneviento House was one big NOPE, especially in the DLC) whereas 4 relied a little more on action and CTE's. 

The setting is absolutely STUNNING, and the detail that went into each environment (oooooo Castle Dimitriscu) was on another level. Each area of the game felt unique, with each Lord adding their own distinct theme to the environment and enemies. No spoilers, but I thought the ending was great and felt the antagonists were fully fleshed out (although I'd love more back story to each because they were just fascinating characters.) Overall, the story was truly one of the best ones in the RE universe, and the twist at the end actually convinced me to replay 7 for some small, hindsight details. Combat felt fluid, the enemies felt balanced, and each boss fight was unique in terms of strategy. The graphics were incredible, and the only con I can say about that is the ray tracing damn near killed my computer (although I believe they patched this because when it first game out the game's performance REALLY struggled while it was enabled.)

Mercenaries was honestly the most fun I've had for bonus content in awhile, and the addition of the DLC characters was SO fun. Shadows of Rose was easily the best DLC to a game I have ever played. The story felt well done, well paced, and sufficiently fleshed out (if not slightly predictable.) The enemies were REALLY creepy, and I actually enjoyed the stealth mechanic that was added in for this, as well as Rose's unique skills. 

Overall: 9.8/10

If Resident Evil VII was a callback to the original RE, then Resident Evil Village is a modern take on RE4. That may appeal to some, and may not to others - the pacing, atmosphere and general gameplay is more fast-paced than before, akin to the switch from classic RE to the shoulder-shooter games. For me personally, it's great - more of a horror-themed FPS than "pure" survival horror.  The hallmarks of Resident Evil are still there, they've just been tweaked to fit into the roller coaster of a campaign that is Village. Again, that may turn off some purists, but the balance of horror, action and gameplay challenges was perfect for me.

The DLC is a little underwhelming, but it was a nice excuse to return to the game. Third-person doesn't really add or detract anything from the campaign, it's just a new way to play. The Rosemary DLC is better in terms of gameplay than anything, and it's slightly disappointing that the story doesn't really mean much in the end. Mercenaries is still Mercenaries, though it's strange that you have to play through so much of the original content to unlock the new stuff (not that it takes that long, I just wasn't expecting it).

Overall, it's a great package. Getting it all in one big bundle is a good deal, and getting it on sale will feel like cheating the system. I paid full price on Day One and loved it - if you like spooky monsters and then shooting those spooky monsters, go buy it.

What I liked the most about Resident Evil Village: 

1 - The atmosphere: RE8 takes place in a snowy medieval-like city in Eastern Europe where you feel traveling back in time. A luxurious castle, an eerie house, an abandonned mine and an underground factory, every part of the game offers an unique experience.

2- The Lords: The four Lords each have a unique personality. Their respective voice actors did a fantastic job. During the early cutscene where we meet all of them for the first time, we direcly discern their relationship.

3- The gameplay: Gameplay-wise, this game is on point. The enemies have the perfect amount of HP to be considered as threat while still providing fun fighting them. You have to think how to defeat heavy enemies while having to deal with basic enemies at the same time. Enemies will drop money or parts of them to be sold to The Duke. You can buy weapons and upgrade them, buy ammunitions and accessories to him.

4- The replay value: For me, it's a HUGE pro. After beating the game once, you can start another game while keeping your inventory (weapons, ammos, health, money). You gain access to challenges that give you points. With these points, you can then buy new weapons, infinite ammos, concept art and character models.

What I didn't like about Resident Evil 8:

There aren't any major issues with the game, but there are still some things that could have been better.

My main issue is that Donna Beneviento and Salvatore Moreau feels overwhelmed by Alcina Dimitrescu and Karl Heisenberg: 

1- My first point here is that Beneviento and Moreau do not put the player in danger. During their respective parts of the game, there are almost no enemies. Playing against Donna Beneviento and her doll Angie really is terrifying the first time, but after starting another new game, you will just want to beat Beneviento as soon as possible because there's not really a lot of things to do: (almost) no enemy, no loot. While being in Moreau's territory, you will aswell feel a lack of enemies. You encounter several enemies at just one location, then nothing more.

2- Beneviento's House and Moreau's Reservoir is just going from point A to point B while you have to explore Alcina Dimitrescu's castle and Karl Heisenberg's factory. There you will find treasure, weapons and weapon upgrades, ennemies, puzzles and mini-bosses. The amount of time spent in the Castle and the Factory is way more important than the house and the reservoir.

Another thing i want to add is that Mother Miranda feels like she's just the main antagonist at the very beggining of the game and at the very end. Otherwise through the whole game, I cared a lot more about the Lords than her.


In conclusion, despite these minors cons, Resident Evil Village is a wonderful game, worth its price and playtime. Definitely one of my favorite game i ever played!

Capcom brought the classic horror survival genre back. but.. for only one game and this ain't it. You will never run out of ammo. You will never have to run from enemies out of desperation. Puzzles are easy. Boss fights are meh and most enemies are bullet sponges, at least at the beginning. The story was okay for a RE game. They replace the suspense with action. Which is disappointing coming off the horror that made RE7 great. The gameplay is fun, for a shooter. which is honestly the problem. This game is more of a action shooter than anything. It has it's fun moments though. 7-10 for me. Def disappointing for all the hype this game had. Capcom could of done better.

A great horror FPS starring Everyman Ethan Winters.  After completing an ill-advised move to a vague Eastern European mishmash country, Ethan's family is attacked by a grizzled Chris Redfield -- and soon after, Ethan finds himself traipsing through a rather RE4-ish village full of werewolves, an incredible castle patrolled by crusty-mouthed vampires . . . and several other interesting places you hopefully did not spoil for yourself by watching a hundred video clips uploaded by overreacting, [i]soy-gaping[/i] twenty-somethings.  It's all great stuff except for the [i]super-scripted[/i] doll bits where the game takes your weapons away and makes you hide from things -- the same goes for the dollhouse sequence in the middle of Shadows of Rose, which stars Ethan's succulent and rather fey-looking teenage daughter (whose hands, apparently, secrete sticky white gunk whenever she gets stressed, giving her jealous female classmates even more ammunition against her.)  Running from the marionette-things just wasn't very fun to me.

But [i]Village[/i] is intriguing, in general very fun, and runs like a dream on my PC.  It's another gleaming-fine game for Capcom's B-horror-adventure series, and I'll be sure to play the whole thing again in the near future -- especially now that I've fixed the mouse sensitivity.  I haven't tried the main Ethan campaign in third-person yet, so there's that too.  

[b]Important advisory:[/b]  if you play this with WASD, which [i]should[/i] be the best control scheme out of the box, you will need to adjust mouse sensitivity or else you will struggle to even [i]aim[/i] the whole way through -- like Ethan's arms are made of lead.  Here's a quick-fix tutorial:  https://youtu.be/dmxfRcLn1b8  I can't believe I actually beat the main campaign like that; I think that says something about how absorbing the game can be!

(And as absorbing as the game is, I [i]still[/i] liked the Baker's house a little better!  Not a criticism of the incredible art or anything, but just a personal preference.  And would it have hurt the developers to give the pseudo-Romanians something other than a bog-standard [i]American accent?[/i]  That part [i]did[/i] annoy me!  It annoyed me a lot!)

The Resident Evil series has changed so much since it's inception and it's fans have strong preferences for the style of some of it's games over others. I'm writing this as someone who adores the horror of Resident evil 2 and the action horror of 4 in particular, I should also mention that resident evil 7 is one of my least favorite in this franchise.

 I'll be making some comparisons to 4 and 7 since those are the two games Village feels closest to. I'll also try to avoid as much spoilers as possible.

The game is separated into 4 main areas all connected together by the titular village. Each area feels like an homage to a specific game in the series, or to a specific genre of horror, which is an aspect of REVIII I rarely see praised, but I love. The 4 areas are the castle, the house, the reservoir and the factory

The castle and reservoir were by far my favorite parts of the entire game. The castle felt reminiscent of RE2R, and the reservoir reminded me of an expanded Del Lago lake fight from RE4. The House was a nice change of pace, and reminded me of a better executed Lucas Baker escape room section and the factory was visually stunning, with amazing art design and really turned up the horror to 11, but to me it dragged on far too long. 

The first four bosses were VERY memorable, the only boss I didn't quite enjoy was the final boss, which was too spongy and not quite as interesting as the previous ones.

Enemy design is all fantastic, the lycans are so much more fun to fight than the molds from 7 and the soldat's were terror inducing until I found out how to fight them.

The game is set in a Romanian mountain village and it's honestly one of the most beautiful and unique games I've ever played. I wasn't much of a fan of the Louisiana hillbilly aesthetic of 7, so I'm so happy they went in this direction with this game. The art style and design is beyond amazing. It is one of the only time's where I kept stopping to take screenshots.

The story isn't the absolute best in the series, but it's very entertaining. And has some fun twists and turns. It felt like it was finding a balance between the RE's B-movie origins and it's new more grounded and serious story approach. 

The game is more action focused than 1,2 or 7, in that aspect it reminds me of RE4. Those that dislike the action horror of 4 might also not enjoy it in Village either, but 2 of the areas do put horror on the forefront so I believe Village does cater to most fans of the series.

Overall Resident Evil village surprised me, it isn't just one of my favorite games in the series now, it's also one of my favorite games in general. In series tradition there's a lot of replay value here if you want to unlock more weapons or infinite ammo and such. There's also hidden mini side quests around the village so there's a lot of incentive to explore. And the new dlc added the ability to play the game in third person so that's also another reason to revisit the game.

A great follow-up to RE7. I'll be honest. RE7 was my first RE game. Just never really was interested in the zombie shtick but 7 got me hooked. It was a blast getting to play as Ethan Winters hellbent on saving his long lost wife. Not to mention all the interesting and surprising twists the story takes. 

I was more than excited to continue Ethan's story in RE8. I was invested in Ethan's family. While the plot of RE8 is sort of similar to RE7, I feel the game goes for a slightly different tone. RE7 is a lot of dodging and running around enemies. RE8 is a much more combat heavy and exploration based game. But the setting, the tone, the interesting cast of characters make for an excellent adventure. 

I know Ethan is not for everyone but I think he is a great protagonist and I personally think Capcom knocked it out of the park. 

Now that the Shadow of Rose DLC has come out, it put a very nice capstone on the story of Ethan and his family. There are still questions left unanswered but I am satisfied with where it leaves things at. The DLC is pretty short, I got it done in less than 4 hours in my first run. There are also some repetitive segments, especially if you just completed the main game. But if you haven't touched the game since the original release, its a nice return to some of the iconic locales, each with some fun twists.I'll be honest some of the combat and encounter designs can be pretty frustrating, so a slight let down from the pretty much excellent base game. However, I really enjoyed playing as Rose, especially after everything that happens in the base game. It feel right, and it ends in what I think is a very beautiful way. I think if you really enjoyed RE8, you'll enjoy the DLC. I am not sure if most people will find the $20.00 price tag equivalent for the amount of game play the DLC provides, but I think the time and effort put into this DLC and the story make it worth the investment if you enjoyed RE8.

Overall, I highly recommend RE8 Village and the Shadow of Rose DLC

[h1] A Great Resident Evil Game [/h1]

I bought Resident Evil 8 on release but couldn't quite get into it when it came out. Originally it came out in May and I prefer to play my horror games in the winter so this game took the back burner and I forgot all about it until the Winter's Expansion.

Firstly, I played the game fully in Third Person Mode and had a great time with it. So much so I think it's better than the first person mode, it doesn't feel half baked or just a tag-on. It genuinely feels very fresh and similar to the other RE remakes.

The story itself is a direct sequel to the events of Resident Evil 7, if you have not played RE7, you shouldn't buy this game until completing it, otherwise you will miss out on a lot of context and nuance the game provides.

For me the best part about the game was exploring the village and seeing what goodies you can find here and there. Sometimes it requires you to progress to different parts of the game to get access to certain parts of the village, but I don't mind that kind of back tracking.

The way I view the game is as such: The Village is your main hub to explore and the four zones are sort of like "Dungeons" to an extent. Very linear for the most part and allow you to progress the story, the only real free-roam you get is within the village and it's not exactly very big to begin with. 

I think the story is quite well written, it's nothing to write home about in comparison to other games like Detroit: Become Human, or Death Stranding, but it's strong enough to keep you wanting to know what happens next.

Exploration is massively rewarded, back tracking in the village after you find certain items is also rewarding. Don't be afraid to go off the obvious path, because there's almost always something there for you to obtain or experience. 

My only complaint is somewhat similar to the one I had for the Resident Evil 3 remake, and that is that there's sometimes just too much ammo in the game, you can easily fight your way through every enemy and still have enough to spare to continue; it really takes away from that element of survival horror in which "Should I fight or should I run?"

The boss design is very cool and the set pieces are wonderful to look at and explore. I found that most, if not all, of the characters are interesting and have their own backstories.

Overall, Resident Evil Village is a great addition to the series and absolutely worth playing, doubly more if you've played Resident Evil 7. 

8/10 - I'll probably do some more playthroughs at some point on higher difficulties.

Village feels like a "Greatest Hits" of the RE franchise and that can be a gift and/or a curse depending your preference. The graphics are incredible and the controls are tight and satisfying. It has a good momentum and it's incredibly fun to play.

My main complaints come from two factors: It's not scary and it's too easy. You can breeze through the entire game in a handful of gaming sessions while only dying a few times. The only portion that gave me any grief was the final boss, who is a relentless bullet sponge. However, even though the game is brief, it does overstay its welcome and I felt exhausted by the end.

The story continues with the Winters' family and is the same gobbledegook that has made my brain glaze over in every entry of this series. While RE7 was incredibly unsettling at times, Village is presented as a fantasy fairy tale that does little to make your spine tingle. It doesn't feel like it's truly connected to RE7. The tone is all over the place and it feels unfocused. There's an action heavy bit at the end that feels like an unnecessary slog. 

While I have my issues with the game, it is a worthy successor to RE7 and lands in the top half of RE series.

Annnnnd finally... hooray for the "skip cutscene" option!

The FOV can't be adjusted and feels really zoomed in. I have a relatively big monitor of 28 inches and I felt a bit sick playing this game. There is a 3rd person perspective but that just feels like a great chunk o' clunk. 

That out of the way, the game is actually pretty nice. The story flows right, the combat is pretty good, reminiscent of RE7 and the graphics are downright stunning. If the FOV was adjustable without modding and the devs thought that through a bit then maybe I would be able to enjoy this game too. I recommend it but I can't play it the way it is.

P.S. To you naysayers who will defend the FOV by saying that its "immersive". Its my choice to break the immersion on a singleplayer game. Its hard getting a good feel of your surroundings if you feel like you're looking through a sniper scope.

Resident Evil Village is an excellent game and if you are considering playing it, I recommend it. The best way to describe this game is if re7 and re4 had a baby that was in the form of a love letter to the franchise.  

As I said, Resident Evil Village, also called re8, is a love letter to the series, giving tribute to every franchise corner. The castle represents classic Resident Evil like 1 and 7, with the layout being a maze full of locked doors with corresponding keys and a pursuer enemy. The haunted house represents the series' best horror. The reserve represents the series’ over-the-top bosses. The factor represents the series’ more actiony side like re4. The section where you play as [spoiler] even pays tribute to the series’ most action side like re5 and re6. All throughout the game is more minor things as well, like the opening village scene being pulled directly from re4. This game actually pulls a lot from resident evil 4, gameplay-wise. The merchant system and inventory system from that game are here as well. 
The game’s story is quite nice and acts as a direct sequel to re7. The villains were a joy to watch when they were on screen and Ethan actually has a personality this time around, through oneliners out occasionally. The story wraps up the duology nicely but leaves certain plot points open for re9 and the future. 
Almost all of re7’s complaints were answered in this game, from a wide variety of enemies to a longer playtime in general. While the horror is turned down for the most part, except for the house that shall not be named and is a threat from Capcom that they can make the scariest horror game ever, this game acts as a bigger and better re7. 
This game has a lot to offer. The large village area acts like a hub for each of the game’s sections and changes as you play. There is a large amount of optional content that can be skipped but allows you to be even more powerful via upgrades and more valuable treasures. There are even mini-bosses that can be found. First-time play-throughs are about 10-14 hours with repeats being 5-8. 
I waited to review this game for when the rumored DLC came out, and now I have played it. Shadows of Rose wraps up the Winters’ story in a nice way since we probably won’t be seeing these characters again in a very long time. The main story got a 3rd person mode which plays like the modern remakes of the series. All things considered, it actually plays quite well like this. Cutscenes are generally still 1st person and swapping between the two gets annoying pretty fast, but it is still a minor complaint. Also, all melee weapons look bad in the third person. 
Mercenaries mode is back and got a major overhaul. It now acts like a rogue-like of sorts, but still leaves a lot to be desired, even with the DLC’s additions. It reminds me of raid mode from the revelations series if progress generally didn’t carry over from game to game. I would have liked it more if the mode took advantage of the series’ other enemies that exist in the RE engine. It would have been cool to see re7’s molded or re2’s zombies. Lickers and hunters would have been fun to fight in first person as well. Resident Evil Revelations 2’s raid mode did this and it was great. Some people will enjoy this mode, but I did not.

The only real issue I have with this game is its pacing. It is atrocious. The game starts off strong with the opening and castle but slows down once you get to the spooky house. This would be fine if we got another chunky section but we then go straight into the reserve, which is a lengthy boss encounter. The stronghold plays right after this and plays like a climax to the game, but is then followed up with the factory section, which is similar in scale to the castle section, if not bigger. The [spoiler] section plays as the real climax and then the final boss is fought. This isn’t a make-or-break by any means but gets tedious on repeat plays. The optional content helps with this thankfully. 
As for smaller complaints, I was super happy to see resident evil 4’s inventory return but it isn’t fully utilized. I rarely had to engage with the game’s inventory, mostly because re4 didn’t have crafting. Crafting ingredients is the most common thing you will find in the world and from enemies. Enemies do not drop ammo at all here. The thing is, crafting ingredients do not take up inventory space, so you basically can store ammo outside your inventory at all times. This is thankfully being changed for the resident evil 4 remake, which does have crafting. 
Another complaint is the weapons. The variety is nice, but they all mostly feel like they are upgrades of each other. The handguns and shotguns are all objectively better than the last in almost every sense. Without counting extra, unlockable guns, the normal game has 3 handguns, 3 shotguns, 1 sniper, 1 magnum, and 1 grenade launcher. Why couldn’t one of the shotguns be a sniper or a handgun be a tmp esk gun? This would also be less of an issue if the handguns and shotguns were unique among each other, filling different roles like re4 and re5, but they act like direct upgrades of each other. Why not make one shotgun slow but powerful with a low ammo capacity, and one fast but low power one with a large ammo capacity. Same with the handguns. One of the handguns even plays like a tmp, but does more damage than the previous handguns before it. Then, the unlockable weapons are generally underwhelming, which is lame. All of this is a very minor thing all things considered, but something I noticed. 

All in all, I am very happy with this game and look forward to resident evil 4 remake and other future resident evil games.

Resident Evil Village is - for those not in the know - effectively Resident Evil 8. The "Vill" part of "Village" is converted into roman numeral overlay for "VIII," which is 8. So yes, this is a mainline game and not just some spinoff. In fact, it's a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7. If you haven't played that one, I would argue that you really ought to before playing this one. You play as the same character in that game, and there are multiple things which come up in the story which won't make too much sense out of context.

Character progression is pretty fun in this one. The RE4 attache case style of inventory is used in this game, with no item box, but a large personal storage and you can flip items if need be to get things to fit better, etc. Enemies drop money and crystals which can be sold for money, and there is a merchant called "the Duke" who will sell you a variety of items and guns, while also offering to upgrade different attributes of your weapons, or even a few character attributes a bit later into the game. I really liked this aspect of the game.

This game takes the first person perspective of RE7, along with the more action-based tone/gameplay of RE4, along with the vital, general creepiness of the series, and blends them all together into a quality product. This game incurred less in-world "dread" for me than some of the other games in the series, but it also includes the most unsettling and frightening moment/sequence for me in the entire series, I think. There are some fun, well-done gameplay shifts in the game, going from an exploratory, exposition opening with some intrigue, a wild RE4-style "village attack" sequence, creepy exploration, A-to-B running-for-your-life, more-so classic Resident Evil exploration/combat/puzzles, high horror focus with lots of puzzles in one area, scripted horror/action, and the incredibly combat-heavy portion of the game which starts and never lets up until the end of the game. I would argue that from the point of the game sending you to an old location that's not part of the village proper, until the ending, there is too much combat and not enough horror or puzzles. 

Aside from that drop-off in what is relatively the third act of the game, the rest of the game is great, and those parts I have issues with are good at times; just excessive. Despite that, I've played through this game multiple times and intend to do so again in the future. I very much liked the ending of the game and found it more fulfilling than other RE games' endings. If you like RE4 and RE7, then I dare say you should definitely purchase RE Village as it is a lot of fun.

Resident Evil Village is a very good game & I am not even close to unhappy with the game.

Village, being the 8th main installment in the RE franchise follows Ethan Winters a few years after the events of Resident Evil 7, and it is a good continuation of the Winters' family & their story.

I have been getting into Resident Evil recently, starting with 7, as I know the franchise is really good & I really want to be into it now. After finishing the freak-horrorshow that was Resident Evil 7, my next game was of course Village. RE Village is not nearly as scary as the previous entry but it does not suffer from that, it still has its scares of course, but it is not near the amount as 7. There is one specific area (that I won't name to not spoil!) that is very scary, not exactly the level as RE7, but quite close.

The main big bosses of Village are very different from one another, but are one big family! You will definitely enjoy meeting this odd group of siblings, and their mother.

The game begins with your baby daughter, Rosemary Winters, being taken to an unknown place. This happens with an intense sequence of events that will be especially shocking to players who successfully completed RE7 and saw the ending. Many things happen until you find yourself walking a very dark, cold and snowy path in the woods. How you got here? I won't tell, but you'll see. It's intense. This path leads you to a Village of course, and your quest begins there: Find Rose. It's an intense ride, and Ethan Winters surely wasn't prepared.

Before witnessing the terror within this mysterious Village, I highly highly recommend you play it's direct predecessor, RESIDENT EVIL 7. There, you will learn all about Ethan Winters himself, his wife Mia Winters, and the journey that led them to this point. That game is a roller-coaster of horror and you will love it, I am sure.

Both RE7 and Village don't connect too much with previous entries in the franchise, as 7 was a soft-reboot of sorts, but you should definitely still play the rest! You witness great terror, many catastrophes and a great cast of characters, all fighting to rid the world of bioweapons.
This game has one returning character: Chris Redfield! He's a lovable character and usually the hero, but he seems to be much more dark and brooding here... just look at that cover art!

Village was a great experience for me and I can't help but love it. I am really hoping you will too.

[h1]” Village is like The Room but you have to play through the movie and can’t fast-forward”[/h1]
There are two sides to the RE series; crazy action, or tense survival horror. Previous games have served one with varying degrees of quality. These design choices are rarely ever mixed because it’s impossible to get it right for this franchise. Resident Evil 8 is one that got it wrong. You rarely get kick-ass action against a variety of crazy enemies and you for sure don’t get a tense item-hunting through excellent puzzle-driven levels like the originals. Instead, you get a game that won’t please either camp. 

Speaking of camp, this game delivers on that front and does not disappoint. The franchise is best when there is no voice acting unless it’s a one-liner. I’ll take the stupid campy route over the boring camp. Looking at you[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/calibrojosh/recommended/21690] RE 5 [/url]&[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/calibrojosh/recommended/221040] RE 6[/url] . The writing is so bad it’s good. Ethan is probably the dumbest character and doesn’t know it, which makes it even better. Some words spoken in this game have to be a translation error. The more they try to explain why everything is happening the less interesting it gets oddly. Remember when it was just fighting zombies from a virus? At least the dumber it gets, the funnier it also gets.

[h1]I’m Just Disappointed[/h1]
The disappointment sets in when that tall vampire lady(Lady D) that all men and some women wanted to get squished by, is barely part of the game. Her level is a linear castle versus an interconnected level like the Baker Mansion, the Police Station, or the Spencer Mansion. Lady D is nothing like Mr. X and her boss fight is the lamest of them all. How they ♥♥♥♥♥♥ so much up with her is beyond me, and the boss fights never get better.

You also get brain-dead puzzles or handed items to progress versus finding them, aka fake exploration. Then most of the time, you don’t get the crazy action the other games added to make up for losing that aspect of the franchise. It tries to be an action horror and fails to execute either in a competent way. Only Dead Space and Darkwood have done it right that I know of. Almost every boss was a slog to fight with the only real threat being falling asleep. Playing Hardcore the first go around in the other games didn’t feel so bad, what changed? Also, the starting action set piece is stupid enough to warrant a refund.

The ending sections should have been the whole game and it would have felt better than trying to be a fake action game masquerading as a fake survival horror. I hated RE 6, but it threw everything at you, but you were a God. The director said he “[i]didn’t want to make Village scary because RE 7 made some people scream[/i]”. Yet, it outsold this game and should speak to what most fans want, but this game is highly praised for some reason, so maybe it’s hard to pinpoint what people want.

[h1]It’s Not All Bad[/h1]
Now it seems like I hate this game with a passion, I’m more disappointed, especially after RE 7 was a great refresh. I’ve played almost every main entry more than once, I won’t ever do it with this one. But for a one-time playthrough, it has some moments. Heisenberg feels like whoever wrote and voiced him tried to take it seriously. His level was also the best, it felt like classic RE with backtracking through an interconnected level for once. I stupidly thought the enemies couldn’t die and decided to run around them like it was a different game. A weird case of the bullet sponge making the game better? Eventually found out, and they do die. The new trader and his comments are equally a highlight too. The upgrades are great, hard to screw that up *cough* RE 6 *cough*
The real kicker is, as I mentioned the developer making the game less scary, yet they put a creepy doll and a “baby” in one location. It’s the scariest thing they’ve ever made to date and was the other huge highlight. I’ll remember it forever whether I want to or not. But the puzzle could have been more, seriously the puzzles in this sucked so hard.

This isn’t the worst Resident Evil game, that’s reserved for RE 6. This might be the worst single-player one, but that’s because most of the mainline entries have more positives than negatives.

Yep.  Great game.  And I don't mean "great" to mean "rather good" - I mean that in my opinion this is a landmark game, outstanding, hall of fame material.

I could pick apart a few flaws: The early game feels annoyingly on rails.  The final boss fight is easily the least interesting in the game.  There's no field of view setting, which means on PC you feel like you're looking at the world through a scuba mask.  The protagonist doesn't have much in the way of a personality.  But these and other minor irritations only stand out because the rest of the game does so much so well.

[list][*][b]Visuals[/b].  A superficial point, but the environments here are lush, diverse, and spooky as hell.  Character designs are convincing and varied, from creepy murder dolls to high-tech agents to a mystical crone to blood-smeared vampires to a comfortably dressed housewife, and much more.  The general presentation here is masterful.

[*][b]Level design[/b].  Location maps range from linear and simple to complex and confusing.  Many areas feel like "your daddy's Resident Evil" but there is a great deal of variety and learning my way around was a pleasure.  Conflict pacing is very thoughtful, with boss fights, minion fights, and "quiet time" balanced to keep the player on their toes, never at ease while exploring, and never doing so much combat at once that it becomes a chore.

[*][b]Overarching design and story[/b].  The four major chapters of the game each feature a very different antagonist, with different relationships to the major story elements, and critically different wrinkles on gameplay which felt wonderful.  The early castle area feels very "classic Resident Evil"; then the second area goes in a different direction gameplay-wise, even [spoiler]taking away your guns[/spoiler].  Again the range here served to keep me interested not just moment to moment but wondering what long-term foundation shifts might come next.

[*][b]Combat and resources[/b].  Guns feel meaty and combat is visceral.  Getting hit often means a very brief cutscene where a monster will grab you and bite your arm for example.  As ever, managing ammunition and supplies is always a concern, with a nice crafting system in place to allow you to make decisions.  Should those chemicals be used for medicine or shotgun shells?

[*][b]Length[/b].  Pacing is great here as well.  My "thorough but not obsessively completionist" playthrough lasted a little over 12 hours.  I felt like I always had things to do and was always in sight of the next major story beat, with a few side activities and treasures to search for when I wanted to take a break from driving the main story.  Things never dragged.[/list]
Very much worth your time, and if you keep your eyes open and have some patience you can get it on sale for $20 like I did.  If the game looks at all interesting to you I urge you to make time for it.

Resident Evil has always been a franchise with short games jam packed with tight level design, decent puzzles and a whole lotta resource management against enemies that just won't die and hit hard... this one's no exception. RE Village feels like the culmination of all their previous (good) experiences distilled into one game, and it really, really shows.

I may have only played 23 hours but I've actually completed the game 3 times, the first one taking the longest and my other two being actually shorter in playtime. Games in the franchise are fine being cleared as is, and at first the playtime may indicate that they're not worth it for the price, but the quality...the quality is just chef's kiss. The level design, the sfx for the enemy growls and wood creaking underneath your feet, the roars of monsters, that one Beneviento level...they'll stay with me for quite a bit.

I'd love to exchange every thousand hour I've spent on MOBA/Online FPS games for one good Resident Evil game, but that's not how the world works.

There couldn't be a better a time for this review with the showcase today.

So why don't we start off with the game play. It feels pretty smooth to play, there wasn't a time where I felt the game screwed me over because of how it plays. The exploration aspect is integrated well into the map and its design as a whole, it all felt pretty organic and when I found a room I couldn't get into before, it was clear that I would be able to at a later time or when I had something that could get me through. The gun play works just like the previous game, 7 and then the REmakes, it doesn't feel overwhelming and is pretty easy to get into the groove. Storage is also the same, you have to keep managing your inventory and make sure you're able to pick up the things you need, nothing too fancy. All the minor details such as things placed in the environment are pretty easy to maneuver around when you've got enemies tailing you and I never found myself cornered.

Game play - 8/10

This game is just visually stunning to look at, especially areas such as the castle entrance, the tower, doll house, etc. If you have a ray tracing compatible GPU, I still wouldn't recommend turning RTX on, it just makes so little difference to the point its barely noticeable and you don't want to tank your performance over that.. Besides that just goes to show that this engine really does exceed expectations in terms of graphics. 

Graphics 20/10

While I don't want to go too much into the story, it is a little lackluster considering what came before. There's quite a bit goofy scenes and some nonsensical things that happened that really shouldn't have or could have been avoided, it does pick up in the later parts of the game and ramps up towards the end and leaves you wanting more, which is always a plus when it comes to story. Just, it could have been more consistent with the seriousness of the story. With its flaws, it really is worth playing through.

Story - 7/10

Overall Rating - 9/10

Resident Evil Village is a great action-horror game strapped to a weak story and missed opportunities for interesting plot developments. Its mechanics are solid and fit its faster pace compared to RE7, though the game has some pacing issues around its midpoint. It has some very memorable characters and scenes, though the main villain and central story focus are big letdowns overall. The pros outweigh the cons for Village, but the game is still a frustrating step down compared to RE7.

Village takes place several years after the good ending of Resident Evil 7. Ethan Winters has settled down into a cozy life in Romania with his wife Mia and daughter Rosemary, only to have his well-earned peace ripped away from him by a close ally. Without warning, Chris Redfield murders Mia, kidnaps Rose, and carts Ethan off to a secluded village in a snowy mountainside. Things only get worse as Ethan delves into the village, encountering monstrous creatures like wolfmen and vampiric ghouls. To rescue his daughter and get answers about Mia's fate, Ethan is forced to confront the inhuman lords of the village, led by the mysterious and godlike cult leader Mother Miranda.

Although Village still has survival horror elements to it, there is a bigger emphasis on combat overall. Ethan handles weapons better than in RE7 and can carry more items on him at once. Money collected from scavenging and from fallen enemies can be spent to upgrade weapons and buy new equipment. You have more opportunities to improve your stats by assembling different recipes. You'll often have to fight more enemies than RE7 would demand of you, but this is balanced out by the increased ammo you carry and the sheer strength of your arsenal. The start of the game grants you a hunting shotgun, a pistol, and a knife - and this quickly expands to a sniper rifle, a magnum revolver, plenty of explosives, and more deadly tools at your disposal. By the endgame, you'll be blowing away mechanized zombies with semi-auto shotguns and automatic pistols.

The game starts out strong but admittedly falters around the midpoint. The initial trek through the village is haunting and sets the tone for the story experience. Ethan's infiltration of Castle Dimitrescu perfectly balances action with tense horror, providing a good mix of close-quarter combat with evasion sequences against unkillable enemies. Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters absolutely live up to the hype while they're on-screen...so it's really unfortunate when she gets killed off about 1/3rd into the game. The cottage level shifts the tone to pure horror, making for some unsettling scenes that sadly slow the game down heavily. The dam level is hit-and-miss, and it fails to answer some crucial questions about why Chris had attacked Ethan's family. Heisenberg's factory is a fun Wolfenstein-like romp against a strong variety of mechanical undead, though it frustratingly dangles an interesting plot thread above you while doing nothing with it.

The entire plot of Village could be resolved with some clear communication between Chris and Ethan. The whole "twist" about him killing Mia isn't resolved until the last part of the game, and the answers you get are a major letdown. He doesn't come across as a villain - just an idiot who should have explained himself to Ethan sooner. Lady Dimitrescu and Lord Heisenberg are fantastic antagonists and steal the show when they're around, but the remaining villains pale in comparison. Mother Miranda is underdeveloped and uninteresting, Lady Beneviento doesn't last long enough to make a big impact, and Lord Moreau is just pathetic compared to his counterparts. Like RE7, the endgame antagonist is much less interesting than the initial antagonist you face. Coupled with the major story hook about Mia being a disappointment, you might come out of Village with mixed feelings about the storyline overall.

The weapon attachment and upgrade system is a nice addition, but it is hampered by some weapons being flat-out better than others. It can be tiring to dump money into upgrades for your pistol only to find a better one a few sections later. RE7's approach of giving balanced stats to alternate weapons is discarded in favor of making them straight upgrades. Why pour money into your initial shotgun when you'll find a superior one before the halfway point of the game? It would have been better if the weapons were balanced around each other, forcing you to choose which strengths matter most in combat. On the bright side, some weapons like the sniper rifle have no better equivalents, making every upgrade you put into them a worthwhile investment.

Despite my gripes with the game, I still think there is a lot to like about Village. Ethan remains a sympathetic protagonist that you'll root for against all odds. The Duke, the strange merchant who'll sell you everything from weapon parts to herbs, is a much-needed friendly face in a hostile environment. Lady Dimitrescu, Lord Heisenberg, and the Dimitrescu daughters absolutely shine as villains and make up for how underwhelming Mother Miranda is. The faster pace of the game's action works well and usually gives you a good balance of exciting action and intense survival horror. In the end, Village delivers a great gaming experience that, while not as well-rounded as RE7, still mostly succeeds at what it sets out to do.

If you loved RE7 and can't wait to see the next part of Ethan's story, I would recommend getting Village at full price. It's a fair deal for a game that took me 12 hours to beat in its first run, not counting the bonus unlockables or the other difficulty options. If you're skeptical about the game, I would wait for it to go on sale for 50% or more. The DLC is mostly cosmetic or pointless aside from Shadows of Rose, so I wouldn't bother spending money on it. Also, if you haven't played a Resident Evil game before Village, I would recommend playing RE7 or the RE2 remake before this. Those will give you a better idea of whether you'll like the series' style of action, puzzles, and survival horror.

I'm fairly new to the resident evil series, I did not play these games growing up because they were 2spooky. I played RE5 and 6 in high school, and thought they were okay time waster couch co-op games that I don't really remember all that well. A little while ago though, I watched a playthrough of resident evil 7 and was really drawn in by it, and so I decided to play RE8 myself.

I am so glad I did, because this game is awesome. The guns are fun, the enemies are scary, and the metroidvania-ish style of opening up the map was rewarding and made me want to keep playing. 

These days I feel like horror games try to ape the Amnesia or Five Nights at Freddy's model where you immediately die whenever you encounter an enemy, and a big scary face comes up on the screen and startles you. As a person who is a big fan of psychological slow-burn horror, I never thought those games were all that scary. Sure they make you jump, but for example playing Outlast, it becomes less threatening because I know what is going to happen. Resident Evil 8 takes a very different approach (mostly) to the horror element, where you HAVE to defend yourself. This simple fact makes me vastly more immersed in the game rather than the insta-kill model, and when I'm immersed, I'm frightened. However the game certainly isn't perfect, and later in the game the horror aspect drops off for me.

Pros:
-Fun spooky times, especially in the beginning when you don't have access to very many weapons
-Cool bonus mode where you fight enemies to try to rack up points, this mode is very addicting.
-Decent enough story that you can engage with to your preference, if you want to go hunting for documents you can, or if you just want to fight monsters you can do that too. The story gets a little deranged towards the end but I think the game earns it
-Bosses are fun and challenging on higher difficulties 
-Lots of "Just for fun" things that you can unlock, like unlimited ammo guns 

Cons:
-The first couple hours of the game are by far the scariest, and the horror element drops off significantly once you get further into the story and it starts going all sci-fi.
-The instant death mechanic is somewhat present
-Significant portion of the game takes place in a factory where the enemies and environments aren't as interesting as in the first area
-[spoiler] The third boss of the game, the doll lady, is clearly meant to be really scary, however I just am not afraid of creepy dolls in the slightest, and again we have that instant death mechanic with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up giant abortion thing.   [/spoiler]

Overall, I loved the game a lot and played it all the way through over the course of one weekend, and have gone back a couple times to do some of the challenges. 8.5/10, definitely recommend.

There's a lot to like about Village. The atmosphere, the enemy (visual) design, the RE4 throwbacks (only works if you've played and enjoyed that game though)...

But there are so many glaring flaws that really make me wonder how this game still comfortably sits on an "Overwhelmingly positive" review status.

Too much action, not enough survival or horror. The writing gets really corny at times, the plot has infuriating holes, Chris is portrayed like a TOTAL DUMBASS just for the sake of the plot... and to be honest so is Ethan on many occasions.

Then there's the Hardcore difficulty. While playing the 2 and 3 remakes on harder difficulties was fun, this one is just... "what were they thinking?" Enemies are just bullet sponges and hit like a truck, which would be fine if other aspects of the game were balanced so you could effectively play around that... but nope. It's like the devs just cranked up some sliders and called it a day.

I don't think it's a "bad" game by all means, I just can't rightly give it a "positive" review given how flawed a game this is. If you're going to get this game, try to get it on sale, first of all, and then either play it on Standard for your first run, or if you REALLY must play on Hardcore, then look up a guide on how to beat the first scripted sequence so you don't bash your head against a wall for an hour or more.

RE: Village quickly became one of my favorite entries in the series less than halfway through. The game perfectly blends both older and newer elements of the series together in a really great way. You'll find yourself exploring an elaborately decorated castle towards the beginning of the game, bringing back nostalgia for the old Spencer Mansion from the first game. The game creates a fairly good sense of progression, with a steady flow of upgrades for your weapons coming along the way. I always felt like my actions mattered.

One particular strong point of Village is the ambiance. The environments you explore in this game are stunning and exquisitely crafted. I often stopped to look around and appreciate the artistry that went into the game. A weak point of the game was definitely the puzzles - they were usually too braindead simple to require much thought. Some puzzles basically had the solution to the puzzle shoved right in your face, making it pointless. This is only a minor drawback, though.

Overall, as a lifelong RE fan, who has been playing the games since the first one on the PS1, Resident Evil Village is an excellent entry in the series, and a splendid continuation of the modern path carved for the series by Resident Evil 7. It adds some more action to the mix than 7, but still maintains a sense of respect for the series' roots.

IMO actually one of the best entries into the resident evil series...

carrying on the first person, Outlast like perspective from RE7, and Ethan's story, Resident Evil Village connects Ethan, and the events of 7 to the rest of the series.

I also really enjoy how this game took lots of elements from RE4; the merchant, mercenaries, food, and more action based gameplay.

The different sections of the village and wacky characters you meet allow for a huge variety in different types of gameplay. The castle gives a stalker like RE2 experience, The dollshouse is like a mix between the tape section of RE7 and an original resident evil puzzle, and is absolutely terrifying. The Lake is like an extended boss fight, the stronghold adds horde-shooter like combat, and the factory adds another level of stress by introducing a bunch of new armoured enemies. Chris' section is fun, purely because it makes you feel invincible with almost infinite ammo and new guns, drastically switching up the gameplay.

The final boss is awesome design wise, and is a decent fight, weirdly reminds me of RE6.

I like the ending and feel that it leaves a lot of open possibilities for the future of resident evil, hopefully we see some returning faces in RE9 and it isnt another soft reboot like 7 (even though that was good).

But generally all I've gotta say is that this was a really good game, and I'm very excited for the DLC coming this October, and if anything I'm just dissapointed that the Ada content was scrapped, but thats probably just me bc I LOVE ADA T_T

Capcom did exceptionally well with this one. Resident Evil Village combines the gameplay of the three previous titles and RE4 to make a unique experience... Ok, maybe RE8 is pretty homogeneous to RE4 considering it has a merchant, gun upgrades, fish murdering, a section where you ride a tiny boat, findable treasures that are also sometimes combineable, similar enemy types to RE4, uhh...

Anyways, that's not to take away from RE8 as the new things it does bring to the table certainly makes it different, and the mechanics that are familiar have been well updated to current video game standards. I should mention that this is primarily an action game with horror element,s so for those looking for something akin to RE7 or the other older style RE games, then you might want to look elsewhere. Contrarily, if you are a fan of the RE games with badass protagonists killing hordes of enemies, then this is the game for you. The common enemies are tougher than in RE4, but there are generally less of them. The intensity of the game picks up towards the end when your arsenal starts to fill up and tougher enemies appear, which force you to use more strategy. 

The plot is also enticing. Ethan Winters is the protagonist again, and this time you are on a mission to go rescue his daughter Rose from a village of mutated people. (Although now that I think about it, even the premises kinda similar to RE4). A good amount of reveals and plot twists make it an interesting story from start to finish. The ending also sets up for future installments, so I'd recommend you give it a playthrough if you plan on playing any sequels. 

To reiterate, Capcom used their magic again to create another solid Resident Evil game. It is very action focused and similar to RE4, but that's essentially the golden goose of the series so does it really surprise anyone that they chose to copy it? Anyways, I think that RE8 is a great game on it's own and certainly recommend it to anyone who is interested.

A continuation of the last title, this one IMO, has more replay ability because of the myriad of choices and ways to dispatch the variety of foes. I liked the atmosphere of Biohazard, but didn't want to replay running and hiding ALL the time. Like most Resident Evil titles, the story isn't perfect, but the visuals and game play make it well worth playing. I'm having a ton of fun with this one. I'm on my third play through, and still smile at all the weird characters and monsters(the giant lady is awesome). The zombies are called wolf creatures this time, and I'm "lycan" it! Yea, I face palmed after that joke too. Yeah, it's weird, but never boring and like most RE titles, it's intense rather than scary, I just don't find most monsters scary. There are ghost-like things happening in parts even though the games are about out of control viruses, but it still adds to the experience of the game. There IS one part of the game that legitimately scared the ba-jabbers out of me, and most who have played this knows EXACTLY which part that is. Ironically, it's the only part of the game in which your weapons are taken away. I was solving some well put together puzzles, hurrying along, when out of NOWHERE came a creature that was not only horrific looking, but made sounds so unsettling, I didn't realize until after I finally escaped it, that my pants where heavy and I had to throw them away (thanks Resident Evil)! I haven't been scared from a video game like that since the first two Silent Hill games. Kudos to you RE, I'm just glad I got the VA to turn to therapy, because I don't know if insurance would pay for my therapy bills. I've always felt that the stories and monsters of the RE universe were a little far fetched, but the action ALWAYS has me coming back to it. I know there are a lot of people groaned at the return of a ton of different monsters and more action, but to me, Biohazard (the last title) wasn't any different, just less insane. More atmospheric, but the story was still far fetched and raised more questions than answered. It still had giant blob monsters the player has to shoot the orange pus bubbles on so I'm not sure why most people say it's different than other titles, besides the action being toned down. I have a ton of hours on the last title, only because I keep dying at the same parts over and over on a higher difficulty, having to watch the same scenes over and over until I had another chance at getting my butt kicked in 10 seconds(that and always looking for the football figurines). This one has more action, and I'm planning on playing it over and over till I'm blue in the face. I'm not sure if the baby's name (Rosemary) was a reference to a specific horror movie, but it's a fun game no matter. It's a bit weird, I'm not sure how the story couldn't figure out Ethan was special, as the "twist" in the end implies, but how could the baby be some all powerful deity out of nowhere? Genetics man, genetics! If Mia was cured, it stands to reason that you should play this game to understand these sentences more. A lot of the story is questionable, but when has that EVER stopped RE from gaining die hard fans? If you like RE 4-6 even though many people groaned at the action and far fetched monsters, I think you'll get along with this title just fine. It's still done in the same fashion as the last tittle, first person view, some running away from certain characters (until you can fight them), plus continues the story after the last one, Biohazard. After Mia and Ethan escape Louisiana, they settle down and have have a cute lil' ol baby. The baby gets kidnapped, cue the father to quest to get her back, fighting off monsters, villains, and werewolf people that need hair gel and a barber. Now, if you'll excuse me, I will get back to the game. The ONLY part I really don't look forward to, is the part that legitimately gave me nightmares, and made me throw my pants away!!! ENJOY!!!

[h1] Well, well, didn't think anyone was left! You must be pretty tough, huh?[/h1]
[h1]Introduction[/h1]
At first, [b]Resident Evil Village[/b] could not run on my PC despite meeting the requirements for the game. I was heartbroken that I could not experience this game at its hype, at launch. However, I was down but not out, as I could get my hands on a [b]Steam Deck[/b], a 256GB model. Finally, I was able to play [b]RE8[/b], and man it was a fantastic game to play from start to finish. I stopped playing the three games I was playing to play it. It’s like [b]RE8[/b] put a hex on me and possessed me to experience what I was missing this whole time.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]A gripping story that will make you question everything around you
[*]Interesting and yet mysterious characters
[*]Fantastic gameplay that incorporates survival horror from RE7 that is mixed with action from RE4
[*]Some fun boss fights
[*]Creepy environments that are beautiful in their own right
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Some of the characters don’t exactly develop much
[*]The third area of the game felt shallow and slowed the pace down
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story takes place after the events of [b]RE7[/b]. [b]Ethan Winters[/b] is living with his wife [b]Mia[/b], and they are having dinner while having a small argument. Then all of a sudden, their house is attacked by [b]Chris Redfield[/b] and his men. [b]Chris[/b] kills [b]Mia[/b] and takes their daughter [b]Rose[/b]. [b]Ethan[/b] is obviously confused and is asking [b]Chris[/b] why he is doing this; [b]Ethan[/b] is then knocked out and the truck he was in crashes. With [b]Chris[/b] and [b]Rose[/b] gone, [b]Ethan[/b] makes his way into this nearby village.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2850616099
In this village, there are these creatures called [b]Lycans[/b] roaming around and eventually, [b]Ethan[/b] finds some survivors who don’t take too kindly to him. There is also this elderly woman who is wandering around the village that the [b]Lycans[/b] seem to ignore. My assumption is that she bakes cookies and hands out candy to them, so they just ignore her.

That shall be all I will say about the story. There is a lot I want to talk about, but I want to avoid spoilers completely. I love how the characters were done as they were all interesting and loveable. The [b]Duke[/b] was a shopkeeper who just had a nice charm to him and gave you a sense of ease whenever you saw him, it made you feel safe, and you could stock up on supplies from him. [b]The Lords[/b] were also interesting, and I liked some of the personalities they had, my two favorites were [b]Donna Beneviento[/b] as she had not just my favorite puzzle, but her segment was also the scariest. Then there was [b]Karl Heisenberg[/b], who was my favorite overall in terms of being a villain, personality, and the level of mystery he had. [b]Alcina Dimitrescu[/b] was also a fun villain and even brought in gameplay elements from [b]RE7[/b] that I loved.

However, not all characters are created equal, [b]Salvatore Moreau[/b] is a character who to me was not developed enough and I personally did not like his area of the game. I can even say the same for [b]Donna Benevento[/b], despite me liking her character, I wish she had more time to shine. This also goes to the main antagonist, [b]Mother Miranda[/b], as she did not really show much of herself, and really, in the end, I just did not care for her.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay for [b]RE8[/b] is honestly fantastic, it combines elements from [b]RE4[/b] and [b]RE7[/b] and they work really well. Shooting enemies is fun as always and you have to try and aim your shots perfectly as they can sometimes make movements to mess up your shots. You are given a few guns to help you out, like [b]pistols[/b], a [b]shotgun[/b], a [b]sniper rifle[/b], and [b]explosives[/b]. You can find ammo scattered throughout the game or craft it by finding materials. You will also be coming across [b]Len[/b], the game's currency that you can use to buy weapons, supplies, and upgrades to help you take out enemies.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2845721839
The boss fights are also fun to fight, my two personal favorites have to be [b]Alcina Dimitrescu[/b] and [b]Karl Heisenberg[/b]. Overall, the former was fun to fight, and I just had a fun time fighting her as a whole, she made me know that she was a threat and could easily take me out if I am not careful. The latter, he had possibly the most unique fight. I would explain more about them, but I would end up spoiling too much of them as a whole.

However, the third area of the game in my eyes did not feel as great as I would have hoped for, unlike the other areas. It was slow and uninteresting, and the boss fight overall was just not fun. It slows down the pace of the game and overall is just not fun to be in. I was just glad to be done with the area and move on to more fun things to do in the game.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
[b]RE8[/b] is a beautiful game, the environments are creepy yet so appealing to look at and explore. You will want to know what other great sights the game has in store for it. Now for the graphics and performance - Well, since I tested it on my [b]Steam Deck[/b], which was the 256GB model. However, my specs on my computer are as follows, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and 16 GB of RAM. I was told by a few people that I could run the game at low settings, but I could not.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2850616236
Take it as you will for this and if anyone has any comments on the specs then you are free to tell me.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
If you enjoyed [b]RE7[/b] and [b]RE4[/b], then I think you will have a lot of fun with this game, I loved the story and its characters. The gameplay definitely hits the mark in terms of fun with its survival horror elements. I highly recommend this game to any [b]RE[/b] fan or someone who loves survival horror games in my opinion, is possibly the best [b]RE[/b] game that I have played so far.

Similar to the previous entry, but with a completely different feel—if the seventh game was more stealth-oriented and built psychological tension through a tight, confined space, [i]Village[/i] is much more action-driven, aiming to impress with a larger, more open map.

Which one you prefer is obviously a matter of taste, but personally, the seventh game had a stronger impact on me. [i]Village[/i] is undoubtedly an interesting game, but the more I played, the more I started wondering if it would ever end. Despite efforts to vary the environments, most of your actions eventually started to feel repetitive. I also didn't find the story all that compelling. A lot of the themes and symbols felt familiar—like I'd seen or played through similar concepts before.

At times, I also felt like the village itself could've been more interactive or alive. Sure, there were a few animals scurrying around that you could shoot for soup ingredients, which added a little something—but I would've liked more to make the world feel less static. Yes, I get that "isolation" is part of the atmosphere, but there's a limit. It's one thing to feel cut off in a small, abandoned location, and another when you have a vast map that feels underutilized. Something unexpected every now and then—a crashed plane, a wandering school bus, something—would have helped break the monotony. Instead, it was just similar-looking houses and occasional enemy spawns.

There [i]were[/i] puzzles, and some areas were locked off until later, which added variety. But I'm also not sure if the four main bosses were introduced in the best order. After Lady Dimitrescu, none of the later sections felt as gripping. That moment also marked a shift—the game moved more toward action and away from stealth, which may have been intentional for pacing, but it left me missing the earlier tension.

That said, [i]Village[/i] is still solid entertainment. Maybe a bit on the long side, but definitely a recommended game for fans of the genre. It also offers good replay value, and the bonus mode, [i]The Mercenaries[/i], adds even more game time.
