Resident Evil 8 is quite possibly my favourite game in the franchise. I have played this game seven times now and know for a fact that I will play it an eighth when the DLC comes out. 

I loved Ethan’s story although I wish we could have gotten more time with the four lords, they’re all extremely entertaining characters when they’re on screen and I couldn’t get enough of them. Plot wise it does feel like some concepts could have been expanded on further but that doesn’t impact the overall quality of it. 

Resident Evil 8 is definitely more action orientated than the game preceding it but when it wants to amp up the horror it does so masterfully. Seven playthroughs in, even knowing exactly what I need to do and what’s coming, certain sections still throw me into a panic.

The combat in this game is top tier and really shines through in Mercenaries Mode. I enjoyed every section in this game and loved the enemy variety. 

This game also provides a New Game + mode where you can take your resources into a new playthrough, as well as unlocking some new weapons to buy in the shop. This is justified by making the harder difficulties a lot more challenging than previous games with scarcer resources, less health and more damage. While it’s possible to complete the game on these higher difficulties right off the bat, I wouldn’t recommend attempting Village of Shadows on your first playthrough of the game. 

This game is a sequel to Resident Evil 7 but provides the option to be given a recap of the previous game before you start for anyone wanting to break into the series for the first time; and ultimately I believe that each game is fresh and unique enough that even if you didn’t enjoy RE7 you may still enjoy this. 

All in all, Resident Evil 8 is an incredibly fun experience that shouldn’t be missed out on. I’m looking forward to the DLC this late October!

[u]What I liked about the game[/u]
[list] 
[*]	 Some really awesome antagonists like Lady Dimitrescu, Heisenberg, and mother Miranda. The voice actors in general did a brilliant job.  The cut-scenes in which the antagonists appear in are very well-done. My favorite antagonist was probably Lady Dimitrescu, because I really liked the idea of being chased by a 9ft 1930/40s vampire mommy.  

[*]	I really like the east European setting.  I liked exploring the old castles, churches, and the resident’s homes.  

[*]	The game has some really cool looking enemies, especially the ones you encounter in Heisenberg’s factory. I like that Capcom have based some of the enemies on werewolf’s and vampires.   

[*]	Plenty of hidden secrets. As you play through the game you will come across all sorts of treasure. 

[*]	 I like that Capcom have brought back the merchant. You can sell your treasure to buy upgrades for your weapons. You can also bring the merchant food to upgrade your stats. 

[*]	A nice selection of weapons, which are fully upgradeable.     

[*]	Tons of bonus content, like Mercenaries mode. You can unlock concept art and figurines. You can also unlock new weapons for the next playthrough. 

[*]	Game has some scary moments. 

[*]	The game play is very enjoyable. I like the idea of a Resident Evil game being in first-person. I think the best way to experience a horror game is in first-person.  

[u]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/u]
 
[*]	Could have done with a bit more horror. 

[*]	Some sections of the game could have done with being a bit longer, for example moreau and Donna section. I think the overall game could have done with being a bit longer. 

[*]	It’s a shame they had to kill off some of the characters. 

[*]	Mercenaries is a bit lackluster, you can only play as Ethan winters. 

[*]	Puzzles were a bit too easy, but I still enjoyed them. 
[/list]
[u]Conclusion[/u]

Overall I really enjoyed Resident Evil Village. The game had some brilliant antagonists. I really liked where the game took place. It was a shame that Lady D was only the first boss. I like that Capcom have carried on with first-person perceptive.   I think the game could have done with being a bit scarier. I would have liked the whole game to have been just as scary as the Donna section. If you enjoyed resident evil 7 and you want a bit more action, then I highly recommend you buy this game.  Can’t wait for the DLC.

I just finished this game and wow what a ride it has been. FOR THOSE WHO WANT THE SHORT SPOILER-FREE REVIEW: This game is one of the best Resident Evil games (in my opinion) out there and the amount of details in this game is amazing. The plot is very good; graphics are stunning; gunplay and gameplay is top-tier and is smooth af; The balance between the horror scares and action is really good; There are some areas that are weaker than the others but are still good; Bonus content is decent for those that want it. 9.5/10.

FOR THOSE THAT WANT THE LONG REVIEW (SPOILER ALERT): I'll be going in a bit more detail here. The "weaker areas" that I mentioned from the short review are Moreau's Reservoir and just before the finale when you battle Heisenberg and play as Chris Redfield. Moreau's Reservoir kinda feels like a filler area which lacks compared to it's predecessor areas, The Castle and House Beneviento. Its Lord, Moreau, also wasn't really developed character-wise but was still decent; and just to add his boss fight was meh. The boss battle between you and Heisenberg is also a bit weird since you're using a vehicle with a cannon and a chainsaw and that made it feel like a standard COD game; but this DOESN'T happen anywhere else in the game which is good. The part where you play as Chris Redfield is also decent at best since you're given fat stacks of ammo just to spray and pray on the enemies and it doesn't feel Resident Evil-like. Other than that, the game is amazing and stunning. The Village, The Castle, House Beneviento and Heisenberg's Factory were all top-notch. The Village was a great opening to the game and as an explorable area; The Castle was designed so well and I loved its stalker enemies; House Beneviento was the scariest part in the entire game and made me terrified for the first time in ages; Heisenberg's Factory had cool enemies and explained more of the lore and also Heisenberg was really well developed. The ending is also emotional and cool in the same time; I do think that Ethan Winters deserves the "rest". This game also has good connections with its prequel, Resident Evil 7, because it explains many things that were left unexplained; like how tf Ethan could flipping stick his limbs back on and how he could survive so much ♥♥♥♥. All in all, it's a great game. 9.5/10.

Village is another step in the right direction for RE. Continuing on with the story of Ethan Winters, it contains a surprisingly well written story, especially for a RE game. 

With multiple antagonists, all of whom are downright unforgettable despite having to share the limelight with each other, a story that adds further lore to the RE verse, and writing that makes you feel emotionally invested in the well being of the protagonist and his daughter, this is debatably the best entry in the series to date. Both Heisenburg and Lady Dimitrescu are especially of note, both having compelling character and motivations while being the definition of polar opposites.

A perfect amalgamation of both new and old school RE. You'll find the classic RE puzzles combined with a map that encourages exploration and contains lots of hidden valuables for the player to sell, including the new mechanic of combinable treasures, adding another layer of choice for the player, whether to sell the initial treasure for a smaller amount right away, or attempt to find the other pieces and combine them for a treasure that is worth more than the sum of its parts. 

In my opinion, one of the best decisions the developers made was the inclusion of the merchant Duke, a mysterious character who attempts to help Ethan throughout his journey in the Village. Initially similar to the merchant of RE4, Duke comes with a whole lot more character, serving as somewhat of a guide to Ethan, and even directly impacting the story at points. Not only does he sell weapons, upgrades and a number of other items, Duke is also able to cook some yummy food, once provided the ingredients, giving the player permanent upgrades to a couple of different aspects, one being an indispensible upgrade to max health.

All in all, RE Village does an exemplary job of combining new and old RE elements, while providing an unforgettable experience that feels both new and nostalgic. I sincerely hope RE continues exploring in this direction, I'm excited for the upcoming DLC and can't wait for further entries!

RE Village is one of the best video games I've ever played. Absolute 10/10. Buy it now. Buy it on sale. You need to play this, fellow gamer. But hear me out. This is more of an action game than a horror game. I mean, Steam's genre for it is literally 'action.' I digress. Review time.

It's also incredibly easier than RE7 was on the equivalent difficulty level--there wasn't an option to heal/craft with the action paused before. Now, not only can you do that but, combined with enemies that reliably drop crafting ingredients; it's hard to not have ammo. 

Ammo was much more scarce in Biohazard and always has been in Resident Evil but, in Village, you can also buy it if you can't find it/craft it. The merchant in this game references the merchant from Resident Evil 4 and for that alone, Capcom deserves the full MSRP. 

Anywho, I loved this game and I guarantee that this title will surprise you. If you've already played RE7, you'll likely predict at least one major plot point as well except, well, let's just say it didn't ruin the story. 

TL;DR--the real horror story here is fatherhood. It's a rough gig. Evil residents make it more rough. Capcom made it fun. I bought this game on sale for less than I paid for Biohazard. 
For the first time as a gamer, I feel like I owe a developer more money. Gimme some DLC, Capcom. You earned my coin.

Resident Evil Village is a great, great game.

The story is fantastic, the characters are great, and the presentation is stellar, and I’m not talking only about the graphics, the art design and aesthetic of this game is incredible, the atmosphere, the different set pieces, the pacing, everything about it it’s just great.

The gameplay is classic Resident Evil blended with some more action focused first person combat, think of a faster paced Resident Evil VII, that is unless you choose to play on harder settings, can’t speak for myself on this but after watching a couple of streamers I’ve heard complains of bullet spongy enemies and a lot of staggering with opponents overall.

Playing the game on normal and casual though, was an immensely joyous experience, it was thrilling at times, terrifying and disturbing in other cases, and plain and simply fun for the most part.

The optimization has been improved substantially since release, it took Capcom to face a public outcry and the “cracking” of their game to fix most issues, but as it stands, despite the Denuvo implementation, Resident Evil Village remains a pretty well optimized game for modern systems, with some minor issues to the ports controls in menus here and there, and the like.

If there is something that annoys me a bit is the fact that the game offers an immense level of incentivizing the player to replay the title, and I did right after my first playthrough, but sadly the game includes a masterstroke of a section, that while beautifully crafted, and stunningly horrifying at that, does hamper the replayability of the game a bit; the whole section last around 24 minutes or so though, so it doesn’t end up being a huge problem either way.

Overall Resident Evil Village delivered an enriching, almost childlike nostalgic experience for me, pulling me further and further to know more about its characters and the world it created, reading through the concept art is eye opening and sheds a light as to the creative process and amount of works that goes into these types of games, I truly cherished my experience with this game as it delivered one that I hadn’t had in a while in games.

Story-wise, the game would make a lot more sense if the 5% that poorly attempts to handwave how this is part of the RE universe didn't exist at all.  "I don't have time to explain" Chris keeps saying, and he's right... he never does.  

I've noted a number of things that Ethan will not do on his quest to save his daughter, but an average 12 year old would have no problem doing when sneaking out of the house.
-Move a half dozen small items blocking a path
-Clear 2-3 inches of snow blocking a gate
-Jimmy open a wooden drawer
-Kick open a rotting wooden door
-Pull up the bucket from a well by pulling on the rope
-Climb over objects as low as two feet fall or over gates with multiple handholds (and no barbed wire) as low as eight feet tall
-Attempt to swim to safety after falling into water instead of flailing around in place waiting to die
I know 'obstacles' like these were part of the series from the beginning, but it's not the 1990s anymore.  Capcom needs to create roadblocks that make logical sense rather than insult the player.

Other random things that bugged me
-Ethan has a flashlight that he pulls out on his own when it's completely dark, but you can't use manually even when it is 90% dark... thanks a lot Ethan!
-Some doors/gates are locked with no key, and you can't unlock them from either side, so they only serve to annoy you when going between areas you've been to before
-Your map shows the locations of chickens, wells, typewriters, locked doors and treasure chests, but not which roads are blocked by debris
-In the intro Ethan makes a reference to going through military training, but I guess he wasn't paying any attention, since he doesn't have any new moves from RE7... maybe that's where they taught him how to stick keys, giant crystals and crafting items into his hyperspace pocket (you can't do it with meat or lockpicks though)

I am pretty sure it is a scripted event but idk, for a first run of a play through it went on too long. But the scenario Mirrors RE4s first visit to its village which is cool. You can upgrade guns, just like in RE4 which is a fun bit of progression. The monsters and bosses are new and unique if, not reminiscent of a few previous ones in the series. There are questions, mysteries, puzzles, combat, backstory and very little backtracking. It really is a well made game

I only have 2 complaints about gameplay.

The first one I have is is with the combat. I do not like it when enemies take 7-15 headshots to kill. They should have reduced the health of all enemies, even bosses, but also drastically reduced ammo. Or how about The first boss taking literally 100s of bullets to kill. Honestly Bullet sponges just take away from horror and turn it a bit campy In my opinion. The first time I spent two full magazines from a pistol on the basic enemy it felt kind of like a joke. That being said it is entirely doable, and later guns do a lot better, but pistols just feel weak all over.

I know that it would change the meaning of gun upgrades, but I think there are nice ways to make it work. For example the starter pistol taking 2-4 headshots to kill an enemy would be good, each damage upgrade reduces the bullets required, for example. Upgrades still mean something, but you are not literally facing a lead faced golem by the time you are done fighting them.

I think having us wonder stuff like, should I spend bullets clearing out this hub, or save it for a particularly hard boss would help add to the horror element. Put enough bullets in the game to kill every enemy, but maybe not when you first meet enemies.

The second complaint, is only a problem with Lady Dimitrescu. The part where she is wandering around the castle looking for you includes a bit of "Player magnetism" which in both of my runs caused me to have to backtrack an entire empty section to get around her. Honestly watching her Go down a set of stairs, then immediately turn around to come back up the stairs and trap me, was just annoying and an Unrewarding player experience. I had been hidden I had not messed up, it made no sense. it just annoyed me and caused me to waste 5 minutes doing an empty already explored loop because the Magnetism ENSURED she did not leave that damn only route stairwell. Every game that has a Big bad Magnetised enemy like this, Alien:isolation, and RE2:Re for example, it is added in for excitement, but When it is natural when it really is just she randomly finds you it is far more exciting. Game designers should realize this. 

Some scripted scenes are ok for example in the dungeon when she literally breaks the wall to cut you off, wonderful Cinematic, but the player hunting magnetism just burned my biscuits.

For Alien:isolation some one made a mod that removed the Alien's player magnetization, and EVERY one who used it and responded said it made the game so much better, it was no longer a waiting game where every 5 minutes the Alien magically finds you, but a Surprise, an OH CRAP moment whenever it appeared and many replied by saying it made the game much more fun AND scary. SO there are real world examples of people actually enjoying the design more.

Neutral opinions
You had a double barrel shotgun modeled in game, and it was even reasonably playable from Development movies in game, I would have rocked that thing for fun if it was in the game even if it was worse than other shotguns.
A stash would have been really nice, if not for the first playthrough the second run through would have been nice, coulda made it an Unlockable in the Challenge Rewards Shop.
Also I want a damn longsword. it is Europe we have LITERAL Castles, ENEMIES THAT WIELD THE LONGSWORDS and I got no longsword(heh). Would have been cool to have.

After about 2-3 hours from the start of this game, my wife started watching me play it, and she didn't let me play alone through the rest. She enjoyed watching just as much as I enjoyed playing it. As far as replayability, I'm sure she won't watch me play through it again, but I'm tempted to do it again one day because of the extras you start to unlock at the end, and I might want to complete some more challenges. Otherwise replayability is not very good, once you're finished you've experienced it all, and it would be like watching a movie over again - you know what's coming and there doesn't seem to be any way to experience variations in playthroughs. Most of the value I place in this game is due to the unique experiences the first time you come across them.

All in all, I'm very happy with the experience I got for the money I paid. I kind of want to go back at least to RE7 and play that, because I found out at the end there are connections between the two. At the very least, some of the characters have a home in both.

I'm usually hesitant to hop on bandwagon games like this, but with Village I was pleasantly surprised. There were times when the game was genuinely scary, but for the most part, gameplay was primarily focused on exploration and combat, and the "puzzles" were not difficult. None of which are necessarily good or bad things- that's just the way they are. The inventory/mercantile mechanics for RE:8 are comparatively well done. Everything feels very well balanced. Enemies posed a significant threat but were not too frustrating to fight.
[hr][/hr]
PROS
- Gorgeous environment featuring an incredible amount of attention to detail
- A comparatively large variety of monsters and fears to face
- Perfect amount of gameplay. Not too long, not to short. Might seem like a small thing to appreciate, but you get what you pay for
- Awesome extras unlocked upon completion (character models, concept art, development shorts)
- Tall women
- Everything is just so well-designed and effortlessly unique. We need more of that in a genre that's so oversaturated, both by indie developers who try too hard to reinvent the wheel and by triple-A studios that just rehash old ideas.

CON (singular)
The weakest link in Village's chain is the story. The game explores new themes (and explores them well) but certainly leaves more to be desired in terms of continuity. There are many instances that feature typical campy horror logic. [spoiler]Ethan is a complete dumbass, but also happens to solo an entire village of godlike supernatural entities because he's made of mold. What.[/spoiler] The dialog is also incredibly weak and senseless sometimes. Example 1 (paraphrased):

[spoiler]Heisenberg: Hey Ethan! I'm the most powerful of the four lords of the village. I've got superpowers like Magneto and an entire army of robot mold zombies at my disposal. Want to team up to defeat our common worst enemy and get your daughter back?

Ethan: Nope! Let's fight until you're dead and I'm so weak that she kills me without difficulty!

Example 2:
Ethan: "I said get your hands off her!"

Chris(literally kidnapping his daughter):  "Ethan, no."

Ethan: *silence*[/spoiler]

I understand that in this particular genre, you'd be hard-pressed to find someone for whom low-quality exchanges like this would be a deal-breaker. But for some of these segments, you really do have to turn your brain off in order to get through. Doesn't need to be perfect- but for 60 bucks, it definitely could be better. Just my two cents.
[hr][/hr]
But despite the game's high memeability, it's still genuinely good. RE:8's shortcomings are vastly overshadowed by all the things it does right. 9/10 (PC) - Any time a series that I care about puts out a great entry, I always suspect that the game that follows it is going to be a let-down. Fortunately, given that the "Resident Evil" series is probably my favorite game series with most of the titles being excellent, the 8th entry is no exception. It took most of the elements that made that previous entry in the series great and builds upon them without making many sacrifices along the way.

The previous entry to the series, "Biohazard", was quite a departure from the normal RE formula in terms of its gameplay mechanics. Most notably switching to a 1st person perspective, it used that new view to really modernize the RE formula while still staying true to its roots. It also made RE a terrifying experience as well. I would put the 7th Resident Evil game right up there amongst the scariest games that I've ever played. "Village" is definitely not in terms of having such a large fear factor. Instead of being surrounded in environments that instill dread, you're now surrounded by environments that are beautiful to look at and contain really cool horror set pieces. If we're comparing them to another favorite series of mine, I would say that "Biohazard" is more comparable to "Alien", while "Village" is like "Aliens". One is more horror-focused while the other is more action-horror. While they are both great in their own way, I definitely prefer the latter of the two. I do still miss being scared like I was playing the previous game, which is really my own big criticism of it. The game has its moments, like the mansion or the doll house, but I wouldn't really say anything other than that it is really scary. Ah well.

One of my favorite expansions that was made to the gameplay over the previous games was adding a lot more to do throughout the game. While it's not truly an open-world setup, it really felt like I had a lot to explore and accomplish through my play-through. It definitely is the least linear of any of the RE games. Exploring each area of the game was a treat because of how great the game looks and how much variety there is with the environments. From villages, to mansions, to factories, everything is designed really well. The graphics are great and the enemies and supporting characters all look top-notch as well. A knock on the last RE game was the enemy variety was really lacking, but Village expands on the baddies that you face off against a great deal and your encounters don't feel stale at all. The sound design, music, controls are all what I would expect out of a AAA title. No complaints.

While "Village" may lack the scary atmosphere of its predecessor, the sacrifice made for a funner gameplay is an acceptable trade-off. This is just a really well-made game and another great entry into a storied franchise.

Resident Evil Village takes place three years after the 7th game. Ethan Winters saved his wife Mia and they had a baby boy. When I say light ball, it really is like a light ball. Even in the brief moment we held the baby in our arms, my cheeks were chapped. Capcom has done a very good job in the design of the doll, as in all the characters. Despite the small problems between the husband and wife who have this beautiful baby, while everything is rosy, Chris Redfield takes the case and, as we can see in the trailers, as a result of a small raid, he shoots Mia on the head. With our eyes dark and Chris taking our baby and leaving, we find ourselves in the middle of the village that gave the game its name. What we need to do next is to find our baby Rose and understand Chris's problem..

We knew that Resident Evil Village would carry traces of both Resident Evil 7 and 4 games as a theme. As you play the game, you see that these traces begin to become more evident. But it's not just about these two games. Capcom, which made a radical change in the camera and gameplay dynamics in the 7th game, continued this order in the new game as well as succeeded in putting the game into different atmospheres. Even though we enter the village atmosphere as in the 4th game, when we look at the integrity of the game, you see that each region actually carries different traces within itself.

Resident Evil Village has managed to bring together different dynamics.
The village part directly resembles Resident Evil 4. Dimitrescu Castle, on the other hand, has a function like the Karakol, Mansion, which we are often familiar with from the series. In these parts, you are trying to open the locked doors and you are actually trying to escape from this place where you are stuck with some small puzzles. The puzzles are not as detailed as in the old games and can be solved very easily. When we leave all these dynamics aside and go to Donna Beneviento's small mansion, the face of the game changes incredibly.

I would also like to point out that this part, which was a big surprise for me, is the part of the game that I love and fear most.

Spoilers review
If you treat this game as a standalone game without the resident evil association and don’t mind generic action, shooting monsters now and then, turning off your brain, then you will have a good time with this game. The world looks beautiful, the environment is amazing to go through, the shooting is fun. 

However, for those expecting this to be a resident evil game, you are going to be very disappointed. Re8 is strange, there are elements of re4 (i.e. inventory system, action oriented, plot over the top, same shop system etc.) but it also tries to be its own thing. The gameplay consists of shooting monsters, managing resources (not really because you will always have plenty of space, making the inventory system useless), doing story objectives, going A to B (which you will be doing a lot of), watching lots of cutscenes, buying and upgrading weapons etc. 

Unfortunately, most of the gameplay doesn’t work for me as I found the game SUPER linear (there were opportunities where maps could have had different paths like the mansion), ridiculous amount of cutscenes and scripted parts, half the game is just watching a movie and not playing, puzzles are non-existent (also super brain dead), and resource management are not scare enough (even on hardcore). My favourite part of the game is the combat situations, I just wish there was more enemy variety so it didn’t feel repetitive killing the same monsters repeatedly. Remember the flying monsters? They only appear like two times and could have been utilised in more combat scenarios acting as a flying enemy that annoys the player to shoot them first (basically doom gameplay lol). Or have various types of Lycan, some can be more aggressive, some defensive, some in between, anything to spice up the gameplay would go a long way. 

It doesn’t help that the entire game treats the player like their babies who can’t think. This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ loves holding your hand giving you all the key items you need to progress throughout the game. There isn’t any backtracking to find key items and figuring out where they belong as you explore the castle/factory/village/dollhouse. Nope, instead, every obstacle that requires an item is just given to you and you just have to go A to B with said item. This makes the game ultra easy and a huge setback from re7 that actually required you to think when exploring Baker’s house (capcom you know we have brains right?). I can’t believe that the castle section in this game was just a A to B with no exploration cause the game forces you to go through certain rooms at certain times (oh so long are the days where re games actually encourages you to explore the world it built). In fact, the optional side quest of finding treasures were my favourite parts of this game. Cause guess what? YOU ACTUALLY EXPLORE kinda, I mean it is still linear and the puzzles answers are given to you so it is still brain dead but it was fun exploring around the village and seeing different parts of it, which the castle section should have been. 

The pacing in this game was also very off, I was expecting to have a dedicated level within the village that would eventually lead the player to the castle. Instead you only hang around the village for a couple of minutes, then suddenly you are already at the castle and a few minutes later you are already fighting one of the sisters. Not to mention the prologue in this game is so slow to get through, that on repeated playthroughs is going to feel like a chore to play again (even when you can skip cutscenes). This type of fast paced action happens throughout the game, and I found it quickly tiring. This pacing wouldn’t be so bad, if I actually got to play the sets out, but sadly, most of the action sequences are scripted or linear. 

My favourite sections were the dollhouse and the factory for different reasons. The dollhouse was cool, because it was creepy to walk through and the gameplay was slow and intentional with no cutscenes. The puzzles were easy, but for once I actually felt like I was playing an re game, slowly going through a creepy location, feeling uneasy, as the location slowly reveals its secrets. The factory was fun to go through because it was action focused without any fixed sequences (unlike the swamp section) so I actually got to play the game for a good while. The factory was also great because you have to backtrack in order to progress through the level, fighting robots along the way. WHY wasn’t the rest of the game like this??? You still have the action but you also have to explore and not just mindlessly walk A to B. 

The plot is so stupid that I honestly don’t want to get into it, otherwise this review would be 5 pages long. Basically, Chris hides IMPORTANT information from Ethan that eventually gets him killed. Chris hides this information because of reasons??? It recommended that you ignore the plot otherwise your brain is going to hurt from all questionable writing decisions. 

Lastly, why did capcom remove qol features like no fov slider??? This game's default fov is awful and would make anyone sick after 2 mins of using it. It so stupid that you have to run a mod just to make the game playable. 

In conclusion, it’s pretty clear that capcom was making a more casual re game this time around. They have succeeded in doing so at the expense of removing/heavily dumbing down all the elements that make resident evil games so special. If you want to play a modern resident evil game that is more akin to the originals then play re2 remake, re7 or re1 remaster (best game ever made :3). If you don’t care about the lack of survival horror elements and just want to shoot some dudes in a snow village, you could get some fun out of this game.

This Might Be the Worst RE Title

─────────────────────────────────────────

GAMEPLAY

• Combat sucks.

• The first combat section has a jarring cut-scene transition if you're indoors.

• The first hour of the game is almost just pressing W on the keyboard.

• Gameplay innovations are nearly nonexistent, with the only new features being shooting while blocking, countering while blocking, and breaking boxes without needing your knife out.

• The gameplay is on rails, offering barely any free exploration — you're forced to fight bosses and unlock doors in a specific order.

• The FOV can't be changed without modding.

• Tons of yellow/white paint instead of good level design and natural navigation cues.

─────────────────────────────────────────

STORY & PACING

• Worse than RE7.

• Horrible pacing and character writing.

• Having werewolves and vampires is extremely unfitting for a Resident Evil title.

• The pacing is very poor, dragging out scenes that should be quick and rushing through moments that could actually build tension.

─────────────────────────────────────────

CHARACTERS

• Ethan is a terrible character — from his dialogue to how he's written — and his inability to leave areas quickly (like in the Moreau cut-scene) makes him feel stupid.

• Chris's character is assassinated for the sake of fake tension. There's no reason he shouldn't have told Ethan why he shot Mia right then and there, but the game forces him to act evil just to push the plot.

• The enemies and villains are too goofy and exaggerated to be threatening.

─────────────────────────────────────────

LOGIC ISSUES & PLOT HOLES

• The Lycans are called off in the opening fight even though they could easily kill Ethan, which makes no sense.

• Trucks drive on a road next to a creepy castle, even though Chris's company should know the village is abandoned due to werewolf attacks.

• The soldiers in the car with Ethan have no guns on them, which is absurd given the situation.

• A villager with a shotgun conveniently has bad aim and misses Ethan.

• Ethan doesn't shoot Miranda in the cut-scene after the Heisenberg fight for no reason.

• He also doesn't stop the old woman who has vital information — even though she's hobbling away and slowly closing a door, he just lets her go because the story needs to continue.

• Miranda doesn't kill Ethan even though she has zero reason to keep him alive, which is just lazy writing.

Alright, I just finished off the game. Please be advised that I am not a professional critic so you may not agree with me on some cases I'd like to mention. The game is very solid from start to finish.

1)Ethan Winters: I dont understand why Capcom insists making this character so two dimensional. I cared about the villans more than I cared about Ethan. There has been no progress made ever since biohazard.

2)Mother Miranda: Cool concept for a villain but she is so detached from the main story line that you are like "okay" when you face-off with her. She should have been embedded to scenes, story better. Imagine you see a batman movie with joker shown in the last 15 seconds of a 2 hour movie. It would have made sense if they used her as a teaser for a follow-up game but as of now, she is the most indifferent, tasteless, odorless villain ever.

3) Physics: I can clearly say Capcom did not put any effort in trying to make the environment interactive at all. %90 of the time you will feel like you are riding a chart in a tunnel of horror. The environment does not react to anything at all. Nothing is breakable unless it can drop a loot -which comes with a preset model so you know what is what-

4) Firearms: I know this is not a simple shooting game but the using firearms is not satisfying. The shooting effects is just not there. Bullets feel like you are shooting a wooden board rather than soft tissue. There is no sense of impact whatsoever.

5) AI: its been one of the worst. Especially that werewolf looking dude where you get the grenade launcher. One moment he acknowledges where you are, starts attacking you. Then runs off after realizing he cant pass through the door treshold. What does he do? ..Goes back to patrol, as if he did not see you at all!  Now I know there has to be a reset mechanic for the game to move forward but seriously, not like this. AI was one of the issues that made me realize that I was just playing a video game. Completely threw me off, and made me abuse the situation. Not to mention how it undermined the atmosphere the game built. 

6) Villains Overall: All the villains have very very cool concepts. Unfortunately the game did not dwell on their concept that much. 1-2 stage of mechanics and you are done. Resident Evil Village continues the iconic survival horror series with a perfect blend of tense exploration, grotesque enemies, and cinematic storytelling. As Ethan Winters, you navigate a mysterious village and the surrounding castle, facing nightmarish creatures and uncovering dark secrets while trying to rescue your kidnapped daughter.

The game balances survival horror with action, offering resource management, puzzle-solving, and combat against a variety of terrifying foes. The enemy designs are grotesque and memorable, from Lycans to the towering Lady Dimitrescu, making every encounter feel intense. The first-person perspective immerses you deeply in the horror experience, while the environments—from eerie village streets to sprawling gothic castles—are richly detailed and atmospheric.

Visually, Resident Evil Village is stunning, leveraging modern graphics to deliver realistic lighting, textures, and horrifyingly beautiful set pieces. The sound design is superb, heightening tension and delivering effective jump scares without overreliance on cheap tricks.

Pros:

Atmospheric and terrifying environments

Balanced mix of horror, exploration, and action

Memorable enemies and boss encounters

Stunning visuals and immersive audio

Cons:

Some combat sections can feel repetitive

Pacing occasionally favors action over suspense

Resource management is minimal for veteran survival horror fans

Verdict:
Resident Evil Village is a modern horror masterpiece that combines classic survival elements with cinematic storytelling and breathtaking visuals. It’s a must-play for fans of the series and anyone who enjoys tense, immersive horror experiences.

To get this out of the way, I think Resident Evil 7 is the better overall experience compared to Resident Evil Village. 7 was a pure survival horror game which lent it a special atmosphere and sense of grounded realism. In Village, the game is much more action-y, which I guess is just a preference, but I didn't enjoy that shift in tone. I liked 7's tone and atmosphere more because it fit everything else around it. The tone here clashes awkwardly with characters like Ethan, alongside the story baggage that follows him and Mia. Village also has much worse writing compared to 7. For example, In 7, Ethan felt like a genuine dude because the way he was written portrayed him as a generic dude that was way in over his head, which contrasted perfectly with the horror tone of 7. Here, he's always cracking one liners and spewing "bad ass" quips which makes him unbearable to listen to, at least some of the time. Village also makes Ethan out to be this special bad ass guy, which was not the appeal of his character, at least to me. Like yeah, he's way more interesting now with his personal connection to Rose and witty one liners, but to me he is just kind of annoying. He's also set in a story that while honestly isn't bad, NEVER gets to the same suspense of 7. In 7, I was constantly wondering what was going to happen next, while in Village's story, ♥♥♥♥ just happens with no real build up and I just begrudgingly accept it. Village also tries to be more ambitiously grandiose than 7, and instead of jumping to the moon and committing to that change, it tries to pay tribute to its horror roots at the same time. This results in a flip flop of tone. For example, In Resident Evil 4, horror and action were woven perfectly together. It never felt like I was playing a horror game one second, and an action game the next. In Village, it constantly feels like that because it never takes the time to build up those horror moments, like in 7. Village just plops in you for a few minutes then moves back into being an action game with a spooky atmosphere. I would sum it up as 7 feeling like exploring a super run down castle at night where anything can go wrong, where as Village feels like your going through a haunted house attraction with your mom closely behind you to make sure you don't get too scared.

However, that is only one side of Village's whole deal. While I think the characters, writing, story, tone and atmosphere are better done in 7, I find the gameplay more fun than 7. 7's gameplay was molded around it being a horror survival game, with little ammo, tight corridors, and dark and dank rooms leaving you with little space to out maneuver your enemies. In Village, you are encouraged to kill literally everything you come across. Seriously, don't spare your ammo, you will ALWAYS have enough, at least on normal difficulty. This makes Village a less tense game than 7, but a more fun game overall because of the stuff you get to play with. For example, the shop from 4 is back and it's fantastic. You get money from killing enemies or looting treasure, sell it to the Duke, and then spend  money on a bunch of sweet guns, modifications, food that permanently increases your stats, etc. This results in you feeling like a power house. I love upgrading my stuff and fighting the healthy selection of regular foes, mini bosses and regular bosses, then going about and exploring this beautiful world that Village has crafted. Even if the middle drags a bit with there being little "explore this place and open doors and get items to proceed" being present, but the beginning and end have that in healthy doses. As a "gamey" game, Village excels in making sure you're never bored and always engaged with a healthy dose of puzzles and action, without going over board in the action department like in 6. 

Resident Evil Village is still a great time, but it's got a lot weighing it down that might turn off some players (like it did me), or attract many others if this type of action is your thing. For me though, I was looking for a true successor to Resident Evil 7, not a more poorly done, albeit still great, Resident Evil 4.

After my experience with Resident Evil 7, I was excited to see Resident Evil Village going in the same direction and continuing Ethan's story. Several playthroughs later I can say that my excitement was well-placed; this is a great Resident Evil game.

The environments in this game are beautiful, from the rolling snowy hills and mountains of the village to the lavish castle interior, you will always feel immersed in whatever location you find yourself in. There are a great variety of environments in this game compared to Resident Evil 7's decrepit house and bayou, making each section of the game feel truly unique.

Resident Evil Village is more action-focused and feels a bit less like horror than Resident Evil 7 does, but it without a doubt still has extremely frightening and heart-pounding moments. The game heavily encourages you to upgrade and sell weapons much like Resident Evil 4, although the weapon progression generally feels more linear. All of the weapons feel satisfying to use and they all serve their own purpose, even if it's just to replace a worse version of that weapon type. There is of course plenty of careful ammo and inventory management as well as scavenging for both supplies and treasure to sell.

The werewolf or lycan on the box art serves as the game's main attraction in terms of enemies, as they are the most common type you'll encounter. They're far more ravenous and agile than the mold monsters of Resident Evil 7, and exploding the head of a lycan after a few well-placed shots doesn't ever get old. But they are not the only enemies, and there actually is a great variety of enemy types to fight. Slow, zombie-like enemies called moroaica, flying enemies called samcas, and even cyborg zombies made from scrap metal just to name a few. The first time you encounter these enemies are well-paced over the course of the game, so you will always be encountering new ones to fight.

Resident Evil Village's characters while bogged down by silly or downright bad writing at times are still quite intriguing, in particular the lords of each house and the Duke. The lords serve as the game's main bosses before the finale and each one is unique. The Duke, on the other hand, is this game's version of Resident Evil 4's merchant. Ethan has a bit more of a personality in this game than in 7, seeming a bit more jaded but he's still frightened by most things as always and isn't nearly as interesting as previous Resident Evil protagonists. Chris Redfield doesn't play as big of a role as the box art might imply in the actual gameplay other than a short section at the end, and in some cutscenes. The story mainly serves to progress the game and has little substance, but it's never too important for understanding or enjoying the game.

There are several challenges to complete that help you unlock rewards for New Game+ runs, which adds a lot to the game's replay value. These include new weapons, character and weapon models to view, concept art, and even additional gamemodes. The gamemode "The Mercenaries" can be unlocked after beating the campaign once, and involves running around arena-style areas from the game mowing down droves of enemies for points and picking up various powerups. While I personally didn't get too much out of this mode, I can see how someone could have fun going for high scores and the SS rank in each stage. With a content update launching in October this year that adds new characters to play as in this mode, it might become more interesting to me.

Resident Evil Village is a great first-person survival horror and is a good entry point into the series. Personally I'd wait for a sale of some kind but this game is a worthwhile experience.

The fear here comes from needing to fight to survive, rather than being on edge due to the scenario.

That still happens of course, being on edge per the scenario you are in. Just less often when compared to RE7. That was the whole game with 7...

Resident Evil Village continues the Ethan Winters story line with the same first person perspective. The story continues with a gruesome beginning and puts the main character (MC) in an unfamiliar land much like the prequel. The premise of the story is a noble one and is quite convincing of both the protagonist and the antagonists motivations. The concept and the theme/setting is amazing with a strong lore backing them up. The other characters are memorable with distinguishable features and personalities along with interesting backstories. The game however has shifted to favor action over horror unlike its predecessor. However, the over the top action makes up for its lack of horror. The game is extremely fun to play and is challenging at the same time. The dialogues have been well written with decent voice acting. The inventory system is the same as the previous resident evil games where you have to choose your gear wisely and use the items available judiciously but compared to the previous entry the developers have decided to give the players little bit more items like ammo, health items etc.. in order for some breathing space. The graphics are surprisingly well executed with the lighting, atmosphere , design, etc... providing truly breathtaking moments and scenery in game for screenshots. The game design hits spot on for the setting and theme of the game. This game runs surprisingly well and even looks good on most PCs including low end ones with great optimization. My only complain is that we have so little of our favorite character Lady Dimitrescu ;) , She is the most notable villain and the game has hardly 30 minutes of her. Overall this is an amazing experience! I highly recommend this game to new players!

So this is not a horror game like RE7 was, this is an action horror game, like RE4... But about 1/4 length and 1/100 the character with the main protagonist being sort of a black void.

A lot of people compare this game to RE4 because of the more action focused elements, like the game insentivising cobat, enemies drop loot all the time, with every kill dropping either a valuable or just straight up money.

The weapon upgrades quickly turn this game into a straight up shooter, as in the beginning you would really consider every engagement due to the fact that the starting gun might as well be a Nerf pistol. But towards mid to late game the guns you use are so powerful that you feel like an action hero and might think you accidentally booted an actual shooter, though not exactly Doom levels of power fantasy, but not a horror game either.

So you have enemies dropping loot, merchant encounters not too far apart and the most forgiving inventory ststem in RE history, where just like in RE4, key items and valubles have a separate inventory with unlimited capacity, but in this game you also get unlimited space for crafting materials, so the main inventory is just for guns, explosives, ammo, and healing items. No need to think twice before picking anything up, and if you clear every location of resources, you'll never run out of ammo, as you can just craft while the game is paused, opening the inventory will pause the game.

Now my other problem is the use of characters. Before the game came out, the internet was real hot for big vampire lady... How disappointing is it to find out that you can go from meeting her for the first time to killing her in big monster boss level in the span of about 30 minutes?
Same thing goes for the next boss, the one after, the one after and the one after that, all the game bosses feel painfully underused.
People keep comparing this to RE4, but finishing that game can take a minimum of 12 hours, when this can bearly scratch 4-5 hours. I played this game for 20 hours, in that time I beat it twice, finished mercenaries, and already started a third run of the main game. A few days ago I played RE4 and it took me 15 hours to beat.
It would be nice if the game was longer, with more enemy variety.
RE4 had a ton of enemies, starting with villagers, to cultists, giants, giant bugs, soldiers, mutants, and all of them had sub classes, I can still remember the first time I popped a villiger's head and a huge tentacle popped out from the neck, or how cold sweat ran down my back when I heard the chainsaw guy coming, knowing he can chop your head off no matter how much health or healing items you have.

Village lacks in the enemy variety department, thoght a step up from RE7, it still can't hold a candle to RE4.

So it this game good? In a vacuum that contains it and RE7, yes, it answers a lot of questions that I won't spoil ftom the last game, but it will live in the shadow of RE4 that did it better over a decade ago.

It's a modern game, so you have fancy graphics, great modeling, solid game play mechanics, just a bit of a shame there's so little of it.

Get it on sale and don't skip on RE7 before playing.

But you really need to check out RE4 HD, as it is a way superior horror shooter. 

I wonder how the RE4 remake will turn out in a year from now.

RESIDENT EVIL: VILLAGE is the 8th instalment of the RESIDENT EVIL franchise.
I'm sure most people know of the RESIDENT EVIL franchise so I will keep this short and sweet, with a few major things to point out:
It is a survival horror game with a rich story-line and character design throughout the entire game.
The art style fits the dynamic of the game adding to the suspense and fear you feel throughout when playing.
The same goes for the sound design, carefully adding to the suspense and fear without shoving it in your face that you're meant to be scared.
And on the topic of suspense and fear, the game does not bombard you with jump scares to cause fear, the mix of methods to do so adds variety to the game and constantly has you watching your back.
My only negative with this game was the short play time; my first completion took only 7 hours even where I was not rushing the main story and took time to explore the many areas.
However, the extra content unlocked after completing the game through, the selection of difficulties to play and many achievements to unlock, this game has clear replay-abilitiy.
As of writing this review [11/06/2022] the entire RESIDENT EVIL franchise is on sale [until 12/06/2022] so I would definitely recommend picking up this game if not more in the franchise.
Last note, on the point of the franchise, fear not if you have not played RESIDENT EVIL VII before playing this game as the story from the previous game is explained to you to fully immerse you into what is going on.

Make no mistake: the environment isn’t interactive, it’s mostly there to set a majestic mood while leaving just enough visual cues to push you forward. This game is far from clever, and the puzzles are about as hard as they were in the recent remakes. But they’re enough to make some players feel clever, and that’s all you can ask. And the backdrop for these simplistic puzzles almost never gets old to tour. Outside of the village and the castle, the story takes you to the expected tropes of past Resident Evil titles, but plays with your expectations enough to keep it engaging and surprising.

A mercantile system also returns in the very large body of the Duke, who lords over the proceedings with a watchful eye.
After buying one of the many upgrades for your weapons (which persist in future playthroughs), the Duke will cheerfully tell you to “have a wonderful adventure.”

The game is the narrative sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, picking up the story three years on. Ethan and Mia are parents now, trying to live out the wholesome family dream. It doesn’t take long for the action to kick in though as Chris Redfield interrupts the happy family and Ethan finds himself wandering into the terrifying hellscape of the village.

Whilst ‘village’ is the name of the game, you are not confined to this one location. It would be fair to say that the village is just the centre of this complicated and intricate world and the game does guide you in the general direction of the story, but you are also free to explore, and you are rewarded for this exploration.

[b]THE GOOD[/b]
- Open-world Resident Evil works well and is complemented by fun optional content
- Remarkable graphics and sound design create a new immersion benchmark for the series
- Face-twisting horror plot with some seriously sinister sequences

[b]THE BAD[/b]
- The story looks the part but doesn’t explore its most interesting ideas

The gameplay is solid for what it is, an action-adventure with few horror elements here and there.

As a Resident Evil game, however, it is disappointing. The maps are extremely linear, there are hardly any puzzles, basically four where one is such that players have solved it by accident, the second so easy that the game locks you inside the puzzle zone and the answer is in the next room. The third has an error in the writing and the fourth one has the solution on the puzzle itself.

There are hardly any route-planning because of its extremely linear design. You might think that the castle (the first section of the game) is a sprawling area with multiple routes and ways to go but in reality there is only one way to go which loops back to the beginning as you collect all the necessary items on this one set path. The next two areas are entirely linear and the last area, the factory, is perhaps the most sprawling of the four but even it is on the low end of openness what comes to the best RE maps.

As an action game it is fine, it does what it sets out to do but as a shooter it is still quite low on the board. As a horror game it is spooky few times but overall it doesn't have that oppressing Resident Evil atmosphere and due to the abundance of items and carrying capacity it lacks almost entirely the "survival" part of the survival horror. You'll never run out of ammo nor do you really need to conserve it either.

The story is nonsensical and the entire premise hangs on Chris not telling Ethan a few crucial things that he never needed to keep from him, a major flaw in character writing. The writers made Chris Redfield a moron in order to make their story possible which means that the plot of RE:Village is "a stupid plot".

Resident Evil 8 takes what worked in Resident Evil 7 and 4, then combines them into a great and memorable experience. Some people have argued that this game sits on top alongside with Resident Evil 4 and the original Resident Evil 2. I can honestly see that. 

This game is a sequel to Resident Evil 7. What they have done is expanded and offered more in this survival horror game. Instead of being in a house, you're in a village that has a castle, dungeons, cabins, water-plant, and factory. On my first play through, there is good amount of tension throughout the game. 

One of the problems of the last game I had was the lack of diversity in the enemies (besides the baker family). Here, they do bring more different variant of enemies, and some requiring a bit more thought than just blasting them. Even including mini-bosses which is bloody great. 

Horror is done about right in this game. I won't spoil it, but there is one part in the game that will utterly scare you with a certain..."creature". Is it scarier than Resident Evil 2 Remake? It doesn't hit that level on all aspects. If it did, this would be like 10/10.  

This game also explains a few things from the last game and tie up a few loose ends. Remember, this is Capcom story-telling, so don't expect something fantastic in terms of writing or story. But for most of the time, you won't really care. 

After a year from release, There is now VR that you can play (not perfect, but good). Which a lot of people were let down when it was released.  Honestly, it's really hard to think of anything negative about this game. I guess the only bad thing is that in the last 3/4 of the game. It can kinda feel a bit subpar and ridiculous. But to me, I never felt that. But I would understand why some might think that. 

But I think this does stand as one of the top-tier Resident Evil Games.

Resident Evil 8, or Village, is a direct sequel to the previous installment. It continues the story of Ethan Winters following his narrow escape from the Bakers. Three years have passed. Ethan and Mia, now under the protection of Chris, are living a happy married life. Their newborn daughter Rose seems to have sealed this happiness. Despite their deep emotional scars, everything seems quite idyllic. So of course, it can't last. Attacked by their own protector, the family is torn asunder, their fragile happiness destroyed and Rose kidnapped. Ethan finds himself tangled in yet another biowarfare conspiracy and has to fight to protect those he loves.

The setting of the game is drastically different from the previous game. Ethan ends up in some eastern European country, ostensibly Romania, on the outskirts of a seemingly abandoned village. Naturally, the village is not abandoned, but instead infested with lycanthrope-looking bioweapons that have killed or infected all the villagers. If you are thinking Resident Evil 4, you are right on the money. Yes, this is obviously inspired, or perhaps even intended as an homage, to that game. The setting similarities don't stop here. There is also an enormous castle that neighbours the village. The lady of the castle, female, tall with an uncanny beauty, is a clear inversion of the male, short and ugly Salazar. The castellan of Resident Evil 4. There are many more parallels, but I would prefer not to spoil. It is certain though that anyone who has played that game will recognize a lot of it here. Even guess a few sequences. 

And this comes with baggage. I know that Resident Evil 4 is a fan favourite. It is indeed an excellent action game, but it has never been a series favourite of mine. It broke with the classic trilogy, it wasn't a survival horror game, it wasn't exactly scary either. If that doesn't sound much like Resident Evil 7, it's because it's really not. In fact, that game was trying hard to return the series to a more horror and survival direction. Village does a 180. It replaces the intimate with the grand, the slow and deliberate with the fast and bombastic. On occasion it even manages to replace the scary with the disturbing, house Beneviento I'm looking at you. The game is a theme park and it invites you on its overblown, campy rollercoaster of large gothic estates and steampunk factories. Thematically, it is as entertaining, as it is inconsistent. The most notable effect this change had was to my mental state when playing. In 7 I was cowed, in 8 I was impetuous.

As expected, the gameplay puts a greater emphasis on action. You are handed guns generously in this game and there are several to discover. The action sequences are more numerous and involved. The gunplay itself is a lot of fun, shooting all those mooks can feel fairly satisfying. There is also a merchant, another throwback to 4. That merchant, aside from selling some useful stuff, can also upgrade your guns to make them more powerful. Though the required resources to do that can be steep and require multiple playthroughs. Frankly, I found it a bit too grindy. Ammunition can be hard to find on higher difficulties, but only on your first run. After that unlimited ammo becomes available. This effectively eliminates the resource management integral to a survival horror. There is even a cooking minigame of sorts. Scour the countryside for hogs and fish and the merchant will cook some gourmet meals for you. Because I guess that's something you do when fighting for your life?

The main problem here is this, the game seems on one hand to want to adopt a much more action-oriented approach, similar to Resident Evil 4, with unlimited ammo, numerous guns and playthroughs, but on the other hand is unwilling to completely break with the Resident Evil 7 recipe. After all, superficially the two games seem to be very close. As a result, it doesn't go all in on the action. It keeps constantly breaking it up with scripted sequences and forced walks. These may work during the first run, but not the ones after. In other words, the game suffers from an identity crisis. It has good action yes, but too much for a scary game and too little for it to be satisfying on its own merit. It's no wonder that one of my favourite sequences was the one right before the final boss, when the game finally goes all in on the action. For a moment there, it seems focused and it was great.

I would be remiss not to mention the game's excellent technical aspects. The graphics are quite beautiful indeed. The environments, which can be at times open and bright, with enough opulence to go around, are very well made and there is a lot of attention to detail. The characters also look great, particularly Chris, 48 years old and more badass than ever. He is who I wanna be when I finally decide to grow up. Soundwise the game is pretty good too. Though the voice-acting specifically, while decent, did perplex me somewhat. I found it odd how everyone in Romania spoke with an American English accent. It would be less of a problem if they hadn't butchered the pronunciation of Lady Dimitrescu's name. But that was just grating. Overall, the game was very stable. Not a single bug or crash encountered. It was also fairly smooth performance wise, with the exception of one notable sequence in the castle. Kudos to Capcom for all that.

In the end, is it worth it? First, I should note, how highly unusual it is for a game in this series to be a direct sequel of the previous installment. Mainline Resident Evil games had never before had the same protagonist for two installments in a row. Even the esteemed classic trilogy, composed of tightly connected games, didn't. To me, this indicates that Resident Evil 7 struck a chord with the audience and Capcom had faith in that game. Whatever my misgivings with it, Resident Evil 7 was a great game. Why then, if they wanted to follow up on it, did they change the recipe in so many ways? I can't even praise them for daring a new direction, it's just Resident Evil 4 they are mixing in, not entirely successfully either. Be that as it may, Village remains a good game and I certainly enjoyed playing it. It is not as good as the previous installment, it lacks its focus and balance, but it is still a good game.

This is just a great twelve hours of solid entertainment. 
Moving from the Texas Chainsaw vibe of RE7 to a more grand guignol atmosphere replete with werewolves, vampires and frankenstein monsters should have been a disaster but somehow it works and even manages to tie the story back to the original games through some tortuous narrative twists.

The RE engine is also pretty amazing in the detail and frame rate it pumps out on even modest hardware, it looks pretty sumptuous wherever you are. Not sure whether it's just the type of game I've been playing recently but this is another one that has a last level where you effectively can mow down everything in your way - pretty cathartic to gun down all the wolfmen that have been causing problems for you all game, though. 
If you can get it for a discount I highly recommend playing through it for the mental story and sitting back for the ride.

RE8 is by far the biggest departure in the series, but I think this installment is not only the best of resident evil, but one of the greatest survival horror games ever created. 

It retains the immersive first person perspective that was introduced in 7, and then amps up the fantasy aspect to 11. It delivers an incredibly creative and beautiful world with unique characters, environments, and one of the most memorable sequences in the history of horror gaming with house beneviento.

The almost metroidvania-like maps are satisfying to make your way through, with a good blend of action, puzzles, and chases to keep you on the edge of your seat. 

Now, my main critique of this game is similar to other fans of the series in that sometimes it can feel too "action horror" over survival, similar to RE4. The game often puts enemies in your path that you have no choice but to fight, removing the strategy element of fight or flight that's critical to survival horror - It wasn't uncommon for me to have 100+ rounds for my pistol so there was rarely a reason NOT to fight and replenish by scavenging.

But the minor downsides are easily forgotten with how immersive and satisfying this is. It's a nearly perfect game and has taken a spot in my top 10 all time favorites.

Arguably the gameplay itself is nothing to write home about, you have a gun, 'pew pew pew', things die. If you played the prequel you would be very welcome to the controls of this game. There's only one negative I can think of that this gameplay would have, and that would be in relation to the first boss; !FIRST BOSS SPOILER WARNING! -> [spoiler] After a lot of hype from fans, it felt a little underwhelming when the Dimitrescu fight consisted of literally running around in circles and looking behind you to shoot her face. Broken by her periodically flying around for a bit. [/spoiler].

There's one point that I felt only after finishing my first run of the game, and that's the flow of the bosses ([b]Possibly major spoilers here so if you haven't played yet you might want to skip this paragraph[/b]. I don't want to have a big black box in the review which is why it's open :) ). The Lady Dimitrescu fight and the area itself is quite fast paced and action packed, there's very rarely a moment where you'll feel at ease in the castle. My issue is this, after that, you have two areas that are quite slow, then another action packed zone, this seems a bit awkward for me. Having a rest from the action in a game is essential, having constant action can be draining and bothersome, but having two whole zones that are largely (I say largely because the second slow zone I'm talking about has quite an action filled boss fight at the end, compared to House Beneviento where the boss fight, while making the player feel anxious, is a game of hide and seek that didn't pick up for the rest of the middle of the game) slow almost felt like a drudge to go through. Obviously I'm no professional and for all I know I might be the only person feeling like the flow is a bit slow in the middle, but why not make the breaks between bosses longer and let [b]those[/b] areas be slow and let all the bosses be more action packed? It felt quite awkward going into the Heisenberg's Factory where there was quite a lot of enemies to kill before making Heisenberg go bang! Though after Heisenberg's Factory, the pacing for the rest of the game feels very fluid.

Other than that previous point, having the gameplay be what it is, will not take you out of your gaming experience at all. The game lets you know to be conservative with your resources very early in the game, which sets the precedence for the rest of the game quite well.

For the non-spoiler explanation I will say this; You won't be disappointed by the games ending, it might not be a completely satisfying ending, but for me it's one of those endings where I didn't leave saying "What the hell?". For the spoiler explanation; [spoiler] Having Ethan's story come to an end I feel is a very bold move, the player base I feel has come to love Ethan and has gone through a lot with him. The saying goes "Don't fix what isn't broken", and while Ethan has been broken in a multitude of different ways in this game, he didn't need fixing. The assumption I feel is that we'll be playing as his daughter in the next game (If this story continues of course), which I have no doubt will be just as fun and interesting as the rest of the RE series. [/spoiler]


         [h1]Conclusion[/h1] 

[b] Rating [/b]:  8/10

The points in rating that were lost is largely due to my nitpicking, and will not guaranteed be things that you will experience in your journey. I wholeheartedly recommend this to anyone who needs a game to play and has some money to spend, it's very easy to get gripped into this game and I highly doubt you'll be disappointed with your purchase.

Resident Evil Village released exactly a year ago, but I wasn’t sure if my old PC would be able to run the game properly, so I decided to wait until I’d upgraded. Now that I’ve finally been able to play it, I can say that it does mostly live up to the hype. This is an excellent game which deserves all the positive reviews and awards.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

-	Feels like a survival horror game. Every enemy is dangerous, and your ammo and health recovery items are limited. Sometimes its better to just avoid enemies and save bullets.

-	Several different weapons that all feel good to use, including dagger, pistol, shotgun, sniper rifle, magnum, proximity mine and pipe bomb.

-	Good enemy variety including werewolves, vampires, flying demons, zombies, and unique boss monsters. Werewolves and zombies can wield weapons such as sword, axe, and bow.

-	Some enemies can be weakened by using environmental effects, or shooting them in a specific weak point.

-	Find hidden treasures which can be sold to a trader, allowing you to buy upgrades for your weapons.

-	Story is better than most Resident Evil games, although that’s not a high bar.

-	Voice acting is very good.

-	Controls are fully rebindable and work great on mouse and keyboard.

-	Took me 13 hours to finish.

-	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]

-	First two hours feel very scripted as you frequently get captured in cutscenes, escape, run down narrow tunnels/corridors, and repeat the cycle.

[h1]The Recommendation[/h1]

Anybody who hasn’t played Resident Evil Village yet should definitely do so when you get the chance. The story is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, so make sure you’ve played that game first.

Imagine you are going on the price is right. There’s nothing wrong with that, right? You have a chance to win some money, a car, a clock radio, mustard that for some reason costs $3 more than it does at your local store, a wardrobe you don’t need, speakers, and a vacation.

But [strike]something[/strike] many things aren’t quite right. Your wife is a soup nazi, you won an all-expenses-paid-trip to Romania (before the show even started) that lasts indefinitely, the models are dipteran, Drew Carey won’t shut the hell up about “family”, and you’re overwhelmed with fear and paranoia when your name is announced. 

Even the games are all wrong. Line ‘em Up results in a heart attack. Plinko has been replaced by Tim Burton's Marble Madness. Take Two makes a baby. Clock Game sounds like Christmas in Hell. Suddenly, it’s time to give the Big Wheel a spin. What’s that? It ripped your prosthetic hand off and now the wheel is jammed? Give us your bid in the Showcase Showdown. What’s that? You don’t want to travel to a castle, manor, mine, goopy pirateland, futuristic factory, or learn about the esoteric history of pharmaceutical companies? Well, it sounds like someone needs to spend their next 60 hours of free-time learning about parenthood and how a being can both predecease and postdecease, and transmigrate.

[b][u]The Good[/u][/b]:
[list]
[*]While the game is more on the action-y side, they haven’t forgotten about the horror elements. It also doesn’t rely on jumpscares.
[*]Do you like weapon variety? There’s more of it this time around.
[*]More enemy variety compared to [b]VII[/b].
[*]The game looks great and has a lot of detail, but interaction with that world is limited.
[*]Remember treasures? There are treasures, and the game tells you when they’re combinable with a piece you do not have yet.
[*]The different areas in this game have differing atmospheres and I think they all work great. There’s one area that has no music, minimal sound effects, and no action, and it manages to have such an unnerving atmosphere that it makes people cry.
[*]Color-coded map helps you collect everything without [i]too[/i] much hand-holding.
[*]The climax.
[*]All the voice acting is great.
[*]Winter time 24/7.
[/list]

[b][u]The Neutral[/u][/b]:
[list]
[*]20 weapons: 3 melee, 5 handguns, 3 shotguns, 2 assault rifles, 1 sniper rifle, 3 magnums, 1 grenade launcher, 1 rocket pistol, and 1 target locator (drone strikes). There is also a handful of throwy booms: flashes, mines, grenades, and pipe bombs.
[*]The game is divided into several parts: Law Abiding Citizen, alternate-reality-Frankenstein-where-the-villagers-are-werewolves, gender-swap Dracula, Silent Hill, Jaws goes to Water World, Terminator goes to Doom 3, and Hellboy.
[*]The game’s soundtrack is largely dark ambient tracks, but there are a few that stand out, such as the one in the trailer.
[*]I think that Moreau’s section is the weakest. While it isn’t bad, I think they could have done more with the character.
[/list]

[b][u]The Bad[/u][/b]:
[list]
[*]Not much in the way of puzzles. While [b]VII[/b] wasn’t exactly a brain-melter, it had some interesting puzzles (Happy Birthday), and a DLC that was essentially an escape room. The second house in the game is more puzzle-oriented, but I wish it had been more challenging.
[*]A remote village in Romania features residents who speak perfect English with American accents.
[*]I feel like they went a bit overboard with the effects on Moreau’s voice. Let the actor come through more.
[*]There’s a room in the castle the needs better optimization. You’ll know when you find it.
[/list]

[b][u]Pro Tips[/u][/b]:
[list]
[*]Don’t sell meats until you know they are no longer needed for recipes which permanently boost stats.
[*]Combine treasures when possible to earn more money from selling them.
[*]I would advise against cranking up the image scaling. It tends to desync the audio and I’m not the only one experiencing that.
[*]Don’t think that you’re going to ace all the Mercenaries levels on the first try. Learn where everything is going to spawn and how to chain it all together. It’s also not as difficult as people make it out to be, but even if you have a rough time, it’s worth it for the double lightsaber.
[*]There’s a post-credits scene.
[/list]

Is [b]Village[/b] worth it? To me it is. On my first playthrough, I thought that replaying it would be annoying after I got to the second area (escape room), but I blazed through it on subsequent playthroughs and it never really got old. I like the gameplay, detail, characters, environments, and the atmosphere. It would be nice if they had tightened up a few aspects of the story that may not make complete sense, or given the Reservoir better treatment (content was cut and a castle rework became the focus), but these in no way ruin the experience. After getting 100% in the game, I still want more.

There is no FOV slider and the default FOV is low enough to induce nausea, so I had to refund. I can't tell if vsync was bugged or what, but the image felt unpleasantly jittery too. This just made the nausea worse. People said this game was a hybrid between RE4 and RE7, but I wasn't expecting RE7 with RE4's FOV. An FOV slider should be a basic accessibility feature nowadays, especially for a big-budget game, so I have no qualms leaving a negative review for this.

Judging by the rest of the reviews the game itself is probably awesome. You may want to play it with a controller on your TV if you have one, though.
