Won't spoil it, but the story is not great. Character development is extremely and disappointingly minimal.

Gameplay is heavily combat oriented with Ethan running around shooting and stabbing in first person. Which could have been awesome, but instead falls short, particularly if compared with RE4. There are no critical head shots that insta-kill enemies. Instead, it is very clear you are just running down health bars, which is plainly shown in mercenaries. There are also no cool melee attacks to punish staggered enemies. Nope, just pew pew and stab stab. The weapon selection is also pretty dismal. You have your standard weapons, and even upgrades, but nothing really stands out. Unlike RE4, the next gun you get is always going to be better than the last, no special upgrades to make each awesome in it's own right. Honestly, I also felt like the sniper rifle was there just because RE4 had them. There really didn't feel like there was much point to it.

Maps. Wow, 99% of maps are just tight corridor mazes. That's pretty much it. Even boss rooms tend to be very confined. That, again, really limited options for combat. RE4 had so many great places to fight, that if used well, the environment itself could be a powerful ally. Not so much in village. Even the village is mostly just tight corridor mazes with snorlax tractors and such forcing a lot of needless backtracking.

Enemies were also pretty limited in design compared to earlier games and many didn't feel like they made much sense. So much of the game felt like it was cobbled together with random ideas that just sounded cool but didn't really mesh well together. This, along with the non-stellar story, made everything feel very ephemeral. Bosses just showed up, and were just as soon disposed of. They didn't really have a purpose in the world outside of getting in your way.

The game did play well enough to see to the end, but I continue to stand by RE4 being a superior title in nearly all respects.

A better mission description to the player should be "Run away from the werewolves for 4-5 minutes".  That at least explains what to do.

Fantastic game. At least a 9/10. Mechanics wise, Village builds upon everything great from Biohazard, as well as some of the best aspects of the Resident Evil II remake. Story wise, Village continues the tradition of expanding upon the overarching story of Resident Evil, while introducing new bio-weapons that take the franchise into new Gothic inspired territory. Resident Evil Village is a near perfect end (supposedly) to Ethan Winter's story. The one and only complaint I have, the one and only thing I can't get over, is the decision to finish Ethan's story without showing us his face. I can't fathom how they came to the decision to kill Ethan off, to have this story end with him sacrificing himself to save his family, only to continually tease the player in the final cutscene, and not finally reveal what Ethan actually looks like. It would've been the perfect way to send the character off. I feel as though by not giving the player that glimpse before ending the story, the game's writers seem to be implying that Ethan  isn't as integral a part of the Resident Evil story as characters whom we do get to see in full, such as Chris or Leon. Indeed, not showing his face before he died just cheapens his entire story arc to me. Other than this one major flaw, I did thoroughly enjoy Resident Evil Village, and I would definitely recommend it (but you should of course at least play Resident Evil Biohazard first).

Honestly, probably the 2nd best Resident Evil right behind 4. It has all the cheese we know and love from the RE series and some great gameplay that's superior to 7. By that, I mostly mean enemy variety and weapon options have been improved. No longer do you fight goop monster, crawly goop monster, fat goop monster, or bugs. Bosses included Mia, Jack, Marguerite, and I guess Eveline is a boss. Oh, and there are technically boss fights against fat goop monsters.

 Instead, you fight the agile, quick lycans, which can be armored and wield weapons, slow moving Moroaica, flying Samca, and the strong Soldats, which have like four variants. For bosses, we have three vampire sisters, a vampire dommy mommy, a creepy puppet, a fat fish boy, a jet engine with legs, a giant mesh of mech and flesh, and a big crow lady. There's also multiple giant lycans, some on all fours being agile and beastial, and others being on hind legs using massive weapons. All of this combined allows for some unique experiences in combat and makes it so much more refreshing than Re7, and highly replayable.

And weapons. Re7 has the G17, M19, and MPM handguns, M21 and M37 Shotguns, the Burner, the P19 Machine Gun, the Grenade Launcher, and the 44-Mag1. Not including DLC, explosives, unlockables, or melee, simply nine weapons. For unlockables, we get... Circular Saw and Albert-1. Including Melee(minus ones you are forced to drop) and explosives, but no DLC, 13. Now with DLC, we do get new weapons, but ONLY in the DLC. For Joe, 3 gauntlets, spears, throwing knives, and stake bombs. For Chris, 3 grenades, one knife, and one shotgun.

Now in Re8, which currently has one DLC weapon, has the LEMI, m1911, and V61 Custom Handguns, M1897, W870 TAC, and SYG-12 shotguns, F2 Sniper Rifle, M1851 Wolfsbane, and S.T.A.K.E magnums, and the GM79 grenade launcher. Not including melee or unlockables, only 10, but a sniper rifle being added is a nice improvement. Now, for unlockables, we get... USM-A1 and Rocket Pistol Handguns, WCX and Dragoon Assault Rifles, Handcannon PZ Magnum, Karambit Knife, and the LZ Answerer. An extra 7 weapons from unlocks compared to Re7's meager 2. Granted, the USM-A1, Karambit, and Dragoon is in Chris's loadout, but that's still 4 unlockable weapons.

Story is... pretty poor, to be honest. Not the best, not the worst either (RE6); however, a lot of the cheesiness is back in the game. Village is to RE7 as RE4 was to Code Veronica. Although, Resident Evil didn't really change a whole lot between 2 and Code Veronica other than adding minor game mechanics  or different graphics. 

Capcom was able to "reinvent the wheel" by translating a traditional RE game into first person with RE7, so naturally Village had to change as many things as possible at once while trying to maintain the same experience. It's still a good game but doesn't feel quite as memorable and often feels like multiple different games combined - not as bad as Resident Evil 6, but not as focused as previous titles. Village certainly lacks any of the subterranean low points of RE6 like an entire level of snowmobiles or HummVee chases or the discombobulated experiences of sneaking around to avoid a knock off Nemesis. In fact, there are really only two gameplay tropes in this title: Run away, or kill all the things. 

Similar to RE4, you can upgrade your equipment and weapons at a merchant and even buy ammo. You'll need it, because you'll be gunning down literally the entire village by the time the game is over. You can also gather resources from animals throughout the map that you can turn in to the Duke - the merchant - in order to craft food items which permanently increase your stats. The story and environment also clearly were meant to evoke memories of RE4 whether it's the creepy European village and castle or the general world design. Almost everything is dark, jagged, and muddy. 

The quasi open world structure of RE7 returns but instead of just one big plantation farm, you now have free reign of an entire "European" village and outside of a few scripted sequences in the game. you can go anywhere in the village at any time, even if there's no reason to. It's loaded with secret rooms and treasure chests that contain unique items or weapons, too, as well as some "secret" bosses. 

All in all, Village is a good game with some decent replay value thanks to challenges and Mercenaries mode, but it doesn't stand out with its own character compared to other titles in the series. The most memorable gameplay sequence in the whole game is the least traditional and would have been more at home in Silent Hill or Evil Within, but it's a strong entry in the series that shows Capcom still knows what they're doing.

What happens when you mix Resident Evil 7 and 4? You get Village. This can be RE 8's both boon and bane, as this solves many issues players have taken with RE 7 like enemy and environmental variety, but replaces them with a new set of problems like toning down the horror aspect of it (which was unfortunately intentional) and pacing. 

Wold I call RE 8 better than its predecessor? Not exactly. It is not better, it is just different which is what makes it fun to come back to but was not able to capture me in a way RE 7 did, mainly because in that game, Capcom knew exactly what they were going for - a concentrated experience akin to original Resident Evil but with that modern polish and flaire. Village, on the other hand, wanted to be more like 4 with action-packed sequences being far more common than in 7, with occasional witted catchphrases and with horror elements being sprinkled in rather little and I simply can not get rid of that nagging feeling that RE 4 has managed to wed these aspects in much more competent and meaningful manner. This absolutely does not mean that Village is not a high-quality game (because it is), but when I compare 7 and it, 7 comes on top, mainly because of its brilliant execution and I hope that Capcom goes back to that style of game-making in RE's next iteration.

[b] [i] Positives [/i] [/b]

+ Immersive atmosphere (although not to the degree of 7, at least not after roughly first 2-3 hours)

+ Main story line does not dissapoint

+ Well written characters (apart from a few that seem to have a strange motivation - hello [spoiler] Chris and Elena[/spoiler])

+ Gameplay improvements that are basically everything we wanted from RE 7's sequel - better weapon variety, actual bartering system and weapon feedback improvements

+ Much needed enemy variety added - this has been mine and most of the RE 7 's player base's biggest gripe with the game - where you have seen exclusively molded of 3 types occasionally spiced with an encounter with a family member as a boss, here you have many different types of enemies corresponding to the area they are located in. Bosses have been made more interesting too.

+ Eerie, well-fitting soundtrack

+ Voice acting and mo-cap is, once again, top notch

+ Amazing and detailed level design

+ Legth of about 12-15 hours

+ Replayability

+ Stellar performance - Capcom really knows how to optimize a game

[b] [i] Negatives [/i] [/b]

- Horror has been toned down since 7 in favor of action, which is a great shame as this was one of the best aspects of 7

- Certain technical decisions that do not make sense - why did they not allow your crosshair to automatically disappear when sprinting, just as it was in 7?

- Certain nonsensical moments in story that are just there to justify some forced story twists

Village, for me, is easily the best game in the modern series. It has a few bugs and glitches that can be slightly annoying, but on the whole this is a very posloshed, atmospheric action horror game that nails modern Resident Evil. 

I say modern, because since Resident Evil 4, the series has struggled with it's identity. Whether it was an action game or a horror game was a constant see-saw act. 

Village strikes the perfect balance of atmosphere and tension, while throwing plenty of action at you, but never allowing you to have enough ammo and resources to feel safe. Even if you find yourself with a lot of ammo, get ready for an incoming hoarde. 

Having the Village as a hub also brings a fresh Metroodvania-esque feeling to the game. Different parts of the village become open throughout the game, giving you access to more resources and weapons and items. 

Replayability is also pretty huge. Mercenaries mode is unlocked after your initial playthrough, alongside the bonus shop that gives you points for each achievement. These points can unlock powerful weapons, character models, infinite ammo for certain weapons you've upgraded and more.

From what I've played so far Resident Evil Village Is a very fun game. It's got a decent story, likeable enough characters, captivating game play, good ambience, enjoyable jump scares, solid puzzles and absolutely beautiful environments. It's been nothing but a pleasure to play through the first quarter of the game.

My favourite thing about the game however is it's revolutionary game mechanics. One day I had just completed the castle Dimitrescu and woke up the next day looking forward to visiting the house with the red chimney (oooo spooky). I booted up the game and what happens? The application completely forgets that I've ever played the game before and my saves are gone. The saves still exist in the game files, but for some reason the application refuses to acknowledge them. 

The game has been out for 11 months and this has been happening since release so obviously this was an intentional game mechanic. It's actually genius, not only does it allow me to go over the story again so I remember what's happening but it also give's me the chance to correct my errors before proceeding with the story. This is EXACTLY what I want out of a game based around progressing through a story, It's like when you're reading a book but you lose the book mark and can't remember what page you were up to. You start at the beginning and quickly scan through the pages you've already read until you get back to where you were. Being able to translate that feeling into a video game format is the sort of artistic genius that rivals the likes of Vincent Van Gogh. 

Watch and learn game developers, this is the future of single player games.

Resident Evil 8 manages to be a beautiful, visual masterpiece, while including overwhelmingly campy writing. With these factors in mind, it personally sorted itself out for me as a horror/comedy in its story. Take that as you will; personally I loved. 

   However, one thing that I must stress to my very core is the very real passion, love, and care that went into crafting this game. It may not have enough horror, depending on your taste, and some people may dislike the heavy emphasis on the action aspect of the game.

   But as continue to play through the game, you'll realize the delicate structuring of every detail that was put into this piece of art. Every area within this game is so stupidly detailed with the new RE engine, and it can't be praised enough for it's style. And, personally, I think its cheesy writing makes a hilariously bad/good story. 

   Could it have done better in some spots, definitely, but when you compare this game to overwhelming amount of cash grabs out there, you'll learn to cherish this fun and replayable experience!

   I should also mention that I played this game on a Dell Inspiron laptop with integrated graphics and a Ryzen 7, and it still looked visually stunning (with 60 fps in closed, indoor areas, and slightly dipping in outdoor areas). This really speaks about Capcom's desire to optimize this game as much as they could for their audience, and I think that should be well known.

Great game, but overall has a lot of wasted potential in my opinion that other entries in the series do better. It's a great hodge podge of the past Resident Evil games that shows everything they've learned about making the series, but it doesn't shine on it's own in much.

Resident Evil 2 does "unkillable" boss chasing through level better
Resident Evil 4 does action-horror better
Resident Evil 7 does horror better

Even if you ignore the horny, the only thing Resident Evil 8 does better than these games is the fact that Lady Dimitrescu is genuinely a very good character, but she's so wasted in this game.

General preception of this game is very misleading on this front, but Lady D is only in the first hour or so of the game, maybe 2 if you're slow. She's a great character with a larger than life personality, pun very much intended, but she's barely in the game compared to the rest of the content given.
There's actually 5 major bosses to fight through in this game and the fact that everybody only knows 1 of them should really show how impactful they were in the story. I'd say the first 2 boss areas are the best the game has to offer as they show Resident Evil at it's best and how far it's grown.

Overall gameplay is much like Resident Evil 4, you have inventory you have to organize through and you can spend money to buy, upgrade, and sell equipment. The game emphasizes the Action part of the Action-Horror genre and with the exception of one part, the game isn't too scary.

Lady D's castle is like Resident Evil 2, a decent sized place to explore with collectibles and an everpresent threat hunting you down the major areas of the location. It's very enjoyable on the first few playthroughs, but I honestly just wish it were bigger and Lady D was allowed to chase you in more areas. Once you know where you're safe and not, it's honestly pretty easy to avoid her.
The second Boss area is much like Resident Evil 7, lots of genuine horror and throughout my 3 playthroughs of the game I dread it every time. Like the castle, I wish it was longer but I think it did what it did well for the amount of time it was there.

Major Bosses 3 - 5 range from either "Okay" - "Awful", the gameplay is still solid in these parts but you'll be longing for the time you spent in Lady D's castle.



It's a good game, overall great value for the money I spent. It runs extremely well and as a Resident Evil vet, I've enjoyed the time I've gotten out of it, but every time I got out of a good area I just wanted more that the game couldn't give.

If you like what you saw in this game, chances are previous games have done it better.

Did you like Resident Evil 7? Village is a lot like 7, but with more enemy variety, more weapons to play with, more of a post-game (not counting DLC, haven't played 7's and 8 doesn't have any yet), but the story is a significant stumbling block. 

My first playthrough was on the normal difficulty, and for the most part it felt like the game would build up my supply of ammo and weapons only to exhaust them during enemy and boss encounters. Guns can be upgraded, with new ones showing up later on in the game with higher base stats, but enemies seem to scale as the game goes along so it doesn't ever feel like I'm ever at a great advantage against the monsters in this game. On NG+ it's possible to spend a special currency to unlock new weapons and unlimilted ammo for the weapons you've fully upgraded, so it's fun to build towards that. Even with unlimited ammo and a fully upgraded magnum, shotgun, etc the bosses on normal seem to really soak up damage without much of a reaction. I haven't looked too deeply into the modding scene for Village, but I would have really liked to have modded in HP counters and enemy health bars into the story, if only to see exactly how effective my weapons actually are at damaging enemies. HP counters and health bars are used in the Mercenaries mode, and they were really helpful for me when I tried that out. 

The story is dumb. Ethan is an idiot, and I hate his one-liners. What I liked about 7 was how it presented itself as a reboot, but 8 clumsily tries to tie itself into the greater Resident Evil series using the awful, "I was behind it all, all along" trope that you might remember from the film Specter: Mother Miranda (the big-bad of Village), the mold, the source of the mold; they're revealed to have been instrumental in the formation of Umbrella and the development of the various viruses developed by Umbrella. A good chunk of the plot, if not the whole thing, could have been carried out by Chris. In fact a lot of the drama could have been side-stepped if Chris has explained everything right at the beginning after that scene you probably remember from the trailer, but instead it seems like every time Chris shows up he delivers dubious lines in a villainous tone for no good reason.

I already said this but I'll say it again, but differently: Resident Evil Village is Resident Evil 7-2. It's bigger, there's more to collect, more enemy variety, more environmental variety, and more to do post-game. It might be more satisfying to play on NG+ but that first time through is also really solid. I'm really cynical about the plot and many of the characters, but the moment to moment gameplay is why I'm recommending this one.

I'm a fan of RE as it is, but I really enjoyed how this game was quite different from the others, yet still managed to pull in elements from the older games to morph it together into this one. It was scary and horrific, and somehow managed to be gorgeous at the same time. These are some notes I have for it:
1. Grotesquely beautiful game art that sometimes I just had to stop and stare in wonder at
2. Confining, tight (well-designed) map layouts that are perfect for building up tension
3. Stunning monsters and villain designs with compelling boss fights
4. The casual level is just difficult enough for, well, casual gamers (me) to enjoy the story and design without ripping out their hair. Although sometimes it felt a little too easy (just toss some mines down and gg)
5. Story was weird, but that is pretty standard for RE. Still manages to be interesting, though!
6. Only main "negative" thing is there are some areas where there are massive frame drops even on my high end pc, I think these areas are bugged out (such as armory in castle). But these drops didn't strongly impact my gameplay or enjoyment of the game.

Despite it's name this is no small Village and you can expect hours of gameplay in a large open world with unique settings for each.

While I skipped Resident Evil 7 (due to my prior GPU being under recommended specs) I was happy to see that the story is largely separated from Village's prequel and didn't find myself lost thanks to a brief optional synopsis that Village provides on the main menu.  Aside from the aforementioned gorgeous environments I found myself thoroughly enjoying the voice cast, especially the variety and unique personalities of each iconic enemy.  There's also plenty of weapons to use and I found that ammo was fairly limited but balanced on hardcore mode as-is synonymous with the games in this series I've played.  Lastly there's a fair amount of bonus content you can experience after finishing the main game like an arcade score attack, new powerful weapons (with infinite ammo unlocks), purchasable concept art, and a model viewer.

I had a lot of fun playing but wished there was a way to increase your Field of View.  I imagine this was an intentional design choice to tighten the combat and suspenseful sections by making the player claustrophobic but this oftentimes made it more difficult to enjoy the scenery and ultimately made combat a bit clunkier than what I'm used to.  I also found the first Lycan fight to be unreasonably challenging.  It happens at the beginning of the game, and you're only given two weapons, starting this game on hardcore meant I needed to deplete all of my ammo just to survive.  

In addition the soundtrack was serviceable but largely forgettable due to it's focus on ambiance over catchy melodies.  Finally [b][i]and I'm also going to probably be one of the only people to say this[/i][/b] but I longed for the Beneviento chapter to be a bit longer in retrospect.  Navigating my way around Village's scariest enemy was one of the best highlights this game had to offer in my experience.  

Overall a great time and after enjoying more of the post-game I look forward to playing the DLC when it's ready!

A fine entry in the series.

It doesn't leave as strong an impression as other recent darlings--namely, RE7 and RE2 '19. The novelty of 7's first-person take has kind of worn off, and there's nothing in here as compactly intricate as RE2's puzzle-box police station. But, it's got everything else an RE fan should expect: lofty production values, slow, deliberate combat, meticulous bullet rationing, and laughably bad writing.

The emphasis on exploration feels lighter here, and long segments are pretty on-rails. Almost every time you get a key, you already know where the door is. The body horror moments now come so frequently that they kind of read like gruesome jokes. The maguffin-guarding area lords have decently cool designs, but other than that big vampire lady, you get the sense that you've seen them all before (they are--no spoilers--Chucky, yet another giant fish, and Magneto). And none have anything to do with the narrative, of course. But what did you expect? RE has never tried to hide that it's just a video game.

For a triple-A series that has reinvented itself so successfully and frequently, an entry like RE8 is always going to feel a little disappointing. But, some of the zombies have jet boosters and drill arms, and that's pretty cool.

This is a good game. It combines RE7 style gameplay with more combat and a snowy village and castle environment. I got it for 29 Euros which is a fair price. I think 59 Euros is too much though. Here are the pros and cons:

Pro:
- excellent sometimes even stunning graphics and good sound
- original and creative environments (village, castle)
- interesting and unqiue characters
- good fighting mechanics
- there is a fun mercenary mode
- RE4 style inventory and merchant
- entertaining boss fights
- interesting puzzles
- refreshing Chris game-play towards the end similar to RE7
- unlockable bonus features like weapons and content

Neutral: 
- the game tries to be scary visually but the fact that killing enemies gives you valuable items makes you the hunter rather than the hunted. Meeting enemies feels more like "how do I kill them effectively" and not "how do I survive this". The hero does suffer pain but feels invinvible nonetheless which also takes away some of the scariness. 
- red explosive barrels (I personally dont like them in survival horror games because they cause a game-ish atmosphere)
- Standard difficulty might be too easy for you if you are good at shooting. Try hard mode right away.

Con:
- The game introduces new characters just to kill them off within seconds or minutes which is a bad story telling style. You dont care about them enough at this point which makes it feel like an unnecessary and cheap effect. 
- Towards the end of the game the style changes very much to a typical game-ish feel. It adds unrealistically huge levels that dont fit the style of the previous chapters. Like that one bad guy who lives in a village has a factory that is so huge that a million people should be working there. 
- The game breaks with the style so much at one point you think it is Battle Field. It was fun to play but imagine sitting in a flying tank with machine gun and tank cannon shooting on a gigantic Transformer-like monster. Yeah, that happens. 
- Many scenes where characters interact - mostly in the later parts of the game - seem so awkward, especially with Chris. 
- The ending is way over the top in scale. It comes out of nowhere and wasnt necessary.

Overall I give this game an 8 score. If it was just for the first half of the game I would have rated it higher but because it breaks with the style so much I had to substract some points. I'd say first half is 9.5 and second half is 6.5.

RE8 was absolutely refreshing. It’s a confidently-designed narrative-focused survival horror game that’s paced within an ideal playtime and is brimming with triple-A polish. 

RE8 offers outstanding situational variety. Unless you want to do a little backtracking, the path forward is always ready to offer you a novel encounter or new gameplay iteration. There was never a point where I didn’t know where to go and I always had an ominous interest in where I was going next. Most puzzles are hardly deserving of the term, but levels are routed cleverly and make the door-and-key structure here quite remarkable.

The story of RE8 is a mix of wild characters, action/horror tropes, and nonsensical sequences that are a thrill to both experience and nitpick. While I didn’t consider myself invested in the content of the narrative, I was still excited to see what was around the next corner. Plenty of it is unintentionally humorous, yet the grander sense of what’s at stake for Ethan always felt real.

Most of the tension throughout the game comes from careful resource management and a heightened awareness of your surroundings. RE8 has an expertly crafted feeling of uncertainty that unfolds as you barely scrape by in a struggle where every bullet counts. To me, it’s one of the most compelling formats for using gameplay to get the player immersed in their surroundings. Moreover, this premise finds its way into loads of other prestigious games that aren't strictly labeled as horror despite how they induce enticing anxiety. As opposed to this delightful form of fear, I also find that running and hiding in anticipation of a jump-scare is more stressful and repetitive than it is engaging, which is why I’m thankful that there’s only one short chapter where RE8 turns into something more akin to Amnesia.

As the plot moves forwards, RE8 gets pretty gung-ho. Including more action makes sense in the context of building to a story’s climax and the game’s overall polish doesn’t leave, but I couldn’t help but miss the subtlety and vulnerability of the game’s earlier portions. Those portions were merely [i]punctuated[/i] by bombastic action instead of completely saturated with it. Here’s hoping this trilogy doesn’t conclude in the same manner as the original Resident Evil games whose final entries devolved into tactless violence.

In terms of software, Capcom’s RE Engine continues to impress. The game never crashed and I never encountered anything I’d classify as a bug. While there was some trouble with pop-in, antialiasing, and getting textures to load quickly, the performance was so solid and the visual composition so impressive that I didn’t feel the need to tweak any of the elaborate settings. With the quick addition of a mod to increase the FOV, rarely did the software-side of the game interrupt the deep, dread-filled immersion of exploring RE8. (I seriously recommend the FOV mod, you can find it with a quick google).

Simply put, RE8 looks gorgeous. There is an excessive amount of detail put into everything from ornate dinner plates to rotting wooden shacks. I feel a little rude for occasionally jogging past views and interiors that must’ve taken countless hours to create. Gunplay may be generally simplistic, but the world in which the methodical exploration takes place is excellently composed.

As more multiplayer games tirelessly compete for player retention while well-advertised single-player releases provide exhausting adventures, I was thrilled to have the chance to play a densely-packed and competent survival horror game with the confidence to tell its story and move on.

AN AMAZING EXPERIENCE

Played in 2022 on Normal difficulty. 
i5-11400, 16GB DDR4 RAM, GTX-1660 6gb
Played in 1080p with all settings on High to Ultra

>>>>> Graphics 10/10 <<<<<
The RE:Engine is a sight to see in action.  The visuals are crisp and immersive.  The character models look fantastic across the board as well.  There was absolutely no unsightly texture pop-in, stuttering, or clipping to be seen throughout the game.    At 1080p with all settings to high or ultra, I was able to get a solid 60fps.  Since the action can get hectic in many places, a good framerate is essential.  Nothing bad to report here; it is a feast for the eyes. 

>>>>> Characters / Setting / Story 10/10 <<<<<
You are yet again playing as Ethan Winters, the man who has little luck keeping ahold of his family and could really use a hand (pun intended). This time we are trust into The Villiage, an eastern-European (possibly Romanian?) location. The rural township and Gothic architecture is a far cry from our last outing in Dulvey, Louisiana.  You are pitted against a series of enemies, each with their own .... shall we say "style" .... of getting in our way.   The trailer did little to spoil past the first few areas so i will not do so here. Much like RE7, The story is very personal.  You get to know these characters very well and even many of the villains ooze charisma.  No spoilers here, but our favorite ex-STARS, ex-BSAA agent Chris Redfield plays a pivotal role.  

>>>>> Music / Sound  10/10 <<<<<
The ambient soundtrack is quite creepy, but the environmental sounds are the showcase.  I would recommend playing with headphones on for the full experience.  Every distant shuffle, scratch, and creak could be an enemy lying in wait. Or it could be nothing but the game keeping you on edge.  I found it to be very effective in any case.  The various boss music is quite good, giving an adequate feeling of tension.  The voice acting is excellent as well.  Kudos to the voice director and actors. The lines felt effectively delivered and not as though they are just reading off a page.   

>>>>> Gameplay 8/10 <<<<<
So did you enjoy RE7 but felt that it would have benefited from more combat with non-boss enemies? Well, RE8 has you covered.  The enemies are varied and some must be attacked in specific ways for your weapons to be effective.  Learning to balance which weapon to use in which situation in which circumstance is the name of the game.  I played on normal difficulty which I felt was a fair challenge.  On Hard or (God save you) Village of Shadows difficulty, you better get ready to run because you will get ripped apart if you don't keep moving.  Ok, so the reason I docked two points.  For some reason, I do not like the running animation in RE7 or RE8. It feels like I am doing a speed walk instead of running for my life.  Also, I found some of the guns to be a bit sluggish to aim and when split seconds matter, that isn't a good thing. 

>>>>> Funfactor and Bugs 10/10 <<<<<
I completed the main quest in around 13 hours.  This may not seem like a long time, but that 13 hours was chocked full of creepy locations, scary enemies, and a story that kept me guessing.  I have played RE since the original released on the PS1 and I can tell you that the franchise has found it's best entry since the fan-favorite RE4.  This is a direct sequel to RE7 in both story and game mechanics, so I would recommend playing RE7 first. For those new to the franchise, there is no need to play the older games to understand what is going on.  However, there are quite a few references and easter eggs for the long-time fans.  (One of the characters makes reference to Chris as a boulder-puncher haha)  Over the playtime, I experiences no bugs, glitches, or crashes to desktop.    

>>>>> Bottom Line 48/50 (96%) <<<<<
If you are a long time fan like more or new to the RE universe, you owe it to yourself to play this game.  It is a really fun ride that is worth the price for admission. With the Mercenaries Mode returning along with unlockables and a NG+, there is a lot of content to keep you entertained.

I can almost pinpoint exactly the moment Resident Evil Village changes from a horror game, to an action game [spoiler] (it's after killing the second Lord, Donna Beneviento) [/spoiler]. For me, this isn't a bad thing as I enjoyed both aspects greatly, it just seems a little funny looking back remembering how initially I was scared of every corner while by the end of my 8 hour play through I was sprinting down dark corridors without a care in the world.

RE8 manages to build incredible tension in it's first half. Saving your [spoiler] baby [/spoiler] is more than enough motivation story-wise but it's the mystery, the brutality and the horror that kept me moving forward, head half tilted away from my monitor and one eye closed.

A big draw is the actual village itself.  It's not just a level, it's an intricate maze of secrets and puzzles, oozing with metroidvania type backtracking that never felt tedious as unlocking new paths or finding new items always felt worthwhile. There are one or two periods of the game that were like elaborate escape rooms and this is when RE8 was at it's best. Using your wits in conjunction with your brawn felt satisfying and thinking on the fly was paramount as there are certain denizens of the village who are never far behind.

This seems to peak in perhaps one of the most horrific sequences in Resident Evil history (that's a bit of a silly statement, I've only played RE4, RE5, RE7 and the RE2 remake, there's LOADS I haven't seen) that left me pausing every few seconds just to gather myself. Sure horror is subjective, but honestly there is some messed up stuff here.

It's after this though, that the game almost knows it's not gonna top that in terms of scare factor and the focus shifts from horror to action. Slowly, your arsenal is bigger and more explosive, there's more fodder to kill and now I can see enemies shuffling down towards me instead of hearing them an inch behind me. This isn't a knock, honestly I was grateful for the let up and lining up head shots was just what I needed. There are side mechanics of crafting and cooking that kept me searching every nook and cranny, just now a lot more liberally.

The story eventually culminates in absolute chaos but I feel that's almost standard for a Resident Evil game. When the credits rolled it was impossible not to directly compare RE8 with RE7, it is a direct successor and RE8 definitely tries to move forward instead of sit alongside but ultimately, I enjoyed RE7 more. 

RE8 is definitely worth your time with it's superbly crafted environments and the continuation of Ethan Winters story. It has some real panic inducing moments and also a shotgun that can blow enemies heads off, something for everyone.

This being my introduction to the Resident Evil games, I absolutely loved every second of it. This game is absolutely amazing and super well made. I set a high bargain to begin with, which was met within the first hour.

Capcom's handling of the Resident Evil franchise has seen its ups and downs, its glories and failures, its hits and misses - For every great game this series has had, it has also had its fair share of missteps. Though it seems like a distant memory now, RE6 nearly brought the series to its knees by trying to be everything to everyone and it belly flopped to an unimaginable degree. Since then, starting in 2017, Capcom has been trying to repair the damage that game wrought in a variety of ways in the form of the newest FPS perspective titles like 7 and Village while also cranking out high quality remakes of classic titles like 2 and 3. And frankly, for my money, Village might just be the best one yet. Right from the get go, this is a game brimming with confidence in itself and the gambles it tries to go for, trading the series signature Sci-Fi horror in laboratories angle for Gothic Horror, complete with the whole shebang of vampires, werewolves, evil puppets, fishmen, wizards and witches. And it works!

Meanwhile, the well executed gameplay of 7 is back here in spades but with even more varieties of enemy types, weapons, level designs and boss encounters. The controls hit that amazing sweet spot between empowering without over doing it and even a standard battle with regular enemies can be quite a challenge. And speaking of the boss fights, each of the main lords (from the iconic Lady D to the diabolical Mother Miranda) pack a punch both in terms of design and combat. It's hard to pick who's the most fun fight, whether it be physical or mental. And to those who might be afraid that the game doesn't offer any worthwhile terrors, don't kid yourself: There's some stuff in this game that gave me a good shock or two I haven't felt since viewing Hereditary back in 2018.

But the biggest surprise here is the relentlessly exciting and emotional narrative that the game sports. We've come a long way from the (admittedly charming) "Jill Sandwich" days, with Village's story being one of a father's ruthless search to rescue his daughter in what feels like one of the bloodiest fairy tales ever put into game form. I won't say anything else beyond this but this was the first RE game I ever encountered to actually make me tear up at the end, which is just baffling for me to write those words for this franchise.

Yet in this time, it tells an good enough story with enough RE game play mechanics to make it worth playing and overlook how fast the game goes.

Gameplay, in my opinion, is very clunky, but yet again, RE games have never been "Smooth" as we know with other shooter games, but it certainly noticable. From using your weapons, to movement, to using actions.

Graphically confusing though.... I would NOT suggest playing this on anything OTHER than the potentially highest graphics. I have a Ryzen 7 5800x and RTX 3070, and anything under what one can consider "High" setting of graphics makes everything look just horrible. There's even a weird issue with FPS that sometimes you only get as much as 50-60 FPS, unless you spam the menu or inventory, which eventually bounces back up to normal (For for me I can run 144 FPS, but the thing is, any attempt to do so ends with a sparatic jumping between 110-140, so it was worth capping it at 120 just to get some stability in that area).

The fights were, honestly, borning. Despite only playing normal, i still only died 3-4 times, most of which was not understanding what was currently happening (which was annoying because I got my 2nd or 3rd death on the 3rd primary boss, which was only one death, and the game made attempts to get met to lower the diffiuculty, which is annoying because the game isn't that great or difficult to be suggesting that). Most boss fights you can kite simply and is nothing more than just throwing enough bullets at the target, which even "weak points", only accelerated the process slightly. Overall, game is worth playing, wish I got it on sale instead of full price though and I don't really see myself playing it again for the NG+ and content that comes with it, just too short of a game with little engagement to enjoy what it has to offer past the first play through.

It is both a success in entertainment and a major disappointment. Since there is no 'middle' rating, I'd go for the thumbs up but my recommendation has clear reservations.

Presentation: 4/5 : In a horror game, presentation is everything and graphically this is a major step up on a technical level from Resident Evil 7 Biohazard. It is optimized to run relatively smoothly and even offers ray tracing technology. You can tell they put a lot of work into textures and settings. However, this game for the most part is NOT SCARY (with one notable horrifying exception I'm sure most agree on) and thematically it is an incoherent mess. I should also say that the improvements in gameplay dramatically get in the way of immersion (see gameplay section)

Story/Dialogue 1/5 : The voice acting, the dialogue, the lazy one-liners, the incoherent story with incredible plotholes - you would think this is a parody of the horror genre, but it is not. It wrecks everything the prequel Resident Evil 7 established (not that it was a masterpiece in storytelling, but at least it had the right tone). Since it plays with a certain level of seriousness, you might laugh through the gameplay - it is unintentionally hilarious!  It is more like Tommy Wiseau 'the room' of horror.  I never thought I would laugh so much as a small detail like the abuse the protagonist hands receives. It hurts that the game depends on cutscenes more than the typical horror game and if you are looking for a story that either grips you or adds to the terror of the game (that is not scary by the way), stay away.

Gameplay 4/5 : In relation to Resident Evil 7 Biohazard, the gameplay is both better and worse. Better in that controls and battle mechanics are less clunky, and better in that you have more flexibility around the weaponry and supplies you need to survive. Worse in that the gameplay enhancements get in the way of horror (do you even run out of ammo or supplies or inventory space?, is your character a trained soldier all of a sudden?) and worse in that the gameplay enhancements make the game feel 'game-y' like the way it tries to force a linear progression, and let's not even start with having a quirky character follow you around to barter with you, cook you meals regardless of where you are, enhance your weapons via tinkering, and so on. So yes, strictly gameplay-wise this is an improvement and it gets better as it progresses, but it sure had to sacrifice a lot to get there.

Game is pretty good and definitely gave me what I expected from the new style of Resident Evil game. Other then a few issues with the game, it was something I do not regret buying. My experience is as fallowed:

Positives 
-The graphics are not disappointing and isn't too demanding on the computer.
-Soooo many things to collect and find in the game, it makes you feel like you will never find everything as there are just too many good places to hide items.
-The game is different from RE 2 and RE 7 in that, the inventory does not really feel as limited in the amount of items you can hold. However, if you as unorganised and reckless like me, you will find a way to plug up your inventory with ammo and guns you rarely use.
-Environment is beautifully ugly, as everything is done so well that it makes me feel like I'm going to either catch a disease or a cold.
-The atmosphere sets you up for a lot of tense moments which is a good thing, as it keeps you immersed in the game play.
-Replay-ability is there for people that like unlocking new guns, infinite ammo, or for the people that really hate their sanity, there is also 2 harder difficulties.

Negatives
-Now with a game that has an atmospheric tensity like this, combined with epic_ly bad mouse sensitivity options by default, you are guaranteed to be doing a lot of panic shooting. Until you have played for a bit, your going to be good at shooting around the enemies as opposed shooting through them.
-For the most part, this game is pretty straight forward. However you will mostly likely find one or two spots that hold you up for a while before figuring out where to go. Okay, so don't think I'm dumb, but some of the hold up's have made me feel that way (like looking up a combination to a lock that was in plain sight).
-This one is not really a negative thing as its part of the design of the game, but when your being chased by an un-kill-able enemy into an area that you makes you realise that your screwed, you just need to take the lose and redo it.
-Despite how long the first play though took me, the game just seemed too short. An objectified play though is going to always feel shorter, but its more like, you want to keep playing the story mode but you can't.
-Replay-ability is there but, after you get a weapon unlock and unlimited ammo to make playing the game easier, it tends to make a person lose interest after repeating this a time or two. The storey mode is exactly the same, no matter how many times you complete it, or weapons you unlock, or difficulty level you play on.

The game is good and deserves praise, but it definitely would have been nice to have a longer story mode or some better replay-ability. However, this game delivered good entertainment for me, and I do have to say that its worth the buy.

[h1]Introduction:[/h1]
[quote]RESIDENT EVIL VILLAGE or RE8 is a horror game developed by capcom, it is a sequel to the previous game (RESIDENT EVIL 7: BIOHAZARD) since it continues the story of our protagonist "Ethan Winters", you don't have to play RE7 to start this game because in your first launch the game will ask you If you want to recap what happened in the previous game.[/quote]

[h1]Difficulty:[/h1]
There are 04 Difficulties in the game (03 at the beginning and one will unlock after finishing the game): 

[b]Casual[/b] is the easy mode If you don't have time and only want to have fun then go for it.

[b]Standard[/b] is normal (I played at that difficulty), I didn't die a lot while playing at that difficulty so I felt like It was easy.

[b]Hardcore[/b] is the hard mode, probably any resident evil fan will go for this first and since I find "Standard" easy I recommend this difficulty instead of it.

[b]Village of Shadows[/b] is the hardest one, and it only unlocks after finishing the game, If you enjoyed the game and the previous difficulties didn't satisfy you, go for this one.

According to gamewith website the differences are:
・Enemy: HP, Speed, & Damage Dealt.
・The ability (or lack thereof) to naturally heal.
・Different enemy placements (Village Of Shadows Only).

[h1]Graphics & Performance:[/h1]
The graphics in this game are so freaking awesome, It's beautiful and the best thing is that its well optimized even for old systems, if you have an old pc you can play it on (High Textures / FXAA + TAA / Others Sets at low / 720p) and still get 45 fps which is playable and with good image quality that doesn't make your eyes bleed, and If you have a beast PC you will find 0 problem running this game on Ultra, to be honest I thank capcom for making this game playable even on old systems since most of recent games doesn't care about optimization, well done capcom you nailed that part!

I also wanna mention that the game has a Camera Mode which Is something I like a lot, It can be found in the pause menu, you might run into a lot of beautiful views and take screenshots of them to share them on Steam.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
RE: VILLAGE is a first person shooter like RE7 (unlike the rest of RE series games which they use 3rd person) the gameplay is similar to RE7 but better a lot, they improved a lot of things and added a lot of content to it, they also upgraded the interface of the inventory and 
the crafting menu and made it easy to use.

Unlike RE7, this game is kinda more open and gives you more content to explore, that factor gives it more Action than Horror since you have a large battle area to use against the enemies.

When it comes to looting, It's kinda like the rest of RE games, you loot ammo and materials to craft healing potions and bombs, and everytime you progress to another area you get new items. There are also puzzles but they don't require to be Albert Einstein to solve them and they are fun to do.

[quote]As a coclusion, RE: VILLAGE did well with the gameplay compared to the previous game, they improved a lot of mechanics and added even new ones.[/quote]

[h1]Story & Horror:[/h1]
During your playthrough you will run from an area to an area, each area has it's unique atmosphere and feels different from the other which is something I like about this game. 

The story didn't impress me a lot so I can't call it a masterpiece but I got attached to some characters and liked them a lot. This game doesn't connect RE7 Story only but the whole series, in this game you will get all your answers for the questions you got from the previous game and It explains everything, there are notes (items that can be read) and pictures in different areas, read and view all of them because they are important and they explain many things.

After completing the game, you will still have more stuffs to do like replaying it on the new difficulty or playing bonus levels and do challenges.

Resident Evil is known for Its horror, and RE: VILLAGE kinda achieved that factor, I'm not that type who get scared easily by playing horror games, played some of them like Outlast so I'm used to jumpscares, I didn't get scared a lot but at least this game made me scream like a woman 2 or 3 times.

[h1]The problems with this game:[/h1]
Overall the game is good but it feels like it misses something, some characters were too good that I wanted to see more cutscenes of them, more encounters with them, It's like I didn't have enough of them I just wanted more but the game only gives you a little of it which make it feel short.

[spoiler]One of my favorite characters in this game is Heisenberg, I wish there are more screen time for him, one idea I found in the internet is a suggestion for capcom to make a DLC where Ethan accepts Karl's offer to beat Miranda together, the game doesn't let you decide and I wish if you were able to do that, like choosing between Mia or Zoe in RE7.[/spoiler]

Resident Evil Village is a wonderful game.

Split into four main sections, each covers different themes, so there is something for everyone to enjoy while playing. The villains are all very well written, and their battles all feel very different from each other, creating unique challenges for each fight. The story is also well intertwined with previous installations and you can tell a lot of time has gone into everything, from the beautiful environments to the lore scattered throughout the various areas. 

Coming straight from finishing RE: Biohazard, it takes a little while to get used to the new systems such as the inventory, but once you do it is a major improvement on the old one. The currency system is also a great way to allow the player to get new upgrades without it feeling like the game just hands it to them when they need it.

The game is also not very demanding, I use a laptop and was able to run the game perfectly with no crashes or frame drops and the game still looked absolutely stunning. 

There is also content in game that you can unlock after completion, allowing you to replay the game with a completely different experience. As I bought the game with all DLCs, I will mention that the bonus content is somewhat lacking, such as the odd choice of safe room music you can enable, but I would not recommend using them anyway, as it breaks some of the game's atmosphere with out of place objects such as tape recorders rather than typewriters for save points, this is of course personal preference.

The positives of this game definitely outweigh the negatives though, and I cannot recommend it enough.

10/10, would definitely play this again.

The game is really solid, let's get that out of the way and other people here have probably explained that well enough. So I'm gonna rant on the one major thing I disliked, the combat and how it tries to be 2 things and ends up with the worst of both worlds. I must admit that I skipped RE7 and I approached this game with the assumption that combat would play similarly to Re4

There have been primarily 2 approaches to combat in RE. The first is the survival method. Combat is purposefully clunky and dissatisfying to encourage you to avoid combat. And perhaps most importantly, enemies drop nothing. So the only reason to ever fight is to preserve your health. This naturally teaches you that combat is only ever a last resort and gameplay is balanced around that. Combat revolves more around planning when to fight and when to flee more than anything else.

The action approach started by RE4 is based around combat skill. Skillful aiming and reaction is the meat of the game. Enemies drop ammo and money so you're encouraged to fight as much as possible, but more importantly, fight skillfully to keep your ammo and health up as much as possible. The stun-counter is critical to this, sparing ammo by stunning an enemy by shooting a certain location, then getting a melee prompt that gives you I-frames and pushes crowds back. The risk-reward factor is not whether or not you can avoid combat, but if you can successfully pull-off manouvers that require you to gamble on being able to shoot accurately when it counts and counterattacking.

So what approach does Re8 use? At first glance, it seems like it wants to follow the action approach. It has a shopkeeper and upgradeable weapons like Re4. But there is one major problem in particular. Enemies drop no ammo, they can drop crafting materials that can be used to make ammo, but it's not reliable. They do drop money usually and the shopkeeper sells some ammo, but it's limited how much you can buy. What this means is that at least on harder difficulties, ammo will almost always be tight. But surely the game is balanced around this right? Well, not really. Unlike Re4 and 2/3 remake where headshots or legshots would stun the enemies to give you a safe escape or a counterattack, most enemies in Re8 don't seem to reliably stun from shooting certain body parts. They do stagger, but usually only after 3-4 shots and the location doesn't seem to matter much. yes, headshots do a tiny bit more damage, but not enough to make it worth the risk of missing. The Lycans especially are very fast on high difficulties and aiming for the head is only worth it with high powered weapons with a chance for a critical headshot. Which never happened with the regular pistol from what I remember so I eventually stopped trying. What also didn't help me is that the game often has periods with little combat where I accumulated 80 bullets and felt pretty good, just to go through a narrow corridor with 8 zombies tightly grouped together and be down to single digits. Leaving me terrified of using bullets because hardcore mode kills you in 2 hits or so. much like Re2 remake. 

But maybe I wasn't supposed to fight everything. Maybe it tries to lean towards survival gameplay you might say. Well, running is very unreliable since you're stuck in first person view and have a hard time telling when enemies are approaching(not helped by that console-grade unchangable FOV). And you rarely backtrack so I often wasn't familiar enough with the area to make those decisions. Backing away from enemies is also risky since you can easily run up against walls or objects that you can't see. And it's easier to get stuck on things than in Re 2/3 remake where you usually fought indoors where walls were more clearly defined. Another thing is, unlike in 2/3 remake where you could find grenades/knifes to give you let you escape a single attack, Re8 has nothing.

Well, I guess there is the block mechanic, but man I do not like the block mechanic. Ignoring the fact that holding up your hands to stop a giant axe is ridiculous even for Resident Evil. Purposefully tanking damage in an RE game just feels so wrong, it's first person as well and imagining yourself holding up your hands to stop an incoming spiked bat does not feel right. Plus, you'd think zombies would just bite your hands anyway so it does not feel intuitive at all. Almost every game in Re has been about avoiding damage, not blocking it like a fighting game. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy blocking in games like Kingdom Hearts and Metal Gear Rising. But blocking in this game isn't based on timing. You just literally hold the block button to put up your hands and that somehow mitigates about %70 of damage taken. There is no reward for timing, all you get is a mechanic where you if you press block right after blocking an attack, you do a shove where you push the enemy back a bit. Which would have been good, if not for the fact it's hard to see when blocking. So you may often be blocking, watching an enemy attack you and then press block again to get the counter-shove, just to be a moment too early and drop your block just in time for the enemy to hit you. It's happened so many times both to me and one of my buddies who I watched stream the game. And on top of that, you can only counter-shove if you have a ranged weapon equipped and the game doesn't mention this if I'm correct. So you're using a ranged weapon to perform a close range action? Blocking just does not feel right.

That might make you think that running away would be the best option in spite of losing out on money. But hey, why upgrade your weapons if you're running away most of the time anyway. You can't really run away reliably, but you can often block and simply walk past enemies, tanking the damage. This is less reliable in open areas where enemies can attack from behind or the sides, but in narrow corridors. This is actually the best option in some cases. You take less damage and spend zero bullets. but it feels so wrong. Another weird development decision, enemies often despawn when you get past the area they're in. Even if you need to go back to that area later for treasure.

I'l try to wrap this up. It feels like the combat is at odds with itself. When I try to avoid combat, I have to deal with a perspective that's not good for dodging and I lose out on money. When I try to fight enemies as much as possible, I feel like I'm wasting valuable ammo for not a big enough reward, with a combat system that does not give me many options for conserving ammo. If I use the block system to walk by everything, I'm not having fun at all. I really feel like the game needed to do one of these things:

-Make enemies drop ammo so you can confidently engage them
-Add combat options to make ammo conservation more feasible
-Give the shopkeeper infinite ammo stock so there is less fear of running out
-Make dodging enemies more fun and engaging
-Add counterattack items like in Re 2/3 remake so you can take more risks

Again, I do like this game. But it frustrates me that this could have been really close to a 10 for me, but it ends up being more of an 8. The silver lining here is, using infinite ammo solves the fear of running out of bullets. Once I started VoS difficulty and could spend more time focusing on actually shooting and less time worrying  about whether or not I would have enough ammo to beat the game, I enjoyed the game far more. In fact, I quite enjoyed mercenaries because I didn't have to worry about getting roadblocked by a lack of bullets.

I recommend you play the game on standard first. Get infinite ammo for at least one weapon. And then play it again on Hardcore or VoS using the infinite ammo as a last resort. That gives you an Re4 like experience where you can focus more on the combat itself and less time wondering if shooting an enemy instead of walking past it with your arms up will come back to bite you in the butt later

Though I’ve never played an RE game before I must say I quite enjoyed my time with the most recent installment in the franchise. It’s short, but the polish makes up for that and while I don’t have strong feelings about the experience as a whole, the moment to moment gameplay is impactful and it’s three most prominent elements: Shooting, Exploration, and Puzzle-solving all blend together in specific ways and while it’s all the same ingredients the recipe is different depending on what part of the game you’re at. After some fine ravioli, the game will serve you some comforting pizza and then shake it back up with a plate of spaghetti. The metaphor isn’t one to one but you get what I’m saying. 

	The gun variety, customizability, and resource management is pretty vanilla. Even with the minigame-esque inventory menu, there’s just not a whole lot of depth to the weapons themselves, but aiming and shooting them is a whole different story. The way the enemies limp towards you and lurch into their attack choreography gives an incredible weight to the experience. It’s almost like the inverse of a bullet hell, especially in post game. And if we’ve learned anything from the Arkham series’ Predator sections, taking a common concept and inverting it onto the player is one that has an incredible effect on how the player perceives the situation. Going back to post game, having the option to try out other difficulty modes with a fully geared Ethan makes things very interesting. I’ve yet to beat Hardcore or Village of Shadows, but from what I can tell it is a basic number change which sounds disappointing on paper but as someone who’s into speedrunning it’s incredibly eye opening to what the rules are of individual segments. Finally figuring out that the Lycan horde at the beginning of the game was dictated by whether or not you loot a Crystal Skull off them was a great “Aha!” moment. But I ended up doing more Standard runs first in order to unlock more bonus weapons from the Extras menu before trying that again.

	The layout of most rooms in the game are essentially linear collectathons; finding valuable items and selling them to Duke. Among obscurities in the ceiling you’ll find Crystal Fragments. The various Wells dotted around the village you’ll find more significant items which would be overpowered, but in order to get what's inside them you need the Well Wheel which requires you to backtrack for said Wells. Every now and again you’ll find something a little more special which sells for a lot, but can be combined with other items later in the game to make said item whole and thus more valuable than the sum of it’s parts. So you have to decide if you want to utilize them as an investment or quick cash. Depending on your skillset you may need more gun parts and upgrades, but if you’re good at shooting you might wait until the game takes things up a notch first. All of these components make exploring the diverse environments that much more exciting and does a great job of incentivizing the player to move forward when they otherwise wouldn’t want to risk it. As I said before, I’m not particularly familiar with the horror genre as a whole, and if there’s any element of a game that subverts my assumptions about jumpscares and cheap deaths then I welcome it.

	Environmental puzzles are where this game really excels. While they are more flavorful than they are chin-scratching, the contraptions you play around with are fun. The biggest difficulty spike was really timing out the collapsing bridges in the Reservoir, and I’m ok with that. What I tend to have a problem with are the inventory-based puzzles where you go to inspect an item, find a button prompt on the back of it, and use that to transform it into an item that’s actually helpful. First of all, there are a lot of these in the first section, and then basically nowhere else in the game except for Winged Key upgrades. I guess learning how these work segways into the items you have to combine in order to sell for more money, but I feel as though the mechanics used to carry this don’t gel well together. While it feels like they tried to help the player learn how these work, more often than not it’s just unintuitive to go into your inventory, scroll to the key items page, find the specific item you’re looking for, select it, scroll it over to the backside, and select the prompt. If they wanted it to be efficient, then this mechanic would be better off automated into oblivion, but if they wanted it to be mysterious then they ruined that by making it too easy; So something like this: When you collect a key item, a preview of it pops up as a notification, inside the pop-up the item preview rotates so you can see all sides of it and you can catch a glimpse of what you need to interact with on it, maybe it’s even lined with that yellow tape that the environmental puzzles have. Then you allow some way for the player to interact with the item without having to ruin your immersion by pulling up the inventory. Maybe when you try to use the Maroon Ring on the eye socket, Ethan automatically pulls the eye out of the ring and that’s that. It would make sense to yadda yadda these details because Ethan has matured since RE7 and already dealt with things like this. If you want something a little more in-depth, maybe examining items puts it in Ethan’s hands and you can see him hold it. You could give inner-monolog voice lines for hints, but having straight-up button prompts is too easy. Having a mechanic like this would make things like the Mia doll flow a lot better. And this “examining items in Ethan’s hands” could also apply to weapons and treasure too for flavor purposes. Sure it’s more motion-capture work, but so what? People love that ♥♥♥♥. 

	As I said before, these 3 things are used in tandem to give the Castle, House, Reservoir, and Factory personality. Castle Dimitrescu is a familiar microcosm of what you expect from a horror shooter, which fits well for a tutorial area. The Village itself gets it’s own sections where you climb around and through what’s simply a combat maze. House Beneviento is a puzzle gauntlet practically dripping with subtext that ends with a stealth section. Moreau's Reservoir is a maze filled with puzzles that caps off with Ethan transforming the maze into a combat arena. Heisenberg’s Factory mirrors this by combat into a maze and capping off with a more cinematic boss fight. When I try to think about all the game’s elements in retrospect they feel homogeneous, but then when I go back to replay moments from the game it ends up feeling robust in it’s variety.

Good, but with some odd and downright poor pacing; virtually no replayability; and an underwhelming antagonist (and, arguably, protagonist). 

The game has trouble knowing what it wants to be: an action game or a survival game. It also lacks the clarity to divide certain aspects between video games and realism - both objectives and gameplay, and certain scripted sequences - which makes things confusing to parse; frantic (in a bad way) in tense situations; and immersion-breaking in common fashion - especially when it is usually most unwanted. The game also suffers from scripted and hyper-linear segments that are undesirable and poor - as many games of this genre, including first-person games, tend to adopt - where certain decisions made during or thereafter by the player (in lieu of what just happened) make little sense or are downright unbelievable; once again, breaking immersion. (The player character could have been eaten many times; and they manage to escape with comical ease at a few points with little consequence. It can feel like running through a "fun-house"; seeing how shallow and inconsequential things are one a "sequence" finishes playing out. It's sad.) A star villain is also greatly under-utilised.

Weapons are very weak, and don't feel good to shoot - especially on higher difficulties. This is padding and is artificial anxiety- and tension-evoking. The FOV (field-of-view) is incredibly tight and makes things claustrophobic, while movement (as is usual for this genre of game - specifically Resident Evil games) is lethargic and ponderous, where it could - and should - be much more responsive and fluid. This is, again, stilted game design to induce anxiousness, and actively fights and hampers the player's experience rather than changing itself and improving.

Great graphics, but with broken anti-aliasing - especially while DoF (depth-of-field) is enabled. (Seriously: I have never seen aliasing so bad since playing games made in the late 1990s to early 2000s. Also, one of the modes does not even work!) Similarly, film grain is of terrible quality - the lowest, again, that I've ever seen in a video game (which can look good if implemented well). Shadow edges and some areas have a stippled overlay that is distracting and can even be seen at a distance. Regardless for the reasons for its implementation, it is unattractive, and breaks realism - especially when the overlay pattern can be made out by the naked eye simply by moving the camera a bit. 

Ray-tracing is minimally used and is quite, to very underwhelming; with shadows; reflective lights; and shadow-casting sources hardly being altered at all. Implementation is low-resolution for the limited reflective assets that there are, while GI (global illumination) seems to be *highly* limited in its bounces and, therefore, effect. Unfortunately, the performance hit - in spite of its numerous shortcomings - is big - higher than that of other ray-traced games with far greater effect and usage. This is just a mediocre implementation of ray-tracing; one that feels rushed and tacked-on.

Great sound design (albeit with missing sounds at times); good performance (now; without ray-tracing); great character performances, albeit with some minor missteps; and great atmosphere (for the most part. The last of the four areas drags on and is largely boring). Flawed, but interesting story that at least climaxes well, even if not fully resolved.

It's a game that could be much better with different decisions made on a variety of factors (including updates to fix presentation problems), but also would need some major restructuring that would prevent it from being the game that it currently is. If it rose above its shortcomings, it could be so much more - and quite a compelling game, in fact. Instead, it's enjoyable, but only marginally - especially if you're looking for something enrapturing, cerebral, and gripping like I was.

I never played the original resident evil games, but I've played the remakes of RE: 2 and 3, biohazard, and now village. This game is the best of them, and I highly recommend it. 

There's a tendency in horror games to make them a powerwalking simulator while you try to solve puzzles along the way. Generally something is chasing you, and it's not mechanically any different from a timer. Solve it in time and you live, take too long and you die, or you have to run around the level and kite the goon chasing you because you can't kill it so you can try the puzzle again. Done well, like in RE 2 and 3, this can add tension (or sometimes comedy) to a game and make it more engaging. Still, by the end of those games I felt like Mr. X and Nemesis were coming to the end of their welcomes, after a while you stop jumping in your chair when you see Mr. X round the corner, and start rolling your eyes instead because it's just an obstacle to progress that you have to literally try to run around. Biohazard suffered from this more in my opinion, but was still enjoyable. Generally though, there were way more opportunities where I wanted to shoot a scary guy in all three games than I ended up getting. 

Being forced into running away from enemies is a good way to feel helpless, which can be good for some horror games, but on the other hand, you don't feel like you have any agency as the player, and at least for me, the stealth isn't as engaging. Village, on the other hand, is the shootiest RE game I've played, and it really enhances the experience. You get chased by a variety of zombie stand ins, and while resource management is still part of the game, you get to blast your way through enemies like never before. There are solid tiers of weapons with standard (damage, reload speed, ect) upgrades to get and find, but it still feels satisfying and rewarding to blow off a head with a sniper rifle, or knock a wolf-man down with a shotgun blast and then empty  your pistol into his head while he tries to get up. If you're a true survival horror purist, then you might take issue with the changes to the gameplay formula, but I think it really enhances the game and makes it significantly more fun. 

Core gameplay changes aside, this ticks all the familiar RE boxes, in a good way. Varied (and disgusting) environments to explore (the castle is my personal favorite but none of them are bad), the occasional cryptic puzzle, examining items closely to find secrets hidden within them, crafting, inventory management, fixed save points, zombies and monsters, reading notes, finding items to unlock/cook upgrades, ect. 

The game has a good core gameplay loop, it has solid replayability by allowing for a NG+ mode where you keep all your upgrades and access a new difficulty, the graphics look great, and it's well optimized, the voice acting is good and you get to hear the actor playing Ethan really try to sell the truly idiotic dialogue he has (it's endearing), overall a really good game and my favorite of the franchise.

The story is severely lacking. It makes no sense. Ethan makes choices that don't reflect his previous encounter in the last game, His actions make no sense a majority of the time. Also having vampires and werewolves. Being bitten, by a werewolf at the start of the game. Having your blood drank by a vampire. None of these alter your character or require special attention. It just is. You don't need silver bullets to kill werewolves. They just die. Vampires are killed by a window breeze and aren't really vampires. They just identify as them.  The most fleshed out level of the game is the castle. The others are quick adventure sets. All puzzles aren't puzzles. The rooms are safe from any attacks so you are fine. Upping your frame rates turns your knife or lightsaber into a fill factory. Because the game directly ties in the weapons damage to your frame rates. 

This game is far from perfect, it sincerely needed a better story and better use of the characters it introduces. Why bring in Werewolves if you won't include a special weapon to kill them.
