It's basically RE:7 but bigger, larger map, more antagonists, more weapons, etc. It has most of the same characters though a different setting. The first thing I noticed was how amazing it looks, especially for a game under 50gb when it appears most devs either don't know how to or don't care to try and compress their games.

The opening hours are fun, unnerving and very interesting, it does draw you in, it's the typical formula of "you are trapped in this area, find puzzle pieces, kill enemies, avoid the main antagonist until a scripted boss fight". It's fun though the horror feels toned down compared to RE:7.

There are two reasons I don't recommend this game, first is the story and second are the boss fights.
RE:7's story was silly, it was this very realistically-rendered world contrasted with laughably bad, Goosebump's level writing where bosses would taunt you endlessly throughout a five minute fight while your character never responds, or where your character would watch part of their body get sliced off, quietly mutter "ow" then pay it no attention again. Village is exactly the same but I feel like they must have hired the junior writers from the last game because the dialogue is painfully bad, it honestly is hard to listen to. Ethan isn't relatable or likeable, Mia is annoying at best, all of the antagonists come across like theater kids rather than grounded villains. I'm not one to let story ruin a game but Village is unfortunately a game where you cannot avoid the story, similarly you can't avoid the boss fights.

Boss fights in RE:7 were bad but usually short. Boss fights in RE:8 are bad but incredibly long at normal+ difficulty. I hated every single boss fight, they all either had super obvious gimmicks that may as well have been quick time event style button prompts to win or the bosses were bullet sponges design to run down your suppliers and leave you re-loading your save so you can go buy more and re-try. The final boss fight was by far the worst, without spoiling it some attacks felt like they were impossible to dodge, the room felt too small to maneuver in and the lack of feedback from the boss to show whether or not your damage was effective made it feel like a grind. I died three times because despite stocking up on supplies as much as I could and re-trying I kept running out. Landing every single shot made no difference, the fight just goes on and on all while the boss espouses dialogue that rivals a James Bond villain, telling me she is going to kill me while not actually doing it despite have ample opportunity. At some stage I got sick of it, dropped the difficulty I had stuck to all play through and was happy to finish up in less than 5 minutes on my next attempt.

Another issue it copies from RE:7 is that it turns into an action-horror game by the end - why did they decide on this? Animations are slow, your character controls like a boat, you're hindered by this to increase tension in one on one combat sections and all of a sudden you have an assault rifle, unlimited ammo, a horde of enemies and the same awful controls, it doesn't work.

The most stand-out section of the game is when you're in the basement with the mannequin, I won't spoil it but the body horror and tension are unrivaled in the rest of the game however it ended too soon.

If it's on sale grab it for an interesting 10+ hour run but I would recommend 7 over this any day, even with all of its flaws. It starts strong but leaves you wishing for its end.

Village calls back to Resident Evil's glory days, for better or worse. It manages to combine the newer immersive first-person action from RE7 with an attempt to recreate the gameplay magic of RE4, all while making some bold design choices along the way.

[h1] Ethan Winters, world's best dad [/h1] 
Once again, the player dons the role (or should I say jacket?) of RE7 protagonist Ethan Winter, who is now far more talkative this time around. Ethan is more developed, going from a blank-slate horror protagonist to an assertive father. This change feels like a natural fit within the narrative as he is no longer just trying to escape, but instead actively pursuing his own goals that take him deep into hostile territory. These personal goals offer a superior narrative hook to most other RE games. As a side-effect of Ethan’s increased presence, he now joins in the long-standing RE tradition of campy protagonist quips. Ethan's smack-talk feels far removed from RE4 Leon's heartfelt camp however-- and reads more like a parent’s self-censorship. Other characters curse like sailors, yet Ethan will call his enemy a 'witch' instead of the obvious alternative (with a 'B'), so he doesn't hurt their feelings. A preschooler's first curse words don’t sell the severity of the situation.

[h1] The baddies [/h1] 
Apart from Ethan (and a certain boulder-punching menace) the most prominent characters are the main antagonist's four lackeys, who are a mixed bag. Up until the point they make their introduction, Village manages to create an incredibly engaging and competent survival-horror experience that improves on the best parts of RE7. The cutscene in question attempts to establish the personalities of the antagonists, but instead paints them as overgrown children throwing a fit. The expertly crafted opening build-up is promptly thrown down the drain due to these character’s complete lack of presence. This scene can't even be called camp -- its about as well-paced as a drummer having a seizure. The writing misses the mark by a mile, as if drafted by a first-year writing student who watches too much anime. This is especially surprising considering the more grounded and well-paced dialog found in the RE2 remake and the start of this very game. This is compounded by mis-castings in the voice department, as certain character’s voices don’t match their appearance. Regardless, the voice talent did deliver some memorable performances.

[h1] Level design [/h1] 
Some of these characters get a lot more screen-time and development than others, which can largely be attributed to the size of their levels. The first sub-section can take an hour or two to complete on your first run, featuring a wide variety of areas, getting chased by unstoppable nemesis-like enemies and even three minibosses. If traditional RE gameplay is your thing, it’s all downhill from here. The second and third areas are easily completed within the hour and feature very little standard gameplay. The last lackey level is the largest and by far the stalest, as its a largely linear shoot-em-up section with a single miniboss. 
This lack of level design pacing feels familiar (just look at RE2 remake's excellent Police Station vs. the subsequent areas) but Village has a valid reason for this; like RE7 was inspired by slasher flicks, each of the lackeys and their levels are themed around a type of horror. These include Vampire, Monster, Psychological and Frankenstein. This was a bold choice that makes for a varied experience the first time around but kills replayability. On subsequent playthroughs the linear, scripted and gameplay-light areas feel like a chore.
Level design in conventional areas is somewhere in between the larger intricate design of RE of old and the small scale streamlined levels featured in RE7. Despite recalling many aspects of RE4, the gameplay area of RE Village doesn't feel quite as sprawling, and neither does the overall playtime.

[h1] What're ya buyin'? [/h1] 
Another aspect in which Village calls back to the classic RE4 is the presence of a merchant. Throughout the game the player finds money with which they can purchase various items. This is a satisfying way to handle power progression, though Village misses the mark on what made this system work in RE4. As you progress, you unlock new weapons in the shop. RE4’s new weapons weren't better than what you had, they simply offered a different playstyle, emphasized by the upgrade system which featured a unique final upgrade per weapon. This added a lot of replayability. Village combines the upgrade system with an RE2 Remake-like attachment system but forgoes both the weapon-altering abilities of the attachments in Remake and the unique upgrades of RE4. Upgrades are simply linear statistical progression, and the same goes for new weapons. The pump-action shotgun is a staple of RE that will carry you through most of the games, but the one in Village needs to be traded out for a better model if you plan on using shotgun shells effectively, losing you money spent on upgrades in the progress. It isn’t terrible, but its oddly regressive and feels like copied homework for the sake of being like RE4.

[h1] Ending nit-pickings [/h1] 
Onto something completely different; nit-picking themes. The game starts with an animated storybook which reads as an inverted version of the events of the game if you squint, but it doesn't offer any substance besides misplaced artistic flair. This story continues during the end credits narrated by a song filled with off-beat, ear-grating “singing” which I can only presume was directly translated from Japanese. You know your one friend who thinks they are a good singer because they add random flourishes with off-key high notes? It reads like someone gave ‘that’ friend creative freedom. The continuation of the story itself offer insight into how the Village came to be, though there’s no relation to the opening sequence besides the art style. Its all style over substance and feels out of place.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1] 
The game takes parts from various Resident Evil titles without understanding them but manages to blend quite well while still having its own unique flavours. The narrative had a few hiccups, but the ending was quite moving, which isn't something that can be said of many RE games. Village certainly doesn't live up to the games that inspired it, but its an enjoyable entry in the series, especially after the rather underdeveloped RE3 remake. I'm exited to see where the 'Winters saga' goes next.
Personally, I'd say its worth about 30 bucks for an RE fan, though the lack of replayability means I can't recommend paying more than that.

I'm writing this review as a test to see if people have had the same problem I had and if my solution works for others as well.

The problem was that whenever I closed the game and started it again nothing had been saved. 
What I mean with this is that I could save in-game but every time I closed the game and started it again the save files were gone along with the settings I've chosen. It was like starting the game up for the first time again.

I spent hours looking through missing files, reinstalling the game and running verifying file with no solution.
Until I looked in the steam settings and saw that I had "steam beta" enabled. I turned it off, ran the game and now Resident Evil Village works properly.

As I said. I'm not sure if this was the solution to my problem so if you have a similar problem like me were the game keeps resetting please do try this out.

You can check if you have steam beta enabled by doing this:
1. Click on Steam in the top left corner of the steam-client
2. Choose Settings
3. Go into the Account tab and you should be able to see "Beta participation"
4. If you have the Beta update choose "change" and pick "NONE"
5. Restart the client and try launching Resident Evil

The introduction of new enemy types and boss battles keeps the gameplay exciting and unpredictable. Visually, Resident Evil Village is stunning, with detailed character models, atmospheric lighting, and chilling sound design that enhance immersion and fear. The audio cues and music ramp up the suspense, making every encounter heart-pounding.

 First of all, especially if you are new to the RE-games here is one thing - don't take the whole story/lore of the game too seriously. This game (and the series) is not about the realism, especially since th 4th part and further. The whole RE-series is a carnivale/fair's haunted house with a smoke-machines and plastic skeletons, made only to entertain guests. No matter what crazy stuff happens they just always point fingers on bioweapons and you are expected to nod and mumble "ah, that explains it". Basically the same stuff that other games and books do with magic. So don't think about all of it too hard and just accept the fact that "it just works". 

 So why do i think this is the best RE game so far?
 First of all i like how we are changing environments often enough - rustic village, gorgeous castle, spooky forests and mansions, caves, industrial plant - you are never bored with the surroundings, which did happen in the previous games, where you spend most of the time in the more or less same locations.

 Next is graphics - i honestly was impressed with the REengine since they made the RE2 remake: crisp, highly detailed graphics with great optimisation, But in the VILLAGE they took the whole "visual fidelity" thing to a whole new level. Absolutely fantastic work! Crazy amount of details, hi-rez textures, photorealism. The castle is especially awesome - with such a level of details and textures you'd think the game would be unplayable on an average machine, but i had a stable 60fps without any issues.  

 Characters in the story have a lot of personality and they are chatty. I like that. They started to do that since the RE7, and upped it even more in the RE8. It's not like they have never talked in the previous games, but due to the limitations of the early games devs could not impliment a lot of dialogues/voice lines and now they can and this is great. Aside from some rare and venerable exemptions i do prefer chatty characters over the silent ones.

 The gunplay is standart for the RE-games so i can't say much about it - it's there and it works. The sound design is very solid, no issues here.

 But overally i think what the game does best - is keeping the overall pace. Player is never bored - game's tempo, enemies, decorations are constantly changing to keep you entertained, involved and on the edge. AND HUGE THANKS to whoever is keeping the series in check making sure that RE-games remain as an adventure packed hamburger, rather than becoming a "who eats more" contest. I'm talking about the playtime here. I don't have a fkn 100+ hours to spend on an every game, but recently more and more of them at least try to make players to do exactly that, otherwise some teenage kid is gonna complain that the game is "too short".  Devs - thank you for making the RE8 a relatively short game, rather than trying to artificially inflate it. Please do so in the future as well. Without any rushing, while exploring as much as i could - i still have finished the whole run in an 18 hours( and out of 'em a few are an afk-time). And this is just how i like it!

 So yeah - graphics, pacing, theme and decorations, diverse characters and bosses, game lenght and the generall "fun factor" - combined are making VILLAGE the best part of the series so far, at least for me.

 So i definitely recommend this game for the full price and during a sale it becomes a "must buy" entry. Cheers!

If I compliment this game i'm just going to be repeating what everyone else says, honestly just buy this game, it is very good and worth the price. However it is not without flaws. Too much action, not enough tension.

It doesn't feel like a "Resident Evil" game, to me it feels more like "Resident Evil 4 2". Despite what the game may tell you, the game is only a sequel to 7 in story alone. As a big fan of the series I have always preferred the true survival horror aspects of these games, Resident Evil Village, simply just does not have this. Does it play like a survival horror game? Kinda. It's more of an action game that has a lot of horror elements. Sure it has horror sections but for the majority of your playtime you will be playing an FPS action game, nothing wrong with that at all, I still love the game it's just to me at least that is not true Resident Evil.

Inventory is not limited (I never filled up my inventory once) which to me takes away from the survival parts of Resident Evil. I love limited inventory as it keeps the player on edge and unsure on what to bring, which is amazing for a horror game. Key items and money is also kept in a separate inventory which i'm personally not a fan of. (you can literally carry an entire village worth of corpses and an arsenal of weapons without any consequence).

I also very much dislike the concept of merchants in these games, you can beat the game completely fine without using them, you never really have to buy ammo from them due to it being plentiful (especially in the action oriented games like this, 4 and 5) but my main dislike for merchants is gun upgrades...

[b] Gun upgrades [/b] , I hate these, especially on a first playthrough. you can upgrade (nearly) any gun you want at (nearly) any time throughout the game, however with weapons like the pistol and shotgun there are always better models of these guns on the map somewhere or available to purchase from the merchant. This just leads to a feeling of frustration because you just spent all of your money upgrading your previous pistol only to find a better one 20 minutes later. (there is nothing else worth buying except gun upgrades too, which makes the merchant even more useless) I also believe the concept of a merchant takes away from horror. I just don't like them in my survival horror games.

[b] I'm really worried about this game. [/b] The game is very good and it was extremely popular, however because of the popularity I fear that Capcom are just going to keep creating action Resident Evil games rather than my beloved true survival horror based ones. I do think they will remake the first game again in the near future however besides that I think they will keep creating action based Resident Evil games because of the popularity of this game. When RE7 came out I was so happy due to it being a true Survival Horror experience ( and it is by far one of my favourite games ) For a while we even got RE2 and 3 remakes with the RE2 remake being my favourite game ever. However this did not last with the release of Village. Village really just is a RE4 again, everything i say about this can be said about RE4, they're both very good games but they just aren't true survival horror to me. I've played and completed every main Resident Evil game (except 6) and have gotten the highest rankings in most. I really like Resident Evil. Here's what I think about 8:

+The game is much longer than I expected.
+It is semi-open world, so there's a lot to explore.
+Weapon upgrades are worth hunting down.
+Gorgeous graphics.
+The castle portion of the game is quite comfy. You explore candlelit environments while the wind howls outside.
+A 9-foot tall woman and her daughters bully you relentlessly

-The puzzles are braindead simple
-The final boss's attacks are very hard to dodge in first-person, especially when she's in spider form
-The ingredients system is introduced far too late. By the time Duke tells you that you can get ingredients and he'll make food for you that grants permanent bonuses, you've already traveled through several areas with critical ingredients (namely, Fish) that you can't travel back to! I thought the fish were strictly environmental dressing. I also killed a few chickens early on, and the description for their meat said that I could give them to Duke. Not seeing the ingredients function because I hadn't unlocked it yet, I figured that all I could do was sell them to him, which I did, forfeiting those ingredients entirely. This is real bone-headed design, imo.
-By far the worst part of the game is the survival segment at the very beginning. You have to survive an onslaught of werewolves while Ethan gives you misleading clues like "There's no end to them!" Actually, there is an end to them and you're just supposed to survive for a few minutes. But there's no indication that this is actually what you're supposed to do. You hear on a radio that there's a house with survivors in it, and I spent my first few attempts trying to find a non-existent way out of the area to this house, getting slaughtered by werewolves because I wasn't playing the right way - I was playing the way the game had mislead me into playing. It is quite frustrating imo, but I recommend sticking it out, because the rest of the game is much fairer when it comes to difficulty.

Overall, it's a very good game that's worth playing, provided you have the patience to put up with some bone-headed and under-tested design decisions, and one especially bad segment at the very beginning.

Very enjoyable yet flawed follow-up on Resident Evil's mainline FPS outings.
Much of the presentation is top notch. Environments look extremely detailed and at times photo-realistic. But while the atmosphere is consistently dense, the horror only sporadically enters the picture. Also, I can't shake the feeling that these games are less and less play-tested. There are a couple of balancing inconsistencies (especially on the higher difficulty settings), and the upgrade path for your weapons and your character are very linear, which is odd since this game tries to emulate RE4 at every step of the way and that game managed to make every loadout viable, while RE Village has a clear set of best weapons and most valuable upgrades.

On the other hand, the level design (especially the name-giving Village) is brilliant, and the sound design does the rest to envelope you into this world. That said, towards the finale the pacing of the game can drag a little, since the story is a bit too convoluted to be engaging till the end (even for RE standards), and the later boss fights uncover some of the weaknesses of the rather bare-bones combat system.

Regardless, I had a really good time and if you can live with a couple of shortcomings, and liked RE7 or RE4, I think you will have a good time as well.

But I have to say, if the developers would have had a bit more time to polish a few ares (especially gameplay wise), and to properly play-test every difficulty setting, these games could easily be modern classics. Basically everything I think is wrong here was wrong with RE3 Remake as well, and I'd love to see the extra effort go into these projects going forward as I really think they can create something outstanding again. They're so close.

First time playthrough of this game is nothing short of amazing, 100% GotY 2021!

Game-play: 
The game-play is quite simple, most bosses and enemies just need to be shot at enough times to die with few exceptions.
Gun play feels good and responsive. Each enemy type has there own flair. The werewolf dudes have an almost aggressive dog like playfulness when they run up to you. They stumble and somersault backwards as you blow them away with your shotgun. The more zombie like dudes are classic to the series and there are a couple variations between them. The robo zombies near the end are an interesting touch and more challenging and visually interesting. The act of finding locked areas and then returning to those areas later with the correct item is satisfying as you unlock more secrets and items. The boss fights themselves are quite simple on the default mode. You run around and shoot the enemy or stun the enemy enough to get a shot at their vulnerable spot. But each boss has there own visual style that each one doesn't feel copy and paste. 

Story:
This is my second RES evil game. I've only played RES 2 Remake and I enjoyed that game too. There was some slight confusion at the start of whos who and why I'm here but that feeling wasn't a problem as i traversed through the game with Ethan as he similarly didn't know what the ♥♥♥♥ was going on. The game really opens up from a plot perspective after you complete the first 2-3ish hours of the game. Going from area to area deepens the world and gives you a different look at how twisted each main antagonist is in their own way. The story has a decent amount of exposition explained through dialogue dumps but its not annoying. Since still a newbie to the RES evil world it sometimes feels like an anime/soap opera in the overall style of the characters but there is a charm to this that grows on you. To be fair but I'm not sure how i would react if a 8ft big tiddy vampire was chasing me around a mansion. I would say a lot of the story comes through the visuals of the game alone.

Graphics/Aesthetics:
The look of this game is stunning and it plays superbly well for how good it looks. I was able to get 100-140fps in the game at full quality (without RTX) at 1440p with a 3060ti. Other games around this time with less visual fidelity struggle to get that smoothness even with DLSS. The aesthetic of the game is cleanly dirty if that makes sense. The dirt and grime and details in this game beautiful. From the inside of the castle with its grand wooden details to its dark and dank dungeons. Also mentioned previously the game is centred around going to different zones to kill that areas boss and collect loot. Each area has a very distinct feel and look but it still falls under the umbrella of the overall aesthetic of the game. From the warm yet creaky interior of the castle with it wealth and riches where lady Dimitrescu is always on your tail waiting to slash at your heels. This contrasts well with different areas like Heisenbergs metal factory of torture where bodies are hanging off of assembly lines ready to fall off and start chasing you as there mechanical parts scrape and spark off the rusty walls. The look of the game is a chefs kiss

Overall:
Scary and tension building but has a good level of action and pacing. The story has a good depth to it with its many characters and areas to explore. The aesthetic of the game carries it for me as its very immersive and detailed. I'm usually not a big fan of horror games but this game has opened my eyes a bit to the genre and I subsequently bought every resident evil game after I finished Village. I'm excited to dive into the other games and see where they take me in the universe of Resident evil.

I have never played, nor been interested in any Resident Evil games. I got into this one because it got great reviews and the videos that I saw of it looked really good.

This is by far the best game that came out in 2021. Set In Romania, this game has an atmosphere and aesthetic not seen in any other game I have played before. The closest thing I can think of is Metro Exodus, another excellent game that I fully recommend especially when you like this one.

The level design is superb and I fell in love with Castle Dimistrescu, an ominous gothic castle inhabited by what is essentially a huge vampire woman. The rest of the areas in the game is also outstanding and by extention, make exploring and going off the intended path a very fun endeavor. You can also be rewarded by finding extra loot and other items that can make your character stronger. 

The gameplay is fairly decent, with a selection of interesting firearms, that you can upgrade with weapon mods and you can improve the stats at a certain merchant. This game also features a new game plus mode, that you can do again and again after each completed run, and you can carry across all the weapons that you had in the previous run, meaning that you can play with fully upgraded late-game weapons from the beginning. In addition, this game has a shop in which you can spent points, which includes options to purchase infinite ammo for certain weapons when you have fully upgraded them in-game. That alone greatly increases the replay value of this game, especially for weapons that have ammo types that are very scarce. The credits for this shop are earned by doing in-game challenges, some of which you will complete when you just play the game normally and others that you really need to go out of your way for.

But not everything about this game is great, unfortunately. The boss battles are definitely one of the weakest aspects of this game, it feels like the gameplay wasn't really designed for with boss battles in mind, with no ability to dodge attacks. In addition there are major issues with hitboxes, and sometimes a boss hits you even if it didn't look that way visually, and other time bosses misses you even visually it seems like (s)he actually touched you. The reverse is also true, where sometimes it looked like you hit a boss but you missed. Regular enemies don't have the same problem. Boss fights are weird and buggy, and if you have completed the game at least once, some of them can be a bit tedious as well. 

In addition the puzzles feel like a bit an insult to the player's intelligence. None of them were difficult as the solutions were often literally spelled out on walls, turning puzzles into more of a speedbump rather than an obstacle in which you really need to think hard in order to solve them. It's not quite on the skyrim level, but it's not far from that either. 

The sound and music is great and really adds to the atmosphere. I will never forget the music that starts playing when you enter a safe room. It's a very soothing tune and I'm certain that if I hear it randomly ten years from now, it will instantly trigger nostalgia.

[h1]PROs:[/h1]
✅ Great design that feels like multiple game genres in one (horror, shooter, puzzle, escape), separately. 
✅ Excellent world design with fun exploration and memorable boss fights.
✅ Fantastic quality-of-life features, especially the beautiful inventory and map systems.
✅ A great New Game+ system with a point-shop for meaningful unlocks.
✅ Very entertaining characters set in an intriguing, vampire-themed world.
✅ Top-notch visual and audio presentation with great voice acting.
✅ Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters. (Ahem, mods.)

[h1]CONs:[/h1]
❌ The character upgrade (food) system isn't clearly explained at first.
❌ A lot of backtracking is required for 100% completion.
❌ There's a major, easy-to-miss point of no return early in the game (in the castle).

[h1]Comments:[/h1]
This is a polished and incredibly fun action-horror experience. What makes it so great is how it feels like several different games nicely rolled into one. The game is divided into distinct sections, each with its own unique tone and gameplay focus. The "horror" area, for example, has a fantastic and genuinely tense atmosphere that rivals the best in the series. This is followed by sections that play like a straightforward shooter with varied enemies, clever puzzle areas, and tense escape sequences. This variety keeps the entire experience feeling just fun and enjoyable from start to finish.

The game is also packed with smart quality-of-life features, from the large, well-organized inventory to the helpful map that marks cleared areas. While there's a lot of backtracking to find all the treasures, it's made manageable by well-placed shortcuts.

I do have a couple of warnings for first-time players. First, the character upgrade system using food isn't explained well. On my first run, I sold my first piece of meat to the Duke, thinking it was just treasure, and lost out on an early permanent upgrade. Second, and this is crucial: fully explore the first main area (the castle) before you leave, as you CANNOT return to it later.

Even playing with infinite ammo on my first Normal run, the game still offered a decent challenge with some of its boss and elite fights. The story is intriguing, the characters are highly entertaining, and the overall presentation is top-tier. It's a fantastic package and a personal favorite.

A quick note on the DLC: Most of it is fluff, but the "All Access Voucher" is essentially a paid shortcut to unlock all the post-game items, if you don't feel like grinding for them on subsequent playthroughs.

Village is exhilarating, horrifying, laugh-out-loud hilarious, and unapologetic in its mission to show the player a great time. A satisfying story sequel to Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, and a brilliant spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4, Village triumphs in basking in the roots of the series, while simultaneously showcasing its brilliant original levels and characters, to the pace of an action-heavy survival-horror beat. From item crafting, to combat, to exploration, the gameplay revolves around extremely satisfying risk/reward loops. The Rogue's gallery is fantastic in terms of each villain's game area and environment, and the performance of the VA's/outstanding fun dialogue and story bring each of them to wicked life (Maggie Robertson's performance as Lady Dimitrescu steals the scene every time). The bar for this franchise has been rather high since the RE Engine titles started releasing, and Village certainly leaps the hurdle- a fantastic video game.

At the time of writing this review, I still haven't completed the game. I intend to, however, and perhaps then I will update this. But as it stands... this game is just not engaging. Pros: sound design, environments. Cons: everything else. Issues I had with the RE2 remake carry over here. Characters and objects feel off where weight is concerned - the way doors open and close is... well, it feels bad.

The story is absurd. Spoilers after this sentence, skip this paragraph if you'd like. But a character reattaches a body part yet shortly after that, seems to be in disbelief when another character is in pieces, that it isn't possible to put them back together. I'm sorry, what. RE has always been zany/campy/dumb but they presented things in such a way that yeah, ok, I can go along with this without questioning it too much. That? Suspension of disbelief is out the window and it ain't coming back.

So in the end, just to give you an idea of how little fun I am having with this game: I am thoroughly enjoying my 25th hour in Pathologic Classic over finishing this. This isn't the Resident Evil I enjoyed in my youth and its taken me RE7, the remakes between, and RE8 to realize that I just need to give up and move on without consuming or sinking money into it anymore. 

At least I'll always have the older games.

Edit: I finally completed the game and yeah, my opinion didn't change.

The latest Resident Evil game, Resident Evil Village returns to the rather controversial first person view that Resident Evil 7 started. While reception of that game was positive, a lot of the feedback was it was a bit too scary. So continue the story of Ethan Winters, Capcom has decided to make Resident Evil Village to be more of a jack of all trades experience. We've been there before haven't we? It only feels Resident Evil 6 was released yesterday....

First off graphics, the Reach for the moon engine (RE Engine), Capcom's in house custom game engine is starting to show its age on this game. The engine works best in small, indoor spaces where it can look photo realistic under the best lighting. Outside however you'll see lower fidelity textures, poor shadows, you lose the quality that the engine is known for when it's moved to larger spaces. You don't even see realistic snow effects like when you're stepping in them. Being a port from console the optimization could have used better tweaking. While my experience was relatively smooth, certain scenes with certain foes that have flies all over them will drop frames to new slide show limits. These moments are very rare, but the random stuttering continue especially the further I get in the game.

Sound effects are an absolute highlight of the game, the crunch of headshots, the ambient noises of the castle halls, the ominous howling winds of a mountain pathway all do a fantastic job portraying the dread of the location you are investigating. Unfortunately the voice acting kills any sense of immersion Capcom has served to get. There's one particular scene (also found on the demo so its no spoilers) where Ethan interacts with the villagers of the game. They are dressed like peasants who live in the 1800s, yet they speak perfect American English. This game is set in Romania right? Yet the people talk like they live in Oregon. At least in older Resident Evils Capcom made the locals speak the language like Spanish in RE4. In Village, not a single voice actor tried to speak Romanian or have a Romanian accent. Whether or not this was due to Covid restrictions or for pure player convenience I'm not certain.

The game design is a bit all over the place which harkens this game back to the most polarizing entry in the franchise, Resident Evil 6. Capcom did not have a cohesive theme on how to lay this game out. Instead they chopped the game up to an amusement park style bits where you have themed areas that lead you to 5 (well, 4 actually since one of them is a pathetically easy game of hide and seek) underwhelming bosses. Many have compared the gameplay flow of Resident Evil Village to RE4 and I simply don't see it. Resident Evil 4 is a masterpiece in game design, the pacing, setup, risk and reward of surviving an onslaught of enemy attacks is simply a master class which is why the game is so revered well over 15 years after it came out. Resident Evil Village couldn't be further from that. Instead of a cohesive theme of gameplay ideas, the developers without legendary producer Shinji Mikami on the helm threw a bunch of ideas or gameplay segments into the game. 2 of the five sections of the game play more like the older styles of Resident Evil, the castle and the very confusing factory. The castle is the absolute highlight of the game as it's the best designed map of the game and where the graphics look absolutely photorealistic at spot. You'll be looking for keys and clues on how to get to your goal along with unkillable enemies that are quite easy to get away from (RE2 remake anyone?). Unfortunately after that section of the game, the experience tanks and tanks hard.

The second themed area you'll be exploring is an escape room type house of horrors location. It's probably the worst part of the game for speed running as it crawls down the pace of the game forcing you to do mundane "puzzles" while trying to jump scare you with the most cliched tropes such as creepy dolls and manequin parts dangling on the ceiling. This section is the devs trying to make a P.T. knock off and doesn't fit Resident Evil's style of survival horror.

The third themed area amplifies the terrible game design of the game. There's a particular section where the player must cross a lake while a lake monster is chasing the player. What entails is a pretty mundane game of you're safe so long as you aren't on the red planks of wood. The monster after you will be swimming around the water, jumping out ever so often, but it won't hurt you unless you're in the red planks when crossing. Any sense of dread is lost when you figure out you can only be killed at certain points of the map. Also a big thing that irked me while playing is the AAA dumbed down game design of color tele prompting. Taken from the 2013 reboot of Tomb Raider items that have yellow stains in them can be interacted with. Instead of naturally placing the items as recognizable interactive ones, they color them out for you which is BAD game design. The game's numerous "puzzles" even conveniently tell you the solution right in front of you it's absolutely a joke of how easy games have become.

Resident Evil Village is I feel a huge misstep for this series. The lack of a cohesive identity feels like the devs tried their hardest to stick all ideas into a wall and hoping to see one of them sticks. I don't mention much of the combat and weapon upgrades and they work well as intended. The monster designs are pretty good all around from the lycans to the armored beasts. After the credits roll there's not much left to do other than the return of the Mercenaries Mode (though it should be called Mercenary Mode lol) which is a fun and fast paced arcade style mode where you need to chain kills to get the highest score possible. The persistent design issues of the campaign is a disappointment. The story was even too off the wall for Resident Evil standards. The lack of an attempt to authenticate the location you're in with locals speaking in perfect American English instead of Romanian destroys any sense of immersion. This game is mediocre modern AAA at it's textbook example.

Preface to the Review:
Resident Evil Village leaves me with mixed feelings. Unfortunately, I can only give it a good or bad rating, and since it has more goods than bads, I have rate it positiv besides all my critics.

Review (may contain spoilers):
Graphically the game is beautiful, you can see the attention to detail and effort in the graphic design. The sound is good and fitting. Unfortunately, this Resident Evil part is the least scary for me with parts 5 and 6, especially after VII I had expected or hoped for more. 
About the story: It is....mixed. (Attention, possible spoilers) Lady Dimitrescu's house (1) and Eisenberg's factory (4) are relatively extensive, you have to solve a few nice (but not too complicated) puzzles, and Eisenberg also has a lot of action. The Angie section (2), on the other hand, is extremely short, although the scenario of her and the dolls would have had a lot of potential in my eyes. Moreau's section (3) is ok, but not particularly entertaining. Boring puzzle and not particularly original either. The boss fights are also very unsteady...Angie and Moreau are through very quickly, the ones against Lady Dimitrescu and Eisenberg are a bit more creative and longer. 
And then comes the last hour of the game...somehow it feels very rushed and too action-packed. The boss fight against Mother Miranda is quite nice, but also over sooner than expected. 
The whole story (if you read a lot of the texts everywhere) is quite nice and fits into the Resident Evil lore. 

Conclusion:
Resident Evil Village is a good game, but it could have been a great or even Fantastic game. If the story of the houses had been developed more, 2 and 3 had been developed more and made a little more interesting, it would certainly have been possible! But as it is, this part of the series only has a place next to Resident Evil 3 - which is good, but doesn't come close to 1,2,4, Code Veronica and 7.

Die ganze Story (wenn man viele der überall sich befindenden Texte ließt) ist ganz nett und passt in die Resident Evil lore.

It definitely falls into the action-oriented dichotomy of the Resident Evil franchise, but the developers didn't want to go all-in and instead the game attempts to appease people like me and those interested in the action part at the same time, leading it into having an identity crisis for 6 hours as it tries to patch together a semblance of atmosphere amidst the four main bosses (the four lords), with the 2nd having the most dedicated attempt at "horror" but falls flat. Before diving right into an action-oriented setpiece for the final hour of the game, which is weirdly the "funnest" part because it drops any pretense of it actually being a horror game or having any depth.

Atmosphere. It's what separates a the best of the best in horror gaming. Alien Isolation took atmosphere to a new level in gaming. Resident Evil 7 did the same. RE8 may not be as scary as these two previous titles, but it definitely has an unforgettable atmosphere that makes the game re-playable. I've already beaten it twice and I'm planning on diving back in for a NG+ Village of Shadows playthrough. 

The boss fights are memorable enough but it's the environments that I keep thinking about. The castle is amazing. I wouldn't have been upset if the whole game was that location. With Ray Tracing it was one of the prettiest sights I've ever seen on a PC, which is another big selling point of this game. It's gorgeous. Now it's not perfect. Capcom has not been known to make the prettiest games and some old textures still managed to get through to the finished product somehow... But THAT RAY TRACING THO! I was getting 120 fps in the castle with max ray tracing @ 1440p. It's the kind of graphical presence that makes you yell at your mom to come see. I don't care what people say these graphics are a damn good reason to play this game if you're otherwise uninterested and sporting a card with RTX support.

While some of the bosses are literal pieces of uninspired ♥♥♥♥ the gameplay is what really keeps me coming back. This game stresses me out in the best way. Not in the way that Dark Souls did, it's not that hard or tedious. If you're like me and love survival games, if want to hit every shot to conserve every bullet and use as little resources as possible just in case... then this is going to be a pleasant task. Other people may find themselves unprepared and running in circles during boss fights. But that's kinda your fault if so!

I haven't felt the need to play a Resident Evil game since 2000 when Code Veronica came out. After that, with the release of the movies and a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games, my interest in the series faded. Even when RE4 reshaped the third person genre, I felt no desire to dive back into the convoluted mess that is the Resident Evil storyline. Yet when RE7 came out my interest was piqued again. Not enough to by the game, mind you, but enough to be interested in the direction it was taking the series. Then RE8 (Village) came out.

This game is pretty great all around. It feels great to play, the pacing is well done, and the sound design is pretty great. The storyline is honestly what kept me interested in the game and I have to say it's probably the best done of any RE game. It's streamlined enough to be mostly understandable (In the whole "I get the gist, but there's obviously deeper lore here" vibe) but still maintaining enough of that classic RE insanity with the plot to feel familiar. While it stays true to the traditional RE tropes (IE: Of course this boss mutates into a giant monster, why not? or Why does each boss have another part of a key that unlocks only the next area?), it still explores newer territory and pushes RE's boundaries a bit. Granted this is the second game in the style so many of these boundary pushes were probably done in RE7, but they still feel good here. My only real complaint about the game is that there is perhaps a bit too much forced direction in the game. While there certain is reason to backtrack and explore, it's minimal and truthfully the game is very direct in where to go. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, it does keep the story pretty tight and consistent, but it's something that I would have liked a little loosened up. There was never a point where I questioned where I was going or what I was doing (even without prompts) which, if we're being honest, should be at least part of the time in a horror game. Don't get me wrong, I don't think I'd enjoy an open-world RE game nor do I think the formula would work in that style. But just a little less hand holding would have been nice, in my opinion.

With all that said I believe this is a fantastic RE game, and a great horror game too. If you enjoy either I recommend playing the game at least once through. I don't know how much enjoyment you'd get out of replays as there's nothing new (outside a few unlockable weapons), but it's definitely worth the initial playthrough if nothing else. By the end of the game I think you'll have found the tale a rewarding one from a narrative perspective, and one with a bittersweet taste upon completion.

Finally, a Resident Evil that tops Resident Evil 4! What's there to say? It's basically Resident Evil 4, cranked up to 11. None of the formula has really changed, as far as fright factor and overall feel of the RE universe. I love this titles, where they break away from the overused T-virus thing. The revisiting of the super natural is always a refresh break, from the usual mutant zombies. The only bad thing that stems from clinging to the traditional RE layout is the "confined trail systems" aspect, that even Tomb Raider suffers from. That and the constantly overused "double back" system. Meaning, every route there is to take is visible off of the main path, but either barred, or locked, the first several times you may pass through the area, until you've either finished a particular objective, or found a proper tool, or key. In many ways this has been an annoyance, for decades. Resident Evil pioneered the model, and it was then adopted by, pretty much, ever survival horror game, including Dead Space. I'd like to see minimized in the future. Alan Wake managed to avoid this, namely by providing a number of different settings and somewhat more expansive areas, making the game feel more like it's continually moving forward, instead of used and re-used again. But I'll not complain because the game freaking hits every note beautifully. I was almost sh**ing my pants in several areas. Especially those segments where all you can do is run and hide, or wait for the boss to finish creepily patrolling a particular zone you were in, so you could move again. 

The game is Resident Evil 4, meets Alan Wake, meets Alien Isolation, meets Tomb Raider (reboot), meets Dark Souls...that's really not a bad combination.  The only other issue, which is probably bigger than the often re-used areas matter, is, you have a crap load of weapons you can collect and upgrade, but no place to keep them all. I would like for there to be a universal storage box, near the merchant. This way I could come back and swap out my gear, as needed. Not sell weapons, to fit other (new) weapons. That's a horrible model. If you're going to have twice as many weapons as there are inventory slots then we need storage containers, so we're not forced to ditch healing salves and ammo for more weapons. So, really? Overall? It's mostly just an inventory issue this game suffers. Especially since some items, like healing salves, don't stack but really ought to and other things that do stack, don't stack nearly enough, like sniper ammo. You're only able to hold 15 in a stack.

Resident Evil Village is a difficult game to rate. My overall impressions of this game were more positive than negative, but it's mainly the price that deters me. I think if you can get this game on sale it's worth it, but at $95AUD it's hard to recommend buying. The higher the price tag goes, the higher your standards should be for the product, and RE8 has some strange flaws for a AAA price tag game.

[b]Pros:[/b][list]

[*]RE8 delivers in spades on atmosphere. The graphics are great, so everything lives up to the creators' artistic vision nicely. You go from frigid, dilapidated village streets to opulent palace halls, spanning lakes and claustrophobic factory tunnels. The settings each feel thematically distinct and have some creative mechanics for keeping the gameplay fresh.

[*]This is then compounded with the incredible character design. Lady Dimitrescu obviously steals the show, but I thought Beneviento and Moreau were also super cool ideas executed perfectly both thematically and mechanically (as in, their zones were fun to play too). The voice actors for the above three characters did a tremendous job in bringing them to life, too.

[*]I like the inclusion of the shop. It lets the devs reward players for exploring / finding secrets, and allows killing zombies to feel like less of a net loss. However, this point leads into some of the game's problems. Because the game is now balanced around the fact that you get money for killing zombies, the game's foundational design choices differ to those of RE7. Combat is now less of a last resort and more of a way to use the vast resources you are offered. This shifts the game's tone and encounters a bit away from horror and towards action. That's fine by me, it still has a lot of both genres, but it's important to recognise what this does to the game experience (see below).[/list]

[b]Cons:[/b][list]

[*]"Good" characters (including Ethan) are clumsily written/voiced at best and hilariously bad at worst. Dialogue and story events involving allied NPCs are strangely paced. I don't want to give spoilers so I won't go into specifics, but without spoilers it's difficult to explain all the little bits of these scenes that add up to a bizarre feeling product. The one liners in particular feel cringey, especially when you consider the seriousness of Ethan's mission. Thankfully all of the above are fairly scarce compared to the rest of the game's writing/pacing.

[*]The devs' idea of endgame difficulty is just to swarm you with the zombie type that detects+dodges when your cursor is on their head. These enemies also dodge and gapclose in the same motion, and have no ending lag or recovery time when they jump across gaps. All of this adds up to infuriating stretches of combat where enemies are zipping up to you out of nowhere, dodging your bullets and biting you.

[*]This wouldn't be so bad if the vendor didn't have a finite supply of all items. If I could use the money I got from killing an absurd amount of zombies to buy more ammo/explosives, that'd be fine. Instead I waste all of my consumables clearing zones and then have a huge amount of money and nothing to spend it on (except underwhelming upgrades for guns I have no ammo for). I was never softlocked by running out of ammo, but I was flooded with cash and scraping for ammo  the further I progressed.

[*] This is a similar point to the above two, but I think worth an extra mention; an aftereffect of having no ammo for your guns is that new guns you find feel less interesting because you can't use them. I picked up a gun in the latter third of the game which I thought looked insanely cool, but I only got to use it maybe two times max, because the game was that stingy with ammo.[/list]

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

My biggest problem with this game is that it moves away from horror and towards action, but without fully thinking through the gameplay changes it makes to accomodate that transition. It floods you with enemies and "rewards" you with currency, but this currency ends up feeling lackluster at best and useless at worst. The combination of ammo scarcity and impractical currency then hampers secret hunting; what is in theory a great framework to reward players ends up feeling like basically nothing because of the points outlined above.

Resident Evil 8 does a lot of really cool stuff, and as a story experience I found it thoroughly enjoyable. But for $95AUD it's competing with Red Dead Redemption 2, or a cart of 3-6 great indie games, or even Biohazard which is only $40AUD. When you stack this game up against its competition, the flaws become a lot more noticeable. Get this game on sale, but think carefully before you buy it at full price.

Thankfully it shouldn't be a problem to get this game at half price since it seems to be constantly on sale. But I also don't agree with that business practice, particularly because there will be times when it's NOT on sale and people will see Overwhelmingly Positive reviews for a $90+ game. I'm reviewing this game at full price, not at sale price.

This game is absolutely fantastic. The developers clearly paid attention when they were remaking Resident Evil 2, and it really shows in this game. Almost everything that made Resident Evil 2 great is present here, but with a movement system that allows for strafing and backpedaling (i.e. you can move in a direction other than where you're looking), giving player motion a comfortably modern feel. The scarcity of ammo, the toughness of enemies, and the intermittent pursuit by enemies that cannot be killed, however, work together to keep up the pressure even as your weaponry advances and convey the idea that every shot matters. 

More than simple gameplay, however, the rich personality of the various villains, well-executed storytelling, and painstaking attention to detail make the game more than the sum of its parts. The environment, especially Castle Dimitrescu, is beautifully crafted, and the graphics engine really brings it to life: the HDR experience is above and beyond better than any other I've seen. Most games' colors look odd in HDR, sometimes too muted, or with too much one one color, but this game manages it beautifully by adapting to the changing light levels of the various environments and using darkness to maintain suspense.

[h1]A Lesson in Horror[/h1]

Resident Evil: Village is a bit like a Halloween-themed amusement park with a twist. It’s a ride, of course, and like most pop-up haunted houses, you feel mostly strapped in and safe. You go from one room to the next and are introduced to something new that pretends it’s dangerous. Maybe it’s a mummy? A zombie? But there’s no real fear that the chainsaw-wielding maniac in the next room will strike you, or that the large plush spider on the wall will actually move, but then again – you have an imagination. And sometimes your imagination cannot help itself. 

And that is where the twist comes in.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2717886804 
 
Horror aesthetics are easy to pull off. Indeed, it’s quite simple to slot in horrific tropes in place of true imagination-induced terror. Any amateur can do it. Simply cut and paste a few severed heads, some gore-splattered weapons, and a few creaky wooden floors. Done and done. But what really matters is how you knot the bow. How do you make your imagery mean something instead of feeling plastic? 

Immersion separates frightening, memorable moments from generic, on-the-rails horror sequences that throw loads of creepy imagery at players (with their fingers crossed and praying) hoping to get a reaction.

It’s also what separates good survival-horror from bad. 

Village checks appropriate boxes. It's alive and dangerous, adding context to all its aesthetics. Even when it’s not particularly horrifying, it’s still gratifying. And interesting. Which is far more valuable than any number of hokey jump scares and faux-spooky monsters.

[h1]Lupophobia[/h1]

Resident Evil: Village is a survival-horror, first-person shooter/adventure game that uses light RPG and weapon customization elements. It’s also the direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, and it improves on its predecessor in a litany of ways. 

For contrast, RE:7 (while still competent) relied heavily on aforementioned tropes. Chiefly, rural hillbilly American archetypes, which were popular horror iconography at the time of its release. The issue with depending upon established horror conventions is that you risk boxing your story in – which was exactly the case with the progenitor. Especially if the player doesn’t find the subject of unwashed, provincial bumpkins scary. Or worse, they find them unintentionally amusing (I’m guilty). 

Village widens the net and completely avoids limiting itself. The throughline is constructed around four or five different zones that each articulate a different thesis. Some areas work better than others, but because the variety is inherent (and everyone responds to different stimuli differently), there is more of a chance the game can produce [i]something[/i] that actually scares you. It’s also able to avoid feeling like a haunted house mishmash because every area sticks to its thesis and supplies context within the game’s narrative. Even if the story is usually silly, things with reason still feel three-dimensional. It’s an effort thing. And Village makes that effort. 

The game is also an absolute clinic on level design. 

Areas that the player will spend time navigating surround a nucleus. That nucleus serves as a safe zone. Well, it’s kind of safe; over the course of the game, the player clears it of enemies. Surrounding areas must be journeyed to via dangerous, corridor-shooting exterior environments, naturally replete with pop-up surprises and unnerving environmental storytelling. And these areas are loaded with unexpectedly dense combat encounters. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2717887156  

Once the areas are arrived at, the player enters (mostly) vertically designed sets that fold back on top of each other as each puzzle is solved, door is unlocked, or boss is destroyed. This gives the player a serotonin-induced sense of accomplishment as they progress, and it also attaches meaning to the game’s shortcuts. It’s extraordinarily well done.
 
Throwing arbitrary, spooky props at players usually isn’t enough to horrify them. And it’s the hardest lesson survival-horror creators must learn: imagery and metaphor must have nuance because that’s what makes them scary.

Everything in Village is mostly deliberate, serves a purpose, and feels earned. 

[h1]A New Kind of Terror[/h1]

The story is doltish as all Resident Evils, and indeed most horror-based narratives, tend to be. However, it far from equals the goofiness that ran amuck through the franchise in its middle years. Village is more grounded. Even when the story beats are not connecting, it still never gives up on them. Particularly in how it frames its themes. 

Whether the story is good or bad is immaterial to the main point: Village tries earnestly to tell one.

You take control of Ethan Winters who is searching for his infant daughter. Village uses the potential trauma of him losing his daughter as the main articulation point for the psychological (and occasionally physical) terror it presents. Which means there’s plenty of baby- and familial-themed horror front and center, but it dodges the “boxed-in” vibe of its predecessor by littering the world with a large variety of other tropes. But these tropes hold their own. Yes, it’s true that many enemies you find will bear similarities to those commonly found within existing Resident Evil titles, but they manage to behave in a manner that is slightly different from expectations. With little effort, Village employs enemies and combat scenarios that feel less familiar, and because of that, more dangerous.

Resident Evil is at its worst when it goes big. At the game’s expense, large enemies, with large hit boxes, that need to be dealt with in a large way, do occasionally sprout up. This tends to happen most often during climaxes or narrative-pivotal encounters. It’s disappointing, but it's not unexpected. And yet, they still created one large creature in particular that horrified me in an entirely novel way. 

It’s commendable that this Resident Evil manages to do the things the series is weakest at, better.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2717887002 

Village's characterization is solid, unexpected, and welcomed. The game features a large cast of characters. And a few show a surprising amount of depth considering the genre. Villains are themed appropriately to the environment in which you encounter them. They never distract either – you get just enough of them and their motivations to keep their presence additive to the overall experience. There are enough layers that, even though it’s not award-worthy depth, you’re still able to reasonably understand how they might behave within the framework of an encounter. 

This means the script is being honest, and perhaps more astonishingly, you’re paying attention to it. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Resident Evil: Village is immersive, fresh, and beautiful. 

It delivers the thrills you expect, along with many you wouldn't, through incredibly deft level design. It’s important, too, as it broadened the series’ expectations by improving on its already famous attributes. And, foremost, it’s a blueprint on how to construct first-person survival-horror games going forward by effectively lacing imagery with reason.

The story is quite silly at times. But the game deserves credit for anchoring narrative gravity to beat changes and character interactions to the point that most of its narrative atrocities can be pardoned, and in many cases, enjoyed. This defaults as a net positive, as the consumer will rightfully wield low expectations anyway. 

Results are undeniable. This is one of the better Resident Evil games. And a marked elevation for the genre. 

The series is in good hands. Hopefully they stay attached. Wink.

One of the most incredible story-driven games I have ever played. It's a perfect follow up to Resident Evil 7 and uses so many story elements from it that it enhances the experience of it's predecessor upon a second playthrough, now knowing things that Village unveiled. Almost all of the sections are fun, creative and fresh, and the puzzles are well integrated into the gameplay. I don't understand why Redfield went through another design change, but his place in the story is enough to enjoy his role, but not so much that it takes away from what is supposed to be Ethan's story.

Ethan is a well done character. [spoiler]As a random dude in RE:7 thrust into a world he had no hand in creating that persevered to the very end. His death too (though is he actually fully dead? I doubt it) was a gut punch that actually gave me pause, the emotions of the characters were very well conveyed at the end.[/spoiler] My only gripe with him is that he's a bit dense for someone that canonically solves all these complex puzzles. I think the community gives him a bit too much of a hard time about it, because most people wouldn't be of sound mind in his situation either, but why did he [spoiler]just go along with everything the Merchant, Heisenberg and Dimitrescu said about Rose? The whole point of the game is getting her back and Ethan essentially hands her to Miranda by putting her parts in the altar.[/spoiler] But besides that, the characters are all awesome and engaging, especially Heisenberg and of course, Lady Dimitrescu. I'd be interested in how the story would have played out if [spoiler]Ethan had teamed up with Heisenberg upon his offer. The hints dropped about Heisenberg throughout the story leaned towards him being a potential ally, but Ethan throws it away saying 'You can't have my daughter!' despite him pretty much giving her to Miranda as I said before. Another example of Ethan not being the smartest, but at least we got an incredible boss fight with Heisenberg out of it.[/spoiler]

Something that improved from RE:7 was the variety of enemies. The last title featured the bosses, Molded, and that's about it. Village has only a slight bit more variety, [spoiler]with the bosses, sub bosses, Lycans, the zombie maid things,  Heisenberg's cyborgs, and variants of most of them,[/spoiler] but it's spaced out enough to spice up the combat when it starts to get repetitive.

However, not everything improved between 7 and Village. I do wish there were a couple extras in the game that had other perspectives, like what RE:7 did with The End of Zoe and Not a Hero DLC, but even without that, there were a lot of extra modes in 7 that added a lot of replay ability; Village lacks that for the most part. The Mercenaries is a fun mode, and it's certainly a blast to go back through the main story to complete all the challenges, use infinite ammo, etc, though a couple more small mode would have been a welcome addition

Overall, this game deserved it's GOTY nomination at the Game Awards, and should've won it in my opinion, but at least it won the Steam Awards GOTY. 9.5/10

Ethan just is not as good of a character as Leon. As a newcomer to Resident Evil, only getting started with the release of 7 (Biohazard), I was really excited to see what this game had in store.

I was not disappointed.

After replaying 7 to death, completing it to the most perfectionist state possible and catching up to date with the lore of the series so far, I wasn't sure which direction Village was going to take me. But I felt ready for the experience nonetheless.

This is an absolutely fantastic game. On a more powerful and reliable PC unlike mine you're in for absolutely stunning visuals and graphics, enough so to stop and take a look at every minor detail carefully crafted by Capcom. Storywise you play as Ethan Winters, the protagonist of Resident Evil 7, back once again as your everyday "everyman". The trials and tribulations you face within the game are well done, the characters come to life and the nature of the plot keeps you gripped and entertained.

I felt easily engaged and placed in Ethan's shoes throughout the course of this game, running through on Hardcore before unlocking the Village of Shadows difficulty. It had so much depth and an insane amount of challenge, something really refreshing to see in a recent triple A title.

I won't spoil the story elements as I believe everyone should play this fantastic game for themselves. Ups, downs, even a few moments of humour and a gripping lore that will keep you entertained and interested as you make your way through the snowy depths of the village and elsewhere.

The gameplay is an interesting new mix of survival horror, showing the prowess and development of your character since the previous game in more confident gunplay and crafting elements, giving you the tension but also power once you've established yourself and your ammunition stocks, weapon upgrades and more. On your first run through, you'll experience the horror - subsequent playthroughs, you can challenge yourself and really test your FPS abilities within the game. It's made going for speedruns, which I've begun attempting since playing (current PB is a 2:25:04 on VoS NG) a whole load of fun and adds a great amount of replay-ability. 

I love this game. The ending was one of the very few times in recent years that a piece of entertainment media (since Gears of War 3!) had me emotional and empathetic for it's characters, while keeping me engaged, interested, and bewildered throughout the whole game.

11/10, I can't wait to see what happens next. I highly recommend this game to anyone, previous fans of Resident Evil or not.

After a dubious remake of RE3 and a series of weird design decisions that marred RE7, Capcom absolutely nailed it with Resident Evil Village. It's an easy 9.5/10. 

Honestly, I think the last single-player game to engage me like RE Village did might have been Bioshock--and that was more than a decade ago. To say I was impressed would be a serious understatement.

Everything about RE8 just works. The graphics are gorgeous, the setting is memorable, the pacing is perfect, and the general gameplay loop is pure joy. The game has notes of RE1, RE4, and RE7, all of which are woven into the experience in a way that highlights the strengths in each of those titles while leaving out the frustrations and weaknesses.

In fact, it generally seems Capcom has (finally) made the effort to identify and fix the glaring problems that have long held the RE series back.

For example: 

-They toned down the frustrating and unnecessary inventory-management aspect of the game by giving players a reasonable (and upgradeable) amount of space. They also separated key and treasure items out from the rest of the inventory so you don't have to choose between ammo and a dead bird on a key.

-They got rid of the sloppy, inaccurate control scheme from RE7 and allowed your character to walk and run and turn at the speed of a normal human instead of forcing you to play as someone who controls like a crippled old dude who just survived a plane crash.

-They removed frustrating puzzles in favor of more straightforward ones that still require thought but do not require YouTube videos, guides, or hours of time to solve.

-They added an economy and upgrade system that gives the player a smooth sense of progression, an actual reason to explore and look for treasures, AND a motivation to kill enemies at the same time. Resources are provided generously enough that you can almost always afford something that will make you stronger, but scarce enough that you have to work for the really big upgrades. 

-They dropped the caricatures and added interesting characters that you might actually remember for more than 10 minutes after the credits roll, and gave each of these characters a unique, memorable location that fits their personalities and backstories. These locations makes RE7's plantation feel like stale bread by comparison.

-They managed to keep pacing tight throughout the game by striking the perfect balance between linearity and exploration, recursive gameplay, and experimentation. 

-Best of all, they managed to write a story that is interesting, thoughtful, and even emotional at times. Hell, they even managed to put together a fun and satisfying ending sequence that you'll actually WANT to play instead of trying to rush through it as you repress the urge to uninstall the game (looking at you, RE7).

Truthfully, I struggle to even come up with any serious complaints about RE Village. I guess I could point out that the game's opening 30 minutes or so aren't the strongest, some areas are a little more amazing than others, and there are a handful of scenes that contain unnecessarily gratuitous violence. I also could have lived with the "labyrinth" puzzles, and there are few relatively unimaginative mini-boss fights scattered throughout the story. But these are tiny bumps on an otherwise immaculate road, and they certainly don't tarnish the overall experience.

In short, RE Village is fantastic. It's one of the best single-player games I've played for many years, and it's one that I'll remember for a long time. It deserves the praise and GOTY awards it has received and is well worth your time and money. If you haven't played it yet, you should.

Okay,

I know that I am going to probably get a little toasted (or a lot maybe) for this review, but I can stand the heat.

Let me say upfront, the last Resident Evil game I played was RE 2 (the original, not the reboot) and I have never watched any of the Resident Evil movies. That should have been my first clue not to purchase this game. I know I am dating myself and that's okay too.

Game of the year 2021, yeah? Not so much in my opinion. Strictly speaking, probably a middle of the road video game. Graphics are good but not excellent. The PC gaming rig I used to play it is an Alienware R12, I9, 32 GB ram with an NVIDIA 3090 video card. Not the very best rig but nothing to sneeze at. Let me get to the review. Also, let me state that this is the first review I have EVER written for a video game on Steam or anywhere else for that matter. My feeling is if I buy the game that is the best review, words are just words. Also, I feel that a review is needed to warn others of the frustration they will encounter as I did. I could not make sense of the game until my daughter explained the history of the game and why the characters were the way they are presently. 

********************************************************************************************************
THERE ARE SPOILERS IN THIS REVIEW, SO PLEASE IF YOU WANT TO PLAY THE GAME WITHOUT KNOWING SOMETHING ABOUT IT, PLEASE STOP NOW!
********************************************************************************************************

Does the player need to play RE 7 prior to playing this game? Absolutely, period; end of sentence. I was so frustrated by the events in the game that I even asked Steam for a refund even after playing for 12 hours knowing that they would probably refuse, but you don't know until you ask. Why would I ask for a refund? The Village as a video game did not make any sense to me. Two examples, 

In the beginning of the game, Ethan has three fingers from his left hand bitten off and is able to:
1. Survive.
2. Wrap the wound and with some help of some chemicals, not die.
3. Not be in any pain.

At one point Ethan has his right hand chopped off and is able to:

1. Walk around with it while bleeding.
2. Not die.
3. Reattach the limb with the help of some chemicals and presto, good as new.

At this point I started to believe that Ethan was the undead. Not a zombie or vampire but not human. Turns out I was right. 

Other issues:

1. When Ethan is attacked, which occurs quite a bit and needs health restored, he pours the 'chemical' over his hand. The same a fore mentioned hand that had the three fingers bitten off. Why doesn't he just drink the 'chemicals'?
2. When opening large double doors and other doors with handles. There are times when the fingers that where bitten off reappear making you think, maybe they grew back.
3. The Duke. I mean the Duke just appears in the most convenient of places. In the village square, the castle, at the sacrificial site. the elevator (in an elevator?)  and just happens to have on hand the things that Ethan needs. Guns. ammo, health, food and can also make improvements to said weapons. It seems the Duke will buy anything that Ethan finds, which is also unusual.
4. Closed maps were very hard to navigate. Tasks had to be completed, sometimes it appeared in a specific order, before progress could be made. 
5. Investigation of objects in your inventory that would or could be broken down or combined should have been made more obvious. I spent a very long time in the first castle because I did not know the stone in the ring I was carrying was the eye of an woman in a door and once the eye was inserted, the door would open and the story could progress. Very frustrating.   

I know there is supposed to be a 'willful suspension of disbelief', like when watching a movie or television show or reading a novel. This video game went so far past my ability to do that, that the immersion one is supposed to feel was completely gone or never started for that matter. Some of this is just plain silly and I found myself saying that out loud while I was playing. Good video games (all of the Half-Life series including VR, Left for Dead, Max Payne 1 and 3, Gears of War 1) one is so immersed in the game play that it can be shocking when the real world invades into the video game world, which is sometime very disappointing. The point I am trying to make is that I was never 'immersed' in the game. It felt more like I was back in college or high school trying to finish a horrible term paper on a subject that no one liked. 

Normally, I gauge how good a game is by knowing that eventually I will play through the game again in the future and be looking forward to it. I am just glad to be finished with this one.

Can I recommend this game to others, Generally no. Specifically for Resident Evil fans who have a good knowledge of at least RE 7 and the general RE history, absolutely.
