I was highly critical of the game when its demo came out. Especially the village scenario seemed convoluted by cutscenes and cringy characters. However, the final game proved to be much much better than the demo let on.  To be sure, the game is at its best when your character – Ethan Winters – just shuts the hell up and doesn’t act like your standard American hero. You also have to cope with all the Romanians speaking perfect American English, and don’t even have an accent. 

Apart from that the game is full of incredible moments and THICK immersion. The animation work is superb, the reloading of guns is on par with MW19 (not a joke) and a late game mission is very reminiscent of MW19, too. I don’t blame Capcom. MW19 is one of the best looking, best sounding and straightforward shooters in recent years. So why not take some notes from it? 

People complained about this game being too heavy on action scenes. I don’t know when they played and on which difficulty but playing it after dark and on Hardcore, I was more than once frightened thanks to the stunning set design/world building and the absolutely incredible sound design. Everything that looks like it should be creaking is creaking, a giant waterfall doesn’t suddenly cut out when you enter a big mansion but becomes a constant background sound. Despite the world being so dead due to monsters having killed everyone, I have rarely visited a world so alive and breathing. RE: Village will suck you right in if you let it and if you have a rather high tolerance for logical errors.
 
There is indeed a lot of action to be had (and thank God for that) but the game is a miracle of pacing done right. In fact, the pacing made me think of a good RPG. By which I mean that the general mix of action scenes, cutscenes, talking, shopping, looting, exploring is very similar to RPGs. There is a lot of pure originality also. The second boss fight and the puzzles leading up to it, for example, don’t include any guns at all. The monsters are very good. From the werewolves that were to be expected to steampunky cyborgs, I never got bored of one enemy type. 

That I don't even bother finishing most games anymore because I get bored of them, I marvel at the fact that I went and played this game and nothing else for 7 days or so straight. And I wouldn't mind playing it yet again come next Winter.

Tl; Dr: Didn't like the demo at all and saw in Village yet another proof of a crumbling AAA gaming industry. I'll readily admit that I was completely wrong with that assumption. The tight pacing, the incredible variation of monsters, weapons and levels, the thick immersion, the superb animations and graphics and sound design all make that this game indeed deserves an overwhelmingly positive rating.

This is another first person RE, following the events of RE7. The setting and story are very thematically different from 7. This game is far more in line with classic RE goofiness. The awkward dialogue returns. Combat is a lot more central to the gameplay of this one, compared to 7 where hiding and running from enemies is typically preferential. There's a little bit of that in this game in the beginning and middle.

As for why it's like 4, the gunplay is fantastic, the weapons are satisfying to use and upgrade. There are unlockables for completing certain challenges, the formula for the story in general is similar to 4, with enough differences to keep it fresh. It was very nostalgic playing this in an odd way.

Same inventory management from 4 is back, almost exactly like 4's but with an annoying downgrade, you can't move an item into an item to move that secondary item out of the way. It's a minor inconvenience but it's there. Very happy to have inventory tetris back.

Collectibles, treasures, side areas to explore. 2 collectibles are devilishly placed, so if you're a completionist keep your eyes peeled even in moments you don't think the devs would be so evil as to place something for you to miss.

This is an extremely good Resident Evil game. 
First and foremost if someone tells you “this is not what the original resident evil were” the guy never played the games. This has everything you want from a RE, if you are a classic fan or If you enjoyed the more “shooting” recent ones. Unironically this game has more in common with the entire RE franchise series and not with the 7th chapter.  
Resident Evil 7 made me lose every hope for this franchise (you can enjoy reading my review on it).
This game simply stylish on the entirety of RE7. The village and the dungeons are fantastic, well realized and with that north-eastern Europe horror vibe, which is delightful after swamps and insects. There is a lot of different places, spooky castle with beautiful women, madhouse, a lake with a monster (and that’s not the only RE4 stuff we will see) and the last levels are simply astonishing on the realization and ambience (but no spoiler).
Let’s just say that industrial horror is not something you see every day, and here is done perfectly.
The characters are all around interesting (and we have more Chris. A LOT more), the story is much more interesting compared to RE7 and it’s an half point between the classics and the new “mainline”. It’s not even a spoiler, there will be a RE9 tailored around stuff that happens in the end of the game. It’s great but I don’t want to guess considering the modern times.
Even if we have another Ethan run this time we have more shooting (not on the scale of RE5, let’s say we are on a RE classic tier), a smiley weapon vendor with upgrades and stuff to craft and find around. Treasures are back, everywhere also with the gems to shoot on the ceiling. Also points and unlockables are back again with a lot of stuff.
And mercenaries mode. I just want to appreciate that we have a mercenaries mode here as fps.
Unfortunately the puzzle stuff is very basic, we don’t have electric power switcheroos, statue guessing or pumps levels, everything is extremely easy but there are a lot of them. Not the best but not the worst. This is really the only thing I want to point cause I have to point the only thing I would like to be better.
The game has a ton of citations from the old RE, story, gameplay and even on the boss fights (the final parts are an absolutely crescendo of wackiness), dialogues and weapons. I don’t know how they do it but they have integrated spooky stuff, shooting, puzzles and some idiotic stuff from all the franchise, mixed everything and served an extremely good game.
This is a very good title which keeps pulling the franchise out of the mud. This time they really know what they were doing and what the fan wanted. For the future, hope for the best, prepare for the worst.

Resident Evil Village is another Ethan Winters journey but this may be the most important one yet. The story begins a few years after the events of Resident Evil 7 following Ethan Winters, who is now living many miles away from Louisiana at a humble home with his wife, Mia, and daughter, Rose, in Europe. The game does a decent job of filling the players in about Ethan's last journey so it isn't necessary to have played the previous title in the series. However, unlike Resident Evil 7, I would not go as far as calling this one a horror game. It does have its fair share of jump scares, ghouls, and zombies, but it is better positioned as an action thriller. And there's plenty of action thriller in this game. The game is divided into four stages where Ethan has to venture into a different area in the map that comes with its own unique themes and presence. Although compared to the first stage of the game the others felt far less significant. The biggest strengths of this game are how it can build tension, the supreme sound stage, and its pace. There is seldom a dull moment as this game puts Ethan through one level of hell to another. The game is at its worst when it comes to dialogues, especially with Ethan. Some of Ethan's responses to everything that is going around him are so poorly delivered and written. However, the performances of some characters like the Duke, Lady Dimitrescu, and Heisenberg were outstanding and made engaging with them that much memorable. There was a lot riding on this game as it sought to conclude the chapter of Ethan Winters. Fortunately it delivered convincingly and I feel content with the way it ended. Overall, the strengths of this game far outshine the weaknesses so it is well worth a recommendation.

[h1] not my favorite resident evil, but far from being the worst either. [/h1]

both thematically and gameplaywise, the latest RE is as far from the early survival horror classics again as a zombie from a Harvard degree in quantum physics, but that is anything but a bad thing. overall, it is much less scary than RE 7 was, but there are a few areas that will make your heart racing as well as one or two well placed jumpscares. with its medieval eastern european setting and werewolf-like enemies it has more of a classical and rather dusty, hackneyed and tame horror vibe, in contrast to the relentless grindhouse horror of RE 7, nevertheless people who are easily scared or startled should avoid RE 8 like an infection with the T-virus.

attentive RE fans will quickly notice that Village is basically one big reference to RE 4, at least when it comes to the setting and story. in terms of leveldesign and atmosphere, especially the earlier parts of the game strongly feel like „back to the roots“ and have that certain „rural“ RE 1 / RE 4 vibe.

The grafics haven’t changed much since RE 7, nevertheless my laptop was not strong enough to max it out on Ultra settings. i went with a healthy mix of high and medium settings, and the game ran perfectly smooth during my entire playthrough, without any crashes, glitches or severe stuttering. still, it manages to look quite impressive even when not maxed out due to the huge care for detail and it is very fun to explore the detailed and extremely atmospheric environments. The sound is top-notch as well and the game has a very high level of production value and overall polish on the technical side. gameplaywise, the gunplay is very satisfying and the puzzles are well designed, not too easy and not too hard.

but like every other RE game, Village is not without its flaws of course. survival horror was definitely toned down again in contrast to the last couple of games and Village feels much more like a slow-paced first person shooter with slight survival horror elements, rather than a pure genre title. the lycans appear very intimidating at the start, but ultimately turn out to be pretty slow and weak losers, who can be dispatched very easily with two or three well-placed headshots. later enemies are a bit more threatening, but nothing that a small mine or skillfully thrown pipe bomb couldn’t adequately handle. Village is one of the easiest and most accessible RE games so far and during the roughly 9 to 12 hours long story, seasoned RE veterans will barely face any true challenges here.

speaking of the story, in typical RE fashion it is a mixed bag. like most other RE games, the narrative starts out tense and mysterious, then quickly looses steam during the middle parts before finally collapsing into a clusterf*ck of contrived plot twists at the end to forcefully tie it in with the already completely messed up canon of the previous games. even on a micro level, the story reaches new heights of stupidity, for example when the main character gets his hand completely cut off, but then literally just glues it back on himself with a healing potion, not even wondering in the slightest why all the severed bones, nerves and muscles work completely fine again not even five minutes later. When he gets captured, his enemies (being the completely moronic imbeciles who they are) don’t take his weapons away and after his quick escape all the bad guys are like: „jeeeeez how could he have gotten away?“ It‘s the completely illogical moments like those which are just too idiotic even for a Resident Evil game, that simply break the immersion at two or three points, despite the fancy grafics and smooth gameplay.

but in the end RE 8 is once again an amazing game which will please long-time series fans and newcomers alike. Definitely worth a buy.

I was a big fan of RE7 and hugely looking forward to playing this one. A lot of people seem to love this game, which is great, but to me that while fun to play for a while it was a very inconsistent and unmemorable experience and found maybe half the game was a bit of a slog to get through. Was definitely very surprised when it started picking up GOTY accolades! The highlight for me was the highly-marketed Castle Dimitrescu section of the early game, but shortly after this I felt the game struggles to keep up the same quality until the final area.

It's hard to deny how incredible this game looks. The attention to detail in the environments is really second to none. The enemy design and variety is also a step up from 7, and some great performances from the cast make it a very immersive experience to play.

The way it plays is essentially a combination of RE7 and RE4. As such, it is more action-oriented than 7 and though RE is always marketed this way, survival horror this is not. I never got to the point where I even really thought about my ammo stocks and it's a similar story with the inventory, which seems to combine the worst aspects of 4 and 7. It is so ridiculously big (unless you plan on carrying every single weapon variant) and you even get an unlimited bucket to keep all your crafting items in. This breaks any concept of inventory management in the game: some people will see this as streamlining, while others would view it as a dumbing-down. The combat is decent but I found the enemies to be very spongy and didn't really respond consistently to being shot.

It is scary in a couple of places, but overall the tension has been taken down several notches, something that has been well publicised as intentional by the developers. Other than the opening 10-15 mins when I wasn't sure what to expect, I did not feel any of the dread that 7 made me feel for its first half. Again, this will be a positive or negative depending on your taste.

The game gives the illusion of being exploration-based, but this isn't strictly true. It's actually very linear, feeling a bit like a ride. You'll often pass a locked door which you can only open from the other side and the game uses these to create the path through an environment, which feels a bit retro in 2021. Bits of the village are gradually unlocked each time you go back, yes, but most of the time in the main story path there's literally only one way you can go. There is no need to search too hard for puzzle items: you are fed these along the way, which will then often be used in an all too simple puzzle 10 mins later along your route. There are however some optional paths to take to collect treasure, which I thought was a nice addition, but these are entirely skippable and not part of the main gameplay loop.

The last thing I wanted to touch on was the story, which is obviously a very subjective topic. I'm normally a fan of the convoluted RE lore, but this felt a step too ridiculous to me, with gaping plot holes and some very questionable character behaviour which just made very little sense. RE7 and RE8 feel a lot like they were created similarly to the Disney Star Wars trilogy, where a different director with a totally different vision comes along for the sequel, and as a result I don't feel like they line up well.

Overall it was a OK game while it lasted, but it lacks cohesion - a symptom of the fact that Capcom are still not sure what kind of game they want Resident Evil to be, and are attempting to please both action and horror camps for the most profit. Unlike the truly great Resident Evils (ie. REmake, RE2R, RE4), I don't feel it offers a consistently good experience to make me want to play it again any time soon, but it's worth the initial playthrough to experience the good moments.

If you liked RE2, RE4, RE7... you might not enjoy this game. Some Resident Evil entries go balls out with action, while other focus on survival and resource management. This one picks an an awkward in between. For the most part, the game only sends a few enemies at a time at you. This works in RE2 or RE7 due to their strain on resources and backtracking nature. Do you kill the enemies now and use valuable ammo, but make this point safe for the future? Or do you try to slip by and risk having to use a rare health item? The spare monster encounters in Resident Evil: Village don't really prompt this choice since ammo is plentiful, the inventory is large and the game is rather linear so you most likely won't need to face them again even if you don't kill them. 

Resident Evil 4, has a more lenient inventory system and is rather linear, but it uses that to be a roller coaster ride, constantly throwing intense and interesting combat encounters at the player. RE:8 simply doesn't do that for the vast majority of the time, and as such doesn't really live up to the spiritual successor of RE:4 it was hyped up to be. The closest the game gets to this is in it's version of mercenary mode, which is in my opinion the best part of the game, and made me really regret the potential this game's systems had. 

The bosses, like most of the game, have stunning visual designs but are very bland gameplay wise. The final boss is the only one that comes across as interesting in any capacity in that regard. On that point, they're rather emblematic of this game as a whole: The admittedly phenomenal and very well polished presentation covers up there's not really much there. I had a decent time the first time around, but where other entries shine with repeat playthroughs that showcase their depth, this one only grows more boring and frustrating as you realize how shallow it is.

Get it on a sale if you're interested in the story, but don't expect anything as good as RE2, RE4 or RE7.

My introduction to the Resident Evil series (i wasnt even alive when the early games came out) recently upgraded my PC and wanted something to flex my specs, really wasn't expecting to get into the game really wanted it as more of a tech demo but quickly got hooked from the start. 

First of all, this game is absolutely f--king gorgeous, all the models seem so lovingly made (with the exception of some mob drops) and this being my first introduction to the "examine item" mechanic in RE games I spent far too much time looking at every little thing. The npc facial animations are insane, fabric physics are unbelievable and every environment feels like a lovingly crafted art piece of its own style. Each different portion of the game has a distinct feel to it visually and game play wise and I really appreciated the art direction above everything, very inspirational. Optimization is pretty good, everything maxed out still got a consistent high frame rate (to be fair I cant tell for sure if it was the game or my overkill setup mmv) with the exception of the later game. There's some "spooky wires" that have fully modeled physics and would dip my fps and cause weird stuttering if I interacted with them, neat concept but mildly annoying when they're everywhere and you need to backtrack through them, nothing major very minor critique might be a different story if you're running it on the minimum specs. But again I cant stess enough just how engrossingly beautiful this game is from an artistic and performance point of view.

Gameplay is very exciting and engaging, I've heard a few fans of the old games critique this and now that this game has made me go back and check out the earlier titles I can understand the disconnect. This game feels much more like metro exodus than it does RE2/3, I think that's in it's favor personally but it depends on what you want out of it. The weapons look, sound, and feel amazing, combat is a blast and always feels gritty and highstakes. The duke is a fantastic character that adds a whole new element of motivation when encountering the spooks of the land, weapon upgrades, new weapons, and supplies can all be bought for money he'll happily pay you for enemy drops, and little treats can find/unlock along the way. Honestly something I really enjoyed about the game was the satisfaction of scraping by a chunk of the game and running back to duke with a stacked backpack knowing I'll be able to go nuts and get all the little things I've lusted after. The cooking system is fine, just didn't find getting the supplies too engaging compared to other parts of the game but permanent stat increases for some exploring are welcome. This barter loop makes the game feel like a horror game that's tempered by rpg game play ala oblivion that's a really nice way of ensuring you're never burnt out on "LOUD SPOOKY AHHH"  it's something I'm really missing playing through RE2.

The sound design is amazing and the spacial audio is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrifying, wear good headphones and turn the game up, that's all I'll say.

The characters are very neat and I really enjoyed the voice acting of most everyone, the story is very compelling but not so controlling that it takes away from game play. It really feels like they wanted to make 4 or 5 different games with different archetypal characters and just said f--- it why not put them all into one, which is something I wouldn't believe would be good unless I had played this.

Really my only critiques are that the fov is locked and makes navigating the world feel a little disorienting at times, and that on pc a lot of the controls feel like they were lazily remapped from console but not nearly as bad as some other ports I've played. The boats are also goofy as hell and feel like I'm wearing a boat shaped shirt instead of actually driving a boat, at times where you are supposed to go can be a bit confusing and require a lot of backtracking but I suppose that's part of the game's charm as well. 

Overall I absolutely got my money's worth and recommend this game to anyone, you do not need to be a fan of the previous games to enjoy this one, and if possible I'd highly recommend playing on max graphics in a nice comfy dark room with headphones. I'm very much not usually the type of person to play these types of games, and primarily play competitive games and don't often value the visuals and general atmosphere of games. So the fact that I got ravenously hooked not just to the game play but the atmosphere of this game speaks volumes about it's quality. 
One of the most compelling titles I've played in recent years, have not felt this much magic in the world of a game since my childhood, could not recommend enough and highly anticipate the next release.

It's a nice addition to the RE line-up, even if it's a mostly short game.
Compared to RE7, which honestly felt weird as a mainline series, it does better to keep in ties with the rest of the Resident Evil games as a full on continuation rather than coming out as a completely different experimentation for the series. Also loved the fact it added in the RE4 & 5 elements into it making it feel like a naturally progressing game. You didn't need to rely on certain weapons for too long while also being able to alternate between the best of both worlds.

In terms of story, I'll keep it brief in spoilers.
[spoiler] Ethan going out of his way to save Rosemary and successfully doing so, only to end himself to save his family is heartbreaking. However, it also makes sure there's a nice conclusion to Ethan's story as a whole while continuing forward with the next generation. The ending of the game is the first time I've seen Resident Evil push itself to not leaving a semi-hopeful ending, meaning there's more coming than we realize. I can't wait for the next installment and curious to see if Chris is even working in the field anymore. [/spoiler]

The game overall is more of a 7.4/10 game however. I would say 7 exactly, but all the little extra content makes it up for replay value. Having Mercenaries return is also a great mode to see feature back. There's not much incentive to replay through the game again other than achievement hunting or beating the game through a higher difficulty, which is a bit of a shame because most Resident Evils are like that.

I'm hoping in the future they add some extra return content to the stories as the whole replay for the sake of a better time or getting more of a challenge is becoming stale. Imagine being able to find some extra little notes or finding another ending because of some context you could've only found after beating the main story (that online sources wouldn't fully be able to help, only hint at) that allow you to return to the main game and find, signifying a greater significance to the plot and providing more details for what exactly happened. I can dream, but more than likely won't happen.

An amazing by-the-book survival horror game that delivers everything you'd expect and more! 

Village looks good, plays good, feels good and features a surprising amount of optional side content for you to explore and/or beat! New set of characters is mostly interesting, my favorite being Heisenberg and Dimitrescu's daughters (yes that's right, tall vampire lady is overrated, I said it, though her voice actress absolutely kills it nevertheless!). 

Locations you'll explore are all tied to this intricate main village area, which you'll roam through several times during the campaign, and uncover more bits and pieces as you progress. Otherwise locations mostly boil down to old dilapidated houses, castles, mineshafts, factories or even a massive lake reservoir area!

As I said before, perhaps the most surprising part of the game for me was how actually non-linear it is and how much side content it offers. There's tons of little bonus puzzles, hidden secrets and treasure to be found. Also tiny "treasure hunts" where you'll find a clue in the form of a message or photo and then have to piece it together to find an especially rare item. There's also a massive amount of items in general. Weapons, weapon attachments, upgrades, food, consumables, crafting materials, various types of ammo for said weapons. There's really a *lot* to find here.

Main campaign sits at a perfect length of about 10hrs. Story is good, didn't have any particular issues with it, aside from good ol' Ethan being as dull of a character as he was in RE7, but I guess that was expected, him being the "player" character. Chris was a little cheesy at first, but turned out okay towards the end. Mia wasn't annoying unlike in RE7. The four lords, our antagonists, were also mostly interesting. Though Lady Dimitrescu and Heisenberg clearly outshine the rest in both story and design. Miranda is a rather dull antagonist, but she doesn't have much screentime anyway.

Perhaps my only little issues with the game is the many graphical glitches I've experienced during my playthrough. I've played on medium-high settings and I've experienced a lot of texture pop-ins, model pop-ins and also unloaded textures/models. They were very frequent, and it seemed to happen more in certain areas. Then the horribly slow mouse sensitivity, where even on the highest setting, the mouse is simply still way too slow for an FPS game. Lastly I also wasn't a particular fan of the FOV, that wasn't modifiable either. The game has a fairly small FOV and it can be a bit hard to see stuff in smaller rooms, so you have to look around a lot, but then that becomes a pain aswell due to the low mouse sensitivity, so that was pretty annoying throughout. None of these issues killed the overall experience for me though.

It's a 9/10.

Resident Evil 8 is a game that builds on Resident Evil 7 in many ways besides the story.  The combat has evolved to be more inspired with some enemies that have harder to reach weak spots or flaws that are more easily detected after reading something. The Atmosphere has grown from the already rich-in-taste Louisiana swamp to a dilapidated European village and its surrounding castles and crypts, filled with little nooks and crannies to explore (and the graphics are top notch if you have the right specs). Some of the puzzles go above and beyond the my favorites from RE7 ([spoiler] The dollhouse basement where you have to dissect a wooden puppet of Mia and the Castle are both tricky and entertaining [/spoiler]). The horror is cranked up by several levels in the beginning with a bunch of clever tricks and utterly creative choices in a monster's design ([spoiler] Like that spawn from hell Fetus that will forever ruin the sound of a happy baby in my mind or the lycans in the village being these beasts of rage in the beginning [/spoiler]). Even some small things like customizing your weaponry and having a more defined sense of progression to egg you on has improved from Biohazard (I know the Duke got me). Resident Evil 7 walked so 8 could run. 

My favorite part is definitely the atmosphere and suspense. I have been conditioned from RE7 to treat every ladder, corner, and door like there is something that is going to jump out at me. In almost every circumstance, you are at a disadvantage and you are very damn aware of it. You might be running low on ammo, you might be in the dark, you are being chased by something but your legs are incapable of running beyond a snail's pace. In the beginning, your pistol is as effective as a squirt gun, but you literally cannot live without it. Shotguns double dog dare you to talk up to a zombie and blow its brains out at the cost of you being closer for it to strike. This game's environment of perpetual danger can require the player to think on their feet and be oh so careful.

This game, however, does stand a few flaws. I'm just gonna say it: Ethan Winters' dialogue and delivery sucks. Dude slays an Eldrich horror on the quest to save his daughter and the best he can come up with is "You're the one who's cursed." But I guess that is a sort of pothole that comes from it being imported from Japan to a different language. I also think the keybinding is a bit odd, but I guess the loss of full control and the doing-away of the player's conditioning from other first person games can add to the suspense in a tight spot (especially when you press ctrl when you want to crouch but end up blowing a bottle of health). This is all small compared to the most glaring issue

[spoiler] [h1]The End[/h1] [/spoiler]

[spoiler] The problem with many horror movies and games, in my opinion, is that they easily run out of steam by the end. Resident Evil 8 starts to lose its luster around the Reservoir level (probably because the dollhouse level pushed the horror up to a maximum and some fat fish guy doesn't pale in comparison). In the beginning, I personally was jumping at every minor zombie that popped up, but by that point, I sorta became numb to basic scares. One major resurgence of fear was at Heisenberg's factory, which made sure you would run out of ammo while facing horrific monsters that have been crafted and experimented on with machinery (which you can tell the historical context behind (Dude is German)) but after that fight the fear was gone. Chris Redfield's mission was a complete 180 in feel, since you are already equipped with a lot of ammo for weapons that can mow down zombies that previously took like 6 clean shots to the head to kill per monster. Then we reach the final boss. This fight was pretty boring except for the cool background the fight takes place in. That's really all there is to say about the Miranda bossfight.[/spoiler]

Overall, this game was dope as ♥♥♥♥, and I would recommend it to people looking for a nice scare, I am looking forward to RE9 where Capcom will hopefully keep this momentum going. Take as much time as you need, devs.

The gunplay is fun. Weapon variety is present, but the end-game weapons are the clear winners here. 

NG+ is an option after completing the game, so you can go and try to max certain weapons and go for infinite ammo to take on the dreaded Village of Shadows difficulty.

Overall, I highly recommend this game. Probably GOTY 2021. Get in now especially while it's on sale.

Being someone who absolutely loves Resident Evil, this game is amazing. Resident Evil has been one of my favorite series growing up, and RE7 has to be my second, if not favorite game in the franchise. I couldn’t imagine a better sequel, the plot was great and everything linked together nicely, but there are things in the game play that counter that. Resident Evil Village, or RE8 is a little mixed for me, despite saying I recommend this game. I won’t lie, This game is a masterpiece but there are some things I would change, or wish was different. 
     Some things I liked were the continuation from RE7, which was amazing. I also enjoyed the castle, I just wished It was a lot longer. I liked the Duke, its defenently a cool new feature but I do feel like compared to the other games, I wasn't running around near death or trying to dodge due to no ammo. One big part of the Resident Evil series, in my opinion, Is trying to savor and search for supplies.
     I felt the game was a little too easy, puzzle and fights wise. I didn't have any bosses that took me more than first, or  second try to beat. i think the puzzles were less extreme than the previous games, but they were good.     The storyline was amazing, as well as the graphics and atmosphere of the game. I loved the ending as it sent me through different feelings. To me, this game wasn't scary either. Just as I thought, RE8 strays into a more action and fantasy area than the previous entry, which kind of makes me wonder why they even decided to do this under the Resident Evil moniker of all franchises. And although this series is not a stranger to jumping the shark and overeaching, RE8 still manages to pull it off quite nicely.

RE8 picks up a couple of years after 7, with Ethan and Mia married with a child who becomes the new center of the story. The game takes us to a very RE4 village but instead of ganados, we find lycans, giants, zombies, vampires and all other sort of very fantastical very not much of a Resident Evil bioweapon style enemies. And somehow, they manage to pull it off. As I mentioned before, the plot overreaches. Not gonna spoil anything, but let's just say that it ties itself with the previous games to give itself a reason for existence and for adding an insane quota of fantasy into the series. It doesn't entirely feel like and RE game because of it, but then again, after all the shark jumping the series has been known for, this comes out as somewhat acceptable. I buy it, what can I say...

Gameplay wise, it leans much more into action than it's previous entry. With RPG elements of course, crafting, and a more open ended world to explore, although retaining every element that has made the series style of map exploration. It tries to balance horror with action (again just like RE4) and even if it doesn't get to do it perfectly, which might offend the more classic fans of the franchise, it does the best it can juggling with both genres. RE8 it's not a scary game, but don't get me wrong, it can be terryfying from time to time: house Beneviento comes out of nowhere, and it's f****** scary man let me tell you that, being chase by Lady Dimitrescu is unnerving and the general atmosphere is enough to keep you on your toes; but you are gonna be much more prepared for most of it, it's harder to be left with no bullets in this one, and the general vibe of it and it's creatures, come out more of a startling vibe than a horror vibe. It is a startling game. It's definitively gonna startle you.

RE8 is a great game indeed, doing it's best to balance two genres and, albeit not having the most sublte of the stories, it still manages to keep you engaged and wondering what's next for the series. One of the best of the year for sure.

TL;DR: 
While visually stunning, RE8 delivers a weak story and misses the mark on most classic RE features like puzzles, inventory management and player path choice. Although this is a negative review, I’d recommend RE8 even to non RE fans with the caveat to only buy it on sale 50% off or more at this point. Read on if you want to specifically know why.

This review will be spoiler free, so you are welcome to read at any point of any subheading. Queue the save room music and the typewriter clacking sounds.

Basis of My Perspective: 
The Resident Evil franchise is something that I enjoy a lot. Personally, I have played nearly every RE game: RE 0-8, Revelations 1&2, Code Veronica, Outbreak, Resistance and the RE-makes 1-3. During my time with these games, I’ve gotten to see what makes for great versions of RE and what doesn’t. Now, this is also somewhat subjective mind you, but I think I have a good handle on what players want out of a RE game. Feel free to disagree with any of what I write in the comments below. If you keep it constructive & civil I may respond to you, but I don’t feed trolls. For the record, I played RE8 on the standard difficulty with a completion time of ~11-12 hours and about 5 hours of Mercenaries content. 

Critique of Pacing:
This game is super linear and it is one of my biggest gripes. It almost feels like it is on rails a good 80% of  the game. There is only ever one path, except for a couple of spots where you can monkey around for extra loot. Every other door you pass will be locked and only opened in one sequence. There is a lack of suspense due to this linearity. In most other RE games, a player is allowed to have a few options simultaneously available to them at all points of the game, except during the ending sequence. This is usually coupled with puzzles that a player is expected to deduce clues to and solve along their exploration. While RE8 allows you to double back, usually it is an irrelevant waste of time.

Critique of Puzzles:
Writing this part will be simple, much like the puzzles in RE8. One of the main appeals in the RE series for me is having to use problem solving skills at the strategic scale in combination with shooting skills at the tactical/situational level. This dual requirement of both skill sets is a key component of what makes a good RE game. In great RE games, I felt like I was using brains and brawn to take down some evil plot. It was like me and my character were out witting and out gunning some cabal of nefarious jerks. In RE8 the puzzles are so laughable that I only had trouble with 1 and that was because I was too distracted IRL to notice when I walked by the object in game. The protagonist in RE8 is no sleuth, the bad guys are just that dumb in this one. Disappointing.

Critique of Story (Still Spoiler Free):
The story for RE8 is only there for ticking boxes. The motivations for the antagonists in this game are never explained well and the explanations that are provided are very weak. Events just seem to happen and the protagonists respond reactively. The plot is very flimsy despite a decent chunk of cutscenes. I don’t think I can write more without spoiling something, so I’ll leave it here.

Critique of Inventory Management:
You almost always have enough space for everything. There is no struggle to pick and choose which guns to bring, you can have em’ all. This makes for a boring experience. Again, going back to deducing as you explore in the other RE games, typically your character isn’t allowed to carry everything. So, this means that you should be paying attention to what is likely up ahead and plan accordingly. Did you just come across a lab note and photo about some experimental bioweapon in the next room? Yeah, normally in a RE game, you’d have taken note of some weakness to acid or flame rounds, or possibly some freezing weakness in fight preparation. In RE8 you get these notes… after you just figured it out on your own by killing a version of whatever is lying dead in the previous room.

Another misstep is the crafting of items. In a world that strives for photorealism, everything appears as potentially scrap metal, or rusted scrap metal. Making it a component of some bullet formula is immersion breaking. On the fly ammo making with garbage from the environment that doesn’t take up inventory space is silly. Why even have a backpack with a grid layout when you make it meaningless? 

Critique of Visuals:
This is where RE8 shines. Like most new games, the tradeoff of better visuals for less substantiative gameplay has been made. The shading, textures, and especially the reflections of metallic/wet surfaces are spot on. It is truly a gorgeous game. For those interested, I ran the game 1920x1080 on a RTX 3060 on relatively high settings. 

Overall Critique:
Personally, I think that RE8 is a slightly above average game for its contemporaries, but only an OK RE game. I do not think it deserves accolades of any kind. It is my estimation that the bar is so incredibly low for games right now, that since this one came out fully completed and is not a total trainwreck, it stands out against the dismal array of other current offerings.

What RE8 tried to do was emulate RE4, but failed. The plot is too thin to not want to poke holes in it as you are playing. It relies on visual aesthetics to induce immersion, but when every other choice seems to somewhat break that immersion, it falls flat. As I sit here writing this review, I am contemplating whether or not to play RE8 ever again, or simply remove it from my hard drive. Honestly, my gut says it is too unappealing to try to play the game again. This is coming from someone who beat RE4 at least 3 times and played countless hours of mercenaries. 

Where RE4 shined RE8 misses. RE4 was more linear than RE8, but it had such better story lines, ammo management considerations, puzzles and special melee moves, that you kind of accepted the linearity as a method to keep the excitement up and not get bogged down in the searching/sleuthing. RE8 takes this linear approach, but then makes the main playable protagonist feel like a couch potato compared to Leon. RE4 also, adds this beautifully crafted, multilayered plot that is intriguing, albeit a bit campy. You knew why Leon was there, but what was Wesker and Umbrella up to? Was Ada a friend or foe? WTF is wrong with Salazar? There were questions you wanted answers to and were willing to shoot endless quantities of mobs in the head for. RE8 does not have this.

Another example of the failure to understand why RE4 works is the Mercenaries game mode. RE4’s Mercenaries mode was a fast paced, white knuckle, explosion filled, roundhouse kick to the face of excitement. RE8’s Mercenaries mode has you waiting for floppy death animations to stop so that you can pick up all of the dumb coin drops that are the basis of the scoring/progression. Frustrating. Not to mention having to revisit the shop after every match. Just gimme the damn guns and let me pew pew some heads until they explode.

There are countless more choices that are off about RE8 that make you wonder #1 where is this franchise going? #2 Do the developers understand their own past successes? #3 Do I even ever bother buying a RE game at full sticker ever again? As to the 3rd question, I’d say no. Not until something amazing comes out from the franchise. I played RE8 for ~20 hours of gameplay and got what seems like zero grand scheme plot development and mediocre entertainment. There are games in my catalog that are cheaper, but yet have enthralled me exponentially more than RE8 did. I can take the low play hours of an RE game if those play hours are fantastic. I’d consider it like breaking out the top shelf liquor, an indulgence that I’d be willing to splurge on, for the right spirit. Sadly, RE8 isn’t it. Capcom needs to look at RE-1&2 Remakes as the future formula of this franchise, or if they want to do a campy, rompy RE4 clone, then do it right.

So, how's the game on its own merits? S'good. Graphically it's certainly the best in series. My system (which at the time of my first play had a 4690k and now has a Ryzen 5 3600) with its GTX 1070 ran it cranked at 1080p on Linux, where it runs flawlessly with no fuss. Good show all around.

The actual basic core mechanics are all as polished as they've ever been. Blocking is still a weird addition, though there is a canon reason why Ethan is so ridiculous in both 7 and 8. It took quite some time to acclimatize myself to the mechanic, and this is having played 7 all the way through twice just before. Once you're aware of it and using it, it's quite nice to have and does give the player the means to stretch their resources a bit further which is good in general.

Returning for one of the aforementioned wiener yanks is a merchant. Not [i]the[/i] merchant, but a merchant. The Duke, a dapper and rotund gentle(man?) you meet fairly early in your adventure. Beyond buying and selling things, there is now a sort of hunting minigame you engage with fairly organically to collect ingredients for the Duke. Collect enough of the correct sort and you get some meaningful upgrades to your abilities. Capcom has in short basically one-upped the merchant from RE 4 in every way apart, perhaps, from the voice acting. I have my doubts any lines from Duke will be recited ad nauseum.

Otherwise, it more or less follows what I'd call the RE 4 formula, collect key items to get to new areas where you collect more key items until eventually the game ends. It's a good formula.

Now for spoilers. If the game sounds good based on what you've read so far though, I think it's safe to say it's a certain hit for you and you should pick it up. Despite the fact that I haven't purchased a game for $60 since 2016, I can say now in hindsight and in confidence that I'd gladly pay that for this game.

One of the most common complaints, apart from this being more "action-oriented" than many in the fanbase would like, is that the game's general pacing, mystique, intrigue, and perhaps even writing drop off after Castle Dimitrescu. I suppose I agree, but when you're going from what is a near-perfect experience that in a vacuum would likely be a 10, anything will seem lackluster. I don't think the writing is perfect, and I don't agree with every decision, but I do believe that the game as a whole is still well above even the average quality of the series as a whole at this point, personal preference for style aside.

The section that follows [strike]boobaville[/strike] Castle Dimitrescu is that of Donna Beneviento, the P.T. inspired true horror section. True horror referring to the fact that Capcom was obviously trying their damndest to spook you, not in that the other games or other styles of games aren't horrifying. It's the "you can't fight back" style of horror, largely popularized by [i]Amnesia: The Dark Descent[/i] and perpetuated by countless others. It begins with you walking through a reasonably and comparatively pleasant segment, until it takes away your arms (or rather your entire inventory) and sends you off to do some puzzle solving. The long and short of it is that the section is a bit of a slog for those playing the game over and over like myself, but is more of an exercise in ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ your pants for the average single-play player.

Between those two sections is village exploration with the normal gameplay loop. You return multiple times with new key items for both progression mandatory and optional searching about. These sections are largely similar otherwise and will not be mentioned in their own paragraph again.

Now you're off to fight Salvatore Moreau. After some scooting around a swampy area that contains a heavily transformed Moreau, you drain a reservoir to fight him head-on. The area is largely fairly simple, but contains a few fun set pieces and the boss fight can be challenging the first time.

Next, and second to last for Ethan, you fight Karl Heisenberg. He's been fairly present throughout the game, scooting to the sideline until he thinks he might have use for Ethan. This is a rather lengthy section of the game, going through Heisenberg's factory. Eventually you come to meet Chris Redfield for the second time, the first being near the beginning of the game. Why spoil the fun explaining why here? At any rate, your fight with Heisenberg is largely on a vehicle that Chris lends you. This ends in Ethan's not-death to Miranda via the violent removal of his heart.

Let's play as Chris! Lovingly referred to by Karl as "that boulder-punching ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥," you can be certain he's a series staple. Why not Jill, Capcom? Chris has his own weapons in a totally separate inventory. He carries a full auto rifle, a fairly strong pistol, and a knife that is [i]way[/i] better than Ethan's. Knife-only achievement good. He also has a laser pointer for designating places to bomb, but you can't use that so liberally.

You stomp through the now quickly burning village, smiting enemies as you pass, and eventually laser designate a giant mold structure to death. This leads you underground where you fight a big lycan (there are werewolves of a sort in this game, which I failed to mention among other things because this game is so absolutely packed) and plant a bomb on the megamycete, a mold (heart?) just causing an entire game series worth of problems. Last for Chris' section, you find that Mia is still alive, just chilling underground in Miranda's lab just past the megamycete.

Mia explains to Chris that Ethan is a special boy, and we return to playing Ethan post his "death." Duke carts you off to where you can finally kill Miranda and reclaim your daughter Rosemary. This was the primary motivation for Ethan. His daughter born of his mold infection and presumably sex with Mia evidently can't die, so Miranda wanted Rose for reasons I don't have the space to expand upon. This led to Rose being chopped up and put into four flasks which you collect in the previous sections. After killing Miranda, she somehow left Ethan dying as well. As Chris tries to get Ethan out Ethan steals the detonator for the explosive, goes back in, and dies in the explosion. Mia and Rose escape, and a cutscene plays where it's clear that Rose is being utilized for her Wesker-esque abilities by some organization or another some 20 years later.

The point of that whole section where I basically just explain the plot is to show how convoluted the whole thing is, and how ridiculous it is. Just how much of it is actually more understandable if you have even a general knowledge of the plot of Resident Evil up to this point. Miranda and [i]Oswell E. Spencer[/i] were working together before the events of the first game. He's the man that owned the mansion from the first game, was a founder of Umbrella, named and given a logo from something that was here, in this game's titular village, before both Miranda and Oswell even got there.

This is exactly what I've personally come to expect from Resident Evil, and I love it. It's got all the hallmarks of the first game, with the polish of millions of dollars. It's as ridiculous a Japanese view of American society and personality as ever, as well as being as ridiculously Japanese in its story telling, and balancing the two in a way only Capcom knows how. It's difficult to express how much I actually like this game. This is coming from someone who didn't even start playing the games until maybe 2018.

Buy this game. Even if you've never played another Resident Evil game in your life.

[h2]Best Non-Resident-Evil Resident Evil Franchise. Recommended 8/10[/h2]
[hr][/hr]
[i][b]For Linux & Steam Deck:[/b] Gold Experience. Requires Glorious Eggrolls’ custom Proton-6.20-GE-1 or newer.[/i]
[hr][/hr]
If you’re expecting a Resident Evil game – inventory management, long tense playthrough in-between saves, challenging puzzles – then you’re going to be disappointed. However, if you’re expecting a first-person-shooting game with horror elements, then Resident Evil Village is going to be the most polish experience you’ll get in the First Person Horror genre. 

While it doesn’t have the great ensemble and atmosphere that RE7 had, RE8 improves its moment to moment first-person combat. The enemies and the boss-fights are fun particularly in the second-half of the game and it’s difficult to not be taken by the sheer spectacle of the set pieces. The analogy that RE8 is like a carnival is very apt. 

If Capcom goes all in on the FPS route, we might just get something quite special. In the meantime, there’s no reason to not get RE8, especially if you’re a Resident Evil fan. Recommended. 
[hr][/hr]
[h3]What’s Great[/h3]

[table]
[tr]
[td]1. Good combat, especially and unfortunately only in the second-half of the game.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]2. Great cast of characters and voice-acting are good but they are underdeveloped.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]3. Graphics is really good. Really good.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

First off, the graphics are gorgeous especially Castle Dimitresque. It definitely able to capture the look of RE1, even if they didn’t quite managed to capture the feel. The lighting is great, the enemies look great, the bosses are design really well. 

The cast of characters is also very well made. Lady Dimitresque, Benivento, Moreau, Heisenberg and Miranda are all iconic with great voice-acting to make these characters come alive. It is very unfortunate most of these villains have little character development and are more like plot devices. This is especially so with Lady Dimitresque as well as Miranda where they don’t feel at all threatening. 

The most striking improvement that RE8 gained since RE7 is the combat. Unlike in RE7, the gunplay here is fun and the enemies as well as boss fights are challenging especially once you finished with Benivento. It's a shame that the combat isn't consistent throughout the game.
[hr][/hr]
[h3]What Could’ve Been[/h3]

[table]
[tr]
[td]1. Villains could’ve been developed to be the best since Tyrant and Mr X.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]2. Tighter gunplay and first-person hack-&-slash could’ve made the combat even more compelling.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]3. Puzzles could’ve been better.[/td]
[/tr]
[tr]
[td]4. The Resident Evil feel and atmosphere is almost completely gone. [/td]
[/tr] 
[/table]

Capcom missed a great opportunity to create a generational iconic villains. Certain Dimistresque, Benivento, Moreau and Heisenberg all had the look and the voice-acting to back it up, but none of them felt threatening or made you feel uneasy. Rather, the appeal is more in their theatrics which is over the top, which is entertaining but ultimately unmemorable within 5 years. 

Another missed opportunity is committing to a real first-person combat experience with FPS like combat complete with melee hack-&-slash mechanics. It’s a shame because this is the very thing that was missing in RE7, and Capcom seemed to have clued in to what actually makes first-person combat good but they seem to lack the confidence to execute it. Well, I guess a slightly above average combat is better than a broken combat. 

Lastly, the puzzles are pretty disappointing considering the pedigree. RE had clever puzzles and while some form of it is apparent in RE8, there are nowhere as interesting as previous franchises. Perhaps they didn’t want to scare all the normies who have never played RE, and this is probably why RE8 has almost none of the original Resident Evil atmosphere or feel. 

As so many have stated, RE8 is a carnival ride rather than an actual survival horror. You don’t get the tension and sense of dread while playing the game. That doesn’t mean that you won’t have a good time, rather you will probably have a pretty darn good one; it’s just that it’s not Resident Evil but a propped-up version of it. 
[hr][/hr]
[h3]Conclusion.[/h3]

It’s a good game, marginally better than RE7 and only beating it by virtue of the potential that I can see the franchise is going. RE8 is probably the furthest away Capcom has taken the franchise from it’s roots. If you can accept that RE8 isn’t survival-horror, rather it has become first-person-horror closer to Bioshock, then you’ll probably going to have a good time.

You can replay this game time and time again and it will still be enjoyable. Speedrunning is more enjoyable than expected especially when you add in your own challenges like 'Village of Shadows Knife Only'.

The only thing that comes to mind as a 'Flaw' would be that sometimes if you are playing VOS mode and fighting Heisenburg the game might freeze. I've tested it myself plenty and it only happens on VOS so remember to save beforehand!

I would recommend trying this game to anyone willing. Even if you don't love horror there can be something for you in here.

EDIT: After working on and off with customer service, they were finally able to find a solution that fixed the game and I was able to reach the main menu and even load my saves. In case anyone else has a similar issue with the autosave bugging the game, I am going to include the solution they gave me:

We would like you to attempt the following steps.
Please note that the operation on the saved data will be at your own risk.

Turn ON the cloud saving

Before you launch the game, move the contents in the saved data folder to another place such as the desktop and make the saved data folder empty.
Save data should be located in the following folder: C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\userdata\(User's ID\1196590\remote\win64_save

Try launching the game

The saved data will recover before the game launches (due to the cloud saving).

Move the recovered saved data in the saved data folder to another place such as the desktop and empty the saved data folder again.
(We would like you to see the RE ENGINE logo that is shown when the game is launched under the condition that the saved data does not exist in the saved data folder.)

When the first setup screen such as selecting language is shown, select the options and start the game.

If this works, you should be able to move your save data back to the save data folder.

When [i]Resident Evil: Village[/i] got announced, I was both enthusiastic and sceptical about it. Even though I adored its premise, I was not fond of it leaning more towards the action, as I would prefer it maintaining the frightening atmosphere from its predecessor. Yet, when I finally started playing it, I could not help to not fall in love with it. Although it is not the first-person shooter horror experience I wished for, its confidence in being its own thing managed to convince me of its qualities.

Simply put, [i]Village[/i] shines thanks to merging constant fast-paced action with straightforward yet rewarding exploration in its varied, beautiful environments, along with a cheesy narrative that is, however, saved by its charismatic antagonists. Thus, it is aware of its strong and weak aspects, balancing them well and delivering a triple-A title that might not be remembered for its complex narrative or revolutionary gameplay, but just for being a damn enjoyable addition to the series—and that is enough. Instead of bloating its players with tons of mediocre or repetitive content, it provides a few hours of honest fun. Perhaps a bit dumb one at times, for sure, but definitely worthy of my time.

Why would it be dumb? Mainly for its plot. I guess one could say that it is in the series’ nature, and perhaps that is why many love it, but I still cannot fully wrap my head around it. The narrative is filled with inconsistencies, where it feels like that its characters behave like feeble-minded individuals on purpose until the story demands otherwise. Due to that, I could not bring myself to care about their problems and goals. However, once any of the villains appeared, I gladly gave them my full attention, as those engrossing (sometimes gross) encounters were the peak of this title for me.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2693929750
With them comes my biggest gripe with this game, though, and that would be the fact that I would love to interact with them more. Yet, its fast-paced style does not allow that, as you are thrown into different situations every few minutes. That is a shame, as I still remember my escapades with daddy Baker from [i]Resident Evil VII[/i], and I missed something like that here; compared to him, the encounters presented here are short and heavily scripted.

Luckily, the rest of the game makes up for it. Just the atmosphere itself is so captivating! Galavanting through an old yet beautiful castle while a snowy storm roars outside its massive walls feels both tensive and cosy. That is only one of the parts of this journey, though, as you will visit various diverse environments, where each tries to represent a different take on a horror genre, some of which truly surprised me. Yet, it would not work well without proper audio, which is, as expected in this series, of top-notch quality again. You can hear all the heavy steps, slow breathing of monsters waiting to bite into your throat—it is haunting. And the voice actors did an outstanding job in making those villains so charming, I will give them that.

Then, there is the gameplay, which excels with its combination of action, exploration and a few horror elements, constantly changing between these every few minutes, creating this swift pace that did not bore me at any moment. Perhaps it could be even described as a nod to the series as a whole as if it tried to combine the best parts of its popular instalments and come up with something for everyone. Such an approach usually ends up being a disaster, but seeing how much I enjoyed playing Village—it proved me wrong in this case. Except for puzzles… those still suck. Like, c'mon, it feels as if the developers made them for a kindergarten event.

While I would surely wish for having more of the terrifying parts, as I felt these were overshadowed by the other ones, I cannot say that its omittance hurts the game per se. Sure, the exploration seems to be easier now, as you are not always chased by some maniac, but it allows for delivering a bit different design approach, where you can search for more treasures and pieces of lore, and then for tons of resources and ammunition, of course. Crafting is important more than ever, as foes come at you in big numbers. Unfortunately, you cannot put items in the storage box anymore, so you have to manage your inventory and either sell or discard the unnecessary stuff. Yet, the loot scattered around looks a bit silly at times. I mean, it usually happens to lie at the most inconvenient place! Like, why does vampiric mama Dimitrescu needs four shotgun shells on her nightstand? To use them as a butt plug? Not judging, but…
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2693928447
Well, at least you can kindly borrow those shells and obliterate any monster that dares to cross your way, whether it is werewolves, totally-not-zombies and… dang, that is perhaps all? Saying more would be spoilies, but the enemy variety manages to keep the gameplay fresh for the whole playthrough, so do not worry about that. The same applies to the boss fights, which usually require a bit different approach to beat them. I mean, sure, you just shoot at them, but at different parts… Eh, it is [i]Resident Evil[/i], do not expect much complexity.

Moreover, you can shoot off weapons from your foes’ hands or even try to immobilize them by hitting their legs, which makes combat more fluid and fun. While gunplay felt a bit clunky at first, it grew on me later on because of two reasons: upgrading your firearms truly matters, and the later ones are just satisfying to shoot. Additionally, you can also use the environment up to your advantage or place mines and such, so there is room to experiment, even if only a little. The good ol’ shotgun is still the best, though!

Yet, the very best thing is that you will not be alone during this journey of yours. Wait, do not panic! You will not get to escort another Ashley, who would constantly scream your name. No! Instead, you will meet someone better, sexier and smarter— I am talking about the Duke, of course, who is the most accurate depiction of the oppressed gamers™. Thus, due to his weight (his body, his choice, you intolerant monsters!), he will not follow you around, but he will help by providing information or trading with you from his cosy basement.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2693931006
If the abovementioned content sounds good for you, then you can look forward to more, as once you finish your first playthrough, a so-called Content Shop unlocks, allowing you to buy new fancy weapons or even cheats, such as unlimited ammo. With these, you can josh around and show those monsters who's the boss here. Apart from that, there is Mercenaries mode, which tests your skills, both in precision and speed, in various arenas filled with aggressive enemies, and it will surely make you hate it once you fail.

Overall, I managed to get about sixty hours out of [i]Village[/i], replaying it three times and then spending more in the Mercenaries mode. Yet, even a single playthrough, lasting for about fifteen hours, is a fair amount of time, especially considering this title’s qualities. It might not be my favourite game from 2021, but it is a damn enjoyable one.

And that is what matters.

While horror games have generally never been my jam, I've grown to really appreciate just how consistently good [i]Resident Evil[/i] games tend to be. I played through 7 back in October, and I enjoyed it, but couldn't help but feel that its limited scope actually hurt the game a little bit, as things like basic enemies weren't that fun to fight, and the story had largely lost my attention by the end. When I got this game, I was eager to see how these criticisms were addressed. And after playing through the game in just about 8 hours, I realized it is basically just an expanded version of 7 in pretty much every way.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

I loved this game visually. It's stunning, just like the previous game, and nails the atmosphere its going for. It's a lot more mysterious and intriguing, but it also knows when it can be scary.  I also really liked the designs of the characters, especially the antagonists. "Vampire mommy milkers" memes aside, each villain got my attention just based off of their appearances alone. The game looks good. There's not much else to say here.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

[i]Village[/i], if you haven't been able to deduce it already, has a lot more action elements compared to its predecessor. The core gameplay mechanics are essentially the same, that being a perfectly competent first-person shooter.  However, everything else is improved upon. Generally speaking, outside of one segment, there isn't really anything that hits the same high points that 7 hits, but the whole experience feels so much smoother here. There's a great amount of variety in the game, and while [i]Resident Evil[/i] seems to have always had a "mediocre second half" problem, which still exists in this game, I found that I had far more fun getting through this game's latter half compared to 2 and 7. And I think part of it is that this game absolutely [i]nails[/i] its pacing. 

As said before, this game has been compared to being at a theme park. Each of the four lords you're hunting has different gameplay mechanics. One is more of a pure survival horror experience where you're unarmed, another is more akin to classic Resident Evil where there is a particularly powerful enemy that's constantly hunting you down, and so on. I never felt that the game overstayed its welcome with any of these mechanics. Some are definitely longer than others, but by the time I'd start feeling bored, the game would end it with a boss fight or throw in a curveball to keep things interesting. Enemy variety actually exists in this game too, which I think helps keep the game from ever feeling dull. I also really liked the level design, as the game emphasizes and rewards exploration in multiple ways, from upgrades to lore, and I felt very compelled to stop and look for secrets. 

Where the game stumbles a little bit are in two areas: the boss fights and the puzzles. The bosses are less egregious, because I wouldn't say they were bad. More than anything, they were just a little disappointing. Considering how good most of the ones in 7 were, I found it a little ironic that this game excelled during its fights with basic enemies and stumbled with its bosses, where its predecessor was the opposite. Most fights were too straightforward, but hey, I'll at least appreciate this game's final boss for (RE7 spoilers) [spoiler]not being a glorified QTE.[/spoiler] The puzzles, however, were almost always way, way too easy. If I wasn't sure of what to do, I'd just trial-and-error it and accidentally get the solution, and I'd say there's only one puzzle that actually made me stop to think for a moment, and that's only because I'd overlooked something obvious. Most of the puzzle answers are basically handed to you, so the puzzles felt more like brief distractions more than actual breaks in combat and scares. But ultimately, it did not break the game for me. 

As I said, while the game doesn't often hit the same high points of 7, it is a more consistent title with better game design in general, as well as great pacing. Overall, the gameplay is largely smoothed out and it made my experience mostly better.

[h1]Story[/h1]

[i]Resident Evil[/i] games don't really have great stories most of the time. They're pretty corny, but weirdly endearing in the process. I think 7 was the exception to that rule, because while the final boss did disappoint me, I really liked the way the main antagonist's motivations were built up (as well as the rest of the Baker family), so I think [i[Village[/i] had some high standards to live up to. And it mostly does. 

Ethan Winters, the protagonist of RE7, has an actual personality now! He does have a tendency to make silly one-liners after surviving yet another near-death experience, but that's part of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] charm in my opinion. The villains were also pretty entertaining, but another big issue I had is that I don't think they were as interesting in the end as the Bakers. They got my attention almost immediately, but I think all of them, barring fan-favorite Lady D who was the highlight character in my opinion, needed some more screentime. I liked all of them, but I wanted to see more of them. 

I also liked the ending, and there was a really cool reveal towards the end that answered a major question I had while playing, and I love when stories explain gameplay mechanics. I will admit I am a bit concerned about where the story goes from here, because I'm aware this series struggled once it derailed into pure action, but I still liked the story overall. It's not amazing, but it's got some stellar twists and turns and I still liked it a lot.

[h1]Audio[/h1]

The sound design and music are both pretty good. There's really not much to discuss in those terms, as they fit what they're going for very well. The voice acting is what I'll be focusing on more here. As I said, Ethan actually has a personality now, and I think part of why it shows as much as it does is due to the solid performance from his voice actor. But, of course, the highlight here is the much-loved Lady D, who completely took control of every scene she was in. However, I was not a big fan of Heisenberg's voice. It felt like they were trying to go for something cool and intimidating, but the accent came off as being overly corny more than anything. However, that's more of a nitpick, as I still liked his character, and the rest of the performances were pretty good. *Sniff* They've come so far from "Jill sandwich!" 

[h1]Content Value[/h1]

All RE games are pretty short, but I think [i]Village[/i] makes the most out of every second of its 8-10 hour playtime. There's a lot more fun side content this time around, and there's also the potential for additional story DLC, which there is none of at the time of writing this. While there's only 1-2 moments in [i]Village[/i] that really stuck out to me compared to 7's highlights, this game feels much more replayable due to the overall polish. I'd say it's a safe buy despite the length, especially if there's even a light discount.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

While it may not be quite as interesting as its predecessor, [i]Village[/i] is a more polished experience overall with much better game design. The "better" game comes down to preference, and I personally prefer this one because it was still memorable in its own right. It's a great time, and I'd easily recommend it [strike]if only for Lady D.[/strike]

Resident Evil Village was one of the most positive experiences I've ever had in gaming. For a series that went a bit off the rails with Resident Evil 5 and 6, the new series of Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil 8 bring a fresh feel to a franchise that has gotten way too complicated over the years. 

Too many people in the Resident Evil fanbase write these games off because they are disconnected from the main Resident Evil storyline, but Resident Evil 7 and Village have created their own in depth and beautifuly frightening worlds in just two games. 

Don't get me wrong, this is definetely an M rated game. This game doesn't hold back any punches on gore, scares, and creepy environments, but where the beauty I talk about comes from is within the world and characters themselves. Not to mention the graphics are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ georgous. 

From a technical standpoint, Resident Evil 8 is an almost perfect game. This game excels in level design, atmosphere, graphics, and audio design. Subtle things like hearing distant doors creaking open in House Beneviento or way the fog and mist works to create a mysterious atmosphere really go a long way. 

The fact that Resident Evil Village is a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7 really helps flesh out the characters and story of this new world that Resident Evil was put into. Ethan changed from a very down low character in Resident Evil 7 to a more complete character in 8. Seeing Chris actually be in the game for more than an end credits scene was great and helped connect this game to the rest of Resident Evil as well. 

Below I will list pros and cons. But before that, I will just say this is a:

9.75/10 - Worth the money. 

Pros: 

- Connected a bit more with the rest of RE and is directly connected to RE7, which was a fantastic game. 

- Graphics and audio design are incredible. Nothing more to say, just amazing. 

- Weapons system doesn't feel overpowered unless you play on casual. 

- Multipule dificulty levels for different styled players. 

- Game doesn't drag on. Perfect length IMO. My playthrough was about 7 hours rushed.

- Each section is varied and has great mechaincs, and most don't involve sneaking. 

- Much more.

Cons:

- Audio Sync - I had a few instances where I had to relaunch my game and change settings because the audio would be about 6 seconds behind the cutscene.

- Heisenberg's Factory drags non - This is my least favorite section of the game. I wanted to leave it about halfway through the total time I spent there. 

- Mia's face animations are just off. They have been since 7 and are just uncanney valley. Chris is much better in this regard. 

- Not as much horror as RE7, last section is a little too action for me.
12/10 for sure. Awesome game play.

This is another Resident Evil masterpiece.

It's a tense fight for survival against hopeless odds as hordes of monsters close in on you; you shakily fire your pistol at them and curse every missed shot as your ammo supplies dwindle...

...but once you complete the game and cash in on NG+ infinite ammo weapons, it's a joyful romp as you blast them right in the face with your shotgun, and send piles of them flying with grenades.

The game neatly splits into several areas, all centred around the unluckiest Romanian village in existence. Each area is the lair of one of the powerful bosses you meet at the start of the game, and you have to defeat each one in turn before taking on the big bad. The gameplay is a good mix of puzzles, and existential threat as you hide and flee from monsters to preserve your meagre ammo... it feels very good once you're strong enough to fight back.

I honestly wanted to play and enjoy this game but the intro sequence is probably the dumbest thing Capcom has ever done in a Resident Evil game. Suffice to say, I wasn't going to spend more than two hours trying to get through that part and miss an opportunity for a refund. If the first impression is sour, it's generally better to be safe and get a refund than struggle through "to the good part". 

So here's a summary (gameplay but no story spoilers): 
Within -minutes- of you getting your first weapon you are introduced to a survival rush that you must succeed or you will not progress the story. You are not told this; in fact during this point of the game you have no idea what is going on and have no written objectives. In essence, your first interaction with any weapons, any enemies, or gameplay et al is a timer-based gate to progress -to the rest of the game- that, if you fail, you will be sent back to the beginning to try again (because you haven't even found the first save point yet). 

This works in games like Resident Evil 4 where the controls are smoother and the game is designed around action combat. It DOES NOT work in Resident Evil Village where you have the field of view of a mole rat, tank controls, limited resources, and no clear idea of what is going on or what you must do. Dropping a new player or returning player into a situation without even telling them what they have to do (survive for 'x' duration; doesn't matter if you even shoot) is a hamfisted attempt at survival horror tension which ironically achieves none of those three words. 

I'm sure the game is great. I'm sure it will be amazing to watch a Let's Play of. It is definitely not for me and I cannot recommend it to anyone looking for that RE7 experience... and I feel a bit justified in saying that from a five-page forum thread of people who said that the intro sequence soured the game for them but they enjoyed the rest.

1. Ich mag keine Full-Horror-Games. Ich finde diese ewige Anspannung einfach sehr nervig und es macht mich fertig. Bei einem Horrorfilm ist es nach 90-120 Minuten halt vorbei, aber bei einem Spiel streckt sich dieses ungemütliche Gefühl halt über 5-10 Stunden. Kein Plan, bin wohl zu alt :)

2. Weil RE7 einfach keine richtige Fortsetzung war. Es wurde nur minimal RE-Lore hinzugefügt, um den Titel zu rechtfertigen.

Nun, Village ist in diesem Sinne komplett anders. Es fühlt sich echt nach einem richtigen Resident Evil-Ableger an. Chris Redfield ist dabei, Es gibt einfach mehr Lore und Anspielungen auf die bekannte RE-Welt. Das hat mir persönlich recht gut gefallen. Ausserdem ist das ganze Spiel leichter verdaubarer. Der Horroranteil wurde stark heruntergefahren und durch Action und Unterhaltung ersetzt.

Zu Village selber: Irgendwie mochte ich den Stil von dem Village erkunden, als Hub und die 4 Lords die 4 verschiedenen Set Pieces anbieten. So sind die Story und die Spielwelt nicht so langweilig.
