Dann die 4 Lords sind ziemlich cool gemacht. Alle haben ihre eigenen Beweggründe und Hintergrundstory, wenn man sich mit ihren Lore befasst.
Gerade die große Lady und das Puppenhaus haben es mir sehr gut angetan. Mochte einfach die ganze Geschichte um die Figuren.

Grafisch war es ein absolutes Meisterwerk. Auf dem PC in 1440p mit 144hz spielt es sich sooooooo verdammt gut. Die Wettereffekte, die Spielwelt selber und die Animation der Figuren und Gegner sind wirklich genial. Für mich sogar das Grafikhighlight 2021.

PRO :

The overwhelmingly positive rating will probably speak for itself, but just in case you A) Haven't bought this game B) Actually want to know why so many people are gushing over it, here are some cliff notes:

1) Satisfying Gunplay: 
This one's a carryover from RE7. Between the sound design, the gun's recoil animations and effect on target they don't get old very fast. The weapon selection isn't that large, but besides the clear-cut upgrades to your shotgun and pistol they mostly feel distinct with their own unique strengths and weaknesses. There's one notable exception, but saying what it is would be a gigantic spoiler so you'll just have to play the game to see.

2) Solid Map Design
If you're a fan of games that reward exploration and reading through everything you find, you'll be well-rewarded here. There are bits of lore and loot scattered everywhere for you to find. Having said that, the maps still do a good job of herding you in the right direction if you're not. 

3) Intriguing Story
Village hops into the canon as a direct sequel to RE7, expanding upon the lore established in Biohazard and adding some fun new twists. The second game's plotline isn't quite as tight as the first, but it definitely has a logical progression and a satisfying ending. If you're a Resident Evil fan you're used to not asking TOO many questions about the plot and this one won't demand too much.

4) Great Action, Spiced with Horror
I will say that one particular segment scared the absolute hell out of me. I won't spoil exactly when it is, but it made me remember playing Penumbra as a kid. That's not a comparison I make lightly and is just about the highest praise I can come up with. The rest is a fantastic action game that can have some real adrenaline-fueled panic moments as you balance conserving ammunition and the horde of enemies trying to use your rib cage as a xylophone.

Village claims to be a survival horror experience. There may be survival horror sections, but a better descriptor would be an action-adventure spectacle with dash of horror. Village is split into several wholly different areas with a village hub. These areas are reminiscent of collecting the lord souls in Dark Souls and adventuring to the underground lava caves of Lost Izalith, or Seath’s castle called the Dukes Archives. These disparate biomes make for memorable areas with clear themes as the bosses, enemies, and set pieces all serve the cohesive vision of that segment. The level design draws obvious comparisons to the classic action-oriented predecessor Resident Evil 4, but that’s not the only connection. Game mechanics like the briefcase inventory system, the vendor that showing up in weird spots throughout, hidden gems and collectibles, and buying weapon upgrades are all stripped directly from RE4 and utilized here. If you loved RE4, Village is for you, if you’re looking for a survival horror experience, look elsewhere. Even the one pure horror segment has zero survival elements and is more akin to the likes of Amnesia or Outlast. I had a similar but different problem with RE7 not feeling like a Resident Evil game and that game had clear survival horror elements. I think, after two entries playing as Ethan, he may be the weak link. Ethan as the guy who went looking for his wife, who also got in over his head worked the first time. But for me, I have zero connection to this character. His one-liners are corny, exacerbating profanities, and the ending reveal just fell flat for me. The developer’s devotion to not showing his face is bizarre and I feel if they went this route, he should have just been a silent protagonist. With all this being said however, Village is a fun action-adventure spectacle while having a little bit of influence from almost every Resident Evil and other horror contemporaries sprinkled in. This one I recommend, but I don’t know how long I will keep playing these games if they continually push towards action and away from survival horror.

I do not recommend RE Village. My thumbs down is, however, a 'soft' downvote. I enjoyed several sections of the game, but there were several others that I did not and sometimes felt rather bored (especially during the first section). At times, it did feel like I was basically pushing forward a scripted cinematic with little player autonomy. 

Part of the problem here seems to be that the game designers weren't sure what kind of game they wanted it to be, so they threw together different styles from past RE games (The 'RE 6 fallacy'?). RE Village seems like an amalgam of RE 7 and RE 4, but one that doesn't really work in the way that each of those two games succeeded. The bland main character, the nonsensical (at times incoherent) story and terrible (sometimes cringey) dialogue didn't help. I hated it when several characters yell out Ethan's FULL name for some strange reason (how many Ethans are there in the Village, I wonder?).

There are certain sections of the game that really shine with the level design and enemy encounters. The graphics are fantastic. Beyond that, however, I didn't find much else to enjoy. RE Village is absolutely not greater than the sum of its (uneven) parts (like RE 4, say). It was a mixed ride for me and not worth the $60 that I paid for it on release.

If you really want to check it out, my recommendation is to get it at a discounted price.

After many years Capcom finally delivers a new Resident Evil game that offers the classic horror experience and manages to satisfy most of RE fans. Despite the first-person view, RE Village still offers the classic horror experience we have been used to, taking a lot of inspiration from RE4, one of the best titles in the series. Having played Resident Evil 7 is not necessary (but still recommended), as there is a good story recap in the settings menu.

The game follows the events from RE7, with Ethan Winters, his wife Mia and their child Rosemary apparently living a happy life in Eastern Europe. Things quickly change after Chris Redfield kills Mia and kidnaps Ethan with his daughter. When Ethan wakes up, he finds himself alone near a remote village controlled by Mother Miranda and four monstrous Lords which must be defeated in order to save baby Rose.

The key word in Resident Evil Village is variety. Starting with the environments, the whole village is divided into different areas that become available once you find a certain item or progress with the story. Some of the other locations include a castle, a creepy mansion, a fortress, a sunken village and more. Most of these are linked to the relevant Lord, but there are some optional areas as well. Backtracking is required if you are looking to obtain all the rare items and collectibles, but it’s also made interesting with the addition of mini-bosses or simply more enemies to shoot down. Speaking of enemies, there is a great variety among them, with new ones being introduced after visiting a new location. There is also a good number of boss fights, each one requiring a different approach and with a very cool monster design.

The gameplay is simply addicting. RE Village still offers a traditional survivor horror experience, with the iconic inventory, items combination and resources management that have always been the hallmarks of the series. There is a great focus on exploration, finding useful resources and more powerful weapons that can give you an advantage in combat. You will often encounter a merchant (taken straight from RE4) where you can sell the treasures you find, as well buying new items, mods and weapons by spending Lei (money that can be dropped by defeated enemies). Gunplay is obviously designed for first-person, which in my opinion works better, but it’s really sad to see that the 3rd person mode is locked behind the purchase of a DLC. Finishing the story unlocks the Mercenaries extra mode, in which you must defeat enemies across different areas within the given time while trying to get the best score.

Music is persistent in Village. It’s often subtle and mysterious, but quickly varies depending on the location and it’s always nice to hear some relaxing ambient music when entering a save room. It’s also perfectly mixed with the impressive sound design, which really sets the tone and gives you enough reason to fear each noise that could potentially sign the presence of an enemy nearby.

What I don’t like about Village is the story itself. The setting is awesome, but Ethan’s personal tragedy is not that interesting, considering he neither has a face or a background to start with. The things happening to him are quite predictable and yet he still reacts in the most unbelievable way. His dialogues are really bad. I lost the count of how many times I heard “I’m going to kill you”, “I’m going to save Rose” or just random insults against giant monsters. Another character who is poorly characterized is Chris Redfield (with his renovated design), whose actions are never properly explained, probably because the writers themselves had no idea what to write or because they wanted to leave a big hole in the story that maybe will be covered up in the next games. Either way, the story of Ethan Winters appears to be meaningless (more like a spin-off), with only minor references to the rest of the series (mostly RE7). I think that Capcom still doesn’t know how to continue the Resident Evil main storyline and carefully moves between remakes and games with self-contained stories that do not add anything to the plot of the series, but to be honest, I am still fine with it as long as they never go back to something like Resident Evil 6.

I've played Resident Evil for years and years, but the longer this series goes on, the more I think it's passed it's prime. While I do think Village is a decent enough game, there's some massive asterisks hanging over certain aspects of it. Spoiler free, tl;dr at the bottom.

[h1] Graphics [/h1]
The game looks great and is easily one of the best looking on the market right now. It runs flawlessly as well. On my RTX 2060 at 1080p, I've got almost every setting maxed out and never once had issues with 60 fps. Not a single crash either. However, the first asterisk I need to talk about is the lack of an FOV slider. The game comes locked at 81. I had to download a mod to bring it up to 95 because it was the first time I'd ever felt dizzy watching a game before. Not having a basic PC graphical setting in 2021 isn't okay. Supposedly the reason behind this was to make the game feel more tense and claustrophobic, but honestly, the game has shifted away from horror and towards set-piece action.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Village built on what made RE7 good and it plays more or less the same as that. Gun goes bang, enemies go down, rinse and repeat. There's puzzles scattered about as well, but as far as combat goes, it doesn't really get more complicated than "shoot until dead/shoot glowing weak point until dead". Puzzles are decent enough, most solutions are straightforward and I never felt the need to go look up answers because of difficulty. My second asterisk comes from the combat however. Combat is either too easy or too frustrating depending on the enemy. Boss fights are lackluster simply because some can simply be stunlocked by hitting their weak points. 

[h1] Story [/h1]
Since I promised no spoilers, I can't really say much about the story, but what I will say is that I think it's a decent story, but a crappy Resident Evil story. I honestly believe if Lady Dimitrescu didn't exist in game and hadn't been the subject of a meme craze for months, the game wouldn't have done near as well as it did. Especially given the fact that she's basically another version of Jack Baker from the last game, but worse since she shows up a total of 2-3 times in game. Her daughters also have next to no screen time which brings up my biggest criticism with the game. Remove her and you're left with bride of chucky, slimeman, and discount dante. They have to share screentime and each one feels one-dimensional since they don't get much dialogue.

When Mr.X was chasing me through RCPD in RE2, I felt far more threatened than any moment in this game. Almost every enemy can be despawned by walking past certain points. There's essentially no horror anymore aside from some spaced out jump scares. There is literally just a single area in the entire game where I felt legit unnerved by the atmosphere (and everyone who's played knows exactly what part I'm referring to) It just feels like we've gone from "evil corporation doing evil science things" to "evil cult doing evil cult thing, but we threw in an Umbrella symbol to force a tie in to the rest of the series". I honestly feel as though I would enjoy the game a lot more if it didn't feel so forced to attach itself to a series I've played for years with completely different expectations.

[h1] tl;dr [/h1]
It's a decent enough game, but not a good Resident Evil game. I think I'd enjoy it more if I wasn't a long time player of RE games. For total playtime, you can expect about 6-7 hours on a first playthrough on normal difficulty. For people wanting 100% completion, you're looking at 30-40 hours.

It's so so satisfying. My system can barely run it well, and I realize that this is probably the last AAA title my 1060 Ti is going to be able to handle. But it runs fine. No lags, etc. It's a very stable game. 

Clunky retro inventory system is clunky and retro. Enemy variety could be more robust and creepy. But the secrets, stories, bosses and world building are just classic.

My biggest gripe is Ethan Winters. Could we have a better voice actor and scripting for the protagonist?!

Finally, just add a jump button and a climbing system. See Far Cry Primal. It's not perfect, but give it up folks,  You want FP survival play? Just do it.

[h1][u]TL/DR[/u][/h1]
Resident Evil should have stopped after the 5th one after the death of Wesker, and maybe come back as some kind of reboot.
This serie is a 25 years old one, and anything this game has to offer are things already done in previous RE games; the worst part being it's done worse. You'll play and constantly have this deja-vu feeling.
This game simply doesn't bring anything to the table, it doesn't work anymore.
If you never played any Resident Evil game and want an ok action game/if you really liked the action side of RE4 and the RE7 approach, you'll probably enjoy this game since it mixes those elements.
If you want to get introduced to the Resident Evil franchise, or if you look for a scary/survival-horror game, forget about it and go for Resident Evil 2 remake which will fit you more.

[b][u]Story/Narration[/u][/b]
The narration and story are barely inexistants so I won't spend lot of time talking about it.
You have a short introduction, and after that… nothing until the very end of the game. You just progress in a scripted world, to finally access the end and learn things that will make you either facepalm or straight up laugh.

[b][u]Game length/Replayability[/u][/b]
- Not too long, not too short : it took me around 9 hours to complete it in Hardcore for a first run.
- The balance between action, more calm moments, exploration and boss fights is good.
- Like in others RE games, you unlock a new difficulty after your first run (the "real" hardcore difficulty).
- The issue here is that unlike other RE games, there is no point to replay it (beside challenges/achievements) : once you played the game once, you basically saw everything. Some areas will do the job for the first time, but it's so scripted, it will just be boring to go through a second time.
- You also unlock Mercenary mode, but it's terrible.

[b][u]Difficulty[/u][/b]
This is one of the worst part of the game. Here is the real difficulty : Normal mode = easy mode / Hardcore mode = normal mode. Here is why :
- I played my first run in Hardcore difficulty, the only hardcore thing being its name. During the first hour of the game, you'll indeed count your ammos, use what you have carefully. But at some point, you realize that the game just throws ammos at your face throught collectibles and merchant : there is no point in saving anything, since spaming your heals/ammos will NEVER put you in a bad situation. Once you kill an ennemy, it basically gives you back the bullet you used in form of coins. Knowing that, it's a big part of stress/management flying away, which is a nonsense in a RE game.
- Even in Hardcore, the game has tons of auto-saves/checkpoint, and you're free to save anytime you want at those typewriters, without having to use some kind of ink.
- Long story short, if you play this game in normal mode, congratulations you ruined your whole experience : you're basically invincible, and you'll carry hundred of bullets within 2 hours in the game. Even in Hardcore, it's very hard to die : I don't think it happened to me more than 3 times.
- After finishing the game once, you unlock a new difficulty. This is the "real hardcore" mode. But why do I have to finish the game first to have the right to play it in hardcore ? What is the point if I already know about how the game works and where to go, what to do, how to kill bosses ?
- You will never have to manage your inventory (maybe once at max), despite carrying an arsenal as big as a military base, don't worry, it will just fit.

[b][u]Immersion[/u][/b]
There is ALWAYS something to break immersion. Here are some random examples, but there is tons of it :
- As said above, the fact that you're pretty much invincible with hundred of ammos and explosive will prevent you to feel any kind of pressure or imminent danger. You will pretty much always run forward, knowing that if you meet an ennemy, you'll just spam it with bullets.
- Where is the usual memorable safe room music ? Where are boss musics ? Where the hell are musics ?
- Obviously, there is no horror in this game. This is an action game, not a survival horror. There is nothing wrong with this, but just be aware you'll never feel any pressure or survival vibe, and you will never be scared except during a single short portion of the game.
- One of the main antagonists captures you and keep you captive without surveillance and let you all of your weapons in case you want to escape… ? Okay I guess.
- Ethan can squeeze between a 5cm gap, guess we're a cat.
- The merchant is free to roam around (teleport ?) without any reasons in the land of the ennemies, free to set his shop, not being scared of the hundreds of dangerous monsters around. Nothing about this is explained.
- I hope you like Call of Duty, because the whole last part of the game is pretty much a COD campaign trailer, and it's terribly done.
- There is no reflection in mirrors…
- A boss who is supposed to be one of the powerfull one is the easiest fight of the game.
- Sometimes you'll get surounded by a lot of ennemies, so you'll want to use your brain and bait them in the next room 3 meters away for a more comfortable place to fight… but your ennemies will just dissapear and respawn in their initial area.
- I can't go on because of review max characters limitation.

[b][u]Gameplay/Interactions[/u][/b]
For some reasons, Capcom decided to step back 15 years earlier.
- The first things you will try to do is to knife/shoot your environment, and you'll quickly notice that your arsenal is made of sponge. No impact anywhere : walls, glass, bottles, even ennemies… nothing. It can be done and it has be done in previous games with the RE Engine, so it's straight up laziness.
- The gameplay is basic and feels very clunky : you move forward, you shoot until it dies, clear the area until it turns blue on your map, repeat.
- In any game with boss fights, you have to use what you learnt during your adventure to be victorious. Not the case here : you shoot until it dies. Sometimes, the game will want you to shoot those red shiny weak points on bosses. Very interesting mechanic (10 years ago).

[b][u]Graphics/Optimization[/u][/b]
- Some areas look very great, lights are well used and look great even without raytracing. Indoor areas are also globally well done.
- Outdoor area in the other hand, If you take a look around you from time to time, your eyes will be burned by disgusting textures not even PS3 worthy (I played in maximal settings).
- You can NOT change FOV (!!).
- The game runs very well and I personally didn't experience any crash or other technical issue.

[b][u]Characters[/u][/b]
I won't talk too much about the antagonists : all of them are very charismatics, but barely/poorly used.
Ethan, the main character, is the less memorable character of the whole RE franchise. There is 0 character developpement about him, you don't even know how he looks like.
His reactions are also ridiculous. For example : [spoiler]the fact he doesn't even listen to what one of your main powerful ennemy has to say. He basically wants to kill the final boss with you. Do you think the ennemy of your ennemy is your friend ? Ethan doesn't.[/spoiler]
Second example : Ethan survives a big ambush, and 15secs later, he meets this old lady drawing satanic glyphs on the floor using her stick with human skulls on it, laughin. His reaction : [i]"hey mam, it's dangerous here, don't stay here"[/i] *facepalm*
When he [spoiler]dies in the game (twice…), you basically won't care at all.[/spoiler]

[b][u]Riddles/Puzzles[/u][/b]
There is no riddles or puzzles, which is a shame for a Resident Evil game. The only kind of "puzzles" I found are : 
- Something about using physics to push a flame against a wall. I personally can't call that a puzzle. The only difficulty being having to deal with this terrible physic the engine can't handle properly.
- Putting a ball in a hole. Wow very intense riddle - for a 2yo kid.

Resident Evil Village is quite simply a quality title, if you're looking for a good action game to play look no further. 

It is probably one of the 'easier' titles in the series but i can image on hard and up many encounters will prove to be incredibly challenging, combined with an increased pressure on resources which is only felt a handful of times on normal difficulty. Even for those that struggle with more challenging core games i would avoid Easy difficulty, the brief taste you get of the game devoid of challenge, a late game dalliance with a rugged series regular; armed to the teeth, was pretty tedious. 

To add a degree of real criticism Resources are perhaps even a little generous on normal difficulty, with money, ammunition and even inventory spaces proving to be very little consideration. I was able to hold a small arsenal of weapons and only needed to switch out 2 obsolete weapons to carry every weapon i found. I was even able to leave one well stocked area completely full of resources should i have had need of them (i didn't). That said i like to think i engaged pretty fully with the mechanics of combat, utilising explosives, crafting regularly, engaging with the guard mechanic, not being afraid to use powerful weapons and avoiding the more obvious ammo sinks.

The often stunning visuals and beautifully handcrafted environments are quite simply a joy to explore and unlocking even a fraction of the treasures it has to offer requires a keen eye and some lateral thinking. If you have a powerful PC this game is definitely up there with the most beautiful titles available and it will ABSOLUTELY add greatly to your immersion to max out the visuals if you can. Most Puzzles never really qualify as true head scratchers but they are satisfying enough for cretinous gamers like myself.

The story is very enjoyable, features well written dialogue and has some good characters, particularly the Duke, alongside some decent twists and turns. In a slight twist on convention optional exploration often yields the most story insights, with key lore hidden beside the treasure you were seeking.

All in All you can tell a great deal of love and care went into the game and that the Resident Evil (mainline) franchise is in good hands for the years to come.

The Resident Evil series continued its personal re-invention experienced in Part 7 and released another first-person game. While super-hardcore fans of the original trilogy might not be happy with this change of core gameplay, Village can still be easily considered one of the best in the series.
The game uses the same engine as RE7 and the remakes, and this time the graphics have been upped once more to near perfection. Textures are incredible, lighting, effects, everything looks amazing, but what really shines are the extremely realistic character faces, which are already showcased in detail at the very beginning of the game. Not many games have managed to reach that excellent mix of texture, animations, and lighting without tapping into the uncanny valley.
Gameplaywise, it is more or less RE7 all over again, which is not bad though. The riddles are far less complex than in the originals, and gameplay is clearly more orientated on the action aspect, although running remains an option that you always need to consider.
The atmosphere is very dense and keeps you on your feet most of the time, and another plus is that jumpscares almost never happen in the entire game, simply because it doesn't have to resort to such simple tricks to create constant tension.
The story can be considered one of the best of all Resident Evil games. That is all I will say about it. If you wish to see what happens, play the game or watch someone else play it for you.
With a first-time playthrough of about 8-10 hours I wouldn't say that the game justifies its high price-tag, but hardcore fans can keep coming back to unlock extra content and achievements. Otherwise get the game on the next sale.

As soon as I arrived in Resident Evil Village’s sinister rural setting, its Resident Evil 4 influence reared its snarling head. Almost immediately surrounded by rabid Lycan locals, I scrambled for shotgun shells and bookshelves to block doorways as the horde closed in, only to be saved a split-second away from death. It’s an intense welcome that serves as a fantastic flashback to the opening of Shinji Mikami’s magnum-toting magnum opus, and one made all the more frantic in first-person perspective. Resident Evil Village might not break much new ground in its own right, but it successfully grafts Resident Evil 4’s best action elements onto the series’ more modern form established in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, making for a genuinely engrossing and increasingly combat-heavy continuation of the Ethan Winters story.

It’s a story that – unfortunately for poor old Ethan – goes from dire straits to dire wolves. Dragged to hillbilly hell and back in an effort to rescue his wife in Resident Evil 7, he subsequently finds himself dropped into a distinctly Transylvanian type of terror in Village. This time it’s his infant daughter who must be saved after she’s kidnapped by a wicked cabal of monster maniacs: Lady Dimitrescu, a vampire tall enough to play center in a Space Jam sequel; Donna Beneviento, a dollmaker with a walking, talking Bride of Chucky sidekick; Salvatore Moreau, a thoroughly repulsive merman; and Karl Heisenberg, a magnetically powered lunatic who runs a factory assembly line of Frankenstein’s monsters.All four report to the mysterious head witch, Mother Miranda, and although admittedly none of them managed to coax out the same kind of genuine scares as the southern-fried psychopaths in Resident Evil 7's Baker family, I found the lot of them to be entertainingly twisted in a slightly cartoonish, Batman villain kind of way. Each presides over their own visually distinctive domain that you must survive, from the opulent gold-trimmed interiors of Castle Dimitrescu to the grungy mechanical works of Heisenberg’s subterranean facility. There are noticeable shifts in mood between each setting, with one demanding a more stealth-driven approach while another leans more into psychological horror than combat. Delving into the darkest corners of Village’s world and uncovering the real reason these fairytale freaks have come into existence in the present day made for a compelling mystery that hooked me throughout my 10-hour playthrough.Aside from the aforementioned Lycans – which come in multiple forms – there are zombie ghouls, flying gargoyles, full-on werewolves, and more waiting to ambush you at every turn. Their onslaught feels like an aggressive response to one of Resident Evil 7’s most notable shortcomings in the lack of variety in its enemy types; its handful of lumbering monsters were referred to as the ‘Mold’, an appropriate name, since they quickly grew stale. Village remedies this by throwing a significantly broader set of nasties into your crosshairs; in fact, the last time there was a line-up of village people this diverse they were singing disco songs about the YMCA.

This expanded roster of bloodthirsty beasts doesn’t just make for a more interestingly evolving series of combat encounters, but it also adds some welcome new depth and decision making to the bolstered crafting system. Should you spend your scarce supply of scrap to cobble together a landmine that will blast the armour off one of the tank-like Lycans, or fashion it into sniper rifle rounds so that you can eliminate nesting gargoyles from afar before they have a chance to swoop down on you?Granted, most of these enemies aren’t particularly clever in their own right – the genetically modified mutants of Heisenberg’s factory might have deadly drills for arms, but they’re far from the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to outmanoeuvring you one-on-one. Still, what Village’s variety of grunts may lack in smarts they certainly make up for in sheer numbers, and although I rarely encountered clusters of more than a handful enemies at a time for the first few hours (outside of the initial overwhelming village reception), at somewhere around its midpoint the size of these enemy swarms started to swell substantially. By the story’s end I was gleefully indulging in chaotic levels of carnage that reminded me more of a run-and-gun Call of Duty campaign than a slow-paced horror game.

Resident Evil 8 is the Resident Evil 4 of Resident Evil 3 in terms of being a sequel to Resident Evil 7. The gun play is more action focused, Ethen is not only given way more ammo than in 7 but also a greater range of movement and gun options. 

Story wise this is several years after 7, quite literally the 3 years and 8ish months after 7's initial release, and it shows in Ethan Winter's overall demeanor and competency. That's not to say Ethan is given the Leon treatment from 2 to 4. Ethan is still very much a "normal" guy. He basically took some basic military training (more like self defense) but he isn't a government agent. 

Gameplay wise while I stand by that this is a more action oriented take on the atmosphere and gameplay of 7 it is not less terrifying or intense. In fact because the enemy variety and enemy population is greater than in 7 you are faced with a lot more head to head situations than Ethan and you would like. The game expects you to take a lot of damage and use up a lot more ammo. The enemies aren't slow mold this time either. Like in 4 the enemies are extremely hostile, fast, and mobile, and hit like a truck. It takes a lot of time to learn the enemies and how to deal with them. 

All in all if you enjoyed 7 you will enjoy 8.

When Resident Evil Village was first announced, I was not especially excited. I was surprised that Capcom was continuing Ethan’s story after Resident Evil 7 instead of moving on to something completely different. Capcom was describing it as a variation on that formula meant to reach a wider audience rather than simply repeat the same kind of horror again.

That shift ended up working far better for me than I expected. Once I actually played it, I realized I had underestimated what Capcom was doing. Village leans more into action than RE7, but not in a way that made it feel like it was abandoning survival horror. Instead, it felt like a more flexible and varied version of that formula, with momentum, more combat freedom, and a structure that kept each major segment feeling distinct. It brought balance horror with a broader, more approachable action experience, and that comes through clearly throughout the game.

What I liked most is that it still carried many of the strengths I enjoyed in Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil 2 Remake while still feeling like its own thing. The storytelling surprised me more than I expected, and I found it emotional, impactful, and genuinely interesting in where it pushed the series next. The atmosphere also did a lot of heavy lifting. Each area had its own identity, challenges, and tone, which helped the campaign stay fresh instead of blending together.

House Beneviento especially left a huge impression on me. That section captured the kind of fear and visual horror that sticks with you long after you finish it, and it was one of the clearest examples of how well Village handled variety without losing tension. More broadly, the game’s environments kept a strong sense of curiosity and dread, which made exploring each new location feel exciting rather than routine.

I could also feel the series evolving here. Village still stands on its own, but it also felt like a bridge between the horror-first direction of RE7 and the more action-forward style that would later make even more sense in the Resident Evil 4 remake. That made the whole experience even more interesting to me in hindsight.

Resident Evil Village ended up being another case where my skepticism was completely wrong. I expected to feel detached from its direction, but instead I got a well-executed action-horror campaign with strong atmosphere, memorable set pieces, and enough surprise and emotion to leave me very curious about where Resident Evil would go next.

After 16 long years and some lowlights in the franchise, Resident Evil 8 is the game that everyone expected and should have gotten after Resident Evil 4 re-invented the series. While Resident Evil 7 was great in its own way, Village feels like an upgrade from 4 in every way possible - the environment, the enemies, and the controls are all finely tuned and improve upon what we experienced when we went up against Los Illuminados and Las Plagas. Even the main character, Ethan Winters, who we met in the previous game and despite being faceless, can stand up in the series as one who is as likable as Leon S. Kennedy. The story, for as convoluted as Resident Evil has gotten over the years, is actually quite enjoyable and might even get some people to buy back in to the series in that regard.

That's all that really needs to be said about this game. It's the spiritual successor and is superior to what was previously the best game in the franchise. Hopefully the conclusion of the Winters trilogy continues to build upon it and improve, so that we don't end up waiting another decade or two for a truly great Resident Evil game. But if we do, I know I'll be anxiously awaiting Resident Evil 12.

A great mixup of the Resident Evil game series in a single package. From the elements of exploration of the first games, the atmosphere of RE7 and a lot of the combat design of RE4, Resident Evil Village works as a love letter to the whole franchise and also as a stand alone title.
The game is played from a first-person perspective just like RE7, but they improved a lot of the combat and speed of the gameplay, meaning that this game is way more focused on action, but don’t worry, the creepy atmosphere and horror elements are still there. The new action speed is a blast, between the item management and resources you still get that survival horror feel, but at the same time you have more options to approach combat and the level design is very well implemented for the use of weapons and enemy design and variety, it’s just plain fun.
The game looks amazing, the Reach to the Moon Engine is just a solid, great looking and optimised Engine, had great performance all the way through and the visual quality is gorgeous. From the gothic/industrial art astyle to the general technical quality of the visuals I have no complaints in this reward with the game, just top of the whole industry.
The plot is ok, It can be campy as hell at times wish is something that I love about this games, but in the more serious emotional moments it falls a little flat, still is an entertaining plot with some fun character and great sense of atmosphere and even references to other games of the series as well as other games and horror movies.
Sound design is great and it helps to sell the horror setting, sadly, the soundtrack isn't that great, nothing awful but also nothing noteworthy, just really average which is a shame because recent RE games just haven’t been able to reach the quality of OSTs of the original games, which was great.
So in the end, a really entertaining game that pays homage to it’s series and horror genre in general, looks great and plays even better, a solid 9/10 in my personal opinion.

I've been playing Biohazard games since the early 90's. They have had their ups (RE 2, RE 4, REmake) and their downs (Most of the spin-off, Code: Veronica, RE 6).

Now, When played RE 7, I thought it was a wonderful step in the right direction going for a more horror kinda game, but the game was far from perfect. It was way too short, the variety of weapons enemies, bosses and maps was poor. Nevertheless, it was a good game.

RE 8 takes everything that made RE 7 great and crank it up to 11 while adding a bit of what made other REs success, then it blend's it all together to get one of the best RE to date.

Mechanically the game doesn't change much from RE 7, your character still feels like a thank (it is intended by design), however it add the progress we saw on RE4 through a Merchant, albeit it is not as robust or "wild" as seen before. 

About the gameplay this game is a masterclass in how to keep your gameplay loop similar enough to have some consistency while changing things just enough to never get bored. This games throws everything at you, full on action scenes, survival horror, straight up psychological terror, while retaining it's core survival horror gameplay (I Played it on Hardcore the first time and I never really became overpowered. Even by the end of adventure I had to keep on managing my resources wisely).

As for the story... I mean, It's a RE Game, it's convoluted, nonsensical yet entertaining , besides, it has many easter eggs for long time fans (I won't spoil any, but it has some really nice callbacks). The story is compelling enough to keep you engaged and looking forward for what's next. Finally, the story is more in line with the story telling of REmake than RE4 if that's worth anything for you.

In short, RE 8 is a successful mixbag of every great RE game to date while retaining the new FPS mechanics and core gameplay. It has the best of the "old" and "new" in the franchise. Easily on my top 3 RE games.

In the technical department. I'm aware the game had some issues at lunch but I played on a 32¨ 1440P monitor using a Ryzen 5600x, 16GB of DDR4 3000Mh and a Vega 64 and the game ran buttery smooth at 80FPS AVG  (65FPS for my 1% low) with every setting max out. The only "issue" I have is the FOV, it's a bit narrower than I'd like, but it didn't cause me any dizziness.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

An otherwise rock-solid FPS game, even with the problems that I mention later.

Castle Dimitrescu is pretty good, but not as great as the Factory.

Heisenberg's Factory. Enough said.

Mommy Dimitrescu, my one true waifu! Always been a sucker for dominant vampire ladies, and Alcina just took it to a whole new level. Especially with her stunning beauty and also with her voice, which is more than enough to weaken me.

Of all the bosses in the game, Lady Dimitrescu is the best one.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]

It's pretty obvious: Alcina Dimitrescu is not the main villain... Or even a recurring villain. It's a real shame that she is the first boss, and that's the end for her...

Would've been nice to have that Dagger of Death's Flowers after Lady Dimitrescu...

There is now a cooldown when slashing with a knife for some reason. No such cooldown existed in RE7. It doesn't make sense when Ethan has had military training.

It didn't make sense in RE7 and it doesn't make sense here, that Capcom won't show Ethan's face. That ending should've had that reveal, but no...

I don't like—at all that they changed Chris' voice and appearance (melding "Chris" and the voice of Carlos into one being = I hereby name this so-called "Chris Redfield" as: Chrissalos), when this is continuation of RE7's story. I almost didn't buy this game because of that asinine change, but Dimitrescu changed my mind. And yes, RE7 version is my favorite, if it wasn't clear already.

Village of Shadows difficulty, without New Game + maxed out weapons before hand. Wouldn't recommend it. Don't know why they added it in Trauma Pack when it's unlockable after beating the game.

Tankiness of enemies for the sake of being tanky, especially in higher difficulties. God have mercy on those poor souls that started their very first playthrough with VoS difficulty... Madhouse difficulty made sense in RE7, where you have to be very precise with headshots and assault coin boosts that damage, especially with just a few enhanced handgun bullets. And why isn't there enhanced handgun ammo in RE8?

Not much horror in the game. Only in the basement in the Doll house section, when I played for the first time. 

I wanted to know more about the history of the Village; the Four Kings who founded that village, and how this Megamycete (also known as Fungal root and Black God) came to be. There's not much of anything...just a few lore snippets. And then there is general information about the four lords and that late introduction to Miranda's past and motivations. Also that very clichéd explanation of how Miranda just happened to find the Megamycete "completely by accident"... From what I've learned, there was originally some kind of flashbacks to the Village's history when the game would "switch between the village in modern day and the past, set in medieval times." That would've been great!

It has come to my knowledge, that the localizer has butchered the lore in the English version. Yes, there are inconsistencies in RE7 too, but nothing this drastic. There's so much more important (and accurate!) lore to be found in the Japanese version (and I don't mean just the lore pages, mind you)! I'm not gonna name them all to you (do your own research!), but... I always wondered, why does Dimitrescu cry out "Flesh... bones! I will devour all of you!" When the English version incorrectly states that she needs human flesh and blood, while in the Japanese version: she needs only other peoples blood. And that she and Heisenberg are both referred to as "outstanding individuals" in those treatment books, while the English version excludes my wife from that for some reason. Don't know why the localizer has some kind of an obsession with the "regeneration" word when that treatment book in reality states that Alcina has increased metabolism. And that the Dagger of Dead Flowers (that's how it translates to) was forged by a "former delusion-obsessed head of the family." Maybe he is that "fallen noble" to whom my waifu is related to? Alcina's diary is also more in keeping with her narcissism - in the Japanese version (obviously), and in the English version it sounds more like she's "in the team" while at the same time she doesn't want to be in that team... it's just so weird when you think about it. And apparently localizer conveniently changed it so (implying) that the heretics are Christians (nothing to see here, am I right?!) and not pagans (as in Japanese version) what the inhabitants of the Village really are. There's a treasure called "Father Nichola's Angel", which in truth should be: Nichola's Goddess Statue. Make of that what you will, but I'm sure you know what I'm thinking about this. If the English version ever gets the accurate lore, then and only then will I change the review into positive. But... I'm afraid it will never happen. Oh, and if the next RE also has watered down lore (i.e. that this localization madness continues), it's also a negative review from me, however good the game might actually be.

[h1]Mixed[/h1]

I wanted to go back to the Castle Dimitrescu! Just like in previous games, to unlock a path to somewhere new and obtaining something, but no... I fancied that Lady Dimitrescu has two boss fights. One in her human form where you weaken her enough times with that special Dagger, that she would then destroy the castle (while mutating) in some parts but not completely. Ethan somehow escapes or gets flung out from there for a time. And when we go back to the destroyed castle, you would have to fight her for the second time when she has fully mutated.

I don't know what even went through their heads when making the Doll house section. Basement part is a very nice experience. Recommending doing a blind playthrough! And the final part, not so good. One thing they have in common: They don't have replay value, at all. It would've been better, if there were more nightmarish creatures; some you would able to vanquish, and then there would be this one thing that you cannot harm at all, it would go away for a time when shooting certain amount of bullets at it or while hiding. I know that would've meant an entirely new objective and all that.

Heisenberg boss fight. It's cool when playing for the first time, but you can easily cheese it in a funny way. In the second phase, just go hug him from the side and then quick-swapping sniper and shotgun like in DOOM Eternal. He will go critical in seconds...

Ethan's healing ability is explained in RE7, so I was very surprised at peoples reaction to it, when he re-attaches his hand right after escaping Lady Dimitrescu. "Like have they not played RE7 at all?" Early in the game you can pick up Ethan's left hand, and it's the same hand that Zoe re-attaches back together. Also, after Jack has severed Ethan's right foot, he's surprised that it healed so quickly with the help of that healing juice. But what truly perplexes me, even to this day: Does that healing juice also fix his clothes?

[h1]Chris' section[/h1]

I would have liked that there was that "three-way battle" against lycans and the BSAA's B.O.Ws, as was shown in the concept art. And that the mold is consuming the village and the lycans alike. Would've been nice to see the other members of Hound Wolf Squad in action, but alas...

As they did nerf Ethan's melee, so too did they nerf Chris' guarding and punching, and I don't know why... In RE7 Not A Hero DLC, you could easily do a just guard (no damage taken) when Mama Molded is charging like a huge boulder at you; stunning her long enough to make some distance. And then when you have just guarded a regular Molded, you can instantly kill it with one punch, but not here...

A fantastic follow-up to the already amazing RE7 that together have basically revitalized Resident Evil. 

To get a few minor issues I have out of the way first:
-There are a few bugs and glitches that virtually every player will encounter but they are more immersion-breaking than game-breaking. 
-One of the more common enemy types has an over-ranged grab attack that gets really annoying to work against but is not game-ruining.
-The game makes it to where you have to sell fully-leveled weapons to make room for your new and improved ones. This isnt an issue when a new weapon is better than its predecessor in every way, but if you really go the distance in NG+ you will encounter the need to pick between beloved weapons due to inventory (unless you use the unlockable infinite ammo perks and literally just load up your inventory grid-square by grid-square with guns)

With that out of the way, the game has exceptional replay value even by RE's standards and you have a lot of freedom to fight and play how you want to. The visuals are jaw-dropping and the environments are some of the most detailed I have ever seen in a game. The entire world feels lived in and storied. The character design was also top notch this time and while RE will never escape its cheesy dialogue writing, the actors and actresses did a fantastic job making it work as best as it was ever going to.

Resident Evil Village obviously took heavy influence from Resident Evil 4. Explore a remote village with a strange religion, collecting treasures to sell to a merchant and purchase upgrades for your weapons. Unlock Mercenaries mode, and get a high ranking on each stage to unlock and overpowered weapon for the main game. It even has the famous opening where seemingly infinite enemies attack until bells summon them away.

There is a decent balance of both horror and action, and in my first playthrough I found myself checking each corner and carefully counting my ammo. I felt that ammo was scarce, but, honestly, that was because I neglected to craft often. The crafting took away from the horror experience, as a limited inventory isn't a big deal when you can hold infinite crafting items. The inventory itself was also massive by the end of the game, and I think at one point I was carrying two pistols, two shotguns, and one of every other weapon type, and still had room to spare.
It should be noted that Village is fairly easy once you get over the horror aspect. The Lycans provide a challenge, but they don't appear often, and many enemies are so slow that you can run circles around them. Tight indoor corridors help to make even slow enemies more challenging, but overall the standard zombies are probably the easiest in the whole series (except maybe Resident Evil Survivor).

Each villain seems to be based off of a classic, Universal-era monster. I noticed nods to Dracula, Frankenstein, and The Creature from the Black Lagoon. Although I'm not sure what one of the villains represented (The Invisible Man?).

Village's Mercenaries mode is probably my favorite version of the series, although it's a bit closer to Raid Mode. Maintaining a combo, finishing with time to spare, and collecting currency all count towards boosting your score. Randomized powerups can turn you into an unstoppable force if you get a decent combination.

The Good:
Beautiful locations.
Memorable villains.
Fun gameplay that jumps between intense action and exploring at your own pace.

The Bad:
Some sections are exactly the same on replays and feel repetitive.
Large sections are completely blocked off as the story progresses, even though the map looks like you should be able to return.
Inventory management trivialized by both crafting and the inventory's massive size.

The Weird:
You can collect ingredients to cook food. Not a problem, but who thought "you know what Resident Evil is missing? Cooking."

[h1] Information / Review English [/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a first-person horror game and the long-awaited sequel to the series, which was developed by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. was developed. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2640843850

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

Four years have passed since the events in Louisiana. Ethan and Mia thought they had finally got through the horror and events of Resident Evil 7 and left it all behind, but they were wrong because it is just beginning .. Ethan and wife Mia have been dating their new offspring, Rose withdrawn from the public. On a cozy evening one day, the intimate trinity is suddenly interrupted when Chris Redfield rumbles through the door with masked mercenaries, shoots Mia and, to make matters worse, steals Rose. Ethan is also led away, but a little later our main character wakes up in the middle of nowhere and goes in search of his missing daughter. Ethan finds the eponymous village of Resident Evil 8, where a familiar, if completely new nightmare awaits him: a biological weapon made by werewolf-like Lycans slaughters the local population, and Ethan is promptly captured by one of the four diabolical counts of the area. Like the Baker family from Part 7, the villains under the mysterious mother Miranda show a disturbing interest in Ethan and his daughter Rose.

Again, the players experience the world from a first-person perspective. The basic controls have remained the same, the gameplay feels familiar. Nevertheless, »Village« comes up with some major changes for the series. For example, the item boxes that once forced players to carefully consider which items to take and which to leave behind have disappeared. Now it is important to get enough in-game currency quickly to buy a larger inventory from the dealer. Like in "Resident Evil 4" such a player appears at various points in the game and sells ammunition, remedies or weapon upgrades to the players. You can also purchase instructions with which you can make ammunition and medicines yourself - from objects such as green cabbage and a chemical that can be found in the game world. In moments of silence, uncertainty, or hesitant exploration, Resident Evil 8 is best. When we crouch under a house in the snow and hide from the hungry, thirsty Lycans or search every inch of an imposing treasury, we quickly forget everything around us. The opposite happens when we discover the yellow packaging tape, which is always prominently distributed, that points to objects with which we can interact.Ethan blows up walls and cuts wood. The remaining majority of the level architecture and objects are made of reinforced concrete, including candles, dishes and rotten fruit. What the title gains in credibility elsewhere is often gambled away shortly afterwards. Titles like "Half-Life: Alyx" or the meanwhile old "Metal Gear Solid 2" demonstrate that pointless interactivity is possible and fun. I could list more, but that would go beyond the scope of this article.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2651845843

[h1] Combat system [/h1]

There are different types of weapons such as knives, pistols, rifles, shotguns, grenade launchers and flamethrowers. Some can be found in the course of the game and for others you need keys or have to solve puzzles. There is the right weapon for every type of enemy. Ammunition is rather in short supply, but it all depends on the level of difficulty, as this varies. Later you will be happy about every available shot in your pocket.

Resident Evil 8 takes what Resident Evil 7 made and continues it. The game embodies the unmistakable gameplay elements of exploration in a tense atmosphere that shaped the “survival horror” genre about twenty years ago. Clear buy recommendation in this genre.


[h1] Information / Review Deutsch [/h1]

Resident Evil Village  ist ein First-Person Horror Spiel und der lang ersehnte Nachfolger der Serie, welches von CAPCOM Co., Ltd. entwickelt wurde. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2651845843

[h1] Gameplay / Geschichte [/h1]

Vier Jahre nach den Ereignissen in Louisiana sind vergangen. Ethan und Mia dachten, sie hätten endlich das Grauen und die Geschehnisse von Resident Evil 7 überstanden und alles hinter sich gelassen, doch sie haben sich getäuscht, denn es fängt gerade erst an.. Ethan und Ehefrau Mia haben sich mit ihrem frischen Nachwuchs Rose aus der Öffentlichkeit zurück gezogen. An einem gemütlichen Abend eines Tages, wird  die traute Dreisamkeit jedoch jäh unterbrochen, als Chris Redfield mit maskierten Söldnern durch die Tür poltert, Mia niederschießt und zu allem Übel auch noch Rose stibitzt. 
Auch Ethan wird abgeführt, wenig später erwacht unsere Hauptfigur aber mitten im verschneiten Nirgendwo und macht sich auf die Suche nach seiner verschwundenen Tochter. Dabei stöbert Ethan das titelgebende Dörfchen von Resident Evil 8 auf, wo ihn ein vertrauter, wenn auch völlig neuer Albtraum erwartet: Eine Biowaffe werwolfartiger Lycans metzelt die örtliche Bevölkerung nieder, und Ethan wird prompt von einem der vier diabolischen Grafen der Gegend gefangen genommen. Wie schon die Baker-Familie aus Teil 7 zeigen die Schurken unter der mysteriösen Mutter Miranda beunruhigend großes Interesse an Ethan sowie dessen Tochter Rose. 

Wieder erleben die Spieler die Welt aus der Ich-Perspektive. Die grundlegende Steuerung ist gleich geblieben, das Spielgefühl wirkt vertraut. Dennoch wartet »Village« mit einigen, für die Serie gravierenden Änderungen auf. So sind etwa die Item-Boxen verschwunden, die Spieler einst zwangen, genau abzuwägen, welche Gegenstände sie mitnehmen und welche sie zurücklassen. Jetzt gilt es, schnell an genügend Ingame-Währung zu kommen, um sich beim Händler ein größeres Inventar zu kaufen. TL:DR
RE"8" follows the story of Ethan Winters that begun in RE"7".
This one is one of the GOOD RE, maybe the BEST, if you are into the more action oriented ones.
The game has GREAT graphics, maybe some of the more realistic in the industry thus far. This means you should get a computer a few steps above potato to really make RE8 come to life.
The story is VERY WELL made, tailored to keep you hooked up along the way, somewhat long, but not overstaying its welcome.
While still having a small share of puzzles and secrets, this is one of the more "dynamic" RE, and it tries to keep the walking back to X to a minimum, trying to show you new things all the time.

The long view:
Resident Evil: VILLage, is as of 2021 the latest installement in the RE franchise, and as the stylized name suggest, the EIGHT game that follows the "main" story of RE, and the "sequel" to Ethan Winthers quest (started in RE7), and the 25th RE game (bar the 3 remakes, that would make the grand total of 28 games!).
That being said: it's not necessary to play ALL games to know your way around, though if you have you'll get a few glimpses to the backstory of the in game universe. 
This game itself gives you a rundown of the previous, so you at least have some knowledge of where the main character, Ethan Winthers, journey began.

SOMETHING OF A SPOILER AHEAD:
If you HAVE played previous games, then know this is one of the more "action oriented" RE, somewhat akin to RE4. Item scarcity is still something of an issue, but it'll more than amount to help you mow down hordes of enemies, while previously you "only" took down a few dozen of them.
RE:VILLAGE is the in game universe take on victorian horror, by explaining the existence of creatures akin warewolfs, vampires, zombies and ghosts, through "scientific" means so the game, like the rest, is more of a sci-fy than a fantasy background. Meaning even though bordering the impossible, it dosn't push the threshold into the supernatural.

As Ethan Winters, you'll navigate a labyrinth of terror, facing off against iconic foes like Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters. The combat is visceral and satisfying, with a balance of action and resource management that keeps you on your toes.

But it's not just the monsters you have to fear; the village itself is a character, full of secrets and hidden dangers. Exploring its dark corners uncovers puzzles and treasures, adding depth to the gameplay experience.

The story weaves elements of horror and folklore into a compelling narrative, though some plot twists may feel predictable to series veterans. However, the game's memorable characters and tense atmosphere make up for any narrative shortcomings.

In conclusion, "Resident Evil Village" is a thrilling journey into darkness, perfect for both series fans and newcomers alike. So grab your shotgun, brace yourself for the horrors that await, and prepare to enter the village of nightmares.

A structured Resident Evil branded journey worth playing
When all else fails you can always rely on Resident Evil games to stick to a rigid formula. Resident Evil Village follows the recipe of many of the previous games: a strong start (slowly poured), a pinch of enemies with imposing, iconic and creative designs, and a final showdown with a well baked, finely greased, too-many-eyed monstrosity. Oh… and don’t forget the icing of classic monsters in ‘bio-weapon’ make-up.
	Resident Evil has consistently followed this recipe for much of the franchises confusing lifespan, and Resident Evil Village is no exception. Village looked like it might break away from its siblings and their focus on zombies, evil swamp people, tentacle monsters and other bio-weapons in disguise. The marketing and begin of Village took several strong trembling steps away  from secret labs and creepy swamps of older Resident Evil games for a jaunt through a gothic setting complete with dominatrix vampires, werewolves and creepy crones. Alas Village does fall back on the typical RE tropes eventually, which ultimately represents the more bland aspects of its run time. However the fresh setting and new direction certainly makes it worth a try, even if you jump ship after the first half of the game.
	When the game is good, it is the pinnacle of what Resident Evil has to offer, topping the best games in the franchise and seating itself as a strong contender amongst other popular survival horror games of this time. This is especially true when Village makes use of the franchise’s ultimate weapon… Great level design. A few quality of life tweaks and a new setting that quite literally drags you into exploring its graveyards and immaculate European castles, makes Village worth the price of admission just for the chance to take the tour around its merry-go-round of level design. 
In this regard, the game is at its strongest when it is giving you time to take a poke around and explore everything at your own pace, inter-spliced with the occasional set-piece chase sequences, dynamic encounters with an un-killable meme vamp-queen, and small scale combat encounters. It is during the linear sequences when the game stumbles – Village falls into the trappings of mediocrity around its mid-point as it begins to feel like the characteristic trudge through the mud that RE games often become by their third act. Luckily, unlike RE 7, Village manages to momentarily pull itself out of the mud and maintain some good amongst the lower points of the game. Resident Evil 7 fell on its face once you complete the Baker house portion of the game with several hours of gameplay to go, but Village only has a few stumbling blocks that momentarily ruin the games inertia. In total the portions of Village that focus too heavily on its combat and weak structure only makes up perhaps 2 hours of campaign.
	During RE Village’s 7-10 hour run time you’ll be making your way through the titular Village, and its surrounding locations as Ethan Winters - the returning ‘hero’ from RE 7. If it was unclear why a faceless milquetoast guy like Ethan was the protagonist in RE 7, then you’ll probably be even more boggled when you realise how much they doubled down on that idea in Village. The plot largely revolves around Ethan and his lost daughter, Rose, for whom you will be scouring the village in search of… while also frantically looking for shotgun ammo and pig meat. Surprisingly the story is deeply rooted in the events of RE 7, although if you haven’t played the previous game, RE Village will still very much make sense. It’s best not to dwell on Ethan or the part he plays in the story for too long, but I will say that he really should have taken some vocal lessons from Gordon Freeman because his dialogue makes you realise that sometimes less is more when it comes to a protagonist. One particularly awkward and jarring line is delivered when Ethan falls through a floor and lands surrounded by dead bodies, for which he exclaims ‘Dead bodies?’, as if the player had no idea that this very clearly haunted and blood soaked village was going to feature corpse piles and blood filled basements. This may seem like a strange gripe, but it really does make the evocative moments of gothic and body horror so much less effective when Ethan is needlessly narrating my reaction for me.
	Switching gears somewhat, Village puts a clear and pronounced effort into its combat, expanding it beyond simply strafing groups of enemies while taking pot shots at their heads. The combat can very much still be boiled down to this basic principle, but there is far more of an emphasis on mechanically complex enemies, utilising your environment through barricading doorways, laying traps and using environmental hazards to your advantage. These mechanical shake-ups make the portions of the game that rely heavily on combat far more effective than previous RE instalments and keep it from going completely stale. While most of the ‘boss fights’ in the game don’t reflect this complexity, there are moments where you almost need to treat enemy encounters and set-piece moments as combat puzzles.
	As great as it is to see expanded combat elements, Village is undeniably at its best when elements of combat are stripped back and the game takes on a ‘solve-the-puzzles-under-stress-of-death’ ethos. While there are combat sections that work effectively, by far the best portion of the game are during the House Beneviento chapter when your weapons are taken away so that genre elements and the thick atmosphere can really flourish. This chapter is so flawless in its execution that the following chapter may give players a bit of whiplash as it takes several downturns before eventually recovering during the Heisenberg chapter. This description of the games high and lowlights may seem a little esoteric, but it is best left to the player to find out what I mean as the key moments of this game are strong tied up in its story. 
	While the game isn’t as perfect as I would have liked, I can dry my tears on how consistently amazing it is as a visual buffet. Some subtle combination of its lowlight, gothic atmosphere and the fantastic fidelity of its world space makes RE Village a stunning theme park ride through the various biomes that the setting has to offer. One of the early peaks in this visual rollercoaster is the Dimistrescu Castle, which feels very much like a crawl through a twisted Beauty and the Beast castle, complete with Lady Dimistrescu as the Beast hunting you through the halls. While this experience has proved voyeuristic for some, these dynamic chase sequences are just as effective (if not more) than the Baker house, Mr X, or other horror contemporaries like Amnesia: Dark Descent that have unkillable big bads chasing you. Another highlight of the games graphical fidelity and level design comes as a surprise in the games latter half; the Heisenberg’s factory, which brings a strong finish to the pseudo-open world portions of the game. You might not think a factory in a horror game is inherently visually striking, but it’s a ‘you have to be there to understand’ kind of location.
	Moving from gameplay and fidelity to story, Village once again starts strong and finishes on its least inspired elements, like many in the RE franchise. The new setting and curious take on gothic creatures feels really fresh, but unfortunately the mysteries of the game’s first half eventually give way to the classic RE motif that everything is a mould/virus bioweapon… which kind of spoils the stories uniqueness. That being said this game certainly taught me something about story and plot in this genre… it’s always at its most compelling when it’s mysterious. Not everything needs to be fully explained, although RE probably wouldn’t be doing its duty if it didn’t relate everything back to Umbrella or bioweapons, so I digress. 
	The story is also where all of the other hallmark wackiness of RE games comes into play

[b]Resident Evil Village successfully strikes out in new, unforgettable directions[/b]
★★★★★ (5/5)
[i]Based on a completed playthrough on Standard difficulty[/i]

Resident Evil Village is a fantastic evolution of its predecessor, a remarkable feat for a follow-up to one of the best horror games in recent memory. It trades Resident Evil 7’s slower-paced haunted house crawl for a more action-oriented romp through a European village steeped in Gothic horror and snowy vistas. While significantly less frightening than the Baker home, Resident Evil Village’s titular locale and its mesmerizing cast of characters are absolutely unforgettable. Many of the events that unfold over the roughly 10-hour adventure need to be seen to be believed; this is a game operating at an abnormally high level of confidence, and its best tricks are better left unspoiled if you can manage it.

Set three years after the torturous events of the previous game, Village sees protagonist Ethan Winters thrust into another nightmare after witnessing Resident Evil long-timer Chris Redfield murder Ethan's wife Mia and kidnap his newborn daughter Rose. Ethan is knocked unconscious and taken too, only for the entire operation to be sidelined by a mysterious attack that leaves a truck overturned and Ethan alone in a forest. It’s not long before Ethan discovers the village and meets its larger-than-life cast of villains, at which point he sets out to take down each of the four village “lords” and their enigmatic leader, Mother Miranda, with the hope of rescuing his daughter. Village's story isn't particularly thick with lore, but its made all the more compelling by its villains and the rather twisted process Ethan must complete to rescue Rose. It also ends spectacularly well; the finale kicks off with one of the most awesome sequences in the history of this genre.

These lords have their own sections of the world carved out for them, each one pulling from an impressive array of horror tropes. Where RE7 had dingy basements, escape rooms, and ghost ships, Village has towering castles, monstrous creatures, and muddy pathways that wind their way through trees. The game takes a more fantastical direction than RE7's more grounded, almost [i]True Detective[/i]-inspired approach. Each “level” of Village presents new challenges, new enemies, and new ways to murder Ethan’s hands. The game only has maybe one or two sections that could be deemed frightening in a vein similar to RE7, and it’s not due to the rest of the game failing to scare. Rather, Village takes inspiration from new sources, choosing to impress with its enemy and environmental design rather than lay out a terrifying experience the entire way through. And these spaces are always rewarding to explore; everywhere you go there are resources to grab and secrets to uncover.

The most significant departure from RE7 is in Village’s focus on action, which will undoubtedly disappoint a few. The combat in Village isn’t amazing--Ethan moves pretty slowly, and there’s still no true aim-down-sights which can leave the shooting feeling a bit dated. But every enemy encounter feels designed around these limitations. There’s a much larger variety of enemies this time around, and each one feels fair to fight. There’s also a larger arsenal of weapons, and they all can be upgraded with attachments that enhance their stopping power, recoil, and magazine size.

Village also sees the return of an omnipresent merchant, a comically large man by the name of Duke. Duke sells items and weapon upgrades and will buy treasures off of Ethan for rather large sums of money. During my playthrough on the Standard difficulty I almost always seemed to have a surplus of cash on hand, which made every encounter with Duke feel like a splendid shopping trip. Duke can also cook for Ethan using meat and fish that can be gathered out in the world. Yes, there’s a mild hunting mechanic in Village, though it really just involves shooting pigs and stabbing fish with a knife. These meals grant permanent bonuses to Ethan’s health and damage resistance, replacing the steroids from RE7.

Unsurprisingly, Village also looks amazing. The environment and character artists absolutely outdid themselves here. Everything and everyone you see just looks [i]so good[/i], with the game’s lighting and texture work being particular highlights. I don’t know that I’ve ever played a game that better fits the “I feel like I can [i]touch[/i] and [i]smell[/i] the things in this room” cliche better than this. Notably, Village takes place almost entirely during the day; unlike RE7, where most of your visual understanding of your surroundings came from a flashlight or dimly lit table lamps, Village discovers [i]sunlight[/i]. It peeks through cracked windows and silhouettes spindly, gnarled branches. The ability to actually see your surroundings, and in turn the things attacking you, necessarily makes Village a less scary game than RE7, but certainly no less an amazing one to look at.

There is a spoiler-filled list I could make of all the things I’ll remember most from Resident Evil Village, but suffice it to say that this game unquestionably lives up to the high bar set by its predecessor. It is equally impressive in its ability to surprise as it is in its boldness to immediately break out of the creepy mold of RE7 into something new. Many have compared this game to Resident Evil 4 for its similarities in setting and action. Though Village necessarily can’t be as groundbreaking as RE4, it matches the classic forebear by just being a startlingly good horror game.

Next to Black Mesa and BioShock Infinite, the third greatest game I've ever played. The combat, empowering and action-packed; the story and characters, unforgettable, emotional and saddening; the environments, breathtakingly beautiful; the variety, challenges, puzzles, dialogue, soundtrack...everything. It's over-the-top and fun as any game can be, yet it knows when to slow down and get serious, all while remaining the best of both Resident Evil worlds: the insane, action-filled hammy fun-fest of RE3-5 and the creepy, slow-paced horror-oriented RE1, 2 and 7.

The bosses, particularly [spoiler]Dimitrescu[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Heisenberg[/spoiler], deserve their own special mention: every single one of them is chock-full of personality and character, their home bases and personalized cannon-fodder enemies seep with enjoyment at every turn, and their dialogue and interactions with Ethan Winters will forever cement them in my memory as some of the greatest villains in gaming. Ethan himself is worth mentioning, too: I went from "eh, he's OK I guess" in RE7 to [spoiler]"♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥...I can't believe he's dead..."[/spoiler] here, and genuinely liked learning his story and hearing his little quips every now and then. He plays the role of a mid-30s systems engineer dad extremely well, and I loved it.

 I can't really put into words just how much this game touched my soul, and it isn't something you can quite understand unless you've played it yourself. This is the best RE game I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing, and a more-than-worthy entry into the series. Would recommend to absolutely anyone even remotely interested in first-person action-horror games looking for emotion, action, humor and character. An unironic 11/10.

in Resident Evil Village we are following Ethan Winters on another adventure, this time it isn't Mia being kidnapped but Rosemary, his daughter. Ethan doesn't know who you are, he doesn't know what you want, he doesn't have money, but he does have a particular set of skills, he will find you, and he will kill you. [strike]Liam[/strike] Ethan goes about exploring the darkest deepest secrets of a village in (eastern?) Europe where he thought he would finally find peace after the events of Resident Evil VII.

The storytelling is excellent and exploring the village to find these extra secrets and lore kept me engaged in the story and with a wish to know more about what's happening. The different antagonists and characters you will meet in the game have great personalities and only contributes to your complete immersion in the Village universe.

While very similar to Resident Evil VII in many aspects, both games differ in the sense that [b]Village[/b] definitely feels like it's packed with action with short horror intermission rather than a horror game with added psychological burn filled with short bursts of action.

My overall experience with the game was wonderful, I wasn't expecting to like it so much and only regret not getting around playing it sooner.

There are werewolves, vampires, robed "vampires" that look like a cross between Emperor Palpatine and Gary Oldman from Bram Stoker's Dracula (but only when he's old), flying bird monsters, ghosts, Tim Burton doll ghosts, a literal crone, some type of goblin/ogre/hunchback, and an able-bodied Dr Loveless from Wild Wild West. Every RE game has bad dialogue and groan-inducing storylines. That's part of the series' charm. I mention the things above because, even for an RE game, there's a lot going on here. 

I would also probably nickname this RE4 Part 2 for the overall setting, though the set pieces look fantastic -- especially the castle. While RE7 was a 9/10 at the time of my review, this one is more of a 8/10 -- though both titles are rated for the series and not gaming as a whole.

[b]Phenomenal, at times exhausting and annoying, sometimes confusing, a lot of backtracking and frequent wandering around and getting lost ... [/b]

... is what comes to mind when I think of Resident Evil (8) Village ... 

The eighth part catapults us into a European backwoods village, which IRL is actually horror enough, I think.
People with strange dialects, drinking parties, farmer's discos, the love of tractors or their own family are really scary enough. But joking aside...

Ethan's flight to Europe with Mia and the baby and the new happiness in the family do not last long. Things get down to business in the first few minutes of the game. Chris Redfield shoots Mia, kidnaps Rose, and Ethan wakes up in the middle of nowhere. Well that's a good start.

Once again and in search of answers, this time we are faced with werewolves and vampires, among others, in RE8 and are supposed to uncover the mystery of Chris, Miranda and the four children. 

The village serves as "the hub" for the entire game world. Over time, new paths open up and we get new gadgets with which we can find useful items. 
There are plenty of different passages in RE8.
From long exploring, the associated “man, now I'm lost again” and “♥♥♥♥, where should / just wanted to go again” to elements of persecution to stealth passages and seemingly endless shootings, everything is included. 

[b]For me[/b] Resident Evil Village is not the game that permanently takes your breath away and it doesn’t come close to the long-lasting terror from the seventh part, but there are sometimes very good moments of horror and disgust.
[b]In summary[/b], I would say, playfully excellent, only a bit boring towards the end, but still well implemented.
