REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS.


THE BASICS

Resident Evil Village was one of my most enjoyable playthroughs of any single player horror game. I loved practically every part of it, from the character design, graphics, world design, sound design, you name it. Even though this is a sequel to the previous release in the franchise (Resident Evil 7 Biohazard) it brought me joy that a recap was made for players that for some reason hadn't gotten round to playing the start of the story. The price can be argued, but for me personally was just fine as I feel I received my money's worth.

THE STORY (SPOILERS)

Of course the main plot twist near the end of the story of Ethan really being dead ever since visiting Louisiana 3 years ago, and being made of the mold was one of the craziests and most intriguing parts of the game for me, but at the same time closed a lot of the holes in the games (Ethan literally having parts of his body chopped off, but just sticking it back on again). The characters all had a unique story to them, showing their backstory and how they ended up slaving away for Mother Miranda, especially Heisenburg. This goes without even mentioning how Mother Miranda disguised herself as Mia to Ethan for possibly a year or more (from what I know).

THE GRAPHICS & SOUND DESIGN

Nothing to be said. Absolutely amazing, the ray-tracing especially.

THE MERCENARIES

The Mercenaries is a time trial sort of minigame which unlocks in the Extra Content shop after you first beat the game. Personally I never found it all that fun, however I can definitely see people enjoying this as a cherry on the top of a cake.

OVERALL

A compelling gaming experience for me, couldn't recommend this enough, extremely good game. Get it!

Resident Evil Village is one of the weirder entries in the series (though not as weird, perhaps, as Code: Veronica), with a focus on gothic horror.  The gameplay is more enjoyable than RE 7, which is why I finished this first.  It's not as scary as 7 because your character is much better at fighting monsters, though one section in particular was quite disturbing.  

This is one of the better looking games I have, so if you own a decent video card you will probably enjoy the graphics.  The village areas are especially beautiful and fortunately that makes up a good chunk of the game.  

As for difficulty, it's one of the easier RE entries, though there are four difficulty settings to provide the right level of challenge.  

The game did remind me a lot of RE4, but it has enough of a personality of its own that it didn't feel like a copycat.  The villains were interesting like most of the ones in RE4, and of course it also takes place in some hidden European village.  The latter half of the game reminded me of 4 the most, however, because the tone switches from horror to action-adventure.  I didn't care much for RE 5 and 6, so it's nice to finally have a sequel that I want to play multiple times like I did with RE4.

It's good. Sometimes brilliant, sometimes predictable but never bad. The problem is, RE7 was a bold, ambitious, wild and brutal game that really brought the franchise back to life, because it wasn't afraid to cross some red lines. RE8 Village isn't the same thing, it's not even trying to step in its prequel shoes. The horror is tuned down, A LOT, the game is still gruesome here and there but the tension, the atmosphere, the dread are just not there, or at least not in the same league of RE7. This game feels safe, focus tested to be just enough to satisfy but not enough to shock or scare in any way, and that's a pity. The core concept with the 4 different kind of horror experiences is a good one, unfortunately none of them really pushes the envelope and 2/4 really make the guns the stars of the show. What really amazes me is how good the game still manages to feel despite being fundamentally disappointing in its approach. The gameplay is good, the graphics are generally stunning (ok there are a few ugly textures here and there but that's the exception) even if the ray tracing isn't pushed too far, it runs smooth as silk and the story kind of keeps it together, it's not exciting like the first half of RE7 and there's some silly stuff but that's just RE after all.
Thumbs up, you should play it if you liked any other game in the series (make sure you played RE7 before because it's all connected), just don't expect this game to push any boundaries because this is truly Capcom playing it as safe as they could to reach more people and getting away with it because the game still ends up being good.

Introduction
Play as a bright, flying, fish-like species called Lumini, as you make your way through a beautiful colourful world, fending off evil creatures wanting to hurt you and escaping the dangers of a hostile planet.

Gameplay
Rather than controlling just a single creature, you play as an entire swarm of Lumini (unless of course you manage to kill them all!). As you progress, you reach large cube crystal-like checkpoints that emit an energy, allowing your force of Lumini to grow. The more little blue flowers you collect along the way, the more your swarm will grow. There are different types of Lumini with different abilities (for example a speed boost, or a bomb-like move which removes damaging objects in your path), and you can change which variety leads the swarm. Though the game mostly involves simply exploring the soothing atmosphere, there are a few puzzles to complete and bad guys to fight off. Some of the puzzles require your swarm of Lumini to separate into 2 groups, both of which you can control at the same time.

Graphics & Art
Honestly, 95% of the reason I play this game is because it is just so beautiful. There are crystals scattered around the Lumini’s path which light up as you pass them, different areas of the map that present a different theme, and bright, contrasting colours (for example the bright colours the crystals emit inside tunnels) throughout the game.
I also thoroughly enjoyed going through the concept art (can be found under ‘extras’), which displays a huge amount of artistic talent.

Replay Value
One play through of Lumini on the easiest setting takes roughly 2 hours. After completing the playthrough on ‘normal’, a harder difficulty will unlock. The replay value is highly dependant on whether you get bored of games easily, as it is fairly repetitive and linear. For me, the artwork is definitely reason enough to play it through numerous times.
There are enough achievements to give you a few playthroughs before you complete the game.

Soundtrack
The soundtrack, much like the rest of the game, is incredibly calming. It’s enthralling, blissful and flows beautifully with the gameplay.

Difficulty & Challenge
The first playthrough of Lumini is on the easiest setting, ‘normal’. It’s honestly very easy, and would be a good difficulty level for someone who is more interested in taking in the art of the game (rather than in engaging in more difficult combat), or even children. Because you have a whole swarm of Lumini, it’s hard to fail; you’re likely not going to lose every single one before the game ends, at least not on normal. After you’ve completed the game on this setting, a harder setting will unlock.
The controls are very easy to use (it is also recommended to use a controller), and the gameplay is very simple with very few dangers along the way.

Overall Verdict
Lumini very quickly became one of my favourite games; I could probably play it over 100 times and it would still have the same serene effect. With the different difficulty levels, I really think Lumini has something to appeal to everyone. For me, it was definitely worth the price.

Resident Evil Village is probably one of the most enjoyable games in the franchise, yet it sadly falls short of some great values that RE7 had. RE8 seems to be the most extensive one out of the whole series and has some really memorable moments. They surely put the most amount of budget into making that game and it totally paid off.

The game's atmosphere isn't as terrifying as in RE7, they specifically did that on purpose because supposedly the previous entry was too horrifying, which is outright dumb thinking in my opinion. Besides that, it still has some cool gruesome stuff but it could've been much more.

The story is interesting, gripping, and has some unexpected plot twists although it is a bit confusing at the end. The puzzled ending absolutely changes the whole vibe of that game and it potentially opens a new door for a sort of continuation of that plotline which is nice.

The gameplay is excellent. It is a top performance of the RE franchise when it comes to that, it's really fluid. RE8 has all of the most important aspects of RE games such as resource management, puzzles, riddles, etc. The return of the merchant was great and it totally expands the players' experience. In conclusion, Resident Evil Village is one of my favorites in the franchise, it has a decent story with incredible gameplay and well-thought-out puzzles. I totally recommend it. 10/10

Fun but buy it when it is on sale. Like most of my reviews I don't feel this game is worth the full $60 price tag. It was fun but it did not have enough content for what I paid for. Even though I waited for it to go on sale. If BlockBuster were still a thing this game would have been something I rented one weekend then returned it a few days later.

The game has some replay value. That was my biggest complaint with RE7. Once I cleared that game I had no desire to play it again. RE8 on the other hand, with all the weapons and upgrades I wanted to play it again. After my 2nd clear I saved up for infinite ammo with wolvesbane. Sadly I didn't feel like playing the game a 3rd time. Maybe when I get bored I might go back on the hardest difficulty.

The game sort of lost it's horror aspect. RE7 went back to it's roots but with RE8 there's more action. I feel action comes at the expense of horror. If something is lurking around the corner I'm not afraid because I can blow it away with a shotgun or a grenade launcher. It starts out scary and it retains that affect for a good while. Even with my various guns there were plenty of times when I was almost out of ammo and I had to kill something with the knife. That too goes away on a 2nd play through when you start with all your guns and can unlock infinite ammo. The section where you play as Chris, the game might as well just be a L4D2 clone.

The guns were plentiful but I felt that was the problem. Whenever I got a gun I would upgrade it. Only to discover a new and better gun later. There's not much debate over which guns are the best. There's like 3 pistols but each one is stronger than the previous. When I found the 2nd pistol I kept using the first because I had upgraded it. By the end of the game my first pistol was maxed and it's stats were crap compared to the final pistol which had no upgrades at this point. I felt like the game punished me for upgrading the early weapons.

Constantly going back to the village got boring after awhile. Sure there were new houses to unlock but I hate having to go back to the same maps over and over. The Castle map felt like the design team spent a lot of time on that and took it easy the rest of the game. Every area after the castle felt like it was rushed. It did not met the expectations of the castle level. Then there's the map that tells you if your missing an item in a room. While I like that feature to a degree but at times I hate it. There were times when I tore a room apart looking for that final item because I didn't want to miss anything important. At times I paused the game just to google what I was missing. Another issue I had were some areas of the map were cut off when you passed a certain point. There were times I missed something to combine a treasure and I couldn't go back to get the piece I was missing.

Boss fights all felt roughly the same. Run away, bang a 180, fire, rinse+repeat. It's pretty hard to be afraid of something chasing you when you aren't looking at it.

The dollhouse was creepy at first but on subsequent play throughs it was just annoying once the scare wore off.

This is a hard one because sure I wouldn't mind recommending this game, but I don't necessarily want to give it a thumbs up either. I just felt like they should have done a much better job considering this is capcom and resident evil we are talking about.


1. The gunplay did not feel/look all that great. I am not a gun expert/connoisseur, but the gunplay for the most part felt very average. Sure some weapons are better than others, but at the end of the day, putting skill/reward aside, I did not find the gunplay all that good in quality.

2. Not a fan of the angle in which you aim/shoot your weapons. I understand that this is how resident evil games are for the most part, but for me it feels off for an FPS game. I would rather have them stick with one or the other, instead of trying to retain a feel from their previous third person view. This ties into why I probably didn't find the gunplay all that great.

3. The villain characters/arcs felt rushed. It was like they were trying to boot you out of the castle as fast as they could, just to boot you out of other areas. There was not enough depth in exploring and character development as I was hoping for. Such a shame because I really wanted to see more of Dimitrescu and her daughters, I understand that people feel like this game has too many cutscenes as it is, but I for one feel like they needed more. I really liked that scene where you are tied next to all the villains, to bad we did not get anymore of that. Remember that scene in RE7 where you are sitting down with the bakers at dinner?, well I would have loved something similar to that with Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters etc. When I look back at this game, ya sure the characters have potential, but they were lost due to its pacing. (most of the characters including chris just felt poorly implemented as well.)

4. Most of the puzzles were too easy. I get that they want to keep things simple for everyone, but I can't help but get offended by some of these puzzles. Would be nice to have puzzles that can kill you if you fail them. 

5. Correct me if I am wrong, but the stealth part of this game is very hit and miss. I am not talking about hiding your body, I am talking about the enemies being smart and reacting to sounds you make. I swear with Lady Dimitrescu for example, I could sprint around, break vases/windows right next door and she won't react to that like I feel like she should. Even shooting your weapon in certain locations in the castle, does not trigger them to run to the location of the shots. it's not like they don't react at all, don't get me wrong, but they could make things much more intense, if they improve their reactions to sound.

6. The difficulty does not sit well with me. My first playthrough was on normal difficulty, now before you guys get all upset, hear me out. When I think of difficulty, I think of smart/adapting AI, not AI that are bullet sponges or kill you in one/two hits. This touches on what I was just talking about as far as stealth. I don't care if Lady demetrius does a crap ton of damage, I just want her to spot me like she should. Many times she should have easily spotted me looking at her from the stairs, or hear me sprinting around and whatnot, she has too many blind spots. Another example would be her daughters, they should be able to counter what I am trying to do and force me to figure out other methods instead of breaking windows. These are the type of things I want for difficulty. Another example would be that they should still see/attack you even when utilizing certain entrances, for example the daughters could send their flies to do damage or force you out even if they can't reach you etc. I would also not mind if dimitrescu could throw a spear at you here and there, doing this would add another layer of randomness/difficulty, and if the spear connects you die instantly, does not matter what difficulty you play on. (Side note: Challenging puzzles are another thing I am looking for as far as difficulty.) Maybe have an option where the inventory screen does not pause the game, random moments where your gun can jam, etc...

7. The knife combat is really boring, I prefer to use knife/melee combat in my gameplays. I typically just save bullets for when I really need them, like when surrounded or for boss/mini boss fights. This should also makes sense if you want to be more stealthy by not having people hear your gunshots. It would be nice if you could have cool finishing kill animations or give players two different ways to hold a knife, and in doing so, give different slicing/stabbing animations with it etc..

8. It sucks not being able to manually holster weapons. Also sucks not being able to change POV settings like they gave players in RE7.

9. I am kind of getting tired of the main character. The villains have so many chances to kill Ethan, but instead they keep choosing to not take things serious, even when they desperately want him dead. They grab him and sling him somewhere and think he is dealt with, when we all know for the 20th time he is not. It is not that he survives that bothers me, it is more about how he survives these engagements that annoy me. I really hope that their new protagonist(daughter) will be much better.

10. From what I can tell, you only have full access to certain upgrades and crafts when you start a new game+. I am not a fan of this at all, having to play a new game+ just to have the magnum recipe sounds really awful to me. What if I didn't want all my things to carry over? Would I still be left with the same playthrough where I am not allowed the magnum recipe, etc?

11. Not a fan of how some of the interactions are being used by an invisible force. It reminds me of older lower budget games. It is not like it ruins the game or anything, but I would like for the character to fully interact with them instead; not only does it look much better, but it forces players to be more cautious about these types of interactions where you are completely vulnerable. Some locations may not matter as much sure, but some things like that jack handle moment, could allow for more player caution. The more the better.

12. Not enough weapons. I really wish they went all out for the people and had a huge collection of weapons. If you are going to have this merchant appearing all over the dang place, might as well make his collection badass. Would like multiple revolvers, multiple snipers, lever action rifles, etc.... (This should be 100% enjoyable as someone's first playthrough, and not mostly a new game+ perk)

 I feel like they need to put more love and time into the pace, character development, weapons, exploring, and difficulty in order for me to want to spend 60$. The last two entries so far are just okay experiences, not bad but not great either, I don't know:( just my opinion. What rating would I give? 6/10 is how I feel about it at the moment.

Long time Resident Evil fans will enjoy this game. It offers a diversified game play experience that continues the story of RE7. It doesn't hold up as well when compared to to some of the other recent releases; however, it does a great job at being a sequel that maintains the spirit of its predecessor while building on its previous success. With that said, it is essential that you play RE7 before playing this game.

This game offers a good mix of horror and action that many fans might find comparable to RE4 but with the engine of RE7. The horror in this game feels very authentic in the fact that it doesn't rely on jump scares. Instead, many of the tense moments in this game come from the fact that players need to actively put themselves in harms way in order to progress through the game and collect certain valuables. The scarcity of resources such as health and ammo keep players on edge and encourage players to fully explore the world around them. These items are often unique and feel very rewarding as opposed to the oversaturated markets of games such as Skyrim. The pacing and balancing of the default difficulty are perfect in that I always felt like I needed more resources, but never felt completely stuck because of it (though that is a very real possibility if you play recklessly)

Much like RE4 and some of the more recent RE remakes, this game encourages you to play thoughtfully and budget resources; however, this game's combat system lacks the sophistication you'd come to expect from the previously mentioned titles. Whereas the other titles gave you combat tools like knifing, knee shooting, kicking, aiming for weak spots and strategically navigating map, this game's combat pretty much boils down to shooting things until they die. Despite this backtracking, the game maintains the player's interest with moody environments, purposeful gameplay, and a sense of pacing that keeps everything feeling fresh.
 
By far the weakest part for me was the main character. Ethan is one of the least charismatic protagonists I've seen from a video game. His dialogue is really flat and void of emotion. It kind of sounds like the voice actor was scared to actually yell while recording his lines out of fear of waking his neighbors. As a result, a lot of moments of intensity and emotion fell flat. It never really felt like there were any stakes. Every stab to the face or disastrous plot development just sounded like a mild inconvenience. At one point, you receive aid from one of the franchise's long-established side characters; however, most of this character's actions don't line up with their supposed motivations and as a result, their actions feel nonsensical. 

On the other hand, I have to give praise to the developers for creating a very memorable cast of villains for this game. Unlike many games where a boss's screen time is limited strictly to their respective battle, the bosses in this game all have unique personalities which are fleshed out throughout the entirety of the game. This character development creates a seamless buildup to each boss battle that feels much more natural than shoehorning a boss battle in at the end of each level. The only boss battle I didn't like was the final one. Much like the protagonist, the final boss feels very stale in terms of emotion, probably due the fact that this boss gets the least amount of screen time out of all the other bosses. Additionally, the battle is slow paced, unimaginative, and offers the player no real room for strategizing. 

Overall, this is a game worth playing, especially if you are a long-time fan of Resident Evil games. Despite its flaws, this game does an incredible job of creating a memorable and enjoyable experience. Just make sure you play RE7 first.

Absolutely loved this game. The only major complaint I could have is that it isn't really a [i]great[/i] follow-up to RE7, in the sense that it's just such a different tone. It's kind of like the Aliens to RE7's Alien, or the Terminator 2 to Terminator. In RE7, despite all the pseudoscience fantasy stuff, the story was pretty grounded, and the challenges you faced felt insurmountable, like you  just barely scraped by (even though really you didn't have much trouble at all). RE8 has a lot more action and a lot more large threats, but at the same time, Ethan really feels kind of ready to face them, so some of that tension is lost. Oh, and another flaw with the game: despite having more varied enemies than 7, it still really didn't have great diversity of enemies. Most of the enemies were just the same sort of AI with different costumes, that stagger more or less when shot.

But overall, it's incredibly fun. The story is compelling enough to keep playing, the setpieces are very refreshingly different with their own unique experiences, and the action is harrowing but - again - not overwhelmingly so. While the emphasis on action  does distract from the horror to me, I'm actually surprised at how effective some of the scares really are. Since the events of the game delve way more into the fantasy side of RE, there was also more freedom to set up scenarios that genuinely toy with you deeper than just a jumpscare. There are tons of secrets to find, and the map is incredibly helpful in finding them without just giving everything away. There was only one puzzle that felt a little obtuse, and unfortunately it comes pretty early on in the game, but everything else is comprehensible enough to piece together without feeling like the game is just holding your hand all the way through. It's got an almost metroidvania feel, where you have the titular village as a hub with 4 main baddie-controlled areas to explore, then as you beat a boss in that area, you unlock something that will grant access to even more of the village. It really makes exploration exciting, and again the map is helpful for finding things you've come across but couldn't access before.

Performance-wise, I was blown out of the water by this game. With a 3060ti, I have moderately high expectations for what I can  run well, but at 1440p plenty of games struggle to stay over 100fps at all times. But, with very rare exception, I maintained a stable 144fps throughout the entire game! The graphics settings are decently comprehensive. I thought it was pretty cool, albeit in a mundane way, that the game has minimum and maximum brightness settings. Great for those who like to pump the brightness up a bit - you don't have to completely blind yourself in lighter scenes now.

All-in-all, I could keep going, but it was just completely fun. It has a kind of slow ramp up, but then the pedal hits the metal and this game never slows down. Simultaneously, I played for an hour or two and felt like it was 8, because I was so absorbed in the game, but then later finished the game in ~10.5 hours and it felt like it just flew by. I wanted more, and yet it never started feeling like it was overstaying its welcome.

I just hope RE can keep up with these last two games. If it goes back to the classic style after these, they'll have lost at least one fan.

I'm guessing that by the end of the story the writers somehow manage to tie the previous game into it's lore. This game is so cool I am thinking this would have been a better stand alone title, completely removed from the Resident Evil franchise. I just don't feel like it has the spirit of the series in the early content of the story which leads to a lot of confusion, where as Bio-hazard at least seemed to reach for the Umbrella links fairly early on and it felt like a natural evolution of the series. Village plays and looks great, however, it is flawed in that it doesn't feel like a Resident Evil title for quite a while. Spoiler alert: werewolves, not zombies, are your first enemy. Yup, that's right, you face off against straight up Lycans, like out of a Gothic horror movie but there is little explanation until like a quarter of the way through the game. I'm not even going to get into the rest of the macabre cast but it doesn't feel like a part of the RE franchise to me. I still think it is enjoyable and some nice eye candy, however, don't think you're getting a true RE game, at least not in the first 4 hours or so. If you have patience you will be rewarded with some cool links to franchise lore once you get past the first major section.

I think this is the new series best. RE2 will always be my first crush until I cheated on her with RE4 but Village is an absolute masterpiece for both gaming and the series. At 5 playthroughs I can tell the developers were all in for this next step in the franchise.  Lets break down the pros and a few cons:

Pros:
-Scariest yet. Back to the roots of a familiar feeling of being hunted as in RE 2.
-Gorgeous graphics and level design. You'll find beauty in the dread.
-More than one excellent plot twist, in fact, there are quite a few.
-The weapons vendor is back!
-Excellent replay value reminiscent of RE 4.
-Boss fights are unique and keep your heart racing.
-Lots of hidden things to find and unlock.
-Brings fan favorites from many RE games into one game.
-Ever-changing game play, nothing becomes repetitive or stale.
-Challenge Point system is incredibly addictive and changed how I went about replays.
-Voice acting is well done with the charismatic and interesting cast of characters.

Cons:
-Some enemy abilities stray away from a RE viral mutation to having somewhat fantastical powers.
-Harder difficulties can't capitalize on NewGame+ upgrades in certain areas of the game where upgraded equipment is irrelevant. Since the harder difficulties were designed around NewGame+ this can bring a full stop to anyone that doesn't have the fortitude to die over and over at the same spot in the game.
-Puzzles are too easy with the exception of one which was very well done.

TL:DR RE Village sets a new bar for the series and if you're a fan it's worth getting a.s.a.p.

Fun game, but less emphasis on the "horror" and more on the "action". Having platinumed RE7 on console, I will say with confidence: don't go into this expecting solely horror. RE8 focuses primarily on the action that was introduced in RE7, but expanded and made the previous system less clunky and more FPS-like, similar to modern FPS games. However, I do not say "focus" lightly. You WILL be forced to confront enemies- no running away, and I'm not talking about just boss battles.

Also, no Madhouse difficulty. Instead you have the "Village of Shadows" difficulty which makes the game extremely difficult, but... that's really all. No remixing things or changing the gameplay loop like RE7. Sad, but what can you do?

Story-wise, the game is "good". Not much like the story of RE7, in which if you played, that game earned the respect of being a thrilling remake of this stagnate corpse of a series. Instead, this game is a "good" sequel. Motives are justifiable and clear-cut, but eventually falls off around a little more than halfway through the game. Also, ending is... meh; hell, maybe even bad. It just... kinda sucks and is underwhelming compared to the nice wrap-up of RE7's end sequence.

Otherwise, graphics are absolutely amazing. Gameplay is reminiscent of a smoother, less clunky RE7. More action focused, and the story is good.

7.5/10, I would recommend waiting for a sale, but if you have the antique coins, buy it!

This is probably the best survival horror game I've ever played.  The graphics and level of detail are nearly immaculate and the range of environments depicted, from quaint and snowy chateaus to dark, dingy subterranean crypts and factories just took my breath away.  The characters and their designs are interesting and memorable, each adding their own horrific theme and set of challenges to overcome. Since Village does continue the story through the eyes of Ethan Winters, having a basic understanding of what took place during the events of RE7 is a must to fully appreciate the story and its conclusion.

It's clear that the horror elements introduced in RE7 have been ramped up considerably, I can recall many "oh-shi*" moments ranging from jump scares to desperately running or attempting to craft supplies with what few raw materials you have while being chased by hordes or giant enemies.  I would definitely recommend to play at a harder difficulty for more fear factor, since ammo is usually pretty easy to come by if rationed well.  The combat system is roughly the same as the previous title, though the introduction of weapon component upgrades and a mini economy provide a nice sense of progress and encourage fully exploring the environment for maximum benefit, though admittedly the scavenging and certain enemy encounters become a bit repetitive at times.

So here are my problems with the RE 8:

1. Story is mediocre at best. Ethan's story was dead give away the moment I saw how he patched up his extremely injured limbs from RE7. So where it would lead was a simple guess work. It was no different then predicting and guessing (right) things like how the Avengers would counter Thano's plan by going into the past using Antman's quantum mumbo jumbo (fancy for time travel), OR how the Big Boss isn't actually Big Boss in MGS5 from David Hayter's interview long before the game even came out (two examples out of many out there). Point being, the cliche story telling isn't anything new. Just rephrased, rehashed, same s**t- different day deal. So why, knowing (predicting) the story I am complaining about it? It's because the game lacks the WAY of telling the story. They really need to hire a good writer for RE9 and on ward. RE is known for cheesy dialogues and poor writing but doesn't hurt to give it a solid, serious tone, albeit with other elements thrown in it. Look at MGS franchise (filled with easter eggs, jokes, etc) for reference Cashcom. Things that Chris could've told in first few min of the story, he kept it till the near end. WHY!? 
Ok, onward with next complain...

2. Gameplay is same as RE7. If it ain't broken, don't fix it. I get it. Doesn't mean it would hurt to change things around. Also they tried avoiding RE5,6 but inadvertantly they put problematic sections in the game that are completely unnecessary. An example of it would be: [spoiler] the little fetus/baby section. It captured the horror but it was extremely short lived AND predictable easy enough to be easily solved without much tension. It gave a taste of horror but again, that was psychological, not BIOLOGICAL as RE is famous for. Then came the horrendous water bridge segment that was completely unnecessary and annoying (try for yourself) that is akin to RE5's alligator/water segment area. Heck RE5 at least gave a simple QTE to overcome the annoyance of dying from silly mechanics, this one didn't. Good no QTE. Bad because it's poorly executed.[/spoiler] Stop bringing back past games' cliche materials. If you must, do it with innovative new mechanics. Keep things fresh.  While at it, make sure the component (action, setting, puzzle) has MEANING behind it. Not just thrown in there for the sake of it.

3. Bosses: Likeable THICC, voluptuous Dragon Mama and her waifu daughters for their obvious attraction(s) but all of the bosses are cliche. We got Alcina Dominatrisexu aka Lust from Full Metal Alchmiest (a literal copy paste); the bug girls (sorry I don't do bugs!) aka Marguerite Baker but sexy version; DIscount Magneto; Discount psycho lady with her dolls (just do a head count of similar boss from RE franchise alone) and Discount Del Lago from RE4. You get the picture! They are just derivatives. Yes its difficult to come up with something new but come on! You can do better. There is a workaround to that problem and that is giving each character huge personality and background story (See #1). Just going from A to B to find key to this and that and then unlock this for that to get those and then X number of stuff to shove in a socket to get the Y components....come on...this is tiresome. RE Village is a splendid follow up to the revitalization that RE VII brought to the franchise.
It's best to play VII before this if you haven't yet though as there are plenty of narrative threads carrying over from the previous game (Plus it's really really good as well).

[h1]What is it like?[/h1]
And well if you have played VII? Village is less of a horror game. Don't get me wrong, it's still horror. It's just a lot more focused on you having a good time than scaring you. You also get to shoot guns a lot more. Otherwise it largely plays, looks (in terms of quality) and feels the same. The less said about the specifics of what you'll encounter the better though - go in and just experience it. These two games (RE VII & VIII) are one of the best examples of AAA as it should be in the gaming industry right now.

[h1]A little more in depth[/h1] 
Compared to the previous installment there are a couple of instances in Village where it felt like things go a little bit overboard into fantasy more than sci-fi. To elaborate, everything in RE VII wrapped up and got explained through in-game lore in a way that felt like "Yeah if chemistry was a little more wild, I could see this stuff happening". The world was also very consistent. And hey largely this is still true for all the things that are important for Village but the game has a lot more style for the sake of style. It's less consistent and really I'm bringing this all up just because Heisenberg's power is ridiculously out of line with what could even be considered plausible. And he's the only instance of this gripe I have. It's not a big deal though, just let the action wash over you and don't think too hard I guess. It does look very spectacular.

Speaking of very spectacular. Graphics are gorgeous and if you happen to have one of those rare RTX video cards, I think RE Village has one the best looking Raytracing implementation of any game sporting this feature that I've played. Voice acting is top notch. Voices are varied and interesting. Sound design is great. You have a post-game arcade mode to shoot guns to your hearts content and a lot of concept are & other behind the scenes goodies to look at.

The sequel to VII undoes everything. (slight spoilers ahead) (Also Edited due to my current outlook)

Resident Evil was the series that made me a horror fan, and in 2021, Resident Evil Village was my most anticipated game. Capcom won me over with Resident Evil VII: Biohazard, and the initial trailers were spectacular. And then, after playing it, as someone who has never played Resident Evil 5 & 6 at that time (I have played 5 and 6 in the years following, and I was initially miffed at the former, but would warm up to it overtime and think the latter stinks), I finally know how it felt for most fans to play them. Resident Evil Village is my personal least favourite entry in the franchise, if not a strong contender for 'Objective Worst'. And it's all because it features one of the franchise's worst stories, if not, THE worst.

It's a shame too, because the gameplay is really good, combining the best elements of 2005's RE4 and the previously mentioned VII: Biohazard. The first person perspective and immersion of one, with the actionised survival horror gameplay and merchant mechanic of the other. It even manages to make the hunting and crafting aspects work by mainly relegating them to optional stuff you can do to increase your chances of survival. It coalesces and feels so good to play, which makes it embarrassing that it sandwiches an atrocious script!

Without spoiling much, Resident Evil Village renders everything you accomplished in Resident Evil VII: Biohazard pointless right from the word 'go'. In fact, as a sequel to VII, it's atrocious. The mold returns as the source of the monsters you face (not a spoiler, you can guess from death animations), but it does things it never did in the prior entry and are impossible to believe. There's a s--tton of dropped plot points from VII, notably Blue Umbrella and The Contractors, who are never even or just BARELY mentioned in DLC this go around. And the believability that VII excelled at is butchered horribly, not just with Ethan surviving attacks that would kill someone like him, but also through the ♥♥♥♥ it pulls to destroy the entire franchise. And Mia, my favourite character from VII, is completely wasted as she becomes sidelined during the idiot plot this game tells.

Speaking of its gleeful despise for YOU, the fans and suspecting players, Resident Evil Village has its main goal as the undoing of everything established and accomplished in the 25 year-long mythology. Franchise rules are buttf---ed repeatedly, as the main monsters, The Four Lords, possess ACTUAL FANTASTICAL SUPERPOWERS, something which goes against the rules of the series and turns Resident Evil into the Anderson film series! The horror is SUPERNATURAL when the main theme of series since day one is meant to be man-made monstrosities and biohazards! Chris Redfield, one of the characters who started it all, is also treated like dirt by the narrative as he begins the idiot plot and undoing of VII's events in the opening scenes. This really makes me mad, as he's my favourite character (see Code Veronica to learn why), and it comes off as a sucker punch after VII gave him such respect.

But by far, the biggest crime Village commits, is that by the time you meet Mother Miranda, everything you did, not just in VII, but in the entire franchise (even the crappy ones), means nothing anymore. In quite possibly the most boneheaded move I've seen in the entire survival horror genre, the writers of this dreck, with approval by Capcom themselves, decided to reveal that Rose Winters, the daughter you're trying to rescue, is the second coming of Eveline, thus rendering Ethan's accomplishments in VII, Leon and Claire's accomplishments in 2, 4 and the animated Degeneration film, and Chris and Jill's accomplishments in the original game, Code: Veronica and countless other stories... POINTLESS. All for the most meaningless, stupid shark jumping reason they could muster. Every rush away from exploding buildings, every unholy monsters destroyed, every zombies/Ganado/Molded survived, every puzzle solved, every measure we took to prevent BOWs from running loose on the world doesn't mean a thing any more. It's all been wiped away just so that Capcom could make Alice a reality and turn the series into a superhero franchise.

And THAT'S why I do not recommend this game. Not because of the gameplay, not even because it's not scary (which it definitely is). It's all because it features the worst story in the entire series, treats you like dirt, and undoes everything you accomplished. I haven't even reached the finale, but after the stunt they pulled in a single monologue, I feel like I need to force myself to. I think I can't even look at 1 - 7 or the spin-offs without thinking of the revelations and outcomes provided by Village, and that is just sickening. 
Thankfully, what Capcom followed it up with (A remake of Resident Evil 4) pissed me off when they announced it, but won me over by turning out to be a massive improvement on both its direct predecessor and Village. So I'm cautiously optimistic for RE9. Hopefully 9 will further set things right, and maybe it will be a damn good time that builds on the strengths of Village whilst ditching the terrible writing that wrecked it. We'll see.

The most resident evil has felt like resident evil since RE4. They have nailed what makes us like the franchise, with a great mix of genuine frights, campy horror, and action moments with a new memorable cast. Take note Silent Hill on how to revamp a game with both old and new gameplay elements,

This game takes everything interesting from Resident Evil 7 and improves upon them and then mixes an unhealthy amount of steroids into it resulting in a game that is immensely fun to play even if the general story and character of Ethan Winters is absolutely awful. 

RE8 has some of the most chaotic game moments from any RE game (and that is including the cluster ♥♥♥♥ that is RE6) and yet they work and result in some really memorable moments like: A mech type battle, a fight with a giant flying creature and a death run gauntlet just to name a few.

This also has one of my favorite opening missions from any RE game as it takes the great opening from RE4 and in my opinion improves upon it as you have to survive a attack from hordes of lycans in a remote and desolate village with only a pistol and limited ammo, this sequence had my heart racing the entire time as the stakes and danger escalates slowly overtime as this attack feels like it seemingly goes on for ever. 

While the main bad villain is really boring and barely in it their side characters / side villains are interesting and fun to watch especially Heisenberg and Lady D.

I'm only voting this down because it's currently sitting at Overwhelmingly positive, which isn't right. It's not a bad game, plays well enough, looks good at times (not so much other times, with characters clipping into the camera, etc) but holy crap is the writing godawful. And not a cheesy "so bad it's good" kind of awful either.
In many respects, this game is a downgrade from RE7, which back then had the balls to try something that had (almost) never been done before in a RE game, with the first person style, Texas chainsaw massacre feel, and everything else. RE8 doesn't even have that going for it.
I loved RE4, which is what this game is trying very hard to be, with the village, castle, merchant, gun upgrades, cultists, etc. But it doesn't land nearly as well. Leon played the "cocky American with fancy gadgets sent to European rural backwater gets in way over his head" a lot more convincingly. Felt very Hostel in that regard.
Ethan is out of his element here. He's not interesting, funny, clever, and he's got no chemistry with anyone here, not even Duke who by all means is supposed to be your bro dude for the whole game. Speaking of Duke, there's no explanation as to why he even helps you, how he knows the stuff he knows, and why he was spared by, well, everything really. Nobody even acknowledges he exists, and even himself says he doesn't know what he is. It's incredibly infuriating because everyone is written as if they only had a napkin worth of characterization and no actual motivation other watching two characters go "my daughter, no MY daughter, NO" and just sort of having to go along with it.
It's a shame because some of the designs and ideas behind them were really good, even if it made no sense. Donna for instance was a huge waste of potential, as her entire area barely takes up half an hour to clear, and then you barely get to see her. Moreau was just a sad waste of everybody's time, and while the remaining cast has a bit more screen time than the rest, they don't really do too much with it.
Even when one character TRIES to explain to Ethan why they're doing what they do, he just goes "I don't care, where's my daughter?" which I suppose makes sense for him in context, but then if even he doesn't get invested, why should we?
Besides, it's not like we get much of a choice. As the only other character we get to play as is Chris, who doesn't bring much to the table other than about 5 minutes worth of CoD bait and "paint the target sir, let's blow this sky high" since that'd be even more out of place for Ethan.
Speaking of playable characters, they even dare to bring back Mercenaries mode... Except you only play as one character. Sure, they make up for that with the money aspect, where you buy your build instead of learning to play as each character, but then that just means you pick one build to min-max and never use anything else.

Bottom line is: This game is to RE7 what RE3R was to RE2R: a rushed production riding on the success and tech of its predecessor (I wouldn't be surprised if most of the code from RE7 was still in there, unchanged) that tries to come off as an epic followup, but just ends up sort of lazy and a waste of potential. It's easy to see how they ripped entire chunks out of 7 to make 8, just as they ripped entire chunk from 2R to make 3R.

Hopefully they cut fewer corners with the RE4 remake (which was pretty much confirmed in the Nvidia leak) because it deserves better than this.

RE7 feels like a modern take on RE 1's gameplay loop. RE:Village is a modern take on RE4'S gameplay loop. This is more action oriented than its predecessor but do not be mistaken it still has some of the DNA of RE7. It is still a Survival Horror game. 

The scope is much grander this time around, as it is set on an entire village with various locales rather than a single house/property. It still has the looping level designs and a sort of semi open village section where you can scavenge for resources. Combat in this game is improved and feels encouraged as Ethan is given a spacing move by pushing enemies away if you successfully guard their attacks , slain enemies also drop items such as money or crafting materials. Item management is easier in this game for better or for worse depending on which gameplay loop you prefer. There is a merchant in the game and you can buy or upgrade items by scavenging for money and/or materials around the various locales of the village. The settings and enemies are more diverse, however some are more interesting than others, I cannot really talk about it without spoiling the game. Ethan is a much more engaging character in this game. The plot is easy to follow but it could get a bit silly/stupid at times.

Overall while it has the backbone of RE4, it has a little something for all RE fans, it is a nice little amalgamation of the ever evolving series that is Resident Evil

P.S. If you are a survival horror veteran play on the higher difficulties, my first playthrough was on Normal and it was too easy.

It's great, no doubt about that. However, I have some complaints.

For one, it's not very scary. It has it's moments, one sequence in particular, but all in all, it's not scary. Compared to RE7 or something like Visage, Layers of Fear, Silent Hill 2/3, Amnesia, Outlast etc, this is basically an action/exploration game with a horror/gothic aesthetic. Maybe if you've never played a horror game before and you're easily frightened you'll feel differently, but if you're a fan of this genre, be aware that it is not particularly scary. I wish they'd put more effort into crafting a horrifying experience and less into creating stimulation for degenerates.

Secondly, the acting is cringey. I mean your local community theater putting on a Halloween play cringey. A few characters are alright, mostly the returnees and a couple of the new characters, but most fit this rule. This does nothing to help the aforementioned lack of horror and is quite immersion breaking in it's own right.

I also ran into issues with audio being out of sync during cutscenes and a few textures looked jarringly poor.

On the plus side, I absolutely love the setting; the world is gorgeous and the gothic aesthetic is very appealing. The gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, the boss fights are mostly well done, and the character/monster designs are spectacular. The story is also engaging. While I found the puzzles to be a bit too easy, they were sometimes entertaining.

I'd highly recommend it for a nice October experience but just understand what it is and what it isn't.

This game was the only one in 2021 what im waited for! The first trailers stunned me so hard. The game mechanics nearly the same as it was in the RE:VII Biohazard back then (fps view, gun upgrades, the saving point as typewriter). The concept art about the game is phenomenal, it is set in a snowy explorable Eastern European Village in Transylvania. This place looks like as the time has stopped there in the middle ages. Near the Village is the Castle Dimitrescu and it's looks so lifelike, outside (even on the roof) and inside as well! INCREDIBLY detailed, well designed. The RE:Village storyline is deep, it continues 3 years after the RE:VII Biohazard's - Baker Family' accident. 

This Transylvanian Village governed by four different mutant lords, each controlling their own forces from strongholds within the village. 

- Alcina Dimitrescu (she is a tall vampiric aristocrat, resides at Castle Dimitrescu with her three daughters Bela, Cassandra, and Daniela)
- Donna Beneviento (rules from her mansion, House Beneviento, and acts through her puppet Angie)
- Salvatore Moreau (operates from a reservoir in close proximity to the village and is described as a "merman")
- Karl Heisenberg (he can manipulate magnetic fields, leads a group of Soldat simulacra from a contemporary factory)

All houses respond to a supreme leader figure called Mother Miranda, the ruler of the village who is a "presence worshipped by the villagers."

All of the gameplay areas are very detailed, the boss fights are difficult enough and they have different mechanics.  Sometimes i felt on some bigger enemys (not boss) that they are a bit undiyng, especially [spoiler]the grave defending "goliat", near Donna Beneviento's graveyard[/spoiler]. I think this is because of the many scripted elements, maybe someday we got a RE game with real physx and variable animation sets (with varied hit animations - the game needs that i think for more realism). My walktrough was about 12,5 hours. Im tryed to check every corners to find collectibles and other stuffs and i wanted to read every single letters. I can say i never saw any game bugs, i never stuck in one place, my i7 8700k & RTX2060 handled the game very nicely on 1080p (maxed with the setting sets to it's 6gb vram), it was smooth on my 144hz display and the visuals was gorgeous. Fantastic game that picks up a few years after RE 7 left off. Personally I thought 7 was much better, but this game still did a phenomenal job.

Pros: 

-Recap: There's an intro that recaps RE 7 so you don't HAVE to play 7 to understand the premise, but RE Village is a sequel and RE 7 is a rather short game at ~10 hours if you want to go play that really quick, RE7 could also be considered a standalone in that you need no information about the previous 7 games to understand. 

-Store: This RE actually features a store which is very useful and something I wanted in the earlier RE series.

-Weapon Upgrades: You can upgrade your weapons, something that was missing in 7.

-Storyline is some grade A writing, you'll enjoy the story the entire game.

-Basic Enemy Variety: this is the most diverse group of common enemies I've ever come across in the RE series. it's not just zombies, plant creatures or Villagers gone insane. The common enemy types you run into are incredibly diverse and have their own strengths and weaknesses. 

Cons:

-Bosses are pretty much the same: With the devotion and time spent developing the regular enemies, you'd think the bosses got the same treatment, however compared to RE7's bosses: (Following spoiler is for RE 7) [spoiler] Chainsaw dueling Jack, Running him over in your car, fighting a she-spider that could climb walls and would lay eggs if you didn't hunt her down and fighting a many eye'd swamp monster that you had to blind while running around a 2 story building to get the perfect angle on each eye. [/spoiler] RE Village's bosses are all boring in comparison, and have pretty much the same win condition. You dodge enemy attacks by strafing, and shooting them after they crash into something. I joke not that this will be the win condition for nearly every boss battle that you encounter.  The list of enemy bosses you beat by letting them crash into something and then attacking when they instead hit a wall/miss you: (RE8 spoilers:) [spoiler] Lady Dom, Propeller guy/Sturm, Urias,  Moreau, even the final boss Mother Miranda sorta falls prey to this, though at least she casts spells. [/spoiler] that's most of the boss battles being nothing but dodge a little and shoot the "unique" vital spot when the enemy whiffs their attack. When you include that one boss battle is [spoiler] Playing a game of tag with scissors and requires no skill to complete [/spoiler] the boss battles are severely lacking in creativity, leaving only 3 boss battles that are unique.

-Store: Seems like the Shopkeeper doesn't add stock as the game goes on but rather restocks to his inventory cap as the game progresses. So if you're like me and you decide you're okay with not spending cash for bullets early on, but then go to buy some later in the game, You'll discover that the shop keeper wont have infinite or even stacks of bullets for sale, rather he will have the same small amount of bullets that you never bought for sale. Left me in a jam late game when I had over 300K currency, was maxed on weapons upgrades and couldn't buy more ammo from the shop keeper.  You will also never be able to buy components for crafting, which is odd, the only way to craft is with components you find laying around the game.

-Food: I found food before recipe crafting was introduced as a mechanic to the game and the option to recipe craft didn't exist. I found a unique food type that never appears again in the game, the food in it's description told me to give this to the Shopkeeper, so I assumed that it was only to be used as a valuable item for currency. This made sense to me as the shopkeeper is a portly man, it wasn't until maybe an hour later that recipes were introduced and I realized I permanently lost on recipe buffs because after you sell that unique resource, it is not available for re-purchase. Combine this with me selling the other "common" food I had come across and I was put at a disadvantage because the game punished me for doing what it told me to do in it's description without explaining that it was a resource, not a valuable. Seems kinda short sighted on the devs part to not explain recipes the moment I get food.

-Personal Gripe that actually is a Spoiler: [spoiler] I feel like the game could have used more of lady Dom and her daughters. Not just because they are sexy vampires, but because they are the ones who the trailers focused on the most and the fact that they are all dead within what is still more or less the intro of the game is a tragedy and disservice. [/spoiler] They are without a doubt the most interesting of the antagonists you face and have the funnest area to explore. Keeping in mind that they clearly have a grudge with the other antagonists, and they could have had a bigger part to play somewhere in the story. I would have loved to see this group of enemies have a more active role through out the game and they could have been a force to be reckoned with.

-Enemies tend to stick to their area for fights: Common enemies usually wont chase you out of their defined area, so if you're on the border between two areas of play, and you start shooting an enemy you see, they occasionally will just let you kill them because they don't know how to get to you. Given that you get a sniper rifle very early in the game you can see how this is a problem. I've killed mini-bosses that put up no fight because they will rush towards me, realize I'm out of their defined fight area, and then they will turn around slowly returning to their idle position, until I reload and put more pot-shots into them.

-I ran into a few glitches during my run, though the game was so fun that I didn't mind it, though others might. one being that I must have perfectly hit 0 HP because I didn't die, yet I wasn't allowed to move, had to manually restart from last save. Also occasionally enemies glitched into walls and were unable to break out of them. However the one glitch that really ticked me off is a known issue that has never been resolved, you can miss beneviento's treasure and the mini-boss fight, I would recommend googling this after the second boss so that you don't miss the treasure/hit the bug. 

Neutral:

-No storage: Every other RE I've played has storage boxes, including RE7, so the decision to get rid of it in this game was a bit of a shock. What you carry on you is all the items you have. You'll have to either destroy items to make room, leave items untouched, or sell to the shopkeeper to make money.

-You may want to have subtitles throughout the game. There's a lot of distorted voices and your character reacts as though he hears them clear as day. You're clearly supposed to understand what is being said by the various enemies who taunt you, but it kinda comes off as silly that your character is understanding a muffled voice with perfect clarity. I musta missed most of the dialogue on the second and third areas because I was too lazy to turn it on.

-This RE is a set story and not an RPG, you'll get to make no decisions throughout this game, unlike 7. Which in unfortunate because I would have loved to betray a character or two given the chance.

-DLC available at the moment seem like cash grabs and micro transaction in nature, which I dislike. One gives you starter items, another unlocks the unlockables you'll get in game anyways, and another is a skin for a gun that apparently most people hate and find difficult to remove.

Resident evil village is an action-horror game. In this game you'll follow Ethan Winters, the protagonist of Resident Evil 7, this time on a quest to get back his daughter and discover why she was kidnapped in the first place.
You will explore the titular village and different dungeons, all while shooting or running your way out of monsters.

The producer of the game called it a "theme park of horror", where it would feel as if you were going to different attractions and experiencing various types of horrors.
This is a very on point description, as each of the areas have different gimmicks that for the most part are over fairly quickly and don't overstay their welcome.
I called this an action-horror game because it feels like a midpoint between action and survival-horror. This is an fps where bullets are not exactly abundant and you have limited inventory space, so deciding what to carry is a decision to make every time you pick a new object, especially weapons.

The game starts very horror like, but as you advance through the areas and amass a greater arsenal it naturally becomes harder to scare the player, so the game focuses more on its action elements, until a certain sequence close to the endgame where the game stops being horror anymore, and turns into an action shooter.

There is a light crafting and upgrading mechanic where you find materials in the game world that you can use to upgrade your weapons, increasing parameters like firepower and bullet capacity.
While this is a nice mechanic on its own, you'll also unlock more weapons while advancing in the game or solving puzzles, and the new weapons supersede the old ones in all practical regards, meaning that if you are able to, you should always use the latest weapons available, even when you had upgraded one of your weapons before.
I'm sure in high levels of play in mercenaries mode, you have to pick the correct tier of weapon and upgrades, but if having to consider a small extra mode to redeem the lack of choice is a lost cause.
Add to this that each type of weapon is either unique or has very few different models, so the weapons diversity ends up feeling very lacking.

The game has puzzles, as all resident evil games do, but the ones in here are very simple and straight forward. 
Only one comes to mind that wasn't immediately obvious how to solve it, but all the others had the solutions right beside them or were simple enough to not warrant putting much thought into it. While I would have prefer puzzles that were a little better, they don't take too long to solve and are there to break the pace of the game in between fights more than anything. 
In this sense the theme park analogy still works because the game isn't as focused in giving you a good challenge as it’s focused in giving you a good time. 

Really I feel the last point is core to the whole game and the biggest reason I would recommend it. The game wants you to have fun with it and enjoy it, albeit sacrificing depth in various parts. I have mostly talked about the flaws I find with the game but I still had a blast playing it on two difficulties and some mercenaries.

If you don't feel any of the cons I have described are deal breakers for you, I would say Resident Evil Village is worth your time.
Although, if you think you'll just play it once (I'd guess the majority of people fall here) then I'd recommend waiting for a sale.

One last thing: if you decide to buy the game, I'd recommend using a mod to increase the Field of View, as I felt the default is too tiny for a monitor. Increasing it to 90 made it much more comfortable to play.

Brilliant! This game exceeded my expectations. I've been a fan of RE since RE2 first came out back in the PS1/Nintendo 64 era. I love every style of each game, classic or modern. But we have to admit the series had become stale somewhere after RE5. Even though RE5 and RE6 weren't necessarily bad, they felt a bit too repetitive, not being helped by the several bland spinoffs that came after.

I was very excited to see how the series would change with RE7, and I was more than surprised to see how unique and refreshed this new RE concept was. New characters, dynamics, camera perspective. It was perfect. A breath of fresh air that was much needed for the series.

But now RE8 (Village) came, and it was time to see how they could expand upon the Ethan universe, and boy they did a magnificent job. This game exudes the same atmosphere than RE7, yet somehow it manages to bring that classic RE flavor, specifically from the masterpiece that RE4 was into the mix. And this is no 'lite' experience full of fan service and references to the RE's of old, this is a game on its own right and one to be remembered.

Is it as impactful as RE7 and RE4 which takes a lot of inspiration from? Not really. But it is an incredibly solid game, with superb graphics, very good controls, engaging gameplay mechanics, memorable characters and a surprisingly long campaign, separated in four different stories styles, all mixed into one semi-open world game. The many challenges and unlockables will also make sure that you come back for more.

It's got that murky atmosphere that RE4 has, also a lot of indie horror cues that RE7 was known for and even a few throwbacks to the classic RE's, with their castles, mansions and puzzles.

All in all, this game was done with love, dedicated to the fans of the franchise and it shows they've put a lot of work into it, considering how difficult it is nowadays to make a solid AAA experience. Color me impressed. Resident Evil is still very alive and well and I cannot wait to see how this Ethan trilogy ends.

As for the technical stuff, the game runs pretty well as expected of the RE Engine. Expect 100+fps on even five year old high end hardware. No stuttering, bugs or glitches that I've noticed now in my second run.

Graphics are extremely polished. This game looks good! My only complaint is that it might be a bit dark sometimes and the game tends to self-adjust its brightness a lot.

The sound is a mixed bag. I'm not sure what happened, but RE2 Remake has been so far the best when it comes to sound. Clarity, balance, etc. Somehow that quality declined in RE3, and although RE8 has improved a bit, it is still not great as RE2. There seems to be balancing issues as well. Things like gunshots being too muffled.

I'm in utter shock at how bored I was playing this game, especially after the back to back successes that the remakes were. I wasn't a big fan of Resident Evil 7, so I suppose I shouldn't be surprised, but this was just awful. After I beat it and unlocked the assault rifle I was ready to get back into it and start slinging lead in the faces of some lycans, only to turn it off after I remembered I would have to sit through the prologue just to get there again.

There is nothing here that recaptures the isolation, conspiracy, or brooding dread that made the Resident Evil series big. Instead, the whole game just feels like theater. It's riddled with just awful over-the-top writing and dialogue, a main character you couldn't care less about, with a mission you couldn't care less about, in a world that quickly gets purged of the only remaining friendly NPCs making it just one more thing you couldn't care less about. Everything feels irrelevant, in fact, by the end of the game you realize that your presence in the story only made things unnecessarily complicated when it could have come to the same conclusion with the loss of a few less human lives, and the plot twists All. Feel. Cheap. I can't get into them without spoilers, so I'll just say that they are numerous and all add plot holes, the chief one being the main character himself.

Mechanically, it runs ok. All the problems just stem from bad design choices. There's a few areas that you just cannot go back to if you forget to loot them. MANY items are annoyingly hidden with no clue as to whether they're crucial, or just another cheap sellable bauble; and it's impossible to tell if you missed something in an area of the map, or if its something you can only find in a later visit which makes it an irritating waste of time to find. You'll spend lots of hair pulling moments sweeping and resweeping rooms and chambers just to make sure whatever item is still there isn't something crucial. The turning controls for the camera or pretty stiff, and it seems to be the only thing you can't edit or adjust in the options. Given that this is an FPS, the lack of peripheral motion is pretty crippling, especially in boss fights, and there's no way to widen your FOV, so get used to it. Mercenary mode, once unlocked, is ok. It leaves a lot to be desired and comes very bare bones. A bonus campaign would have been better.

This was not worth the staggering price tag it came with, and I feel cheated. If it was half the price, I wouldn't feel so bad about it.

Gameplay wise again its solid its a blend of resident evil 4s action and inventory management combined with the horror of 7. Its leans more on the action side but the inclusion of enemies not dropping ammo leaves encounters still on the tense side at least for the first playthrough. Mercenaries mode seems fairly tacked on and is no where as fleshed out compared to other entries or no where near as fun as say the raid modes in the revelation series.

In all resident evil 8 is yet another great entry in the RE franchise and I woukd highly recommend you play it.

It's a successor of RE7 story, so if you enjoyed RE7, go play Village, you'd like it.
Interiors are detailed as hell and light works are also mostly awesome.
Outdoors aren't that visually cool, textures are blurry and geometry sometimes looks lame.
Puzzles are mostly in 1st half of the game, the late part becomes kind of slow-paced survival shooter, not a horror-quest we expect from RE series.
Story isn't really inspiring. This sentimental 'saving my family'-motivation gets boring pretty quick, in fact, Ethan is an ultimate murder machine that can defeat strongest and ugliest zombie behemots with knife and bazooka, his balls are bigger than [spoiler]Lady Dimitriescu's boobs[/spoiler]. And still every 30 minutes there is a cut scene shows him crying and praying for [spoiler]saving his poor little daughter[/spoiler]. Meh.

Typewriters are there, but the storage box is replaced with travelling merchant who sells you ammo and buys any fancy stuff you steal from village bosses.

Concusion:
Interior graphics 10/10 (oh, these lighting shaders!)
Character visuals 10/10 (very impressive texturing, a lot of details in motion capture)
Immersion 9/10 (keeping you stressed all the way)
Sound design 9/10 (must-have for this genre, use headphones)
Level design 9/10 (returning to old locations to look at them from different perspective, RE-way)
Music 7/10 (atmospheric, but not self-sufficient)
Puzzles 6/10 (RE games usually have some puzzles other than 'find-a-proper-key-for-this-door')
Story 6/10 (there are some memorable characters, but main plot isn't much captivating)
Outdoor graphics 6/10 (snow and wood textures are from 2007)
Difficulty balance 5/10 (some big bosses are weaker than their minions)

Overall 8/10. This game doesn't bring much fresh air to horror genre, but it's made with love to RE-series and especially to every aspect we enjoyed in its ancestor, RE7.

I really enjoyed this game. If I had to compare it to another game in the series I would say it is the most like RE 4, but it has the over the top cheese taken out and it has more tension and scares added in. There's a lot less John Woo type stuff in this one too. I like this one a lot better than RE 7. They're both great, but the atmosphere of this game just makes it so much more fun.

The plot of this game is good as far as RE games go. It definitely has it's flaws and gets pretty weird towards the end. What I like the most about this is that all of the characters in the game definitely have their own plans. This isn't a game where you're up against a unified team that keeps bringing out their special moves and telling you that you'll never beat the big boss. In this game the four lords are each unique. Some of them are closer to each other than others. There are rivalries in the group. Some like mother Miranda and some do not. It helps make each one more distinct. 

The game play through each section is different enough to do that as well. In the castle you spend your entire time sneaking around and trying not to get slashed or eaten by Lady D and her daughters. In the little house it's Ethan verses his fears. There isn't really any combat in that section, but it's certainly memorable. Then there's fish guy that. That is essentially a Shadow of the Colossus boss fight. And then there is Hiesenberg. His section is mostly just combat challenges with an over the top boss battle at the end. Well really two boss battles at the end. That helps keep things feeling pretty fresh throughout the play through. 

I played through on Village of Shadows difficulty. I had infinite ammo and that barely helped on that difficulty. On Village of Shadows pretty much every enemy in the game can either one shot you or instantly take you down to danger status with one attack. They are stupid aggressive and they come in large packs. The tension in that difficulty made the play through very enjoyable. The game is relentless in that mode. There's definitely skill checks throughout too so that if you do have infinite ammo it isn't an instant win. Just getting to the merchant the first time took me a few hours. I got stuck at the first siege section. There are similar sections that push player skill later on. If you are looking for a challenge I would definitely recommend that difficulty. Personally I would rather use infinite ammo on it because it is tuned so high, but if you're up for it knock yourself out without it. 

I very much enjoyed my time with this game. It is definitely one I plan on replaying in the future.

I really enjoyed playing this game as a long-time fan of this series. Village is much more action oriented than it predecessor RE7, and it has much more of a RE4 feel in that it gives you enough ammo to take on pretty much all of the enemies in the game if you are careful with shots and use the right weapon for the right job. There are also lots of moments and mechanics in the game (such as weapon upgrading via the merchant and finding hidden treasures) which will really take you back to playing as Leon Kennedy in his own rural European village. It has a great attention to detail in terms of the level design and puzzles and each environment feels different from the last with the village acting as a sort of hub you return to after each section. The boss design for each of the characters is enjoyable as well as challenging and unique in comparison with the other bosses. Enemy design throughout the game is quite varied and avoids the stale feeling of killing the same enemy over and over as you play through the story. The game is very nice looking, a slight graphical improvement over RE7. NG+ and Mercenaries modes gives the game extra play time once you're done with the story. All in all I would highly recommend this game to fans of the series and newbies looking for a fun, action-based house of horrors style puzzle shooter.

Stellar looking, very atmospheric horror game with some solid and some very questionable design decisions and also, unfortunately, appallingly awful story. Worth playing as it is as an amazing experience, just do yourself a favor and don't look into any logic within the story (or just walking around the village in general). 

(+) Top of the line art direction: lighting, assets and monster and environment design
(+) Looks amazing also from the technical point of view
(+) Amazing setting, stellar atmosphere
(+) Top-notch first-person cutscenes
(+) Good level design. Not annoying to move around, the scale of the levels is just right, the setting changes often keeping the experience fresh. Not much backtracking.

(-) The menu UI is very awkward (and bugged when using mouse)
(-) The fake barriers keeping you from progress are painful as there's village full of crap laying around but you need that one, story-based lever to use for basic mechanic tasks. In story, the character can prone (and swim and so on), during gameplay you can't thus some barriers are simply cringy as they pose an insurmountable obstacle to someone who can fight mutated monsters with a knife, survived his own death 200 times, and casually walks off falls from spine-breaking heights. The biggest barricade (and the real boss of this game) are wooden-plank doors no bomb can destroy and god-save you if they're LOCKED FROM THE OTHER SIDE! Don't mind that any teenage rascal can open these old, big-ass locks with a twig, your character cannot even with a shotgun, high-caliber rifle, grenade launcher or a -- for this task specifically developed -- lockpick.
(-) Some backtracking can't be done as the game restricts an entrance through doors/gates you just used to move forward (but for no good reason you can't use them to go back). Some parts of the map simply close down (and the loot you left there is unreachable), paradoxically, other parts can't be explored fully unless you backtrack. This inconsistency was a very poor decision as you don't know if you should look for some tool to help you open the locked out loot (before moving forward) or if you must move forward as you can only access that tool later on in the story. Very confusing and subsequently very frustrating.
(-) The inventory system feels out place in this game. First, it's just a nuisance but when you carry a bunch of objects that literally have 'too heavy' in their description, you'll roll your eyes.
(-) Shooting is uncomfortable, weird. Mostly due to some animation-related trigger restrictions that feel like bugs. There's no view through sights and the HUD crosshair is one of the worst any game ever used.
(-) Way too corridory, scripted, narrow.
(-) Enemies are bullet sponges.
(-) Lack of any player agency.
(--) The story is unbelievably horrid. It makes no sense, it's full of plotholes and braindead characters. It's a B level zombie storywriting which would be fine if the narrative admitted it and didn't try to sell itself as a serious one. The art and tech people who made wonders with this game deserve better. Screenwriters and designers of the game dropped the ball here.
