This is my first Resident Evil game so I had to do some research to understand every context, but nevertheless, it was an overwhelmingly positive ride. The game has everything horror fans will enjoy, I’ll cover the most important topics:

- Outstanding character design. There are so many memorable villains (one could even argue whether Moreau is a villain or rather a victim), each of them unique regarding boss fights, backstory, motivation and aesthetic. Actually I can’t tell who’s my favourite. My inner simp says it‘s the blood-thirsty, fashionable Vampire family, but I found Heisenberg’s hatred towards Mother Miranda most interesting and plausible. Moreau’s appearance may be disgusting and repellent, but also pitiful. I feel equally bad for killing Donna after I find out about her background story. None of the Lords deserved what they became.

- While the boss fights are pretty similar regarding mechanics, they are very unique conceptually. For example, you open a window to eridacte a bunch of troublesome flies. Or beat the ♥♥♥♥ out of a scrap Transformer. This may sound weird and not Resident Evil like at all, but works surprisingly well and and ensures many unique and memorable settings. At one point, I felt like Ethan/the player is the true monster for chasing down a mentally ill young woman and stabbing her to death with a pair of scissors while she clutched her childhood doll. Is this how Ethan treats Rose too?! These are completely different circumstances compared to other games where you take pleasure in killing off the bad guys. 

- Without doubt the level designers had great fun creating the village and each of their boss areas. I honestly can’t tell which looks more fascinating: is it the giant Castle Dimitrescu which seems spooky from the outside but turns out to be absolutely gorgeous from the inside, with valuable furnishing being a stark contrast to the shabby village you visit at first? Or is it Donna and Angie’s psycho house in which I encountered one of the vilest creatures I’ve ever seen? Or Moreaus‘ swampy and stinking wasteland which hides an entire fishing village? Or Heisenberg’s rusty and metal af factory (my secret winner) because I adore styles like Steampunk, Mad Max and Cyberpunk and this combined them all??

- The game is a perfect mix of immersive cutscenes full of super realistic face animations, a suspenseful walking simulator, free exploration possibilities and sweaty gameplay which mostly consists of climbing, shooting, solving riddles and panically figuring out where to find the next Duke safe spot is just right. 

- A moderate number of really good and unexpected jumpscares, most of them produced by the Duke whilst browsing your inventory, will keep you awake. Surround audio on top of this is eargasmic. And finally the constant feeling of being underpowered, overwhelmed and chased made me feel uncomfortable and in danger most of the time, well done Capcom. Surely, there are some safe spots and the village is pretty empty once you killed every enemy, but being chased through the castle and especially through Heisenbergs factory when the lights go down were one of the most intense chases I’ve experienced in a game. The sound of those drillers still haunt me. 

All these factors lead to RE8 being a great game that covers both the horror and the shooter genre really well. It creates an immersive, cold and dark world with lots of hidden paths, items, treasures and (mini) bosses. Ethan‘s dry humour was gold and fitted really well. Probs to the other voice actors as well (RIP Jeanette Maus). Many quality of life aspects perfect the fun to play aspect, e.g. no fall damage, the upgraded weapons don’t lose their modifications after selling, higher difficulties drop better loot etc. Speaking of which, there are lots of nice extras and incentives to try multiple playthroughs apart from achievements. For example, the models and concept arts are a precious addition to the awesome character design and imagery. And also the hardest difficulty, Village of Shadows, is worth trying after you complete the game if you love sweaty PVE gameplay (though, ♥♥♥♥ you Heisenberg, I love your character design but screw this boss fight lol). The only issues that bothered me were the tedious inventory management and the fact that you can only have one automatic save point at a time. 

In conclusion, I had an amazing experience and even though I’m not a Resident Evil veteran, it seems to me as if this game was pure fan service. The insane story reveal in the end makes it a 9.5/10 for me. Bought it for the Lady, stayed for the plot.
In the end, everyone wants to either
I) date one of the Dimitrescus
II) pet poor Moreau
III) save Donna
IV) or side with Heisenberg.
Which one are you?

I don’t think I can really say anything about Resident Evil Village that hasn’t already been mentioned. But I’ll give it a whirl anyway so here goes:

Having played through the game twice now (once on PS5 and once on Steam) I can say it truly enjoyed it. It has a perfect mix of horror and action, unlike Resident Evil 7 that seemed to be more focused on horror. The game feels great, plays great and looks great. 

Just like its predecessor the game plays out entirely in first person view, immersing you into its exceptionally weird story. After just a short introduction you end up in a village and from there you start your journey, a.k.a. horror story.

There’s been a lot of talk of Lady Dumitrescu before its release and while it’s a great character that looms over you and follows you throughout the castle it’s only a short part of the game, taking just several hours in this 10 hours or so adventure. This happens quite early in the adventure so there’s still much to look forward to afterwards, thankfully.

There’s an entire village to explore with secrets, animals and loot to be found that you can then sell or trade with a gigantic merchant. There are quite a few mini bosses to be killed, and, of course, actual bosses, all of them in their own environment (industrial and water, for example). But still all of it connected to the village where you’ll return to frequently. It think it’s safe to say this can be seen as some sort of hub where you can relax after the initial onslaught of enemies.

Crafting also plays a big part of the game. Stuff you find along the way can be used to make ammo, medkits, pipe bombs and mines alongside other stuff that can be unlocked by purchasing the recipes from the merchant. It does remove some of the game’s tension, though.
Later on you can also find and kill animals that can be used to give you small bonuses like adding permanent extra health.

You are probably wondering if there are cons in this game and the answer is yes. While I enjoyed it and think it was great - really great - it isn’t perfect and there are always things that can be improved (upon), namely:
- The story. It’s weird and doesn’t make much sense if you’ve never or hardly played Resident Evil before.
- SPOILER The part where you switch characters near the end of the game wasn’t fun to play and really stood out (obviously because it’s a different character). I didn’t like it.
- It wasn’t always clear if you were damaging a boss, the feedback seemed really poor, but if you keep in mind that all of your weapons will do damage - no matter what - you’ll probably survive. Some bosses require a different tactic, though.

Since Resident Evil Village is a cross-gen game you wouldn’t expect the game to be all that as far as graphics are concerned but nothing is less true. They’re detailed and gorgeous with the exception of a few low resolution textures. All of the characters are excellently animated and the village oozes atmosphere and somehow also looks naturally connected.
About the voice acting I can be short (as always): it’s excellent. Talented, delivered convincingly and fitting with the actual characters. None of them felt out of place.

Resident Evil Village is a brilliant horror action game that’s almost perfectly paced. It’s really very similar to Resident Evil 4, except for the fact that it is shorter. The gameplay of this new Resident Evil is great, the graphics amazing and the story… well, weird. But everything else is *chef’s kiss*.

This game has a 12 hour campaign with very little replay value, the mercenaries mode is so simplistic it's barely worth talking about. I would only recommend this at a (very) reduced price. 

The gunplay is fun and satisfying, definitely the best part of the game, but enemy variety is very low, so you'll be fighting the same werewolfes from beginning to end. Bosses are standard Resident Evil fare, not great, not terrible.

By Resident Evil standards the story is decent enough, some interesting ideas, lots of cliché. The game can't quite decide whether it wants to be a campy shooter or a suspenseful horror-game and doesn't really commit to either. 

Level Design is good during the first third of the game, but afterwards it becomes pretty much completely linear with some light backtracking, so if you enjoyed the dense, interconnected world of the re2 remake this might not be the game for you.

The whole bonus point system suggests that this game is supposed to played multiple times, but this clashes severely with the games many cinematic sequences, which might be ok the first time but kill the pacing on replays. These include but are not limited to:

- a long opening sequence. Even when you skip all cutscenes it takes a good 10 minutes for the actual game to start

- a PT-esque horror sequence. Very spooky the first time, annoying and tedious every other time

- a Call of Duty-style shootout against dozens of enemies towards the very end of the game. Chaotic, exhausting and ends the game on a bit of a sour note.

All in all I'd give the game a 6/10. A fun, but superficial shooter that sometimes feels like Resident Evil, oftentimes not. If you're looking for a horror experience, there are games with much better value available. If you're looking for a more "traditional" RE experience, stick to the excellent RE2 remake or check out the Evil within 1 & 2.

Resident Evil: Village is one of the most commercially and critically successful games in the franchise and is likely to win Game Of The Year. If you enjoyed this game, more power to you for getting your money's worth. Unfortunately, I did not have the same experience as everyone else playing this game. Now, don't get me wrong, its an adequate game and the final third of the game is really good which is what kept me playing and got me to finish it. Sadly, it was too little, too late.

While Resident Evil 7 was inspired heavily by the first three entries in the franchise, Village, going by its marketing, was supposed to be the spiritual successor to Resident Evil 4. You can see similar DNA with the attache case, the merchant, weapon upgrade system and pivot towards action horror. Sadly, its not fit to lace Resident Evil 4's boots. The problem is that Village attempts to do too much instead of focusing on one style of gameplay. It shares DNA with 4 and 7. Most reviews have stated it takes the best of both games. I would disagree completely and instead say its stuck in a gray area of not doing either style of gameplay particularly well.

Resident Evil 4, as you probably know, was an action horror title which threw hordes of enemies at the player and presented them with numerous combat options with several weapons, enemy types and contextual melee attacks. As a result, combat always felt fresh and distracted the player from the linear level design and removed puzzles. Village, on the other hand, has so few enemy types in comparison to the Gonados of Resident Evil 4 which minimises the amount of interesting encounters that can be constructed. To make matters worse, these enemies are only ever thrown at you in stacks of 2-3 for the first two thirds of the game. These encounters also happen infrequently. As a result, you never really get to feel the satisfaction of your fully upgraded arsenal for the first 2/3 of the game. The majority of the game feels like Resident Evil 4 with unengaging combat. The lack of contextual melee attacks also takes a way one of the many options the player had in RE4. As I said earlier, the final third of the game is when the action is firing on all cylinders with the game throwing hordes and hordes of enemies at the player and lets them fully unleash their firepower and its almost as satisfying as RE4. Truly a great sequence. However, by this point, there is only two hours to go until you've finished it. A counterpoint, could be to play on New Game Plus but the first two thirds of the game are so slow with almost two hours of walking forward and interactive cut scenes that I would never want to experience it again. Once you get past that part, you have to play the woeful Castle Dimitrescu and Moreau's Lake sections to get to the good part. No thank you.

The problem lies in the fact that Capcom wanted to please every demographic with this game. It wanted the old school fans and it wanted mass appeal rather than just picking one and going with it. They should have ditched the survival horror sections entirely as those sections are a joke to anyone that's played the original games. Either go all the way on survival horror like in Resident Evil 2 Remake or don't do it at all. Castle Dimitrescu is the worst level in the entire game honestly. It presents itself as a labyrinth like the Mansion from the original game with doors to unlock, puzzles to solve and a stalker enemy in a similar style to Mr X from the RE2 remake except with no resource management required. The problem is that this section is designed in a linear fashion with zero exploration required for progression. Each key item unlocks a single door in the castle with no thinking or route planning required. The worst offender is the mask item you acquire before one of the daughter boss fights. The solution to to the puzzle is in the exact same room as the puzzle. There is no exploration required in the castle in which you need to find the item you need to piece the puzzle together. Every solution is basically right in front of you. The worst offender being the piano puzzle where you can literally just mash the keys and the puzzle autocompletes. This is no RE2 Remake where they give you the Diamond Key, which unlocks six different doors, and then asks you to figure out which puzzle item in each of those rooms goes where. The problem is that the route forward is always obvious and your brain could literally be hanging out your head and you'd be fine. I have no problem with Village being a dumb game honestly but if they want to go that route, fully embrace it and go full action horror. Ditch these puzzles and this level design and do what's done later in the final third of the game.

Basically, this game is in a weird grey area between RE7 and RE4 and doesn't really satisfy me as an action game or a horror game. It just sort of exists and then it ends. As I said, at the top, its fine if you like it. You are no less a Resident Evil fan than me. Its just, if this is the future of the franchise, which is likely with how successful it was, then I'm afraid I'm going to have to give it a skip unless to they commit to either a horror game or an action game.

Resident Evil Village is what a Next-Gen game should be, Beautiful Graphics, Captivating Gameplay, and Amazing story. 

It's clear that Village takes direct influence from RE4, however the action is very low-key in comparison as the game inserts a feeling of dread from an empty village, with nothing but the wind and snow breezing over. Once you enter the Castle, you feel safe, as you get to meet the 5 main antagonists of the game who on there own, have so much depth and story to, that leaves you wanting more. The game plays with your emotions, connecting with your senses of depression, fear, and heroism. It's one of the first video games that manages to successfully pull off Genre Hybritiy in the Gaming industry. 

The story feels very disconnected from the main franchise, which is not a bad thing, it actually allows you to breathe, and start with something fresh, it doesent suffer from the issues of a typical sequel, as its almost impossible to compare this game to RE7. The story is very much focused on the characters and there motivations, you don't have to play the other games to understand the story, which as I mentioned before, a good thing, being disconnected allows for new ideas to take place, and allows you the player to connect with each and every character in the game.

My only critisism is the writing and the dialogue, at times it can feel really feel cringy or just stating the obvious, often the protaganist just says "wHaT Is gOiNg oN?????" and it can feel a bit repetitive if you play for long periods of time. The Average story time is 7 to 8 hours, however this can be strectched to around 9-10 if you collect EVERY single item in the game.

Overall the game is a solid 9/10 "Short but Sweet"

This game is a phenomenal example of a solo-player horror game. It has positives and negatives, but even with it's negatives, it is a MUST PLAY in my book. 

Let's start with the positives.
The aesthetic of this game goes so far beyond anything I have ever played. From props, to environment, to stunning characters, it is an absolute win for the visuals. The character designs are brilliant and tell you lots of information just from looking at them. The Dimitrescu Lady and Daughters are by far one of the best examples of this, but Mother Miranda truly does take the cake. The environment is unique and sets the tone beautifully for the story telling. 

The game play is next. It is engaging, fast-paced, unique, and moderately tricky. Some of the puzzles are similar to other RE games, and others are new and exciting. There's not much to say about the game play other than it is exactly what you should expect, in a good way.

Next let's talk about the story. They decided to make a direct sequel to the game before this, and I think it went very well. The story is extremely interesting, fleshes out the world more, makes us love (and hate) returning characters, and lets us fall in love with new ones. Resident Evil Village continues Capcom's hot-streak. Starting with RE7 Capcom has been releasing hit after hit for the Resident Evil franchise and Village is no different.

In Village you once again play as Ethan Winters from RE7 as he's thrown into another horror show, this time trying to save his daughter. Village is a direct continuation from RE7 with critical plot points directly referencing RE7. It is advised that you play through RE7 plus its free Not A Hero DLC before starting Village if you care about story.

Village follows a very similar formula to RE7 right down to the first person perspective. The game takes place in an unnamed Romanian Village, whoda thunk, and as you progress more parts of the Village open up. There's lots of returning to places to finish puzzles, or to open door you now possess the key for, or just for hunting secrets. There are five lords of the Village, and you must take down each of them. Each lord has their own unique theme and boss fight. All are awesome well design characters. You'll almost feel bad for putting them down as you'll certainly fall in love with each of their charming personalities.

Village's story is decent and fairly well written. There are some spotty character motivation, namely Chris', but pushing that aside this is quite a unique tale for the RE franchise. Never has there been this direct of a continuation, besides maybe Code Veronica, and there's some surprising revelations for past RE games delivered here. Ethan is more present here than he was in RE7, and despite a cheesy line here and there I find him to be quite a like-able and unorthodox RE hero. His motivation is pure and unwavering. He's a dad on a mission. And all the villains as stated before are absolutely delightful.

Gameplay is an evolution of RE7's with some inspirations from RE4. General combat has a similar feel to RE7 just with the pace being cranked up a bit, and with much more enemy variety to boot, The RE4 attache case returns as well as the joy of tetris item management. There's also crafting, similar to the past three games, but this time around crafting materials no longer take up inventory space. Neither do key items and treasure. Speaking of treasure there is a currency system in Village, much like RE4, as well as a charismatic merchant named The Duke who you'll sell your loot to in order to purchase items and upgrades from.

The difficulty of Village I think is a little bit underwhelming. I played on the Hardcore setting for my first run, and the challenge of it felt on par with the normal difficulty of the past three entries. I did a second run on "Village of Shadows" difficulty and it felt similar to past titles Hardcore setting. It seems Capcom has lowered the baseline difficulty for Village, likely to make it more newcomer friendly. If you're an RE veteran, even if you've only played say the RE2/3 remakes on normal, I recommend playing on the higher settings for Village for an adequate challenge. There's also new game+ which also allows you to raise or lower the difficulty. So you can play through on normal, unlock all the weapons and upgrades, and then new game+ into Village of Shadows if you wanted to.

The Mercenaries game mode also makes a welcomed return, however it is locked behind completing Village's story. In The Mercenaries you'll run through locations ripped from the campaign while on a timer as you face a gauntlet of enemies, collecting power ups and time extenders along the way. Once finishing a map you'll be sent to the Duke so you can restock and upgrade your weapons before heading to the next map. Village's Mercenaries is quite addicting as you try to break your previous high scores, and learn how to most optimally 
run each map. Earning S ranks also nets you new power ups granting more reasons to go back in for one more run.

The graphics and performance of Village are also top notch. I'm running a 1660 Super, i5 8400, 16 GBs of RAM with the game on a SSD, and with a mixture of medium and high settings I can run Village with 80-150fps at 1080p on my rig. I could easily crank everything to high and still achieve a locked 60fps, but with my mixed settings the game looks and feels great on my freesync monitor.

However, even with everything great about Village, there's one great big stain that must be addressed. That great performance I mention wasn't the case at Village's launch. In fact performance was downright miserable as the game was plagued with a persistent stuttering issue that would occur every time you defeated an enemy or performed certain actions. There were also certain enemies who could cause prolonged drops to your frame rate into the single digits when they performed specific actions. These performance issues were exclusive to the PC version of Village, and weren't patch until 3 months after launch. It was discovered that Village's DRM was the cause of the stutters and poor performance after a pirated version of the game was shown to have none of these performance issues. For how much Capcom should be praised for turning around the Resident Evil IP and returning it to its survival horror roots, they should also be reprimanded for allowing such severe performance issues to persist for so long, let alone ship in such a state, and for basically punishing paying customers for legitimately acquiring their product. It is appreciated that these issues were eventually addressed, but it shouldn't have taken everything that it did for Capcom to do the bare minimum.

All in all Resident Evil Village is a fantastic addition to the franchise, and has quickly become one of my favorites for series. Solid gameplay and story paired with excellent graphics/atmosphere and performance. Truly a treat all around.

"Resident Evil 8 is a call back to Resident Evil 4"
This was the phrase parroted in the period leading up to the game's release. Thankfully this turned out to be on the larger end of untrue, otherwise the game could have been many times worse than it is.

While the game has "a creepy castle and a village" that's largely the end of the similarities. In general the whole tone is a lot different and more serious (though it still has its moments) which I apprecated. There's no Meme cracking Leon deflating any tone or pace out of every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ moment of the game.

The game does have its problems however, one is once again, its length. The game feels heavily rushed in many ways and feels like it does tricks to feel fuller than it is. I note this the most in the second and 3rd areas, both are heavily on rails that are really not very long or that interesting yet try to jazz the area up with stuff to make the player deliberately slow down so it feels longer. 

The second area (which I'll refer to it as this cause its spoiler heavy) is the most guilty of this because while its neat the first time you ever go through it, subsequent play throughs will have you banging your head going "GOD CAN I SKIP THIS PLEASE!?" every single time. It incorporates a trick that only works once, and they honestly should have given a way to skip it in NG+ because while it'd not made the game any longer, it'd at least not dig at you. 

The 3rd area isn't as annoying but still pretty annoying because of the on rails dodging it is with almost no combat to it. Ironically? Had this been RE7 that'd been totally fine, but this game trains your brain out the gate to expect more combat than the 2nd and 3rd areas want to give you. Its like the game doesn't really know what it wants to be and switches its tones constantly. Some would say this is the game giving you variety but... when it feels like different teams made each area due to how much contrast the variety provides... I dunno about that.

Then there's the return of the much clamored for mercenaries mode... which is ok I guess... the only mercenaries mode I ever truly liked was the one in the original RE3, so its inclusion here means very little. I'd rather have had a more full main game than this mode if I am being perfectly honest.

However, I'd rather have a mercenaries mode double the size it is now and a main game the same size than have the stupid RE:Versus the game is packaged with. Versus isn't even playable yet and I hope it honestly gets scrapped and they are forced to add more content to 8. Because they didn't seem to learn their lesson from RE:sistance. RE:sistance was the main reason I was not an early adopter of 8 and only am playing it this early even because it was gifted. Capcom needs to learn selling half a game and expecting a MP plugin to pick up the slack does not work.

So while this is an overall enjoyable experience there are problems and I air caution to people and maybe wait for some pretty decent sales on this one.

A Visual Masterpiece!

      Resident Evil: Village is a absolute sight to see on new hardware. Level design is at it highest in this installment, providing the player with vast eye-popping castles and mountains and close-quartered detailed houses and rooms to make you stop and look around. The combat is nothing to complain about. Controls are smooth and responsive, ease of access is present and weapon-swapping is swift. The story is something that must be told to everyone who is an avid horror fan. 
      Providing the player with a rich and vibrant variety of environments to help push the narrative. Now you might have asked yourself, "Do I have to play Resident Evil: Biohazard to understand this?" Yes and no. Simply put, I would personally encourage one to play Biohazard before Village due to the same attention to detail and brilliant level design that it shares. However, In the beginning of Village, the player is provided with a recap of the event of Biohazard. One can play Village and understand the story without playing Biohazard but you'll miss out on some references and events that took place in that game. Adding onto that, the gravity of some key moments in Village's story won't hit as hard due to the lack of experience in the Biohazard. After completing Village, the player is given the option to play challenges to unlock more weapons to use in the story and other modes! Replayability is present in this title. 
      The potency of "Scare Factor" (as I call it) is a bit lacking. I blame myself for that since I've played dozens of horror games in my years. I found Biohazard to be more terrifying than Village however, Village really did shoot their shot in the visuals and nailed that bullseye. Compared to other games, the sense of vulnerability and helplessness is absent due to your arsenal of weapons at your disposal. Compared to the Outlast franchise, I didn't feel many moments of pure anxiety. If you're new to horror, this is for you! If you are an avid horror fan and haven't played any of the Outlast games? You're in for the ride of your life. 
     All in all, This game is f-ing fantastic! Runs amazing on new hardware and is an absolute masterpiece! It is 100% worth the full price tag. 10/10

Resident Evil Village is loaded with atmosphere. If you appreciate an intricate level of detail bordering on excessive in your video games, then this is the title for you, especially if you're well-versed in classic horror tropes. Village has baroque castles with dark secrets, a creepy blockaded Eastern-European town full of terrors, and traditional monsters pulled from fairy tales  and tweaked with the series' mutated theme. Seven foot tall vampiress Lady Dimitrescu took the internet by storm, but she's joined by lycans, giant werewolves, blood-sucking witches composed of flies, possessed dolls, and a humongous amphibious catfish that vomits acid. Unlike the last Resident Evil game I played, Village uses a first person perspective, which heightens the horror without taking away the signature gamplay of the series. You'll still have to search rooms for loot and ammo, scrounging what you can while dealing with the occasional puzzle. The shooting feels solid, although the frame of view is too narrow, and Ethan, your doofus protagonist,  moves at the pace of a wounded buffalo, which is fine most of the time, except when you're trapped in a cave or narrow rampart and you have to outmaneuver a giant mutated dragon. The story is nigh incomprehensible, especially for someone who didn't play Resident Evil 7. The game opens with Ethan sitting down to a nice dinner with his wife after putting his infant daughter to bed. A bunch of spec-op guys break in, shoot Ethan's wife, and steal his baby. You start following them, only to discover that they were ripped to shreds by a pack of werewolves. Looking at the reviews of Resident Evil Village, one would think it a masterpiece of design and storytelling, with an ‘overwhelmingly positive’ verdict from Steam users.

Unfortunately, I’d have to drastically disagree and describe this game as silly, derivative, bland, and extremely formulaic.

I’m a massive RE fan, played the lot, and my heart most definitely lies in the original Playstation generation of the Jill Sandwich, but it doesn’t mean I can’t handle the contemporary models.

They’re ok, not great, but they’re ok – but Village is outright poor and gives me zero incentive to return for more.

Graphically it’s nice, but we take stuff like that for granted these days and visuals aren’t a credible way to rate a game any more, but gameplay and design are.

And here’s where this silly game completely fails. The plot, while initially thoroughly intriguing, falls to pieces as the stupidity of the story starts to unravel with the Village itself and the weird monsters plaguing the place, before the idiocy of the first ‘twist’ appears. When it’s reveal, said with a straight face, I actually found myself laughing.

But it’s the terrible voice acting of Ethan, not to mention his absurd dialogue, which really goes furthest in ruining this game. He’s just an annoying emo in this game, just shouting like a brat and it is utterly jarring. In short, while his voice actor did a decent job in RE7, this one was bad. Real bad. Plus that stupid dialogue. Take the Heisingburg stuff, the guy is actually saying he wants to work with you to beat the bad guy, and sure, while his wording about Rose was maybe not the most sensitive, Ethan’s reaction is to shout at him like he’s the enemy. It literally made no sense. 

And the plotting throughout the game was just a mess. The exposition at the end ‘revealing’ all the secrets was like the game spoonfeeding the audience the answers in one go, and it was incredibly crude.

As for the actual gameplay? Rubbish. Too many illogical paths blocked, far too many doors ‘locked from the other side’, and the combat was mediocre. 

The atmosphere was ok, I’ll give it that, and it did a bit of a job of paying homage to the Spencer mansion via the Castle.

And I did actually love the Dollmaker section, which was by some distance the highlight of the whole game.

But overall it’s the worst RE of the RE Engine age, and quite how this hot mess scores so highly among both critics and gamers alike is beyond me.

Which is fair enough. Can’t speak for everyone.

The visual design for bosses was fantastic and they were quite different in terms of gameplay, I especially enjoyed the final one. It is worth mentioning however that some mini bosses get repeated, although only once from what I've personally experienced.

I think there are two compelling action sequences that are worth mentioning which contrast eachother very well, one in the beggining that had me on the edge of my seat, trying your best to survive while getting overwhelmed and one at the end where you're a complete badass, mowing down enemies with high tech equipment to make your way towards your objective.

The environments were beautiful, loved the medieval romanian architecture and attention to detail, game has a great sense of atmosphere as well.

Story was a blast, I didn't expect these developments, I don't wanna spoil anything but it does have some "holy ♥♥♥♥" moments especially if you're familiar with the previous games.

The graphics were improved from 7 in many ways but I especially liked the facial animations and model quality in this one.

As per usual with RE games, if you hate puzzles you will probably get frustrated with this game, although I thought they were done pretty well all things considered. Besides for some of the more classic RE ones where you have to find different components and keys, it also had a few physics based puzzles and a detective one that involves a mannequin which was pretty decent. Puzzles usually offer a moment of respite where you can take recent events in, away from all the action and horror.

The game did freeze once for about 5 seconds right after defeating a boss. It also suffers from weird controls on mouse and keyboard and it doesn't offer to rebind some keys such as middle mouse button for moving the map. 

As with most other Resident Evil titles, the survival horror aspect makes the gameplay quite meticulous and slow if you're used to other games like Doom for example. You have to conserve resources, go for aiming precision and headshots, time blocks, avoid attacks, sometimes avoid fighting enemies altogether and so on. Keep that in mind if you dislike this type of gameplay.

Overall an enjoyable time, I'll play it on the two higher difficulties as well and the other game mode and try to complete challenges too since the gameplay is quite fun.

I'd say this is probably my favorite RE title since 4.

Usually I would leave some stupid one-liner review like "I don't got friends. I have family..." or something along those lines but Resident Evil Village genuinely made me want to take the time to write something meaningful about this game. A heads up - most likely I'll be mentioning some of the important plot points of the game and areas.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The gameplay for the most part follows the same first-person aspects and gunplay from Resident Evil 7. However, a distinct difference between 7 and Village is the return of a bigger inventory (no item box) and a shop where you can buy supplies or upgrade your arsenal of weapons just like how it was done in Resident Evil 4. One of the main gimmicks of this game is that there in total four lords you'll have to fight: Big vampire lady, Creepy Doll Lady, Swamp Thing, and The Heisenberg (my favorite lord). Each lord fight always felt distinct and different from one another which in turn made them more memorable. While Lady D and Heisenberg were the coolest, the Doll Lady felt like the lowest point as there was little to no challenge whatsoever when fighting her. Overall, I love the return of this system from Resident Evil 4 because I always felt a sense of progression with my items and would love to continue to see more boss fights on the scale that Village created in future games.

[h1] Atmosphere [/h1]
The game does a phenomenal job at creating throughout the game to always create these anxiety-inducing areas such as the village, the castle, and many other areas. The game felt like a mash between the horror of Resident Evil 7 and the action parts of Resident Evil 4 which was something that constantly made the game entertaining at every turn. While it may not be as scary compared to RE7, I still do think that they managed to keep aspects of what makes Resident Evil what it is through the environments and atmosphere created in this game.

[h1] Narrative [/h1]
The story is one of the best, in my opinion, in the Resident Evil franchise and a great end to Ethan Winters. I constantly felt that I had to keep on going to find out more and more about the setting, the character, and Ethan the most. I liked that Ethan felt more developed as a character who's a father that'll do anything in order to restore the family he wants to keep together. As a story as a whole, I felt that while it serves as the end of Ethan Winters, it also does well to set the foundation for future games to continue the story with Chris Redfield and possibly any other returning RE characters in the franchise.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
Overall I would give this game a solid 9/10 for such an investing story line with characters that felt alive and an ending that felt satisfactory by all means. I would most definitely recommend this game for both its narrative, music, and gameplay that come all together to create this amazing game.

Resident Evil Village is an incredible game with a very strong identity.
RE8 combines so many of the best features from the franchise while still offering a new and refreshing experience. I have always been a long time fan of resident evil which could lead to me having a bias towards this game but I truly believe anyone with an interest in the game or RE in general, should definitely pick this game up at some point. At the time of writing this review, I have just under 30 hours which is a few playthroughs along with going for some out of the way achievements. While most people may only do one to two runs coming in around 12 or less hours for a "full experience run", I would still highly recommend this game. However, purchasing at full retail price (60 dollars) may be a bit high if you plan to only play once or twice. However, for someone like me who will 100% the game as I have with previous, it was money well spent. It may be in your best interest to wait for a sale if you only plan to play once or twice. In my opinion, this game has two very prominent features that make it stand out from other RE games. This game seems to be a well balanced mixture of required and optional combat along with an incredible story. I find that some of the other RE games and games nowadays in general, sometimes struggle with finding the balance between the story and combat but I believe this game does a great job of implementing both. Its not uncommon for games to have a hard time to truly find their identity but RE8 takes a very firm stance on the survival horror genre and plays into it perfectly. Thus far, I have enjoyed every run I have played and have found no moments to be dull or repetitive. It has been said that this game specifically does not have good replay - ability but I would highly disagree. I would argue that the second or third time are the most fun, especially if you crank up the difficulty. It makes me sad to see the end of the winters story but I am hopeful that it will potentially continue in the form of Rose as the protagonist. Capcom has outdone themselves once again in my opinion and I think this game got a lot more negative feedback the it deserved. My only real critics would be that it would be nice to have an FOV slider (Note: The FOV is not nearly as bad as some people say and there are mods to help if you find it truly unbearable) and it would have been nice for the game to be a bit longer. I don't believe most people are going out of their way for challenges and achievements and the boss fights aren't all that hard. Therefore, it can lead to the game being quickly finished which can turn people off that were looking to buy a more lasting experience. As I mentioned above, I plan to 100% this game over time and may update the review once finished but my parting words would be that this game is fantastic and offers something very different then any other game. That dollhouse truly unlocked a new fear in me. I employ you to consider purchasing this game and to take all negative reviews with a grain of salt. Hope this helps!

This section is a boring shooter with the same enemy over and over, and it leads into the worst part of this supposed horror game: The Black Ops shooter run and gun section. Combined with laughable dialogue and terrible story the game struggles to keep interest throughout the whole game. [h3]Of Fat Babies and Fairy Tales[/h3]
The Village feels like a proper sequel to RE4. It further deepens the intricate atmosphere of an Ass European countryside, boasting a rich, zany fleur of protestant paganism, which isn't always an oxymoron... but it's a complex issue and here we have no space for a theological discussion. Things are strange in this fairy-tale Romania with realistically sprouted potatoes is what I'm saying.

So, hooking back up with Mia and having a fat baby with her seems to be the canon, sadly. I don't like her, but at least as a character she's not as useless as Elena. Anyway, they didn't let me ponder for too long before, uhh, 'that boulder punching a-hole' happened, which I found hilarious. But let's just leave the plot alone for now and speak of the characters instead.

I adore The Duke, the glorious leviathan of a man is a scenery-chewing spectacle by himself! His larger-than-life personality stole the show. Naturally, I appreciated lady Dimitrescu and the claws she snatched from FMA's Lust. However, the gold goes to Magneto as Heisenberg. Or was he inspired by the 1990's 'Hardware'? The game has top-of-the-line voice acting overall, but his voice I deem the greatest. Too bad that facial animations appear trashy, especially the lip sync.

At least we don't see Ethan's face. I love his reactions, his snark, even his screams of pain. The man wallows in misery, getting through more mutilations than the toys of my childhood. Alas, he's a bit of a one-note dad figure and I didn't find his surface-level commitment to saving his daughter the player barely sees that emotionally investing.

I still enjoyed the roller coaster though. You get into a predicament, get out, get in, get out... And despite that the plot doesn’t budge until the end, the game expands on the universe greatly. I'm not an expert on RE's lore, but this game managed to answer a couple of my questions about the world along the way. Speaking of world-building, I'm on board with how they keep integrating health potions into the setting instead of leaving them a concession.

[h3]Jolly Excitement[/h3]
RE7 could be funny at times while paying homage to its grindhouse roots, yet it was a horrifying game that left a deep footprint on my soul's face. Being an impressionable man, the accurate testament to the lack of horror in RE8 is that I could play it alone at night with the lights off. The panic horror, gross-out, and disturbing creatures are still there and the sound design is so good that I periodically spooked myself by touching dry shrubbery.

But typically, I felt nothing but jolly excitement throughout. I say "typically" because RE8 also happens to feature the most soul-piercingly terrifying sequences ever designed. The memory of what transpired during the second-best scene after the pig scare, "that P.T. on steroids moment", keeps turning my stomach when I write these words. It's peak horror, no doubt, yet it's spread unevenly.

[h3]How I Stopped Worrying And Started Blasting[/h3]
As a diamond crutch, the action density is higher than ever. I started on Hardcore, but it ran its willy over my teeth like they're a xylophone. Hence, I had to revert to Standard after the tanky Lycans swarmed me 20 times in a row. As it turned out, this was the hardest moment in the whole game on any difficulty. They throw stronger enemies at you early on, then heads easily pop left and right in the second half of the game if you're a thorough explorer.

In comparison, scrawny ghouls and harpies that you encounter later are a joke. Yes, the monsters aren't just blobs of mold, there's a decent variety! Enemies evade your bullets, block timings can be tricky, you have to think on the go - use explosive barrels to clean up the screen and bags of flour for distraction, barricade the doors. The combat is fast-paced, frantic fun, just like in RE4.

Most of RE7's bosses were kinda difficult when you didn't know what you were doing. Here, I only died to the first insect lady since I didn't realize I had to run. It went smoother with the Lords. They are an extravagant bunch of narcissistic psychopaths and their residences each present you with a somewhat different gameplay style. You will be delighted to find out more about them by yourself.

[h3]You Wanted Puzzles But Ba-Da-Ba-Da-Ba-Be-Bop-Bop-Bodda-Bope[/h3]
Respectively, they've dumbed-down the puzzles. The authors acknowledged and accepted the derp, which would rub me the wrong way if it didn't benefit the pacing. And undeniably, they were going for the latter above all. You get pulled through the game at lightspeed. The epic views and dreadful events flash before your eyes like subtitles in Scatman John's video. They could've made the game smarter and longer to please the fans more, yet I won't condemn the devs for not doing so since it was an insanely wild ride from start to finish.

Even the persistent puzzle of item management could not escape its peers' fate. Gone is your canonical stash chest, you are compensated with a much bigger inventory to carry loads of classical RE guns, from pistols to a grenade launcher. Not even once in the whole game, I had to decide what to leave and what to take, there's enough space for everything. I'm not down with this change.

[h3]Ooh, shiny![/h3]
So, you come to this godforsaken village, everything's despicably locked, teasing you, and you can't open a thing! Hours later, you come back with a vengeance - with bundles of keys, a wheel, and a crank in your pockets - to confidently take back the denied satisfaction and make every last door, every single box, even the wells that dared to reject your advances tremble before you in primordial fear. Now, that's what I call delayed gratification! I hope it didn't come off as some incel's manifesto.

As usual, corpses and other containers hide valuables. Lei or something you can sell for Lei, which is the local currency. Things you can buy with it are standard: weapon upgrades, schematics, supplies, and crafting recipes. But the best thing is that the shiny treasures are back! They are usually hidden in plain sight, which makes them harder to notice. Almost left the house, turned back for one last look... aha! A gem among the ashes in the stove! Precious.

Crafting is as unassuming and tactical as ever, allowing you to make what you need depending on the circumstances. Being able to hunt is a new, yet self-explanatory feature: kill animals, they drop the ingredients you should hand to The Duke, so he could cook you the most exquisite dishes that give you permanent stat upgrades. Not brilliant but nice.

[h3]The Beauty of the Grotesque[/h3]
The environments are as gorgeous as they are noninteractive, it's an all holes barred experience. The game's world could end up feeling like a museum of luxurious assets if the scenery wasn't so atmospheric. The BDSM dungeons of Disneytrecu's castle gave me the Martyrs\Serbian Film vibes. The insane Beneviento's mansion and flooded village of Moreau left an impact. Not to mention the Heisenberg's factory where the game becomes System Shock for a brief moment. As much as I'd like to, to say more would be a spoiler.

At some points of the game the artistry was so stunning that I couldn't believe how smoothly the game performed. The lighting and modelling are perfect. The weapons, in particular, feature all these neat details: the weathered look and the manually added scrapes. I'm also a sucker for cool god rays and The Village exploited my weakness every step of the way.

[hr][/hr]
This whole game is one huge weakness of mine! It's a sight to behold as well as a joy to play. It has raised my spirits high, now I'm sure that Capcom won't crap itself when remaking RE4. I'll allow myself a drop of optimism just this once and I hope not to choke on it later.

P.S. [b]BRING BACK[/b] some [b]INVENTORY MANAGEMENT.[/b]

Over the past two weeks, I played through both Resident Evil 7, and I just finished playing Resident Evil: Village yesterday. I will say first that when it comes to the Resident Evil franchise, I'm not a hardcore fan. I have always known of Resident Evil, but I only really played the Demo of Resident Evil 2 on my original Playstation, and then I played the Leon half of the RE2: Remake on my PC back in 2019.
This is the reason why I asked, about a week ago, what order I should go about playing the other RE games because I really do want to go back and experience them all, especially after just finishing Village.
That being said, here are my opinions opinions on Resident Evil 7 and Resident Evil village. I feel that between two games, that Resident Evil 7 was a better game. I really enjoyed 7 more because of the fact that I was always on edge playing it. (I would like to add in here that I wore headphones while playing both games on PC, to immerse myself more.)

When it came to 7, there is just something that is very terrifying and uneasy about the game...from beginning to basically the end of the game. Unfortunately I never really got that feeling while playing Village. Instead there were really only certain sections of Village where I felt scared while playing it.
Throughout a majority of 7, there was this feeling of being afraid to turn a corner because of the fact that Jack, or  Marguerite, or Lucas might be there waiting for me. I honestly only felt this way at the beginning of Village. After dealing with Beneviento in Village, that uneasy feeling disappears and I really feel like the game just somehow loses steam when dealing with Moreau and Heisenberg.

While I feel like Village is still a good game...it felt like it went from being a Horror game, to some sort of weird Call of Duty game at the end, especially when you end up playing as Chris.

Because of this, it really made me not want to finish the game. I had the same sort of issue with 7. Everything was going great, right until the end when Jack turns into this massive mutant thing, and then all of a sudden we are on this ship...which I found super boring...and then we are dealing with Eveline as some sort of massive monster coming out of the house.

Now I know that things becoming massive monsters, is nothing new for Resident Evil. The same thing happens in RE2 with Mr. X, but at least there it made more sense. Especially because Mr. X has been THE major threat throughout the entire game. So the finally battle with him becoming mutated works because he has been the major threat throughout the game.

But when it comes to RE8, having Heisenburg become some massive mutated monster made no sense to me. I would have rather of dealt with him in his human form first, before the big battle as some kind of metal maniac.

I honestly wish that we got to deal with Lady D a bit longer. Especially with how much she was used in the marketing for the game...to me it was a real let down to not only have her as the first boss that you deal with, but to be in the castle for what seemed to be such a short period of time.

Honestly the amount of detail that went into making that castle is so beautiful...that it's really a shame you can't go back and visit it later in the game.
The most terrified that I felt while playing Village, came while exploring Beneviento's house. I have always had a MAJOR fear of porcelain dolls, and so having to go through a house surround by them...well lets just say there were a couple times I saved and quit the game and came back to it later. As scary as that section of the game was, that was another part that I felt was just to short. Especially because I was able to beat her section of the game and Moreau's within what felt like an hour.

Overall, I feel like Village, while still a great game and worth playing, jumped the shark a bit with all of the over the top action at the end. If I had to pick between playing Resident Evil 7 again or playing Resident Evil Village again, I would probably pick 7 because of how terrified it made me feel.

Again, Village is a great game...but I felt slightly let down because I feel like it was overhyped a bit. I wish that we got more of the terrifying parts like dealing with Lady D, and exploring Beneviento's house, and less of the over the top action of Heisenburg and Chris Redfield.

Hopefully they will fix these problems, if and when Resident Evil 9 comes out.

As a game, I'd say yes, it's decent enough to earn my thumbs up, as a port however - it's bad - REALLY bad.

Took CAPCOM months to fix it and even now there are issues which I really doubt will be addressed regardless on how many patches or excuses they make.

Now, as a game, this one suffers from a weirdly tonned down identity crisis we all know and saw on RE 6 - you know, the game that tried to appeal pretty much every kind of fan at the same time, while almost killing the franchise in the process.

What holds the game together despite all that is the plot. I really enjoyed it, and made me appreciate Ethan far more as a character, his depiction on RE 7 was rather shallow, specially compared to Mia. 

Sadly it's the only positive thing I can think of.


You can't put two very different RE perspectives on one game and hope it will work. RE 4 is a landmark of a game, bought and played far more I'd be proud to admit it. It defined pretty much an entire generation - yet It's no survival horror, not the kind RE 7 was by essentially rebooting the core gameplay. And that's what happens here - the game shifts from RE 4 mechanics to 7 - sometimes so fast and clumsily - that you may start asking yourself if the devs themselves struggled on how or what the game should be about. 

By no means I'm a hater of the over the shoulder action packed RE days, quite the contrary, I love RE 5 to the point I'd put it on my top 5 of my all time favorites on PS3 - but I can't in good faith call it a good RE, not by survival horror standards. If RE 8 decided once more to shift into that territory and stay with it - fine by me, even though I prefer full horror aesthetics - but trying to appeal both sides while struggling to balance is such a naive move from CAPCOM it almost seems they learned nothing from past mistakes.

There are 3 eras of Resident Evil;

The Survival Horror era - RE1/2/3
The Big Scale, Fast Paced Action era RE4/Code Veronica
The Co-Op purely action Era RE5/6

With Ethan Winters, we are given a taste of the 2 best eras of RE. RE8 gives us the fast action but scary and tense gameplay. The game has some of the most stunning visuals and incredible atmosphere. Ive not seen a game do it like this since RE2 remake and Alien Isolation. It is a scary game 

RE8 gives use the scale and puzzles of RE4 too. You can tell they really wanted to take a lot of inspiration from RE4 from the collectables to other things like inventory management, the in game store and the weapons and upgrades. With new ways too, but the DNA is there. 

As for the survival horror aspect, you can feel it. But you will not be running out of ammo. And if you understand how the currency system from RE4, then you will have quite a lot of money throughout. But in regards to the survival horror, capcom did a pretty great job with the difficulties so i know people will get their fix through that. 

The villains are great. Some better than the others... Lady Dimitrescu is as good as you hope she would be. All the internet hype really came through. Funny enough, she is the first villain you will go up against and i can tell you, there is a reason why. Capcom wanted to keep your butts in your seat. She did that. She is the Mr.X of RE8

I wont get into the others just because of spoilers, the way you face them is better to be experienced.

And Finally, Ethan Winters. I thought he is in the lower end of Resident Evil playable characters. But you really get behind him in this game. In the first game i kept thinking he  was wasting his time. But his motivations in this game are a real driving force in keeping you playing. 

Ethan really came through and my only problem with him is that he is a faceless protag. Its a technique devs use to make the player feel like they are the character. I dont like it, another one i hate is the silent protag for the same effect. Just never enjoyed those style of narrative. 

Ethan Winters story is over, i wanna see some Leon, Claire and Ada for the next RE games.

After completing and unlocking everything before the 'buy the rewards' got popped out, I think this is a great game.  With RE3:Remake coming between 7 and 8's release, my hopes in Capcom were pretty low.  But let's not discuss that flaming bag of god knows what.  Resident Evil 8 really feels like survival horror again.  Or at least it's like a punch to the face of nostalgia for RE4, yet with the more posing threat of enemies that can hurt you way worse than you can hurt them, in 7.  

It's one of the few games, such as outlast, to really creep me out at a certain part of the game.  Pushing that feeling you get at the start of the game, being completely helpless against the onslaught while having no way to really fight back other than to just leg it.  It's good.  I really did enjoy Ethans story.  Still don't know why they turned Chris into a total beefcake, but it works.  And wonderful hidden treasures everywhere just begging to be found and sold to the Duke for his lovely trinkets.  Very Memorable characters, I really hope we learn more about the Duke in the DLC.  Although it's weird how many people are stuck on Lady Dimitrescu for what a small part she plays in the overall game.  It's weird, guys.  Duke is Far hotter.  And have you seen Salvatore's smile?

My biggest complaint, as with most Capcom games that come out these days, is when it finally starts feeling like you've got a hang of the game, and really have a fighting chance, like you can't wait to beat down some baddies, and that's usually where Capcom ends the game.  I think they make the games too short, and the replayability, i.e. the unlockables and rewards that actually get people to replay it, are now all for sale on the store page.  I get that some people have busy lives and don't have time to waste a whole evening between shifts unlocking things.  But Capcom just shot them selves in the foot with that by killing the games replayability with a pay to win.

Besides that DLC, the other one which gives you some extra ammo and healing items and a lock pick, that can only be redeemed once.  That seems like kind of a harsh restriction.  Especially when, it seems when you collect something not randomly generated, it doesn't come back for further playthroughs.  Plenty of their past games have done that, allowing you to get a trophy in RE4 for having all treasures in your inventory in one playthrough, grinding respawnable guns in 5 or, again, the re spawning treasures to make the monotonous grind of getting the unlocks a little better.  Which, again, my complaint that they're shooting themselves in the foot by selling all unlockables and removing any real reward for further runs.

But, as with seven, Hopefully they'll be pumping out some DLC that fleshes out the game, or even adds more fun modes.  I really enjoyed "Feeding Daddy" in seven.  Although more story would be nice.  Will update if further DLC gets released.

Resident Evil has finally made its way into eastern lands of Europe, more specifically one unnamed village in Transylvanian Mountains of Romania. You're left off with Ethan from the previous installment now settled with Mia in his relatively modest home somewhere classified location, taking care of their very so normal baby girl. All of the enthusiasm you're experiencing in the beginning will slowly dissipate as you're thrown at the heart of swarm, unknown beasts and monsters alike roaming your surroundings like rats amidst harvest. The dreadful, sinister and abandoned looking village will entice your gaze on every single yard corner, remnants of bodies from farm animals and wasted grains paint slowly and intensively the vicious encounters you'll partake. The visual fidelity through protagonist's eyes is an experience to behold, life-like artwork and animations worthy of unique appraisal. You're provided with a powerful arsenal to choose from which allows you to annihilate every single grotesque creature paving the path to your precious daughter. Raw true survival horror experience occurs and indulges my expectations, I can attest it stands firm from previous titles in the series. There are several areas to explore each with its own theme and ridiculous but thrilling traps that will coax flight or fight responses, leaving oneself more often than not forced to improvise and adapt to each situation. 

The whole system of first person shooter is vastly improved from Ethan's previous adventure as mentioned earlier with lots more weapons to behead ghouls, everything feels more responsive especially when you're blocking enormous werewolf claws with your bare hands; obviously enhanced by the fact you're superhuman with fast regenerative abilities fully recovering your endurance after every encounter. OST & sound design as always is at the peak creating and augmenting the already intensified terror you're forced to withstand. The major character actors being into their roles one hundred percent strengthens the attachments and bonds you'll feel towards their personas, there's a tragedy lying in wait getting you to only empathize through their harrowing stories. Location & characters lore is well written to emulate further involvement, boosting the immersion as if you're there yourself strolling with your own feet and smelling the cold appalling environment. A worthy journey with authentic design of local tradition and culture (approved by a romanian native™) there's lots of fun things to explore, decently difficult puzzles and high variety of monsters to go decimate in most gory manners.

On a whole, the game is a linear hectic experience, and although I have enjoyed it even with the fps breaking the pace every now and then, you cannot deny the fact that you are mostly going in a single straight line all the time, disguised by some nuances of 'would-be' exploration and a lot of packed up action.

You have a variety of places to go throughout the game, but you actually are lead to these places in a same order. There's not really something that you can do before or after, the option of choice. You must do this, then do that, then do another thing. In the between, you pick this and that, fight this and that, read this and that. The main example is the first large area of the game, the castle. You enter it, there are many doors and basically all of them are 'locked on the other side'. You are basically led by the game to go where they planed to. Not to mention many cutscenes breaking the pace quite constantly. The exploration of said castle is pretty much linear, because you need certain items to keep on going, and these items appear, sometimes quite too conveniently, around your path. This sort of realization might not occur when you are first playing the game. But when you replay it, you'll notice that things are pretty much straighforward. You don't need or have to explore anything because there's nothing to explore. You just go, because eventually, key items will spring up before you. And some other things feel kind of ... useless? Like that old lady? She's quite random, if you think about it. She's neither here nor there. And I'm not talking about her casual appearances. I mean her, herself. She's another element that sort of helps you in chaotic moments, and she seems to find chaos funny, then she reappears, give you a keyitem out of the blue, then the last boss turns herself into her too during a speech. So, the old lady seems not to have any roots and you won't find her ever again, making you wonder what the heck was her. At the same time, wondering or not makes no difference at all.

Like many other people here in the reviews, the most heart-pounding moment is at Beneviento's house, exactly because you are defenseless, vulnerable – and dolls are ever so creepy. Not to mention that baby introduction, of course, the mutated giggling and so forth. And although it was also another linear experience, it was the only moment that caused some sense of panic and horror. The rest of the game is basically action.

I did like the factory part because it had moments of double backing and more exploration, not mandatory too, to get some unique items, if you wished. The area boss, however, was quite underwhelming. Again, you were given tools to win, basically. 

Regarding the story and characters, I was ever a Chris fanboy, not much akin to Leon that much (maybe because he just sprang up from a rookie to a special-trained-badass guy?), and I have some strong bindings to characters that are guided by their instinct of protection, because that's my feeling regarding others as well, which is why I also like Ethans with his fatherly drive. The Resident Evil franchise for the past 10 years, give or take, has faced a multitude of backlash, especially since the disappointing Resident Evil 3 Remake’s release in early 2020. Despite the harsh comments and disapproval from fans, CAPCOM managed to secure another hit and continue the success of Resident Evil 7 and arguably RE2 Remake, with various improvements - not just from the design and the storytelling, but from game mechanics and accessibility. However, it is important to note that this is a continuation of the Resident Evil 7 story, and it’s designed to feel that way with its First Person POV. If you enjoy the more "traditional" 3rd Person format of RE, you may be a bit disappointed.

It’s easy to tell at first glance that CAPCOM experimented with the gameplay in this latest installment, and not all of the elements succeeded. Still, they leave pleasing results when executed flawlessly, and the game has many moments for die-hard fans alike. At first, I was slightly apprehensive and confused by the story, but questions and mystery in the beginning segments fueled my drive to keep exploring. I just had to venture deeper to understand what was exactly happening. The answers to the questions that the game presented, while somewhat cliche at times, did satisfy me, though only to a certain extent due to certain lore elements revealed. The story's flowing was smooth, pacing somewhat fast, and at times messy - but the end: impactful.

The puzzles are not complex and can easily be perceived as far too slow and barren compared to the high-action shooter segments. They’re not like the puzzles you’d find in standard horror / thriller games in that instance, but they do help break up the action to take a moment to breathe and lose yourself in the scenery. 

The environments are incredibly stunning. The world isn't large, and so, it shouldn’t be referred to as ‘open-world,’ though it is larger than previous RE games and does give you the initial impression. Still, the way the levels are intertwined with clever designs and hidden areas help cease curiosity as you progress only to go, "oh, so that's where this goes!" The enemy design is demanding, and the attention to detail for the most part is impressive, with CAPCOM’s history. There's a good chunk of variety in here, so you won't feel like you are fighting the same enemy over and over, but it's just large enough that you will think, "oh god, not this guy again." As for standouts: I think we all can agree that Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters are the perfect example.

As a die-hard horror fan, the most significant moment that I appreciated was the first time the game decided, "okay, you've had fun shooting your way through here. now get ready to be terrified." And fortunately, it leaves you helpless; it plays mind-games with you and surprisingly creates the sheer terror of a genuine psychological horror during plot points of the game. I would've loved these moments more if the story had been a little more cohesive and more thought out, but when they did pop up, I was both terrified & filled with adrenaline.

What sets RE Village apart from other horror games is the balance of action and fear, which are designed to complement each other to provide varied and engaging encounters - the years of experience from the development team truly show. There are certain parts of the game where you will not be able to shoot your way through, no matter what’s in your arsenal. That may be a negative for some players, but this was nothing but a positive for me. 

It's rare nowadays to find a game that takes on a risky approach to blend two genres and do it successfully. Once you complete the story, you unlock Mercenaries mode. The Mercenaries, a personal favorite “mini-game” in the Resident Evil franchise, is incredibly fun with lots of replayability. CAPCOM even went the extra mile to make a second or third run more enjoyable beyond the usual ‘you’ve unlocked a new superweapon to use next round.’

Moving on to difficulty - I finished on "Standard," which was surprisingly challenging but not overwhelming. There are harder modes beyond that if you dare, such as Village of Shadows. Still, I enjoyed not having the burden of having to min/max everything and potentially spoil things to understand what I would be facing. During my livestream, I died plenty of times - enough to reconsider strategies and re-adapt my style beyond my usual running and gunning. The bosses themselves, I felt, were on the too easy side of things, but I know most Resident Evil fans play for predominantly the storyline and lore, so keep that in mind.

The lack of a Field of View slider in the settings has been voiced as a major flaw by many people, including myself - due to this, I can’t defend CAPCOM since it’s pretty common in today’s video game culture that newly published titles do, in fact, have this feature. I agree with many others that it's unacceptable that a game in 2021 requires a mod for this; hopefully, though, this will get patched in. While this was annoying, I admit that it did not detract me entirely from enjoying the game in full and was merely a minor inconvenience at best.

For me, there have not been many good "horror" games as of late, and the Resident Evil series as a whole has been lacking. While Resident Evil: Village may not fit the standard of what a horror game is expected to be, it created an enjoyable journey of emotions for me. 

For this, I will say, Well done, CAPCOM. It may be just me being a huge fan of the series since I was a young child, but I would definitely consider this installment a success in my book. I thoroughly enjoyed every minute and only wished there was a bit more.

Now, let’s wait for the DLC.

Remember in other RE games where you would find a puzzle piece and not need it until 30 min later or it's needed for something on the other side of the map? The only map that feels like Resident Evil is the factory (which so many people shockingly hate). It was the most fun for me and had the most replayability because you actually had to backtrack, check the map, and make meaningful decisions about how to deal with enemies (run away, run around, fight, target weakpoints, etc.) Add item management to it and it would have been one of the best RE maps in the franchise. 


[h1][b]Not enough combat to make up for the things the devs took out[/b][/h1]

Even playing on hardcore, it feels like you never face enough enemies. RE4 and RE5 may have been linear and had huge inventory spaces, but they made up for it with a lot of combat. Outside the opening lycan horde, the game is devoid of any challenging combat until you head to the factory where you fight large groups of lycans and deal with the factory enemies which were awesome because of what I mentioned earlier. The bosses aren't challenging either. They just take forever to die. I was mostly disappointed with the 3 witches as they all fight the same way and aren't unique from each other at all. 


[h1][b]Benevito's house is just a giant cutscene[/b][/h1]

There was so much potential here but it was wasted because the game decides to take away your weapons and give you quick time events instead. Imagine having to fight possessed dolls flying in the air that tested your aim? Imagine having to fight horrific illusions of monsters you fought earlier but now they look different and have different attack patterns because Benevito put Ethan's mind on acid? Imagine having to maneuver around the giant deformed baby like Mr. X on top of all of that while frantically trying to get out the house? But no, the devs want you to watch a glorified cutscene instead. Maybe you'll have actual control in fighting Benevito? Nope. It's a QTE. 


[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]

Village is boring, way too easy, and doesn't feel like an RE game. CAPCOM tried to combine old school RE with RE4/5 and failed miserably because they don't know what made those games great. The challenge in old RE games (1-3, 0, etc.) came from exploration, item management, and picking your battles wisely. The challenge in games like RE4/5 came from combat even though it didn't have what the older RE titles had. Both were fun, even if I prefer the older RE titles' gameplay. Village just made me want to fall asleep for most of the game until I got to the factory. There's so little decision making in this game and they completely missed the point of both experiences. Playing Village is like trying to drive a ferrari with no gas. It looks great but it doesn't work. Even then, a pirated version of this game has better performance than the official one. If CAPCOM continues down this path, the future of RE looks bleak.

Got into the series with 7 and this improves on every aspect. This game's best trait is its variety -- while in one or two parts genuinely horrifying, mostly the game's horror is just a well maintained tension, especially in the early sections and the Castle, which most closely mirrors the classic Resident Evil formula. As you hit the midpoint, though, the game gets even better as it opens up into a larger metroidvania format, before making its way through a tense corridor shooter into all-out balls to the walls action territory. In just under ten hours of actual playtime I feel like I've wormed my way through a good story (that appropriately follows up to the previous game), good horror, decent puzzles, fun action, comically insane reveals and surprises, and beat a whole bunch of great bosses, which is the makings of a great, good old-fashioned singleplayer romp.

My biggest complaint is the difficulty balancing. I recommend playing on Hardcore, but expect the opening to be unreasonably punishing. After that, the game is pretty easy--I rarely ever died--until you reach the end, where the difficulty ramps up appropriately. I just wish the difficulty curve was... well, a curve, and not a zig-zag nonsense line. 

Also beware that there are some issues with the port apparently related to the DRM, most notably stuttering--although a recent patch seems to have largely solved this and the game maintained a good, consistent frame rate with few technical issues after that. But YMMV.

But these small problems had no serious effect on my playthrough, this game is just a straight up blast. Well worth it.
