Alright, let’s not waste any time or try to kid ourselves. Resident Evil Village is a masterpiece. There, I’ve said it. It’s out in the open now. In the wake of so many AAA titles being released in a half-baked or broken state, it is the very epitome of a relief to see a game with this much hype released not only working, but excelling at nearly everything.

The story picks up several years after the events of RE7. If, like me, players had not experienced RE7, there is a recap available that broadly goes over the events to bring the player up to speed. It’s enough to let one know what happened without spoiling the experience. Players are then treated to a Tim Burton-esque sequence before revealing it was a bedtime story for new parents Ethan and Mia Winters. 

Following what seems like a pattern of trilogies in the RE series, Ethan stars as the protagonist in his second outing. Events quickly turn things sideways and he’s set upon a quest to track down his missing daughter, Rose. The search leads him to a small European village, hearkening back to Leon’s trip in RE4. Along the way, Ethan is subjected to a litany of monsters, creatures, and larger-than-life characters. In fact, aside from the stunning views Village consistently delivers, it are these characters that I found most enthralling.

It’s not just the Lords and Ladies governing the town that are so engrossing. Mysterious characters like The Duke and even the villagers Ethan encounters are so completely fleshed out. Motivations are as unique as the mannerisms and models. There is a level of detail in every aspect that only helps to decorate this decadent experience. Everyone has a story to be told if the player digs enough.

But, Village follows the traditional Resident Evil format. Players are introduced to a starting area that was shown primarily in promotional materials. From there, the shock and horror subside a bit before revealing secret labs and conspiracies. It’s formulaic, to be sure, but it’s a formula I love all the same. The primary reason for this is the execution in each of the areas players visit. Each has a distinct theme and story-telling method. From the Dracula-inspired halls of Castle Dimitrescu to the Silent Hill levels of creepiness in House Beneviento, each area and mini-story is nearly a masterpiece in its own right.

The story moves along at a good pace without any noticeable slogs or portions that felt tired. Even after three play-throughs I found myself still exploring every nook and cranny, hoping to learn more. Much like any RE title, there is an abundance of notes to be found that flesh out the events of the world. Towards the end, certain pieces are set up for a third entry in the Ethan Winters trilogy. Not a cliffhanger, but more an aftertaste that left me hungry for more.

Village was my first foray into FPS Resident Evil. I skipped out on RE7 as the demo was far too scary and I wasn’t sold on hillbilly horror in a series primarily about zombies and biological monsters. After playing through Village, I realize how wrong I was. It was shocking how well the game lends itself to first-person as well as it did third-person. While I don’t necessarily see a benefit to either perspective, the take-away I had was that neither was a detriment. The only odd thing (that I quickly got used to) was that despite being a FPS, Village doesn’t utilize the iron sights when aiming. Rather, it opts for an arcade-like crosshair system that can be zoomed in. Otherwise, the game handled extremely well with controller.

The inventory system and crafting are nearly identical to RE4, so it was quite intuitive to navigate around and manage my stuff. One fantastic addition was the “bounty” system offered by The Duke. By tracking down and hunting certain animals, The Duke is able to whip up dishes that offer permanent stat bonuses to Ethan. It gave the back-half of the game a little extra life as I tracked down chickens and fish for my next feast.

Combat is fast, fluid, and frantic. From the first attack by “werewolves” on the village to the mutant soldiers found later on, each encounter is tense and terrifying. Ethan has a bevy of weapons at his disposal and he’ll need them to overcome the horrors he’s faced with. The bulk of the enemies are melee-focused with only a handful having ranged potential. That being said, most of the fights then rely on them having superior numbers that must be whittled down and engaged strategically in order to survive.

My first play-through was on the easiest difficulty as I wanted to experience the story and not worry about my skills failing me in a critical spot. From there, I took advantage of the unlock system and equipped infinite ammo for the starting shotgun. On my second play-through, I bumped the difficulty to normal and quickly found it was going to be a walk in the park. When play-through three occurred on hard mode with my infinite ammo magnum, the game was laughably easy. All of that tension and strategy I had mentioned earlier had completely gone out the window. So, subsequent play-throughs will lose the terror, but present a different form of fun as players become the monster beset upon this remote village.

Along those same lines is the Mercenary mode. Rather than be subjected to the horror of monsters, players must fight against another kind of evil: a time rush. Racing against the clock and trying to rack up kills, perks, and points as fast and efficiently as possible is the key to this mode. Players are scored at the end of each run. Doing well will unlock bonuses for use in the main game.

I mentioned Village’s beauty earlier and it cannot be overstated how gorgeous the game actually is. Pictures fail to do it justice. The amount of detail each character, environment, and weapon receives is unreal. Capcom’s proprietary RE Engine is on full display here and it truly shines. I am consistently astounded at the level of quality and fidelity Capcom is able to put into a game without performance suffering. 

Perhaps knowing that players would be so enchanted with the world they had created, Capcom did add a photo mode to the game. There are a number of options available, however, the end result is always tragically marred by Capcom copyright info boldly displayed at the bottom of said photo. I’ve not found a way around this and it is a shame. This single inclusion made the entire option pointless.

That being said, despite taking place in a relatively small village and the surrounding area, the number of environments available was surprising. From the run-down village to dank dungeons to industrial labyrinths, it’s all a visual feast.

Your eyeballs aren’t the only ones in for a treat. Ears get a special experience as well. Gunshots crack and monsters roar and howl. The surround sound options bring the horror to another level. All manner of nastiness bumps and creaks and shrieks in the dark before bloodied talons and fangs leap forth. Voice-acting is sublime with a masterful performance from each member of the cast. The accompanying soundtrack is a horror masterpiece, falling just short of the majesty that was the Bloodborne soundtrack.

By now it’s no secret the love I harbor for Village. It is a perfect balance of action, adventure, horror, and grand ambiance. Seven months into the year and it is an incredibly strong contender for my game of the year. I can’t recommend it enough to anyone remotely a fan of the genres it occupies. It only helps that the game does well enough to loop in the larger world without making new players feel lost. Again, it’s a taste that will leave you hungry for more.

I am a fan of the Resident Evil franchise since the first game and, to be honest, I was sceptical about Resident Evil Village.
The trailer didn't make me feel excited at all, and while the themes such as vampires as werewolf were new for the series, I wasn't really sure if it was going to work out. Also, hearing that the developers would turn down the horror and focus once again on more action just confirmed my doubt even more.

But let me tell you, my doubts were for nothing.
Yeah, compared to VII, there is a lot more action. But it's not like Resident Evil 6 and more like 4. It doesn't feel like you're in an action movie, gunning down everything in your sight with no worries whatsoever. Instead, you feel like your arsenal for survival, carefully managing your ammo and resources.
This game surely has its problems, such as a lack of enemy variety, lack of oustanding music (the older games all had an amazing soundtrack, but this time I don't remember a single track), technical difficulties (at least for me) and a weird plot (which was always a problem for the series I guess). But they nailed the atmosphere, as you panic, fear, run, shoot and escape out of this hellhole.
I just wish the first areas of the game were bigger, since they were the best out of all the areas.
There's a good amount of weapon variety and the gunplay is satisfying everytime you hit a juicy headshot.
The weapons are upgradable, there's a merchant, the old inventory system, a lot of aspects from older games that fans loved.
It motivates you to play more than once with so many unlockables it's crazy. 
One more thing that I really didn't enjoy is the running speed, it's seriously so damn slow.
There are more things to cover than the points that I mentioned, but for me those were the biggest ones I could think of.

I do recommend Village for people that can play horror games, but I'd recommend playing the previous parts first, especially VII.
I'm sure you can still enjoy Village without prior knowledge, but I also think that you would be able to appreciate the 
ties to the overall story more if you had that knowledge beforehand.

Don't let the thumbs down fool you.  If there was a neutral option in the rating system I would have picked that.  Resident Evil Village is an ok game.  While the game wants to be the new Resident Evil 4 it ends up more like 5 and 6.  Especially writing wise.  The game leans heavy on the over the top action and gun play, feeling more like a FPS with some light resource management.  Only one very small section of the game feels like classic tension filled Resident Evil with the rest of the game feeling like Zombie Call of Duty.

The resource management feels very tacked on and not well thought out.  Because you no longer have a secondary storage box they give you a lot more inventory space now, and make inventory upgrades practically mandatory if you want to carry around your much needed weapons.  But you can't really manage anything, if you don't have room for something either you throw away an item or you leave it behind and never come back for it.  But considering how bullet spongy the enemies are that shouldn't be a problem.

Combat feels fine, although some weapons can feel a bit glitchy.  The puzzles are pretty brain dead easy to solve and while the game is a step up from Resident Evil 7 in terms of enemies looking different; outside of bosses they all feel the same in terms of how you fight them and deal with them.  A weird thing to note about the game is that it doesn't tell you about the cooking upgrade feature (which is the only way to get health upgrades) until after you kill an anime and get the food.

This wouldn't be a problem except that some animals become gate locked since the game has this weird thing where it won't let you reenter previous boss lairs so if you missed something in them you're screwed.  I feel bad for anyone trying to 100 percent this game.

Special note though the running sections in this game are garbage.  Ethen's movements feel very awkward and weightless which means you don't get that precise motion you look for in running sections.  This is made worse when you have to crouch, which is a different button prompt and with no slide option.

Ok now the elephant in the room.  The story.  Without spoiling anything the game has TERRIBLE writing.  Made even worse by the fact the director/game designers have let the success of Resident Evil 7 go to their head.  Granted their were signs in Resident Evil 7 that the writing was just barely being kept good (worse cop ever, Crazy punching uncle etc.) but they have dialed up the stupid to 11 here.  Characters will constantly act like morons acting in very round about ways to achieve their goals.

People, will just do things or tell Ethen information he needs to know so he can continue the plot.  Which is a damn shame because there is a lot of interesting character ideas in the four lords that never get fully realized.  Even Ethen has some more stuff going on personality wise that I wish we could have explored more, to really flesh out his character.

With that said the worst to get it is Chris and the BSAA.  Chris and the BSAA get completely character assassinated (also if you wondered what ever happen to Blue Umbrella keep wondering because the writers forgot they existed).  If you thought RE6 Chris was bad you haven't seen anything; not only is Chris stupid with how he tries to achieve his goals, he's also an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for no reason.  And they play up the tired soldier stereotype with him up to 11, stress smoking and everything.   And I don't even want to talk about what they did to the BSAA.  And the worst part was that it wasn't even needed.  They could have easily written Chris and the BSAA out but they included them in anyway.

Thank god someone higher up stopped them from ruining Ada too.

My final thoughts on the game is that it's ok.  The gameplay is fine for an action game, but for a Resident Evil horror game it's disappointing.  The story however, while having potential, is bad and clearly not thought out at all.  So I say pass or wait for a deep sale on this game.

as someone who only got into the RE series recently, i really like this game, but not in the same way that i liked RE2Make and RE7 (in a more general sense though, i like it more than 7 and less than 2make). it's still clearly a horror game, but it is one that focuses a bit more on the action and is compromised of several sub-experiences (think of 7's different sections but each section is even more distinct) rather than 1-2 larger experiences (like RE2make)

i didn't think 7 needed a direct sequel, but village justifies its own existence not only with a good story, but also by improving upon 7's gameplay systems in almost every way. combat is better, there are more enemies to fight, and you are given a lot more options with how to take fights (probably too many if you played on standard like i did).

in addition, it knows how goofy it is at times and chooses to celebrate the more absurd aspects of horror while taking care to not stray too far away from its horror aesthetic. i actually found this game to be much less scary than 2make, but this game nails its environment and tone so well that i don't really mind that very much. this game does want to scare you and stress you out, but it also goes out of its own way to make sure you're still having fun with its amazing world, entertaining characters, and the fact that you are playing as an incredibly regular dude reacting to the most insane story twists in the most regular dude way (it's funnier than it sounds, trust me).

despite the semi-silliness, less scary tone, and more action-oriented combat, this is still a horror RE game through and through. i wouldn't consider it to be my favorite horror game, but it's incredibly polished and is most definitely a grand old time.

also, i highly recommend using a mod that lets you increase the fov and remove the vignette. i experienced headaches while playing 7 due to the vignette and limited fov, so installing a mod that let me tweak both of those thing greatly improved my experience with village. you don't even need to set the fov much higher, just set it to something small enough to still be somewhat claustrophobic but large enough for you to play without a headache

I've beaten this game on multiple platforms, have gotten all of the achievements (excluding Mercenaries), done all of the challenges, and have played through Village close to 20 times now. But, even on Village of Shadows difficulty, I did not find it to be very hard. Only on VoS does any game play change. A few enemies are added for intensity, but on Hardcore, nothing changes except the enemies being harder to kill. 

I really love the challenge/store system. After you complete the game for the first time, you're able to buy items using in-game points from challenges to get weapons, infinite ammo, etc. Personally, that made me re-play the game multiple times to beat every challenge, get every story achievement, and unlock all of these new guns.

On to the review. This is a fantastic Resident Evil game, in my opinion. It pulls very heavily from a few other titles in the franchise, most notably 4 and 7. It uses the elements it pulls from the prior entries to great effect, and really builds on the solid foundation that was laid by 7.

The story, while a bit cheesy, was really enjoyable. Some of the dialogue was a bit goofy, but I was heavily engaged throughout my time with the game and it was a fun ride start to finish. The handling of Ethan was great, and it gave him much more of a personality than he had in 7. He truly felt like a character, rather than a vessel for the player. The conclusion was satisfying, if somewhat predictable. Overall, big ups to the writing team because they did some great work. There is some fantastic info hidden in the notes, too, and it really helped build up the image of the Village, and added depth to the big bads.

Gameplay wise, this is a truly fantastic successor to 7. The overall feel is much the same, but the guns felt weightier, and Ethan feels a bit less stiff during combat. Village also does a fantastic job at having you bounce between weapons, as ammo can become scarce within moments. Conservation is key, and knowing how and when to use your knife to it's fullest potential will save your behind in later sections. Enemy design and AI is more varied and well done than in 7, leading to even single enemy encounters being more engaging. There are some cheese strats. but that's to be expected of just about any game and I don't feel that it detracts from the experience in any way.

Bonus content is a bit lacking, as this game has no DLC at the time of the review, but what is included in the game (NG+, VoS difficulty, The Mercenaries, and progression earned from in-game achievements/goals) are a lot of fun. The game continues long standing series traditions by giving you bonus weapons for replays after meeting some requirements, and gives you ways to unlock infinite ammo for your favorites which is always welcome. A small touch that I love is the fact that weapon progression is carried between purchase and sale, so if you sell the base handgun for room in your inventory but choose to buy it back later you'll still have the upgrades you purchased for it. 

Overall, the game is fantastic, and I highly recommend for both series veterans, people who only enjoyed some of the later entries, or those of you who only enjoyed 7. If you're looking for an entry point to the series, I recommend 7 more, but because you can get caught up on the key notes of the story if you haven't played 7 you can definitely start here too.

[h1] Story [/h1]

Personally I loved the story, it was well paced, and gives you a good reason to want to push forward. Ethan is as usual kind of meh, and sometimes seemingly brain dead in what he says. But honestly, I enjoy a bit of silly and nonsensical moments to break up the tension of these games. If you want serious survival horror through and through, then you might not enjoy some of Ethan's lines and thoughts.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Gameplay is tight, I didn't notice anything that felt off or working incorrectly. The gun play felt great, yes some guns are slower than makes sense IRL, but it adds to the tension of high stress moments. The game does pause while you're in your inventory, so you can take a breath and craft some items you may need, or equip something you don't have in your four(4) quick select slots. The POV is quite tight, but I didn't mind it to be honest. It works in a lot of the areas, and adds to the feel in my opinion. The settings for sensitivity are a little weird to understand, or they were for me anyway. Movement Camera Sensitivity with Mouse is your standard sensitivity without aiming, just moving the mouse without touching anything else. Aiming Camera Sensitivity with Mouse is your sensitivity when holding aim/right mouse button. It took me awhile to figure out how to set those correctly to work how I wanted.

Overall, if you are on the fence about this game, and you enjoy first person survival horror games, I would recommend this one. It's high quality, looks amazing, plays incredibly well, and the difficulties work very well for what you're looking for. Minus Village of Shadows difficulty, that just feels bullet spongy. Which is alright to get more unlocks and challenge points for bonus content, but it would've been nice if the hardest difficulty added more than just greatly increasing enemy health and the damage they deal.

[h1] Not All Monsters Lurk In The Shadows [/h1]

[b] Overview [/b]
The Resident Evil franchise has continually changed and evolved over it's 25-year history. Most often, those evolutions have been fascinating as Resident Evil tries different mixes of survival-horror and action gameplay. With Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, Capcom venture into first-person perspective territory together with a more narrow scope and horror-focused experience. The eigtht installment, Resident Evil 8: Village evolves that idea to make something that feels very different from it's predecessor but still is just as engaging. Though the perspective and mechanics of the game remains the same, Village branches off in it's own direction from RE7 and manage to capture the things that were great about that game while still not make a straight up copy. Like other people have mentioned, RE8 Village is RE7 Biohazard through the lens of RE4.

RE8: Village picks up on RE7's story three years later and once again features the protagonist Ethan Winters. After the incident at the Baker house in RE7, Ethen and Mia went into hiding in Europe in an attempt to restart their lives. They've since had a daughter named Rosemary and are trying their best to forget the terrifying past. But unfortunately, that past strikes back at them aggressively and Ethan is, once again, on a mission to save his family. Though, this time won't be as easy...

[b] Gameplay [/b]
Just like Resident Evil 4 from 2005, the opening of the Village is a big frightening gunfight that really puts you in a defensible position which you also run a high risk of losing. It's a completely different experience from that of the slow paced RE7 whose combat was built on the fear of knowing that the number of bullets you have on you are not enough to kill the molded creatures lurking around the building. Even though Village feels like such a turn away from RE7 it perfectly works as a sequel. Village uses the same movement system which can sometimes be REALLY stressful if you're, for example, being chased. Ethan isn't especially agile and doesn't sprint very fast. Despite the fact that Ethan more trudge than run, Village is mindful and is designed so that enemies also approach cautiously and slowly. This can make it easy to keep your distent from enemies since most of them are focusing on melee attacks. But thanks to the first-person perspective, your awareness is narrowed and you need to be more hypervigilant about your surroundings. All of a sudden you can be stuck in a corner and nowhere to run. However, I want to point out that the controls are definitely not clunky. They're very responsive.

Resident Evil: Village has far more variety of enemies to fight this time around than previous titles. In Village, it's not all shooting and has a lot of varied pacing and challenges throughout. There are four different areas to unlock during your adventure and story progression. Each headed by one of four lords with different backstories, styles and approaches to the player. I love the idea of mixing the experience with the different horror ideas. You don't just shoot your way through hordes of different enemies and call it a day, you're also engaging in stealth in some areas. Later portions of the game throw different obstacles into your path and you need to solve puzzles instead. You might have plenty of weapons, but can you handle what you're about to face? Will they even work against the next creature you encounter? That's excellent balance between providing lots of action and maintaining that dread.

Bullets and resources are easy to come by and if you're short, you have the ability to craft more from the materials you find in the world in your menu. If resources are what you need, you can even purchase them from the Duke, a traveling merchant with a habit of showing up when you need him the most. The world is scattered with guns and upgrades and you'll be revisiting the central village, who acts out as a central hub-area, to scour it for new hidden items. All that stuff you're carrying around has to go somewhere, so RE8 brings back the inventory manegement system from RE4. You can now move items around to make sure they all fit in your case. Like tetris.

[b] Length and Replayability [/b]
I have played through this game once which took me around 16 hours to complete on standard difficulty. Taking my time to explore all locations in my own pace and do secondary activities like hunting and scouring. The length of the game is, according to me, the perfect length of a game. Especially when the game encourage replaying.

Then we do have "Mercenaries Mode" which is a standalone game mode who is unlocked after finishing the game once. Re-using maps from the main game and put players against hordes of enemies in various locations with objectives and scores. A wonderful edition to the game.

I feel deprived. Deprived of excitment. How can I ever feel anticipation for another game again? After playing the seventh game of the Resident Evil series (Biohazard), which to me differs from the others, I went head first into it's succesor with the mindset of an enthusiastic golden retriever and a bunch of questions. What happened to Ethan Winters and his wife Mia? How will this issue connect to the previous ones? etc. I got the answers I needed aswell as a feeling of emptiness and loss after the game's ending credits had started, this game really got to me and I wish I could play it all anew.

[b] Story [/b]
As predicted, we first meet the Winters couple in their new house somewhere in a European scenery. Mia is preparing a late night dinner while Ethan is putting their newborn daughter, Rose, to bed. After a few minutes of wandering around the house a big explosion appears out of nowhere and through the now big hole in the wall Chris Redfield's squad enters, only to shoot Mia several times and kidnap the two other members of the family - Ethan and Rosemary Winters. 
Ethan later finds himself at a crash site. The vehichles which were used for the abduction of Ethan and his child were now found in the deep snow by the side of the road and without any sign of Rose or Chris Redfeild and his remaining squad members. Here is where Ethan's long hunt to retrieve his daughter Rosemary begins and the story that follows is absolutely amazing. It captures you and will take you along on a journey of emotions; excitement, fear, sadness, anger, hope and relief.

[b] Gameplay [/b]
- To me, the gameplay felt very action-based. Lots of running, fighting and so-called "boss music", but with a fine touch of solving puzzles that wont turn your brain into mold *insert laughing zombies*. 
This part of the Resident Evil franchise also gives you the opportunity to side-step from the story if you need a little breather (or a heart attack depending on where you decide to side-step), maybe loot some houses, catch up on lore or get some easter egg-achivements. 
- Village includes a great variaty of scenery which makes the game more exciting aswell as stressfull, because new enviroment comes with lacking knowledge of hiding spots. But in a story-based game as this one, repeating settings would get tiring. 
- How the characters were written and executed, by the voice actors and actresses, actually made me grow fond of them even though they are supposed to be portraid as evil and vile monsters. The amount of dialogs between player and characters were, without exaggeration, perfect! Sometimes you can hear the characters talk amongst themselves  which gives the game vivacity and not the lifelessness of an Oblivion NPC.
- The game took me approximatly 16 hours to complete, but I'm a slow gamer who wouldn't refuse a chill-pill if offered.

It's a mix of RE4 and RE7 in terms of gameplay. The gun play is surprisingly satisfying, probably the best aiming has ever felt in a Resident Evil. The game is split into about 5 sections, between each of which you'll go back to the central area to gain access to parts you previously couldn't explore.

The characters are interesting, with Heisenberg probably being my favorite. The exception is the second boss as that section is too short to get invested. Although, that second section is one of my favorite parts - I just wished there was more to it.

The graphics are obviously the best the series has looked. There is so much detail put into the game world. It might be the first time in a game I've seen rock formations that are convincing. If I had only one complaint it is the textures can be kind of meh in some spots. But overall the game is beautiful.

The first playthrough there can be a lack of materials/ammo in some spots. That shouldn't come to a surprise if you've played RE before. But, with NG+ the subsequent playthroughs are just a blast to do. After completing the game once you are able to use an in-game currency to unlock art and weapons, not to mention unlimited ammo for weapons. Each time can offer something different thanks to that along with various difficulty options. To earn that currency you complete various challenges. Trying to complete those challenges, or lower your best completion time, add to the replayability.

I wouldn't call it a bad game, but it hardly does anything innovative and some thing are lacking. I'll try to keep this review as spoiler free as possible.
-DISCLAIMER-
I am not an artist, musician, or game designer so please forgive any weird or overused vocabulary. 

Graphics/Design
Firstly, the game is gorgeous. The village, all locations, the characters; it's all stunning. I'd love to see this pushed to maximum settings, but my current PC can't handle that.            - 5/5 

Story/Atmosphere
It plays largely the same as Resident Evil 7, even copying a few story beats. Ethan Winters is searching for a person very important to him and finds himself in a strange village (vaguely European) where there are spooky werewolf type creatures and some bosses claiming they're part of a family, which Ethan is introduced to early on. Everything revealed to you is all incredibly vague untill the end of the game, but in my opinion, it's not worth finding out. I wasn't expecting an "amazing" story from a series with Jill Sandwiches and Boulder punching, but things are either confusing, so cheesy it hurts, or at times boring. The biggest killer to me in this story is the voice acting. The only characters that I think do a good job are Ethan and Dimitresque. The rest of the cast is either only ok or completely unfitting, with Heisenberg being the worst offender of this. This village is somewhere out in Europe, but everyone has a perfect American accent? Even this "family" which has been in charge for generations under this "Mother Miranda" who is also a village legacy? It just creates sort of a disconnect. Furthermore, the tone is inconsistent. I can't tell if this game is trying to imitate the "return to horror" tone of Resident Evil 7 or the more action packed Resident Evils. Credit where credit is due however. Each level, while tonally inconsistent with each other, each provide a unique feel that would be great if allowed to linger over the game as a whole. Some of the story feels rushed; as though the writers were somehow making it up as they went along instead of having a plan. "We'll figure that out later." Chris Redfield             - 2.8/5

Music
The music is fine. Nothing really stood out as memorable to me, but it was all servicible and inoffensive to the ears. 3/5

Game
This game progresses in a very linear fashion. Just to clarify, this isn't always a bad thing, but I feel like this game's environments would've been much more "alive" with a simple ability to backtrack. Maybe even incorporate it into the game. You CAN backtrack over 60% of the village, but to no specific "level" once beaten. There are 4 levels and essentially 2 "sub-levels". You beat the big bad in each level and move on. Resident Evil 7 had more advantage in this where, even though it was the same deal, things felt more connected than a glorified overworld. Exploring is limited as most of your path is railroaded with a side corridor every now and then. If you're paying even a little bit of attention, you shouldn't miss most extras. This brings me to the difficulty of the game. At the time of this review I have only played the game on the "standard" difficulty, which for all intents and purposes should be the developers intended way to experience the game, thus the name "standard". Resident Evil 8 at no point offers any challenge, feels genuinely threatening, or clever. This game is EASY. Puzzles amount to "turn this object over. bring object back. match da shapes." The only section I would really call a PUZZLE is when you're forced to use a hanging brazier's physics to swing it to light some fires. This was an ok puzzle... the first time. It only shows up maybe 3 or 4 more times, but why reuse it at all if you already taught us the solution? Combat is the staple Resident Evil slow and methodical, and it's just as easy as the puzzles. I never felt threatened by the enemies. Enemy types all do the same, predictable patterns that are thwarted by just holding the space bar when they get close. The knife is fine enough on most enemies, even in groups of as much as 3, and the starter pistol is the only gun you really need for anything that isn't a miniboss or boss. I was never worried that I was going to run out of ammunition in this game where ammo is supposed to feel limited. This is mainly for two reasons. There is a crafting system that allows you to make ammo and healing items. I'd say a good 90% of enemies drop an herb or gunpowder or scrap, allowing you to constantly stay restocked on ammo and health with no worry. If the enemies dont drop any components, then you'll be sure to find WAY more than you need by quickly scavenging the incredibly limited areas. Remember how I said there was a shop in this game? Enemies drop treasures for selling almost as much as components, and ammo is cheap. It isn't even just ammo; you can buy and find and make large quantities of powerful explosives to breeze through. Inventory management is all but gone. Your inventory is never really too small to hold everything you need. No sacrifices here. Mostly the game feels rushed. It feels like all the focus went into Dimitresque's castle, and that section was good fun. The second level, ill call it the doll house, had some genuinely good and fun psychological horror gameplay, and is likely my favorite level, but it ends as quickly as it begins.  After Dimitresque's casle, it feels as though less care went into the later areas.  3.5/5

Overall this game isn't bad; it's okay. Middle of the road. I know I mostly spoke negatively, but that's because the things that are okay about the game are just that: okay. If you've played Resident Evil 7 and you want to see a continuation of a story, you'd likely have a better time watching a Let's Play on Youtube, If you really want to pick it up yourself, I'd say wait until the base price is 30 USD instead of 60.  The game took me around 12 hours to beat on a first playthrough, but would probably only take somewhere around 4-6 if you know what youre doing on a second playthough; even less if you're dodging treasures. I'm an advocate for making a fantastic 5 hour game over a run of the mill 50 hour game, but this game is run of the mill AND short... and currently 60 dollars... with DLC for this underdeveloped game announced before release.

Overall  -  3/5

They miss the mark on pretty much everything great about the games that inspired this one. It has a great combat loop inspired by Resident Evil 4 that is marred by mostly boring enemy encounters. It has incredibly simplified level design which does a decent job of imitating what good classic Resident Evil maps are supposed to feel like without actually making good classic Resident Evil maps (with the exception of one of the later sections in the game). There is some sense of ammo scarcity at points, but if you purchase inventory upgrades (these are not hidden), you will never have to make difficult decisions on managing your inventory. I played on hard, and there was not a single item in the game that I could not pick up. There was not a single moment in the game where I had to even rearrange my inventory to pick up an item. The boss design ranges from passable to objectively terrible. 

The puzzles are embarrassingly easy and trivial, even for Resident Evil. You will never have to use your brain to solve any of them.

The game constantly changes its rules and gameplay mechanics to suit one-off set-piece encounters. The scariest section in the game strips the player of all weapons and inventory, which breaks all of the tension because you no longer have to manage ammo or healing at all, meaning that you know there will be no combat. Any time the spooky monster shows up, hide under a bed or in a locker. And, by the way, if you're ever low on health ('in the red'), just wait for a few seconds - the game will heal you up to medium health (yellow) just by not being hit.

The story is convoluted and full of plot-holes. The only way to make sense of why characters do certain things is to make assumptions that the translation is bad. Seriously, even within the fantasy setting, none of it makes sense.

If you're looking for a consistently well-designed action game with cool weapons and good combat encounter design, this is not it. If you're looking for a good survival-horror experience with puzzle-solving and intricate levels, this is not it. If you're looking for a little mix of both, well, this is it, but it's painfully shallow on both fronts, and it handles itself with seemingly no understanding of what makes those genres work.

I have had great time playing the story mode. This review is spoiler free (I think).
Graphics: great. Very good looking. No major complaints except for occasional frame drops. FOV a bit too small and causes motion sickness especially on the small boat.
Story: has some clear plot holes but in general no huge issues. Great to see they try to tie the story to the old RE lore.
Characters: RE8 improves Ethan as main protagonist a lot compared to RE7. Human villagers are interesting but short lived. Main antagonists are interesting but inconsistent - a couple are more interesting and have much much longer screen time than the others.
Combat: It feels great and it is satisfying to shoot and to upgrade the weapons at the merchant. Enemy variety is not amazing but good enough, and some rooms are interesting with environmental hazards and enemy placement. Boss fights are okay. There is one boss fight that just feels like interactive cutscene, but same can be said for RE7 final boss fight. Final boss definitely better than RE7 Eveline or Lucas.
Puzzles: designed pretty well. Not brain-dead easy (maybe the piano one is) but most importantly not feel like a chore to go through in repeated playthroughs. I see some reviewers say that some puzzles should have had more backtracking, but personally I think that would just be a forced backtracking and a chore especially in repeated playthroughs.
Horror: the start of the game and one part in the game are very unsettling. That one part is really nice and the length IMO is good too. Compared to RE7 I think the two games are "different". All places in RE7 are dirty and disgusting while RE8 has some beautiful and gorgeous locations so RE7 is more demanding. The tension is higher in RE7 but it is constant tension throughout the first half of the game so the scare feeling wears out fast (at least for me). RE7 becomes quite bland for me after Margurite, but RE8 is still quite interesting in latter sections (maybe the part when you don't play as Ethan is a bit chore). The pursuer in RE7 and RE2R are much more aggressive, but RE8 pursuer is literally invincible so it makes sense that they make the pursuer less terrifying.
Length: 10 hours to 12 hours if you fully explore the game and read the documents. On metacritic some complains the game being too short (<8 hours) they are probably rushing through everything too hard.
Replayability: extra weapons are expensive but only takes a few runs to get enough funds for them. Challenges and achievements are reasonable. Highest difficulty is interesting but I wish they change things a bit more like in RE7 mad house.
Mercenary mode: RE8 shotgun is heavily nerfed compared to previous entries and I think this affects the mercenary mode.  I find myself just selling everything and only using the pistol because other weapons don't feel as effective. I have only SS'ed two stages as for now, but can't find the urge to play more. It kinda feels repetitive. I will update this review if my view on this mode changes after I 100% the game.

To summarize I definitely recommend RE8.

anyone who has played RE2 or RE7 knows that this game is capcom forgetting everything that worked well in their previous games and experimenting with an odd formula. its not bad but it is certainly not worth the price nor should it be rated above RE7 or RE2. There is a foundation here for a good game (the castle was pretty good and the beneviento house was also some the best survival horror ever) but the latter game lacks so much its ridiculous, I can barely recommend just because of two good parts, despite how good those parts are. 

The body horror 'moreau' seems like an interesting concept and then you enter a boring linear stage with an uninspired puzzle. Then the game tops it off with a boss fight that is weak and boring. This section just feels like 'take some cheapass shooting gameplay because you've had such a hard time with our boring ass non survival horror gameplay'. Then you fight that big king lycan thing, like the one earlier in the game. There's another depth to gameplay here (airstrike) which is nice and makes this fight interesting instead pure sh*t like the one earlier in the game which is possibly the worse boss fight ever. The room you fight in with Chris and the lycan is stupidly small and its not even scary its just inconvenient and annoying. 

The game then does that stupid thing RE7 did and capcom CLEARLY didn't learn as they dump exposition and plot holes filling in a whole scene by making you READ a bunch of f*cking papers. Instead of telling a story through the actual gameplay and characters it uses possibly the worst way to convey a story ever. Please capcom, next time just tell the story climax through characters or at least do it in parts so the player can piece the story together. It's just lazy writing and lazy game making. [spoiler] Mia's alive, in what they thought was a twist but it was so poorly executed [/spoiler] and then you end up playing as Ethan again in what is a probably the best dialogue in the game between the merchant and Ethan and then you fight Miranda at the end which appears to be a challenge at first but once you figure out her move set it becomes stupidly easy for a last boss fight. 

Mercenaries mode is a lazy way to make you unlock weapons and ammo to replay the game. I'll eventually have the will to finish the game again, when I can be assed to sit though mercenaries mode to make replaying the game slightly more fun. 

There is a good game here somewhere, but capcom threw too many ideas in at once, forgot what worked really well in RE7 and what didn't work well and, in my opinion, made an underwhelming and weak game. What I mean when I say there is a good game here somewhere is: the 'village' hub is not creative and the game would've been ten times better just making and expanding on the castle idea. This is my first Resident Evil experience so I'm unsure how it compares to the other games, but as a stand alone, I would say I thoroughly enjoyed the experience. It took me about 8 or 9 hours to finish the story, but the post-game will probably keep me going until I hit around 30 or 40 hours. There wasn't a moment in the game where I was underwhelmed or negatively frustrated, and even though I'm running this game on a severely outdated laptop, the graphics and gameplay, even with occasional frame drops on my end, are splendid.

The aesthetics of the game are great. Each zone felt like a drastic change in theme, but it wasn't too jarring to displace my immersion. It genuinely feels like a lot of effort was put behind the design on both an artistic and gameplay level. And by gameplay I mean primarily exploration. There is a lot to explore. Never did exploring feel like a stall, instead, it was satisfying and right in tune with the progression of the game. To be honest, it was the best part for me. There wasn't anything rushing you, so you could wander at your own pace. That's not to say that the action is very stop and go, rather I'd say it keeps up the mood with enemies. Enemies would pop up here and there. With most weapons, shooting felt responsive and strong. Killing enemies and grabbing drops from them felt rewarding enough. Selling and upgrading felt even [i]more[/i] rewarding. As for the puzzles, they don't really stand out to me. I could barely remember a few if I tried... with exception to one or two of the ball puzzles that took a while to do. Some puzzles are required to progress through the story, and they're relatively straightforward. Not much else to say for that.

Character and creature designs are nice but I find the latter a bit lacking. For the main antagonists and the mini-bosses, they work and they're good, no complaints there. I'll spoiler the next few parts, but it's not really that important to the game, just notes on the enemies.

[spoiler]Where I had hoped to find more enemy variation is during the second and the third zone, with Donna Beneviento and Salvatore Moreau. After completing the creepy baby area, monsters appear on your way back to the altar. They simply look like the Moroaice you fight in Lady Dimitrescu's blood cellar were you to take their hoods off and give them a sickle. Honestly, not that big of a complaint, since the second zone was practically entirely puzzles and story. I didn't really notice until I played it a second time.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Then you have Moreau's part, which I felt had way more potential than it showed. The only variation in monster design I see here were the armored lycans. I suppose I was hoping for monsters with a bit more of a grotesque side. I feel there were many opportunities to put them in: more in the mines, during the boss fight, even after the boss fight if you were to go back to the wreck. Perhaps that's why I feel this is the weakest point of the game. Heisenberg's factory was nice. Map layout could get confusing, but with the monsters, as you get through further into the zone, the Soldats' attachments change their silhouettes enough. Combine that with the sound design of their attacks, feels like a completely different fight.[/spoiler]

Story... I suppose it works? It justifies enough of where Ethan Winters go and why he goes to places, and that's about it as far as I can tell. There's also maybe an element to it, at least I think, where it tries to frame Ethan as a very righteous and honorable character, and yeah he does go through a lot of sacrifice, but as a character I didn't really empathize or find him very likable. I didn't feel as though there was an underlying message or some kind of moral to the story—and I don't think it matters if there isn't any. I find that the gameplay itself shines enough to warrant a minimal narrative. Cutscenes have some strange lines of dialogue, but it's a smooth enough transition into the action that you can dismiss it. As you go through the game, there are a couple of files lying around that can give insight into what's happening, and I guess that's fun.

Finally post-game. I'm still going through it as I write this review. As of currently, I finished my second run and picked up a few achievements and I am now on my third. My interest in the game is slowly dwindling, but I'll probably 100% it anyway. Completion points are plentiful at the moment, I don't find it too hard to unlock what I want. Mercenaries, the gamemode of just killing things, is fun, I find myself enjoying the grind to better scores. Unlocking concept art and models is very interesting to me, doesn't cost too much to get them all so that's great. A few of the challenges aren't on the achievements on Steam, which is a bit confusing to me. I'd imagine having an achievement to break 19 windows, you'd also include the challenge to kill enemies with certain weapons and so forth. But that's just me. Excited to play VoS when I feel prepared.

[b] Summary [/b]
First up, I don't complain about games' directions, and often enjoy it when sequels try new things and have different themes.  RE8 is a radical departure from the P.T. inspired horror of RE7.  RE8 has more action, brightly lit areas, and insanely unique characters.  Technical flaws aside, I personally loved this game, and really enjoyed the setting and direction they went with.  I definitely recommend this title, as it was a blast from beginning to end.  I broke down more details into Design, Gameplay, and Technical below.

[b] Design [/b]
The art direction and level design are top notch.  Every inch is detailed to the max, rivaling that of the Dark Souls franchise.  Characters have interesting properties and come to life, it's both a terror and a joy to see them.  I really enjoyed how every "boss" had their own themed level.  Castle D. Sparkles was medieval and massive, P.T. house was terrifying and creepy, Fish-man felt like a huge RE4 homage, and Frankenstein/Terminator factory was unique (although my least favorite).  Voice acting, animation, sound design, all of it is polished and impressive.

[b] Gameplay [/b]
The semi open-world/hub world setup they went with worked out well.  Gameplay is as smooth as ever, and it was simple to craft, swap weapons, navigate menus, solve puzzles, etc.  Weapon upgrades felt useless because you'd find a weapon that was better at every stat without any upgrades, wish there was a more strategic pro/con setup for the weapons.  Other than that, shooting had impact and felt good.

[b] Technical [/b]
The technical aspects are however a disappointing negative for an otherwise fantastic experience.  Framerate is great with ray tracing on, and game looks incredible.  But the technical issues bring it down a few notches.  Capcom's awful decision of DRM setup causes hitching when you take damage, when you kill an enemy, and random times throughout the game (literally stood in one spot and hitched).  I can ignore level loading hitching, but this kind of hitching made the action a bit less enjoyable.  The PS5 version has none of these problems, so it's a shame Capcom went this route for PC players who want the best experience possible.  As of today, July 4th 2021, there have been 0 patches from Capcom and I am doubtful we'll get anything other than DLC.

RE8 builds on its' predecessor in many positive ways; a somehow even more optimised version of the RE Engine (seriously, I run a very average Ryzen 5 2600x based PC and I played this entire game at 1440P, as good as max settings, never dropping below 60FPS the entire run) provides a gloriously grotesque village environment which plays central hub to this bizarre new world to explore, and then it throws you into the over the top opulence of Lady Dimetrescu's mansion. Every environment looks amazing and is all designed to add to the relentless horror and the never-ending feeling of helplessness so quintessentially Resident Evil.

Where the game fell down mostly for me was the slight shift from pure horror to action. Sure, there are many times during the game where you're running for your life and looking for ANYWHERE to hide from the monster pursuing you! Sadly, even though I was quite profligate which my ammo usage, ammo management (an absolute staple of RE games) was never a concern of mine and in most circumstances, even against bosses, I felt more than equipped to easily dispatch with any risk to my health. Maybe I've just played too many of these games, I'm old enough to just about remember the release of the original Resident Evil and other than RE5 or 6 (easily the worst entries into this fine series) I have completed them all, most of them many times, so perhaps I'm being harsh in my assessment.

Bottom line, as experienced as I was, I still had 12 hours of great fun working my way through this game. I easily could have shaved 2 hours off that time if I wasn't as explorational as I was, but for me, half the fun of these games is exploring every nook and cranny of the macabre world being presented to us!

I can be difficult to separate reviewing the game and reviewing the technological aspects of a game. No one reviews a movie and talks about the film or cameras used, and no one reviews a book and talks about the type of paper, however games have a unique aspect where technological issues can interfere with the enjoyment of the game.

The game is amazing. This game takes all of my favorite parts of Resident Evil (treasure, merchant, gun upgrades) and applies those concepts to the Resident Evil 7 style gameplay. RE8 is really not a horror game in the same way 7 was, it's mostly an action game, and I would compare the experience to RE4. It can be creepy, and there may be a few jump scares, but the answer is always shoot, and if you are good at shooting, enemies won't really bother you.

It was a good length, had good pacing, and exploration was rewarded with treasures in order to upgrade your stuff. It was a lot of fun.

Technologically speaking, I had a really hard time. The biggest issue was a bug where after some time playing, it would enter a slow motion thing, where it wasn't just bad fps or something, but everything was happening in slow motion, and I would have to run back to a save point (in slow motion) and save, exit the game, restart the game and it would be back to normal. I've got a great computer, running an rtx 3080 with an i7 10700, so I run the game mostly on max settings, with all ray tracing stuff on, image quality at 1.2, etc. It runs at 60fps or higher, and it looks amazing. But that damn slow motion bug just kept happening, and so I tried a ton of things to stop it, which lead to more issues. If I try to change the refresh rate in the menu, it hard restarts my computer. If I wait until the slow motion happens, and I go in and turn ray tracing off, it goes back to working. So I was spending a ton of time in menus trying to get this game to run properly, only to deal with the computer restarting if I changed the wrong setting, to lowering settings that didn't need to be or shouldn't need to be lowered.

If there was no technical issues, this game would've been a perfect experience. Because of the issues, there was always that feeling that at any second my experience was going to be ruined by some technical problem.

The game itself is a perfect Resident Evil.

I am a huge fan of survival horror.  This is not survival horror but an action horror game.  Of course that alone does not make the game bad.  What this game does do however is remove every aspect of resident evil that i love that often makes resident evil unique.  I will also state that i find resident evil 4 very boring for similar reasons, however if you like that style of game you will likely enjoy this more.

-  This game is very linear, all key items are handed to you and outside of treasure no exploration is required  Basically the main game does not require your brain at all.

 - No decision making required with enemies and you are rewarded for killing them.  This goes against survival horror, you should not be encouraged to slaughter everything.  You basically get endless resources and space in this game so you might as well.  In a survival horror resident evil typically if you see an enemy you need to make a risk evaluation of that enemy to determine if its worth killing ( for example maybe a zombie by a save room you kill, while one at a dead end you dont).  And on top of this you dont even get creative ways to deal with enemies, its just shoot or run.  unlike say revelations 2 (stealth, shoot, run, stun with 1 character finish with the other).   

 - The map is not a puzzle, and the only puzzles are basically all in one section.  That puzzle section is very good and makes people think of PT, but one of the best parts of resident evil it the map itself being the big puzzle, where basically to beat the game you have to keep finding key items and slowly unravel how to get through each location.  The best examples of this are the mansion and guard house in re1r, the RPD in re2r, the city in re3og, and the prison and arctic in code veronica.  One thing the map being a puzzle does is make it so when you dont kill an enemy you might see it again, this mixed with limited resources makes for an engaging experience with a lot of decision making

Essentially what we have is a very scripted, cinematic, go forward and shoot experience.  It is not really bad as much as it is disappointing because it removes the biggest factors I love about resident evil

Also the difficulties are lazy and essentially based on bullet sponge's, replay value is poor in part because of this, mercenaries is basically a bad raid mode with no progression like the revelations games

-The villains, while Heisenberg and Lady D do stand out a ton, the other 3 just don't feel nearly as interesting, whereas the Baker family all felt unique and stood out, that's not to say the 4 or 5 big bads don't stand out, it's just that they feel a bit less special.
-The story

What I liked less:

Resident Evil Village clicked for me the more I played it. After my first run (coming from RE2 Remake), I thought it was a little subpar. But now, after four playthroughs, almost every achievement unlocked (except the “heal only four times” one—way too annoying), I can say I enjoy it just as much as RE2.

Mercenaries mode is a blast too, even though I’ve only dipped into it a few times. Scoring SS on the first two maps was fun and shows it has good replay value.

At first, I wasted time comparing Village to other RE games, especially RE2 Remake (my first and favorite in the series). But after multiple playthroughs, I’ve stopped doing that. On its own, Village delivers a story and gameplay loop that’s just as fun as RE2—and that’s what matters.

For context, I’ve played RE2 Remake, RE3 Remake, and RE7. Haven’t touched RE4 yet, but I’m looking forward to the remake when it drops. If you’re on the fence, Village is absolutely worth it.

[b]Resident Evil Village[/b] is one of the best emotional horror games I've ever played.

It goes without saying that the characters, the Lords, are amazing, each character is the embodiment of something. Donna is based on tropes of gothic literature; stories of ghosts and haunting dolls. Moreau is an obvious reference to the H. G. Wells novel and works of H. P. Lovecraft with his fish-like form. Lady Dimitrescu, who refers us to Tyrant, what connects us with early REs, and also represents the Blood Countess, Elizabeth Bathory, who killed girls to enjoy their blood. And Karl Heisenberg, of course, a direct reference to Werner Heisenberg, the theoretical physicist. 

Moreover, relationships in Mother Miranda’s "family": we see a "daughter" who wants to be like a mother, a "son" who wants an independent life, a "son" trying to do everything so that his mother will like him and a "daughter" who is stuck in childhood and doesn’t want live in the real world. At the same time, there is competition between all the “children”, and the actions are somehow concentrated on the mother. And each model of behavior can be easily transferred to real life. 

A few words about the general atmosphere, another strong side of this game. Locations are both old and new at the same time. Walking around the game, the feeling that everything around is familiar won’t leave you, you probably will think about other games like Call of Cthulhu, The Evil Within or the previous parts of RE: the mansion from the first game, the village of the fourth.

The soundtrack is astounding, it conveys the atmosphere of the game very well. It diversifies fights, walking across locations, and conversations during cut-scenes. The soundtrack is pleasing to the ears - and this is the most important thing.
Is it scary? No. Are the jump scares scary? No, as well. Nevertheless, I was constantly in an anxious state, in a good way, oppressed by everything: whether it was the plot twists or just my thoughts about what was happening. Also, any of the above things kept me on my toes and intrigued. The Benevento Manor was the most memorable in terms of the atmosphere since it was there that many things pressed on the psyche, but no spoilers.

[b]Resident Evil Village[/b] is probably not the best game in the RE series, but definitely one of the best games this year, which I highly recommend playing.

Resident Evil 8, or Village as it is called. Is this a good game? Yes. Oh my yes. Is it better than 7? Maybe. Lets get into it.
RE8 is set in an Italian village from the start, and within the first half hour you are already beset upon by your numerous enemies, starting with vampire women, and moving on to various others that I will not spoil. The game continues the RE formula of exploration being rewarded with resources that you can use or trade. The trader returns, though not in his RE4 glory, this one is a large man named Duke who will gladly buy up treasure you find, and you will find a lot. Puzzles galore, bonus encounters, hidden secrets everywhere, this is a real return to form continuing the RE golden age we find ourselves in, but with that comes some issues. 
This is not as focused a game as 7. 7 took place in one location that was polished to a mirror shine and this one goes for escalation of what was in that game in the style of 4. More enemies, more bosses, more everything. Does it all work? Mostly yes, but there are some issues. The first and most obvious is that the increased focus on gunplay and enemies means that the horror elements have been stripped away a bit to make room for it. Ethan is much more capable in this game than 7, and this is reflected in his more powerful attacks and weapons, and increased damage potential overall. Does this detract from the game? Not to me, but someone wanting a hardcore horror experience may walk away disappointed. 
Now as for the good. This is a beautiful game that runs like a dream, the ray tracing in particular makes this game a standout showpiece on PC, especially a high end one, and the work in the background to make the game look its best has really paid off. 
The increased enemy variety over the molded makes every encounter more interesting as you can't just rely on the same three enemies popping up over and over again, and the increased weapon variety makes fighting much more rewarding as you find your playstyle. In addition the challenge modes return, letting to unlock various new weapons for subsequent playthroughs. 
And now on to the story. No spoilers of course. 
The four lords are a joy to watch interact, each is unique in their personality from the high and mighty Dimitriscu to the pathetic simpering Moreu, and they all have their setpieces and amazingly realized locales. This is truly where the game shines. The story is layered and amazingly well told and the beginning cinematic that plays out like a children's storybook is honestly one of the most beautifully animated things I have ever seen in a video game. 
Final thoughts. Buy this game, it is amazing. If you like Resident Evil, you will like this. If you like story based games you will love this. If you want horror, there is some there, but it does get drowned out a bit in the combat, but the body horror aspect of these games is back on full display. Get this game as soon as you can, because it is honestly one of my new favorites.

I had never played Resident Evil until the beginning of this year when I played RE2 Remake for the first time. Ever since, I went and binged every other RE game I could get my hands on, for the most part, my marathon happening to end right when RE8 was released a few weeks after completing 7. I went into RE7 blind, with the only knowledge I had of it being Lady Dimitrescu because (duh, the meme). I say this because I come in with a very loose understanding of what Resident Evil is, and very little nostalgia to influence my opinion. I didn't like 7 all that much, so I wasn't expecting to have such a good time with RE8, but I did.

While frustrating to navigate at times, the level design feels much bigger than the Baker estate from 7. The truly scary scenes showed me that not every horror game has to rely on jump-scares to be scary (RE7 was... somewhat scary, but more startling than genuine terror). I also enjoyed the gun-play a lot! For a horror game, it was surprisingly good and I found myself willingly fighting hordes of zombies just to practice my aim or play greedy for that extra loot. The game isn't exactly difficult I'd say, but I heard I was a bit of a rare case where most people found many parts of the game challenging, whereas I didn't. 

Being able to fight things other than the 'stalkers' of the game also makes you feel more powerful and in control as you navigate an otherwise out of your control situation. When I was playing RE7, there was a pretty heavy lack of 'fodder enemies' so it felt like when you got weapon upgrades, they didn't do all that much. It feels much better to use guns in this game. I compare RE7 and RE8 a lot because they're intrinsically connected storyline-wise, as this will be a 3 part series (with RE9 presumably capping things off), so it feels logical to compare them in comparison to previous RE games which have vastly different tones and gameplay styles.

The inventory system felt MUCH better than 7, where you had the flexibility to carry more while also having to be careful of not over-filling with too much stuff. There's no chest box to store items, so you had to be careful with your organization. 

I'll finally talk about the story, but I'll avoid spoilers for the most part. All I will say is that I HEAVILY enjoyed the plot of this game though it is a bit heavy at the end (a lot of information is dropped at once, but it makes sense story progression-wise), and I think the antagonists were a lot better. Please DO NOT get into this game to expect Lady Dimitrescu to be the only antagonist, and don't expect to stay in the castle the whole time. I know some people didn't like its tone or just came into the game hyped about the whole game is in the castle, but it's not. The advertising material doesn't tell you much but just anticipate something much cooler. 

Honestly 9/10 game it's my second favorite Resident Evil game right after Resident Evil 2 Remake, with Revelations 2 being a very close 3rd. Even if you're not into Resident Evil as a franchise, it feels a lot different from most RE games that you can play 7+8 without missing too much context as to what's going on other than a few easter-eggs flying over your head.

Pretty fun, ultimately short but for what it is I'm satisfied with what I paid.  My final in-game playtime clocked in at around 8 hours which included completing many side missions, a little bit of easy achievement hunting, collecting new weapons and more resources, and generally seeing most (if not all) of what the game had to offer.

Weapons feel decently satisfying however aside from 6's stupid-but-fun gun-kata/melee combat and 4's Best In Class mechanics I wasn't blown out of the water.  It does that Resident Evil thing where you can't shake the feeling that some enemies take more damage to kill than others of the exact same type, as if the game is artificially rationing your ammo.  If I shoot a Lycan dude twice in the head for a headshot, it feels less satisfying to shoot the same Lycan dude standing right next to him 5 times in the head for the same thing.  Sometimes attacks even with powerful or fully upgraded weapons won't even stagger similar enemies and it can lead to you feeling like you've either wasted currency on that weapon or that you're just wasting ammo.

Graphically gorgeous.  I'm not lucky enough to have a "modern" graphics card but my 1070ti gave me a solid 70-90FPS on Higher settings with a few tweaks for certain ones that I personally deem unnoticeable.  The level designs are very well realized with secrets passages leading to small staged areas giving a bit of environmental storytelling.  I'm going to assume that if you have a card capable of RT that it looks even better.  There are certain scripted set pieces that really showcased some impressive tech, the artistic direction as well elevated those moments.

This isn't necessarily a spoiler but I was slightly caught off guard by how the game splits it's chapters and sections up.  Until launch Capcom heavily featured Lady. Dimistriciosuosuiosue (not looking up how to spell that, sorry!) in the ad campaigns (for good reason, and I'm not complaining) but what you'll find out is that her area is just one of 4-5 entire split areas that last for about 2 hours each.  If you've seen some of the first trailers with the antagonists huddled around Ethan just know that each one there has their own section of gameplay that differs from the last.  In between each of these areas you'll spend about half an hour exploring new areas of the village, upgrading your gear and hunting animals for stat boosts, and completing side missions.

1. Dimitryusc plays more like RE2R, personally I didn't find her gimmick of chasing you down nearly as oppressive and anxiety inducing as Mr. X, but there were more than a few moments where she caught me off guard and I needed to hide for a minute or two.  It would have been nice to have her roam around and be more of a presence in the castle but I wasn't upset by it.
2. Maureo or however you pronounce it is the gross little dude.  You do some puzzling on floating bridges while avoiding his fish form, collect electrical switches in classic RE style, and fight him in an interesting arena.  It's short and not that bad but very much the weakest section.
3. The Dollhouse section is extremely short and the actual "fight" at the end isn't that great.  That being said aside from being shorter than the others and being mostly a cutscene it flips over from being a Resident Evil game to more of a Silent Hill type of psychological horror.  It's the closest thing we'll get to a certain Playable Teaser.
4. The last Metal Guy has some neat close range combat in a massive, changing underground factory.  It reminded me a bit of the Labs in RE4 with the Regenerators where you have to hit small weak spots while they hound you through tiny corridors.  The final boss is a neat concept and from what I understand a reference to an older manga or movie, it's cool and "drives" home the metal-base body horror theme quite well.
5. The gameplay changes up for a bit towards the end in a similar manner to RE7's late game area and it's DLC.  It's a fun change of pace.

As for being actually "scary"? It's a step down from RE7.  The first half of that game was excellent and truly set the bar for more modern horror titles.  Being chased down by Jack throughout the Baker home is still very well done and I'll be going back to that more soon.  

All in all, I'm satisfied with what I paid for.  It's a highly replayable (if you know what you're doing and have the right upgrades you can rush the game in less than 3 hours, and get achievements for it!) and contains some moments of real fun.  I wouldn't say it hits the highs that 7 did, but don't let that stop you.

This game is a major step up from Resident Evil 7 which introduces a simple crafting mechanics, revamped inventory system & larger world to explore. It's kinda like a combination of Resident Evil 4 in terms of the visual theme & Resident Evil 7 in terms of the core game mechanics with a few new elements like the inventory system & shopkeeper from the aforementioned.

The story mostly focuses on the main character introduced in Resident Evil 7, Ethan Winters. Unlike Resident Evil 7, Resident Evil Village doesn't focus on the horror aspect as much but Castle Dimitrescu does have some resemblance to the Baker Ranch & is pretty early in the story if you're into that. However, it does switch to Chris Redfield for a small segment near the end of the story which is a bit more action-oriented & takes place in the village. Interestingly, the story doesn't just cover the present Resident Evil timeline but also dives deep into the past for anyone who's into the lore.

The Mercenaries does make a return, requiring the player to finish the game for the first time & then unlock it in the Extra Content Shop for 10 Completion Points (CP). The Extra Content Shop also has Special Weapons, Infinite Ammo, Figures & Concept Art allowing the player to spend their hard earned CP. Overall, the Extra Content Shop & it's challenges does add some replay value to the game. However, I don't see myself doing more than 2 playthroughs at most.

I was able to use a workaround to get the game working on Windows 7 with some additional files & tweaks to the executable file. I'll admit that my system specification & the operating system is obsolete. But I've been able to run Resident Evil 2 (2019), 3 (2020), 6 & 7 which is effectively different iterations of the same engine, the fact there's no DX11 or Vulkan support is a joke.

The game also comes with Denuvo Anti-Tamper which is pretty anti-consumer as this can affect the performance & modding capabilities. There's no reason for a game to have more than 1 DRM as Steam DRM comes as standard with most games on Steam. If you're not sure how much Denuvo Anti-Tamper affects the game's performance, just play the demo & see for yourself.

It is, to date, one of the top examples of what Resident Evil has to offer and why the franchise is so relevant, even to this day.  The game is satisfying and leaves you wanting more.  Succinctly, the game borrows the best elements of Resident Evil 4, Resident Evil 7 and merges them into an excellent first person shooting experience.

Aesthetically, RE: VIII has nigh-photo-realistic graphics that elicit dropped jaw after dropped jaw.  Normally, excellent graphics are hobbled or tempered by poor character/environmental design but, in the case of RE: VIII, the game's ambiance and atmosphere take center stage, creating a vibrant and singular world vision.  Unlike so many other beautiful games, based on Unreal Engine 4 and CryEngine, which run dog slow and exhibit a litany of technical issues, RE: VIII is not only easily one of the most beautiful games on the market but also one of the best performing.

RE: VIII ran at locked 4K, Ultra settings on my Radeon VII (make sure you have plenty of VRAM, as it needs at least 13 GB) and demonstrated excellent frame consistency and frame times.  Character models are especially good, with Alcina, Mia, Chris, and Miranda showcasing uncannily spectacular levels of realism.  The game was stable, didn't crash, exhibited minimal issues/slow downs and did so running graphical circles around games with far more fanfare.  The soundtrack, voice acting and sound effects were all excellent.

Shooting play is good.  It may not be the best shooting play you've ever experienced but it is certainly responsive, communicative and fluid.  Most weapons feel really good and the animations/sounds are evocative.  The inventory system works.  Melee and blocking add a layer of needed complexity.  Upgrades, collectibles and secrets abound that reward careful and exhaustive play throughs.  The lore is substantially improved over many other nonsensical iterations.

The game is supposed to present a Romanian and classical interpretation of the Resident Evil monster stable and it all works beautifully.  The story has some twists and turns and while you won't experience any surprises compared to, say, Bioshock, the game still works hard to keep the player invested and attentive.  The story ending is satisfying and ties up most loose ends well.  Unlike Resident Evil 3, RE: VIII seems to be crafted with purposeful intent and care.

For those players that don't want to replay the entire 20-22 hour campaign again, hunting for hidden goodies, there is the multiplayer component which will be unlocked by the end of the summer in 2021.  The mode is sure to add some replayability but, to be clear, the single player campaign for RE: VIII is worthy of the price of admission purely on its own.  

What a treat.  Yes, the game isn't as terrifying as Resident Evil 7 (although it still has scares and panic).  No, the game isn't the most accessible title of the franchise.  Yes, it's a shooter.  It's also the best single player game of the year, bar none.

Highest possible recommendation.
