Look... this game is a 10/10. Graphics are great, performance is great*, story is great, gameplay is great. This is a Resident Evil game through-and-through and it is a wild and satisfying ride. Big ups to Capcom for taking an iconic series and having the stones to do different things with it. In particular, 8 is a wonderful blend of 7 (creepy, in your face horror) and 4 (more on the actiony side) and hints of RE1 and Code Veronica. Level design is stunning. Capcom have done it again and this is a must play for any fan of the series. If you're new to the series -- what are you waiting for!!! Jump in!!!

*Now to address the elephant in the room on performance and "bugs". In my play through, I've not found any bugs or issues. Performance is rock solid and buttery smooth. My secret? Turn off ray tracing... I too spent a lot of money on my RTX 3070 and 5800X and would love to use ray tracing in every game but... this is Capcoms first attempt at integrating RT into the RE engine and well.. it's their first attempt.. It's not perfect and experience tells us first attempts at RT in engines usually isn't perfect. 

If you feel you're going to miss out on visuals, you're not... RT here - even if it worked at high performance - is just not that good. I find CACAO actually gives better visuals, the lighting itself is still stunning, even with RT on it uses screen space reflections AND light rays have finite bounces.... this just isn't a high quality implementation like Metro. But you know what... that's fine. RE engine looks amazing and runs amazingly well and you still get SSR and beautiful lighting with CACAO. 

If down the road the RT is rewritten in RE engine (like what 4A did with Metro), then I'd turn it on. That's not what we have here. Instead of getting hurt over that one very tiny detail, buy the game, turn RT off, know it looks incredible and ENJOY IT!!!!

Okay, where do I even start? It's gorgeous. The ambience, the enemies, the visuals, and the story. All of the antagonists are uniquely designed and integrated into the story and I was shocked to see that the village itself had new stuff to do throughout the entire game. Like, you could clear one section and kill a village lord, and then you pick up a key or something that can be used to unlock new houses and areas for treasure and new experiences. I easily spent at least an hour running around looking for things to pick up.

SPOILERS AHEAD:

The lords of the village are by far the most intriguing part of the story. Sure, Ethan grows on me, and Duke is my boy, but the real character fleshing comes from understanding the people you're trying to save your daughter from. 

I will die on the Heisenberg bandwagon because he's the best lord, hands down. He has a goal, he wants to be free, he wants things that makes me relate to him. Yeah, the others have their quirks and to this day I dream about Lady Dimitrescu and Heisenberg fighting over me because holy hell, I am whipped and simped up, but Heisenberg is just such a good character. 

Miranda is kinda eh. As is Mia. Chris sounds like Carlos, but has returned to his RE5 and RE6 badass levels (after taking a saddening break from being cool in RE7, and I also miss his old voice, but that's okay). I'd eat lunch with the Duke anytime, just lemme know. 

WORD OF WARNING AND SPOILER FOR RE7 AND RE8: This is basically the only flaw I noticed, so I was confused going into this game. I literally played Resident Evil 7 the day before I started Village, and Mia wasn't my favorite, so I cured Zoe with the vaccine, as I was given a choice. So Mia died in my game, but without knowing that she did because I cured Zoe (who also died, like 2 seconds later), I came into Village confused as to why Mia was suddenly back and why we had a literal child. Unless you cure Mia, the rest of the story won't line up, which is disappointing and makes it feel like an actual Telltale game without forcing you into one ending. I'd rather it force Mia to be saved, anyway, because then the next game would at least make sense.

But I love Resident Evil Village, and it's made it to my top 10 games at least, possibly my top 5.

Similar to RE4 (Duke even makes a reference to the merchant!), you obtain a special currency called Lei and use it to buy first aid, bullets, upgrades, weaponry, etc. acquired from killing the lycans and other enemies. He'll take those crystal skulls happily ! The character himself, The Duke,  is a pleasure to interact with - he's mysterious yet helpful along the way, not revealing anything but giving you a helping hand to help you go from point A to point B and so on and so forth. 

With that in mind, all of the characters are wonderful - each are unique and are all memorable. Lady Dimitrescu herself is insanely popular (for... obvious reasons..) but her personality is something to love, and her overall design is great. A tall vampire lady with a motherly comfort for her daughters yet a bloodlust for Ethan. [spoiler]Revealed by some of her lines after killing the daughters such as, "It was cold... wasn't it, Daniela?" or "How much blood and sweat do you think it took to raise those daughters? You have incurred an impossible debt!"[/spoiler]

As well, Angie, Moreau, and Heisenberg - all of the main four - are all unique and serve their purpose. Whether it be how, [spoiler] Moreau wants to be loved by Mother Miranda and seen as a worthy subject for the vessel or Angie playing hide and seek like a child with (who is revealed to be after killing her) Ms. Beneviento, or Heisenberg going against the orders and plotting to kill Miranda with Rose and Ethan.[/spoiler] All of them serve a purpose to the story and guide it along and give it a flow in a consistent order, slowly revealing information along the way. 

Onto the graphics - the game itself is absolutely gorgeous. The village interior design and exterior are amazing, filled with obstacles that you slowly progress through. And, each gives off a distinct vibe and new sort of feel. [spoiler]Dimitrescu's castle is royal and divine, filled with beautiful red colors and royal accessories along with a sort of dim lighting. Beneviento's home is dark, set aside and under a waterfall - sort of calming yet underground it is horrifying with a very creepy mysterious presence as you explore through the doll workshop. Moreau's lake is swampy, green and overrun with damaged buildings and machinery. Heisenberg's factory is filled with metal contraptions and enemies along with machinery and a huge area, connected by gears, metal and more. Miranda's final section with dim lighting and darkness, representing her character as she wants only Rose and to kill Ethan and obtain Eva.[/spoiler]

For bugs, the only thing I encountered was a Samca getting stuck under the rooftops. Other than that everything ran smoothly aside from some lag here and there during closeups of enemies, when a lot of particle effects are present. Overall the game ran really well!

Overall, I absolutely love this game. It's an amazing take on the RE universe and series and, although not that scary compared to something such as RE2 (constantly having Mr. X on you) or other games (RE3 Nemesis where he chases you at random points and increasingly gets more violent), the game has its moments. I recommend it to anyone who wants to begin playing the RE games - it's a very very good entrance into the series for newcomers, especially since it recaps 7 and goes off from it and continues the story. Even though you might miss some references here and there, the story is pretty simple to follow.

Don't get me wrong the game is excellent, the environment is visually beautiful, the enemies are horrifically gruesome looking, the pacing is rather fitting for the story and the story itself is above average for a RE game.  

However some thing to note about this game is this;

1.  The "treasure", in this game is hopelessly boring.  There's no challenge to getting these items other than running back and forth or killing something, not to mention the fact that the developers overlooked their own unique system of examining items for the possibility of finding new and unique sub items for other items.  This retention of valuables causes the player to inventory manage much more tightly therefore exploration is wildly encouraged and has a higher payoff.  Not only do most of the treasures not use this examine system but the items themselves are one offs you just sell for money, nothing interesting about them.  The mini-games the sub quests and "things to do" are like mindblowingly bad.  The LABYRINTH puzzles are pointless to do. The little treasures scattered around the world are literally pointless to do, The minigames are pointless to do.  When you scour for an item to do a mini-game and that scouring takes more than an hour of time I expect some type of unique reward, even if its a bottlecap or some type of figurine that is later tied to something like an achievement or costume.  Like 85% of the "Items" you get from doing this stuff reward you with Lei and that's it, and then maybe peppered in there are some items where you need to combine some other items with it.  I remember in Resident Evil 4 there was a specific item that carried over for multiple chapters before you could finish combining the items for the finished sellable, pretty crazy inventory management.

2.  The gun-play in this game is just so boring, the developers encourage environmental damage and using explosives to take down large groups of monsters, but there's a pool of like 15 guns in this game you can choose from, not to mention we're back to the progression system of weapons so the first 10 guns you run into will never be used again in your playthrough, unlike some predecessor that use a system to encourage other gun usage by giving these guns unique traits once fully upgraded which Village does not use.  However I hate playing survival Resident Evil games that highly encourage environment fighting like moving things or constantly running and throwing grenades, if you're giving the player a system where they can choose from multiple upgradable guns and then throwing them into a universe where the guns really aren't that effective, go figure people cheese and ONLY use the most powerful strategy moving forward instead of being open ended with their gameplay.

3. Realistically speaking, there's like no content in this game that's worth exploring for, everything is set out for you on a platter in a little line of candy to the next boss fight.  So linear, so mind numbing.  I was super excited for the world exploration when the map finally opened up with the keys to only find out the different areas are literally houses or enclosed locations with one items worth finding, and it just gives you Lei in return.  I basically gave up exploration about after the second major boss and did the story.

[h1] Hands-On (Off?) Review of the Potential GotY [/h1]
[b] Overview [/b]
Resident Evil Village is a masterpiece in every way and is one of the brightest entries to series to date. Capcom finally succeeds in combining and utilizing different types of horror into one comprehensive story after failing miserably in trying to do so in Resident Evil 6. Without going too much into spoiler territory, let's just say that Mr. Winters will have his hands full with a variety of entertaining and harrowing encounters on his journey to piece together what happened to his daughter.

[b] Gameplay [/b]
This game has perhaps some of the tightest and well-woven gameplay I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. Every weapon feels unique to shoot and utilize, keeping you on your toes and forcing you to think carefully about each encounter. With limited ammo and crafting materials in the environment, I was constantly rotating between my weaponry and trying to optimize my resources to get the job done. There are also various ways to use the environment to your advantage, such as the classic red explosive barrels, movable shelves, and bags of flour.

A useful mechanic that returns from Resident Evil 7 is the blocking mechanic. As series veterans know, it reduces incoming damage. To adjust to the more action focused nature of Village, Ethan is capable of pushing enemies away immediately after blocking, a wonderful addition that opens up new layers of strategical combat. Another upgrade over RE7 is the move away from item boxes to a RE4-like attache case. Being able to constantly carry your weapons and sub-weapons allows for experimentation with different weaponry whenever you want and allows you to utilize different approaches to solving enemy encounters. Thankfully, crafting materials are placed in a different menu from your weapons along with treasures and key items, freeing up much-needed space.

Speaking of enemies, there are a variety of threats that blow RE7 out of the water. Werewolves, nuns, and zombies comprise many of the basic enemies and they are capable of closing in on you quickly and efficiently, taking off sizable chunks of Ethan's health. There are also many different sub-bosses to deal with, each having different weak points and approaches to fighting. They often come out of nowhere as well, adding to the suspense. Last but not least, the five main bosses are perhaps the best encounters of them all. They offer a satisfying ending to their respective areas, witty and entertaining banter and personalities, and of course, difficult to reach weak points. 

A final notable gameplay element is the Duke, Village's version of RE4's merchant. He is personable, likable, and mysterious and provides many useful services such as weapon, ammo, and healing purchases, weapon upgrades, and even cooking up feasts that upgrade Ethan's stats. These meals are made with the help of hunting for animals, another new mechanic. Animals are often hidden in optional areas that require backtracking and sometimes even solving puzzles. However, it is well worth it to collect their meat for the permanent stat boosts and high selling value of meat. Backtracking and scouring the environment should be done anyways because there are also valuable hidden treasures and additional resources to find as you progress through the game and village slowly starts opening up new areas. These resources will likely be the difference between survival and death, especially at higher difficulty settings.

[b] Difficulty [/b]
Casual is the lowest and easiest difficulty. This is recommended for players brand new to the series and/or brand new to shooters in general. For achievement hunters, this is also the go-to choice as none of the achievements besides the difficulty achievements are difficulty-dependent. Ammo and resources are plentiful, enemies have significantly reduced health, and Ethan takes less damage. Enemies are also slower and less aggressive in general, sometimes just standing there and taking damage without retaliating. Another notable difference is that Lei pickups from enemies are low and less common than in higher difficulties. 

Standard is the "normal" difficulty although series veterans and veterans of other shooters might find this difficulty a little too easy. Ammo and resources are still easy to find and enemies are still relatively passive although they do hit harder. Lei pickups are a little more frequent and of higher amounts than what is found in the Casual difficulty.

Hardcore is the difficulty I recommend RE veterans to start off at. It is the highest difficulty offered at the beginning with the standard version of the game. It is a lot more tense and satisfying than Standard, as enemies make an effort to get in your face to take you down. Ammo and resources are more scarce than in Standard and even common enemies will be capable of taking multiple shots before dying. Thus, smart weapon upgrades are needed, blocking will need to be utilized often, and running may be resorted to more often to save precious resources. Lei drops are frequent and higher amounts than in Standard.

Village of Shadows is the highest difficulty in the game and can be unlocked by completing the story once or by buying the Deluxe Edition of the game. It is not recommended to start on this difficulty, as that is quite masochistic and an exercise in frustration. That is likely because this difficulty appears to be made unbalanced unless you have infinite ammo. Enemies will not hesitate to kill you, sprinting up to you in droves and making frustratingly well-timed dodges to waste your valuable and scarce ammo. They are also found in new locations around the map and previous "late-game" enemies will spawn earlier in the story as well. On top of that, you can only take two to three hits before dying, even with all of the cooking upgrades and with perfectly timed blocks. Some bosses also have new tactics up their sleeve and are tanky to the max, which makes things excruciating especially in the late-game and this is regardless of you having infinite ammo. To help soften the blow a bit, enemies drop generous amounts of Lei early and more often, making weapon upgrades a breeze. 

[b] Length and Replayability [/b]
On my first playthrough, I took around 14 hours to complete the game because I wanted to explore every nook-and-cranny of the game and find all of the hidden files and treasures. Even when skipping this optional stuff, a first playthrough would average around 8 to 10 hours. Additional playthroughs are definitely recommended to unlock some sweet new weaponry, finish upgrading your weapons, trying new difficulties, and unlocking achievements. There is also the Mercenaries (an extra minigame) and cool figures and documents that give a behind the scenes look behind the production of the game and an expansion on the game's lore. As you can see, I've put in a little over 80 hours into this game trying to unlock everything so there's quite a bit of content to stick around for.

[b] Performance and Issues [/b]
GPU: GTX 1660 ti
CPU: Intel Core i7-9750H
RAM: 16GB

The game ran consistently smooth with very little in the way of stuttering and tearing. My frame rate fluctuated between 70 to 120 FPS, even during intense sequences. Only when my PC ran a little too hot were there any noticeable frame drops, notably when the sisters and their flies appeared or if there was a mass enemy spawn. I have so far not come across any bugs yet so the game is clean in that department as well.

Issues with the gameplay and story itself that I hope will be addressed is adding a FOV slider (it's currently locked at around 85 or so), adding more characters to the Mercenaries, and adding some story related DLC to expand upon the Lords or explore how the Village came to be before Ethan's arrival.

[b] Conclusion [/b]
Overall, Village gave me plenty of great moments and scares and I have thoroughly enjoyed my time with it, 10/10!

Resident Evil Village was one of the few games I was looking forward to this year aside from Cyberpunk, and I have to say it did not disappoint. 

[u] Pros: [/u]
+Amazing graphics and beautiful imagery/scenery (You feel completely immersed in isolated, cold Europe)
+Fun engaging combat (Satisfying kills, weapons have weight, plenty to kill)

+Interesting characters with diverse personalities (Lady D, The Duke, Heisenberg)
+Big mommy milkers - and that waistline.......yes. (need I say more?)

[u] Cons: [/u]
-Lack of horror (More of a personal taste and not a deal breaker, but I do wish it was more horror focused like RE7 with a tense atmosphere)
-Relatively short game (First play-through took about 6-7 hours collecting and searching everything, but you can finish it in less than 2 hours if you rush it)
-Some parts felt rushed (I would've liked to see more of Beneviento's residence/ could've done more with it imo)

All in all it's a solid game with fun combat and good storytelling and I'm excited for the DLC!

Resident Evil 8, a.k.a. - RE: Village... A mix between the old and the new :)

Honestly... my favourite, and subjectively best Resident Evil so far, and I've played all of them up to date, from the classics, RE0 - all the way to RE: Village... but that's just my opinion.

It starts off a little slow, but the action picks up shortly after. It has many segments with puzzles which require thinking and backtracking, much like in RE7. At times, the horror element is even better than in RE7, to be honest, especially towards the middle of the game. There were lots of unexpected parts that made me jump or feel uncomfortable/vulnerable. And I loved it! :)

Of course, the game isn't all just puzzles and suspense, etc... it's a throwback to the more action-oriented Resident Evils, such as RE4. Classic RE ridiculousness :) 

The gameplay and animations are also nice, they feel very "weighty". The Merchant shop is a nice addition, again, just like in RE4, which makes for a fun and repetitive gameplay loop in the background - always looking to upgrade your guns, sell treasures, buy supplies in preparation for a boss fight, etc...

The art direction is the best of any Resident Evil game ever, hands down! CAPCOM's really pushing their RE Engine! Being a 1st person game, some textures are incredibly high-resolution up-close which is much appreciated. The lighting does wonders to the models / textures and materials, and it's clear it was designed in a way that naturally guides your path. Very, very solid art direction! Every scene and character tells its story! Honestly, a real treat to look at!

And always running at around 60fps (4K resolution, maxed out settings, with Ray-Tracing & HDR enabled) sometimes going as high as 90-100fps. 

Some odd stuttering here and there, from Lady Dimitrescu's daughters' flies / insect particle FX, or a millisecond stutter upon killing an enemy, but I'm sure it'll get patched soon... I know many people reported this issue on PC... hopefully CAPCOM is aware...

And it features a very touching story, with memorable and badass characters, too - many references / lore / easter eggs related to previous games. Also, being a Romanian, I loved how our culture was represented in the game, haha! Some parts were hilarious! A solid experience! 

Starting a NG+ playthrough soon, on Village of Shadows difficulty... wish me luck!

This is a great installment to the series and now perhaps 'tops' as one of my top three Resident Evil games. My usual order goes RE Remake, RE 7, and RE 4. However, RE 7 now may be replaced by the sheer epic magnitude of Resident Evil 8. Village was more than I expected, and I was glad to see Ethan return. The gameplay is thoroughly entertaining and the enemies are the smartest I've ever seen in a horror game. The graphics are amazing, Ethan is at his absolute best, the merchant system is simple, effective and pleasing; great guns, tensity and epicness.

Yes, I use the word "Epic" to describe RE 8.

I wouldn't say this is much of a horror game, however. It is more of a robust collision of action and everything else that makes Resident Evil: RESIDENT EVIL. It is so much Resident Evil in one game it is almost to STUPID proportions of RESIDENT EVIL, but all the while VERY pleasing (because that's what we want) and leaves you thoroughly satisfied as any fan, or even a new comer to the series would. 

Unfortunately, like I said, it's not very scary.

But, it is still a survival horror game and that's what counts. There are a few things I will say though, that aren't perfect about it. For example, the story line isn't ENTIRELY ludicrous, (but is a far cry from the simplicity of the original Resident Evil) and is STILL ludicrous, nonetheless. 

Chris Redfield is probably at his absolute worst in this game and almost to the point of his "plans" being so stupid its comical. Yes, our beloved Chris Redfield is back and looking better than ever after his plastic surgery from RE 7 (seriously what was with that?), he's tougher, harder and DUMBER than ever! He makes the laziest, most unplanned, unsound and JEOPARDIZING decisions that totally screws over Ethan.

I know anything past Code Veronica is NOT PLAYED for its story so the somewhat laughable plot is acceptable thanks to the game play; a few quirks; and Ethan himself. The Four Lords, (along with Mother Merinda), do add a layer of story-telling to the game that is very fun and unique, but Chris Redfield adds an unsuspected layer of "WTF" and "Why'd you do that?" to the point of making him out to be one of the biggest jerks ever.

Thanks for destroying my dreams, Chris!

However, I will say, he is a little redeemable for a portion of the game IS spent playing at him and IS very fun.

A few OTHER things, such as some CANON left me VERY ticked off. It seems Capcom turned around and immediately switched things with the previous (RE7) installment in order for it to fit with a narrative that changes Ethan completely. The ending was a little dramatic and unsettling, as well. 

As for its length and replayability, as any RE fan knows you can typically beat  the first run around 7 hours. No, for an RE game this isn't too short and left me satisfied. However, don't expect it to be longer than something like Resident Evil 4, which is one of the longer games of the series.

Also, for speed runners: there are moments (in the beginning) where you will spend A LOT OF TIME ... wasting ... time. Yes, the game has a rather slow START UP and if you are a PC user, perhaps you can find a mod it to skip past it? 

Other than that, this is one of the best Resident Evil games to come. My personal rating: 8.5/10

I originally recommended this game.  Having had more time to think about it, and having spent some time on the RE4 remake; I realized.  This game... isn't very good.  Oh, don't get me wrong; it's not BAD.  There's a fair bit that they did right.  The environments are suitably creepy and the graphics are good.   The problem is; it's basically RE4, with a less interesting protagonist, mold in stead of bugs, and less satisfying combat.  Oh, there are other differences; after all, it's in Romania, which is totally different from Spain!  Sure, there's a run-down village, a big castle, a merchant, and all that, but it's different, okay?  The major issue I have is this; the RE4 remake makes it clear that someone who works with the franchise understands having weapons that are just FLAT OUT better than the weapons that use the same ammunition is not fun.  The LEMI is completely made useless by the 1911, and the 1911 is made completely useless by the Vz. 61, or whatever they call it.  There's simply no reason to use anything other than the best weapon.  I also don't care for the (admittedly tense) Beneviento house.  Don't get me wrong, it was fun the first time through, but between just having some weapons flat-out better and that section bringing the pace of the game to a grinding halt while the protagonist works through his fear of fatherhood; it removes virtually all replay value for me.   Which is what this series has mostly been about.  Oh sure, they tried to make up for that by adding unlockable weapons, but guess what?  Those are either a joke weapon (the gyrojet pistol), a totally better than the magnum automag (or a revolver that fires rifle rounds), or... an automatic rifle.  They're also kind of boring.  Also, I pointed out in my original review that the "Not a hero" DLC for REVII proved that ADS is possible in the engine.  I don't know why they just did the tightened reticle in first person rather than having the character use the sights.  Which is another issue; you don't need to aim to shoot, although given the speed of the basic enemies I see why they went that way.  In any case, not the best RE game, and not one that I can really recommend, with the benefit of hindsight.

Resident Evil 8 would have been an amazing groundbreaking game if it was released in 2012. But in 2021, it feels half baked. Capcom is not the developer I remember. 

The game runs good enough, and other than some odd spots where I felt the game perhaps didnt load LOD's correctly, for example later in the game there are areas with a lot of stone bricks in the road, I always felt they never reached a high enough resolution (Playing in 4kHDR) and it just looked... Odd against the nice assets in the rest of the area. Which was also stonework. 

A lot of people talk about the 2nd area of the game as being the scariest. But if you played Amnesia/Penumbra back in its heyday, you'll realize this part is just a very shallow version of that gameplay. You literally hide in 2 closets, complete the puzzle, and its done. It was the most anticlimactic part of the game for me.  But yet, this is praised as being one of the, if not the best part of RE8, but it lasts not even 10 minutes, and again, its just a worse, shorter Penumbra/Amnesia section (look those games up if you never heard of them) all I can say is that it was disappointing. But yet, this is the most praised section, and I say its the worst. I think that says a lot. 

Another thing I didnt like about RE8 was the very 'Gamey' aspect of it. Which isn't itself a bad thing. But for example the beginning of the game is an arbitrary 'Survive against an unseen timer' and all it did was frustrate me because it felt arbitrary, the intro actually turned me off so bad I regretted my purchase but was past 2 hours at that point. It went unplayed for a month  until I forced myself to beat it since i bought it.  
The absence of an FOV slider in 2021 is unacceptable from a AAA company, let alone one that has given us FOV sliders in previous releases!!!! WTF is up with that!!! Also, I have NEVER had to increase my mouse DPI just to have a comfortable sensitivity in game (With in game sensitivity at Max) so WTF!?

The main Villain's in the game are very well done I would say, the performance from the actors is good, about what you would expect from a AAA game in 2021, although the entire game Mia felt off, it literally felt like she was a different person completely from RE7.  Was this intended? 

The gameplay itself is a more action based than RE7, and one thing I have to give RE8 is the boss fights, while not super crazy or anything, but they required you to think just a little. So thankfully it is more than just shoot until dead. The normal enemies are mostly just generic zombie/lycan/vampire/bad humanoid thing, but there are a few exceptions later on in the game. Nothing too memorable, but I wouldn't say immediately forgettable either.

One thing I did not like before this game even released is how the actress that played as far as I can tell, at least one of, but seems to be credited for most of the 3 Daughters, passed away before the game released, and while I don't know what was discussed or in a contract. But if it was me, and I passed away before being able to give my approval on the final product, I would want my likeness removed from the game. Think for yourself on that one. Maybe she would have wanted have her likeness in the game. But this is a game made for making money, and to me, not removing her likeness, likely to just not have to re-cast and do all that work again, seems disrespectful. But again, for all I know, she wanted this. All Capcom did was make a tweet, yep, because that's how we show respect and grief these days. 

This whole game felt like a B film. It shined in some areas, but then right after something stupid in the story would happen, or Ethan would get basically killed again (and just because they explain that at the very end of the game does not make it ok) and just take me completely out of it and go "Oh yea, this is a game" It flipped back and forth between action and not very good attempts at horror. The only scares in this game where when you got jumpscared, that beautiful atmosphere of impending doom that I love RE for, is absent completely.

I had read before buying this, that RE8 is like a theme park of horror, sure, if you were living under a rock for 10 years maybe, or maybe if you are 10, and that's ok, but for an adult who grew up on RE. I enjoyed the RE3 remake more than this, and I will be the first to tell you the RE3 remake is far from perfect, but it still felt like they knew what RE was supposed to be. Or maybe we were blinded by nostalgia. 

At the end of the day, for maybe 20 - 30 bucks, ok. But THIS from Capcom? I can't be the only one who has been seeing this slow decline from the Capcom of my childhood, to this stranger with a mask on. This game is needlessly overhyped, if RE 8 is your first RE game, or first horror-ish game, then you will probably not be disappointed. But from a fan who truly misses Survival Horror, and has not been getting that from the Grandaddy of Survival Horror, I just feel shafted.

Not much to say here as the 95% overwhelmingly positive rating pretty much says it all. RE Village isn't as innovative as some of the other titles in the series but it's an extremely well done hybrid. This game makes sense and plays well on every level. A couple of things I'll mention, even though they're basic points: I love how Cap-com made this game so you can play it without having a fancy, high priced rig. There's no reason, really, why more games shouldn't run on a 1050 ti or whatever. The other thing that I love is the various difficulty levels mean what they say. Some of us just don't have the time to keep replaying and replaying boss fights, etc., we just want to be able to complete the game within a reasonable amount of time and enjoy the story. In RE Village, casual means casual. The most times I died in the course of any boss fight was three, if I remember correctly. Also, the puzzles in this game were very well thought out and so fun to solve. I'm not the biggest fan of survival horror because I hate--this is a point a lot of other players have made-- not being able to fight back. RE Village isn't very scary at all, except arguably in a couple of segments. This game is just fascinating in it's own way and FUN to play. $60 is a lot to pay for a game but considering how a lot of games aren't this good, or aren't as good as they should be, in my view it's worth the full price. Even in RE 7 you had Mia (more or less) and Zoe supporting you, but here not even Mia had many appearances except at the start where she is 'different'. Furthermore, the antagonists had little to no depth. This game should have focused on the Dimitrescu family like RE7 focused on the Baker family. But instead they ended up just as some forgettable HP bags to bring down with almost no back story. Just to add some more 'bosses' of questionable quality. I still liked the doll house, but the werewolves could have been better and Heisenbergs robot army didn't fit at all in the scenario.

Well, part of the problem might have been my expectations. I also don't get the name of the game. The 'village' stops being a village about 30 minutes into the game. Then everyone is dead and the only thing left is a big graveyard of abandoned houses. Overall, I enjoyed my play through of Resident Evil 8. There were some tense moments the game designers expertly created through out the game which kept me on edge. I particularly enjoyed the [spoiler] doll house [/spoiler] segment which was an exceptionally eerie set up for a really disturbing scene.

Having said that, I didn't think the game was perfect and had issue with the following points:

1. Vast segments of the game are filled with 1-2 standard enemies which become tedious to deal with very fast. They don't have much difference in terms of attack patterns and are easily dispatched by running and blasting. It isn't till later in the game, and only for the briefest of moments, do we encounter some variety in combatants.

2. It didn't really feel like a survival horror game. RE8 gives plenty of inventory space from the start, so space management was never really a thing and we were given so many guns and ammo that it never really felt like much of an issue. Also it was easy enough blasting past enemies. 

3. I wish they had included a field of view option. It was available in RE7, not so sure why it was missing here. I got a bit dizzy being unable to change the FOV. Had the same issue in RE7, but increasing it helped.

4. Ethan seems different in this game, and not his cool self from RE7. It was strange hearing him utter cheap comebacks after defeating a boss OR being defiant by simply cussing an antagonist. i.e. "Well NOW you are the cursed one" OR "F#@K you B@!#H" I am OK with cussing, but here it feels lazy, almost tacked on.

5. Story wise, it starts of well enough but by the end it just all comes crashing together, and is a bit too wacky for my tastes. The end scene teases that we aren't quite done with the winters family, but it left me with questions as to how someone who never [spoiler] met their father is so attached to them, regularly paying them visits [/spoiler] 

If you got through those points, you might think I didn't like the game. But I did, it was a good overall experience and worth playing though hence my positive recommendation. For me RE7 did it better, and that's just my preference.

Resident Evil Village takes the same formula, gameplay, and style that RE:7 did and improves on almost all aspects! The Story of Resident Evil: Village continues with Ethan Winters, however instead of trying to save his wife - he is now dragged into another conflict way above his head to rescue his newborn baby Rosemary. The Story takes place over the course of four main acts covering different "rulers" of the village who each feel completely unique from one another, although it clearly feels as though some got more love over others. If you were a fan of Resident Evil 7, I cannot recommend RE:Village enough! As a whole, I would rate RE:Village a 7/10 [with 5 being average]. A game that is COMPLETELY worth the full price of admission, but I will not revisit anytime soon! The finale left me excited for the next entry

[h1]Environment[/h1]
I was initially skeptical about moving from the horrifying location of the Louisiana swamp to an open & well lit village/castle that we see in Village. My skepticism was quickly dismissed as I found myself loving the environments in RE:Village significantly more than the previous entry. A perfect example that not all games scary need to take place in pitch black corridors.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
RE:Village utilizes the same gameplay formula from RE:7 and fine tunes elements of it to make everything feel just a bit better. Nailing headshots felt rewarding, blocking enemy attacks provided a much better option for defending, and boss fights in the game, while all following the same formula of "run, shoot as much as possible, then run again" still were exciting by the variety of final bosses that you will come across. The game took my just over 10 hours to complete, and that is as much time as I felt it deserved. [The additional time you may see on record was capturing footage for video content purposes] By the end I did feel as though it overstayed its welcome - more on that later. Changes to crafting from the previous entry, and the introduction of the Duke and his marketplace were greatly welcome! While they didn't necessarily add any additional value to the experience, I was happy that Capcom did not simply stick to the same exact thing. For a game that borrows a lot of elements from its predecessor, these small changes helped significantly to make the experience feel new. Scavenging for resources and supplies felt rewarding, as every corner there may hide an unseen danger which, if not prepared for, could be your demise. The game felt tense the whole way through by always keeping you just short of the resources you think you need.

[h1]Visuals & Sound[/h1]
You only need to look at the trailers to see how beautiful this game is. As for sound - the sound design is one of the best I've heard in a long time. Sound in horror games is one of the most important aspects and RE:Village nails it. 

[h1]bugs[/h1] 
I am happy to say that I didn't run across any major bugs while playing on PC. Maybe a small visual error here and there, but nothing significant enough that I remembered it by the end of my playthrough.

[h1]Negatives[/h1] 
*Some Minor Spoilers Ahead*
While Resident Evil Village is a great game it is not a perfect game. The variety of enemies, and the separation of its villains [more detail on this in just a bit] hold it back from being something truly spectacular. Starting with the enemies: In RE:7 we fought through mutamycete monstrosities that would shamble towards you weaving around so as to not walk directly into incoming bullets. In RE:Village - you will fight 3 varieties of enemies...Zombies that behave exactly the same as the previous enemies in RE:7, Lycanthropes who, although faster (and some have bows) behave mostly the same as the zombies, and Mechanical monsters who try to break up the tedium by forcing you to target a weak spot. In small moments there may be some bird monsters as well. By the end of the game, the lack of variety in enemies grew tiresome, and I couldn't wait to just run past every zombie that jumped out who existed simply for the sake of slowing player progress, or consuming player resources. A great example of this (spoiler ahead) [spoiler] during the factory segment of the game, Ethan calls out multiple times dialogue along the lines of "are you serious there's more of this!? Simultaneously me, as the player, was thinking the same thing in a negative way. I was ready to be done and move on just to progress the story more. [/spoiler] Like a vacation that lasts a few days too long, by the end I was more than happy to finish the experience. All of this culminated to an ending that was nothing short of fantastic.

The division of the games main antagonists also proved to be a major weakness. While each villain and their respective areas in the game felt wholly unique, this seemingly came at the cost of dividing gameplay elements. What I mean by this is: each main villain can be categorized into their own gameplay element. Lady Dimitrescu represents survival, Beneviento represents horror, Moreau represents puzzles, and Heisenberg represents combat. This does not mean that they were mutually exclusive to their respective areas, but each one particularly highlighted one gameplay element over the others [with lady Dimitrescu being the best of all of them, subjectively. No, not because she is the tall vampire lady...] Each of those four game elements combined [again most prominently featured in Lady Dimetrescu's area] are when the game is at its best. Separated, you have 3 individual and, albeit unique areas, but areas that stand weaker alone. I can't help but feel as though the game gave massively interesting characters like Heisenberg the short end of the stick. Possibly there were too many to cram into the game, possibly the developers gave more love to some over others, but the final result, although filled with potential, left me wondering what could have been if there was more time spent to each of them. With all that said, I still loved and respect the diversity that each area brought.

While Steam says I played the game for 19 hours, it actually took me 8 hours and 30 minutes to beat the game, and I did almost everything: I found almost all treasures (except for one which I couldn't get because I progressed to far into the story to trigger a certain thing), I found almost all guns (except for the ones you can buy) and I have been pretty much over the entire map. So, the game is only around 2 and a half hours longer than last year's very disappointingly short game Resident Evil 3 Remake. But does that make it bad? And is that why I am bit disappointed? No. 

I always enjoy my time with these games. No matter how weak an entry might be. I never finish a Resident Evil game with the thought that I wasted my time. This game is no different. And truth be told, it is better than 7 and 3R but not by much. 

The gameplay loop is exactly like it was in 7. Resident Evil 8 is a first person shooter with inventory management and "limited" (more on that later) ressources, it has puzzles (more on that later too) and levels that a structured like Metrovania levels, you know where you (although recent games have unfortunately had less of that compared to the first couple games) backtrack through the levels in order to progress to new areas from the main hub level. 

The shooting is solid enough, it can be a little stiff as to be expected with a survival horror game. If the combat was too good then we would have a Dead Space (read my reviews for those games to see what I mean) situation where you don't feel any tension in the fights due to being too much of a beast yourself to be afraid of the actual beasts. You get a arsenal of weapons as you play through the game that you either buy from the merchant or find. You can upgrade these weapons by either paying said merchant or add attachments on them that you either buy from the merchant or find. What do you use to buy stuff? Well just standard cash that you get from either finding it or selling treasures/items to the merchant. Well, so far so good right? 

While I do enjoy this loop I do have some complaints. Resident Evil 8 throws a lot of enemies at you, but at the same time it also gives you a LOT of ressources so they aren't really ever THAT limited. I don't really like that. It makes it feel more like a regular shooter than a survival horror game. The stiff aiming and all that wasn't really a issue tho, no matter the amount of enemies the game threw at me so at least that's a plus. Overall, I enjoyed the combat in 7 and I also enjoy it here despite the issues I got with it since it is exactly the same.

The puzzles were a big weakness of 7. Resident Evil generally moved away from them after 4 but 7 kinda brought them back-ish. They weren't particularly challenging and overall they were very same-y. However, while the puzzles in this game aren't hard, they are a nice break from the action and they do have some variety to them.

The same can be said about the enemy variety and design. This was another thing that sucked hard in 7. Besides the Baker family, the enemies were really bad, just different shapes of black goo basically. While this game doesn't have the same insane variety of the games of old, it is at least a step up from the previous game and it never really got too repetitive.

The bosses, however, have not improved. There are more of them than in 7 but they straight up suck for the most part. I attribute this mainly to the arenas where you fight them. Since movement is very limitedand since they more often then not are either too big or too small. The fights themselves are also often tedious ranging from bad to alright. I didn't really care for their designs either and it didn't help that they have so little screen time that they hardly made an impact on that front. You can read notes about them or from them that you find through out the levels but that hardly adds much besides some back story and maybe also a little bit of their motivation. Even the big vampire lady (who was totally overhyped btw, since she barely appear in the game). I did appreciate that we got a scene where they were all together, like in Metal Gear Solid 3, I really like when games do that. It makes me feel like I am taking down a actual team instead of just a string of villains that appear one by one. 

As far as the levels are concerned. I feel like the first 2 levels were solid that being the village which is also the hub level and the castle, the middle portion was alright and the ending levels were tedious. That is EXACTLY what I felt about 7 as well. Although, it doesn't become THAT bad but you can feel a dip in quality after you leave the castle level (which is ironically also the one they showed the most in the promotional material). The house level afterwards is also pretty solid but kinda short.

The story isn't good. But that is hardly a surprise. It's Resident Evil after all, it's been the case since the first game. These games tell their stories through their levels and their atmosphere. The actual written story that plays are usually pretty campy and the characters are paper thin. I like that because it usually contrasts the actual game quite well. That is why it feels especially odd that this game takes itself so seriously. This is bad, yes, but not in the way as the previous entries. The graphics and facial animations look pretty good in 2021, the voice acting isn't terrible but it isn't exactly good either especially from Ethan Winters, the protagonist, who is not convincing more than half of the time, the music and sound is solid and the dialogue is generic, but hardly bad. There was a charm to the previous games that I feel like the newer games really lack. Oh, and every frickin villager speaks perfect english even though they appear to be in East Europe. Contrast that with 4 where they either spoke spanish (since it took place in Spain) or english with accents. That kinda broke the immersion for me a couple times too. 

So to conclude. I had a fun enough time with the game. Despite all the issues I got with it. If you enjoyed 7 then you are likely gonna like this one too. The gameplay loop is solid enough, it looks and sounds great, the puzzles are a nice addition and getting loot and better gear while traversing the Metrovania styled levels is always fun. Before you read the below, I will say I did enjoy many parts of RE Village, but my overall consensus on it is negative, particularly in comparison to RE 7. LOTS of spoilers below. You have been warned. 

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[olist]
    [*]FPS Elements
The FPS transition in Resident Evil is still alive and well. I personally enjoy this because it increases the nature of perceiving horror directly instead of seeing it inflicted on a character you watch. I really don't have any negatives on this - I enjoy first person in any horror game. The weapons were mostly fun to use and I didn't have any problems with that. Well... except for the knife. Why is there a pause after swiping it twice? I mean...really? Why? That's just a mood-killer. 
    [*]Merchant System
So, this is where I differ greatly from many players. Where some may absolutely love a merchant system, I never wanted to see it in Resident Evil again. Why? Because it ruins the "horror survival" aspect of the game. It's not really horror survival when you can purchase goods and services from somebody that follows you around with the intention of profit. It just doesn't make sense, and [spoiler]the merchants' background or take in the story is never revealed at the end anyway.[/spoiler] Resident Evil 7 does not have this system at all, and I found the gameplay more enjoyable when I had to scavenge for hidden items to actually "survive". I felt more accomplished when I found guns & ammo hidden in the Bakers house.
    [*]Open Atmosphere
I enjoyed the extended exploration in the game. I didn't feel like I was stuck in one small area always like in RE:7. However, I will also say that may have lowered the intensity of fear I had in the game too. Feeling more open and free with random enemies jumping around is not as scary as being trapped in a small, condensed bog-land of molded that follow you every which way. At least RE: Village enemies knew how to open doors. 

But the elevators. Seriously. Mass Effect: Legendary Edition reduced elevator time, and RE: Village brought slow elevators back into my life? UGH! STOP. 

[/olist]

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
I really had no issues with the graphics - I think they did a fine job and I'm not really expecting more here.

[h1]Horror Quality[/h1]
Ok, this is where it gets messy and relates to what I mentioned before about the merchant system too, but it's more than just that. Overall, I must say that this game rarely scared me at all. Most situations were predictable, and the enemies annoyed me more than scaring me. The molded were far more terrifying opponents, and Jack still surpasses any antagonist I faced in Resident Evil. The personalities of most villains were boring and predictable. 

I will give credit to the giant baby fetus monster. That was one moment that actually did scare me A LOT! Also, the dolls are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wicked. I loved the soundtrack that played at that point in the game. Why couldn't the game consist of more enemies like this? Create more Regenerator / molded type enemies. That's the kind of ♥♥♥♥ that scares me. Hyper-Meth infused zombies? No. Just no. I wanted more pure molded. They were far scarier and demented. 

[h1]Replay Value[/h1]
This game does possess a solid New Game+ system. However... I just sent through the game a second time, and I already had infinite ammo for my big ass shotgun and grenade launcher. I was already like. "Wtf. There's no challenge here. Peaceout. I'm done." I liked RE7 more, where you had to beat MadHouse to receive infinite ammo. The prizes you obtained from completing the game alone were not overpowered - beating it under 4 hours provided some stronger gifts (like the circular chainsaw). But I still find RE7 more enjoyable to replay because the fear aspect sticks stronger to it than RE:8 Village. I immediately grew bored in my second playthrough. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
I am happy that the story concluded the power of the Molded and where it originated. The concept of Ethan always being "Dead" was pretty grim, but I liked it! I think that the game got carried away with some strange aspects... I didn't expect Gears of War to make it into RE:8. I think the game branched out too far - they need to back up and look at what made RE:7 fun. RE:7 was more enjoyable story-wise because it was simplistic to it's nature and didn't overthink anything. It could have used improvements here and there, and I will say I liked how RE: Village was longer (or felt longer) than RE:7 did. 

[h1]Ethan's Character is Lame[/h1]
I didn't like Ethan as much in this game. His character rarely let out F-bombs, which was disappointing and they kept portraying him as this "Good father that wants to protect his daughter" Through the ENTIRE game. No other character revealed in him - this is literally all they emphasize on every waking second. It gets really old. What happened to the badass "♥♥♥♥ YOU TOO!" and "♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥. Jesus ♥♥♥♥!" Ethan? Also... he seemed to get over Mia's death pretty fast (who is really not Mia). His character was very boring to say the least and I did not feel too sad when he died at the end. I was actually happy the repetition of the story finally came to an end.

Instead of a horror survival game, this should be labeled as a "Search and Rescue" game. Yup, another Ashley situation. That's all it felt like 95% of the time. At least Rose wasn't an outright dumb **** like Ashley.

Spoiler-Free review
[u] TLDR [/u]
Resident Evil Village is the 8th Resident Evil game in the main installment, it's a massive improvement over RE7, I enjoyed it much more and its visuals are stunning. But has its shortcomings.

[b] Gameplay [/b]
RE8 is a first-person shooter with horror elements, inventory management and sometimes puzzles. As you progress, you find keys, unlock more areas, fight against new types of enemies. All while the story unfolds and becomes more exciting.

[b] Story [/b]
You are Ethan Winters, you and Mia Winters recently got a baby girl, which they named Rose. One evening while they decide to eat dinner, Chris and his soldiers storm into their house, Chris killing Mia. He takes Rose, and knocks Ethan unconcious. He wakes up nearby a village, where he quickly finds out beasts have invaded. Can he put an end to the reign of the monsters and save his Rose? 

[b] Compared to previous installments [/b]
Gameplaywise, RE8 is a lot like RE7. A first person shooter. However, it has been streamlined to play better, and environments  have been scaled up big time. I'd say RE8 is a huge improvement. It still holds that RE7 DNA, but works much better.
Compared to RE5-6, there's not much that's comparable, with maybe the exception of the game having action based scenes where tons of enemies are thrown at you.
Compared to RE2 and RE3 remakes, it also runs on the RE-engine, has the same sort of discoverability for puzzles and keys, but still misses some of the atmosphere RE2 brings on through. RE3 however, it's much closer to that, RE8 gives much more freedom however.
Compared to the classic RE's (RE0,1,1HD,2,3) there's not much in common with the except of the game being connected to them lorewise. 

[b] Graphics [/b]
The graphics are absolutely beautiful in this game, with my i5 3470 and GTX 1060, the game runs on 60 fps average and so is one of the best looking, and one of the best perfoming games I've ever played. While you might not need something like my setup, I'd recommend atleast having a mid-end setup, but I have a feeling people with low-end systems can enjoy this game as well as long as it's not too low-end.

[b] My opinion [/b]
RE8 is a beautiful looking, wonderful sounding, big game. There's so much to discover, so much to see if you pay attention. While I wouldn't call it my favorite game, it's definitely is up there for one of my favorite first-person games. There are a few issues I have with it, though. Like RE3, Village sometimes has some exploration issues. Once you complete an important area, say, the castle, you can't return to re-explore, to get items you forgot to get, making the game feel smaller. Second, I feel like the areas are underutilized, puzzles are solvable in the same or an area nearby, making the places not feel very connected and less of a "village" and more of "levels". This might be because my favorite RE games are RE1 and 2, in which some doors, or puzzles are locked till you find the solution or key in a different area. I really wish RE9 allows for more flexibility in puzzles and objects. Sure, it'll create more backtracking, but I enjoy that as long as it rewards.

[b] Conclusion [/b]
RE8 is a great game, my favorite 2021 game so far. It's close to becoming an RE favorite, but still has some ways to go to become what it wants to become. If you enjoy First Person shooters with horror elements, buy this.

It runs reasonably well, I didn't encounter any glitches or bugs that I saw, other than an enemy corpse clipping through a wall or something. 

You don't need to have played 7 to play 8, there is a recap of the main beats of 7 at the beginning of this if you need it, although having played 7 would definetly help in the more emotional moments and to connect some dots. 

The only real downside I would say for this is I think the pacing is off, or at least too fast in some areas. You don't get much time at all to just have a second to reflect on whats going on before being rushed into the next gameplay area (its a semi open world, but you'll have a cutscene/story moment and then immediately be back out mowing down enemies). 

The boss fights are alright, if you've played any of the games I listed above it's nothing really new.

There's a New Game + so that's nice. Overall I'd recommend it if you're ok with the things I talked about, and even though it only lasted for 10 hours on normal, I still feel as though between that and the new game + mode I got my monies worth.

Let me tell you, this game is freakin amazing. If I should describe this game in one sentence, I´d probally said it´s mix of the best re 4´s and re 7´s features, but the game is a lot more than that! Devs basically gambled when they introduced this exploring system ( wich was partly already in the previous parts) and let me tell you, it paid off!!! You can backtrack to every area, wich I would strongly recommend. The backtracking is fun, gives you a tons of rewards and you´ll explore some lore + find extra encounters with some new foes. The gunplay is SMOOTH. Of course, you can´t expect doom players to be satisfied with it, but comparing it to other resident evils, it´s just soo good. The graphics are AMAZING. In the first sequence you wouldn´t recognize whetever you´re playing a game or watching a horror movie. The sounds are super realistic, like I´m living in the cellar and oh GOSH, I had extreme paranoia thanks to the amazing AUDIO side of the game. The map is well made and so are the villains. Every villain is very remarkable and each of them actually has motivation for his actions (unlike in Re7 and well, most of the series games :D . )I like the way how you´re going threw the game, every Lord of the vilage has really unique and breathtaking are wich you will remember for a long time, one of them being extremelly spooky.  Your personal merchant, the Duke is mysterious and funny guy, his shop system is working well alongside with the new feature, wich is cooking: You hunt animals throughout the whole map, then bring em to the duke and he will cook you a food that will raise your health/speed etc. The ending is well... As you would expect from the Resident evil, not a masterpiece, but it´s a nice dot behind the whole game I guess. Bonus game mode Mercenaries is good, but won´t entertain you for more than 4 hours. Replayability is nice, you have lots of ingame challenges wich rewards you with completion points. You can spend CP in the BONUS menu tobuy new guns, infinite ammos or artworks. The village of shadows difficulty is HARD, but other than that I feel like you should play HARDCORE right off the bat, it´s not extremely challenging and you´ll get the right horror feeling, just like in Alien: Isolation. Conclusion: I believe in Heisenberg supremacy :D the game is 9.5/10, I only found like 2 bugs in 2 playthrougs and I miss the decision choice from Re 7. STILL, I think that this game could potentially be game of the year and I don´t regret single penny spent on this masterpiece.

In RE4, there's multiple weapons for each type (3 shotguns, 4 handguns, 2 rifles, etc). Village did the same, But here's the issue: when you unlock a new gun, it's straight up just a better version of the previous one. What's the fun in that??

In RE4, the weapons ACTUALLY FELT different from each other: they even had unique features if you fully upgraded them!
In the internet, you can even find forums where people discuss what's their favourite weapon. That's how decision-making comes to place! RE4 put you in different situations and based on your play-style, you had to carefully choose your equipment. This also contributed a lot to replay value, because you could try the game again with a different combat style.
Also, each enemy encounter in RE4 felt unique and satisfying to play. In Village, fighting lycans is stressful, i got tired of them within the first half of the game.

In classic Resident Evil games, you also had to constantly make decisions. For example, you had to do tight inventory management and you had choose which doors you were going to enter. In Village, the inventory is absolutely huge (Why did they place the crafting items in a different inventory?).

Also, there's always only one way to go!!! I thought the castle was going to be something like the RPD in RE2, but it was really disappointing. It felt linear and short. (The only section where i could actually do exploration on my own was searching for treasures in the village, that was probably my favourite part in the game.)
Also, Lady Dimitrescu is really easy to avoid and isn't nowhere as menacing as MR.X from RE2.

The chemical fluid in RE7 was used to make both ammo and health, so you actually had to think before combining it. Now, ammo & health are made from different ingredients, so everytime i found an herb, i instantly made a First-Aid Med (without thinking twice).

[h1]Now some good things :)[/h1]

- Lots of optional stuff: I absolutely loved searching for the treasures scattered around the Village. There are even secret bosses!

- Variety: Each section of the game is unique from the rest.

- Interesting characters: Ethan is way more interesting in this game than in RE7, and all of the the 4 Lords have strong personalities.

- Interesting Story: Village's ending is BY FAR the best one in the entire franchise. RE games used to always end in a generic way (like with a helicopter in a sunset). This is probably the first time a Resident Evil game made me feel curious for what's to come.

[h1]Final Veridict[/h1]

Even though it could have been better, Resident Evil Village is a solid experience and i recommend it to everyone.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a first-person shooter survival horror developed by Capcom. The game is set in the present time, three years following the events of RE 7. Once again, the player assumes the role of Ethan Winters, who, after an unfortunate series of events, finds himself separated from his family and stranded in a remote Romanian village. Here, he will set himself on a journey to save his family and, at the same time, survive the dreadful and unforgiving place.

By far, its story is my favorite in the entire series. The writers have surprisingly taken the Resident Evil narrative to a whole new level, and that’s something I didn’t think I’d ever say. Ethan’s arduous journey to rescue his family is convincing, immersive, and full of mysteries and twists, with memorable moments and characters — definitely an experience that will stick with me for a while.

[h3]A True Horror Experience[/h3] 

The game’s heavy, bleak, and terrifying atmosphere is remarkable. Wandering within the various bewildering and interconnected rooms of Castle Dimitrescu, exploring decrepit sheds, and running in the claustrophobic corridors of a colossal factory definitely felt like a dose of adrenaline. At all times, I couldn’t help but feel this eerie and disturbing feeling of vulnerability and anxiety — always expecting a jump scare or something of the sort at every turn and corner. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2483196646

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]

Gameplay-wise, this title is beyond excellent. From frantic combat to exciting exploration, everything is fluid, well-crafted, and entertaining. Once again, Capcom opted to deviate a little from their last iteration and give Village a more significant focus on the action. At first, I was slightly skeptical about it, as the last thing I wanted was this to be just another mediocre title, with some cheap Michael Bay-style sort of action segments and uninspired gameplay — yes, I’m talking to you, RE 6. Though, to my surprise and satisfaction, it wasn’t anything like that. In Village, they flawlessly attained the precise equilibrium between action and horror, essentially creating the perfect incorporation of RE 4 and 7 into one. Hence, even if you are not fond of this slightly more action-focused turn the game took, you shouldn’t be all worried; because, in the end, the game still manages to be a true survival horror, truthful to its roots.

The pleasant combat mechanic is one of the key features that made this title stand out the most. Whether gunning down a crowd of enemies who dare stand in your way, or just trying to protect yourself with a mere knife, Village’s combat plays fluidly and actually strives to keep the player engaged at all times. In order to stand your ground against the myriad of repulsive monstrosities, you can count on an immense and diversified arsenal that will help you send your foes to the other plane of existence. I’m really fond of the game’s large weapon assortment and how the guns work; each weapon in the game, from shotguns to hand cannons, is unique and feels totally authentic and pleasant to handle and shoot. And things don’t end there: during the journey, the player can additionally find a plethora of attachments to enhance their guns, these varying from extended magazines, barrels, foregrips, and even scopes.

While the game indeed recycles some of its predecessor’s core gameplay mechanics, it also brings plenty of additional features to the table, as well as tweaks to pre-existing ones. One of my favorites is that Ethan can now parry basic enemy attacks in addition to blocking them — which can be pretty useful; it certainly saved my life countless times. The crafting system was also further improved, and it is much simpler and quicker to craft your items this time. Instead of the old mechanic of “combining items” present in pretty much all previous iterations, here, crafting has its own exclusive tab where you can quickly assemble your items by pressing one mere button. And, surprisingly enough, Village has a pretty interesting hunting and cooking mechanic — which works in a very simplified manner. 

Scattered throughout the map, you can find a variety of animals to hunt, ranging from pigs to fishes and even goats. Once you kill any of the animals, it will drop a piece of meat, which can be delivered to the merchant to brew your selected desired meal. Eating certain dishes will highly improve Ethan’s overall stats permanently, such as health, movement velocity, and even how much damage he can take in fights. This cooking mechanic is indeed a very welcomed feature; even with its simplicity, it still is one of the best additions to the title. 

One aspect that the RE series is well known for and nearly constantly delivers in great fashion is, definitely, the boss fights — and here, it’s no different. Village has some of the most charismatic bosses and thrilling battles of the series. Every boss encounter plays uniquely, with each one of them having their own distinctive move sets, attack patterns, and weak spots the player must exploit to prevail in the fight. Even though I didn’t find them very arduous opponents (besides the final one), standing your ground against all the daunting monsters on the hardest difficulty certainly made me break a sweat. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2513232711

To my surprise, the optional bosses are back in Village. There are five of them you can encounter as you progress in the narrative. Even though they aren’t as creative or their fights as unique as the main villains, I still had lots of fun facing them.

The revamped level design is one of the best aspects of the game. Most areas are much more open now — with a surplus of broader sections to explore and secrets to unravel. This novel approach regarding the levels is excellent and also refreshing to the series. Though, what caught my attention the most, was the much more extensive exploration system. Fortunately, that mechanic is excellent, and very much worthwhile. Similar to various horror titles, exploring each part of the map is essential for your survival. Here, investigating and exploring the various intriguing and breathtaking areas in search of crafting resources, ammunition, and all sorts of supplies can be the only thing that determines whether you die or stay alive to fight another day.

[h3]Performance & Issues[/h3]

[quote][i]PC Specs
GPU: RTX 3080
CPU: Ryzen 5 5600x 
RAM: 32 GB[/i][/quote]

Throughout my multiple playthroughs, I, fortunately, had very few performance problems. I played the entire game on the max settings (RTX On) and had a pretty decent overall frame rate; it usually fluctuated around 85-100FPS with no stuttering. The only time where my PC struggled a bit was in a particular section with a bug swarm. Regarding the game’s performance with the RTX turned off, it ran smoothly, far above the 100FPS mark with no problems whatsoever. 

On the topic of bugs, I encountered few of them. Those I came upon were mere collision bugs that caused enemies to clip through environmental props. I also had this weird glitch where every time I’d alt-tab, the frame rate would lock at 20FPS; though it was fixable, however, by just setting the game to borderless.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

Resident Evil Village was, undoubtedly, my most delightful surprise this year thus far. I surely had a great time and have solely good things to say about the game — it absolutely has surpassed any expectations I had. Capcom did everything right this time, from the narrative and atmosphere to the gameplay mechanics; everything was made with the utmost care and attention. Therefore, with all that said, even at full price, I can’t recommend this game highly enough. Village is, without a shadow of a doubt, one of the best survival-horror experiences out there.

Resident Evil Village is 8th installment in mainline Resident Evil series. After two reamkes of older games in the series and the pretty good soft reboot with RE7 it was really interesting to see where the series would go next. Returning to the RE7's first person perspective RE8 is an interesting blend of design from both action focused RE4 and more horror and exploration focused classic RE. And I have to say, this game is really good.

You play as Ethan Winters, the returning protagonist from RE7, who after the incident in Louisiana now lives under protection of BSAA and moved with his family into a remote, unspecified country somewhere within Eastern Europe. Winters family semm to get along nicely, although the trauma after Baker Estate is still haunting them. But everything falls apart when Chris Redfield, iconic character and the veteran of RE, attacks Ethan's home, kills his wife and abducts his child. After the attack Ethan finds himself in the unknown village, controlled by 4 lords and religious leader of the community Mother Miranda. Ethan now has only one goal, find his daughter, who is also stuck in this village, and get out of there alive. 
The marketing for the game was hiding a lot of story elements, I can't really go deep with it without spoiling the whole thing. but despite a few issues with this title, I have to say that the story of this game was really satisfying for me. Ethan's quest ot find and save his daughter and his determination really spoke to me. Maybe that's because I'm also a father to a two younger children. And the character of Ethan really grew after RE7, where he was mostly blank and wasn't reacting to what's happening around him. The four lords of the village are also very charismatic personalities. Each one of them have their own themes and styles and they were developed in a very interesting way. For most people of course Lady Dimitresku stole the show, but I felt like each of the 4 villains left their mark on the game in a meaningful way. And Mother Miranda was actually one of the most hateable villains in the series. And then there is just incredible third act that drops one twist after another. 

The game looks just gorgeus. The village is really detailed, with houses, that tell each their own story, to the castle Dimitresku, to the factory in the late game. I'm sure people, that are fans of photomode, had a lot of wallpapers after a playthrough with the amount of beatiful views you can capture here. The characters and monsters also look great, with a lot of small details that make them really memorable. I also really loved how guns look in this game. There is a range from simple peashoters, to the old weapons with engravings on them, to some "tactical" weaponry that military personell used. And the animation on them looked really good. And the game is very well optimised just like how the rest of the RE Engine games are. There is a lot of different options you can manage to make the game look good and run good. There is even ray-tracing now, although I'm still wasn't impressed with it. The only complaint I have is that the FOV is way to zoomed in, bu on the other hand this is supposed to be a horror game and not a fast-paced FPS. I think that developers still should include FOV slider and give us ability to manage it to at least some extent, like FOV of 90 won't break the immersion, I'm sure of it.

Now the game uses interesting idea of using the blueprint of RE4 and applying it to the gameplay of RE7. There is now much more emphasis on action, killed enemies are dropping loot for a player and there are places to explore where you can find treasures that can be sold. Now that being said, i wouldn't say that the combat is as good as RE4 was. RE4 not only had much better response from enemies after shooting, there was also this element of combat sandbox, that is mostly gone from this title. At the begginning of the game you have section where you have to fight off a horde of lycans, and you have to run from them, hide and barricade in houses, there are red barrels and flour stacks that can be used as a diversion to avoid a group of enemies. But most of the time you will be stuck in a tight corridor fighting few enemies that can be just shot at and outside of picking which weapon to use, you don't really have that much variety in your tactics. 
The crafting is back, but now it occupies it's own part of the invertory entirely and you just need a recipe that will automatically produce you what you need. There is this weird dsibalance in how you can craft a bunch of pistol and sniper ammo, but shotgun ammo was actually so scarce. Crafting it gives you only 3 shells, which is nearly not enough for most of the time. 
The invertory from RE$ is also back and you can upgrade it as well. And placig every item how you want in it, giving you self a personal layout off all the things you need. And that's really cool, RE4 had my favourite invertory system, so I'm glad to see it again.
The big part of the game, just like in RE4, is the merchant. The Duke, as he known as, is a crucial part of the gaem, because he sells you additional supplies, weapons and recipes and also upgrades your weapons. He also can cook food with the ingredients you can find around the village, that you need to hunt-down, almost Far Cry style. Each of the dishes he cooks give you passive upgrades, that are really useful, but you can get all of them only if you actively look for them, since getting the most powerful upgreades you need to find rare animals that are hidden from you. The progression system here is really satsfying, almost more than RE4. you actively feel how your character gets stronger with each new upgrade, but the enemies also ramp up. 
The level design of RE8 is really what sold me here. The main village area is used as a hub between the areas of four lords. And it's not only just an area you just run back and forward, you actually can find here a lot of good stuff for yourself, from treasures, to weapon upgrades, to animals for you to hunt down. But this is not only major area, since it connects you to four different big areas, including of course Castle Dimitresku, House Beneviente, the Reservoir where Slvatore Moreau lives and Heisenberg's factory. Each with their own secrets to find. The game is really packed with what you can do, and even if the main campaign is mostly linear, you still have a choice to find much more. The main village opens up more and more after each lord is taken down, and you get more key items that allow you find more interesting stuff here. It's this metroidvania approach that makes exploration so satisfying. 

Resident Evil Village is a really good game, that I personally really enjoyed. That being said, the response to the game was so lukewarm. I don't really know why so many people find it just "fine" as RE title, because for me this is probably my top 3 favourite RE games that I've played. So take my opinion with a slight grain of salt. This game maybe wasn't a masterpiece that some hoped it would be, but I really enjoyed it. And I hope whoever reads this finds it fun too.
