Let's get this straight. This game has a really lazy game design. If someone tells you it is like RE7 + RE4...well..these people have no idea what they are talking about. In short, without going in-depth: Re7 is all about thoroughly exploring your surroundings, finding stuff hidden within interior or exterior (something can be literally hiding under the desk, you have to crouch to spot and get it), solving puzzles to access new locations, crafting decision and ammo conservation. Re4 is linear, no puzzles if we are being realistic, but is all about CONSTANT INTERESTING COMBAT SITUATIONS, it always throws something new at you and you can deal with it differently, approach situation your way. Both of these games are about decision-making. Re8 is NONE OF THAT. It is Linear. Don't let map layout confuse you thinking it has lots of explorations and thoughtful map design! Scripted events will lead you to key items often and you just have to backtrack through that one corridor in order to open locked door you've seen before to progress using the key which was just freely handed to you! Next, it has dumb and lazy puzzles which toddlers can solve, it has very little amount of enemy encounters and all of them are shallow and uninspired, no interesting or creative situations. Also, there's no point in having inventory similar to RE4, because all the important crafting components are getting stock in a separate inventory menu with no amount restrictions. Back to combat, when I said it is atrocious, I meant it - shooting feels really bad, almost no impact from it. Your character is really slow and there are situations when you naturally want to dodge because enemies are moving fast, but no dodge for ya, only stupid hand block. I mean, when someone giant-sized jumps at ya from above, back in your mind you don't really expect to use hand block, you want to dodge/roll quickly to the side. These character controls are taken directly from slow-paced RE7 and ain't working here. Combat just does not feel good or satisfying. There are no tactics to be made too. There are no clever level designs you could use to your advantage, or interesting enemies to experiment with.

From technical points of view: this game is very primitive for something that has been released in 2021. Yes, the picture is pretty but it is stale as hell. Also not polished perfectly: I had some enemies often clipping through stuff and getting stuck.And where the Hell is FOV slider? In conclusion, I don't hate this game at all, like I stated before - it's just mediocre - and considering the amount of ridiculous positivity towards it for no good reason, felt like I had to speak out.
Btw I like that Village at least tries to be varied in terms of the locations and its length is fair. That is fair to mention.

This is one of those games where Steam's thumbs up/down system is woefully inadequate. It took me quite a bit to decide if I should put one or the other and ultimately decided that thumbs down is too negative for what this game offers. Yeah I would recommend this game but I have my reservations regarding it.

Due to long history of this franchise and the review's word limit, it makes it difficult to put down everything I found problematic or lacking, but in essence it is lack of consistency in the design when compared to previous entries. For those coming into this series at this point, I would actually recommend watching videos and if it suits your fancy chances are you will enjoy it. The game doesn't really lie or try to overshadow its faults. It's more because I'm picky and because I expected more from people who made so many games that outshine this one in the franchise.

The series in general has two major design directions (ok not counting offshoots like Survivor and such). It either follows the atmosphere/tension/puzzle/item management of games like 1-3, or it follows a more linear combat saturated approach such as 4. Games like 5 and 6 for example follow 4 but fail to capture the reasons it was well made. While something like RE2 remake captures the essence what made the original games so good but in a more up to date experience. This game simply can't make up its mind which it wants to be. It is broken into multiple sections that can be complete different ends of the spectrum. One second you might be mowing down  a horde, another you won't have a weapon and you will be running away playing hide and seek under the bed.

The linearity of the level design is in a bit like RE4. Puzzles are simplified, you find a solution for each pretty close to where it is. There is little backtracking or thinking to actually progress, all backtracking is optional for resources. This isn't navigating RPD where you find different bits and bobs that open up things in different ends of the place and you have to figure out how to navigate it to conserve resources (or time). This is fine, as I said RE4 did it much like this, but this game doesn't have NEARLY as much combat as RE4 did. It has good bits in some sections, but again, that whole pacing issue just makes it a disjointed experience.

Some sections are just downright bad or gimmicky. One of the opening segments is to survive endless amount of enemies for a period of time. This ends up far more frustrating because the game did not set a good precedent what to expect out of resources. RE4 did something similar but this felt like a really bad copy paste of it where the missed the point. Kind of like the copying someone's homework and not really reading if the questions matched the answers. Top down is the same, execution, not so much. 

I can't really go into some other segments without spoiling, but the difference in design for them is too stark. I am not quite sure what I'm playing in the moment. Am I playing an action game, am I playing an atmosphere horror game, or am I playing a resource management survival game. It's neither of them.  It doesn't always work.

(I do have to point out that FoV is awful. I understand why, but it doesn't work when you start to lean on combat). You can mod this though.

What does work is adoption of the upgrade system. Even if it isn't as good as RE4 (no exclusive upgrades, and guns are more tiered than sidegrades). It makes combat and replayibility good. To me that sort of thing is fun. Running around in RE4 with the handcannon blowing everything away. Same thing here. In general combat is pretty good but I'm still unsure why they made only Lycans have their heads explode on final headshots. Why not other enemies too. Also enemy variety is sorely lacking as well as how you approach them. RE4 had plagas which could be killed with flashbangs, or you could suplex to make sure they don't spawn. RE2 remake you could walk to avoid lickers. Nothing like that here. You get your gun and shoot.

Look. It's not a bad game. I am recommending it. It does have a severe identity crisis though. I do kind of wonder where the overwhelming praise is coming from. Maybe people never really played much in the franchise? If you want great examples of what the series has to offer play RE2 Remake (if originals are outdated for you) and RE4 (still holds up). They are probably also cheaper than this. But again if you want to watch a dude suffer absurd trauma to his hands (honestly, the hell Capcom...) look no further.

Resident Evil Village is the more action-packed sequel to Resident Evil 7 and the first semi open-world game in the series, featuring optional areas to explore. It is an immensely satisfying adventure, yet has a few flaws desired to be improved when you look at the details.

Pros:
The semi open-world is well integrated. Optional areas are basically loose ends for each session, so they come very naturally. They enrich the game contents a lot as exploration is always a fun part of Resident Evil.

Basically, each session of the game features different level designs offering different experiences. I really enjoy that because it gives a game better pacing and prevents players from feeling exhausted from doing the same thing for long.

Game mechanics such as the merchant, treasures, upgrade etc., are well-thought and well-designed. They help balance resource management and encourage players to do more exploration. 

The resource management design is very smart. It is aligned with progression and learning curve so that the game maintains a consistent sense of tension from resource rarity without causing any difficulty spike.

Key bidding is as comfy as usual. Shooting feels so much better than Resident Evil 7.

Enemy is designed to have attack pattern similar to action games, making combat extra fun.

This game is such eye candy with beautiful visual details. Optimization is very good as well.

This game is more on the intense side instead of being scary. The number of horror session is significantly reduced compared to Resident Evil 7, however, it gets even more horrifying. It is so well done with the atmosphere and pacing, making great use of elements of psychological horror and corridor claustrophobia inspired by Silent Hill P.T.

Music like save room music and the credit song are good to listen to. There are some easter eggs from past games that make old players happy.

It is the first time Resident Evil story gets so emotional and empathic with the protagonist and I like this aspect of it. Lines are also well-written to fit each character’s status and personality.

Cons:
Its map design is more on the simplistic side. It is fairly linear and doesn’t provide enough challenges even it is still the Metroidvania-like design. I wish it was more like RPD in Resident Evil 2.

Puzzles are very easy and not challenging enough. 

Your pursuer(s) is not as stressful as Tyrant in Resident Evil 2 and doesn’t pose much of a threat as there are so many “off-limit” safe areas. This very design makes stealth basically non-exist.

Heisenberg’s design and his boss fight are very Wolfenstein but not very Resident Evil.

Default sensitivity is extremely low. Even you turn it up, aiming with sniper rifle still has low sensitivity, making it my least enjoyed weapon to use. If you are one of those guys like me using low mouse DPI (I use 700), you have to turn up DPI to move the sniper rifle crosshair swiftly.

Weapon-wise, I don’t like some of the design choices, but they are not necessarily a problem for everyone, other than the bug.
•	Sniper rifle doesn’t have enough recoil to feel right, making it more like the laser-like sniper rifle in Resident Evil 4.
•	It is for balance reason, but shotgun is too slow for my liking, taking forever to burst out one shot.
•	There is a bug regarding grenade launcher. You need to press F and right mouse button to change ammo type, however, the game only shows pressing F. 

The map is more important than ever due to the big world scale, but it has flaws. 
•	The color-coded searching indication only works indoors, you don’t get any notice for missing outdoor items.
•	Some large areas are marked as an entire section in the map (e.g. castle rooftop), making item searching in these areas very hard if you miss any.
•	Finding paths in cross-layer area (i.e. factory has many places you need to travel up and downstairs to get to) is inconvenient because you can’t see two floors directly. 
•	Moving map with middle mouse button is inconvenient, Map moving sensitivity is too high (not sure if it is user setting related).

There are some performance issues.
•	Ghosting still exists.
•	Drastic frame rates drop or stutter happens when enemies grab and bite you. It gets very severe when you are bitten by the vampire sisters.
•	When you kill an enemy, the game stutters for like 0.2 seconds. It is more noticeable when you blow up a Lycan’s head.
•	For low specs machines, audio and video desynchronize during cutscenes, probably because rendering characters takes too much VRAM.

I think the game could have done better in these details.
•	Some hidden treasures are so damn well hidden. It is quite frustrating that you know it is there but you just cannot find it.
•	When you kill flying enemies or those on the rooftop, their drop items can be dropped to where you can see but cannot reach.
•	Some items such as iron insignia key and Dimitrescu’s key won’t discard automatically even they have no further use, while most used items will.
•	Other areas have significantly fewer destructible environments and items than the castle.
•	For me, when entering a dark area from a bright place, the brightness change is very uncomfortable, and it takes too long.
•	Some background music is too predictable. Nothing has happened yet the music has already spoiled everything. Also, some of them are very cliché, like straight from popcorn horror movies in the 2000s. The transition between different music can sometimes be very abrupt and unnatural.
•	Strangely, in one session the character would keep repeating the same line. [spoiler]When you have killed three daughters, the Lady will chase you and repeat “The entire bloodline of House Dimtrescu is done in? By the likes of you?!” again and again. [/spoiler]
•	I don’t like the game switching back and forth between first and third person perspective in the latter part of the game. It is not immersive and kind of throws me off. I know it is hard to do some scenes from first-person perspective, but I wish they can stick with it to the end.

The story is not bad, but there are some flaws I just can’t ignore.
•	The whole plot about Chris raiding the house is just marketing clickbait. I mean if you do a second playthrough, you can see it is absurd that he could have explained everything to Ethan in the beginning, he just didn’t. It is unreasonable and pretty ridiculous when you think about it, and makes Chris looks stupid and reckless.
•	Chris’s inconsistency. [spoiler]Chris is like “I don’t want a civilian to be involved”, and then “take this buggy that has rocket and machine gun and fight”. I know the actual plot is a little different (he just asked Ethan to leave in the buggy), but the outcome is the same, [/spoiler]so it doesn’t justify the inconsistency.
•	Lots of things are unexplained. Such as, the history of the village. [spoiler] What is the story with the dagger, the war maiden and four statues? Why Chris moved the Winters to somewhere so close to the village? Who is EVE 002? Etc. [/spoiler] The game teases some of those to players, but never fully explained. I don’t know whether Capcom has a bigger plan for these settings in the future, but for now, the story setting is surely incomplete.

Those are all my take with Resident Evil Village. I am much more nitpicking than normal people because I am a big fan of the franchise, but in fact, I am quite happy with how the game turns out (just do better with the details next time). There are so many memorable sections everywhere and I genuinely enjoy all of those. However, I wish the future Resident Evil:
•	Bring back the stimulus from Resident Evil 7 for any future game with hidden treasures.
•	Bring back the sub-weapon button from Resident Evil 2 so that we don’t have to toss around inventory for explosives and knife.
•	MORE LADY DIMTRESCU PLEASE.

Overall, I found Ethan a little too weak to be believable in his anger. I also wasn't crazy about the 1st person view. CAPCOM had broken ground with two different 3rd person playing modes, but I doubt they would bring anything new to the table with 1st person, and like RE Survivor, they didn't. 

Ethan and Chris are easily my LEAST favorite RE characters in the franchise, so I wasn't expecting much.
So I went into RE8 immediately jaded and found cons quickly:
CONS:
[list]
    [*]Ethan's demise is almost comical. The amount of times he gets severely injured and patched back up is laughable. Without giving away any spoilers, I will say they attempt to address this later in the story, but still, it seems like an 'easy way out' explanation rather than something that closes the loop holes. 
    [*]Shotguns seem useless. Way too slow to reload, didn't make anything more scary, just an inconvenience. When you replay the game with clear data, don't be surprised if you skip shotguns completely.
    [*]Story was not my favorite. Too many holes... too many AWESOME tangents they could have made but just didn't. Felt like a lost opportunity. For a game about a village, you never learn a whole lot about the village and villagers themselves. Nothing of their religion or customs. All you get is an ending slideshow similar to RE4, but even then, you have to go into the un-lockables to get an explanation of that.
    [*]Didn't jump once, was never scared. This one is VERY subjective, so take with a grain of salt. I never have been afraid of werewolves, witches, or vampires personally. So I found it easily the least scary game of the series. Pictures would fall off the wall, bodies would drop suddenly to the floor from nowhere, and not a single one of them had me jump :( I guess the mood wasn't there. Maybe if they had gone a more satanic route, I would have been more frightened. 
[/list]

I was quickly consumed by the pros though
PROS
[list]
    [*]A merchant!!! And an actual interesting/mysterious character he is!
    [*]Variety of challenges
    [*]A money/commerce system for the items!
    [*]Customized weapons and un-lockables
    [*]Gorgeous level design, like the castle
    [*]Superb voice-acting
    [*]Positive RE4 throwbacks like breakable crates, treasure combinations, shooting a sparkly to get jewels, etc
    [*]Great pacing/flow
[/list]

Overall, for better or worse, everybody knows RE4 changed the series. The fact that they took so many things that worked for RE4 and brought them back made this a VERY welcome game for me. After the amazing revival of Resident Evil that was Resident Evil 7: biohazard, Capcom was met with reviews rightly calling this game one of the scariest video games of all time. Unfortunately, this game does not live up to the legacy of the previous game. Is certainly has many scary moments, but the unrelenting terror of the Baker Farm is gone here.

This game is separated into four major sections, and I think that every player will be able to find something in them. From a similar section to the Spencer Mansion to full-on psychological horror, this game uses its variety in setting beautifully.

The gameplay and weapons are wonderful. It controls very well and many points are very satisfying to play. The guns work well and upgrading them is rewarding. There is very good weapon variety and all of the boss fights are memorable and fun, although there is one that very much stands out as not fitting well with the others.

This game has one of the most engaging and emotional stories in the history of Resident Evil. Throughout the whole game you will be rooting for Ethan and becoming genuinely invested in his struggles. Todd Soley's performance as Ethan Winters is wonderful and heartbreaking. None of the issues with Ethan from the last game appear here; he expresses himself and you can hear the emotion in his voice whenever he talks. The rest of the cast is very talented, particularly Jeff Schine as Chris Redfield, and the four lords of the Village, Dimitrescu, Beneviento, Moreau, and Heisenberg. Although, the main antagonist, Mother Miranda, leaves a little to be desired from her performance.

There is a wonderful balance of Horror and Action in the game which, although not what I wanted, is a wonderful place for people who are unfamiliar with the series to join in. I truly hope that Capcom keeps this same balance of genres in future games, because it will keep the series from going downhill again.

Overall, while not quite what I wanted, this game sets out to do exactly what was intended, and is immensely fun. Whether you're familiar with the series or considering playing it for the first time, this is the game for you.

I don't think it will reach higher than some of my favorites in the series due to its sensible downsides, such as more action styled setpieces, pacing and a couple of "What the hell, Chris?" moments here and there. SO MUCH better. SO MUCH more than I was expecting! 

This game is a near perfect marriage of Resident Evil VII and Resident Evil 4 as far as it's aesthetic, tone and the way it plays. The terror factor has been turned down a little from the last game, but instead we get a much more expansive story, a robust weapons/gear system and some of the most memorable new characters the series has offered up in a good while. I normally won't replay new games right away, but I think I'm on my 11th run in the game now (partially thanks to its tough but manageable achievement challenges) and I'm still discovering little details and touches each time. 
Keeping it simple:

Pros: The story is bigger and more involved than VII while not becoming a bloated mess. The characters here are also much more varied and colorful than before. The combat system is simple to learn the basics for, yet harder to master, especially on higher difficulties. The in-game puzzles and challenges (more often than not) hit the sweet spot of being very solvable in the moment while not being too dumbed down or simplistic to enjoy. All of the in-game extra tasks, side missions, side bosses and the rewarding exploration factor are key to replayability. You can do absolutely everything and take your time, stretching the game time to 11-12 hrs or more. You can also fire through only the essentials and finish the story in the time it would take to watch a movie if you so desired.  

Cons: The Main plot of the story can be a little convoluted at times. Some characters don't get fleshed out nearly as much as you'd hope while others make blatantly boneheaded choices to suit their respective motivations. Ethan Winters as a protagonist can get a bit grating with some real eye-roller one-liners and often milktoast characterization. Ethan is a more multidimensional character than he was in VII but that's not saying much on it's own. You do, however, gain more of an appreciation for Ethan as the story goes on and if viewed through the proper lens, he can end up being one of the more sympathetic protagonists the series has ever had. It's just a slow burn to see what the writers are really doing with him and I wouldn't blame some for no longer caring enough when the bigger moments come to really appreciate them. 

Overall, I think RE:Village/RE:VIII is the best addition to the main line of Resident Evil titles since RE:4. There's a lot to love for longtime fans of the series as this seems to fit into the larger Resident Evil world a little more neatly than it's predecessor. New fans shouldn't have any trouble jumping in here without getting lost either. While this is a direct sequel to VII, this game starts off with a quick recap of past events and thats really all the context you'll need for a fully rewarding experience.

I wouldn’t describe myself as a Resident Evil fan, or even really a horror fan. It’s not that I have anything against the Resident Evil series or the horror genre, it’s just not usually my cup of tea. Consequently, if you’re really big on the series or on horror in general, I’m probably not the right person to look to for impressions on this game. That being said, I actually really loved the game, and I think it’s partly because the developers decided to tone down the horror elements a little bit after getting some player feedback about Resident Evil 7- but we’ll come back to that. 

For now, let’s talk about what Resident Evil Village actually is. It’s the latest entry in the Resident Evil series, serving as a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7. Ethan and Mia are together again, and they have a baby named Rose. Predictably, things go bad pretty much right away, and Ethan is thrown into yet another horrific situation, much to his dismay. You start off in a mostly destroyed and abandoned town which serves as a bit of a hub area throughout the game – at the start it’s almost entirely closed off, but you see all the spots you can come back to later with the requisite item to explore. As you play through the game and complete each main “area”, you’ll return to the village hub again and again, each time able to explore a few more of those spots. It’s a really clever and enjoyable system, particularly because it avoids a big issue I often have with metroidvania games – having to remember all these obscure little spots to trudge all the way back to later on. Instead, the flow of gameplay and exploration here is much more natural – you go off to complete part of the story, and always return with something new in hand you can use to unlock more of the hub, which in turn better prepares you for the trials you’ll face as you go back to chipping away at the main objective. 

This part is super subjective, but for me (read: somebody who normally isn’t huge on horror, the only horror game I’ve beaten is RE2: Remake), Resident Evil Village strikes the perfect balance between horror, action, and comedy. I know there are a substantial number of people out there that absolutely loved Resident Evil 7 (which apparently was significantly more scary), but I don’t think I would’ve enjoyed this game nearly as much if the horror dial had been turned up many more notches. I felt like it struck this amazing balance of throwing in a lot of spooky moments and using a wide variety of tools to really build up the suspense and tension on the way there, but also cleverly spreading those out a bit between moments of rest, development of the plot, and points of extreme silliness. The restraint was absolutely critical to my enjoyment of this game – the developers were really clever about knowing when to really amp up the pressure and when to ease off and give you a chance to reset. 

Another thing I really love about Village is how it (apparently) treads more in the footsteps of the more action-heavy Resident Evil 4 as opposed to some of the more horror-heavy games (presumably like 7). Conservation of ammo is still somewhat important, but you’re not necessarily expected to leave things alive, and in most cases doing so will actually put you at a disadvantage. Killing enemies costs you a few bullets, but they also drop treasures that you can sell for money which you can use to get better stuff. This might come off as though the horror-level of the game has been significantly dialed down (if you can just kill everything, how is it scary?), but don’t worry – I assure you it is not that simple. There are plenty of enemies that are not so easily dispatched. 

There are so many other things about Resident Evil Village that I appreciate – the quality of life improvements such as the attache inventory system (and key items not taking up space), the map marking areas of interest and rooms changing colour when you’ve found everything they have to offer, and the generous save points all contribute towards a significantly less clunky Resident Evil than some of the others I’ve messed around with (such as the recent remake of 2). On top of that, the game is absolutely gorgeous, and runs like a dream – I had no problem getting a smooth framerate on 1440p with the settings cranked up pretty high. Lastly, the sound design is just as good as you’d expect from a Resident Evil game.

In all seriousness, I could go on for ages about all the things I love about this game. Resident Evil Village feels like the culmination of the developers working hard to understand a lot of the issues people had with previous entries in the series, and doing their best to correct those things and keep the game out of its own way. The story is awesome and silly, the graphics are gorgeous, the sound design is amazing, and there are plenty of suspenseful and horrific moments to enjoy. Oh yeah, and the boss fights are actually a ton of fun too. 

The game clocks in at about 10-15 hours long if you're not completing absolutely everything, which for me is actually a big plus. It comes in with a bang, stays fresh throughout, and goes out on a really high note without overstaying its welcome. If that sounds too short for you, completionism will amp that up to at least 25-30 hours, and there's also the mercenaries mode for some extra fun.

Of course, no game is complete without its flaws, and Village has several - the most prominent of which being that the puzzles are a bit of a joke. I solved most of the puzzles in seconds, and it feels like a better balance could've been struck here between making them easy enough for people not to get stuck on and making them interesting and challenging - as they are, I don't really see what the point of including them was. There are some other minor gripes, too, I just don't really care - the rest of the game more than makes up for any little annoyances I might have had.

With that being said, this review is going to be one big hot take because I am a little conflicted about my feelings after playing it… I can’t decide if this one dethrones [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] as my favorite RE or not!

This is not a decision I take lightly. [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is one of my favorite games ever made. It’s one of very few games that I’ve played over and over again throughout the years. It's recognized as a classic that innovated games for years after it came out. Hell, over-the-shoulder cameras are still the standard for third-person games and QTEs are still used today – for better or worse. [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] does not do anything that innovative.

But [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool. From start to finish, every environment is engaging. Each of the villains is interesting and entertaining (even Moreau, in my opinion). The story is, of course, nonsense – but it's compelling nonsense that had me wondering what was going to happen next. These are all things that I’d be hard pressed to say about [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. (Remember Krauser and how the only memorable thing about him is the crappy QTE boss battle? Remember the yawn inducing island area? I’d rather forget those things, honestly.)

The humor is back from RE4, and I couldn't be happier about it. Horror comedy is my favorite genre of… well, any medium. This game is absolutely ridiculous and still manages to be spooky. I think Sturm encapsulates this well: he made me laugh as I pissed my pants and that's just the best feeling in the world. 

The action feels fluid, though, admittedly, I missed Leon’s roundhouse kick to stagger big groups of baddies. One of the achievements alludes to pushing an enemy after blocking – maybe it functions the same way? I'm not sure; I didn't know about it before beating the game.

Then there's the hot button issue: this game is not long. It's not massive. Maybe some DLC will make it girthy in the future. However, it doesn't overstay its welcome, either, and I'm glad that this one avoided that issue, unlike others in the series. It's part of why I felt this one is consistently good; Capcom trimmed all the fat and put put out an excellent product.

A really good, RE4-inspired entry in the RE franchise that's only hindered by some issues with the story and a lackluster Mercenaries mode.

The game's strengths are the gameplay and the atmosphere. The game is just really fun to play - even after finishing it multiple times and having mostly everything memorized, it was still fun to start a new game to try to complete certain challenges or difficulty levels. The gunplay is great, guns feel great to use and upgrading them feels satisfying and there is a lot more to unlock in the game after beating it once. Plus, as it is with many RE games, you can have a challenging and scary experience on your first playthrough, then just enjoy steamrolling enemies using the stuff you've unlocked or use them to survive the highest difficulty (which is very challenging).

RE Village's "horror factor" relies a lot more on atmosphere than on jumpscares. It does have a few "jumpscary" moments, but for the most part, it's the atmosphere that makes the game feel oppressive and scary. Even if it's not a game that relies too much on darkness and where you can see everything (for the most part), it still feels like a horror game. Overall, it feels like a Resident Evil game (in a positive manner).

The issues start with the story. It has its up and downs, there are some truly great characters present, but there are also certain parts of the story that are just completely awful (though I'll avoid spoilers here).

The game is split into "sections", with the village serving as a sort of "hub" for the player (though not exactly one). Each of these "sections" are based on a specific type of horror. The game's first half is fantastic: it's scary and the two first sections are very well made. After that, it starts to lose steam gradually: one section barely has any enemies to fight (huge missed opportunity) and another has enemies that are too tanky - which is actually great in making the player feel helpless, but the number of enemies in that section is a little overdone and eventually the feeling of helplessness just turns into frustration and an ammo drain. It ends in a boss fight that is way too action-packed and it's then immediately followed by the worst part of the game, which is even more based on action (rather than horror) and just feels reminiscent of RE5 and 6.

Mercenaries mode is kinda meh, as this time around you only get to play as Ethan. I don't mind that levels have limited number of enemies instead of being survival arenas and I like that you can use money to buy/upgrade stuff, but it feels unbalanced - feels like it wasn't tested out properly. There are 4 stages, then those same 4 stages again on a harder difficulty. The enemies being stronger is fine, but the problem is the very limited loadout you get for those stages and it just doesn't feel very fun to be playing against the odds.

One of the good things about the game is that I didn't notice a single bug in the entire game, which says a lot about how well designed and tested the game is. There were however a few issues with framerate drops in some parts of the game.

Despite the issues the game has, it's still an easy recommendation. It just feels like it would have been so much better if the issues with the story were fixed and if the Mercenaries mode was more fun.

I'm feeling some pretty strong buyer's remorse with this one. This game has an incredibly strong opening, but the pacing takes a dive about halfway through and drops like a rock for the last act, culminating in what might be the biggest and dumbest ending of the series, RE5 aside. It also introduces some glitches at the end for good measure, making me feel like Capcom has hoodwinked me - just as I had restored some of my good will towards them.

Like everyone else who has played this game, I immediately noticed a strong Resident Evil 4 influence, which I didn't mind, as the game also builds up a pretty effective horror atmosphere. The first portion of the game (the titular Village and Castle Dimitrescu) is classic Resident Evil level design with more modern mechanics, albeit with fewer and easier puzzles. I was having a great time exploring and finding secrets, while the controls, inventory management, etc. were largely fluid and intuitive. I will not surprise anyone by saying that I found a strong PT influence with the next area, the Beneviento House, which was a surprise and generated some good scares and filled a Silent Hill sized hole in my heart. I was all set to call this one of the best entries in the series since 2004's Outbreak File #2.
Then the game runs out of ideas, and decides to go the action route, largely dropping puzzles and opting for bland and uninspired locations, with bigger and more over-the-top boss battles. Near the end, I was reminded of the final boss of The Evil Within that had me laughing at how ridiculous it was. The final boss is even aware of how stupid it all is...
[spoiler]Making reference to Chris Redfield's boulder punching exploits from RE5. I can abide by some camp, but that was just too much. [/spoiler]
And then the game somehow takes an even more perplexing tone, turning into something akin to a Call of Duty Zombies scenario - ammo drops, marking targets for air strikes, witty radio banter - it has it all. At this point the game doesn't even let you bring up the map, I suppose because you won't even need it in such a straightforward area with no treasures to find.
Here also is where my audio sync problems began, during at least three cutscenes, having a lag of up to 3-4 seconds. Moreover, I ran into some really ugly looking graphical problems during the cutscenes, including texture popping, frame rate drops, and some distracting texture problems that caused grid-like patterns to appear on helicopter blades patches of grass. I would chalk this up to my computer, but I'd had almost no issues for the rest of the game, nor for the actual gameplay sections at the end. 
I would be curious to know what the development process of this game was like, because it sure feels like the five or six discernible chunks of it were all designed by different teams who didn't talk to each other much; that, or they began to run out of time starting at the Reservoir, and [i] really [/i] had to rush things for the last hour or so. 
And so, I got to experience what might be the most polarizing game I've ever played. I can't think of another time that a game started out so strongly and sputtered so much in the mid-game. I can't bring myself to hate it, as it does so many things right at some point that it felt at least somewhat worth it. It feels like drinking a nice, frosty milkshake, only to discover a big, juicy fly at the bottom of the glass. You can still taste the creamy chocolate in your mouth, but you also feel kind of queasy.

If you're [i] really [/i] curious, I would recommend getting it on a very generous sale, playing until the end of the Beneviento house, and then just watching the ending online.

I am a big Resident Evil and a Capcom fan, and I really enjoyed the recent efforts by Capcom in the franchise, especially RE7 and RE2R.

I unfortunately didn't enjoy RE8. If i had to describe this game in a few sentences, I would say that:
The game feels rushed, and unfinished. This game doesn't play like an RE game, it has a very promising premise, which it disappointingly fails to deliver. 
The design of the game feels cotradictory to itself, it has a lot of cool ideas and designs, none of which it manages to properly set-up and pay-off. 

The long version is below.

The Good:
1) Art-direction - the game has VERY memorable and well made area, monster and character designs. As far as art is conserned - the game is a 10/10.
2) Exploration is fairly well made, you get to back track a lot in particilar areas of the game, and the game rewards you for it with lots of hidden and missible items, upgrades, and even secret mini-boss encounters.
3) The first 3-4 hours of the game are VERY well made, the atmosphere is consistent, there is a right amount of tension and suspense, and the game actualy plays and feels like an RE game.

Cons:
1) The gunplay is average in the begining and is fairly dismall by the end. You have more guns then you have hot-keys to bind, just like in any RE game, but in a well-designed RE game, you have those extra guns not because you will be forced to switch to them in the middle of standart encounters, it's because the ammo in the game is scarce and you choose which guns you will be taking out of your inventory box for the next section of the game, while you collect ammo for the guns you didn't take.
However, this game starts to consider itself a full-fledged action game towards the latter half of it, and starts throwing at you increasingly more enemies, and/or tougher enemies, so if you play on Hardcore, and you collect EVERYTHING, you still often find yourself needing to switch to other guns, that are not in your hot-key selection. The game pauses everytime you go into the inventory menu, so it comes off as very contradictory, because the game expects you to have this fast-paced action scenes, where enemies are fast, or brutal, or both, yet in order to deal with them it gives you almost a turn-based combat system with a slow and clunky protagonist and, a need to constantly go back to the inventory/crafting menu, which pauses the fast-paced action. It doesn't make sense.

2) While we're on the subject of inventory management - there is none. You always have more space than you need, you can basically carry almost all the dublicate weapons (i.e. 2 shotguns, 2 pistols, etc) in the game and still have room for extra. But you won't be carrying dublicate weapons, you will be carrying whatever pistol or shotgun is most powerful in that point of the game, and with 6 weapons in you're inventory, healing items, cooking items, ammo and etc, you still have 20-30% of spare space everytime, no matter what. At this point, why even bother having an inventory system then?

3) The latter 2/3 of the game, after the castle section, is a mess of poorly fit together, different desings. The game shifts to a horror, into a combat puzzle, into a horde survivor mode, into a semi-RE design level with poorly designed enemies, into a Call-of-Duty section (I kid you not).
RE always tried to play with different designs, and that is not a bad thing, but the tone of the game is all over the place, it doesn't fit, it feels like you're playing 5 different games in one, you don't feel like all this places are connected and exist in one Village, there is just no way that that could be. And aside for the Doll House section, and perhaps the first fort encounters, everything else feels poorly designed, you can see what will happen in the room before you walk in to it, all the set up is barebones, all the pay-off is obvious, all the gameplay elements that are waiting for you there are mostly dissapointing and unsatisfying.

4) I have to mention the boss and mini-boss designs. They're mostly horrible, you are usually locked in a tight room with a mini-boss or boss, and you only have and NEED 2 mechanics to beat them, walk to either side to dodge their slow and limp attack, or run away to dodge their slightly faster attack. That's it. 90% of bosses are defeated like this! This is absolutely ridiculious! RE7 had AMAZING boss designs! There were numerous mechanics to defeating Jack (in any of his 3 forms) or Marguarete. They had numerous attack patterns, you could traverse the fighting arenas in many possible ways, use environmental object to gain advantage and etc . These were very well designed battles.
In RE8, they drop you in a small or slightly big circle arena, and all you have to do is move left-right, or run and then shoot. The majority of bosses don't even have any weak points to shoot, you just... shoot them... dodge their attack by walking or running from it... then shoot them again...Until they die... 
I didn't believe it at first, but after the 5-th or 6-th boss fight with the same design, I understood that it was an intentional decision and it was very dissapointing.
Out of all the bosses, the only one that actually has some sort of interesting combat mechanics - is Marou. And Donna Beniviento has a good puzzle-boss design.
The only well designed mini-boss encounters, are probobly the first  big werewolf fight, and perhaps the Otto's windmill fight. That's it.

5) The story. It's nonsencial. They try to make it feel like it was all planned out, but it obviously wasn't, it was written as they went along with the games, and it was written VERY poorly. It makes no sense, characters motivation makes no sense, and the way it is told is abysmal. They just dump on you the plot in the last 30 minutes of the game, and wrap up the show. Horrible plot.

6) While we're on the subject of writing. The character writing is abysmal too. Out of the four lords that are supposed to be the main event of the game, the only one that has actual character arc, a set-up, a culmination, and a closure, is Lady D, that again, makes me believe, that the development was rushed, since she is the first lord you will be going through. Every other Lord, is basically introduced to you via 1, or 2 (if you're lucky) 10 to 20 second cutscene, after which, you go through his area of the map, you fight him, and... his gone. No motive, no character development or character relationship to grow between them and the protagonist, you just go through them like they're an amusment park, and forget about it the second the ride is over.

7) PC technical issues - last but not least of the games problems. It has micro-stutter on most of the enemy kill-shots, a porblem the majority of people playing on PC are having, and Capcom didn't acknowledge or fix the issue in almost a month since the release of the game, as of the time of this review. Very uncharacteristic behaviour from them, their recent PC ports were pretty flawless, and they addresed any issues they've had very timely, don't really understand what happened there.
it is not gamebraking, but it is somewhat immersion breaking, and is pretty noticeble.

For closure - I feel like this game could've been special, and they had VERY cool ideas, but, it seems like the development was rushed, or severly damaged by the COVID-19 epidemic. A shame, I hope Capcom will not only see the sales and praises the game gets, but also listens to the critisicm, so that the next installment will be much more consistent, fun and engaging.

If you are a fan of Resident evil 7's horror element, you will find Village's attempts at horror lackluster. Granted, there are very few scare moments and the developers openly stated that they would not make Village scarier. What intrigued me most with this game was the parallels they made with previous Resident evil games. For instance, Resident evil 8's introduction, castle environment and merchant feature is very reminiscent of RE4. I also loved the replayability of this game as certain weapon upgrades are not available unless you complete the game. The CP system allows noobs like myself to have an edge when playing the game on harder difficulties, though infinite ammo dragoon is way too OP. I did however find that some of Ethan's interactions were a bit weak and some elements of the story could've been replaced with more intriguing events or interactions. 

Positives:
- Fantastic Visuals (I was running this on a 2070)
- Audio has been programmed well
- Replayable
- Very fun final boss fight
- Intriguing story (though not the strongest)
- The enemy designs and models are amazing
- Hilarious line by Heisenburg that references RE5

Negatives:
- Ethan has some very odd lines that I did find strange
- Little to no horror moments except for one boss area that did make me uneasy
- Village of shadows difficulty is harder than taking a watermelon ♥♥♥♥

Overall, this is one of my favourite Resident Evil games. It is a very different game to 7, and I would have to replay 7 to determine which one I would prefer. I would definetly recommend this game, especially if it lands on sale one day.

I have played all previous Resident Evil games, but my favorite prior to this one was Resident Evil 7, the characters, atmosphere, level design, bosses, and overall story of that game was amazing. But somehow Resident Evil Village took what made Resident Evil 7 good, and made it better. 

Level design in this game is some of the best you'll ever see in any horror game or any game in general. Only downside of the 7th game was there was basically one type of enemy, a black venom monster, but in this game it is expanded upon to the extent that I couldn't even imagine the time it took to make this game, There are at least 3 different main types of enemies, and without saying too much, each set of enemies has multiple different variants of said enemy, usually stronger, and bigger. Not even including all the mini bosses in the game, I can think of at least 4 different ones, each one is just as challenging, as not every enemy does the same thing. They will sporadically move left and right, stumble to make you miss your shots, the different animations when you get hit, its perfect.

The main bosses are also another amazing part of this game, the first one you face is pretty hard, but my god, I tried so hard to be scared of her but I couldn't and it wasn't because she isn't scary, its because she has the fattest ass and tits ive ever seen on a video game character. I mean Jesus, they knew what they were doing with that character model, alright, back on track, Every boss offers a different challenge when it comes to defeating them, which makes it hard, but fun. 

Another thing this game does wonderfully is the Duke, which is the merchant you come across many times in the game. Its fun to be rewarded for completing a complicated labyrinth puzzle, or defeat a challenging boss and be compensated for doing said objective. Another thing good about this game was the set up, and pacing all throughout, you spend a considerable amount of time wandering around trying to find every item in every room, doing everything you can to make that room go blue instead of red.

With all that being said, the only fault I see with this game is the lack of puzzles, now I say a fault, but It didn't really bother me, you still have the ball puzzles, and the code lock puzzles, which aren't to hard. But I like to see some more challenging puzzles, like in the RE 2 remaster, which had many hard puzzles, but it was fun. I am also so glad we got to play as Ethan Winters again, It felt good playing as him again, as I loved his character in the previous installment.

In all, this game was suspenseful, scary, confusing at times, very interesting, and very, very well paced. I can say with 100% confidence, this is the best RE game you will ever play. This game, hands down is a 10/10. If you are looking to play an fps horror game, or you want to play it just because its the new resident evil game, or even just a horror game in general, then choose this one. You will not regret paying $60 on this masterpiece of a game. It is simply put, the perfect horror game.

🎮 First Impressions
Resident Evil as a series started losing me for a while.

It drifted away from survival horror and leaned way too far into action.

Unlimited ammo, constant shooting, less tension. It just didn’t feel the same.

This game pulled it back.

👻 Horror vs Action (Finally Balanced Again)
This actually feels like survival horror again.

Limited resources
Slower combat
Real tension

You’re not just running through enemies. You’re thinking about every encounter.

You can fight, but you don’t always want to.

⚔️ Gameplay
Combat is slower, but it makes sense.

Ammo matters again.

Every fight feels like a decision, not just something you breeze through.

You can:

Avoid enemies
Or fight and get rewarded

That balance works.

🧟 Enemy Variety
This was a surprise.

Instead of the usual “same enemy, different color,” there’s actual variety here.

Different designs, different behaviors, it keeps things from getting stale.

Way better than just endless zombies.

🎨 Graphics
Overall, the game looks great.

There are moments where it looks a little grainy, even on higher settings, but it doesn’t ruin anything.

The atmosphere carries it more than anything else.

🏆 Final Thoughts
This brought back my interest in Resident Evil.

I went in already kind of over the series, expecting more of the same.

Instead, it actually felt like a return to what made it good in the first place.

Slower, more focused, and actually tense again.

Now I’m actually looking forward to what they do next.

Brilliant Resident Evil game.. The liking from this game would really depend on your taste in a Resident Evil game. The franchise has had it's fair share of changing genres as the series progresses and both Biohazard and Village (The latest installments) has primarily covered the horror genre for the most part. Regardless of the preferred taste, this game honestly seems to have all of the Resident Evil elements that makes the concept so original. Survival, horror, action, and psychological are all aspects that this game had. I don't think a Resident Evil has ever done that before, at least not THIS good. This game also surprised me with the story, it takes a sharp turn as it wraps up and it caught me off. Needless to say, I was invested and enjoyed the game just as much. I went straight from RE7 to RE8, so my experience is largely comparative. So far, 8 is not as good as 7 was. The Bakers are a hard act to follow. That said, 8 is still good. 

Unfortunately, the opening is exasperating. Where 7 opens with a title sequence over a car ride, and then drops you immediately into a creepy swamp, 8 opens with a tense domestic scene between Mia and Ethan that does very little to set the tone of the game other than immediately "fridging" Mia and kidnapping baby Rose. After so much time spent focusing on Mia in RE7, killing her off in the opening minutes of 8 bugged me (yes I'm aware of later spoilers involving Mia. They don't make the opening scene any less tiring).

After the opening in Ethan's house, the actual intro begins. It's effective. Trudging through the dark in the snow was appropriately unsettling. Pushing through the dead birds hanging from the trees was reminiscent of RE7 enough that I expected Ethan to mutter "not again." When the first enemy shows up, the game does a good job establishing them as not your average mindless zombies. They're fast, animalistic bullet sponges that make you work to survive right away.

Surviving the opening attack is difficult. There's no obvious goal. The village is a maze of dead ends. The enemies come in numbers you can't hope to defeat. Running around and using barricades where you can find is the only option. I died four times before completing it. I'm still not sure what I did to trigger the end of the scene. 

After that scene, it's a bit of exploration and exposition, meeting the game's big bads, and a fun escape sequence through a trap filled dungeon. After that is off to Castle Dimitrescu, to face off against the much-hyped Giant Vamp Mommy Dom and her three daughters.

The whole sequence lives up to the hype. The castle is beautiful and atmospheric. The enemies are typical mindless zombie types, but are used effectively. The four unstoppable ladies of the house punctuate the exploration with intense sections of running and screaming. The fact that they are hunting you, so they show up all over the place, adds effective paranoia to the whole castle. 

My biggest complaint about the gameplay is that now the enemies drop money, or consumables. I feel that design choice was a mistake. Hunting down all the corpses you left behind after a bit fight slows the momentum of the game. With the flying enemies in particular, I found myself trying to kill them when they were close to me, just so I wouldn't lose whatever they drop (they tend to drop a lot of money). I felt like the game was pushing me towards a gameplay style better suited to an action game. The enemies tend to drop more than enough money to stock up on bullets and health stuff, so I haven't felt the extra layer caused by being low on ammo and medicine. In this aspect of gameplay, RE7 did much better.

Where Village really excels is with the atmosphere. Many of the environments feel like they were pulled from Bloodborne (which I mean in the most complementary way possible). They designers absolutely nailed the gothic horror feel. 

Overall, I think it's a fantastic addition to the franchise.

Takes about 9-11 hours to do a complete play-through.


[b][u]The Good[/u][/b]
• Graphics look pretty good. Even on older hardware it is pretty easy to max out the graphics settings and still get a steady 60 FPS, other than a few key points in the game where heavy lag is inevitable.

• The map design is pretty good. One of the few times you can actually have fun while playing this game is when you have a new section of the village to explore.

• This is the first Resident Evil game where inventory space isn't a massive issue. Key items, treasures, and crafting ingredients are all stored in their own sections (with unlimited capacity), so you don't need to spend half the game running back to an item storage box.

• No adaptive difficulty.


[b][u]The Bad[/u][/b]
• There is almost nothing in the game that is "horror" outside of its very excessive use of sound effects. The few attempts that they do make at horror are really poorly done and just seem really low effort.

• There aren't really any puzzles in the game, which is supposed to be a staple of Resident Evil games. The two types of "puzzles" that the game does have are either just pick up an item then take it from point A to point B and use it, or read a note that is directly next to the "puzzle" for the exact solution to it.

• The writing is some of the absolute worst in the series. The way they try to connect a story involving werewolves, mech soldiers, and people with super powers with Resdient Evil 7's story feels, as you'd expect, very forced.

• The characters in this game are introduced and discarded so quickly that none of them have any depth. They only give you a tiny bit of background information on each of them, usually in the form of a bit of text on a scrap of paper somewhere.

• The combat in this game is not fun at all. The developers clearly wanted to make a DOOM-like game, not a Resident Evil game. You're constantly fighting hordes of bullet-sponge enemies, making any progression in the game very annoying and tedious.

• Hardcore difficulty doesn't seem to be much different from normal difficulty except enemies are a bit more bullet-spongie. This doesn't really make the game harder (especially with the ridiculous amount of ammo that is available), it just makes it more annoying and slower to get through the game.

• There are several times in this game when it lags very heavily regardless of how good your PC is or what your graphics settings are. Certain characters have special effects or attacks that will lag the game very heavily. There is also a very noticeable lag spike for just a half-second every single time an enemy dies, for some odd reason.

SO LET'S TALK ABOUT RE VILLAGE
First things first, if you want to buy this game go for it, it became one of my top 3 favorite RE,so yes it's excellent.
Second this review will not have any spoilers of the plot, but I'll talk about game mechanics that you may consider spoiler so caution. Let's start.

INTRODUCTION
RE Village is the newest RE made by Capcom, it is a direct continuation of the events of RE 7 and a spiritual successor of the famous RE 4, in a such way that you can say that this was going to be the remake, or they will use this game as base for a future remake, basically almost all the mechanics and aspects of RE4 are in this game.
The game offers you 8 hours + campaign, with a nice variety of enemies, "variety" of weapons, puzzles, collectables.
Also, a post game with the comeback of the Mercenaries, unlockable weapons and cool concept arts and models, in total if you want to "plat" this game will take you more or less than 40 hours+ to do all the stuff.
It's not a horror focused like 7, it is more a "tension" focused, with a few jump scares, but it delivers the survivor horror that we love really well.

HISTORY
The game has an excellent plot, with memorable characters and locations, also as I said with 8 hours+ of duration, which in my opinion is kinda bad, the game suffers a little of what I call the RE 3 remake syndrome, where the game is rushed, not as rushed as R3 remake of course, but  important plot parts are really fast if you took a closer look, and because of it lost potential of a more deep history, the one that we have is good, really good, but it could be better, the sad part is that it would be, when you unlock the concept arts you see that they were planning a lot more, and this "more" would be fantastic for the game, if RE Village won't win this game of the year, will be for this little lack of content that were missing for sure.
In short the history is fantastic, and probably you will like it, but  it could be a little longer.

MECHANICS
This game being a direct continuation of RE 7 implies that it uses the same first person point of view of it and all of its features, does not present any significant change, they add a "push" mechanic were when you block an enemy attack if you press the button again Ethan will push the enemy away. Besides of it will you have basically the same gameplay of the 7 with the little differentials  being the RE 4 implemented features.
We have the merchant back, so we can sell, buy, and upgrade our weapons in the same way we did back in the day, with the sad part that we don't have the "Exclusive upgrade" for weapons THIS IS AWFUL, I'll talk more about later.
Because of the merchant, enemies drop money, and we have the treasures back, our inventory uses the suitcase mechanic (and yes we have the inventory Tetris back), the health/defense upgrades are based in a new dish feature, were the merchant will cook for us if we bring the right meats of the animal that we can hunt in the map.
In the end the game uses a mixture of RE 7 and RE 4 to give you a really cool gameplay.

COMBAT
As I said, the combat is the same RE7 one, with the "push" feature being the new thing, enemies will take more damage in the head, with the removal of the "critical hit" feature, shooting in the legs will not drop the enemy and shooting in the hand can make enemies drop their weapons, but nothing more than this, so always shoot in the head.

WEAPONS
Oh, yeah the good part, weapons directly influence the combat gameplay and in RE 8 it is good, but could be better.
We have in total 9 weapons in the main story that you can buy, get, and upgrade.
3 pistols
3 shotguns
1 sniper rifle
1 grenade launcher (explosive, flash)
1 magnum
we also have land mines and pipe bombs.
You can upgrade the weapons with attachments, and improve its stats in the merchant in the same way in RE4, but again we don't have the "Exclusive upgrade", and as I said this is terrible.
For you that haven't played previous RE, the exclusive upgrade is a feature when you full upgrade a weapon stats a last one appears that give that weapon a differential, this is perfect because make every weapon unique, and player choice based, but not in RE 8, because of the lack of it, every weapon that have more options of the type make the previous ones obsolete for the rest of the game and future game plays, because the last one will always be better, also trivializes the upgrades that you buy for then, this kill completely the replayability factor of the game with different weapons.
Also, we have more unlockable weapons post game, in total are 7 more weapons, that once you unlock you can buy at the merchant.
The game packs a cool variety of weapons, but in the end you will always be using the same ones.

AMBIENCE
This for me where the game shines the most, I just love the ambience of this game, the RE 4 concepts made this game environment so good, you really fell like you are in a village in Europe, the air, the builds, everything give you a wonderful time, the environment is one of the most important parts of a horror game, it is what make you uncomfortable, tense and anxious, as I said RE 8 is not a horror focused game as 7 were, but certainly  delivers to you a fantastic experience with regard to the environment, this game is beautiful.

GRAPHICS
The game is beautiful, the RE engine always deliver gorgeous graphics for us, this is also the first RE with ray tracing, a cool feature if you can afford it.
But if you talk about optimization the game could be a little more optimized, I have a RTX 2060 SUPER, and the first time I played the game set the graphics to high + RT, in some closed ambient the fps were 70 +, but in the open world was terrible, with a 40 - 50 fps, so if you want to play this game with RT on, you will need a strong card, after I turned off the RT the fps went high, but in the open world and some closed places was little instable again, being 80 fps + almost everywhere and dropping to 50 - 60 fps in those specific cases.
The main problem that I was able to see is some effects that make the fps drop in these cases, and in the open world a general lack of optimization, but nothing serious really.

I only started playing RE games last year, so I do not have the same attachments or feelings of nostalgia towards the franchise like most avid fans do. I AM a fan of RE, however, just not that crazy about it. Therefore, I do not have the belief that all RE games should be the same kind of survival horror that were the original games from the 90s. When I play a game, all I want is just to enjoy the hell out of it, regardless of genre. Did I enjoy RE8? Hell yes. Is it an RE game? Definitely. I have a lot of praises to sing for this game, but most of it has already been said. So, let's talk about some my issues with the game.

1) Unbalanced difficulty across different types of enemies. Some enemies are just a lot harder to kill than others, and I'm not even onto the boss fights yet. Also, the enemies that ARE supposed to be harder to kill are not so. For example, you will not meet a harder enemy in this game than the Lycans (or werewolves if you don't know what they're called). There is a segment in the beginning of the game that involves a lot, a lot of Lycans. It is very tough (absurdly tough depending on which difficulty mode you're on), and you might think that that is a precursor to a harder gameplay. But no. That is probably the hardest moment in the entire game. Compared to that, everything else is a breeze. I am not exaggerating. The boss fights are also absurdly easy. Yes, there are some with their unique challenges, but some are so easy that I personally felt as if the developers did not put much thought into it. It's not a spoiler to say this since they are in every marketing campaign and you know you're gonna fight them at some point - the Dimitrescu daughters. They are so easy to kill no matter which difficulty mode you're on, and a room full of Lycans would have been a much tougher battle.

2) It is a relatively very easy game to beat, unless you deliberately challenge yourself. Let me explain. The hardest difficulty mode is the Village of Shadows mode. Unless you are some pro gamer, you would probably not play the Village of Shadows mode without carryover weapons/ammo/effects from your previous save. Along with infinite ammo which you should be able to unlock (by your own choice) after the first playthrough, you are practically invincible. But, if you like challenges and you play the Village of Shadows mode from a new gameplay, yes it is going to be very difficult to beat. However, it will not be because the game is difficult, but because the enemies have steroids and morphine injected and their health bars are jacked up. The gameplay is still the same - aim and shoot. No ammo? Run. There is not much to think about. Unlike RE2 Remake where you actually had to strategize your routes to certain places, knowing what was in store for you, especially on Hardcore mode. RE7 also required some sort of strategizing despite its linear gameplay. 

3) Replay value is not very high. Yes, if you liked the game enough like I do, you would want to replay it to explore places you've never been to, to get all the other achievements, etc. But there are a lot of unskippable "walking simulator" moments that ruin the experience and pacing of the game. These moments are great for the first playthrough where everything is an experience, but on repeat playthroughs they are boring as hell and serve absolutely no purpose. This is honestly something the developers should have thought of. I have replayed RE8 about 8 times now and I am officially bored. There is nothing new to do. In comparison, I've played RE2 Remake many more times than I can count. There were so many things I could do and experiment in RE2 Remake that I didn't replay to complete the game anymore but just to have fun with the enemies, especially with mods and stuff.

4) Mercenaries mode is just a pain to go through. Granted, I only played it twice on RE4 so this mode didn't really interest me from the get go. But for RE8, I made a decision - I was going to get all the achievements so I'm going to make it through the whole way. After completing 5 stages, I gave up. Everything felt like a chore. From Stage 5 onwards, things get a whole lot tougher and really, at that point, there is really no real reason to play it anymore unless you are really adamant on unlocking one of the weapons or you just like challenges. Like I mentioned earlier, I just want to enjoy the games I play and I do not find joy in grinding. Especially for this Mercenaries mode which really has no payoff for all the grinding. 

5) Enemies take way too long to drop their loot after you kill them. I find that I spent a long amount of time just waiting around the enemies I've killed to finish their death animation so that I can collect my loot. It's a small nitpick, but it does ruin the pacing and adrenaline that's been built up over time. And this is even more important in Mercenaries mode because time is a factor and you also need to collect the loot to purchase/upgrade weapons and for extra points. I don't understand why the loot can't appear instantly when an enemy dies. Probably an oversight from the developers.

6) Lady Dimitrescu. Anybody who's seen the trailer and/or played RE2 Remake would have probably guessed her role in the game. But for the benefit of the minority, I will brand this as a spoiler. [spoiler] For a stalker enemy, she poses absolutely no threat to the player. None at all. She is easy to evade and there are so many safe rooms which are easily accessible in no time. This confuses me because it has to be a mistake. Stalker enemies are usually more challenging than this. Or am I wrong?[/spoiler]

7) The castle segment is truly, truly not fully realized. I'm no game developer, but even I can think of many ways to make this segment even more amazing with the unique villains we have. [spoiler] What would have been really fun is if Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters (when they appear in the castle) can tag team and combo you instead of only individually attacking you, which is sad especially when the daughters would disappear to make way for Lady Dimitrescu to deal with you alone. Also, instead of making Lady Dimitrescu the stalker enemy, why not have all three daughters appear in the castle and chase you at the same time from all directions? Wouldn't that be heart pounding? [/spoiler]

These are the main issues I have with RE8. Now, with the praises. First of all, I absolutely love how unique it is and how bold the developers were to combine very different and unlikely genres into a single game. You get a medieval castle, [spoiler]spooky doll house[/spoiler] and [spoiler]mecha[/spoiler] all in one! How cool is that! Yes, it makes for an inconsistent gameplay. However, I was able to treat the whole thing like 4 mini games in 1, which totaled about 11-12 hours on my first playthrough. That is great! It felt like the developers just wanted to make a really fun game and they decided to go bonkers with it. It's a similar kind of crazy that is found in anime series' like Kill la Kill and Gurren Lagann. It's out of left field but amazing at the same time! The biggest surprise to me was the entire last boss map where I totally did not expect to see what I saw. It is not unique in the grand scheme of things, but definitely unique for an RE game. This will definitely divide fans because it is not very RE-like. Therefore, how you feel about it will depend entirely on the emotional connection you have with the franchise. As a casual gamer, I absolutely loved it. It was a breath of fresh air I never thought I would get.

I would go on but I am reaching the word limit. In summary, I'd say RE8 absolutely knocks it out of the park. It's brilliant for what it is, and it is also a shame because it is so flawed. Imagine what a kickass game we could have gotten if more was done to it and some of its flaws fixed. Regardless, I enjoyed all the time I've spent in RE8 and I have high hopes for the next instalment.

The fact that it's very much a throwback to the fast-paced action of Resident Evil 4 also means it largely takes a step back from the slow-burn scares of Resident Evil 7's excellent opening hours, which may well disappoint those who prefer more psychological dread to blowing off heads. But if you have an itch for action-heavy survival-horror, then Resident Evil Village will scratch it like a fistfull of Lady Dimitrescu’s freakish fingernails.

My rating: 9/10

*  Having completed the game three times across varying difficulties—casual, hardcore, and the formidable Village of Shadows—I can confidently assert that this game is meticulously crafted. The level of detail in design, from visual fidelity to the strategic use of color to guide players, is exceptional. Capcom’s penchant for yellow—from paint to ropes and ledges—subtly directs players through the environment, enhancing navigation without breaking immersion.

Audiovisual Excellence

The game excels in audio design, with its soundscapes effectively building tension and heralding threats lurking just out of sight. Graphically, the game dazzles on higher settings with a remarkable attention to detail visible from the dust on your gun to the natural environment. Even reused assets from RE7 are cleverly integrated, contributing to a rich, cohesive world rather than detracting from the experience.

Gameplay Experience

My gameplay was largely smooth, marred only by a single crash triggered by an exploit I used to unlock unlimited ammo for high-tier weapons early. This allowed for an easier completion of several challenges in my final playthrough. While Village of Shadows difficulty promised heightened challenge, it often felt predictable, with insufficient enemy variation until later stages, particularly in Heisenberg’s factory. Despite the increased difficulty setting, access to powerful weaponry like the M1851 Wolfsbane and the S.T.A.K.E Magnum made even this challenging mode feel less daunting.

Potential Improvements

Despite the game’s overall excellence, a few quality of life improvements could enhance the experience further:
1. **Storage Box in Safe Rooms**: A small storage box for managing weapons and ammo would be beneficial, especially for those looking to unlock specific bonuses.
2. **Dynamic Enemy Spawns**: More varied and dynamic enemy placements on higher difficulties would elevate the challenge and replay value.
3. **Skippable Intro Cutscene**: After the initial playthrough, the option to skip the intro would streamline subsequent runs, reducing repetition and maintaining pacing.

Closing Thoughts

While the game does not revolutionize its genre, it refines and polishes the formula to near perfection. Minor tweaks could elevate it even further, ensuring that both new players and series veterans find continued enjoyment and challenge. The thought of in-game characters facilitating player progress as a tongue-in-cheek nod to game design is a humorous and intriguing suggestion that could add a layer of meta-commentary to future installments.

In conclusion, while not without its flaws, the game stands out for its craftsmanship, engaging gameplay, and immersive world. It’s a commendable installment in the series that most fans will appreciate.

Another great addition to the Resident Evil franchise, Resident Evil Village takes the formula of the last game and builds upon it, making a great action horror game that works as a first person shooter with tense fights and exploration of eerie locations. While Resident Evil 7 was a bit more focused on the horror and survival aspects, Village feels like a natural progression from that as you once against play as Ethan Winters who is now more experienced and confident, making Village feel more like the Resident Evil 4 of this new wave of Resident Evil games. 

The art and sound direction of this game is great, presenting you with a highly detailed world that has a macabre beauty to it as you explore a decaying village and its surrounding locales that are in various states of decay, giving your an uneasy feeling as you explore them. Enemy designs are great, nothing overly flashy or stand outish, fitting right in with the environments that they are found in. The art and design of the weapons is also good, and they feel satisfying to use with good sound design complimenting their impact on enemies. 

As for the horror aspects, I feel like this game is a little worse off in that department than Resident Evil 7 due to there being greater focus on the action portions, and I personally have a hard time actually feeling scared in Resident Evil games to begin with, but a lot of the horror in this game comes from being in tense situations. The game does a fairly good job at making you feel vulnerable to attack if you mess up especially on the higher difficulties, as well as when you are in sections of the game where you can't hurt certain enemies and need to run from them. 

Overall, Resident Evil Village is one of my favorite games from 2021, and whether you like horror games or shooters, I think you should consider giving this game a go, it has a good amount of replay value to it and overall the story is satisfying and the gameplay is great.

I absolutely loved this game, the atmosphere it set was so different from anything seen in RE7 and a lot of games i've played recently tbh. It managed to give you the feeling of fear playing a first person horror game with the tanky and powerful enemies (especially if you play through it on Village of Shadows) that have erratic movements and awesome "scary" designs while also still letting you feel partially in control of situations with the strong weapons and multiple options to clear or get past groups of enemies, even more so if your playing new game plus and have purchased some of the bonus weapons (Handcannon PZ, S.T.A.K.E, infinite ammo for most any weapon etc.). The ability the game demonstrates to switch from one setting to the other seamlessly is also great; to go from running around a luxurious European castle, to trying to find my way out of a massive factory while making them feel both right at home in the Resident Evil universe is really nice. RE8 not only has the amazing setting and atmosphere but the plot and story to back those up as well, it kept me very interested throughout my playthroughs and the lore scattered around to read kept me even more sucked into the game. Although the main layout of events is very predictable after you get out of Castle Dimitrescu there's enough things in between and little surprises to keep the story from getting stale.There is so much more to write about the game but to sum it up this game is a 9/10 for me only not getting a 10/10 because i felt there could have been some more traditionally hard RE puzzles and secrets added in.
