[h1] Resident Evil Village [/h1]

After playing the game on the hardest difficulty available to my first playthrough (Hardcore), and finishing with a playtime of 10.53 hours, I finished off with an experience that had such an impact on my view of videogames today that I felt it necessary to for the first time leave a review.

[h1] I give this game a very strong 9/10.
And here's why: [/h1]

[h1] The Pros [/h1]
Resident Evil is a longbound series that stretches so far back as to 1996, and to keep such a series alive and refresh the interest which each releasing title, is a feat in its own - and Village is no exception. Starting off on the highest difficulty, the game throws you into a world of comfort, which quickly pulls a 180 on you and you're instantly forced to brave the dangers ahead, much like previous titles such as Resident Evil 4. This game doesn't just try to work as a First-Person Shooter - it ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ owns it! The Combat is smooth, the whole world is one big map, and not once did I have FPS issues. The game force you into a realization that you're against all possible odds and invite you to take your first babysteps to take control. Wonderful Character introductions flourish in this Capcom masterpiece as I was both laughing, gasping and downright yelling (sorry neighbors) as plottwists were delivered right left and center. Even when you feel like you have braved the worst, it throws you back in the lion's pit, and a fresh hell awaits you - but each time you pull through, you have more to show for it, and the merchant system offers rich rewards for those who dare to venture where none have returned! Already when I entered the first major area of the game, I was presented with a choice: Either do what you're here to do and leave - or leave no stone unturned and loot all that isn't nailed down! Being the absolute sociopathic hoarder I am, I went with the latter, and I was not disappointed with the resulting bounty I had at the end of the area! It is said that one should not overstay their welcome, well I say they're wrong - stay for as long as you want and loot all you can, and you'll find that the biggest dares offers the richest fruit. Each time I went into a new area of the game I felt like something new was waiting for me, and after hours of playing I went from pissing myself from having to confront two enemies at once, to laughing as they came at me in dozens. Resident Evil has always been a series to make you choke on your own breaths, and Village is definatly no exception! You want horror? You've got it right here!

[h1] The Cons [/h1]
While Village definatly is a masterpiece by today's standards, it is unfortunatly not free of the plague that are cons, and while there aren't that many, the ones there are did unfortunatly ruin my experience enough to knock of a whole point from the final result. To begin with the game does an amazing job at producing the helpless scenario you find yourself in, yet with helplessness comes panic, and with panic comes irrationality, and with irrationality comes mistakes - and mistakes can ruin the immersion quite a bit if you do them too much. At one section of the game, which shall remain unspoken for the sake of spoilers, the game pushed me into a situation that forces me to put as much ♥♥♥♥ between me and the enemies. However, the enemies continue to bash it down, forcing me to flee from house to house until I have nowhere left to run. With no options left, I decided to just jump off the building and run, yet I had no idea where. A few deaths later, and my immersion beginning to be exchanged into frustration, my friend tried to aid me best he could. Yet since he didn't 100% what to do, I died a few more times and this was where my immersion was broken, a total of 6 deaths before I asked my friend to google for me, and he found out what I was supposed to do. I was apparently supposed to survive for long enough until a certain enemy emerges, at which point I was supposed to run to a certain place, where apparently an arrow would be shot into my leg. As I made my way to the place however, RNG reared its ugly face, and I almost died a 7th time. Make note that none of this was affected by the difficulty - I just didn't have a single clue of what to do, there wasn't even an objective going up saying "Survive" or "Escape". The second thing which ruined the immersion was during a perticular chase scene which I shan't forget until the day I perish. The chase section was indeed panic-inducing, yet when I hugged the elevator's gate and tried to find a key prompt I was presented with nothing. I panicked and ended up smashing my F key against everything - the power box, the elevator's bars, the button, but nothing happened. The enemy caught up and I died, and there goes my immersion yet again. So what was the solution? Apparently you must stand right infront of the elevator button, right deadcenter infront of it, in order to get the prompt. This infuriated me beyond words.



[h1] Final Verdict [/h1]
Despite the small cons, I only had those two moments in the game where I felt my immersion and experience ruined. I had no issues with the enemies, the weapon system, the merchant system, the treasure rooms, the areas, the map layout, the exploration, the combat system, the bosses, the upgrading system, none of it. And I have to be honest with you; it's been a really long time since I enjoyed a game this much. I will definatly be playing it again, with the new items you can get from the Bonus Shop, where you can use the points you gather from the game you play and buy new items you can use in future playthroughs. I can't really say the game is worth it's 80€ on steam, but if you can find it for a cheaper price, it's definatly worth it.

Here's my spoiler-free review of Resident Evil Village. At the time of writing this I've finished the game 5 times, completed all available challenges, went through all difficulties and checked pretty much everything the game has to offer. I've enjoyed the overall package, so I'll be focusing mostly on its faults.

[h1][b]Fine Status[/b][/h1]
For those that are concerned about the duration of the game, I can share some good news: depending on your picked difficulty + play style approach, the game could be anywhere from 10 to 20 hours. For my first impressions I picked Hardcore, did tons of exploration and sightseeing, ended up with 15 hours of in-game timer, even more on Steam playtime due to restarts and deaths. The quality of the segments always felt top-notch throughout the experience and there wasn't a segment that felt particularly rushed.

While RE7 had like 3 goo monsters for the whole game, in Village the variety is back on the menu. It's not as mutation-rich like RE6, but the roster is decent, and you don't get the "not this same-looking thing again" feeling that plagued 7. If I had to complain then I'd mention that some enemy design in terms of attack patterns is a bit annoying, especially during the first playthrough.

Exploration is really fun in this one, as Village looks gorgeous. You can see the areas that you're going to visit in the distance, similar to Souls. It's possible to explore at your own pace and the visuals are a consistent eye candy unless you start noticing recycled assets from previous RE engine games. The pacing is excellent, as it balances between action, exploration and horror.

The gunplay is okay. There are a couple of things holding it back: as of now there's stuttering (see PC Specifics) and on higher difficulties B.O.W.s become far too spongy for my taste. I would rather prefer more dangerous and aggressive behavior or at least increased numbers, but not basic spongy ORC-style B.O.W.s that rarely flinch to begin with. On the flip side, the firepower arsenal has been expanded, you can carry more weapons and they are upgradable. Weapons progression is satisfying, it's possible to do the old RE4 ammo refill trick, the selection of weapons is versatile yet traditional. It gets expanded even more once you finish the game and unlock bonus content.

[h1][b]Caution Status[/b][/h1]
Standard difficulty showers the player with ammo, Hardcore provides much better resource balancing, but also gatekeeps new players with an unfair difficulty spike right at the beginning of the game. It's not representative of the overall difficulty and is rather frustrating experience for an unsuspecting player. As a whole package Hardcore provides just enough resources to keep the player on the edge, giving something I'd call "resource management anxiety": the player being scared of spending ammo too inefficiently, rather than being scared by B.O.W.s themselves. A satisfying survival horror game won't force you to run away unless it's a scripted/timed sequence.

Village of Shadows difficulty is the arrange mode of this game that shuffles B.O.W.s around, throws in extra surprises, and you'd think it would be similar to RE7's Madhouse, but it ain't. While it is possible to finish your first playthrough on this difficulty, I wouldn't consider it to be an "enjoyable" experience, as the balancing is geared towards returning players that have completion unlocks. See it as RE3's Infernal difficulty.

[h1][b]Danger Status[/b][/h1]
It's time for the annual soundtrack complaints. RE7, RE2 and RE Village share a common approach to audio design - ambience during exploration, a suspense theme when B.O.W.s are alert or searching nearby, battle themes for the boss fights and a dramatic last stretch theme. Only RE3 breaks this mold by utilizing a remade original soundtrack, which gives the game a deeper atmosphere that the other titles lack. I didn't expect much, but Village sounded really generic and nothing caught my ear except for maybe The Mercenaries theme, similar to how the best themes of RE2 were in the DLC content. I believe that a distinct soundtrack would compliment a survival horror title, classic RE titles and Revelations did it right.

There were quite a few scenes that were painfully cliché. You enter a room and see all the set pieces in place: the trigger, the ambush and the place where things will go bad. Is this supposed to give the player awareness and cause anticipation anxiety? This happens a bit too often and even in some cutscenes it's possible to accurately guess the outcome. I can't say that predictability is a good quality in a horror title, but then again I've heard rumors that Village has been intentionally toned down, since RE7 was "too scary". If so, then I disagree with such decision entirely.

[h1][b]PC Specifics[/b][/h1]
Reach for the Moon Engine scales well with older hardware. If you've played any of the previous games using this engine then chances are you're going to experience a similar performance profile. I was pleasantly surprised that the demo and the main game ran mostly at locked 60 FPS, which is also the target frame rate on consoles. The options menu is vast and there's a nice amount of tweakable settings.

However, as of now there are a few performance bugs that can negatively impact the player's overall experience, depending on how sensitive the player is to them.
Every single time you land a finishing blow on a B.O.W. the game will stutter, and it's certainly ain't yet another implementation of Capcom's Hit-Stop technology from Dead Rising. Does it occur on consoles? No. Does this make the game unplayable? Also no, as I've went through all the game's challenges while having this bug.
Whenever there are a lot of insects on your screen, the frame rate nosedives to the point of being barely playable. This can be avoided by not nearing the bugs, but even then it's not something that can be ignored.

Temporal Anti-Aliasing is not working correctly, since any other RE title will have visible ghosting when there's some kind of motion. This means more aliased image unless you bump up the resolution or resolution multiplier.

I can agree that most video games should have an FoV slider and that it is not acceptable not to include one. We should not be resorting to 3rd party patches for such basic accessibility option, considering that narrow FoV can cause motion sickness.

After watching Digital Foundry PC port review done by Alex Battaglia, I can agree with everything said in the video. So here are a few things that I'd want to highlight.
When I first booted up the game I was confused by the slowest license agreement scrolling I've ever seen, then following by a menu that clearly was not designed for a snappy keyboard and mouse experience. The in-game default key binds are comfortable enough, though.
Variable Rate Shading is completely messed up and defeats the purpose of the setting. It's not configured properly and should be not used as of now.
Ray tracing settings lack any sort of future-proofing, allowing a console-like experience at best. I personally enjoy pushing old games to their limits, especially if they offer options that would absolutely destroy the frame rate on hardware of the time. In this case the resolution of the effects is so low that it can look worse than traditional rasterized graphics.

Sincerely hoping to see the game receive the necessary performance, graphical and QoL patches.

[h1][b]Conclusion:[/b][/h1]
For the duration of my 100% challenge completion I've mostly had fun and I didn't experience burn-out. The game has good levels of replayability thanks to its distinct locations, the player's arsenal of weapons and balanced pacing. As the developers said, Village is certainly more action-oriented and it's good at what it does, same as Resident Evil 6.

So, here is a pretty detailed review WITHOUT SPOILERS. First of all, I have to say that I absolutely LOVED Resident Evil 7. I have finished it half a dozen times on PlayStation and I had very high standards for this new installation. To be brief, Resident Evil Village might not have been as good as its predecessor, but it was very fun and I will surely continue enjoying it.

The first thing you notice while playing the game is that it is much more "open" that the last installation. Instead of being in a house, or residence, you are in a wide open area, except in some parts. The lighting is very different than in other horror games, making it a bit more "friendly". There is ammo everywhere in the map, so you don't have to worry about being left without weapons and the addition of the merchant helps you get whatever you need. The story and all the characters are well developed, not as much as the ones from RE7, but pretty good nontheless. The only thing that I didn't like in that part is Ethan's voice-acting and some voicelines of his that just ruin the vibe and seem completely out of place. The story is well driven, until a point, at which point it just seems ridiculous. The atmosphere is much lighter and the game isn't scary at all, except for a part around mid-game that most players pinpoint as the scariest part of the game, if not the series. I finished the game in around 8-9 hours without rushing.

What I enjoyed very much at the last game is the fact that it doesn't end when you finish the story, but continues through countless extras. This game doesn't have that much extra content, so far, but it is enough to keep you busy and is pretty fun, too. I really hope that CapCom makes more content on RE Village.

So in conclusion, the game is not as scary as others in the series. Although there are some flaws in the writing and voice-acting, I had fun playing it and will continue enjoying it. As for the price I don't know if it fits this game. I think that it is worth it, but if you don't want to pay full price, it's better to wait for an offer. I would recommend it to anyone, whether they are a fan of the series or not. I would rate it 8.5/10

I'm just going to leave a  somewhat short review for the time being, until I have the time to write my full thoughts. 

With that said, RE8/RE Village for me was absolutely phenomenal. It truly is a blend of RE7+RE4; while still feeling like it's own thing (Because it is). I finished my first playthrough on Hardcore, which is the difficulty I recommend starting on *if* you're a RE/survival-horror veteran like myself. Even though during the first Lycan fight/interaction on Hardcore it can feel frustratingly tough especially if you're unaware of what to do to progress. 

Though, after that sequence the game is very well balanced in it's difficulty on Hardcore, for me Standard/Casual enemies are a bit too easy to put down and ammo/crafting resources feel a tad too plentiful. TL;DR Standard/Casual will have the game feeling like it's leaning harder towards RE4 vs. RE7, whereas I'd say the opposite on Hardcore.

RE Engine shines once again, RE8 is absolutely beautiful graphically and it's art style is very well realized. Combat/gameplay is responsive and fun, Guns have a lot of punch to them and feel great (Much like RE7) which makes the combat that much more engaging and satisfying. 

There's also quite a lot of weapons to get your hands on, which also boosts replay-ability given the fact some weapons won't unlock until you've finished your first playthrough, some will also become available to buy in the bonus shop. So, NG+ is totally worth it IMHO, and there's also an unlockable (Unless you bought the deluxe version, in which case it's available from the start) harder difficulty called "Village of Shadows" which is very tough, but all your NG+ weapons/gear make it quite fun.

Each area has it's own detailed, well realized style. Generally speaking also quite varied which I found to be a great thing, especially the way each area interconnects with the Village, which also is very fun to explore and unlock sections of. Some areas (Especially one area in particular) being scarier than others, but all of them have their own mood and atmosphere. And I personally loved all of the locations. 

For story/characters, this is IMO arguably the best Resident Evil has ever been, especially the last Act of the game. I never thought a RE game would make me emotional but hah, RE8 proved me wrong. Is it over the top in that vintage RE sort of way? Sure, sometimes. But RE8 does have it's darker, more serious moments, and for me it was very effective in pulling me into those moments.

Highly recommended. It's a great RE game, and just a phenomenal game in general.  Though numbered reviews aren't my personal thing, if I were to give RE8 a score out of 10, I'd say for sure a 9/10

The bosses are fairly simple and don't require too much preperation so if you are looking for a challenge I recommend not starting on the normal difficulty.
When it comes to graphics and sound this game is a masterpiece but please be aware that even with the latest hardware you can expect some FPS drops here and there, I'm hoping this will be patched somewhere in the future.
For me the game has crashed twice in my current 14 hours of playtime but the auto-save this game offers should save you from losing any important progress.

I highly recommend this game and I am unable to stop thinking about all the details I might have missed on my first playthrough! So I'll jump right back in to this wonderfully created world of horror once again!

Oh man, where to begin?

For the record, I never really paid much attention to [i]Resident Evil[/i]. I vaguely remember the days of [i]Operation Raccoon City[/i] and wrote it off as just another franchise being run into the ground.

I'd played a bit of the first game and found it clunky and annoying to play, mostly because of the fixed cameras. I did manage to finish RE4 and, at risk of being crucified, it was pretty forgettable with painfully cheesy writing and an arcade-style gameplay loop that'd well and truly forgotten its supposed roots in survival horror.

So, life story aside, I was never a big fan of [i]Resident Evil[/i] - or horror games at all, for that matter - and didn't exactly have the series on my radar. Until quite literally a week ago. 

I was bored and had heard good things about the new one, so I decided to check out 7. It was good. Really good. The change to first person was a huge improvement, gameplay had nice progression and damn, did they nail the atmosphere. Not to beat a dead Lycan or anything, but the reboot has proven to be the best possible thing for a previously stagnating series. 

Capcom should be applauded for throwing away the established formula and experimenting. As we've seen with [i]Demon's Souls[/i], [i]Spec Ops: The Line[/i] and similar titles, creativity rather than overbearing executives and enough of a budget to back it up leads to some fascinating and memorable games.

And so we come to [i]Village[/i]. Going into it with little knowledge or expectations beyond what I'd played of 7, I was interested to see what all the fuss is about. 

Ethan Winters just can't seem to catch a break. Now out in the backwoods of Europe, an attack on his family has brought you to the titular village where shadowy forces have overrun a once tight-knit, if reclusive, community. Desperate to find Rose and get out alive, it soon becomes apparent that things aren't quite what they seem. 

Looks like you'll have to do this the hard way.

[i]"Just go out and kill a few beasts. 
It's for your own good."[/i]

In terms of moment-to-moment gameplay, not a whole lot has changed from 7. Ethan no longer feels like the bumbling idiot that could barely hold a gun at the start of the previous game, but if you're expecting this to be a bombastic, run-and-gun affair, [i]Village[/i] is very much its own beast.

You'll scavenge for supplies, craft items and slowly navigate the township as the cramped spaces of the Baker house have been traded in for roads full of bloodthirsty maniacs. Speaking of which, there's a nice range of enemies on show here, with many of them acting erratically and forcing you to time your shots carefully. 

Looking at the screenshots, it should comes as no surprise that RE8 is absolutely gorgeous to look at. The art team deserves serious props for the attention to detail they put into each of the locations. If you're lucky enough to be playing this with ray-tracing, the lighting is really something else as Ethan travels through dark crypts, opulent halls and ruins caked in muck.

Backtracking is sometimes a necessity, but thankfully the environmental puzzles don't affect the pacing that much and there's good incentive for players who are willing to explore off the beaten path. Duke signals the return of the merchant; a likeable character that gives you a reason to trade all that hard-earned loot and upgrade your arsenal of weapons.

Sound design is also great and the whole cast did a great job with their performances, although Lady Dimitrescu seems to have taken centre stage in the game as much as she has in marketing. I can't really speak to how effective the scares are because I find horror very predictable. There is one moment, however, that was insane. If you've played the game, you know what I'm referring to.

But what about the story?

This is difficult to talk about without getting into major spoiler territory, but I've seen a lot of talk around [i]Village[/i] becoming too focused on action over horror. Even ignoring the RE4 in the room, I disagree with the idea that it's lost sight of what the new trilogy was meant to be.

The whole point of 7 was to build Ethan up from basically nothing. At the beginning of the game, you were brutally beaten into submission and shown just how laughably outmatched he was in comparison. Jack shrugged off gunshots and, even when he [i]was[/i] killed, would quickly regenerate.

By the end of the previous game, Ethan had been forced into becoming a hardened killing machine. Even the quips in dialogue reflected this, as he went from being a scared survivor to just pissed off, before ultimately facing down far more than a zombie or two.

As [i]Village[/i] is a continuation of his storyline, it makes sense then that he wouldn't be back in the same disempowered position he was previously because it would completely ignore the growth of his character.

Sure, a lot of this depends on the difficulty you play on, but I enjoyed RE8 a lot... specifically [i]because[/i] it rode that line between action and horror so beautifully. I don't want to spoil anything but the final part of the game in particular was brilliant. 

I was psyched up as things began to converge for some much-needed payoff. One twist might not sit well with longtime fans of the series, but [i]Resident Evil[/i] always seemed kinda bonkers anyway with the viruses, Umbrella and a certain boulder so it didn't bother me that much.

The game itself is very polished, only a few visual bugs like hair jumping a bit when loading in or some clipping but nothing significant enough to detract from the immersion. In the age of half-baked ports and Early Access, it's nice to see a game that has clearly had so much love put into it by a team that genuinely cares.

[i]"Fear the old blood."[/i]

As a whole, [i]Resident Evil Village[/i] is well worth a look with a good chunk of gothic horror to really sink your teeth into. Or claws. With the potential left open from its ending, I'm looking forward to seeing where the series goes next, but for now, I reckon I'll be checking out the remakes.

I want to preface this review by saying I thoroughly enjoyed this game and hope to see DLC that can expand on certain characters present and cut. Anything I might say past this might contain a few spoilers so read at your own discretion.

The games pacing was decent, weapons feel good, inventory management is satisfying, the replayability in some sections is lacking since you'll know for certain what to do (you will know the sections as you complete them). There are certain sections in which the tension is ramped up to 11 and it really sets a great tone, unfortunately afterwards you never quite hit the same high. The inability to go back to some certain sections and check everything after it is done is a small disappointment as it could lend to the game being more fleshed out. As for the tonal shift for certain lords,  I understand the decision to switch from periods of high tension and low tension to accentuate the high tension areas, but I feel like they could have ratcheted it up a little more often toward the end. 

The only major gripe I have is playing the game on Village of Shadows difficulty, it isn't very fun to get through after having beaten the game on Hardcore/Normal/Casual. I am eagerly anticipating DLC for the game, hopefully a continuation of Chris's involvement in the background of the games events as is eluded to when you play through. [h1]Resident Evil Village: Just a Nibble, or Maybe a Bite?[/h1]

Well, it's finally here. Only announced a year ago in June 2020, but what a long year it has been. The sequel to Capcom's stellar return-to-form Resident Evil 7 promises pulse-pounding action, spine-tingling horrors, and of course buxom vampires to die for. But is it worth the price of admission, or should you grip your cross tightly and wait for a sale? These are my thoughts:

[u]The Nitty Gritty[/u]
Standing as a direct sequel to Resident Evil 7, Ethan Winters and his wife Mia escaped the Baker plantation and have spent the past three years living in secrecy with their newborn daughter, Rosemary. Despite his best efforts to keep his family safe Ethan is separated from his daughter, and now must journey through a quaint Eastern European town bordering an imposing palatial castle filled to the brim with lycanthropic monstrosities. And oh, there's a swamp and massive foundry nearby, whod've thunk. Ethan quickly finds himself pitted against the Four Lords led by one Mother Miranda, an imposing figure that seems responsible for both the destruction of the town's inhabitants and the kidnapping of Ethan's daughter. Now Ethan must struggle not just to save Rosemary, but along the way survive the onslaught of these terrifying baddies. Any lucky gamer that has had the treat of experiencing Resident Evil 7 will know that the game oozed horror. 

Resident Evil Village doesn't skimp on this, but it doesn't gorge itself either. The first half of the game is reminiscent of Resident Evil 2 Remake's constant fear of the imposing Mr. X in constant chase, and Resident Evil 7's terrifying atmosphere and sound design to make even walking around an empty village nerve-wracking. And yet, in cozying up to RE's previous action titles, Ethan eventually finds himself running and gunning like an action hero, slaying hordes of monsters like Doomguy (on a slow day). It's not a bad presentation, but by the end of the game there is no question the title strays far from any semblance of survival horror. Complete with action-man one-liners, Ethan feels less like an everyman and more like a John Rambo. It's not bad, but it is worrying given Capcom's past record with the series.

[u]But How's the Gameplay?[/u]
For better or worse, Resident Evil 4 was a watershed for the series. Beloved not just by Resident Evil fans but also action fans, its gameplay loop is recreated in beautiful fashion here. Whereas its predecessor Resident Evil 7 featured limited inventory space and equally limited weapons choices, Village brings back 4's attache case in all its glory. The player collects funds from downed enemies or suitably hidden valuables, and trades them in to a local merchant in return for medicine, ammo, and upgrades of their weapons. Sound familiar? Well it should and that's the point, our resident merchant "The Duke" even quotes RE4 cheekily ("What are ya buyin? Hehehe"). 

Innovating further on the formula however, Ethan will have to scrounge for materials laying around which can be combined to form ammo, healing salves, or even explosives. It's a fantastic addition to an already addicting system, allowing the player to adapt and construct whatever they may need moment to moment. Out of ammo but you spent all your money on upgrading your pistol? No problem, just make some pistol ammo and blast away. Finally, there is the addition of cooked meals which The Duke can prepare for Ethan, so long as he brings him suitable materials. Upgrades range from increased health, blocking damage, and even increased movement speed. By game's end, Ethan will be running like an Olympian blasting opponents with a veritable arsenal of cannons.

And therein lies the problem: The moment-to-moment gameplay is spectacular, and there are moments when you will be begging for more enemies to endlessly mince with your shotgun. In return however, as this gameplay loop becomes more prevalent any survival elements are eschewed in favor of frustratingly-designed dungeons and frenetic action.

[u]Wait...You Said Frustrating?[/u]
That's right. For all its graces, Village is not without is flaws. The terrifying atmosphere we're treated to at the game's intro, along with the persistent danger of Lady Dimistriscu and her three psychotic daughters, all evaporates in the latter half of the game. Each of the Four Lords Ethan must defeat have their own demesnes he must traverse in order to defeat them. The first two are positively chilling, with suitable level design and moments of terror which can only be seen to be experienced. But by the time Ethan sets foot into the swamp to battle the disgusting Lord Moreau, the game veers heavily into action setpieces, and once you enter Heisenburg's Foundry all pretense of horror flies out the window. Blasting monsters cranked out on assembly lines, the only terror you will feel is that of frustration in trying to navigate its confusing hallways. 

[u]Just Give it to me Straight, Should I Buy it?[/u]
Yes. Resident Evil Village is worth every penny of your $60, perhaps then some. It is not a long game, easily beatable in under 15 hours even collecting every little do-dad, but by the end you'll appreciate the love and care that Capcom brought to bear in constructing the conclusion to Ethan's story. Though it slips up here and there with its tonal shifts and approach to gameplay, Village is a worthy entry in Capcom's 26-year-old series (yes you are getting old aren't you?). Where the series is headed anyone can guess --it's going to be Resident Evil 4 Remake by the way-- but Village isn't just another shoddy attempt at slapping the name on the box and cashing in. You should definitely play it to see the fusion of RE4's gameplay mechanics and RE7's terrifying atmosphere.

Im giving this game a thumbs up for the sole reason that as a GAME its good.  Graphics are beautiful, gameplay is solid and extremely well optimized, and most importantly the combat is fun.  It also has a lot of "tip of the hat" moments to Resident Evil 4 that I really appreciate to see devs doing.

But trust me when I tell you (and I know I'm gonna end up getting some hate for this...so I will open the comments up for anyone who would like to rebuttle).  But,  I have a lot of negative things to say about where the STORY of this game is going.

Before you stand up and try to smack me across the face with your keyboard!!!   Let me explain:

Lets rewind a bit to 1996.  Im 12 years old, hanging out with one of my best friends back then doing a sleep over at his house.  He wanted to show me a new game he got (Resident Evil).  He popped it into his PlayStation, I mean the old PlayStation too (not the newer slim ones) the fat one.  We had to play it on his parents TV in their room (his brother was on the TV in the living room playing Need for Speed), so we were forced into the parents bedroom by default.  The TV was  up on an unneccessarily high dresser.  So we sat indian style on the bed, controller in hand.  

The game fires up, and we start playing....WOW!!! The game literally blew me away.  Mind you graphics back then weren't anything special, but for a 12 year old who didn't know any better I must say I was impressed to see what computer graphics were becoming.  The bad acting in the cut scenes didn't phase us because we were locked into the story.....and we were 12 so we didn't really know what bad acting was.

But still, the game was great for us.  I think I can speak for all of us when I say the first time we experianced the dog crashing through the window in the hallway for the first time none of us got any sleep that night!  The story of the T-Virus infecting the human race as zombies was such a basic premise of a story and easy enough to follow.  It had nothing but horror elements, all the way up to the game over screen.  Needless to say I was hooked.   I jumped on Resident Evil 2 and 3 when they came out and loved them just as much.  (lets not get into the others, lets be real, I'll be here all night....I love this series).

Anyways, lets fast forward 25 years.  Its now the year 2021....and Resident Evil 8 comes out.  Holy effing ♥♥♥♥ batman!  I'm excited!  I played RE7 the one before it, and I loved it.  I'm ready for another blockbuster RE game.  I get Resident Evil 8.......install it, hit play:

(not getting into first few scenes for sake of spoilers) but...

The first moment you walk out of the bushes and see the castle....the first thought that goes through my head is Castlevania.  When I think of Castlevania, I think of Vampires, and Werewolves, Bats, The Grim Reaper.  It had the same look, but im thinking wait a minute.   THIS IS A RESIDENT EVIL GAME.  Their cant be any Vampires or Werewolves.  I don't remember that being a thing in ANY past RE games (at least from recent memory).  But I'm thinking, whatever, they just going for the aestitic to set the atmosphere.  So I keep playing.....

The first enemy I encounter is........a werewolf?   what?

Then the next enemy type I get introduced to is......a vampire?  wait......WTF is going on???  This isn't Resident Evil at all.

So needless to say, I got a few hours into the game.  I did enjoy the time I played.  Like I said, top notch graphics, really good gameplay, smooth and optimized.  Its just....

I feel like this game is kind of a slap in the face to all of us OG Resident Evil fans.   The T-Virus turns humans into zombies.  Even with the different variations of the T-Virus that came after was always geared somehow to turning humans into zombies (for the most part).  Other than a few freak accidents and heavily mutating people (Berkin) or engineered as a super weapon (tyrant/mr.x).

What type of virus is Umbrella making now that makes Vampires and Werewolves? Anyways, I didn't care enough of the story to continue playing.  The lack of horror elements was disturbing for a Resident Evil game (i dont know why they try so hard to get away from horror). I have about 10 hours in, but i restarted about halfway through cause I got confused and frustrated so I never finished.   I'm sure i'll eventually go back to it to finish, but I'm not in any rush.  The story really lost me at Vampires and Werewolves.....like I said.  As a GAME, its great!  But it should NOT be called Resident Evil.  Whatever story they are trying to convince me with by having Chris go rogue for some reason I really could careless if Vampires and Werewolves are apparently a thing now in the RE universe.  This game should just be called Castlevania: Eternal.

But....nevertheless, the game was enjoyable for the part of it I played.  Just the story I do not like.....at all.

The developers this time grew some balls and stopped pretending they wanted to make the first Resident Evil again. The past three games couldn't commit to a pure action or survival horror experience, so you wound up with a weird half-way house of both that felt neither challenging or satisfying (still good games though!).

You never feel like you're running fast enough, or shooting well enough, yet you wind up coming out the other end alright, generally. The rest is an ever-escalating sequence of setpieces and flowy pathfinding through labyrinthine halls that culminates in an awesome climax. 

REmake is my favorite because it's terrifying and realistic, but Village may be the best Resident Evil for none of those reasons. If you like macabre themes and good action, this is a great purchase.

“His story comes to a close…” The next mainline Resident Evil title is finally here: Resident Evil Village. After its announcement in 2020, Capcom has been very secretive with what this game exactly is, drip-feeding small details into the fanbase, while keeping most of the story and gameplay shrouded in mystery. The game returns with the first-person gameplay like its predecessor, 'Resident Evil 7 Biohazard' and its main protagonist, Ethan Winters, while giving it a completely different vibe: Gothic Survival Horror. Is it a good survival horror game? Is it a good Resident Evil game? Let’s find out. 

As mentioned, the game returns the first person camera like in Resident Evil 7, giving it a more claustrophobic feeling and adding a little bit of extra horror vibe like in Resident Evil 7. In the game you’ll encounter a ton of different enemy types, which is a huge improvement from the lack of enemy types in Resident Evil 7. There is also some variety in weapons with tons of upgrades, to kill said enemies (obviously). Furthermore you can find treasures again like in Resident Evil 4, which you can sell to a merchant (called ‘The Duke’) to get some money to upgrade your weapons.

Like in every RE title there are key items that you can find to solve puzzles or make some progress in the area you’re in. The puzzles are not really that hard unfortunately. The area’s in the game are huge and beautiful (graphics are good), well designed and they are all/feel unique, making moving through the different environments interesting and exciting; what will the game offer me this time? The gameplay, things like moving, shooting the whole circus is well done, not too special but well done, and it feels smoother than RE7.
 
Now its story time. The game begins with Ethan and Mia’s home being raided by the one and only, Chris Redfield. After having murdered Mia in cold blood and having taken his daughter, Chris retreats into the night. After the home invasion, Ethan wakes up in the night in a strange place and then the survival-horror begins. Ethan in this game is a much more improved character, he’s much more relatable because of the better and more realistic voice acting; The voice acting and the characters of the main antagonists are great and interesting respectively, but it does feel like missed opportunity: Capcom could have done much more with the antagonists than they did now, and the idea that they didn’t is just sad. They’re still great though, don’t worry. The game is much more action packed like RE4, but it is still scarier than RE4. The game balances the horror parts and action parts, adding to keeping the game interesting, besides story, environment and characters.

Besides the return of Ethan, Mia, Chris, first person, RE7’s guarding, action and horror stuff, there is something else waiting for you, ‘The Mercenaries’ mode! To play this mode you have to first finish the game at least once. Then you can buy it with CP, the game's currency which you obtain through completing challenges, like in Resident Evil 3: Remake (so no real money!). The mode is fun and adds some extra stuff to do after finishing the game, besides going for all the challenges, beating the game at different difficulty levels, NG+ and completing achievements. The story itself is fun replaying; there are always little details that you missed previously in for example: files, cutscenes or dialogue, and there are also side-areas which you can explore if you didn’t do that in your first run. 

Some final things to mention: The game runs on pretty steady FPS on the ‘high setting’ on PC, I’ve only had two frame drops in this 15 hour experience, from 60 to 20 fps for just a second before it jumped back to 60 fps. The music is great and fits the moment of the game you’re in and the voice acting is like always awesome. The transaction from gameplay to cutscene does feel weird at times.

Verdict: Resident Evil Village is an awesome game that brings back great horror and great action as seen in previous titles in the series. The story is interesting just like its characters, which could have been more interesting if they added more story to the characters. The game runs on steady fps, without almost any frame drops, while you walk through a beautiful and exciting environment, and where every different place in the game really feels unique. Game/gunplay feels great, puzzles are ok (nothing too special), music fits the moment of the game and the voice acting is just awesome.

While I had fun with this game, only about half of the content in the game really drew my attention. As somebody who was a fan of RE5 and 6 but not first person games as much, I knew this one was always going to be lower on my list as a Resident Evil experience goes. There will be some spoilers in here, but I'll try to keep it to a minimum.

The gameplay and battle mechanics are okay. Nothing spectacular. You can block and shoot, crouch and run. Movement in this game can very weird and stiff. Sometimes moving against an object I can't see will seem to halt my movement entirely. Sometimes trying to sprint out of a situation will leave my character hanging half a second before he starts moving. There were some enjoyable fight experiences later on with some harder enemies. But as a whole, nothing really stood out as being a very engaging experience. The camera was very narrow and gave a hard tunnel-vision effect, which made experiences with all aspects of the game more disorienting than anything else. Not as bad as the small bit I tried of RE7, but still not my cup of tea.

The level design was quite nice as whole. Some very strong retro Resident Evil takes in a couple areas. Some middle sections were less enjoyable. Felt more like I was playing psuedo-Quick Time Events instead of doing actual gameplay. With that and getting locked out of some areas for exploring later, I felt torn between trying to 100% as much as possible or replaying these sections again in another run.

Plot delivery was a miss for me. This is largely because of how first-person and tunnel-visioned everything was for a majority of the game. It was told more like a first-person book than a horror movie like most Resident Evils did before it. Ethan experiences things that I just can't relate, largely because of it being first-person and the absurd things happening. Felt like he would have been a less boring character as a whole for everybody if you could see his face or body language at times, but he was intended to be a faceless protagonist (which is weird when he still talks). Most people talking to my character felt like they were staring straight through me, giving me a strange second-person vibe to most encounters, especially the longer the game went. Along with having very few interactions with anybody who wasn't an enemy (I almost forgot about the throw away characters put there for... some reason...), Ethan feels much like a lone-gunner everywhere he goes and the whole experience feels empty.

Pacing of the game is extremely weird. The first part is a large amount of cutscenes with moments you get to walk along between them (minus the HUGE survivor sequence early on). The amount of cutscenes thrown into the game became more tedious than immersive. They kept happening but I know what happens in them doesn't really matter as I don't do anything until my WASD and mouse start responding. It made me miss QTEs of older games with the over abundance of tunnel-visioned cutscenes. Middle parts of the game were good for one go and I was glad when they were done. A lot of boss fights felt like me unloading way too many bullets into one enemy, but that's probably because of the downtime with walking and cutscenes.

The end part of the game finally utilizes some third-person sequences, which feels more jarring at that point. I can see how this might have been an artistic choice, but it really didn't work for me. Most of the end felt frustrating with some battle sequences that were thrown in and a plot that had lost me by then. After actually doing more of the third-person perspective cutscenes that I kept saying early on would have caught my interest more, the game started to interest me more. I ended feeling frustrated that they could have done more the whole game and actually wanting more after it was over.

I was very cautious when starting RE7 as it was a big change from the norm which I’d grown to love. But after playing through (one of multiple play throughs) I’d quickly came to respect and enjoy the new direction the game was going in. 

So when RE Village released I was eager to see how the story of Ethan would progress, and it didn’t disappoint. 

*Visuals*

From the vey first moment I was amazed by just how beautiful this game is visually. Textures, lighting, characters are all incredible, and ray tracing adds a nice atmospheric effect which I would suggest using if you have the hardware. 

Photo Mode is worth taking advantage of if you enjoy that type of thing. It offers a lot of options and you can grab some stunning screenshots.

8/10

*Gameplay*

Gameplay is almost identical to RE7. I did however find it slightly more difficult, which was a good thing. One issue I did have was the lack of herbs, which made certain parts of the game a frustrating.

7/10

*Story*

Story wise I thought it was incredible. It grips you from the first moment and doesn’t let do until the final second. Characters are well developed, and you genuinely care about them. A few twist and turns along the way require you to think a bit, which I liked. The jump scares are well done, even if they are a bit predictable to a RE veteran. 

The ending will leave you counting the days until RE9 releases. Which it most definitely will.

8/10

*Performance*

This is where the game falls short. Usually the RE Engine is flawless for me so I was shocked to see the performance in this game was not up to standard. 

Playing on a RTX3080 I could easily max everything out with RT on at 4K and got a good 75-90fps in most areas. However, the game has certain areas where fps tanks. This is most notably when there are aggressive particle effects such as the daughters. 

I also noticed a memory leak issue which requires a reload to fix. 

Hopefully these can be patched to make the game a smooth experience.

5/10

*Sound*

It’s fantastic. Suspense is built brilliantly. Sound effect such as the footsteps are clear and precise, which helps a lot in certain areas. 

8/10

Overall the game was a fantastic 12 hour experience. Although performance let it down in some areas, it was worth putting those issues aside to play what will undoubtably be one of the best games this year. 

Final Score 8/10 (Must Play)

RE Village isn't a bad game. I enjoyed playing it in some areas. But maybe my mistake was expecting it to be as fun as RE7 or RE2 remake was because I was severely underwhelmed by this game. 

Like I said, it's not a bad game. It's just not as great as it could've been or as great as I was anticipating it would be.

I am admittedly a new fan to RE games so my best experiences were with 7 and RE2 remake, so I really enjoyed the tension of the ammo and inventory management of those games. In RE8 as well as RE3, the game gives you an overabundance of ammo and it takes away all the tension of the game's encounters when you never really feel in danger because you'll likely never dip below 10 bullets worth of ammo. I don't know why Capcom is going this direction by making RE3 and 8 so Shooty and Looty focused but it's a lot less fun and a lot less tense than RE2 and 7.

Also, the puzzles in this game are ridiculously easy. There are so many interesting puzzle sections that could have incorporated into a European style castle in a snowy village but the castle section was incredibly linear and underwhelming. The puzzles in the game are garbage and take less than five minutes to solve. Even the locker combination codes from RE2 required more searching/thinking to figure out.

Honestly, the structure of the story is also bland and predictable. All the villager NPCs are worthless and literally an entire roomful of them are killed off within the first three minutes you get to meet them. 

The boss battles are dry and unimaginative. There's not even a whole lot of BOW chase action like with Mr. X/Nemesis, because Lady D [spoiler] doesn't even make it to the halfway point of the game [/spoiler].

I just feel like RE8 abandoned so much of what made RE7 and 2 fun. No focus on inventory management. No fun or challenging puzzles. Not even good chase sequences. An overabundance of ammo. Underwhelming boss fights. Boring story.

This game is easily 2021's Game of the Year, a work of art, and a masterpiece.  I bet this will be the new Resident Evil 4, the gold standard every subsequent RE game is evaluated against.  The visuals are some of the best I've ever seen, with breathtaking set pieces and realistic textures and lighting that make this terrifying adventure a joy to look at. 

The game play itself is also some of the best (if not the best) in the RE series.  With the Village acting as the center of the adventure, several areas branch off complete with its own aesthetic, atmosphere and flavor of game play.  The game play range is almost an ode to survival horror as a piece of any title in the genre exists here.  Segments range from run and gun segments to a having nothing at your disposal but your wits while the game recruits every possible psychological trick it has at its disposal to terrify you ... and it succeeds.

It definitely helps to play Resident Evil 7: Biohazard first (or at least read the synopsis of events in the Options of RE8), as this story picks up where the previous entry in the series leaves off.  Still, Village is playable (and absolutely enjoyable) without the background story.  It might just motivate you to go play 7 ... that's what I'm doing after my Village playthrough.

Resident Evil 4 is one of my favorite games of all time. Now the Resident Evil team has decided to take the formula from RE4 and combine it with the new style from RE7 to make Resident Evil Village. Here is a game that gives a great blend of horror, action, and campy writing.

The game is not a nonstop ride of horrors that will chill you to your bones for hours on end (though your millage may vary). However, that isn't to say the game won't get under your skin. There were plenty of times I found myself creeped out and even dreading the next step forward. 

Sometimes that fear comes in the form of not having enough ammo and having to consider how you will proceed. While at times you may have enough ammo that you feel like a super soldier. One fight between a tough enemy may drain you of much of your supplies. The action is very robust and satisfying. Enough so that they welcome you to an arena shootout after the game in Mercenaries. 

The story is very much on brand for Resident Evil. If you're not into a B-movie plot that got a massive special effects budget, then Resident Evil in general probably isn't for you. Village once again introduces us to colorful characters that stick with you long after the credits roll. It's just unfortunate that Capcom did not see how much of a powerhouse Lady Dimitrescu (tall lady) would be with the masses. Many people may be (and are already) disappointed with how much of a role she has to play in the overall game. Still the story in intriguing and keeps you wanting to find out more, solve the next puzzle, and blast the next ghoul. 

If horror is a genre you can play through, then I absolutely recommend Resident Evil Village.

*Spoiler Free Review*

Compared to the Last Game:
This game took every problem I had with RE7 and fixed them.
The pacing is faster. There are more enemy types. There are more weapons, and more ways to improve them. There's the Duke. There's a Thicc, Tall, Dommy Mommy vampire. There are also werewolves. Ethan is significantly improved as a protagonist. Literally it's RE7 but better in every way. It's similar to how Assassin's Creed Odyssey is just an objectively improved Origins.

Performance:
Game runs fantastic on high settings, even on my aging rig. You shouldn't have any issues unless you're on a potato. Lots of flex and customization options. The game defaults to a window mode on first launch which is weird but, Capcom games have a history of doing so for me. Easy fix to full-screen, runs flawlessly. 

Potential Story Issues:
The one thing that people may not like are the late story twists. To my estimation there are three. One involves a shift in game-play, one involves a retcon to the previous game (RE7), and one involves a retcon to the wider RE universe lore. These are all very much a case of YMMV. Personally, I liked the first two and I am ambivalent towards the third.

TLDR:
It is RE7 but better and with a dash of RE4. If you thought RE7 was boring then you should like this one. Highly Recommend.

Resident Evil Village feels like a mixture of Resident Evil 4 and 7 but not as good. 
I'll quickly start with the PC settings, it bothers me how lazy Capcom is to not include a FOV slider.  
Playing this game in its default fov, left me disorientated and frustrating at times when evading enemies or missing item because everything felt so zoomed in. Graphically, I didn't feel there was much improvement with everything cranked up to max, edges or textures just seemed off, just by going what my eyes can see. 
I would later find out, the anti-aliasing seems to be broken as mentioned from Digital Foundry finding. 

Although I gave this game a negative, I would prefer to give this game an okay rating if there was an option. 
The direction, the things that bothered me, the improvement I wanted from this game, are what impacted me the most. 
It doesn't quite deserve the high praises and the faults with this game, shouldn't be ignored. 

I'd still argue that Resident Evil 7 has it's place in the Resi franchise, RE7 came at a time where Capcom needed to revitalise Resident Evil and they achieved that with the horror element. Something that was lacking from 4, 5 and 6. They manged to create a sense of vulnerability from a first person prospective in 7, the horror, the atmosphere and the layer of tension, which is mostly missing in RE Village. 

RE8 direction focuses too much on the action and I already knew this leading up to launch as it was mention many times from developers but with too much actions, takes away from the horror element. The combat itself, felt very stiff to me, none of the weapons stood out or felt unique so on the horror and combat element, I'm left disappointed on both fronts.

I know this will be subjected but I really don't care much for Ethan Winters, I kinda didn't mind him in RE7 just because he was a regular guy, trying to survive in the Baker house. Which I always felt Ethan was in danger and never safe behind any walls. I feel like RE7 (First Person View) works best in a close quarter horror in a claustrophobia sense. The openness in RE8 derail from that. Something that was also a let down, was the characters. They just didn't quite have the impact as RE7. Boss battle wasn't anything special, the game doesn't give you enough time to build up to why these bosses are scary because frankly, they are not.  I even completed RE8 in the hardest difficulty setting in my second playthrough, (Village Of Shadows) in hopes of added an extra layers of fear in gameplay and boss battle but it never achieve that for me. I won't go too much into details, I felt Lady D was a miss opportunity and the castle was probably the most fun section. Rest of the boss battle was very lacklustre to me. Same could be said for Heisenberg, a boss character that looks interesting but you don't see or get enough from him. I didn't find him scary and maybe more suspense could of been done to add a layer to his character.  I would quickly say, Mia and Chris were the biggest missed opportunity in RE8. Hell, Zoe Baker was more of a interesting character than Ethan Winters. 
I'll end this review by giving my final thoughts on what I want from Capcom. I'll like to see an OG character return to have their own unique game, Jill (not RE3-Remake Jill), Chris, Claire, I would like to see more of young Leon, perhaps before RE4 or Ada Wong with a bit of dynamic to her personality where she doesn't always have to have an iron front barrier to her personality.  An RE game in 3rd person like RE2-Remake. I still want Resi to have first person view as a side project to experiment for the franchise, though I would prefer if they chose a direction that mostly focus on horror, rather than action.  

So, those are my thoughts.

Overall: 7.3/10

Positive:

Story 10/10 - I don't want to spoil the story for others, but it was the best part of this game. A few twists and turns and through the entire experience I couldn't put the game down and wanted to keep on playing to find out more.

Graphics 9/10 - The graphics on this game are really good, the first time you enter the village and look over the area is truly breath taking and helps build you up for whats to come.

Gameplay 7/10 - I love the first person aspect of this game (like Resident Evil 7) and found the combat very fun, I find the first person nature also adds to the immersiveness of the game that has been executed very well.

Replayability 8/10 - There is alot to see in this game and many things to miss, though the game can be short (managed 2 hours 15 for my speed run attempt for the Dashing Dad challenge) it is also a very fun environment to explore and take your time with, my first play through took around 10 hours and felt full of content with practically no areas where something wasn't going on (whether it be npc's, items or puzzles).

Sound effects 6/10 - The sounds are good, but many felt like they were taken from an open source default sound pool (like vase smash sounds). Nothing wrong with them, but nothing amazing.

Music 6/10 - Similar to the sound effects, there is nothing wrong with the music but nothing amazing either, some games you can picture a boss and hear the soundtrack that went with them, unfortunately I can't really remember any of the music from this game even after 3 runs.

Neutral:

Re-visiting: 5/10 I love to try and explore 100% of these games in my first run if possible but found certain areas are locked off to you once completed, this is common in many games but I would have liked the ability to re-visit a couple locations to give a 2nd look over without needing to do this on New Game+ (though I suppose, this did encourage me to do additional runs of the game)

Negative:

DLC - I purchased the Deluxe edition and got the Trauma pack DLC and tbh, it's over priced and useless imo. The gun you get with the trauma pack is useful for about 1 section of the game on your first run and can then be sold as the starting pistol with a couple of upgrades will be better. Personally, this weapon should have either been made upgradeable or just bundled as a pre-order bonus not a purchasable extra. I won't count this on my grading however as it isn't necessarily part of the game (if you don't purchase it).

This isn't really a resident evil game at this point, but it's more than 7 was. I thought 7 was really well done but I didn't like it at all. This game, I like parts, and hate others. The combat is fun just like the old RE games so if you are coming from pre RE7 or are a fan of RE4, you will probably like this game. My biggest issue is just how little care the devs gave certain parts of the game. At a glance the game is beautiful, but if you look beyond initial shock and awe you will see tons of weak cover up for really poorly done things. Cut scenes are hit and miss as well. Some run great and look great, while others desynch with audio, or show how little the designers cared if something clipped horribly (Look at Moreau's death scene for the best example of this). I'm really conflicted on whether I should recommend this or not. I like this game quite a bit compared to 7, but I don't like it anywhere near as much as the previous titles. If you are a casual difficulty player of RE, you will laugh at how stupidly easy it is in RE8. I played through on the normal difficulty, and it was a challenge at most times, not that the game was hard, but just like 7 I never really had that much ammo and enemies are bullet sponges. There's also not a great mechanic surrounding guns. The magnum is unbelievably strong. The pistols are surprisingly weak. The Sniper is dead in the middle and I don't even know what to say about shot guns. They are strong one shot, then the next almost worthless. It's hard to even use a pistol, but you get so little ammo for other guns that you have to use the weak POS. I know pistols are meant to be the primary weapon so they can't be OP, but ffs, they are waaaay too weak. On the normal difficulty it takes over 40 hits to fight slightly harder than the general ads. On village of shadows I tried fighting the first daughter with guns... that didn't happen. After about 30 pistol rounds, 20 shotgun shells, 4 magnum hits, and about 5 heals, I died and then just dropped mines until she died and stopped playing that difficulty. I was on new game + so I had upgraded gear but holy hell is that hard. If you like a game with a decent combat system, absolutely no direction as to where you are supposed to go or what the hell you are doing when you need it, but an overly straightforward direction that is really well displayed, so you are constantly lost when it counts this is the game for you. I don't like horror games but I have to say, for that being a focus they did a great job. Screw that damn doll house man... 

Long story short, I like this game, but it's not really worth $60. And ffs, don't buy the extra content. Holy hell is that a really bad money grab. The hanging ornaments can't go on any guns but the first pistol and shotgun, which are both absolute trash from the moment you get them. On that note, what the hell is the logic behind making weapons fire so damn slow? The first pistol by all means should likely be the fastest, but the 1911 is way faster and then there's the suped up glock that fires fast as well. And the SYS, semi-auto shot gun that is an AK platform, is the slowest out of the box. HOW IS A PUMP FASTER? There's so many little things that just ruin what this game could have been. Try not to look at the giant holes in the terrain or the floating rocks, and you will have a wonderful visual experience, but be lost to the depths of hell in the mansion and factory.

It feels like in some cases the developers had all these ideas but didn't know how to incorporate them all into a game that didn't take one hundred hours to complete. I will break this review down into Story, Game play and Endgame content. The story section will spoil the plot line so avoid that section if you have not played RE8 yet from start to finish.


[b]Story[/b]

The story expands upon the ending of resident evil 7, Ethan is now living quietly somewhere with Mia and their child and we learn that they have been relocated their by Chris Redfield. Ethan has been receiving combat training as well so he is more of a killer in this game than in RE7.

The story goes much bigger in this entry with new multiple large locations instead of the small baker's house from RE7. One of the things I quite liked about RE7 was the ability to condense and entire game into the 1 house area. It had some charm to it that RE8 lacks, but nonetheless, still great in the location department. Chris then breaks through the front door, killing Mia and is taken by Chris.

This is what kicks the events of the game into action. Ethan wakes after the transport van crashes and stumbles into the new area of RE8. A little while on, Ethan is introduced to the lords of the village. Each of the lords has their own distinct back stories and lore and throughout the game, it was a joy to learn about each one of them. Ethan is then tasked with finding and killing the four lords, each in their own areas to gather the parts of of his daughter (it’s complicated). He proceeds to hunt all of them down 1 by one before facing Miranda.

[b]Summarized[/b]

This aspect of the game can be weak at times and the game can take quite a long time to pick up pace in the story department until the very end where almost every single question gets answered very quickly as well as a great twist to pull the events of both games nicely together and answering some longing fan questions. The ending alone is worth the price of admission

[b]Gameplay[/b]

Game play is a mix between the survival horror of RE7 and the action of RE4 blending these two together into a hybrid. The game has way more action sections than horror sections with big set pieces for some great moments. You have a wider arsenal of weapons available as well as a large collection of new enemies to face. Weather throwing grenades planting mines or mowing enemies down with a semi-automatic rifle, it’s clear that the game lies more on the action end of the spectrum. With that being said, the game still has sections of fear and tension and these sections are a welcomed break of pace from the more action sections of the game.

The puzzle solving is back but this is quite a weak part of it and the puzzles require little to no thinking to solve and this aspect should hopefully be improved in RE9.
There are tons of secrets and collectibles to be found similar to RE2 and Re7. Item management and secrets are still stellar in the series and RE8 is no different. Finding an item in a late game area which gives you access to something you found right at the start of the game is always cool and great when it gets pulled off in this fashion. Weapons sound fantastic, and the meaty pop of shot gunning something in the face is always very satisfying.

[b]End Game[/b]

This area of the game is very strong. Upon completion of the game, you unlock Village of Shadows difficulty and this is a whole new way to play. Meaner enemies and new placements as well as unlocking some new weapons to play with adds some extra depth and is very welcomed. 

You gain access to challenges which reward you with completion points which can be used to buy special items, new weapons as well as unlocks mods for the weapons. 

On top of all of that you also get access to a new mode called mercenaries which tasks you with killing a certain number of enemies in a specific time frame. Chaining enemy kills together increased your timer and you can find money and abilities to use through each stage. You only have access to a specific set of weapons each stage so planning which weapons to take into the stage and weather to upgrade it or use the case for another weapon is all strong question which keep the game play interesting and varied. But this is just an extra on top of everything

[b]Final Thoughts[/b]
The game is not as strong has RE7 and does not have the same charm but is still an incredible game worth the admission fee and a great entry for old and new resident evil fans.

[b]Pros[/b]
-Still a resident evil game to it’s core

-Slow to get moving in the story department.
-Can sometime be too action orientated and moves to much away from survival horror.
-Some framerate problems in the castle area with the daughters and flies.
-Some weak boss battles

Ok so let's start this review off with a metric for grading. I will be grading the game on qualities that have their place in every game. These categories are going to be Graphics, Story, Dialogue, Environment, Characters, Bugs/design flaws, Mechanics, replay-ability, side content, and sound design. these will be rated x/10 for a total of x/100

1. Graphics: This game has pretty good graphics, it isn't like playing a movie but you can look at the matting of Lady Demitrescu's make-up. things in game have believable textures and don't look painted on. the game is pretty high poly and has effects (will be explored more in environment) that look less cartoonish than other games. For example [spoiler] when Ethan get's his hand bit off[/spoiler]. but many of the other gore effects are cartoonish like when you [spoiler] get hung up on hooks and have to pull yourself down[/spoiler] the "holes" have no pass through like they would in real life. 

over all score: 8/10

2. Story: without giving much away, this story is less ambitious than 7. it goes back to RE's roots at having the same general ending of blow up area at the end, but it also tries to tie in ethan's story a bit more with the other games in the franchise. this stuff all feels sort of flat. the twist at the end, which i will not explain. feels sort of shoehorned in at the end as an explanation for a plot hole in this and the last game. I do like the ending of the game because [spoiler] ethan dies and i didn't like him [/spoiler] over all the story is just over average and kinda forced at times 

over all: 6/10

3. Dialogue: Those of you familiar with resident evil, (i myself am not) may know that they are definitely not known for their dialogue. The voice acting itself is pretty good. i remember actually feeling guilty for killing certain characters because they said they didn't want to die. However, Ethan's lines couldn't be more cheesy. making him a backseat character when it's a first person game. he was like this in the last game, but he talked less. Heisenberg's VA sounds like he was constantly inhaling sulfur hexafluoride to make his voice DEEPER and it made it hard to take him seriously. Also, all of the Voice Actors are american which makes no sense given the story taking place in Norway. But the stage presence of the members of House Demitrescu, Bienviento, and even Moreau are excellent and, despite Heisenberg's weird voice, the performance was on point and I liked his sequence. 

over all 9/10 (not fair to dock every category because of Ethan)

4. Environment: There are a few things that make this category. 1 is the screenshotability of every location in the game. any room you are in is interesting to look at and actually encourages your brain to explore because of how good stuff is to look at. In the factory you are met with hues of orange and shiny black and dark silver metal along with yellow and red flakes to communicate the heat. The halls in the castle Demitrescu is adorned with beautiful ornate furniture and doors. the entrance to the village instantly gives you a distant view of the castle. House Bienviento has a creepy uneasy feeling like the dolls inside are watching your every move. The game manages to capture masterful design at every point.

Conclusion: 10/10

5. Characters: While the characters are interesting, more so if you read the in game books. They don't really mesh well with poor stupid Ethan. They have the player solve puzzles meanwhile the character they play is such a blithering idiot it's surprising he doesn't choke on his own drool. If Ethan were more well written or didn't speak at all, the other characters would have been more interesting. You could make up your own reasons why the character makes decisions that Ethan makes that would normally be poor decisions.(like when he refuses the deal, also i will not elaborate on this for spoilers) all of the issues that Ethan causes in other categories are going to this one because he is a bad character. He gets OP protag vibes and doesn't grow. he's a mary sue. 

conclusion: 2/10

6. bugs/ game design: i didn't experience a single bug throughout my 3 playthroughs (except for the demitrescu sisters who are made of them) the game design however is why this section gets any lost points. The placement and pace between the 4 lords didn't feel right. Beware spoilers for order of the segments and length of fights. skip to the score or next number if this would bother you. I feel that there can be an argument that the order the fights were in made sense because demitrescu lives in the big castle and so she needs to go first to set the mood. But I feel that Moreau should have been the first up since he was the most initially motivated to take down Ethan. also he was the weakest willed character and therefor easiest to trick and kill. also unlocking the rest of the village would have been nice so i can get everywhere. then simply put demitresu third so she can have more screen-time. also making the Bienviento section longer because it was the scariest, and scary worked well in res e 7. Where the mom sequence was the longest and she was the most uncomfortable character to be around in a good way. The game did clearly have a lot of thought put into the design of the village working around the given plot. and i can't fault the team who designed the layout if the writers wanted the order so only minus 2 points, 

Conclusion 8/10

7. Mechanics: The game is really fun to play, it takes away your weapons at the right times so that you have to learn and use other mechanics to help yourself. there are a few interesting puzzles. and there's a merchant that allows you to upgrade your weapons. while the save rooms are immersion breaking, they feel mechanically necessary for things. i wouldn't want to be attacked while i am buying something, and i don't want every creature to be the same difficulty to kill. you feel like you become more powerful in this game and it works.

overall: 9/10

8. replayability: this game does not allow you to finish all of the achievements in one run, which is fine. but the story is kind of bland and lacks options. you can't change the order in which you defeat the 4 lords which makes it the same thing the 3 times you need to complete the game for all of the achievements. luckily, the game isn't a chore to play through after your first run. so when you replay, paying attention to the story the first time you realize some things throughout the second play through. If Resident Evil 7 was the game that revived the series and its survival horror roots, then Resident Evil Village is the blockbuster follow-up. The developers have stated that Village was heavily inspired by RE4, and it shows — from the action-horror opening sequence, to the inventory system and weapon upgrades, to the European-medieval setting — Village feels like RE4: 2021 Edition at first.

But just when you think you've seen it all, Village performs a U-turn, venturing into new territory previously unexplored by the series, while borrowing a lot of elements from past titles and other horror games. By the endgame, it feels like you've experienced a "greatest hits" collection of the genre. Your enjoyment of these drastic changes in tone and gameplay will vary greatly depending on your personal tastes.

Overall I enjoyed what Village had to offer — the gameplay is solid, the story has some baffling moments but is redeemed by strong character drama and themes. A great continuation of what RE7 started and I'm curious to see where Capcom will take RE9 next.

I'd be lying if I said I wasn't entirely skeptical about Reaident Evil Village when it was first announced. I'm a 90s kid so growing up I loved the Resident Evil franchise for that classic zombie survival horror essence.

Even to this day in my opinion some of my favorite games were the classics and the remakes of 2 and 3. Don't get me wrong, 4 was a great game as well which leads me to my next point. This game heavily reminds me of a mix between 4 and 7. Granted, Resident Evil Village is nowhere near as scary as some of it's predecessors. But it makes up for that in content, atmosphere, setting, story, and sheer replayability.

The graphics are awesome, combat is definitely fun although less geared towards survival once you make a dent in progress, and the enemies are extremely interesting.

I love how it has that classic Resident Evil feel of backtracking to uncover new secrets and items. Because of that I spent practically all my time making sure I completely swept an area clean or backtracked once I had certain key items to make sure I didn't miss anything important.

At the time of this review it took about 27 hours for me to beat the game. I know people have claimed they've beat it in 10 hours, 8 hours, even 5 hours or less. But if you're anything like me and spend most of your time soaking in each area of the map and exploring until your hearts content you'll find it's definitely worth the $65 price tag.

I only had 2 very minor slight hiccups performance wise during my playthrough. During certain segments in the game my frames dropped to 40 fps despite me playing on a 2070 super with very good hardware. Outside of that fact the game ran smooth as butter with everything on max settings.

Now do I recommend it? Absolutely! As soon as I post this review I'll be hopping right back on to complete a second playthrough and have some fun with all the goodies you unlock after you initially beat the game.

Capcom you genuinely surprised me with this gem and I thank you for it!
