When compared to it's extremely popular predecessor (RE7: Biohazard)  RE: Village falls short in some areas but shines brighter in others. It is its own diamond in an already well established series. 

[b] Positives: [/b]
- The story is quite compelling and interesting to follow, Especially when paying attention to the documents and letters scattered across the world. Eliot becomes a lot more human during the prologue and end-game which helped a lot.
- Every character is unique, with their own quirks and personalities. I found myself in a bitter rivalry with the first main antagonist, Lady Dimitrescu. I experienced pitty on the bullied Moreau. And with Duke, I was excited to see him every time he appeared knowing his advice and stock would further my ability in the coming missions.
- THE ITEM SYSTEM! The item system is a massive improvement on the previous game. With the addition of upgradable weapons and the extended arsenal the game feels ever-changing in how I approach certain situations. For example, in the early game, when approaching a group of enemies I might panic switch to a pipe bomb for mass damage. But, late-game I would probably opt for the [spoiler]  grenade launcher [/spoiler] or upgraded 
[spoiler] sniper rifle [/spoiler] to tap their heads off one-by-one. 
- Replayability (STORY) is something that I worried about with this game. But, i have decided that RE8 does this well (enough). The story is very replayable with the multitude of challenges. Personally, I had a lot of fun with the 
[i] Knives Out [/i] challenge and [i] Dashing Dad [/i] challenge. Both were exciting. The latter brought out the mediocre speed-runner within me :).
- Visually this game is amazing. Even without all the fancy settings this game achieves a level of atmosphere that I don't think any other game has in the past. This has been achieved with the layers upon layers of dimension from the mountains in the distance foregrounded by the Dimitrescu castle, further foregrounded by the various elements of the village. All of this is brought together by the fine mist and perfect light that saturates the village. The most outstanding internal environment was (no surprise) the castle. Part of me wishes we spent more of the game inside the castle as this is where I had the most fun exploring every nook and cranny in hopes to find the next secret or valuable piece of ammo. 
- Boss fights on HARDCORE offered a nice challenge while still maintaining the narrative flow that more casual players might look for in such a game. I enjoyed most of the boss fights to varying degrees (including the mini-bosses).

[b] Negatives: [/b]
- Dialogue, at times, is very generic and comical at times with Ethan pointing out what is happening right in front of him. [spoiler] 'Why does everyone keep dying one me!' [/spoiler]
- The only boss fight that I found a little monotonous was the Moreau fight. I get that his health pool is supposed to be BiG for such a big boy but the opportunities for crit damage (which is especially valuable on Hardcore and VOS) were few and far between. I feel an increased frequency of this window would help with this. But that's just me being picky. 
- MERCENARIES is a bit poopoo. I was expecting to be able to unlock playable characters and possibly some entirely new arenas and weapons but this was not the case. We are stuck with little-old Ethan and the guns we know (one of which is pretty much useless after the first level). Other than that the game mode is a lil fun if you dont mind the lack of incentive to play other than the Ranks. 

[b] Summary: [/b]
RE8: Village is a brilliantly enjoyable game with a lot to offer and a lot of potential for further expansion. Don't go into the game expecting the constant nail biting tension of RE7 and you will fall in love like I did. It is its own monster and has made its mark in the RE universe, a pretty unique one at that.

Easily one of the best games I've ever played and the second best Resident Evil game in my book (RE2Remake is still king).

RE Village is an amalgam of previous RE titles, combining the survivor horror aspects from the first couple games with over the top action set pieces and weapon customization of 4 and 5. The first few hours are very tense and challenging, culminating in one of the scariest moments in all of the franchise [spoiler] House Beneviento [/spoiler] and from that point it goes on a more action heavy approach.

I loved the gunplay as well. The weapons are a bit janky and heavy with slow reload times and fire rate until you spend enough money to tweak or trade them for new weapons. They have a nice feel and weight to them. You'll know what I'm talking when you play it.

Another aspect I really liked is the openness of the game. The Village is brimming with secrets and collectibles and every new key item you get in one of the four lords subareas opens up new opportunities to search previous inaccessible houses, boats, caverns and discover new puzzles and mini bosses throughout the village. This game really triggered my OCD lol. I kept searching every nook and cranny for items such as ammo, weapon attachments and treasures until every area was colored blue (the areas colored red in the map are those you still have items to find). Believe me, it is worth the effort. You'll find secret weapons, ammo, story documents, animals to hunt and valuable treasures to sell and tweak your guns and health pool/defence capabilities.

Now for the story, well. It's amazing. I confess I wasn't sold on the story and overall aesthetic of the game when it was first revealed. But boy was I wrong.

[spoiler] Right from the start you see the hero (or is he?) Chris murdering Mia in cold blood and seemingly kidnapping Ethan's baby daughter. As the game goes on, you learn that the village is an experiment of the evil Mother Miranda (one hell of an antagonist) and that Chris' actions were all justified. The final hour is gut wrenching with emotional moments, lots of shooting and a plot twist that ties the RE7 and RE8 story in a way that the game doesn't leave any loose ends. The connection between Mother Miranda and Oswell Spencer from RE1 is also incredible, making her one of the more important characters in all of the franchise [/spoiler].
Almost every RE game ends suddenly and with poor explanation of what has happened. This is not the case with RE8 that has the best ending of the franchise IMO.

Aside from the main game there is The Mercenaries Mode, a welcome return of one of the best extra modes ever. I found it to be lots of fun with rogue like elements that kept every run fresh and challenging. You also unlock a huge list of challenges and achievements to complete after you beat the game that will please completionists. If you want to play the story again, you can hit New Game+ which lets you carry over all weapons and upgrades from previous runs.

I'm really looking forward for RE9. I think Capcom outdid themselves with this one, both gameplay and storywise. RE8 gives closure to Ethan/Mia/Mold story but sets the stage for a sequel in a very subtle way.

One quick word of advice: I suggest you play in the hardcore difficulty. I chose that difficulty in my first run and thought it to be just right. I saw some people play in standard and I think it is too easy, the enemies die with much fewer bullets and inflict a lot less damage. From what I saw, people rarely died or ran out of ammo in standard difficulty.

All in all be it standard of hardcore, the game is amazing. It's a must play.

Wow, just a fantastic game. I absolutely loved Resident Evil 7 and had been anticipating a sequel ever since finishing it. When they first started showing previews and some walkthroughs for the game I was a little ambivalent as it look way different than the previous game. The tone felt different and didn't really seem like a horror game. Just an action game with horror elements. I can safely say that it wasn't the case at all. While the game definitely seems a bit more action oriented it is a disturbing and unsettling game that had me pausing to take break every hour or so. 

My favorite aspect of the game was the thing that worried me earlier, the enemies. The faster lychen characters seemed like they would require speed and quicker movement rather than the need for accuracy like the previous games' enemies. While that is somewhat true, the enemies are terrifying and the need for accuracy is necessary along with the need for speed/quicker movement. The bosses are also a ton of fun with a different "feel" for each one that brings back elements from previous Resident Evil games. Not to spoil too much you have the classic "puzzle" mansion, a more on rail boss that really brings the horror elements, a more action oriented boss and a newer "Lovecraftian" boss that hasn't really been explored as much in RE. 

Overall it's a ton of fun and feels fresh. While the horror fans might be a bit more disappointed with the more "Jack of All Trades, Master of None" direction they went with rather than just leaning on horror, I think everyone who has enjoyed and played a handful of RE games will walk away completely satisfied. Only bigger issues I have are the shorter length and the Mercenary mode being ridiculously short. So short that I couldn't help but laugh after I finished it in less than 10 minutes. I'm sure they're flesh it out with updates or DLC, but now it might as well not exist.

I'd say a 9/10. Finishing it under 10 hours was a bit disappointing so if you want more bang for your bucks and you're not sure if you'll like the game then wait til it drops to $40-$50 but for me it was a blast and I will be playing again and looking out for future DLC.

so lets talk about Resident Evil lineage for a minute and then get back to Resident Evil 8 : VIllage

Firstly i must say, much has changed. old technology gave more scares and more clunky/choppy gameplay but brilliant frustration and replayability value but the newer games have at times been a hit and miss. the series has progressed beautifully in terms of storyline, character arc, gameplay, music scores etc. but truly one thing Resident Evil franchise has managed to capture is its ability to make the game lovable or hateable.

Resident Evil Village is one such game which players will eventually come to love or hate. dont get me wrong, 7 and 8 are 2 of the most beautiful games made by capcom and trust me when i say youre paying worth every penny for the gameplay. but there is always a hit and miss.

i dont know whether the directors and producers constantly choose to ignore customer feedback or they just want to indulge in their own "Xperiments".

The game itself is well written, makes sense, nothing mind boggling about the narratives. characters are nice, and their layers etc are beautifully designed as well. i really wish the puzzles ARENT cheesy ffs. i want to be challenged in puzzles. the only puzzle that really made me think more then 5 minutes was [spoiler]Heisenbergs Horse Door Key[/spoiler] .

the characters are magnificent in their own maniacal way. Alcina moreau donna and heisenberg are good villians. and heisenberg tops the cake for the fights. donnas layer, is well... wont reveal spoilers, ...the best EVER part of all the Resident Evil parts. trust me when i say that its saddening when the part comes to an end. <3 

the areas are well, typical of resident evil imagination. but nice to see that the game blends in well with gameplay and doesnt concentrate on one area all the time. the back-forth pacing is what RE is loved about. the frustration to complete a puzzle by realizing "OHHHHHH so thats how this works" , these little things have a small but meaningful impact on the game.

the guns and their animations are nicely designed but i feel the "aiming" has some glitchy responses. at one point i couldnt even shoot GOAT point blank with my shotty.  and the recoil seemed to far off. same goes for all the weapons, even the rifle, whos open view shooting seemed ridiculous, even at close quarters. -.- 

the cold bitter theme of the outside village during the first half of the game is what is RE all about, sending shivers. the slow pace and constant feel to expect something out of nowhere. dont get me wrong, the scares are plenty, but.. not really VERY scary. 

missions are good. i wont lie, this game didnt seemed dragged or anyway short. it was well balanced. i DO wish and pray for a longer run for Resident Evil 9 in future. want more then 30-40 hrs of gameplay. want puzzles back with a vengeance and i want one of those "nemesis" type c*nts following everywhere i go. i want constant fear on me that if i wait in a room too long, its not going to end well. sadly RE8 lacked this. and you could explore and hunt at your own will and pace. it didnt make you "run for your life" nor did it make you feel scared. it was... relaxed lol. and RE series is anything BUT relaxed. 

the music score is one of the best of the series. i loved the music especially during the [spoiler]lycan fights[/spoiler] and i honestly felt there was some great fighting sequence about to be had. action was great. felt RE4 all over again.

overall, more improvement from RE7, and definitely there is more potential for future titles <333

Resident Evil Village marked every box that I needed it to mark. (NO SPOILERS)

Village is a wonderful blend of RE7's first person mechanics, and RE4's iconic setting. We play as Ethan Winters, the newly added protagonist from RE7. In my opinion, this game launched Ethan into the ranks of the most beloved Resident Evil heroes, alongside Chris/Claire Redfield, Leon Kennedy and Jill Valentine. 

Gameplay wise, RE Village feels a lot cleaner than RE7 in terms of mechanics. Capcom definitely took some time to refine the first-person combat that was introduced in 7. You will definitely have to tinker with some of the options to fit your preferred sensitivity, aiming speed and the like. One issue (and really the only issue) I had was during my time in the Castle, and certain bug-related enemies caused rather heavy frame drops.

Story wise, Village crafts a wonderful narrative around Ethan and his life after the Baker Incident in RE7. It is fairly well thought out tale, and one that even sticks a landing within the wider Resident Evil universe. Personally, at no point did I feel like the story was dragging or was moving too fast, but I understand a few peoples gripes with some of the middle points seeming a little quick (without revealing any plot).

Overall, I would recommend Resident Evil Village to series veterans and newcomers alike. It is a solid story with solid villains. It has some spooks, it has some action. A little something for everyone, especially those who love the Resident Evil story/lore.

Spoiler-Free Review: I simply cannot recommend this game enough as a long-time fan of the series. RE4 + RE7 = RE8. There is no denying that math. The RE4 vibes in this game are real. The good and bad are below. I'm very critical of games, so the 'Bad' section seems a little long. Mind you, I would still strongly recommend this game in its current presentation. I'd give it a solid 9/10. 

THE GOOD: The narrative is actually very well-done in this entry and might leave you with a few emotions to process before the credits roll and even after. Gameplay-wise, this is the best RE title in the series. It combines the survival horror elements that we are used to with the series, and plays into some exploration themes as well. There is an entire sequence that pays homage to P.T. and it might be one of the most memorable of the game (for me, at least). The shooting in this game is fantastic; the best the series has offered yet. The Mercenaries game mode in this installment is very addictive and I can only describe it as Resident Wick. You can clearly see with the amount of time I've logged into the game so far, it has a high replay value. 

THE BAD: My biggest complaint with this game is the complete lack of a FOV slider or FOV adjustment option. The FOV in this game is incredibly narrow, but it is easily fixed with a mod available on Nexus. There are also some technical issues that ran into during my playtime. I'm running a RTX 3070 with an Intel i7 10870H and there are a few points in the game where I encountered significant frame drops into the 20s. They are very rare and only occur during very specific sequences for a matter of seconds. It doesn't kill the game experience, but it might break your immersion for a moment when it happens. Overall, I maintained a steady 90 FPS throughout the rest of the game using about 7.5 gigs of my VRAM (I capped my frame rate at 90 FPS on this particular machine. A powerful PC can get much more FPS on this title). The most frequent issue that I notice is the presence of a brief (and I mean incredibly brief) stutter upon killing enemies. It doesn't happen with every enemy, but it happens often enough to make you wish it didn't.

RAY TRACING RANT: This game further solidifies my belief that ray tracing is a completely unnecessary trend in gaming that bears too little merit in relation to the increased performance demand. I turned ray tracing on maximum at multiple points in the game, and the difference in visual presentation is barely noticeable, yet the performance decrease is more than obvious. I'm fairly certain that the industry push towards ray tracing is being done primarily to save developers the time and effort normally required for setting up in-game lighting.

An enjoyable experience. This game definitely feels like an evolution of the previous game, RE7. The gameplay is a great mix of classic RE and modern RE, with certain sections being slower paced and other sections being action packed, especially near the end, right before the final boss battle. 

My favorite section is Castle Dimitrescu, a slow paced area offering numerous rooms fulls of puzzles. That area is essentially a classic RE map and experience and definitely the highlight of the game, especially for being the first part of the game. The only negative is that the castle offers a strong start for the game that it undermines the rest of the game, I believe the game could have benefited if this area was the midpoint and not the start.

The setting is another highlight for me, the mysterious village full of monsters in the outskirts of Europe sounds something out of a fairy tale and it feels so well within the game's universe. Not to mention the many great characters this village offers, with every main character there having their own moment to shine. I highly recommend this game. The story is not the best but it's a good end to a character's story, it gave me the feels. Gameplay is an improvement from the last game, with improvements to mechanics. Gameplay is faster and more intense I like the ability to push off enemies from successful blocks, I like how the enemies move more they feel more organic rather than a stumbling meat sack to avoid. Enemy variety is good, you have fast moving enemies, slow moving enemies, hulking big boys and ammo sponge. Bosses have their own theme which is very good, I like the cat and mouse with Lady D, the puzzle solving, psychological aspect with Donna, traditional boss fight with Moreau and rail shooter with Heisenberg. 

Excellent level design, you can experience a lot of different environments. Returning game mechanics make the game much more enjoyable. I love getting my equipment from either exploration or by purchasing from the Duke. The Duke ensures you can get the edge on your adventure and even helps you out with showing you locations of treasure; that you WILL NEED if you want to do some serious damage. The game is relatively long for your first playthrough around 10 hours for me because exploration is what I like about games. You can also play the Mercenaries game mode that can be unlocked after clearing the game the first time, as well as unlocking the extras menu that allows you to purchase concept art, character models, gun models, guns that were not in the first playthrough, Chris' weapons, infinite ammo and much more; all while using in game credits allowing you to earn the items which I am a fan of. There is a New Game+ mode allowing you load a cleared save and starting the game with all your items and money. 

Overall I can safely say Yes, I highly recommend this game, and eagerly await the next iteration of this franchise. I can only pray that Capcom stay on the straight and narrow and continue to release AAA releases like this, this game has restore my faith to this series.

To preface this review;

This is the first Resident Evil game I have played. That being said, I have watched both a speed-run and a long play of Resident Evil 7. I was always interested in Resident Evil 7, but never had the spare money to buy it. After watching multiple play-through's, reviews, as well as reading deeply into the lore, I didn't have the itch to play it when I finally had the opportunity to.

Resident Evil Village wasn't on my radar at all, until a friend of mine mentioned it to me a week before release. I watched all the trailers and read everything there was to read about it. I even watched another Resi 7 speed run. Needless to say I managed to hype myself up for this game.

I don't play horror games, usually preferring to watch others play them, so take my opinion with a grain of salt. If you want to know how good of a horror game this is, or how good of a Resident Evil game this is, I may not be the best person to ask. That being said, I've been playing video games for a long time, particularly interested in single player experiences. 

Resident Evil Village is a damn good video game. Its a damn good single player experience, and I would venture to call it a solid horror game. From what I know about Resi 7 and what I've read about previous entries in the series, I would also guess it's a great Resident Evil Game.

It seems that people's biggest problems with this game are; it isn't scary enough, Lady Dimitrescu and her castle aren't a big enough part of the game, there aren't enough puzzles, the gameplay is too action-oriented, and the pacing/gameplay shifts drastically towards the end. That's at least what I have gathered from the past few days of watching and reading reviews. 

I personally find that the majority of people saying the game isn't scary enough are avid horror gamers and youtubers/streamers. Clearly these people would have a higher tolerance to this kind of thing, but that doesn't detract from their complaints. I would argue though that this game is plenty scary for your average player. On my first play-through, I felt a constant tension while wandering Castle Dimitrescu. Going through the Village felt eerily quiet and empty at times, heightening my paranoia, and then the game capitalized on this with Lycan encounters and jumpscares peppered throughout. House Beneviento was one of the scariest things I've experienced in a game, playing more towards psychological and gore horror. The first half of this game really emphasizes tension and surprise. House Moreau is a quick sunny cake-walk that felt like the weakest house, in my opinion, as far as horror goes. It was still very fun, and what it lacked in scariness, it made up for in action and scenery. House Heisenberg is probably the longest or second longest section of the game, being on par with Castle Dimitrescu. This house is a return to horror, but keeps all the action packed pace of House Moreau. The horror of house Heisenberg definitely feels less thrilling and suspenseful and more terrifying because of the enemies you face and the frequency with which you face them. The last two sections of the game definitely heavily lean towards action and stray away from horror, I won't deny that at all. All that said, I don't think someone can objectively say this game "isn't scary". Sure, it may not scare you if you have a higher tolerance to this kind of stuff, and that's a valid point to make against something that's meant to be a "horror" game, but I and many others like me would probably say this game is as scary as it needs to be and certainly deserves to be called horror.

As for the complaint that this game doesn't feature Lady Dimitrescu and her castle enough, that's less a problem with the game and more a problem with you and your expectations. Of course, I could see how someone could watch all the trailers and think that Chris and Lady Dimitrescu are the two big bad's of this game, but I just personally interpreted that build-up as being good marketing that doesn't give away the whole story. I was very happy when I first escaped Castle Dimitrescu and realized there was much more left to play and more enemies to face. I won't deny however that Donna Beneviento and Salvatore Moreau were underwritten and underutilized. This wasn't a huge deal to me however, because it felt like capcom was just working under a "quality over quantity" mantra. Beneviento has the shortest house in the game, but it was certainly the scariest and most puzzle-dense. For those that felt her and Moreau were underwritten, I recommend reading all the lore the game offers throughout. Moreau's character was as deep as he needed to be, given his incredibly low mental capacity. I felt that his section of the game was great for advancing the plot and letting the player have fun with their weapons. This is a nice little change of pace, and contrary to a lot of negative reviews, I don't think much needed to be added to be honest. I just couldn't disagree more that the game would purely benefit from capcom shoehorning in more and more for Beneviento and Moreau. I think each section of the game was curated very well: 
- Castle Dimitrescu is tense and suspensful, there are plenty of rooms, corridors, and levels to explore and get lost in. There are a few puzzles, several mobs, three sub-boss fights, and a boss fight. This was the best place to start the game since the player is inexperienced. It is also a pretty decent chunk, I would say you spend somwhere between 1/5 and 1/4 of the game here.
- House Beneviento takes you out of Castle Dimitrescu's "tutorial" part of the game and strips you of your weapons. You have to solve puzzles and be quick on your feet in this deeply atmospheric and terrifying doll house.
- House Moreau, as previously stated, is a pretty quick section of the game even on your first play through. There's nothing overly confusing to solve here, there's not much distance you have to cover, and you really just end up shooting a lot of things and use everything you've learned about the gunplay in this bossfight.
- House Heisenberg is comparable in length to Castle Dimitrescu. This section of the game appropriately follows the first three. At this point the game knows that you have an understanding of solving puzzles, using your weapons, being quick on your feet, and running through big confusing places. The game knows this and tries to strain you a little further in all regards. The scenery here is arguably the best, but I personally think Castle Dimitrescu takes the cake. 
- The rest of the game after going through all four lords drops a lot of the horror elements of the game, but remains creepy in it's imagery and plot. The game-play really amps up here and the pace kicks in. The ending of this game is pretty fast compared to the first and final houses. It definitely feels like a sprint to the finish line, and I'm not mad about it. 

There is no doubting that this game has far fewer puzzles and is far more action-focused than Resident Evil 7. I'm not entirely sure how this could drastically effect the way you view this game. For those who think this way, I guess just go replay Resident Evil 7. I've always felt that some series need to stick to the formula, and some need to freshen things up. For example, the borderlands series got really dry for me after a while because it felt like I was buying the same game every time. In contrast to this, I haven't played any Assassin's Creed game from Origin onward because too much has changed about the series. I think Resident Evil benefited from such a change of gameplay and atmosphere, although I would agree that the game could use more puzzles, and puzzles of higher difficulty.

This game is incredible and I didn't even get into all the post-game content and replayability. I could write a review of equal length applauding the writing, directing, imagery, and more.

Updated review upon reflection: 

- The story and writing was a major let down. Messy - This story is very obviously made up different ideas from different producers, bolted together. Feels like one producer wanted the game to star the same protagonist as Resi7 - but another producer wanted to this game to be an adventure game. Ethan WInters was designed for a horror game. He's written to be a victim type of dude, crying, whining, etc. This is great when you insert him in a horrorific scenario - but Resi8 is an adventure game - and Ethan Winters just doesn't play. He whines, complains, acts victmized as he would in a horror game - it doesn't work at all. 

- As an adventure game Resi8 is fun. There's lots of combat, and the combat feels great. The exploration aspect is put on rails - you are forced fed key items and progression is very linear - gone are the days of funding multiple puzzle items out of order and backtracking to get things solved. You lose of a lot of Resident Evil's tradmark suspense - but you do get a faster pace - this is an arcady blast compared to past Resi titles. 

- Resi's item management mechanic is almost gone. Key items don't take up space, nor do crafting items or treasures, so no more carefully calculating what you will need to bring into new areas. This mechanic feels included purely as tradition. 

- The art direction is gorgeously rendered, as you'd expect from a AAA game running on the RE engine. But it was samey. Only the castle really stands out. Everything else:  Lots of snow, debris, and rundown shacks. So many rundown shacks. 

-The artwork of this game depicts an open looking world but there too many invisible walls - you're not in an open world at all - it's a dungeon. it's irksome when blocked paths are rendered as a a shrub and a flimsy piece of wood. Why not drop in a big brick wall and make it clear?  Again, it felt like one producer wanted the game to look like an open world, another producer wanted strict dungeon game design - Resi8 is not unified in its concepts at all. 

- There is one area where you play for an hour or so without guns and the focus is strictly on puzzle solving. It was great fun and stood and really stood out as a memorable part of the game particularly because the game is mostly an action adventure game. Another highlight of this area is that it contains the game's more genuinely scary monster. The climax to this section is a puzzle boss which is irksome - i feel these scenarios penalize unique play style, and are tedious on repeat playthrus. 

-  Other gaming publications have been highly critical of the last section of the game, but I thought it was great fun. It was a good balance of shooty bang action and a main puzzle that required backtracking. 


-------------- CONCLUSION -------------


Resident Evil 7 was a quantum leap forward in re-asserting the series as horror for a new generation. Resident Evil 2 (Remake) was another risk that paid off, showing the world that horror games with AAA budgets are viable. 

Resident Evil (8) Village feels like a course-correction. The problem is it feels as tho they have over-corrected. This is all very conventional and silly. It feels geared toward a younger audience, and it might be just right for them. As for me

I give it a marginal thumbs up recommendation, if you're craving a spooky game with AAA polish, this game will do. If you can do without the spookiness - there are much better action shooters out there.

== ORIGINAL REVIEW
I wish Steam had a "meh" rating, since I would recommend this game to a certain type of player, but I certainly didn't like it, hence the thumbs down.

Ok, so I want to make some things clear first:

- I don't think it's a bad game, in fact I think it's very well done and I can see why most players like it.

- I'm not biased towards "old school" or "new school" RE. My top games are 4, 1R, 2, 2R and 7, and the ones I hate most are 6 and 0, so it's not the style that makes me like or hate a specific game.

- I'll obviously talk about spoilers.

So, my main gripe with this game is, funnily enough, what most people seem to like: the variety in horror. As I mentioned, I don't mind RE trying new stuff, but I just wish they committed to just one or maybe two styles. For instance in RE4, the horror "theme" stopped being virus/zombies and became parasite/mind control, so they took this and exhausted every single type of enemy this would entail, and the limitation allowed them to be very creative with tons of memorable, unique enemies like the blind claw, chain-saw dude (which gets an update in every game since), cultists etc.

In 8, it's pretty clear (even from the art designs comments) that they went for a horror show approach with a variety of monsters, like Castlevania. I don't think this is bad per se, I just don't think it fits RE. How I wish they just committed to the Vampire and/or Werewolves theme and created a ton of stuff with that!  When I saw Lady D daughters, the lower medieval prisoners zombies and the fly/bat thing I was genuinely hyped, but then this theme suddenly dropped and got replaced with Child's Play and I was "waa?". This means that every enemy just get its basic trope interpretation and not much else. Also I know the fetus is a lot of people favorite scene, but on-rails horror where you have to hide and wait a timer just don't do it for me, I just find it mind numbing and on repeated playthroughs it'll be a slog (just like Sherry's in RE2R). In the end, it feels like the fungus is now a pretty lame excuse to do whatever, like give Magneto powers to humans, and I just don't know how I feel about something that can do whatever, whenever with no rules. Cyber zombies were funny though (even though it's basically Doom).

Another gripe is combat. It is definitely better than 7, but I would make the point that in 7 you're not supposed to be good at combat for two reasons: Ethan is just a regular dude, and an awkward combat helps making you feel helpless in a horror game, like old school RE (not trying to excuse it, I see why people wouldn't like it). However, It's still so limited compared to 4, 5 and 6! I'm not very fond of 5 and 6, but the combat in these games are fun. The one I like most is 4 though, and it's the more limited of the three, so why do I complain 8 is limited but praise 4 for being limited wtf? The thing is, all combat in 4 was built around the limitation of having to stop to shoot, so every enemy acts and has a singular strategy you have to uncover to fight against, tailored for your movement as a player. And variety. Enemy with projectiles, enemy with shield, dynamite enemy, blind enemy, OHK enemy, giant machine gun enemy, among others. It was common to have to fight multiple enemy types at once, making you think about how to tackle each situation. Am I wrong or in 8 you ONLY fight one enemy type at a time, except for the occasional projectile dude and a few bosses? Also, my strategy for all enemies was the same: walk backwards and then the enemy whiffs, or just block, occasionally running forward. Even bosses.

And finally, I thought the story was just meh. First of all, I think it's pretty fanfic-y how Umbrella went from just being a pharmaceutical company with shady bioweapon labs, to this almost cabalistic thing that involves ancient ruins and rituals, Spencer being a mythical figure in search of immortality that's related to every BOW incident in the world, and Chris coincidentally always finding the document that says that (I wouldn't be surprised if Spencer comes back at some point; and Miranda just casually have a 60 year old letter sitting on a table for others to read??).

I don't get how Ethan being a fungus is that big of a deal since to me it was supposed to be pretty clear with 7, as both he and Mia clearly had regeneration. Also I think Mia got robbed of being the one to save Ethan and her daughter at the end, since I think Chris was there just for fan service (but no Jill...).

Well, I said my piece and I'm at ease, agree to disagree with most people I guess. Thanks for reading anyway!

EDIT: honestly the more I think about it the worse it gets. RE never had outstanding stories, but apart from a few exceptions they usually made sense in of themselves, even all the silliness of 4 was explained in one way or another. This game though... is just nonsense.

What was Miranda's plan after all? Why did she need to disguise as Mia? Wouldn't it be easier to just sneak in and take the baby, since she did this anyway? Then she makes a challenge for Ethan to kill all 4 lords... why? Miranda had no use for Ethan, just straight out killing him. Then again, why didn't she just do the ritual when she got to the village with the baby? Why divide it in four and give Rose to the 4 lords? She just makes the ritual without Ethan, and without the lords... she just needed Rose. It's not like it's magic, it's just a fungus.

And then there's Chris. What was his plan again? Why just not tell Ethan outright that it wasn't Mia? It would take like, 3 seconds? The game even acknowledges this was stupid, but it sounds like the writers realizing this made no sense more than anything. Then he trained Ethan for combat... and tells him to not do anything? But Ethan did MUCH more than Chris and he was still unwilling. Did Chris purposefully let Ethan and Mia have a fungus baby? So he knew the baby was a fungus, and also Ethan and Mia? How did he know Miranda would come for them, and disguised as Mia?

Ugh, my head hurts...

Although not a masterpiece, one of the best Resident Evil games we've seen in the last 20 years.  The environments and lighting effects are some of the best I've seen on current gen hardware, and the story is one of the best efforts Capcom has put forward to date.  That said, nearly every positive has a "but" to go along with it, with loads of missed potential.

The one example I'll touch on is the second major area you get to explore.  Although it is incredibly well done, it's also incredibly short and would likely have done better to have been the third section of the game rather than the second for pacing's sake (grounding/humbling the player as they were starting to rise heading into the final section[s] of the game).  Felt like they put it that early to appease RE7 fans and it was a mistake, imo. 

That said, if you're looking for a step into what's to come moving forward for gaming, this is an outstanding video game and worth your hard earned $$.  If you love action / horror style games, don't miss this one.   

+ Pros
Incredible Lighting/Environments
Ambient noises are well done
Story is one of the best RE stories we've gotten
More Gunplay
Pacing is incredibly well done
Bonus mode (Mercenaries) is tons of fun and a great post game reward

- Cons
Some sound effects feel very "stock" and phoned in 
A little cheesy
Gunplay feels a little meh overall outside of Mercs
Could have been GOTY with better directional choices

TL;DR: Both old and new RE fans have things to like here, and if you've never played a RE game before, the only thing you'll miss are a few references here and there, with even a recap of RE7 existing in this game.  Don't feel like you need to play the previous titles to give this one a go.  Solid 8.5/10 for me.

 The atmosphere of this one to me is even better than 7 for various reasons. Overall RE:Village is a must for fans of the series as well as newcomers, it does excel at what Resident Evil is known for and it offers a satisfying horror adventure. Resident Evil Village:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ 

After being rescued three years ago from the Baker’s house by Chris Redfield and his commando units somewhere in the Louisiana countryside, Ethan and Mia Winters have relocated at Chris’ request and recently welcomed their first child, Rosemary. The event that occurred three years ago is still fresh in their minds, and a sense of insecurity and fear is constantly looming over them even if they are trying hard to forget, to move on and enjoy their little bundle of joy. But one night, the living nightmare starts again for Ethan after Mia is gunned down in their apartment by their saviour, Chris Redfield, who was after Rosemary. Ethan refused to see his daughter taken away and tried to put up a bit of a fight but was knocked out cold by the butt of a sub-machine gun. When he woke up, he was somewhere close to a Resident Evil Village!

Resident Evil Village is the 8th game of the iconic first-person survival horror/ puzzle-solving series developed and self-published by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. The game was released on the 7th of May 2021 on Steam as well as on PS4, PS5, Xbox Series X and Xbox One.  

The game consists of the main story and the Mercenaries mode, which will unlock once you have successfully finished your first playthrough. There are four levels of difficulty, which are Casual, Normal, Hardcore and Village of Shadows. In my case, I decided to play my first playthrough on the Normal difficulty, and it took me around 11 hours to complete the game. 

What an absolute piece of art this game is. From start to finish Resident Evil Village provides stunning graphics and entertainment with exquisite cutscenes, great gameplay and several  jump-out-of-your-chair moments. In terms of puzzles, it is more or less finding keys or objects that can give you access to a new area within the village or in the buildings you’ll be visiting during your gameplay. I was surprised about the amount of action this game provides! The element of horror survival is there, but it is far more subtle than the action you encounter playing this game. Don’t get me wrong, I didn’t mind it at all, and in fact I think the balance between the two is pretty much spot on. Nonetheless, it startled me a little bit as I was not expecting to be frequently attacked by a horde of enemies. But I did really enjoy the different types of enemy that I encountered in each of the main locations in this game. 

Regarding the story, you play Ethan Winters who is on a mission to save his daughter and does not know why his daughter has been abducted by a woman named Mother Miranda. Very quickly into the piece, Ethan will be brought to Mother Miranda by one of her four Lieutenants name Heisenberg. There, he will meet the entire gang painfully, and he will be given a chance to escape at that cutscene. That will bring on a frantic pursuit which Ethan need to be quick to find his way out by navigating into dangerous rooms and make sure to keep moving ahead and not being caught. There are a couple of these pursuits in this which are very fun.  
 
To save his daughter, he will have to defeat all four Mother Miranda Lieutenants in four different locations and retrieve the four parts of his daughter, which will be in four yellow glass rectangles. I must say that I personally enjoyed Dimitrescu’s Castle stage the most, and the boss fight with the Mutated Alcina Dimitrescu was absolutely a hell of a battle. Then, the Reservoir and the Factory were pretty good too, but I am afraid the Donna Beneviento and Angie stage were a bit dull for me liking and frankly very easy. 
 
Ethan will start this chilling story without any weapons, and he will be given a gun by an NPC relatively early on upon arriving at the village. Unfortunately for him, he will have a small amount of ammunition, goods and money at first. So, he will need to search houses, open draws and wardrobes to find some new goodies. Don’t worry too much, a small black arrow will highlight the compartments he is able to open. He can also find goodies on surfaces and in wooden boxes with yellow paint on them. Most of the time when Ethan kills an enemy, the foe will most likely drop either some Lei (money), an object or ammunition. Don’t forget lo look up at the trees and on ceilings, you might also find interesting goodies. 

In a few locations, you’ll be able to sell, buy and upgrade weapons, buy recipes for making ammunition or increase your inventory slots at the caravan of Duke the merchant. But all cost serious Lei, so bear that in mind. You can also get perks by providing Duke with specific meats so he can cook one of his recipes. 

As I mentioned before, all aspects of the game are extremely well-done, and it was such a pleasure to run this game on my 4k monitor on the 3840 X 2160 resolution and using my Astro A50 headset. Unfortunately, I had a few crashes during my gameplay. The game just froze, which is always a bit frustrating. Thankfully, the game autosaves right after cutscenes, before encounters and after fights. You also save your game at the iconic typewriters. The game has full controller support in terms of the controls, but I personally prefer playing these types of game with my mouse and keyboard.

Positives:
~~~~~~~ 
+	Stunning graphics and atmosphere
+	A good story with amazing cutscenes
+	A good variety of enemies
+	Four levels of difficulty
+	Mercenaries mode unlocked after finishing your first playthrough
+	Full controller support
+	Achievements and trading cards

Negatives:
~~~~~~~~ 

-	I experienced a few crashes.

A first-person survival horror with plenty of action, great gameplay, stunning graphics and amazing cutscenes. It would be sacrilege to miss Resident Evil Village!

WARNING: Review will contain spoilers. 

Overall I would say that I have mixed feelings about this game, it's not great, but it's not bad. If I had to pick one word to summarize Village it would be inconsistent. The gameplay and presentation of the game is fantastic, but the tone is all over the place, It doesn't feel like Resident Evil. It honestly feels like the developers had a lot of ideas for different horror games, but mashed them all together and slapped the Resident Evil title on it. 

The game starts strong, but loses itself quickly, for a game called Village, the actual village is quite boring and doesn't have any lasting presence, it is not on the same level as The Spencer Mansion, The RPD, or the Baker Estate. The village feels half baked, presumably because there are 5 major areas in the game. Of these 5 areas, the only one that really stands out is Castle Dimitrescu, but even that feels like a missed opportunity.  

Tonally the game is all over the place, it starts off very strong but quickly loses it's identity. We are introduced to an eerie setting and a mystery begging to be solved, but then the game abandons the established tone in order to create sequences that, by themselves, are interesting, but together form an inconsistent experience.

[spoiler]Castle Dimitrescu is by far my favorite part of the game, the castle is beautiful and evokes feelings of classic Resident Evil. The dimly lit dungeons, and the ominous silence of the castle halls create a sense of wonder and tension. Couple this with the amazing Lady Dimitrescu, an antagonist with a foreboding presence and overall great character design. The castle is over quickly, which is disappointing as I wanted to explore more of it. Donna Beneviento's section feels like something that belongs in a game more akin to Silent Hill, it feels so out of place thematically. Creepy dolls are not reminiscent of Resident Evil, it feels like it was put into the game because the developers thought it would be scary. The area aims to be more puzzle focused, but fails as there is no real thinking involved and devolves into, find item and put it where it's supposed to go. Moreaus's area is quite generic, nothing special about it. However it was during Heisenberg's section that the game really lost me, it basically turns into Wolfenstein and loses all semblance of horror. While the enemies and atmosphere are cool, it isn't scary, at this point the game is a full on action game. The boss fight with Heisenberg has you piloting a tank with infinite ammo and a cannon. Chris's section is basically Call of Duty, which is fun, but feels out of place.[/spoiler]

I often see people say that Village is what would happen if Resident Evil 4 and 7 had a baby, but I feel like that statement is a disservice to both games. While Resident Evil 4 is an action game, it knows it's an action game and doesn't take itself too seriously. It embraces it's silliness and resulted in an amazing game (but not an amazing Resident Evil game). Resident Evil 7 was a brilliant return to form, harkening back to the tension and panic of classic Resident Evil. Village feels like it tries to do both, but doesn't really succeed in either.

The story is ok, but I won't go into it because I don't think it's as crucial to Resident Evil as the scares, but I can appreciate Capcom for putting more emphasis on the story. 

While I did enjoy my time with the game, I find it difficult to recommend as I have mixed opinions about it. I think Resident Evil fans will enjoy it for expanding on the characters and lore, but some might be disappointed in the games direction. Newcomers will probably enjoy the game if they enjoyed Resident Evil 7. I wish there was a neutral option for whether or not I would recommend it, but as I did enjoy the game, and I feel like it is something that many people would enjoy, I would recommend it. 

If I had to give the game a score, I would give it a 6.5 or a 7 out of 10.

This is probably the best form of a resident evil game, as far as graphics, gameplay, inventory management, setting, atmosphere, antagonists, etc., at least in my personal opinion.

I can't speak much to the story in comparison to the other games, but it has been engaging enough to keep me coming back.

As far as pacing goes, it does seem a bit odd.  They set up that there are 4 main objectives prior to facing the main baddie, however that first one is probably 1/3rd+ of the game, wheras the others are relatively short in comparison.  I haven't quite finished the game myself, but this does seem like a bit of an odd discrepiency, and mabye they were rushed / couldn't put quite the same level of detail into the later parts of the game.
Overall however, this certianly doesn't hurt the game, as it's not like it's lacking for content.

While it does seem to be pretty well balanced, some enemies are definetly more bullet sponegy than they need to be.  I get taking down a boss should be an achievement and all, but if it takes 10+ headshots to take out one basic enemy, and they drop 1/4th of the recipe for 15 bullets, it definetly feels like you're constantly losing resources.  I know that's an aspect of the survival horror resource scarcity but it does seem odd, especially considering this is on standard difficulty.

As far as real "horror", there's really only one memorable section, though there are a few places where they successfully make you feel powerless, and in fear as a result of an enemies seeming invincibility etc.

Irregardless of those nitpicks, it is fun, and I'd absolutely reccomend it.

I originally played Resident Evil Village on release day, and as a huge fan of the Resident Evil series, I was pretty excited. As a big fan of Resident Evil 7 in particular, I had high hopes. When I originally finished Village however, my thoughts were ultimately inconclusive. I knew I liked the game, but overall I wasn't sure how I felt on the whole experience. The game sat in dormant in my library for a while, but recently as part of me revisiting the series as a whole, I decided to replay it.

What I didn't expect however, was that I would really love this game upon my revisit. I played through the game 4 times over, first beating it on standard, then twice on hardcore and then I finally beat it again on Village of Shadows. While not perfect by any stretch, Resident Evil Village is an incredibly fun and engaging game and I think its far better than I originally thought.

The story of Village is a bit of a mess. Naturally, in a series this long and complex, the story was bound to get lost somewhere. It follows Ethan Winters again, taking place multiple years after the previous game. Without spoiling anything, a series of bad events leads to your daughter being kidnapped and you needing to go rescue her. The plot follows familiar beats to what you might expect from Resident Evil by now. There is conspiracy, bio weapons, Umbrella is of course involved in some way and your daughter is somehow stuck in the middle of it all. The story is solid overall, with the only issues lying with some occasional odd pacing and characters sometimes acting out of order. Chris Redfield in particular acts incredibly off for much of the game and had me scratching my head at a few moments. Dialogue is a mixed bag, with some amazingly cheesy lines, and some god awful ones as well. Provided you don't take it too seriously, it stays consistently enjoyable throughout.

As you would expect, the graphics in this game are absolutely amazing. Character models have a crazy amount of detail to them, the environments are far more detailed and dense than previous entries and the visual style is perfect. This truly does set a benchmark for the series in the graphical department and I have no clue how they would manage to up it from here.

To talk about sound, its fairly solid all around. The soundtrack isn't present very often, but it is really good when it does show. The Gothic music style fits the world really well and can make the boss fights pretty incredible. The guns also sound really great and combat has a really good punch to it all in all.

The gameplay is technically a mix of Resident Evil 7, and Resident Evil 4. It keeps the first person perspective and control style of 7, but the gameplay design and action focus is pulled straight from Resident Evil 4. If you loved Resident Evil 4's gameplay, you will most likely also enjoy Village. There is much less of an emphasis on puzzles all around. The game instead focuses on action gameplay and exploration. The Village itself acts as a hub for you to explore in between your actual objectives outside of it. Originally, I felt the gameplay sections were uneven, however after playing, I don't feel so harsh. The only section I would call lesser, would be the swamp section, due to its basic platform puzzle design and unappealing environment. All other sections however are far better and hold the game up. Lady D's castle at the beginning is a big standout in particular and it is a shame this didn't make up more of the game.

One place where some people had issue was the game's length. On my first ever playthrough, I remember the game taking me around 7 hours to beat. I did a bit of extra exploring, but not a ton. On my average playthrough now, I can beat the game in around 3 hours. One may complain about the short length overall, however the game is tailor made for replayability. I beat this game multiple times back to back and had a blast the whole time. If you beat the game only once and complain the content is lacking, you are genuinely playing it wrong. The true way to play is through New Game Plus. You beat the game again, this time on a higher difficulty and bringing your upgraded weapons with you. When you are facing the tough battles with your max upgrades and special weapons from the bonus completion menu, it all reaches a new level.

With all my replays and extra time spent playing, I've gotten almost 30 hours total and I definitely think I got my money's worth from it overall. Resident Evil Village quickly became one of my favourite games in the whole Resident Evil series, and this is one I will be revisiting very often

Full disclaimer and warning: 
-I will be giving spoilers about the first six hours of the game further down in this review
-This is the very first Resident Evil game I have played
-I have not played the game beyond the first six hours

If you have not already lynched me entirely for any of the above, I will be laying out my experiences both positive and negative with this game and my view on it as someone who has freshly picked it up with no prior experience in the series.

First things first. Do I consider Resident Evil Village to be a bad game? Not entirely. I think it has a lot of parts that deserve a lot of credit and I am sure even casual fans of Resident Evil could enjoy it far better than I did. Beyond a brief desync between audio and visuals in the first few cinematics I experienced no major technical issues with the game. It flowed smoothly, the audio was of high quality, the graphics were very good even with my playing on 'performance first' setting. While the game is undeniably more of a campy exploration of various set pieces that are either action or horror than than the 'survival horror' it is advertised as, I do not see this as a bad thing. It had me laughing and uneasy at various points and I can only give the game props for that. 

What are my issues then? I'll lay them out as plainly as I can.

1. I feel deceived as to what the game was about. With all the trailers and promotional material I have seen, I went into this game expecting a horror game centred around the subject of eastern european folklore. Vampires, Witches, Werewolves, so on. This is not to say that I was not ready for a Resident Evil game however. I was fully aware and accepting that everything about this was going to be explained by the crazy science of umbrella or related. As it turns out? I was quite ready to accept all of that. There Werewolves are this games infected zombies. The fly witches are a result of a biological experiment on corpses. The big mommy vampire turns into a big tentacle dragon monster. All of this and more I was quite ready for. What I was not ready for was for seemingly all of that to be dropped before I was even through a quarter of the game. The vampires and witches were gone, the werewolves disappeared for large sections and it seems we were moving on to entirely different subjects. Fish monsters, spooky doll houses and what I shall playfully describe as 'cowboy magneto with a hammer'. I do feel deceived as to what this game was about, and I am sure I am not the only person to feel this way. This is not to say that I wanted the vampires to be the only part of the game, though I would not have argued with that. That is not to say I wanted the trailer to give everything away, that certainly wouldn't work. What I am saying is that I would like more of it to stick to the setting and themes that were advertised. Zombie werewolf boss. Gargoyle creatures. More witches. All of it with crazy umbrella science behind it I am sure but not...not factories with telekentic gear cowboys.

2. The quality of the horror. The dollhouse is what lost me. I am sure it did wonders for other people, but I could only describe it as cheap youtube or twitch bait. The tension of walking through a dollhouse was quickly lost after the first floor when nothing was seemingly going to happen. It was empty space for tension. Nothing moving in the corner of my eyes. Nothing disappearing as I turned back around. I understand building tension, and it did a good job....but it then went on for twice as too long. Then right as tension built back up again, it was lost. A few moments of the lights going off enough for the main character to lose all their weapons in some inexplicable way. Things teleported. Stuff appeared as it shouldn't and normally I would not mind this in the slightest, if it wans't for the fact that this is a Resident Evil game. Science is meant to explain it all and using cheap supernatural scares just seemed ill fitting for me. The taking away of the weapons to me seemed as though the game was admitting it couldn't maintain horror without making me defenceless, while at the same time advertising that there was no threat at all. Not until everything turned dark...and I was met with something that was not terrifying, not scary, not unsettling, just unpleasant. I came for a game with eastern european gothic horror laced with crazy mutant science. I did not expect a giant fetus baby suddenly in the dollhouse. I don't think anyone could have expected that. It was certainly shocking, but not in the way that it should have been. It was a cheap unpleasantness that had no thought or craft behind it, just shock value. The monster was certainly well designed, but it took me out of the moment entirely. It was at this point I closed the game and so far I have no further intention of pulling it back up, as it seems that the quality and the build up so far could only further degenerate.

I am sure many people will have things to pick away at this review with, or simply spout that I should have expected all of this from a resident evil game and perhaps I did make a mistake to put any faith in this game to not go in this direction, but it is what it is. People can read and decide for themselves, I am sure many people will enjoy this game. But for those who are of a like mind with myself, I advise you to give this game a skip. It's not what you think it is. At the very least go in expecting something very, very different.

TL:DR, the advertisement of eastern myth and gothic horror is quickly replaced with cheap shock horror and basic scare tricks. If you are looking for a resident evil game, then you shall get what you want, I hope you enjoy the game. If you saw the trailers and saw this as a unique gothic horror, I advise you to adjust your lens or skip this game.

Two steps forward one step back. Village addresses almost every complaint and problem with RE7 yet there are some minor set backs which are puzzling. 

1. The inventory system now pauses the game. Why? RE7s great strength was that you were only able to take a breath in save rooms. Sure, pausing the game to exit or adjust settings is fine but it does hinder the flow when you can stop time and fix your inventory. 
2. That leads to the second step back, inventory, it feels as if the RE4 tetris inventory was brought back but not fully finished for this game. Some features like being back to swamp items with each other has been removed and the overall navigation of the inventory is clunky. 
3. The pickup item and interact with lock triggers are atrocious in this game. You see this problem clearly by watching any speedrun. This was not an issue with RE7.
4. The weapon latter in this game is not good. Every weapon is a direct upgrade to the last. Part of what made RE4 (which this game takes a lot of inspiration from) so fun with it's weapons is that there are multiple options for end game. With RE8 each time a new gun appears it's minimum damage is the max that is currently available for your gun. This means there really isn't a reason to not always use the next weapon you find.
5. The middle game (Lords 2 and 3) feel rushed and short. It's shame as the Reservoir and Garden have a lot of atmosphere and potential.

These are the most objective faults of an overall pretty good game. I have nearly 100% this game  so I have played through many times. If you like 7 and 4 you will like this game.

As of the time writing this, I have beaten the game twice now.

I really did enjoy my time with this game. It felt unique and I had a blast uncovering every nook and cranny of collectible I could find, or scrounging up ammo to handle the situation at hand. Brought me back to moments when I played RE7. And that's about it for me. 

Personally, I didn't mind the switch to first person, and still don't. What I don't like is Ethan Winters. I think he is easily one of the worst protagonists I have ever seen in a game. He will make stupid comments and will not take action at various times when there is seemingly no good reason. Minor spoiler for the early game: [spoiler] When Ethan first arrives at Luiza's house it is revealed that the father of the woman you just rescued turns into one of the Lycans and begins murdering everyone in the room. At this point, even in your first playthrough, Ethan is carrying a pistol and a shotgun and chooses to do nothing and instead gets "saved" by the daughter who suddenly has a shotgun [/spoiler]. 

The writing is really laughable at times. I streamed this game for a handful of my friends the first few days it came out. Admittedly we enjoy poking fun at things, and perhaps we could've been harsh at times. Yet the story is so driven by the need to connect itself to the universe of Resident Evil, I think it falls flat on its face. If this game was just The Village, and had no prior connections to the Resident Evil universe I think I would've been more impressed. This has the same faults, in my opinion, as Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag. That game was a really poor Assassin's Creed game but an amazing pirate game, why not focus on that element instead? Studios are afraid to walk away from an established title franchise, because it will simply still make money if it is titled Resident Evil 8, even though this game has only one real reason it's even remotely connected to the plot. 

The game isn't scary to me, but I don't blame anyone on that behalf. Most people have seen the Tweets talking about the design team taking into consideration how people were scared to play the previous title and they didn't want that. Or it could be that I grew up playing horror games and had nightmares of the monsters and creatures I've fought and now very little seems to scare me anymore. Regardless of the answer, this game is much more action based for certain, especially with the amount of guns you can unlock, there are so many of them it's somewhat overwhelming. 

I loved the characters introduced and the design of the Village. It felt very natural to explore, even though the Village itself is a bit of an awkward maze to get through. I never felt like I wasn't excited to see who I encounter next, but Ethan is just so unlikable to me that the dude wastes times taunting the antagonists, or just being downright stupid at times. Maybe it's just the script was bad, and perhaps in other languages it is okay, but something about the way Ethan responded to some horribly supernatural things, along with a dash of Resident Evil classic tentacled monsters and the like, Ethan never really felt like he was actually fighting for his life.

The Duke being the new Merchant similar to RE4 was an incredible inclusion. I love shopkeepers in games and this guy certainly is the reason why I love them. A huge air of mystery around the character, he has everything you could need, offers new upgrades as the game progresses, and even offers permanent upgrades for subsequent playthoughs to unlock more toys to play with. Perfect in every way as far as I'm concerned. 

The extra mode after beating the game, Mercenaries is simply mediocre. It can be fun, but it isn't my cup of tea and I think unless I decided to go for 100% completion of the achievements, I will never return to play that mode. 

Though I do have my complaints and didn't enjoy this as a Resident Evil game, this game was still amazing to play. If they leaned more on the horror elements the franchise has shown they can do, I think this game would've been so much better. Of course there is nothing more Resident Evil than running around with an infinite ammo Grenade Launcher and Revolver just decimating your foes for the fun of it, so maybe I just don't like the Protagonist? Hard to say.

Just leaving some spoiler-free thoughts (story-wise) after completing the game on Hardcore difficulty:

First of all, I do recommend playing on Hardcore if you are initially just thinking of doing a single playthrough even though there is a sequence in the beginning that can be quite challenging as you get used to the mechanics of it all. However, past that point, the rest of the game feels very balanced for this difficulty as you are always teetering on just having enough resources (that is, somewhere in between being a little short, and having some extra to spare that makes up for missed shots/unnecessary damage).

In terms of the experience, the game does feel more action-oriented than its predecessor but not too much like what we saw in the transition to RE5 and RE6. Like many have described this one feels like a mix of RE7 and RE4, but if I might add, with a Van Helsing-esque skin applied on top. Overall, very much enjoyed the campaign and is probably one of the best survival-horror titles that I've played to date - it had a good mix of environments/settings, some truly memorable and terrifying sequences (one in particular brought out PT vibes), a variety of puzzles as one would expect from an RE game, and many battles/struggles leaving you in question as to how you pulled that off in the chance that you got it on the first try.

As for minor critiques - sometimes the mechanic of pushing away enemies is a bit finicky, there is a particular gun scope that I felt was designed confusingly because of the offset crosshair markers, and even with an RTX 2070s I had to turn off ray-tracing to be able to guarantee above 60fps at all times (with it on, certain places/events would kill frames even though I was mostly getting above 60fps)

Observations:

1. Action-packed with emphasis on combat, like RE4.
2. Inventory, upgrade system, treasures, and map system borrow from RE4.
3. Extra weapon upgrades through weapon attachments, increasing weapon stats.
4. Level design is larger than in RE7, using an open map (akin to a hub world), allowing for some exploration.
5. Somewhat unique gameplay experiences in different parts of the map.
6. Crafting system to create ammo and other items (actual scrap metal needed to craft)
7. Skill upgrades are via the Merchant in-game, using ingredients from hunting birds and animals.
8. Light to medium difficulty puzzles present to break up the game flow a bit.

Pros:

1. Larger enemy variety compared to RE7.
2. Gun handling is solid.
3. Combat is fun, especially using Guard and Knock Back to create space.
4. Action sequences well thought out.
5. Mercenaries Mode similar to older entries.
6. Cutscenes can be skipped or paused.

Cons:

1. Enemies can be bullet sponges at times.
2. No stun melee attacks.
3. Horror factor is reduced (compared to RE7).
4. Mercenaries Mode has only one playable character.
5. More exploration could have been added (light relevant sidequests would have been welcome)

Technical observations on PC version:

1. Default FOV is too low. FOV slider is missing. Forced Vignetting with no option to turn it off. (The FoV mod fixes these 2 problems).
2. Variable Rate Shading makes image way worse than it should (suspect it is a Tier 1 implementation). AMD FSR works as an alternative.
3. No Quit Game menu option. Del button is mapped to quitting the game.
4. No DLSS (due to this being an AMD-oriented Raytracing implementation). AMD FSR is present, though.
5. Default mouse sensitivity is low. Control scheme feels like the mouse is emulating the joysticks on console controllers.

Overall, a great game that lives up to the RE name. This is basically RE4 lightly sprinkled on top of RE7. The PC port performs well now, thanks to the patches and the addition of AMD FSR.

Given that I'm not recommending this game, from the outset, I'd like to clarify that the game, in and of itself, is solid and worth a purchase if you're into Resident Evil, survival horror games, or just want a solid AAA game to eat up some time. The PC version, however, is a bit of a mess. 

I'm running an RTX 2060 and a ryzen 7 2700. The recommended system requirements include a GTX 1070 or equivalent to run, so I'm certainly within the sys requirements threshold. I was playing the game at 3440x1440 resolution at medium settings with all ray-tracing features turned off (which, to be honest, when I toggled them to see how they added to/detracted from the game's rasterised presentation, didn't impress me all that much). For the majority of the game, I would hover around 75-90 fps with some dips to the mid 50s during intense scenes and some jumps to the 110s during less demanding scenes. Pretty acceptable performance for a game targeting consoles with roughly RTX 2070S levels of GPU power. HOWEVER, after the first area, I began to get massive hitches, consistently 75 seconds in length roughly every 5-7 minutes. I searched for others finding similar problems and all I could find was one video on Youtube suggesting to turn off RTX (ok, already done) and turn down the model quality. This didn't work. My initial assumption was that it was too VRAM hungry and I needed to drop my resolution and be more aggressive with texture/model quality. Bumping down, aggressively, did nothing. This is why I'm not recommending this port. Unless you have the patience of a saint, or are enjoying the game enough to slog through the hurdles, I would not recommend the game at all. 

Now, I played this in a couple chunks, over roughly 4 days, finishing today over the course of the first half of the day. Today, in the final fourth of the game, RE8 ran smooth as butter. No hitches, no stutters, no (presumably) VRAM-bound lock ups. I can't tell you why. No updates or patches were issued to fix the game. I haven't yet checked to see how many people playing on PC are reporting similar problems to what I faced. But, it is worth keeping in mind that, if you play this game on PC, especially if you are at or around the system requirements' recommended threshold, you may be in for an experience that is borderline unacceptable. OR, you may be fine. 

As for RE8 itself, I'm a big fan of RE1 Remake. It's tightly designed, with some of the smartest level planning in any game ever. Every inch of that game is carefully sculpted to craft thick atmosphere and nail-biting tension. I love its looping design, it's smart economy of resources, and its uncompromising vision. RE7 is the only other RE game I've played that has come close to that tightness of design. It's my second favorite. But, it, like RE2 Remake, RE4 (a franchise favorite that I appreciate, but don't love for its more linear levels, revolutionary combat, and breakneck speed), and RE3 Remake, falls flat in its final act. RE8 similarly falls flat in its final act. It seeks to be an amalgamation of the dread-filled halls of the Baker mansion and the sillier, mechanics-driven romp through Spain of RE4. It nails that aim. But, because it leans heavier into RE4, the final act becomes, basically a Call of Duty level, with bombast, explosions, and a bizarre tonal shift that seems driven by a need to elevate series mainstays to the status of godhood, instead of crafting ever-escalating scares. What I'm most disappointed by, particularly after replaying RE7 in anticipation, is how that feeling of adrenaline highs, the shakes and weak knees I was left with after a session of RE7 - particularly in its first half - are basically totally absent. Even the scariest portion of RE8, a great scene to be sure, lasts just a short while and, so, doesn't have enough time to truly experiment with its scares. 

What kept me going was the combat and the level design. The hub and spokes approach is interesting, every main area of the game branches off from the village square. It never gave me the 'aha' moments I had while playing RE1 or even RE7, but it gives the overall level design a cohesion that RE4 lacked. This is, in essence, a massively blown-up version of the approach taken with RE7, where it's all one contiguous map, even if it's hard to see at the beginning. What I think works less well about RE8's design is the size of the map. In RE7, the treasures and resources hidden in plain sight were condensed enough, that it was feasible to search every nook and cranny. More often, than not, in RE8, I just looked for stuff that was manageable to reach, gems on the ceiling, ammo in the drawers or in plain sight. There are whole optional areas here, but more often than not, when I did go searching, it felt like it was conflicting with the game's pacing, because of the map's size. Bigger isn't always better. Still, the interlocking areas are a joy to explore, even if you aren't combing through every hallway and turning over every rock. The combat is essentially unchanged from RE7. You shoot enemy limbs to slow them down, you shoot enemy heads to stun and eventually pop (though, here, the satisfying head 'pop' makes less sense than the molded), you block incoming attacks to reduce damage taken. It's still satisfying, enemies still duck in and out of the line of fire, and precision is still the name of the game. If you liked RE7 or RE4, you'll like this. 

So, I'm conflicted. It's a fun game. One that builds on what I liked about RE7, but doesn't entirely nail the elegance and simplicity of design that made that game sing. But, hey, at least I got to see a cute goth girl munch on my neck. And, that's worth the price of admission alone.
