First of all this review will be spoiler free so you can read safely, I will not contain any spoilers regarding the story. And now onto the review.
So the game begins as you would expect in your house with Mia and your daughter Rose, then long story short you end up in the first area of the game, The Village.

[h1] The Village [/h1]
In here if you have played the demos you need to open the big door leading to the castle. One thing I would say for The Village is that it's the connecting all other locations in the game and keeping the story together, without it the game wouldn't be the game it is. So in here you meet with the most common enemies in the game the Lycans which were people before, well everything went to sh*t. I think if you haven't played any of the RE games, this is a pretty good game to start with. Anyway, If you are worried that the game looks like it's too action focused, don't, trust me the scary is in here but yes it is a bit more action focused than other entries. The Village when you play for the first time you will be scared as with most areas in the game, one thing to note is you will go back and forth in this area as i said it connects everything else.

[h1] Castle Dimitrescu, her daughters and the Big Momma herself [/h1]
So remember Mr. X you could compare him to Dimitrescu, at some point she'll start roaming around the castle, after you kill 2 of her daughters if I am not mistaken. Now I wanna tell you the sound design in this game is fantastic in this game. You are literally going to want to exit the game, yes it's that good, you will sit in a room and hope she doesn't find you and you will hear every single step she does and be like: Is she going downstairs or upstairs or is she next to the door? Another thing I would Dimitrescu is such a interesting character but the game is not centered around her, about after 2-3 hours you are done with her. Anyway this is not the scariest area in the game in my opinion, let me tell you which is it.

[h1] Donna & Angie Beneviento in the House Beneviento [/h1]
So in the trailers you probably saw that white doll, that doll is Angie. This area has the most puzzles in the whole game, which are pretty good, but it also has some great scares that will probably make you pause or stand up from your chair (that may be too much but there is one specific thing here that is just insane when you see it for the first time). I'm not gonna tell you what it is since this is spoiler free. Anyway onto the other areas.

[h1] Moreau, Heisenberg and the greatest boss fight in the game in my opinion [/h1]
So you are probably a little confused, Moreau is one of the bosses in the game, he is ugly and throws up everywhere and he is the dumbest of all of the lords, the boss fight with him was interesting, not great but good enough. Heisenberg is the lord that has the purpose to kill his creator, so he is the good looking guy with the hammer from the trailers and he controls metal. And I really, really liked the boss fight with him, you fight him close to the end of the game, but for me this battle was the best in the game. I liked it more even than the last boss fight which I'll leave for you to discover.

[h1] Story & Difficulty of the game [/h1]
So about the story I won't say much but it gets really, really interesting in the last few hours and it has a unexpected twist and ending, but it was great at least for me. About the difficulty i recommend playing on Hardcore, I played myself on Standard and I died 3 or 4 times during the whole game. So I think this game is definitely easier than other games in the franchise if you play on Standard, so as I said I would recommend going with Hardcore but that's your choice.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
So I know this review is kind of all over the place and I might have missed some important stuff to talk about but this is my first review on a game like this, there is so much to appreciate in this game and for 60$ it's so worth it, trust me. It's a top down completely new RE experience than the ones we're are used to and I really liked it, even loved it. This was a little experiment from Capcom that turned out to be successful and great and I think a lot of people will say the same. Good job Capcom! Really good job after RE3 Remake, but you come back strong as always! Thank you for reading out this review, stay safe, have fun and I hope this review was useful for you!

This game is the most splendid execution of the RE formula to date. Everything is there, and it's all done wonderfully well.

The RE gameplay loop is something to marvel at from a game-design standpoint. It's truly incredibly how engaging it is, how it forces the player to use everything at their disposal, to explore every inch, every nook and cranny. The horror elements are baked in to the very core of some sections, and one feels a special sense of accomplishment once they overcome them, precisely due to how they are designed. 

Village takes all of these things and polishes them to the extreme. Everything that makes an RE game is here, and it's all done so well that you can truly appreciate the years of work and learning that the devs have put into this series. RE8 is the culmination of everything we've seen and learned from previous RE titles, and it is executed splendidly.

The only gripe I really have is that enemies are leashed to certain areas, allowing you to cheese them and taking away some of the horror elements. Other than that, I can't see anything they've really done wrong. 

RE8 is truly excellent, a exemplary specimen of game design done right. Others should study how this game does what it does and why it is so much fun for the player.

honestly a major improvement in every way over resident evil 7. this game has an insane amount of replay value, which is something i loved about the resident evil 2 and 3 remakes, and something i felt RE7 was lacking. 

this is the best story and characters i've found in an RE game, they actually took the boring and flat character of ethan winters and turned him into one of the best RE characters. chris redfield is also great in this game, the way he's presented makes perfect sense for his character. the villains are all fun and original, but you'll find lady dimitrescu and heisenberg steal the show. every character has their own theme and aesthetic, leading to every area having a completely different gameplay style and theme. every once in a while the game throws a curveball and puts you in a brand new scenario that keeps things fresh, even the lowest points basically boil down to "the action arena part" which is fun in its own right even if it's unimaginative. 

the visuals are stunning, even running at medium-low graphics on my system the art style shone through, making every area and character memorable and screenshot-worthy (i got my money's worth out of the photo mode!)

the gameplay is a massive improvement, every gun feels good to use, and most of them are incredibly useful. the exploration is fun, and the puzzles are interesting. the shop and treasure system fits this game well, and the upgrades help you keep using weapons well after they could have stopped being useful. the standard difficulty isnt massively difficult, but the higher difficulties provide a decent challenge, even with overpowered ng+ weapons.

the mercenaries mode is fun as well, as a sort of "easy to learn, hard to master" mode. i felt like my strategies made it fairly easy, but i usually only get around an A or an S, so it takes a lot of practice to get higher scores.

within ~50 hours i completed all of the campaign challenges and the majority of the mercenaries challenges, right now i'm only one achievement short of 100% achievements (i still have to get an S on every mercenaries stage)

the default FOV is a bit frustrating and there is no in-game slider, so i installed a mod to increase the FOV. i completed my first playthrough with the default FOV and still enjoyed it, but adjusting the FOV definitely made the subsequent 40+ hours more enjoyable

i recommend this to any RE, shooter, or horror-action game fan

Resident Evil is a series that has had its up's and down's as well as its moments of experimentation, which is typical with most long-running series. Whether its video games, movies, or shows, they will usually mix the formula up a little to keep things feeling fresh. Resident Evil Village at it's most basic is sort of a pseudo Resident Evil 4 in what's no being called by some fans as the "Winters Saga" since it follows Ethan Winters and his family. If you're like me, you probably had the literal ♥♥♥♥ scared out of you by Resident Evil 7 simply because it was a very raw and unnerving experience that set the stage for the remakes and subsequent sequels primarily with repeated gameplay mechanics, and Resident Evil Village is no different. When I said the game was a pseudo Resident Evil 4 I meant it because the jarring horror of Resident Evil 7 is almost completely removed, and instead replaced with more action than horror, so much so that the devs commented on this shift in tone because too many people were scared by the previous entry which is fair for a wider audience but for the majority it could single-handedly kill interest.

For me, the game is "fine". I say it bluntly because after finishing the game a whopping four times, especially on the hardest mode, I began to pick up a lot of flaws and shortcomings that first time players won't notice. For starters, this game's structure is very much "drag and drop". From start to finish it just feels like you're running a gauntlet or a checklist of locales that needed to fit the more Romanian folklore with Lycans (Werewolves), Vampires, haunted manors, water logged villages with an aquatic monster, and Frankenstein monsters, and even with continuous play-throughs it all just felt jam packed, congested. You go from point to point so quickly that sometimes the action just slows to a crawl for me, granted I know some people love that since it breaks things up and helps to change the experience, but for me, it just goes by so quickly that by the end I was kinda scratching my head. It's certainly not bad, but when you notice it, it does become a little tedious. And by no means am I knocking the design team that made these locations because they are all dripping with creativity that does indeed make things feel unique. Don't get me wrong, the Baker house in Resident Evil 7 is permanently seared into my mind as one of the most haunting places I've seen in recent memory, simply because it's set in a real location with a lot of real world influence and compared to that the mountain town of Resident Evil Village is cool on the surface, but I just felt like I was playing a diet Resident Evil 4 sometimes. 

Outside the set design, I can say the hallmarks of Resident Evil are here. From managing your inventory, solving puzzles, fighting big bads, and of course exploring the world all feel great! Whether it's upgrading weapons with money or parts you find it always feels satisfying to pop some sorry bastard with a cannon you find or send them flying with a stray shotgun blast to the chest, it could never feel so much better! The best part is that for the first time in a very long time, Mercenaries has made a welcomed return, and it's just as fun as you would expect. So overall, if you want to ignore my tirade about the setting or pacing, I can wholeheartedly recommend Village on the basis that it just feels good to play the first time around, and even when you play through it a second time it still feels good when you've unlocked some powerful weapons to play around with. Just keep in mind by the third or fourth time you might begin to see what I ranted about.

I won't lie. As a diehard fan of this saga since the first game, i was skeptic about this game, but it surprised me big time.

This game takes off what Resident Evil VII left and gives it renewed value, bringing the story forward in an extremely well narrated and well paced game.

[h1]Postive aspects of the game.[/h1]
- You don't need to play any other game to understand the story even if it's the 8th in the main series. You could play RE7 for a full picture of this game story, or watch the RE7 recap you find ingame here.
- I'm not one to pay attention to it, but the graphics were simply gorgeous. 10/10
- The characters are well designed and some are quite likeable, even the damn villains.
- The world design is stunning. Wandering off in the world can make you discover eerie and gorgeous locations. Some may induce curiosity, making you explore further and further, others may induce anxiety and claustrophobic feelings that will make you want to bolt out of there. The mix between beauty and danger is perfect, at least for me.
- The feeling of progression reminds me of Resident Evil 4, in sense of tuning up your weapons until you can  get the next best thing.
- The merchant is not just a "Whaddaya buyin?" guy, he has cute and funny interactions. He even cracks a joke once or twice. A real personality that brings you moments of company from time to time. 
- The stress inducing situations are truly ones of survival horror, where you have to manage your resources and path in order not to ♥♥♥♥ up your progress. You may end up spending one hour exploring the map trying to get some currency to buy more items because you were reckless before, or you may be able to sell some stuff to upgrade your favourite weapon to feel more secure going forward.
- The story is well paced and very well narrated. The main character grows on you like a good friend or a brother and you can truly feel his dispair through out the game, with the ending being something you can truly empathise with.  
- Some apparently ridicolous stuff happens during the game that arises questions by design, and the plot-twists are real.
- I loved the final boss design, simply epic, can't put to words how much i loved the design.

[h1]Negative Aspects.[/h1]
- The background music could have been better, seems like they did not pay much attention to it which is weird in a Resident Evil Game.
- There is one specific plot-twist that was designed just for marketing and it shows, leaving one big plot-hole or inconsistency.
- The marketing hype for Lady Dimitrescu will cause some mixed feelings after beating the game for reasons that shall be rather obvious.
- The FPS for some people seem to fall harshly when the vampires are around, I had no issues with this though.
- First person, i hate first person and i know this is a problem for me not for the game, but still, negative in my book. Looking forward to the third person mod.
- Field of view is pathetically bad, there are mods to fix this available already that make the game much, much better.
- Game is incredibly good for my taste and im sad i finished.


[h1]In conclusion, [/h1]
 If you like story driven games, and do not mind the first person, definitely try Resident Evil 7; then Resident Evil 8. Playing 7 before 8 wiil truly make a difference for how you feel during this game and after. The other games in the series are not needed in order to understand this story arch at all. 
RE:Village was an experience i did not have in years from a story perspective. Being a hardcore fan of the saga, specially the originals, this game has brought me back some hope for CAPCOM and curiosity for the future of the saga.
Truly looking forward for the next installment in the series, and for now, probably busy trying to hunt down achievements.

-My Short History with Resident Evil-
Heard a lot about it but never played any until 5, and it was great fun if only because it was something that was co-op. As I grew older I've grown to love every bit of the franchise, no matter how varied. 5 remains special to me but like most people I consider 4 to be the best, or at least the most fun. I've played every mainline entry that's on PC at this stage, including Revelations. I've been drawn to similar games too like Evil Within. Resident Evil made me love survival horror.

-Reviewing The Game (Spoiler free)-
It's definitely less scary, while i am a veteran and i appreciate the similarities to RE4, the fact that every single enemy drops loot without fail in all difficulties removes a big question of when exactly they die. Of course there have always been other tells, audio or visual but having something so concrete removes much of the fear from the enemies themselves. Along with neatly placed documents that tell you how to kill whatever's in the next room. The franchise has always had hints like this but i don't feel like it's ever been so detailed and conveniently located. This also removes a lot of the spooks. There's some new additions to the formula with a shove ability after you block certain attacks. If you are looking for a survival horror game and not an fps with a horror dressing, play on hardcore right from the start. Obviously doing so won't entirely erase the fact that this game is more action and exploration focused. With that said, the range of environments, like most RE games will surprise you. Sometimes you will wish you could spend more time in some versus others, and a strong complaint for me in this game is just wanting more. Many of the threats you encounter are kind of isolated. 

There's several notable hostile NPC's but it's extremely little the amount of internal interaction they have. When you are in X persons area, they and their particular cronies are the only threat you will face. In RE7, it felt like the family was really toying with you as a collective. There was times when it focused on one more than another but it felt more unpredictable on a first time through and even replaying it, it feels more interesting being able to see them all more often. Basically in 8, the characters are just as interesting but really not built upon as much as the Baker family was. It feels too cookie cutter. I don't think a narrative/puzzle driven game like Resident Evil could handle a "pick your own adventure" approach to which threat you went toward, but if they were determined to quarter them off in their places as they did, maybe it would've been worth trying? 

But besides the quality of spooks, it's a great game. The story is great, and it's a decent sequel from a franchise that doesn't really do them. It's still funny, it's still surprising and shocking. But it's game-play at least, isn't as spooky. It feels like the combat really has become too formulaic in this entry. Even in RE4 you were dealing with tank controls if combat became too predictable. In this, to it's detriment, it's too fluid and easy. About the only thing limiting you is the fov, but even then enemies don't seem too dangerous when you can't see them. 

In the end it's a fantastic entry, a great starting point for newcomers and a great continuation of the franchise and Ethan's story. While being at times both a subtle and heavy handed homage to earlier titles in a truly endearing way. Sometimes it's cool, sometimes it's meta, sometimes it's respectful and at times downright hilarious. Even without comparing it to the rest of the franchise, it's like a love letter to classic horror aesthetics (not so much thematically though, this is still Resident Evil). The references to RE4 and 5 in this make for some interesting discoveries both in the games lore and stories about the real life development of the games. The potential for dlc and a sequel is strong. Also the mercenary mode this time around features almost rogue-like combat elements. Makes replaying it more fun despite the fact it's still kind of just a time trial in a preset location from the story.

-Summary-
I love this franchise, I love this entry. If you liked 7, you will enjoy this without a doubt, but bear in mind it's differences. I have no idea where Resident Evil goes next, but you will see me there.

I finished this game late last night as of writing this review and I did a live stream series for it on Twitch, whilst it was a lot of fun to stream it playing it however had it's pro's and con's. 

Resident Evil Village is a game with some interesting things going on in regards to it's story telling that has potentially set the foundation for a sequel and it also made me be in complete awe at how graphically satisfying it looks.

But I simply cannot deny that there are a handful of flaws this game has and because of that I want to address them in this review and explain in my own opinion why this game doesn't come close to deserving a perfect 10/10 score but instead it should be scored a very modest and generous score of 7/10.

So with that said grab a beverage of your liking, sit down and read on.

First let's start off on the positive portion of this review, the pro's of this game.

- PROS

1. Graphics

The graphical fidelity of this game is absolutely amazing in max graphic settings providing  you can run it on a computer that can perform such graphical prowess, which mine can.

From Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters to Mother Miranda, the character models in this game are absolutely rich in detail and they are all absolutely engaging to look at when they are on screen.

The world locales in this game albeit very visually bleak look absolutely stunning when running the game in max graphical settings especially in Castle Dimitrescu, I was in absolute awe when I was making my way around the various parts of the Castle from the lighting to the chilling Gothic vibes the Castle has going on, it's quite a visual spectacle. 

2. Story

I won't divulge deeply into the story because obviously spoilers but I can assure you when I finished the game, I was really taken back at what happened and I can say it definitely sets up the premise for a sequel.

Now we get into why I think this game is flawed and doesn't deserve all the overwhelmingly positive reviews it's currently getting.

- CONS

1. Game Play

 A good game needs to have good game play that's how it goes right? 

Unfortunately, Resident Evil Village carries a bag containing a small portion of good game play elements and a noticeable sizeable amount of flawed game play elements.

Controlling Ethan Winters felt more like a tedious chore then being actually fun, his walking speed can be slow as molasses and his running momentum can feel very floaty and that can be a huge disadvantage when you are trying to run away from a certain character or a horde of monsters.

In the years I have played various Resident Evil games, I feel that the gun play in each game has never been the strongest game play feature as gun play in the handful of Resident Evil games I have played all felt really clunky and finicky to aim and shoot.

Whilst at it's core the Resident Evil franchise has been survival horror first and foremost with gun play attached to the core game play, once again gun play in this game feels clunky and finicky when it comes to aiming and shooting and it to me it feels like a big disadvantage when you're trying to kill hordes of monsters and in the various boss fights you encounter through out the game.

WARNING THE FOLLOW CON IS A STORY SPOILER, PLEASE DO NOT READ ON IF YOU DON'T WANT TO BE SPOILED, IF YOU'RE OK WITH SPOILERS THEN PLEASE CONTINUE TO READ ON. 


2. Capcom really over hyped Lady Dimitrescu's story involvement in all of the advertising of the game leading up to it's release

When this game was being advertised leading up to it's release, Capcom really put a major focus on Lady Dimitrescu's involvement in the game's story.

While yes she is a villain in the story of this game, she is not the main villain that you are tasked to track down and kill.

Mother Miranda is the main villain of Village and Lady Dimitrescu get's killed off fairly early on in the game's story.

I feel Capcom falsely advertised Lady Dimitrescu's involvement in the game's story and I also feel she got heavily cheated by being killed off so early.


                                                END OF SPOILER


3. The game is no way near as terrifying as Biohazard and that kind of sucks

I wasn't a huge fan of Resident Evil 7 Biohazard mostly due to how claustrophobic it was and how a lot of the rooms in the house it's set in felt way too identical and because of that, I got lost fairly quickly and gave up in the end but I absolutely loved how intensely in your face it was with how spooky it was.

Upon playing Resident Evil Village, I feel like Capcom really dialled down the scare intensity.

Sure there were a handful of genuine jump scares but they were really scattered through out the game, the level of horror felt really unbalanced. 

- CONCLUSION

I highly recommend playing Resident Evil Village if you have played Biohazard and are wanting to know what happens next in the Ethan Winters saga but can I recommend playing Resident Evil Village as a standalone game in the franchise?

Yes but don't expect the game to really break any barriers when it comes to game play as it is very flawed. 

My Score: 7/10

An Honest No Frills, No Memes, No Mommy Milker Issues Review of REVillage.

I've been an RE fan since i first booted up director's cut on the PS1 two decades and some change ago. I enjoyed the clunky controller fear, the item management fear, the locked camera angle fear, and the following fears that accompanied and adapted with technology to the RE Franchise. I can safely say that RE6 was insane garbage, and that most of the spin-offs can be played or dismissed with time put into an RE Lore video. 

That being said I feel like I can express a fair opinion on RE8 without sounding like to much of a whiny gamer, and more of an observational why it's worth it's weight in price...so here we go.

RE8 is basically RE4 gameplay with RE7 atmosphere and spooky vibes. Anyone who says otherwise is lying to themself. The graphics are good (although the current memory leak issue, which will hopefully be patched soon, make playing it a pain in the ass unless tweaked a specific way), the surroundings and backdrop are awesome, and as long as you take off aim acceleration and aim assist the gun play is nice. 

THE GAME IS NOT MEANT TO BE RATED BASED OFF THE FIRST PLAY THROUGH IMO.

Once you start New Game + that's where a majority of RE8's capability shines. It's typical RE fare with acquiring unlimited ammo guns, speed running, achievement hunting, and trying to find all the treasures on the map and discovering the lore. 
You unlock the Mercenaries mode after you beat the game through the bonus options menu and that definitely provides a lot of replayability to the game. The only REAL problem with Mercenaries is that the first Two areas Village and Castle can easily get an S or SS rank with Shotgun/Sniper rifle combo and some kiting. Other than that you can run around and use different weapon combos to try and get the highest score. I don't know if there is a worldwide leader board but it IS a fun take on the Mercenaries mode RE is famous for.

If you're feeling froggy enough you can TRY to beat Village of Shadows mode. It's extremely unforgiving, and i'm currently trying to beat it myself at the time of this writing with the STAKE maxed out with unlimited ammo.

While I'm unsure of their DLC Path (Is there going to be any? i don't know to be honest...haven't looked into it) I can safely say they dropped the ball with the pre order for the Samurai Edge Wesker Edition. I mean at the end of the day you still payed $70 for a pre order and they GAVE you a pistol and some shrubs and ammo. The Samurai Edge should've provided some sort of fresher game play but you can't upgrade it, so by the time you level up the first pistol you get in the game, the pre order bonus is already worthless. It's unfortunate but since you're not really paying anything extra for some cool nods to RE lore it's a toss up on worth and mostly forgettable.

Speed running the game is easy enough as a majority of the time spent in the initial run through (mine was clocked in at somewhere around 15 hours) is going back and forth to find weapons, treasures on the map that the Duke marks for you to get ammo and upgrades, and finding the extra little "sub bosses" around the map. My current speed run time without much effort clocks in at 2.34 hrs on hardcore mode with no infinite ammo weapons unlocked yet, so it's entirely doable.

I like how Capcom has basically decided to chunk off the RE Franchise in terms of story and lore. RE 1-3 is part one, 4-6 is part 2, and RE 7- what im assuming will be 9 is this current run of lore. It's a genuinely enjoyable lore this chunk of story telling and I'm glad to learn more about the origins of everything resident evil. If you look at it all very concavely, the RE lore is basically about Mother Miranda wanting her kid back from the dead. Literally, it's all her fault everything from RE 1-7 happens...at least that's what i've picked up from the lore. 

A few gripes listed regarding immersion are as follows:

- despite Lady Dimetrescu being a major portion of the advertising (you know what you were doing Capcom, don't lie), the Castle area and her story only sit for about 1/5 of the game.
- unless you've played RE7 you don't really understand why Ethan's hand can do the things Ethan's hand does, and the big reveal is a bit whack otherwise.
- when you're popping off rounds in the Castle area it's underwhelming that neither the sisters or Lady D don't immediately navigate to the locations of a pistol, shotgun, rifle, or whatever your using. Their interactions are very RE3 Remake Nemesis...and that's not good.
- capcom REALLY hates Ethan's hand
- video Memory Leak NEEDS to be addressed, I'm running a 3070 TI and I'm fairly certain the graphics quality of the game aren't the best they can be which is a major bummer.

REVillage is an amazing game despite it's...odd pacing. Personally if they did more of the spooky house area I would've enjoyed it a LOT more...but apparently Capcom got the thought from a bunch of Pu55i35 that RE7 was TOO SCARY?!?!?! and toned down the scariness for RE8...let that sink in...and imagine how great RE8 could've really been.

8/10

Considering the fact that I am a loot rat in many of the games that I have found myself indulged in, I have been blessed with the time to fully analyse each and every feature of games that I have found myself obsessed with. With this being said, Resident Evil: Village is an excellent blend of both RE4 and RE7, and it does NOT hold back from throwing any punches. Each and every environment genuinely ropes in the attention of the viewer, the architecture of the castle in particular really stood out to me, openly pulling inspiration from Romanian structures with extreme attention to detail. Without spoiling much, you will find yourself entering areas that you have previously trekked through only to find unexpected changes in environment and, potentially, new threats as well as new treasures to unlock that metaphorically unhinge your jaw. There are multiple segments to the storytelling that utilise significantly different themes, with drastic changes that I truly felt were integrated very well, and as it stands, I would honestly claim that it is well worth the full price having pre-ordered the game. 

If you are on the fence about purchasing at this point, I will gladly be the individual who stands on the sidelines and eggs you on problematically, as I took breaks from my usual routines just to binge this game for 3 days due to everything that it has to offer. Get to it as soon as you possibly can, RE8 is very impressive, CAPCOM clearly knew what they were doing, and I will likely find myself returning for New Game+ mode just to clear out more achievements as well as to gain further insight on the lore itself. In conclusion, Resident Evil: Village is now arguably a pillar to the franchise and will continue to stand pretty damn strong, and I invite anyone who can handle a good action horror game to play and enjoy whenever they can find the time. Hopefully, I have convinced you to unload your wallet onto this masterpiece, have an amazing time, and I thank you for reading my late night bumbling. I hope that I was able to drag you on-board the hype train without revealing too much, and if I was, that means this review was a solid success.

After four playthroughs, unlocking all of the achievements, and completing all of the challenges, I can definitely say that Resident Evil Village is a very solid entry in the RE franchise. With satisfying gunplay, likable characters, and beautiful environments, RE Village manages to always be entertaining. In fact, even after thirty hours of game time, I never once felt bored; there is always something to unlock, explore, or mess around with. Along with this, from a technical perspective, RE Village is pretty solid. From the ultra-realistic graphics to solid performance, Capcom did a good job making this an enjoyable game to play on PC. However, even though RE Village does a lot right, there are a few things that hold it back from being one of the best RE games ever. The main problem, in my opinion, is the lack of direction. For example, the castle area feels like classic survival horror, House Beneviento is solely focused on environmental horror, the swamp area is reminiscent of RE4, the factory is all about exploration, and the section at the end is pure action. Even though this amount of variety keeps things from feeling repetitive, it also ruins the pacing. For a franchise that has been all about replaying them over and over again, by having poor pacing, it can make RE Village a pain to replay. Besides the lack of direction and poor pacing, there's also a lack of some basic graphical options. The main one, and the one everyone has probably heard of, is the lack of an FOV slider. Yet, RE Village also lacks SMAA anti-aliasing, which was present in previous RE engine games. Furthermore, as for technical issues, whenever you kill an enemy, the game severely stutters. At first, I thought this was an issue on my end. However, after doing some research, it looks like this is a problem for nearly everyone. Still, though, considering that this will probably be fixed soon, it's not too big of a deal. Overall, even though there are some problems with Resident Evil Village, I had a great time with it. Whether you're a fan of old-school RE or a fan of the more action-oriented entries, you'll have an excellent time.

Resident Evil 8, I think, is the best Resident Evil game to date, all nostalgia for older games aside. Many people are saying that this game is not a "Good Resident Evil" game, but a good horror adventure shooter. I think these fellas are mega wrong. Allow me to explain in this review.

Story: 

The story, without spoilers, is quite expected of resident evil, starting off of very little information and being thrown into an eventual revelation and flurry of plot twists once you hit the end. Either way, its basis was extremely well set up in re7 and it ended just as well. There's not too much to say about the story because much of it happens at the end, but just know it was a very good sequel to 7. 

Gameplay:

The main gripe from the community appears to be from a gameplay perspective, with resident evil fans claiming that the game isn't a good resident evil style game, which i think is extremely dumb for 2 reasons. First, the game is expanding and pressing on it's own direction (as shown with 7 effectively being a reboot, after the disaster that was 6), with many ideas taken from Resident Evil 4 and other games in this particular game, this is not a bad thing, remaining with a set concrete playstyle in a series is a good way to kill it and by adapting but keeping some things the same (eg, first person, horror orientated game, but keeping puzzles and the bio-weapon theme of resident evil), RE7 and 8 have been very good to the series. Second reason is that, as i have previously mentioned, it is very much like a RE game, it doesn't need to be third person to make it a RE game. The puzzle / horror-survival focused game play is enough to make it a RE title, even if it leans horror (much like RE4 did).

The gameplay is much like 7 however Ethan's learned some new tricks to make the shooting (which'll be alot more common) much easier, he's received combat training allowing you to shove enemies away which is good and means you can make distance, he can also climb over fences and vault windows as well as barricade doors or use the environment, allowing for many ways to beat hordes or strong enemies. 

Additionally, crafting makes a return in a more clear manner, moving away from combination and opting in for a traditional crafting screen allowing you to see what recipes you have, and what is required to make them.

The shop and guns present in the game are very cool, including collectibles, each gun is unique and weapons in the same class are different enough to encourage a different playstyle with them. E.g. One pistol might be strong but low in ammo and fire rate initially, and another might be high in firerate and mag size with low damage. The shop and treasure system is great because it rewards you for being thorough and it  gives you a direction to progress in outside the story.

A small change is that enemies more commonly drop items now, meaning you have reason to remain and kill them all, which leans to the re4 side.

Finally, bosses are much better this time around, whilst ultimately they are still shoot / run away deal that RE has always been plagued with, bosses have specific mechanics which you need to think about outside of this traditional boss cycle. E.g. hiding behind objects, destroying parts of the arena to use to your advantage, shooting enemy projectiles etc. 

Conclusion, I think this game is GOTY, even though its this early. So many parts are very good, even the worst parts were very enjoyable for me. The game keeps its horror theme quite well, not the kind that you will be scared out of your mind but instead you'll be uncomfortable and on edge at all times, which is really well done and adds to the experience. Minutes in this game can  sometimes feel like hours especially if you've been through a certain stressful section. The post-game content (and 100%ing, which i've done) is surprisingly fun, i played through the game 3 times and did the extra content for about 5-6 hours and it's worth the shot. 

Overall, for me, a 10/10. If you are new to Resident Evil, play Resident Evil 7, then Resident Evil 8 (Village), and then the other games. These two games are a perfect entry point, but also very fun for an experienced Resident Evil fan with an open mind.

Resident Evil 4 was the first horror game I can recall playing, back when I was still far too young to have rightfully played it. I loved it on the gamecube, I loved it on the Wii, and now that I own it on PC I love it there too. RE1 is still my favorite, but something about the village aesthetic, iconic characters, and upgradable weapons stuck with me, and I still consider it the most replayable of the series. It goes without saying, then, that I was extremely excited for Village, which seemed largely cut from the same cloth as RE4. Having finished it four times, I can now safely say that Capcom has gotten me to purchase RE4 not three, but four times.

Mechanically, it's very similar to RE7, but with elements from 4 blended in; the progression is still largely one big puzzle box, with keys and items for you to find that let you slowly unlock the rest of its map and find its secrets. But while RE7 took a lot of inspiration from RE1 respectively, RE8 really doesn't care much for its puzzles. The game is much more action-based with a heavier emphasis on shooting, and in that regard the weapon selection has been greatly increased as well. Along with finding them, you can also purchase and upgrade them courtesy of a lovable merchant using money dropped by enemies. It was a formula that worked great in 2005, and it still works great now; I can't say I don't miss the more horror-focused approach that 7 took, but if it had to be different they picked a great option to base it off of. While it's hardly as scary as anything in the series prior, it succeeds well in just being fun, instead. There's a load of challenges and things to be unlocked in repeat playthroughs, and The Mercenaries makes a return as well, offering a series of time-based score trials with a bit of inspiration from the later games' Raid Modes. 

The story has been broadened quite a bit since 7, showing more of the inevitable corporate conspiracies lurking under the surface and the general state of things that weren't really expanded on in 7 until the DLC, but don't expect to get too deep into it just yet. You play as Ethan Winters again, and he's still just as loveably dumb; he's the type of protagonist who, when faced with a truck in a garage, would try to floor the truck through the house's brick walls instead of reversing it through the wooden back door. He has all the sense of self-preservation of someone who just learned they can reattach their limbs with funny green goo, and even by the end of everything he doesn't seem to know, nor really care about what's going on in the neighborhood. He's about as far from a typical RE protagonist as it gets, barely even getting a face of his own, and I love it -- I miss the old gang, of course, but from a player perspective it's nice to go back to someone who's still wide-eyed and innocent, rather than going in expecting to be hunting down bioterrorists. For a horror game in particular, I think that's an important quality.

Like RE7, the game's opening moments are dotted with oddly jarring moments of torture
porn, this time revolving almost entirely around Ethan's hands. It's all just as out of place as it was before, largely because Ethan recovers from most of it almost immediately; his hands should be about as useful as two mounds of ground beef affixed to wrists by the time you're through the introductory chapters, but with the power of Green Goo he soldiers on with only minor alterations to the weapon viewmodels, ready to open the top right drawer of every dresser in the village just fine. From there, however, you're left much more free to wander than 7 allowed; the map is pseudo-open, and rather than being the first series of "levels" like in RE4 the village serves as a hub that you frequently return back to, with a fair amount of side things to loot and explore. It's hardly a sprawling open world, and you shouldn't expect "open map" to mean the game lasts any more than the usual 10-12 hours for a Resident Evil game (for a first playthrough, at least), but it's plenty appreciable in its own right. The plot that follows isn't exactly groundbreaking, but it's still fairly good, leaving me particularly hopeful about where it's all going from here.

But as much as I loved RE8, enough to have already completed it four times and unlocked all of its achievements, I have to admit that it isn't perfect. Its biggest flaw by far is also one of its positives; while I loved the similarities to RE4 in style initially, Village really just doesn't want to let the past go. Stop me if you've heard this one before: You start the game with a large timed shootout in the village, only to be interrupted by a bell that calls everyone away. Then you solve a few puzzles, move on to a large castle, where you meet the first of the main villain's henchmen, etc, etc. It would be spoilers to go into just how deeply ingrained RE4 is in the game's DNA, but if you've played RE4 you've practically spoiled most of the setpieces for yourself anyways. They're fairly blatant, from almost start to finish. 

It's not that Village is completely devoid of originality, and most of its original concepts are great -- it just seems afraid to show them very often, in favor of letting its reverance slip into the fanaticism of a stalker wanting to copy their idol to a T. It gets to the point that it makes me wonder if maybe Village was originally meant to be the oft-mentioned remake of RE4 people always talk about, with new takes on the same concepts and setpieces, only for it to have been made a new game entirely later on. The one section that doesn't fit the mold is also the shortest, with its villain more or less coming and going with no fanfare. That applies to one of the other villains, as well; it's not that I don't like Lady Dimitrescu and her utterly luxurious curves, and in fact they could've simply made her the villain throughout the game and I would've been more than happy to see it, but instead they tease these others, similarly interesting but in different ways, only to treat them extremely unevenly. It results in them being a bit less sympathetic than the Baker family was in the end, if only because by the end of the game you'll probably have forgotten about some of them.

My other complaint, as mentioned earlier, is the lack of any real puzzle work. Resident Evil has never exactly been a master class at that, leaving anything more difficult than key puzzles largely to Silent Hill (may it rest in peace) instead, but it at least knew how to keep a secret. RE8 has no qualms with simply marking every rare treasure chest on the map from almost the beginning of the game, even on the harder difficulties, seemingly thinking that anyone would need, or even want such a thing. Any treasures that can be combined are now marked as 'Combineable', removing any guesswork or experimentation there. It's a forgivable change, given that the focus is much more on combat this time anyways, and there are still plenty of unmarked lesser secrets to find, but I can't properly explain the difference between finding an important hidden treasure through your own exploring and experimentation versus being told where it is and asked to go fetch it. It's exacerbated by the lack of any particular differences in the higher difficulties except for enemy health and damage; even Village of Shadows, seemingly the equivalent of RE7's Madhouse, only really changes a small handful of enemy placements. None of it really affected my enjoyment that much in the end, but I would happily pay extra for a "treat the player like they're smarter than Ethan" mode DLC later down the line.

Ever since the original Resident Evil 2 I feel this series has taken a turn for the worst. They all seem to follow the same formula and plagiarize themselves constantly. The mutations were all played out and overdone soo many times it just looks ridiculous and often pointless. The FOV is always annoying and the reticle has often been a constant annoyance. And my biggest gripe has always been that one person is always invincible which makes it not even worth playing.

But this one is different. This game seems to be a huge step in the right direction. I walked through the demo thinking, "well, this is exactly the same as the others" and saw all the hype surrounding its release. I immediately found a deal for $30 on the day it was released and passed it up. A friend said they bought it and sort of talked me into it with their excitement over it. So I found another copy for $40 on release day and gave it a shot. I was not disappointed.

Near the beginning it feels like a completely different game from the franchise as well as the rest of the game. Enemies come in packs of a few different categories which repeat at different times. Such as in town, there are only a few different characters you'll notice as they spawn, they could have definitely taken more time on this as well as the destruction of environments. 

A lot of the assets and things seem very rushed and they still got the FoV completely wrong but thankfully modders were on the scene to take care of this right away. "Invincible guy" in this one, I suppose there probably IS one in the form of a girl but it's not exactly to the point of trapping you and overbearingly annoying as it usually is. And it's only temporary, not all throughout the game. 

Then there are the bosses. There is such a build up for each one and they turn out to be really easy to beat. Which isn't an immediate deal-breaker for me, but they could have been more creative. I could elaborate a bit more on this review but I think I've addressed most everything I wanted to say. The whole "vagina-faced" enemies with long tongues and all that crap they've been regurgitating for years has been replaced with enemies that actually seem actually interesting. The story isn't really all that special but the gameplay makes up for it. Cutscenes didn't go on forever and you have the option to skip them.

One major buzzkill was the [SPOILER] part where you control Chris. You feel no real threat and it feels like Call of Duty rather than Resident Evil. You have an endless amount of health and ammo and it really feels as though you're accomplishing nothing. Then the last boss... That was a pretty big let down. I faced a bug during the entirety of the game where cutscenes wouldn't align with the words spoken which was really annoying but overall I got through it.

Overall, I give this game a 9/10, which if you've seen my other reviews on these titles says a lot for the direction they're taking. It's as though they're beginning to actually do things right. Give it a try, I didn't want it to end.

[b]CASE ONE:[/b]
In game design, it's important to think about how you think a player will engage in a certain situation. Think about your demographic; are they going to be given the gameplay functions to run, or to hold their ground and fight? The most important thing to remember as well is to make sure that the player can survive long enough to get through a scenario in their first try, but not make it too easy that they just breeze past it. In a survival horror especially, this is quintessential for a successful game.

However, Village really bit the bullet and decided to take one of the paths that was the hardest to create, but one of the most rewarding. They implemented a specific route to take, the one and only you could really take, and made you have the illusion that it was being done on a wing and a prayer. Subtle nods to what you are supposed to do are given to you subconsciously and you just... do  them. It makes the game much more immersive. The only place where this tactic really failed is the Lycan ambush at the very beginning of the game. But after that, it's pretty much perfect.

[b]CASE TWO:[/b]
Sequels are always very hard. Rather than consider this as Resident Evil 8, I'm considering 7 as more of a game of it's own and having this really just be Biohazard 2 (If you dare say 'actually...' at me I will go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥). Game developers are always stuck with the idea of "How can we make this bigger and better than the last game?" when the better question is "How can we make this different from the last game?" The former question is a question you need to ask when your game didn't perform well. But since Biohazard was such a success, we need to be asking the latter.

And Village is a huge step in a different, unique direction from Biohazard. It's thrilling, it's full of action, but plenty of storytelling moments and horror to fill the adrenaline. It doesn't feel like there is a dull moment to be had. It's a plenty of a different pace from 7 that new players who didn't enjoy the previous one will enjoy it, but players who enjoyed 7 can still enjoy this too.

[b]CASE THREE:[/b]
Pacing in a story has always failed to have a good middle ground. In a game like Borderlands 3, you are constantly filled with a sense of ugh, because it's so blatantly clear that filler content was placed just so that the game could reach a certain hour mark just to get the time right. Game developers are so overcome with the idea of extremely long campaigns that they don't realize that the game is being deteriorated by it.

However, Village knows how to stop filler content from being so consuming, and makes sure that the pacing of the story if fulfilling and not wasting your time. You're always learning something new, and Ethan is always developing as a character. Capcom, just lay off the man a little. You're meant to torture your protagonists, yes, but not literally.

I have had an absolute blast during my first playthrough. The highlights for me were:

- The combat is fast paced and exciting* with a load of different enemies that are a ton of fun to fight.

- The merchant is an interesting character who provides services that allow for a lot of upgrades and weapon customisation and selling and buying items. Money is in abundance which allows for a lot of choice and exploration of upgrades.

- There are a few secret areas and even more secret items that can be constructed and sold to the merchant for a high price just like in RE4

- The environments are beautiful and pleasing to look at. 

- There are some interesting characters such as lady D and Heisenberg. 

- There is a huge amount of replay value because of the vast amount of unlockables and upgrades available. 

However

This game does have some minor flaws. most of which stem from pacing and start to become more evident in subsequent playthroughs such as:

- The slow intro which drags on and becomes a slog after you've seen it a couple of times. 

- The doll house section which deviates from the overall action thriller structure of the game and attempts to add horror elements that become a chore to play after going through it a couple of times.

- The Call Of Resident Evil section which gives me PTSD of the abomination that is RE6. 

- The village itself can be a pain in the arse to navigate upon revisiting and there should've been some options made available to make it easier to get through e.g. being able to destroy the broken crusty tractors and carriages blocking the paths.

- The game suffers from some weak characters such as Mother Miranda, Moraeu and Donna who needed to be explored and expanded upon further or scrapped in favour of strong characters such as Lady D and Heisenberg (with lady D and her castle feeling particularly under utilised) imo. Ethan is also a bit meh in this game and has some goofy dialogue now and again.

Overall this is a fantastic experience with great gameplay that old and new Resident Evil fans will enjoy with some replay value but some sections/elements will require quite a bit of patience after you've already beaten the game once or twice and the overarching story is a bit meh.

*the fast paced combat on a keyboard and mouse is very enjoyable but I can see that people who prefer to play with a controller might be left feeling frustrated by twitchy enemies such as the lycans and flying creatures.

There are no details about the story listed below, however there are some generalizations about certain points of the game that may be interpreted as a spoiler.

Pros:
- Incredible graphics
- Intense monster skirmishing
- Some great boss encounters
- Terrifying ambiance/sense of dread in some areas
- 97% of voice acting is amazing
- Soundtrack is brilliant
- Lady D and Heisenberg carry the first time experience & keep you playing
- Achievements are not out of reach for casual players & can be completed while infinite ammo unlocks are being used in NG+ replays
- Replay value is emboldened by challenge points system
- Enemy (non-boss) AI appears to scale with difficulty, i.e. Lycans get faster/dodge & lunge more
- Village of Shadows difficulty adds more enemies in areas to increase replay value
- Bonus Content Mercenaries game achievements allow the unlock of a LIGHTSABER to use in the story mode
- Area content attempts to offer something for everyone, showing adaptation within the series/franchise, which gets an A for effort.


Cons:
- Hardcore is not difficult at all.  Playing the game on Village of Shadows and not using NG+ appears to be the real challenge within this installment.  
- No puzzles are difficult and require next to no effort to solve or find the answers.  Solutions do not change with difficulty.  Hard fail for an RE title to be honest.
- Game is disappointingly linear.  "On-rails shooter" is a very good description.  You literally cannot take a wrong turn in this game.
- Critical choice is irrelevant.  There is never a spot where you feel like you need to dodge an enemy to conserve ammo.  
- Inventory management can be wonky at times, i.e. unable to swap weapon positions when moving things around, even if you have plenty of space in that area.  Once inventory space is maxed the survival aspect of space management is gone.  It doesn't really make sense.
- Item click/examine/pick up hit boxes are also wonky at times, i.e. open a cupboard and you have to crouch and put your cursor on the bag to grab some Lei, but you can grab a crystal skull on top of an 8 foot ledge you're not even directly facing
- Lady D, while overwhelmingly popular and a tremendous villain, is unfortunately non-threatening prior to her mutation.  Her AI during chases within the castle is super predictable and she is very easily kited/avoided.  Being able to walk right by her in narrow halls without punishment deteriorates her value.
- Heisenberg's voice over actor (English version) sounds completely out of place, making him difficult to take seriously until he mutates.  The character simply does not look like he would sound or speak in that fashion or with that accent.  Nothing against the actor, just sounds/feels like a fit that could have been better.
- Story and character development after the castle is seriously lacking.  Donna and Moreau feel like fillers and there is zero care for why they are even in the game.  They are basically loot bags.  
- Not a fan of the Heisenberg boss encounter.  Silly, pointless, and absurdly easy.  An overwhelming departure from what one may consider a classic RE boss fight.  It feels like so much more could have been done with him. 
- The final 10-15% of the game and its story direction is very strange and may dissuade/turn-off classic RE fans.  Its really absurd, opens up a box of questions & serves as a major speed bump in the flow of how the game actually feels up until that point.  

Overall:
- Feels like RE 4, plays like RE 7. 
- Could have easily been a 10/10 with better UI optimization, more character development and a less "hand holding" game exploration experience.   
- Story was a huge nonsensical mess after the factory, but the overall experience was great.
- Solid game.
- 7.5/10

Ok, so I just 100%ed Resident Evil Village and it has been one of my favorite gaming experiences as of late.

Story- As per Resident Evil stories, this one is goofy and dumb, but I love it. Along with having that classic RE feel to the story, it also has a lot of emotion and heart to it. I won't spoil but the ending here is great and really heartfelt. (Story Spoilers Ahead) A few issues I had with the story were a few missed opportunities with characters. This, for me, is only felt with the villagers at the beginning of the game. They seem to be there just to die and didn't have much significance to the plot. It isn't that bad of a problem but from the trailers, it seemed these characters would do much more.

Characters- The characters are great for the most part. Returning characters from previous RE games such as Ethan, Mia, and Chris are much more fleshed out personalities and characters in RE8 especially Ethan. As for the four lords, they all have distinct and fun personalities, but I wish Donna Beneviento got a little more screen time.

Gameplay- Gameplay is fun and has been modified and upgraded from RE7. Now there is being able to push enemies away while blocking and also returning mechanics from other RE games such as the inventory, merchant (in the form of the Duke), and weapon upgrades which all serve as a refreshing return to RE4 like mechanics. Shooting feels responsive and satisfying. The game also has good replay value with new game+, an unlockable difficulty, challenges which earn you points to buy various extras from the extra content shop, and the return of mercenaries. The game also has a perfect balance of horror and action.

Graphics and Environments- The graphics on display here are gorgeous. The expertly crafted environment make for an excellent experience admiring and exploring the various areas of RE Village.

Negatives- Some areas of the game may drag for some people. The unlockable difficulty, Village of Shadows, is near impossible for normal players on a new save. The story may be too out there and goofy for some people. The first person perspective is not for everyone. Chris gameplay segment is just call of duty. No FOV slider. The different areas of the game are very different in tone and in gameplay, so that may be jarring or off putting to some people. 

Conclusion- From gameplay, to story, characters, and graphics, Resident Evil Village has been a remarkable experience for me. From start, to finish, this game has engrossed me since the release and even though I have played this game to 100%, I will still return to play this game over and over. Thank you Capcom, for Resident Evil Village.

The game wants to be so much... exploration and puzzles like in Resident Evil 1, the setting from part 4, the craziness from part 7, action, horror, steampunk.... and somewhere in the middle of it all is a fairy tale. In the end, however, it's nothing half and nothing whole. If you look behind the imposing scenes and the outstanding graphics with all the effects, there's not much left of the actual game. Even the vampire/werewolf setting doesn't change that much.

The partially charismatic and interesting villains that are presented to you relatively at the beginning of the game only turn out to be victims of a hastily thrown together gameplay with even worse dialogs and monologues. Imposing or eerie locations like the castle or the doll maker's house are unfortunately so short that they remain mere footnotes and exceptions in an otherwise monotonous gameplay. What starts out as a Resident Evil 4 vibe launching setting becomes more and more of a pointless action shooter. The problem with this is your rather sluggish controls in direct comparison to the mostly swift enemies. What still worked in part 7 and fit well into the game now just doesn't feel good anymore, as enemies sometimes don't react to your hits at all. It's not so bad with single enemies, but when you're only fighting hordes, the whole system fails.

However, the game also left me relatively early with everything else. For every "puzzle", the appropriate answer is practically right next to it. The interesting story at the beginning of the game becomes more and more absurd and unrealistic (in the context of the realism of Resident Evil in general). The game makes it virtually impossible to identify in any way with the main character or emotionally relate to what he is experiencing, due to the story and dialogue. 

However, it is also carried by the numerous allusions to previous events or characters without creating anything memorable itself. Everything you need to know is served to you half-baked at the very end, without leaving you room for your own reflections. The soundtrack is practically absent, unlike other games in the series. If you come out of the cinema and afterwards you think about what just happened, the producers have done everything right. That's exactly what many games manage to do, even if they don't have the same budget. Resident Evil Village doesn't do that. When the credits roll, the game is over, in every sense of the word. 

But even the small things can have a big impact. While in part 7 the character opened the doors by hand or simply leaned against the wall, here the doors open or close mostly by themselves. When you quickly switch between two weapons, the character seems to have 4 arms instead of 2. The boat ride in part 4 felt more realistic, as the boat here seems to ride on rails rather than water....

In the whole game there were maybe 2-3 areas that still had anything to do with horror. That means if you expect darkness, oppressive atmosphere or a dense scary atmosphere with an exciting story you will be disappointed here.

For a game that wants to continue a story, it fails in too many ways. It is a game without a soul of itself.

Tested by the Youtube channel Digital Foundry in the video "Resident Evil 4 PC: Is New DRM Impacting Game Performance?" has been found that the Enigma Protector DRM causes an average of -10% in framerate drops, with dips of -40% in certain scenarios, way more than the original Denuvo DRM.

This is not the first time that Capcom decided to put Enigma in some of their older games: RE Revelations suffered major backlash from customers because of the major dip in perfomance, so much so they had to remove Enigma from the game for good and recently they released the original Dino Crisis series on Steam, a quick scouring of the forum will reveal a lot of customers unhappy with the perfomance of said games. Why a 25 years old single player game that should run flawlessly on a phone had to be "protected" against "cheating" is everyone's guess, especially when you realise that a GOG version of both games was already available, without the Enigma Protector and without issues.

Here's my grievances with it:

-Retroactively degrading perfomances of a game or a product is an unethical and fundamentally anti-consumer practice that should be illegal. Imagine your car having less hp out of nowhere because the car company decided to update the software that way

-Capcom degraded the game for no reasons at all, Enigma Protector doesn't prevent cheats or mods in any capable way and it's openly mocked by the mod communities

-All Capcom's game that have been "protected" by Enigma suffered of significant perfomance loss and the DRM can be easily removed by the cracking scene. The customer is therefore presented with this funny scenario: would you rather download the game for free or pay money for a degraded version that runs worst than the pirated copy?

-There's a very likely possibility that in future all Capcom's games will eventually incorporate the Enigma DRM years after launch, the system that you used to play them could eventually not being capable of the same perfomance as before, forcing some to spend money on very costly upgrades (due to the AI craze)

-Enigma Protector devs in the past have behaved very unprofessionally, mocking and insulting whoever questioned the validity of their practices and their work, raising more than one red flag on the true purpose of their work and their true intent

I don't know who and why at Capcom signed a contract for this to happen but they clearly got scammed and it's time for them cope with it. The opening section to RE8 is a recreation of the same opening in RE4. You go through a few buildings in the village and are then met by an unending wave of enemies that you need to survive until the bell tower rings. After the bell rings you are then able to freely explore and figure things out.

The game has 5 areas that you will end up exploring. The Village, Castle Dimitrescu, [spoiler]House Beneviento[/spoiler], [spoiler]the Reservoir[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Heisenberg's Factory[/spoiler]. The village itself acts as a central hub of sorts for getting into the other areas that are connected to it. A couple of things that I disliked at first was that you are unable to go back into the castle once you leave it and cannot go back to the village once you go to the factory.

Another comeback from RE4 is the inventory system. Here you can manage your weapons, meds and any other items found in it. Items can be moved/rotated around and some can be stacked/unstacked. The subtle changes they have done to it however do make it rather simplified.

One change that RE8 has made from the general inventory management of previous RE games is that all crafting has been separated into its own menu. There is no cap as to how many of each crafting resource you can hold so there is no inventory management required. This applies to any Key/Treasure items as well.

RE8 also includes a merchant who you will meet at very convenient locations which is another feature from RE4. You can buy items from him such as ammo, weapons and crafting blueprints. He can upgrade your weapons to have more damage, increase reload times, increase the rate of fire and increase the magazine size. You can sell any of the items from your inventory and treasures. As you progress through the game the merchant will offer you inventory expansions, new weapons, modifications and upgrades.

Sadly the merchant does not offer unique weapon features for completing all of the weapon upgrades for a single weapon like in RE4. However The merchant in RE8 has a new addition where he offers to cook you meals. These meals require meat from different creatures that can be found by exploring the world. These meals give you permanent upgrades to your health, defense and speed.

Yet another feature from RE4 that is making a return are the treasures. They function almost identical to how they work in RE4. Most can be sold as is, while others can be combined into a complete set so that they can be sold at a higher price.

The enemies of the game really only consist of Lycans. There are several other enemy types with a few of them having different variants that can be found in different locations but you barely come across them. Lycans outnumber everything 9 to 1.

There is really nothing special about their design as the enemies are mostly just there for you to shoot at something from time to time. However I did love the Soldats that you meet in the Factory portion of the game.

The Boss fights themselves are pretty straight forward just like the enemies. [spoiler]Dimitrescu is a mix of activating certain triggers to progress her to the actual damage phase. Beneviento is a hide and seek game where you simply press F on a doll a few times. Moreau is just a bullet sponge that you can shoot till he dies. Heisenberg is an on rails shooter sequence with unlimited ammo. Miranda is also a bullet sponge that you keep shooting till she dies.[/spoiler]

After completing the game you can play through it again on new game+ where the merchant will now offer more items for you to buy. You will also get access to the challenges and points shop that was seen in the 2020 Resident Evil 3 Remake. It's identical to the RE3R points shop where you complete challenges for points that can be then be used to buy figures, artwork, unique weapons and unlimited ammo options.

The Mercenaries mode can be purchased from the points store. It functions the same way in almost every other Resident Evil game. You have a set amount of time to kill at least half the amount of total enemies to spawn in the extraction. You can chain kill enemies to build up your combo score and collect time orbs for additional time. One addition to this mode is abilities which act as a passive perk making you more powerful as you progress through the area.

In terms of difficulty the game is probably the easiest Resident Evil game that has been released so far. I'm not sure why they made it this simple as they have also removed the limited save feature that is usually found on the hardest difficulty, along with the rankings/scores. The only challenging thing that I found in the game was the Hardcore variant of the Factory area in the mercs mode (Factory II).

The game checkpoints nearly every minute which makes the save locations completely pointless. This means that if you die, you will load back in with barely any time loss or consequences. This is the same on the harder difficulties which removes any further challenges.

The visuals of RE8 are the best in the series by far. The game also comes with a few Ray Tracing features; blending lighting together, Some reflections, however most reflections still use screen space techniques, and ambient occlusion gets replaced with a RT variant that looks much nicer and more accurate.

The optimization is almost perfect aside from two very annoying things. Having RT on can sometimes cause the frame rate to drop in some areas. The Bugs swarming around the daughters also cause the same issue. This can usually be fixed by toggling RT off/on but repeatedly doing this does get annoying after awhile. So I've just decided to play the game with RT off until they fix the issues.

The games audio quality is the same as what you got in RE7, RE2R & RE3R. The soundtrack used in the game mainly consists of low ambient noise but sadly isn't used in the game that often. [spoiler]The part where you play as Chris is fantastic tough. Reminded me of the HUNK theme from RE2R[/spoiler].

The gameplay itself is almost identical to RE7 but... There is a slight delay to all the foot movements you do which can make the game feel clunky. However there are no delays when it comes to aiming and firing the weapons. I think this is what makes the game even easier because you can pull off headshots very easily.

Sadly when you [spoiler]play as Chris his gameplay is the same as when you play as Ethan. Where as in RE7, playing as Chris or Joe offered their own unique gameplay mechanics[/spoiler].

The story itself is alright... The writing is complete trash in most areas. The Duke (merchant) was really the only character who seemed to have decent lines. The game ends [spoiler]on a cliffhanger where the BSAA seem to be using bioweapons as their soldiers/cleanup crew, so Chris wants to head to BSAAs HQ to find out what they are doing. After the credits we get one last cutscene where we are now in the future and Ethans daughter Rose is grown up. Her handler and her lil outburst seem to suggest she is much more powerful than the mold. There is also a 80 page document you can read called the "The Baker Incident Report" that turns out to be written by Zoe from RE7. She seems to be working as a journalist and is been sent documents and messages warning her that it's not over yet.[/spoiler]. This ending leaves more questions than answers. It feels like its only the first part to some bigger story.

The games current release state has a perfect amount of content to keep you playing and replaying for the NG+ content but not worth the $125 price here in New Zealand at least.

As a big Resident Evil fan, I thoroughly enjoyed this entry to the series. It gave me a lot of ratatouille moments, reminding me of when I played Resident Evil 4 as a young lad while also being a unique entry into the RE series. 

The premise is pretty simple: Ethan has another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up day, arrives at village, and has to kill 4 lords to get his daughter Rose back and defeat the super baddy witch lady. The 4 lords might truthfully be my favorite parts of the game. Each represents a horror trope, ranging from werewolves, vampires, creepy haunted dolls, swamp monsters, and Frankenstein. It was really cool to see these concepts in a Resident Evil game and see all of them connected to the (admittedly messy)  mythos Resident Evil has constructed.

I also thought the backtracking in this game was really well done. Every time you would return to an area, it would feel safe, but then the game will throw some sort of challenge at you to make the horror still feel fresh. All the areas were really unique and interesting, with my favorites being the castle and the factory.

So yes, I do recommend this game. But there are a few cons I think people should consider:

1. I do not believes all the lords live up to their fullest potentials. A lot of the areas feature a decent amount of content, but all end up feeling really short. All the lords are really interesting characters and I wish we got to explore them more. Dimitrescu is going to be remembered as a very iconic horror villain (thank you r34) but I really wish there was more of her. Same for Donna and Moreau. Heisenberg gets the closest to reaching his potential, but just does not make it for me due to a lackluster boss battle. It was still an enjoyable experience for me, but I believe they could have all been so much more.

2. Ethan is not a very engaging character. He was designed to be a self-insert for the player. So when the story is about him trying to rescue his daughter, it just does not reach the emotional impact it could have. Ethan does not react to horror like any normal human would; he reacts like a gamer who is just tried of running into bullet sponge enemies.

3. I have not played through the game a second time yet, but I can already tell second-playthroughs for this game are going to be a drag. The intro is very long and there is not a way to skip it as far as I know. There are also areas that will drag on second-playthroughs, such as a certain (terrifying on the first go) stealth section.

4. You need to play through Resident Evil 7 for the best experience in this game. Which can suck, because who wants to buy another game to enjoy a game?

5. THE COOKING MECHANIC - So when you kill an animal and pick up its meat, then you will get a prompt that says "Give meat to the Duke" or something on the lines of that. I mistaked that for selling the meats to the Duke. As it turns out, the cooking mechanic was story-locked. So I lost access to some very nice upgrades, such as HP increases, movement speed increases, and increased damage resistance when blocking. This was pretty frustrating because I lost access to nice stuff because the devs did a very poor job of communicating what to do with the meats. The game was still beatable without most of the upgrades, but it did make things more challenging. It didn't help when food took up inventory space.

Overall, I do not think this was the best Resident Evil game, but it definitely is in the top 10 for me. It's a very memorable game and I'm glad it sold well due to people simping over a 9 foot milf vampire.
