This is a non spoiler review: 

The game starts extremely strong, you're put into a pretty harrowing, high energy and tense opening that immediately kept on edge until the game truly started. One of the most fun Resident evil openers since RE 2's intro!

Once you get into the game itself, past the intro section's many cutscenes (this does effect replayability unfortunately) you're once again in a semi open world area where you need to find items to unlock doors and puzzles throughout the game world - this element of the game is very strong, with many optional areas for extra items and treasures, something I really appreciated on my first playthrough and is consistent through the entire game, minus some majorly scripted sections. 

In terms of horror, you will be in much suspense throughout, fighting a variety of monsters from a basic Dark Souls like zombie to wolf like creatures that swarm you with intensity. My only issue with the horror aspect is there are too many scripted set pieces, once you realise how scripted the game world is when replaying the game, the world feels much less threatening. 

I also appreciated the villiage hub world itself, it's brimming with details and unlockables - it's one of the best central hub areas I've seen since firelink shrine or the earlier lego games. I absolutely loved opening it up throughout my progress, a huge improvement from previous games. 

In terms of the PC Port... this is where things get tricky.

In many sections of the game you will get a huge fps drop when getting attacked by certain monsters or killing certain monsters... this will happen regardless of your settings and was absolutely immersion breaking. 
Hopefully this aspect will get fixed in the future as it's a real game breaker for me. 

In terms of the plot... I enjoyed uncovering it. I did not enjoy the actual reasons behind the many mysteries the plot laid out. The ending felt utterly mind boggling to me but it didn't detract the game for me too much, this is an RE game afterall... you come to expect some strange stuff. Regardless uncovering the plot was really well handled and would recommend at least one playthrough to get a really cinematic experience of the world. 

Gameplay wise the game is strong, building from RE 7 and combining the best elements of RE 4. I really enjoyed the currency aspect of the game, upgrading and buying weapons, selling treasure etc. This really pushed me to get all the extra content in the game. You also have a huge variety of weapons this time around - from a simple pistol to an unlockable lightsaber... there's so much to unlock and refine that requires multiple playthroughs to fully complete - a superb decision giving me reason to play it over and over.

The gunplay is also pretty good, the guns feel right to use and impactfull - though certain monsters don't react to shots and are basically bullet sponges but this doesn't apply to all monsters... an inconsistent decision to say the least.

There is also mercenaries mode, one of my favourite versions of the classic arcade mode. All I will say here is you will have a blast! 

Overall i'd give this game a solid 8 out of 10. I haven't given too much away but the quality of the game does gradually get lower as it progresses, it also has an extremely long intro, which is superb going in for the first time but will drive you crazy on repeat playthroughs. It also suffers from too many set pieces but the game looks and plays gorgeously, has much to unlock and explore, and fantastic character interactions + a lengthy story mode that is a good apology for the RE3 remake.

Pros first, and one con:

The environment and encounter variety is great, with a few standout sequences that are really memorable, and you never know what weirdness the game will throw at you next, keeping you engaged throughout. Some firefights are really intense, you're never bored, exploration is fun and rewarding, and the game has a grand scope that keeps it constantly entertaining. It's a decent length too (took me 13 hours without finding everything, and there's a lot to find).

That said, it isn't "scary", per se, which was a bit of a shame (minus one particular level that's still burned into my eyes). Sure, there's tension in hoping you have juuust enough ammunition to make it through some of the tougher battles, but if you got excited by Resident Evil 7's shift towards a more intimate, slow-burn and psychological approach to fear (like I did), you might be a little disappointed, as it doesn't continue down that route. For some, this might be good news, I know Resi 4 is the best in the series for many, but for me, this aspect was a slight let-down.

Still, my time was far from wasted playing it, it's a very well made and very entertaining action game.

TLDR: If you’re looking for a solid spook fest, and don’t mind some plot weirdness, then Resident Evil Village has a satisfying core loop and an engaging story that’s worth the price of admission.

I haven’t played many of the Resident Evil games, I played Resident Evil 5 on the Xbox 360, I played a bit of Revelations, and I managed to steel my nerves in 2make. I don’t really have the investment in Resident Evil as much as series fans might, so I consider myself an outsider to the series continuity and characters. Resident Evil 7 looked a little too gross for me, and as such I didn’t play it, as a result I didn’t get to see the start of the plot of this new arc. Thankfully, there is a “Previously On…” movie in Village, so you can get a general idea of the plot without having played the previous entry. Village is a direct continuation of the plot in Resident Evil 7, so I guess if you want the full story and you were basically pulled to this game because of the aesthetic, then I recommend buying the bundle or watching someone else play it if you want the fullest experience.

I won’t get into plot details, but what I will say is that the plot is very… anime.  In the way that characters tend to explain things to the player when they’ve already figured them out themselves, and characters take not explaining things as a good way to make a plot happen. That being said, I still enjoyed what plot there was, and a late game revelation did a good job of explaining a complaint I was going to have about something else.

If you asked me to describe overall mechanical feel of Village, I’d say it’s probably closer to games like Zelda, in that while yes, combat is an important element, a greater portion of the game is focused on environmental puzzles and backtracking, and those puzzles can even be used to kill or avoid enemies. If you go into Village with the mindset of Call of Duty, you’re probably going to be disappointed. 

Like most survival horror games, the combat comes down to resource management and finding yourself with 11 bullets and 4 enemies that each take 7 shots to kill. You’ll almost never be flush with ammo, and if you are, you won’t be for long. Even going into the finale, I had to be extra careful where I placed my shots and I was franticly running around scrounging and crafting supplies, while trying to not get impaled. Careful use explosives and ammo, environmental objects, and even good ol’ fashioned running, are the name of the game here. The gunplay of Village is good, although some of the guns lack sonic punch. The shotguns feel meaty, but the pistols and sniper rifle really sounded like I was launching spitballs at the enemies even after I had upgraded them. Weapon variety is a minor complaint, by the end of the game, you basically have 2 pistols, a magnum, 3 different shotguns, 1 SMG type thing, and a grenade launcher. I know that sounds like a lot, but by ammo necessity, you’re going to be using one pistol, one shotgun, and the grenade launcher for more intense situations. You also must carry all of the weapons you find if you don’t want to lose them. You can’t just store them somewhere and come back, you must keep them in your inventory or sell them. I would have liked to see some more weapon variety, but, I will say none of the guns feel out of place for the vibe of the game, so Ethan isn’t finding an M4 in a pile of dirt and going to town on the werewolves.

Gunplay isn’t the only part of the game though; a lot of your time will be spent doing puzzles and backtracking to find, or create key items to progress. I can’t really get too much into this without spoilers, but the environments did that Dark Souls thing, where if you go into an area see something and can’t access it right now, you will probably be able to come back later and go there and find something inside. Which really made the different areas feel like places I could explore and poke around in without feeling like I was just wasting my time.

What really drew me into Village was the visuals. When I saw my friend playing this game, I was almost immediately reminded of Bloodborne. The gothic architecture, the literal werewolves, the gloomy snow-covered village, it’s all great stuff and sharply realized. Technically, there are some problems, even with playing around with the settings, I got some massive frame drops in areas that weren’t even technically overly complex. When I watched my friend stream the game, there were some moments where looking at a certain character would plummet his framerate into the twenties, whereas my less powerful computer had no issues. There were also some frequent animation bugs and hit detection issues, but those were minor compared to the performance problems. I feel like this is probably something that will be smoothed over with patches, but it is worthy to note if you’re particularly sensitive to framerate issues.

There are things I’d like to mention about the gameplay and story, both good and bad, but doing so would probably ruin parts of the plot, and I was pretty invested in the story from the outset, so I don’t want to really get into them since I don’t want to spoil anything. But suffice to say that those points wouldn’t really make or break my opinion on the game even if I could talk about them without giving away anything.

For those of you out there who are avoiding this game because of its genre, I’d say that Village is closer to an adventure game than something like Outlast or Amnesia, despite some of the same gameplay notes being hit. Overall, I’d highly recommend Resident Evil Village.

Before playing this game I really wasn't expecting a whole lot more than what Resident Evil 7 offered but boy was I in for one wild ride.

The gameplay loop is extremely satisfying for a few key reasons and these are, enemy variety, treasure hunting, boss battles and weapon modifications with the latter being more akin to that of Resident Evil 4. Treasures are located all over the well thought out hub area of the game which is the village. These treasures can be collected and sold to a charismatic merchant who is more than happy to buy your wares in exchange for the game's currency, Lei. Lei is spent on weapon modifications or even other supplies if you’re in a pinch. You’ll need these modifications too because the enemies of the game are no joke, they’ll dip and dive out of your crosshairs while attempting to get close enough for a quick bite to eat. I won’t specify what enemies you’ll face but just know they never get old and there’s enough variety to keep you on your toes.

The game is extremely well balanced in terms of the amount of items at your disposal so you’ll never feel too overpowered in any given situation, you’ll always have just enough ammunition to take care of whatever the game throws at you. This all adds to the games great pacing and atmosphere which is fantastic. I won’t spoil any areas but the quality of the village itself is by no means ‘as good as it gets’ and there is enough environmental variety to keep your eyes glued to the screen with amazement because the art direction is on point. The weapons in the game are a joy to use, whether you’re popping heads with the sniper rifle or unloading pistol rounds into a Lycans head you can rest assured you'll be having a blast. The game is a charming mix of gore, horror, action and campy voice acting but this by no means detracts from the overarching story and there’s a lot here to keep you engaged.

I’m yet to sink my teeth into Mercenaries or the new game plus modes but for my first playthrough I have nothing but praise for this game. From a technical standpoint the game runs great and I have experienced no crashes or weird glitches, the game is well optimised and comes in at 25Gig which is impressive these days.

If you’re looking for a story driven FPS with a lengthy campaign and what is no doubt stella replay value, pick this game up and go get’em.

 Resident Evil 7 was my initial introduction to Resident Evil, back when I used to watch playthroughs since I couldn't play anything myself. Not long ago, I revisited the game and played it for myself for the first time, and I loved it. 7's story left a mark on me and the gameplay was some solid RE horror survival. When I heard that 8 was to continue the story of 7, I was not as excited as you might think. I was actually quite indifferent. But when the game released, I got it just a day after and played it. And my indifference was not warranted at all.
 Gameplay wise, 8 is very fun. 8 borrows a lot from Resident Evil 4, both in setting and function. The inventory system works very differently than 7's did, as there are now multiple tabs for crafting items, key items, and normal items like guns, ammo, healing items, etc. 8 has a wide array of guns, and I mean a lot. There are multiple pistols to find, as well as shotguns and other extra guns. Most can be upgraded and some have slots for attachments which help beef them up. They all feel nice and sound nice. 8, however, is very easy. And I mean very. I played twice, once on standard and the next on hardcore (which, by the way, doesn't have the limited save function most RE hardcore difficulties have) and I never once ran out of ammo. I always had something to use, partly because of how many guns you can carry (you can have like 5 or more at max inventory space) and how much ammo you're given (and able to craft). There is even a trader, named Duke, who lets you buy weapons and ammo, among other things. As such, there are treasures to find that can be sold for good amounts of money, or Lei. Even on hardcore, enemies aren't as powerful as you might think. I died maybe a total of 10-15 times throughout both playthroughs together. This does not diminish the game's quality at all, but it is worthy to note. I cannot speak for Village of Shadows, however (the fourth difficulty level), so perhaps that offers a bigger challenge. This game is not very long either, perhaps 8-10 on average. But it is very fun to simply explore and find everything that the game keeps hidden away from you. I was up for hours just looking around for anything to loot only because it felt so fun to do so. As a game, 8 is very fun and while not very hard it has a lot in store, from multiple boss fights to a wide array of enemies and locations that 7 did not have.
 But what of the game as a narrative? Truthfully, Resident Evil has never been known for its narrative prowess, or at least I don't think it should be. But 8 is some of RE's best. Taking the base that 7 laid out with the story of Ethan Winters, we follow him to a Romanian village after his wife was killed and his child abducted by Chris Redfield of all people. So you spend your time pissing around in a village, then a castle, then some underground tunnels, then back into the village and even into a factory and a resevoir. All the while, Ethan has to collect these "flasks" which house parts of his daughter Rose's body. Ultimately, Ethan comes face to face with Miranda, the architect of all this madness that Ethan has been subject to. Here we learn that Miranda's goal is to remake Rose into her own daughter, aka Eveline from 7. The mutamycete (mold) from 7 has followed us here, as well. When Ethan has his heart ripped out, and we follow Chris through the village which is overrun with BSAA bioweapons and lycan people (note also that Mia wasn't killed, but taken hostage and imitated by Miranda who survived the initial attack by Chris in the beginning), we learn that Ethan has been dead all this time, having been killed by Jack back in Louisiana. The mold has kept him alive this entire time. So as Chris makes his way to Miranda, Ethan learns of his condition from a dream with Eveline and then awakes to find himself being brought to Miranda by Duke. Here, Ethan and Chris meet at the heart of the madness and put Miranda down (or rather Ethan puts her down).
 There was a very quiet sadness to 7. A simple family infected by a child who just wanted a family, but instead received a life as a literal weapon. Ethan is simply caught in the middle, looking for Mia. But 8 is not like that. The game is far more action like, and does not have the thick oppressive atmosphere of 7. But the ending is what sells it for me. After Miranda's death, Chris has to carry Ethan to the escape helicopter. Ethan, now knowing his fate, realizes that there is no real point. He is quite literally falling apart, and in one last show of loyalty to his family, he sends Chris and the rescued Rose away to detonate the mutamycete infestation in the village. And it is in this way Ethan ends, in a final show of self sacrifice to save his daughter. So in a way he accomplished what he set out to do, having rescued Mia and Rose, but he did not get to live to see it.
 I explain it poorly, and I omit a lot of details, but I assure you that it was executed perfectly. The ending hours to this game are simply amazing, both narratively and gameplay wise. 8 may not have 7's atmosphere, but it has gameplay and narrative power that 7 couldn't dream of, albeit it was only possible because of 7. Play 7 before 8, and you have yourself a Resident Evil package like nothing else.
 8.5/10, R.I.P. Ethan Winters

First of all, play this on Hardcore. Especially if you want a more "survival horror" experience.

Secondly, while I enjoyed this game very much, I don't recommend getting the PC version unless you have a good rig for it. There are some serious frame drop issues here and there, even when I cranked my settings as low as I could, and I'm hearing and seeing other people who have good rigs experience this as well. I seriously hope they can patch these issues as I nearly considered refunding the game after having it freeze up EVERY TIME an enemy grabbed me!

But despite that huge headache at the start, I really loved my time with this game! I honestly didn't expect to enjoy it as much as I did, especially since when the game was first unveiled I had some slight concerns about not only the whole "lycans and vampires" angle they were going for with the enemies, but also hearing about the more "action" approach this game was going to take. The last few RE games I played were the HD Remaster of Resident Evil Remake, RE7, and RE2 Remake, the latter two being HUGE strides back in the right direction for the series in terms of survival horror. Especially after the more action-heavy approach of 4-6. 

Yes, this game has a more action-oriented approach... in SOME areas. Especially towards the end. To me, it's a horror game in the same sense that something like Bloodborne can be considered a horror game... Speaking of which, I got really similar vibes to that game not just from most of the enemies and environments, but also the lore you uncover at the end regarding the discovery of the pathogen and its use in the village. But if you play it in Hardcore like I recommended above, it will add a bigger emphasis on resource management and making sure you have enough of the good stuff on hand for bosses and tougher enemies. Enemies will also be more spongy and will hit harder. I ended up having to reload earlier saves just so I could get more First Aid and a better arsenal for two particular boss battles that were giving me trouble.


As for the base gameplay... really solid! It's got the classic RE (and also SoulsBorne) map format where all the areas are interconnected and you keep unlocking doors and passageways to use as shortcuts to earlier areas as you go. Exploration is further encouraged as there are not only hidden treasures and collectibles, but also some optional side areas and mini-bosses. Definitely encourages replayability and gazing at the gorgeously crafted environments.
I also enjoyed the cast of villains in this game and found myself feeling sympathetic towards some of them. (Anyone else feel kinda bad for Moreau?) 

As much as I loved this game, though, there are a few gripes I have aside from the frame-rate issues:

- Some environments are a bit confusing to navigate at first, especially the village itself. Heisenberg's area turned into a frustrating maze at one point all because one section was blocked off halfway through.

-I was a bit taken weirded out at first when I found out that Herbs were no longer consumables, but crafting items instead. So... if you don't have a Chem Fluid to combine with them, you can't heal. While it does add to the tension of the game, it's still a bit weird considering they were always healing items in the older games. I wish that were still the case... like being able to use Herbs to slightly recover health (Red to Orange/Yellow) and combining them with Chem Fluid to make a First Aid and fully recover your health. 

-I'm not a fan of how most interactable and breakable objects are marked with yellow paint or tape... like breakable boxes, wells (Every single one you can use the Well Wheel on and they get crossed off the map once you used them anyway so what's even the point). and even SIGN POSTS, FFS. 

TL;DR - This is a really solid RE game, in my opinion. But the PC version definitely needs some patching up.

I've beaten the campaign a few times, from normal to the hardest difficulty 'Village of Shadows', done a vast majority of the challenges, and beaten the first 4 maps to Mercenaries mode. Originally I felt that RE8 properly earned its spot next to greater RE titles like 1 and 4, but having done more playthroughs of the game, I believe that the game sits a bit further below those titles.

Getting visuals and aesthetics out of the way, they are great and all that so no need to ponder whether it looks good or not (If you're one of those people that are just into visuals)

RE8's main flaws, to me, come from its approach to tone, level design, and more so of what the game could have been.

 - The story's shift in tone acts up in various parts of the game especially with Ethan's dialogue. RE7 had this same issue, with Ethan writhing in pain to acting like what ever happened wasn't a big deal. At one point he even saw his wife get taken by Lucas while she screamed for help and all said was 'Damn it." like he tried throwing a piece of trash into the bin and ended up missing it. RE8 even had this moment when Mia was shot to death right in front of him at the beginning of the game with no sign of emotional shock like screaming "MIAAAAAAA!!!!" or something like. Then there's quips in the danger moments, which are a whole other thing that just make you think, "Ethan!, could you at least be a bit scared at the fact that you could die at this moment?!". Even story moments that tie into the rest of the RE universe like [spoiler] when you find out Umbrella was basically founded here through Spencer and Miranda in 1 note at the final moments of the game [/spoiler] I feel it should have been spread out throughout the game with small hints towards it unlike the obvious 'ok something happened here but I don't know exactly what it was' motif.

- Level Design was a bit under utilized especially after Castle Dimitrescu. While the castle was sort of a puzzle to get through with back tracking in between, the rest of the game is just a 'keep moving forward' type design, which isn't always a bad thing, but how its executed determines this quality. Areas after that just felt too straight forward and not all that interesting in terms of layout. Also you aren't exactly able to return to previous play areas either once you took out that area's boss. You miss something in any of those areas, say for instance a shootable object or treasure, you'll have to get it on your next playthrough. I've seen other people talk how the interconnected area where you go to other bosses' domains could have been a choose your own route type thing as well, which would have been a nice touch to the game. 

Other nitpicks for me include variety in difficulty (like having different solutions to puzzles, item placement, maybe a secret area or two that could only be accessed on this higher difficulty) just small changes to make it feel different, not 'making every enemy have more health and hit harder', this concept is so overdone in so many games nowadays. 

In conclusion, RE8, while flawed to a degree, is still a good entry in the RE series. It makes a name for itself and has its own identity, but not really that impressive to where it exceeds expectations. I had a fun run at the start for sure (first runs are always wonderful despite the flaws listed above) It just could have been more though, and hopefully the DLC addresses a few of these issues later on.

 I do have a couple of gripes with the PC port's UI and the odd omission of a Field of View slider is a real head scratcher. First let me begin by saying I have always been a bit of a "skeptical fan" of the RE series. Love the idea, intrigued by the lore. Atmosphere has always been great. Puzzles were usually fun and interesting, etc. That being said, I have had issues with some of the titles. Mechanics I did not enjoy such as being forced to run from certain enemies that you cannot kill (Tyrant in RE2, for example) and in some of the games the movement mechanics are so terrible it ruins the experience. It was the movement itself that made me never want to finish RE4 for example. So trust me when I say what I have to say next. 

I LOVED THIS GAME!!!!!

Transitioning from the 3rd person views of the old days of RE to the new 1st person view was awesome to begin with and though, again, there were aspects of RE7 I did not enjoy, the change of pace made me keep going. I'm glad I did because I needed the knowledge of the story from 7 for this. 

Right from the start I noticed the movement was faster and easier to maneuver than RE7, but still not completely free of some clunkiness which is fine, it's part of what makes these games challenging and scary. Knowing you can't move the way you feel you could IRL definitely adds to the terror. Now that I can move just a bit faster and easier though made the game play much more fun for me and made me more confident during the game's various combat scenarios. 

I of course also noticed the graphics were much sharper than in RE7 which I found to be a very welcome improvement. I liked the quality of RE7 don't get me wrong but this game took it to a whole new level imho. Everything was beautifully built and detailed and that of course in turn makes the game that much more intriguing, impressive and terrifying. I also loved the fact that this game featured a good variety of characters from the villagers to monsters to bosses and so on. It never felt stale. 

The story behind Village is fantastic. I thoroughly enjoyed the story itself and how everything was presented and how well it all ties to the previous title. The level of balance they were able to achieve here is no small feat. There was enough mystery that not everything could be guessed by any means, but they also gave enough to keep me wanting more. Of course even at the end not everything has been revealed either and there will definitely be another game. I still have questions of course, but I know enough that I don't feel robbed.

Overall I think Capcom has finally found the perfect balance of horror, story, combat, and strategy to make RE a series that can truly shine in my eyes which is a fantastic feeling as I have ALWAYS wanted to be more into these games. If they can keep this model and just improve upon it I will anxiously await the next game and unabashedly shout to my Steam account, "TAKE ALL MY ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ MONEY!!!" 

If you are like me and hesitant to get this because of previous titles leaving a bad taste in your mouth, don't be. It's absolutely worth the 60 dollar price tag, especially if you have the RTX card and surround sound system to REALLY enjoy it.

Resident Evil Village is a hard game for me to form an oppinion on. On one hand, it has some of the best level desing in a Resident Evil game to date. It's balance between action and horror is just perfect. It still manages to be unnerving and scary. One sequence in particular, being one of the greatest horror moments in the entire franchise. It even has a few legitimately clever jumpscares.

But the horror is balanced well enough that I actually look forward to play it when turning it on. Unlike the Resident Evil Remake or RE7, which mostly fill me with dread.

Comparisons to Resident Evil 4 are obvious. Not only is the european setting similar. But, the game even brings back the merchant and the briefcase based inventory. The tone of the game is far more grounded than RE4. Which, to be fair, is something that can be said about most games.

Village has a fair bit of tongue-in-cheek silliness, but it's not all ridiculous. The tone of the writing lies somewhere between Resident Evil 7 and the Resident Evil 2 remake. For some reason, I found myself being reminded a lot of Howling 2: Your Sister is a Werewolf while playing. Maybe it's the way that movie also confuses werewolves with vampires. I don't know.... It's hard to place the game, really.

I look at it in sort of a similar way I would look at Call of Duty: Black Ops 2. It's a very very strong entry within it's franchise, one that doesn't reinvent the wheel but, mainly because it doesn't have to. The foundations of the franchise are strong enough to support it, and the game does a great job living up to them. But, much like Black Ops 2... It's just another Resident Evil.

It's not the major reimagining of the franchise that RE7 was, or the fantastic old-school adaptation that the RE2 Remake was. Neither is it the disapointing letdown that Resident Evil 3 was. It's a strong product that paves the way for what will most likely be an excellent sequel, aka Resident Evil 9.

But, it's not in any way revolutionary, it's just another good Resident Evil game. Just like Black Ops 2 was another good Call of Duty game. There are abysmal Resident Evil games, there are exemplary Resident Evil games. Village is a good one. And it's definitely worth your time. I usually only play games once. But I ended up starting a new playtrough literally the second the credits ended. I loved playing this game and it makes me really excited to see what the series will bring in the future.
One thing I'd strongly reccomend is playing the game on hard difficulty. Medium difficulty just becomes far too generous with ammo towards the end. Ennemies also tend to lack agression on medium. The way they stand around waiting to be shot can be somewhat distracting.

The AI and ressources at your disposal on hard are far better balanced. And differences go further than that. During the Castle Dimetrescu sequence, for example. Tall Lady seems to restrict her movement to the main hall, on normal difficulty. Whereas, on hard, she'll follow you all around the Castle, much like Mr.X did.
The Mercenary mode is also tons of fun. I usually wouldn't touch Mercenary in these games. But the weapon you unlock for achieving a Double S score on all challenges intrigued me. Trying it made appreciate the combat a lot more too.
A big downside on PC is the lack of an FOV setting. There are mods that allow you to expand the FOV. But native support would be welcome. Performance wise, the game is very well optimised. Hitting 100 frames at 1080p on PC is pretty easy. Especially with the interlaced rendering option, which looked terrible in other RE Engine games, but actually looks really good in Village.

WARNING: There may be mild gameplay SPOILERS in this review. I won't spoil any story details, but I will be discussing the different areas in the game, and in which order they appear. 

  So, let's start with the negatives, so that I can end on a positive note. The first issue I noticed after starting the game was menu navigation. By default, It's a little strange. Having to hit "P" to skip scenes (for that Dashing Dad Achievement...) is pretty awkward, and having it default to ESC would have been more in line with almost every other game made today. RE Village is definitely a console port for PC and that is very obvious in some of its design. Expect to rebind some controls. 

  My second and most technically obvious issue is how the graphics settings were configured on the recommended preset. Using an RTX 2070 Super at 1080p resolution, I was able to get 160fps off and on without ray tracing. The game mostly looked and played great at these settings, except in the games first (or second, depending on whether you count the prologue) area, Castle Dimitrescu. The decor of the castle includes a lot of gold accenting. This gold had some very bad jagged edge aliasing and shimmering that looked terrible, and was extremely distracting. I played through the entire game with these settings, and after the castle, I didn't really notice this shimmering anywhere else. 
  Before I started a second run through, I watched a video by Alex Battaglia from Digital Foundry where he listed his recommended settings. These settings cut my frame rate to about 90fps, but the aliasing issue completely disappeared and also included the ray tracing options. I'd check out his video on YouTube. 

  Finally, the last issue (and also, not. Keep reading) I had with the game was its overall pacing. Beware, this is possibly SPOILER territory, so proceed with caution. After a short playable cutscene, the game starts much like its predecessor Resident Evil VII. Moving slowly through the dark, listening to nothing more than the ambient sounds of an old house settling, et cetera, BUT, the developers quickly let you know that this is not your typical RE game (5 and 6 aside, because Capcom has come to their senses since then). You suddenly get a taste of Village's combat,and just as fast as it appeared, it's gone. There are sections of combat sprinkled through the mid game periodically to keep you on your toes however, in the last few sections, Village suddenly turns into some kind of RE meets Wolfenstein meets Van Helsing with a little Call of Duty thrown in.

I hesitate to throw "best" around, especially when picking the best in a series. It is very easy to argue that Village is not the best game in the franchise, it's a claim that one could contest with almost any other entry in the series. However, what I can confidently say is that Village was my [i]favorite[/i] game in the franchise. 

Every review for this game seems to mention how it's RE 4 + RE 7. And, for what it's worth, they're right. But I think it goes a bit deeper than 7's gameplay in 4's general sort of setting. This isn't just a game, it's a fun game. For many horror games the enjoyment comes from the thrill, the scares, the tension. And while Village has this in spades, in particular in one certain area that many are calling the scariest RE has been, it also has genuinely fun gameplay. This is where I think it borrows the most from 4, not in setting, but in game design. 

You are rarely fully helpless in Village, you can be outgunned or outnumbered, but only on a few occasions will you have no means of putting up a good fight. The gunplay is tight and fair, leading to situations where you're less scared of what's around the next corner, and more concerned with the best way to clear out a group of enemies. It's fun, you feel strong when you should and can quickly feel inferior to your challenge in moments in a way that just feels right. 

The game's far from perfect, there's one area early in the game that's just frustrating due to lack of clear direction and from what I've seen is a nightmare on hardcore going in blind. It also can sometimes fail to point out a certain aspect to progression, meaning that sometimes the "puzzle" stumping you is missing a pressable button or unlockable door. But these faults are, in my opinion, very minor and only are the occasional frustration in an overall satisfying romp. 

The story is pure Resident Evil, which is to say full of shlock, scary moments, and the occasional bombastic monster encounter. All of the villains absolutely steal the show, with everyone's favorite vampire and Mr. I Can't Believe It's Not Nic Cage in particular being highlights. It's not a very deep story, and feels very loose up until the story's final hour, but the cast carries it in a way where it never feels dull. 

All in all, I cannot say Resident Evil Village is the best game in the franchise: but I can say it is the one that I view the most fondly.

I started this game in hardcore difficulty, and I highly recommend it if you have plenty of experience with first person shooters

-Story-
Intriguing, different and interesting from the beginning, feels like a fresh experience.The end is very emotive and pulled out a tear from me. The game's world building is beautiful (in its own creepy way) and also visually astonishing in a very similar fashion to the way dark souls games are built, could get a 10/10 from a graphic/technical point of view alone. 

-Horror-
At this difficulty I would place the degree of "horror" somewhere between around re2 and re3 remakes (which I played in normal difficulty) since resources and ammo are VERY limited. but there are specific sections in the game where the experience goes full sillent hill and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it gets scary. 
But more than fear, the game succeeds in keeping you tense and alert all the time, this is definitely close to the experience I had in RE4. The only time the horror factor fades in this game is towards the ending, but only because by then it is possible to manage enough resources to have 1 and a half extra magazine for every ammunition type.

-Action-
The action is a core element of the experience. If you are like me who DOES NOT really like a pure horror experience, but also some degree of action, then this is definitely the game for you (I would say it is similar yet slightly less frenetic than the Metro series). If you look for a 100% horror game then I wouldn't be sure you want to spend full price for this game.

-Weapons and familiar mechanics-
The game brings back the storage and weapon upgrades mechanics from RE4, money is not abundant and I had to spend it in the smartest way possible based on my situation, sometimes I would not upgrade some weapons or buy extra storage space if I lacked ammo or had 70% of my bag empty (again, no ammo nor healing items etc..) . I really liked this degree of frustration since the game does not make the combat too easy and it forces you to think how to use your money.

I try to give u several ways to compare if this is a game you really want to buy at full launch price, If you are the kind of player I am (based on what I wrote above) then I highly recommend it. But in general IF you find this game at least at 30% off, It is without a doubt worth it.

Let's just get the cons out of the way early:  The game's story is a bit short.  Probably 10-20 hours depending on your playstyle.  For some, especially those that didn't care for previous resident evil titles, this may be a deal breaker and/or a good commercial for a rental services like Gamefly.

The story is tropey and uninteresting if you take it at face value.  But fans of the Resident Evil series will recognize the plot as a near-perfect Resident Evil story.  Ridiculous evil conspiracies, shadowy teams of mercenaries, horrific creatures, bizarre traveling salesmen, and a world that is conspicuously populated with weapons, ammo, a particular green plant, and explosive barrels for, like, no reason.  The story captures that unique campy aesthetic that made the original Resident Evil universe so fun to obsess over, and it still manages to be utterly terrifying while it does so.  In particular, it perfectly captures that gradual transition from survival-horror at the game's start to action-horror by the end.

Gameplay is nothing novel or groundbreaking, but it's still good.  However you felt about the gameplay of RE7 is probably how you'll feel about this one.  Bosses are creative and interesting affaris.  Ammo placement is well-done.  I consistently found myself with *just barely* enough ammo for most sections of the game, with a few dry spells that had me relying on the knife more than I was comfortable with.

Visually, the game is excellently done.  They create a host of different environments, from luxurious castle to ghost town to dingy factories, and the more cinematic portions of the game are a treat.  They borrowed a lot of RE4's visual design when it came to the more common monsters, but they always look good even when they don't look original.  The bosses are largely an exception: almost every unique enemy in the game, of which there are many, is both original and spectacularly designed.

If you can afford to buy a game that you'll only play for about 10-20 hours, or if you're the type to play a game multiple times, I recommend this.  Especially if you feel like you haven't got enough good singleplayer games in your diet.

Resident Evil Village is, in many ways, a game of two halves. The previous 25 years of Resident Evil games varied enormously,  from stripped-back survival horror, to a more explosion-laden style of action horror. To mark the 25th anniversary, it feels as if the developers attempted to accommodate both ends of this spectrum. The result is a game which has some moments of brilliance but also some extreme unevenness. 

Without giving any spoilers away, the game could be divided roughly into six parts. The Introduction, four distinct areas each concluding with a boss (each with their own tone and style), and the Finale. The introduction is incredibly strong, and has survival horror printed all over it. It serves as a great introduction to the village setting. The four middle sections are very different from each other. One dabbles in romantic Gothic horror, one focuses on stripped-back Silent Hill P.T-style horror with the removal of weapons (and a brilliantly twisted encounter in a basement), one focuses on grotesque body-horror and the final one occupies an industrial setting with experiments in man and metal. The Finale introduces a significant shift and ends in full-on action-horror, tonally a long way away from the beginning.

How much you enjoy it may vary on what your preferred style of horror is. There's likely something in here for everyone. The first half is more classic survival horror, the second half is much more action-horror. I much preferred the first half and would have enjoyed having it stay in that vein. The shift is gradual, so there isn't a single standout jarring moment, but there are moments in the second half where the scares retreat and the action clearly takes over. 

My opinion is that in attempting to include both styles, they created a somewhat uneven experience. Resident Evil 4 achieved that balance, but it's a difficult trick to pull off successfully, let alone twice.

Four new mainline Resident Evil games in just 4 years… Even during the heyday of the series in the late 90s it didn’t happen quite as often. After trying to recapture the essence of the classic survival horror with flawed but wonderful Resident Evil 7 we got not less wonderful reimagining of Resident Evil 2, both of which managed to recapture the glory of the genre, while attempting new things. Then last year we had a disappointing attempt at a remake, but a very solid and fun linear survival action Resident Evil 3. And this year we get an attempt to mix 7 with 4, in Village (or as they stylize it VII.l.age, to show that it’s RE8). And it’s a really good, really well put together game. That I struggle to care much about.

I liked my first playthrough of RE Village a lot, mostly because of its strongest aspect – the exploration. It is genuinely fun to run around the beautiful locations of the game, finding treasures, new weapons or upgrades (just like in RE4) and just enjoying the views. And I did like the attempt to constantly spice things up – every “act”, so to speak, of Village works differently, focusing on different aspects of gameplay. It’s not exactly new for the series, and even 7, which this game is serving as a direct sequel to in terms of story, was very clearly divided into sections, each of which felt different. So Capcom tried to go even harder into this concept and on the first playthrough it is pretty fun and surprising.

Unfortunately, it is here, where I went from this really positive first playthrough impressions into the usual meat of any Resident Evil – the replayability. And quickly found myself utterly bored, even though I couldn’t quite understand why at first. I mean, there are multiple challenges and unlocks, most of which sound fun. There’s the return of The Mercenaries minigame that I never liked, but hey, it’s pretty well done too. There are additional difficulties that I could try. And there were still a couple things that I’ve managed to miss on my first playthrough. But none of it felt fun or exciting. And I’ve realized that the seeming variety of each act was extremely surface level. And, in fact, all of these acts just felt like they could be separate games that don’t fit into a whole experience when combined together. Which made me realize the core of my issues – the main gameplay of the game is really plain and boring.

What made RE4 tick was the fact that it’s core gameplay of running and shooting/kicking enemies was fun. It was somewhat clunky and the skill floor in that game was higher than, I’d argue, it should’ve been. But at the same time, it’s core mechanics and unique mix of weapons, each of which had it’s exclusive upsides and downsides, meant that you could find your own way of playing the game, that constantly challenged you. Even on its easiest difficulty with new game plus weaponry, there was fun to be had with its basics.

RE Village instead takes RE7 core, that was made with specific weapon, enemy and level design in mind, and drops more enemies and more weapons on top. All newer weapons in the game are straight up upgrades to the older ones. All enemies feel the same, despite seemingly having unique elements to them. And killing enemies feels like the most blandest FPS you’ve ever played. Sure, it’s challenging you far more on harder difficulties, but it’s more frustrating than fun specifically because the basics are plain and uninteresting. Where’s the counter punch from Not a Hero? Where are some clever tricks with specific weapons to learn as you play? Where’s the management of resources that’s actually fun?

And sadly, the story, which is always the least important point for enjoying RE games, is really boring too, despite having promise. Ethan is as much of a non-character as he was in 7, except this time the game goes to such great lengths to avoid showing his face in cutscenes, that it feels like a bad b-movie that’s not showing the unmasked villain to keep the mystery until later. Connections (no pun intended) to older games feel shoehorned and are simply dropped in files you can walk past. Chris remains the least interesting main character of the series, despite yet another attempt to give him something. And the villains lack the charisma and screen time of the Baker family or even the characters from RE3 (2020). I guess, it’s fun that all of those RE4 prototypes, the so called RE 3.5 demos, have been finally made into a game.

Resident Evil Village is a really well made, really good game that is fun to play once. But it’s also the only RE title I can think of, that doesn’t have anything special I could really hold on to, while even the worst or most frustrating games in the series before this one usually had something. It is weird to think that an RE game would have such bland action mechanics, especially one being so focused on the action aspect. But here we are. And even though it’s a really good game, I don’t really care much about it.

Resident Evil 8 is hands down the best game in the series. If you haven't already, play Resident Evil 7 then give this game a try.

While not the best Resident Evil in the reboot/revival series, it is still a great addition that is well worth your time.

First the positive: The design, especially Dimitrescu's castle and the village are amazing. The detail and the graphics are some of the best that I've ever seen in a game before. These environments truly add to the game in a way that make it feel like the story couldn't be told anywhere else. The village has the feel of being like a location in a gothic fantasy novel, lost in specific period of time. I really enjoyed this portion of the game. I also like the open-endedness of the Village, giving it a unique spin on the Resident Evil formula. I found myself going off the beaten path to find a hidden treasure, lore, or secret weapons. I did quite a bit of this in my first playthrough and I still feel like I missed a lot, which lends itself to more playthroughs to find more hidden content.

The four lords were all great and complex characters, with Lady Dimistrescu, her daughters, and Heisenberg being highlights. The mysterious Duke is also a great character. You never know what he really is after which adds to his mysterious persona.

As with other Resident Evil games, there are a plethora of unique enemies and puzzles throughout. This game doesn't rise above the rest, but definitely isn't lesser than any of the other entries in the reboot series.

There are some truly scary moments. Especially during the 1st 3/5 of the game. The last 2/5 of the game also has some scares here and there, but it morphs into more of an action game a bit, which I will talk about in the not so positive portion of my review.

Finally, performance wise the game runs extremely well on my pc at 2k. No hiccups or FPS drops. I do have a 3070 so I'm not sure how the game will run on an older graphics card.

Not so positive: Most of the boss fights were underwhelming to me. Resident Evil boss fights usually give you a series of minor conditions, such as use this weapon to inflict this type of damage, or shoot this specific spot on the boss, which gives the boss fights a unique feel so it doesn't devolve into bullet sponge encounters. While there are some fights like that here, there are more "bullet sponge" boss fights in Village than in previous games.

I also feel like they used weaker characters too much and some of their strongest characters not enough in the story. There were some characters that we only see for an hour or two and then they're gone, never to be seen again. I feel like they could've found a way to use them better. Ethan Winters is a boring character. I know some people like him, but he is a far weaker protagonist than Leon, Claire, Chris, and Jill.

Finally, the final boss and last 1/5 of the game is not up to par with the rest of the game in my opinion. Some of the decisions that were made storywise at this point weaken some of the characters and story elements from earlier in the story. It takes away from that feeling of being in a gothic fantasy that they had built up throughout most of the game. Also, it becomes less survival horror game with some action to straight out action game. I don't feel like the gunplay and movement of Resident Evil games is good enough to support straight out action, which is why to me it feels slightly lackluster.

Including Village, this is how I would rank the last 4 Resident Evil Games:

1. Resident Evil 2 Remake 9.5/10
2 (tie). Resident Evil 7 Biohazard 8.5/10
3 (tie). Resident Evil Village 8.5/10
4. Resident Evil 3 Remake 7.5/10

Even though I had some issues with the under utilization of some of the stronger characters in favor of weaker characters, and the last 1/5 of the story not living up to the rest of the experience, I still enjoyed Resident Evil Village. With it's beautiful environments, open-ended world design, and some truly horrific moments, it is an excellent addition to the series, and has me looking forward to more games down the line.

I’ve been with the [i]RE[/i] universe since the very first game came out, which was around 25 years ago. The franchise has seen some highs and lows since then – my personal favourites are [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] (both the original and the remake) and [i]Resident Evil 7[/i], which managed to revitalize the franchise while at the same time returned to its roots.

Now, [i]Village[/i] is almost nothing like Ethan’s previous adventure, unfortunately. Don’t get me wrong, it’s really fun (you can see that I gave it a thumbs up), maybe so far the best AAA game this year. However, instead of the creepy, atmospheric gameplay, this time we got an action-adventure shooter. 

[spoiler]Sure, there are some parts, especially in the castle and House Beneviento, that still gave me goosebumps all over, like a real survival horror should, but everywhere else I was just going around shooting everything, while not feeling scared at all. Towards the end, in the factory, the game straight up turned into [i]Doom[/i], not to mention that insane, over-the-top bossfight with Heisenberg…[/spoiler]

With that said, the graphics are beautiful, the story is great (including many additions to the overall lore that will definitely blow the minds of all long-time [i]RE[/i] players), the fights are fluid, and there are tons of secrets all over the village that are worth discovering. You can also replay the whole thing if you’re aiming for the achievements, or spend some time with [i]The Mercenaries[/i] mode.

All in all, I can safely recommend this to all action lovers, just keep in mind that you’ll not get the same survival horror experience as in [i]RE7[/i].

Unfortunately after the indie horror approach taken for RE7 (which was excellent btw because it went for a more rural a la Texas chainsaw massacre slasher experience ditching the absurdly over the top anime shenanigans that plagued 6) the devs decided to bring back some schlock, albeit in more moderate quantities this time. This leaves RE8 with some experience disconnecting moments as on one side, it's dark, serious and downright horrible (in a good way) and on the other, it's cringey, hilariously bad and unamusing when it tries to be funny. The constant back and forth between those 2 gets tiresome as you can't be in grave danger doing your best to save your family while being chased by horrific creatures one moment, witness a bad soap opera drama banter between "lords" the next, back to "Oh this is serious and horrible!" after that while your character, out of the blue starts spewing "Fk you!" quirky one liners. 

The gameplay is basically a RE7 (improved) rehash though this time it has some questionable mechanics: even though now Ethan has "military training" he's still moving like he's stuck in water all the time and some enemies are clearly programmed for a quick dodge/roll response that probably ended up on the cutting floor. You can now push immediately after blocking but you can't do a quick attack (let alone a finisher) along with it but hey, you can now quick turn in a flash which makes the whole tanky movement even more jarring. I won't bore you with the story because frankly, at 60 euros, that's what you're playing this game for but expect it to be as the whole experience itself: bipolar, with a rushed exposition/explanation dump towards the end and self-contradictory at times if you look back. Good thing there's a whole Chris Redfield and his team segment toward the end to shake things up because by the time it comes, the whole thing was getting stale. 

Now a few words about the marketing for this game: if you're expecting Lady Dimitrescu to be some kind of Nemesis, you'll be very disappointed - she's in fact quite tame, boring and has a hilariously bad boss form ripped straight from some 90s B horror. Truth be told, she's kinda the least interesting thing that this game has to offer as there's one segment further down the line that will seriously creep you out especially if you're a parent (no kidding, it's probably the most horrific and well made encounter i've seen in a game for a long time) and while the game constantly ups itself it still can't help fall flat on his face on the final boss, which again, is such a bad B movie clicheic bullet sponge that it makes you think you're playing a completely different game. There's another personal issue i have with this game and it ain't a "cancel culture" one but in fact a "missed opportunity" one: If you decide to go full on rural Romania aesthetic (though it's more like 1900s) and lean heavily on it's linguistics (yes, the Duke's chef menu is in romanian as well as some other terms peppered along the story, like the "Cadou" Mcguffin, which means "gift"), at least do your homework and call werewolves "strigoi" (they stole the moon from the night skies in our folklore) not "lycans", because you'll rarely hear that term in eastern Europe and this ain't Underworld. Still, kudos to the team for not going Vlad the Impaler/Dracula bananas on Lady Di and her offsprings, which are just blink and you miss it mentioned as being vampires. 

So, all that said, why am I recommending it? Because i had fun with it, cringey story and voice acting aside (looking at you Heisenberg), because it's still a predominately well made game (borders on photo-realism with RT on) and because it had the Chris Redfield segment to save the day. Then again, 60 euros for a stretched out 17h game (hardest difficulty, a lot of wondering around and exploring) is about 20-25 euros too much for what this game has to offer so i'd wait for a more down to earth price. 

Lastly, Capcom, please get the hint and give us a fully fledged Chris Redfield standalone adventure - it's the 2nd time the guy elevates games with not that interesting protagonists (sure, Ethan is....fine at best but i couldn't care ♥♥♥♥ for the after credits Rose stinger) or downright detestable characters (looking at you Mia).

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Resident Evil 8 is a decent horror game, one that relies less on the fear/panic factor compared to the previous one however it slightly improves in almost everything else. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+The gothic-inspired atmosphere is fantastic. 
+The combat and the weapons are pretty fun. 
+Fixes some of the plotholes I had with the 7th game. 

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-Less scary and more action-oriented. 
-Weak PC port. 
-The villains were idiotic and the game was nothing but a horny-jail marketing bs. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
You play as Ethan Winters, yet again, a few years after the events of the 7th game. You now have a kid and are living happily in Romania with Mia when things go to ♥♥♥♥, again, and your daughter, Rose, gets kidnapped by some crazy woman. Fast forward, you end up in a fictional village in Romania along with its surroundings such as a factory, the castle of the marketed villain, lady Dimitrescu and other places you will soon discover.

The overall story, without spoiling, does not rely just on lady Dimitrescu so make sure you set your expectations accordingly. Besides the fact that she's quite the hot lady, her plans and all the other villains you encounter are absolutely dumb as hell. They will constantly complain that you keep killing them and foiling their plans while at the same time whenever you get caught by them they just toy with you or let you go. Ethan has the most ridiculous, dumb, and obvious plot armor I've seen in any game. At some point, I felt like I was basically the Doom Guy of Resident Evil. In the previous game, nothing was certain, you'd feel panic, scared, it was an unknown a lot of times, the plot armor was not as obvious but in RE8 you are a f*cking God. This is why most Resident Evil games after the 4th started getting less and less good because you were no longer in a survival horror game, but instead it was a dude-bro action game and it seems the 8th went in the same direction, mostly. 

Now that isn't really a bad thing, it depends on the players taste because there are certainly fans of RE games that like the action ones and there are those that like the horror ones. I am one of the latter and while Resident Evil 8 has some scary moments and some cheap scares, overall it's the Call of Duty of horror games. I did enjoy the fact that they explained some of Ethan's plot armor even from the 7th game because it was getting ridiculous. 

Story rating: 7.5/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
So I already mentioned RE8 is more action than scary but I'll go a bit more into detail. Apparently, based on some articles, the devs went on a different route compared to the 7th one because a lot of critics were too scared to play it and as such most of the game takes place in an abandoned village in daylight while you shoot zombies and other types of generic enemies walking or running towards you in an obvious less scary manner.

There are very few times where the survival-horror aspect has a presence and I played and finished the game on Hardcore. You press forward and shoot waves and waves of enemies, figure out where to go, and repeat. There are however times and by that, I mean two specific chapters one with lady Dimitrescu and one with another villain, where shooting has less impact and you simply have to run away. But let us be realistic here for a moment. Looking at the videos and marketing are you really going to be scared of running away from lady Dimitrescu? Mr. X and Nemesis were panic-inducing. Lady D. gives a different kind of feeling. The other villain or chapter is scary because your guns are being taken away and it has a more psychological impact than anything else which I liked but it's short. 

But moving aside from the direction they chose which I was not a fan of, the combat is still really fun and quite challenging at times. I highly recommend going with Hardcore from the start since saves are no longer limited by difficulty and it adds a bit of survival due to scarcer resources and tankier enemies. Compared to the 7th game besides finding upgrades for all the arsenal, you can improve their stats at the Duke, who is a shop owner. You can also buy guns from him, improve your health and other various things which gave the game more depth than its previous "brother". Exploring the map is also much better and I enjoyed looking for everything I could find in all the places I ended up. The boss fights overall are good some boring but you'll enjoy them. 

Overall if you have no issues with the direction RE8 went and prefer the combat focus, I can guarantee that you'll enjoy it more than the predecessor. 

Gameplay rating: 8/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
I won't go into many details regarding audio due to limited space however when it comes to voice acting, they range from bad to ok. Surprisingly lady Dimitrescu played quite well, however, everyone else, including Ethan, did not act very well. Chris and some other dude sound exactly like Keanu Reeves and just tried to be cool but did not do a good job at it, quite poorly I'd say so. 

The music is good, some boss fight songs do sound quite nice and give you that Bloodborne feel, as well as the overall music, fit well with the gothic style. Sound effects and everything from the atmosphere are all good, nothing to worry about. 

Audio rating: 7.5/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
The worst aspect of the game is the port. Just like in the demo, there is no fov and by default, it comes with a 60 fov or something close which is fine for TV, blind and ignorant people but most of us prefer some control especially in an FPS.  Luckily modders fixed it. Also apparently when Ethan equips a weapon they all come with a set of new hands. Swapping weapons does not actually swap the weapon but it brings a new pair of hands holding the said weapon. It's hilarious and bad. 

Performance-wise, it runs ok at best for the most part but it does have a lot of random frame drops with nothing going on on the screen. If you're wondering about the level design, it is superior to the previous game but still in a very linear fashion. You have a lot more to explore and the game does certainly look very detailed in a lot of places, especially the main village where almost every house can be explored. 

Graphics, performance and tech analysis score: 7/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Obviously, this may come as a shock as I am a reviewer myself but I would say avoid steam reviews. Most of them are filled with either huge spoilers and no warnings or people just upvoting because of the hot lady. I'd say 80% are pointless and the overall score on Steam does not reflect the quality of the game. The marketing team knew what they were doing with lady Dimitrescu and it worked. Go watch ACG's review and why he did not recommend it. I do recommend it because I did also recommended the 7th and this is certainly a bit better if you exclude the horror/scary factor but you should keep in mind, it's not as good as you might think it is. Maybe wait for a sale if you're not a fan. 

[h1]Final score: 7.5/10[/h1]

Resident Evil Village is a survival horror game set in first-person perspective just like Resident Evil 7. The game is of course developed and published by Capcom. The story is about Ethan who have had his daughter Rose kidnapped, Ethan and Chris finds themselves in a europe in a village which is filled with mutants creatures.

[h1] Pros : [/h1]

-The game is beautiful, the environment, the snowy theme. This game really feels like a Resident Evil game, it gives out big Resident Evil 4 vibes.
-The action in this game is amazing! In Resident Evil 7 I felt that the weapons could sometimes be useless. In this game you will probably make use of every weapon and bullet you have.
-The first half of the game with Lady D and her castle is ONE of the best moments you will ever have in any Resident Evil game.
-The exploration in this game is really rewarding, you can easily find weapon attachments, treasures, rare animals and other cool stuff around the environment which makes the exploraing in this game really satisfying.
-The lengthwise it's on par with other Resident Evil games and there is absolutely nothing wrong with the game, you will probably finish the game in 7-14 hours depending on rather you're focusing on the story or the exploration.
-Just like Resident Evil 4, the game features a merchant aswell as foundable treasures that are valuable. Unlike 7, here you have a currency which you spend to buy weapons, weapon attachments, supplies and updrages.
-The character artwork in this game is extremely well done. Every character has its own unique outfit, I also have to give credits to the voice actors for doing such an amazing job.
-Without spoilering, I think the ending to this game is one of if not the best ending in the whole series.

[h1] Cons : [/h1]

-The biggest problem that I have with this game is that Resident Evil Village ISN'T a horror game at all. There is only one small selection in the game that comes close to scary but unlike RE7, the game misses the horror feeling/vibe.
-Some of the characters felt extremly flat and was there only to make the game longer with their own selection and boss battle. Important to add that I am not talking about Lady D or Heisenberg, I think those two characters are the high point of the game.
-For the dead hard Resident Evil fans, the story isn't really involved with any of the older games expect for 7 and therefore all this craziness can feel a little meaningless.
-The amount of puzzles is very small in my and many other options, Capcom did a better job with the puzzles in 7 and many other games in the series.
-After the first half, when Alcina Dimitrescu's part is done the game begins to feel like a glow down. The same problem had Resident Evil 2, after escpaing Raccoon Police Station you begin to feel a little bit more bored because you're done with the high point of the game.


[h1] Worth buying? [/h1]

This game is mostly what you expect from a Resident Evil game, if you enjoy Resident Evil 7, 4 or almost any game in the series then you will definitely enjoy this aswell. The game misses a lot of things but it also gives us even more new stuff. It's not the best game in the series but it's not the worst one either. Like most of the games, it's simply just a good game. Expect for the ending of the game, Village doesn't stand out too much in the series. I will give this game a 8/10, I recommand but I personally think Resident Evil 7 is a tiny bit better.

Resident Evil: Village is as much a dark fairytale as it is a homage to various flavors of horror. Starting with the beautifully animated children's tale “Village of Shadows” being narrated by Mia to little Rose to lull her to sleep that foreshadows your upcoming journey, and gave me some strong Coraline vibes, to Ethan Winters’ ultimate motivation of recovering his stolen daughter, it starts more Brother’s Grimm than Night of the Living Dead. By the time you’ve found your way to the village besieged by lycans, the tone moves towards gothic horror as you’re introduced to some survivors and a bit of the unorthodox religion built around the mysterious Mother Miranda.

While Capcom’s marketing campaigns were heavily centered around the Internet’s thirst for the 9-foot-6 Alcina Dimitrescu, she’s just one of five colorful characters that stand between you and your daughter and you’re introduced to the lot of them very early in your journey. The ghostly doll-maker Donna Beneviento who interacts with the world through her doll Angie, the self-loathing fish man monstrosity Salvatore Moreau and the over-the-top charismatic egomaniacal inventor Karl Heisenberg are each given a slice of the game to chew the scenery, some far more than others, before you get your meeting with Miranda. Each of these Four Lords are given their own environment inspired by different horror tropes for you to travel through and unload ammo into the various monsters that want to see you dead. Gone are the mold people of RE7, or the Moulded, and in their place is a far more varied cast of bullet sponges. Snarling lycans, shambling Moroaică, and drill-armed cyber-zombies are just a few of the things you’ll be facing while looking for your daughter. Don’t worry though, ammo tends to be plentiful if you’re landing a decent number of headshots and it’s usually the bosses, mini-bosses and optional mini bosses that really soak up a good deal of it. The latter are especially spongey and can tear through your carefully hoarded stash with ease before finally going down. The relatively generous amount of ammo and the swarms of enemies moves this title further away from the expected gameplay limitations of survival horror and is more of an action title for better or for worse. If you were looking for a more classic RE experience, this isn't it. There are a few tense moments in the game, with House Beneviento being a fantastic standout sequence for atmosphere—very reminiscent of a polished version of all the PT clones we’ve seen over the years done exceptionally well—but the game is more glorious B-movie camp than psychological dread. There are few moments where avoiding enemies is preferable to making their heads pop and most of them are near the end of the game.

Capcom also continues its sadistic vendetta against Ethan's poor hands. If you thought they'd gone through a lot in Resident Evil 7, you haven't seen anything yet.

Village wears its RE4 influence proudly on its sleeve with its rural, Eastern European setting and the returning merchant, this time embodied by the Duke, a far more talkative ally in Winter’s quest to rescue Rose. The inventory system is also reminiscent of RE4 and they’ve separated crafting materials, key items and the new treasures that you can sell to the Duke for more Lei (the local currency) from your ammo, weapons and consumables. For people coming from RE7, this might give you a sigh of relief. Unless you’re a masochist who enjoyed inventory juggling with the item box in the last title, the larger inventory is probably a welcome change. There’s also no item box to store excess items and no real need for it. You’ll have plenty of space for everything you pick up, especially if you’re increasing your storage capacity regularly.

The Duke is also able to upgrade your weapons in exchange for Lei and there’s a new way for Ethan to boost his stats. Instead of the injectables from the last game, you can hunt various animals in order to harvest their meat which the Duke turns into delicious meals to increase your max health, your speed and absorb more damage when you’re blocking. 
The game is easily the most beautiful Resident Evil yet and its max settings are beyond the capabilities of my gaming laptop. Still, with a bit of tweaking, it was still gorgeous to look at with detailed interiors and environments where you could almost feel the biting cold. You really get the sense that these places are lived in, with small environmental details that helps bring the sets to life. Castle Dimitrescu is especially impressive with its mixture of opulent interiors and bloody dungeons. I imagine with a powerful enough rig it’s probably one of the most visually impressive games made so far but it easily holds its own without the latest technology.

My first playthrough clocked in at 9 hours and 6 minutes of playtime and I didn’t discover every secret by any means. The game also offers you a New Game+ mode where you’ll start off with your inventory, minus key items for progression, after going through the introduction. Beating the game also gives you access to the extra content menu which allows you to unlock various goodies by spending points gained through achievement hunting. This gives you access to a few more powerful weapons (that are quickly outclassed if you start sinking cash into upgrading your endgame guns—especially the New Game+ exclusive S.T.A.K.E. super Magnum that the Duke has on sale for a hefty 300,000 Lei) in the Duke’s shop and the extremely useful infinite ammo upgrade if you want to tackle “Village of Shadows” difficulty as well as concept art, models and the like. Village is worth replaying if only to soak in the beautifully haunting scenery again, this time while heavily armed to easily dispatch all those creatures standing between you and your sightseeing, but the staggering number of collectables is another great incentive.

By the time the ending credits roll to the sound of singer Aga Ujima recounting your journey in the beautiful “Yearning for Dark Shadows”, calling back to the “Village of Shadows” fairytale at the start, you’ve gone through a veritable theme park of horror. The game also ties itself into the broader Resident Evil lore for people who care about that sort of thing outside of the connection to Chris Redfield and his Hound Wolf Squad. A post-credit scene also presumably sets up the final entry into what’s rumoured to be a trilogy (starting with RE:7) or some form of future DLC in the pipeline. Speaking of DLC, something akin to a longer House Beneviento sequence would be a great addition as the insane and murderous doll-maker was given a woefully short time in the spotlight despite being in one of the most memorable parts of the game.

This is a title that’s well worth picking up if you have the means to and a must buy the second it comes on sale if you can’t right now.

Resident Evil Village: A Rollercoaster of Emotions and Zombies

🎮 Main Game Review

Hey, gamers! Buckle up, because we're diving into the twisted, terrifying, and sometimes hilarious world of Resident Evil Village. First off, let's talk about our boy Ethan Winters. The guy's as bland as a rice cake, but hey, that just makes the village's wacky residents shine even more, am I right?

👻 The Good Stuff
1. Variety is the Spice of Death: One minute you're in a haunted castle, the next you're in a factory that even Elon Musk would find creepy. The game keeps you on your toes like a cat on a hot tin roof.
2. Action-Packed: If you're the kind of person who likes to shoot first and ask questions later, you're in for a treat. This game has more action than a Michael Bay movie, minus the explosions.
3. Audio Bliss: The sound design is so good, you'll think the zombies are right behind you. Spoiler: they probably are.

🤡 The Not-So-Good
1. Where's the Horror?: For a game that's supposed to make you wet your pants, it's surprisingly light on the scares. It's like going to a haunted house and finding out it's run by clowns.
2. Boss Fights: More like "Boss Frights," because they're not that scary. Kinda feels like the developers ran out of coffee during this part.

🎮 DLC: Shadows of Rose Review

Alright, let's switch gears and talk about the DLC, Shadows of Rose. You know, the one where Rose tries to live a normal life but ends up freezing zombies and destroying goo. Sounds like my last relationship, to be honest.

🌹 The Good Stuff
1. New Mechanics: Freezing enemies? Destroying goo? Sign me up! It's like they took the base game and sprinkled some magic dust on it.
2. Intensity Level 100: This DLC has some of the most intense moments in the Resident Evil series. You'll be gripping your controller so hard, it might just snap.

🤔 The Not-So-Good
1. Short and Not-So-Sweet: With a runtime of just 2.5 hours, this DLC is shorter than my attention span. 
2. Déjà Vu: No new areas? Really? It's like going back to your hometown and realizing nothing's changed. A bit of a letdown, if you ask me.

Final Thoughts
So, should you play Resident Evil Village and its DLC? Absolutely, especially if you're a fan of the series or just love a good action-horror game. Just don't expect to be sleeping with the lights off anytime soon.

And that's a wrap! Whether you're here for the scares, the action, or just to see Ethan get his butt kicked, Resident Evil Village and its DLC have something for everyone. Just maybe keep a change of pants handy, you know, just in case. 😜
