[h1]RE VIllage: A Tribute to Resident Evil[/h1]
The newest entry to the Resident Evil Series is a great game that takes a lot of things from several past entries. This is why many people have considered this game as a love letter to the entire franchise as it takes elements from past games like the first-person perspective from RE7, traversing a mansion-like environment like in RE1/REmake, to a more action based gameplay like in RE4 through 6.  Some may think this have caused the game to be a somewhat unfocused experienced which i do agree to a certain extent, but with all that said i still enjoy this game thoroughly, even though it stumbles a lot of the times. With all the content this game offers, i definitely recommend buying it at full price. Though as of now, the PC port is not the greatest as there are some key PC features missing and if you're unsure of buying the game because of this, then i suggest getting it on sale.

[u]Pros[/u]
+ A very stellar art direction and a more interesting setting when compared to the previous game, RE7.
+ Exploration and backtracking. The exploration in RE8 is very rewarding and satisfying, and the backtracking is barely an issue as it isn't tedious at all and rewards you for it. Except for one level which i will get into later.
+ Fun combat. If you've played RE7, then you'll feel at home with this game's combat. The guns are satisfying to use and the small additions like being able to push enemies away is pretty handy.
+ Good difficulty balance. I've played the game on Hardcore mode and i feel like it's probably the best difficulty to play on as you're forced to think what to use and what to keep for later.
+ Chris Redfield. For the small screentime that he had, the boulder-puncher alpha chad was a joy to behold.
+ Mercenaries. Its back with a few extra bells and whistles and its a fun mode to go through once you're done with the game.

[u]Mixed[/u]
+/- PC Port. Like i said before the PC port isn't really all that great as there are important key features missing like an FOV slider. Though i didn't personally ran into other issues besides that as i got pretty good performance whilst playing.
+/- Cast of villains. We all know the big tall vamp lady mommy, Lady Dimitrescu who her and her daughters were heavily marketed before the game came out and they are probably the most memorable antagonist in this game. The game's other villains beside her are sadly kind of disappointing. This is because they lack screen-time and have barely any build-up to their respective boss fights. Though i suppose Heisenberg was pretty cool, i just wish there were more to these guys.

[u]Cons[/u]
- Disappointing puzzles. The puzzles are honestly fairly easy through out and there weren't too many of them which was kind of disappointing for me personally as I've always really liked the puzzle-solving aspect of Resident Evil.
- Lackluster Boss fights. Like the puzzles, the boss fight are quite easy and not that memorable except for a few.
- The factory level. This level is a slog as it's too long and you're forced to backtrack to face some of the most annoying enemies in the entire game. Its also a really boring area visually compared to the other areas in the game.
- Ethan as a protagonist. I didn't like Ethan that much in RE7 but he wasn't as annoying as he was more of a blank-slate back then. Now, the game asks you to really sympathize with him while he shouts cringy one-liners and losing body parts like its nothing while also never showing his face once to the audience. I understood what they were going for with Ethan's character but i just personally can't stand him.
- A very dumb and somewhat predictable plot twist. Like, really man?

Resident Evil Village is an imperfect fusion of the RE7 and RE4 styles of gameplay. Sadly the game attempts to combine the two and never manages to quite live up to either.

The action is not as fast or fluid as Resident Evil 4 and the game lacks the depth of weapon upgrades that RE4 had. New guns are always directly better than predecessors, and there are no exclusive upgrades for any of the weapons, just some weapon mods that offer minor improvements.

Also gone is the satisfying dismemberment and gore that was present in the remake of 2 (and RE 7 to a slightly lesser extent). You can't blow the legs off Lycan as you could molded or zombies. This may have been for ratings reasons, but it's disappointing as it makes the combat less visceral and satisfying.

On the horror side, this is an area that has taken a downgrade from RE 7. Whilst the game does have some undeniable tense sections (including a very short but fantastic sequence around mid game), it misses the overall horror of RE 7. The game has some effective jump scare sequences, but none of the constant tension that RE 7 instilled.

Setting wise, the game is basically a modern "theme park" style game. You have the central European village as a hub and then four areas that all have different themes. A Gothic castle, a creepy Victorian-esque house filled with dolls, a swamp and finally (and probably the most action heavy sequence in the game) an industrial factory.

The game is cheesy to the extreme, but this is nothing new for RE titles. Personally I felt Ethan's story fell flat as he's never been characterised well, and therefore the sense of urgency was completely missing from his storyline. Anymore said about the story would be to create spoilers, I'll just say that Chris features fairly prominently throughout.

The game has a mercenaries mode which is more like the raid mode from revelations than the one from RE 4. It lacks character selection but has an interesting random perk system, and completionists may enjoy the experience of completing all the maps with the highest ranking. Challenges completed in both merc mode and the main game unlock points to spend in a bonus store much like the one in RE3 remake where you can unlock new weapons for future playthroughs.

Overall it's probably worth at least one playthrough for fans of the series. I'd prefer a return to either RE 7 or the third person style of the newer remakes in the future, but Capcom never seems to do what you expect, so who knows that they'll do next.

Jumping straight in: 

Resident Evil Village is the direct sequel to 2017's Resident Evil 7: Biohazard and follows Ethan Winters in search of his daughter. 

The presentation is stellar. Lighting and texture work are great to gawk at even at lower settings. 
Game looks gorgeous and runs pretty smoothly on medium with my 1070. 
(I had a couple some pretty bad frame drops during some of the more elaborate weather effects, but those are few and far in between) 
Sound design is amazing from the growls of the enemies to the sound of the gunshots and subsequent impacts on their heads. The main cast and side characters are all well acted. Ethan's dialogue can be a bit cheesy at some point, but by the end he's become one of my favorite protagonists in this series. 

Gameplay is RE7 turned up to 11 and feels both tense and satisfying. There's more weapon variety than in RE7 and the all feel great to use. With great guns, comes challenging foes to use them on. Thankfully Village delivers in that. Just when you think you're getting the hang of it, the game throws a new enemy at you. I played on Hardcore, early on enemies do feel a bit bullet spongy, but it as you level up, it becomes a bit more well balanced.

The bosses are well themed, well designed (not frustrating or an absolute joke) and really help to serve the story and atmosphere. Each boss has its own area within the village and they and not a single one of them that felt out of place. 
It really makes you want to explore the whole village and seek out some of the many treasures that feel grounded within the places that they are found. 

You honestly have go hunting for these treasures because the late game weapons and upgrades are incredibly expensive and if you aren't careful you can end up spending all your money on early game gear only to get better versions of the weapon you already upgraded a couple of hours later. 

My only gripe was the lack of a "point of no return" notification. I wont spoil it here because it is available online at your own risk but if you miss anything there is a new game plus mode and plenty of unlockables, including a 4th difficulty mode to justify a second or third run. 

Throw in the time attacked based Mercenary mode and you've got yourself a game that's going to keep you entertained for a good amount of time. 

On a final note, a lot of people have made comparisons saying this is basically RE7 + RE4 and that's very evident in its setting and mechanics. But there's some serious Silent Hill Influences with some of the more psychological aspects and atmosphere of the story. Not to mention the basic plot being about a father going to some weird town to rescue his daughter from some cult [spoiler] before a rebirth ceremony [/spoiler] 

I'm excited for the future. This feels like a return to classic survival horror, before the days of boulder punching and elaborate matrix style fight scenes. This game feels just as fresh as RE7 did on release. If you didn't enjoy RE7 because you felt a lack of combat and slower pace, pick this one up. It may surprise you.

Village is finally here, the next big installment in Capcom's flagship horror franchise. Let me share my thoughts.

[h1] PROS [/h1]

The graphics, voice acting, and the sound design are all top notch here. This really helps this game nail it's atmosphere and it feels like a truly next gen game. Every actor who mo-capped did a fantastic job, I loved the voices and movement of these characters (even if it was a big exaggerated).

The story was pretty great (not a RE mega fan only played 2R and 7 so can comment on how it compares to any other RE games besides that), there were obviously some 'jaw-dropping' ridiculous moments, but stuff like that tends to happen in these games so... The antagonists here are some of my favorites in a long time (not even joking here), I loved Heisenberg especially. My point is, without giving anything away, I enjoyed the story.

My spoiler thoughts: [spoiler] Ethan being dead was a neat and crazy twist, I saw nothing wrong with it. I also feel he went out appropriately, and his conclusion was satisfying. [/spoiler]

Gameplay is what it is, if you've played RE7 you know what to expect. It's a first-person survival game, with horror as a minor aspect this time around. You'll be doing most of the hunting and killing here, versus avoiding certain enemies or conserving ammo in RE7. Ammo and materials are indeed still limited, but they are in greater quantities here. Be prepared to kill and shoot things. A LOT. the entire last fourth of this game turns into Call of Duty and it sucks, but the game really nails everything up until that point so I can forgive it myself.

The game itself is the same RE length as per usual, you'll probably finish a first playthrough of this game in 10-12 hours. After finishing the story, as with the other REs, you can earn a metric crap ton of new content by beating challenges in the storymode, or earn brand new weapons by completing the game on new difficulties. Point is, you'll have a lot to do here even after finishing the game.

The game is relatively easy, I managed to get through on normal murdering absolutely everything in my path, and I scraped by two endgame sections with barely any ammo and some mines. If you're experienced with survival horror games, I'd say start with Hardcore, if you're new to RE start with standard and you'll be fine. I haven't tried the coveted Village of Shadows difficulty yet, but I hear every enemy gets quicker, beefier, and upgraded enemies appear more frequently (so basically harder hardcore).

[h1] CONS [/h1]

The last fourth of this game man. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. I was fine with [spoiler] the factory level [/spoiler] for the most part, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ do things go off the rails after that where [spoiler] you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mech fight, then it turns into a Call of Duty level with Chris. [/spoiler]

The second area [spoiler] the doll house [/spoiler] was particularly scary, but sadly seems to have gotten the short end of the stick when it comes to length, so if they expanded on that more I would've loved that section of the game.

[h1] FINAL THOUGHTS [/h1]

Overall though, I honestly have barely anything bad to say about this game. It's fun, I liked the story and characters, there's lots to do, and I would definitely come back to this game in a month of two. I would say it's worth that full 60$ and you should pick it up.

I'm a pansy when it comes to the horror genre, but I have always loved Resident Evil games. Resident Evil Village is easily one of my new favorite games in the series, as well as in general. The story is well-paced, and the enemy varieties are introduced with precision. Sometimes the game can feel a bit clunky when it comes to the guns, and I don't like that the enemies can grapple through melee attacks that should otherwise kill them (Karambit swipe to the head). However, I still find combat satisfying and fun. Gunshots have a punch and the reload animations feel nice to pull off. Boss fights are the same style they've been in typical Resident Evil fashion, but that doesn't mean they are bad. In fact, I quite enjoy taking on each boss (Yeah, baby! Ha, get it?) in their respective zones. 

Most of the writing for the game is pretty good, but I have my gripes here and there. The voice actors are all great, I think, but the lines they were given sometimes don't feel right when they are delivered. For instance, the beginning has a line after you are introduced to the lycans that just seems out of place. Another example of this is during an intense sequence involving a boss and Ethan just spurts out a one-liner out of nowhere. I guess you could attribute that sort of thing to the writers trying to make Ethan relate more to the player, but to me it seems like the dad jokes are just taking over his life now that he's a father.

Mercenaries in this game is okay, but I wish they had done more in it in terms of playable characters. The fun aspect of it is still there, and I enjoy the power trip you can have while racking up a good combo. All in all, a fun little extra mode as it is, but would not be against seeing more added to it in the future. 

I'm rambling and have no real direction for this review, and I keep getting distracted. I guess watching Shrek the Third can do that to you? So, all in all, this game is great and I wholly recommend it to anyone that is a fan of Resident Evil. Worth the money, even with the dad jokes and sometimes clunky guns.

For every RE4 we get an RE6 and for every RE2R an RE3R... which is to say Capcom have not been generally been very good at following up the good games. Now lets see what we have in this RE8, it feel like we have a bit of everything from each RE series 

But first, the overall game design :-

- An inventory system like the good old RE4, and also with a lovely merchant that speak more then just "Welcommmeeee"
- Good variety of weapon to slowly progress when the story goes on. Too bad it didn't have the old "hidden" weapon bonus after fully upgraded each of the weapon.
- The map design is comparable to RE2 remake, few area will be revisit but provide different enemy and content to explore. A well design idea of creating the feeling of spending your entire day on the village.
- Combat, you have the mixture of good old RE original all the way to the FPS action shooting that looks like doom. There is ambush, jump scare, horde of enemies swarming at you, LARGE enemy that is very tension to fight with. Everything from horror to action you can ask for, RE8 delivered.
- So, all the gun and run feel like action game ? nah, there is one section of the game throw you back to the classic horror, where the enemy is darkness and the environment.....and......a .......[spoiler] baby [/spoiler]
- Replay-ability is also good, although I wish they could shuffle more monster on a higher difficulties. But stil, there are plenty of challenges to make a new run completely different and make the game fresh.
- Boss design is VERY GOOD. You have the al-classic nemesis enemy, the large fish/croc/whatever, humanoid and also ghost. Too bad there is no hunter (or there is ? the wolf...? hmmm)
-Story is.....ok....but Ethan need a closure/conclusion to his story, so ....yeah.
- Mercenaries mode is a bit disappointed, as it is linear and does not have a sense of progression.

Here is the rundown of how each stage feel like compare to others RE series :-

1. First village visit : This feel like the old RE4 beginning, but with more violence on our poor Ethan.
2. Castle : This area feel like the RE2, trapped in a mansion/PD, constantly running from Nemesis type enemy and finding keys to slowly open more areas. 
3. Village second visit :  Same village, but more stuff to grab, start to get use to the village layout. (Wish there was more enemy so the place will feel fresh).
4. Mansion : This is the good old "no weapon, jump scare" episode, almost no gun fight, just good old run or die. 
5. Village third visit : At this point, the village is basically just a staging area for next stage.
6. Flooded fisherman village : This area is more about navigating environmental puzzle, but a refreshing change of pace. I wish there was a fight with the boat like the RE4.
7. Village #4 : The same old.
8. Stronghold : This area feel more like an action game then horror. Feel like the Castle section with Krauser in RE4.
9. Factory : THIS IS THE GEM of the game. On my first run I was thinking the game feel like ending soon, but nope. Factory is a multiple level stage, each with distinct theme and introduction of new enemies making this area a breath of fresh air compare to the 4th visit of the village. It is comparable to the "Lab" section of the RE game, with switch between action and horror/dark area.
10. [spoiler] Chris section [/spoiler] : This feel like RE6 now. Shoot everything that move, bomb large enemy and move on. After all, it does fit well with the character here :). Also [spoiler] when Heisenberg say "boulder punchy guy" I cannot stop laughing anymore, well played Capcom, well played [/spoiler]
11. Final boss : Kinda boring, I was hoping for multiple stage fight, but oh well, at least it is the only [spoiler] non large monster type of boss. (Doron was't even a boss to compare with) [/spoiler]

Overall, I would say this is among the top 3 of RE franchise. If the story is more engaging and if the extra content was better design, I would say this can be the best title of the series. Hope that the DLC will remedy some of the shallow content problems.

This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥ slaps. Just like how RE7 was a return to roots with the horror aspects, which it does pretty well, RE8 brings back a lot of stuff, like the shop, weapon upgrades, actually good varied environments, and thanks to the village theme it can bring back the truly wacky puzzles, which is great. This game is excellent, and I think if you like resident evil at all, you'll like Village.

The Highlights:

-One big issue with 7 was the lack of enemy variety. In that one, there was like, 3 enemy types, not counting bosses. In this one, there are a ton of enemy types, and a bunch of ways you have to counter them. Some use ranged weapons, some are really fast, there's a type that wears armor and you have to get the armor off, there's the flying guys, and also the werewolves.

-weapon tiers and weapon upgrades are back. The pistol and shotgun each have 3 variants, each with different niches. For example, the first shotgun you get is balanced, the second has a wide spread for dealing with multiple enemies, and the third has a super focused spread for bosses. One minor issue is that all the shotguns have frankly ridiculously slow firing speeds. Like, i'm talking almost 3 seconds between shots with the 1897. And that's WITH the mod that increases firing speed.

-One of the bosses mentions the boulder punching scene from RE5 which is just the best

-I know that comparing something to dark souls isn't even beating a dead horse, it's hitting the horse's headstone, but Village feels a little bit like Dark Souls. Scratch that, it's more like Sekiro. As in, the setting feels like dark souls, but the gameplay is more like Sekiro. Specifically, blocking is extremely important, as well as timing those blocks. Also, after successfully blocking, you can knock enemies back for a clear and easy shot(like breaking an enemie's posture). Also, when like 3 or more enemies get right in your grill you're basically done for, just like sekiro.(no I'm not bad at sekiro its just an oversimplification for review purposes)

-The Duke.

Some minor issues, though:

-This review is being written immediately after finishing Village for the first time. I played on the standard difficulty. Resource management was almost never an issue. For the vast majority of the game, I had over 100 pistol ammo at all times. Not until the very end, for some reason. Like, the final section, the factory part, has very very few resources for crafting medkits, I don't know why. Maybe resources become a thing on the higher difficulties, I dunno.

-Maybe I'm just not scared very easily, but during this whole ~10 hour game, I only got genuinely scared twice. Maybe it's just me... 

-Soundtrack feels weak to me. I dunno. It was especially noticeable during the final boss fight. Some people say the saferoom music is bad too but I disagree wholeheartedly.

-The game isn't perfectly optimized. I have a pretty decent rig here, and at some points my poor computer was chugging along at a buttery smooth 4fps.

-The story has some minor pacing issues, I know it's sort of intentional, but a lot of stuff seems rushed, while other things seem really slow. Sections 1 & 4 take ages, while sections 2 & 3 are each like 45 minutes, even if you're not in a hurry. Also some things feel like they're poorly explained or not explained at all. 

Nitpickery:

-Honestly I kinda feel bad for poor Ethan. The absolute suffering the man goes through in this one. Like he just gets horribly maimed so often in the cutscenes. And he just pours some Feel Good Juice over the horrible, gaping wound, and continues on. 

-On the subject of Ethan, they never ever show his face, and I have no idea why. It made a little more sense in 7, cause it was almost exclusively in first person. But this one has third person cutscenes, and the lengths they go to to keep Ethan's face out of the frame are such that it gets in the way of immersion. 

-The post credits scene sets up minor sequel bait, which is a given for post credits scenes, but they way its made heavily implies that the hypothetical RE9 will take place some time during the 2030-2040s. Are they gonna make the next game take place in the future or something? Seems weird.

Resident Evil Village (still think they should have officially included the 8 in there) is like a combination between Resident Evil 4 and 7, with a little bit of Bloodborne sprinkled in as well. If this sounds promising to you, play the game ASAP! It's an extremely polished and entertaining experience from beginning to end.

Generally speaking, it may not be as spooky as 7, but it offers much more content and replay value, with potentially the best boss line-up of the entire series. Big vampire lady and her hot daughters are not exactly the scariest bunch, but there are other things that will successfully deliver some spooks your way. I've seen many people mention that the campaign is only 8 hours long, and I'm 90% sure that people just keep looking at the in-game clock that makes it seem shorter than it is. If you explore a lot, you can easily spend 12-15 hours on your first run, especially if you play on harder difficulties. 

Basically, if you loved the style of the previous game or RE2 remake, and you dislike the action-horror seen in RE4 and the like, this may not be your cup of tea. Personal preferences also heavily affect which parts of the game will shine for you the most, because this game goes through a lot of phases you could say. Personally, I think it's among the best entries in the series, and I'm glad that Capcom is still bold enough to try different directions with Resident evil. In many ways, this game is like a celebration of Resident evil and it's 25 year history, and that's a party that I'll gladly take a part in.

If you're reading reviews for the new Resident Evil game then you probably weren't a huge fan of Resident Evil 7 for the following reasons: bland protagonist, lack of enemy variety, and that AWFUL ship level. Right? Let's address those right now.

1) Ethan will be easier to like if you're a mom or a dad because he's looking for his daughter and he is PISSED! He also has military training now, so he's a little more competent. However, he is still a little bland until you learn more about him later in Village. Look at it this way, if you hate the guy, you can at least laugh at how badly he gets maimed and beaten during the many cutscenes.

2) RE7 has 6 enemy types (2 of which you likely forgot about) without DLC and 5 unique boss fights. RE Village has 9 enemy types (all of which are memorable), 4 unique mini boss types, and 5 (arguably 6) unique boss fights. That is a definite improvement and helps make the game feel a lot more like a world.

3) I personally did not dislike any level in the game on quite the same level as that stupid ship from RE7. However, I have seen several people voice criticism regarding a particular level later in the game. I actually REALLY enjoyed that level, but it's all preference I suppose. It kept my interest far more easily than the ship.

There is a major point I would like to address: the difference in gameplay between RE7 and Village. It's no secret that Village has more action; that's by design, and Capcom was very transparent about it after the game was officially revealed. There is a minority group of dedicated Resi fans who prefer the horror of the classic games over the more "arcade" feeling of RE4, 5, 6, etc... RE7 helped "reboot" the horror for many, but Village takes it right back to that focus on tighter gunplay and facing numerous baddies at once.

I am also a longtime fan who started playing Resi games back in 2002-3 as a child, and while horror is a key element of the atmosphere in these games, in my personal opinion the actual tension mostly stems from a lack of ammo/resources -- that is, being forced to choose between using precious ammo on enemies or trying your luck at evading them, for fear of being literally unable to finish the next boss fight due to a lack of the required ammo to kill it and progress. It's a thrilling and very understated part of those older games, and it has certainly diminished with newer games.

If you are like me, and those other minority group Resi fans, then I have this to say to you: PLAY VILLAGE ON HARDCORE MODE!! I made the mistake of starting on Standard, and I was a walking arsenal by the end. I have seen more energy and positivity coming from players who chose Hardcore for their first playthrough. There is still one more difficulty setting after Hardcore, you unlock it by beating the game once. I feel that Hardcore will keep things challenging enough for the average Resi veteran, but it shouldn't ruin your experience. I've heard it can sometimes be more difficult than Madhouse in RE7, but I never played Madhouse so I wouldn't know.

In conclusion, I am satisfied with Village and I will continue to enjoy it as I make my way through New Game +. I do prefer Village over RE7, but that's because I am willing to forsake some spooks for more fun as long as the tone of the game hasn't changed too drastically (plus there ARE a few legitimately scary parts in the game, one in particular that has gone viral by now). I think that while there may be a couple things that will disappoint some players, most will agree that Village is a very nice addition to the Resident Evil franchise.

Resident Evil 8 is full of references to the entirety of the RE franchise, but it also does a really great job in tying all the games' stories together. While it can be a bit complicated or confusing at certain moments, the story as a whole isn't too bad, and really does go the distance to tie in all the previous Resident Evil games. (TL;DR at the bottom)

In terms of gameplay, the game obviously plays a lot like RE7 due to the first person perspective. Though, compared to RE7, this game is far more action than it is horror, especially towards the end of the game. To be fair, the RE franchise has pretty continually leaned towards action more than horror since RE5, so I don't really find it to be a bad thing. It even makes for some really fun and interesting fights and encounters. The game also tends to feel a lot like my favorite Resident Evil game, RE4. From the spooky village and castle, the currency system, valuables, vendor/merchant, upgrading your weapons through them, the briefcase-looking inventory system, even down to the sounds that play when you pick up and inspect a new item. There are countless other similarities to RE4, and the detail is very apparent throughout the game. As I mentioned before, there are plenty of references to most if not all of the previous RE games as well (even some pretty funny ones). It's all very nostalgic while also feeling extremely new and fresh. I'm not that big into graphics but if that is something that you value, this game is beautiful - even when not running on the highest settings.

By the time you get to the end of the game, things will really start to make sense, especially in the overarching RE universe and origins. If you haven't played a Resident Evil game before, some things may not make as much sense but there is a RE7 recap video you can watch before starting your playthrough that I definitely recommend. Though, I honestly do recommend at least playing RE7 before this (not only for the context, RE7 is really good!). Even better, if you can get all of the RE games for cheap during a Steam sale, and play through all, this game will serve as a bow to tie all the games together.

First of all I want start off by saying i'm stoked they chose to continue the story of Ethan Winters. Resident Evil 7 left a huge impact on me and made me a bigger fan of the series than I ever could have been.

Fortunately for many 8 has taken a huge step away from the relentless horror found in 7 and has gone back to a more classic Resident Evil style flow. Fight some enemies here, solve a few puzzles along the way and occasionally come across a minor scare or two. As much as I would have loved another heart pounding scare fest, I still found myself falling in love with this new entry. It was an absolute blast that I couldn't pull myself away from.

I just beat the game a few minutes ago so I will just right down my immediate spoiler free thoughts :)

The main Village itself is rather basic honestly and I found the surrounding areas you visit to be where to most memorable moments occur. There are some really cool locations you visit especially in the later sections, some even being my favorite locations period in a Resident Evil title. This is one of those games where things just get more and more interesting the further you progress. Which is a shame really because the game shines so bright in the final 4-5 hours. It's one of those things where you kinda wished the game had just started off in those locations. Not a huge deal at all, the Village is small and serves as a good way to learn the game more or less. But look for the real fun outside of it.

One minor gripe (depending on who you are) is the abundance of ammo you can find and craft. I guess this is more of them shifting away from the horror elements but I do miss having to really consider reserving ammo. It's everywhere in this game and when you can't find any you'll surely be able to craft or purchase enough until you do. It is a combat heavy game so this does make sense, and the weapons are badass as usual with plenty of upgrades you can make along the way. My style however is more of a restricted ammo supply. 

The game play is top notch, I never felt bored while playing. A lot of the enemies do require you to be tactical in where you shoot them. Shooting a leg can cause them to slow down, giving you a good opportunity to shoot the small piece of armor off their head to go for the kill. I believe once I even shot the weapon straight out of the hand of an enemy, that was really cool and gives you a lot of room to approach situations with some real strategy (which could have been heightened with less ammo oh well). There is a MUCH better enemy variety in 8 than there was in 7 which is a very good thing. They all behave differently and some offer up a wonderful challenge that I thoroughly enjoyed. I always looked forward to the next encounter.

So of course let's talk about the infamous Tall Lady Dimistrescu. She and her daughters make for some fairly interesting antagonists. No where near as impactful as the Bakers (from 7) themselves but they all serve their purpose in the world and definitely make the experience more enjoyable. Just don't expect nothing too amazing from either one other than a few key segments from each. They get the job done but in my opinion they aren't the real stars of the show, i'll save that for you to figure out when you play.

Don't want to touch on this much for obvious reasons but the boss fights are super fun and super memorable. I loved each and every one that was presented and they really showcase just how exciting a title like this can really get. They found a great balance between subtle exploration and combat to something a bit more over the top.

The overall story itself was extremely interesting. I found myself really wanting to know what was going to happen next and many times craving the story more than I ever have in previous titles. There is a lot going on here and everything ties together very well especially with the previous game (RE:7). Although it isn't paramount to play 7 (there is a recap at the beginning) I would say you are missing out a good deal by not having played it (which you very much should seriously, top tier game). The game leaves you with a lot to think about by the time the credits roll.

Honestly buy this game. Whether you are new or a returning veteran to the series you will not be disappointed what so ever. I really love how this franchise has made a massive comeback in recent years and i'm officially more excited for the future of Resident Evil than I ever have been.

[h1]The Game is Made up of Parts of All Past RE, With a Little New to Bring it All Together[/h1]

This isn't the normal RE1, RE2 (remake and original), or RE7 type of gameplay where you always manage your inventory and go back and forth in an intricate mansion. It isn't the type of gameplay of 3, 4 or 5 either where you run around in a fully linear way destroying people in front of you. It's somewhere in between. 

*The first 1/4 of the game is in the mansion (RE 1, 2, 7) and it does trick you really well into thinking you're the one deciding where to go and what to do first but in reality [b]it is very linear and there is no real puzzle solving/backtracking[/b]. Although I enjoyed it, I wished it was a little bigger with more elements of player choice and backtracking/puzzle solving.

*The second 2/4 is a linear horror mansion where your stripped of your weapons (P.T, Outlast). It's very scary but only the first time. The horror isn't all cheesy jump scares, and even though you can't use your weapons you can still outsmart your enemy. You aren't just supposed to go forward and close your eyes.

*The third 3/4 is a [b]chaotic action movie[/b] (RE 3, 4, 5) where you run around solving puzzles on the fly just to go into the other section where you're chased around by a big fish (RE4) and trying to kill it.

*The fourth 4/4 is a factory that is atmospheric, horror, and action. It also has puzzles and a little backtracking. It's honestly the best part of the game, I think it's the part where everything blends together.

*The semi-open world is really well done with hunting, enemies, treasure, and puzzles.


*The boss fights are fun but [b]enemy variety is lacking in an action/survival horror game[/b]. 

*The story is good.

Resident Evil Village is the rare game that's so good and engaging that I instantly had to start a second playthrough the moment I finished the main story. It takes some of the best parts of RE4 and RE7 and combines them into an almost perfect game. There are some bumps in the road, for sure, but overall is a spectacular experience worth visiting several times.

A direct sequel to RE7, this game follows Ethan Winters as he tries to establish himself into a peaceful life with his family but sees himself dragged yet again into another life-changing misadventure full of monsters, terror and pain. No spoilers here because Village contains what's probably the richest, most surprising and emotional story in the entire franchise. The game doesn't really require you to have played the previous games to understand it, but your experience will undoubtedly be better if you did, since there are a lot of callbacks to the series' overarching plot. Helpfully, the game has an optional recap of the previous game at the start.

Gameplay is, again, a combination of RE4 and RE7's strong points. The first person perspective of RE7 is retained, but the inventory system and the weapon upgrading / customizing from RE4 make a comeback, and it has all been helpfully improved and streamlined. Furthermore, a crafting system has been added. While you can expand your inventory to hold more weapons and items, certain kinds of items have their own menu and don't take valuable space. Crafting isn't anything out of the ordinary, but it works. Since materials are shared between different items you always run into a situation where you have to consider if making more offensive or curative items is the best idea. There's also an upgrade system for yourself, allowing you to become faster and more resilient. Pro-tip: DO NOT SELL THE MEAT OF THE ANIMALS YOU KILL. You'll thank me later.

This is a more action-focused game than RE7, but it certainly retains that game's sense of horror. The story never reaches the campy style of RE4, so you might be disappointed if you wanted more of that, but I assure you what this game delivers is excellent in its own right. Besides the action, there's a bigger focus on exploration. Like the more classic games in the series, there's a lot of returning to previous parts of the map to unlock new areas, find new items or fight new enemies. There's rarely a sense of padding, fortunately.

The challenge/points system from the latests games makes a comeback as well. As you complete certain challenges inside the game you acquire points. Once you finish the main story once the points store is open and you can exchange those points for new guns, infinite ammo, concept art or character models. You can also unlock the Mercenaries mode here (which also allows you to get points). Finishing the story will also allow you to play in New Game+ mode, which is always a nice treat

As for the negatives, there are a few. They don't ruin the experience, but they can be annoying. For one, the aiming system is a bit off. You need to point somewhere and wait a moment for the sight to set and have a chance to have a perfect shot. This is standard for many FPS games, of course, but the problem is that the majority of the enemies have the tendency to dodge your aim (much more than they did in previous games), so the moment you set your aims on them they will strafe and ruin your chance at a good headshot. As a consequence, the system cannot be perfected. How good your headshots are will depend a lot on luck. The tradeoff here is that you have better chances while aiming at the body, but we all know headshots are the strongest attacks in these games. Granted, it's all part of the experience, and you get used to it the more you play, but it will certainly be a point of contention.

Another negative is that the game has a few "forced walking" areas. These are getting too common in many games these days despite the fact that no one likes them. There's really no point to these, since any bit of ambience they could generate is instantly negated by just how sick we all are of them, and I wish they had an option to skip them, like cutscenes do.

Performance in the game is surprisingly good. Despite the game having more detailed models and animations and greater numbers of enemies on the screen at the same time than any previous game in the series it runs quite well. It certainly runs better than RE7 did. That being said, and this is another negative, sometimes the game will suffer from sudden massive slowdows. with the fps dropping into the single numbers. I don't know what causes this, because it seems to happen entirely at random. There's a certain area of the game where it happened to me the most, but it's otherwise not possible to predict when and for how long it'll happen. Sometimes it'll happen when fighting enemies, sometimes when alone. Sometimes it'll go away in a few seconds and sometimes it'll need you to quit to the main menu and reload a save for it to fix itself (thankfully, the area it happened to me the most is right next to a save point). Sometimes it'll happen a couple of minutes into your session, and sometimes you can play for hours and never encounter this problem. I suspect it's a memory leak, but I'm not really savvy enough to be sure.

Those gripes aside, this is still a fantastic game, and one of the best one in the entire franchise. Top 5 for sure. The basic story mode will take you between 8-11 hours, depending on how much you explore, but the subsequent playthroughs in NG+ and/or higher difficulty levels and the Mercenaries mode add a lot of replayability. I wholeheartedly recommend it, and I can't wait for a follow-up DLC (edit: it has been announced!).

I'm not that big a fan of Resident Evil. I wasn't all that impressed with RE 7 or the 2 recent Remakes. I really enjoyed RE 4 but more as an exciting action game than a survival horror. But this was the first game to finally click with me as an enjoyable, well structured and well balanced survival horror experience.

I thought the environments were varied and very well designed, I loved the structure of the village being this central area you frequently visit and explore in between venturing to each of the lord's territories. I loved how each of the lord's sections were very different in style from the more RE1 style backtracking puzzle zone of Lady Dimitrescu's castle to the more psychological horror environment in the Beneviento house. Wasn't that big a fan of Heisenberg's section but I still thought it was passable. Most of the enemies and bosses were fun to fight and very well balanced and accompanied some solid atmosphere, sound design and music. Just like RE4 the game makes great use of downtime in between hordes of enemies making the pacing for the most part damn near perfect.

I like how the gameplay basically combines the more action-heavy weapon upgrade and resource management elements from RE4 with the denseness and tighter scope and atmosphere of RE7. The Duke was honestly a joy to interact with and mirrored the spark provided by the Merchant in RE4 very well. It's these systems and environments that actually gave me incentive to explore and not rush through the game which is more than I can say for the other RE titles I've played. The length of the game really varies depending on how much you want to explore the environments to collect treasures and ramp up your arsenal providing a range of 7-12 hours for the main story.

What I will say on the more negative side is the story, while kind of interesting for most of the game, really started to lose me towards the last couple of hours where they try to connect the overarching plot to previous established canon, which is done quite poorly. And the ending was just plain confusing and a bit anticlimactic at least in my opinion.

Overall I enjoyed Resident Evil Village a lot more than I thought I would. It's pretty much the only RE game besides 4 I can confidently say I like.

I honestly loved this game more than Resident Evil 7, which was already one of my top Resident Evil games. However, this game does take a lot of risks and diverges from the regular Resident Evil formula. Many of the parts (specifically the Village and the Castle) closely resembled the games of the past, while a few others stray somewhat far from what we've been used to (which I won't go into detail as these locations weren't revealed to a great extent in the trailers). However, there are very action heavy parts where you're just gunning down enemies and running into new rooms as well as parts where the suspense is almost too much. The use of several different locations also makes the enemy cast very diverse, not just game-play wise, but actually lore wise. I find this to be much less tedious than Resident Evil 7, as in that game every single enemy was apart of the mold and pretty much had no variety. In Village, lycans move side to side, dashing around quickly to avoid your bullets and the most powerful lycans wear armor or carry hammers. Zombies are much less mobility dependent, relying more on tight quarters to deal damage. Some enemies (which are found further in the game) charge at you with near invincibility and require hitting weak spots to take down quickly. Overall, enemy variety made this game always a joy to play.

The Village itself is also a great addition to the game, with its expansive open world. Every house has something worthwhile, whether it be ammunition or treasure to sell to the Duke. It also greatly rewards people who love backtracking. I'm pretty sure only a few of the houses are actually required to progress the story. Some doors are locked and require specific keys to open (which usually aren't in your possession when you first find them), encouraging you to go back once you do have the key. Other houses are locked from the inside and require you to be creative and explore your surroundings to find a way in. While it may seem like good idea to just explore every single inch of the Village and stock up on resources, the game throws enough lycans and other beasts to make you decide whether or not its worth it. Overall, the Village acts as a central hub where you constantly come back to, but it also rewards the players willing to explore.

While I really did enjoy this game, there are just a few gripes. One minor one is the lack of optimization in specific parts of the game. I'm not playing this game on the best rig, but I can average around 100 FPS 99% of the time. However, during encounters with the daughters in the castle, my frames drop to unacceptable levels. Even with I applied a mod to get rid of the bugs (which I thought was the problem), the frames continued to drop. However, this only happens with the daughters and Moreau. Second, despite the amount of hype that Dimitrescu garnered, she doesn't really feel like a main antagonist and feels sidelined by the other important villains. This might be partially due to how quiet she is when she's walking around the Castle. She doesn't stomp like Mr. X does, despite being much taller. I guess this is supposed to show how lady-like she is, but I feel like it detracts from the tension and fear. Lastly, the Deluxe Edition was kind of a let down. I got the Resident Evil Village and 7 Bundle, so I got the Deluxe Edition. While it does have a lot of things to satisfy the fans that love lore, it really doesn't give much else to make it a good option over the regular edition. I thought the gun you got for the deluxe edition would be a beast (since it's literally the same gun as the one you used against Eveline in the final battle in Resident Evil 7). However, it's really only better than the starting gun for a few hours at most, as only a few upgrades will make the LEMI much better than the DLC gun. While I did enjoy reading all of the lore and looking at the concept art, I just don't feel like buying the Deluxe Edition on its own is a good idea. It would be much better to get the RE7/8 Bundle, which basically makes RE7 and all its DLC only $10. I also really wish they would add some playable DLC in a season pass, but there have been no mentions of DLC in the future. While Mercenaries was a blast (and I'm still trying to get high scores), the upcoming RE:Verse feels out of place. I feel like a co-op game mode would go so well in the RE Universe and Deathmatch just isn't the way to go.

Hands down the best Resident Evil I've played. The story was brilliantly written and made me drop my jaw a few times, the combat and movement was incredibly smooth, and the game is amazingly optimized. Besides a few frame drops when a bunch of flies swarm me in the Castle section, I don't remember any stutters or frame drops bothering me.

I'll list the pros and cons below.

Pros:

- As said above, amazing story with some pretty damn good twists.
- The characters are all lovable, even the "villains".
- This is possibly the least linear Resident Evil I've ever played. It has you going back to explore the Village multiple times, and there are tons of optional bosses, treasures, and explorable areas.
- The cheesy lines were absolutely spot on for a Resident Evil game and if anything made it feel a lot like Resident Evil 4, I loved it.
- Amazing optimization, small download size. There are a few frames drops when being swarmed by flies, but the fact that I maintained 60 FPS+ throughout the majority of the game with a GTX 1060 in 2021 is worthy of some praise.
- The environment is beautiful, atmospheric, and immersive.
- Good mix of horror and action. The horror moments scared the ♥♥♥♥ out of me, and the action parts only made me want to keep playing over and over again.
- Amazing replay value for a Resident Evil game that doesn't even have an DLC yet. I'm 62 hours in as of writing this review and still have more things I want to accomplish even though I've 100% the achievements.
- The soundtrack is some of the best I've heard in the series.

Cons:

- Picking up and interacting with objects can be kind of weird sometimes, especially if you're speedrunning.
- There is only ONE saferoom in the game with save room music. I was hoping to hear more of it, but the music was nice.
- Mercenaries was kind of disappointing. It's cool how you can gain certain abilities as you move through stages, but it doesn't have the same competitive feeling that RE4's Merc mode has. Along with that, there aren't any online leaderboards for it, so there isn't really any point competing.


SPOILERS BELOW




- I wish Lady Dimitrescu, Heisenberg, Luiza, and Elena had more screen time. I was pretty disappointed when the villagers were all killed off within the first hour of my blind playthrough. As for Dimitrescu, I was hoping she would sort of appear throughout the game, hunting you down like the Nemesis. Instead she was the first boss and only had one mutation. As for Heisenberg, you basically only have one confrontation with him as well. It would be nice if they had more boss fights for the two of them but oh well.



SPOILERS OVER

In all, I really enjoyed the game and it is definitely my favorite Resident Evil already. I'm excited for future DLC to come out to add to the replayability of this game. Also. if you're reading this and heard other people call this game "bad because it's too short", don't listen to them. They clearly have never played a Resident Evil game in their life. Every Resident Evil game is a short experience with amazing replay value. Plus, it's better to have a short memorable experience with little to no filler, rather than a long and dragged out playthrough where you get burnt out in the middle of the story.

Resident Evil Village is the sequel to Resident Evil 7 and my favorite game in the Resident Evil franchise to date. While I may be biased towards the newer games, having only played RE2R, RE3R and RE7, this game simply took the best of those games and combined it into one. 

I really liked the map design, which seems to be based on Romanian themes, and how the environment felt. The village seemed cramped and forlorn, the castle eerie and towering, while the factory was imposing and confusing. The fact that each villain had their own "area" in the map meant that I could do things at my own pace and explore the map to my desire, which I did. My first playthrough, on Standard, clocked in at around 7 hours in-game time, and I enjoyed every minute of it. I explored most of the areas that I could have, though I definitely missed the occasional treasure or enemy. What struck me in particular was that I didn't dislike any part of the game. While there were definitely parts I preferred, there was nothing that I didn't enjoy while playing the game. In RE7, I didn't really like the Marguerite fight, but this game has none of that. Every moment is packed with suspense, action, fear or awe. I found myself spending a lot of time staring at the scenery and looking for things to screenshot, as opposed to continuing forward in the story. 

The game also has surprisingly good replayability for a story-driven singleplayer game. After completing the game for the first time, you unlock the Extra Content Shop, where you can spend points earned from completing challenges. I really like that Capcom took over this system from RE3R as opposed to the Unlockables in RE7. Infinite Ammo is purchased per weapon and not unlocked across all weapons like it was in RE7. Additionally, to be able to buy Infinite Ammo in the first place requires you to have fully upgraded the weapon in the story mode. I was able to upgrade the starter pistol and shotgun in my first playthrough, which meant I needed to replay the story if I wanted to purchase Infinite Ammo for other weapons. Being encouraged to complete challenges adds a lot more replayability and enjoyment, which I felt was lacking in RE7 (made up for by the very well-made DLC). 

RE Village also allows you to "stack" your save files, meaning you can complete the story multiple times and your weapons will carry over each time, allowing you to slowly build your arsenal of weapons until you feel ready to take on Village of Shadows, this game's hardest difficulty. I unlocked Infinite Ammo for the Wolfsbane before hopping into my first VoS playthrough, and even then, it was quite difficult. Playing this difficulty on New Game will definitely pose a hefty challenge, one that I hope to undertake soon. 

[spoiler] In terms of the story itself, I think that the ending was fitting. The reveal that Ethan in-fact died in RE7 and has since been nothing but a walking Molded was not exactly surprising considering his very advanced regenerative abilities; however, it also puts Mia into the spotlight as being very tolerant of the Infected, as she was with Eveline in RE7 (since she even had a child with Ethan). While a lot of questions are answered, even more questions are raised with regard to grown-up Rose, and I look forward to seeing what the RE franchise has in store for her future. [/spoiler]

The game brands itself as survival horror, which I would not entirely agree with, as it was predominantly "survival". My first playthrough definitely had me scared at some points, particularly [spoiler] the Beneviento residence [/spoiler] (I was scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the first time I played that), and the goosebumps continued into the next two playthroughs. Some jumpscares caught me off guard, but most of them were relatively expectable. There is also a large focus on action as opposed to simple horror, which I don't necessarily disprove of given that I enjoy a bit of action in horror games. Nonetheless, the game is fantastic at being what it is, that being a very convincing sequel to the well-received RE7.

I originally had gotten this game because of Lady Alcina Dimitrescu, I hadn't expected to really care for the game much past her. 
Castle Dimitrescu was an amazing area and certainly lived up to my expectations. I have not played any previous Resident Evil games and so I was stuck in there until I realized that the game had a fair share of puzzles. It was a very nice surprise to realize this, as I love games with puzzles (it is what made me fall in love with the Tomb Raider series). None of the puzzles were frustrating but nonetheless remained challenging enough to give me satisfaction when I completed them. 
The areas after were similarly entertaining and passed my original expectations. The story was easy to follow despite me having no previous knowledge of the series (they offer a summary of the previous game in the beginning which was very helpful). It was a very fun story to learn and experience. Though some of Ethan's lines were kind of lame (but not bad enough to ruin immersion).
Combat started out slow, you aren't given many weapons and it took me a bit to get used to the low mouse sensitivity. Later on, it picked up with the addition of more weapons, greater variety of enemies, and the variance of enemy weak spots.

Beneviento's estate however, specifically the basement, is genuinely horrifying. It is the only place in the game where I wasn't just on edge, I had my heart pounding as I tried to get out of there as quick as possible. Turns out, I was a little too fast and didn't realize I could pick up Angie to sell. Frankly, the extra money (lei) was worth giving up to get out of there.

For any concerned about bugs in the game, I didn't encounter any. Except the swarm(s) of literal bugs, who were beautiful.

If you're looking for a pure horror experience this one is just ok, however if you're looking for a creepy fps its a great game. Unlike most Resident Evil games this is a direct continuation of the previous entry, keep that in mind.

After playing this game for quite some time, and replaying it multiple times, I felt the need to revise my original review for this game. Would I still recommend it? Yes. As evident by my hours put into the game, it's enjoyable, and I feel like it has a good bit of replay value; I'm even considering speedrunning the game myself. But the more I play this game, the more glaring problems I find with it and the more I play, the more I'm weary of Resident Evil's future.

First, I want to talk about what's great about this game. For me the best thing about this game is the pacing, in past RE games there were sections that I felt were too long and overstayed their welcome. The most immediate example that comes to mind is the ending portion of RE7, where I felt it was dragging the game out for a bit too long. No part of this game felt like it was too long for what they were trying to do. It's the main reason why I keep coming back and doing new playthroughs and trying to unlock everything. The game just flows really nicely. That extends to the level and world design.

Second, and no spoilers of any kind here so you're safe, I really liked the story. It was nice and enjoyable, the writing could have been a bit better as Ethan was still pretty one-dimensional. But overall it was an enjoyable story, and the lore-text scattered throughout the world was nice to read as well, as sometimes lore text can just be boring. That's really all I can say without spoilers.

Unfortunately, now that's about the best praise I can give it, as the more I play the game the more flaws I find with it. For me, the biggest thing I'm starting to dislike about this entry in Resident Evil, is that while it feels like a step forward in some ways with story and gameplay, it feels like a step back when it comes to the horror aspect of the game. It is still a horror game, there are some tense moments in this game, but looking back to RE7 and REmake2, it feels like a big step back.

One major way it's a step back is the fact that supply scarcity doesn’t seem like a thing in this game. As one of my friends who watched me play this game, even remarked on how surprised they were when they noticed how much ammo I had (I was playing on Standard for a first playthrough). And during the first playthrough ammo and healing wasn’t that big of an issue for me, if one gun was low, another had more than enough ammo to last a while. Compare this RE7 and especially REmake2 where if you weren’t careful with your ammo, you would have to roll with the knife for a bit, making upcoming sections more tense. A big reason for this not being an issue is that the merchant can sell you some ammo, there’s limits to what he will sell you, but regardless, you can boost your ammo if needed. And another big reason is that enemies can drop crafting supplies, and I feel like they drop them too often. In RE7 and REmake2 crafting felt more controlled and it meant that you had to be more careful, especially in REmake2.

Another thing that I dislike about this game is that although they listened to feedback with RE7, and how that game had a lack of enemy variety, there was one major problem with it. With this game, there are plenty of different enemies here, but the AI sucked and they dropped the ball big time. It feels like roughly ninety percent of the time, enemies will just stand/slowly strafe back and forth and wait for you to shoot. I get that they want the feeling of the enemy sizing you up but they do that for too long, then when they move in they still don’t move in that fast.

As far as how they handle the enemies, another big thing, and what got me the most worried for RE9, is how they use enemies and in a way, how they design weapons. There are a few sections of the game where it becomes a mini combat arena. They throw a good bit of enemies at you and you either have to kill them or try your luck at avoiding them. So killing enemies in these sections, if you decide to kill them, just becomes a DPS check. This might not seem like a big problem, I thought this design was contained within these sections. But the more I played the more I realized this idea of killing enemies through a DPS check extends to the entire game. This takes RE7 and REmake2's more slow and methodical approach to combat (haven’t played REmake3 yet), and the type of combat you expect from this type of horror game, and pushes it towards action. This is why I’m weary of RE9’s future.

This is because they took a lot from RE4, and I mean A LOT. From inventory design, the merchant, to literally copying story beats and elements from RE4, it takes a LOT from that game. And regardless of whether you love RE4 or not I hope you may agree on two things. As good as you might think RE4 is, it’s not so fun to have a retread of that game, they still do a lot of things differently and have new ideas, but they do take a lot from RE4. And regardless if you like that game or not, we can agree that RE4 was the reason Capcom pushed the series into a more action oriented direction for a while. I’m weary that this game will also do the same, as this already feels like it’s dangerously close to becoming an action game (which is how I felt about RE4, although it’s a horror game and a good game, it came dangerously close to action). And that is my main concern with Resident Evil going forward.

Is this game good? Like, really good? Yes, I think so. Is it still a horror game? Yes, but it gets dangerously close to feeling like an action game at times. There are things I love about this game, but other things I dislike about this game and gets me worried about the series’ future. I would still recommend this game to anyone who loves horror or Resident Evil, but I hope Capcom doesn’t make the same mistake of pushing the series too far into action. There are also a few other minor gripes I have with this game but I think they aren’t relevant to this review. As far as what I talked about, these are the only major points I want to talk about. In a way, I hope RE9 feels more like REmake2 rather than pushing forward with the design of this game, and in a way, the design of RE4.

Much like Resident Evil 7, Resident Evil 8 is an absolutely phenomenal game, right up until the last bit, which is... Fine. 

Every level is an entirely different genre of both horror, and gameplay, from classic Resident Evil exploration being chased by a nemesis in a gothic castle, to puzzle box level design in tight hallways that remind of P.T., to the more action and set-piece driven camp horror of RE4/5/6, to a psuedo-open world exploration of the village itself which reminded of the way Bloodborne would change old areas as the game went on, revealing new secrets.

I imagine some people will be disappointed by the lack of focus on a specific style of gameplay, or genre of horror, but changing up the game entirely every few hours felt engaging and kept me wondering what was coming around the next corner every time. It's a good version of each of those things, and never really feels like it drops the gameplay ball at any point.

The biggest problem is the writing, specifically the protagonist Ethan Winters. I liked Ethan in Resident Evil 7, he was a bit bland, maybe, but felt like an adequate everyman trapped in a nightmare scenario. In Resident Evil 8, Ethan Winters is the stupidest protagonist I've maybe ever seen. It really pulled me out of it, as he makes a number of decisions throughout the game that make no logical sense whatsoever, other than just, "the plot needs this." It's baffling.

RE8 is a 9/10 game with a 4/10 story, but the story isn't what anyone was really coming to it for in the first place, so it still pushes through to being an absolute delight, one of the highlights of 2021 gaming releases so far.

I played through my first playthrough on standard so I could enjoy the game without it being too difficult on the first run and soak in the story as I was playing. I went at a reasonable pace I completed my first run trying to complete every room I entered. I backtracked a little bit too for some secret and treasures. I finished my run at around the 11-hour mark (in-game timer).

RE8 is by far one of the best first-person action-horror games I've played in a long while. As a fan of horror and Gothic victorian aesthetics, the setting and all the different areas of the game kept me awestruck. There wasn't a time where I walked into another part of the village and go, damn this ♥♥♥♥ looks cool.

The village itself acts as the centre of the web, where it all begins and each little strand that comes from it is very fun and keeps you wanting to explore every nook and cranny you see. It works as a hub and as a place you can at most points just take a breather from whatever horror you just unveiled last. without the village, I don't think the game could have worked as well as it did if it was linear sequence to sequence as some of the other RE games.

The introduction to the game starts you off in a very cinematic horror type of way, how it keeps you hooked with a new mystery, who? what? where? why? and as you progress through the intro you get gripped by the atmosphere and the situation you've been presented as you enter this strange snow cloaked village that’s too silent for comfort. The start of the game reminds me of how I felt when I first played the remake of 2 and how it’s you vs the unknown.

Castle Dimitriescu is an ode to the old fashioned gameplay of RE2 where you wander into a certain place find something for something, a thing to put in a thing, a box to open that contains something rare and a looming threat of the internet's favourite 9-foot tall vampire lady stalking the halls as you scramble around picking up the final pieces of the puzzle you need to get 3 more shotgun shells. 

[spoiler] Beneviento's house on the hill. What a beautiful display of psycho horror fundamentals, this whole sequence is one of the best if not the best segment for me. This escape room type horror segment is perfectly crafted and a breath of fresh air when leaving the castle. Your weapons removed as you're plonked in a weird workshop deep in the basement of this gloomy house. Creepy noises loom over you while your eyes play tricks as you see after images of Ethan's loved one walking past clouded windows as you try and figure out all the little pieces you need to escape this horror. all to be stopped in your path by a monster you cannot face so you must run and hide. Creepy and unsettling dolls watch your every move as you crawl through this nightmare only to be met with reminders of Ethan's past with Mia. slowly getting drip-fed something isn’t right, people are keeping things from me, flooding Ethan with paranoia as he's close to ending this seriously bad time. this segment is genuinely such a fun part of the game if you enjoy psycho-horror escape rooms like the DLC in RE7 but much more expanded on and doused in atmosphere.

Moreau’s Reservoir, I will say off the bat I think this segment of the game is, unfortunately, its weakest but that’s not to say it's bad, I still think it’s decently good and does deserve its place in this game. The zone itself is just one big boss fight, you walk across makeshift "raft-bridges" dodging the big bad of the zone while picking up loot and trying not to fall into the deep murky water. in this part I never really felt like I was in a lick of danger, I felt as long as I take my time not to get grabbed by the baddy I felt like I could take as much time as I needed to look around and see what was going on. once you've traversed all the wooden beams and wooden boxes you finally reach the exit you have a boss fight that I enjoyed, in a way it felt like I was playing hide and seek with the boss, having to hide under terrain so I didn’t take damage from certain attacks while also trying to take potshots at the bosses weak spot it was enjoyable and the most engaging part of the whole segment.

the lead up to Heisenberg's Factory was really fun, some really fun action parts of the game here. The stronghold is arena fight after arena fight, a lot of action while you're trying not to run through the mass of ammo you've collected and you will run through, it was at this point where I found use in what I thought was a useless weapon but it helped push me through this segment.

Heisenberg's Factory felt like I was really trying to survive this utter maze of machinery and bodies augmented with metal and gears, this is where the monster variety kicks in for me. You see an enemy unlike ones you've fought before in this game but every time you find one like it, it’s been upgraded and more menacing than the last. this threat of "oh ♥♥♥♥ I hope there’s not a bigger and much harder version of that guy coming up, I'm running out of ammo here" hits hard as you traverse this steamy factory to end up fighting a really fun mini-boss that leads onto one of the most cheesy over the top stupid but fun boss fights.

and finally the last segments of the game, you take over Chris Redfield as he's also been in this village trying to figure out the same mystery as you. It’s pure action, they try to make you think damn Chris is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ badass. Look at all the ammo he has, why are all his weapons so damn powerful and why is he SO DAMN COOL?! 

You're then given the reins back to Ethan as you stumble your way to the final boss and a good final boss indeed. they took the comments about RE7 not having a good final boss and said, let’s improve and work on it and they sure did. The entire fight is fun to run but has a bit of a challenge on it, it has a few mechanics you have to try and think about while also unloading the last remains of your ammo stock into the boss. [/spoiler]

all in all, I really enjoyed this game, but I have some gripes with it also, it’s not the perfect game but it’s perfect enough for me. 

I wish the villains got more screen time, they all seem like complex characters that are underutilised other than to be here’s the bad guy who holds the key. Because of this most of the game feels like it’s all over the place but what brings it back together is the village, for some reason it makes all the different tones and characters fit in this seemingly mish-mashed part of the world.

Ethan finally feels like a character and no longer a blank slate for you to say "hey I’m playing this guy, why do I care about this person" He's finally fleshed out and made seem like an actual character in the game.

As one of my anticipated games of 2021, my hype wasn't let down. I don't think its the perfect game but I think its easily worth of GOTY
