Gameplay: In a lot of ways the gameplay of RE Village is similar to the gameplay from RE7, just a lot more streamlined and refined in ways that make RE: Village a real joy to play. A lot of those refinements come with the game's protagonist, Ethan, and the way he controls. With the experience gained in RE7 and some military training with Chris' wolf pack squad in between games, Ethan is now a much more capable survivor than he was in his last appearance and this is conveyed very well during the gameplay. You can see this in the way Ethan now handles firearms and even in his reload animations, saving magazines that still have bullets in them for later. Ethan can also push and kick enemies away after performing a block, this gives you a few precious moments to get back on target and save yourself from getting gnawed on like a fresh ham on Christmas. 

The enemies you fight have likewise received an overhaul and are now powered by a fairly intelligent AI system. Enemies no longer walk slowly towards you as you take potshots at their heads. They will flank you, hang back, overpower you with numbers, sprint at you, and even make strategic retreats to regroup if you kill enough of them. There is a wider variety of enemies in Village compared to the four variations of the molded we had in RE7 and you will fight many different types of beasts during your time in and outside of the Village and even the boss fights are spectacular. 

There have been a lot of people of comparing RE: Village to RE4 and I think that it is an apt comparison. RE: Village is more on the action side of the Resident Evil spectrum, which might make some fans angry after the more horror-focused RE7, but it's nowhere near the action hell that was Chris' campaign in RE6. The blend of action and survival horror that Capcom went with here is a great mixture and works well without going too far into action territory. Also, the inventory system of RE4 is back in Village and you will be playing Tetris to fit that last bit of handgun ammo if you're not careful with your inventory management. 

In yet another likeness to RE4, a merchant character makes a return to the franchise in the form of The Duke. A very rotund man that can also upgrade your weapons and cook you meals from resources gathered while hunting to permanently buff your stats like the steroids injectors from RE7. Yes, you heard that right, there is hunting in RE Village. Of course, it's less like actual hunting and more like running up to animals and stabbing them repeatedly until they die a horribly painful death. That's how I did it at least. Bullets don't grow on trees, man. 

The Duke does also play a bigger part in the overall story of the game, but I'm not gonna spoil anything about that in this video. 

Puzzles do have a bigger relevance in Village, and while not being anywhere close to the hair-pulling annoying puzzles of past RE games, some of them will flex your brain a little bit. 

Presentation: The developers of the Resident Evil series have always been extremely talented at crafting incredible and interesting locals for their main characters to develop severe PTSD in and RE Village is no different in that regard. There are five main areas that you will explore that all stem off of the titular Village. These areas are all varied and beautifully realized, with each environment being well designed and interesting to navigate, but you'll always come back to the village allowing you to explore it even further with new items. The game does a good job of slowly opening the village as you gain new items to traverse it. 

Village was made using the same game engine that they used to make RE7, RE2Remake, and RE3 Remake, so of course, the graphics are going to be amazing, but I think RE Village takes it to the next level and it feels like it's reached it's the pinnacle. I played this game on PC with the settings on max and I was completely blown away by how good it looked. 

I did, however, have some glitches while playing RE: Village. There were a few cases of the audio losing sync with the characters during cutscenes, dips in frame rate, and there was a point where the game wouldn't let me use my controller to aim. It wasn't anything that reloading a checkpoint couldn't fix. 

Story: Picking up a few years after the events of Resident Evil 7, Ethan and Mia have settled down somewhere in Europe and are raising a daughter named Rose. Everyone seems to be happy until Chris "Boulder Puncher" Redfield, along with a squad of soldiers, storms the Winter's home. Chris shoots Mia dead, knocks Ethan the ♥♥♥♥ out, and peace out with Ethan's baby. What an absolute chad move. 

Ethan awakens in the outskirts of the Village after Chris' convoy crashes for some unknown reason, with seemingly the only survivor. He heads farther into the woods, making it through the Forrest, Ethan finds himself on a cliff overlooking the Village. Making his way down, Ethan quickly realizes that this is no ordinary village, and finding his daughter isn't going to be an easy task. 

The story of RE: V has a very strong start and you feel invested in the characters right away. Ethan is a much more vocal character this time around and in turn, he becomes a lot more likable. Capcom, however, still insisted on not showing Ethan's face and I really can't understand why. Why would they go through so much effort to make Ethan more of a relatable character and not show his face? It works for games like amnesia and outlast because the characters that you play as are conduits for the players. It's supposed to make you feel like you're the one who's in that situation and therefore those characters are mostly silent throughout those games, but Ethan is an established character with dialogue, a personality, and motivations. Why not give him a face? Sorry, rant over. 

The rest of the cast is stellar too in the four lords of the village. You have Heisenberg, Moreau, Donna, and finally, the one that the whole game was marketed around the tall lady herself, Lady Dimitrecu. They are all well-realized and developed characters that have interesting backstories that keep them from being generic villains. Lady Meranda, the matriarch of the four lords, is also a very intriguing character and while she has her reasons for committing all of the atrocities that now plague the village, it doesn't stop her from being just a terrible person in all the worst ways. 

By the end of the game, there are many questions presented, and not all of them are answered and that's not a surprise as Capcom has already confirmed that there is another game coming that will wrap up this story. But it seems to me that at certain points, they just decided to have something be mysterious to have a mystery, and it doesn't really add anything to the story, but who knows, maybe they'll do something crazy with it in the next game and I'll look back and be like "Wow, the pieces were all there from the beginning.". 

I've noticed a lot of people say that RE: Village isn't a scary game and for the most part that is true. It is more atmospheric than RE7 and you have this feeling that you are never quite safe no matter where you are, but there is a sequence in this game that is single-handedly one of the scariest sequences in any Resident Evil game and it was shocking to me that it was in a RE game. 

Resident Evil: Village does do some interesting stuff with the lore of the RE universe that I'm positive will piss a lot of hardcore fans off and I can see where they're coming from, but I didn't really have a problem with it. 

Verdict: Resident Evil is a long-running franchise with a storied past with games ranging from masterpieces to garbage fires. RE: Village, however, is an incredible entry into the series and one that has a terrific mixture of both action and horror and it will be looked at as one of the best Resident Evil games ever made and a strong contender for game of the year.

I have been a Resident Evil fan since the 1990's when Resident Evil 2 came out. I was pleased that they returned to their survival horror roots in RE VII, and they have largely continued with RE VIII. This game doesn't quite have the same horror feel as the last game, because it relies more on action, they have some new things distinguishing it from the last game. 

First, you rely much more on crafting. Secondly, there is a merchant in the game (the Duke). He even has a dialogue that connects him to the mysterious merchant in RE4. While that isn't of itself remarkable, it does help it feel more connected to the RE universe lore-wise. The game is largely linear, and I wouldn't quite agree with some other reviews calling it a semi-open world. It may feel that way on the first playthrough because they do encourage backtracking to discover certain paths (of which some are necessary and others contain treasure). 

There is some replayability in completing challenges to unlock items and content (Mercenaries mode, infinite ammo, A DAMN LIGHTSABER, etc.) New Game + (NG+) enables you to carry over all of your acquired items. As another note, there is a slight cooking element to the game where you find ingredients, and a few of the rare ingredients are hidden well in the world (with a hint to each) to grant you additional buffs when you give them to the Duke. 

I do so wish that a certain character who I will only refer to as "Mommy" was in the game more. I also wish her castle was utilized more as I am a huge fan of the Victorian goth feel. My very first little review:

Lore of my relationship with RE before review: I love Resident Evil, it's one of my favorite franchises. RE: 4 was my first resident evil so when I heard RE: Village was going to take a lot of inspiration from 4 I was all for it.

Review: This is not really a horror game. Like Resident Evil 4 is overall scarier than this game. However, Village has a horror section which I would rate as one of the scariest horror experiences in gaming to date. At least that I played. So it did that section extraordinarily well. 

UPGRADES AND LEVEL DESIGN: The other bits, the main game, the action was very well paced. Upgrades were frequent, but not too frequent. The levels had a ton to explore, optional treasures to find, keys that lead to treasures, weapons you can find optional. You can totally just end up passing quite a few of them up. The levels are intricately designed and jam packed in dense little areas. Hard to navigate until you learn the layout then it gets really easy to maneuver. Especially when you unlock shortcuts which I enjoy. IT feels like you're progressing. 

GAMEPLAY: The gameplay is also great. It's not Call of Duty, you're not meant to sprint around, slide, jump and shoot. For what the gameplay and enemy design is, the combat feels great.

STORY: I'm not a story analyst and chances are most people aren't. So speaking for your "average enjoyer" and not your "average fan" (maybe you'll get that) the story is quite enjoyable. The writing isn't a masterpiece like The Last of Us Part 1, but the story felt good, right and quite understandable. Better than most Resident Evil games for sure, but that isn't saying much because RE isn't really known for their main stories so much as the interesting lore surrounding it.

Characters: I loooved the characters tbh. Lady D had a brilliant performance and we can't forget her "larger than life personality". Heisenberg was really interesting and a joy to witness. Also he kinda sounds like Keanu Reeves or is that just me? Ethan, I actually LIKE Ethan. I know it's a love or hate thing with him. He's a bit whiny at the beginning and he also has a bit of an attitude. But I think that is what makes him more relatable and it's understandable. He's done with everything because he's been thrown into two situations he wants no part of. He's also heroic yet imperfect. Duke is also amazing. Awesome character and he helps me out.

Setting: I won't dwell too long on this, all the settings were fantastic. I loved the art direction.

Boss Fights: These are not the best bosses of any game, HOWEVER. These are the BEST boss fights of the Resident Evil series. Most of them are quite fun and tense though there is a gimmick boss or two. Also there are optional sort of mini bosses that guard certain treasures. Won't go into spoilers but they're also quite fun even if a bit easy to avoid. Mostly bullet sponges, but I appreciate their placement and their purpose.

MERCENARIES: Holy crap I love mercenaries mode.

[b] No spoilers in this review [/b]

Overall, I think Resident Evil Village is one of the best solo triple A games that came out in the last few years, and I highly recommend it. I have nothing but praises in terms of story and gameplay. 

The game looks and run amazingly well. I've got a good configuration (RTX3080, 16gb RAM and a Ryzen 3600X) but surprisingly, a lot of the games that get released lately don't really run well. COD Black Ops Cold War, Red Dead Redemption 2, Cyberpunk 2077 for examples. In Resident Evil Village however, I can easily get 100fps+ with Raytracing. The game is super stable too.

I've seen lots of comments about the length of the game, with some calling it too short. If you compare this to big triple A games like GTA5 or The Witcher 3, where the main story of these games can easily keep you busy for 40+ hours, and there are tons of additional contents in the form of side missions/quests, I guess I can understand why you would say that. RE8 main story took me approximately 12 hours to complete. I was playing on hardcore (the hardest difficulty available at the start) and took my time, explored at lot. If you plan on playing in normal/casual and be more focused on the story than me, you can probably expect 8 to 9 hours of gameplay.

Personally it's the kind of duration I expect from this kind of solo experience, so I wasn't too surprised. What I really like about RE8 is the pace, the rhythm of the game. I feel like CAPCOM has really nailed this notion in the few last Resident Evil games that they have made/re-made. I never feel like there is any filler.  You know when you play those solo games, and you do these kinds of quests/objectives that you feel are there to just to add content ? Where you feel like it's just the same area copy pasted and you're doing the same thing for another hour ? Well, RE8 doesn't have any of those. It feels like watching a great movie. It's super intense, there are constantly new mechanics/zones/enemies to discover and that renew the experience. You constantly want to see what's next. 

The game also has replay value in the sense of hidden content/places in the game. After finishing the game, you can replay it with all of the equipments/unlock from your previous run (NG+/New game+). CAPCOM implemented a list of challenges to complete which can unlock a bunch of bonus content in the game, in the form of artworks, new weapons, cheats, etc. There are a lot of them, for example : 
- Finishing the game in the hardest difficulty 
- Beating bosses under a certain timer
- Finishing the game using only the knife
There's also the classical "Mercenary" mode that makes its return, which is basically an Arcade mode. You are dropped in an area of the game, and the goal is to score the most points by killing enemies. It's alright, but it's definitely not the highlight of the game.

On the negative side, I thought that the difficulty of the game was weirdly calibrated. The puzzles are ridiculously too easy. You know this game for newborns where you have to put the shape in the hole that corresponds to them ? Yeah... that's pretty much the difficulty of the puzzles in this game. Fights also tell the same story, at least in the hardest difficulty settings. For example, I one-shotted almost every boss, but I got stuck at one of the intro sequences for almost an hour. Weapon damage is also super weird. One sniper shot does 10 times the damage of a single bullet of your handgun. The game also lacks an FOV slider.

Honestly a really good game, but I do have some gripes with it:

-While the game did a good job of keeping me on my toes the entire playthrough (save for a certain "spooky" section I won't spoil), I had to install an FOV mod to be able to even enjoy it, because apparently CAPCOM thinks giving their players motion sickness is somehow making the game "scary". Needless to say, I wasn't very scared and spent the first 30 minutes of the game thinking about how sick I was feeling. Oh, well...

-I'd like to praise the game for doing a decent job at showcasing traditional Romanian culture through its visual design (although a bit cliche at times), but it all kinda falls flat for me when 90% of the Romanian words spoken by the characters in the game (including names) are mispronounced. I would cut them some slack for it, but it really wouldn't have taken long to do research and give the voice actors some direction. Even worse, while the pronunciation is incorrect, different characters in the game will pronounce things differently. Why? Did the voice actors not receive any guidance at all? It's really disappointing when a character can't even pronounce their own name correctly (looking at you, Lady Dimitrescu...)

-You would think that making a game set in a specific country would mean that some of the people in the game would speak the language, but no. Honestly, maybe it would've been too much to expect Romanian dubs. It would've been a great time to introduce them to the franchise, but we couldn't even get some locals speaking it. They did it with RE4 and RE5, so why not this game?

-This game's graphics are really good; especially the interior areas. My only gripe with the environmental design however is that a lot of the outdoor areas suffer from being too... detailed? The game is pretty open, but I still found myself running into invisible walls a lot trying to go places I couldn't. Maybe it was just me, but the outside could've used a more clear design at times.

-There are some really clever puzzles in the game. Some of them even made me say "That's cool!" out loud. Unfortunately though, like any RE game, most of the game is just finding keys or key items to put into slots to progress. Not necessarily a bad thing, but just something I'm kinda getting tired of in the series.

-The story was pretty well told, but I found it hard to get into because it's very poorly written, in my opinion. Like RE7, most of the game's plot can be summed up by just saying "it was the mold virus all along", which to me is really lazy writing. Essentially a Deus Ex Machina. It gets a bit crazy later on and I start to wonder if it's even a Resident Evil game anymore.

-The characters are pretty interesting, but a lot of them get the short end of the stick. Some of them are either not present enough to mean anything or they just act like a characterization tool for the main character. A good example, without spoiling anything, would be the villagers. The ragtag team of survivors gets wiped within the first hour of the game and it really makes you wonder why they were there in the first place, besides being a reason for Ethan to "mourn" someone besides his family. While on the topic of Ethan, it really seemed like they wanted to go all out with his character this time around, but his lines were either really poorly written or just not delivered well. The game tries to portray him as a "badass" later in the game and it feels really forced to me. Yeah, he got military training. Why is he suddenly an action hero though? His character arc is supposed to be him overcoming his fears and leaving his past behind, but none of it means much when he barely reacts to anything. I think they missed a huge opportunity by not having him monologue more. Maybe I would've actually liked him this time around.

-There are A LOT of reused assets. Most if it is basic stuff like boxes or just things you wouldn't really care about. Hilariously, every dead body in the game seems to be a reused and/or altered model of Samuel Jordan from RE: Resistance and maybe Clancy from RE7. This was fine for the most part, but in the beginning act of the game you run into a pile of corpses which are reused models of the villagers you're supposed to meet later. This honestly confused me because I saw DEMO footage prior to playing the full game and for a second I was wondering if the DEMO was some sort of alternate reality or a marketing ploy to deceive, but I later met them and it just felt really awkward. I was anxious throughout the game, wondering if that was somehow part of the story, but it was never touched upon. I guess you could also explain this with "it was the mold virus all along". Wonderful...

-I don't find the game to be very replayable, like most of the recent RE titles. Other than the standard stuff like difficulties, shop items and NG+, the game only really offers Mercenaries mode. This mode was in prior games as well and I'm very thankful that it's back, although it lacks a lot of the energy from said prior Mercenaries modes, simply because the game wasn't really built for action combat, which is what the mode is all about. It was still quite fun though, as the gameplay is still fast paced, and honestly unlocking the figurines for viewing in the gallery mode is always a joy in any game.

Not much else I can talk about without having to spoil the game, but I hope you pick it up and play it because it was a fun time. If this is your first Resident Evil game, don't expect the others to be like this one, at least storywise.

Imagine Star Wars Episode 7 The Force Awakens, but instead of being just a re-skin to A new Hope, it's actually unique and fun.

Resident Evil 8 is child of Resident Evil 4 and 7. It continues the story of Ethan Winters from RE 7 but makes you play RE 4 in first person. At least that what it feels like.
At times the similiarties between RE 8 and 4 feel almost cheap, "hey that's just like RE 4" doesn't come to mind just  a few times.

However gameplay wise, at leat to me, this is a huge improvement. While I liked the atmoshere and creepiness of RE 7, I didn't enjoy playing the game a lot. In my mind, RE 7 always felt like those horror games that want to make you feel powerless and avoid combat but like in good old RE fashion this is not really the case. Instead of running from monstrous enemies you (are suppose to) Rambo them down like a madman.

In RE 8 on the other hand the "survival-horror" comes from dealing with enemies, managing ammo, weapon and health. While this is actually not very different from RE 7, you always know when the game wants you to run or fight and you know that you are suppose to fight a lot.
So gameplay wise it's very similiar to REmake 2 where you are constently on the edge of enemies appearing to avoid getting ambushed, losing health and wasting ammunition.
Defeated enemies always drop either money, treasures or crafting materials so you are expected to defeat whatever you encounter.

The only thing I didn't really like about the gameplay was that weapon upgrades didn't really feel balanced and new guns didn't really feel like alternatives but the obvious choice.
The default PIstol and Shotgun fully upgraded are barely better than the next set of guns that replace them stock. Since there's no point in carrying two of the same weapon type you can just sell the old guns for an immediate improvement.

Nevertheless, the game is quite fun to play and another great entry in the Resident Evil series.

Please ignore my short playtime, my PC cannot handle this game (the quality of the PC port is also questionable, some areas are extremely badly optimized), so I bought it for PS5 and have since platinum-ed it.

Another masterpiece from Capcom that unfortunately puts the series on the edge of a very steep cliff.

We really have to be grateful for that horrible mess that was RE6, because without it we would not have the modern horror classics like RE7, RE2make and now RE8. And make no mistake, just like RE7, RE8 is a proper horror game that uses it's structure (5 main villains) to incorporate 4 various horror subgenres and styles without even breaking a sweat.

RE7 started as a mish-mash of American horror influences (Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Wrong Turn, Evil Dead, Hills Have Eyes, Saw, The Blair Witch Project, The Frogs etc.) that slowly became it's own thing.

RE8 starts as a mish-mash of Gothic horror (Dracula / Lady Dracula, Frankenstein, Wolfman, Creature from the Black Lagoon, Island of Lost Souls, Frankenstein etc.), Hammer horror, Euro-Horror... but with plenty of influences from modern horror movies (Deadly Silence, Frankenfish, Frankenstein's Army, The Descent, Wolfman remake, IT remake etc.) and, surprisingly, comic books (the late game twist regarding one of the main characters is straight out of Swamp Thing, the villain reminded me of Locke & Key in more ways than one.

Yes there is more action and the game is very weirdly paced (the action heavy parts are back loaded into the last 1-2 hour of the game. Still, the game has atmosphere to spare, even in the later, more shooty parts. People expecting nonstop attack on the senses do not really understand how horror genre works and adapts and should never be allowed to gatekeep this or anything else.

This game was clearly made by people who understand how the genre works and how horror can be fun, not just endless wallowing in misery and jumpscares like 99% of the Steam horror output.

[h1]Introduction:[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil Village[/b] hits it's mark, I just wish they'd aim a little higher.  


[h1]Pros:[/h1]

The [b]Graphics[/b] are Breathtaking, Raytracing has been used to [b]perfection here[/b], turn it on if you can. 

The [b]Performance[/b] is [b]FANTASTIC[/b], I have a 3080 coupled with an old Ryzen 7 1700x which tends to give me problems from time to time, especially if a game is badly optimised ([i]Badly optimised games tend to be CPU heavy[/i]). This game, however, is beautifully optimised, a near perfect PC port. I ran it at 90-144 frames ([i]Frames vary from area to area[/i]) throughout the game, at the MAXIMUM graphics settings, bar 4K. 

The [b]Sound Design[/b] is great, the atmosphere is thick and every sound has it's place. 

The [b]Enemy Design[/b] is interesting and there is enough variety to keep you somewhat on your toes throughout the experience.

The [b]Voice Acting[/b] is good, bar Ethan at times. 

The [b]Story[/b] is fairly interesting, not the best they have to offer I'm sure but it keeps you relatively hooked. 

The [b]Level Design[/b] is impressive at times, it never quite reaches the heights it should with all the experience CAPCOM has but it definitely flows well enough. 

The [b]Gameplay[/b] is definitely good and a step-up from it's predecessor, though I can't help but wish there was more complexity to it. 


[h1]Cons:[/h1]

[b]Ethan's Voice Direction/Acting[/b] was decent at the best of times and often fell far short of the mark. Most of his lines felt out of place, like the voice actor had been directed to speak a line but his direction had withheld the context. 

The [b]Horror[/b] was sadly missing from a large portion of the game, it still remains an enjoyable survival "horror" experience but there were very few sections where I was genuinely scared. There are some good moments here and there but If you're looking purely for a horror game you'll seldom find it here. 

The [b]Gunplay[/b] while not bad, feels like it's been ripped straight from a game with much less action, if they're going to take the action route, they should refine and diversify what your character is able to do. Hopefully they do this AND bring the horror back. 

The [b]Length[/b] of the game left a little to be desired, it took me just under 10 hours of actual gameplay to complete it, well worth the money, though I fail to rid myself of the desire for more. There are Five main areas in the game, each with their own sub-"plot", [b]Two[/b] of these areas feel fleshed out and earn their length, the other [b]Three[/b] while undeniably complete, fall short of their potential and aren't as grandiose as the other Two. 


[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]

[b]Resident Evil Village[/b] is certainly worth it's price-tag and CAPCOM remains relatively consistent in executing this sub-genre of Survival Horror, though I can't help but wish they'd shoot for the stars from time to time, it feels like they're so close to creating masterpieces with near every release, yet they fall short on a few fundamental things that bring their score down too low to be considered as such. 

I urge them to continue with this formula, refining the Story, Dialogue, Gunplay and Horror and elevating it to the next level, these are good games, I just wish they'd make them great.

I must admit I’ve never played Resident Evil, so my review will be based on my impressions of the game alone, and not its relation to other games in the series etc.

Given I like dark things, I was immediately drawn in by the aesthetics, atmosphere (and of course, Lady Dimitrescu), that Capcom presented in their trailers. I was already looking for a new game to play, so I decided on this one. I don’t play much horror, and hearing the reputation Resident Evil has for being the champion of horror games, I expected to have sleepless nights ahead of me. I was wrong. I jumped in my chair a few times, but other than that, I felt this was more an action game than a horror one. Which I don’t mind, I like action games, but when the game is tagged as horror, you should expect horror.

It started off very good and promising, faltered in the middle, then just tanked at the end. The graphics and aesthetics were amazing, but the gameplay and characters were just blah. I enjoyed some aspects of the gameplay, like crafting bullets, the inventory system, etc, but most of the time I was just shooting things in the head, and that gets old very quickly if there’s not a great story to hold it up. Or characters, for that matter, and Ethan Winters has got to be the worst protagonist I’ve ever played. For a guy who lived through the horrors of the previous game, he is weaker than a wet paper bag, with the personality of one to match. Keanu Reeves in Bram Stoker’s Dracula has more than this guy. Seriously. Jack Dawson delivered the ‘Rose!’ line much better, too. 

Then there’s the fact that he’s basically immortal. He can sustain pain that would make the average joe faint or DIE without so much as an ‘ow.’ [spoiler] The part where he got half his hand bitten off, and he doesn’t faint once, and walks around continuing to use it like a normal hand is just silly. [/spoiler] It breaks immersion (which is arguably the most important thing in any game, ESPECIALLY a horror game), but not as much as the voice acting.

This game is set in Romania, but the whole village is full of American ex-pats. Surely a company as big as Capcom with a hugely successful franchise as this could afford to hire Romanian voice actors, or at least get the American ones to put on Romanian accents, or at least, any European accent? I should have played the game in German. Maybe then I would have enjoyed it better. A lot of the dialogue was cringe too, given the whole premise of the game. Every monster Ethan encounters is met with ‘What the ♥♥♥♥ is that thing?’ or words to that effect. I would have thought he was used to such things by now.

Overall, I am disappointed in this game. It has its moments, but they are far too fleeting. Lady Dimitrescu, given her hype, was criminally underused, and the only truly scary part of the game, the Dollhouse, was also a wasted opportunity. Still worth a play, but at a reduced price. 

Also, Mia’s hairstyle was simply awful. Long hair is not a static thing.

So let's get the obvious thing out of the way: no, I don't hate this game. All told, I've definitely played worse, even just among the Resident Evil series. That said, I really can't call Village very good, and the only reason I'm fine with having bought it is that I did so at a considerable discount. The best way to summarize it is to imagine someone very carefully mixing RE4 and RE7 in a lab, and then halfway through they accidentally knock over a big bottle of RE6 and dump the whole thing into their mixture.
I'm not really going to discuss the story in much detail because the parts of it that aren't spoilers can basically be found in any and every other review, but I will say that (apparently contrary to most players here) it's pretty terrible. It's difficult to fully support that statement without giving away some pretty wild plot twists, but in general Village's plot problems stem from three core areas. Firstly, it feels rushed and disjointed. One of my few criticisms of RE7 was that the Baker family didn't really interact with each other much, and mostly felt like separate, loosely related characters who would calmly wait for you to kill one of them before the next one tagged in. A sequel, I had hoped, would have the antagonistic party act as a more cohesive unit, with the various individuals occasionally tag-teaming you to provide extra challenge and give all of them some more interesting dynamics, as well as just more screentime. Village took the opposite approach, with each major character not only barely tolerating their co-conspirators, but literally being in entirely separate maps from them. These maps, which vary slightly in length but (almost) never go beyond two hours apiece, are the only instances in which each villain, one at a time, appears. You enter the place, you find the villain, you kill the villain, you move on. By now, you've no doubt heard that everyone's favorite tall vampiress is only around for the game's first three hours--incredibly, Dimitrescu still has the second-most-developed character of all five antagonists.
Secondly, Village's plot has an interesting problem in that it legitimately would not occur if three particular characters didn't display a frankly shocking lack of critical thinking skills at multiple important junctures. Again, very difficult to discuss this without giving away most of the final act, but just know there were multiple times as the story came to a close that I just put my head in my hands and sighed.
And finally, on a related note, Village bravely endeavors to connect its increasingly bizarre and isolated events to the Resident Evil series as a whole, which is at this point to be expected. Unfortunately, while careful connections can cause you to re-examine the plot of not just the game you're current playing, but previous ones as well, these ones managed to complicate the already absurd lore of the Resident Evil series, while simultaneously adding nothing of value. By tying itself in knots to make a place for itself in Resident Evil, Village made me like the series as a whole less than I did before I started playing.
So the story is a mess that, not unlike a particularly dangerous mold, contaminates and fouls every good thing it touches. If the game is fun, though, you can at least just get some popcorn and enjoy the ride, right? Fortunately, playing Village is a pretty good time...at first. The game's opening act is ripped directly from RE4, but still feels as harrowing as it did back in 2005, and, Castle Dimitrescu, the glorious land of the promotional material, brought back joyful memories of the Baker mansion. It's after this when things get strange. As mentioned earlier, every major enemy has their own little world that is separated from the rest of the map, sometimes literally. These worlds vary widely in content and quality, with one being a surprisingly good pure horror experience (those who remember PT might get some deja vu, or perhaps trauma), while another is an excruciatingly long slog through an enemy infested factory (side note, somehow the map in this game is terrible. No idea what happened, the RE games have never given this much map trouble before). It leads to game design that feels as flighty and inconsistent as its story. The levels only get worse as the game progresses, and the environments, enemies and cutscenes get more bombastic and, as a result, infinitely less interesting. The second half of this game especially is just so...loud. At the end of Village, there were three different games that I rapidly jumped between, and none of them were Resident Evil.
The bosses are just as disappointing, but the specifics vary greatly. During one so-called boss fight I legitimately don't think I was ever attacked, while another had abilities I'm certain Ethan actually can't avoid. To the game's credit, the visual designs of the bosses are all pretty interesting (except one), but basically all of them turn out to just be bullet sponges, with a handful having attacks that will instantly kill you unless a person who has already beaten the game sits behind you and points out when you should start running for cover.
So what about Village did I like? Well, it looks nice. Furthermore, I don't know what Capcom did to pull it off, but this is the first triple-A game I've owned that supports ray tracing and doesn't destroy my framerate when I use it, so a high-end pc can get all of Village's mediocrity to at least look real crisp. I also liked the early game as whole, and there are several characters that I think I would have enjoyed if they had just been given more screentime. 
That's what bums me out the most about this game, honestly: the potential. There were so many places Resident Evil could have gone after 7, and it really seemed like they were reaching for greater heights with this game's trailers, demos, and even opening. Unfortunately, maybe Capcom just bit off more than they could chew; they flew too close to the sun, and, like Icarus, their wings melted, and they were cast down into the abyss. And once they landed in the dark, they found that they could not see, because Ethan keeps shining his flashlight on his gun instead of where he's looking, so I can't figure out where I'm supposed to go, much less if there's anything in my way that will do yet another terrible, terrible thing to my hands.
Please don't pay full price for this game.

A great RE title in recent years (at least original and not a remake). Ethan's story continues bringing forth new characters to the RE Universe (nothing wrong with the OG crew but new faces and their stories are always welcomed and a breath of fresh air). The Setting is greatly made, with the work on it very detailed. Areas that I'm made to feel disgusted present it well and same with areas I'm meant to feel cold. All in all the setting is nice, and well put together that feels like an authentic eastern village. The Weapons are fun, from you normal weapon types you would see in RE (pistols, shotguns, assault rifles, etc.) and with the introduction of the Merchant again we see the hunt for finding resources to upgrade said weapons (or more so resource management on which weapon would best be powered to suit me better in the future) The Story was well done and kept me entertained looking forward to what was coming next, what new question will arise and what answer will come forth. Has high replay value like most other RE game titles. The concept arts, and behind the scene videos really add to the work as it does a good job showing the work they put into for the game.
Though beyond the good points there are some rough spots. Some of the backstories for some of the characters you encounter hardly felt to be there. The more I played the more I felt the want to learn more about the antagonists. However besides 1-2 notes you can find you hardly ever get much info on them as characters rather then their abilities or combat styles in the game. Wish there was more in terms of lore in that department. Though the writing is still good in terms of the overall story I felt that individual writings for important characters were either scraped or hardly touch on. Another big issue I had with the game would be that whenever you go into your item inventory and come out your characters momentum just stops. Even if you hold down the 'W' key to move forward it still takes the game a second or two after closing the menu to give you back controls of your character. Which can be a pain when you are in a tight spot and need to grab something not hotkeyed in your 4 hotkey slots. Moreso when you play on higher difficulties where a single hit could take you down from Health to Danger. Another issue would be the lack of I-Frames. Multiple times I was put in a situation where I got tapped by an enemy causing my character to stumble just to be insta-grabbed by another enemy and my health lowed down to near danger (playing on the hardest difficulty but the lack of I-frames doesnt matter the difficulty to my knowledge). It can be annoying to see one mess up result in you geting stun locked. Though it adds a challenge and its the biggest of deals to me but its good info to know going in. Another problem I had though doesn't really take away anything from the game. But the more i progress the more I felt like I felt like it was RE4 some of the areas remind me of the different areas in 4 (maybe testing the assets to later be used in the RE4 remake? I don't know, not really a full issue for me but something I cant help but point out).

To preface, my rating is based on two runs: once in Normal, and the second in Hardcore. I'm not going to touch the Mercenary mode for now and will update the review when I finally touch that. I will refer to Resident Evil 8 - Village as RE8. I'll try to be as general as possible to avoid spoiling it.

Game Mechanics
>
+ Parry was added to blocking. Parry won't do any noticeable damage, but at least it exists to provide you the option to push enemies back.
- FOV. I feel like this feature is badly neglected. I genuinely hate the current fixed FOV. It's way too low, and I'm not downloading a mod to turn up the FOV.

Game Content
>
+ The shop System finally added back. Good god, how I've missed this. The game takes some inspirations from Resident Evil 4, like having the locale take place in a Village near a huge Castle, and it seems like they also took inspiration in making a shop system. Like in RE4, the Shop offers a menu where the player could, in exchange for currency, purchase [limited] supplies, upgrade weapons, and sell items to the duke. Unlike RE4, RE8's shop provides a nice little kitchen menu where you can have the duke cook up food in exchange for your ingredients. These foods provide permanent buffs, which I find nicely.
+ Atmosphere. I think I can say that, without a shadow of a doubt, that I am playing inside an actual village. Ridiculous thing to point out considering the game's name is Resident Evil Village, but I genuinely feel like I'm in some old country side village. Not too much technology is scattered about, and the technology you do see is either owned by some militant force, or is super old. The only thing that takes me out of immersion is a certain main bosses' area. Not going to say whose, but it'll be obvious when you see it.
+/- Bosses. I've honestly become numb to these bosses. Without going into specifics, it feels like I've seen almost all of their attack patterns before. The most unique of the main bosses are probably the 2nd and 4th bosses.
- Mapping & Game terrain. Okay, so if we have a map that develops as we explore the area, it'd be great if it could map out blocked paths. If a road leads do a blocked path that isn't blocked by a door/gate, it won't be updated on the map. Whenever I need to backtrack, my monkey brain cant handle remembering alternate paths to certain areas if it's been long enough. Sorry, this might be a superficial/un-needed commentary on this feature, but it's been bugging me enough that I need to comment on it.

Post Game Content-
>
+ Challenge Points & Challenge Shop. You can get challenge points by completing challenges which can vary from doing weird, random fun stuff like opening all the outhouses in one playthrough, to beating a boss under a desired time. These points can be used to purchase unlockables like the Mercenary mode (a whopping 10 CP! By the time you've finished your first play through, it is almost guaranteed that you have at least this much CP), infinite ammo (requires that the gun has all upgrades & weapon parts), and cool collectibles like figures you can inspect.
+ Cutscenes you can rewatch. 
+/- Mercenary. N/A, not played yet.

Little backstory: RE4 was my first RE. It was released in 2005 when I was 13 years old. I didn't play it until Christmas of that year, and didn't finish it until I was probably 15.

The intro of the game scared me ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, mob of zombies, chainsaw, stuck inside a house. It was too much. I finally got brave enough and forced my way through it with my sister, all the way until the Regenerators. Once again, scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and took a small break again. Once I grew some balls, I pushed through that section and beat the game. "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that was awesome" as I restarted with new game+, then eventually professional mode. A friend and I started having competitions for The Mercenaries. Love for horror games took root.

Eventually, curiosity overtook me and I looked into the other games. Resident evil 0 and the first Remake came out in 2002, 3 years before RE4. Of course, being a Gamecube owner, I snatched the games up at the first chance. The cheesy writing, the atmosphere and thrills, I was absolutely hooked. 

RE2 and RE3 were ported in 2003, so of course those were next. It would be years before I played Veronica, and I wasn't missing much there.

RE5 came out in 2009, and the buddy I competed with and I both picked it up, and co-oped through the whole thing in a weekend. Once again, The Mercenaries competitions began.

Re6 was in 2012, and once again we played through it and The Mercenaries tournaments happened again.

RE7 came out in 2017 and absolutely turned the series around. The intro to the Baker house was absolutely terrifying. The Molded were horrifying. I still get chills thinking about the Basement and Slaughterhouse area. It was a relatively short title, even for a Resident Evil game. The Baker House, and getting chased by Jack was a thrill. Going to Marguerite's guesthouse and dealing with the bugs made my skin crawl. Then into Lucas' funhouse with the room escape, which you were given the solution in a VHS tape. Fantastic all the way through the final battle with Jack, then the boat section where is slogs a bit. Then you kill Eve and the game is over, fly off into the sunset with the house exploding in the back.

RE8. Whoo boy. I know it gets the moniker of "RE4 2.0" and it's not too far off. This is absolutely not a bad thing. 

We're gonna start with the characters:

Ethan, who a lot of people say is dull and a boring character, is quite likable in my opinion. Being sort of a blank slate allows for a better self insert. Henry is my favorite Silent Hill protagonist for this reason.

Mia is your typical damsel in distress, not too much here.

Chris is still the lovable boulder punching beefcake. The years have taken the toll on this man, all the horror he's seen since 1998.

The Duke is your shopkeeper. He's a bit of a mysterious one, even after beating the game. He has a bit more of a role to play than the RE4 shop keeper, and he has more of a personality than "STRANGER, STRANGER! NOW THAT'S A WEAPON!"

Lady Dimitrescu is the first baddie you'll come across. She's an absolute unit of a woman and dear god you already know about this woman she's the face of all the ads and trailers. 

Heisenberg sounds like Deputy Dangle and I can't get over that. He's very energetic and kind of quirky. He's also Magneto. 

Moreau is a bit of a dummy, but he's really pitiful. Kinda felt bad killing him tbh.

Donna Beneviento is a combination of Jigsaw, Scarecrow and those puppet users from Naruto.

Mother Miranda is a neat lady you should give her your children. Nothing bad will happen I promise.

Now we'll go through each level design:

The opening of the game is VERY reminiscent of the intro of RE4. You're in a village in Europe, a horde of monsters attack and you feel hopeless with just your pistol, that takes 10+ bullets to down a single enemy. It's a frightening situation! The of course a loud howl is heard and all the enemies retreat. This is now your hubworld for the rest of the game.

Lady Dimitrescu's castle is your second level. It plays a lot like Remake2, you go around, solve some puzzles, get chased by the large lady. Overall, pretty fun.

House Beneviento is a house.A house filled with dolls. This place plays like a "Escape the Room" type games, with a bit of hallucinations to go along with the dark, dank atmosphere. 

Moreau is the lake level from RE4, enough said here.

Heisenberg is a combat heavy level. Lots of his personal experiments hanging around. None of them are friendly. Give them buckshot as gifts.

*First I have to say I played Resident Evil 8 on Hardcore and on a beefy computer.*

Resident Evil 8; There is so much to say about the game and yet so little to say about the impact that RE:8 has on anything. Right off the bat I have to say that RE:8 features some of the worst implications of Re Engine yet. 

I often talk about how much I love the engine Capcom has created for the new Resident Evil IP's. Resident Evil 7 was the first of the series to implement Re Engine to the series and by the gods it is glorious. Item management was quick, pickups were quick and easy, crafting was not frustrating and actually meant something, the list really does go on but Ill save you the time. After RE:7, Capcom decided to use the same system for the Resident evil 2 and 3 remakes with slight modifications but nothing that made the UI clunky or strange. Then Resident Evil 8 decided to mess all that glory that the 3 previous games had brought to the franchise. One major example was the accessibility for the 'Key Items' menu. In RE:2 and 3 for example (I'm more familiar with those over 7 due to my recent playthrough of 3 and countless speedruns of 2) Key Items took up an inventory space once the item had been used, the player was prompt to discard the item for more space and declaring that that item was used and not needed anymore. it was a perfect balance of finding all the implications of that item and then throwing it away. RE:8 decided that instead of that system you are not only forced to hold on to key items but also there is a separate tab in your menu for Key Items. It was not such a nuisance until the player had to look at pictures of locations for rare birds or rare fish. The flow to look at key items was Tab>Key items>scroll down>click on picture>look at what you want>close menu>find where that is. It also did not help that Ethan never discarded used key items so by the end there was easily 10 items before the picture you wanted to look at which is just frustrating. Further more scrolling down the menu was hard to do due to scroll wheel did not work for any menu what-so-ever. I do have to say that when a key item was needed, simply pressing "F" next to a door that needed a key would bring up the key item menu but with so many useless keys and junk in that menu I often clicked on the wrong item and was stuck in a "Item could not be used here" text box that would disable movement keys and interact keys for a solid 2 seconds, which shouldn't be so bad if it didn't happen so frequently. Everything else about the UI was more or less okay.

Carrying on RE:8 has some amazing graphics. I run a pretty beefy computer at the moment and in my playtime I had a pleasant 100 FPS on High graphics. One spot particularly brought my FPS to 70 but it was only for 10 seconds or so. Really there isn't much to say about graphics in RE:8, its just as good as RE:7, 2 remake, and 3 remake. They all had great visuals that brought their respective games to life. Final note on graphics I found that my computer was being WHIPPED on this game. Easily one of the most taxing games I have run on this computer and my tower was screaming at me while I enjoyed the game.

Moving on to the gameplay. I've said this to my friends and I have been trying to keep an open mind on the game but, Resident Evil 8 is NOT a horror game, it is an action adventure. RE:8 felt more like RE:4 and RE:6 in the sense that horror was an element in the game but only utilized via cheap tactics and unsettling chase sequences. There was never a moment where I stopped, accessed the situation, feared to move on, and then close the game saying "Not tonight Satan!" Which was something Resident Evil 7 did perfectly. See, it is really hard to make a player terrified of a situation when they have a hand cannon and an abundance of bombs, ammo, and health ups, but RE:7 showed the player that no matter what you can do, you are not prepared. Similarly Silent Hill was amazing at creating scary situations while still giving the player a chance to fight what they are afraid of. It is not weakness to have a weapon, it is weakness to take away the players gun and expect them to be scared. Resident Evil 8 had a section where they stripped your weapons from you. It is one of the cheapest ways to scare the player. Of course the player is going to be afraid to progress when you take away the thing that makes them feel safe but ultimately, as a player I know, that if you keep on moving forward you will get your guns back and you will persevere. It really killed the scariest part of RE:8 for me and immediately after you get a water level :D The gun play in RE:8 was decent, it didn't add to anything to the series and I would even go as far to say that the previous games did it better. The knife is worthless. guns don't feel like they impact anything until the end game guns. 

lastly, the story line of RE:8 was absolutely atrocious. It was cliche, typical, and even after the plot had thickened I was already too checked out to even care. Whoever was the director of this game should just be fired. They took the face-value simple story of RE:7 into this uninspired hot mess that just had twists to have them. I really hope Resident Evil will continue on as a Survival Horror game instead of the Action Adventure they have given us. I have to say I am truly sorry for you if you think that RE:8 is a horror game. Go do yourself a favour and play RE:7 or P.T.

My opinion of this game changed about three times over the course of my 12 or so hour playthrough. My initial thoughts were disappointment. I was a huge fan of RE Biohazard. What made it great was it's constant feeling of suspense, terrifying visuals, and an immersive atmosphere. It was obvious that Village was quite toned down. I was relatively relaxed through the first 1/3 of my playthrough, almost to the point where I felt bored. 

And then things picked up. And then they really picked up. The setting of Village is so incredibly detailed. It is gorgeous, but also horrifying. The game runs very smooth, and it has a variety of unique landscapes and visuals. There were a few parts of the game where the action became a little over the top. You shoot the same identical looking zombie about 50 times. At some point it starts detracting from the experience. But that is really my only gripe. For some, that may be even seen as a positive. 

The final third of the game is where we reach the climax. Much is revealed about the story, and there are clues and revelations that link Village to the other games in the franchise. The final third is also the most intense. This is where the game went from mediocre, to good, to actually pretty great. 

All in all, try to resist comparing this game to Biohazard like I did. You may or may not be disappointed. Instead, enjoy it for what it is. Resident Evil has explored like 5 different genres within its arching story and series of games. While its not always perfect, I have to marvel at their ability to create a totally new and exciting experience. If you're a fan of the series, I would say this is worth the $60 purchase. If you are just getting into RE for the first time, maybe wait for a $40 sale.

One final note: there is a ton of lore packed into this game. It is tempting to speed through the game. But you can appreciate when you slow down a bit, and take everything in. It is clear that a lot of work went into every moment of this game. And then after its all finished, hop on Youtube and discover what you missed (or play through it again)!

Resident Evil has faced a myriad of backlash after the slightly disappointing Nemesis (which I have not personally played) but CAPCOM secures another hit and continues the success of 7 with various improvements (both under-the-hood & in design/story telling). It is important to note that this is a successor and continuation of 7 and is designed to feel that way so if you enjoy the more "traditional" over-the-shoulder format of RE, you might be a bit disappointed.

You can tell CAPCOM experimented a bit with mechanics in this iteration and not all of them succeeded but boy did they have an impact when executed flawlessly and the game has a lot of those moments for me, personally. At first, I was a bit apprehensive and confused by the story but questions & ambiguity in the beginning hours fuelled my drive to keep exploring. I just had to venture deeper to understand what was exactly happening and the revelations (whilst somewhat cliche at times) did satisfy me. The story's ebb & flow was smooth, the pacing somewhat fast but the end the delivery: impactful.

The puzzles are not hard (it's not like your traditional horror in that regard) but they are somewhat interesting and help break up the action to take a break and lose yourself in the scenery. Have we spoken about environments? They are gorgeous. The world isn't large enough to be considered open or even semi-open but the way the levels are intertwined with smart blocking & locks help to pique that curiosity as you progress only to go "ooh, that's where this leads". Enemy design has been meticulous and the attention to detail impressed me immensely. There's a good chunk of variety in here so you won't feel like you are fighting the exact same enemy over and over but it's just large enough that you WILL think "not this guy again". As for standouts: I think we all know and can appreciate the "lovely ladies of the castle" as one prime example.

As an avid horror fan, the biggest aspect I appreciated is when the game decided "okay, you've had some fun blasting your way here, now buckle up and put your diapers on". It leaves you helpless, it tortures your senses and creates the sheer terror of a truly psychological thriller during segments of the game. I would've loved more but when they cropped up, I was both terrified & filled with adrenaline. What sets RE:8 apart from a lot of other horror games is its balance of action & horror which are designed to complement each other to provide a varied & engaging experience. There are specific sections where you will simply not be able to shoot your way through, no matter what weapons you have or how good you are. If that is a negative, so be it but for me this was nothing but a positive. It's rare to find a game that employs a risky approach of trying to meld the two genres in such a unified manner. After you are done with the story, Mercenaries mode is a lot of fun with a heap of replayability & CAPCOM has gone the extra mile to make a second run more enjoyable beyond the usual "here's a crazy weapon for the next time, enjoy".

Let's talk difficulty. I finished on "Hardcore" which is the "Hard" version of RE and it was challenging but not overwhelming. There's a steeper mode beyond that if you truly wish but I actually enjoyed not having the burden of having to min/max everything and potentially spoiling things just to understand what I would be up against. I died a good amount of times for me to reconsider elements of strategy and adapt my approach beyond running into everything and gunning things down. The bosses themselves are probably on the easy side but again, the story was what I was there for primarily so take heed.

The lack of a FOV slider is a big no-no for a lot of people and I cannot defend CAPCOM here. I do agree it's unacceptable at this point in time that the game requires a mod for this but hopefully with time, this will get patched in but whilst this was inconvenient, it did not detract me from enjoying the game in its full glory.

There's not a lot of good "horror" games lately and whilst this may not fit the full bill of what a horror game should be, it created a VERY fun run of emotions for me and for that, I say "well done". I might be easily pleased for some standards but I would consider this a huge and welcome success in my eyes. I thoroughly enjoyed every minute and only wish there was a bit more.

As for that and in closing, m8, I r8 this 8/8. Recommended purchase from me if you enjoy a healthy mix of horror & action in a first person perspective. Think of this like a love-child between Resident Evil 4 & Resident Evil 7.

This is one of if not the best horror game I have played in recent memory. The story is very well paced, characters are extremely likeable and believable with some incredible voice acting. The environments are created with so much attention to detail with Lady Dimitrescu's castle obviously being one of the best areas in the game. The bosses you face are artistically unique and staying true to the RE series with it's gruesomeness at the same time. 

There is a lot of environmental storytelling for you to find off the beaten path as well. It will give you some early information on things that you would usually learn later on if you hadn't found it. It makes exploration worth doing as you'll get extra bits of lore that you usually wouldn't have been able to get if you hadn't explored. A lot of the history of the different areas in the game are given to you through written notes or books. They will also tell you about enemies you may face as well as hints for puzzles you might find on your way through. 

This game could easily be a 10 if it wasn't for some minor issues such as frame rate drops during some attacks from specific enemies (which can easily be cleaned up with a patch of course, however I'm judging the game based off of the condition it was sold in) and some oddly vacant gameplay options such as an FOV slider. This doesn't necessarily damage the game in any way however to have some quality of life gameplay options is something I would have definitely personally appreciated as a lower FOV can mess with my eyes.

It seems like the game is setting itself up for another in the series which is no surprise but is done really well without feeling like they're forcefully creating another game when the story does not need one. It fits really nicely and I am super excited to see what they do with the characters in the future!

I'd easily recommend this to anyone! Be that new players to Resident Evil games, or older fans of the series. It's a definite change to the regular 3rd person games you may be used to in the series, however it is done masterfully with combat feeling super gritty and it's survival elements being in play as well.

After I played Resident Evil 7, I was very exciting to see what Capcom had in store next. and seeing the reveal trailer for this game, I was excited to see that Capcom was taking notes from their previous games like Resident Evil 4 in terms of the mood and tone of the game. I waited and waited for the game to come out, and the final product did not disappoint. 

This game obviously follows up the previous release and continues the story of Ethan Winters, Ethan as a character is also expanded and we learn more about him and how Louisiana took a toll on him and the things that he had done to prepare for another event. After a certain event, Ethan is once again thrown into the world of monsters, but this time in a cold, desolate village somewhere in England, where the village people are turned into Lycans and speak about Mother Miranda and how she abandoned them.

The atmosphere is absolutely stellar and is sure to chill you (no pun intended). The monsters are excellently designed with incredible amounts of detail. The game structure is also more refined in my opinion compared to RE7. The graphics as well are vastly improved from RE7, where that games textures can be muddy at times and everything seems to have a shimmer to it, RE8 improves everything, textures are high resolution and look almost realistic (if you don't look really hard at it), the thing I noticed most was Ethan's hands, which have immense detail compared to his hands in RE7, which almost immerses me more in the game.

As I mentioned earlier, this game takes notes from previous games, mostly RE4, where instead of mainly focusing on the horror aspect, it takes a more loud action and rambunctious tone. Characters are now more focused and lean more into the wacky side, and this works very well and makes the game from a cheesy found-footage horror flick, into well, a cheesy action-horror flick. Gameplay is also inspired by RE4, as now Ethan's arsenal is expanded and improved, Ammo is now more plentiful and Ethan can now mantle over certain obstacles and run faster, this also makes sense as by this point, Ethan has had military training. Reload animations are polished and guns feel punchy and powerful.

I really enjoyed this game and I prefer it to RE7, for me, it was engaging from start to finish and I didn't feel that at any point that I wished the game was going to end. I'm excited to see what they have in store for the next Resident Evil, whether it is a remake or a new entry, I am down for it. I'd give this game a 9/10, my only real issue with the game is that on lower difficulties, it is way too easy, but obviously that can be fixed with patches and/or just playing on a harder difficulty. I would also like to see DLC for this game in the future to help expand the lore of the village.

Village is the perfect follow up game to biohazard in every way. Ethan this time around crashes into a village after his baby was taken and wife killed. from there, his mission becomes to save his daughter, rose. This game not only paints Ethan as a interesting character it builds on it. He goes through the four lords and mother Miranda with that one goal of saving rose. The sections of the game each had their own unique charm. All of the areas in Village are apart of this overarching gothic theme (keep that in mind).  house dimitrescu being the first major area to explore besides the village itself, It is home to the tall lady herself and her three daughters. This area is the perfect combo of having puzzles, tense chases from dimitrescu herself, and one more thing (and my personal fav part). there are a few scenes of the family meeting in the main hall where she speaks to the daughters, the last one in particular, where she expresses her feeling of loss after realizing that you killed her daughters. This really builds her character. next up, house beneviento, this house creeped me out. There wasn't much story to go off here except for ethan being tortured by beneviento mentally, but the horror in this house scared the crap out of me, Im not even gonna spoil it here for anyone reading who hasn't played it yet. Just go play it and you'll know what I mean. House moreau, This one was interesting. I personally am really scared of water stuff but i'll leave that out of this because its just me personally. The story of this one jump starts the beginning of mother miranda's character and how the 4 lords interact with one another. It was kind of a tragic story, he was the runt of the group. But he loved mother miranda with everything he had. Next up, heisenberg. There isn't much here either gameplay wise, but story wise it really showed the inner workings of what mother miranda has done. And after that, chris unfolds the rest of the story to ethan before the final showdown. But even after all of that, what really sells the game for me is that to the average player, the story is shallow. But the diaries you read along the way of the story really bring everything together and explain a lot of stuff. Also the duke, a very interesting choice and a cool character. Overall though, I think capcom really hit the spot with this game. And I hope they can continue to keep up the scary games with great stories. :)

An enjoyable (but somewhat short) AAA action game. It's clear that a lot of time was spent fine-tuning the visuals and atmosphere.

There's not much survival horror gameplay; Supplies are plentiful and the player character is required to fight enemies at many points in the game. There's rarely a feeling of being helpless or overwhelmed. Any attack in the game can be blocked and shrugged off by the player character, so even the larger or more gruesome-looking enemies don't feel anymore dangerous than the others.

There's also a pretty low skill ceiling for the action gameplay. Unlike RE4, there are no combos or dodging or reflex-intensive interactions that reward masterful engagement with the combat scenario. Instead, you have your very powerful and easy to use 'block' action and guns with lots of ammunition. The combat loop almost always boils down to blocking the enemy and then shooting them during their recovery animation and then blocking them again. This makes combat feel tedious at times.

Despite the above criticisms, I enjoyed playing through the game. Someone expecting a game like RE4 will be disappointed, as will someone expecting an earnest survival horror game. It's more like Half-life or Half-life 2: a game where the action primarily drives the story instead of being the main focus.

Incredibly strong game, a great entry into the Franchise and I highly recommend it to anyone looking to get through the AAA drought going on right now. It takes everything that made RE7 great and builds upon it, making for an incredibly fun and often tense experience.

If I were writing this after playing 2 hours, it would be a glowing thumbs up. But this game has some essential pacing issues (first half is almost all puzzles/horror with maybe 30 mins combined of combat, second half is almost all combat and cutscenes). And the second half is FAR less memorable and well-designed than the first half.

But more than that, it really fails to engage as a survival horror game -- you're never managing resources, making choices about whether to expend ammo on an enemy you know you'll need to go past again, etc, etc. 

OK, fine, it's not a survival horror, but it also fails as a shooter. It shouldn't need the variety of weapons/enemies/skills as DOOM, but when the endgame is 3 solid hours of combat, you start to notice all that it's missing. It's a mediocre shooter tacked onto some slow-paced exploration and puzzle solving (really not much puzzle solving; most of the puzzles are bleedingly obvious). 

It doesn't help that instead of one really well-realized location, it has 6 half-finished ones. Just as you're getting into an area, you're already done with it.

The story is good. The graphics are good. The setting is good and reasonably well-realized. If this is what you're here for, then by all means pick it up; it delivers on that. But it doesn't maintain the survival horror momentum of RE7 and the remakes, nor does it succeed as a shooter. The gameplay of both halves of the game is inconsistent and weak. In my mind, this is a huge step back from RE7.

This is a good game, not a great game.  I would recommend it for fans of the series and genre, but I think comparisons to RE4 are drastically overselling it.  I love RE4. I played and beat it maybe 20 times or so on the gamecube when I was a kid.  It was my first Resident Evil game, and it remains my favorite, even after beating RE8. I also recently replayed RE4 on the PC, so I know I’m not blinded by nostalgia in making this comparison.   

I’m not a megafan of the series in general, but I have recently completed RE2 remake, which I loved; and RE7 which I played in VR on PSVR.  RE7 was terrifying but captivating throughout.  I enjoyed it for the most part.  It was just very intense and absolutely terrifying pretty much 100% of the time. It is a game that will put hairs on your chest for sure. 

So I'm a longtime fan of RE4, and have recently developed a deeper love for the series as a whole, which I guess is why I found RE8 to be so disappointing.  Maybe my expectations were too high?  But if I could summarize the game, I would say that it is pretty much a hallway simulator and feels very much on rails the majority of the time.  The game just feels so claustrophobic.  I’m sure some of that is intentional to increase the tension and horror, but I feel that it is important to understand what this game actually is, and most comparisons to RE4 are kind of superficial.   

Basically, I was hoping for a game that was 80% RE4, 20% RE7; but what we have here is more like the opposite.  It’s maybe 70% RE7/30% RE4.  There are some systems that come from RE4, like the merchant and weapon upgrades.  I appreciated these, but they really do not feel meaningful at all.  We are talking about reducing reload time from like 2.4s to 2.3s.  They just do not have the impact that the upgrades had in RE4.  They are also very expensive, so you spend a lot of time exploring for items to sell so you can afford upgrades, then you get some meaningless upgrade.  For example, from the starter pistol, to the fully upgraded pistol at the end of the game; I found it took about the same 4-6+ shots in the face to take down a zombie or lycan.  That’s just not satisfying progression.  It’s the illusion of progression.  

Other comparisons to RE4 are surface level.  Like the fact that it takes place in a “European village.”  First of all, the majority of the game does not even take place in the village.  I don’t want to spoil anything, but suffice it to say that I think the name of this game is kind of silly given how little time you spend in the actual village. Another point I would like to make is how RE4 actually felt like a remote place.  The ganados all speak Spanish constantly, which gives them a ton of personality and really helps to establish the fact that you are in Spain.  The RE8, nobody even has an accent.  If this is supposed to be Transylvania basically, why does every character/villian have a bland American accent?  The graphics suggest a remote village, but this is not supported by the characters or voice acting; unlike RE4, which nails all of this.  You felt out of place and hunted.  In RE8 everything just feels really familiar.  Vampires and werewolves... spooky castles... etc.  It’s a little bit trite with European horror tropes.  In RE4 you are being pursued by a cult whose heads explode into parasites that try to hack you apart.  In RE8 you are fighting disparate factions that don’t really feel like they have a sense of place. 

I know this sounds very negative, but I want folks to understand that this game is not as similar to RE4 as some would have you believe.  Sure if you played through RE4 once 16 years ago it might seem comparable, but I lived and breathed that game for years, so trust me when I say that RE8 ain’t that.  RE8 has much more in common with RE7 and other modern 1st person horror experiences.  It feels much more like an on rails horror thrill ride; and less like a real game.  You get to do some shooting in hallways between set pieces and boss battles, but that’s about it.  There really isn’t much in the way of level design.  For every battle you can pretty much back pedal a bit to a choke point then slaughter every enemy.   

Also, there are a TON of boss battles.  I can’t believe how many boss battles there are, and they are all so boring and repetitive.  Basically pump them full of all your ammo then the battle ends.  I swear that’s how they are designed.  It really feels like the battle just goes on and on until you run out of ammo then the game ends the fight.  There is no sort of boss health bar, or really any visual way to determine how much damage you’ve done.  The bosses don’t fall apart like in Doom Eternal for example.  They just go on forever, sometimes with multiple phases, but they all feel like a war of attrition as opposed to opportunities to be tested and offer skillful play.  This wouldn’t really be a problem if there weren’t so many of them, but I swear half of this game is boring boss battles.  It’s pretty much 50% boss battles, 30% exploring, and 20% hallway shooting. 

Let’s talk about graphics and performance.  I have to give Capcom credit here.  The game ran pretty much flawlessly on max settings on my system.  RTX 3080, Ryzen 5 5600X.  RTX on.  I got 80-120 fps pretty much the whole time at 3840x1600 resolution on an LG OLED w/ Gsync enabled (I highly recommend ultrawide aspect ratio for this game due to the really narrow FOV).  There was only one room where my fps just randomly dropped to like 30, but it seemed to be a bug.  It was one small room, and as soon as I would exit it went back to normal and it was repeatable.  The game looks incredible, but I did notice a lot of aliasing.  I tried all sorts of different settings, CAS on/off, TAA+FXAA vs TAA only.  No matter what there is a lot of aliasing, particularly on specular edges.  Not sure what’s up with that, and at times I definitely found it distracting.  But as a whole, I found the game to be stunning to look at with tons of vibe and great performance.  It was probably the highlight of the game to be honest, but I’m a bit of a graphics ♥♥♥♥♥.   

I think I could go on forever about this game, but to summarize:  it’s a good game, but I would probably wait for a sale if you aren’t really invested in the series or horror games in general.  Don’t go into it expecting anything like RE4 or you will find yourself as disappointed as me.
