This game lives up to being a sequel to RE7. While it's not slow paced through out the entire story (like RE7 was to keep the horror vibes), this has plenty to put your average horror gamer turning on the lights at night. 

It is clear that this game had been inspired by RE4 (yes I know they stated it as well), which is definitely my favorite RE game. It actually plays out similar to it (in terms of action/horror). Early on it's horror, action, horror, finishing off with action. So if you loved RE4, you'll love this game. 

REV does a good job of introducing new characters explaining why they act the way they do. While some did feel underdeveloped and others felt had so much more potential to be more than they actually were, the ones that they did great more than make up for it. 

One issue that many RE games have is that there is never really an explanation as to why things are happening other than "someone created a new virus and is testing it and/or someone got infected and couldn't contain it". REV does an excellent job of explaining why the events are happening (though you certainly feel like you aren't getting enough information up until the last hour or 2 of the game). It all connects into a full circle that RE7 started. With each installment feeling disconnected despite sharing the same world, REV adds more story-wise than most of its predecessors to feeling like it's all connected (not just connected via diaries/logs). 

Lastly, a lot of people (especially big companies in their reviews) say that there is too much action, especially towards the end of the game. However, it is not because they ran out of horror ideas. It's because the story calls for it. That is ultimately my main gripe about the series. Sometimes it focuses too much on being a horror game that the lore of the RE universe is almost non-existent (except in notes and diaries of why things are happening, like in RE7) or there is too much lore explaining the state of the RE universe that horror kind of just takes a back seat (RE6). Thus, RE is always having an identity crisis as to what it wants to be and that's OK. You don't have to always do the same thing to be a good RE game (RE Chronicles were amazing and I want more).

Okay okay, admittedly I started playing Resident Evil since the release of RE2 remaster so I do not have any nostalgic feelings lingering around so take this in perspective when reading this review.

The game is a continuation of the events in Resident Evil 7. So if you haven't played this game I advise you to do so or watch some background video's. You play as Ethan Carter who is looking for his missing daughter in a medieval village after a brutal house raid.

The graphics of the game are stunning and really feel next-gen. There is so much atmosphere and detail. Sometimes I just stand still to take in the scenery.  I'm playing this game in 4k on ultra with Ray Tracing on Ultra on 5950x and 3090. The game runs absolutely flawless. No framedrops, stutter or bad framepacing. The fps is around 80 / 90 fps outdoors and 120+ indoors.

The game plays like a typical RE evil game. There's blood, gore and weapons. The game is mostly action oriented with some puzzles. The puzzles are very easy to solve so expect no brain breakers there. Most of the time clues of what to do or instructions to open a chest are hidden in the same room.

New to the game is that you earn an in-game currency (LEI) by picking op treasures and items from chests and slain monsters. With this currency you can buy upgrades, items and weapons from a vendor on various locations in the game. It's a nice addition to the game and makes exploring hidden area's much more rewarding.

[i]Resident Evil[/i] has taken many shapes since its inception. Survival horror, light gun shooter, third person adventure, online cooperative game, and, with 2017’s [i]Resident Evil 7[/i], first-person horror. This latest shape was fitting, in a way: the very first [i]Resident Evil[/i] was conceived as a first-person game, before the limitations of the PlayStation forced Capcom to abandon it. At the time of [i]Resident Evil 7's[/i] release, though, it was a return to the survival horror that once defined Capcom’s multifaceted franchise.

And it was quite good.

Now, after two years of remakes, we at last have the eighth instalment – [i]Village[/i]. It, too, is good. Very good, actually.

We’re back as [i]Resident Evil 7's[/i] Ethan Winters, three years on from the horrible events in Louisiana. He’s living with his wife, Mia, and their newborn daughter, Rose, in Romania. It’s all domestic bliss until masked operatives suddenly assault their home and kidnap Rose. That’s a bummer, but it all gets much weirder when it’s quickly revealed the operatives are led by none other than one of [i]Resident Evil’s[/i] steadfast heroes, Chris Redfield, now older, gruffer, and sporting nothing less than one of the finest jackets to ever grace gaming.

Ethan’s search for Rose takes him to a snow-swept village that’s shielded from the world by great sierras and dense pine forests, overlooked by a dark castle that you just know bodes ill; let’s hope he doesn’t have to go inside! The whole village, rotten and dilapidated, is strangely absent of its inhabitants… At least, human inhabitants. Soon enough Ethan is assaulted by hordes of canine-like Lycans, and the game is on.

But he does have one friend amidst all the blood and mayhem: the genial if mysterious Duke, who is on hand to sell supplies and upgrade your arsenal. He’s a tremendously effective character, and I always enjoyed seeing him; like the village itself he’s an anchor for the player in-between all the crazy.

I talked at the start about [i]Resident Evil's[/i] experimentation with different genres, and naturally some turn out better than others. To my delight [i]Village[/i] is an assured and explosive combination of two of my absolute favourites, namely the original [i]Resident Evil[/i] and the genre-defining [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. Both are two of the best games ever made, so I was super curious as to how they’d blend together.

The result, at least for the most part, is that the blend works beautifully. Where [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was a more cautious tale that dripped tension as you ventured farther into the Bakers’ house, [i]Village[/i] is keen to strike a balance between slow burn horror and all-out action.

The opening sequence sees the players beset on all sides by Lycans, dashing between houses and barring doors with closets for a temporary reprieve. Scrambling up a ladder to the roof once the deluge overcomes the meagre defences, the player is met with Lycans firing flaming arrows across the rooftops, gnashing their teeth and calling for your death. It’s mad and frantic and nail-biting, until at last some unknown event calls them off, and the cacophony of howls gives way to the shrill wind and the trickle of a shallow river.

It’s no mistake the opening resembles Leon’s arrival in rural Spain back in [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]; Capcom mean to forewarn players that further gunfights lay ahead, and so should arm themselves accordingly. I enjoyed the first-person shooting that runs through the game, although it’s arguably less graceful and intuitive than [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. There’s a certain clumsiness that comes with the first-person perspective, especially when your enemies rarely used range weapons and want to get up close and personal.

I know some players found the game’s final stages the weakest – when the guns come out and the survival horror takes a back seat. But that wasn’t my experience of it; all the madcap shooting felt like a suitable payoff to everything that had gone before it, changing gears at just the right moment.

The Lycans, as with the zombies of old, are only the beginning; there are crazier, nastier monsters lurking in the darkest corners of the village, a few of which manage to be genuinely creepy. A visit to Donna Beneviento’s house, for instance, is guaranteed to shake even the hardiest of players. Lynchian in its inspirations, it amplifies the game’s themes of parenthood and loss, successfully eliciting the existential dread of it all in horrifying fashion.

The narrative itself, in which Ethan has to locate four vials containing his daughter (don’t ask), is surprisingly decent for a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game. Sure, there’s plenty of abysmal lines and corny acting, but I feel like the series is at long last starting to mature. It may be at a snail’s pace and rife with clichés, but we’re thankfully a long way from the pure trash of old. [i]Village[/i] does start taking itself a bit [i]too[/i] seriously by the end, but even that, in all its weirdness, seems like an improvement.

[i]Village[/i] does have a protagonist problem, though. I didn’t like Ethan Winters in the last game and I liked him even less here. He’s a generic, whiny twit, who literally starts the game reprimanding his wife for reading Rose a spooky fairy tale, then goes on to aggressively whine at everyone else he comes into contact with. He’s the bland white hero of many a mediocre horror film, treating each new encounter with tiresome incredulity.

I kept wishing I was playing as Mia instead, who had successfully won me over by the end of [i]Resident Evil 7[/i]. The women in this series are always better than their male counterparts. Always. Capcom should take that to heart and adjust their priorities accordingly!

Before rounding off I’d like to credit the superlative RE Engine. Whether you’re skulking through Lady Dimitrescu’s haunting castle (yes, it, and she, are as good as you hoped), wading through the village or just admiring the snow-capped peaks, [i]Village[/i] is a stunning game, laced with detail and oozing ambience. I didn’t have any performance issues on my AMD Radeon RX 5700 XT, keeping most of the settings on high without eating into performance. I did have some trouble getting the brightness right, but I reckon that may have been user error.

Judging from the closing scenes there’s plenty more of the Winters’ story to come, and I’m genuinely looking forward to it. [i]Village[/i] might be one of my favourite [i]Resident Evil[/i] games, even if some of that is surely down to my love of isolated, snowy settings and baroque castles. But more importantly here is a sequel that broke the series’ curse, which often saw a truly great title followed by a shallow and uninspired imitation (see [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] to [i]Resident Evil 5[/i] or [i]Resident Evil[/i] (2002) to [i]Resident Evil Zero[/i]). One step forward, two steps back – that’s usually [i]Resident Evil’s[/i] MO.

Gratifyingly that's not the case here. [i]Village[/i] takes what was great about [i]Resident Evil 7[/i], expands it, and creates a terrific new title of its own. Hooray. More please.

(SPOILER FREE)( You need to be online to play the single player game, but if you connect the game to an online server and then disconnect it while the game runs, it will keep running so my play time is a lot bigger than what is shown on my profile.) Have you ever played Dead Space 3? It's essentially the same thing here. Resident Evil 7 felt more like a passion project because they sort of reinvented the wheel when it comes to the license and everything felt unique, well implemented and everything was thought off extensively! It's a masterful product that even to this day is worth replaying and playing on different plateforms. I would easily compare Res7 to Dead Space 1 with a bigger production value. If you haven't played Dead Space, it still holds up really well after all this time.

Resident Evil Village feels like a mix of Resident Evil 2,4,5,6 and 7. The combat is a mix of Res 2 and 4 because the enemies are spongy and they're often a lot of them at the same time. Enemies need about 6 headshots on normal mode to die and the game tries to make you feel like you're going to miss ammo and health packs but, you can find ammo really often and you can build resources on the fly. Also, the dismemberment aspect of Resident evil 7 is gone. Enemies also lack variety in their animation patterns. For example, in the second layout which is the castle of the vampire queen (Tall woman from the trailers), you can find skeletons for which get stunned when you knife them on the face 4 times. Therefore, if you keep aiming correctly, you will never get hit because the stun cancels their attack. There are also rooms where, if you lead them far from their original area, they will turn around, never attack you and walk slowly back to their original area so that their programmation kicks back in... The lycans in the game wait in line one behind the other and, most of the time, you will be fighting them one at the time even if there are 3-4 of them. Lastly, even if the lycans have different skins, they all share the same animation.  Basically, the combat is very systematic and felt boring. I decided to skip enemies entierely until I realized that you gain A LOT of money from the loot that they drop... Speaking of loot, the upgrade system  and loot system is ripped straight from resident evil 5. Spend too much money on an upgrade that will be useful for an hour because you'll find another gun which is stronger (the game contains a lot of guns). When enemies die, they drop crystals and other trinkets that serve as extra money. You will also find crystals hidden on walls that you need to shoot down. It's a little too grindy for my taste but, it does the job. I just believe that the lack of upgrade system in Res7 made that game seem more fresh... 

Bosses also are disappointing! Remember the three witch daughters of the vampire queen in the trailers? Well, the three girls are mini bosses which behave the same way and one of them glitched out on me by refusing to leave the end wall of the room and, therefore,  never even tried to attack me. The room contains a switch that opens up a top window for those that played the game. On a similar note, the tall lady walks around the house trying to kill you but she walks the same speed as you walk so, as long as you keep walking, she will never catch you. There's also a shop next to the main lobby to which resets her chase animations making her leave the area because she can't enter the room. She's also too fat to walk around in tight corridors so, if she unfortunately corners you, you won't be able to escape. Her boss battle is very reminiscent of Resident Evil 6. Big monster with a WAYYY to easy battle cycle. I didn't get hit once until I got to the last phase which is at the end of her health. Very anticlimactic! 

The save system is also wierd. The game contains manual saves similar to most resident evils and it also has auto saves. The game auto saves in important moments and therefore I didn't make manual saves often but, once you get into the castle, you will lose a lot of progress if you die while trying to 100% the area. I died 4 times getting a lot of stuff and then getting killed by the tall lady because I got corned... The manual save is also located super far and in a random room which is located in an area that you won't revisit unless you want to manual save... Iwould have honestly switched the shop keeper and the manual save station. That way, the tall lady would be scarier because you wouldn't have access to a ridiculous jail free card and you would have to think twice before going to buy stuff from the shop. It's not super frustrating and It doesn't happen often but, when it does... it sucks.

The game also attempts to add puzzles to solve and, when I mean that it attempts to make puzzles, the solution is almost ALWAYS next to the puzzle or in the same room...

Lastly, THIS ISN'T A HORROR GAME! You're often in sunny/cloudy areas. Enemies don't look menacing, when you combine it with the mediocre gameplay, it removes all tension from the moment. The story doesn't build up the characters that much either and I don't get why other reviewers say that the story is good. You get one or two cut scenes to introduce the enemy and then you kill them... The Jack build up from Resident evil isn't there and the story feels like a retelling of Res7 without the build up. Don't get me wrong, it does the job, but its also nothing to brag about... 

On the opposite end, I need to give the game where credit is due! The game is beautiful and it runs almost flawlessly on my RTX 3070 and Intel Core I7. The game comes with an EXTENSIVE options menu to the point where I believe that you could run this game on a super low end computer. Gameplay, as much as I don't like it, plays exactly as the developers probably intended it to play. Everything is done well and it's in a much better state than 90% of 3AAA games and that is really appreciated! 

I could go on and talk in more detail about the other stuff that just feels off but, if I had to summarize it, it would go something like this! If you were expecting Resident Evil 7 quality, you won't find it here. If you liked the more shoot don't think or feel Resident evil games, then you will like this title a lot more! If you played Dead Space 3, then you understand the quality difference that I'm talking about! It has everything that it needs to be an awesome horror title, but its excecution makes it change the genre and turns it into another competently made meh shooter. Buy this game when it drops to 40$ IF YOU WERE EXCITED TO PLAY THIS TITLE BEFORE THE RELEASE. If you end up not liking the game, I feel that 40$ isn't really that much of a waste. I'm lucky! My brother split the cost with me and I was able to get the Deluxe for 80$ so 40$ each. Btw, my brother and gf didn't like this title.  Wait for a deep deep sale if you can wait for playing the game.

This game is really a mixed bag. If there was a "meh" option regarding recommendation, I would choose that. In hindsight, I don't really think RE is the right franchise to do Gothic horror. The combat almost feels like padding in between Village's various set pieces, which are pretty memorable to be fair. I don't think this is a bad choice for people who are new to the franchise. If you want a resident evil game that's a bit heavier on action and less anxiety inducing, Village, Resi4, and Resi5 (if you can put up with co-op) aren't bad options. Resident Evil Village: Ethan must die
There are many good things about this game, and its a good Resident Evil game, but its just 'OK'. While I enjoyed the setting, gun-play and plethora of characters, the game lacks in certain departments as far as a protagonist. 
Ethan is the dumbest character in any video game, just when you think its a good time to stop, he says something, or throws himself into another stupid situation. I know its a horror game, but its hard to root for someone who is dumber than a bag of rocks. 
The story is centered around you trying to feel for Ethan, but I find it hard when he says the dumbest lines at the complete wrong moment. A perfect example is after you reach the village and enter the house with the injured people. If you've played you know what I am talking about. But I am making this point because of how it affects the overall story, and I personally felt no connection with Ethan. The ending turns into this mess, and even if I wanted to post a spoiler review, I would find it hard to explain what happens. 
There are good and interesting characters, like Duke, and Lady Dimitrescu, but they are mostly background characters and that's fine. They did a good job building on these characters, and I personally found them more interesting than Ethan. I think the game would've been better if he didn't talk.
Apart from all that, the gameplay is a cross between re7 and re4 and it works good. The inventory management from re4 is back which is a huge plus, but weirdly enough I found myself organizing a lot to save space, but never run into a situation where I ran out of space or couldn't pick anything up. I assume they did this because there is no item box, but this is minor compared to everything else. Gun-play and progression is excellent, once again straight from resident evil 4 A+. Exploration, combining treasures, all good things. There's a cooking system, where you hunt animals and make meals to improve stats, and its simple and straight forward. The different settings you play through really immerse you in the world of Village. The map is a perfect size too, for a resident evil title, not to big, but big enough to explore and support later speed-runs for neat endgame unlockables that you get and blaze through the story with, very fun. 
Overall, very good title, not the best story, but nothing too terrible(aside from Ethan). If you're thinking on holding out for a sale, I would stick with it, re titles usually come out and receive sales pretty early on because of a promotion so wait a few months, its a short game so everyone will get through it and the sales will go down and they'll sell low to get new people on board. The wait for Resident Evil Village has been a bumpy ride, with my anticipation being all over the place after each leak and official reveal. Now that I've finally played it...

[b]Here are the Nifty things I liked, and the Lame things I didn't.[/b]

[h1]The Nifty[/h1]
✪ Though I'm disappointed by the game toning down its scares so it can feel accessible to a wider audience, this is the first time action-horror has been appealing to me since Dead Space 2, which is my shining star in the mismatched genre. This is especially true during the game's absolutely phenomenal first half, where there's a near perfect blend of both.

✪ Quality of life features that were added to improve 7's formula are very much welcome and make the game feel a lot more fluid. Key items no longer taking up inventory space, the ability to shove enemies, having an expandable suitcase instead of universal storage boxes and the return of shops are just a few things that will make returning to older games a bit more difficult than I anticipated.

✪ Enemy variety, excluding bosses and DLC, was disappointing to me in Resident Evil 7. Molded never clicked as an appealing threat despite there being 3 different versions, and the bugs you squashed at The Old House felt underused. Village fixes this issue relatively quickly by not only giving me a lot more enemy variety, but also throwing a lot more enemies my way at once. It was nice to have a horror game where I got to choose between fight or flight again, especially since the genre has been painfully void of that for quite some time.

✪ Resident Evil Village has some of the most fun boss fights I've ever done, which often had me wondering if I was still even playing a Resident Evil game. That isn't a bad thing since all but one matched the game's style and tone, but Resident Evil often struggles to provide memorable boss fights for me. I always remember their cool designs, but nothing about the vast majority of encounters stood out because you'd shoot the boss until it died. Village gives each boss interesting mechanics, similar to 4 and 7, that make it so you can't just shoot your way through, and that's the kind of excellent boss design I'd love to see more of going forward.

✪  I'm all for extra content and things to do once I finish a game's main campaign, and Resident Evil Village scratches that itch as soon as the credits start rolling. Mercenaries returns with a questionable name, considering the fact that you can only play as one mercenary at the time of writing, but is still a blast to play. You also get access to Village of Shadows mode, which plays a lot like Resident Evil 7's Madhouse difficulty without being as punishing; saves remain the same as they were in other difficulties and you can use your inventory from prior runs. Bonus content, including 3D figures, concept art and special weapons can be unlocked as well if you'd like, including a lightsaber that requires you to get a SS ranking in every Mercenaries mission.

[h1]The Lame[/h1]
✘ It's a shame how much the second half of this game seems to completely drift away from the first half. When the game starts, you get this intense, action-packed body with horror pumping through its veins. However, shortly after defeating the second boss, a lot of what made the game spooky just gets turned into more action with whimsical charm. Fortunately the story holds up throughout, but from a gameplay perspective, I couldn't help but feel underwhelmed by the second half. 

✘ Even when using the optimization settings suggested by Nvidia's GeForce Experience with minor tweaks on my 3080, there were times when the game would spontaneously drop frames from steady 90s to low 20s. This usually occurred a few steps prior to triggering cutscenes and going into new areas. Then, depending on how low the frames were, the game's audio would end up 5 to 10 seconds ahead of what I was seeing on the screen. Fortunately fixing it wasn't too much of a hassle. I could often just reload my last checkpoint thanks to the game's saving system being overly generous, but there were some instances where I'd have to restart the entire game.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Resident Evil Village has everything it takes to be considered a solid game; a great story, enticing gameplay, variety and a decent amount of replay value. However, it also loses its spark halfway through, and feels much more like an action-thriller than the action-horror I was anticipating. Regardless, I'd say it's a must-play whether you're a long-time fan or someone completely new to the franchise.

Story wise its fun and light, the main protagonist is like a theatre drop-out that can't believe he's in a RE game, not sure if intentional or just bland VA. The antagonists and the setting is the real highlight here. The Village, the Castle, the Damn, the Factory, the Doll House, they're each fun to explore in the their own right. The Big Mommy and Heisenberg are the standouts of the cast of characters, the rest are forgettable and don't leave a big impression like the previously mentioned (which is probably why they were chosen for the Mercenaries DLC). Overall the base game is fun and sometimes tense, the story is fine for what it is, and I still enjoyed my time on my 4th and 5th playthroughs.

Now the DLC came out much later and I never gave it much attention, but since I've managed to get through it, I can summarise as follows: Shadow of Rose is a neat story that heavily reuses content from the base game, and concludes the Winters story-line. The Mercenaries expansion could be great if only they allowed the characters to be played in 3rd person. I doubt it was a technical hurdle, since you can play in 3P in the main game. Besides that, its neat using each characters abilities and powers to take down waves of enemies. As for the rest of the extra content, I think its a waste and adds no real value for the Expansion.

Would I still recommend this title? I mean, yes, its a fun game that borrows heavily from RE4 while being its own thing. It's worth playing, especially during the winter season.

Game's not very scary unless you're 12. Not a huge flaw, though I do wish RE would stay RE. This game is what RE4/5/6 should have been when they tried to become an action game. In RE8, you will find a shooter thriller with lots of busy work in clearing the map, playing efficiently and inventorizing. The game offers replay value in new equipment to use and difficulties to play on, but it is a weak form of replay value, as the campaign doesn't quite lend itself to it. You have numerous set-piece moments in the story where you can either do no damage to your enemy or you're playing through scripted sequences or just have your inventory taken away from you. These moments were interesting the first time, but will make repeat playthroughs a slog. The combat also isn't really design to make new equipment interesting. You can use a pistol, shotgun or rifle, etc. - different weapon types are there and are fun to utilize, but what KIND of shotgun you use, what KIND of pistol you use, these things don't actually matter much, so again, you're not really getting much for replay value by unlocking them. There isn't much leeway in how you play through the game either. E.g. in Dark Souls games you tend to have choice on what area you go to next - there's no such thing of any meaningful capacity in RE8. So to recap, yes - they attempt to give you replay value, but no, I played 2 hours into New Game + and got bored, so...

The game's presentation is a mixed bag. Everything looks crispy and the game runs great without meme-tracing. The sound design would be good, if not for the sloppy weapon noises. Everything sounds like an airsoft gun. Really hurts the feel of combat. Enemies behave in interesting ways that make them hard to aim at, but something feels off. They're a bit too rigid. You don't have the flinching and gore that zombies did in REmake 2/3 or the moulded in 7 had. You have an inventory suitcase where you can sort your items, which is FUN - yet by the end of the game I realized there wasn't actually much point to doing so, other than scratching some busy work OCD itch I had. You will never be threatened with not having enough space, unless you make really dumb shopping decisions.

The plot is honestly the worst part of this game. It's just about servicable. It's there to drive the game forward but pretty much a child could have wrote it. The whole "Chris killed my wife" thing is explained in a throwaway plot point and it's all just basically an event that happens to make the trailer of the game interesting. 

Back on the bright side, though, this feels like the longest and most solid Resident Evil title that this engine has had so far. REmake 2/3 and RE7 are inferior games to Village, if only by a little - with the caveat that the previous 3 were MUCH better horror experiences. Exploring and collecting everything and exhausting what's on offer in the environment feels very nice and rewarding. The pacing of the game for one playthrough is also done very well. Past games tend to front load the interesting level(s) and close out the game with 2-4 hours of linear hallways. This game has a few linear sequences inserted numerous times but they are short and you get more open, less railroaded levels for most of your play time. Key word is *most* though and it's still not exactly a Dark Souls game in terms of level design, and not anything like Resident Evil 1 either where you have one massive labyrinthine structure to explore.

[h1]VILLAGE OF THE DAMNED GOOD[/h1]

Visual fidelity, PC performance and Gunplay are all great, Enemy designs are much stronger than RE7 & enemy variety as a whole is greatly improved although does feel a bit front loaded. I had complaints with the narrative that I felt were adequately addressed by the end, in fact Village has maybe one of the strongest endings of any RE title. Exploration is light, the pacing feels top notch in game counter says it took me bang on 10 hours to complete and I dont think there was any down time at all not one section of this game felt like filler. There is a healthy dose of exploration with a light bit of backtracking for optional collectibles, this is an Action RE title in a similiar vein to RE4&5 so while you can, will and should revisit areas its not going to be a case of tracking which key opens which door on which floor like say in classic resi or the resi 2 remake. 

Yes there are a ton of Resi 4 callbacks but I dont feel they make the game feel derivative at all, RE8 finds its own personality from the get go. The action focused gunplay for sure invokes RE4 but there is no knockdown mechanic for staggered enemies pretty much the only thing missing really, and thats for good reason as this game is a lot easier than those previous games. I played REmake 2 from the get go on hardcore and found it a gruelling but enjoyable experience, i didn't fancy going that hard again on a first playthrough for Village so I went with standard and other than the first real group Lycan encounter I found the whole game a breeze. Not necessarily a bad thing but if your an experienced action game fan or just a longtime RE fan I would recommend hardcore for a first playthrough to keep the stakes up, especially if 10 hours sounds too short for you. 

Honestly my only real complaint is with the hunting mechanic, you can find animals in revisited areas and killing them gets you meat you can use to make meals for permanent health, defence and speed upgrades. While the game mentioned to me that I had to take these pieces of meat to the Duke for some particular reason it never told me why. So when i got to him i just sold them expecting something to happen, nothing did so i carried on regardless, only to then find that the next time I visited him a whole new cookery tab was available after I had now sold a pretty large set of various animal meats. Why the game didnt just unlock this as soon as I had meat in my inventory is beyond me and very frustrating as I locked myself out of most of the upgrades in this tab. I managed to get 2 upgrades before the end of the game 1 to health and 1 to defence (a blocking mechanic i hardly used to be honest) the game was so easy though that those upgrades werent necessary at all but just something to consider. 

The game is great but short, pure popcorn I streamed it to my friends and they were just as hooked watching it as I was playing it. Think of it like a Horror uncharted in that regard but with actually competent mechanics, gameplay and level design. The merceneries mode, additional difficulties and bonus unlockables have kept me playing for a few more hours and I look forward to another playthrough on greater difficulties. I do wish the merceneries was the multiplayer component instead of RE:verse but even in single player its a great time too and Im very grateful for its return. I love re-running areas watching my high score improve on each successive run. 

Next id like to finish up by addressing  some grievances I had with the plot while playing and much to my surprise how i felt the game did a good job of actually addressing and resolving them. so [b]spoilers ahead[/b] you have been warned! 

[spoiler]Immediately I was shocked at how awful I felt Mia and Ethans relationship was she seems quick to anger which is a red flag and she snaps at him a bit too quickly. she even taps his hand with what should surely be a scalding hot spoon at one point but ethan is seemingly not actually burned by it. I thought that who ever had written this segment maybe needed to a see a relationship councillor but no, and this really should've been obvious in hindsight but its not actually Mia thats in these scenes. 
Another Issue I had with the plot is that it felt like a lot of this could've been avoided had Chris simply told Ethan what the situation was, but obviously wheres the fun in that. Years of playing video games have kind of left me expecting plot hole filled stories and honestly im kinda willing to just overlook stuff like that and not let it drag my experience down but much to my surprise late in the game one of Chris' companions actually scolds him for not just telling Ethan what the situation was and Chris even agrees that he's made a mistake. Cool nice to see that the writer was also aware that alot of this couldve been avoided and we weren't just supposed to ignore it and it actually becomes a moment of self reflection for chris. 
Lastly my complaints with Ethan himself, I was pretty disappointed to see Ethan & Mia return in Village on announcement. Im not against RE introducing new protagonists infact the anthology aspect to the series is something I enjoy greatly but i felt no real affection towards Ethan & Mia by the end of RE7. So its nice to say that Ethan Winters has grown on me now, i still think hiding his face is silly but I like how every enemy refers to him by his full name now, Ethan WINTERS you hear it constantly does a good job of bumping Ethan up with the other Protagonists like Claire Redfield, Jill Valentine, Leon Kennedy etc. I kinda love some of the campy corny B-movie lines he spouts throughout too I couldnt help but chuckle when he cried out about how this is all happening again its corny trash like RE1 & RE4 and I love it personally. 
Another immersion breaking issue that the internet is currently memeing to death that I just assumed was a consequence of this just being a video game is the absurdity of Ethan Winters being able to recover from so much brutal body damage. He literally has his hand completely cut off from his body and within minutes he just pours some disinfectant on that bad boy and glues it straight back on, its so ridiculous that you cant help but laugh at it and stuff like this happens to Ethan constantly. Again like with Chris' remarks i didnt expect a follow up to this absurdity but there is one and a satisfying one in my opinion, i actually guessed it the minute he glued his hand back on as its the only way that could ever make sense but to see it actually come up in a conclusive way during the ending hour was very satisfying[/spoiler]

Yeah if your still reading, thank you for your time I highly recommend the game I had a great time with it, Shop around for a cheaper option as it is quite short if you intend to play it once and move on I found it for £36 the day before launch, know that you dont need any of the special edition DLC it all looks pretty mediocre and a waste of money. for £36 and just the base game I had a great time and felt I got my moneys worth!

Originally I wasn't interested in this game but when I heard it continues from RE7, I felt that I had to play it to see what more story they would have with Ethan. There's a lot of twists and turns but overall I felt that the story was alright. There's a lot for discussions in terms of lore and what's coming for RE9.

I had a problem with the game at the very beginning. The game's FoV is set to 81 and Capcom for some inane reason decided to not add a FoV slider. According to some people, this helps make the game more scary. Excuse me while I go puke in the toilet from the motion sickness. I'm used to playing First-Person games with at least 90+ FoV so having the FoV that low made me incredibly nauseous. I had to go and download a external mod made by the community called Lazy FoV and Vignette Fix from ModNexus and no more motion sickness. 

The game itself, in my opinion, suffers from an identity crisis. It tries to be scary but that ends in 15 minutes of the beginning. Seriously it goes from night-time so dark you can't see ahead without a flashlight to daybreak and then daylight the entire game through. You just run through the place and shoot monsters. You should play this on Hardcore because then the 'Survival' part of the game comes in full effect while managing your ammo. You can shoot at the monsters' legs to stun them while you pull out your knife for some free damage or even kill to save ammo. 

There are 'puzzles' in the game but they're so simple that I not sure if I like it or not. To be fair I wouldn't really want to get stuck in a puzzle for 10+ minutes when I could be enjoying the story but I digress. Simple puzzles. 

There's a stage in the game where you have to run and hide in a closet or under the bed. That part was pretty interesting. When I opened the closet and saw nothing inside, I tried to step in it and close the door. To my surprise, it worked and I thought, "There's going to be a run-and-hide section. Alright."

Then it's just back to shooting, more shooting, throw a few explosives, and shoot some more. The protagonist, Ethan, which should be prey felt more like the Terminator instead. You don't die and you carry a couple or three pistols, a shotgun or two, a bolt action sniper rifle that uses 7.62mm, and plenty of explosives on you. I want to complain about a section of the game later on which you use a cannon that's literally welded in place with a few screws and bits and pieces of metal... more than once. Physics begone! 

Overall the story was interesting, the gameplay's there and it's whatever. If you've played RE5, RE7, RE2 remake, you'll know what to expect. One thing I like though is that the crafting materials have their own separate inventory like The Last of Us which was a huge problem in RE7 trying to manage the inventory. The game has its own immersion and immersion breaking things like monsters dropping money or crafting materials. Whatever. You're not provided with any military-grade weapons until you beat the game which you unlock in the Extra Contents shop: The Dragoon (Which should be a AN-94 or something of similar) and the WCX (MCX, a 5.56 assault rifle). There's also the USM (USP) and the kramabit. They're really powerful for Standard difficulty and Hardcore is about just right. For the hardest difficulty, Village of Shadows which you unlock by beating the game or pay more money, it's truly about Survival of the Fittest. 

I've beaten the game on Standard and I'll go back into it on Hardcore. I enjoy popping heads with the sniper rifle.

Taking a lot of cues from Resident Evil 4, and combining them with the modern gameplay that Resident Evil 7 had seems like a no-brainer now. But, that is mostly due to how well Resident Evil Village (RE8) pulls it off. It's an action-horror game that leaves you to decide how much action you want usually, but it is definitely possible  (and usually rewarded) to hunt down all the crazy beasties the game throws at you. And in direct response to the lackluster enemy variety of the seventh entry in the series, this game has A LOT of different abominations to destroy.

Overall, it's a great looking game that will tickle an RE4-shaped hole in your heart. If you are looking for the slower, more-nuanced horror of early RE, you might not like it as much. But, generally, this game can and should find a wide audience of fans as it can be a competent single-player shooter.

This is easily the most original and most enjoyable RE game I have ever played.  RE2 and RE3 Remakes were great and it was fun to see how things were changed and what is now considered canon, as well as the nostalgia attached to them, but RE8 is by far the most creative and original in my opinion.  I will not get into too much detail, but I will say that there are some constructive criticisms that need to be addressed and opinions corrected.  
The pacing I think works perfect.  This game is meant to be played again and again, so breaks in action and storyline to walk around and find treasures and whatnot is expected and welcome (especially after some of the areas).  I do, however, think there could have been a better order for the bosses.  It would have made more sense to take 2 bosses in particular and make them first, as they have less content than what was anticipated.  This would also help with easing people into the sort of game play that will be expected from them.  Coming off of one MASSIVE area to find yourself in another area that takes (if you really suck at these games like I do), 45 minutes at best, after having just spent the better part of 8 hours going through arguably the most complex area of the game is jarring.  Two of the bosses are nothing, in my opinion, so making them the first two would have been much more satisfying and ramps us up for the main events.  
While streaming this game, I heard from a lot of people who played it as well as those who were experiencing it for the first time with me, talk about how they weren't a fan of Ethan and Mia.  I can't blame them, but the problem is not with the characters as they were portrayed in RE8.  Instead, the problem is with how they were portrayed in RE7. Ethan has more of personality this time round, but the bar was pretty low.  He had zero personality in 7, so they worked with what they had.  Regardless of whether he was meant to represent "the player(s)" in 7, his personality was non-existent, which is what set the bar pretty low.  This time round, he's pissed.  He's mad at a lot of people and just wants a normal life and it shows. His attitude in this game would be what i would expect from someone who has been beaten to hell time and time again and just wants to live in peace. Is it perfect?  No, but it is leaps and bounds over what it was in 7.  Mia, I think was demonized way too much in 7, and the surprise was ruined for us.  We all knew Mia was going to be in 8, because 7 ruined the choice we made in the game by putting in DLC that Zoe gets rescued after, and then ruined it again when they showed Mia FIRST THING in the trailer for 8.  So now the bar for 8 is a man who had no personality and a woman whom almost no one felt anything for...AND THEN had the major choice we could make to rescue her ruined by the game itself.  The bar was set pretty low, so to see the characters be who they are in this game is a night and day comparison.  
Story-wise, the game is amazing and I would love to play a game that had so many twists are turns and revealed EVERYTHING the way it did again.  This game proves that CAPCOM knows exactly what they're doing and the RE Franchise will be around for a very very long time.  

Technical stuff:
If you are running a lower end computer, BE WARNED: The game has a tough time of running everything exactly when it needs to run, so at the beginning when you have to "wait it out" for a certain thing to happen, it's possible that you can be soft-locked, as the timers either start way too late or don't start whatsoever.  I was stuck in this "survive" part for 3.5 hours before finally giving up and starting over.  If you find yourself at the start of this game in a world of hell that never ends, this could be the reason why.  Just start over at that point because you can't fix it.
This game also has an issue with multiple monitors, especially while using the map/inventory screen/pause screen.  You CAN click out of the game, which will shrink back into windowed mode.  I've tried it on many different resolutions and this occurs, without fail, every time.  This, however, should not be confused with what is being brought up next.
Alt-tab: DO NOT DO IT.  Many people, including myself, have made the fatal mistake i this game of alt-tabbing.  The frames will go down to almost nothing in some areas and, especially if streaming, will turn your stream into a slideshow and make you wonder if you're losing frames because your net is taking a dump, or the game is dying. The answer is that the game is trying not to die, but barely. The only fix is to restart the game entirely and the problem will be fixed.  

Even with the order criticisms, the bar for characters being set pretty low before we play the game and the technical issues, I would still give this game an 8.9/10.  Story is great and kept me coming back for more.  The extra stuff was a lot of fun, the breaks in action were much needed and welcomed, and the reveals and surprises at the end nailed it.  I don't typically go back and play RE games after having beaten them, but even with all the issues I feel this game has, I plan on doing just that.  If you've been on the fence with buying this game, do yourself a favor and get on the train.  The journey is completely worth it.

Resident Evil Village is a great mixture of classic and present Resident Evil. Village takes the modern Resident Evil feel of Resident Evil 7 with the first person perspective, and even has the more horror feel that RE7 also went for. However Village isn't as scary as Resident Evil 7, it still has its moments. It also takes heavy inspiration from Resident Evil 4 with even the settings and overall gameplay. It improved very well on the treasure and merchant system from RE4, and Village has a perfect balance of classic survival horror RE, and the more action focused RE games. 
 
Overall story:
The overall story and characters of Resident Evil Village are amazing, I truly was surprised with how the story turned out, it didn't really follow the normal Resident Evil plot development, but I personally enjoyed that it deviated from normal. I also felt like this game grounded itself in the Resident Evil universe better than RE7. The villians of RE: Village are also all well done and have unique segments dedicated to them, and pretty fun boss fights. Ethan Winters himself, while I didn't dislike him in RE7 he just didn't have much personalty to him unlike other RE protagonists. However in Village, Ethan had much more personality and overall a much better character, definitely making him one of my favorite protagonists in Resident Evil.

Bonus content:

Resident evil village is a solid entry into the RE franchise, it grabs what worked from RE 7 and expands upon it while using elements from RE 4 to make this game equally fun and scary. The game feels bigger in scope compared from the last entry as the game moves away from the baker home and takes place in a remote European village. 
Like in previous entries there are plenty of reasons to back track and explore your surrounding to collect money to buy upgrades. Combat feels good while still hold on to a sense of frantic helplessness that will create tension in the moments you are surrounded or facing a tough baddie while keeping it fresh with an assortment of different monsters to fight and adapt around unlike the last game with it's generic venom looking mold creatures. The games still holds on its horror elements with some moments being genuinely terrifying such as Beneviento segment where you're being chase by a silent hill like deformed baby. Each area feel different from the next while taking pages from different horror films, like Dimitrescu castle feeling like Bran stroker's dracula to Heisenburg(no not the meth dealing professor though I wouldn't mind that Heisenburg as a horror bad guy) feeling like a mix of Tetsuo and a NIN music video. 
The story is pretty good, leaving you guessing at each step of the way. Ethan feels like a more flesh out than the last entry but at times still feels like the definition of vanilla but I think that on purpose to allow the player to insert themselves in the shoes of Ethan for immersion sake. Each boss has their own different personality that keeps you invested in them, with a minor complaint on the last boss having a generic marvel villain "I'm going to rule the world you fools, bow to me!" forgettable vibe and the fact Lady Dimitrescu didn't have a bigger role... because she was such a great character.... yeah. but I'm sure you modders will make her ummm more present in the game. if you know what I mean ;). No spoilers: the games does ties loose ends from the last game while leaving things open for a sequel. So there is that to look forward to. 
All in all, I highly recommend if you like the last RE or just a fan of the series or the genre.

It's a solid game with a fantastic art direction, but some people are praising it as if it's the best entry in the long standing franchise and it just isn't. 
The first problem is a loss of identity. Been playing Resident Evil since the first game on the PSX. I think this might be my favorite one ever, although it's a bit early to tell. Despite starting with the classics on the Playstation, I've always preferred RE4's approach, just hoped it would go more down a horror route. Loved RE7, and the RE2 Remake was stellar.

This is like an excellent combination of 4 and 7, with a few areas of some pretty darn good horror mixed in to boot. Loads more enemy types and weapons than 7, plenty to unlock after you beat the game, etc. Game is fairly difficult to start in just about any difficulty, but quickly gets much easier as you get kitted out. I was able to just blast my way through Hardcore difficulty after a couple hours in the story, which was a lot of fun, but a greater challenge would've been appreciated. Village of Shadows, on the other hand, is much more difficult. New enemy placements, items in different places and less of them, but more money available from enemy drops. The enemies become very, VERY tanky, which means it's a lot harder to methodically clear out rooms, and the defenses you may have ignored on lower difficulties become far more useful.

The game is a pretty good length (took me roughly 14-15 hours to do a relatively slow exploration playthrough on Hardcore, in-game timer said 11 hours, Steam said 17.7, I know for a fact that time in menus and retries are not tracked per save, and I never left the game idle for too long.) and unlike most RE games, it, at least in my opinion, never loses steam. It manages to keep an excellent pace all the way through and there's no section I'm groaning about going back to. One I look forward to least I know I can through in just a few minutes.

Capcom really outdid themselves, and the game mode you unlock after beating it is my favorite incarnation of that mode so far. Just great stuff all around. I was worried they would lose their way after 7 and 2 Remake, just because Capcom historically is unable to release great game after great game in most of their series for too long, as we saw with the fun-but-very-flawed RE3 Remake, but I'm happy to say that they went all out and it paid off in spades.

As someone who has been a fan of Resident Evil since playing the very first game and hasn't missed an installation since, let me just say "Wow". It's a pity this game did not come out last year as this would of hands down stolen the show from a lot of the overhyped and/or disappointing releases that came through last year; Cyberpunk, The Last of Us 2, you all know which ones I'm talking about. There'll be spoilers but I'll be sure to tag them.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Story & Characters:[/h1]
I have to be honest, while there are one or two questions I still feel are unanswered for me, the story is in my opinion one of the best ones we've seen in a while. Unlike 7, this game ends with a feeling of progression to the overall story of the franchise. We're seeing the origins of some organisations, the current state of others, and are getting a better understanding of where we are at and where we will be going. 

I've seen some articles where people complain that Ethan is faceless and boring but I actually think this works in the games favour. Often times I found myself less worried about [b]Ethan[/b] finding his daughter and more worried about [b]Me[/b]  finding [b]my[/b] daughter. The same kind of relatability I can find with other faceless protagonists is definitely present here. As opposed to the previous games where it was Chris' story, Jills' story or Claires' story, this felt like a universal story. One which Ethan was a big yet silent part of. 

The villains were all very memorable and all had distinct personalities and themes. I absolutely adore the fairy tale book tie in they included. Alcina and her daughters were, of course, my favourites. Moreau was however, my least favourite. Bad by no means but not quite as fun to meet and fight as the others. 

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
I played through this game on Hardcore and I am currently going through it again on Village of Shadows, so I'll be speaking in regards to this. As someone who typically prefers the third person or fixed camera angle seen in previous games, the first person camera is a refreshing and welcome return. Ammo was something I was definitely being mindful of since I eventually had to reload to a previous save after being a bit too trigger happy. When they said this game will provide more action than the last instalment they weren't joking, but boy do they do it well. 

The action sequences by no means work as an opposing force to the horror, in fact the two compliment each other very well. There are two sequences in the game that perfectly sum this up. The first being [spoiler]Chris' first playable segment. You are given an incredibly powerful assault rifle, pistol, plenty of grenades and a laser designator. Usually I wouldn't be a fan of shooting galleries like this but I had an absolute blast mowing down everything in the village. Bonus points for Karambit Knife and Boss Battle.[/spoiler].

The second instance was [spoiler]in the Beneviento Mansion. Your weapons are taken from you, and you are left defenceless as you solve puzzles using a mannequin of Mia. After a bit of suspense building, you return to the area shrouded in darkness and streaks of blood across the floor, with a trail of intestines leading out. The monster in this section was downright horrifying, and having the game turn into a horrifying form of hide & seek was brilliant.[/spoiler]

[h1]Sound and Music:[/h1]
Okay let me start this by saying, as I was watching the credits, my friend pointed out they had one foley artists. ONE. FOLEY ARTIST. Someone needs to give that man a medal as the sound in this game is phenomenal. Guns sound impactful, critical headshots sound meaty and satisfying, and even small details such as the wooden dolls creaking and the minor differences in terrain and movement. All of it comes together perfectly and really adds to the immersion here.

The music, like most Resident Evil games, never really stuck with me save for a few songs. I noticed during [spoiler]Chris' segment[/spoiler] that the eerie noise playing sounded a lot like the music from the very first title but, that is just me speculating. If so it's a nice little addition as being the first time we play as him in the more progressed universe. The ending credits however... oh my the end credits song. Using the same song from the launch trailer, "Yearning for Dark Shadows" is perhaps a step above Aunt Rhody from the previous game, at least for me. So much more grim, much darker and felt far more impactful emotionally. 

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
If you liked RE4 or you like RE7, you will love this game. This feels like a perfect amalgamation of both titles and this game has definitely taken it's place as my favourite Resident Evil game, above the RE2Make and RE4. If you are at all a fan of Resident Evil I cannot recommend this title enough to you. While I understand it won't appeal to everyone, I feel like it's one of those must plays for anyone who wants to call themselves a Resident Evil fan.

So, to put this into context, I hadn't played a Resident Evil game before, although I'd played the entire original Alone in the Dark trilogy, which was the inspiration for the originals. I also knew a bunch of things about most of the games at a surface level, but not much.

What made me decide to purchase this game is that I saw someone said it wasn't too scary. I saw this as a good thing. And yeah, it has the perfect blend of action vs. horror vs. what I'd like to call "old-school running around". By that I mean, exploring, solving light puzzles, etc.

And what I really liked about this whole blend is that it really felt like one of the older games transposed faithfully to modern sensibilities and tech. For one, I could imagine a RE1-style demake of this super easily. But most importantly, to use the Fallout franchise as an example... you know how Fallout 4 is arguably more a "Fallout-themed" game than an actual Fallout game? RE8 doesn't suffer from this problem at all, when you might have expected it to. It feels super faithful to the DNA of the series. And yeah, the caveat is that this is coming from someone who DIDN'T play any of the other games, but my point is that it felt enough like an older horror game made modern, in all the good ways.

The writing is good, the characters are good, the art direction is very solid, the technical presentation a liiiittle bit uneven (but good), the music is... forgettable, but that's fine, sometimes it's just not meant to be. No complaints about any of that.

My only complaint would be that I would've liked to have a "natural" way to tell when you have completely looted a room. Near the end of the game I was basically constantly opening & closing my map every time I picked something up to see if the room I was in had turned blue. Maybe a little chime or a line from Ethan would have been far better.

Overall, I have to say I would definitely recommend this game just on the basis of being a really great middle point between horror and action. And 90% of the horror is more "tension" than "psychological". There is only ONE straightforward horror segment in the entire game, and believe me, you'll know when you get to it... haha.

I've gotta say, Resident Evil Village isn't necessarily a bad game. It's just made a lot of departures from the things I liked and it has some pretty bad parts of it. This is operating under the assumption you've played RE7. 

Pros: 
- Sticking with first person view, still dig that! It's decently pretty aside from a couple of texture issues, but solid! 
- Audio design is great. I love the ambient sounds that actually make sense. If you're in a house/building you can hear footsteps and sometimes a door opening which can make you a bit paranoid (at first, more on that later)
- If you're a fan of action like RE4 with a bit more action mixed with RE7, that's roughly what you're looking at here. Combat feels good and you're definitely forced to manage your ammo. 

Cons: 
- The boss mechanics. Holy crap. First boss. Run in one direction mindlessly. Then run the other direction mindlessly. Shoot boss. Rinse repeat. That's all. Sad to say very few of the other encounters are more engaging than that. That's such a let down. It's not tense, it's not scary, it's just drawn out and really, it's just boring. The minions are more fun and tense to fight. 
- The puzzles aren't really puzzles at all. Literally one of them is a 3x3 or 4x4 (I forget) grid of lights. The "puzzle" is there's a paper next to you with the solution, but it's turned sideways. Really. That's what passes for player engagement here. Just give me a key to turn if you're going to boil down a puzzle to literally having the solution next to me. 
- The ui is actually horrendous. The game doesn't remember I play in fullscreen instead of windowed mode. It randomly changed my graphics settings and cranked the VRAM requirement/recommendation way up and I had to menu dive to figure out what it changed. Playing mouse and keyboard is annoying if you like to use the mouse wheel to scroll up and down and when you're in a menu, the game lets you mouse off screen (if you're using a dual monitor setup) that's a minor complaint, but it's a peeve. 
- There's almost no horror here. Okay. Well. Let me preface that, as a horror enthusiast, there's almost no horror here. My perspective is a bit skewed as I played RE7 in VR. There was a lot of pleading for my life in shrilly high pitched voices, but I emerged victorious and a wee bit more brave. Now, I would love RE8 to be VR...not because of tall lady in vr....but it would've been at least instantly a bit scarier. The game telegraphs the few "jumpscares" it has? There's even a section of the game that seems to be dedicated to horror. I got excited, created a separate save file so I could replay it, but ultimately, it was just creepy and not really scary. Some people might be afraid because of just moreso phobias, but not really nailing the atmosphere there at all. 
- You may enjoy it more that this game leans heavier on action. I'm not a fan. I feel like the move to RE6 to RE7 was a solid reset to go back to being a proper horror game with still solid combat mechanics that made sure you managed your ammo well. This game still makes you manage your ammo, but it's pretty shooty mcshooterson. It's not bad, just not what I wanted out of Resident Evil. 
- There's some story/character elements that really make no sense, but I won't go into that because spoilers. There's just weird character choices that seem super out of character and actually make no logical sense. 

TLDR; It's not like more of 7 sadly. It's far less scary, more actiony, and the story/characters are more nonsensical than the campy charm of Resident Evil. The boss fights feel like they were rushed and VERY VERY basic and not very engaging. As a Resident Evil fan, I can safely say that 8 was not remotely worth $60 for me. It's not bad, just not what I wanted at all. Tons of people love this game so maybe give it a shot anyways!

Resident Evil Village carries the burden of following up not just the  critically acclaimed Resident Evil 7 but also the series' 2 & 3 remakes. These games all vary drastically, and their different degrees and takes on the classic Survival Horror formula prove only to make this challenge more daunting. 

Right at the start, Village proves itself to be of a different mettle. Taking notes instead from the ever-classic Resident Evil 4, Village instead seeks to mark itself as another Survival Horror / Action hybrid. While that may stir insecurities in certain series fans, Village itself is an astoundingly good example of how solid these titles can be.

Similar to Resident Evil 4, Village bombards players with a thorough depth of mechanics, mostly returning from 4 itself. The opening combat segment alone steals its gameplay from Resident Evil 4's hard opening, a scary village, filled with creatures, and only one objective: SURVIVE. 

Barricading myself into the buildings, pushing furniture in front of doors, and shooting the all new Lycan (Werewolf) main enemies, I quickly realized that this game was more of an homage to the Resident Evil 4 and 5 days, of horror-esque environments with tough as nails combat and an exaggerated, fun story. Don't take those words as an affront to the horror and quality of Village, however, this game can be outright dreadful, with one specific gameplay sequence reminding me more of a Silent Hill title. 

PROS:
-Unique, Gothic Horror Aesthetic
-Plenty of gross-out body horror
-Outright beautiful graphics, comparable to that of Alien: Isolation and The Witcher 3
-Combination of Resident Evil 4's action gameplay with 7's control scheming
-Fantastic, somewhat exaggerated story with interesting plot twists
-Wealth of unlocks and the inclusion of The Mercenaries optional gamemode
-1 Incredibly fun, challenging difficulty unlock

CONS:
-Controls can sometimes feel slightly loose
-No FOV options on PC (I recommend using Fluffy Mod Manager's built-in trainer)
-Performance issues with Lady Dimitrescu's daughters
-A dumbed-down Mercenaries mode

Conclusion: Resident Evil Village is definitely a step in the right direction for the series. As much as 7 captured that same classic survival horror feeling, Village does a perfect job of meshing it with action. In my opinion this is the second best action game in the series, next to Resident Evil 4.

FINAL SCORE: 9/10

Resident Evil Village is a borderline great game. Here's some pros and cons.

Pros
1. It has a great story, one of the best in the series.
2. Fun gameplay that doesn't get stale with the upgrades for your weapons and new weapons.
3. 90% of the game was extremely fun to explore.
4. One of the highest replayabilities I've ever seen in a Resident Evil game or any game for that matter.
5. Genuinely scary moments without deriving too much from the Resident Evil universe.
6. One of the more unique design of enemies and bosses of the series.
7. The references and Easter Eggs will leave long-time fans with a smile on their face.
8. The return of a fan favorite game-mode.

Cons
1. The story-line structure could've been handled better. [spoiler] The game decides to wait until the final 30 minutes to hour to explain everything. [/spoiler]
2. The one part of the game that was not fun at all for me was [spoiler] the factory. That place has boring enemy designs and was the only part I didn't want to pick everything up. [/spoiler]
3 1/2. My #1 complaint with the game is that you cannot re-explore an area that you've already been to. For example if you get done with Castle Dimitrescu and leave you cannot return until NG+. I see no story or gameplay reason as to why this is even a thing. 
3 2/2. If you didn't pick up a treasure when it becomes available, it might become locked later on. Once again, I see no reason as to why this is even a thing. For example [spoiler] the stone tablet for the Beneviento's Grave becomes locked out after a certain point in the story. [/spoiler] This genuinely frustrated me.
4. They [spoiler] never show Ethan's face, however you can view his face via a mod on nexus in the model viewer. [/spoiler]

Overall I'm really close to calling this a great game but some of the cons really make it difficult. If Capcom patches some of the issues I have and fixes gameplay problems with framedrops then I would easily call this one of my top 5 Resident Evil games.

I do recommend this game, but it does come with a disclaimer for those who came into it expecting what I did. This game is NOT a horror game like RE:7 was, but rather more an action thriller with horror elements sprinkled in. So if you are expecting that level of spookiness that 7 had you will be disappointed. Apparently Capcom had said that 7 was too scary for people, so they wanted to dial it back. I understand why they did it. Horror is not one of the most popular genres. Generally can't be marketed to children and so many adults are just wusses that can't handle more than a few chills. Basically this game was dialed back so that they could make more sales. Anyway to the review:

[h1]Enemies/Difficulty[/h1]
As mentioned above this game is more of an action thriller, but it does that part pretty well. From early on in the game they throw enemies at you at least 2-3 at a time in the more chill parts. Then when things ramp up they will come in droves. There are quite a few enemy types and none of the basic enemies are particularly hard. You just need to make sure you kite the enemies well and try not to get yourself cornered. The only basic enemy that can throw you off are the lycans, because they are pretty mobile and will actively try to dodge your shots. I won't go into the details of the boss battles, but none were a challenge and it is pretty easy to figure out their mechanics and read their patterns. I only died to one boss and it was because I hadn't figured out one part of it's sequence the first time.

The game gives you a lot of tools to deal with the more active combat style and for me at least playing on standard I hardly ever felt challenged. I haven't played it on a harder difficulty yet, but if you are like me and were expecting standard to be challenging enough, you would be wrong and should just play on hard. The main reason for this is that you are rewarded pretty handsomely for killing enemies, especially special types. Since there is a bartering feature in the game now it is smart to kill enemies for treasure so that you may upgrade your weapons, buy blueprints for crafting, and even upgrade your inventory. Speaking of which, inventory space is not an issue in this game.

[h1]Story/Puzzles/Collectibles[/h1]
Without spoiling anything I will say that the story kind of fell flat. The best part of the story and character was Lady Dimitrescu, yet your time spent in her area and the time her character got in the game was way too short lived. Two out of the four main areas you go to (aside from the village, which is like the hub) were hardly entertaining and seemed almost rushed. One of them seems interesting at first cause it's in this slightly creepy house. The focus is on puzzles, which were just okay and did not make up for the fact that it's a no combat zone basically. The puzzles throughout the game did not require much thought to solve. If you played 7 you kind of know the formula so they're ez pz. The other bad area was also so short and pointless cause neither area added much at all to the story and the "Bosses" were totally uninteresting characters. And it's not that they couldn't have been interesting, it's that the writing for these characters were just terrible and their role in the plot was insignificant. They just seemed like stepping stones rather than actual characters. The Duke is pretty cool and I thought Heisenberg's character had a somewhat interesting backstory.

Speaking of writing, Ethan's character is even more cringe than in 7. Just the things he says and some of the choices he makes are like wtf? Don't get me wrong, he's a badass as far as what he's able to accomplish, but you're just left scratching your head a lot of the time watching his character. I wish the villagers got to have a bigger part in the story, but with the way the story ended up going I can see why they didn't. If you are someone who is willing to explore and backtrack there are a lot of extra things you can find and tidbits of the story that piece together the lore. The surface of the story is ok, but when you find all those extra things it really helps flesh it out.

Miranda is hardly seen in the game, but mentioned a lot. Though for me she's kind of an afterthought in the game and her impact on my experience was insignificant. I thought the ending was pretty decent actually. It closes out this chapter of the story quite well and opens up a whole new avenue for future RE games. I have an idea of where they will be taking this next and I think it will be totally changing the RE formula.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall this is a very visually stunning game, especially the lighting and details on the characters. Personally I wish the game had more of that visceral horror we saw in 7, but as an action thriller this does hold it's own place in the RE franchise. There is a ton of replayability with this game because of the main menu shop that allows you to unlock new guns and many other things with points you earn from in game achievements. I'm looking forward to hopping back in on a higher difficulty and seeing what other challenges await in the mercenary mode.

For now I give this game a 7.5/10
