Resident Evil 8 is not only one of the best games in the entire franchise, it is also one of the best action horror games in recent memory AND a worthy tribute to its seminal predecessor, Resident Evil 4. A must-play for fans of the series and highly recommended to fans of horror games, shooters, and over-the-top dramatic storytelling.

Warning, this review will contain spoilers, but I'll spoiler tag them.

I did my playthrough on Hardcore difficulty, I went slow, explored, did nearly everything, took me 23 hours (16 hours on the in-game timer). The reason my review says around 17 hours is because the first session I did completely logged off so I could *cough* play it a bit early.

RE8 is a fantastic game. The biggest compliment I can give it is there's not a section of the game I thought was bad. There's sections I prefer, but I think the whole game is good.

I find it strangely hard to compare the game to other RE games because of how... "fresh" a take some aspects of the game are. It does lack some tonal consistency & trades this off with variety & excellent pacing. The "Village" of the game works as connective tissue to help bring it together though, I don't know if the game would've been as good if you, for example, went linear straight from area to area. The hub Village works to help transition you from the different tones of each area, I actually think without the Village the game would've been a lot worse. It's made me think a lot about game design, since in earnest the developers words of, "Theme Park of Horror" describes RE8 near perfectly.

I do notice each part of the game taps into aaspect of Resident Evil.

The opening prologue hour taps into the sorta "cinematic opening" chapters RE has been doing recently, between RE7, RE:2, RE:3.

Dimitrescu's Castle is an expansion on the "Classic RE Unlocking Survival-Horror" area, like Baker's House in RE7, or RPD Police Station in RE:2, giving a stalker enemy with rooms to solve, puzzles, shambling enemies.

[spoiler]Beneviento's House is an expansion on the Escape Room idea that RE7 had, in Lucas' Birthday Tape section, or the Banned Footage Bedroom DLC piece, except they decided to increase the horror aspect of it.

Moreau's Reservoir is basically an expansive boss fight, something the series has tried a few times to accomplish, but go through an area with the monster harassing you, ultimately ending with its boss fight. I do think his area could've done with a bit more to it, but I think it actually is the most successful attempt at "cinematic horror, monster build-up" the series has done to date.

The Stronghold actually has some of the best battle arenas in the game, & I actually ended up loving it. It felt like taking what they learned from RE4 & RE5's more intense battles, & making a few really well designed combat encounters with tension & crowd control.

Heisenberg's Factory felt like working on labyrinth-esque design & trying to blend tension further into the combat, making trickier to face monsters (a few I noticed pulled from series history, like beserk Chainsaw Majini, a little Garrador-esque for the mini-boss). Then capping it off with an over-the-top dumb but fun battle.

Chris' section feels like an expansion on the side character segments in many RE games, when they tried to go for more action-packed sequences, to make it feel good & empowering, but with new mechanical hooks to play around with in a brief exchange.[/spoiler]

And finally, the final boss & sequence just felt like they wanted to make a good final boss fight, & a better than usual RE ending.

I can actually see pretty clearly that RE8 was them further developing a lot of individual elements the series has toyed around with in the last decade, & the biggest compliment I can give RE8 is I feel it's a successful one. I think each area pretty successfully manages to be an improvement of what came before.

And I think the Village helps round it out. I've concluded I really like horror games with "small hub areas", I personally loved it in Silent Hill Downpour, Evil Within 2, & now Resident Evil Village, where there's side areas to do, mysteries to solve, hidden events off the main path to just explore. The Village in RE8 isn't big, but it's very dense, and as I said, I actually think it was the perfect solution to help connect the tonal contrast and help the game feel thematically consistant and connected, as otherwise the huge tonal whiplash between the various areas could've been done a lot more poorly.

I do think the boss fights also end up being stronger than usual for the series, it does feel there's a bit room for improvement, but the series has a rocky, uneven history with boss fights, & I can say Village has more consistently good boss fights than other entries, helped they're all pretty varied to each other.

I really like Ethan's story, [spoiler]I think the reveal how Ethan was essentially a BOW ever since the beginning of RE7, just he and no one else outside of Mia was aware of it, is interesting. It also puts an interesting spin on Mia, who seems to sympathize with BOWs, as she did with Eveline, & seems to still accept Ethan as her husband (& I guess even conceives a child with him) knowing he was essentially a perfected Molded all along.

Speaking of that, I like how RE8's ending does a lot of, "Show, don't tell," answering questions but raising a lot, & they're legitimately interesting questions & answers. I suspect RE8 will leave a lot of questions & uncertainties for the time being, but I think it makes the future of the series more interesting.[/spoiler]

RE8's story is kinda' out of focus until the last hour or so, but I think it's held up by an interesting cast of villains. I'm actually sad the RE8 villain cast only get so much screentime, each one of them felt like they had potential to do more, but that's a huge step up from boring villains the series had going for it compared to some of the recent past entries.

I know I loved RE8, but I need a bit more time to digest where I'd place it on my series chart. Most RE games have a consistent tone that kinda degrades in the last third. RE8 doesn't suffer this problem, but in exchange it switches multiple tones during its course. The Village does help connect them, but they're still quite different to each other. Village is held by its core themes, Village setting, & characters, but the actual gameplay experience goes a bit all over the place.

Compared to, say, RE7, which nailed its hillbilly found footage horror aesthetic & focus on the Baker Family, RE8 is a bit more all over the place. This leads to greater variety, & I think RE8 nails what it's going for, but it's very different, & actually makes them hard to compare for me. I think RE8 virtually solves all of RE7's problems, IE it has a good final boss fight, Chris is really interesting in RE8, new much more interesting enemies, with new enemy types introduced through the whole game, with a better back-half, but it's such a different game than RE7 in so many ways I still find it hard to compare the two.

Which I guess is also interesting, since RE8's foundation is so clearly RE7, that the fact it feels so different speaks to them doing a lot with that foundation to make it something entirely new that doesn't feel like a retread at all.

I'm very curious what fans & Capcom ultimately pull from RE8, but my immediate impressions are glowing. I think it makes the series future exciting. I think it's a very good game, a weirdly experimental RE, but a successful one.

This game did not make me sick, the environments were great, the enemies were really interesting, the sounds were top-notch, and so were the levels. I had a lot of fun going into new areas. I also really enjoyed being able to level up weapons and having no main box, just your inventory you can expand. I know those last two things were homages to RE4, but I actually haven't played that yet. And after playing this one, I really am excited to get it when 4 is remastered and released.

I really dislike stories that just plop children and women down to be used as emotional props. There's no real development, it is just expected for you to care because "SHE WIFE. SHE BABY. YOU LOVE." This says what I thought in a nutshell about Resident Evil 8: Village. I’ll warn that there will be [b][u]spoilers ahead[/u][/b] due to me talking about the storytelling, but I will put a spoiler tag over them to ensure that the game isn’t spoiled for anyone just simply looking for my talk about things that are unrelated to the plot. That being said, my enjoyment of the storytelling is critical to the high feelings and marks I have of this review. This was a game where I truly felt gratified by the experience I had from beginning to end with this game. I felt a palpable excitement for playing a horror video game. I had visceral experiences of dread. I have plenty of good things to say about this game. I can’t wait to share them. This will probably be my longest review.

✅ [h3][b] Quality development of their engine. [/b][/h3] -- I'm not a game developer and I don't think I will be, but after making a new engine with the previous game, they showed so much that they could do with it in this game. I'm sure that if I knew the mechanics behind what they're doing, I'm sure I could understand it better. We can certainly feel this with certain puzzles in the game. The puzzles with finding the balls and being able to use them to open the little colored skulls is so cool and that requires a fine attention to detail with physics in the game, I'm sure. There's a few other things too like the moving objects in the game that can go up and down. I'm thinking about the elevator in the Heisenberg section of the game and I'm trying to think of if there's an equivalent in the previous game. I know there are elevators that move up and down, but I'm not sure how difficult it is to create one that moves between three floors upon meeting certain conditions. Seems interesting. I just.. feel it. Also with the [b]hugeness[/b] of the environments in this game as compared to the previous title. Not to say that they didn't make strides with it, but this one is palpable [i] in the base game[/i] and that to me is incredible.  

✅[h3][b] A tremendously good execution of the lighting. [/b][/h3] -- If I seriously counted how many times that I said "wow this lighting is amazing." I would probably have said it about 20-30 times realistically. It was just so cool to see how the lighting of each environment was. I'm separating this as a specific bullet away from environment/atmospheres as well because of how stark it was when it came up in the game. The lighting in and of itself with the different colors just struck me as being an element that could have changed an environment entirely. Like whenever you're in the wine cellar, there's shin-high wine or blood, and everything is bathed in this diffuse red light from behind a box. I felt this tangible trepidation of "I am not at all sure about what's going to happen" and it felt really great.

✅[h3][b] Establishing shots and micro-establishing shots are amazing, as well as brilliant scenery and atmosphere. [/b][/h3] - So... what is an establishing shot? Usually this is a thing in filmmaking, but this was apparent in this game that it seemed to be a device that was used. Usually an establishing shot "sets up or establishes the context for a scene by showing the relationship between its important figures and objects." ( [url=https://filmanalysis.yale.edu/editing/#establishing] Source [/url] ) In the beginning of this game, there is somewhat of a mirror/parallel from the previous game with the opening establishing shot and the previous one. (I don't consider this to be a spoiler as I've mentioned nothing, but please comment if you find this to be frustrating or would like me to tag it.)

Lastly was going to tackle the atmosphere of this game and the scenes. Well, it certainly lives up to its name: [spoiler] it takes place in a village. [/spoiler] But I think the fact that you think about the full map of the entirety of this game versus the previous game, and you can consider just how gigantic things are in this game. Each of the houses of the Four Lords has a different atmosphere to it and creates different types of tension. It's like watching mini horror films inside of one big overarching horror film. It's masterfully done. I was satisfied. 

✅ [h3][b] Final boss fight of this game as a vast improvement from the previous installment.[/b][/h3] -- So basically there is little to no comparison between the Eveline fight in the previous game and the Miranda fight in this game. I realize that there are phases to the previous game, but I feel like you genuinely had to be strategic in this game with this fight. With the previous game it felt like I was ticking boxes like. Okay, cool.. I got that done... I bopped her and shot her. and Oh.. I got a gun, and boom, boss fight done. Whereas the thing with this game was like I was chipping slowly away at this massive health bar that wasn't apparent, I was starved of ammo the entire time, and was brought especially low with hope and everything, but eventually conquered. It was so much more gratifying, too! 

✅[h3][b] The storytelling flourishes [/b][/h3] – A robust and sprawling land filled to the brim with breadcrumbs of lore throughout. -- This is yet another section that I feel as though will be riddled with spoilers because I want to talk about it at length so I will put a spoiler over this one as well. I almost don't know where to begin?! Genuinely. I felt as though I read a wonderful novel between the Four Lords and Mother Miranda and how the previous story linked with this one. AND THE ENDING? I mean, man. I was so drained I didn't feel as though I could play anything else for a little bit and I had to get all of this out by typing it out. I was so excited by the story in this game. 

I had a preference for Karl Heisenberg as well. I liked his character and his personality most out of all of the Four Lords and Mother Miranda as well, as far as the antagonists are concerned. 

I could probably break this out so much more, but I think for now what I've really said is genuinely sufficient for at least a glance without writing much more about it.

✅ [h3][b] Difficult puzzles that left me stumped, but weren’t unintuitive. [/b][/h3] – Usually something being intuitive is part of playing a video game for me, because I would prefer things be intuitive and not forced, unless a highlight of the title is the fact that it is creatively unintuitive. In this case, it had a mixture of both. As for the puzzles, they were so much fun. I felt like they made sense and they made me think outside the box and use my critical thinking for every single time. 

✅[h3][b] Upgrade to the special edition is optional and mostly only provides cosmetic changes [/b][/h3]

✅[h3][b] Genuineness and engaging nature of the characters, immersion [/b][/h3]

➖[h3][b] Maybe the areas with The Dollmaker, Donna Beneviento and certain other areas of the game could have been longer? [/b][/h3] But this really isn't even a complaint. I'm simply trying to find something that could be improved upon. Usually if I have a direct complaint or frustration about a game, I'll address it. In this game, there doesn't seem to be much of that.

[h2][b][u] Overall [/u][/b][/h2]

I think this was a pretty good game, with a few issues keeping it from being great. Overall it was incredibly atmospheric and interesting story wise, and I think it's a better game than RE7 for sure. The first half of the game really shines, with my favorites being Castle Dimitrescu and the House of Beneviento. I feel like this section of the game was more horror based, whereas the latter half felt more action orientated. In the end it strikes a better balance than RE7 did, which is why it's a better game in my opinion.

My biggest gripes are probably some of the scripted scenarios that can be immersion breaking. In the intro there was a scripted cut scene which was meant to occur outside, however I was inside at the time causing my camera to warp through some of the textures which was pretty jarring. There was a few more examples of these, however it was only mildly irritating. My second biggest issue is some of the voice acting and sounds, which can be flat out bad at some points. The most notable ones for myself was some glass shattering in the intro, which sounded like a desktop recording, and a few lines in the closing cinematic, which had some very audible distortion over it.

Some other issues were definitely the mouse sensitivity, which I had to crank up on my mouses DPI for it to be comfortable, and the locked FOV. I had to download a mod in order to unlock and customize it, however it's pretty ridiculous a game doesn't include this in 2021; the low FOV actually made me slightly motion sick in the demo. I also had a few frame drops in some of the boss fights, however it was smooth otherwise.

Negatives aside, this game does a great job at drawing you in and keeping you interested. All of the characters were very  unique, and I felt like all of the lords had something to add without feeling out of place. The Duke was a great addition, and I really enjoyed the shop aspect and upgrading which weapons you preferred. It was also nice to see a wider variety of monsters and enemies, which was a great change up from only the molded in RE7.

Overall, I think Resident Evil Village is a pretty good game. It has a few glaring issues, however the story and atmosphere that it creates was well worth the purchase. I wouldn't call it incredibly scary, and would advise you to look elsewhere if you are only interested in the horror elements. However, if you are looking for a blend of both horror and action I think this game really scratches that itch and recommend it.

I played Resident Evil 7 very late, and after playing it I can't believe it took me so long to play it because I fell in love with the game. It was a downright terrifying game. The Baker family and their home were wonderfully terrifying and that experience enjoyable, horrific, and anxiety inducing. It was the horror experience that made me fall in love with the Resident Evil series in the first place. It wasn't a perfect game, but the core of the game was great and greater than any faults that existed. So again, I couldn't believe it took me so long to play it.

I couldn't believe, until playing Resident Evil Village, that is. Playing RE Village reminded me, for a lack of a better word, just how stupid the Resident Evil series could be. I haven't finished the game, but very early in and increasingly through the 4 hours I have played, the game is turning out to be same schlock that Capcom started pumping out for RE4, 5, and 6. 

The reintroduction of a shop and the game being littered with ammo lowers the stakes and reduces the threat considerably.  Enemies dropping money and items to sell (to support the shop mechanic) is incredibly immersion breaking, and mechanically it encourages killing enemies instead of conserving ammo and engaging in combat as a last resort.

All of the monsters come off as comically stupid and there appears to be no internal consistency to what they can and cannot do. I feels like horror-themed fantasy instead of making one conceit to build the threats that appear in the world. Going back to RE7, once you learn about what the driving force is behind all of supernatural beings you come across, it's not hard to picture that they all come from the same thing, and it feels rooted in reality (again, except for the one conceit) and is internally consistent.

Lastly, everything about the characters I've come across and the world just seems campy. Now, Resident Evil has a long history of camp and I believe the camp can be used well to relieve some tension in an otherwise tense game, but this game just overall feels like B-horror-movie campy schlock. This game has a cartoony sense of horror that is not engaging and not really all that actually scary. It's a slow, set-piece heavy first person shooter with puzzles and a Halloween coat of paint.

I guess I'll go back to being skeptical of Resident Evil releases despite how great RE7 and RE2 Remake were.

Set a few years after the events of Resident Evil 7, Village has Ethan & Mia Winters moved to Europe for a fresh start and to give birth to as well as raise their newborn daughter Rose. This peaceful family is promptly shattered when Mia Winters is shot in cold blood by none other than Chris Redfield. Ethan & Rose are scooped up but are separated shortly after and Ethan is charged with finding his daughter as he approaches this snowy village in the shadow of a foreboding castle.

Village is a 1st person survival-horror experience as a natural continuation of RE7 but does tend to feel a bit more responsive as Ethan has been studying in firearms training after the events in Louisiana. There is a lot more weapon  variety that's improved from RE7 that becomes more apparent later on in the game. Ammo can be in short supply depending on what difficulty you start with but RE8 as includes a crafting system you can use in a pinch if you have the required materials to proceed. RE8 is also much more puzzle heavy compared to previous entries in the series and was a welcome surprise as a form of downtime while still being engaged in the game.

Map variety has really stepped up as you'll have 4 main areas to tackle as you progress guarded by 4 lords. They as well as each area is very unique visually, enemy types, & even game-play at times. Enemies react differently depending on where you attack them but also approach you to attack dynamically by rolling or sidestepping as they close the distance. While this all takes place in a village, Resident Evil has never felt bigger with large maps rife with detail. Exploring houses in the village gives you an impression that they felt very lived in and the generations of people that have come and gone there.

Speaking more on visuals, the character & enemy models look fantastic. The mega-scan tech that Capcom is using looks amazing with even minor things that can be made out like eyelashes or pores and the more supernatural elements like claws & fur in fine detail.

The actors that did motion capture & voice acting did a great job here especially with some characters having starkly different heights or other different physiques to convey in the game. Music is great when used and never felt overused as you progress.

RE8 could last around 8-12 hours depending on how much of the side content you complete. When you eventually beat the game is where the extra content comes in.

You'll be rewarded with Completion Points based on what challenges you beat, similar to RE2R & RE3R. These challenges include and expand on the achievement list and the Completion Points that you get are used in the Extra Content Shop. A fan favorite mode that you can unlock is The Mercenaries, try to build up your high-score against the clock that you tackle in a handful of maps with the opportunity to gain weapon upgrades & power-ups along the way. Other unlocks from the Extra Content Shop include some exclusive weapons, infinite ammo for each weapon (that doesn't affect achievements\challenges), character models & concept art.

I'm going to include some tips that are just generally good to know before you start.
[list]
[*]The color yellow is your friend: This is expanded beyond RE7 or the remakes and could be a quest hint, breakable object or could lead you to a hidden area.

[*]Leverage those save slots: You have 20 save slots available with each of the 4 main areas & the village changing each time you return after completing one of those areas, make sure to make a separate save before you leave each main area if you want to hunt for challenges later.

[*]A few Resident Evil 4 tips are back: If you see a sparkle somewhere, shoot it. If you are out of ammo on a weapon and upgrade its ammo capacity with The Duke, it'll refill your ammo.

[*]The Animal Kingdom: Kill all animals and do not sell the meat, you'll eventually need these for passive upgrades. There are a limited amount of animals to hunt for each play-through so make sure you hunt as much as you can.

[*]Explore: As I mentioned earlier, the village changes each time you return after taking out 1 of the lords. Not just coming back with more key items that allow you to access more areas, but a few changes in familiar areas could happen too....[/list]
I really don't have anything negative to say about Village, its a fantastic game and my personal favorite so far in the series. However there is some less than ideal results in PC performance.

For some reason, the retail release performs worse than the game-play demo that was released a week ago. Ray-tracing in particular really tanks performance, I was getting a frame-rate in the single digits at times on a 3070 when enabled and yet when I enabled it the demo, the frame-rate was very smooth. Performance with Ray-tracing turned off also performs slightly worse as well compared to the demo, lowering texture memory usage helped the most but it's a baffling situation. Unfortunately, I highly doubt we'll get DLSS as a workaround since Capcom went with AMD's Fidelity technology instead.

UPDATE: Turns out Capcom had their own layer of DRM separate from Denuvo, this home-grown DRM was the source of all the strange performance issues the game has had unlike the demo. Capcom has since patched the game to either remove or perhaps turn off their DRM and performance has improved quite a bit. Denuvo is still here but doesn't have any perceivable impact, Denuvo likely will stick around for a while with RE8 DLC in development.

Resident Evil Village is a direct sequel to the very successful Resident Evil 7 Biohazard and is set in - you guessed it - a village.
The game follows the tragic story of Ethan Winters who already risked his life trying to save Mia from the mansion in RE:7. In this game though, he is on a mission to save his daughter Rosemary. 
With a 10ish hour story it's not as long as many other AAA single player titles out there but instead focuses on quality, fun gameplay and replayability. 
The main villains of village have very interesting designs and backstory to them which you discover later on in the story. The boss fights differs greatly from one another and feel hectic, fun and even disgusting at times but always manages to make you on the edge of your seat on the first playthrough, 
As for the setting they've chosen for this game, I'd definitely say that this is headed towards the right direction. The setting is very similar to a game every RE fan knows by this point which is the classic Resident Evil 4 released back in January of 2005. The game was set in a village somewhere in Spain and had us play as Leon Kennedy, the main protagonist of Resident Evil 2. The game had a very grim setting to it and felt extremely eerie at times. Although it has a 3rd person perspective, it shares a lot of similarities with Resident Evil Village. From the location to the grim setting and color scheme and many other things. This makes the game so much more enjoyable as it really feels like it fits in the REvers.
One thing I'm gonna point out though is that the story felt a bit rushed at times. It only took minutes for it to go from a bit peaceful to extremely serious and grim. I mean, (SMALL SPOILER) my man loses two of his fingers barely 20 minutes in. 
I personally think they should have eased us into the whole shebang and let some bosses get a bit more showtime before they were gone from the story. Despite this though, I'm totally fine by the pace of the story and action and absolutely love what they've done here as it ties very well into the rest of the REverse.
Speaking of action, the game focuses a lot more on action than its predecessor. 
The game lets you choose between a variety of different weapons, some of which you can unlock through completion points you get from doing challenges. The way they implemented this was extremely nice in my honest opinion as it adds a lot more depth to the game. BUT, I'd absolutely say that the game needs a harder difficulty than the "village of shadows" difficulty as the weapons that you unlock infinite ammo on makes the game way to easy.
Anyways, based on my experience I'd definitely say that this is a mix of RE:7 and RE:4 that absolutely succeeds. From RE:7s first person perspective and gory story to RE:4s village, grim setting and combat. 
This makes me very hopeful for an RE:4 remake since I think they wanted to test the waters with this game to see if people would like the direction they are headed. Especially with the setting of village.

DISCLAIMER: This game is in first person, but Capcom thought it would be best to NOT add in a FOV slider for their game, because getting motion sickness with a very narrow field of view is "mOrE CIneMaTiC!" However, there is a mod you can download to fix their game, and ultimately helped me enjoy the game significantly more. Now, let us get started -

Pros of what I thought made this game awesome:

1). The enemies. When I first heard that this game was announced, I thought this was the stupidest thing I ever heard, Lycans and Vampires. However, upon playing this game, this worked amazingly well. The Lycans are creepy, scary, and can appear at a moment’s notice sometimes without you even noticing. They are fast, they get in your face and they are relentless. The other enemies are varied, and they keep things changing, helping the game stay fresh. Especially toward the end of the game, the enemies are awesome to fight including some of the bosses, resulting in fun fights. 

2). The locations: The location that Capcom marketed the crap out of, is incredible. The Village really sets the tone right from the get-go. Everything is destroyed, ripped to shreds, houses left abandoned, giving that tense and uneasy feeling of what could be lurking behind that door or around the corner. The locations here are breathtaking at times and is fun to be exploring in. There is one location near the end of the game, that I really did not care for, it was something that I did not care about being in. And we all know the castle, another beautiful location that was very fun to explore and try to complete puzzles. The locations in this game are very memorable and a blast. 

3). Gameplay: There is a lot here, so this one I will try to keep condensed down. The game almost feels like Resident Evil 4 but in first person, the gun play is fun and fighting the enemies, which you will be doing a lot, is very enjoyable for 8 plus hours. There is a "decent" amount of weaponry in the game to kill enemies with. The new merchant you will interact with is an awesome character, not as awesome as the merchant from RE4, but there is a hidden gem that he talks about in that regard. The game play in terms of shooting mechanics is self-explanatory and pretty bog standard when it comes to first person shooters. No aim down sights unless you are using the sniper. There are things I will not spoil, but there are items for each location that you will find and be able to use in the game. I thought that was a very nice addition to the game. 

4). The exploration: This is where this game truly shines. A big component of Resident Evil has always been exploration, looking for treasures or for key items to continue with the story. This game probably has one of the best exploration components in a Resident Evil game because of the amount of it you can do, and you very well might come across some new sightings too. 

5). The characters: The characters in this game are fantastic. The last few Resident Evil games have been doing such an awesome job when it comes to their characters. I already knew the characters of RE2R and RE3R, so I knew what to expect with them and they were on point. And with this game with newer characters, they were awesome, and I really enjoyed when they appeared on screen. There are a couple that I will get into later during my complaints/negatives. But overall, I really liked most of them, that includes the new merchant as well. 

6). The Environment and tone they set I love the environment they go for in each of the levels and they all have a distinct stress and fear factor involved, always wondering when the next enemy was going to pop up. There was one location, that took this beyond my expectations and was one of the most tense and horrifying experiences I have played in a video game. Also, adore the gothic and medieval setting. I loved how they took something like that would be in Bloodborne or Dark Souls, and brought it into RE. The best part, it works. 

My complaints and negatives of the game:

1). This is the first complaint or negative aspect that I will combine into one, because I believe they are both just as bad as one another. That is the aspect of first-person camera views in a Resident Evil game. One of my biggest fears with RE7 was that was going to create a terrible new trend in Resident Evil where first person becomes a focal point, and the survival horror elements go out the window. While focusing on more horror like Outlast and Amnesia. Resident Evil can and HAVE done their games in 3rd person and made them scary, a prime example is Resident Evil 2 Remake. They showed that it can be done, and now with RE8, who knows when they will drop this garbage first person perspective from this awesome series. There were times I completely forgot I was playing a Resident Evil game, that is because of the camera angle and who our terrible main protagonist is. 

Continued...

The second part is Ethan Winters. In fact, the whole Winters family is terrible. The thing about this game is that it tried so much to be a Resident Evil 4 spiritual successor, but they have this bland, unfunny, boring personality of a character as a main protagonist instead of someone like Leon. I honesty could not care or less about the Winters story, his backstory, everything. At least with Leon, in RE4 specifically, when he made a funny one liner, he was funny and never took himself too seriously. Capcom, stop putting in main protagonists that represent "the player", I do not want to play as a character that more or less "represents the player" like Outlast or Amnesia does. I have those games, if I wanted something like that, I would go play them or Penumbra. This is Resident Evil, give me a legendary character like Chris, Jill, Leon, or Claire, etc. Not this character that we cannot put a face to, it's stupid, and doesn't work in RE.

2). Any bugs/glitches, or bad game design? No bugs or noticeable glitches. There were times where bad game design came into play. There was a section later in the game where I was exiting a corridor and if enemies were to appear, all I would have to do is back pedal and they were not able to follow me farther into the corridor, so they would just run away. In that same instance, the enemies ran away, stopped and were looking away from me. So, I proceeded to shoot them, and they did not even react, they just stood there until they died. And that is not the only instance, it happened multiple times where if you back peddled into a certain room or hallway, the enemies would not follow, they will just go back to walking around forgetting you are even there. I was able to cheese a few enemies, including some powerful ones. C'mon Capcom. If you were not able to do that in 2005 for RE4 and cheesing enemies was not allowed, you could not do it in a game that was released in 2021? Unreal. It honestly just took me out of the moment at times. 

3). The opening hour or so, is a drag.

4). The audio: There were times that the audio was terrible. The gun sounds sucked and sounds like there is no depth to them. One instance there at the start of the game, where a loud crash was heard, made me chuckle more than it did frighten me. I wear a pair of 7.1 surround sound headphones because audio is very important in video games. But this effect sounds like some cheap effect they pulled off the internet somewhere. Even the crows sounded terrible sometimes. Plus, on some of the characters, it almost sounds like as if you can still hear them in the recording booth, the editing seems like it was hit and miss. 

5). The music, or lack thereof: There was only two major sections in the game where I noticed any decent noticeable soundtrack playing. Other than that, its atmospheric sound effects.

Overall, with my complaints of how I feel about this game, and if you're a not a Resident Evil fan or have been playing since the 90's, I still think the game is great, a must buy.

PLEASE NOTE: I am typing this review with full intentions to explain in moderate depth a personal review of this game. I do not intend to post spoilers- but Reader, please be advised!

At time of review- I had just finished the first story run. Completion consists of Story, handful of collectibles, and a bit of Mercenaries game play to get a full taste. This review is to break down my pros and cons (if any) Also note- I am a long time Resident evil Fan. 

Now, some of you may have Played RE 7: Biohazard as your first and only installment in the series due to the first person and totally different perspective aspect. I completely understand that. And with that, Resident Evil 8 is exactly the same.. eh, well, mostly. If you experienced the emotional roller coaster that was 7, you can recall the jump scares, nerve shredding tense moments, and all of the above that made it a great title. This time, the details unravel, you get a better look at the story and continuation of Ethan Winters, and FOR YOU RE LOVERS OUT THERE- some loose ends that finally get tied after what I found (No comment due to potential spoilers) as some gaps or oddities that yes, RE has known to carry.. but also lacking explanation in the entirety of RE7.

A con for some would be the lack of storage or stash containers that you find in select chapters of RE:7, but the older fans like me fully enjoyed the use of sole inventory like previous titles themselves, with the ability to expand inventory in exchange for Lei ( in game currency.) Another con, yes.. the cheeky reviews were right- The boss fights were EASY. and I mean Barely lift a finger and just shoot the mf type easy. Pro to this? The story telling in each fight was phenomenal. 

Like ALL resident evil games, lore is everything. I will say it again with more meaning.. THE LORE IS EVERYTHING. This story is one of it's own, but please take the time to look at as many files, docs, pictures, pages, etc that you can possibly find in game. Backstories, total linkage, etc will make perfect sense if you do. Everything really had a purpose and although the story explains the surface... that is all it really will do unless you dig in and read. I honestly completed the story in 7 hours- and spent the other 3 just reading all I could find. CONTEXT but no intend to spoil- Close to the end of game, you will find a rather legendary piece of lore and if you read it, you know. I loved RE:7.. but I did feel the lead to this game was a major curiousity.. and it was. It was worth the wait. SERIOUSLY.

For some context of what I value in my Resident Evil games, here's my updated franchise rankings:
[olist]
[*]RE1:Remake
[*]RE2
[*]RE3
[*]RE0
[*]RE1
[*]RE:CV
[*]RE3:Remake
[*]RE2:Remake
[*]RE4
[*]RE7
[*][b]RE8[/b]
[*]RE5
[*]RE6 (the only game I [b]DON'T[/b] recommend playing)
[/olist]

[u]Pros[/u]
[list]
[*]I enjoyed the moment to moment gameplay more than RE7. Having much less of a focus on unkillable enemies does wonders for the fun factor.
[*]The inventory management solved the inventory bloat problem from games like the RE2 remake by not cluttering up your limited inventory space with key items and crafting ingredients. No more getting mad that you picked up EVEN MORE gun powder.
[*]I loved some of the boss designs. I love monsters and this game had some really freaky looking ones.
[*]The graphics are great. I still don't have an RTX card but I imagine this game looks even better with ray tracing.
[*]I like having some defensive options in games. The guard system in this gives the players another mechanic to juggle that makes combat more engaging. It does feel a little OP when upgraded though.
[/list]

[u]Cons[/u]
[list]
[*]There are critical parts of this game's story that completely fall apart if you think about them at all. Giant franchise timeline events are shoehorned in. It also paves the way for RE9 to have some RE6 levels of nonsense.
[*]Its direct connection to RE7 made me like that game less. RE4's fun but dumb, franchise poisoning ass just jumped up a spot in my rankings.
[*]The game gets very action heavy as it goes on. One boss fight in particular is super out of place. There were parts that just made me want to play RE4 if it's going to just lean into action over horror.
[*]The game feels very fragmented in both story and gameplay depending on the area you're playing through. The whole castle area is the clear winner for me. The remaining 6 or so hours of the game didn't capture that same feeling I was hoping for.
[*]The map for the main village area is trash. You are going to get lost thanks to the map not marking things like blocked roads.
[*]Why can't I drop one item over another in my inventory? Diablo 1 solved this issue in 1996.
[/list]

Big Resident Evil Fan here, could not of been more excited for this title after a couple of years of remakes (Albeit, fantastic remakes.)

First off I'll start by saying that this game is gorgeous. During the entire run I was constantly stopping to comment on the weathered, worn and lived in textures of the environments. Character models, skin and clothing look fantastic but the games biggest strength is in its lighting which is absolutely mind blowing. It definitely sets the scene in all exterior and interior environments.

Secondly, I will agree with most people that I just cant get behind Ethan Winters. Ethan has almost no charisma or likeability and the way he reacts to what is going on just isn't realistic and makes no sense...it's almost as if he is self aware and realises that he is a video game character. The fact that Capcom goes to extreme lengths, even in official pictures to not give Ethan a face provides even more of a disconnect. I like Mia though. And I really don't see the obsession with Lady Dimitrescu, like how could people find that attractive and not Mia??.

The story is kinda predictable but I felt was more enjoyable then RE7. Chris definitely is the most enjoyable character in this game by far but by this point in the series canon he is 48 years old and you start to wonder about how much longer he can keep doing this. I look forward to hopefully seeing Claire, Jill and Leon in upcoming games but with there characters ageing it seems like we need some new characters. At times I thought this game was scarier than 7 but then it would feel like a full blown action game...

Overall I would say the story seems to close the Umbrella arc and take the franchise in a new direction although I am still undecided if I like where it is going. If anything but the time the credits rolled I kinda missed the whole umbrella, t virus zombies and Racoon City/Lab aspects of RE. I will end this review by saying that I probably like this game more than 7 and would play it over it but its not a vast improvement, but any resident evil fan should definitely play it.

This is one of the best games in the Resident Evil series. Many complain that it's much slower and tedious than the previous games, but that for me is what makes it so unique. I'll answer some problems that people seem to ask me.

Q: The game is not fun in first-person mode.

A: Yes, the game is annoying in this mode, but personally, it makes the game a whole lot scarier. You'll be spending most of this game in dark hallways and crowded spaces, and third person wouldn't work well here. Sure, if this game was an RPG, first person would not be the best choice, but this mode is the perfect experience for a horror game.

Q: This game is really slow.

A: Again, this is correct. Village is way slower than the other games. Ammo is scarce and enemies are uncommon. But this is what makes it so fun and different. Taking your time through these long and beautiful roads and slowly worrying what's going to happen next. That's why I love this game so much. You never know what crazy thing will happen next.

Q: The story is bad

A: Not really. Sure, it's not perfect, but it's extremely creative and interesting for a horror story. Ethan is definitely not a memorable character, but Capcom is aware of this, so the game is more focused on the side characters and villains, like the sisters and Lady Dimitrescu (or as the Internet calls her, Tall Lady). 

Q: The boss fights are boring.

A: Yes. That is one of the weaker aspects of Village. The boss fights aren't anything amazing, or nothing we haven't seen. But absorbing them in first-person, along with some of the puzzles and lore behind the bosses, is why I wouldn't judge the game too hard off of this.

Q: The game isn't scary

A: I can understand that compared to Resident Evil 7, this game pulled less jumpscares and such, but I wouldn't say it's "not scary." There are plenty of moments that made me shiver down my spine. 

This game is worth buying 100 percent. Village is a perfect game for fans and first-timers to the series, with it's perfect controls, it's beautiful graphics, and it's creepy tone. I highly recommend this game (and that's not just because of Tall Lady).

Resident Evil 8 The Village is a good game. That's it, that's all there is to say really. It's just good, not great, not amazing, but good. It tries to be like its big brother, 4, but it just falls so short. In fact, if I closed my eyes, I could probably imagine playing as Leon hunting down Ashley in a nondescript Spanish countryside. Instead, I open my eyes and see myself as Ethan hunting down his daughter Rose in a nondescript <insert European region here> countryside. Both 4 and 8 have castles, they both have a mysterious magical cult, but there are a few inherent differences between both of them.

[u]Let's start with the negatives shall we?[/u]
1. I hate self-insert characters in a series like Resident Evil. Ethan in Resident Evil 7 was just weird to me, I didn't like it then, didn't like it now, but at least the storyline provides adequate reasoning for him to be the main character this time rather than Chris or Leon or Jill or any of the other characters I love.

2. Lady Dimitrescu is abhorrently over-hyped. Like, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I LOVE BIG VAMPIRE WAIFU, but, first boss? There's a challenge that requires you to kill her in under 5 minutes? If you paid attention to the ad campaign, she was a fan favorite and everyone wanted to know more about her. They played her as this grand figure that would be involved for a good portion of the game, but then just kinda uses her as a knock-off Mr. X/Tyrant from Resident Evil 2. I want so much more about her, I want to know who she was before she became the giantess. She has to be more interesting than just the first boss.

3. Consistent bugs. I've discovered at least 4 consistent bugs in the game, 3 of which can make the game impassable at certain areas, but can be fixed with save/reload mechanics. Mainly, the biggest culprit, is a monster in "Chapter 3" that gets stuck in a hallway and blocks the exit.

4. The Settings Menu. RTX Mode resets your graphics settings and the graphics themselves can look like Playstation 2 graphics at times. It's weird, like, the first time you get into the game you of course fiddle with the graphics settings to make sure you're getting the best experience and what-not, but it took me about 5 minutes to set up graphics. I get in game, the graphics look almost PS1 era. Back to the menu, I see RTX mode set to "Off", so, I flip it to "On". All my settings reset, I don't notice this because it's not that apparent. Back to game, now I'm in PS2 era graphics. Go back to menu, fix all the graphics settings after another 5 minutes, back to game, and the graphics are now tolerable. Get to a point in the game where they give me a gun. Up until this point, I had assumed that aim/look sensitivity was contextual, you know, like, because I wasn't in a spot with danger they turned the sensitivity down. Nope, it's slow as hell all the time. Back to the options menu. Find the mouse sensitivity, crank that bad boy to 11, and boom, doing great. Wait, no I'm not, because there is a SEPARATE SETTING FOR AIMING SENSITIVITY! Back to the options menu, set that to 11, and finally, the game is playable.

5. Chris Redfield - Why is he a ♥♥♥♥? Why is he a military genius? In Resident Evil 1 he was an ex-military marksman who joined STARS and then joined BSAA and started travelling the world destroying bio-weapons. Since when did he become some badass super soldier? I know, nit-picking, but I never really pegged Chris for the "tall, dark, and brooding super soldier" type, you know?

6. [spoiler]MOLD? REALLY?![/spoiler] You can always tell when the writers start to run out of ideas. They reuse old concepts, they stay away from anything new or anything too old, and they just beg for dear life that no one asks any questions. Umbrella is hardly mentioned, BSAA is tossed around willy-nilly, viruses are passe, and anything that isn't supremely over-the-top isn't worth mentioning or doing. Just get to the final boss and you'll see what I mean. [spoiler] When your boss is literally capable of creating giant MOLD TENTACLES that can tear up the Earth within a 10 km radius, how in the ♥♥♥♥ is that not a "SEND IN THE ARMY" moment? How does no one notice these villages just going poof, or that these villages happen to even exist?! [/spoiler]

[u]Now, not everything about this game was a negative, so let's look at the positives:[/u]
1. This is a decently fun game, it has some awesome creep factor (Chapter 3 (the second boss) in particular gave me flashbacks to the Seaside Hotel from Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines. I literally had to pause the game, stand up, and walk away to collect myself. The fights are fun, the gameplay is challenging, and it feels like Resident Evil 4's younger, less cool brother.

2. Lady Dimitrescu - Seriously, she's probably my favorite character of the game simply for the amount of character development they put into her. In fact, all of the bosses were just fun. They each had their own quirks, their own personality, and aside from some voice acting issues from Heisenberg's weird gameshow host voice, I love all the bosses. They needed way more character development like Lady D got, but each one is memorable... Except Moreau... Moreau was just... weird. You'll understand when you see him.

3. The Meta - There are a lot of references to previous games. The merchant makes a joke about "What are you buying?" from Resident Evil 4, during Heisenberg's fight, he makes a passing mention at Chris' boulder-punching past (I swear, I feel like I hallucinated that moment, but I know it's there!), and the big reveal at the end [spoiler]where they explain why Ethan has survived everything from Resident Evil 7, including that he regrew his fingers and hand (which he loses again during this adventure), because he's made of magic moss [/spoiler]. The Meta elements in this game are fun, but can break immersion if you're someone who really likes that in a game.

4. It is a different kind of Resident Evil. The fact that Ethan is some faceless protagonist and is some weird self-insert for the player, I had a hard time connecting with this game. Resident Evil has always been, "Here's Chris/Jill/Leon/Claire, they are trapped in a nightmare, now help them survive", but RE8 gives the feeling of a diet version of Outlast 2. It's creepy, but not scary. It's less survival-horror, more action-horror. It has story, but it's not story-based. I think that this being different from RE2, RE3, and RE4 is a positive. It gives Capcom some new directions. They don't have to always stick with their roster of characters, they can throw a new character in every so often, and when they do, it can wind up being fun.

5. Replayability. While, technically, this game has slightly less replayability than RE4, but theres still some great reasons to play RE8 more than once. It's a chance to unlock guns, infinite ammo, and bonuses like concept art and character models.

So, for my final ruling, I'd say if you really want to play it, then go play it right now, but other wise, I'd wait a bit to see if the price drops or if any DLC makes some more fun available. As I said at the beginning, this is a good game, but it's just that, just good.

Resident Evil Village is definetly worth getting. 

Some people are complaining that it's not enough like RE7. What these people want is a "boo! haunted house" format of horror game with almost zero gameplay where it's essentially like a big interactive movie. RE: Village has parts that are like this, but does not overinvest in it. It also does not make the mistake of being too action oriented where you are bombarded by mobs constantly taking all the horror and suspense out of it like RE: 5. 

RE: Village I believe delivers a very balanced experience of survival horror where there are parts with a lot of gameplay and action, but it takes time to build up some suspense so when you get to the action it has more impact.

The atmosphere of the game is awesome. This it does very well. It is incredible to look at visually. The controls are not the best though, but I don't think it ruins the experience. When you are running away from a giant monster you aren't sitting there thinking about how the movement is a little clunky.

The biggest downside of the game for me personally was the fact that it takes a very long time to find all the items hidden within the levels. They really seem to want you to stay in each area for awhile and explore, but I wish they would of made items a bit easier to find so the pacing isn't constantly broken up by searching every nook and cranny of a room to find one tiny jewel embedded on the ceiling or a piece of scrap metal in the corner that blends in with the wall behind it.

The payoff though is well worth it. The game does a great job of putting you in the setting and it's a pretty wild ride from start to finish. Once you get into the world the game puts you in you will quickly forget about all it's minor flaws.

Resident Evil Village is the 8th main installment of this series, and it brings some awesome things to the table.  I was very close to giving it a 10/10 for the first few hours I played, but some glaring issues came about that kept bugging me and hindered my enjoyment of the game.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
-Resident Evil 4 inspired inventory and gameplay that is great to see return.
-Beautifully crafted, varied environments.
-An interesting story that kept me engaged which continues the events of Resident Evil 7 directly.
-Exciting combat counters with punchy weapons.
-Some intense boss fights.
-Guarding is required more often in this game compared to RE7 which keeps you on your toes.
-New characters that are mostly interesting and likeable.
-Tall Vampire Lady!!  Jokes aside, Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters were awesome.  [spoiler]I think they should have been the main antagonists like the marketing for the game made it seem.  I didn’t care about Mother Miranda as much[/spoiler].
-Some earned scares, and moments where I really felt afraid.

[h1]Things I was mixed on:[/h1]
-Kind of silly, but you can't assign the Mr. Raccoon/Mr. Everywhere charms on more than 1 weapon, the first pistol and first shotgun.  That just seemed strange to me.
-Base enemies don’t feel that varied.  They all behave pretty much the same way, but have a different model to fit the area they’re in.
-Some parts leaned too much towards the action side of things, and felt more on-the-rails than I would have liked.  I get nervous when that happens in this series, because I don’t want it to go back in the direction of Resident Evil 6.
-The game frequently told me I could press LB to push an enemy away, but I couldn't get it to work at all.  I tried several times but I just never got the timing of it.  As of 5-10-2021, I still don't have the achievement for doing it once lol.  
-Story issue: [spoiler] Chris being really mean to Ethan for the first 3/4ths of the game, and not filling him in on what was happening on despite having ample opportunity to do so.  It’s like he reverted back to meanie pants poopy face alcoholic amnesia Chris from RE6.  This is only made worse by how they acknowledge it towards the end of the game, where Ethan and another character say Chris should have told Ethan what was going on.  Yet, despite those moments of the story’s self-awareness, it doesn’t provide any meaningful reason as to why Chris acted the way he did.  It basically just boils down to ‘he messed up’ because he’s human and his emotions got the better of him.  That plot point can work very well in some stories, but it falls flat here.[/spoiler]. 
-The story moves [i]very[/i] quickly towards the end of the game despite moving pretty slowly for most of it.  It suddenly goes from 0-100 and throws so many revelations at you I found it kind of hard to keep up.
-The voice lines for Chris and Heisenberg lacked good direction at some points.  The actors did great work with what they were given.  But, there were some lines where if I was the director I would've called for re-recordings.  The most notable one for me was when Chris is talking to [spoiler]Mia about Ethan being gone, towards the end of the game[/spoiler], and he sounds like he has a Boston accent.  I felt like that delivery just didn't work for Chris's character.  There were also times with Heisenberg where his sentence inflections really stood out to me as odd, but this may have been intentional.  
-The RE4-style inventory is really cool, but it doesn’t work as well as it did in RE4.  In RE4, if you were moving an item and pressed the button to place it down over another item, for most item pairs it would swap them so you place down your currently held item and pick up the other one.  This was useful if you wanted to place a gun in a spot but there was a grenade somewhere in that space – it would put down the gun and pick up the grenade so you could put it somewhere else.  In Village, this [i]only[/i] happens with ammo over other ammo, after pressing the button multiple times.  This got frustrating fast, as my muscle memory from RE4 kept kicking in (I beat it 3 times before Village came out).  It makes organizing the inventory slower.
-The game is really linear.  There is rarely a moment where you have to stop, look at your item inventory, and think about what you have to do to progress.  The way forward is always pretty clear.  It makes the Resident Evil 4 influence obvious, and I felt like it didn’t work as well for this game.  It’s still a really well done game world and its areas flow from one to the next.  But, the no-loadscreen open world design gives the impression that it will be more like a bigger version of the RPD from RE2 Remake or the Baker House of RE7, where you’re having to run back and forth through areas you’ve opened to solve new puzzles as you acquire more key items.  I suppose this could be true about the Village in the middle, but [spoiler]you really just run through it aside from unlocking some bonuses.  Nothing mission critical is present there after the beginning of the game[/spoiler].

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
-Mia. In RE7, she was a badass double agent who put up a cute wife façade for Ethan while fulfilling her own Ada Wong-style agenda with her other secretive work.  In this game, [spoiler]she gets completely sidelined, and turned into a damsel in distress.  Her involvement in the Eveline mold project is never explained.  She does nothing noteworthy and gets no development because for most of the game you think she’s dead[/spoiler].  I wasn’t a huge fan of that.
-Sometimes after getting grabbed by an enemy, another one would grab me immediately after I got let go, before I could get a chance to guard or heal.  Uncommon, but really lame when it happened.  Broke immersion.
-We still do not get to see [spoiler]Ethan’s face, despite there being a cutscene where he is with Chris where there was a perfect opportunity to do so – we see 95% of his head, just not his face.  Literally all he had to do was look up at Chris while he spoke, but for some silly reason he just looks at the ground[/spoiler].  That really annoyed me because it felt like we were going to see it, and then we don’t.  
-[spoiler]Lady Dimitriscu (and her daughters)[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Heisenberg[/spoiler] were criminally underused.  I felt like you could’ve cut out [spoiler] House Beneviento and Moreau’s Resevoir [/spoiler] entirely to focus more on expanding [spoiler]the Castle and the Factory[/spoiler].  On that note, I found the castle to be really short despite marketing making it seem like it would be one of the game’s main recurring areas, which was disappointing since it and Lady Dimitrescu are two of the best things about this game.  I really didn’t like that [spoiler]it’s completely blocked off once you leave and you are not allowed to go back.  Why?  I could understand if the game was even more like RE4 where you completely leave the village/castle and go to another place, but you don’t.  The castle just sits there, barring you from entry[/spoiler].  Lame.

Despite my criticisms, I did enjoy my time overall with Resident Evil Village.  It is a welcome entry to the series and a polished experience.  It's an impressive feat to keep the series feeling fresh and fun despite being over 20 years old. It's not a bad game, it's a good game in its own right. It's just not a great Resident Evil game.

Resident Evil 7 brought the series back to life, RE2 Remake was the best yet, RE3 Remake was pretty good despite some content cuts, and now Resident Evil Village continues the trend of excellence. Where RE7 leaned closer to old-school Resident Evil, Village plays more like RE4. It is more action oriented but still feels like a Resident Evil game, with plenty of scary moments.

You play as Ethan once again. He is still not the most compelling protagonist, but his character is improved this time. The story continues from RE7, and Ethan is once again thrust into chaos. The areas are diverse and interesting, and the enemies are varied and numerous. Unlike the Molded in RE7, which became repetitive, Village keeps fights fresh with a wide range of enemies. Most boss fights are fun and engaging, and the merchant system from RE4 works very well here.

The first person gunplay is solid, and the story is compelling enough to make you wonder where the series will go next. The game also includes a free mode called Mercenaries Mode, where you defeat as many enemies as possible while collecting new abilities and weapons. This mode is fun and unlocks after completing the story.

I really enjoyed this game, even more than RE7, though I still consider RE2 Remake the best. Resident Evil Village is a strong entry and a must play for any Resident Evil or horror fan.

Summary / SPOILERS
I wasn't really looking forward to more Resident Evil, although it is perhaps the only game franchise I have any interest in anymore aside from Elder Scrolls. But I got the game anyway since I probably won't buy another game in years. I really liked the idea of returning into the world of Dracula Resurrection game but in a more dynamic manner, though honestly RE7's story was pretty conclusive so I wasn't jumping from excitement. The first moments of the game were really bleh with a long walk in a tiny path fogged by blizzard that I expect from a Steam greenlight asset flip. In the town the game picked up and the game's really solid combat and gameplay were instantly enjoyable. At first I need to cower in the broken houses with my handful of ammo, nervous of where are all the noises coming from and if the beasts will come through roof or window or floor. I'm pushed in cold water as I need to learn to swim in unfamiliar environment against savage predators. The barricade system and flour sacks are a great addition to the normal shoot or run gameplay familiar from RE7 along with the upgrade system. 

The intro is even a bit too busy with the survivors who conveniently get all killed, making me sigh along with Ethan. After that the gameplay is kind of uneven but mostly good. As the game calms down and I learn the ropes and gain control, it never stops being satisfying to shoot a couple of rounds into enemies' knees to make them stumble, followed by a couple of headshots, or a shotgun blast directly to the face or playing cat and mouse with the terminators luring them to show their weak spot. The game has plenty of puzzles and various kinds from key finding to pushing objects to deciphering poems, all of which I enjoyed a lot and improves on RE7. Otherwise too the game has variety, from the packs of beasts wandering around the town to the few immortal vampires inside the castle to the huge frog fish to the near indestructible robot-men to the mind games. All of the segments are excellently crafted, but it is too formulaic and gamey. I didn't care for the Grimm/Fable/Nightmare before Christmas type of intro and when Duke explained to me how the game will play out: These are the guys in the game, I mark them on your map, you need to kill them, and oh there are also lot of other collectibles I will also mark on your map. Even before that, while I greatly enjoyed Dimitrescu's castle, her daughters very nearly felt like nameless lieutenants in any subpar open world game and the multiple "get multiple keys and bring them in this one room" certainly didn't help. At that point the game efficiently lost me, it felt like I'm suddenly playing Fable or Arkham Origins or Assassin's Creed instead of a very story-centric and unpredictable horror game. I thought I understood why the game is called Village instead of VIII, Capcom kind of was lazy and didn't dare to call this actual VIII. So the game is lucky that the following hours with the actual bosses and levels were so well done because this could have ended ugly. But the Silent Hill orphanage is a very tense and disturbing mockup, the vomiting frog prince RE4 fish tribute also has its moments plus the boss fight with acid rain and blocked paths is exciting. 

After that "hiatus", Heisenberg finally actually shares some story even though he is also kind of annoying Joker-wannabe with his ridiculous signs and whatnot, or as if Capcom wanted to add Dante into RE universe. But the trip to lycan den to wipe out their leader and destroy the tribe is the moment the game kicks into high gear for me and I felt like Neo even though death was always near. Afterwards Heisenberg's factory setting fits Resident Evil with heavy iron hell vibe, and it kept the high quality for the rest of game. The game starts to have good, although half predictable twists, Chris Redfield comes back and totally redeems his so-so appearance in RE7. Now Chris looks like believably aged version of RE5-66 Chris and he also sounds to be in the same ballpark. This amount of of 2% veteran badassery vs. 98% "squeeze your pistol and fear" is exactly the right ratio, although Capcom still doesn't quite nail the concept of "squadmates". I was delighted that RE8 is confirmed to have tight roots with Oswell's legacy and the lore from RE1-RE6, although it was like 1 room that contained all the lore so it's like Capcom ticking yet more boxes, at this point the laboratories at the end of games telling everything is a bit of a predictable trope I hope something is done about, though same time I really enjoyed it. The finale of Ethan coming back was kind of predictable considering the lengths his regeneration went to especially in this game, but the way it happened even without heart and the outcome certainly wasn't as I was expecting him to become a boss or triumph. The end boss is one of the better ones in the franchise with cool hellraiser vampire morpher thing and the moments after it were really touching. It wasn't Chris who passes the mantle to the new hero, but actually Ethan was doomed and went face to face with death in a way Mass Effect 3 wishes they handled Shepard. Ethan put down a demi-god with his last strength, knowing he is probably doomed anyway and let Chris and others carry the torch. 

The game was a good 11 hours long with a very conclusive and satisfying end that clearly ends this game but leaves room for interesting ways for the story to go. Mercenaries and the other unexpected unlocks at the end were a cherry on the top. Graphics are good with some really nice romanian town and castle scenery and it runs well even on my quite weak PC, although there is some desyncing with cutscene animation and voice acting present. Audio is good quality and A.I. never felt broken but contributed a lot to the suspense. So in short I'm extremely satisfied having paid full price for RE8, and even though this would be a fitting swansong, I'm still interested in seeing what RE9 will be. They have interesting immediate options, Chris is back as a leader and despite some setbacks this game has good foundation and enough effort and creativity to make another game work. 

But I really hope they are done with the Grimm thematics: the accursed doll girl, the fish king comic relief, the giant mobster merchant and the animation book all were blergh. To me Resident Evil is about urban and science based horror, which can be augmented with some mysticism smokescreen, but this many smokescreens in one place doesn't work and it just feels like gipsy magic and that soon our main character grows angel halo or devil horns depending how you play. Also while I like Metroidvania, not every game needs it, at least not in the Assassin's Creed way. Fighting against the same boss 3 times, who never learns of her previous (sister's) downfall is bad. Having 15 conveniently placed wells all with the same mechanics and contains is bad. Having a jokey storyteller telling me what is the plot of the game and then sending me to it almost without surprises is bad. Having a GPS map with exact statistics of which rooms still contain undiscovered things in a transylvania based game is bad. Fortunately the game doesn't tell me when is the point of no return so while I was sort of OCD about collecting the things (but after a while decided that keeping the horror universe alive in my mind is more important than collecting gems and meat), at one point it became impossible and then I just went on enjoying the plot as it unfolded. Otherwise I would still be collecting the things and ruining the feel of this horrific world. For when I'm running the same town streets for the 30th time without enemies, or with the same rinse and repeat respawning enemies, the game turns into a life-tourist-egg-hunt-simulator and not horror.  Anyway, Resident Evil Village still keeps the series going strong, which makes the series special. Are numbered games and many spin-offs are great or better.

Storyline, dialogue and horror elements could be improved but it's a really good action thriller title. 
Combat feels very responsive and deliberate and the weapon/resource progression is satisfying, even if it doesn't take too long to go through the story. 

It's got good pacing between fights as well, giving you enough breathing room to explore, gather items, read bits of backstory and solve puzzles while still giving enough tension and enemy encounters to keep you invested. Feels a lot like a mixture of RE: 7 and RE: 4 Combined together. 

An odd downside is that the game isn't too difficult, at least on normal so far. Resources are forgiving and enemies have a tougher time reaching you. And even when they do, blocking (or headshotting to stun them), nullifies or even prevents damage being dealt in the first place. For veteran players, you might as well start off on Hardcore. It's a small nitpick however.

The game also seems to be pretty short which can be seen as either a good thing or bad thing. You could argue that since it's short it's more replayable and might even bring more reason to attempt speedruns or new game+ modes, along with other personal challenges or 100% runs. But again, still subjective. So if you were looking for a very long, thought out and intricate story you might find that elsewhere. Despite some technical issues that will hopefully be addressed in the near future (and no FOV slider in a first person game in 2021? wtf capcom), this is a very good game. At first I was a little bit worried due to the amount of cinematics used within the first hour of the game, but I had faith that the game would become a bit less overly scripted, and it did. 

I think there's something to appreciate about a big triple A release deciding not to fill their game with a ton of bloat for the sake of making the customer feel like they got their money's worth. RE Village aims to be a fun, replayable game that respects the intelligence of the player, and for the most part I think it succeeds. There is some flaws here and there, and I think the opening could have been structured a little better, as it doesn't give the most amazing first impressions in my opinion, but once the game opens up, it's a whole lot of fun. 

One thing I have to say though is that if you're on board the Dimitrescu hype train, this game is probably going to disappoint you.  I was personally never really attracted to her at all (but found her endearing in a campy way), so it's not a disappointment to me, but it's clear that Capcom saw the popularity of the character on the internet and decided to roll with it in the game's marketing, making the game's marketing a little bit deceiving. I've seen some reviews of this game negatively impacted by this one aspect. While I think that's a shame, since I think there's a great Resident Evil game here, I can understand the frustration a little bit. 

As a Resident Evil game, I absolutely love it. Sure, it trips up in a few areas (there's a couple points I don't look forward to on replays), but most RE games do. Besides the RE3 remake, Capcom has been really consistent with their output for the last 4 years. I think it really says something when I have a really hard time deciding whether RE7, RE2 remake, or RE8 is my favorite RE Engine Resident Evil game. 

TL;DR If you liked RE7 and RE2 remake, I don't see how you could dislike this game.
