[h1] This game is interesting. As an RE fan, I am quiet conflicted about it. [/h1]

This game feels very, and I mean very, heavily inspired by RE4. So let's just get that out of the way, if you enjoyed RE4, you will love this game. If you are not an RE4 fan, keep reading as this game might still be an RE game you enjoy. 

Now if you've read this far, I will go over why I am so torn about this game. 
Overall I would give this game a positive review, giving it a solid 7.5-8 out of 10 for a modern RE fan. 

[b]The parts I enjoyed: 
Overall good story, especially if you played RE7. 
Well designed puzzles. 
Really well designed characters (Except Chris, it feels like he was thrown in there as a fan service).
Beautiful art style and graphics. 
Incredible Atmosphere of each level. 
Incredible sound staging and design. 
If you can get over the fact that this is more of a shooter than a horror game, then the guns are actually well balanced. 
Each weapon has it's own use and feels distinct. 

Things I really didn't like about this game: 
The very heavy influence of RE4 made this feel in a lot of parts as more of a shooter first, horror second type of game. 
The AI for some of the monsters on the hardest difficulty, just doesn't make sense. It feels hard just to be hard, rather than due to properly well designed monster AI. 
Certain levels on the hardest difficulty just feel like a zombie horde shooter, where you will go through ALL of your ammo, healing and ect, unless you cheese the encounters by some mechanic. Basically, it feels like this game was designed to be played on the standard difficulty, and then the monsters are just made bullet sponges the higher the difficulty you go. 
AWFUL, and i mean AWFUL UI design. I understand that they made it for consoles, but if you had the time to spend making this game as beautiful as it is graphically, which is obviously designed for PC, then the least you could do is proper UI design. It's borderline unusable with a mouse and keyboard. [/b]

My favorite parts of the game, where the 1st, 2nd lords, and to a lesser degree but still enjoyable the 3rd lord, as well as the in-between exploration and puzzle solving. My least favorite thing was the opening level, it's borderline unwinnable on the hardest difficulty, unless you cheese the level, and I do mean cheese it. If you play it as it's meant to be played, you will die, over and over again. And the 4th lord, including everything leading up to him. It's just a shooter, and not a very good one at that. 

So overall, if you're an RE fan, I think the compelling story (if you ignore Chris), and beautiful setting, graphics, sound and lots of great puzzles will keep you happy and feeling like you didn't waste your time or money after you beat the game. I just wish they would move away from this RE4 shooter first, horror second design. Or at least if you're going to force me to shoot through 40 enemies in a row, make the shooting mechanics good.

Really enjoyed this game start to finish. Just incredible. And it really does feel like a tribute to many past RE games all put into one package. People are making the comparison with 4 and 7, which is mostly right, but there is so much more going on behind the curtains. It isn't particularly scary all the time, I'd say it's mostly stressful, but it does have one bit that effed me up after playing. I loved it all the same. The setting is probably the best the series has ever had too in my opinion, it feels very bloodborne-esque (which is pretty much just a combo of old European/Victorian architecture) both in the level design and the enemy designs. 

My only real complaint with the game (and it's a nitpick) would be enemy variety. You sometimes encounter the same enemies over and over, in some cases they don't even have different skins/designs. It's just clones of the same ones copy/pasted for a few sections. But again, this is minor, and what already is there is still a huge improvement over the lack of enemy variety 7 had.

Lastly I have to talk about how graphically impressive the game is, and how well it ran on my Geforce 1060 on mostly high settings. I only had one area in the game where my framerate dropped immensely, and it was in a single room in Lady D's castle that didn't have much going on. I don't really know what happened there, there was a bossfight in it too which really made the experience all that more difficult.

To close, amazing game. Absolutely worth the money and time. And don't listen to those complaining that it's too short, I spent 15 hours searching every nook and cranny, and for my 60 euros I'd say that's perfectly acceptable. For the last few years, Capcom has been releasing hit after hit. Sure, they stumbled a bit with RE3 Remake and its rather content-lean release, but Resident Evil 8 represents a return to form for Capcom. The world has been upside down lately and Capcom is signaling that times are changing and we are getting back to normal by releasing the sort of quality game we would expect from the developers of Resident Evil 6, Umbrella Corps, and Devil May Cry 2. 

The attempt at recapturing the genre-bending fun and camp that was Resident Evil 4 goes horribly wrong in a game that is at once too goofy AND too serious. The attempts at humor fall flat as the game tales itself far too seriously elsewhere, so the wink and nod that came with the much-beloved Resident Evil 4's campy moments is largely absent in a game that thinks its subject matter is of the utmost seriousness, and is indeed quite frightening.

Horror really isn't something that comes into play in this game. There are some jump scares, and some set pieces that, if allowed to breathe, might have been creepy. But this game won't slow down enough to allow for the horror to really set in. Unfortunately, it doesn't do so well on the action part either, as the enemies are horrifically bullet spongey even on lower difficulties where even the fodder enemies you may fight in droves can take almost a full clip of head shots to take down.

Don't expect too much from this rather blind attempt at emulating what made Resident Evil 4 work, and certainly don't go in looking for followup to Resident Evil 7 in any sense other than that both games [i]truly[/i] go off the rails in their respective final segments.

Resident Evil Village (Resident Evil 8, depending on your persuasion) is by all means a technological marvel. The game uses the RE Engine which has been used for the RE2 and 3 remakes, and once again this engine proves its magic. Saying this game has good graphics is an understatement to the highest degree, this game is immersive by design. What's more is that despite it's visuals the game remains optimized and rarely drops frames. Going past the visuals, this game pulls its weight as a true Resident Evil game and takes everything that didn't work from 7, and fixes it. It's fair to say that this game is like if 7 and 4 had a baby, which is an amazing combo to have. The first person survival horror that worked so well in Biohazard returns with small, but important features from 4 such as inventory management, a proper merchant (who is a great character, I might add), crafting supplies, and so on. The game is also a great entry way for people who have never played an RE game, as it gives explanations on the events of RE7 that are necessary to understand this games plot. Resident Evil Village really does have all the necessary ingredients to make a modern day classic, and I feel will be a huge turning point for the future of the series. The game is divided into 5 "acts" so to speak, split between each of the antagonists and their respective fights. None of the villains overstay their welcome and as soon as it starts to get old, they wrap up and send you flying to the next mission. On the contrary however, this may be a detriment to some as if you enjoy the theme of one area, you unfortunately won't be there for long. That's more a nitpick than anything, but I still found it worth bringing up. Take for example Castle Dimitrescue, or as most people online know it, the hot vampire milf section. This area is fantastic and serves excellently as the first real threat you face. Unfortunately this area is only about an hour to two hours of the main story. Resident Evil games however are not known for their amazingly long length, so I find it silly to get worked up over such a thing. 

I feel Village is one of the first AAA releases in a while to feel completely finished. It never feels rushed and doesn't show any signs of corners being cut. It fires in all cylinders and completely delivers in everything it promises. A game being finished shouldn't feel as big of a deal as this, but my God does it feel it refreshing to see a game come out that feels like it was methodically thought out and prepared. One of the few recent AAA games that I bought for full price, and feel like I fully got my money. I believe the game is fully worth the $60 price tag (Don't let Steam fool you, the game is actually $60, just hidden under the $80 bundle) and you shouldn't wait for a sale. But hey, it's 2021 and money is tight, I get that. I think this game would go on sale for at most about $45 and that is still a great price for the game. Please do yourself a favor and experience this.

The story is grasping and will keep you wondering what's next. Of course the iconic cheesy one liners from all Resident Evil games are still here in full force. And what's an RE game without stupid one liners? Of course with the games shorter length, some characters don't feel like they are as fully fleshed out as possible. However, this is Resident Evil, not a JRPG. I'm here to kill monsters and zombies and the game gives you just that experience. 

If my gushing hasn't told you enough already, this game is fantastic and absolutely worth the price of admission. Truly, a modern classic

Some context:
I see a lot of Resident Evil fanboys rating this game negatively because it "doesn't feel like a Resident Evil game." So I'm going to be writing this review about how the game performs as a game, NOT as a Resident Evil game. Also I'm going to be rating it on four different aspects, the game play, the combat, the spooky, and the story.

The actual review:

THE GAME PLAY 8/10: The game play in RE: Village is pretty similar to other RE games as in you go around searching for different keys or items that open doors or unlock different items you need to progress. You usually find these by searching the village or by doing puzzles. The actual exploration of the village was very fun as there were many secret paths and many areas for you to search. The map is pretty big so you will spend a lot of time exploring. The puzzles are not very difficult and pretty underwhelming in most circumstances.

THE COMBAT 9/10: The combat was my favorite part of this game, it was so satisfying to walk up to a zombie and blow its head off with a shotgun. The gunshots felt responsive when you hit a zombie in the head, and just overall felt good. You will be doing a lot of shooting things in RE: Village, so if you like shooting things you will not be disappointed in this game.

THE SPOOKY 5/10: The weakest part of RE: Village is how un-scary it is. There were a couple parts in this game when I did feel pretty scared, but after you get all your weapons and gear nothing is very scary anymore because you know that anything the pops out at you, you can just blow its head off. I do wish there a little more spooky parts in this game but the rest of the game makes up for the lack of it.

THE STORY 8/10: I really enjoyed the story in RE: Village, I felt that the devs definitely did a good job with the story. There are some emotional parts and there are some spooky parts, but the overall plot was the best part for me. It did a great job continuing on from where RE: 7 left off but at the same time it felt like its own story in general. 

OVERALL 9/10: I really enjoyed my time playing this game and I definitely feel like I got my moneys worth. If you are looking for a pure RE experience maybe this isn't the game for you. If you are just looking for a solid 12 hour game that you can really have fun in, I highly recommend Resident Evil: Village.

Ethan is a pretty unconvincing protagonist and seems so out of place in the RE universe and the amount of missable stuff in this game is quite staggering.

I've seen other reviews point out how Ethan is able to withstand so much punishment and further I've seen comments point out on these reviews that it is explained in the canon when you complete the game. Now for my main complaint. I have missed so many damn things in this game. How are you supposed to find some of these things without consulting a guide? I wanted to do those ball puzzles, but it appears the way you can do them is by pushing something out of the way in a level that becomes unaccessible once you fight the boss. I get this game is all about multiple play-throughs, but there is no way I would have found these things without looking at a guide. I am not a fan of that type of game design, I want to be able to find this stuff out as I play.

[b]Uncharismatic protagonist Ethan Winters, who survived the Hillibilly swamp hell from Resi VII, has moved to an idyllic  Romanian village with his wife Mia in order to forget the traumatizing events from Louisiana. [/b]
This game has had a mixed reception thus far given that some of the more hardcore fans of the RESI franchise have always felt that "horror" has fallen short in many titles of the saga. On top of that, ammunition is looted en masse by killing zombies, unlike in its predecessor [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/418370/Resident_Evil_7_Biohazard/] Resident Evil VII[/url] 
This does indeed diminish the claustrophobic survival horror effect in the game design, and its invoked paranoia, since one rarely has no ammo. 
Likewise, with certain more bullet-spammy sequences of the game and the fact that the inventory is hugely expandable through backpacks, this renders the incarcerating terror feels mute at times unlike in the recent remakes [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/883710/#] Resident Evil 2 [/url] and [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/952060/Resident_Evil_3/] Resident Evil 3. [/url]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2481115184
One may equally criticize that while the initial premise with the Romanian village and the Vampire Castle Dimitrescu is absolutely amazing, that it feels like Capcom is playing a manic circus director who wants to show off as many different beasts, clowns, puppets and stunts as possible.  The game design may be described as one of those horror Rollercoasters 
many of us visited in childhood for most of the game. Horror on rails so to say.
This leads to the  plot having inconsistencies and the umbrella plot being integrated quite randomly and without much plausibility. This desire to fulfill different demands in the horror genre makes the different parts of the story difficult to link. It is a pity that the Romanian folklore disappeared during the story as it could have been used to connect the very different characters and arcs in an overarching way with more plausibility. The story is flawed if one looks at the writing as a whole. The story and the occult rumanian angle converge quite well initially, until the developers have problems consolidating this dualism of fantasy and bio-weapons later on.
[b] However, this explosive kind of directing and presentation is exactly what appeals to me; may it lack subtlety or not. [/b]
I do understand the frustration of some with the premise and lack of horror factor consistency through the game..
Furthermore, this game suffers from backtracking that may feel too much at some moments and fps drops when changing the settings in its current state.
It would have been good to incorporate more local Romanian folklore into the game and specifically into the meals of the Duke. They would have benefited from cultural lore and animations instead of the sketched images in the Duke's book.

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/21690/Resident_Evil_5/] Resident Evil 5 [/url] was heavily in critique for this and seen as a military action shooter, rather than a horror game.

[h1] [b]  Personal Rating: 87% [/b] [/h1]
Capcom totally nailed it when designing the four lords and their respective arcs; both from a game design perspective but also just judging the characters themselves.
[b] Even though they can't measure up to House Dimitrescu, I have enjoyed the character arcs of the house Moreau, Beneviento and Heisenberg all the same! [/b]

[h1] [b]  Diversified Psychological Horror via Selective Phobia [/b] [/h1]
A remarkable consequence of that is that the horror angles of the game are completely diversified, as the 4 lords are totally different.
[b]  Psychologically the horror is very different from one lord to the next since Capcom attempts to tap into different kinds of fears and incorporates this into the game design. 
It is almost as if Capcom is a winemaker who distills a scarlet concoction from phobia grapes. [/b]
One lord boss battle did not even consist of gunplay for most of the time for instance, but rather made use of of subtlety in environmental storytelling of the horror.

Especially the majestic Lady Dimitrescu and her daughters in the castle  are voiced and designed so well they justify an entire game dedicated to them.

Easy contender for GOAT.   It's rare that a game truly gets its genre and gives players exactly what they want from it.  Village is one of those games.  

Performance:
It's worth noting I'm running the game inside of a VM with passthrough on an RX590.  You will probably get slightly better performance on a bare iron machine.  Specs are as follows:
RX590 - 8Gb
E2xx-v3 series Xeon running at 3.4Ghz - 10 threads pinned to VM.
16GB RAM
Cruicial 1TB SATA/SSD using virtio drivers. 

Game runs at a solid frame rate of between 30-45 fps on 1080 medium settings.  Audio desyncs during cutscenes.   Using latest Radeon drivers to drive audio over displayport.

Pros:
-Atmosphere and scenario design are top notch, as stated previously it's just the right mix of action and genuine horror.  
-The combat system is carried over from 7,  it's pretty good to average, but workable when you get your hands on it.  Gunplay is valued over melee, but that's to be expected.  
-Guns can be more easily customized by exchanging in game currency for stat boosts.  
-Perm. stat boosts to walking speed and max health can be done through a hunting sub-quest.  You can easily find prey to hunt along the main story-line.  I didn't need to go out of the way to much too get the max health buff.
-Story is excellent.
-Boss battles are varied and challenging as well as cinematic and engaging.
-Missed treasure is marked on the map as you explore the village. 
-Enemy variety is much better than 7 with each scenario having its own unique enemies to deal with.
           
Cons:
-Major problems with audio desyncing during cutscenes.  Once again my setup is abnormal, but it's been seen on some bare iron setups running 1060s or slightly lower/mid end cards.
-Weapons customization is kind of a waste on all but endgame weapons.  Your first shotgun isn't going to be as good as your base second shotgun, same with third shotgun.  My advice is to just wait until you get the 1911A to start upgrading your pistol.
-Your backpack is all you have.  I didn't find a crate to store anything in.  So you will need to either sell your guns if you don't have room for them or buy more space. 
-Some essential routes/passages are hard to find/notice.

Misc:
-There's a Mr X/Jack Baker/Old School Nemesis type character in this game who tracks and chases you around a certain scenario, and while they are programmed/stated excellently.  This type of mechanic is starting to get a little bit stale.

Welcome to Resident Evil 8, where Capcom once again try to physically break a divergent path in their story back into line with the rest of the canon, even though everyone has been happy with the ending of certain plot points 3 games ago. Also witness as Capcom try their hardest to explain away the complete apathetic attitude and utter invulnerability of their new main protagonist in a so-called twist which sees the head of everyone who witnesses it turn 142 degrees in a direction though impossible in utter disbelief. Aside from this, behold a game which takes what RE7 does for it’s gameplay, improves on it, give you a bigger area to walk around in, more weapons to slap ♥♥♥♥ around with but still keeps pulling from its past games for every single one of its ideas. Old ideas, done very well.

In this game you will be fighting the following:
•	Furries
•	Bigger furries
•	Hammer furries
•	Meth addicts
•	The gargoyle gremlin from Gremlins 2: The New Batch
•	Aggressive gardeners 
•	The Internet’s new waifus for the week
•	Silent Hill’s cast off
•	Raggidolls
•	Your fish supper from last week
•	Meth addicts hired by Facebook
•	Wolfenstein’s  Supersoldaten
•	A B52 bomber on legs
•	Jim Carey’s Dr Robotnik

The majority of the game’s first run will be trying to figure out where the hell you are going, fighting off attacks from one or more of the above and cackling in laughter as you watch Ethan get battered, thrown and mutilated throughout. Not much has changed from RE7, it’s still first person, you still can only have 4 weapons in your hot-swap bar at any one time, you craft ammo and healing items out of stuff you find on the ground. Adding to this is a health dose of RE4 mechanics. Enemies drops stuff, ammo, craftables and money, the inventory system is a straight copy of RE4’s attaché case and there is a merchant dotted around the area that you buy things from, never explains how he’s able to move around as quick as he can (Which is even more impressive given this guy’s size) and allows upgrading of your weaponry.  It all comes together to make a game which is functionally good and works… mostly. Odd glitch here and there, but it works.

The story is… typical Resident Evil. As said before, RE8 is trying to break what was done in RE7 into line with the rest of the canon. There was something said way back when in a Zero Punctuation video on a RE game, RE 5 I think. RE had a twisted mess of plot threads and non sensical stuff, then made a game only tangentially related to that mess. It sells gang busters, and the next game follows up on that, but then bogs down the narrative with all the mess from the previous games. That last game was RE4. Then e had RE5, which really should have finished off the whole ‘Umbrella’ arc, and then RE6 which was RE 6 and had Neo Umbrella and bioterrorist dinosaurs and we do not talk about it. Then, we get RE7. Fresh take on the series, tangentially related story wise to the previous games. And now we have RE8, which tries to shoehorn the previous game’s canon in like a demented baby trying to push its own bulbous head into a square hole two inches wise. You can see the strains, and the contrivances are just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ridiculous. Capcom needs to make this the underline point. They have a world where bioterrorism exists. They have the opportunity to do something fresh with it. They almost made it this time but could not help themselves and had to go back to their crutches. As well as that, the whole deal with Ethan is hinted at throughout the game, but the big reveal actually had me stop playing for five minutes before saying ‘That is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stupid’. One story beat does have me interested in what I am hoping is the DLC and not the next main game, but only time will tell

All in all, this is as close gameplay wise as you’re going to get to RE 4 in the modern age. It’s an enjoyable game to run and re-run, trying to blast past bosses and obstacles with New Game Plus and the god like arsenal you acquire, or start fresh on harder difficulties with self-imposed rules. Aside from one or two characters, however, there is not a lot of charm in the characters that would make this a 100% RE4-like for me. Ethan is still a brick with an affinity to reject fall damage. Chris has not changed since RE5,. The internet’s latest waifu, giant vampire lady, has presence for the short time he’s around but it is short. The other bosses are given even less screen time aside from Heisenberg (Who is given about the same amount of time as Vampire Lady) and the overall antagonist is just… there, really. The Duke, the vendor for the game, is the only one with any sort of charm that you can like and you actually want to know more about him.

Overall recommended game if you want something to enjoy for gameplay but don’t care on story

RE VIII is strange. Its a game with an identity crisis that can't decide what it wants to be
I should note this review contains spoilers, and is intended more for postgame catharsis

It kicks off with slow paced cinematic immersive roleplaying which segways into an utterly brutal introduction, for the first hour or two the game seems intent on leading you by the nose along a linear path full of setpieces and intense action.

Then suddenly, really too suddenly, you're in a beautiful gothic castle. Pretty but claustrophobic. The one you've seen in all the trailers. For a while, the game is fairly quiet exploration and puzzling, you'll start to miss the combat. Then the combat comes back without explanation and it's suddenly stealth versus invincible pursuers. The castle is home to some of the best boss fights, especially the last one

Before you know it though, Castle Dmitrescu is over, it feels too soon. This is what everyone was looking forward to, and its barely a third of the way through the game. This is like opening a concert with the headline act. Really tough to follow. 
Unfortunately, i'd say it doesn't quite manage it, though a few points come close. The castle really should have been later in the game, its kind of blown its load too early, and set the bar too high. Not to mention killing off the best character in the game

After the castle, the game suddenly goes into Open World mode, you're finally given freedom to explore, shop, hunt treasure and do side activities. Here you'll quickly discover that enemies don't respawn, and probably scour the map of all life before the next major story beat. You will unfortunately also discover that the titular village is really not very big, and that you've already seen most of it in the introduction.

Then there's a truly bizarre sequence where the game forgets what it was supposed to be doing and tries to be Amnesia. Suddenly all your guns are stripped, and its all atmosphere, puzzles and forced-stealth in the wake of horrible things. This chapter is pretty effective and spooky, but its also entirely divorced from the rest of the game. Theres no loot, no combat, no exploration really. When all's said and done, you leave that place almost as empty-handed as you went in. Its like someone went off and made their own seperate game, and capcom somehow tried to cram it into this one.

The next chapter after that is wildly different but has a similarly seperated structure. Again no combat (until a bossfight at the end), it suddenly turns into a platforming adventure, hopping across driftwood and rooftops.

These two chapters are wierd. The villains in them are also wierd. But they don't really feel like they fit. They're kind of filler to pad out the game, lacking the length, depth and especially the freedom, that the parts up until now have afforded

things kinda return to form from there, there's a much heavier focus on combat, the factory level particularly is huge, complex and full of things to explore, but its kinda too big and not nearly as pretty or interesting as the castle

The finale with chris is amazing, and the final boss is great too

Where was i going with this....
RE 8 is wierd. It's definitely not a bad game, this review is positive. It is a very good game. But I think, not a great game. 
It's just long enough that you wouldn't call it a short game. It has just enough upgrades and exploration to not be called linear. It has a pretty classically great overarching story, the sort you'd expect mythology about. But the hour-to-hour details of it are lacking. Generally, this game lacks in overall vision, pacing and design.

It's like someone wrote the beginning and the end, then handed their half finished script over to a team of other writers who each got to make their own piece to fill out the middle. The result is a wildly inconsistent hodgepodge of ideas that really doesn't fit together. But as a whole, it is fun and compelling

Story is generally the weakest point. RE games were already pretty reliant on text and audio logs, but this game is severely lacking in even those. Most of the villains you kill, you won't understand the slightest thing about who they were or what motivated them. Some of this is explained later, though a lot is left mysterious.
The common enemies get even less treatment.  Almost nothing is explained about what they are or where they came from. In the introduction it feels like the Lycan army is going to be your nemesis, but they eventually get sidelined by half a dozen other things. 

By the endgame you've seen werewolves, vampires, zombies and cyborgs. Yes, all in the same game. At times it feels like a child just making ♥♥♥♥ up as they go along without any care for continuity or reason. Very little of this is explained, the zombies in particular get literally no explanation, or even acknowledgement, from any character or document in the game. I guess zombies are just a universal seasoning you can sprinkle on anything and not have to justify it. They just appear, in your way, and you've gotta shoot them. nobody talks about it.  One criticism of RE7 was that the normal enemies just felt like filler to pad out the game, and that's only slightly less true here. The lycans seemed like they were going to be a major plot point, but they just peter out like the writers lost interest

For all of its flaws though, RE: Village has sheer quality on its side. Everything is pretty, photorealistic, well made, well acted. well choreographed, well animated, etc. If it had a lower budget it might have been a bad game, but it's too big to fail and capcom's infinite money helps to keep it above water. 

The gameplay is fun, when the game can decide what its gameplay is going to be today
The exploration is fun, when the game graciously allows you off the leash to sniff around a bit
The combat is fun, when it deigns to give you things to shoot
The story is a grand classical tale in broad strokes, with details colored in crayon by a bored child

It's a shining example of design by committee muddying the waters, and using excessive funding as the glue to hold everything together. This is not a well designed or well planned game, but it somehow results in a fun product in the end.

Resident Evil has been perfected at last. Whether you're a fan of the survival horror entries or the action-packed ones...Village satisfies both kinds of players.

This game continues the story of 2017's Resident Evil 7: Biohazard and sees Ethan Winters on a mission to recover his kidnapped daughter Rose from a mysterious and ghoulish European village. It's highly recommended that if you're a newbie to the Resident Evil franchise, you should at the very least play Resident Evil 7 before picking this one up. If you don't have the time or money for that though, the game does feature a short video recap of the previous game to get you caught up. However, to truly appreciate the game's huge lore reveals in its final couple hours, you should probably watch a recap on the entire Resident Evil timeline which you can find on YouTube.

Each of the 4 houses you must fight your way through are incredibly varied and enjoyable as is the main village hub area itself. The pacing of the game is excellent too. Resident Evil 7, perhaps in an attempt to distance itself far away from the campy action of Resident Evil 5 and 6, was incredibly scary...perhaps maybe TOO scary. Resident Evil Village tones the horror back a couple notches and is better for it. Don't get me wrong. The game is STILL scary. You will jump. You will get scared. Your skin will crawl and your spine will tingle. The horror that made Resident Evil what it is...it's still here in abundance. However, the difference this time though is the constant dread of RE 7 has been spaced out with incredibly fun action and character sequences that give you a moment to breathe.

This game wears it's influence of Resident Evil 4 right on its sleeve and it isn't afraid to show it, from the briefcase inventory management, to the merchant you can purchase supplies and upgrades from, to the way Ethan cracks occasional one-liners like Leon Kennedy. If you're and RE veteran who has fond memories of the GameCube classic, you'll feel right at home in Village. The game even features the return of the fan favorite Mercenaries arcade mode that you can unlock after completing the story. I've played quite a few RE games, but this is the first one I've actually been tempted to revisit thanks to this Mercenaries mode.

Many reviews have also made a note about the repetitive boss battles and the game's last hour or so, which turns into Call of Duty for a little while. Personally, these issues didn't bother me much. The bosses are all interesting and while the manner for defeating most of them is just pumping them full of lead until they scream out and keel over dead, I found it enjoyable. It kept me from getting frustrated at boss encounters cause I was never really at a loss on how to beat them. That's not to say the bosses are particularly easy, even on Standard difficulty. Some of them are fast and hit hard, so you have to be on your toes and quick on the trigger. As for the "Call of Duty" section, it was a welcome change of pace to finally have the firepower to take on the horrors that had been scaring me all game, even if it was just for a brief moment.

While the Resident Evil formula has finally been perfectly balanced between action and horror, that's not to say the game is perfect. Personally I found the second house that you visit a bit too short for my liking with too little combat. Also, many of the puzzles throughout the game don't give you a clear enough hint on how to solve them. I'm no stranger to RE puzzles but there's a difference between a difficult puzzle and a puzzle draped in cryptic riddles that don't even attempt to point you in the right direction. Village likes to favor the latter and I found myself more than once just cheating my way through them by looking up guides cause the game left me so confused. I also didn't really need to interact with the briefcase inventory as much as I did in RE 4. In Resident Evil 4, I would often have to move items around, turn them, combine them to make more room, and really try to maximize space and make the inventory as efficient as possible. Here, due to my crafting components not taking up inventory space and the fact that you can shortcut your weapons to the number keys like in RE 7, I had little need to go in and re-arrange my inventory like I did in RE 4. So long as I kept purchasing the briefcase size upgrades as they became available, I didn't need to worry about running out of space. This essentially just made the whole inventory management system a nostalgic skin and nothing more.

These flaws didn't take away from the overall experience, though, which was much stronger than RE 7 and might just be my new favorite entry in the series. If not my absolute favorite, easily in the Top 3. Without delving into spoilers, the ending both connects this new soft reboot series that started with RE 7 back to the original games as well as gives fans plenty to speculate on about where the series could be headed next. I had a blast with Village and if you have any interest in this series at all, this is a must play.

[i]Resident Evil 8[/i] is a game about experimentation, not only for evil genetic mutations as per the plot, but for this legendary survival horror franchise. Its predecessor [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was also about experimenting, but where that game played with touches and notions of what the franchise could be without fully committing to anything, [i]Resi 8[/i] feels like a burst of creativity and unrestrained vision.

 The game confidently presents new gameplay idea after new gameplay idea to the player, switching gears from open exploration, to linear shooting, to indie-horror style puzzle solving with gusto and flair. There's quite literally never a dull moment in this game, even during the down time between Lords back in the village. This breathless pacing is easily the games greatest strength, and is more than capable of elevating it's relatively simple puzzles and gunplay. Outside of the linear sections, exploring the village and the surrounding countryside is rewarding and fun. The game dishes out ample rewards for anyone who returns back to earlier areas, which feed back into the Duke and his merchantry shop. Choosing to do all of the side content (of which there is a fair bit) makes for the longest [i]Resident Evil[/i] game in recent memory, though the game still commits to the rapid pace and ends long before it overstays it's welcome. Thankfully, players who want to return to [i]8[/i] will find it chock full of replay value, as the Village of Shadows "super hardcore" difficulty tosses remixed encounters at the player from the get-go, up to including lategame enemies in early-game fights. Plus there are achievements which transform into currency for the unlock shop, returning from RE2make. There's even an unlockable Mercenaries mode, which has seen a fun remix from the usual fare and comes with it's own unlocks too.

 This is all tied together with a presentation that I can only describe as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ phenomenal. The artistic design of the village and the surrounding areas are just amazing, and the level of detail in the environments is above and beyond, even for the already impressive RE Engine. Audio design is similarly excellent, with 3D audio and great clarity making each environment seem sinister and imposing. Character design and animation are above and beyond, while effects look just gorgeous. The game even has no loading times outside of death or loading a save, which is a great touch. The presentation elevates [i]Resident Evil 8[/i] into a truly excellent experience, and coming from a person who doesn't care much about graphics, that should say something.

 [i]Resident Evil 8[/i] is not perfect, though. In choosing to experiment with different gameplay styles so much, the games great pacing can falter. Moreau and Benevito's areas in particular are very fun, but struggle on repeat playthroughs thanks to their linearity. In addition, the end of the game is backloaded with action to an uncomfortable degree, which is par for the course for this series, but here feels like it could have been better managed. The focus on action, while gripping, can also be a burden as the gameplay has not changed much fundamentally from the purposefully clunky [i]Resi 7[/i]. The game's great presentation has also caused some technical issues for some. Certain effects like the vampire women's bugs or lycan hair can cause huge framerate drops for my rig, which thankfully never impaired gameplay in any way. Outside of these dips the game runs perfectly, but you get the sense that the RE Engine is being pushed to it's limits and the game could have used some better optimisation. Lastly, the games story is standard fare for this franchise (read: stupid), but can be enjoyable if you turn your brain off. Ethan is a dull protagonist for the most part, but his performance can be surprisingly moving and seeing him slowly transform into a ball of rage and determination by the endgame is enjoyable to watch. 

 Ultimately, [i]Resident Evil 8[/i] feels like the culmination of every idea that the previous game attempted, but failed at. This game is a celebration of the franchise and what makes it special, while also stretching the legs of what the Resi franchise might be capable of. It's not an entirely bump-free ride, but it is a confident and engaging one from start to finish, and one I can easily state is one of the better games in a franchise of masterpieces.

RE Village feels like a mixture between RE7 and RE4, but with an identity of its own. In general, there is less horror than RE7 (except for one specific house) and far fewer jump scares. Sniping enemies from afar and being in an isolated but ample region brings memories from RE4.

Comparisons aside, RE Village excels at graphics and environment design. As with most modern RE titles, production values are high and the game feels polished. There are plenty of in-universe references, and the upgrading and cooking mechanic is decent. The soundtrack is ominous and gunplay is OK, but both feel slightly less impactful than RE3 Remake's. The Bonus Shop is more prominent, as models are not unlocked automatically as in the recent remakes. Unfortunately, just like in RE7, pacing is uneven, and there is a lot of exposition and plot twists towards the final part of the story. Also, Capcom completely forgot how to make puzzles, which used to be a big part of classic RE.

I would recommend RE Village to those who enjoy games in the style of RE4 or RE7.

As soon as I arrived in Resident Evil Village’s sinister rural setting, its Resident Evil 4 influence reared its snarling head. Almost immediately surrounded by rabid Lycan locals, I scrambled for shotgun shells and bookshelves to block doorways as the horde closed in, only to be saved a split-second away from death. It’s an intense welcome that serves as a fantastic flashback to the opening of Shinji Mikami’s magnum-toting magnum opus, and one made all the more frantic in first-person perspective. Resident Evil Village might not break much new ground in its own right, but it successfully grafts Resident Evil 4’s best action elements onto the series’ more modern form established in Resident Evil 7: Biohazard, making for a genuinely engrossing and increasingly combat-heavy continuation of the Ethan Winters story.

It’s a story that – unfortunately for poor old Ethan – goes from dire straits to dire wolves. Dragged to hillbilly hell and back in an effort to rescue his wife in Resident Evil 7, he subsequently finds himself dropped into a distinctly Transylvanian type of terror in Village. This time it’s his infant daughter who must be saved after she’s kidnapped by a wicked cabal of monster maniacs: Lady Dimitrescu, a vampire tall enough to play center in a Space Jam sequel; Donna Beneviento, a dollmaker with a walking, talking Bride of Chucky sidekick; Salvatore Moreau, a thoroughly repulsive merman; and Karl Heisenberg, a magnetically powered lunatic who runs a factory assembly line of Frankenstein’s monsters.

Update 10/3/2021
I have had zero inclination to revisit Village since I finished the main campaign.  Once the wow-factor of the technical side wears off, this could be any action game. Village blends into the background of forgettable AAA action games just as soon as it became a sensation. The game is simply too westernized and drab, lacking any soul or sense of legacy every game prior to RE7 had. Village is a game you should rent, not buy, which is why I can't recommend it. Get it on Gamepass and save your money.
RE: Village is a technical showcase for RE Engine and an enjoyable series of set pieces. A handful of fun little puzzles are interspersed, along with some genuinely unsettling scares. Newcomers will enjoy the excellent graphics, solid performance, tight gameplay, and mesmerizing sound design. This is an incredible game when taken on its own merit.
Old school fans shaken by the game's advertisement blitz will be pleasantly surprised with how the game progresses. As a fan of the Playstation trilogy of games, I was left cold by the game's conclusion, and believe that, despite what's sure to be a blockbuster hit for Capcom, this franchise has completely lost its soul. RE4:R might be a good game for fans of the original, but RE9 might be the first game in the entire franchise that I sit out. RE:Village is what happens when RE6 and RE7 meld together and wear RE4's clothes, only without the latter's charm and humor. On the other hand, RE9 is set to be "The Last of Chris 2." Until then, enjoy this game, and hope RE4:R manages to bring back some of the campy humor and heart this series once had.

What I write for this review is the experience I had with the game, everybody will experience things differently. This is my honest review if you don't like it well tough. Also no game is safe from a review whether its early access or 
full release, also i'll try not to spoil anything in the game by leaving out information now onto the review.

The Game: I want to say this is 3rd best Resident Evil game has been made, Resident Evil 4 & Resident Evil 7 & Resident Evil: Village is taking things from both games to create Resident Evil: Village & its been done so well.  

The Story: Resident Evil: Village is continuing the Ethan Winter story three years later after the Baker family incident in Resident Evil 7. The story involves Ethan trying to find his 6 month old daughter Rosemary in a weird messed village that has these's mutated werewolf human like monsters. Upon investigating Ethan learns there are 4 lords (bosses) that know something about Rosemary & you are determined to find out what's happening. 

Bosses: there are 5 bosses, 4 you have to defeat in order to get to the main boss. Four of these bosses each control different sections of the map that you must go (by script, can't choose who to fight) The bosses are Lady Dimitrescu, 
Donna Beneviento, Salvatore Moreau, Karl Heisenberg. The final boss, well i'll leave that out & because again no spoilers.

Saving: this game uses the same save system as resident evil 4 did with typewriters. The typewriter placement in the game seems to fairly well placed, you can always find it with the merchant but it can be found in places just before 
important/long events.

Weapons: The game gives you your basic loadout a knife, pistol & the M1897 shotgun in the village & gives you better weapons later on, which are pretty sweet. Each weapon can be upgraded to have more firepower, faster fire rate, faster
reloading & more ammo capacity. Some of these upgrades are buy-able & some have to be found by exploring.

Treasure: there are valuable treasure to be found, some being low value to being very valuable. Finding these can be sold for Lei which is the currency to buy/see in this game & can be sold to the merchant that is your biggest help
in the game. 

Merchant: this game is using the merchant function like Resident Evil 4 game did with Leon. This merchant will have thing from health, ammo, craft-able blueprints, weapons, weapon parts.

Crafting: you can craft health, ammo & explosives. Each using similar components except for explosives has 1 extra component then the ammo.

Storage: well there isn't any storage system which is the result of the Resident Evil 4 system where you kept everything on you until you decide to sell it to the merchant but luckily Capcom isn't too mean here, they do allow you to sell
your unused weapons & can buy them back later if you desire but for a price of course. I think having no storage is kinda bad, Capcom should have given us a storage but limited to still force us to choose what to leave for later & take now but no storage wasn't an issue with me, I was able to storage manage everything & sold things I didn't use. 

Graphics: the graphics of this game is just amazing, so detailed & so clean. I really didn't see anything wrong with the games graphics but some people did experience fps drop in some sections of the game but I didn't experience any
fps drop at all.

Sound: the sound was just fantastic, the fun sounds, glass braking, liquid splashing, just I didn't have any horrible sound problems at all. Nothing looped glitched or lingered or nothing.

Controls: I had no issue with walking but I did have an issue with looking around. The game defaults look sensitivity to 4 or 5 which caused me to swipe huge causing me to pick up my mouse to recent to still keep swiping. After changing look sensitivity to its highest set 9, I still had small look problems but nothing I could really do other then just adapt to the horrible sensitivity. I believe this was an issue in Resident Evil 7 but not sure, its been 4 years since then so not sure.

Acting: the acting with Ethan was & is a problem in both Resident Evil 7 & Resident Evil: Village. His reaction to things are just of someone who doesn't seem to have no emotions. Hoping Capcom took the acting more seriously this time around but seems like they didn't. Like when Mia getting shot by Chris's team, Ethan just stood there not doing anything or when Rose was being taken he didn't have any real anger. He just saw his wife get murdered in cold blood & his daughter being kidnapped, Ethan just had a numb reaction, not doing anything. Not reacting to having his hand chopped off or having his heart ripped out, Ethan just showed lack of emotions which made it difficult to have any emotions to anything happening in the game as a player. A good story needs to have awesome emotions in order for the game to really hit the player emotionally.

Final thoughts: Resident Evil: Village is the third best game I have played & loved every bit of it. The enemies were different & unique & made game-play thrilling. With Resident Evil: Village taking best parts of Resident Evil 4 & Resident Evil 7 just made this game so awesome.

Game Score: taking things I listed into consideration, Resident Evil: Village gets a 8/10. It would have gotten a 9/10 if the acting was better & for it to have gotten a 10/10 if the game was 100% smooth but an 8/10 score was just
right from my experience & would suggest you pick this game up if you like horror games & pick this game up if you are a fan 
of Resident Evil 4 or Resident Evil 7.

That's the Pony review for Resident Evil: Village.

Ethan Winters... you are a man among men because this game shows how far your willing to go for your family... 

The game is intense with gameplay (Have yet to play hardcore so going to do so soon now that I know where to go thanks to a Standard run), you need to watch where you aim because the enemies (Mainly Lycan's will swerve a lot to avoid fire), Bosses are intense firefights so try and save Ammo for them.... and watch out for the River/Dam part of the game... got killed twice from the enviroment puzzles than dying to enemies... oi... 

Finally do NOT expect this to be a simple run, even if it seems open ended, big tip, go from the giant lady (Cannot spell her name off the top of my head but you will be forced to go through her level first anyway), the doll controller, the hunchback lake monster man, and finally Magneto (Seriously not trying to make a refrence the guy early on is like Magneto, even his boss fight and the level before are metal incarnate.)

Finally... do not hold back on upgrades... may be a bit of a redundant thing but the order is as followed, get cases to increase inventory first and foremost... second is the weapon attachments and recepies for crafting items (order of prefrence will vary), and finally are the ammo and other items that will come from the shop... though bit of a tip... do not sell meats or fish meats... made that mistake when I first played the game, didn't know they would help with power ups until the menu with the duke (Shop keeper) updated to allow cooking items to be used... missed out on two of the four upgrades because of that.

Resident evil Village took aspects from Resident Evil 4 and Combined that with Resident evil 7. It's tense, horrifying and quite engaging. If you liked Resident evil 7 and/or liked Resident evil 4 then you'll have a thriller and a fun experience. But if you haven't played those game and still looking for a decent horror game then this is worth your time. 

The game is absolutely beautiful, If you seen the trailers then you would already know that the environment is amazing. The Castle and the Village are just stunning and even other locations (Which I won't spoil). Which something they took feedback from RE:7. 
People complained that there wasn't any variety and you just fought against the same kind of enemies over and over again in locations that looked the similar as in previous locations. For RE:Village, they took it to heart and added more. Each location you enter has something new to throw and new kind of threat. It prevents the game from going stale and it bring this idea to thought like; "What will the next location be like, What kind enemies will I encounter, What is the boss like?" I'm happy to say, Not like ones you fought before. Each with their own strengths and obstacles. 

The only con is the story and the characters. The story isn't unique and most likely while playing, you can imagine or figure out certain key points and know where the plot going. You've probably already seen this kind of story before and you can risk losing care. Especially in some part where it can be argued that they jumped the shark with that idea and don't explain other key points in the story.

Another flaw is the Characters. In Resident evil 7 you got to learn more about the baker family. What came to be and their role in that game that makes them iconic, Especially unique characteristics that make them so funny, threatening and worth investing your time into them. In RE:Village, It seems to be glossed over and not really much is known about the villains. There are some points and mentions now and there but its not fully fleshed out enough to fully grasp the characters role here. 
What I mean is, When you saw Jack Baker RE:7, He was sadistic, intimidating, dedicated, funny and quite daring. You remember he used the car in the garage, doing whirly-twirly's to crush you. But before all that (If you played the DLC or not) you saw he was caring, hard work, Stern but fair, A family man. So you felt sympathy for him, You became invested in him. 
The same isn't applied here, For the Tall women... besides her huge.......size....  She isn't fully fleshed out to know her personally. and when you think you're close to getting to know her backstory, You're at the boss fight, Killed her... and isn't mentioned again until at the end by finding a book that talks about her. At which I too nearly forgotten when I proceeded to the other parts of the game. It seem she was lacking in the writing department for people to remember her (Besides her size). 

But despite the flaws I experience on my first play on Normal Difficulty (And not dying once), The gameplay was amazing and horror was still there. Worth my time 

(Right now as I wrote this, I'm experimenting with Darkness of Village. So I'll likely update this review to showcase the "Village of Shadows" Difficulty... So far, You need to learn the exploits of the game and mechanics to preserve as much resources and ammo for each part, otherwise you'll die so easily...  Basically, Learn to Speedrun) 

TL:DR    It's a great horror and a Fantastic Game. Might be recommended to play Resident evil 7, If you liked that, then you'll like this one.

While being good overall, Resident Evil 8 does have a couple of major sections that are primarily puzzle-based that would get cumbersome on additional playthroughs.

In addition, the game lacks any sort of cathartic purpose to grind for unlimited ammo weapons. Resident Evil 1 or 2? Yeah, get the unlimited weapons and cut loose. No need to manage each shot. In Resident Evil 8, you feel prepared for each engagement to where you can kill all of the enemies with little ammo management.

Mercenaries is enjoyable, but is different this time around. Instead of getting to choose from different characters with different loadouts for each, you go through a series of stages as Ethan and purchase weapons / upgrades between stages. Does it work? Sure, but it feels more like an exercise in optimizing purchases between rounds rather than enjoying specific characters and loadouts.

Overall, you will enjoy your first playthrough of Resident Evil 8, but subsequent playthroughs will feel like an absolute slog through the lengthy puzzle sections.

I'm giving this game a thumbs down because the developers does not seem to know what the game is supposed to be. 

Action horror or bullet sponge looter shooter?

The initial game starts well with nice pacing. Basic mystery, unknown events, overwhelming odds, inventory management and "make every shot count" kind of thing. The art and audio is quite nice on max settings and performs really well (I did not have any of the issues people have been posting about). It does however start to crumble from there. A reskinned Nemesis opponent, looter shooter mechanics with an upgrade shop, minibosses with gameplay tropes making them look stupid (if you have lived in a place for quite some time, you know what dangers to avoid in your own home... but not these guys). At first some of these characters are overwhelming to the protagonist, but in the mini-boss fights all they manage to do is walk around?... Also add the odd detail with the protagonist being kinda mortal at first, but later behaves completely indestructible thanks to the magic herb juice (he can't regenerate a "mere" bite at first, but can later regenerate acid wounds and repair major dismemberments)... It's such a mixed bag. The game tries to establish a pseudo open world hub, the village, but it becomes apparent that it is only there to pad the play time. The pacing is completely slowed down by the "I can barely jog" speed, which feels completely ridiculous in the boss fights. Which by the way has a very odd difficulty curve. One of the later bosses, that you think will be the hardest one to beat, can be beaten without any effort. This does not come close to the pointless damage scaling however... You start with the mechanic of upgrading your weapons and get a sense of progression. But little do you know that the game throws away all the work you did to max out your weapons, because you will automatically be able to buy a better one after a certain point. You also learn that maxing out your weapons is actually a bad move, because it is better spent later in the game when everything becomes a bulletsponge mess. It is incredibly frustrating when you can afford all the upgrades for most of the game but can't afford to upgrade the final versions of the weapons for the end game because you don't have enough loot, because you completely wasted it on the earlier upgrades.

All this and I'm not even getting into the details of the RE universe.

The game IS enjoyable to a certain extent, but is not proportional to the hype train the game is getting. I'm giving the game a thumbs down as a headsup to those who wants to know the less pretty details.

Resident Evil Village is like how Doom Eternal improved upon Doom 2016.  

They took elements from 4, such as the outside village, the treasures and shop along with the variety of guns, and took the horror elements from 7.  It's not as scary as 7 is, and it's not as action packed as 4, but it's a good blend of the two that just feels like the right step forward in the evolution of Resident Evil games.  I don't want to talk too much about things that happen in the game as if you play this, you want to know as little as possible.  Don't look up anything, just play it.  

The only cons I can think of is that the early game does feel a bit rushed.  I don't want to get too into it, but when or if you've played this, you have to agree that the early game feels incredibly good but then feels rushed.  Thankfully that doesn't impact the rest of the game too much, but I wish the early game was a bit longer.  The four lords also seemed a bit lacking in some aspects, as there wasn't too much to them at all in the grand scheme of things.  One thing that is less of a con and more of a weird curiosity is that I have 16 hours on steam playing the game, yet my playthrough was only 9 hours.  I didn't AFK or anything for my playthrough, and I could understand maybe an hour being dedicated to benchmarking or using menus, but I think the timer is off.  

My tip for you is that you should upgrade your weapons and later on sell them, as you don't get the full amount back for it, but you'll get a majority of your money back and you'll be able to kill enemies faster and conserve ammunition, which saves you money in the long run.  The other tip is to make sure to fully explore a lords area fully, as you can't go back to it unlike the hub and most of the areas.  You can miss out on permanent weapon upgrades if you're not careful.  Make sure to also use your map and if a area is red, you're missing something, and sometimes it can be gems that you shoot from a wall or ceiling.

I liked RE:Village so much.

It continues to be an incredible experience. Seriously.

Every area in this game is fun to explore and structured pretty uniquely. It treads the line between being pretty linear but having these bits that open up and allow for backtracking for better items and resources, which felt like classic RE in a way. The gameplay loop of finding ♥♥♥♥ and powering Ethan up through the meal system / the Duke's upgrades is so satisfying and implemented well.

In terms of replayability, this game has it (probably) the best out of any Resident Evil game. NG+ rewards and a reasonable achievement list does this game wonders. I have a feeling that both completionists will love this game, and even people that don't usually go for 100% completion may want to complete Village. I know I do. The game is short enough to make it reasonable to really anyone.

The game itself is visually striking. The graphics are great, as to be expected from anything in the RE Engine at this point. Some areas are drenched in deep color while others are drab, gray, and devoid of life. Stylistically, it just works and it's exactly the kind of contrast that RE7 needed.

More or less, Village focuses on action. The gameplay is finely tuned, and the gunplay goes from good to great once you start to get upgrades for your weapons. It keeps you on your toes, of course, but there's only one explicitly "scary" section of the game. Even disregarding the scary bits, Village feels like it was made for Resident Evil 4 fans, and its influence shines through.

The story is bombastic and campy and blockbuster-y but I'm not sure how it stacks up to 7.

A definite 9/10 and a must play.

RE Village is yet another solid entry in the main series of Resident Evil series, continuing in the same vein as RE VII's first person shooter setting, with many of the same characters transposed to an entirely unfamiliar setting.  It has few weak moments but otherwise does most things well, but never quite attains the legendary status of some of the other heavy hitters in its list of predecessors.

Personally I would say RE VIII is a mix between the RE3 remake and RE7, borrowing the more action oriented feeling of the former and combining it with the claustrophobic first person view of the latter. 

Visually, the game is very impressive and with a few scattered exceptions runs very well in all areas. 

The enemies are creative, varied, and interesting, leaving behind the nonstop boring sludge monsters of RE VII.

The game is essentially divided into four different zones, each with a boss, and capped off by the final boss of the game.  Each zone is wildly different in setting and how you approach it.  The first, Castle Dimetrescu, is a large game of cat and mouse a la Mr. X in the RE2 remake.  The second is a much more jump-scare oriented horror fest that leaves you without your weapons for most of the section.  The third feels very much like the water parts of RE4 and RE5, where you're dodging a giant aquatic monster until you can find a way to even the odds.  And the final area is very much like the more industrial areas of the latter parts of RE5, with monsters ripped straight out of the B Horror movie "Frakenstein's Army".

The game also tries very hard to feel like RE4 in a lot of ways, but tends to fail to attain that kind of greatness, with each of its various systems being a little more shallow for the sake of... accessibility?  Ease?  Not quite sure.

And herein lies what is likely RE VIII's greatest weakness - it removes almost all of the difficulty that isn't directly related to actually fighting.  There's no longer any meaningful inventory management of any kind.  Unless you're a very bad shot, you will have more than enough supplies to carry you through.  Crafting and key items are now kept in their own separate and endless inventories, so they're never competing with your guns and ammo for space.  

Weapons, while fun enough, are boring in the sense that there's a VERY clear upgrade path, and virtually no reason for deviating from it.  When you find a new gun of the same type as one you already have (Pistol or shotgun basically, as there's only one sniper rifle and one grenade launcher), they always start with more damage than their predecessor and often more ammo capacity.  Sure, the upgrades are expensive, but since there's no advantage whatsoever to upgrading both at the same time (Assuming you even had the money to do so, which you don't), you can sell your already upgraded inferior guns for a nice chunk of change.  Money is the one area in which you do have to make some decisions, at least on your first playthrough, because even after gathering all valuables to sell, you stop well short of being able to afford all upgrades in a single playthrough.

Speaking of playthroughs, unless you just want it to be, only your first one will be any kind of difficult.  Not only can you buy super weapons with currency earned by completing challenges, and infinite ammo versions of them if you so desire, you also start with ALL your weapons, ammo, and consumables that you had left from your previous save file when you start a NG+.  Yeah, the enemies are slightly harder, but upgraded late tier weapons will make that seem like a joke in no time.

Mercenaries mode is also a let down in my opinion.  There's some light progression in that you unlock more areas, abilities, and more starting cash as you get good ranks on the levels, but it lacks the fun of RE3 or RE4 in that there's no choices of different mercenaries, and the environments aren't nearly as fun to play in.  Where is Hunk for crying out loud...  You can only play as Ethan Winters, and you're basically handed all the ammo you need to make it a non-challenge.  Sure, getting the higher ranks still requires a great deal of planning and coordination, but it's a shadow of its former self.

That being said, this is a more than solid entry in the series that puts RE 6 and even 5 to shame.  It's not super long, coming it at maybe 10-20 hours on your first playthrough, depending on how thorough you are in exploring the side areas, but it is a well made game with some good scares here and there, and good if not overly easy gameplay.  A must buy for a fan of the series.

Resident Evil Village is not only the best Resident Evil I ever played since the very first release on the first Playstation. it is one of the best games ever made and the new standard for the Action-Horror genre. 

From the first moment Village draws you into its intense atmosphere and world building. "Good graphics" doesn't cut it here anymore, it's more like interactive art in fluid motion from start to finish. Especially Lady Dimitrescu herself and her castle and daughters are iconic and unforgettable character and location designs up there with Bioshock's Rapture and Big Daddy. Village covers a wide range of European history from the mentioned exterior medieval and interior Victorian Age castle, the title giving village itself, but also deep woods and mines, dungeons, rivers and lakes, finally a steam-punk factory crossing into Terminator territory. And the Capcom team just nails every single one. You can also really tell the team respected its characters, Eastern European, Slavic and Orthodox source material which, mixed with some Japanese Oni anologies, feels very fresh. Only From Software also does it this good.

For years I was somewhat skeptical of the Resi games. I found them okay, but forgettable and sometimes very cringe when it came to writing - the "b-movie flair" was never my thing. The Remakes were too action focused for me and they actually lost all horror and dread for me, in Resi 7 the terror was there, but it could play tedious and slow at times: although this fit for where Ethan was at the time, it often wasn't a great fun experience for me. I was also never a fan of achievement hunting for replayability. But Village is different! Revolutionary for the series even. And it has converted me from a skeptic to an admirer.
I was very impressed how the team managed to orchestrate a design symphony that almost perfectly mixes all of its elements to a fresh, captivating and smooth experience that is more than the sum of its parts: from exploration and treasure seeking, riddles and survival-combat, to Nemesis like unbeatable enemies, some stealth and passages of naked terror. As varied as the locations and atmospheric experiences are, so is the gameplay. Ethan through his tour de force developes from the normie fighting for his life as in Resi 7 to a commando soldier and monster slayer hero at the end. Every location feels great and you always do something new and interesting.

I also can't understand why some people think Village has less horror than Resi 7. Not only has it equal peaks in shock and awe, Village varies its themes greatly: classic survival-horror, Blairwitch Project like helpless isolation, Silent Hill and existential dread, body horror in all varieties from Dead Space and Alien, over Cronenberg to cyberpunk and Terminator. 

Somewhat negative were only two things: [spoiler] Heisenberg's factory [/spoiler] felt too drawn out to artificially make the game longer and it is not quite up there with the other locations (too many identical looking tunnel and box levels), and I wasn't too fond of the one shooting passage with [spoiler] Chris Redfield [/spoiler], but it's still thematically interesting and certainly didn't ruin the game for me. 

And although the writing isn't exactly The Brothers Karamasow, it didn't ruin the atmosphere for me, but supported it this time. Finally we can only be thankful that Japanese games do not try to force a political agenda on you like so much that is coming out of the USA and wider West since several years. Resident Evil's cosmos of terror and dread is certainly still perferable to Clown World.

At the end I could tell myself: these are the experiences for which the pioneer technologies and humble beginnings in the 90s and around the turn of the millenium were made, when everything comes together now and starts to bloom. Making gaming to the most interesting entertainment medium on the planet. Who needs Hollywood anyway?

Resident Evil 7 gave the RE series a much needed fresh coat of paint, bringing the franchise all the way back to it's true survival horror routes. Resident Evil 8 had a lot to live up to after it's incredibly successful predecessor, and I can whole heartedly say it 100% lived up to my expectations, and even managed to surpass them in some ways. 

RE8 does little to hide it's clear inspiration from RE4; from it's setting, trading and weapon mechanics to it's large variety of crazy and creepy enemy design, it truly feels like a spiritual successor not only to RE7 but to RE4. And, as a diehard fan of those games, I can't help but fall in love with this one too. 

The experience oozes atmosphere from beginning to end. The gothic horror nature of the village and Castle Dimitrescu were definitely the highlights of the game for me, bringing back the feeling from classic entries like the original Resident Evil as you desperately search beautifully crafted areas whilst solving a plethora of wonderfully fun puzzles and evading unique and terrifying (or attractive, depending on your preference) enemies throughout. This game unashamedly takes great ideas from the past and reinvigorates them in so many awesome ways.

Ethan, trained under Chris after the events of RE7, is now significantly more experienced in weaponry and combat. And so he should be. Village  expands heavily on the action side of RE7, with so many new weapons and enemy variety that you'll almost certainly be needing everything you can get your hands on. Despite leaning into this action aspect more than previously, the game doesn't forget it's horror routes and is packed to the brim with some genuinely terrifying enemies and areas. One area, without spoiling anything, contains the scariest experience I've ever had in a videogame, hands down. I adored it, as it really set the bar for the kind of pure horror experiences the Capcom team are capable of putting together.

I had very few gripes with Village. The primary one I saw others also show concern over was a level later in the game. Without spoiling anything, it's primary issue is that it overstays it's welcome quite a bit and becomes rather tedious, though admittedly this isn't as noticeable on your first run as there's more than enough tension to keep you too focused on the game to realise (at least that was the case for me). This level also takes a turn away from the gothic horror tone that persists throughout most of the game up until this point, which I did also find a little disappointing.

Overall, RE8 is an astounding success in my opinion. If you're going into this game as a new player I'd definitely recommend checking out RE7 first as that game is also stellar and knowledge of it's events is fairly integral to the plot of Village (though there is a recap included if you're desperate to play this game). I really can't fully express how much I appreciated so much of what RE8 does, especially it's huge inspiration from RE4. It expands on so many elements of RE7 and feels like a true successor with all of it's changes, all of which elevate the experience meaningfully.

After beating my first save file from start to finish I'll have to admit this is likely now in my top 3 favorite Resident Evil games - Maybe even top 2.  It's almost perfect I dare say as I genuinely couldn't think of a single thing to complain about throughout the whole thing.

The game had excellent world building, environments, enemies, scares, surprises and a decent amount of puzzles.  It's almost like a journey from start to finish rather than a game - And I mean that in the most endearing way possible.

A lot of the game mechanics mimic both Resident Evil 4 and Resident Evil 7 - This isn't anything new to talk about as by now everyone who has played Village so far has come to realize this - There's even mentions of this in the concept art from Capcom themselves about how this game emulates a bit of Resident Evil 4.  With that being said if you were a fan of Resident Evil 4 this game delivers on what you may have been wanting more of from that game.  There's treasure to find, weapons to buy and upgrade and items to trade with the Duke who acts as Village's Merchant.

The environments look amazing and each area feels like its own little set piece that will awe you - Not to mention aside from this game looking beautiful in almost every environment the game runs amazingly smooth.  Capcom was even so confident in their world building this time around that they've included a photo mode for you to take pictures with.  So it makes capturing those special moments easier so you can view or share them later at your own convenience.

The weapon handling and movement feels pretty nice - All the weapons feel like they have an oomf to them when attacking enemies - The gore is admittedly a little lacking in combat [spoiler]With good reason if you pay attention to the story[/spoiler]  but it's not the biggest loss and doesn't detract from the game.  Each boss in the game was a unique experience with plenty of intense moments.  I could easily say this is one of the few Resident Evil games where Capcom didn't neglect the boss fights.

Overall though I could praise this game all day but it's easier to just say try it out yourself - This likely will be my favorite game of 2021 and I'm looking forward to see how Capcom continues the story.

Will probably add more to this post later but for now go buy Village - It's a great game.

Also post game content is awesome - Especially the developer comments on concept art - Please do more stuff like that Capcom
